en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
This immeasurable [work] has issued from the lips of Dvaipāyana.
For one who hears the *Bhārata* being recited— which is meritorious, purifying, a destroyer of sin,
and auspicious— what need is there for consecration with the waters of Puṣkara?
One who gives a hundred cows with horns made of gold to a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and possessed of great erudition,
and one who listens to the entire narrative of the *Bhārata*— [the merit of these two is equal].
The fruit for both of them becomes equal.
I bow to Vyāsa, the grandson of Vasiṣṭha, the great-grandson of Śakti, the sinless son of Parāśara,
the father of Śuka, and a treasure-house of austerity.

Salutations to Vyāsa, who is a form of Viṣṇu; salutations to Viṣṇu, who is in the form of Vyāsa. Salutations indeed to the treasure-house of Brahman, to the descendant of Vasiṣṭha; salutations again and again.
Salutations to the Great Dharma; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Creator.
Having paid homage to the Brahmins, I shall proclaim the eternal Dharmas. Homage to that Blessed One, Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
by whose grace I shall recount this narrative of Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśampāyana said: Having offered water for all their friends, those sons of Pāṇḍu,
as well as Vidura, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and all the women of the Bharata lineage, [performed the funeral rites].
There those great-souled descendants of Kuru dwelt for one month outside the city, intending to complete their period of ritual purification. Then,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous soul, performed the water-libation ceremony.
The high-souled Siddhas and the best of Brahman-sages arrived—
Dvaipāyana, Nārada, the great Ṛṣi Devala,
Devasthāna, Kaṇva, and their most excellent disciples.
And other twice-born men, learned in the Vedas and perfected in wisdom—
householders and *snātakas* alike— all beheld that best of the Kurus. Having approached the high-souled one, they were honored by him according to the prescribed rites.
Those great seers sat down upon costly seats;
having then accepted the hospitality appropriate for that occasion,
they sat around Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounding him according to the prescribed custom.
On the sacred bank of the Bhāgīrathī, hundreds of thousands of brahmins were consoling the king, whose mind was overwhelmed with grief; then,
at that time, Nārada spoke to the righteous Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having deliberated with the sages, words appropriate for the occasion were spoken:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, by the strength of your arms and through the grace of Mādhava,
this entire earth has been conquered righteously."
"By good fortune you have been released from this battle that strikes fear into the world.
O Pāṇḍava, do you take delight in being devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya?
And having slain your enemies, O King, do you gladden your friends?"
"Having obtained this prosperity, I hope that grief does not afflict you.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This entire earth has been conquered by relying on the strength of Kṛṣṇa's arms."
Through the grace of the Brahmins and by the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna,
this great sorrow dwells constantly in my heart:
that I have caused this vast destruction of kinsmen, brought about by greed.
"Having caused the death of Saubhadra and the sons of Draupadī— my beloved children—
this victory, O Blessed One, appears to me as a defeat.
What indeed will my daughter-in-law, the daughter of the Vṛṣṇis, say to Madhusūdana?"
Dwelling in Dvārakā, she will hear that Hari-Kṛṣṇa has departed from here;
this Draupadī, whose sons have been slain and whose kinsmen are lost, is wretched and,
though ever intent on our welfare and pleasure, she seems to afflict me even more now.
"O Blessed One, O Nārada, listen to this other matter which I shall tell you:
I have been joined with grief by Kuntī through the concealment of the mantra.
He who possesses the strength of ten thousand elephants and is an unrivaled chariot-warrior in battle—"
The wise one, whose gait is like the playful stride of a lion, compassionate, self-controlled, and firm in his vows;
the refuge of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, proud and of fierce prowess;
intolerant and ever-impetuous—he is the one who will strike us down in battle after battle.
Skilled in swift weapons, a versatile warrior, accomplished, and possessed of wondrous prowess—
he is the son secretly born to Kuntī and our uterine brother,
whom Kuntī described as the son of the Sun during the water-rites.
In former times, having placed her son— endowed with every virtue— within a basket and cast him into the water,
she set it adrift upon the current of the Gaṅgā;
he whom this world considered to be the son of a charioteer and the son of Rādhā.
"He was indeed the eldest son of Kuntī, our own uterine brother;
yet, out of ignorance and greedy for the kingdom, I caused him to be slain in battle.
That act burns my limbs like fire consumes a heap of cotton."
"Indeed, even Pārtha Śvetavāhana does not know him as his brother;
neither do I, nor Bhīma, nor the twins. Yet he, firm in his vows, knows us.
We have heard that Pṛthā has indeed gone into his presence."
"Indeed, you desire peace for us, and you are my son"—
thus Pṛthā’s wish was not granted by that high-souled one;
we have heard that he spoke these words to his mother only very late.
"For I shall not be able to abandon King Duryodhana in battle; indeed,
it would be ungentlemanly, cruel,
and ungrateful on my part if I were to make peace with Yudhiṣṭhira according to your counsel."
"People will think that I am afraid of the one with white horses in battle. Therefore, he said, "Having defeated Vijaya along with Keśava in combat,
I shall afterwards make peace with the son of Dharma."
Pṛthā spoke again to that broad-chested one:
"Grant safety to four; fight Phalguna at your will.
The wise one, trembling and with palms joined in reverence, replied to his mother:
"O mother, I will not slay four of your sons who have come within my reach;
for it is certain that you shall have exactly five sons remaining—
either with Karṇa if Arjuna is slain, or with Arjuna if I am slain."
Then his mother, longing for her son, spoke once more to him:
"May you bring well-being to your brothers, those for whose welfare you desire to act.
Having spoken thus to him and dismissed him, Pṛthā returned to her home.

That hero, his own uterine brother, was slain by Arjuna; yet, O Sage, the secret counsel was revealed neither to Pṛthā nor to him. Then that brave and great archer was struck down by the son of Pṛthā.
"But later, O best of the twice-born, I learned from the words of Pṛthā, O Lord, that Karṇa was my own uterine brother and my elder sibling; because of that,
my heart burns intensely as I have slain my brother."
With Karna and Arjuna as my allies, I could defeat even Vasava himself. When I was being tormented in the assembly hall by the evil-minded sons of Dhritarashtra,
the anger that suddenly arose within me subsided upon seeing Karna.
For when I hear his harsh words, bitter in their outcome,
as he speaks in the assembly during the gambling match seeking the welfare of Duryodhana,
my anger vanishes upon beholding his feet.
"It is my conviction that Kuntī’s feet were indeed similar to Karṇa’s; yet,
though I search for the cause of this resemblance between Pṛthā and you, I cannot find the reason for it by any means, no matter how much I reflect."
"How indeed did the earth swallow his wheel in battle, and how was my brother cursed? You ought to tell me that here.
O Blessed One, I wish to hear everything from you exactly as it happened."
"For you are all-knowing and wise; there is no doubt that you know everything done and undone in the three worlds, both in the future and the present.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the sage Nārada, the best among speakers,
related all of that— how the son of the Sūta had been cursed.
"It is even so, O mighty-armed Bhārata, just as you say."
"Nothing whatsoever would have been unbearable for Karṇa and Arjuna in battle.
However, O King, I shall tell you this secret of the gods;
listen, O Great King, to how this occurred in the past."
"O Lord, how may the *kṣatra* go to heaven purified by the sword?"— thinking thus,
he produced a maiden's womb, which gave rise to intense rivalry. That boy, endowed with splendor, came to be known as the son of a *sūta*.
He [studied] the science of archery under your preceptor, the best of the Aṅgirases;
he [observed] the strength of Bhīmasena, the lightness of hand of Phalguna,
your own wisdom, O king of kings, and likewise the discipline of the twins.
Reflecting upon his friendship with Vāsudeva since childhood and the affection of the subjects for the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, he burned with envy. Indeed,
in his youth, he had formed a friendship with King Duryodhana.
Though you have always been his constant enemies, both by fate and by nature,
Karna, perceiving that Dhananjaya was superior in knowledge regarding the science of archery,
approached Droṇa in private and spoke these words.
"I wish to know the Brahmāstra, along with its secret methods of withdrawal.
Ah, how strange! How very strange is this world, turned upside down, wherein the virtuous man feels shame, while the wicked man finds satisfaction!"
"It is my conviction that I shall become equal to Arjuna in battle.
Your affection for your sons and for your disciples is surely equal.
Through your grace, the wise shall not say of me that I am unskilled in weapons."
Thus addressed by Karṇa, Droṇa, who felt a sense of regard for Phalguna and was aware of Karṇa’s wickedness, spoke to him:
"A Brahmin who has duly observed his vows should know the Brahmāstra."
"Or a Kṣatriya who is an ascetic— one whom no other could know by any means.
Having been addressed thus, he took leave of the best of the Aṅgirases and, having honored him in return,
went swiftly toward Mount Mahendra to see Rāma.
Approaching Rāma and bowing his head in salutation,
he addressed him with reverence, saying, "I am a Brāhmaṇa of the Bhṛgu lineage.
Rāma received him, having inquired after all matters, such as his lineage and so forth.
"Stay; you are welcome," he said, and he became exceedingly joyful.
While Karṇa was dwelling there on Mahendra, the best of mountains, he had encounters with Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and gods.
There, he received the science of weapons according to the prescribed rites from the best of the Bhrigus;
he became exceedingly dear to the gods, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas.
Once, while wandering near a hermitage on the shore of the ocean, he—

With sword and bow in hand, the son of the Sūta roamed about alone. O Pārtha, he happened by chance to kill the sacrificial cow of a certain Brahmin teacher who was intent on his *agnihotra* rites, having done so out of ignorance.
Considering that it was done out of ignorance, Karṇa informed the Brāhmaṇa and,
seeking to appease him, spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, this cow of yours was killed unintentionally."
"Show me favor in this matter," he said again and again.
To him, that brahmin spoke, enraged and as if reviling him with his words:
"O man of evil conduct, you deserve to be slain! O wicked-minded one, receive the fruit [of your actions]!"

"O wicked one, while you are fighting with him with whom you always vie and for whose sake you strive incessantly, the earth shall swallow the wheel. Then, when the wheel has been swallowed by the earth, your head— bereft of consciousness— "
"Exerting his prowess, the enemy will strike you down; go, O lowest of men!
Just as this cow was struck by you, O fool, while you were heedless, so shall another strike off your head while you are likewise heedless."
Then he again sought to appease that best of the twice-born with cattle, wealth, and jewels; but he spoke to him once more:
"Not even all the world could make this word uttered by me false."
"Go, or stay, or whatever task you have, perform that.
Thus addressed by the Brahmin, Karṇa, with his face cast down in dejection,
approached Rāma in fear, reflecting upon those very words in his mind.
Nārada said:
The tiger among the Bhṛgus was gratified by Karṇa’s prowess of arm, his humility, his self-restraint, and likewise by his service to his preceptor.

To him, that ascetic, with undistracted mind, duly taught the entire Brahmāstra, including the method of its withdrawal, in its entirety to that son of great penance. Then, having mastered the weapon, Karṇa took his pleasure in the hermitage of Bhṛgu.
He of wondrous prowess indeed exerted himself in the science of archery. Then once, the wise Rāma, emaciated by fasting, was wandering near the hermitage accompanied by Karṇa.

The son of Jamadagni, his mind weary and his head resting on Karna’s lap, fell asleep, having developed a sense of intimacy and friendship through his trust. Then, a worm born of phlegm appeared, feeding upon flesh and blood.
Terrible and with a dreadful touch, it approached Karna's vicinity.
Reaching his thigh, that blood-drinker tore it open;
yet, out of fear for his preceptor, he was unable either to cast it off or to kill him.
O Bhārata, although he was being thus bitten by that worm,
the son of the Sūta, fearing the awakening of his preceptor, overlooked it;
Karna, however, suppressed that unbearable pain through his fortitude.
Unshaken and unperturbed, he sustained the descendant of Bhṛgu.
But when the scion of Bhṛgu’s line was touched on his body by blood,
the radiant one awoke and, feeling tormented, spoke these words:
"Alas! I have fallen into impurity; what is this that you are doing?
Cast aside your fear and tell me the truth of this matter.
Then Karṇa told him that he was being devoured by a worm.
And Rāma beheld that worm, which resembled a boar,
having eight feet, sharp fangs, and covered as if with needles;
its limbs were completely bristling with hair, and it was known by the name Alarka.
As soon as he was seen by Rāma, the worm gave up its life-breaths;
it was like a marvel that it did so right there, drenched in blood.
Then, Viśvarūpa, the terrifying one, was seen in the sky.
The Rākṣasa Lohitagrīva, whose body was black and who rode upon the clouds, with his heart’s desire fulfilled, stood before Rāma with palms joined in reverence and spoke:
"May it be well with you, O tiger among the Bhṛgus; I shall now depart as I came."
"O best of sages, I have been liberated from hell by you.
May it be well with you, and may there be joy; you have done what is pleasing to me.
To him, the mighty-armed and powerful son of Jamadagni replied:
"Who are you, and for what reason have you entered hell? Tell me that.
He replied, "Formerly, O dear one, in the age of the gods, I was a great asura named Gṛtsa, almost equal in age to Bhṛgu."
"Having forcibly abducted Bhṛgu’s dearly beloved wife,
I fell to the earth as a worm due to the curse of that great ṛṣi.
Then your great-grandfather spoke to me in anger:"
"O sinner, you who eat urine and phlegm shall enter hell.
"O Brahmin, when will there be an end to this curse? I asked him.
Then Bhṛgu said to me, "It shall come to pass with Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu."

"O virtuous one, having encountered you, I have reached this state; though it was not a favorable one, I have been liberated from that evil birth. Having spoken thus and paid his respects, the great asura departed for Rāma."
12,003.024c Rāma, however, spoke these words to Karṇa with anger:
12,003.025a "O fool, this is an extreme sorrow that a Brāhmaṇa could never endure;
12,003.025c you possess the fortitude of a Kṣatriya. Out of my desire for the truth, let it be told."
Then Karna, fearing a curse, spoke to him while seeking his favor:
"O Bhārgava, know me to be a *sūta* born from the union of a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya;
people on earth call me Karna, the son of Rādhā."
"O Brahmin, descendant of Bhṛgu, show favor to me, who am greedy for the weapon. There is no doubt that my father is my preceptor, the lord who bestowed upon me the knowledge of the Vedas;
therefore, I spoke of your lineage as 'Bhārgava' in your presence."
To him, who had fallen upon the ground, wretched, trembling, and with palms joined in reverence, the best of the Bhrigus spoke with anger, as if laughing:
"Since you have treated me falsely here out of greed for the weapon..."
"Therefore, O fool, this Brahmāstra shall indeed manifest itself to you,
except at the time of your death when you encounter an equal;
for the Brahmāstra never remains permanently with one who is not a Brāhmaṇa."
"Go now; no place for falsehood exists here for you. There shall be no kṣatriya on earth equal to you in battle.
Having been addressed thus by Rāma, he departed in accordance with justice.
Having approached Duryodhana, he declared, "I have mastered the weapons.
Nārada said:
But Karṇa, having obtained these weapons from the descendant of Bhṛgu...
Accompanied by Duryodhana, O bull of the Bharatas, he rejoiced. Then, O King, at one time the kings gathered for the *svayaṃvara* (self-choice marriage) of King Citrāṅgada in the kingdom of Kaliṅga.
12,004.003a There, O Bhārata, is a city named Śrīmadrājapura;
12,004.003c there, hundreds of kings assembled for the sake of the maiden.
12,004.004a Having heard that all those monarchs had gathered there, Duryodhana [set out].
Accompanied by Karṇa, he departed in a chariot with golden parts.
Then, O best of kings, when that great festival of the *svayaṃvara* had commenced, the monarchs assembled for the sake of the maiden.
Śiśupāla, Jarāsaṃdha, Bhīṣmaka, and Vakra; Kapotaroman, Nīla, and Rukmin of firm prowess;
Sṛgāla, O great king, and he who was the sovereign of the kingdom of women.
Aśoka, Śatadhanvan, Bhoja, and the one known as Vīra—
these and many others, O Bhārata, including kings who are teachers of the Mlecchas from the east and the north, have taken refuge in the southern direction.
All wore golden armlets and were adorned with garlands of refined gold; all possessed radiant bodies and were as fierce with pride as tigers in rut.
Then, O Bhārata, when those kings had taken their seats...
Accompanied by her nurse and the eunuch, that maiden entered the arena.
Then, O Bhārata, as the names of the kings were being proclaimed,
that fair-complexioned maiden passed over the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.
But Duryodhana, the descendant of Kuru, could not endure that slight;
he rejected the maiden after having insulted the lords of men. Intoxicated by the pride of his own prowess, he relied upon Bhīṣma and Droṇa.
Having placed that maiden upon his chariot, he summoned the lords of men.
O bull among men, Karna— the best among wielders of weapons— followed behind him on his chariot, sword in hand, wearing leather arm-guards and finger-protectors.
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, there arose a great clash among the kings as they donned their armor and yoked their chariots;
filled with rage, they rushed toward both Karṇa and Duryodhana.
Releasing showers of arrows like clouds over two mountains,
Karna struck down each of those oncoming warriors' bows— along with their arrows and quivers— to the surface of the earth using a single razor-headed shaft.
Then Karna, the best among strikers, having confounded some who were without bows, some with raised bows,
some carrying arrows, and others likewise bearing chariot-spears and maces,
by means of his lightness of hand—
Having slain the majority of their charioteers, he overcame those lords of men.
Urging on their horses themselves and crying out, "Go!
Go!", those kings fled from the battle with broken spirits.
Duryodhana, protected by Karṇa,
then advanced joyfully toward the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura), taking the maiden with him.
Nārada said:

Knowing that Karṇa had manifested his full strength, King Jarāsaṃdha, the lord of the earth and ruler of Magadha, challenged him to a single combat on chariots in battle. A duel then took place between those two, both of whom were experts in divine weapons.
As they showered one another with various weapons in battle,
their arrows exhausted, their bows broken, and their swords shattered, both of them,
endowed with great strength, fell to the earth and grappled with each other using their arms.
Then, as he was fighting with Bāhukaṇṭaka,
Karṇa split the joint of his body that had been joined together by old age.
Seeing this transformation of his own body, the king—
"O Bhārata, casting aside their enmity, he said to Karṇa, 'I am pleased.
Out of affection, he then gave the city of Mālinī to Karṇa.
O tiger among men, that conqueror of enemies became king over the Aṅgas."
Karna, the crusher of enemy forces, protected Campā with the consent of Duryodhana— this is also known to you. Thus,
he became renowned upon the earth for the prowess of his weapons.
For the sake of your welfare, the Lord of the Gods requested the armor and earrings;
deluded by the illusion of the god, he gave away those divine, innate, and most highly honored earrings as well as his innate armor.
Freed from his two earrings and his natural armor,
he was slain in battle by Vijaya while Vāsudeva looked on,
due to the curse of the brahmin and of the high-souled Rāma.
Due to the boon granted to Kuntī, through the illusory power (*māyā*) of Indra,

because of Bhīṣma’s disregard for him during the enumeration of chariot-warriors, because he was mentioned as only half a chariot-warrior, because his energy was suppressed by Śalya, and through the policy of Vāsudeva.
Having taken up the divine weapons of Rudra, the king of the gods, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, Droṇa, and the high-souled Kṛpa, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow [confronted his foes] in battle.
"Karna Vaikartana, whose splendor was equal to the sun, has been slain.
Thus was your brother cursed and deceived by many;
that tiger among men is not to be mourned, for he met his death in battle."
12,006.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus, the celestial sage Nārada ceased;
but Yudhiṣṭhira, the royal seer, remained lost in thought, overwhelmed by grief.
To that hero of dejected mind, with his face cast down and afflicted, sighing like a serpent and with eyes bathed in tears,
Kuntī— her limbs overwhelmed by grief and her consciousness stricken by sorrow— [approached].
12,006.003c She, speaking with sweet words, spoke these meaningful words at the proper time:
12,006.004a "O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, you ought not to grieve for him. 12,006.004c Cast off your sorrow, O highly wise one, and hear these words of mine."

O best among the upholders of dharma, I previously endeavored to make you recognize our brotherhood, as did the divine Bhāskara, your father, who is the foremost of the righteous; for that which was to be said by a well-wishing friend desiring your welfare and prosperity.
Likewise, at the end of a dream, Divākara spoke thus in my presence:
"Neither Bhānu nor I was able, through reasons of affection,
to persuade him in the past, nor to lead him to unity with you."
"Then, overcome by time, he took delight in fanning the flame of enmity;
because he acted as your adversary, he was overlooked by me. When his mother had spoken thus, Dharmarāja, his eyes clouded with tears, [listened].
The righteous-souled one, his mind agitated by grief, spoke these words to her:
"I am pained because of your concealment of the secret counsel. Then, that one of great splendor cursed women in all the worlds.
Thinking, "They will not preserve the secret," the king was overcome with extreme sorrow; remembering his sons, grandsons, kinsmen, and friends, he became agitated in heart and lost his composure.
Then, his soul overwhelmed by grief like a fire enveloped in smoke,
the wise king, tormented by anguish, fell into despondency.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But Yudhiṣṭhira, the righteous-souled one, his mind agitated by grief and tormented by sorrow,
lamented as he remembered the great car-warrior Karṇa;
possessed by pain and grief, he sighed again and again.
Seeing Arjuna, he, emaciated by grief, spoke these words:
"If we had lived on alms in the city of the Vṛṣṇis and Andhakas after depriving our kinsmen of their men, we would not have fallen into this miserable state."
"Our enemies have achieved their goals, while the Kurus, having accomplished their purpose, are indeed [victorious]. Having slain ourselves by our own hands, what fruit of dharma shall we obtain?
Fie upon the conduct of the kṣatriyas! Fie upon innate strength!"
"Fie on this indignation by which we have been brought to this calamity!
Patience, self-restraint, purity, non-hostility, freedom from envy,
non-violence, and truthful speech— these are the constant virtues of forest-dwellers."
But we, out of greed and delusion, have resorted to arrogance and pride;
having fallen into this state through the desire to enjoy a mere fragment of sovereignty,
nothing could gladden us even with the kingship of the three worlds.
Having seen our kinsmen, who were seekers of flesh, slain upon the earth,
we— having abandoned those who were not to be killed and who were equal to the earth itself for the sake of the earth— now live on, deprived of our purpose and with our kinsmen destroyed.

For us who are greedy for material gain like dogs, we are like dogs indeed; our prey has been lost, as has the one who would enjoy that prey. Neither the entire earth nor heaps of gold [could satisfy us].
Not by all these cattle and horses that have been slain here should you grieve;
for they were possessed by desire and passion, and filled with anger and resentment, they mounted the vehicle of death and went to the abode of Vaivasvata.
Desiring much welfare, fathers long for sons through austerity, celibacy, reverence, and endurance; likewise through fasts, sacrifices, vows, auspicious rites, and blessings.
Mothers conceive embryos and carry them for ten months;
if they are born safely, or if once born they live,
and if, having attained their full development and gained strength, they should grant us happiness.
"Both in this world and the next"— thus do the wretched act, motivated by the desire for rewards.
This undertaking of theirs has come to naught, entirely fruitless,
since their young sons, adorned with polished earrings, have been slain.
Without having enjoyed earthly pleasures and without having discharged their debts to the ancestors and the gods, they have gone to the abode of Vaivasvata. Indeed,
O dear one, when their parents were born, they were as if filled with desire for them.
At that very moment, when their strength and forms had fully emerged, those kings were slain—
men joined by desire and passion, and unbalanced by anger and joy; they shall never at any time enjoy even the slightest fruit of their birth.
Of the Pāñcālas and the Kurus, those who remain unslain are indeed as good as dead;
we, however, by our own deeds, shall fall into the lowest worlds. We alone are considered the cause of the destruction of this world.
We have been treated with deceit by the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. He is always wise in dishonesty, a hater who lives by guile,
and is constantly false in his conduct toward us, even though we have done him no wrong.
"We desire shares, and they [desire them] too; yet neither have we conquered, nor have they. Neither have they enjoyed this earth, nor women, nor song and instrumental music.
This is not to be discussed in the assembly of ministers, nor has it been heard by those who are learned."
Neither most precious jewels, nor land, nor the acquisition of wealth—
tormented by his hatred for us, he finds no happiness here. Having seen that prosperity of ours, he has become pale, wan, and emaciated.
It was reported to King Dhṛtarāṣṭra by the son of Subala;
out of greed for his son, the father consented to that man who stood upon an unrighteous path,
even though he disregarded his father, Gāṅgeya, and Vidura as well.
Without doubt, Dhṛtarāṣṭra has met his end just as I have,
having failed to restrain his impure and greedy son who followed the dictates of desire,
and having caused his own brothers to be slain, he has fallen from radiant glory.
Having cast these two aged ones into the fire of grief, that Suyodhana—
ever possessed of a sinful mind and filled with hatred toward us—
who indeed, being a kinsman of noble birth, would speak thus to his own friends?
Just as that base man spoke while desiring to fight in the presence of the Vṛṣṇis,
so too have we been ruined for eternal years through our own fault,
burning all directions with our splendor like suns.
"That man of enmity toward us has fallen under the influence of evil counselors;
indeed, for the sake of Duryodhana, this family of ours has been brought to ruin. Having committed the slaughter of those who should not have been slain, we have incurred censure in the world."
Having made that evil-minded evildoer, the destroyer of this lineage,
the lord of the kingdom, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra now grieves. The heroes have been slain, sin has been committed, and his own realm has been ruined.

"O Dhanañjaya, having slain [them], my anger has departed; yet this grief now overwhelms me. A sin committed is neutralized by a virtuous act—either through confession, repentance, giving, or even through austerity."

"By returning [to the path], by visiting sacred fords, and by the recitation of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, one who possesses renunciation (*tyāga*) is not capable of committing sin again; such is the *Śruti*.
When the *Śruti* declares that one who possesses renunciation does not undergo birth and death..."
"O Dhanañjaya, when one has attained the path, made firm in resolve, and reached Brahman, then that sage, endowed with knowledge and free from the pairs of opposites,
shall depart for the supreme state after taking leave of you all, O scorcher of foes."

"O destroyer of enemies, it is revealed in the sacred scriptures that the entirety of Dharma cannot be attained by one who possesses worldly attachments; this has been witnessed by me personally, for I abandoned even my sense of sin while desiring to maintain such attachments."
"The scripture declares that it is possible to attain the cause for the destruction of rebirth.
Therefore, having abandoned all possessions as well as my entire kingdom,
I shall go forth, liberated, free from sorrow, and free from fever."
"Rule this earth, secure and with its thorns removed. O best of the Kurus, I have no need for the kingdom nor for enjoyments.
Having spoken these words, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [remained silent].
12,007.041c Then Pārtha, the youngest, ceased speaking and replied.
12,008.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
12,008.001a Then Arjuna, as if insulted and unable to endure it, spoke these words.

Displaying his own fierce nature, the son of Indra, possessed of fierce prowess and firm resolve in speech, spoke these most eloquent words; and the one of great splendor, smiling and repeatedly licking the corners of his mouth, addressed him.

"Alas, what suffering! Alas, what hardship! Alas, what supreme despondency, that having performed superhuman deeds and slain your enemies, you should abandon the highest sovereignty obtained through your own dharma!"
Having slain your enemies, how can you now abandon everything all at once out of a lack of resolve?
For where is there sovereignty for one who is impotent, or again, for one who procrastinates?
And for what purpose did you slay the protectors of the earth while overcome by anger?
For he who would live by begging, without any action whatsoever, and who would desire to prosper through undertakings— he, possessing nothing, has his well-being destroyed;
he is renowned throughout all the worlds as one devoid of sons and cattle.

"O King, what will this world say of you, who have abandoned a prosperous kingdom to live by adopting the most wicked livelihood of a skull-bearer? Having cast aside all undertakings, with your well-being destroyed and possessing nothing,"
"O Lord, why do you desire to wander for alms like an ordinary man? Born in this royal family and having conquered the entire earth,
you now abandon both dharma and worldly prosperity in their entirety and set out for the forest out of folly."
"If these sacrificial offerings,
deprived of you, are plundered here by the wicked, the sin will surely fall upon you alone.
Thus did Nahuṣa speak regarding this state of destitution, which is not to be desired.

For cruel magic rites are indeed practiced by those without wealth; fie on this state of poverty here! You surely know that even the sages possess only enough for a single day, yet they say that this dharma proceeds from wealth.
"He who takes away another's wealth destroys that person's merit;
O King, when our wealth is being taken from us, whom could we possibly forgive? People look upon a poor man standing by their side as if he were a criminal under accusation."
12,008.014c Who in this world ought to declare that poverty is a sin? 12,008.015a O King, one who has fallen from grace is pitied, and one who is destitute is also pitied;
12,008.015c I perceive no difference between the outcast and the indigent.
For from wealth that has increased and been gathered from here and there,
all activities proceed, like rivers from mountains.
From wealth, O lord of men, come both dharma and desire, as well as heaven itself.
For the maintenance of life in this world does not succeed without wealth.
Indeed, for a man of small intelligence who is deprived of wealth,
all his activities are cut off, like small streams in the summer heat.
He who has wealth has friends; he who has wealth has kinsmen. He who has wealth is a man in this world; he who has wealth is a wise man.
Wealth cannot be acquired by one who is destitute, even if he desires it and seeks it.
12,08.020c Meanings are bound together by means of wealth, just as great elephants are bound by smaller elephants.
12,08.021a Virtue, pleasure, heaven, joy, anger, sacred learning, and self-restraint—
O lord of men, all these proceed from wealth.
From wealth the family prospers; from wealth righteousness proceeds.
For one without wealth, O Supreme Person, there is neither this world nor the next. One who lacks wealth cannot properly perform religious duties.
For from wealth, indeed, righteousness flows like a mountain river from a mountain.
O King, he who has emaciated horses, emaciated cattle, emaciated servants, and emaciated guests—he alone is truly "emaciated" (kṛśa); one who is merely thin in body is not truly emaciated.
Consider this according to what is right; observe how it was with the gods and asuras.
O King, what else do the deities prosper from than the slaughter of their own kin? If one were not permitted to take [life] from another, how could one ever undertake such a dharma?
This alone is the conclusion established by the seers regarding the Vedas:
the triple knowledge (trayī vidyā) must be studied, one must become wise,
wealth must be acquired by all means, and sacrifices must be performed with diligence.
"By means of treachery, the gods have obtained all their positions in heaven.
What else is there besides treachery by which the deities covet their kinsmen? Thus the gods have resolved, as do the eternal declarations of the Vedas."
They study, perform austerities, sacrifice, and officiate at sacrifices;
indeed, whatever excellence they acquire from elsewhere is entirely that very [merit].
Yet, we do not see any wealth anywhere that has not been taken away by others.
In this very way, indeed, kings conquer this earth;
having conquered it, they claim ownership over it, just as sons do over the wealth of their father.
For it is declared that for these royal seers (rājarṣis), who have won heaven, this [conquest] is their dharma.
Just as water flows from a full ocean in all ten directions,
so does wealth from a royal family spread throughout the earth.
This [earth] once belonged to Dilīpa, Nṛga, and Nahuṣa.
That earth which belonged to Ambarīṣa and Māndhātṛ now rests upon you.
That sacrifice consisting of material wealth, complete with all sacrificial fees, has arrived for you.
If you do not perform it, O King, you shall incur the sin of having offended the gods.

When a king performs the horse sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, all those who approach his final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) become purified. Viśvarūpa Mahādeva [is present] at the great sacrifice known as the Sarvamedha.
He offered all beings as oblations, and likewise his own self by means of his self.
This path to prosperity is eternal; we have heard that there is no end to it.
Great is the path of Daśaratha; O King, do not follow a wrong path.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For a moment, focusing your mind and ears one-pointedly within your inner self, listen to my words; having heard them, may they be pleasing to you."

"For your sake, I shall never again travel upon a path frequented by caravans; rather, I shall go having abandoned worldly pleasures. Ask me: what path is there that is secure and fit for one to travel alone?"
Alternatively, if you do not wish to ask, listen to me even though I am unasked:
having abandoned the pursuit of worldly pleasures and performing great austerities,
I shall dwell in the forest with the deer, subsisting on fruits and roots.
Offering oblations into the fire at the proper times and performing ablutions at both dawn and dusk,
he became emaciated, restricted in his diet, and wore skins, rags, and matted hair;
enduring cold, wind, and heat, he was steadfast against hunger, thirst, and fatigue.
Wasting away his body through austerity prescribed by rule,
he constantly listened to various sounds pleasing to the mind and ear—
the cries of joyful beasts and birds dwelling in the forests.
Sniffing the delicate fragrances of flowering trees and creepers,
beholding various beautiful forest-dwellers in the woods,
and even seeing the forest-dwelling ascetics living with their families, he wandered.
I shall not perform any unpleasant acts, much less toward those living in villages; dwelling in solitude, reflecting deeply, and subsisting on both cooked and uncooked food,
I shall satisfy the ancestors and the gods with forest produce, prayers, and water.
Thus, practicing the fierce and even fiercer rules prescribed in the forest scriptures, I shall await the end of this body. Or else,
I alone shall dwell for a single day beneath each individual tree.
Wandering for alms, a shaven-headed sage, I shall wear away this body—
covered with dust, taking refuge in empty houses or making my dwelling at the foot of a tree, having abandoned all that is pleasant and unpleasant.
Neither grieving nor rejoicing, regarding blame and self-praise as equal,

having become free from expectations, free from the sense of "mine," free from the pairs of opposites, and without possessions; delighting in the Self, with a tranquil mind, appearing like one who is dull, blind, and deaf.
Never entering into any conversation with anyone else,
and not harming any of the four kinds of beings, whether moving or stationary; remaining established in his own duty toward all creatures, he was impartial toward all living beings.
Neither mocking anyone nor ever knitting his brows, he was always cheerful of countenance and perfectly restrained in all his senses;
without asking the way of anyone, he proceeded by whichever path presented itself.
Desiring to go to no particular place or direction,
indifferent to travel and not looking back, he proceeded straight and composed, avoiding all living beings, both mobile and immobile.

But his own nature goes before him; even when foods arise and opposing pairs of conditions appear, he does not think about any of them. Whether the food be meager or tasteless, he never laments its prior non-attainment.
Wandering for alms even among others, fulfilling seven [houses] even when there is no gain;
when the smoke has ceased, the pestle is laid aside, the embers are extinguished, the people have finished their meal,
the movement of the bowls has passed, and the time for begging has ended.
Wandering for alms at a single time, visiting only two or five houses,
I shall roam this earth, having released the snares of longing; whether there is gain or loss, I, a man of great austerity, shall maintain equanimity.
Acting neither like one who wishes to live nor like one who wishes to die, neither rejoicing in life nor hating death,
he remains the same whether someone hacks at one of his arms with an axe or anoints the other with sandalwood paste.
Thinking neither of the inauspicious nor the auspicious regarding those two,
and having completely abandoned all those worldly activities for prosperity that can be performed by one who lives, he remained fixed as if in a mere moment.
Always unattached to those things, having abandoned all sensory activities,
with all volitional thoughts completely relinquished and the impurities of the self thoroughly cleansed,
he is liberated from all attachments and has transcended all snares.
Not remaining under the control of anyone, sharing the nature of the wind,
and wandering thus with passion departed, I shall attain eternal contentment;
for through craving, out of ignorance, I have been made to commit great evil.
12,009.030 Having performed various wholesome and unwholesome deeds, men maintain what is called their "own kin," which is bound together by the relationship of cause and effect.
12,009.031 At the end of their lifespan, they must abandon this body that is nearly exhausted.
For he receives that evil, which is indeed the fruit of the doer's action.
Thus, in this wheel of saṃsāra, which revolves like the wheel of a chariot,
this collection of beings comes together with other collections of beings for the sake of their respective tasks.
Happiness belongs to one who abandons this essence-less and endless cycle of existence (saṃsāra), which is afflicted by the pains of birth, death, old age, and disease;
for even the gods fall from heaven, and the great seers (maharṣis) fall from their stations.
For who indeed, desiring worldly existence and knowing the true nature of its causes, would act thus?
Having performed various deeds characterized by diverse marks,
a king is bound by earthly rulers for even the slightest of reasons.
Therefore, this nectar of wisdom has finally presented itself to me. Having attained it, I pray for that state which is imperishable, eternal, and firm.
Practicing constantly in this manner, by means of this very way of life—
"Established upon the fearless path, I shall cast off this body.
Bhīma said:
"O King, [this speech of yours] is like that of a dull-witted and ignorant reciter of the Vedas."
"12,010.001c This intellect of yours, struck down by mere recitation, does not perceive the true meaning. 12,010.002a For one whose mind is set on idleness and who censures the duties of kings,
12,010.002c what fruit would there be, O bull of the Bharatas, in the destruction of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?"
For one who follows the path of the kṣatriyas, even toward a kinsman such as you, there is found no patience, compassion, pity, or kindness— if we had known that your mind was such as this.
"We shall not take up weapons at all, nor shall we slay anyone;
we shall subsist solely on alms until the release of our bodies.
Had this been so, there would have been no such terrible war among the rulers of the earth."
"The wise indeed know that all this is food for the vital breath (prāṇa);
everything, both the stationary and the moving, is the sustenance of the vital breath.
Therefore, whoever are obstacles to one who is seizing a kingdom—"
"Those who know the duty of the Kṣatriya understand, O wise ones, that they must be slain. They were full of fault, they were our enemies to the kingdom, and they have been killed by us.
Having slain them, O Yudhiṣṭhira, enjoy this earth in accordance with dharma."
Just as a man who, having dug a well but not yet reached water,
might turn back covered in mud— our action is comparable to that.
Or as one who, having climbed a great tree and gathered honey from it...
This task of ours is like one who, without having reached his destination, meets his end; it is similar to this.
Just as a man setting out on a long journey might turn back in despair, falling away from his hope, so too is this task of ours.
"O best of the Kurus, just as a man who, after having caused his enemies to be slain,
might afterwards cause himself to be slain— such is this deed of ours.
It is like a hungry man who, having obtained food, should not eat it by chance."
And having obtained his beloved, the lover performed this deed of ours;
for we alone are to be blamed here, O Bhārata, we who are dull-witted that we follow you, O King, thinking, "He is our eldest."
"For we, who possess the strength of arms, are learned and high-minded;
yet we abide by the words of a eunuch, just like those who are powerless.
We, who have no other recourse and have lost our purpose—what other way is there for us but this—to strive for the accomplishment of our goal?"
"How indeed could people not perceive what they see? For it is taught that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) should be performed in times of calamity by one who is overcome by old age and ruined by enemies."
Therefore, those of perfected wisdom in this world do not disparage renunciation;
rather, those who perceive with subtle insight consider it to be a transgression of dharma.
How then can one who has arisen from that [dharma], who is devoted to it, and who relies upon it, [be considered otherwise]?

One should remain censuring that very [system], for faith is held elsewhere. This knowledge of the Vedic doctrine, promulgated by those devoid of prosperity, destitute of wealth, and nihilists, is like a semblance of truth that is actually false.

But it is possible for one who has adopted the tonsure and maintains himself by his own self, having assumed the outward guise of dharma, to remain [in that state], yet not to truly live. Furthermore,
it is possible for one to live happily alone in the forests.
Those who do not support their sons, grandsons, divine sages, guests, and ancestors—
people say that such men, even if they kill deer, boars, and birds, have not conquered heaven; nor do people say that merit accrues to them by this means.
"O King, if anyone could attain perfection through renunciation alone,
then mountains and trees would also quickly attain perfection;
for these are seen to be in a state of constant renunciation and free from affliction."
Free from possessiveness and always acting according to their own nature, if one does not attain success through one's own efforts but through those of others,
then action alone must be performed; for there is no success for one who is inactive.
Even aquatic creatures and those born from moisture shall attain success;
for those men who have only themselves to support and no one else at all,
they indeed are the ones in this world comparable to mountains.
12,010.028a Behold how the world is occupied with its own respective actions;
12,010.028c therefore, action alone must be performed; there is no success for one who is inactive.
12,011.001 Arjuna said:
In this very context, O bull of the Bharatas, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Śakra and certain ascetics.
Some twice-born men, having abandoned their homes, went to the forest.
Those dull-witted men, born into noble families but still hairless, went forth into homelessness;
thinking, "This is the Dharma," they remained established in the life of celibacy.
Having abandoned their homes and even their fathers, Indra felt compassion for them.
The Blessed One, having become a golden bird, addressed them:
"What has been done by these men who subsist on the remains of offerings is indeed very difficult to achieve.
Oh, how meritorious is their deed, and how praiseworthy is their way of life!"
"Those who were devoted to dharma have attained perfection and reached the supreme goal.
The sages said:
"Oh, how this bird praises those who eat the remains of sacrificial offerings!"
"Surely he is instructing us, for we are eaters of remnants.
The bird said:
"I do not praise you, who are smeared with mud and covered in dust."
"Those who eat leftovers are dull-witted; others indeed are those who eat the remains of sacrificial offerings.
The sages said:
"We ourselves worship this very thing, thinking it to be the supreme good."
"O Śakuni, speak that which is for our welfare; we truly place great faith in you.
Śakuni said:
"If you do not suspect me, dividing yourselves by your own will,"
"Therefore, I shall speak to you words that are beneficial and true to reality.
The sages said:
"O dear one, we listen to your words; the paths are well known to you."
"O righteous-souled one, we wish to abide by your command; please instruct us.
Śakuni said:
"Among quadrupeds, the cow is the foremost; among metals, gold is the best."
The mantra is the most excellent of sounds; the Brāhmaṇa is the best of bipeds.
This mantra is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa from the birth-rite onwards, throughout his life until his death at the cremation ground.
Vedic rituals constitute his unsurpassed path to heaven; furthermore,
they declare that all rites are perfected through mantras,
and thus success in this world is sought through those whose words are firmly rooted in the sacred tradition.
The months, the half-months, the seasons, the sun, the moon, and the stars—
all beings strive after these; this is the field of success for those attached to ritual action, this is the holy place, this indeed is the great stage of life.
Now, those men who, censuring ritual action, have entered upon a wrong path—
sin indeed belongs to those fools who are devoid of purpose.
[They disregard] the eternal lineages of the gods, the ancestors, and the Vedas.
Having abandoned [this], the deluded act, and thereby they go to a path not heard of in the scriptures.
"Let this be your appropriate austerity; I shall give it," so was the seer impelled.
Therefore, when one resolves upon that, it is called the austerity of the ascetic.

Having divided the eternal lineages of the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins, he performed the service of his teacher; that indeed is called difficult to accomplish. For it was by performing what is difficult that the gods attained supreme sovereignty.
Therefore, I declare to you that the life of a householder is difficult to undertake.
For austerity is the highest good, and this is the root of all creatures; of this there is no doubt.
It is upon this domestic order, by means of its prescribed rules, that everything is established.
The learned Brahmins who have transcended the pairs of opposites and are free from envy know this to be austerity;
therefore, the middle forest among the worlds is called austerity. Those who subsist on the remains of sacrificial food attain that state which is difficult to reach.
Having divided the food daily between morning and evening according to rule for his own family,
and having given portions to guests, the gods, the ancestors, and his kin,
those who eat what remains are called *vighasāśins*.
Therefore, by adhering to their own duty, being firm in their vows and speakers of truth,
they become teachers of the world and remain unblemished.
Having attained the third heaven of Śakra in the celestial realm, they dwell there free from envy.
"Those people who perform difficult deeds dwell for eternal years.
Then, having heard those words of his which were consistent with dharma and artha,
they abandoned the path of nihilism and took refuge in the dharma of the householder's life.
"Therefore, O invincible one, best among men, relying upon eternal fortitude, rule the entire earth whose enemies have been slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:

Having heard Arjuna’s words, Nakula, the subduer of enemies and possessor of great wisdom, looked toward the king— the best among all upholders of dharma— and, out of deference to his brother’s mind, spoke these words.
Broad-chested, mighty-armed, with a copper-hued face and measured speech—
know, O great king, that all the fires of the gods were piled at Viśākha-yūpa; therefore, know that the gods abide on the path of action.

Even those who are not atheists, who give life to theists and act as fathers to them, they too perform only ritual action; behold the rule, O King! But know that those who are cast out by the Vedic injunctions are extreme atheists.

"For a Brahmin who abandons what is declared in the Vedas in all his ritual acts does not reach the back of the celestial realm by the path of the gods, O Bhārata. Those certain of the Vedas say that he surpasses all stages of life."
O lord of men, learn from me of those Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with Vedic learning:
they bestow wealth acquired through righteous means upon the foremost of sacrifices for those of perfected self; O great king, such a man is indeed remembered as a renouncer.

Without regard for the acquisition of pleasure, established likewise in the higher state, O Great King, he who abandons even his own self is a renouncer characterized by darkness (tāmasa), O Lord. Wandering without a fixed abode, the sage takes refuge at the roots of trees.
O Pārtha, that yogi who never cooks for himself, who is renounced and lives as a mendicant,
who disregards anger and joy as well as malice, O lord of men—
that brahmin who studies the Vedas is a renouncer and a worshiper of his guru.
12.012.011 Wise men say that all the stages of life (āśramas) have been weighed together on a scale:
O King, those three are on one side, and the householder’s stage (gṛhasthāśrama) alone is on the other.
12.012.012 For he who truly considers the goal, O Bhārata, as well as pleasure and heaven—[it is the householder who achieves them].
"This is the path of the great seers; this is the way of those who know the world"—
he who maintains such a disposition is a true renunciant, O bull of the Bharatas,
and not he who, like a fool, abandons his home for the forest.
When one who is crooked and a hypocrite regarding the Dharma looks upon sensual pleasures,
then the King of Death binds him by the neck with the noose of death.
Action performed out of pride is said to be fruitless.
O Great King, everything joined with renunciation yields great fruit:
tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, charity, truth, purity, and straightforwardness;
sacrifice, fortitude, and righteousness—this is remembered as the eternal ordinance of the seers.
An undertaking here for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and guests is praised;
for in this very path, O Great King, the threefold aim (trivarga) is the exclusive fruit. For one who abides by this rule practiced by the Brahmins—
For one who is renounced and active in this world, no destruction exists anywhere. Indeed,
O King, the stainless Prajāpati, with a tranquil soul, created offspring with the thought, "They shall worship me with sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees."
Climbers, trees, and likewise medicinal herbs for the sake of sacrifice; sacrificial animals fit for offering, as well as the oblations intended for sacrifice—
these are obstructed by those in the householder stage of life who perform such sacrificial rites.

Therefore, the life of a householder in this world is both difficult to perform and difficult to attain. Having attained that state, O Great King, those householders who possess cattle and grain but do not perform sacrifices incur eternal sin.
The seers perform the sacrifice of Vedic study, while others perform the sacrifice of knowledge;
yet others extend the great sacrifices by means of the mind alone. Furthermore, O Great King, this other matter has been told to me by the wise.
Neither earth, nor fire, nor wind, nor water, nor the sun;
neither the stars, nor the moon, nor the quarters of space, nor time itself;
neither sound, nor touch, nor form, nor smell, nor taste exists anywhere.
And there are no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which an object of cognition (*prameya*) could be established:
neither perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor inference (*anumāna*), nor comparison (*upamāna*), nor scripture (*āgama*);
neither presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), nor tradition (*aitihya*), nor example (*dṛṣṭānta*), nor doubt (*saṃśaya*).
O King, there is no final certainty anywhere regarding what is unrighteousness or what is indeed righteousness;
there are neither animals nor immobile beings, neither gods nor humans;
there is no division of castes and stages of life, nor is there any agent or performer of action.
There is neither purpose nor prosperity, nor any activity directed toward purpose;
O King, this entire world has become shrouded in darkness and is without light.
Even though the Self exists, it does not attain union with the mind.

The mind was indeed unconscious, while the Self alone was conscious; the Lord alone is consciousness, and by Him this world has been made profound. And the mantras, O King, were conscious, yet they were not joined with a body.
And those sages named Viśvasṛjs were the deities of the mantras;
having received consciousness from the Lord, the cosmic egg was fashioned by them. Having performed the sacrifice to the Viśvasṛj, the Great-Grandfather (Brahmā) was created.
By him, through the grace of the Lord, the creation was undertaken;
this is the consciousness of the Lord by which this world is conscious,
and the entire world has been pervaded by Śambhu through yoga.
Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa were briefly explained by the Supreme Lord, the Sovereign, according to his own will;
yet the ignorant creature is powerless, a mere vessel for pleasure and pain.
Impelled by the Lord, one may go either to heaven or even into a pit.
Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and the Self of all embodied beings,
as well as the mind and the object of sense— all these are impelled by consciousness (cetanā).
Driven by their own actions, they are joined with pleasure and pain; the division of social classes and stages of life was set in motion by the Lord;
this world, including the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, was created by him.
O Great King, you and others alike abide under the control of the Lord;
we live and we die, and are in no way independent.
Having abandoned and having abandoned all beings, and having destroyed this entire world—
He who worships the deity through such action is not smeared by sin.
Although the rituals of all householders are inherently violent,
those who perform them for the sake of the deities and the sages attain the supreme goal.
In the past, enemies were struck down everywhere by rulers of the earth who desired the welfare of their subjects and sought their own well-being;
if there were sin in that, how is it that they have attained heaven?
O King, those who are enveloped by evil deeds do not fall into hell; O ruler,
the denizens of heaven envy that twice-born man who abides in the path of the concentration of giving and has become one with Brahman.

Having gathered various kinds of jewels from here and there, you do not bestow them in sacrifices; O lord of men, you utter words of atheism while remaining devoted to your family, yet I see no true renunciation in you.

O Great King, perform sacrifices with the Rājasūya, the Aśvamedha, or again with the Sarvamedha, and whatever other rites are honored by the Brāhmaṇas, O dear one, so that you may become like Śakra, the lord of the gods.
A king who, through the fault of his own negligence, allows his subjects to be plundered by robbers,
and who provides no refuge for his people, is said to be the personification of Kali.
[He seizes] horses, cows, female slaves, and well-adorned female elephants.
O lord of the people, with minds possessed by envy, we shall become those who ruin kings, failing to bestow villages, districts, fields, and houses upon the twice-born.
Those who do not give, who offer no refuge, and who share in the king's transgressions,
shall experience only sufferings and never any pleasures;
for they have neither performed the great sacrifices nor offered the ancestral *svadhā* oblations.
If you then go forth into homelessness without having renounced [worldly attachments] at sacred fords (tīrtha),
you will vanish like a cloud torn asunder by the wind;
fallen from both worlds, you will remain suspended in the intermediate space.
Having abandoned whatever exists internally or externally that causes attachment of the mind, one should be a renouncer— not he who merely departs after leaving behind his home.
For one abiding in this rule practiced by the wise Brahmins, [there is liberation].
"O Great King, there is no destruction whatsoever for a Brāhmaṇa.
Having swiftly slain his enemies in their prosperity, just as Śakra [slays] the hosts of Daityas in battle."
O Pārtha, who would grieve when one is devoted to his own duty,
which was remembered by the ancients, O King, and practiced by the wise?
And one does not grieve even for those slain while performing their own duty.
Having conquered the earth through the duty of a warrior and through valor— just as it was done by the foremost of kings of old— he bestowed it upon those learned in the sacred mantras.
"O lord of men, you shall go to the back of the celestial vault;
O Pārtha, you should not grieve today.
Sahadeva said:
"O Bhārata, success does not come about by abandoning external objects;
nor does success come about, or perhaps not, by abandoning the bodily objects.
For one who is liberated from external objects yet still covets those pertaining to the body,"
Whatever dharma or whatever happiness may belong to our enemies, let that be ours as well;
and whatever dharma or whatever happiness may belong to our friends as they rule the earth, having renounced their own bodies and possessions, let that be ours as well.
That which consists of two syllables is death, while that which consists of three syllables is the eternal Brahman.
"It is mine" is death, and "it is not mine" is the eternal. Both Brahman and death, O King, are situated within the self alone.
"Even if they remain unseen, they would undoubtedly cause living beings to fight. O Bhārata, if the indestructibility of this being were certain,
then even after piercing the bodies of creatures, no violence would ensue."
Moreover, if the arising and the dissolution of a sentient being were simultaneous,
then upon the destruction of the body, [the being] would be destroyed, and the path of ritual action would be in vain.
Therefore, having abandoned this absolute [view], [one should follow] that which was practiced by those of old and even those before them.
This path, frequented by the virtuous, should be followed by one who possesses discernment;
it was likewise trodden by Svāyambhuva Manu and other universal monarchs.
For if this were indeed an inferior path, why would it have been pursued by them?
O Bhārata, this earth has been enjoyed many times by them, O King, throughout the virtuous ages beginning with Kṛta and Tretā;
yet even after obtaining the entire earth, together with all its moving and unmoving beings, [it remains unsatisfied].
The life of that king who does not consume [the fruits of his rule] properly is fruitless. Or rather, O King, even for one dwelling in the forest and living on forest produce,
if he possesses a sense of "mine" regarding material things, he dwells in the jaws of death.
"O Bhārata, behold the true nature of all things, both external and internal;
those who perceive that nature are liberated from great fear.
You are my father, you are my mother, you are my brother, and you are my teacher."
Therefore, you ought to forgive these lamentations of one who is afflicted with grief.
Whether what I have spoken here be true or false, know that it was said out of devotion, O protector of the earth, O best of the Bharatas.
12,014.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
While Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and King of Dharma, remained silent,
his brothers spoke various diverse conclusions derived from the Vedas.
12,014.002a Endowed with a noble lineage, illustrious, and large-eyed,
12,014.002c Draupadī, the best among women, addressed the king of kings,
12,014.003a as he sat there, a bull among monarchs, surrounded by his brothers.
Like a leader of a herd surrounded by elephants resembling lions and tigers,
she was always full of self-respect, especially toward Yudhiṣṭhira;
cherished constantly by the king, she was a knower of dharma and a perceiver of dharma.
Addressing her husband with most beautiful and conciliatory words, she whose hips were broad looked at him and then spoke these words:
"O Pārtha, these brothers of yours are like withering *stokaka* birds."
"They stand crying out piteously, yet you do not rejoice in them.
O Great King, gladden these who are constantly partakers of suffering with appropriate words, like great elephants in rut."
"O King, how is it that previously in the Dvaitavana forest, after speaking such words to these brothers who were together and afflicted by cold, wind, and heat, you said:
'Having slain Duryodhana in battle, we shall enjoy the earth'?"
For those seeking victory in battle, [the field] was filled with all their desires;
having deprived chariot-warriors of their chariots and slain great elephants,
those subduers of enemies covered the earth with chariots and riders.
"By performing various sacrifices, abundant and accompanied by ample sacrificial fees,
the suffering caused by dwelling in the forest will lead to our happiness.
Having spoken thus to them yourself, O best among the upholders of dharma—
"How is it, O hero, that you now strike down even our hearts?
A coward does not enjoy the earth; a coward does not partake of wealth;
and in the house of a coward, sons do not dwell, like fish in the mud."
A Kṣatriya does not shine without punishment, nor does he attain prosperity without punishment;
O Bhārata, the subjects of a king who lacks punishment do not thrive in happiness.
[This world], adorned with gods, asuras, gandharvas, and apsarases, is [ruled by him].
Adorned by *rakṣas*, *guhyakas*, *nāgas*, and humans,
and filled with the three aims of life (*trivarga*) as well as the attainment of those three aims, the entire world, governed by the rod of punishment, is fit for enjoyment.
O protector of the earth, listen to this eternal scripture concerning the Self-Existent One (*svayaṃbhū*). This is known to the Brahmins and to you as well, O lord of the people;
for when this world is without a king and everything runs away in fear from all sides...
For the protection of this world, the Lord created a king—
of massive body and great prowess, capable of guarding the universe—
who possessed the qualities of Anila, Agni, Yama, Ārka, Indra, and Varuṇa.
Having extracted the eternal measures from both Candra and Vitteśa,
O King, because this lord of men arises from a portion of these lords of the gods,
he therefore overcomes all beings with his splendor.
He blazes like the sun, scorching both eyes and minds;
no one on earth is able even to look upon him.
He becomes fire and wind, he becomes the sun, the moon, and the King of Dharma.
He is Kubera, he is Varuṇa, and he is the majestic Mahendra; indeed, the splendor of the divine Grandfather, of Viṣṇu, of Śarva,
and of all the ṛṣis is established within him.
A king must not be despised even if he is a child, thinking "he is merely a human being," for he is a great deity dwelling in human form. Fire burns only the man who approaches it carelessly.
The fire of a king burns the family along with its accumulation of livestock and wealth;
the house of Dhṛtarāṣṭra has been consumed by the fire born of his own wrath. This is evident to the whole world, and there is no doubt about it.
A king who is of noble birth, endowed with virtuous conduct, and righteous,
who is devoted to the protection of his subjects, is honored even by the gods—
provided he examines the task at hand, as well as his own power, place, and time, according to their true nature.

For the sake of accomplishing dharma, he repeatedly assumes manifold forms. Prosperity (Padmā Śrī) dwells in his favor, victory in his prowess, and death in his anger; for he is composed of all splendor.
But that man who hates him out of delusion perishes;
for even the king sets his mind upon his swift destruction. Therefore, the king applies himself to that dharma which he desires for those who are dear to him.
Even when facing what is undesirable among those things that are undesirable, one should not swerve from that dharma.
For the sake of all beings, the Lord created in the beginning Dharma as his own son, the rod of punishment, which is composed of the splendor of Brahman, to be its protector.
Out of fear of him, all beings— both stationary and moving— are fit for their respective enjoyments, and they do not deviate from their duties;
this occurs after he has truly considered the place, the time, the capacity, and the task.
He should exercise restraint toward men who act unjustly according to their deserts;
he is the king, he is the personification of punishment, he is the leader, and he is the ruler.
He is the imperishable lord of dharma for the social classes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*).
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them. The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be dharma.
When wielded after careful deliberation, the rod makes all subjects delighted.
But punishment applied without due consideration destroys everything on all sides. If the king were not to apply punishment tirelessly toward those deserving of it,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
A crow might eat the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and a dog might lick the oblation (*havis*). There would be no ownership anywhere, and the superior would descend to the inferior.
The entire world is kept in order by punishment; a truly pure man is difficult to find.
For it is through fear of punishment that the entire world is fit for enjoyment.
Even the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, rākṣasas, birds, and serpents—
they too are made fit for enjoyment only when restrained by punishment.
All social classes would become corrupt and all moral boundaries would be shattered;
moreover, the entire world would fall into turmoil through the misuse of punishment.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment (Daṇḍa) moves about, destroying evil—there alone does order prevail.
The subjects do not go astray there when the leader perceives rightly; they call that king their guide who speaks the truth,
who acts with deliberation, who is wise, and who is skilled in the matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
When a king administers that [punishment] properly, he advances toward heaven;
but one who is self-indulgent, a slave to sense-objects, and base, is destroyed by punishment itself.
For punishment possesses great majesty and is difficult to be wielded by those of undisciplined soul.
One who has strayed from righteousness destroys the king himself along with his kinsmen; thereafter, he harms the fortress, the kingdom, and the world of moving and unmoving beings,
as well as the sages and gods dwelling in the intermediate space.
He cannot be led by right means by one who is without companions, who is deluded, greedy, and of unrefined intellect, nor by one who indulges in sensual pleasures; rather,
he must be guided by one who is pure, true to his word, and follows the treatises on statecraft.
For punishment can indeed be administered by one who is wise and well-assisted;
he should act with justice within his own kingdom, yet be exceedingly severe toward his enemies.
He should be a friend to those who are crooked, affectionate toward his loved ones, and endowed with patience toward the Brahmins.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning grains from the earth,
his fame shall spread throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water; but for a king who acts otherwise, being one whose self is undisciplined, [his fame does not spread].
One's fame in the world would be diminished like a drop of ghee in water—
[so it would be] by Rudra, the god of gods, by Brahmā, O lord of the earth,
and by Viṣṇu the god and the high-souled Śakra.

O King, the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who had deviated from dharma, were struck down by the world-protectors, the spirits, and the high-souled Pāṇḍavas; those unrighteous men of evil conduct were overthrown along with their armies.
O Lord of the Earth, having slain them, not even the slightest fault attaches to you—
whether by means of guile, illusion, or according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, O King.
Benevolence toward all beings, charity, study, and austerity [are the virtues].
O best of kings, this is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa, not that of a king: the restraint of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous. This is the supreme duty of kings, as is not fleeing from battle.
He in whom both forbearance and anger, giving and withholding, fear and fearlessness, as well as both restraint and favor reside— he indeed is called a knower of Dharma.
Neither by sacred learning, nor by charity, nor by conciliation, nor by sacrifice [is he to be known].
This earth was obtained by you neither through bribery nor even otherwise;
for that force of the enemies, so prepared by heroes,
endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, and superior in its three constituent parts— [was overcome by you].

"O hero, that [kingdom] which was protected by Droṇa and Karṇa, as well as by Aśvatthāman and Kṛpa, has been slain by you; therefore, enjoy the earth. O great king, Jambūdvīpa is filled with various provinces."
"O tiger among men, O Lord,
Krauñcadvīpa, which is equal in size to Jambūdvīpa,
has been crushed by your rod on the western side of Mount Mahāmeru."
O lord of men, Śākadvīpa is equal in size to Krauñcadvīpa;
it was crushed by you with your staff to the east of Mahāmeru,
and it is commensurate with Śākadvīpa to the north of Mahāmeru.
O tiger among men, Bhadrāśva has been subdued by your rod;
and having plunged into the ocean, O hero, you have subdued with your rod the islands along with their intermediate islands, which are the abodes of various peoples.
O Bhārata, having performed these incomparable deeds,
O Great King, you do not rejoice even while being honored by the twice-born; therefore,
O Bhārata, look upon these brothers of yours and greet them with joy.
Like bulls in rut, like powerful lordly elephants,
all of them are equal to the immortals, capable of enduring enemies, and subduers of foes;
it is my conviction that even a single one among them would be sufficient for their happiness.
How much more so my husbands, those tigers among men and bulls among men,
who are like all the senses combined in the movement of a body? My mother-in-law, who is all-knowing and all-seeing, did not speak an untruth.
"O Pāñcālī, Yudhiṣṭhira, having slain many thousands of kings through his swift prowess, will establish you in unsurpassed happiness;
yet, O lord of men, I perceive that [his victory] has become futile because of your delusion."

"O Indra among kings, those whose eldest brother is mad follow his lead; therefore, because of your madness, O lord of men, all the Pāṇḍavas have become mad. For if your brothers were not mad, O ruler of people,"
Having bound you together with the atheists, they would rule the earth;
for indeed, he who acts thus like a fool does not attain what is beneficial. [They treat him] with incense, applications of collyrium, and even nasal therapies.

He who walks the path of unrighteousness should be treated with medicines; O King, madness must be removed by whatever means necessary. O best of the Bharatas, I am the most wretched of all women in the world.
"O King, since I desire to live even though I have been thus treated with hostility by my enemies—
the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who are always treading the path of unrighteousness— I see no fault whatsoever in the slaying of such as they."
O lord of men, hear these verses sung by Uśanas:
"The one who kills himself, the one who destroys wealth, the one who kills a kinsman, the one who administers poison, the one who kills with Atharvan rites, and he who violates his wife."
The Blessed Lord Brahmā declared to the high-souled Bhārgava that the killing of even these six types of aggressors is blameless,
O King— even if they belong to the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya castes and are walking upon the path of the righteous.

Having forcibly entered a house, one should put to death the murderer, as well as the poisoner, the giver of forbidden food or drink, and the arsonist; this is the path for rulers even in cases of the killing of cows or Brahmins.

Even for the sake of seizing the hair of women, one should fight against the Grandfather (Brahmā), the Lord of the gods; how much more so against a sinner? For the sake of cows and Brahmins, and during the calamities of kings—
Even a Brahmin of great power should fight when his own body is threatened by the destruction of the kingdom, or upon hearing the cries of distress raised by women.

One may slay a Brahmin who has deviated from the Dharma if he is an assailant; a wise man should not even mentally contemplate his death in any other circumstance. This same conduct applies in the case of killing a cow or a Brahmin, as well as for the purpose of protecting those who recite the sacred mantras.
A Kṣatriya must not kill a Brahmin, even when his own family is in peril, unless that Brahmin is a thief, a cruel man, or one who has strayed from the Dharma.
A base Kṣatriya, however, may fight with a Brahmin in battle to the best of his ability.
Even if an assailant (*ātatāyin*) approaching in battle is a master of the Vedānta, one may slay him with the intent to kill; by that act, one does not become a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*).
This applies whether he is a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one of the lowest castes.

One should never strike a peaceful Brāhmaṇa even with a blade of grass; if one should threaten a Brāhmaṇa, the offense becomes more serious when contact is made. For three hundred years, that sinner finds no firm standing.
Having struck [another] even once, one would fall into hell for a thousand years;
therefore, one should never threaten another, nor should one ever strike with a weapon,
for it is a settled rule that [the sinner remains there] as many years as the number of particles of dust the blood takes up.
For that many years, that wicked man shall wander in hell.
He who would pierce the skin or the bones of a Brahmin, or cause it to be done, should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin; he is the lowest of men and must perform penance.
Having killed a learned Brāhmaṇa as well as a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī,
one who has killed a Brāhmaṇa shall observe the vow for twenty-four years;
this is declared by all the wise to be double the gravity of the offense of killing a Brāhmaṇa.
If he does not perform penance, the king shall banish him after branding him with a mark.
Whether it be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, the king shall put him to death,
so that a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa or a thief may not think, "He will act in this same way."
Having cut off both hands and feet, as well as the nose and lips, the king should further deprive the slayer of a Brahmin— who is the highest sinner— of his eyes;
this is declared to be the punishment for a Śūdra, and likewise for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya.
But a Brāhmaṇa who does not perform penance should be banished;
a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra [who commits such a crime] he should cause to be slain with a weapon.
The king should banish Brāhmaṇas who have killed a Brāhmaṇa after branding them with a mark.
One should cause those with impaired faculties and those of the three [lower] castes to dwell together with Caṇḍālas.
