Whoever drinks from the same vessel as them becomes a slayer of a Brahmin by that very act of drinking. Furthermore, no funeral offerings (piṇḍas) should be given to the deceased by anyone [on their behalf].
Dark-complexioned, deformed, and with disheveled hair hanging down, she torments the perpetrator when unseen; they know her as "Brahmahatyā" (the personified sin of killing a Brahmin).
And by the one who has slain a Brahmin, the Brahmins, the lands, and the cities are all defiled.
Very soon they will be afflicted by famine, disease, and thieves. One should subject a Brāhmaṇa of evil deeds, an assailant of other Brāhmaṇas,
as well as a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, to the extraction of the eyes.
The king is the strength of the weak, as are those who are strong and virtuous;
for the wicked, whether they be powerful or powerless, death is desired. He who would slay even one guilty of a fault without first informing the lord of the earth—

Whether he be weak or strong, he deserves defeat; likewise, one who disregards the king’s command, the judge, or flees from the court, as well as one who refuses to acknowledge a witness of truthful speech— one such as this should be declared defeated.

He who escapes from bonds and he who, being a surety, does not pay; he who is of noble birth and wealthy—such a person deserves defeat. And that man who, summoned by the king’s command, does not go to the court.
Having relied upon a powerful man and being armed, he was defeated;
having conquered that man of great audacity with punishment,
one should send him to the next world, stripped of his body and all his possessions.

No one should offer funeral rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for one who is already dead; having committed such an act, he should be made to pay the middle amercement, the first level of the fine for violence. [This applies to] the adultery of a woman of noble family and the plundering of the kingdom.

The sages declare that killing a Brahmin, theft, treachery against the king, and fifthly, [the consumption of] liquor— these are indeed the great sins (mahāpātaka). This applies to acts of violence other than in battle, as well as to the public proclamation of one who has drunk liquor.
One must never overlook a man who commits a great sin such as violating the teacher’s bed or betraying a friend;
having swiftly confiscated all his property, one should then deprive him of his life.
The punishment ordained of old by Brahmā for the three castes is as follows: one who commits a great violence against a Brāhmaṇa should be branded and banished;
or else, the fine shall be one thousand gold pieces as ransom for his body.
Thus has the wise and high-minded Uśanas declared for the four castes,
as well as for women, children, and the elderly, regarding the death penalty; and Bṛhaspati has declared that for the wicked and ill-behaved, the end of life itself is the punishment.
O highly fortunate one, you have declared the punishment for all *ātatāyins* (assassins),
for all those of evil intent who commit sinful deeds in this world;
the punishment of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons is held to be faultless.
O King, while the evil-minded son of Subala and the wicked-souled Karṇa looked on,
and even while those heroes were watching, I was brought into the assembly hall during my menses by you.
O King, she was clothed in a single garment because of your fault; let there be no destruction of dharma for you through the ruin of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s lineage,
nor let [the city] be consumed by the fire of your wrath along with its herds and stores of wealth.
Thus, for your sake, I have encountered such suffering;
yet, by the grace of Āditya, I have not been deprived of my life,
protected by the God of gods, the cause of time for the world.
At that time, King Divākara did not leave them naked;
for those who strive with diligence, prosperity arises. But you, having obtained the entire earth, have brought this calamity upon yourself.
O King, just as Māndhātṛ and Ambarīṣa— those two best of kings— were esteemed by the rulers of the earth, so do you shine forth. Rule the divine earth, protecting your subjects with righteousness.
"O King, do not be despondent over this earth with its mountains, forests, and islands. Perform various sacrifices, offer oblations into the fires,
and bestow cities, enjoyments, and garments upon the twice-born, O best of kings."
12,015.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard the words of Yājñasenī, Arjuna spoke once more,
after having paid due respect to his mighty-armed elder brother and lord.
The rod of punishment governs all subjects; the rod alone protects them. The rod remains awake while others sleep; the wise know the rod to be Dharma.
O lord of men, the rod likewise guards both Dharma and Artha.
The rod of punishment protects desire; the rod is said to be the three goals of life (trivarga).
By the rod grain is protected, and by the rod wealth is protected. O wise one, accept this and observe the natural order of the world.
Some evildoers do not commit evil out of fear of royal punishment;
some do so out of fear of Yama’s rod, and others even out of fear of the next world;
yet some evildoers refrain from evil out of mutual fear of one another.
Thus, in this world created by destiny, everything is established upon punishment.
Out of fear of punishment alone, some do not devour one another;
for if punishment did not protect them, they would sink into blind darkness.

Because it tames the untamed and punishes even the undisciplined, the wise know it as *daṇḍa* (punishment), owing to its function of taming (*damana*) and punishing (*daṇḍana*). Out of fear of the next world, these wicked people do not commit evil.
For Brahmins, punishment is by word; for Kṣatriyas, it is the application of the arm;
for Vaiśyas, punishment is said to be by means of fines; and the Śūdra is declared to be exempt from punishment.
This is for the sake of preventing the delusion of mortals and for the protection of property.
O lord of the people, the boundary known as punishment has been established in the world;
where the dark, red-eyed Punishment moves about truthfully,
there the subjects do not go astray, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
it is only through fear of punishment that these men remain on the path. O King, one who is not afraid does not sacrifice, nor does one who is not afraid desire to give.
No man who is not fearless desires to abide by his agreement.
Without piercing the vital organs of others, without performing a cruel deed,
and without killing like a fisherman, one does not attain great prosperity.
For one who does not strike, there is no fame here in this world, nor wealth, nor even progeny.
It was by the slaying of Vṛtra alone that Indra became Mahendra;
he obtained the Māhendra cup and became the lord of the worlds.
The world worships most intensely those very gods who are the slayers:
Rudra is a slayer, as are Skanda, Śakra, Agni, Varuṇa, and Yama;
likewise, Kāla, Vāyu, Mṛtyu, Vaiśravaṇa, and Ravi are slayers.
O Bhārata, the Vasus, Maruts, Sādhyas, and Viśvedevas—
people bow down before these gods, humbled by their majesty;
but they do not worship Brahmā, nor Dhātṛ, nor Pūṣan in any way whatsoever.

Some men, themselves tranquil and having desisted from all activities, worship those who stand as mediators among all beings, who are self-controlled and devoted to peace. Indeed, I do not see anyone living in this world who lives by non-violence.
12,015.020c Living beings subsist upon other living beings; the stronger prey upon the weaker.
12,015.021a The mongoose eats mice, and the cat likewise eats the mongoose;
O King, the dog eats the cat, and the wild beast eats the dog.
A man eats them all; behold how dharma has come to pass! All this—whatever is moving and whatever is stationary—is food for the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Regarding this ordinance ordained by the gods, the wise man is not deluded.
"O Indra among kings, you ought to be as you were created.
For those who have subdued their anger and joy, who have retired to the forest and become mild,
such ascetics do not sustain their lives by taking life."
In water there are many living beings, as are those on the earth and within fruits;
yet there is no one who does not kill them—what else is there but the sustaining of life? Some beings have subtle origins that can only be reached through inference.
Even by the falling of a single eyelash, the destruction of their entire bodies might occur.
Having departed from their villages, sages who are free from anger and envy are seen wandering in the forest, deluded and still clinging to the duties of householders.
Having broken the earth, cut down plants, trees, and the like, and [killed] egg-born animals,
men perform sacrifices and thereby attain heaven.
When the science of government (daṇḍanīti) is properly administered, all undertakings succeed.
O Kaunteya, regarding all living beings, I have no doubt on this point:
if punishment did not exist in the world, these creatures would perish;
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish on a spit.
And this truth was spoken by Brahmā in the past:
"Punishment, when properly administered, protects the subjects.
Behold, even the fires grow calm and lose their fear.
Threatened by the fear of punishment, they tremble;
for if the king were not vigilant in inflicting punishment upon those deserving of it, O King,
this world would be like blinding darkness and nothing could be discerned.
If punishment did not exist in this world to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous,
even those who have violated the bounds of conduct, who are atheists, and who revile the Vedas,
would still be fit for the enjoyment of life only when kept in check by punishment.
The entire world is kept in check by punishment, for a truly pure man is difficult to find. Indeed, out of fear of punishment, people here apply themselves to their livelihoods.
This is for the sake of preventing confusion among the four social orders and for the proper guidance of men.
The rod of punishment was ordained by the Creator to protect both dharma and worldly prosperity.
If they did not fear the rod, birds and beasts of prey would devour livestock,
humans, and the sacrificial offerings intended for the rites.
If punishment did not protect, the student would not study, the auspicious cow would not be milked, and no maiden would go to her wedding;
universal chaos would prevail, and all social barriers would be shattered.
If punishment did not protect, people would not understand the sense of ownership;
they would not be able to perform year-long sacrificial sessions (*sattras*) free from fear,
nor could they conduct them according to rule with the prescribed sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), if punishment did not protect.
They would not practice the dharma in the hermitages by relying on the prescribed rules, if punishment did not protect learning from being lost.
Neither camels, nor oxen, nor horses, mules, nor donkeys [would exist].
If punishment did not protect, even yoked [animals] would not draw vehicles;
servants would not obey their commands, nor would a child ever act at any time, and one would not abide by the dharma taught by the fathers, if punishment did not protect.
All subjects abide by the rod; the wise know the rod to be fear. In the rod are established both heaven for men and this world.
Neither fraud, nor sin, nor even deception is seen there [in its absence].
12,015.044c Where the rod of punishment, well-applied, moves about as the destroyer of enemies;
12,015.045a A dog might boldly drink the sacrificial oblation if the rod were not raised;
12,015.045c A crow might carry off the *puroḍāśa* cake if the rod did not protect it.

Whether this kingdom has been acquired through righteousness or through unrighteousness, you should not feel grief in that regard; enjoy the pleasures and perform sacrifices. The prosperous, dressed in pure garments, practice dharma with ease.
Dwelling with beloved wives and enjoying excellent food, all undertakings for the sake of wealth depend upon it—of this there is no doubt;
and that [wealth] depends upon the rod. Behold the majesty of the rod!
The proclamation of Dharma here has been made solely for the sake of maintaining the course of worldly life;
"non-violence" and "the violence of the virtuous"—this is the superior adoption of Dharma.
No one is possessed of absolute qualities, nor is anyone entirely devoid of qualities.
In all their activities, both the good and the evil are seen:
having castrated the bulls, they then pierce their noses;
they make them pull heavy loads, bind them, and subdue them.
In this world thus confounded, led astray upon a worn-out path,
O Great King, practice the ancient Dharma through various means.
Sacrifice, give, protect your subjects, and uphold the Dharma.
"O Kaunteya, slay your enemies and protect your friends. Let there be no anger in you as you strike down your foes, O Bhārata;
for in that act, O Bhārata, no sin whatsoever accrues to the doer."

For he who would slay an approaching assassin does not thereby become a killer of an embryo; rather, it is wrath that encounters wrath. There is no doubt that the inner self of all beings is incapable of being slain.
Since the self is indestructible, how could it ever be slain by anyone? For just as a man might enter a new house again,
even so does the living soul enter various bodies.
"Having cast off old bodies, one assumes new ones;
thus do those people who perceive the truth describe the mouth of death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard Arjuna’s words, the highly indignant Bhīmasena, endowed with splendor, summoned his fortitude and spoke to his eldest brother:
"O King, you are one who knows the dharma; there is nothing on earth unknown to you."
"We have always endeavored to train ourselves in your conduct, yet we have not been able [to master it]. 'I shall not speak; I shall not speak'—this was the resolve fixed in my mind.
But out of extreme distress I shall speak; listen to that, O lord of men."
But because of your delusion, everything has been rendered doubtful;
we have fallen into a state of distress and likewise into weakness.
For how could the king of the world, who is learned in all the scriptures, [act thus]?
Out of dejection, he falls into delusion just like a base man. The coming and going of the world is known to you;
O Lord, there is nothing unknown to you regarding the future or the present.

"Since this is the case, O Great King, O lord of men, regarding the matter of sovereignty, I shall declare the cause here; listen to it with a focused mind. Disease arises in two ways: physical as well as mental."

The birth of these two from one another is not found to be free from mutual influence; a physical disease arises from a mental one—of this there is no doubt—and a mental disease arises from a physical one: this is the certainty.

He who grieves over past physical or mental sufferings obtains suffering through that very suffering and encounters two misfortunes. Cold, heat, and wind— these three are the qualities born of the body.
The equilibrium of these qualities is said to be the characteristic of health;
when any one of them is in excess, the following treatment is prescribed:
cold is countered by heat, and heat is countered by cold.
By both [means] the wind is bound; this is called the method.
Goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*)—these are the three qualities of the mind. By passion goodness is pacified; by goodness passion is pacified.
Grief is overcome by joy, and joy is overcome by grief. Someone dwelling in happiness desires to remember suffering;
someone dwelling in suffering desires to remember happiness.
Therefore, you should not be sorrowful for sorrow, nor joyful for joy;
you should not be sorrowful for that which has arisen as happiness, nor joyful for that which has arisen as suffering, O descendant of Kuru, for destiny is indeed most powerful.
Or perhaps this is your very nature, O King, by which you are dragged away—
having seen Kṛṣṇā brought into the assembly hall, clad in a single garment and in her courses,
while the sons of Pāṇḍu looked on— you ought not to forget that.
His exile from the city, his dwelling in deerskins,
and his residence in the great forest— you should not remember those things; nor should you recall his suffering at the hands of Jaṭāsura or his battle with Citrasena.
How have you forgotten the suffering caused by the Saindhavas? How have you forgotten the kick from Kīcaka’s foot during our life in concealment,
and how have you forgotten Princess Draupadī?
"O King, we are powerful and difficult even for the gods to conquer;
remember how we have fallen into the state of servitude in the city of Virāṭa.
And recall, O subduer of enemies, that battle you had with Droṇa and Bhīṣma."
"O you who possess a single mind, this terrible battle has now arrived for you—
a battle where arrows serve no purpose, nor do friends or kinsmen; you must fight alone, for that battle has come upon you."
If you should abandon your life while this battle remains unconquered,
you will take on another body and fight with that very same person once again.
For he who is not wealthy is fallen, and that which is meager is like the leavings of another.
Even for the powerful, much that is unwholesome exists; wealth protects nothing at all.
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, you must go this very day to the further shore of battle, having abandoned the manifest through your own actions toward the unmanifest.
If this battle remains unconquered, what state will you reach?
Having conquered this, O Great King, you will have accomplished all that was to be done. Having resolved upon this understanding, [consider] the coming and going of all beings.
"Rule the kingdom as is fitting, following the conduct of your fathers and grandfathers.
By good fortune, the wicked Duryodhana has been slain in battle along with his followers;
by good fortune, you have followed the path of Draupadī’s braid."
"Perform the horse sacrifice according to the rules, with abundant sacrificial fees;
we are your servants, O Pārtha, as is the heroic Vāsudeva.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Discontent, negligence, intoxication, passion, lack of tranquility,
force, delusion, arrogance, and even agitation in every respect—
possessed by these evils, you desire sovereignty.

Be free from worldly desires, liberated, tranquil, and truly happy. Even for that sole sovereign who might rule this entire earth as his pupil, there is but one stomach; why then do you praise this [earth]?
O bull among men, this desire cannot be fulfilled in a single day, nor in a month;
one could not satisfy it even in a lifetime, for it remains unfulfilled.
Just as a fire blazes when well-kindled, it is extinguished when not fed with fuel.

By eating little food, one should pacify the digestive fire that has arisen in the belly; yet the ignorant man, for the sake of his own belly, makes a great deal of leftover scraps. Conquer the belly, O Earth; by conquering it, you have conquered what is truly beneficial.

"You praise human sensual enjoyments and sovereign power; yet those who do not indulge in such pleasures and are devoid of strength go to the unsurpassed state. Furthermore, the security and prosperity of the kingdom, as well as righteousness and unrighteousness, rest upon you."
"Free yourself from this great burden by taking recourse in renunciation alone. For the sake of a single belly, a tiger kills much prey;
other animals of slow movement and gait depend upon that for their livelihood."

Having withdrawn from sense-objects, the ascetic practices renunciation; yet kings are not satisfied—behold the difference in their understanding! [Some live] on leaf-food, some who grind with stones, and likewise those who use their teeth as a mortar.
By those who subsist on water and those who subsist on air, this hell has been conquered. A king who might rule over this entire earth in its entirety,
and one for whom stone and gold are equal— such a person has achieved his purpose, not the monarch.
Be free from undertaking in your intentions, free from hope, and free from the sense of "mine. Abide in that sorrowless state which is imperishable both here and in the hereafter.
Those who are free from worldly attachments do not grieve; why then do you grieve for what is an attachment?
By renouncing all sensual pleasures, you shall be liberated from falsehood. The two paths, the path of the ancestors (pitṛyāna) and the path of the gods (devayāna), are well known;
those who perform sacrifices travel by the path of the ancestors, while those seeking liberation travel by the path of the gods.
Purified by austerity, celibacy, and the study of the Vedas,
they indeed shine forth after casting off their bodies, having reached a state beyond the reach of death. In this world, worldly gain is called a bond, and likewise, action is said to be a bond.
Freed from those two bonds, one attains that supreme state. Furthermore,
they cite this verse sung by Janaka,
who was free from dualities, liberated, and perceiving liberation:
"Infinite indeed is my wealth, though I possess nothing at all.
While Mithilā is in flames, nothing of mine is burned. Having ascended the palace of wisdom, I do not grieve for people who grieve."
Standing upon a mountain, one looks down upon those of dull intellect as if they were standing on the ground;
he who sees what is to be seen while seeing is truly sighted and wise. And because it brings about the discernment of the unknown and full awakening, it is called "intellect" (*buddhi*).
But he who understands speech indeed attains great honor among those learned ones of purified self who have attained the state of Brahman,
when he perceives the diverse states of beings as abiding in the One.
From that very [source], Brahman then attains expansion;
those people go to that state, but not the ignorant, nor those of small intellect,
nor those lacking wisdom, nor those devoid of austerity— for everything is established in the intellect.
12,018.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
When the king had become silent, Arjuna spoke to him once more,
tormented by grief and sorrow, and pierced by the arrow-like words of the king.
12,018.002 People relate this ancient history,
O Bhārata, a dialogue between the King of Videha and his wife, concerning that lord of men who had resolved to renounce his kingdom for the sake of living on alms.
12,018.003 [They tell of] that lord of people who, having abandoned his kingdom, set his mind upon seeking food by begging.
The distressed queen replied to the King of Videha:
"Having abandoned wealth, offspring, friends, and various kinds of jewels,
Janaka has adopted the tonsure and set out upon the path of purification."

His beloved wife saw him, who was living on alms and possessed nothing; he sat near a handful of parched grain, free from desire and devoid of envy. Approaching her husband, who was fearless of anything, she spoke to him.
In private, the high-minded wife, filled with anger, spoke these reasoned words:
"How is it that, having abandoned your own kingdom which was filled with wealth and grain,
you have adopted the life of a skull-bearer and wander in the forest on a handful of parched grain?"
"O King, your promise is one thing, yet your conduct is another.
O Ruler of the Earth, having abandoned a great kingdom, you find satisfaction in something so small.
O King, it is not by this that guests, celestial sages, and ancestors [are honored]."

"O King, it is possible for you to support [them] today; this exertion of yours is in vain. Abandoned by the gods, the guests, and the ancestors—by all of these—you wander as a mendicant, devoid of ritual action."

"You, who were once the master of thousands of Brahmins learned in the three Vedas and the protector of the world, now seek sustenance from others. Having abandoned your blazing splendor, you are now looked upon like a dog."
Today your mother Kausalyā is without a son, and you yourself are without a lord. Eighty kṣatriyas, desiring righteousness, wait upon you— pitiable men who, seeking rewards, place their hopes in you.
And by rendering them fruitless, O King, what worlds indeed will you go to? Since liberation is uncertain and embodied beings are dependent on others, for you—
a man of evil deeds— there is neither a higher world nor a lower one.
Having abandoned a lawful wife, you who desire to live—
why do you renounce garlands, perfumes, ornaments, and various garments, and wander forth as a mendicant devoid of action?

Having been a great purifier and a drinking-place for all beings, you have now become a wealthy lord of the forest and sit here attended by others. Indeed, many flesh-eaters even devour an elephant that has been left as a deposit.
There are already many worms [in this body]; how much more so for you, who are useless?
If someone were to break this water-pot, take away your triple-staff, and carry off your garment—how would your mind react to that?
"But as for this grasping of a handful of grain, having abandoned everything—
if all this [world] were equal to it, why is this being given to me?
If a handful of grain is the goal here, your promise is destroyed."
"Who am I to you, and who are you to me? What favor do you have for me today?
O King, rule the earth wherever your favor may be bestowed—be it upon a palace, a bed, a vehicle, garments, or ornaments."
Why indeed do you renounce those riches accumulated by those who, devoid of prosperity, penniless, abandoned by friends, and possessing nothing, yet sought only pleasure—
riches that one might as well accept forever or give away forever?
Know the difference between these two: which of them is said to be superior?
When gifts are given to those who are always begging and are free from deceit, it is like a poorly offered oblation cast into a forest fire.

O King, just as the fire Jātavedas is extinguished without having burnt anything, so too does a twice-born man who is constantly begging find no peace. In this world, the Vedas and food are the eternal foundation for the virtuous.

If there were no giver, how could there be those who desire liberation? From food arise householders in this world, and from that very food, monks likewise. From food life arises; thus, the giver of food is the giver of life.
Arising from householders and depending solely upon householders,
those who are self-controlled sit censuring their very source and foundation.
One should not recognize a mendicant by his renunciation, nor by his shaven head, nor by his begging.
But know that mendicant who straightforwardly renounces wealth to be happy.
Moving about unattached as if attached, free from worldly ties and released from bonds,
equal toward enemy and friend— he indeed is liberated, O lord of the earth.

Shaven-headed and clad in saffron robes, they wander about for the sake of alms; yet, bound by various snares, they vainly accumulate the bait of worldly gain— those who, having abandoned the three Vedas and the means of livelihood, even forsake their own sons.

Those of little intelligence accept the triple staff and the saffron robe; know that their wearing of the saffron robe while their impurities are not yet removed is merely for the sake of gain. It is my opinion that these shaven-headed men who carry the banner of dharma do so only for the sake of a livelihood.

O great king, by supporting virtuous men— whether they wear saffron robes, deerskins, or rags, or whether they are naked, shaven-headed, or wear matted locks— conquer the worlds, for you have mastered your senses. [Support those who maintain] the sacred fires, perform sacrifices for their gurus, and offer animals and priestly fees.
"Who indeed is more virtuous than he who gives three thousand five hundred gold coins every single day?
King Janaka is celebrated in this world as a knower of reality;
yet even he was once possessed by delusion—do not fall under the power of delusion."
Thus, this Dharma has been successively handed down by men who are ever devoted to giving,
endowed with the quality of compassion, and free from desire and anger;
they protect their subjects and remain established in the highest form of charity.
"Devoted to Brahman, truthful in speech, honoring our elders and teachers, and offering oblations according to the rules to the gods, guests, and servants, we shall attain the worlds we desire."
"We shall attain the desired state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O father, I know the scriptures, both those that are lower and those that are higher."
The Vedic injunctions are twofold: "Perform action" and "Renounce action.
The scriptures are also confused and variegated with various arguments. Therefore, I shall declare to you, according to the rule, the exact extent of that certainty which the Veda establishes.
But you, though skilled solely in weapons and observant of the vow of a hero,

are in no way capable of understanding the true meaning of the scriptures as it really is. Only one who perceives the subtle meaning of the scriptures is proficient in determining the nature of dharma.
"Therefore, you should not speak to me in this way, even if you perceive it as dharma.
O son of Kuntī, the words you have spoken out of brotherly affection are just and appropriate; for that, O Arjuna, I am pleased with you."
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a being equal to me, equal to Īśvara, equal to Brahmā, or equal to Vāsudeva; likewise,
among the foremost of warriors, you are said to possess the highest strength.
The strength that exists in Indra and Vāyu, and the strength that exists in Janārdana—
that same strength is found in Bhīmasena and in you, O Arjuna.
O Pāṇḍava, you are a versatile warrior equal to him, and a long-range shooter as well.
Endowed with divine weapons, what other man is equal to you?
In all the laws of war and in the skillful execution of actions,
there is no one found in the three worlds who is your equal.

That which is righteous and endowed with dharma is known by me in its entirety; however, that speech concerning the subtleties of dharma is difficult for you to cross over. O Dhanañjaya, you ought not to harbor doubt regarding my intellect.
"You are merely an expert in the science of war; you have not served the elders.
You do not know the definitive conclusions of those who understand both the concise and the detailed.
My dear son, for the wise, the conclusion is this: asceticism, renunciation, and the prescribed rule."
Each subsequent one among these is superior; this is the path to the highest good (*naiḥśreyasī gati*).
But you do not think thus, O Pārtha, that there is nothing superior to wealth. In this regard, I shall explain to you how this is not the primary concern.
For righteous people are seen to be devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas;
there are sages endowed with ascetic power for whom eternal worlds are secured. Likewise, there are wise men who have not yet grown beards and others who dwell in the forest.
12,019.012c Those who were infinite in number and destitute of wealth have gone to heaven by means of sacred study. 12,019.013a But by the northern path, the noble ones—
having abandoned the darkness born of ignorance through the restraint of the senses— have gone to the worlds of those who practice renunciation.
But that radiant path which you see to the south—
these are the worlds of those who perform ritual actions, who have resorted to cremation grounds. However, that destination which those seeking liberation behold is indescribable.
Therefore, renunciation is held to be the primary goal, yet it is difficult to realize.
Poets, however, remain established in their positions by following the scriptures, desiring to discern the essential from the non-essential, thinking, "It might be here; it might be there."
Having transcended the declarations of the Vedas and the Āraṇyaka scriptures,
they split open the trunk of a plantain tree and saw no core within it.
Then, by means of absolute exclusion, [they analyzed] the body composed of the five elements.
They say that the self is endowed with desire and aversion, as is known through its gestures;
yet it cannot be grasped by the eye, nor can it be defined by speech. Preceded by the cause of karma, it transmigrates among living beings.
Having made one’s sphere of activity virtuous and having restrained the thirst of the mind,
and having cast off the continuity of karma, one may become happy, free from support. On this very path, which is subtle to perceive and practiced by the virtuous—
"O Arjuna, why do you praise that which is full of misfortune?
For people who know the ancient scriptures, O Bhārata, always perceive it thus:
they are constantly devoted to ritual acts, such as giving, sacrifice, and religious duty."
Even those who are wise and possess the causes for understanding are very difficult to turn back;
though they have firmly mastered what was heard before, the deluded proclaim, "This does not exist," rejecting the nectar while speaking thus in the assembly of people.
"12,019.024c They wander over the entire earth, eloquent and deeply learned;
12,019.025a those whom we do not recognize—who here is capable of knowing them?
12,019.025c Thus it is with those who are wise, virtuous, great, and most proficient in the scriptures."
"Through austerity one attains greatness; through intelligence, indeed, one finds greatness;
through renunciation, O son of Kuntī, the knower of dharma always attains happiness.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In that interval between speeches, the eloquent Devasthāna, of great asceticism,
spoke these even more refined words to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"As for the speech uttered by Phalguna— that there is nothing superior to wealth— "
12,020.002c Here I shall relate this to you; listen with a one-pointed mind.
12,020.003a O Ajātaśatru, by means of righteousness (dharma), the entire earth has been conquered by you. 12,020.003c Having conquered it, O King, you ought not to abandon it in vain.
For this four-stepped ladder is firmly established upon action;
O mighty-armed king, conquer it step by step in due order. Therefore, O Pārtha, perform great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.

"O Bhārata, you should understand that some sages perform the sacrifice of Vedic study, while others perform the sacrifice of knowledge; yet others are devoted to ritual action and devoted to austerity,
O King of kings, as is heard in the words of the Vaikhānasas."
For one who strives for the sake of wealth, non-striving is superior;
for whoever would rely upon that wealth, a greater evil would increase.
And for the sake of wealth, they undergo the accumulation of property with great difficulty.
Thirsting for wealth and lacking wisdom, one does not perceive the sin of destroying an embryo. Because one gives to the undeserving and does not give to the deserving,
the duty of giving is difficult to perform due to the failure to distinguish between the unworthy and the worthy.

Wealth was created by the Creator for the sake of sacrifice; the person who performs the sacrifice is both its intended recipient and its protector. Therefore, everything should be employed solely for the purpose of sacrifice.
Immediately after that came wealth, and then desire.
With various sacrifices accompanied by abundant food, the mighty Indra surpassed all the gods.
Having attained the state of Indra through that, he shines resplendent;
therefore, everything should be employed in the sacrifice.
The Great-Souled Mahādeva [is present] in the Sarvamedha sacrifice.
Having offered himself as a sacrifice, the god of gods, manifesting his power,
pervades and supports all the worlds with his glory; radiant and clothed in animal skins, he shines forth.
Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, was indeed a king among mortals who, through his prosperity, conquered the king of the gods;
at his sacrifice, Fortune herself took up residence.
In which all the vessels were made of gold—
12,020.014a— you have heard of Hariścandra, the lord of kings,
who, having performed sacrifices, was a doer of merit and free from sorrow.
"That mortal who conquered Śakra through his supernatural power (ṛddhi) must consume everything at the sacrifice.
Devasthāna said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history of what Bṛhaspati said when questioned by Indra at the time of their meeting:
"Contentment is indeed the highest heaven; contentment is the supreme happiness."
Nothing external to contentment stands perfectly firm;
when one withdraws all desires from every side, as a tortoise draws in its limbs,
then the self alone, being the light of the self, becomes serene through its own self.

When he does not fear, and when others do not fear him, and when he conquers desire and hatred, then he perceives the Self. When he neither becomes angry nor feels malice toward any living beings, [then he perceives the Self].
Then, through action, mind, and speech, one attains Brahman. Thus, O Kaunteya, beings perceive each respective dharma at each respective time; therefore, understand this, O Bhārata.

Some praise tranquility, while others likewise praise physical exertion; some do not praise one nor the other, while still others praise both. Some people praise sacrifice, and other people praise renunciation.
Some praise giving, while others praise receiving;
some, having renounced everything, sit in silent meditation.
Some praise sovereignty, the protection of all beings.
Having killed, having pierced, and having cut—some [practitioners] are devoted solely to such ascetic conduct.
Having observed all this, the wise have reached this conclusion:
that dharma which consists precisely in non-injury toward living beings is what is esteemed by the virtuous.
Absence of malice, truthfulness of speech, sharing with others, fortitude, forbearance,
procreation within one's own wife, gentleness, modesty, and lack of fickleness—
Manu, the son of the Self-existent, declared these to be the wealth desired by those for whom Dharma is paramount.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, protect [the kingdom] with such effort.

For that Kṣatriya who is ever established in sovereignty, self-controlled, to whom the pleasant and unpleasant are equal, who eats only the remnants of sacrifice, and who knows the true meaning of the science of kingship— [he alone is a true ruler].
Devoted to the restraint of the wicked and intent on the support of the virtuous,

the knower of dharma should establish his subjects upon the path of righteousness and conduct himself accordingly. Then, having transferred the royal glory to his son, he should dwell in the forest, subsisting on the products of the wild.
Following the very discipline of a recluse, he should pass his time without sloth.
For the king who conducts himself in this way, firmly resolved upon the duties of a king,
both this world and the next shall be fruitful, O monarch.
But I consider Nirvana to be very difficult to cross and fraught with many obstacles. Thus have they followed the Dharma, being devoted to truth, charity, and austerity,
endowed with the virtues of compassion, and free from desire and anger.
Devoted to the protection of their subjects and established in the highest self-restraint,
they attained the supreme goal through battle for the sake of cows and Brahmins.
O scorcher of foes, it was thus that the Rudras, along with the Vasus and the Ādityas, [attained their state].
The Sādhyas and hosts of royal seers, having relied upon this dharma,
became vigilant and thereby attained heaven through their own meritorious deeds.
Vaiśampāyana said:
In that interval between speeches, Arjuna spoke once more to his eldest brother, the lord, whose mind was despondent:
"O knower of dharma, having obtained this unsurpassed kingdom through the duty of a kshatriya..."
"O best of men, having conquered the enemies, why do you grieve so intensely?
O great king, death in battle is ordained for Kṣatriyas;
it is superior to many sacrifices—remember the duty of a warrior."
"O Lord, for Brahmins, austerity and renunciation are recorded as the prescribed dharma for the afterlife;
for Kshatriyas, death in battle is ordained. The dharma of the Kshatriya is known to be extremely fierce and constantly centered on weapons."
O best of the Bharatas,
even for a Brāhmaṇa who abides by the duty of a Kṣatriya, O King,
death by the sword in battle at the proper time is praised in this world; for the Kṣatriya is established in the Brahman.
"O lord of men, neither renunciation, nor begging, nor asceticism,
nor living off the wealth of others is prescribed for a Kṣatriya. You, O bull of the Bharatas, are a knower of all dharmas and the soul of all."
The wise king, skillful in the world and having seen both the higher and the lower,
should abandon the grief born of distress and be girded for action;
for the heart of a Kṣatriya, especially, is as firm as a diamond.

"O lord of men, having conquered your enemies in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya and having obtained a kingdom free from thorns, you, who have mastered your own self, should be devoted to sacrifice and charity. Indeed,
Indra was the son of a Brāhmaṇa, yet he became a Kṣatriya through his actions."
He slew ninety-nine kinsmen of evil conduct;
and that deed of his, O lord of the people, was indeed worthy of honor and praise. By means of it, he attained the sovereignty of the gods—so we have heard.
Therefore, O great king, perform sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
just as Indra does, O lord of men, so that you may be free from distress for a long time. Since this is the case, O bull among kṣatriyas, do not grieve at all.
Purified by weapons in accordance with the duty of a Kṣatriya, they have attained the supreme goal.
O bull of the Bharatas, that which has occurred was destined to be so;
for destiny, O tiger among kings, cannot be transgressed.
12,023.001 Vaiśampāyana said: O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, the Kauravya son of Kuntī said nothing; thereupon Dvaipāyana spoke.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, these words of Bibhatsu are entirely true.
The stage of life known as the householder’s state is recorded in the scriptures as the highest dharma.
O knower of dharma, practice your own duty according to the scriptures and according to the prescribed rules."

"For it is not ordained that you should abandon the life of a householder for the forest. Indeed, the gods, the ancestors, the seers, as well as your dependents, always subsist upon the householder; therefore, O lord of the earth, devote yourself to them."

O lord of the earth, birds, domestic animals, and all living beings are sustained by householders alone; therefore, the householder is the foremost among those in the stages of life (āśramas). Indeed, this stage is the most difficult of these four stages to practice.
O Pārtha, perform that [vow] with an undistracted mind, for it is difficult to practice for those with weak senses.
You possess complete knowledge of the Vedas and have performed great austerities;
now you ought to bear the burden of the kingdom inherited from your father and grandfather.
Austerity, sacrifice, as well as knowledge, living on alms, restraint of the senses,
meditation, solitary conduct, contentment, and giving according to one's ability— these,
O Great King, are the activities of Brahmins that bring about perfection.
And I shall speak further concerning the Kṣatriyas, which is already known to you as well:
sacrifice, learning, exertion, and lack of contentment regarding prosperity; the wielding of the extremely fierce rod of punishment, and the protection of the subjects.

O lord of the people, complete knowledge of the Vedas, as well as austerity, virtuous conduct, the acquisition of great wealth, and its bestowal upon worthy recipients— these are the meritorious deeds of kings.
"We have heard that they bring success to both this world and the next;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is said that for them, the wielding of the rod of punishment is the superior duty,
for strength always resides in the Kṣatriya, and within strength, the rod is established."
O King, these activities bring about the success of Kṣatriyas;
and Bṛhaspati also spoke this verse:
"The earth swallows these two, just as a snake swallows creatures dwelling in holes."
One who does not oppose the king and does not exile a Brahmin [attains success]; moreover,
it is heard that the royal sage Sudyumna attained supreme perfection through the wielding of the rod of punishment, just like Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, by what deed did Sudyumna, the lord of the earth, attain supreme perfection? I wish to hear about that king."
Vyāsa said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history:
there were two brothers, Śaṅkha and Likhita, who were firm in their vows.
Each of them had a delightful dwelling,
situated separately along the Bāhudā river, provided with trees that bore flowers and fruit in all seasons.
Then, on one occasion, Likhita went to the hermitage of Śaṅkha.
Then, by chance, Śaṅkha emerged from the hermitage.
Having approached his brother Śaṅkha’s hermitage,
Likhita then gathered fruits that were perfectly ripe.
Taking them up, that twice-born man ate them with confidence. While he was indeed eating, Śaṅkha also arrived at the hermitage.
Seeing him eating, Śaṅkha spoke to his brother.
"From where were these fruits obtained, and by what means do you eat them?
He replied to his elder brother, touching him and saluting him, as if laughing: "I have taken them from right here."
Then Śaṅkha, filled with intense anger, said to him:
"This theft was committed by you yourself while gathering these fruits.
Go, approach the king, and proclaim your own deed."
Then, O King, having been urged by his brother's words, Likhita went to the kingdom of Sudyumna and, deeply distressed, spoke these words:
"O best of kings, this act of taking what was not given has indeed been committed."
"Knowing me to be a thief, uphold your own duty;
O lord of men, quickly inflict the punishment for a thief upon me.
Having been addressed thus, [the king] acted upon his words toward Sudyumna, the ruler of the earth.
O mighty-armed one, Likhita, firm in his vows, approached him.
But Sudyumna, the lord of men, having heard from the frontier guards that Likhita had arrived,
went out on foot together with his ministers.
Approaching that best of those who know Brahman, the king said to him:
"Tell me, O Blessed One, for what purpose have you come? That [purpose] is already accomplished.
Thus addressed, that brahmin-sage spoke this to Sudyumna.
"Having promised, 'I shall do it,' you ought to fulfill that once you have heard it. O bull among men, O King, I have eaten fruits not authorized by my preceptor; punish me for that without delay."
Sudyumna said:
"O bull among brahmins, if the king is considered by you to be the authority in the administration of punishment, then he should likewise be the cause for granting permission."
"You, whose deeds are pure and who observe great vows, have been granted permission; speak of other desires, for I shall indeed carry out your word.
Vyāsa said:
Although he was being entreated by the high-souled king, the Brahmanical seer did not choose any other boon than that [spare] life of the great-souled Likhita.
Thereupon, that protector of the earth [addressed] the high-souled Likhita...
Having had his two hands cut off, he departed;
having gone to his brother Śaṅkha, he spoke these words in a state of distress:
"O Blessed One, you ought to forgive this evil-minded Dhṛtadaṇḍa."
Śaṅkha said:
"O knower of dharma, I am not angry with you, nor do you defile me. O Brahmin, my lineage is perfectly pure and renowned throughout this world."

"You have indeed transgressed against dharma; therefore, an expiation has been made for you. Go quickly to the Bāhudā river and offer libations according to the prescribed rites to the gods, the ancestors, and the seers, and do not set your mind upon unrighteousness."
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife—
they say these are the great sins (mahāpātaka), as is association with those who commit them. O Brahmin, there is indeed no great sin equal to theft.
O highly fortunate one, in this world, that [act] is indeed equal to the killing of a Brahmin.
O Brāhmaṇa, for all evildoers, corporal punishment is declared to be the penalty;
specifically for a thief, no other punishment is ordained.

Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or even one of the twice-born—if he has committed a sin out of desire, he must be punished; there is no doubt about this. Indeed, men who have committed sins and been subjected to punishment by kings [are purified].
"Free from stain, they go to heaven like virtuous people who have performed good deeds.
O Brahmin, our lineage has been uplifted now that you have upheld the rod of punishment.
Vyāsa said:
Having heard those words of Śaṅkha, Likhita then entered the holy river and proceeded to fetch water. Thereupon,
his two hands appeared, resembling lotuses.
Then, filled with wonder, he showed those two hands to his brother.
Then Śaṅkha said to him: "This has been accomplished by me through asceticism;
let there be no doubt in you regarding this, for it is ordained by fate alone."
12,024.026 Likhita said:
"O you of great splendor, why was I not purified by you even earlier,
O best of the twice-born, since the power of your asceticism is such as this?"
Śaṅkha said:
"It is indeed so; this must be done by me, for I am not the wielder of punishment over you.
That king shall be purified, as will you, together with your ancestors."
Vyāsa said:
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, by that deed, that king— being preeminent—
attained supreme perfection, just as Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, did.
This is the duty of Kṣatriyas: the protection of the subjects.
O Great King, do not set your mind on grief regarding this deviation from the path; listen to these beneficial words of your brother, O best among those who know the Dharma.
"For the duty of a Kshatriya, O Indra among kings, is indeed the staff [of punishment], not the shaven head.
Vaishampayana said:
"The great seer Krishna Dvaipayana spoke to him once again:"
"O son of Kuntī, Ajātaśatru, these meaningful words were spoken:
'O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, O Great King, while your brothers were living as ascetics in the forest, they had certain desires there.'"
"O best of the Bharatas, let these great car-warriors attain those [kingdoms];
rule the earth, O Pārtha, like Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa.
A life of hardship in the forest has already been experienced by us ascetics."
"O tiger among men, let these [people] experience happiness at the end of their suffering;
O Bhārata, lord of the people, after you have experienced dharma, wealth, and pleasure together with your brothers, you shall then set forth."
O Bhārata, O son of Kuntī, attain freedom from debt toward guests, ancestors, and the gods; then you shall go to heaven. O joy of the Kurus, perform the Sarvamedha and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
"O great king, after that you shall attain the supreme goal;
and having united all your brothers with sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
O son of Pāṇḍu, you will achieve incomparable fame."
"O tiger among men, O joy of the Kurus, we know your word. And hear from me, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, how a ruler, while taking wealth and exercising restraint, does not fall away from his duties."
O Lord of Men, those skilled in the Dharma establish [the means of valid cognition] as follows:
perception, inference, comparison, and likewise scripture; as well as presumptive testimony, tradition, doubt, and ascertainment.
Appearance, gesture, gait, and movement, O Bhārata;
likewise, the proposition, the reason, the example, the application,
the conclusion, their expression, the object of knowledge, and the purpose.
They say that these means of proof are for the sake of establishing many categories;
perception and inference are held to be the source of all.
For one who knows the means of valid cognition and is discerning is able [to establish them] within the scope of the staff [of punishment].
A punishment meted out by one who lacks moderation may destroy even a lord of the earth. However,
that king who, while awaiting the proper place and time, displays his power against a bandit by relying on the wisdom born of the scriptures, is not joined with sin.
The king who takes a sixth part as tax but does not protect his kingdom,
incurs a fourth part of that people's sin. Listen now to how a king, by abiding in his duties, does not fall away from righteousness.

O you of great splendor, when a king is struck by fate at the time of action, he should remain free from fear, following the injunctions of the Dharmaśāstras, disregarding desire and anger, and looking upon all with equanimity like a father.
If one causes that action to be neglected, they say there is no transgression therein. Whether by force or with deliberate intent, enemies must indeed be suppressed.
One should not form alliances with the wicked, nor should one allow the kingdom to be treated as a commodity for trade.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, heroes, noble men, those worthy of honor, and the learned, as well as those possessing cattle and wealth, must be especially protected; and those of great learning should be appointed to matters concerning righteous legal proceedings.
O protector of the earth, those who are experts in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and rely upon the treatises on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), O King,

those who know the true meaning of the Vedas and are highly learned in the treatises on reasoning (*tarkaśāstra*), should be appointed by one who possesses discernment to matters of counsel and legal procedure.

The intellect cultivated through the treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*), that which is cultivated through the treatises on dharma (*dharma-śāstra*), and that which is cultivated through the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*)— even with these, O King, one may conquer the three worlds; therefore,
let those who know the true essence of the Vedas be appointed to the sacrificial rites.
O King, those who know the Vedas and those who know the Śāstras are of great intelligence;
they have mastered Ānvīkṣikī, Trayī, Vārtā, and Daṇḍanīti. They should be employed in all matters, for they have reached the highest state of wisdom.
Even toward one endowed with many virtues, a wise man should not place his full trust in a single individual.
A king who fails to protect, who is ill-behaved, arrogant, stubborn, and envious, incurs sin and is called "uncontrollable."

When people perish while unprotected because the king is struck down by fate, or when they are slain by thieves, all that is the sin of the king. But when [the kingdom] is well-counseled, well-governed, and established according to the prescribed rules...

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, when human effort has been exerted, there is no unrighteousness. Undertakings may fail or they may succeed through destiny; however, when human exertion has been performed, no sin touches the king."

"O tiger among kings, O ruler of the earth, I shall here relate to you this story concerning what occurred regarding the royal seer Hayagrīva in former times— concerning that hero of unwearied deeds who, having slain his enemies, was himself killed in battle."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, the deed performed by that wise man who was without allies and had been conquered in battle— namely, his suppression of his enemies and his supreme application in the protection of men.
Having performed his duty and attained fame in a fair fight,
Vājigrīva rejoices in the world of the gods;
he who has surrendered his life in battles against those who attack him.
Though cut by weapons and oppressed by bandits,
the high-souled Aśvagrīva, devoted to his duties and perfected in self, rejoices in the world of the gods.
The bow is the sacrificial post, the bowstring the cord, and the arrow the offering-spoon;
the sword is the small ladle, and blood is the clarified butter. The chariot that moves at will is the altar, and the battle is the fire.
Having offered the Cāturhotra sacrifice with four preeminent steeds into that sacrificial fire,
the powerful lion among kings was then liberated from his enemies and his sins.
Having offered his life as a final oblation in battle,
he whose neck was like a horse’s rejoices in the world of the gods;
protecting the kingdom with wisdom and policy, he likewise attains that state.
Having renounced his own self, devoted to sacrifice, and high-souled,
that wise one, having pervaded all the worlds with his fame,
rejoices in the world of the gods with the neck of a horse.
Having protected the earth through divine success, human policy, and the principles of yoga,
therefore the high-souled king is one whose nature is righteousness.
Hayagrīva rejoices in the heavenly world—
he who is learned, renounced, faithful, and grateful,
having abandoned the human world and performed his duty.
The king, esteemed by the wise, the learned, and those of great intelligence, having conquered the world and abandoned his body,
attained the Vedas perfectly and studied the Śāstras.
Having protected the kingdom correctly and having established the four social orders in their respective duties, that great-souled one with the neck of a horse rejoices in the world of the gods.
Having won battles and protected his subjects,
having drunk the *soma* juice and gratified the foremost of the twice-born,
and having wielded the rod of punishment over his people with justice;
One who has been worn down in battle rejoices in the world of the gods;
his conduct is praiseworthy,
and virtuous, learned men— those worthy of honor— pay him their respects.
Having conquered heaven and gone to the worlds of heroes,
the high-souled one of meritorious fame attained perfection.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the words of Dvaipāyana, and while Dhanañjaya was enraged,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, addressed Vyāsa and replied:
"This kingdom is not for me, nor are these various kinds of enjoyments."
"O Sage, today my mind is filled with joy, yet this grief torments me;
having heard the lamentations of women who are heroless and childless,
I find no peace."
Thus addressed, Vyāsa, the best among those who know yoga,
the knower of dharma and master of the Vedas, replied thus to the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira:
"It is not attained through action, nor by reflection;"
Nor is there any giver for this man;
it is ordained by the Creator through the application of successive turns:
a human being receives everything in due time.
It is not possible for ordinary men to attain [success] at the wrong time through the study of intelligence or the scriptures;
even a fool sometimes attains his goals.
For time is indifferent toward what is to be done;
it does not grant fruit at a time when there is no manifestation,
nor do crafts, mantras, or likewise medicinal herbs.
Those very [elements], when brought into harmony by time, succeed and blaze forth during the period of prosperity; by time,
the winds blow swiftly.
In due season, rain falls from the clouds;
in due season, there is water with lotuses and lilies; and in due season, the trees in the forests put forth their blossoms.
By time, nights become dark and bright;
by time, the moon’s orb becomes full;
and not out of season do trees bear flowers and fruit.

Rivers do not flow with untimely force, nor do birds and serpents become intoxicated out of season; likewise, wild beasts, elephants, mountains, and great celestial bodies do not deviate from their proper times.
Conceptions do not occur among women out of season;
the cold, heat, and rains do not arrive out of season;
and no one dies or is born out of season.
A fool does not speak out of season;
youth does not arrive out of season;
and a sown seed does not sprout out of season.
The sun does not enter into conjunction out of season;
it does not go to the setting mountain out of season;
nor does it wax or wane out of season.
The moon and the ocean, garlanded with great waves—
regarding this, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history sung by King Senajit when he was afflicted by sorrow.
This insurmountable cycle touches all mortals alike;
for all human beings, when ripened by time, must die.
And men kill others, O King, while other men likewise kill them.
This is a worldly designation, O King; it neither harms nor is it harmed.
Some think that it kills, while others think that it does not kill. However, by their very nature, the birth and destruction of beings are fixed.
When wealth is lost, or when a wife, a son, or a father has died, one should perform the rites for alleviating grief while reflecting, "Alas, what misery!
Why do you, being yourself a fool, grieve; why do you mourn for that which is itself an object of pity?
Behold the sufferings within sufferings, and the fears within fears.
Even this self is not mine; even the entire earth is mine [only in name].
Seeing that "as it is for me, so it is for others," one does not become deluded.
Thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for joy assail the fool day after day, but not the wise man. Thus,
these beloved and hated things come in their turn with the passage of time.
Among living beings, both sufferings and pleasures revolve;
there is only suffering, no pleasure, for it is perceived as such. Suffering arises from the affliction of craving, and pleasure arises from the affliction of suffering.
After happiness comes suffering; after suffering comes happiness.
One does not experience suffering eternally, nor does one experience happiness eternally.
For at the end of sufferings there is happiness, and at the end of happiness there is suffering.
For happiness indeed ends in suffering, and sometimes happiness arises from suffering;
therefore, one who desires eternal happiness should abandon both of these. Suffering originates from the end of happiness, and happiness originates from the end of suffering.
Whatever cause there may be for grief, or for burning anguish, or for the fainting of suffering, or even whatever is the root of exhaustion— one should abandon even a single limb that is its source.
Whether it be pleasure or pain, whether it be dear or not dear.
One should attend to whatever comes to hand with an unconquered heart. My dear friend, perform even a slight unpleasant act toward your wife or your sons;
from that you shall know who belongs to whom, by what means, or in what manner.

"Those who are the most deluded in the world and those who have gone beyond the intellect—only they prosper in happiness; the one in the middle is joined with suffering. Thus spoke the highly wise Senajit to Yudhiṣṭhira.
He who knows the high and low of the world, who knows the Dharma, and who knows pleasure and pain—
he who finds happiness in the suffering of another shall never truly be happy;
for there is no end to sufferings, as one arises after another.
Happiness and suffering, existence and non-existence, gain and loss, death and life—
all these touch everyone here in turn.
Therefore, the wise man should neither rejoice nor be angry.
They say that initiation, protection during a sacrifice, and battle constitute *yoga*;
likewise, [the application of] the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) within the kingdom is *yoga*.

One should know that the renunciation of wealth and sacrificial fees at a sacrifice, as well as perfect knowledge, are means of purification (12,026.032c). Protecting the kingdom with deliberate wisdom and policy; (12,026.033a)
Having renounced self-interest, devoted to sacrifice, and being a great soul who moves through all the worlds in the form of Dharma,
he rejoices in the world of the gods after leaving his body.
Having won battles and protected the kingdom,
having drunk the Soma and caused the subjects to prosper,
and having wielded the rod of punishment over the people with justice;
Perished in battle, he rejoices in the world of the gods;
they perform sacrifices, conquer kingdoms, protect their realms, and these things are dear to them.
Having properly acquired the Vedas and studied the treatises,
and having properly protected the kingdom, the king established the four castes in their respective duties.

The man whose conduct even while dwelling in heaven is honored by men, by the citizens, the country folk, and his ministers, rejoices in the world of the gods as one whose soul is purified; he is the king, the best among kings.
In this very context, Yudhiṣṭhira, the noble-minded one, addressed Dhanañjaya with these most refined words:
"O Pārtha, as for what you think— that there is nothing superior to wealth."
"The claim that for one who is destitute there is neither heaven, nor happiness, nor prosperity— that is false;
for many people are seen who have attained perfection through the sacrifice of Vedic study,
as well as sages devoted to austerity, whose worlds are eternal."
O Dhanañjaya, those who constantly observe the covenant of the ṛṣis,
who are devoted to them and know all duties— the gods recognize those as true brāhmaṇas. Others are sages established in the study of the Vedas, while still others are established in knowledge.
O Dhanañjaya, you should always observe those who are devoted to action;
O Pāṇḍava, all duties should be established upon those who are devoted to knowledge,
just as we previously learned from the words of the Vaikhānasas.
O Bhārata, the Ajas, the Pṛśnis, the Sikatas,
the Aruṇas, and the Ketavas have likewise gone to heaven through the study of the Vedas.
Having performed these deeds prescribed by the Veda, O Dhanañjaya, they attained that state.
Charity, study, sacrifice, and the restraint of the senses— difficult to master—
are the means by which those who have gone to heaven by the southern path of Aryaman reach these worlds of the performers of ritual action; this I have declared even before.

But by the northern path you behold that which begins with self-restraint; these eternal worlds of those who practice renunciation shine forth, O Pārtha. Regarding this, those who know the ancient lore praise the northern course, O Pārtha.
Through contentment comes the attainment of heaven; contentment is the supreme happiness.
There is nothing superior to satisfaction; it is firmly established when one is free from anger and joy. For one who has subdued both anger and joy, there is constant and supreme success.
In this regard, they also cite these verses sung by Yayāti,
by which one may withdraw all desires from every side, just as a tortoise withdraws its limbs:
"When one does not fear, and when others do not fear one..."
When one neither desires nor hates, then one attains Brahman. When one does not harbor any evil intention toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman.

For the virtuous one whose pride and delusion have been subdued, who has abandoned all attachments, and whose self-luminosity is manifest, liberation is attained. But listen to this from me as I speak, O Pārtha, with your senses restrained.
Some seek righteousness, others seek conduct, and still others seek wealth.
For one who would strive for the sake of wealth, non-striving is superior; for there is great fault in riches, and even that dharma which rests upon them is likewise flawed.
We perceive this directly before our eyes; you too ought to see it.
For one who strives for it, the avoidance of things that ought to be avoided is difficult;
it is exceedingly hard to achieve even among those who have acquired wealth.
They say that such conduct toward one who harms is truly contrary to the truth. But a man whose behavior is corrupted, who is devoid of sorrow and fear,
being thirsty for even a trifle and acting with malice, does not perceive the sin of killing an embryo.
Servants are constantly suspicious of one who takes [wealth], as if from fear of robbers;
and having obtained wealth that is difficult to acquire, one suffers great remorse after giving it away.
Who can reproach the man without wealth? He is liberated from all things and is happy.

Even by seizing the property of the gods, one would not become happy through wealth. Regarding this, those who know the past recite a verse sung at a sacrifice, which relies upon the Three Vedas and effects the preparation of the sacrificial ground in this world: [The verse follows: "O King, do not seize the property of the gods; for by seizing the property of the gods, one does not become happy through wealth. In this regard, those conversant with antiquity proclaim a verse sung at a sacrifice, which rests upon the Triple Veda and serves as the foundation for the ritual.
Wealth was created by the Creator for the sake of sacrifice;
man was created as its protector for the sake of sacrifice.
Therefore, everything should be employed solely for sacrifice.
Wealth is not praised as beneficial for the sake of desire;
rather, O son of Kuntī, best among the wealthy, know this:
the Creator bestows wealth upon mortals for the purpose of sacrifice.
Therefore, people do not truly understand that [the world] is not fixed for anyone;
hence, one who has faith in this world should both give and sacrifice.
They say that the true purpose of what is acquired is renunciation, neither enjoyment nor its depletion.
What need has he for accumulation when a more important task remains? Those of small intellect who give to those who have strayed from their own duty,
those people, after death, consume excrement for a hundred years.

That which one gives to the unworthy, and that which one does not give to the worthy— because of the failure to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy, even the practice of giving is difficult to perform. Regarding the various kinds of material goods acquired, two transgressions are to be understood.
Bestowing gifts upon the unworthy and failing to bestow them upon the worthy.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Now that the youth Abhimanyu has been slain, as have the sons of Draupadī..."
In Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and King Drupada;
in Vasuṣeṇa, who knows the dharma, and King Dhṛṣṭaketu;
and likewise among other lords of men from various lands in that battle.

Grief does not leave me, who am afflicted by the slaughter of my kinsmen— me, who was once so fierce in my desire for sovereignty and the one who brought about the destruction of my own lineage; I, in whose lap he used to roll while playing as a child.
Greedy for the kingdom, I struck down the son of Gaṅgā;
for when I saw him reeling from the arrows of Pārtha,
trembling as if struck by thunderbolts while looking toward Śikhaṇḍin.
Seeing my grandfather, that lion among men, tall as a withered lion,
being struck by sharp arrows— facing eastward, sinking down, and fallen from his chariot by those shafts— my mind was deeply distressed.
As he reeled like a mountain, a faintness came over me then;
for that Kauravya, bow and arrows in hand, had fought the descendant of Bhṛgu for many days in a great battle at Kurukṣetra.
In Vārāṇasī, the hero, the son of the River, challenged the assembled host of earthly kṣatriyas to combat on a single chariot for the sake of the maiden— by whom King Ugrāyudha,
the invincible universal monarch, had been defeated.
Consumed by the heat of weapons, he was slain by me in battle. He who,
protecting his own death, did not strike down Śikhaṇḍin, the prince of the Pañcālas, with his arrows— he has now been struck down by Arjuna.
O best of sages, when I saw him fallen upon the ground, drenched in blood, a most violent fever entered me at that very moment—
by whom this child was nurtured, and by whom we were protected.

By me— a sinful slayer of my preceptor, deluded and greedy for sovereignty— he was caused to be slain for the sake of a kingdom lasting but a short time; he who was a great archer and honored by all the kings of the earth.

Having encountered me in battle, you spoke falsely and wickedly regarding my son. O King, that which the preceptor said to me— that you are a man of truthful word— burns my limbs, provided that my son still lives.
"May the Brahmin not touch my truth; he questioned me about that very matter.
Yet, having placed an elephant between us, I treated him falsely—being a sinner, greedy for the kingdom, and a slayer of my preceptor."
Donning a cloak of truth, I told my preceptor in the midst of battle that Aśvatthāman had been slain when his elephant was struck down:
"To what worlds shall I go, having performed such a cruel deed?"
And since I caused the death of Karṇa, who never fled in battles,
my eldest brother and most fierce warrior— who could be more sinful than I?
And since I [caused the death of] Abhimanyu, a mere youth born like a lion among the mountains...
Driven by greed, I led the army into the force protected by Droṇa. From that moment on, I have been unable to look upon Bībhatsu or the lotus-eyed Kṛṣṇa, like a sinner who has killed an embryo.
And I grieve for Draupadī, who does not deserve such sorrow, now deprived of her five sons;
I grieve for the earth, which is like the earth deprived of its five mountains. Thus am I, a sinner and a wrongdoer, the cause of the earth’s destruction.
"Remaining seated in this very manner, I shall wither away this body.
Know me today to be one who has sat down to fast unto death, a slayer of his guru,
so that even in other births I may not be the destroyer of my lineage."
"I shall not enjoy excellent pleasures, nor the kingdom, nor its appurtenances;
I shall neither eat nor drink in any way. Remaining here, O ascetic, I shall wither my dear life-breaths."
"Go wherever you wish; I grant you leave with favor. All of you, give me your permission: I shall cast off this body.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To Pārtha, who was speaking thus and overwhelmed by grief for his kinsmen,
Vyāsa, the best of sages, restrained him and said, "Do not speak so;
O great king, you ought not to indulge in excessive sorrow."
"O Lord, I shall speak again of that which has been ordained:
for all living beings who are born, unions and separations are certain;
like bubbles upon the waters, they come into being and then cease to be."
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall. Unions end in separation, for life indeed ends in death.
Laziness results in suffering at the end, while diligence brings about happiness despite initial hardship.
Prosperity, fortune, modesty, fortitude, and success dwell indeed in one who is not indolent.
Friends are not sufficient for happiness, nor are enemies sufficient for suffering;
wisdom is not sufficient for wealth, nor is wealth sufficient for pleasures.
"O son of Kuntī, perform those very actions for which you were created by the Creator;
for it is from this alone that your success shall come, O King, and not through your own power.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To the eldest son of Pāṇḍu, who was tormented by grief for his kinsmen and desired to cast off his life-breaths, Vyāsa dispelled his sorrow. Vyāsa said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history, O tiger among men; listen to that song of Aśman, Yudhiṣṭhira.
King Janaka of Videha once questioned the wise Brāhmaṇa Aśman.
Overwhelmed by suffering and grief, he asked about his doubt.
Janaka said:
"Whether it be the arrival or the departure of kinsmen and wealth..."
"How should a man who desires what is auspicious conduct himself?
Aśmaka said:
"Immediately after this self has arisen for a man..."
Those various sorrows and joys come revolving around him;
when he encounters either of them, whatever he indulges in carries away his discernment, just as the wind carries away a cloud.

"I am of noble birth! I am accomplished! I am no mere mortal!"—with these three reasons, his mind becomes intoxicated. With his mind thus intoxicated, he squanders the enjoyments accumulated by his ancestors.
One who is destitute considers the seizing of others' property to be virtuous;
kings restrain such a person who has transgressed the bounds of propriety and seizes what is improper, just as hunters strike down a greedy deer with arrows.

O King, those men who are twenty or thirty years of age shall not exist beyond a hundred years. For those who suffer such extreme miseries, one should prescribe a remedy through the power of the intellect.
Observing everywhere the conduct of all living beings,
[he saw that] for those of mental origin, the source of sufferings is the delusion of the mind;
or else it is the onset of the undesired— no third cause is possible.
In this way, these various sufferings, as well as those arising from contact, beset the human being here; indeed,
old age and death devour all beings like two wolves.
Neither the strong nor the weak, neither the short nor the tall— no human being ever transcends old age and death,
even after conquering this entire earth bounded by the ocean.
Whether it be happiness or suffering that has befallen living beings, O lord of men,
all must be experienced helplessly; there is no way to avoid it,
whether in early life, middle age, or the final stage.
Those objects which are desired will indeed be unavoidable, and their opposites as well; separation from what is very dear and union with what is unpleasant, gain and loss,
pleasure and pain— all follow the dictates of destiny.
The manifestation of beings, as well as the casting off of the body,
attainment, exertion, and yoga— all this is established [in this].
Odor, color, taste, and touch cease according to their own nature.
In the same way, pleasure and pain follow their fixed destiny. Sitting, lying down, traveling, rising, drinking, and eating— all these for all living beings occur only through the power of time.
There are physicians who are themselves afflicted by disease, and those who are strong who are also very weak; there are those with wives as well as eunuchs—the revolution of time is indeed diverse.
So too are birth in a noble family, valor, health, and even fortitude.
Good fortune and enjoyment are obtained through destiny;
there are many sons for the poor who do not desire them,
yet they are absent for the wealthy who strive for them and long for them.
Disease, fire, water, weapons, hunger, wild beasts, poison,
death by rope, and likewise falling from a height—
by whichever cause a creature's departure is ordained, by that very means it goes.
He is seen neither as one who does not transgress [the law], nor again as one who has transgressed it.
For here, O lord of men, a wealthy man is seen perishing while still young,
while another, though poor and afflicted, lives for a hundred years.
Men who possess nothing are seen to live long, while those born into prosperous families perish like moths. Generally, in this world, the wealthy lack the capacity to enjoy their riches.
O lord of men, even pieces of wood are consumed by the poor; yet,
impelled by time, the wicked soul thinks, "I am doing this," as he commits sin out of discontent for whatever is desired.
Women, dice, hunting, and drinking—these are censured by the wise due to the addiction they cause;
yet even many who are highly learned are seen to be deeply attached to them.
Thus, in the course of time, all things—whether desired or undesired—[arise].
They touch all beings, yet no cause for this is perceived. Who creates or sustains the wind, space, fire, the moon and sun, day and night, the luminaries, the rivers, and the mountains?
Cold, heat, and likewise rain revolve according to time;
even so, O bull among men, do pleasure and pain come to human beings. Neither medicines, nor scriptures, nor fire-oblations, nor recitations of mantras can [alter this].
They do not protect a human being from death or even from old age;
