just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and,
having met, drift apart, such is the meeting of living beings.

Whether they are attended by men and women with songs and instrumental music, or whether they are destitute and dependent on the food of others— Death treats them all with equal action. Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives [are likewise subject to it].
Experienced throughout the cycles of existence, to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
No one will ever belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone. This meeting with one's circle of wives, kinsmen, and friends is merely a chance encounter on the road.
"Where was I? Where am I? Where shall I go? Who indeed am I? What am I established for here?

For what reason, and for whom, should I grieve?"—in this way one should steady the mind regarding this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), which moves like a wheel, where dwelling with loved ones is impermanent.
This meeting on the path is merely a chance encounter; a brother, mother, father, or friend—the wise know that the next world has never been seen before by direct perception.
Desiring one's own welfare, one must have faith, without overstepping the sacred scriptures.
One should perform rites for the ancestors and the gods, practice the duties of dharma, and the wise man should sacrifice according to the rules and pursue the three goals of life;
for this world is sinking into the deep ocean of time.
In this great sea whose crocodiles are old age and death, no one remains awake;
though they study the science of life (Āyurveda) along with its entire ancillary literature,
many physicians are seen to be overwhelmed by diseases themselves.
Though they drink decoctions and various kinds of clarified butter,
they do not transcend death, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore;
even those who know the elixirs of rejuvenation and have properly applied such elixirs [are no exception].
12,028.046 Like trees broken by mighty elephants, they are seen shattered by old age.
12,028.047 Likewise, those endowed with austerity, devoted to the practice of Vedic study, generous, and habituated to sacrifice, do not cross over old age and death.

For indeed, for all beings that are born, days do not turn back, nor months, nor years; nor do fortnights or nights. Thus, this unstable being travels along that vast path by means of time, which is itself constant.
Helpless, a man approaches that which is inhabited by all beings;
either the body departs from the living soul, or the soul departs from the body. This meeting with wives and other kinsmen is merely like a chance encounter on a road.
This constant companionship can never be obtained by anyone,
even with one’s own body, let alone with anyone else.
Where indeed is your father today, O King, and where is your grandfather today?
You do not see them today, nor do they see you;
for indeed, a person is not the seer of heaven or hell.
O King, the scripture is the eye of the virtuous; follow it here.
Having practiced the life of celibacy, he should procreate and perform sacrifices,
free from malice, in order to discharge his debts to the ancestors, the gods, and the great seers. He, being devoted to sacrifice, should be intent upon procreation.
First, as a celibate student whose wings are fully developed,
one should worship both this world and heaven,
having cast off all malice from the heart.
For a king who practices the Dharma correctly and acquires wealth in the proper manner,
his fame increases as his wheel of sovereignty rolls forth.
"Among all the worlds, both moving and unmoving," Vyāsa said:
"Having thus understood this, the King of Videha..."
Having addressed the stone with these complete words, his purpose fully accomplished, he of pure intellect,
his sorrow stilled, departed for his own home.
In the same way, O Acyuta, you too must abandon your grief;
arise, O equal of Śakra, and take up joy! The earth has been conquered by you through the dharma of the kṣatriya.
"Enjoy it, O son of Kuntī; do not despair.
Vaiśampāyana said:
While Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī and the son of Dharma, remained silent, [Yudhiṣṭhira spoke].
Guḍākeśa, the son of Pāṇḍu, addressed Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O water for the forest fire of grief! O filler of the well of sorrow! O axe for the creeper of lamentation! O you whose very fame destroys grief!"
"O Mādhava, this Dharmarāja, the scorcher of foes, is tormented by grief for his kinsmen; he is submerged in an ocean of sorrow—console him.
O Janārdana, we all have once again fallen into a state of uncertainty."
"O mighty-armed one, you ought to destroy his grief.
Thus addressed by the high-souled Vijaya, Govinda—
the lotus-eyed Acyuta— turned toward the king.
For Keśava is not to be bypassed by the King of Dharma;
from his childhood, Govinda has been dearer to him than Arjuna.
Grasping his arm adorned with sandalwood paste, the mighty-armed one—
Śauri spoke to him, who resembled a pillar of rock, seeking to console him:
"His face, with its fine teeth and beautiful eyes,
shone like a clearly blossomed lotus awakened by the sun."
"O tiger among men, do not give way to grief that withers the body;
for those who have been slain on this field of battle cannot be recovered by you again,
just as gains obtained in a dream vanish upon waking."
"O King, thus have those Kṣatriyas who passed away in the great battle—
all of them heroes facing their foes, the ornaments of the field—
departed; not one among them was struck down while fleeing or with his back turned."
Having fought in the great battle and renounced their own lives, all those heroes, purified by weapons, have attained heaven; you ought not to grieve for them.
Those heroes were devoted to the duty of the kṣatriyas and had reached the further shore of the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

They have attained the meritorious state of heroes; you ought not to grieve for them. In this very context, they cite this ancient history of how Nārada spoke to Sṛñjaya when he was afflicted by grief for his sons.
"O Sṛñjaya, I, you, and all living beings shall experience happiness and sorrow;
we shall move about in the state of non-liberation—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Listen as I proclaim the supreme good fortune of kings."
"Pay close attention, O King, and you shall then cast off your sorrow.
Upon merely hearing of those high-souled lords of the earth who have passed away, and having heard this, dispel your anguish; listen to me as I speak in detail."
This is the supreme pacification of malefic planets and the best means for increasing longevity;
it is a captivating account of the foremost of kings.
O Sṛñjaya, hear from me how Marutta, the son of Avikṣita, passed away.
The gods, including Indra and Varuṇa, led by Bṛhaspati, went to the sacrifice of that high-souled king, the creator of all beings;
he who provoked a rivalry with Śakra, the king of the gods and performer of a hundred sacrifices.
He whom the learned Bṛhaspati, seeking to please Śakra, had refused;
he whom Saṃvarta officiated for, for the purpose of causing distress to Bṛhaspati— while that best of kings was ruling, O most excellent of monarchs.
The earth, garlanded with sacred shrines, shone forth, yielding crops without being ploughed.
At the sacrificial session of the son of Avikṣita, the Viśvedevas were the members of the assembly,
the Maruts were the attendants, and the Sādhyas were present for that high-souled one.
When the hosts of Maruts drank the Soma of Marutta, his sacrificial gifts surpassed those of gods, humans, and Gandharvas. If even he died, O Sṛñjaya, who was four times more blessed than you;

"Even more meritorious than a son—do not grieve for your son. Thus he spoke, referring to Suhotra, the son of Vitithi, who had died without having performed sacrifices or given sacrificial fees, O Sṛñjaya; so we have heard.
For twelve years, Maghavan rained down gold upon him;
O lord of men, having obtained him, the earth became true to her name and possessed of wealth, for the rivers carried gold to that ruler of the realm.

O King, Maghavan, honored by the world, cast down tortoises, crabs, crocodiles, sea-monsters, and even porpoises into the rivers. Seeing those golden fish, sea-monsters, and turtles fallen there, [the people were amazed].
Then, by the thousands and by the hundreds, the son of Vitatha smiled;
that boundless gold was spread out across Kurujāṅgala as he, composed in mind, performed his sacrifice and bestowed it upon the Brāhmaṇas during the extended rite.
O Sṛñjaya, if he has died— who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son;
O Śvaitya, be at peace and do not mourn for him who gave no sacrificial fees and performed no sacrifices.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Bṛhadratha, the lord of Aṅga, has died—
he who bestowed a thousand times a thousand white horses and a thousand times a thousand maidens adorned with gold.
Performing a sacrifice during an extended ritual,
he bestowed as a sacrificial fee a thousand times a thousand elephants, each like a lotus-lake;
performing a sacrifice during an extended ritual, he bestowed as a sacrificial fee [that vast number].
Ten million bulls adorned with golden garlands,
followed by thousands of cows, he bestowed as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) while Aṅga was performing a sacrifice on Mount Viṣṇupada.
Indra was exhilarated by the Soma, and the twice-born were gratified by the sacrificial gifts;
O Indra among kings, in his sacrifices numbering in the hundreds,
those gifts indeed surpassed those of the gods, humans, and Gandharvas.
There is no other man born or yet to be born who will bestow that wealth which Aṅga bestowed during the seven Soma-sacrifices; for he has died, O Sṛñjaya, who was four times more blessed than you.
"Even he was more meritorious than your son; therefore, do not grieve for your son.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that even Śibi Auśīnara died—he who had enveloped this entire earth like a piece of leather."
Making the earth resound with the great roar of his chariot,
he who brought the world under a single umbrella by means of his victorious single chariot—
whatever there may be today of cattle and horses, along with the wild animals of the forest.
Śibi Auśīnara gave away that many cows at his sacrifice; O Bhārata, among all the kings, Prajāpati considered no one— neither of the past nor of the future— to be able to bear his burden.

Except for Śibi Auśīnara, that royal sage who possessed the prowess of Indra— if even he died, O Sṛñjaya, being far superior to you in the four virtues and more meritorious than your son, do not grieve for your son.
"O Sṛñjaya, do not grieve; indeed, pacify yourself for that one who gave no sacrificial fee and performed no sacrifice.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that even Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta—the great archer, son of Śakuntalā, possessed of abundant wealth and splendor—has died."
He who, having bound thirty horses for the gods along the Yamunā,
twenty along the Sarasvatī, and fourteen along the Gaṅgā,
[performed] a thousand Aśvamedha sacrifices and a hundred Rājasūya sacrifices—
In ancient times, that highly energetic Bharata, son of Duḥṣanta, performed great sacrifices.
Among all the kings on earth, other monarchs were unable to emulate Bharata’s great deeds,
just as mortals are unable to reach the sky with their arms.

O Sṛñjaya, even Bharata, who was far superior to you in the four auspicious virtues, died— he who, having bound more than a thousand horses and having prepared the sacrificial altar, gave a thousand lotuses to Kaṇva.
"Even more meritorious than your son, do not grieve for your son.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, has died—
he who always had compassion for all creatures as if they were his own biological sons."

While Rāma ruled the kingdom, there was not a single widow or a person without a protector in his realm; he was like a father to everyone. The rain-clouds poured forth at the proper seasons, and the crops were full of flavor.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, there was always an abundance of food;
living beings did not drown in water, nor did fire burn them for no purpose,
and while Rāma ruled the kingdom, there was no fear arising from predatory beasts.

While Rāma ruled, the subjects lived for thousands of years and likewise had thousands of sons; they were free from disease and all their goals were accomplished. There was no mutual dispute even among women, let alone among men.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, the subjects were constant in righteousness;
they were contented, had all their goals accomplished, were fearless, and moved about according to their own will.
While Rāma ruled the kingdom, men were devoted to the vow of truth.

While Rāma ruled the kingdom, the trees were free from calamities and always bore flowers and fruit; all the cows yielded a drona-measure of milk. Having dwelt in the forest for fourteen years, that man of great asceticism—
Rāma slew the Rākṣasa, the descendant of Pulastya, who was a thorn to the worlds;
he performed ten unimpeded Aśvamedha sacrifices with the Jārūthī rite.
He was dark-complexioned, youthful, with red eyes, and possessed the prowess of an elephant in rut.
With arms reaching to his knees, a handsome face, the shoulders of a lion, and mighty arms,
Rāma ruled the kingdom for ten thousand years and one hundred years.
O Sṛñjaya, if even he who was the lord of Ayodhyā and was far superior to you in the four auspicious virtues,
and was more meritorious than your son, has died— then do not grieve for your son.
And we have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that King Bhagīratha also died—
he at whose sacrifice Indra, the best of the gods, having drunk the *soma* juice, became intoxicated with pride and [slew] many thousands of Asuras.
By the strength of his own arms, the blessed subduer of Pāka conquered [the world]; he,
while performing a sacrifice with its altar spread out, bestowed as a sacrificial fee a thousand times a thousand maidens adorned with gold.
All the maidens were mounted on chariots, and every chariot was yoked to four horses.
In each chariot there were a hundred elephants, adorned with golden garlands and marked by lotus-signs;
and a thousand horses followed behind each and every elephant.
For every horse there were a thousand cows, and for every cow there was a thousand goats and sheep;
she who once sat upon his lap while he dwelt in the secluded forest became,
in former times, Urvaśī, the Gaṅgā Bhāgīrathī.
O Sṛñjaya, if even Bhagīratha— the descendant of Ikṣvāku, who gave profuse sacrificial fees while performing sacrifices,
and to whom Gaṅgā, flowing through the three worlds, became a daughter— died, he who was far more distinguished in the four virtues than you; [how much more so others?]
"He was even more meritorious than his son; therefore, do not grieve for your son. We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Dilīpa and Ailavila also died—those whose many deeds the twice-born recount."
In that great sacrifice, the lord of the earth, being composed in mind, bestowed this earth, rich in wealth, upon the Brahmins. At every sacrifice of that patron here, the domestic priest—
He bestowed as a sacrificial gift twelve thousand golden elephants.
At his sacrifice, there stood a magnificent, glorious sacrificial post made of gold,
which the gods, led by Śakra, approached as they performed their ritual duties.
Upon that golden sacrificial post, which had a pith of gold,
six thousand celestial Gandharvas danced in seven groups;
there, Viśvāvasu himself played the lute in their midst.
"All living beings thought, 'He is playing for me.
This is what the other kings did not emulate of King Dilīpa:
that women adorned with gold lay down intoxicated upon the road."

Those men who beheld King Dilīpa— the wielder of the formidable bow, the speaker of truth, and the great-souled one— they too were conquerors of heaven. Three sounds never ceased in the palace of Dilīpa.
The sound of Vedic recitation, the twang of the bowstring, and the cry "Let it be given!"—
if even he has died, O Sṛñjaya, who was more distinguished in the four virtues than you and more meritorious than your son, then do not grieve for your son.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva, is dead—
he whom the Marut gods extracted as a fetus from the side of his father,
he who had grown within the womb of the high-souled Yuvanāśva.
The illustrious King Trilokavijayin was born from the *pṛṣadājya* [clarified butter mixed with curds].
Seeing him, who possessed a divine form, lying upon his father’s lap,
the gods said to one another, "Whom will this child suckle?"
"He shall sustain me alone"—thinking thus, Indra descended [to assist him].
Then Śatakratu gave him the name Māndhātṛ. Thereafter, for the sake of the great-souled one's nourishment, a stream of milk [flowed forth].
The hand of Yuvanāśva flowed into the mouth of Indra, as did the hand of Indra;
drinking from that hand of Indra, he grew day by day. O King, in twelve days he became equal to one twelve years old.
In a single day, this entire earth came under his sway—
he who was righteous-souled, high-minded, a hero equal to Indra in battle,
and the king Āṅgāra, Marutta, Asita, and Gaya.
Māndhātṛ conquered Aṅga and Bṛhadratha in battle;
when Yauvanāśva fought against Aṅgāra in combat,
the gods, by the twanging of his bow, thought that heaven itself was being split asunder.
From where the sun rises to where it sets,
all that is called the domain of Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva;
having performed a hundred horse-sacrifices and a hundred royal consecrations.
The lord of the earth gave to the brahmins golden rohita fish, one yojana in height and ten yojanas in length; the other people divided among themselves those that remained over.

If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son. We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that even Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, has died.
O King, having conquered this entire earth together with its oceans,
he traversed it by the distance of a single throw of a sacrificial pin,
adorning it with altars and wandering across the earth while performing meritorious sacrifices.
Having performed a thousand sacrifices and a hundred horse-sacrifices,
he gratified the Lord of the Gods with three mountains of gold after slaying the Daityas and Dānavas in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, divided the entire earth into twelve parts;
having settled his sons, headed by Yadu,
Druhyu, and Puru, at the borders, he consecrated Pūru in his own kingdom and departed for the forest accompanied by his wives.

If even he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son. We have also heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Ambarīṣa, the son of Nābhāga, has died.

12,029.093c O best of kings, he whom the subjects chose as their meritorious protector; 12,029.094a who, with a concentrated mind, performed sacrifices for ten thousand times a thousand kings who had themselves offered ten thousand sacrifices, while himself performing a vast sacrifice for the sake of the Brahmins.
"Neither have men of former times done this, nor will others do so in the future"—
thus did the sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇās) applaud Ambarīṣa Nābhāga.
There were a hundred thousand kings and a hundred hundreds of kings.

Having all performed horse-sacrifices, they departed for the southern path. O Sṛñjaya, since he has died— he who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— do not grieve for your son.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Śaśabindu, the son of Citraratha, has died— he,
the high-souled one who possessed a hundred thousand wives,
and whose sons numbered a million Śaśabindus.
All were clad in golden armor, and all were excellent archers.
One hundred maidens followed behind each prince.
For every maiden there were one hundred elephants, and for every elephant there were one hundred chariots.
For every chariot there were a hundred horses of noble breed adorned with golden garlands;
for every horse there were a hundred cows, and for every cow, likewise, a hundred goats and sheep.
This was the boundless wealth bestowed at the great Horse Sacrifice.

O great king Sṛñjaya, Śaśabindu bestowed [his wealth] upon the Brahmins; he died, though he was more distinguished in the four virtues than you and even more meritorious than your son. Do not grieve for your son.
We have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that Āmūrtarayas died at Gayā—
he who had been king for a hundred years and subsisted only on the remnants of sacrificial offerings. To him, Agni granted boons, and thereupon Gaya chose his boons.
"May my merit be inexhaustible as I give, and may my faith in the Dharma increase. O Consumer of Oblations, by your grace, may my mind delight in truth.
And we have heard that he obtained all those desires from the Purifier.
Possessed of great splendor, he performed the Darśa, Paurṇamāsa, and Cāturmāsya sacrifices again and again for a thousand years;
he gave away a hundred thousand cows and ten thousand horses.
Rising again and again for a thousand years,
he gave gifts; O bull among men, he gratified the gods with Soma, the twice-born with wealth, the ancestors with *svadhā* offerings, and his own wives with all their desires.
Having fashioned a golden earth ten vyāmas wide and twice as long,
the king gave it as a sacrificial fee at the great horse sacrifice (vājimedha),
O King, O bull among men— as many as are the grains of sand in the Ganges.

Gaya, the son of Āmūrtarayas, gave away as many cows; yet he died, O Sṛñjaya, though he was more distinguished in the four virtues than you and even more meritorious than your son. Do not grieve for your son.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that Rantideva, the son of Saṅkṛti, died—
he who, having perfectly propitiated Śakra, obtained a boon as one of great fame:
"May food be abundant for us, and may we receive guests."

"May our faith never depart from us, and may we never have to beg anything from anyone. To that high-souled and illustrious Rantideva, who was firm in his vows, domestic and wild animals presented themselves of their own accord.
From where the great river flowed forth due to the swelling of the heap of hides,
that great river became renowned as the Carmaṇvatī.
In the extended assembly, the king gave gold coins to the Brahmins.
"Where the twice-born indeed cry out, 'A golden coin for you! A golden coin for you!
and having said, 'A thousand for you,' he would approach the Brāhmaṇas; [there he provided] the materials for the Anvāhārya offering and whatever other articles were required."
Pots, cooking vessels, cauldrons, plates, and even pans—
there was nothing belonging to the wise Rantideva that was not made of gold.
On whatever night he stayed in the house of Sāṅkṛti Rantideva, [it was filled with such wealth].
Twenty thousand and one hundred cows were slaughtered there;
the cooks, adorned with polished jeweled earrings, cried out,
"Eat your soup in abundance today, for there is no meat as there was before!"

If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son. And we have heard, O Sṛñjaya, that even the high-souled Sagara has died.
That tiger among men, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, possessed superhuman prowess;
sixty thousand sons followed behind him as he went forth,
like hosts of stars following the king of constellations when the clouds have cleared at the end of the rainy season.
He under whose single umbrella the entire earth once bowed down; he who gratified the deities with a thousand horse-sacrifices;
he who gave away a palace made entirely of gold, supported by golden pillars.
It was filled with women whose eyes were like lotus petals, crowded together upon their couches;
and by his command, the twice-born distributed that wealth among worthy brahmins in various ways according to their desires.
He who, out of anger, caused the earth to be dug until it was marked by the ocean—
he after whose name the sea attained the state of being called *Sāgara*— if even he died, O Sṛñjaya, though he was four times more blessed than you;
"You are even more meritorious than your son; do not grieve for your son.
O Sṛñjaya, we have heard that King Pṛthu, the son of Vena, died—he whom the great seers, having assembled together, consecrated in the great forest."
"He shall indeed expand the worlds," thus he was named Pṛthu; and because he protects us from injury (*kṣata*), he is therefore remembered as a Kṣatriya.
When the subjects saw Pṛthu, the son of Vena, they said, "We are attached (*raktāḥ*) to him."

From that affection [of the people], the name "Rāja" (King) arose for him. While Vainya was ruling, the earth yielded crops without being ploughed, there was honey in every leaf-cup, and all the cows yielded a *droṇa* measure of milk.
Free from disease, having all their goals accomplished, and fearing nothing from any quarter,
men dwelt according to their desire both in the fields and in their homes. The waters solidified for him as he desired to cross the ocean.
The rivers did not overflow, nor was there any obstruction of the banners.
At the great horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), the king gave to the Brahmins twenty-one mountains made of gold, each three *nalas* in height.

"If he has died, O Sṛñjaya— he who was four times more blessed than you and even more meritorious than your son— then do not grieve for your son. Why indeed, O Sṛñjaya, do you sit there lost in silent thought?"
O King, you do not listen to these words of mine,
even though I have spoken this meaningful discourse correctly,
like wholesome advice given to one who is about to die.
Sṛñjaya said:
O Nārada, I hear these words of yours,
which possess wonderful meanings like a garland of holy fragrance.
For the sake of destroying my grief, you have recounted the fame of those great-souled royal sages who performed meritorious deeds;
O great seer, your discourse has not been in vain.
"O Nārada, upon seeing you alone, I am freed from sorrow.
O expounder of Brahman, I wish to hear your words; I am never satiated by them, just as one is not by drinking nectar."
O Lord Amoghadarśin, if you would grant your grace to me, who am consumed by the sins of my son,
may there be for me today the restoration of life to one who has died.
"And through your grace, there shall be a reunion with your son.
Nārada said:
"This beloved son of yours has departed;"
"The mountain Svarṇaṣṭhīvī gave him to you;
I now give that son back to you—
Hiraṇyanābha, who shall live for a thousand years."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How did that son of Sṛñjaya become Kāñcanaṣṭhīvī? For what reason was he given by Parvata, and by whom did he die?
When the lifespan of humans was ten thousand years,
how could the son of Sṛñjaya have died before reaching youth?
Or was he merely named Suvarṇaṣṭhīvin?
"Is it true that he spat out gold? This I wish to know.
Vāsudeva said:
"In this regard, O lord of men, I shall relate to you what occurred as it happened."
In former times, the two great sages Nārada and Parvata, who were honored by the worlds,
came here from the realm of the gods— uncle and nephew—
desiring to sport with delight among human beings.
By means of the food of the sacrificial oblation, the food of the purifier, and indeed the food of the gods—
Nārada and his maternal uncle Parvata, who was the son of his sister—
both of them endowed with ascetic power, wandered upon the surface of the earth.
Enjoying human pleasures as was fitting, they wandered about, full of affection and joined by joy; there they made an agreement:
"Whatever thought may arise in the heart, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious,"
"That curse must be told to one another; otherwise, it shall become false.
Having promised "So be it," those two great seers, honored by the world, approached King Sṛñjaya Śvaitya and spoke these words to him.

"We two shall dwell with you for some time for your benefit; O protector of the earth, attend to our needs properly. Having agreed, saying "So be it," the king honored them and attended to them with hospitality.
Then once, the great-souled king, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to those two Tathāgatas: "This daughter of mine, of excellent complexion, is my only child; she shall serve you both."

"12,030.012c She was beautiful, with faultless limbs, endowed with virtuous conduct and character; 12,030.012e tender and youthful, resembling the filaments of a lotus. 12,030.013a Addressed by the two of them as 'most gentle,' the king gave her his command."
"O maiden, you must attend upon these two Brahmins like a god and like a father.
That virtuous maiden, having replied "So be it" to her father,
honored and served them both according to the king's instructions.
By her such conduct and her incomparable beauty,
the god of love suddenly and instantly took possession of Nārada’s heart;
thereupon, desire grew within the heart of that great-souled one.
Just as the lord of stars gradually waxes at the onset of the bright fortnight,
so too that knower of dharma, feeling ashamed, did not disclose his intense passion to his high-souled nephew Parvata.

Then, through his ascetic power and by his gestures, Parvata understood that Nārada was afflicted by passion; enraged, he then cursed him most severely. "Having made an agreement with me, you were indeed composed and remained together with me."
"O Brahman, whatever intention should arise in the heart— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
it must be disclosed to one another; that promise of yours has indeed been rendered false, and therefore I speak these words."

"Previously, you did not tell me that you were acting out of desire; therefore, I shall cast this curse upon you for [approaching] your delicate daughter-in-law. For you, though being a teacher, a knower of Brahman, an ascetic, and a Brāhmaṇa,"
"You have violated the agreement that was made between us two in private.
Therefore, being greatly incensed, I shall curse you; listen to it from me:
your wife shall become Sukumārī, of this there is no doubt."
"O Lord, from the time of your marriage, both the maiden and other men shall see you as a monkey,
deprived of your natural form.
Having understood those words from Parvata, Nārada then [departed].
Out of anger, that maternal uncle cursed his nephew as well:
"Though you are endowed with asceticism, celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint, and though you are ever devoted to dharma, you shall not attain residence in heaven."
Having thus cursed one another, those two, exceedingly enraged and intolerant,
returned toward each other like two furious, pre-eminent elephants;
the great sage Parvata then wandered over the entire earth.
O Bhārata, being honored according to custom by his own splendor,
Nārada, the most excellent of the righteous, then obtained that blameless maiden Sukumārī, the daughter of Sṛñjaya, in accordance with dharma.
But that maiden, in accordance with the curse, beheld Nārada as a monkey immediately upon the recitation of the marriage mantras;
and Sukumārī saw the celestial rishi with the face of a monkey.
She did not despise him at all, but remained full of affection;
she attended upon her husband and did not go to anyone else even in her mind—
whether a god, a sage, or a yakṣa— for she was devoted to her husband.
Then, on one occasion, the blessed Parvata was wandering through a somewhat desolate forest when he beheld Nārada there. Thereupon,
having offered his salutations, Parvata then spoke to Nārada.
"O Lord, may you show favor toward me for the sake of reaching heaven. Then,
seeing Parvata seated there with palms joined in reverence, Nārada— himself even more dejected than the wretched man— spoke to him.
"First you cursed me, saying, 'You shall become a monkey.
After you said this, I in turn cursed you out of resentment,
saying, 'From this day forward, you indeed shall not obtain residence in heaven.'"
"This is indeed not worthy of you, for you stand in the place of a son to me.
Then those two sages withdrew their mutual curses.
Having seen Nārada, who was endowed with splendor and possessed a divine form, they were filled with wonder.
Sukumārī fled, fearing for her offspring;
seeing that blameless woman running away, Parvata then said to her, "This is your husband; there is no need for hesitation here."

The sage Nārada, the blessed lord whose soul is supremely righteous, is inseparable from your own heart; let there be no doubt in you regarding this. Thus was he entreated in many ways by the high-souled Parvata.
Having heard that curse of her husband, she returned to her own natural state.
Then Parvata went to heaven, and Nārada went to his home;
for this great Ṛṣi Nārada is a witness to the deeds of all.
12,030.042c "When questioned, O best of men, he will indeed relate exactly what occurred.
12,031.001 Vaiśampāyana said: 12,031.001a Thereupon, the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, replied to Nārada.
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the origin of Suvarṇaṣṭhīvin.
Thus addressed by Dharmarāja, the sage Nārada related exactly what had occurred regarding Suvarṇaṣṭhīvin.
"O Great King, it is exactly as Keśava has said.
However, I shall tell you, who asks, what remains to be done regarding this matter.
Both I and Parvata—the great sage who is my sister's son—"
Desirous of wealth, we two went to Sṛñjaya, the best among victors; there,
honored by him with rites prescribed by rule and provided with all our desires, we dwelt in his house.
When the rainy season had passed and it was time for my departure,
Parvata spoke these meaningful words to me at that time:
"We two have been highly honored in the house of this lord of men."
"O Brahman, we have dwelt here for a long time; let what is appropriate now be considered. Then, O King, I spoke to the mountain of auspicious appearance:
"O Lord, all this is fitting for you, my sister's son."

"Let the king be enticed with a boon; let him obtain whatever he desires. If you so think it right, let him attain success through our ascetic power. Then, having summoned King Sṛñjaya, who was of auspicious appearance—
12,031.010c The bull among sages, Parvata, spoke these approved words:
12,031.011a "O King, we are both pleased by your honors, which are born of your sincerity;
12,031.011c permitted by us both, O best of men, consider a boon."
"O Great King, accept that which may be appropriate for humans, provided it does not cause injury to the gods; for you are considered by us worthy of worship.
Sṛñjaya said:
"If you two are pleased with me, my purpose is accomplished by this much alone;
this itself is the supreme gain, a great fruit already realized for me.
Nārada said:
To him who was speaking thus, Parvata replied once more:
"O King, choose that resolve which has long resided in your heart.
Sṛñjaya said:
"I desire a heroic son, one who is powerful, firm in his vows, long-lived, highly fortunate, and equal in splendor to the king of the gods. Parvata said:
"This desire of yours shall come to pass, yet he shall not be long-lived;
for this resolve was formed in your heart for the sake of surpassing the king of the gods. And because of his spitting gold, he shall be known as Suvarṇaṣṭhīvī."
And he, possessing splendor equal to that of the king of the gods, was to be protected from the king of the gods.
Nārada said:
Having heard those words of the high-souled Parvata, Sṛñjaya—
Then he sought to propitiate him, saying, "May it not be thus;
O Sage, may there be a long-lived son for me through your ascetic power. But Parvata said nothing to him out of regard for Indra.
To that distressed king, I spoke once again:
"O Great King, you must remember me; when remembered, I shall appear to you. I shall bring back to you your beloved son, who has fallen under the power of the King of the Dead."
"I shall restore that form once more; do not grieve, O lord of the earth.
Having spoken thus to the king, the two departed as they desired, and Sṛñjaya entered his own palace according to his wish.
Then, after some time had passed for the royal sage Sṛñjaya,
a son of great heroism was born, blazing as if with splendor.
In due course, he grew like a great lotus in a lake.
He became known as Kāñcanasṭhīvī, for that was his name according to its true meaning.
O best of the Kurus, that most wonderful thing spread throughout the world;
and Indra, the lord of the gods, learned of that boon granted to the two high-souled ones.
Then, fearing defeat and abiding by the counsel of Bṛhaspati,
the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra became intent on seeking a vulnerability in the prince;
he then urged forth the thunderbolt, that divine weapon personified.
"O Lord, become a tiger and slay this prince!
For once he has grown in prowess, he will surely overcome me—
just as Parvata gave him to Vajra, the son of Sṛñjaya."

Thus addressed by Śakra, Vajra, the conqueror of enemy cities, constantly followed the prince, watching for an opportunity. Sṛñjaya, too, having obtained a son whose splendor was equal to that of the king of the gods, [was filled with joy].
Then, together with his inner apartments, the king became constantly devoted to the forest, filled with joy.
Thereafter, one day on the bank of the Bhāgīrathī by a forest waterfall,
that boy, accompanied by his nurse, ran about for the sake of play.
A boy of about five years of age, possessing the prowess of a lord of serpents and endowed with great strength, encountered a tiger that had suddenly sprung upon him;
crushed by it, the prince trembled.
Lifeless, he fell upon the earth, and then the nurse cried out in distress. Having slain the prince,
that tiger, concealed by the illusory power (*māyā*) of the King of the Gods, vanished right then and there.
Hearing the cry of the nurse as she wept in extreme distress,
the lord of the earth himself ran toward that place.
There he saw him lying lifeless, his blood having been drained away.
[He saw] the prince, devoid of joy, like the moon fallen from the sky. Placing his son— whose chest was crushed and who was drenched in blood— upon his lap, he lamented in deep distress.
Then those mothers of his, weeping and emaciated by grief,
ran toward that place where King Sṛñjaya was.
Then that king, with his mind turned inward, remembered me.
Knowing that he had thought this, I went into his presence;
and I, O lord of the earth, spoke these words to him as he was overwhelmed with grief— words which had been told to you by the hero of the Yadus.
And then, with the permission of Vāsava, I restored him to life;
for that which was destined to be must happen thus, and it could not have been otherwise.
From that time forward, that highly illustrious prince became known as Svarṇaṣṭhīvī.
The heroic one gladdened the hearts of his father and mother;
when his father had ascended to heaven,
that powerful lord of terrible prowess ruled the kingdom for one thousand one hundred years.
Then, having performed many great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees,
that one of great splendor gratified both the gods and the ancestors;
and he begot many sons who ensured the continuation of his lineage.
After a long time, O King, he has passed away according to the law of time. Therefore, O Indra among kings, dispel this grief that has arisen within you,
just as Keśava and Vyāsa of great asceticism have told you.
"Having ascended the kingdom inherited from your father and grandfather, carry it far;
by performing meritorious great sacrifices, you shall attain the worlds you desire.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To King Yudhiṣṭhira, who was silent and grieving,
the ascetic Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who knows the essence of dharma, said:
"O lotus-eyed one, the protection of subjects is the duty of kings."

Dharma is the eternal authority for the world; one must always follow dharma. O King, indeed, maintain the station of your fathers and grandfathers. And that dharma which resides among the Brahmins is eternal and determined by the Vedas.
O bull of the Bharatas, that is the eternal authority among all authorities;
the Kṣatriya is the protector of that entire dharma. Likewise, whatever man in his realm opposes its command, [he must be restrained].

He who, having fallen under the sway of delusion, would subvert the authority of the authoritative— whether he be a servant, a son, or even some ascetic— is one who obstructs the course of worldly affairs and should be restrained by force with both arms.
By all possible means, he should restrain those evildoers or even have them executed;
for a king who acts otherwise incurs sin.
Indeed, he who does not protect the Dharma when it is being destroyed is a destroyer of Dharma.
Those destroyers of righteousness have been slain by you, along with their followers. Abiding in your own duty, O Pāṇḍava, why do you grieve?
For a king should indeed slay, give, and protect his subjects in accordance with dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O one rich in asceticism, I do not doubt the words you speak;
for Dharma is directly perceived by you, O best among all upholders of dharma."
"Indeed, for the sake of sovereignty, I have caused many who should not be slain to be killed. O Brahmin, those wrongful acts burn and torment me.
Vyāsa said:
"O Bhārata, is it the Lord who is the creator, or is it the individual soul?
Is it chance that prevails in the world, or is the fruit known to be born of action? For it is by the Lord, O King, that both the good and the evil are ordained."
Men perform an action, yet its fruit goes to the Lord (Īśvara).
For just as if a man were to cut down a tree in the forest with an axe,
the sin would belong only to the cutter and not to the axe in any way whatsoever.
Alternatively, if [the soul] were to obtain the fruit of action by taking that [body] as its substrate,
then the sin committed with a staff or a weapon would not reside in the person;
yet this is not accepted, O son of Kuntī, that a fruit produced by one [should accrue to another].
One might attain [this]; therefore, entrust that to the Lord.
Or else, the person is the agent of both auspicious and sinful actions;
since there is no other [agent], perform another auspicious deed accordingly.
"O King, for no one anywhere ever turns back from destiny.
That sin which is caused by staff or weapon does not reside in the man;
or if you think, O King, that the world is established upon chance (haṭha)."
Even so, unwholesome karma has not existed, nor will it exist;
nevertheless, the world must apply itself to both the auspicious and the evil.
Among all things practiced in the world, the raising of the rod of punishment by kings is the most essential.
Moreover, O Bhārata, it is my conviction that in this world actions continue to revolve, and these beings experience the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds. Thus,
it is true that the fruit of action is certain, arising from the auspicious or inauspicious instruction of one's own conduct.

"Abandon that, O tiger among kings; do not set your mind on grief in this way. O Bhārata, for one who abides in his own duty even when it is subject to reproach, such self-abandonment, O King, is not fitting for you."
"O Kaunteya, expiations have been ordained here for those who perform ritual acts;
one who possesses a body may perform them, but one without a body would fail.
Therefore, O King, while you are still alive, you shall practice expiation."
"O Bhārata, if you do not perform penance, you shall suffer after death.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"My sons, grandsons, brothers, and fathers have been slain."
O Grandfather, fathers-in-law, teachers, maternal uncles along with grandfathers,
high-souled Kṣatriyas, as well as relatives, friends, companions, kinsmen, and brothers— [all these must be honored].
"O Grandfather, many lords of men gathered from various lands have been slain by me alone, who am greedy for sovereignty. Having killed such kings as those, who were ever devoted to righteousness— "
"O one rich in asceticism, what shall I attain by repeatedly drinking Soma,
while I burn incessantly today, thinking again and again of this earth now bereft of those glorious lions among kings?"

Having witnessed this terrible slaughter of kinsmen, and hundreds of enemies slain, as well as other men by the millions, I am consumed with grief, O Grandfather. What indeed will be the condition of those excellent women today?
Deprived of their own sons, husbands, and brothers,
they— emaciated and miserable— cried out against us, the terrible Pāṇḍavas joined by the Vṛṣṇis, who were like agents of death, as they fell upon the ground.
Not seeing their fathers, brothers, husbands, and sons,
all these women will abandon their dear lives and go to the abode of Yama;
O best of the twice-born, because of my affection for them, I have no doubt in this matter.
"Because of the subtlety of dharma, it is evident that we shall incur the sin of killing a woman. Having killed our friends and committed an infinite evil,
we shall surely fall headlong into hell."
"O best of beings, we shall cast off our bodies through fierce asceticism. O Grandfather, tell me specifically about the various hermitages.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, the seer Dvaipāyana then, having examined the matter skillfully with his intellect, spoke to the Pāṇḍava:
"Do not despair, O King; remember the duty of a Kṣatriya."
O bull among Kṣatriyas, these Kṣatriyas were indeed slain according to their own dharma;
desiring complete sovereignty and great fame upon the earth,
they met their end through Time, joined by the decree of destiny.
"You are not the slayer, nor is Bhīma, nor Arjuna, nor even the two Yamas;
it is Time, by the law of succession, that takes away the life-breaths of embodied beings.
For him, there are no mother or father, nor is there anyone who is exempt from his grasp."
He who is the witness of the actions of all creatures was withdrawn by that Time;
O bull among men, this [destruction] is merely the instrument of that Time,
for that he destroys beings with beings is his sovereign form.
Know that he is the witness of both good and evil, whose nature consists of the embodiment of karma;
he is Time, which results in the qualities of pleasure and pain, and which bestows the fruits of time.
O mighty-armed one, reflect also upon their respective actions.
"Those who acted as the cause of destruction have themselves fallen under the power of time; recognize for yourself the nature of your own self-restraint, vows, and conduct,
since you were made to perform such an act by the force of destiny."

Just as a machine fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ remains under the control of its maker, so too is this world made to revolve by action joined with time. For, having observed this birth of the person to be without a [prior] cause...
Accidental destruction, grief and joy which are useless,
and whatever offense you have here through the deception of your mind—
for that purpose, O King, expiation is required; therefore, perform it.
And this, O Pārtha, is heard regarding the ancient war between the gods and the asuras:
the asuras were the elder brothers and the gods were the younger;
among them, too, there was a great struggle on account of sovereignty.
It is said that the battle lasted for thirty-two thousand years;
having turned the earth into a single ocean drenched in blood,
the gods then slew the Daityas and regained the celestial realm.
In that very same way, O Bhārata, having obtained the earth, Brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas—
deluded by pride— resorted to the Dānavas for the sake of assistance;
they were known throughout the three worlds as the Śālāvṛkas.
Those eighty-eight thousand,
who desired the destruction of Dharma and were promoters of unrighteousness,
were also slain by the gods; those evil-minded ones must be killed by the gods, like the fierce Daityas.
If, by killing one individual, the well-being of the remaining members of the family may be secured,
then even the destruction of a family or a kingdom does not constitute a violation of ethical conduct (*vṛtta*).
For there exists, O lord of men, a certain form of dharma that appears as adharma.
Dharma can also take the form of adharma; this must be understood by the wise. Therefore, steady yourself, O Pāṇḍava, for you are learned in the scriptures.
You have followed the path previously traversed by the gods, O Bhārata.
"O bull among the Pāṇḍavas, such as these shall not go to hell;
O scorcher of foes, comfort these brothers and your friends. For he who, at the commencement of a sinful undertaking, is permeated by the intent for that deed—"
Even while performing [the rite], he would remain just as he was; and having performed it, he would be devoid of shame.
It is declared that all that impurity remains complete within him;
for such a person of evil deeds, there is neither expiation nor any diminution of his sin.
But you, belonging to a pure lineage, were compelled by the fault of another;
having performed this deed against your will, you now suffer remorse.
The great horse-sacrifice (Aśvamedha) is declared to be the atonement for such an act.
"O Great King, bring him; thus you shall be free from sin.
Having conquered his enemies along with the Maruts, Maghavan, the subduer of Pāka, became known as Śatakratu after performing a hundred sacrifices, bringing each one individually."

Having purified his sins and conquered heaven, Śakra, having attained worlds that bring forth happiness and being surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, shone brightly while illuminating the quarters. Thus did the Lord of Śacī receive great honor from the Apsarases in the heavenly world.
The sages and the gods wait upon the Lord of the Immortals;
you, O sinless one, have now transferred yourself here to the earth by your prowess,
and the rulers of the world have been conquered by your valor.
"O King, having gone to their cities and kingdoms surrounded by your friends,
consecrate your brothers, sons, and grandsons each in their own kingdom;
and even for those who are children or still in the womb, offer words of consolation."
Delighting all your subjects, protect the earth.
For those who have no sons, consecrate their daughters there;
for the hearts of women are full of desire, and in this way they will abandon their grief.

Having thus offered consolation throughout all the kingdoms, O Bhārata, perform the horse sacrifice (vājimedha), just as the victorious Indra did in ancient times. Those high-souled Kṣatriyas, O bull among Kṣatriyas, are not to be mourned.
Deluded by the power of destiny, they have met their destruction through their own deeds.
You have attained the duty of a Kṣatriya and acquired a kingdom free from stain. O Kaunteya, practice that dharma which is most excellent for the life hereafter.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, by performing what actions in this world does a man become subject to expiation? And by doing what may he be liberated? Tell me that."
Vyāsa said:
By failing to perform prescribed duties, by practicing those that are forbidden,
and by conducting himself falsely, a man indeed becomes liable for penance.
He who is a religious student (brahmacārī) at sunrise,
as well as one dismissed by the sun [at sunset], one with deformed nails, or even one with black teeth;
one who has been superseded in marriage (parivitti), the superseder (parivettā), one who abandons the Veda (brahmojjha), and one who is a reviler— [these are those who must not be invited].
Likewise, one who marries a woman whose husband is still living, as well as one who marries a woman previously married to a younger brother while the elder brother is alive;

one who has broken his vow of celibacy, as well as a slayer of a twice-born man; one who abandons a Brahmin at a place other than a sacred site, and one who fails to bestow [his daughter] upon a worthy suitor at a sacred site.

O Kaunteya, one who performs sacrifices for a village, one who sells the king’s goods, one who kills a Śūdra woman, and one who [kills] a Brahmin— the former is more censurable than the latter. One who slaughters animals in vain and one who sets forest fires [are likewise censured].
One who behaves falsely toward others, one who opposes his guru,
one who abandons the sacred fires, and likewise one who sells the Veda—
all these are as sinful as one who violates an established agreement.
I shall also declare those actions that ought not to be done; learn them from me.
Listen with an attentive mind to those things which are contrary to both worldly custom and the Vedas:
the abandonment of one’s own duty and the performance of the duty of another.

Sacrificing for those for whom one should not sacrifice, as well as eating what is unfit to be eaten; abandoning one who has sought refuge, likewise failing to support one's dependents; the sale of liquids, and also the killing of animals.
O Bhārata, he who, though capable, does not perform the rites such as the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), and he who constantly fails to bestow all things that ought to be given;
he who withholds sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and who violates the property of a Brāhmaṇa— [these are likewise fallen].
Those who know the Dharma declare that all these are improper acts:
a son dividing the inheritance with his father, one who violates the teacher’s bed, and a person who, failing to procreate, acts unrighteously; such a person becomes an unrighteous man.
12.035.015 These actions have been described both in detail and otherwise—
those which, by performing or not performing them, a person becomes liable to penance.
12.035.016 Indeed, these very same actions, when being performed by human beings...
Listen now to those specific circumstances under which they do not become stained:
even if one kills in battle an approaching man who has mastered the Vedāntas and comes with a weapon raised,
desiring to kill, one does not thereby become a slayer of a Brahmin.
Moreover, O Kaunteya, this mantra is recited here in the Vedas;
I shall declare to you that dharma which is established by the authority of the Vedas:
that one who kills an assassin who has deviated from the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa.

By that act, he does not become a slayer of a Brahmin; rather, it is wrath that encounters wrath. Likewise, one who, when his life is at stake, drinks even liquor through ignorance—not being incited by others and remaining devoted to dharma—deserves purification once again.
12,035.021a All this has been told to you, O Kaunteya, regarding the eating of forbidden food;
12,035.021c by means of this entire ordinance for penance, one becomes purified.
12,035.022a For even violating the teacher’s bed does not defile a man if it is for the sake of the teacher.
Uddālaka begot Śvetaketu from his disciple. One who commits theft for the sake of his teacher during times of distress is not bound by the law,
provided he does not act out of habitual desire for such conduct.
One does not incur sin by taking property from others, except for the property of Brahmins;
and he who does not consume it himself is not smeared by that evil. Untruth may be spoken for the sake of saving a life, whether one's own or another's.
For the sake of a preceptor, among women, and in the performance of marriage rites,
the vow does not need to be repeated under any circumstances even if semen is emitted during sleep;
instead, an oblation of clarified butter into a kindled fire is prescribed as the expiation.
There is no sin in the elder brother remaining unmarried while the younger marries, nor in one who has fallen from his caste, nor likewise in one who has renounced the world;
begging for alms and adultery do not corrupt the Dharma. One should never perform the useless slaughter of animals, nor cause it to be performed.
For the consecration of sacrificial animals, as enjoined by the sacred rules, is indeed an act of grace.

A gift given out of ignorance to an unworthy Brāhmaṇa does not cause defilement; likewise, the bestowing of gifts—whether with a specific motive or otherwise—at a sacred ford or at a non-sacred place [is not defiling].

In the case of women who act improperly, there may be an expiation that leaves them undefiled; by that, she is purified, but the husband is not defiled. Having understood the true nature of Soma, its sale would likewise be non-defiling.
The dismissal of an incompetent servant is faultless;
setting fire to a forest for the sake of cattle is not a transgression.
These are the actions that have been described, performing which one does not incur blame.
"I shall describe the penances in full detail, O Bhārata,
by performing which a man shall become purified, O lord of men.
Vyāsa said:

O Bhārata, by means of austerity, ritual acts, and indeed by giving, a man purifies his sin; once purified, he does not engage in it again. Eating but once a day and subsisting on alms, he performs his own duty.
Carrying a skull in his hand, bearing a staff (khaṭvāṅga), remaining celibate, and always alert, free from malice, sleeping on the ground, and making his penance known to the world—
the slayer of a Brahmin is fully liberated after twelve full years.
Or he may become an object of observation for weapon-bearers, according to his own wish, or for learned men;
or he may throw himself headlong three times into a kindled fire while reciting one of the Vedas;
or he may walk a hundred *yojanas* while reciting one of the Vedas.
One should bestow one's entire property upon a Brāhmaṇa learned in the Vedas,
or wealth sufficient for a lifetime, or a house together with its furnishings;
the protector of cows and Brāhmaṇas is liberated from the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa.

A man who has killed a Brahmin is purified by eating sparingly for six years; however, by eating [only once] every month, he is liberated in three years. One who eats [only once] every month is purified in one year; there is no doubt about this.
Likewise, O King, by ceasing [evil] even for a very short time, one is liberated;
there is no doubt that one is purified by the Aśvamedha sacrifice. And those men of such a kind who bathe in its concluding purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) are likewise purified.
"All these become purified of sin," so says the supreme Śruti.
One who is slain in battle for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa is liberated from the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, one who bestows a hundred thousand cows upon worthy recipients [attains the same].
A killer of a Brahmin shall be liberated from all sins indeed;
he who gives twenty-five thousand Kapila cows that yield milk is likewise liberated from all sins.
By giving a thousand milch cows with their calves to virtuous and poor men when one's life is in danger, one is indeed released from sin. Furthermore,
he who bestows a hundred horses of the Kamboja breed upon the Brahmins [is likewise freed].
O protector of the earth, he is liberated from sin by those who are self-restrained;
and O Bhārata, he who would grant even a single wish to another,
and who does not boast after having given it, is likewise liberated from sin.
If a twice-born man, having drunk liquor even once, should drink [liquor] that is the color of fire,
he purifies himself both in this world and in the next. Or, by throwing himself down from Mount Meru or entering a blazing fire, he attains purification.

By undertaking the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*), one is liberated from all sins. Having performed the *Bṛhaspatisava* sacrifice, a Brāhmaṇa who has drunk liquor may again enter the assembly of Brāhmaṇas; such indeed is the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) for a Brāhmaṇa.

O King, that man who, having drunk liquor, makes a gift of land without envy and never drinks it again, is purified once he has undergone the purificatory rites. One who has violated the Guru’s bed should lie down upon a heated iron slab.
Or, placing his penis in his hand, he may go forth as a wandering mendicant with his gaze fixed upward;
by the liberation of the body, he is released from unwholesome karma. Women who remain self-restrained for a year are likewise liberated from their karmas.
He who observes the great vow (mahāvrata), or gives away his entire possessions,
or is slain in battle for the sake of his guru, shall be liberated from evil karma. Likewise, one who serves with falsehood or opposes his guru [is also freed].

By offering what is pleasing to him, one is released from that sin; however, for the sake of one who has violated his vow of chastity (*avakīrṇin*), he should perform the penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-vrata*). Clad in the hide of a donkey for six months, he shall likewise be freed from the transgression.
One who has stolen another's wife, as well as one who misappropriates another's wealth,
shall be freed from that sin by becoming a practitioner of a vow for one year.
However, he who has committed theft should give back to the owner property equal in value to what was taken.
By that various means,

O Bhārata, he may be released from his transgression; by performing the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, well-practiced for at least ten [days], both the younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*) and the elder brother superseded (*parivitti*) become purified.
By performing this, he shall always be a deliverer of his ancestors;
yet there is no fault in the woman, nor is she defiled by it.
For the Cāturmāsya sacrifice is prescribed as pure when performed during her fertile season.
Those who know the Dharma understand that women are purified by this;
however, women suspected of sins should not be approached by one who knows [the truth],
for they are purified by their menses, just as a vessel is purified by ashes.
A bell-metal vessel defiled by the feet, or even one smelled by a cow,
or one defiled by the remnants of mouth-rinsing, shall be purified by ten [cleansings].
The entire four-footed Dharma is ordained for the Brāhmaṇas.
When a Kṣatriya has committed an offense, the law is ordained to be reduced by one quarter;
likewise, for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, a quarter is ordained for each. One should understand the determination of the gravity or lightness of these offenses according to this principle.
Having killed an animal of the lower realms or having cut down many other trees,
a man should subsist on air for three nights and proclaim his deed. O King, this expiation is prescribed for approaching women who should not be approached.
Having lived for six months wearing wet clothes and sleeping on ashes,
this indeed shall be the rule for all forbidden acts,
according to the procedure declared by the Brahmins and supported by examples, scriptures, and logical reasons.

Even one who studies the Sāvitrī mantra, eating moderately in a pure place, being non-violent, not dull-witted, and remaining silent, is liberated from all sins. During the days he should constantly stand facing the open sky, and at night he should sleep there.
Three times during the day and three times during the night, he should enter the water while still wearing his clothes. While engaged in this vow, he must not speak with women, Śūdras, or outcasts.
By performing such a vow, a twice-born man is released from the sins committed through ignorance.
After death, one receives the fruit of good and evil deeds, with the elements as witnesses;
whatever exceeds between those two, the doer receives that fruit.
Therefore, through giving, austerity, and righteous action, one attains auspicious fruit.
Having committed an inauspicious act, one should increase its merit so that it becomes superabundant;
one should perform auspicious deeds when signs of evil karma appear, and one should constantly give away wealth; thus, one shall be liberated from sin.
For an expiation has been declared that is proportionate to the sin; however, an expiation is prescribed for all matters except for the great sins (mahāpātaka),
whether they concern things fit or unfit to be eaten, or likewise things that should or should not be spoken.
O King, for those who act out of ignorance and knowledge, different rules are prescribed and permitted. However, a sin committed knowingly becomes grave in every respect;
whereas for a fault committed through an error of ignorance, an expiation is ordained.
Sin can be removed by means of the ritual procedure as it has been described;
however, this procedure is prescribed only for those who are believers and full of faith,
and never for men who are atheists or lacking in faith.

O best of the upholders of dharma, O tiger among men, this rule is not seen to apply to those in whom deceit and vice predominate; rather, the conduct of the virtuous and the virtue of the virtuous must be followed by one who desires happiness both in this world and after death.
"O King, by that former reason, you shall be released from sin—
either through their slaughter for the sake of protection, or by the performance of your duty as a king; or else, if you feel some compassion, you shall perform an expiation."
"May you not, however, meet your end through an act practiced by the ignoble.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, [remained silent].
Having reflected for a moment, he replied to the one whose wealth is asceticism:
"O Grandfather, tell me what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten, what gift is praised as worthy, and who is a worthy recipient and who is not."
Vyāsa said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
the conversation between the Siddhas and Manu, the Lord of Creatures.
In former times, at the beginning of the age, the Siddhas, devoted to austerities and vows, approached the Lord Prajāpati as he sat and questioned him regarding dharma:
"How is food [to be prepared], how is giving, how is study, and how is austerity?"
"O Prajāpati, please tell us everything regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Thus addressed by them, the blessed Svāyambhuva Manu said:
"Listen as I describe dharma according to its nature, both in detail and in brief."
In the absence of specific instruction, there shall be recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, and likewise fasting;
self-knowledge, meritorious rivers, and those who are devoted to such [virtues]—
these are the merits for mountains in the absence of specific instruction.
The consumption of gold, as well as bathing with jewels and other substances, visiting sacred shrines, and the consumption of clarified butter—
these quickly make a person pure; of this there is no doubt.

A wise person should never be arrogant, even for a moment; for one who desires long life, he should drink hot water for three nights. Refraining from taking what is not given, generosity, study, and austerity [are the means].
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, forbearance, and sacrifice are the characteristics of Dharma.
That which is indeed Dharma becomes Adharma when established in an improper place or at an improper time.
Taking what is not given, falsehood, and violence are recorded as Dharma only when they are situational.
For those who understand, both dharma and adharma are of two kinds:
non-engagement and engagement; this twofold nature belongs to both the world and the Veda.
Immortality results from non-engagement, while mortality is the fruit of action.
One should know that the fruit of the impure is impure, and likewise, the fruit of the pure is indeed pure.
Furthermore, for both of these, there may be results characterized as pure or impure,
as well as destiny, that which is joined with destiny, vital breath, and dissolution.
From performing an unwholesome act unintentionally, a wholesome fruit arises;
whether it occurs in a future life due to doubt, or as a visible result in this very life,
expiation is prescribed for an act performed unintentionally.

Furthermore, the affliction of the body and the pleasant and unpleasant experiences of the mind, which arise from anger and delusion, are pacified through examples, scriptural authority, and logical reasoning, as well as by medicines, mantras, and rites of atonement.

If a king has released a condemned person, he is purified by fasting for one night; for the sake of his own purification, the domestic priest (purohita) must fast for three nights. When a man, having experienced decay and grief, does not die, [he should perform these rites].

One should prescribe that those who have been afflicted by weapons and the like remain there for three nights. One should avoid the family customs of all those residing in various castes and guilds; indeed, one should not follow that practice among those for whom no [higher] dharma exists.
When a legal matter arises and there is doubt regarding the dharma, what ten experts in the Vedas and Shastras or three reciters of the Dharma declare shall be the dharma.
Likewise, red clay and ants [are also to be considered].
Likewise, the *śleṣmātaka* fruit, O Brahmins, and poison itself are not to be eaten;
those fish which are devoid of scales are not to be eaten by Brāhmaṇas; nor are four-footed creatures other than the tortoise, nor frogs, nor any other aquatic animals.
The *bhāsa*, swans, eagles, ruddy geese, cranes, and water-fowls;
the *kaṅka*, the *madgu*, vultures, as well as crows and owls;
all carnivorous birds, and four-footed creatures with fangs.

A Brāhmaṇa should not drink the milk of those animals that have teeth in both jaws and four fangs on each side; nor the milk of ewes, mares, she-asses, female camels, or even cows that have recently calved, nor that of human women or does.

The food of a hungry ghost (preta), the food of a woman who has recently given birth, and whatever food is less than ten days old—these are unfit for eating and unfit for drinking; likewise, the milk of a cow that has not passed ten days after calving [is forbidden].
The food of a king takes away one’s splendor (tejas); the food of a Śūdra takes away one’s Vedic luster (brahmavarcasa).

The food of a goldsmith, of a woman who has no hero (husband), and the excrement [of such a woman]; the food of a usurer, the food of a courtesan, and the food of one who tolerates a paramour; and the food of those who are entirely conquered by women.
The food of one who has been initiated for sacrifice, of a miser, of one who sells sacrifices,
of a carpenter, of a leather-cutter, of a libertine, of a washerman,
of a physician, and likewise of a guard, is unfit to be eaten.
The food of those accused by a village or a guild, of those who live as stage-women, of those who have married before their elder brothers,
of eunuchs, and likewise of bards and gamblers;
as well as food taken while being forbidden, and that which is fermented or stale.

That which is followed by liquor, that which is leavings, and whatever remains [of a meal] are unfit for consumption. Likewise, preparations of flour, meat, sugarcane, and vegetables, as well as products of milk, and groats, parched grain, and *karambha*— these are not to be eaten if they have stood for a long time.
Milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, meat, and cakes prepared in vain are unfit to be eaten and forbidden as food for Brahmin householders;
[they are offered] to the gods, the ancestors, men, the sages, and the domestic deities.
Only after having performed worship should a householder then eat.
Just as a renunciant monk dwells in his own home, so too a householder who conducts himself in this manner, living with his beloved wife, shall attain dharma.
A righteous person should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to one who has done him a favor,
nor to those whose character is devoted to dancing and singing, nor to jesters; nor to one who is intoxicated, nor to one who is insane, nor to a thief, nor to a physician.

A gift given to a Brahmin who lacks Vedic learning (*aśrotriya*) and does not discourse on the Brahman is as if dead; it should not be given to one who is deficient in speech, nor to one who is discolored, nor to one who is deficient in a limb, nor to a dwarf, nor to a wicked person, nor to one of low birth, nor to one who has not been refined by vows.
Whatever is given improperly and whatever is received improperly will lead to the ruin of both the giver and the receiver alike.
It is like one who attempts to cross the ocean by clinging to a piece of khadira wood or even a stone.
In that same way, both the giver and the recipient sink down. Just as fire covered with wet wood does not blaze,
so too the recipient who is devoid of austerity, Vedic study, and virtuous conduct [does not shine].
Just as water in a skull, or milk in a dog-skin bag,
[becomes impure] due to the defect of its container, so too is sacred learning [rendered useless] when placed in one who lacks virtuous conduct.
He who is devoid of mantras, devoid of vows, ignorant of the scriptures, yet free from malice— [such a person is not fit for instruction].
Out of compassion, one should give even to such distressed men; yet,
one must certainly not give out of compassion even to an injurer who is distressed,
merely because it is the practice of the virtuous or because it is the law.

That gift was given without cause to a brahmin devoid of dharma; it would become [fruitless] due to the fault of the unworthy recipient—of this I have no doubt. Just as an elephant made of wood, or a deer made of leather, [is no real elephant or deer].
A Brahmin who has not studied the Vedas— these three are merely bearers of names.
Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a cow is fruitless with another cow, and just as a bird might be wingless, so too is a Brahmin devoid of mantras.
As a village is empty of grain, as a well is without water,
and as an oblation poured into what is not fire, so too is [an offering] made to one who has been excluded;
it is a destruction of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings for both the gods and the ancestors.
A foolish enemy who steals one's wealth does not deserve to attain the higher worlds.
All this has been told to you exactly as it happened, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
for this great matter, O bull of the Bharatas, ought to be heard in its entirety.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, O Great Sage, O Best of the Twice-born, I desire to hear in detail the duties of kings and all the duties of the four social orders."
"How should policy be enacted by a ruler in times of calamity? Adhering to the path of righteousness, how may I conquer the earth?
For this discourse on atonement has been expanded by the distinctions between what is fit to be eaten and what is not."
This [news], inclining toward curiosity, produces as it were a joy within me;
yet the practice of dharma and kingship are constantly in conflict,
by which my mind becomes bewildered as I reflect upon them perpetually.
12,038.005 Vaiśampāyana said:
12,038.005a Beholding Nārada, the highly effulgent Vyāsa, the best among those who know the Vedas and knowing all that is ancient, spoke to him.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, if you wish to hear the Dharmas in their entirety,
go to Bhīṣma, the mighty-armed elder and grandfather of the Kurus. He will [dispel] the doubts residing in your mind regarding all the secret mysteries."
The son of Bhagirathi, the omniscient knower of all dharmas, who cut [the path],
was begotten by the divine goddess, the river that flows through the three worlds;
he was one who beheld all the gods in person, headed by Śakra.

Having repeatedly gratified the celestial sages, headed by Bṛhaspati, with respectful service, the Lord studied the science of statecraft (rājanīti). That twice-born preceptor of both gods and asuras, Uśanas, knows whatever treatise exists on this subject.
The best of the Kurus acquired all of that,

along with its etymological explanations; moreover, the one of great intelligence received from Cyavana Bhārgava the Vedas augmented by their auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), as well as [the knowledge] from Vasiṣṭha, who was firm in his vows.
He formerly studied under the eldest son of the Grandfather, Kumāra, who blazes with radiant splendor and knows the truth of the path of the supreme self;
from the mouth of Mārkaṇḍeya, he obtained the entire dharma of the ascetic.
O bull of the Bharatas, he obtained celestial weapons from Rāma and Śakra;
though born among men, his death was at his own will,
and it is heard that despite being childless, he attained the worlds of merit in heaven.
He whose holy Brahman-sages have always been the members of his assembly,
and for whom nothing remains unknown among all things to be known through wisdom— he who knows the dharma and understands the subtle truth of the meaning of dharma, will speak to you.
"Go to him before he, who knows the Dharma, gives up his life-breaths.
Thus addressed, the son of Kuntī— possessed of long-sighted wisdom and great splendor—
spoke to Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, the best among speakers.
Having caused a truly great slaughter among his kinsmen that made the hair stand on end, he— having committed an offense against the whole world and being the cause of the earth’s destruction—
was himself slain in battle by deceit, though he fought with straight weapons.
"For what reason am I worthy to question him?
Then, desiring the welfare of the four castes,
the mighty-armed and most radiant best of the Yadus spoke again to that foremost of kings.
"O best of kings, you ought not now to persist so intensely in grief; do that which the venerable Vyāsa has said. O mighty-armed one, the brahmins and your brothers of great prowess [are with you]."
Like those afflicted by the heat who wait upon the rain-cloud with hope,
so do the kings who remain after the slaughter, and the entire assembled fourfold order of society, O great king, wait upon you, their sovereign of the Kurujāṅgala kingdom.
And for the sake of these high-souled Brāhmaṇas,
by the command of our preceptor Vyāsa of immeasurable splendor,
and for the sake of our friends such as ourselves and of Draupadī, O scorcher of foes.
"O slayer of enemies, do what is pleasing and bring about the welfare of the world.
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa, the lotus-eyed king,
a man of great asceticism, rose up for the benefit of all the world.
Thus exhorted by Viṣṭaraśravas himself,
as well as by Dvaipāyana, Devasthāna, and Jiṣṇu—
Yudhiṣṭhira, that tiger among men, was thus entreated by these and many others.

Having heard those words, the high-minded son of Pāṇḍu— a treasury of sacred learning, skilled in all that is heard and worthy of being heard— abandoned his mental anguish and distress; having resolved within his mind, he attained peace.
Surrounded by them like the moon by the stars, the king, placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at his head, entered his own city. As he was about to enter,
that knower of dharma, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, [did so].
He worshipped the gods and thousands of Brahmins.
Then he [prepared] a new, bright chariot covered with blankets and deerskins,
yoked to sixteen white oxen endowed with auspicious marks.
Honored with sacred mantras and praised by the great seers,
he ascended the nectar-filled chariot like the god Soma;
then Bhīma, the son of Kuntī, possessed of terrible prowess, took hold of the reins.
Arjuna held up a radiant white umbrella;
that white umbrella being held over his head shone like a cloud white as the king of stars in the sky.
Then the two heroic sons of Mādrī, adorned and radiant as moonbeams, took up the two white yak-tail fans for him. Those five brothers, all beautifully adorned, mounted the chariot.
O King, at that time all beings appeared as if they were a single mass;
then, mounting a brilliant chariot yoked with horses of great speed,
Yuyutsu followed behind the eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, O King.
