Mounting a bright golden chariot yoked with the horses Sainya and Sugrīva, Kṛṣṇa followed the Kurus together with Sātyaki; meanwhile,
O Bhārata, the eldest father of the son of Pṛthā proceeded by means of a palanquin.
12,038.040c Accompanied by Gāndhārī, he went at the head of Dharmarāja.
12,038.041a And all those Kuru women— Kuntī, Draupadī Kṛṣṇā, and the rest— 12,038.041c proceeded in various kinds of vehicles, preceded by Vidura.

Then numerous chariots and well-adorned elephants, as well as foot-soldiers and horses, followed behind. Then, with the eloquent recitations of bards, heralds, and panegyrists, [the procession moved forward].
Being thus praised, the king went to the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura).
That departure of the mighty-armed one was peerless on earth;
it was a grand procession, teeming with joyful and well-fed people.
As Pārtha set out,
the city and the royal highway were duly adorned by the city-dwellers with white garlands, banners, and sacrificial altars.
The royal highway was enclosed and exquisitely perfumed with incenses; moreover, the royal palace was completely covered with powdered fragrances, various flowers, *priyaṅgu* blossoms,
and suspended garlands of flowers.
At the city gate, sturdy new jars filled with water,
maidens, flowers, and goats were stationed here and there;
thus did the son of Pāṇḍu find the city with its gates well-decorated.
Being praised with auspicious words and surrounded by his friends, he entered.
Vaiśampāyana said:
But upon the entry of the sons of Pṛthā, the people dwelling in the city—
Then many thousands of people, eager to see him, gathered together;
that royal highway, with its squares beautifully adorned, shone,
O King, like the great ocean swelling at the rising of the moon.
O Bhārata, the vast mansions along the royal road, filled with women and richly adorned with jewels, seemed to tremble under their weight. They praised Yudhiṣṭhira slowly, as if with modesty.
"Bhīmasena and Arjuna, as well as the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī—
blessed are you, O Pāñcālī, for you attend upon these best of men, O auspicious lady, just as Gautamī attends upon the great seers."
"O beautiful lady, your deeds are never in vain, and so too is your observance of vows," thus did the women praise Kṛṣṇā at that time, O great king;
and by means of those words of praise and their mutual exclamations, O Bhārata, [the king was moved].
The city was then filled with sounds born of joy. Having traversed that royal highway as was fitting, Yudhiṣṭhira approached the decorated and resplendent royal palace.
Then all the subjects, both those from the city and those from the countryside,
gathered from here and there and spoke words pleasing to the ear:
"By good fortune you are victorious, O Indra among kings, O slayer of enemies!"
"By good fortune, the kingdom has been regained through both righteousness and power.
O Great King, may you reign over us here for a hundred autumns;
protect the subjects with righteousness, O King, just as Indra protects the triple heaven."
Thus, honored with auspicious rites at the gate of the royal palace,
and having accepted from all sides the blessings uttered by the twice-born,
the king entered his residence, which resembled the abode of the King of the Gods.

Having heard this account of victory, he descended from his chariot. Entering the inner apartments, the illustrious king approached the deities and honored them in every way with jewels, perfumes, and garlands.
Then the illustrious and highly renowned one emerged once again;
he beheld well-formed brahmins standing before him.
He was then surrounded by those brahmins, who were desirous of pronouncing blessings.

He shone like the stainless moon surrounded by hosts of stars. Placing his preceptor Dhaumya and his eldest father at the forefront, the son of Kuntī honored those brahmins according to the prescribed rites.

The king entered the assembly hall like Vāsava entering Sudharmā; O Indra among kings, he did so with jasmine flowers, sweetmeats, jewels, abundant gold, cattle, garments, and various things desired by each.

Then, O Bhārata, there arose the sound of the proclamation of a holy day (*puṇyāha*), which seemed to pierce the very heavens; it was auspicious, generating joy for friends, and bringing delight to the ears. There, O King, the speech of the twice-born ones resounded like the cry of swans.

O King, there was heard the sound of those learned in the Vedas, with their words, phrases, and syllables full of profound meaning; then there arose the resonant blast of kettledrums and the delightful sound of conchs,
as those proclaiming victory made their voices heard.
When the assembly of brahmins there had become silent once more,
the Rākṣasa Cārvāka, disguised as a brahmin, spoke to the king;
he was a friend of Duryodhana, concealed there in the form of a mendicant.
Wearing a topknot and carrying a triple staff, the Sāṃkhya ascetic was bold and free from fear;
O Indra among kings, he was then surrounded by many thousands of brahmins who were established in austerity and self-restraint and desiring to offer him blessings.
That wicked man, harboring evil intentions toward the high-souled Pāṇḍavas,
spoke to the lord of the earth without even taking leave of those Brahmins, saying:
"All these twice-born ones have placed this speech upon me."
"Fie on you, a wicked king who has slaughtered your own kin! O son of Kuntī, what use is this kingdom to you now that you have brought about the destruction of your relatives?
Having caused the death of your elders as well, death is better for you than life."
Having heard these words of that terrible Rākṣasa, those twice-born ones trembled and cried out, overwhelmed by his speech. Then all those Brāhmaṇas and King Yudhiṣṭhira [were likewise affected].
Ashamed and extremely agitated, O lord of the people, they remained silent.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"May you be gracious toward me, who bows down and entreats you."
"You ought not to reproach me, who am fallen into such distress.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, O King, lord of the people, all those brahmins..."
They said, "This word is not ours; may prosperity be yours, O King.
Then those high-souled ones—Brahmins learned in the Vedas and purified by their austerities—perceived him with the eye of knowledge.
The 12,039.033 Brāhmaṇas said:
"This Rākṣasa named Cārvāka, a friend of Duryodhana,
desires to act for his benefit while disguised as a wandering mendicant."
"O righteous-souled one, we do not say that such fear as this should remain;
let auspiciousness attend you along with your brothers.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all those pure brahmins, overcome with anger by their *huṃ* sounds, reviling him, struck down the sinful rākṣasa. He fell, utterly consumed by the splendor of those who discourse on the Veda.
Like a budding tree consumed by the thunderbolt of the great Indra, [he fell].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, while the king stood there with his brothers...
Janārdana, the son of Devakī and all-seeing one, spoke [as follows].
Having been honored, the brahmins departed after congratulating the king;
and the Pāṇḍava king, together with his circle of friends, attained great joy.
Vāsudeva said:
"O dear one, in this world, Brāhmaṇas are always to be honored by me;
they are gods walking upon the earth, whose speech is poison, yet who are easily propitiated."
Long ago in the Kṛta age, O dear one, a Rākṣasa named Cārvāka performed austerities at Badarī for many years, O mighty-armed one. Then,
he was repeatedly invited by Brahmā to choose a boon.
O Bhārata, he chose as his boon fearlessness from all beings;
with the sole exception of insulting the twice-born,
the Lord of the World then granted him that unsurpassed boon of fearlessness from all beings.
Having obtained that boon, that wicked Rākṣasa of immeasurable prowess, fierce deeds, and great strength, began to torment the gods. Then the gods, having assembled together, spoke thus to Brahmā:

Then, O Bhārata, the imperishable God, seeing them distressed by the power of that Rākṣasa, spoke to them for his destruction: "I have indeed ordained there how his death shall come to pass before long."
"O King, a king named Duryodhana will become his friend.
Bound by affection for him, he (the son of the fisherman) will show contempt toward the Brahmins. Thereupon, the Brahmins, provoked by his mistreatment, will become enraged."

"Those whose strength is speech shall burn away his evil, and then he will go to destruction. This very Rākṣasa, Cārvāka, lies here slain by the Brahma-staff, O best of kings; do not grieve, O bull of the Bharatas."
"O King, those kinsmen of yours have been slain according to the duty of the Kṣatriyas;
those high-souled heroes, the bulls among the Kṣatriyas, have gone to heaven. Therefore, O Acyuta, establish yourself in what is auspicious; let there be no despondency in you."
"Slay your enemies, protect your subjects, and support the twice-born.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thereupon, the king, the son of Kuntī, was freed from anger and relieved of his fever.
Delighted, he sat down upon a supreme golden throne facing the east.
Facing him on a seat covered with a soft rug sat Sātyaki and Vāsudeva, those two subduers of enemies.
Having placed the king in the center, both the high-souled Bhīmasena and Arjuna sat down upon two smooth jeweled seats,
bright with ivory couches and adorned with gold.
Pṛthā also sat together with Sahadeva and Nakula;
Sudharmā, Vidura, Dhaumya, and Dhṛtarāṣṭra the Kaurava sat down individually on seats that resembled blazing fires.
Yuyutsu, Saṃjaya, and the illustrious Gāndhārī—
everyone sat down where King Dhṛtarāṣṭra was. Seated there, the righteous-souled king touched white flowers.
12,040.007c Swastikas, unbroken grains, earth, gold, silver, and jewels;
12,040.008a Then all the subjects, placing the family priest at their head, beheld the King of Dharma, who had brought many auspicious objects with him.
The earth, gold, and various kinds of jewels;
the vessels for the consecration, gathered with every necessary material;
and there, [vessels] made of gold, copper, silver, and earth.
Full water-pots, flowers, parched grain, sacred grass, products of the cow,
*śamī*, *palāśa*, and *puṃnāga* wood for fuel, honey, clarified butter,
a sacrificial ladle made of udumbara wood, and conch shells adorned with gold.
Upon a jeweled throne made of udumbara wood and covered with a tiger skin,
the family priest Dhaumya— having been authorized by the scion of Daśārha—
smeared the sacrificial altar, which sloped toward the northeast, according to the prescribed marks.

Having seated the high-souled one and Kṛṣṇā, the daughter of Drupada, upon a smooth, auspicious *sarvatobhadra* seat covered with a tiger skin— firmly established on its feet and glowing with a brilliance like that of fire.

The wise one offered oblations into the purifying fire according to the prescribed rites and mantras. Then, rising up, the descendant of Daśārha took the honored conch shell and consecrated Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, as the lord of the earth.
And the royal seer Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as well as all the subjects,
having given their consent, the Pāṇḍava, together with Kṛṣṇa and his brothers,
was consecrated by means of the Pāñcajanya conch; and the king became one whose face was like nectar.
Then they sounded the paṇavas, ānakas, and dundubhis;
Dharmarāja also accepted all that in accordance with dharma, and he,
who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, honored them according to the prescribed rites.
Then, with a thousand gold coins, he had the Brahmins recite blessings—
men perfected in Vedic study and endowed with virtuous conduct and character.
O King, those pleased Brahmins pronounced blessings of well-being and victory upon him.
Crying out like swans, they praised Yudhiṣṭhira:
"O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, O Pāṇḍava, by good fortune you are victorious! By good fortune, O you of great splendor, you have recovered your own dharma through your prowess."
"By good fortune, O King, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow and Bhīmasena the Pāṇḍava are well, as are you yourself and the two Pāṇḍava sons of Mādrī;
and all your brothers, together with their friends, are safe with their chariots."
O bull among the Bharatas, by the grace of Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the World,
having conquered all enemies and delighting the subjects through righteousness,
protect the eternal earth with its forests and islands.
"Released from this battle through the destruction of the heroes, with your enemies slain,
quickly perform those duties that follow in due time, O Pāṇḍava.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, was honored in return by those virtuous men.
O Bhārata, he entered into his great kingdom together with his friends.
This narrative known as the *Śrī Mahābhārata* bestows the fruits of desired objects;
it promotes longevity, generates nourishment, and grants the increase of sons and grandsons.
Bestowing all prosperity upon men and warding off the flood of all sins,
it is the sole means for achieving constant devotion to the illustrious Vāsudeva;
[it belongs] to both Śiva and Vāsudeva, the God of gods.
It is adorned on all sides by their pure majesty—
that of the royal sages who performed meritorious deeds, of the high-souled sages,
of their great majesty, their vast merit, and the skill displayed in battles.
The proclamation of sacred fields, holy fords, and rivers;
the narrative of the Mahābhārata, a history of great fruit,
beginning with the birth of Śantanu and the high-souled Pāṇḍavas.

From the beginning until the chapter on royal consecration, one who is restrained and well-composed should listen for the sake of accomplishing his goals; he shall obtain all desires. Having heard this chapter on consecration, one should always remain concentrated.
One should feed the preeminent Brahmins with milk, clarified butter, and various collections of hard and soft foods, for that is indeed the means to attain spiritual welfare.
One should honor the speaker of the Mahābhārata with the same reverence one reserves for Vyāsa himself.
With a concentrated mind, [he worshipped] with offerings such as garments, ornaments, and perfumes.
Vaiśampāyana said:
That speech of the subjects was appropriate to the time and place.
Having heard this, King Yudhiṣṭhira then replied to Uttara:
"Blessed are the sons of Pāṇḍu in this world, for whom the preeminent Brahmins,
having assembled, speak of their virtues— whether they be true or even untrue."
"It is my conviction that we are surely worthy of your favor,
since you, free from envy, speak of us as being endowed with such virtues. The great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra is our father and our supreme deity."
"Those who desire to do what is pleasing to me must remain devoted to his service and to what is dear to him.
For it is for this purpose that I live, having committed this great slaughter of my kinsmen;
I must constantly serve him without weariness."
"If I am worthy of favor from you, my friends,
then you ought to behave toward Dhṛtarāṣṭra exactly as before. For he is the protector of the world, as well as yours, along with me."
"The entire earth and all the Pāṇḍavas belong to him alone;
this word of mine must be kept in your minds. Having followed the king, you may now depart as you please."

Having dismissed all the citizens and country-folk, the joy of the Kurus, the descendant of Kuru, appointed Bhīmasena to the position of heir apparent (*yauvarājya*). [He was superior] in counsel, in decision-making, and in the deliberation upon the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*).
With great affection, he appointed the wise Vidura to oversee what had been done and what remained to be done, as well as the consideration of income and expenditure;
and he assigned Saṃjaya, who was endowed with abundant and excellent qualities, to similar duties.
The king appointed Nakula to oversee the size of the army as well as the food and wages, and to supervise the laborers; he was also charged with resisting foreign invasions and crushing the arrogant.

The great king Yudhiṣṭhira gave instructions to Phalguna regarding the Vedic rites of the twice-born and indeed all other duties; likewise, that scorcher of foes assigned Dhaumya, the best of domestic priests, to oversee the affairs of the chaplains.
O lord of the people, the king always gave instructions to Sahadeva, who stood by his side; for the monarch was protected by him in every situation,
in whatever tasks he deemed him fit for.
The lord of the earth, being well-pleased, assigned them each to those very positions;
that slayer of enemy heroes, whose soul was righteous and who was devoted to dharma, spoke to Vidura, Saṃjaya, and the high-minded Yuyutsu.
"Rising again and again, you must all, with vigilance, perform exactly and in due order whatever duties belong to this king, my father,
as well as those tasks that concern the citizens and the people of the provinces at all times."
Having obtained the king’s permission regarding those duties according to dharma,
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira [performed the rites] for those kinsmen who had been slain in battle.

The noble-minded King Dhṛtarāṣṭra caused the funeral rites to be performed for them individually; he provided food endowed with every desirable quality, as well as cattle and wealth, for the sake of his sons' post-mortem rites.
The highly illustrious one [took] various jewels of great value;
Yudhiṣṭhira, however, [took those] of Karṇa and the high-souled Droṇa,
as well as those of Dhṛṣṭadyumna and Abhimanyu, and of the Rākṣasa son of Hiḍimbā.
Together with Draupadī, he bestowed gifts upon Virāṭa and his other well-wishing allies, as well as upon Drupada and the sons of Draupadī;
addressing each one individually, he gave thousands of Brahmins to each.
He gratified them with wealth, garments, jewels, and cattle;
and for those other rulers of the earth who had no kinsmen,
he performed their funeral rites, naming each one individually.
The Pāṇḍava caused various assembly halls, water-stations,
and tanks to be built for all his friends as funeral rites;
having thus discharged his debt to them, he attained freedom from reproach in the worlds.
Having fulfilled his duties while protecting his subjects according to dharma,
the king honored Dhṛtarāṣṭra as before, as well as Gāndhārī and Vidura,
and he likewise paid due honor to all the Kaurava ministers and servants.
And whatever women were there whose husbands had been slain and whose sons had been killed,
the compassionate Kuru king honored them all and protected them;
likewise, he provided dwellings, clothing, and food for those who were distressed, blind, and miserable.
Devoted to compassion, the powerful king bestowed his favor.
Having conquered the entire earth and attained freedom from debt toward his enemies,
King Yudhiṣṭhira, now without rivals, lived happily.
12,043.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having been consecrated and having obtained the kingdom, the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira,
pure and with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the lotus-eyed descendant of Daśārha.
"O Kṛṣṇa, O tiger among the Yadus, through your grace, your policy, your strength, your intellect, and likewise through your prowess,
this ancestral kingdom has been regained by me."
"Salutations to you, O lotus-eyed one; again and again, O subduer of enemies!
They call you the one Puruṣa; they call you the Lord of the Sātvatas. The supreme ṛṣis praise you with many various names."
"O Viśvakarman, homage be to you, O Soul of the universe, source of the universe!
O Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, Hara, Kṛṣṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣottama!
In ancient times, you entered the state of being an embryo within Aditi for seven nights."
You alone are Pṛśnigarbha; they call you Triyuga as well.
You are called Śuciśravas, Hṛṣīkeśa, Ghṛtārcis, and Haṃsa. You alone are Tricakṣus, Śambhu, Vibhu, and Dāmodara.
Varāha, Agni, Bṛhadbhānu, Vṛṣaṇas, Tārkṣyalakṣaṇa,
Anīkasāhas, Puruṣa, Śipiviṣṭa, Urukrama,
Vāciṣṭha, Ugra, Senānī, Satya, Vājasani, and Guha.
The infallible one, the shaker of enemies, the creator, the transformer, the bull;
you alone are the one who has made the path, the mountain, the one containing the bull, and Vṛṣākapi;
the dweller by the rivers, the wave, the three-peaked, the three-aboded, the triple-formed, and the infallible.

You alone are the sovereign ruler, the universal monarch, the self-ruler, the king of the gods, the bestower of dharma, and the source of existence; you are the all-pervading lord, the earth, the conqueror, Kṛṣṇa, and you are indeed he whose path is black.
You are the maker of good offerings, the physician, Āvarta, Kapila, and Vāmana.
You are called Yajña, Dhruva, Pataṅga, and Jayatsena; you are Śikhaṇḍin, Nahuṣa, Babhru, Divaspṛś, and Punarvasu;
you are Subabhru, Ukṣan, Rukma, Suṣeṇa, and Dundubhi.

You are Gabhastinemi, Śrīpadma, Puṣkara, and Puṣpadhāraṇa; you are Ṛbhu, Vibhu, and Sarvasūkṣma, and you are recited as Sāvitra. You are the ocean, you are Brahmā, you are the sacred abode, and you are the bow.
O Keśava, they call you Hiraṇyagarbha, Svadhā, and Svāhā. O Kṛṣṇa, you are the womb and the dissolution of this universe;
you alone create this entire world in the beginning.
"O Source of the Universe, this entire world is under your control;
homage be to you, O wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the sword.
Thus was Kṛṣṇa praised by Dharmarāja.
In the midst of the assembly, the lotus-eyed one,
filled with joy, greeted that eldest Pāṇḍava, the descendant of Bharata, with abundant words— the foremost of the Yādavas.
This hundred names of Viṣṇu was proclaimed by Dharmarāja;
whoever should recite or even hear it is liberated from all sins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the king dismissed all his subjects;
having received permission, they entered their respective homes.
Thereafter, King Yudhiṣṭhira [addressed] Bhīma of terrible prowess.
Consoling them, the wise one spoke to Arjuna and the twins:
"In this great battle, your bodies have been mangled by enemies with various weapons;
you are utterly exhausted and tormented by grief and wrath."
"O best of men, you have endured painful dwellings in the forest for my sake, just as base men would; now,
let this victory be enjoyed by you according to your pleasure and as you wish."
"Once you have rested and regained your composure, I shall meet with you all again tomorrow.
Then [he went] to the palace of Duryodhana, which was adorned with lofty mansions,
filled with many jewels, and crowded with male and female servants.
Authorized by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and given by his brother, the mighty-armed Vṛkodara took possession of it, just as Maghavan takes Mount Mandara;
for it was like the house of Duryodhana, and likewise that of Duḥśāsana.
Adorned with rows of palaces and decorated with golden archways, filled with male and female servants and abundant wealth and grain,
the mighty-armed Arjuna entered it by the king’s command.
He entered the residence of Duḥśāsana, which was endowed with every prosperity; then he went to the palace of Durmarṣaṇa, which was superior to the house of Duḥśāsana,
resembling the abode of Kubera and adorned with jewels and gold.
O great king, the righteous King Yudhiṣṭhira, being pleased, gave to Nakula— who was worthy of the best and had been emaciated in the great forest—
the foremost mansion of Durmukha, which was magnificent and adorned with gold.
He gave to Sahadeva, who was ever intent on doing what was pleasing to him, a residence filled with women whose eyes were like lotus petals;
having obtained it, he rejoiced just as the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) does upon reaching Kailāsa.
Yuyutsu, Vidura, and the highly effulgent Sañjaya,
as well as Sudharmā and Dhaumya, each went to their respective abodes;
while Śauri, together with Sātyaki, went to the residence of Arjuna.
That tiger among men entered [the cave] like a tiger entering a mountain cavern. There, provided with various foods and drinks, they dwelt happily;
having awakened in comfort, they waited upon King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Janamejaya said:
O Brahmin, you ought to tell me here what else the immensely radiant Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira did after he had regained his kingdom.
"O Sage, you ought to explain what that hero, the Blessed Lord Hṛṣīkeśa, the supreme teacher of the three worlds, did.
Vaiśampāyana said:

"Listen, O sinless Indra among kings, to what the Pāṇḍavas did after placing Vāsudeva at their head, as it is being told by me in truth. Having obtained the kingdom, the highly resplendent Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira— "

He established the four social orders (*cāturvarṇya*) each in their respective duties as was appropriate; he stabilized the castes through both policy and discipline. And he [established] a thousand high-souled *brāhmaṇas* who were accomplished in the ritual baths (*snātaka*).

The Pāṇḍava caused each person to recite [the Veda] while giving them one thousand gold coins (*niṣka*). In this manner, he fully satisfied his dependents, servants, those who sought refuge, guests, the wretched, and even the seekers of logic with their desired objects.
He gave ten thousand cows to the family priest Dhaumya,
as well as wealth, gold, silver, and various garments;
and toward Kṛpa, O great king, he behaved with the conduct due to a preceptor.
The righteous-souled one, firm in his vows, offered worship to Vidura;
that best of givers satisfied all who had sought his protection by providing various kinds of food, drink, garments, beds, and seats.
Having brought about the pacification of those who had been provoked, that king of great renown, O best of kings, paid honor to Yuyutsu, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra;
and he entrusted that kingdom to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Gāndhārī, and Vidura.
Having reported [all this], O King, King Yudhiṣṭhira remained as if at ease;
and having thus gratified the entire city, O Janamejaya,
he approached the high-souled Vāsudeva with palms joined in reverence.
Then, upon a great couch adorned with jewels and gold,
he beheld Kṛṣṇa seated, dark-hued like a cloud upon Mount Meru,
his body blazing with splendor and adorned with divine ornaments.
Clad in yellow silk, he shone like a gem set in gold;
his chest was brilliantly adorned with the Kaustubha jewel,
and he wore a crown as if the rising sun had ascended the mountain of sunrise.
There is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that can be compared to him. Approaching the high-souled Viṣṇu, who has the form of a person,
he then spoke these words with a sweet voice and a smile.
"O best among the wise, has the night passed peacefully for you?
O Acyuta, are all your cognitions clear?
For it is by relying upon that divine intellect of yours, O best among the wise," [he said].
"O Blessed One, through your grace— O you whose prowess is the refuge of the three worlds— we have attained sovereignty, and the earth stands under our control.
We have achieved victory and preeminent fame, yet we have not fallen away from dharma."
To Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira, who was speaking in that manner,
the Blessed One said nothing at all, but instead entered into meditation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O you of immeasurable prowess, what is this supreme marvel that you meditate upon? O refuge of the world, is all well with these three worlds?
O Supreme Person, having taken recourse to the path of the fourth dhyāna..."
"O Lord, because you have departed, my mind is filled with wonder. For the five-fold wind within your body has been restrained,
and all your senses have been established in the mind."

Your senses and your mind have been merged into your intellect; indeed, O Lord, the entire host has been placed within your *kṣetrajña*. Your body hairs do not quiver, and likewise your intellect and mind are steadfast.
"O Mādhava, you are as motionless as a pillar, a wall, or a stone; you are devoid of all exertion.
O Acyuta, just as a lamp placed in a windless spot burns without flickering, so too, O Blessed One, O God, are you unmoving and firm in resolve."
Nevertheless, O Lord, to me who has sought refuge and entreats you— If it is fit for me to hear here, and if it is not a secret of yours, O Lord,
sever the doubt of me who has sought refuge and entreats you.
For you are indeed the creator and the transformer; you are both the perishable and the imperishable. You alone, O Supreme Person, are without beginning or end, the primordial one.
To me, your devotee who has sought refuge in you and bows his head in prostration—
"O best among the upholders of dharma, speak of this meditation according to its true nature.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then, having fixed his mind and his faculties of perception and intellect upon his own domain,"
Preceded by a smile, the Blessed One, the younger brother of Vāsava, spoke these words:
"Bhīṣma, lying upon his bed of arrows like a fire about to be extinguished, that tiger among men meditates upon me; therefore, my mind is fixed upon him."
"Even the King of the Gods could not endure the sound of his bowstring, which was like the crash of a thunderbolt; it is to him that I have turned my mind.
By him, having rushed forward with speed, the entire circle of kings [was overwhelmed]."
In my mind, I have gone to him who formerly married three maidens;
I have gone in my mind to him whom Rāma, though he fought the descendant of Bhṛgu for twenty-three nights, could not overcome.
O King, my mind has gone, dear father, to that prince whom Gaṅgā bore according to the rite of pregnancy— that disciple of Vasiṣṭha,
the wise and highly energetic one who wields the divine weapons.
O Pāṇḍava, with my mind I have gone to that beloved disciple of Rāma Jāmadagnya, who has mastered the four Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
and who is the repository of all branches of knowledge. I have gone to him with my mind.
Having unified the collection of the senses and restrained the mind through wisdom, he sought refuge in me; therefore, my mind became fixed upon him.
For he, O bull among men, is the past, the future, and the present.

The best among those who uphold dharma knows this; therefore, my mind is fixed upon him. For when that tiger among men has departed to heaven by his own deeds, O Pārtha, the earth will become like a night when the moon has vanished.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having approached Bhīṣma, the son of Gaṅgā, who possesses terrible prowess, and having saluted him, ask whatever is in your mind—
concerning the four Vedas, the four sacrificial offices, and the four stages of life.

"O lord of the earth, ask him about the dharma of the four social orders (cāturvarṇya). Once Bhīṣma, that leader of the Kauravas, has set, all forms of knowledge will diminish; therefore, I urge you."
Having heard those excellent and truthful words of Vāsudeva,
that knower of dharma, his throat choked with tears, spoke to Janārdana:
"O Mādhava, regarding the power of Bhīṣma that you have described..."
"O giver of honor, there is no doubt in my mind regarding this;
for I have heard from great-souled Brahmins as they recounted the immense fortune and the power of the high-souled Bhīṣma."
"O slayer of enemies, O delighter of the Yādavas, whatever you, the creator of the worlds, say is indeed so; that word is not to be questioned,
since your mind, O Mādhava, has been inclined toward showing me favor."
"Placing you at our head, we shall behold Bhīṣma;
for when the divine sun has turned its course, he will depart for the other worlds.
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, that Kuru elder deserves to see you."
"For the sight of you—the primordial deity, both the perishable and the imperishable—would be a true gain; for you are a treasure-trove composed of Brahman.
Having heard these words of Dharmarāja, Madhusūdana [replied].
Standing by his side, he said to Sātyaki, "Let my chariot be yoked.
Then Sātyaki, having stepped out from the presence of Keśava,
spoke to Dāruka, saying, "Let Kṛṣṇa's chariot be yoked as well."
Having quickly heard the words of Sātyaki,
[he mounted] that best of chariots, its parts adorned with gold and featuring side-panels made of emeralds and cat's-eye gems.
Adorned with wheels bound in gold,
possessing the radiance of the sun's rays, moving swiftly,
and decorated with various wonderful jewels and gems.
Like the newly risen sun, he was radiant;
he possessed a variegated banner of Tārkṣya and was adorned with flags,
led by excellent horses at the head of Sugrīva’s army.
With palms joined in reverence, Dāruka, that lion among kings, announced to Acyuta that the chariot was well-yoked with horses swift as thought, their limbs adorned with gold.
Janamejaya said:
While lying upon the bed of arrows, how did the grandfather of the Bharatas cast off his body, and what yoga did he maintain?
12,047.002 Vaiśampāyana said: Listen attentively, O King, having become pure and composed,
to the renunciation of the body by the high-souled Bhīṣma, O tiger among the Kurus.
O King, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha,
under the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), when the sun had reached the meridian,
and just as the sun had turned toward its northern course, [the wheel appeared].
Composed in meditation, he absorbed his self within the Self alone;
Bhīṣma, covered with hundreds of arrows like the sun with its rays scattered abroad,
lay there endowed with supreme splendor, surrounded by the best of Brahmins.
By Vyāsa Vedaśravas, by the celestial sage Nārada, by Devasthāna, Vātsya, as well as Aśmaka and Sumantu,
and likewise by Jaimini and the high-souled Paila.
And by Śāṇḍilya and Devala, and by the wise Maitreya; by Asita, Vasiṣṭha, and the high-souled Kauśika;
and by Hārīta and Lomaśa, as well as by the wise Ātreya.
Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and the great sage Cyavana;
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, Vālmīki, Tumburu, and Kuru;
Maudgalya, Bhārgava Rāma, and the great sage Tṛṇabindu.
Pippalāda, Vāyu, Saṃvarta, Pulaha, Kaca,
Kāśyapa, Pulastya, Kratu, Dakṣa, Parāśara,
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Kāśya, Gautama, and the sage Gālava.
Dhaumya, Vibhāṇḍa, Māṇḍavya, Dhaumra, Kṛṣṇānubhautika, Ulūka the supreme brahmin, the great sage Mārkaṇḍeya,
Bhāskari, Pūraṇa, Kṛṣṇa, and the most righteous Sūta.
And by that great-souled external sage Gālava,
by the illustrious Yājñavalkya, by Śaṅkha, and by Pulaha—
by these and other hosts of highly fortunate and great-souled sages.
Surrounded by those distinguished for their faith and self-restraint, like the moon by the planets,
as well as by other sages and the high-souled Pulastya,
Bhīṣma— that tiger among men— [honored them] in deed, thought, and speech.
Lying upon a bed of arrows, he stood with palms joined in reverence and meditated upon Kṛṣṇa;
with a voice of full resonance, he praised Madhusūdana—
the Lord of Yoga, Padmanābha, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, and the Lord of the World.

Then Bhīṣma, the most excellent among those skilled in speech and supremely righteous in soul, having become pure and with palms joined in reverence, praised the Lord Vāsudeva— the victor who is without beginning or end, self-born, and eternal.

Desiring to propitiate Kṛṣṇa, I wish to utter that speech— both detailed and concise— by which Puruṣottama may be pleased. [With this] pure [speech], [I praise] the pure one, the swan dwelling in purity, the supreme lord who is devoted to the highest.
Having yoked my self with my whole being, I take refuge in that Prajāpati,
the supreme Brahman without beginning or end, whom neither the gods nor the sages know;
the Lord Dhātṛ, Nārāyaṇa Hari alone knows him.
From Nārāyaṇa [proceeded] the hosts of ṛṣis, as well as the Siddhas and Mahoragas;
the gods and divine seers who know him as the supreme, immutable one;
and the gods, Dānavas, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Pannagas.
Who indeed is this Blessed One, and from whence does he come— this one whom they do not know,
in whom all beings abide and into whom they enter,
as clusters of gems upon a thread, existing as qualities within the Lord of Beings?

In that eternal, extended, and firm thread upon which the universe— composed of both the existent and the non-existent— rests like a garland, [I meditate] on Hari, the architect of the universe, whose every limb is the universe,
who possesses a thousand heads, a thousand feet, and a thousand eyes.
They call him the god Nārāyaṇa, the supreme refuge of the universe, who possesses a crown upon a thousand arms and is radiant with a thousand faces;
he is the smallest of the small and the most massive of the massive.
He who is the weightiest among the weighty, the most excellent among the excellent, and the best even among those things that lead to the highest good—
him they praise as the one whose actions are truth, as Truth itself, within the *vākas*, the *anuvākas*, the *niṣads*, and the *upaniṣads*, amidst the *sāmans* dedicated to Truth.
[They worship] the fourfold Self with four [means], the Lord of the Sātvatas who abides in purity,
whom the gods worship with divine and secret supreme names;
in whom austerity is eternally practiced, and which [taste] resides within his limbs.
He who is the soul of all, the knower of all, the All, the omniscient, the creator of all— him,
the God whom the goddess Devakī bore from Vasudeva,
as the fire-drill produces the blazing fire for the protection of the earthly Brahman.
He who, free from desire and devoid of impurity, having worshipped Govinda— who is none other than himself— beholds Him established within his own self for the sake of infinity;
he is called Puruṣa in the Purāṇas and Brahmā at the beginnings of the ages.
In the Kṣaya [Yuga], he is proclaimed as Saṃkarṣaṇa; we worship him, the one to be worshipped,
who is the single Adhokṣaja manifested in many forms,
whom those devoted to no other, being observant of ritual acts, worship for the fulfillment of all desires.
That which they call the treasury of the world, in which all creatures are contained; in which these worlds flutter like birds upon the water;
that Truth, the single-syllabled Brahman, which is beyond both being and non-being.
Neither gods nor sages know that which is without beginning, middle, or end; that which the gods, asuras, gandharvas, along with the perfected ones (siddhas), rishis, and great serpents (mahoragas),
constantly worship with devotion as the supreme medicine for suffering.
The god who is without beginning or end, self-born and eternal; Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, who is beyond ratiocination and incomprehensible;
whose deeds surpass those of Vāyu and Indra, and whose splendor exceeds that of the sun and fire.
I take refuge in that Prajāpati, whose nature transcends the faculties of the intellect,
whom they indeed call the creator of the universe, the lord of all that moves and stands, the overseer of the world, the imperishable, the supreme state.

Salutations to that one whose essence is the Sun, who was born as twelvefold from the single womb that is golden-hued, which Aditi bore to destroy the Daityas. He who, in the bright fortnight, gratifies the gods and in the dark fortnight, the ancestors, with nectar.
Salutations to him who is the king of the twice-born, whose essence is Soma;
salutations to him whose nature is the Hotṛ priest, who is meditated upon by the gods with fire as their mouth, and who is the first enjoyer of the oblation throughout the entire world.

Salutation to that Self who is to be known, beyond the vast darkness, the Person of blazing splendor, by knowing whom one transcends death. Salutation to Him whom they praise in the great *bṛhatī* hymn, in the sacred fire, and in the great sacrifice.
Salutation to Him who is the Self of the Vedas, whom the assemblies of sages sing;
salutation to Him who is the Self of Sacrifice, whose abode is the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, who takes the form of the five oblations, and whom they extend as the seven-threaded sacrifice.
Salutations to Him whose essence is the oblation, who is offered with four, four, two, and five [verses], and again with two;
He who is Suparṇa, named Yajus, whose limbs are the Chandas and whose head is the Trivṛt.
Salutation to him whose eyes are the *rathantara* and *bṛhat* [sāmans], who is the self of the hymn of praise;
salutation to that golden-colored bird, the seer of the world-creators, who was born at the sacrificial session of a thousand offerings— he who is the self of the swan.

Salutations to that Self of Speech, whom they call the eternal syllable (*akṣara*), whose limbs are the words, whose joints are the sandhis, and whose characteristics are the vowels and consonants; he who,
becoming the sacrificial boar, indeed lifted up the earth.

Homage to him whose essence is vigor, who acts for the benefit of the three worlds; homage to him whose essence is sleep, who reclines upon a couch adorned by a serpent, fashioned with a thousand hoods, having established himself in *yoga*.
To the Viśvedevas, the Maruts, the Rudras, the Ādityas, and the Aśvins;
to the Vasus, the Siddhas, and the Sādhyas—to that Self of the gods, salutation!
The unmanifest, the intellect (*buddhi*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the mind (*manas*), and the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*).
Salutation to Him, the essence of the principles (*tattva*), who consists of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the gross objects (*viśeṣa*).

Salutation to Him, the essence of the elements (*bhūtātman*), who is the past, the present, and the future, and who is the source and the dissolution of the elements and all other things; He who is the first-born of all beings.

Salutations again and again to those who offer obeisance at the sacrifice of Viṣṇu, the Boar of immeasurable splendor; for even they are worthy of reverence. Indeed, those people who know the subtle investigate Him as the most subtle.

Salutations to that subtle Self, the Brahman which is both subtle and non-subtle. Salutations to that Fish-form, by whom the Vedas situated in the subterranean realm were swiftly recovered and restored to Viriñca.
Salutations to that one whose nature is the Tortoise, who, when the churning for the nectar of immortality had begun, supported Mount Mandara with his exceedingly firm body; salutations to him who,
assuming the form of a Boar, [upheld] the earth together with its forests and mountains.
Salutation to Him in the form of a boar, who lifted up [the earth] with a single tusk;
salutation to Him in the form of a lion, who, having assumed the body of a Narasiṃha that strikes fear into all the worlds, slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.
Salutation to that proud-souled one, whose form is endowed with tawny eyes and mane, as well as fangs and claws, who brings about the end of the lords of the Dānavas; salutation to him who,
having assumed the form of a dwarf, bound Bali by means of his illusory power.

Salutations to Him who has traversed the three worlds, the one whose very nature is to traverse; salutations to Him who, having become Rāma, the son of Jamadagni and the best among wielders of weapons,
rendered the earth devoid of Kṣatriyas— salutations to Him whose nature is Rāma.
Salutations to that embodiment of wrath who, out of a sense of pride regarding his transgression of the Dharma, thrice seven times slew the Kṣatriyas in the assembly; he who,
having become Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, [slew] the delighter of the Pulastya clan.

Salutations to him who, in the form of a Kṣatriya, slew Rāvaṇa in battle; salutations to that glorious one who stands as Halī and Musalī, clad in blue garments. Salutations to Rāma, the son of Rohiṇī, who exists as the soul of worldly enjoyment.
Salutations always to the bearer of the conch, the bearer of the discus, the bearer of the Śārṅga bow, and the one clad in yellow garments;
salutations to that Kṛṣṇa-soul who wears a forest garland. The glorious son of Vasudeva played in the cowherd settlement of Nanda.
Salutations to Him who is the soul of play, for the sake of the destruction of Kaṃsa;
salutations to that Kṛṣṇa-nature, who, having entered the state of Vasudeva and being born in the lineage of Yadu, performed the removal of the earth's burden.
Acting as Arjuna’s charioteer in battle, he bestowed the nectar of the Gītā;
salutations to him, whose nature is Brahman, who acted for the benefit of the three worlds. Having brought the Dānavas under his control, he returned once more to the state of a Buddha.
Salutations to that one of pure self for the sake of protecting the creation;
salutations to him who, mounted on a horse, shall slay the Mlecchas when the Kali age arrives; salutations to that Kalky-ātman who is the establisher of Dharma.
Salutations to Him whose nature is play, who slew thousands, millions, and billions of Kṣatriyas in the Bhārata war; salutations to Him who,
in the lineage of Tārā, having slain Kālanemi, the foremost of the Dānavas—
He gave the kingdom to Mahendra; salutations to Him, the Supreme Self (mukhyātman).
Salutations to Him, the Witness-Self (sākṣyātman), who dwells as the witness within the bodies of all living beings, and who is the witness of the imperishable and the perishable breaths.
Homage be to you, O Mahādeva; homage to you, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees! Homage be to you, O Subrahmaṇya; be gracious, O Supreme Lord!
O All-pervading One, everything is pervaded by you in both unmanifest and manifest forms.
To Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-eyed one, the great lord of all worlds,
whose navel is golden, who is the limb of sacrifice, the immortal, and whose face is turned in every direction—
for those [who worship him], there is never any inauspiciousness in any undertaking.
In whose hearts Hari, the Lord of Gods and the abode of auspiciousness, resides— Bhagavān Viṣṇu is auspiciousness; Madhusūdana is auspiciousness;
Puṇḍarīkākṣa is auspiciousness; Garuḍadhvaja is auspiciousness.
Salutations to that one whose essence is truth, who builds the bridge for the virtuous by means of the eternal *ṛta*— the source of immortality— through the constituent parts of dharma, artha,
and legal procedure; he whom those practicing various religious paths and seeking various fruits of dharma [approach].
They worship him with various attributes; homage to that Self of Dharma!
Homage to that Self of Desire, from whom all embodied beings—though their bodies are formless—are born, and who is the intoxication of all living creatures!

Salutation to that Self of the Field (kṣetrātman), whom the great seers discern as the Unmanifest residing within the Manifest, seated as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) within the Field; salutation to Him who is the nature of pure vision, established in the Self, and encompassed by the sixteen qualities.
The Sāṃkhyas call him the seventeenth; salutation to him whose nature is Sāṃkhya.
Salutation to him whose nature is Yoga, whom those who practice yoga—sleepless, with breath conquered, established in purity, and with senses restrained—behold as light.

Salutations to that Self of Liberation, whom those peaceful renunciants— free from the fear of rebirth— attain when both demerit and merit have ceased. He who, at the end of a thousand yugas, becomes the fire with blazing flames.
Salutation to that terrible-souled one who devours all beings;
salutation to that one who, having devoured all beings and made the world a single ocean, sleeps as a child alone— that one whose nature is *māyā*.
Salutation to that Puruṣa of infinite self, who has a thousand heads, whose nature is the yogic sleep that encompasses the four oceans,
and upon whose single navel the entire universe is established— [the navel] of the Unborn.
Salutation to that lotus-souled one, the Puṣkara of Puṣkarākṣa. Salutation to him whose hair consists of clouds, whose every limb and joint consists of rivers,
and whose belly consists of the four oceans— to him, the soul of water, salutation!
Salutations to Him, the causal Self, from whom all transformations of creation and dissolution are produced, and into whom they are dissolved;
He who remains seated at night and stands forth during the day.
Salutations to that Self who is the witness of both the desirable and the undesirable;
salutations to that Self of action, whose form is Vaikuṇṭha, unimpeded in all tasks and ever-exerted for the sake of dharma.
Salutations to him whose soul was cruel, who, enraged in battle, thrice seven times slew the kṣatriyas who had transgressed the dignity of dharma; salutations to him who,
having divided himself fivefold, became the wind residing within the body.
Salutation to him whose nature is wind, who impels all beings;
salutation to him whose nature is time, the creator of creation and dissolution, who revolves through the ages by means of his portions consisting of days, seasons, solstices, and years.

The Brahmins are his mouth, the Kṣatriyas his arms, the Vaiśyas his thighs and belly, and the Śūdras rest upon his feet; homage to him, whose nature is the social orders. Fire is his mouth, heaven his head, space his navel, and the earth his feet.
Salutation to him who is the soul of the worlds, whose eye is the sun and whose ears are the quarters;
salutation to that protector-soul whom the Vaiśeṣikas call the guardian of the objects of the senses for those abiding within their spheres through specific qualities.
Salutations to that Prāṇātman, who consists of food, drink, and fuel, who increases the vital fluids and the life-breaths, and who sustains all living beings;
salutations to him who consumes the four kinds of food for the purpose of sustaining the vital breaths.
Fire cooks while remaining within [the fuel]; homage to him whose nature is that of the cooked.
Homage to him whose nature is pride, whose form has tawny eyes and mane, and whose weapons are his fangs and claws, bringing about the end of the lords of the Dānavas.
To the glorious, all-pervading Lord Ananta, who dwells in the subterranean realm (rasātala) and sustains the entire universe— to Him, whose essence is valor, obeisance!
And to Him who is the master of the ears and other senses as they operate upon their respective objects.
Salutations to that one of manifold nature who experiences all objects;
salutations to that subtle self whom neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the daityas, nor the dānavas truly know.
Salutation to Him whose essence is light, who outshines the splendors of fire, the sun, the moon, and the stars— those luminaries of divine form;
He who is beyond time, beyond sacrifice, and beyond both the existent and the non-existent.

12,047.047c Without beginning, yet the origin of the universe—to that Soul of the Universe, salutations! 12,047.047d*0084_01 The lightning-fire, the digestive fire, the purifying fire, and indeed the bright fire; 12,047.047d*0084_02 The burner of all things consumed—to that Fire-Self, salutations!

Salutations to Him in the form of the Fish, who, standing upon the surface of the waters at the center of the earth, slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and by whom the Vedas were indeed recovered; salutations to Him who bears the earth with its seven continents, its oceans, and its mountains.
Salutations to Him who bears [the earth] upon His back; salutations to Him whose nature is that of the tortoise.
Salutations to Him who, assuming the form of a boar, lifted up the earth submerged in the single ocean; salutations to Him whose nature is that of the boar.
Salutations to that one in the form of a lion, who, having assumed the terrifying Narasiṃha form,
slew Hiraṇyakaśipu; salutations to that lion-souled one who,
having assumed the form of Vāmana, bound Bali through his illusory power.
These three worlds have been traversed by him; homage to that one whose self has traversed all.
Having become the son of Jamadagni, the Lord Rāma, wielder of the axe, who was the slayer of the thousand Arjunas—homage to that fierce-souled one.

Having become Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, he slew Rāvaṇa—the delight of the Paulastya clan—in battle; homage to him, the soul of the Kṣatriya order! The glorious Vāsudeva, the son of Vasudeva, is the Lord of the World.
Salutations to Him whose essence is Kṛṣṇa, who removed the burden of the earth;
salutations to Him whose essence is delusion, who, assuming the form of Buddha and being devoted to all dharmas, bewilders all beings.
At the end of the Kali age, he who rides upon a horse will destroy the Mlecchas;
salutation to him, the soul of time, for the sake of establishing the Dharma. Salutation to him, the beginningless origin of the universe, the soul of the universe.
Salutations to that one whose nature is delusion, who deludes all beings through the bonds of affection and passion for the sake of protecting creation;
salutations to him who is eternal consciousness, ever-present in the hearts of all living creatures.

Salutations to that subtle Self, who is more transcendent than all else and subtler than the subtle. Salutations to that Knowledge-Self, whom the wise attain by knowing this knowledge of the Self which is established within the five [elements].

Salutations to that secret Self, whose true nature is not known even by the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, nor by the supreme ṛṣis who have reached their goals; salutations to him whose body is immeasurable and whose infinite vision extends everywhere.
Homage to Him, the inconceivable Self, who is boundless and immeasurable;
homage to Him whose essence is Brahman, who eternally bears matted hair and a staff, who possesses a protruding belly, and who carries a water-pot as his quiver.
Salutation to Vāsudeva, the joy of the Yadus, who was born of Vasudeva and Devakī, holding the conch, discus, and mace in his hands;
salutation to the great-souled Tryambaka, the lord of the thirty gods, who wields the trident.

Salutation to that Rudra-soul, whose upward-pointing *liṅga* is smeared with ashes; salutation to that Rudra-soul, who wears a garland of skulls on his head, is clothed in a tiger skin, and whose body is smeared with ashes.
Salutation to that fierce-souled one, whose head is adorned with the crescent moon, who wears a serpent as a sacred thread, and who holds the Pināka bow and the trident in his hands;
salutation to him who has become the self of the five elements, and who is the self of the origin and destruction of all beings.

Salutation to him who is free from anger, malice, and delusion, whose nature is peace; salutation to that Self of all, in whom is everything, from whom is everything, who is everything, who is everywhere,
and who eternally consists of everything.

O Viśvakarman, homage be to you, O Soul of the universe, source of the universe! You are the liberation of all beings, standing beyond the five elements. Homage to you in the three worlds; homage to you beyond the three worlds.
Salutations to you in all directions, for you are indeed the ultimate refuge of all. Salutations to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu, the source and the dissolution of the worlds;
for you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, are the unconquered creator and the destroyer.
"By that [vision], I behold your divine manifestations throughout the three paths;
and I behold in its true essence that eternal form of yours,
by which heaven is pervaded by your head and the goddess Earth by your feet."

By your prowess, you have [conquered] the three worlds; you are the eternal Puruṣa. The quarters are your arms, the sun is your eye, and Śukra and Prajāpati are your virility. The seven paths of the wind of immeasurable splendor have been obstructed by you.
O All-pervading Lord, everything that is unmanifest is pervaded by you in manifest form;
O All-pervading Lord, everything is pervaded by you in the nature of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
The unmanifest is the form of Brahman, while this world of moving and non-moving beings is the manifest.
Resembling the *atasī* flower and clad in yellow garments, you are the infallible one;
we measure your forms like a cloud accompanied by lightning. Homage to the one who creates a protective circle against the terrors of hell!

Salutations to Viṣṇu, who is like a raft for those tossed in the whirlpools of the river of *saṃsāra*; salutations to the God who is benevolent toward Brahman, and who brings welfare to cows and Brahmins;
repeated salutations to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, who brings welfare to the world.

The two syllables "Ha-ri" are provisions for the wilderness of living beings, a medicine that cuts through saṃsāra, and a protection against suffering and grief. Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa [is sufficient].
Equal to the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of ten horse-sacrifices,
one who performs ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth;
but one who bows to Kṛṣṇa does not return to existence.
Those who observe the black vow, remembering Kṛṣṇa at night, and who, having risen again, [meditate on] Kṛṣṇa,
they— possessing black bodies— enter into Kṛṣṇa.
Like clarified butter offered with mantras into the sacrificial fire,
[he is] Nārāyaṇa, the thousand-eyed one, honored by all the worlds,
whose navel is golden, who is the limb of sacrifice, the immortal one facing in every direction.
For those who pay homage to Govinda, no fear exists.
Just as all is truly composed of Viṣṇu, just as the sacrificial oblation is composed of Viṣṇu,
and just as everything is composed of Viṣṇu, so may my sin be destroyed.

Salutations again and again even to those who offer obeisance to that Viṣṇu, the Sacrificial Boar of immeasurable splendor. To me, your devotee who has sought refuge in you and desires to attain the cherished goal, [grant it].

"O lotus-eyed one, O best of gods, meditate upon that which is the highest good. Thus has Viṣṇu—the source of knowledge and austerity, yet himself without origin—been praised. May the god Janārdana, worshipped by this sacrifice of speech, be pleased with me.
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme austerity.
This entire universe has Nārāyaṇa as its highest goal and Nārāyaṇa as its very soul.
Having spoken these words, Bhīṣma’s mind became entirely absorbed in Him.
Then, with the words "Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa," he performed his salutation. Having perceived Bhīṣma’s devotion through his yogic power, Mādhava,
Hari, went there to bestow upon him divine knowledge that perceives the three periods of time.

By constantly praising Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the Overseer of the universe, one is liberated from all sins. This King of Hymns to Viṣṇu, whose deeds are wonderful, is now complete.
In ancient times, this [teaching] which destroys great sins was sung by the son of Gaṅgā.
When that sound had ceased, those exponents of the Veda,
their throats choked with tears, honored the high-minded Bhīṣma with words of praise.
Those foremost of Brahmins, offering praise to Keśava, the Supreme Person, all slowly and repeatedly extolled Bhīṣma as well. Then, having understood Bhīṣma’s yoga of devotion, Puruṣottama—
Suddenly rising up in great joy, he mounted his chariot;
Keśava and Sātyaki departed on one chariot,
while the two high-souled ones, Yudhiṣṭhira and Dhanañjaya, went on another.
Bhīmasena and both the twins (the Yamau) were mounted upon a single chariot;
Kṛpa, Yuyutsu, the Sūta, and Saṃjaya were on another chariot.
Those bulls among men set forth in their chariots, which resembled fortified cities.
Making the earth tremble with the great roar of their chariot wheels,
O best of men, he then heard on the road the auspicious words uttered by the twice-born, which were in harmony with you.
Then the slayer of Keśin, with a joyful mind, greeted another person who stood bowed with palms joined in reverence;
thus he recited, remembering the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
Whoever hears this hymn to the delighter of the Yadu clan,
that wielder of the discus, having all his sins destroyed,
enters Janārdana at the dissolution of the body.
At the time of the separation from life, that which yogins diligently fix within their minds—
he beholds Hari standing before him.
Having attained his goal, Bhīṣma indeed gave up his life-breaths.
This King of Hymns to Viṣṇu, the performer of wondrous deeds, is now complete;
it was sung of old by the son of Gaṅgā and is the destroyer of great sins.

12,047.072d*0099_11 A man desiring liberation, being pure, should recite this King of Hymns, which removes the stains of defilement; 12,047.072d*0099_12 having transcended the great worlds that have come together, [he shall attain the supreme state].
The foot of the Great-Souled One attains the immortal state.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Hṛṣīkeśa and King Yudhiṣṭhira—
Kṛpa and all the others, as well as the four Pāṇḍavas,
set out quickly for Kurukṣetra on chariots resembling cities, adorned with banners and flags, drawn by swift-moving horses.
Having descended upon Kurukṣetra, which was strewn with hair, marrow,
and bones— where those high-souled kṣatriyas had laid down their bodies— it was heaped up like mountains by the piles of the bodies and bones of elephants and horses.
It was strewn with human heads like conch shells,
covered by thousands of funeral pyres, and filled with armor and weapons,
appearing like the banquet ground of Time (Kāla) after he has finished his feast and abandoned it.
Beholding Kurukṣetra, which was frequented by hosts of spirits and inhabited by throngs of Rākṣasas, those great car-warriors proceeded swiftly.
Even as he went, the mighty-armed one, the delighter of all the Yādavas, [proceeded].
He spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira of the prowess of the son of Jamadagni:
"O Pārtha, those five lakes of Rāma are visible in the distance,
in which he gratified his ancestors with the blood of Kṣatriyas."
Having cleared the earth of the Kṣatriya caste twenty-one times,
the Lord Rāma then desisted from that task here on earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Yadu clan,
regarding what you have said— that the earth was cleared of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times by Rāma— and that the seed of the Kṣatriyas was burnt by Rāma, I have a great doubt in this matter."
O one of immeasurable prowess, how did the kṣatriyas arise again?
O bull among the Yadus, by the high-souled and blessed Rāma,
how was the kṣatriyas exterminated, and how did they attain growth once more?

"In the Mahābhārata war, indeed, kṣatriyas were slain by the millions; O best of speakers, the earth was likewise strewn with kṣatriyas. For what reason was this kṣatriya order destroyed in the past by the descendant of Bhṛgu?"
"O tiger among the Yadus, by the high-souled Rāma at Kurukṣetra—[this was told] by him.
Thus, O Vārṣṇeya, whose banner bears the emblem of Tārkṣya, sever this doubt of mine;
for our supreme authority, O Kṛṣṇa, younger brother of Vāsava, is indeed you."
12,048.015 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, while proceeding on his way, the lord, the elder brother of Gada,
related everything to him exactly as it was.
Then, to Yudhiṣṭhira of incomparable prowess, [he spoke];
at which time the earth became crowded with Kṣatriyas.
Vāsudeva said:
Listen, O son of Kuntī, to as much as I have heard regarding Rāma—
from the great sages as they recounted the cause of his birth and how,
by the son of Jamadagni, millions of Kṣatriyas were slain.
Those who were born in royal lineages and subsequently slain in Bhārata— Jahnu was the son of Ajahnu, and Ballava was his son;
the son of that righteous one was the lord of the earth named Kuśika.
He performed fierce austerities, equal on earth to the thousand-eyed Indra,
thinking, "May I obtain an unconquered son who shall be the lord of the three worlds. Seeing him engaged in such fierce penance, the thousand-eyed Purandara [approached].
O descendant of Bharata,
the Lord of the lords of the worlds himself came there, capable of procreating a son; O King,
he became his son, known by the name Gādhi, the Kauśika, who was like the subduer of Pāka (Indra).
O King, O Lord, he had a daughter named Satyavatī.
The lord Gādhi gave her to Ṛcīka, the son of Kavi.
Then, O Kaunteya, descendant of Kuru, the descendant of Bhṛgu was pleased.

For the sake of obtaining sons, he likewise cooked a sacrificial oblation (*caru*) for Gādhi. Then Ṛcīka, the descendant of Bhṛgu, summoned his wife and said to her: "This oblation is to be consumed by you, and this one by your mother."
To her shall be born a son, radiant, a bull among kṣatriyas,
unconquerable by the kṣatriyas of the world, and a slayer of the foremost of kṣatriyas.
O auspicious lady, you too shall have a son who is steadfast and endowed with ascetic power.
"O best of the twice-born, this sacrificial oblation (caru) shall produce one whose nature is tranquility," said the wise Ṛcīka,
the descendant of Bhṛgu, to his wife; having spoken thus,
he departed for the forest, intent upon ascetic penance.
At that very time, O King, King Gādhi, intent on a pilgrimage to sacred fords, arrived at the hermitage of Ṛcīka together with his wife. Then,
O King, Satyavatī took two portions of sacrificial charu.
Then, at her husband’s word, she joyfully and calmly informed her mother.
But her mother, O son of Kuntī, gave her own sacrificial oblation (*caru*) to her daughter;
and she, in turn, unknowingly placed that *caru* within herself.

Then Satyavatī conceived a fetus that was to be the ender of the Kṣatriyas; she bore it with a radiant body, and its appearance was formidable. Seeing her then, Ṛcīka indeed perceived [the truth] through the power of meditative concentration.

O tiger among kings, he said to his own wife of excellent complexion: "O blessed lady, you have been deceived by your mother through the exchange of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*). For a son of cruel deeds and great strength shall be born to you."
"For a brother shall be born to you, one who has become Brahman and whose wealth is asceticism;
for by means of my ascetic power, the entire universe has been entrusted there to Brahman,
and all the heroic vigor of the Kṣatriyas has been entrusted to your mother."
"O blessed lady, it shall not be so by way of reversal;
let your mother become a Brāhmaṇa and you yourself have a Kṣatriya son.
Thus was the highly fortunate Satyavatī addressed by her husband at that time.
She fell before him with her head bowed, trembling, and spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, you ought not today to speak such words as these,
that you shall obtain a son who is the lowest of Brahmins, O Great Sage."
12,049.022 Ṛcīka said:
"O blessed lady, this desire was not intended by me for you in that manner;
[if so], the son would have been of fierce deeds, and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) and the mother would have been the cause."
Satyavatī said:
"O sage, O best among those who recite prayers, if you so desired, you could create even the worlds; how much more so my own? May I obtain a son who is self-controlled and upright."
Ṛcīka said:
"O blessed lady, never before have I spoken a false word, even in jest;
how much less so now that I have kindled the fire for the preparation of the sacrificial oblation with the recitation of mantras?"
"O blessed lady, this was seen by me long ago and known through my ascetic power:
that your father's entire lineage shall indeed become one with Brahman.
Satyavatī said:
"O best among those who recite prayers, it may indeed be so that my grandson here shall be yours as well; however, may I obtain a son who is self-controlled and upright.
Ṛcīka said:
"O lady of excellent complexion, there is no distinction for me between a son and a grandson;
O blessed one, it shall be exactly as you have spoken.
Vāsudeva said:
Then Satyavatī gave birth to a son of Bhrigu’s lineage, Jamadagni, who was devoted to asceticism, tranquil, and composed in spirit. He,
in turn, begot a most formidable son of Jamadagni.
And Gādhi, the joy of the Kuśikas, obtained as his heir Viśvāmitra, who was equal to a Brahmarṣi and endowed with the universal Brahman. Ārcīka begot Jamadagni, who was most formidable.
He begot a son upon Jamadagni, that treasury of asceticism— a preeminent youth who had mastered all branches of knowledge and reached the further shore of the science of archery.
Having gratified Mahādeva on Mount Gandhamādana, Rāma— slayer of kṣatriyas and like a blazing fire—
chose as boons divine weapons and an axe of exceeding brilliance.
With that axe of unyielding edge, blazing with the luster of fire, and immeasurable, he became peerless among all beings in the worlds. At that very time, however, the powerful son of Kṛtavīrya—
The radiant Kṣatriya named Arjuna, of the Haihaya lineage,
was a king possessing a thousand arms through the grace of Dattātreya;
he was a wheel-turning monarch of great splendor for the Brahmins during the horse sacrifice.
He scorched the entire earth with its seven continents and its cities by the strength of his own arms and weapons in battle, through supreme righteousness; yet,
O Kauravya, he was begged for alms by the thirsty Citrabhānu.
The valiant and powerful Sahasrabāhu then gave alms to Agni;
the heroic one offered villages, cities, cowherd settlements, and towns.
And with his arrows, Citrabhānu blazed forth as if desiring to consume them.
By the power of that lord of men,
Kārtavīrya, that great ascetic burned the mountains and the forests.
He [then] saw that hermitage and forest of Varuṇa’s son was empty.
Fanned by the wind, Citrabhānu, together with his horses,
consumed [the forest]. Then, O Acyuta, Āpava, out of anger, cursed Arjuna when the hermitage had been burnt by Kārtavīrya, O Great King, though he himself was full of prowess.

"O Arjuna, because this forest of mine was burnt by you out of delusion, though it was not spared by you, therefore Rāma shall sever your arms in battle. But Arjuna, O great king, is powerful and always devoted to peace."

Devoted to Brahmins, a protector, a giver, and a hero, O Bhārata, he did not then consider the curse bestowed by that high-souled one. His sons, though exceedingly powerful, were [doomed] by the curse for the slaying of their father.
O bull of the Bharatas, those arrogant and ever-cruel men brought away the calf of Jamadagni’s cow without the knowledge of the wise Kārtavīrya, the lord of the Haihayas.
On account of that, a battle took place with the high-souled son of Jamadagni. Then, having severed the arms of Arjuna despite his great prowess,
the son of Jamadagni led the crying calf back to his own hermitage.

"O Indra among kings, let the lord bring them back from their inner apartments. But those sons of Arjuna, being unwise, then gathered together and went to the hermitage of the high-souled Jamadagni, who was unaware of their arrival.
O lord of men, with the tips of their broad-headed arrows, they struck off heads from bodies while the high-souled Rāma had gone out for the sake of sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass—
right before the eyes of Rāma’s mother and likewise those dwelling in the hermitage.
Having heard that matter, Rāma became enraged like the fire of cosmic destruction;
for he was indeed peerless in the science of archery and adorned with divine weapons,
the descendant of Bhṛgu took up his axe which resembled the crescent of the moon's orb.

Then, filled with supreme indignation due to the resentment over his father’s slaughter, Rāma vowed to rid the earth of the kṣatriyas and took up his weapon. Thereupon, that powerful tiger among the Bhṛgus [encountered] Kārtavīrya.

Displaying his prowess, he swiftly slew all the sons and grandsons on every side. Having killed thousands of Haihayas, O King, that descendant of Bhṛgu, filled with supreme wrath, turned the earth into a mire of blood.
Having thus rid the earth of the Kṣatriya caste, he who possessed such great splendor,
overcome by supreme compassion, departed for the forest.
Then, after some thousands of years had passed...

The lord Parāvasu, the grandson of Viśvāmitra and son of Raibhya, who was by nature prone to anger, became violently agitated, O great king; having been insulted in the assembly of people, that man of great asceticism spoke thus.

O Rāma, were not Pratardana and the others who were present and assembled at the sacrifice during Yayāti’s fall Kṣatriyas? O Rāma, you are false to your promise; you boast thus in the assembly of people.
Out of fear of the Kṣatriya heroes, he had taken refuge on a mountain. Then, hearing that the earth was once again covered with hundreds of Kṣatriyas, the descendant of Bhṛgu took up his weapon.
12,049.053 Then those hundreds of Kṣatriyas, O King, who had been restored to life by him, grew up with great prowess and became lords of the earth.
12,049.054 But he, O ruler of men, quickly slew them once again, even as children.
Then the earth once again became filled with those remaining in the womb;
as each child was born, he indeed slew it again. And at that time, he did not protect certain Kṣatriya women from their sons.
Having cleared the earth of the Kṣatriyas twenty-one times,
the Lord then gave it as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to Kaśyapa at the conclusion of the horse sacrifice;
Kaśyapa, however, designated it with his hand for the sake of preserving the remaining Kṣatriyas.
O King, holding the sacrificial ladle, the illustrious one then spoke these words:
"Go to the far shore of the southern ocean, O great sage;
you must never dwell here within my domain, O Rāma."
"By you, the earth was given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) in my horse-sacrifice (*vājimedha*).
Indeed, having already given this earth away, I am no longer the master to give it again.
Thereupon, the ocean created for him the region of Śūrpāraka.

Out of fear of the son of Jamadagni, he [Rāma] went to the western region of the earth; but Kaśyapa, O great king, having accepted this earth and established it under the governance of the Brāhmaṇas, entered the great forest.

Then, O bull of the Bharatas, Śūdras and Vaiśyas, acting according to their own will, began to consort with the wives of the foremost among the twice-born in that world of living beings devoid of a king; thus the weak were oppressed by those who were stronger.
They are oppressed, and no one here possesses mastery over wealth. Some Brahmins drink liquor; fools who consider themselves scholars;
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras all treading upon the wrong path.
Relying upon one another, those who stand on the wrong path cause destruction;
having abandoned their own duty (*svadharma*), the Brahmins have taken refuge in heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍa*),
and they all practice theft, falsehood, and deceit.
Having slain the twice-born who were established in their own duties as well as those dwelling in the hermitages,
and the Vaiśyas who remained on the path of truth, and even those Śūdras who were righteous—
they, being of evil conduct and utterly fearless, caused them all to be killed.

They destroy those who are devoted to sacrifice and study, the ascetics dwelling in hermitages, and even cowherds, the elderly, and women; furthermore, the sciences of logic, the three Vedas, commerce, and political ethics no longer function.

Indeed, many twice-born men have fallen into the state of *vrātyas*; through their inverted conduct, they have become *mlecchas* in every respect. Consequently, in the course of time, the earth entered the subterranean realm (*rasātala*).
Oppressed by the wicked,
they were swiftly brought to ruin through that perversion,
as they were not protected according to the law by Kṣatriyas who should guard the Dharma.
Seeing her flowing away there, that high-minded Kaśyapa was greatly agitated; he then supported the earth with his thigh,
O King, as she was sinking, and for that reason the earth is known as "Urvi."
Then the goddess Earth, having propitiated Kaśyapa, made this request on behalf of the protectors:
"O Brahmin, there are among men certain bulls among Kṣatriyas who have been protected by me."
"O sage, may those born in the lineage of the Haihayas protect me!
O Lord, there is a descendant of Paurava, the son of Viḍūratha,
O Brahmin, who was raised by bears on Mount Ṛkṣavat."
Thus, out of compassion, the sacrificer Parāśara, possessed of immeasurable splendor,
protected the heir of Saudāsa;
for he performed all the tasks for that ṛṣi like a śūdra.
Known as Sarvakarman, may that king protect me. The son of Śibi, possessed of great splendor and named Gopati by name,
who was protected by cows in the forest— may he protect me, O Sage.
The son of Pratardana was the highly illustrious Vatsa;
may that king, who was reared among calves in the cow-pen, protect me.
And the grandson of Dadhivāhana was the son of Diviratha.
That Aṅga was protected by Gautama on the banks of the Gaṅgā;
the mighty-armed Bṛhadratha, honored for his prosperity on earth,
was protected by the illustrious golāṅgūlas on Gṛdhrakūṭa.
In the lineage of Marutta, there were three Kṣatriyas descended from Turvasu;
equal to Marutpati in prowess, they were protected by the ocean. These heirs of the Kṣatriya line became renowned here and there.

May those who are constantly dependent upon the castes of smiths, goldsmiths, and others protect me properly; through them, I shall remain steadfast. And likewise, may their fathers and grandfathers [protect me].
"12,049.076c Those who were slain in battle for my sake by Rāma of unwearied deeds—12,049.077a I must certainly perform their funeral rites; of this there is no doubt.
12,049.077c For I do not desire constant protection from one who lacks valor."
"Let that be arranged quickly so that I may rule by means of one currently existing.
Then Kaśyapa, having summoned those Kṣatriyas renowned for their prowess whom the earth had designated, consecrated them as protectors of the earth.
Their sons and grandsons, whose lineages remain established— thus,
O Pāṇḍava, is this ancient account regarding that which you ask me.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Even as he was speaking thus,
that hero of the Yadus departed swiftly on his chariot toward Yudhiṣṭhira, the foremost of the upholders of dharma, like the sun.
Entering the three worlds with his splendors, the Blessed One [shone].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, having heard of that deed of Rāma...
Filled with supreme wonder, he replied to Janārdana:
"O Vārṣṇeya, oh, how great is the prowess of the high-souled Rāma, who, like Śakra himself,
has by his valor rid the earth of Kṣatriyas through his wrath!"
12,050.003a Protected by cows, by the ocean, and likewise by langurs, bears, and monkeys, 12,050.003c the upholders of the Kṣatriya lineages remained anxious with fear of Rāma.
12,050.004a "Oh, how blessed is this world! And how fortunate are the men upon the earth!"
"O Acyuta, since such a righteous deed has been performed by this twice-born man,"—
thus, O dear one, as Acyuta and Yudhiṣṭhira proceeded,
they went to where the lordly son of Gaṅgā lay upon his bed of arrows.
Then they beheld Bhīṣma lying upon a bed of arrows,
like the evening sun enveloped in its own web of rays, resembling a fire;
he was being attended by sages as Śatakratu is by the gods.
In that most righteous region along the river Oghavatī,
Kṛṣṇa, King Yudhiṣṭhira the Dharmarāja, the four Pāṇḍavas, and Śāradvata and the others beheld him from afar.
Then, leaping down from their mounts and restraining their restless minds,
they concentrated their faculties and approached the great sages.
Having offered their salutations, Govinda, Sātyaki, and those Kauravas stood before them.
Afterwards, those sages, Vyāsa and the others, approached the son of Gaṅgā.
Then, having inquired about the increase of his ascetic merit, all those bulls among men, the Yadus and Kauravas, sat down surrounding the son of Gaṅgā.
Then, perceiving the son of Gaṅgā to be like a fire being extinguished,
Keśava, with a somewhat dejected mind, spoke thus to Bhīṣma:
"O King, are your faculties as clear as they were before?"
"O best among speakers, is your intellect indeed unconfused?
Is your body not tormented by the pain of the arrow's impact?
For physical suffering is indeed more powerful than mental suffering."
