"O Lord, by the granting of a boon from your father Śantanu, who was of virtuous character, you possess the power of death at will; yet this is not a cause for peace. For even a very minute thorn in this body indeed produces pain."
How much more so, O Bhārata, for you who are covered by heaps of arrows?
Indeed, it need not be told to you that living beings have their origin and their passing;
for you, O Bhārata, would instruct even the gods in what is beneficial.
O bull among men, whatever has been, whatever will be, and whatever is now—
everything is placed as if in the palm of your hand, you who are mature in wisdom. So too are the cycle of existence for all beings and the arising of the fruits of dharma.
"O one of great wisdom, you are known to me; for you are a treasure composed of Brahman.

Indeed, though I see you established here in a prosperous kingdom, with all your limbs intact and free from disease, surrounded by thousands of women, yet you remain one whose vital energy is drawn upward."

O King, except for Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu— who is true to his promise, possessed of great heroism, a hero devoted solely to righteousness, and who lay upon a bed of arrows having forcibly stayed death— there is no one else in the three worlds [who could do so].
We have never heard from our father of anything that was innate or self-evident [in him],
whether in truth, austerity, charity, and the performance of sacrifice;
or in the science of archery, the Vedas, and constant supervision.

We have never heard of anyone like you— a great chariot-warrior who is compassionate, pure, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings. For you [could defeat] the gods along with the Gandharvas, as well as the Suras, Asuras, and Rākṣasas.

"O Bhīṣma, O mighty-armed one, you are capable of conquering [the enemy] with a single chariot alone; of this there is no doubt. For you, O Bhīṣma, are like Vāsava among the Vasus, and are always proclaimed by the Brahmins as the ninth [Vasu], yet not inferior in qualities."
"O best of men, I indeed recognize you,
who are renowned even among the thirty gods for your own great power;
O lord of men, such a person has never been seen nor heard of by me among human beings."
"O King, there is no man anywhere on earth who is your equal in virtues;
indeed, you surpass even the gods in all qualities. For by means of your ascetic power (*tapas*), you are capable of creating the worlds, both moving and unmoving."

How much more so for one who possesses worlds superior to his own through supreme virtues? Therefore, O Bhīṣma, dispel the grief of this eldest son of Pāṇḍu, who is now burning with sorrow due to the destruction of his kinsmen.
O Bhārata, for all those duties that have been proclaimed for the four social orders (cāturvarṇya) and are connected with the four stages of life (cāturāśramya), they are all known to you;
as well as those declared for the four Vedas and the four officiating priests (cāturhotra), O Bhārata.
The eternal duties prescribed in Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
and that single dharma which is not contradicted by the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya)— that primordial dharma, O Gāṅgeya, is already known to you.

You know the dharma-characteristics of those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), as well as that which is prescribed for the *mlecchas*, and you understand the dharma-characteristics of regions, castes,
and families; both that which is declared in the Vedas and that which is declared by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) is known to you.
Both the path of worldly engagement and the path of renunciation are known to you;
the Itihāsas and Purāṇas are known to you in their entirety,
and the entire Dharmaśāstra dwells eternally in your mind.
"O bull among men, there is no one else in this world besides you who can cut through those various matters that cause doubt in this world.
[He knows] that which has arisen in the mind of the son of Pāṇḍu;"
O Lord of Men, dispel this sorrow with your wisdom; for those like you, possessing the full extent of supreme intelligence,
exist for the sake of bringing peace to people who are bewildered.
12,051.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard the words of the wise Vāsudeva, Bhīṣma slightly raised his face and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words.
"Salutations to you, O Blessed Viṣṇu, the source of the origin and destruction of the worlds! For you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, are the unvanquished creator and the destroyer.
Salutations to you, O Architect of the Universe (Viśvakarman), the Soul of the Universe, and the Source of the Universe!"
You are the liberation of all beings, standing beyond the five elements.
Homage to you in the three worlds; homage to you beyond the three. O Lord of Yoga, let there be homage to you, for you are the supreme refuge of all.
"O best of men, because of those words you have spoken concerning me,
I behold your divine manifestations throughout the three paths;
and I see in their true essence that which is your eternal form."
The seven paths of the wind of immeasurable splendor have been blocked by you.
The heavens are pervaded by your head, and the goddess Earth by your feet. The quarters are your arms, the sun is your eye, and Śakra is established in your prowess.
Resembling the flax flower and clad in yellow garments, we perceive your imperishable form like a cloud accompanied by lightning. To me,
your devotee who has sought refuge in you and desires to attain the supreme goal, [grant that goal].
"O lotus-eyed one, O best of gods, meditate upon that which is the highest good.
Vāsudeva said:
"Since you indeed possess supreme devotion toward me, O bull among men..."

Then, O King, my divine form was revealed to you by me. For I do not reveal myself, O Indra among kings, to one who is not a devotee, nor to a devotee who is not upright, nor to one who is not self-controlled, O Bhārata.

But you, O Bhīṣma, are my devotee, always established in uprightness; you are pure and devoted to self-restraint, austerity, truth, and charity. By virtue of your own ascetic merit, O King, you are worthy to behold me.
For the worlds from which there is no return have been placed before you,
O hero of the Kurus; fifty-six days remain of your life.
Then, O Bhīṣma, having cast off the body, you shall attain [the realms] through the arising of the fruits of your auspicious deeds.
For these Vasu gods have their celestial chariots;
Having taken their positions, all of them, resembling blazing fires,
remain invisible while waiting for you as the sun approaches the northern quarter.
When the Blessed One has turned away, and the sun has reached the northern quarter by the power of time,
you shall go to the worlds, O hero among men.
O Bhīṣma, O hero, when you have departed, this world and all branches of knowledge will utterly perish once the wise man has passed away and returned no more.
Therefore, we have all come into your presence for the sake of discerning the dharma,
for you whose learning has been impaired by grief for your kinsmen.
Speak words consistent with dharma and purposeful meaning, joined with composure, to Yudhiṣṭhira who is devoted to truth; dispel his grief with these beneficial words.
12,052.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having heard those words of Kṛṣṇa— which were beneficial and consistent with dharma and artha— Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, replied with palms joined in reverence.
"O Lord of the World, O mighty-armed one, O Śiva, Nārāyaṇa, Acyuta!
Having heard your words, I am overwhelmed with joy.
And what more shall I say in your presence, O Master of Speech?"
When everything that has entered speech is concentrated within your own speech—
whatever has been done in the world, whatever is to be done, and whatever is currently being done—
all that has issued forth from you, O God, for the worlds are indeed composed of your intellect.
He who could describe the world of the gods in the presence of the king of the gods—
he would explain the meanings of the treatises on dharma, kama, and artha before you. My mind, O Madhusūdana, is distressed by the impact of these arrows.
My limbs are failing and my intellect is not clear;
I have no inspiration at all to speak anything,
O Govinda, as I am being tormented by arrows that are like poison and fire.

My strength fails and my intellect falters; my vital breaths hasten toward their end. My vital organs burn with pain, and likewise my mind is utterly bewildered. Because of this weakness, my speech falters; how then can I venture to speak?
"O delighter of the Daśārha clan, please be gracious toward me.
Forgive that, O mighty-armed one; I shall say nothing more, O Acyuta, for even Vācaspati himself would falter while speaking in your presence."
"I do not perceive the directions, nor the sky, nor the earth;
I stand here solely by your power, O Madhusūdana.
Therefore, O Lord, whatever is for the welfare of Dharmarāja, [do that] yourself."
Therefore, speak quickly, for you are the source of all scriptures. While you,
the eternal creator of the world, remain present, how could anyone like me speak [against you], as a disciple might when standing before his teacher?
Vāsudeva said:
"These words are fitting for the leader of the Kauravas,
who is possessed of great heroism and great being, and who stands as a seer of all purposes."
"O Gāṅgeya, as for what you have said to me regarding the pain from the wounds of the arrows—
accept here, O Bhīṣma, a boon granted by my grace, O Lord:
let there be no exhaustion for you, no fainting, no burning sensation, and no agony."
O son of Gaṅgā, hunger and thirst shall not prevail over you, nor indeed shall they arise;
O sinless one, all forms of knowledge shall manifest within you,
and no attachment whatsoever shall appear in your intellect.
O Bhīṣma, your mind will always abide in *sattva*,
free from *rajas* and *tamas*, like the lord of stars released from thick clouds.
Whatever is endowed with righteousness (*dharma*) or even with worldly purpose (*artha*), [you shall perceive it].

"O tiger among kings, as you reflect upon this, your intellect shall become preeminent; and by relying upon divine vision, O one of immeasurable prowess, you shall behold this fourfold host of beings."
"O Bhīṣma, endowed with the eye of knowledge, you shall see the fourfold net of creatures in their true nature, like a fish in clear water. Vaiśampāyana said:
Then all those great seers, together with Vyāsa, honored Kṛṣṇa with words joined with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. Thereupon,
a divine rain of flowers belonging to all seasons fell from the sky.
Where the descendant of Vṛṣṇi fell, along with the son of Gaṅgā and the Pāṇḍavas,
celestial musical instruments were sounded and throngs of Apsarases sang; nor was anything harmful or inauspicious seen there at all.
A pure, auspicious, and pleasant wind blew, carrying all fragrances;
and as the quarters became tranquil, the beasts and birds cried out in peace.
Then, after a moment, the blessed thousand-rayed sun appeared.
Like a forest fire burning in a secluded spot, he was seen approaching from the west.
Then all the great seers, having risen, addressed Janārdana,
Bhīṣma, and King Yudhiṣṭhira.
Then Keśava, the Pāṇḍava, Sātyaki, Sañjaya, and Kṛpa, the son of Śaradvat, performed their salutations. Then those devoted to righteousness were duly honored by them.
Having said, "We shall meet tomorrow," they departed quickly as they pleased.
Likewise, having taken leave of the son of Gaṅgā, Keśava and those Pāṇḍavas circumambulated him and ascended their splendid chariots.
Then [they set out] with chariots whose poles were tipped with gold, with rutting elephants resembling mountains,
and with horses swift as Garuḍas.
That army marched with its foot soldiers holding bows and other weapons in front of the chariots,
and likewise moved in great numbers behind them.
Just as the great river Narmadā, having reached Mount Rkṣavant, flows both before and behind it,
so too did the divine Moon appear in the east.
Having arisen, he gladdened that army,
just as the sun, having drained the sap from the medicinal herbs during the day, restores them again with its own very quality.
Then, having entered that city which possessed a splendor like the city of the gods,
those bulls of the Yadu clan and the Pāṇḍavas each entered their respective excellent palaces as was appropriate.
Like lions exhausted in caves, [the Pandavas lay down].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, having entered the palace, Madhusūdana fell fast asleep.
When only one watch of the night remained,
Mādhava awoke; having resorted to the path of meditation and surveyed all forms of knowledge, he thereafter meditated upon the eternal Brahman.
Then those learned in the Vedas and Purāṇas, well-trained and possessing melodious voices, praised Viśvakarman Vāsudeva, the Lord of Creatures;
likewise, those who clap their hands recited, and the singers sang.
Conch shells, lutes, and drums were sounded by the thousands;
and the exceedingly charming sound of lutes, small drums,
and flutes was heard from that palace like a vast, spreading laugh.
Likewise, for King Yudhiṣṭhira as well,
sweet words accompanied by auspicious rites and joined with song and instrumental music resounded aloud.
Then, having risen and bathed, Acyuta of the Daśārhas stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having recited the secret mantra twelve thousand and five times, the mighty-armed one took refuge in the sacred fires and remained there.
Then Mādhava caused a thousand Brahmins, each of whom was a knower of the four Vedas, to recite blessings, providing a thousand cows for each one.
Having performed the auspicious rites of touching and having looked at himself in a stainless mirror, Kṛṣṇa then spoke to Sātyaki:
"Go, O descendant of Śini; having gone to the royal residence, find out [the king's condition]."
"Is the highly energetic Yudhiṣṭhira ready to see Bhīṣma?
At these words of Kṛṣṇa, Sātyaki went in haste;
having approached King Yudhiṣṭhira, he spoke to him.
"O King, the excellent chariot of the wise Vāsudeva is yoked; Janārdana will proceed into the presence of the son of the River (Bhīṣma). O Dharmarāja of great splendor, that Kṛṣṇa awaits you."
"Whatever task must be done hereafter, you ought to perform it.
Thus addressed, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma, replied.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Phalguna of incomparable splendor, let my excellent chariot be yoked;
no soldiers shall go, for we alone shall go. And Bhishma, the best among the upholders of dharma, must not be harassed by me."
"Therefore, O Dhanañjaya, let even the attendants turn back.
From this day forward, the son of Gaṅgā will discourse on the supreme secret;
henceforth, O Kaunteya, I do not desire the presence of common folk."
12,053.017 Vaiśampāyana said: 12,053.017a Having heard those words, Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī,
O bull among men, pointed out to him a suitable and excellent chariot.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the twins, Bhīma, and Arjuna—
like all living beings together— went to the residence of Kṛṣṇa.
And as the high-souled Pāṇḍavas were arriving, Kṛṣṇa also [came forth].
Accompanied by the descendant of Śini, the wise one mounted his chariot. Standing upon their chariots, having consulted with one another and inquired after the comfort of the night,
those great car-warriors set forth on their excellent vehicles, which rumbled like the clouds.
Dāruka urged on Vāsudeva’s horses— Meghapuṣpa, Balāha, Sainya, and Sugrīva. Those horses of Vāsudeva were driven forward by Dāruka.
O King, then those mighty and impetuous warriors proceeded along, scratching the earth with the tips of their hooves as if devouring the sky;
they descended upon Kurukṣetra, the field of all righteousness.
Then they went to where the lord Bhīṣma lay upon his bed of arrows,
sitting together with the celestial rishis like Brahmā among the hosts of gods.
Then Govinda and Yudhiṣṭhira descended from their chariot.
Bhīma, the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, the twins,
and Sātyaki likewise honored the sages by raising their right hands;
surrounded by them, the king shone like the moon amidst the stars.
Like Vāsava approaching Brahmā, he approached the son of Gaṅgā;
that mighty-armed one beheld him lying upon a bed of arrows like the fallen sun, his own courage overcome by fear.
Janamejaya said: O virtuous-souled one, O being of great essence, O you who are true to your promise, O self-conquered one— O illustrious Devavrata, O infallible one, now lying upon a bed of arrows!
While Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu and Ganga, that tiger among men, lay upon his hero’s bed attended by the Pāṇḍavas,
what conversations took place in that assembly of heroes?
"Tell me that, O great sage, when all the armies have been slain.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"When Bhīṣma, the bearer of the burden of the Kauravas, had fallen upon the bed of arrows..."
O King, the perfected seers led by Nārada arrived,
as did the surviving kings headed by Yudhiṣṭhira,
along with Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Kṛṣṇa, Bhīma, Arjuna, and the twins.

Having approached the grandfather of the Bharatas, those high-souled ones lamented for Gāṅgeya as if for the sun fallen from the sky. After reflecting for a moment, Nārada, who possesses divine vision, spoke.
He spoke to all the Pāṇḍavas and the kings who remained after the slaughter:
"I declare that the time has come; let this Bhīṣma be questioned, for the son of Gaṅgā is setting like the sun, O Bhārata."
"12,054.009a This man is about to cast off his life-breaths; all of you, approach him and question him.
12,054.009c For he knows all the various duties of the four social orders (cāturvarṇya). 12,054.010a This aged man shall before long attain the worlds of those who have cast off their bodies."
"Quickly interrogate him regarding the doubts residing in your minds.
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, the lords of men approached Bhīṣma;
yet, being unable to question him, they looked at one another.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu, said to Hṛṣīkeśa:
"O son of Devakī, no one other than you is capable of questioning the Grandfather.
O invincible Madhusūdana, do you speak first."
"For you, O dear one, are the best among us all in the knowledge of all dharmas.
Thus addressed by the Pāṇḍava, the blessed Keśava,
the infallible Acyuta, then approached the invincible [Arjuna] and spoke.
Vāsudeva said:
"O best of kings, has the night passed for you in comfort?
Has your intellect, with its characteristics made clear, become fully present?"
"O sinless one, do all branches of knowledge appear clearly to you? Is your heart not weary, and is your mind not agitated?
Bhīṣma said:
"O sinless Govinda, by your grace, burning, delusion, exhaustion, fatigue, languor, and pain have all immediately vanished.
And as for that which has been, that which is to be, and that which is now present, O You of supreme splendor— "
I perceive all that as clearly as a fruit held in the palm of my hand. O Acyuta, by virtue of your boon, I behold all those duties declared in the Vedas and those established in the Vedāntas.

Whatever dharma has been proclaimed by the learned remains in my heart; O Janārdana, I am a knower of the dharma pertaining to countries, castes, and families. Furthermore, whatever purpose resides within the duties of the four stages of life (āśramas) is likewise established in my heart.
"O Keśava, I understand all the duties of kings;
indeed, whatever is the essential meaning among all dharmas, that is established in my heart.
And wherever it ought to be spoken, O Janārdana, that I shall speak."
"Indeed, through your grace, O Śubhā, my mind and intellect have entered [into wisdom]. Strengthened by your meditation, I have become like a youth once more;
through your favor, O Janārdana, I am now capable of speaking what is beneficial."
"Why did you yourself not speak of what is beneficial for the Pāṇḍava?
What is it that you wish to say in this matter? Tell me that quickly, O Mādhava.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Kaurava, know me to be the root of both fame and the highest good. From me all states of being, consisting of both the existent and the non-existent, have come forth.
When one says 'the cool-rayed moon,' who in this world would be surprised?"
"In the same way, who would be surprised that I am filled with glory?
Yet, O one of great splendor, I must further bestow glory upon you;
therefore, O Bhīṣma, my vast intellect is fully concentrated upon you."
"O protector of the earth, as long as this firm earth shall endure,
so long will your imperishable fame circulate through the worlds.
And whatever you shall speak, O Bhīṣma, to the inquiring son of Pāṇḍu,"
"Like the proclamations of the Vedas, they shall endure upon the surface of the earth.
And whoever, by means of this authority, shall unite himself with the Self,
he shall experience the fruit of all meritorious deeds after death."
"For this reason, O Bhīṣma, divine intelligence has been granted by me to you,
so that your fame might spread even further.
For as long as a man's fame spreads upon the earth in this world,"
It is certain that his station shall remain inexhaustible for that long.
O King, the kings who survived the slaughter sit around you;
desiring to inquire about the duties of righteousness, speak to them, O Bhārata.

For you are advanced in age and endowed with learning and proper conduct; you are skilled in the duties of kings, both those of the ancients and those of later times. Indeed, from the time of your birth, no one has ever seen any transgression in you.
All the kings know you to be a knower of the dharmas; O King, speak of the supreme policy to them as a father speaks to his sons. For both the ṛṣis and the gods have been constantly attended by you.

"Therefore, you must certainly speak here; I see that you should explain the dharmas in their entirety to those who wish to hear them. For the wise have declared it a duty that a learned person, when questioned, must speak."
O Lord, for one who does not respond, there is indeed a grievous fault.
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, being learned and being asked about the eternal duties by your sons and grandsons who desire to know them, you should speak.
12,055.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then the highly effulgent delighter of the Kurus spoke these words:
"Indeed, since my speech and mind are steady, I shall proclaim the duties (dharmas)."
"By your grace, O Govinda, you are indeed the eternal Self of all beings.
Let King Yudhiṣṭhira, however, question me regarding the duties of righteousness;
in this way, O sinless one, I shall be pleased and I will speak of those duties."
When that bull among kings, the high-souled and righteous one, was born,
all the sages rejoiced; let that Pāṇḍava question me—
he who is the foremost of all the Kuru practitioners of dharma, renowned for their splendor.
"Let that Pāṇḍava who has no equal ask me;
let that Pāṇḍava in whom there is always steadfastness, self-control, celibacy, forbearance, and righteousness, as well as vigor and splendor, ask me."
Truth, charity, austerity, purity, tranquility, skillfulness, and composure—
in whomsoever all these qualities reside, let that son of Pāṇḍu question me.
He who does not act out of desire, nor out of anger, nor out of fear, nor for the sake of material gain;
May that son of Pāṇḍu, who is righteous-souled yet might perform unrighteousness, question me;
may that son of Pāṇḍu question me who honors his kinsmen, guests, servants, dependents, and those seeking refuge by treating them with hospitality.
"Let that Pāṇḍava question me, who is constant in truth, constant in forgiveness, constant in knowledge, and fond of guests; who constantly gives to the virtuous,
and who is ever devoted to sacrifice, study, and righteousness."
"Peaceful and having heard the secret doctrine, let that son of Pāṇḍu question me.
Vāsudeva said:
"That righteous-souled Yudhiṣṭhira is possessed by great shame."
Fearing the dread of a curse, O lord of the people, he does not approach you; having caused the destruction of the world, the Lord of the World,
fearing the dread of a curse, does not approach you.

"Having slain with his arrows those who are worthy of worship, those deserving of honor, those devoted to him, his gurus, kinsmen, and relatives— all those entitled to the guest-offering— he does not approach you.
Bhīṣma said:
O Kṛṣṇa, just as the duty of Brāhmaṇas consists of charity, study, and austerity,
so too for Kṣatriyas is the casting down of the body in battle.
[One should not slay] fathers, grandfathers, sons, teachers, relatives, or kinsmen.
He who slays in battle those who act with deceit— that is indeed righteousness.
O Keśava, that Kṣatriya who slays in combat wicked men who have abandoned their agreements and are greedy, even if they be his own gurus, is a knower of dharma.

He who, out of greed, does not regard the eternal bridge of dharma— he who slays him in battle is indeed a Kṣatriya who knows the law. [Such a one crosses] the river whose waters are blood, whose grass is hair, whose mountains are elephants, and whose trees are banners.
That Kṣatriya who makes the earth [his] in battles is a knower of dharma. When summoned to battle, a scion of the warrior class must always fight;
for Manu has declared that war is righteous, leads to heaven, and secures the world.
12,055.018 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having been thus addressed by Bhīṣma, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
approached him with humility and stood before him in his presence.
Then Bhīṣma grasped his feet and greeted him with joy;
having smelled the crown of his head, he then said to him, "Be seated.
Then the son of Gaṅgā, the bull among all archers, spoke to him.
"Ask me, my dear, with confidence; do not fear, O best of the Kurus.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having prostrated before Hṛṣīkeśa and having saluted his grandfather, [he spoke].
Having paid homage to all his elders, Yudhiṣṭhira questioned them:
"Those who know the Dharma declare that sovereignty is indeed the supreme duty;
yet I consider this a great burden—speak on this, O King."
"O Grandfather, tell me specifically about the duties of kings;
for the duties of kings are the ultimate refuge for the entire world of living beings. O Kaurava, the three goals of life are fully contained within these royal duties."
The entire doctrine of liberation (mokṣadharma) is clearly set forth here in its entirety.
Just as reins are for a horse and a goad is for an elephant,
so the dharma of kings is traditionally held to be the means of restraint for the world.
If this dharma practiced by royal seers were indeed to become utterly confused,
there would be no stability for the world and everything would fall into disorder;
for just as the rising sun destroys the darkness of the asuras.

"O Grandfather, the duties of kings likewise cast one into an inauspicious state after death. Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, you who are the foremost among the wise, first explain the true essence of the duties of kings."
"And for all of us, O scorcher of foes, you are the supreme authority;
indeed, Vāsudeva regards you as the highest in wisdom.
Bhīṣma said:
Salutations to the Great Dharma; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Creator. Having paid homage to the Brahmins, I shall declare the eternal duties.
Listen to me fully, O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding the duties of kings.
O best of the Kurus, whatever else you desire to hear as it is being explained, [know that] at the very outset, out of a desire to please the king,
it was ordained that one must behave toward the gods and the twice-born according to the prescribed rules.
O best of the Kurus, by indeed honoring the deities and the Brahmins,
one attains freedom from debt toward dharma and is held in high esteem by the world.
O son Yudhiṣṭhira, you should always exert yourself in rising early.
For without exertion, destiny alone does not bring about the success of kings' aims.
Indeed, these two—destiny and exertion—are common to all;
yet I consider human effort to be superior, while destiny is said to be merely that which is determined by fate.
And when an undertaking has failed, do not indeed give way to grief;
for discipline, my dear, is what prevails—this is the supreme policy for kings.
For there is no cause for the success of kings other than truth.
For a king devoted to truth rejoices both in this world and after death. O Indra among kings, even for the sages, truth alone is the supreme wealth;
likewise, for a king, there is no cause for inspiring confidence greater than truth.

One who is virtuous, possessed of good character, self-controlled, gentle, righteous, and has conquered his senses; one who is pleasant to behold and liberal in his aims—such a person shall never fall away from prosperity.
O joy of the Kurus, you should resort to uprightness in all your undertakings.
Endowed with straightforwardness, the sages rejoice in heaven;
likewise through discernment of policy and the preservation of the triple Veda.
For a king who is always mild is disregarded by everyone in every respect.
The world trembles before severity; therefore, practice both.
O best of givers, the Brahmins must always remain exempt from punishment for you;
for the Brahmins, O Bhārata, are a supreme being in this world.
O Indra among kings, two verses were also sung by the high-souled Manu;
O Kauravya, you ought to keep them in your heart regarding your own duties:
"Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone."
Their all-pervading energy is extinguished within their own sources:
when iron strikes stone, and fire encounters water; likewise, when a Kṣatriya hates a Brāhmaṇa, those three perish.
Knowing this, O Great King, those twice-born ones are indeed worthy of your reverence;
for the best of the twice-born, endowed with tranquility, uphold the Veda that dwells upon the earth.
And thus it is, O tiger among men, that they do not cause obstruction to the course of the world.
"Those who are such as these should always be restrained by the strength of one's arms.
O King, O highly wise one, listen with a focused mind to these two verses sung in the past by the great seer Uśanas."
Even if one who has mastered the Vedanta approaches in battle with weapon raised, a lord of men who regards righteousness should restrain him according to his own duty;
for he who protects righteousness when it is perishing is a knower of dharma.
By that act, he does not become a slayer of an embryo; rather, it is his wrath that reaches the offender.
In this very manner, O best of men, the twice-born must indeed be protected; even when they have committed an offense, one should banish them to the borders of the realm.
O Lord of the People, one should indeed show compassion even toward those who have been accused of these crimes:
the killing of a Brahmin, violating the teacher’s bed, and likewise the destruction of an embryo;
as well as for a Brahmin who has acted against the king, his banishment should take place at the edge of the realm.
Shaving, the taking of wealth, and the departure from their own city are ordained for them;
never do they experience physical danger. And those men, O best of men, shall always be beloved by them.
For there is no treasury superior to a collection of men for kings; and regarding the six types of fortresses determined by the treatises, O Great King,
they consider the human fortress to be the most difficult to overcome among them all.
Therefore, a wise man should always exercise compassion toward the four social orders. A king who is righteous in soul and truthful in speech delights his subjects.
Yet, O best of men, you must not be constantly forgiving.
"For a king who is mild is unrighteous, like an elephant that is merely patient.
And in the treatise of Bṛhaspati, verses were indeed established in ancient times regarding this matter;
O Great King, listen as I recite them to you."
A base person will constantly seek to humiliate a king who is ever-forgiving,
just as an elephant-driver seeks to mount the very head of the elephant.
Therefore, a king should never be exclusively mild, nor should he be exclusively harsh.
Like the glorious sun in spring, he was neither cold nor heat-giving.
O Great King, you should always examine both your own people and those of others through direct perception, inference, comparison, and authoritative instruction.
O giver of profuse sacrificial fees, you should abandon all vices; yet, while not failing to apply yourself to your duties, you must utterly avoid attachment.
For one who is constantly addicted to vice is indeed held in contempt in this world.
A king who is excessively hateful causes the world to tremble.
A king must always behave in the same manner as a pregnant woman;
hear now, O Great King, the reason why this is desired.

"Just as a pregnant woman, setting aside her own dear and cherished desires, secures the welfare of the fetus, so too, O best of the Kurus, must a king who constantly follows righteousness act without doubt."

O Pāṇḍava, you must never abandon your fortitude, even at the cost of sacrificing what is dear to yourself; for the command of one who is steadfast and whose punishment is clear is never thwarted. Furthermore, whatever may be for the welfare of the world, that is what you should pursue. You must not ever forsake your resolve.

"O best among speakers, O tiger among kings, you should not constantly engage in jesting with your servants; hear from me the fault in this. For, out of excessive familiarity, dependents come to despise their master."

They do not remain in their own place, for they indeed transgress his word; when sent on errands, they hesitate, and they pry into secrets. They beg for what should not be asked for, and they consume what should not be eaten.
They become enraged, they flare up in anger, and they sit upon his very land;
by means of bribes and deceptions, they subvert his affairs and bring his realm to ruin through counterfeit measures.
Women gaze at him with their eyes and assume his same attire;
in his presence, O tiger among men, they spit and blow wind, and being shameless, they speak such words.
When a king is joyous and mild, people mount horses, elephants, or even chariots esteemed by monarchs without showing him due respect.
O King, this is difficult for you; this is a difficult feat for you.
Thus do those present in the assembly address him as "friend";
yet when he is angry, they merely laugh, and they feel no joy even when honored. Furthermore, they are always prone to rivalry with one another for various reasons.
They disregard his counsel, reveal his misdeeds,
and treat his commands with contempt as if they were mere playthings.
They likewise show disdain for his ornaments, food, baths, and ointments.
O tiger among men, O Bhārata, they listen to him with derision while remaining at ease; they revile their own offices and abandon them,
and they are not satisfied with their livelihoods, even taking what is due to the king.
They desire to sport with him as if with a bird bound by a string; moreover, people in the world say, "The king is led by us.
Thus, these and other faults indeed manifest.
"When King Yudhiṣṭhira was endowed with gentleness and cheerfulness," Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, a king must indeed be ever-vigilant."
For a king who is devoid of effort becomes like a woman and is brought to ruin.
O lord of the people, the venerable Uśanas has spoken a verse on this matter; O King, listen with an undivided mind as I recite it to you.
The earth swallows these two, just as a snake swallows creatures dwelling in holes:
a king who does not oppose [his enemies] and a Brahmin who does not travel abroad.
Therefore, O tiger among men, you ought to take this to heart.
Make peace with those with whom it should be made, and oppose those who should be opposed. Furthermore,
regarding the seven constituent parts of your kingdom— sovereign, minister, ally, treasury, realm, fort, and army— whoever should act with hostility toward them, [you must deal with him].

Whether it be a teacher or even a friend, he must indeed be struck down. For this ancient verse was sung long ago by King Marutta regarding the exercise of royal authority, O Indra among kings, according to the doctrine of Bṛhaspati.
"Even a guru, if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path— his abandonment is ordained.
This was done here by the wise King Sagara, the son of Bāhu."
Asamañja was the eldest son, yet he was abandoned by the king who sought the welfare of the citizens.
O King, Asamañja had previously been casting the children of the citizens into the Sarayū;
therefore, having been rebuked by his father, he was exiled.

Even the great ascetic Śvetaketu was abandoned by the sage Uddālaka as his beloved son for having behaved falsely toward the brahmins. In this world, the eternal duty of kings is solely the pleasing of the people.

The protection of truth and straightforwardness in legal proceedings; not seizing the wealth of others, and giving or causing what is due to be given at the proper time— a king who is valiant, truthful in speech, and patient does not deviate from the path.
One whose mantras are guarded, who has conquered anger, who has reached certainty regarding the meaning of the scriptures,
and who is constantly devoted to dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—
such a king, with his vulnerabilities covered by the three Vedas, is worthy to rule.
For kings who act with wickedness, there is nothing more [sinful] than concealment [of their faults]. The duties of the four castes must be protected by the ruler of the earth;
for the protection against the confusion of dharma is the eternal duty of kings.

A king should not place his trust [in anyone], nor should he place excessive trust; he must constantly examine the merits and defects of the six measures of policy with his intellect. A king who perceives the vulnerabilities of his enemies is always praised.
He who understands the meaning of the three-fold group of aims, who employs spies and stratagems, who delights in the accumulation of the treasury, who resembles Yama and Vaiśravaṇa,
and who knows the ten-fold group characterized by its stability, increase, and decline.
The king should be the supporter of those who are not supported and the overseer of those who are supported; he should be pleasant-faced and speak with a smile;
he should attend upon the elders, conquer sloth, and be free from greed.
With his mind established in the conduct of the virtuous— for the virtuous indeed observe proper behavior—
he should never take wealth from the hands of the virtuous; rather,
he should take it from the wicked and bestow it upon the virtuous.
He himself is a striker and a giver, self-controlled and a master of the means of subduing others;
he is a giver at the proper time and an enjoyer, as well as one of pure conduct. [He should employ] those who are brave, devoted, incorruptible, born of noble lineage, and free from disease.
[He saw] those remaining who were associated with the learned, who were self-respecting and not contemptuous; who possessed knowledge, knew the world, and looked toward the next world;
who were virtuous, devoted to their duties, and as immovable as mountains.

A king who places prosperity foremost should always appoint companions; he should be equal to them in enjoyments, being superior only by his royal umbrella and his command. His conduct toward them should always be both manifest and behind their backs.
By acting in this way, the lord of men indeed incurs no weariness here.
But that king who suspects everyone and who seizes everything from all is quickly overcome by his own people— being crooked and greedy as he is.

But the pure protector of the earth, devoted to winning the hearts of the people, does not fall when seized by enemies, and having fallen, he recovers his standing. He is free from anger, devoid of vices, mild in punishment, and has conquered his senses.

He becomes a king of all beings, as trustworthy as the Himalayas— wise, endowed with the qualities of justice, intent upon the vulnerabilities of his enemies, pleasing to behold for all social orders, and likewise a knower of right and wrong policy.
He acts with promptness, has conquered anger, is gracious, and high-minded; he is healthy by nature, disciplined, active, and free from boastfulness;
his undertakings are indeed brought to completion and never left unfinished.

That king in whose realm men roam about without fear, like sons in their father's house, is the best of kings. That king is the best of monarchs whose citizens and rural subjects do not conceal their wealth and who understand both right policy and its opposite;
he is the one whose people dwelling in his realm are devoted to their own respective duties.

He is a king in whose realm men delight not in social cliques, are self-controlled, protected according to the law, obedient, tractable, disciplined, and free from contentiousness; and who take pleasure in giving charity.
In that realm of the protector of the earth where there is no fraud, no deceit, no illusion, and no envy, there exists the eternal Dharma;
he who honors the sciences, who is guided by wisdom, and is devoted to the welfare of his citizens.
That king who follows the dharma of the virtuous and is generous deserves the kingdom; that king whose spies and secret counsels, regarding both what has been done and what remains to be done,
are never known by his enemies, deserves the kingdom.
O Bhārata, this verse was formerly sung by the high-souled Bhārgava in the narrative of Rāma’s life concerning the king:
"One should first seek a king, then a wife, and then wealth."
12,057.041c If there were no king, from where would the people have wives? From where would they have wealth?
12,057.042a Therefore, O King, for those lions among kings, there is no other eternal duty 12,057.042c than clearly manifest protection; protection is the very sustenance of the world.
These two verses were also cited by Manu, the son of Pracetas, regarding the duties of kings, O Indra among kings; listen to them here with a focused mind:
"A man should abandon these six, just as one would a leaking boat in the ocean."
One should avoid a teacher who does not instruct, a priest who has not studied the Vedas, a king who does not provide protection, a wife who speaks unpleasantly,
a cowherd who desires to live in a village, and a barber who desires to live in the forest.
Having spoken thus, the wise Bhīṣma, the grandfather of the Kurus, spoke once more,
words that contained the essential essence of everything.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the very cream of the duties of kings;
for the blessed Bṛhaspati praises no other duty."
The blessed Viśālākṣa, and Kāvya of great asceticism,
the thousand-eyed Mahendra, as well as Manu Prācetasa,
the blessed Bharadvāja, and the sage Gauraśiras.
O best among the upholders of dharma, those who compose treatises on royal polity— those devoted to Brahman and exponents of the Veda— praise protection alone as dharma.
O king with copper-hued lotus-eyes, hear now the means for this.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, [these are]: conduct and resolve, giving at the proper time without stinginess, taking what is appropriate through right means and not taking through improper means,
the gathering of the virtuous, heroism, skillfulness, truthfulness, and the welfare of the subjects.
The sowing of dissension within the enemy's faction through both dishonest and honest means;
the non-abandonment of the virtuous and the support of those of noble birth; the accumulation of things that ought to be stored; and service even to the wise.

Constantly gladdening the army, looking after the subjects, lack of weariness in affairs of state, as well as the increase of the treasury; guarding the city, maintaining distrust [of enemies], and preventing dissension among the assembly of citizens.
The inspection of dilapidated monuments and the care of those in distress;
the timely application of the two kinds of punishment; and the proper observation of enemies, neutrals, and allies.
Sowing dissension among one's own servants by observing those of others; maintaining distrust toward oneself while likewise inspiring confidence in the enemy;
constant adherence to the principles of policy and righteousness; and perpetual industriousness.
"Never showing contempt for enemies and always avoiding the ignoble— this,
Bṛhaspati declared, is the exertion of kings. Learn from me these verses concerning that which is the root of the duty of kings."
Through exertion, the nectar was obtained; through exertion, the Asuras were slain. Through exertion, Mahendra attained preeminence both in heaven and here on earth.
A man who is steadfast in exertion stands above those who are merely steadfast in speech.

Those wise in speech delight in attending upon one who is steadfast in exertion. For a king who lacks exertion, even if he be possessed of intelligence, will be constantly vulnerable to his enemies, like a snake deprived of its venom.
An enemy must not be disregarded, even if he is weak, by one who is stronger;
for even a small fire burns, and even a small amount of poison kills.
An enemy, though joined with only a single horse, becomes formidable when taking refuge in a fortress.
It torments every region, even that of a prosperous king.
Whatever secret counsel a king may speak for the sake of victory and the governance of the world, and whatever crookedness may lie in his heart for the sake of some purpose— [all this is revealed].

Whatever wrongful task he may have, he should maintain it through integrity alone; for the sake of deceiving the world, he should perform righteous deeds. For kingship is a very great system, difficult to be maintained by those who have not disciplined their souls.
This supreme position of authority cannot be borne by one who is mild;
sovereignty, which is a constant source of alluring temptations, is maintained here through straightforwardness.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you must always conduct yourself with a mixture of both qualities.

"Even if there should be misfortune for him while he is protecting his subjects, that too is a great merit for him; for such is the conduct of the protectors of the earth. Thus has this brief summary of the duties of kings been described to you."
"O best of speakers, tell me further that in which you have doubt.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Then the venerable Vyāsa and Devasthāna, together with Aśman,"
Vāsudeva, Kṛpa, Sātyaki, and Sañjaya likewise, with faces blooming as if in great joy, cried out, "Excellent! Excellent!
and praised Bhīṣma, that tiger among men and best of the upholders of dharma.
Then, with a dejected mind, that best of the Kurus spoke to Bhīṣma,
his eyes filled with tears, slowly touching his feet:
"O Grandfather, tomorrow I shall ask you about my own doubt."
The sun also sets after having drunk up the terrestrial moisture.
Then Keśava, Kṛpa, and those others, Yudhiṣṭhira and the rest, paid their respects to the twice-born.
Having circumambulated the son of the great river,
they then ascended their chariots with joy;
and having plunged into the Dṛṣadvatī, those of virtuous vows—
Having performed their water-libations and completed their prayers and auspicious rites,
those subduers of enemies, having worshipped at the twilight hour according to the rules, then entered the city named after the elephant.
12,059.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
12,059.001a Then, having risen at dawn and performed their morning rites,
those Pāṇḍavas and Yādavas set out on chariots that resembled cities.
Having reached Kurukṣetra and approached the sinless Bhīṣma,
and having inquired after the welfare of Gāṅgeya, the best of chariot-warriors, during that pleasant night,
they saluted Vyāsa and the other ṛṣis, being greeted by them all in return.
They sat down on all sides, surrounding Bhīṣma completely.
Then the king of great splendor, Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma,
having honored and saluted Bhīṣma with palms joined in reverence, spoke to him.
"O Bhārata, this sound 'king, king' that circulates—
tell me, O Grandfather, how did it originate?
For [all beings] have equal hands, heads, and necks, and are identical in their intellect, senses, and self."
He is one whose nature is equal in suffering and happiness, with a back, arms, and belly of equal measure;
he has equal semen, bone, and marrow, as well as equal flesh and blood;
his inhalations and exhalations are equal, and he possesses a life-force and body that are identical.
Sharing the same birth and death as all men, and equal to them in all qualities,
how does he alone preside over those who possess distinguished intellects and are heroic?
How does he alone [rule] the entire earth, which is crowded with heroes, warriors, and noble men?
The world protects him and desires his favor;
by the favor of one, the entire world becomes gracious. It is certain that when he is agitated, everyone becomes agitated.
"O bull among the Bharatas, I desire to hear all of this in its true essence;
O best of speakers, tell it to me exactly as it is. For this cause, O lord of the people, cannot be a trivial one."
12,059.012c Since the entire world bows down before him like a god, 12,059.013 Bhīṣma said:
12,059.013a "O best of men, you are self-restrained; listen to everything in its entirety."
Just as sovereignty first arose in the Kṛta age:
there was neither kingdom nor king, neither punishment nor one who inflicts it;
by dharma alone all subjects protected one another.

O Bhārata, while men were thus protecting one another according to dharma, they fell into extreme exhaustion; consequently, delusion (moha) entered them. O bull among men, those human beings, having fallen under the power of delusion, [became negligent].
And because of their delusion regarding right practice, the Dharma perished for them. But when right practice was lost, those men, then subject to delusion,
O best of the Bharatas, all fell under the sway of greed.
Then, O Lord, as men began to touch her though she was unattainable, another passion named *kāma* (desire) arose there;
and when they had fallen under the power of desire, that which is called *rāga* (attachment) touched them.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who were intoxicated did not distinguish between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; likewise, O Indra among kings, they failed to avoid approaching women who should not be approached, speaking what should not be spoken, eating what should not be eaten, or committing what was a fault and what was not.
When this world of men had become utterly corrupted, the Veda (brahman) was then lost;
and because the Veda was lost, O King, Dharma likewise met its destruction. When both the Veda and Dharma were lost, the gods then fell into terror.
Terrified, O tiger among men, they went to Brahmā for refuge;
having approached the Blessed One, the Grandfather of the worlds,
all those gods, afflicted by pain, grief, and fear, spoke with palms joined in reverence.
"O Blessed One, the eternal Brahman residing in the world of men has been lost;
because of states such as greed and delusion, fear has entered us.
And with the destruction of Brahman, O Lord, Dharma too has perished."
Then, O Lord of the Three Worlds, we attained equality with mortals;
for our rain falls downward, whereas mortals rain upward. Because of the cessation of their ritual activities, we then fell into a state of uncertainty.
"O Grandfather, contemplate that which is our ultimate good; for this power of ours, arising from your own majesty, is now perishing. Then the Blessed Self-born One spoke to all those gods.

"I shall contemplate what is most beneficial; let your fear depart, O bulls among the gods. Then, by means of his own intellect, he composed a hundred thousand chapters in which dharma, as well as artha and kāma, were fully described.
This group is proclaimed by the Self-born as the "Triad" (trivarga);

liberation (mokṣa) is the fourth, having its own distinct purpose and being a distinct group. Furthermore, another triad pertaining to liberation is declared: goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).
Position, increase, and decrease, as well as the threefold set born of punishment;
self, place, time, means, and the task itself;
allies, and the cause—this is known as the sixfold group arising from statecraft (*nīti*).
O bull among the Bharatas, the three Vedas, metaphysics, economics,
and the extensive science of government (daṇḍanīti) are demonstrated therein; as well as the protection of ministers, secret missions, and the safeguarding of the prince.
Espionage with its various means and diverse types of secret agents, as well as conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force, O Pāṇḍava—
these, along with indifference as the fifth, have been fully enumerated here.
The entire mantra has been described, as well as its various meanings and divisions; likewise, the failure of a mantra and the fruits of both success and failure have been explained.
Furthermore, the various types of conjunctions—whether inferior, middling, or superior—have been detailed.
The [chapter] titled "Fear, Honor, and Wealth" has been described in its entirety;
likewise, the four seasons for expeditions, the detailed exposition of the three aims of life (*trivarga*),
and both righteous victory as well as victory for the sake of material gain have been set forth.
The victory of the Asuras has been described in its entirety;
here, the threefold characteristics of the five groups have also been described,
as well as the open and the secret forms of punishment, which are proclaimed as the *daṇḍa*.

The manifest [army] there consists of eight divisions, while the secret division is very extensive. O Pāṇḍava, these eight consist of chariots, elephants, horses, and infantry; as well as laborers, boats, scouts, and guides on the road.
O Kauravya, these are the manifest components of the army;
furthermore, the mobile and immobile applications of powders, poisons, and the like have been described.
Secret weapons are recorded as being of various kinds, both for touch and for consumption.

That which is spoken with a playful intent in battle or at dice, accompanied by confidence, is called *kaitavya*; this is the ninth expedient according to the wise. Indifference toward all undertakings and the performance of actions [is the tenth].
That by which the three aims of life are destroyed when undesirable things arise—
such as the illusions of sorcery and the like employed by those who live by their wits or by actors—
and that which is accompanied by auspicious omens, inauspicious omens, and portents.
Hypocrisy (*ḍambha*) is employed against a group of enemies by resorting to outward signs; deceit (*śāṭhya*) is said to be a lack of activity that corrupts the mind with defects.
Furthermore, the enemy, the friend, and the neutral party have also been described.
All the qualities of the path and likewise the qualities of the stages; self-protection, encouragement, and the inspection of scouts;
and also the various arrangements of men, elephants, chariots, and horses.
Various battle arrays of diverse names, wonderful skill in combat, portents of victory and defeat, fair fighting and fair retreat,
as well as the knowledge of tempering weapons— O bull of the Bharatas, all these were taught.
O Pāṇḍava, [I have taught you] the release from calamities concerning the army, as well as the gladdening of the army; the time for siege and assault, and the time of danger;
likewise, the construction of trenches and the strategic movement of troops.

The oppression of a foreign kingdom by fierce forces from forest-dwelling thieves, by arsonists, poisoners, and spies in disguise, by the instigation of guild leaders, and by the cutting down of vegetation.
By the disparagement of the elephants, by causing apprehension,
by obstructing the devotee, and by seizing the path,
there occurs the decline, increase, or equilibrium of the sevenfold kingdom.
The employment of the power of envoys, the expansion of the kingdom, the detailed exposition of the treatment of enemies, neutrals, and allies,
as well as the methods for crushing and resisting those who are more powerful.
Legal proceedings and the very subtle administration of justice, as well as the removal of thorns [criminals],
tranquility, the application of physical exercise, the acquisition of wealth,
the maintenance of those who are not supported, and the supervision of those who are supported.
Giving at the proper time for a purpose, and refraining from addiction to vices;
likewise, the qualities of a king and those of a commander-in-chief,
as well as the merits and faults of both the cause and the agent.
The various evil signs and the conduct of one's dependents,
suspicion toward everyone, and the avoidance of negligence;
the desire to obtain what has not yet been gained, and likewise the increase of what has already been obtained.

The giving away of what has been increased to worthy recipients according to the rules, as well as the distribution of wealth for the sake of dharma, for the sake of wealth, and for the sake of pleasure—
the fourth [type], which is for the destruction of calamities, is likewise described here.
O best of the Kurus, ten vices have been declared here: those born of anger, those that are fierce, and likewise those born of desire;
namely, hunting, gambling, drinking, and women, O bull of the Bharatas.
The teachers say that these were spoken here by the Self-Existent One as arising from desire:
harshness of speech, as well as ferocity, severity of punishment,
self-restraint [in the sense of suppression], renunciation, and the spoiling of wealth.
Various types of siege engines and their operations have been described:
the crushing, the repelling, and the breaking of standards;
the destruction of sacred trees, the assault on fortifications, and the ruin of workshops.
The chariot-fittings, the marching forth, and likewise the encampment have been described;
O best of warriors, the sounding of the paṇavas, ānakas, conchs, and kettledrums, the acquisition of materials, and the vital secrets— these are the six.
The pacification of what has been acquired, the honoring of the virtuous, unity with the wise, knowledge of the procedure for the morning oblation,
the touching of auspicious objects, and the tending of the body.
12,059.066c And constant application to food-restraint, as well as perpetual faith;
12,059.067a Rising at the proper time alone, truthfulness, and sweet speech;
12,059.067c Likewise, the performance of festivals, social gatherings, and rites involving the dedication of offerings.
O tiger among the Bharatas, conduct in all legal matters— whether direct or indirect— and constant supervision,
as well as the immunity from punishment for Brahmins and the infliction of punishment with due deliberation, [must be maintained].
The protection of one's own people and kinsmen according to their merits,
the protection of the citizens, and the expansion of one’s own kingdom; and that deliberation concerning the circle of twelve kings, O King— these constitute the duties of a ruler.
The seventy-two-fold intelligence that was proclaimed by the Self-Existent One has been declared,
as well as the duties of various countries, castes, and families. Furthermore, virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation have been described herein.
Expedients, the desire for wealth, various large-scale sacrificial fees,
the practice of root-magic (*mūlakarma*), illusion (*māyā*), and the application of yoga are described here; likewise,
the pollution of rivers with stagnant waters is described in this work.

"O tiger among kings, whatever means there may be by which the world does not stray from the path of the noble ones— all that has been described in the treatise on political ethics (nītiśāstra). Having composed this auspicious scripture, the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign, [proceeded]."
Greatly delighted, he spoke to all the gods, headed by Śakra:
"For the benefit of the world and for the establishment of the three aims of life,
this intellect has been manifested as the fresh butter of Sarasvatī."
Accompanied by Daṇḍa, she indeed performs the protection of the world; devoted to restraint and favor, she will move throughout the worlds.
She is led by Daṇḍa, and she also leads Daṇḍa.
That which is called *daṇḍanīti* (the science of government) follows after the three worlds;
this essence of the qualities of the sixfold policy shall abide foremost among the high-souled ones. Because of the greatness of that *daṇḍa*, this science possesses clearly defined characteristics.
The vast movement of the stars by which all this is pervaded;
the tradition of the Purāṇas and the origin of the great seers;
the lineage of the sacred fords and the lineage of the constellations, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
The entirety of the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) and likewise the four sacrificial offices (cāturhotra),

as well as the four castes (cāturvarṇya) and the four Vedas (cāturvedya), have been described here; and the histories (itihāsa), the secondary Vedas (upaveda), and the entire system of logic (nyāya) have also been described.
Austerity, knowledge, non-violence, truth and falsehood, supreme policy, service to the aged, charity, purity, exertion,
and compassion for all beings— all this has been described herein.

Whatever exists on earth that has been expressed in speech, all of that is contained within this scripture of the Grandfather; of this there is no doubt, O Pāṇḍava. Indeed, dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa are all fully proclaimed herein.
Then the Blessed One Śaṅkara first received that policy;
he who is multiform, large-eyed, auspicious, Sthāṇu, and Lord of Umā—
the god who is without beginning or end and endowed with consciousness and other attributes.
He who has all the *jñānas*, beginning with the *tāraka*, under his control; he who possesses the sovereignty endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā*, which is not artificial;
the Lord, the son of Brahmā, who arose from his forehead for the sake of [Brahmā’s] satisfaction.
The imperishable Lord of the universe wept with a terrible sound;
for when he was born as the son, the father indeed [wept] in the son, and the son likewise in the father—
He by whom the cosmic egg was fashioned, having bestowed his intellect upon the Creator of the world.
In whom the golden swan, the bird, was manifested—
that creator of the entire world, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
that god who is the self of all beings, Mahādeva, the eternal.

The imperishable abode of twelve thousand five hundred and nine Rudras was [established]. Then, perceiving the decline of the lifespan of the Yugas, the Blessed Lord Śiva abridged the scripture of great significance composed by Brahmā.
That which is called the Vaiśālākṣa,
consisting of twelve thousand five hundred and eight chapters, was received by Indra; the venerable Purandara, a master of great asceticism, then condensed that treatise into ten thousand chapters.
O dear one, having received from the god Maheśvara that which was spoken by the five thousand [sages] seeking the welfare of all creatures— that is the Bāhudantaka.
The lord Bṛhaspati, by means of his intellect, condensed it into exactly three thousand chapters; that is called the Bārhaspatya.
Kāvya then spoke a further condensation consisting of one thousand chapters.
That scripture, consisting of 12,059 verses, was composed by the teacher of yoga, possessed of immeasurable wisdom and great ascetic power.
Thus, O Pāṇḍava, out of consideration for the world and knowing that the lifespan of mortals had diminished, this scripture was condensed by the great ṛṣis.
Then the gods, having assembled together, spoke to Viṣṇu Prajāpati:
"Point out that one who alone deserves preeminence among mortals.
Thereupon, the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, the sovereign, reflected deeply.
From him, Taijasa begot a mind-born son named Virajas.
O illustrious one, Virajas did not desire sovereignty on earth;
rather, O Pāṇḍava, his intellect was directed solely toward renunciation.
Kīrtimān was his son, and he too transcended the five [elements]. Kardama was his son, and he also performed great penance. The son of the patriarch Kardama was indeed named Anaṅga.

A virtuous protector of his subjects and expert in the science of governance, Anaṅgaputra— possessing great strength and being well-versed in policy— having indeed attained the sovereignty over the earth, subsequently fell under the power of the senses.

O King, having obtained a highly fortunate woman who was beautiful and deluded by passion— a virtuous lady endowed with good fortune and unsurpassed qualities— Mṛtyu’s mind-born daughter named Sunīthā [approached her].

She who was renowned throughout the three worlds gave birth to Vena; the sages, exponents of the Veda, struck him— who was lawless toward his subjects and subject to the sway of passion and hatred— with kusha grass purified by mantras.
The sages churned his right thigh with the recitation of mantras;
from it was born on earth a deformed man, short-limbed,
resembling a burnt stump, with red eyes and black hair.
"Sit down," thus said the sages who discourse on Brahman to him;
from that, the Niṣādas were born— cruel beings who dwell in mountains and forests,
as well as other Mlecchas by the hundreds of thousands who inhabit the Vindhya range.
Those great seers churned his right hand once more;
from it was born a man whose form was like another Indra,
clad in armor, with a sword girt to him, and equipped with arrows and a bow.

He was a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and he had reached the further shore of the science of archery (*dhanurveda*). O King, the entire science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) rested upon that best of men.
Then Vainya, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to those great seers.
"A very subtle intellect has arisen within me, perceiving both dharma and worldly purpose.
Tell me truly what I ought to do with it. Whatever task you shall command me to perform, provided it is consistent with our purpose—"
"I shall certainly do that; there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
Then those gods and the supreme ṛṣis said to him:
"Practice that dharma which is established as constant, without any doubt."
Having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant, remaining equanimous toward all living beings,
and having cast far away desire, anger, greed, and pride— whatever man there may be in this world who would deviate from dharma; [he shall go to hell].
"He must be restrained by your two arms, as you constantly keep your eye on dharma.
Ascend to your vow through mind, deed, and speech, repeatedly declaring: 'I shall protect the earthly Brahman.'"
"Whatever principles of legal conduct based on the administration of punishment have been declared here,
I shall carry them out without hesitation and never under my own arbitrary will. Furthermore, O Lord, you must promise that the twice-born are not to be punished by me."
"O scorcher of enemies, I shall protect the entire world from all disorder.
Then Vainya spoke to those gods, who were preceded by the sages:
"O bulls among the gods, let it be so, provided that the Brahmins are my allies."
When those exponents of the Veda said to him, "So be it," Vainya agreed;
Śukra, a treasury consisting of sacred knowledge, became his domestic priest,
while the Vālakhilyas became his ministers, and the host of Sārasvatas likewise became his attendants.
The venerable great seer Garga was his astrologer;
among men, there is this supreme tradition that he was the eighth from himself. And before him were born two bards, a Sūta and a Māgadha.
The powerful King Pṛthu, son of Vena, being pleased with those two,
gave the Anūpa region to Sūta and Magadha to Māgadha.
The high-souled and venerable Atri was his preceptor for the Vedas.
Nārada constantly recited the Itihāsas and other sacred histories;
he properly leveled the earth,
for we have heard that there was previously a great unevenness in the ground.
In all the Manvantaras, the earth becomes uneven; therefore, O Great King,
Vainya extracted the masses of rocks from all sides with the tip of his bow,
and by that means the mountains were increased.

O Pāṇḍava, he was consecrated for the protection of subjects by the god Viṣṇu, by Śakra together with the deities, by the ṛṣis, and by Brahmā; and the Earth herself appeared before him in person, bringing precious gems.
Sāgara, the lord of rivers, and Himavat, the best of mountains,
as well as Śakra, O Yudhiṣṭhira, gave him inexhaustible wealth;
and Mahāmeru himself, the mountain of gold, gave him gold.
And the Lord Naravāhana, the master of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas,
bestowed wealth sufficient for virtue, worldly prosperity, and pleasure;
likewise, horses, chariots, elephants, and men by the tens of millions.
O Pāṇḍava, by the mere thought of Vainya, [these things] appeared:
there was neither old age, nor famine, nor mental afflictions, nor likewise physical diseases;
and never from reptiles, nor from thieves, nor from one another.
Fear arose there because of that king’s protection;
the waters solidified for him as he marched toward the ocean,
the mountains yielded the path, and his banner was never broken.
By him this earth was milked for seventeen kinds of grain;
and by Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas, each obtained whatever they desired. By that high-souled one, this world was made preeminent in righteousness.

Because he delights all his subjects, he is called a *rājā*. Because he protects the Brahmins from injury (*kṣatra*), he is called a *kṣatriya*. And this earth is remembered by the virtuous as "Pṛthivī" because it is spread out with wealth.
The eternal Viṣṇu himself established this [oath]:
"O King, O ruler of the earth, no one shall ever overstep you. And through his ascetic power, the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu entered that protector of the earth.
O King, because that world constantly bows to the god-like lords of men as it does to the gods,
and because it is perpetually protected by the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), no one can overcome it; furthermore, this is due to his constant observation through the employment of spies.
12,059.132a Even for a ruler of the earth here, together with his own self and his instruments,
12,059.132c what cause could there be for the world to remain under his control, other than the quality of destiny?
12,059.133a At that time, from the forehead of Viṣṇu, a golden lotus came into being.
From whom the goddess Śrī was born as the wife of the wise Dharma;
and from Śrī, O Pāṇḍava, Artha was born through Dharma. Thus, Dharma, Artha, and Śrī are established in the kingdom.
Upon the exhaustion of his merit, having descended from the heavenly world to the earth, O dear one, he is born as a king who follows the dictates of the science of government;
and that man on earth is endowed with greatness derived from Viṣṇu.
Endowed with such intelligence, he attains greatness;
indeed, no one can overstep the established order of the gods. He remains under the control of that one alone, provided he conforms to his will.
For auspicious action, O Indra among kings, leads to auspiciousness. This world abides by the word of such a single peerless man;
for whoever has beheld his face, O gentle one, becomes subject to his will.
One beholds him as fortunate, wealthy, and handsome;
therefore, O Indra among kings, he is constantly proclaimed by the wise in the world:
"The gods and the god-like men (kings) are equal," O lord of the people.
"12,059.141a All this has been told to you regarding the greatness among kings, 12,059.141c in its entirety, O best of the Bharatas; what else should be discussed here?
12,060.001 Vaiśampāyana said:"
Then again, Yudhiṣṭhira, having saluted his grandfather, the son of Gaṅgā, and becoming restrained with palms joined in reverence, questioned him:
"What are the duties for all the social orders, and what are the specific duties for each of the four orders?"
12,060.002c And what are considered the duties of kings among the four stages of life?
12,060.003a By what means does a kingdom prosper, and by what does a king flourish?
12,060.003c By what, O bull of the Bharatas, do the citizens and the servants thrive?

What kind of treasury, army, fortress, allies, and ministers should a king avoid? Likewise, what kind of officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers should he shun? In what circumstances, and during what particular calamity, should a king place his trust?
"From where, O Grandfather, is the self so firm that it must be protected? Tell me that.
Furthermore, what kind of oath should there be when beings are divided by duplicity? And what is the fruit of unrighteousness, as well as the consequence of violating an oath?"
"O Grandfather, explain all this according to its true nature and likewise its conventional usage, both in brief and in detail. Bhīṣma said:
Salutations to the Great Dharma; salutations to Kṛṣṇa, the Creator.
Having paid homage to the Brāhmaṇas, I shall proclaim the eternal Dharmas.
Freedom from anger, truthfulness of speech, sharing with others, and likewise forgiveness—these are they.
Procreation within one's own wife, purity, and freedom from malice; straightforwardness, and the maintenance of dependents—these nine duties pertain to all social classes.
But I shall now declare to you exclusively that which is the duty of the Brāhmaṇa.
"O Great King, they say that self-restraint alone is the ancient dharma;
in it, the duties of private study and teaching are fully accomplished.
If wealth should come to one who is thus established in his own duty,"
One who refrains from improper acts, who is tranquil and satisfied by wisdom,
should produce offspring, give gifts, and perform sacrifices;
for it is held by the virtuous that wealth should be enjoyed only after sharing it with others.

But a Brāhmaṇa who has completed his duties through Vedic study alone may or may not perform other [rites]; such a Brāhmaṇa is said to be a "friend" (maitra). O Bhārata, I shall now declare to you that which is the duty of a Kṣatriya as well.
The king should give, not beg; he should sacrifice, but not officiate as a priest for others;
he should not teach, but should study; and he should protect his subjects. Constantly exerting himself in the destruction of bandits, he should display his prowess in battle.
Those kings who have performed sacrifices, who are learned in the scriptures,
and who are victors in battle— they are the greatest conquerors of worlds among them.
He who returns from the field of battle with an unscarred body [is likewise supreme].

Those who know the past do not praise that deed of a Kṣatriya; for they say that the primary duty of those born of the warrior class is indeed the slaying [of enemies]. There is no task more essential for him than the destruction of bandits.
Giving, study, sacrifice, yoga, and security are ordained [for all];
therefore, a king who desires to attain righteousness must especially engage in battle. Having established all his subjects in their respective duties, the lord of the earth [should do so].
One should cause all duties to be completed according to the Dharma.
A king should have his tasks fully accomplished through the protection [of his subjects].
Whether he performs other [duties] or does not perform them, he is called a Kṣatriya belonging to Indra’s lineage.
O Bhārata, I shall now declare to you that which is the duty of the Vaiśya here in this world:
giving gifts, study, sacrifice, and the accumulation of wealth through purity.
A Vaiśya, being diligent, should protect all cattle here as if they were his own children.
Any other action he might perform would constitute improper conduct (vikarma). Indeed, by protecting them, he shall obtain great happiness.
For Prajāpati, having created cattle, entrusted them to the Vaiśya.
He entrusted all his subjects to the Brāhmaṇa and to the king. O lord of men, I shall now declare his mode of life and what constitutes his livelihood;
for the Vaiśya must certainly be supported by the king.

One should drink one cow from six [cows], and from a hundred, one should take a pair; furthermore, at the time of threshing, the seventh part is the share, as is a sixteenth part (kalā) for the horns and the hooves. This is the annual wage for all seeds of grain.
A Vaiśya should not entertain the desire, "I will not tend cattle";
if a Vaiśya so desires, they must by no means be tended by anyone else.
O Bhārata, I shall also declare to you that dharma which belongs to the Śūdra.
For Prajāpati ordained the Śūdra as the servant of the social classes;
therefore, service to the classes is prescribed for the Śūdra.
And by serving them, he shall attain great happiness.
A Śūdra, free from malice, should serve these three castes; he should never, under any circumstances, engage in the accumulation of wealth,
for a base man, having acquired riches, might bring his superiors under his control.
Or, being righteous, he may fulfill his desires with the king's permission.
I shall now declare his means of livelihood and what constitutes his subsistence;
for the Śūdra is said to be one who must necessarily be supported by the other castes.
An umbrella, a turban, sandals, and fans made of *uśīra* grass— these,
when worn out, should be given to a Śūdra servant. Furthermore, tattered garments that are no longer fit to be worn should be discarded by the twice-born.

12,060.033c These [duties] are indeed to be prescribed for the Śūdra, for that is his wealth of dharma. 12,060.034a And whatever Śūdra may come as a servant to the twice-born, 12,060.034c those who know the dharma say that a livelihood must be provided for him by them.
A maintenance allowance of twelve thousand and sixty-three and three-quarters paṇas should be given to one who has not departed; the aged and the infirm must be supported.
A Śūdra must never abandon his master in any calamity;
even when his wealth is exhausted, he must support his master with extra effort.

For a Śūdra possesses no property of his own, as all his wealth may be taken by his master. O Bhārata, it has been declared that for the three [upper] castes, sacrifice is performed with the three Vedas;
however, for a Śūdra, the *svāhākāra*, the *namaskāra*, and mantras are prescribed.
A Śūdra, observing vows, should himself perform the *pākayajña* sacrifices with those two [wives].
They say that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for a *pākayajña* consists of a full vessel.
A Śūdra named Paijavana gave a hundred thousand of these.
"We have heard that the sacrificial fee is given according to the ritual procedure for Indra and Agni; therefore,
O Bhārata, the sacrifice of faith is ordained for all the social classes, and it belongs to him alone."

In all sacrifices, faith is indeed the foremost deity; it is the great purifier for those who offer worship. O Brahmins, each deity is supreme in relation to its own respective [offering], even among one another.
12,060.040c They performed sacrifices here with sessions for those eternal desires.
12,060.041a Among the three social orders, the created beings were indeed associated with the Brāhmaṇas.
12,060.041c Those who are even the gods of the gods—whatever they might say, that is indeed supreme.
Therefore, all sacrifices are performed by means of the Vedic classes (*varṇas*), not out of mere desire.
A twice-born man who knows the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas should always be honored like a god;
however, one who lacks the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* is a calamity brought about by Prajāpati.
O dear one, O Bhārata, sacrifice is performed through the power of the intellect among all social classes.
Neither the gods nor other people seek out those who destroy the sacrifice;
