therefore, the sacrifice of faith is ordained for all classes.
The Brahmins always worshipped their own deity with their own [means]; thus it was that they sacrificed for other castes as well. That very great dharma has been made known to us.
Created by Brahmā and seen among the three social orders (varṇas),
the Brāhmaṇa is indeed to be honored and is delighted among the three varṇas. Therefore, the social orders are upright, for such is the nature of their birth.
These things are mixed together; this is their maturation.
Therefore, from that very [source], the dharma of birth and caste is indeed mixed together;
this is its very agitation.
There is one *sāman*, one *yajus*, and one *ṛk*;
and one sage is seen among them who is free from doubt.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung at the sacrifice: 12,060.046a Here, those who know the ancient lore proclaim the verses chanted at the sacrifice.
O King of kings, among the Vaikhānasa sages who desire to sacrifice, there are twelve thousand, six hundred, and four and a half [thousand].
Whether the sun has risen or not yet risen, one who is faithful and has conquered his senses offers oblations into the fire according to dharma; indeed, faith is the great cause.
That which was spilled of it is the former; that which was not spilled is the latter.
There are many forms of sacrifice and various fruits of action. He who thoroughly understands these, being firmly established in the certainty of knowledge—
A twice-born man endowed with faith is worthy to perform the sacrifice—
whether he be a thief, a sinner, or even the worst of evildoers;
whoever desires to perform the sacrifice, him they call truly virtuous.

The seers praise him, saying, "This is certainly excellent; there is no doubt about it. For it is the settled conclusion that sacrifices must be performed by all classes in every way. Indeed, nothing equal to sacrifice is found in the three worlds."
"Therefore, they say that one should sacrifice with a man who is free from malice,
relying on the purity of faith and giving according to his ability.
Bhīṣma said:
O mighty-armed one of true prowess, Yudhiṣṭhira, hear now concerning the four stages of life (āśramas) and the duties of the four castes in this world:
the forest-dweller’s life, the life of mendicancy, and the great stage of the householder.
They declare the stage of the student (brahmacarya-āśrama) to be the fourth, chosen by the Brahmins;
having undergone the sacrament of wearing matted hair and attained the status of the twice-born, and having performed the rites such as the establishment of the sacred fires and studied the Veda.
Whether with his wife or without her, the self-possessed man who has restrained his senses,
having fulfilled his duties in the householder stage, may enter the forest-dweller stage of life;
there, that knower of dharma, having thoroughly studied the Āraṇyaka scriptures, [should practice].

Having procreated while remaining a perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*), one attains the nature of the imperishable. O King, these very signs of the sages who are perpetual celibates must first be practiced here by a wise Brahmin.

O Lord of the people, for a Brahmin who has practiced the life of celibacy and seeks liberation, the practice of wandering for alms is praised in this world; he should sleep wherever sunset finds him, maintaining no sacred fires and possessing no fixed dwelling.

A sage who lives on whatever is obtained, who is self-controlled and has conquered his senses, should be free from desire, equal toward all, free from enjoyment, and devoid of transformation; such a Brahmin, having reached the stage of peace, attains the nature of the imperishable Self.
Having studied the Vedas, performed all his duties,
procreated offspring, and enjoyed pleasures,
he should, with a concentrated mind, practice that difficult discipline.
Regarding the dharma of the householder as seen in the dharma of the sages:
he should be content with his own wife, approach her only during her fertile period, follow the prescribed injunctions, and be neither deceitful nor crooked.
Eating in moderation, devoted to the gods, grateful,
truthful, gentle, compassionate, and patient;
self-controlled, obedient, and vigilant in the offerings to the gods and ancestors;

A householder should be one who constantly gives food to the twice-born, who is free from envy, who bestows gifts upon all who bear outward marks of religious life, and who is ever devoted to the sacrificial fires.
12,061.013a Now, O dear one, the great seers of exalted power have here recited the song of Nārāyaṇa;
12,061.013c it is of great significance and is intensely applied through austerity.
Listen then as it is being spoken by me:
truthfulness, straightforwardness, and the honoring of guests; likewise, righteousness, wealth, and pleasure are found in one's wife.
"Worldly pleasures are to be enjoyed in this world and indeed in the next; this is my opinion. Likewise, the maintenance of one's wife and children, as well as the mastery of the Vedas,"

The supreme ṛṣis declare that this is the best of hermitages for the virtuous. For indeed, the Brāhmaṇa who is devoted to sacrifice and dwells in the householder stage of life according to the rule [attains this].
Having thoroughly purified his conduct as a householder,
he attains the pure fruit of heaven;
upon the abandonment of his body, his desired objects are considered to be inexhaustible.
With eyes, heads, and mouths on every side, they stand for the sake of infinity.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one eats, another mutters prayers, another moves about;
yet all serve that very same teacher, covered in dirt and mud.

A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should always be observant of his vows, constantly devoted to initiation, and self-controlled. Always following the shadow of his teacher, studying diligently,
and remaining well-restrained, he should dwell [with him] always performing his duties without questioning the Veda.

Constantly performing service to his guru, he should bow down before him; wandering alone without a fixed abode, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he should remain entirely withdrawn from the six worldly activities and not engaged in them at all.
"He does not act out of a sense of entitlement, nor does he serve those who hate him;
O dear one, this is considered the state of life for a celibate student (brahmacārin) in this hermitage.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"Speak of those dharmas that are auspicious, pleasant, of great ultimate fruit, non-violent, and esteemed by the world; speak of those dharmas that provide easy means for people like me and bring them happiness.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Lord, four stages of life (āśramas) have been ordained here for the Brāhmaṇa; O best of the Bharatas, the other three castes follow them. Many duties have been declared, O King."
These lead to heaven and are devoted to the Kṣatriya;
they are not recorded as precedents for other rules,
for everything is ordained according to rule within the Kṣatriya duty.
Performing the duties of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya,
and even those of a Śūdra while being a Brāhmaṇa,
that dull-witted man is censured in this world.
And he goes to hell in the next world.
O Pāṇḍava, apply that designation which is used in the world for a slave, a dog, a wolf, or a beast, to a Brahmin who persists in improper conduct.
Of one engaged in the six duties within all four stages of life, endowed with every virtue, perfected in self-mastery, a pure Brahmin devoted to asceticism.
For the worlds designated as imperishable belong to the generous man who is free from desire.
Whatever kind of action a person performs, by whatever means, and in whatever place,
he obtains a corresponding result through that very same quality.

O Indra among kings, you ought to understand the great calculation of Vedic study through the increase [of wealth] by means of agriculture, trade, and the livelihood of a servant. Time, impelled by time and determined by the cycle of time, has arrived.
Helplessly, one performs actions that are superior, inferior, or middling. Gifts are finite, yet in the past they were conducive to welfare.
For the world is devoted to its own karma; the Imperishable (Akṣara), however, faces in all directions.
Bhīṣma said: Drawing the bowstring and the destruction of enemies,
as well as agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing.
Furthermore, serving for the sake of wealth—
this is the highest improper act for a twice-born man.
However, the wise householder should practice the six duties of a Brahmin.
For a Brahmin who has fulfilled his duties, dwelling in the forest is commended.
He should avoid service to kings, wealth from agriculture, living by trade, crookedness, the company of unchaste women, and usury.

O King, he who is a friend of Brahmins in name only, who is of evil conduct and has strayed from dharma, who is the husband of a low-caste woman, a slanderer, and a dancer— such a person becomes a Śūdra.

O Lord of the Kauravas, a Brāhmaṇa who is a village servant, one who follows forbidden occupations, or one who is dull-witted and has fallen away from his proper conduct— such a person is likewise [excluded].
O King, even if one studies the Vedas or recites them,
such a person is equal to Śūdras and may be fed like a slave;
all these become equal to Śūdras.
O King, one should avoid these [persons] at rites for the gods:
those who eat without restraint, those of cruel conduct,
those whose nature is violence, and those who have abandoned their own dharma and livelihood.
O King, whatever offerings to the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*), and whatever else there may be—
whether they are things to be given or not to be given— they all belong to him.
Therefore, this duty is ordained for the Brāhmaṇa.
Self-restraint, purity, and straightforwardness as well, O King—
all these stages of life (āśramas) for the Brahmin were indeed ordained by Brahmā in ancient times, O King.
He who is self-controlled, a drinker of Soma, of noble character,
compassionate, all-enduring, free from desire, upright, gentle, merciful, and patient;
O King, he indeed is the true Brahmin and no other, though he may be a performer of evil deeds;
for all the worlds, desiring righteousness, depend upon him— whether he be a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a prince.
Therefore, O son of Pāṇḍu, considering that the castes are attached to the duties of their respective births, Viṣṇu does not desire this [confusion] in the world,
lest it should happen to all people in the world.
The four castes and the declarations of the Vedas would not exist; all sacrifices and all worldly activities would cease, and none at all would remain established in their respective stages of life.

And whoever among the three social classes should desire to practice the stages of life (*āśrama*) and perform the duties prescribed for those stages, listen to them, O Pāṇḍava. [This applies to one] who has fulfilled his obligations through service and completed the duty of procreation.

Having obtained the king’s permission, O lord of the earth, all the stages of life (āśramas) are prescribed for a Śūdra— even one who has entered them only slightly or who follows ten of the duties— excepting that which is free from desire for rewards.

"O Indra among kings, those who practice dharma do not say that the life of begging is prescribed for him, nor for a Vaiśya, nor indeed for a prince. Having fulfilled his duties, having passed his youth, and having exerted himself in service to the king,"

Having studied the Vedas according to dharma and the treatises on statecraft, O sinless one, and having performed the rites for progeny and other duties, as well as the Soma sacrifice, a Vaiśya may, with the king’s permission, proceed to the circle of hermitages.
O best among those who speak, having protected all his subjects with righteousness and having likewise performed the Rājasūya, Aśvamedha, and other sacrifices,
he bestowed sacrificial fees upon the Brahmins according to the prescribed texts.
O Pāṇḍava, bull among Kṣatriyas, having achieved victory in battle— whether it be small or great— you should install your son as the protector of the subjects in the kingdom,
or another Kṣatriya of a different lineage who is highly esteemed.
Having properly honored the ancestors with ancestral rites according to the rules,
and having diligently worshipped the gods with sacrifices and the sages with the Vedas, he who,
when the time of death has arrived, desires to enter another stage of life—
O King, having proceeded through the stages of life (āśramas) in due order, one shall attain perfection; O Indra among kings, by following the path of living on alms as a royal seer (rājarṣi),
even one who has abandoned the duties of a householder may live if he desires to survive.
"O bull among the Bharatas, O tiger among kings, this ultimate duty is not prescribed for only three of the four stages of life, as they say; rather,
much depends upon the Kṣatriyas for the welfare of all mankind."
By those who practice the dharma that is supreme in the world,
all dharmas along with their subordinate dharmas [are derived] from the three;
I hear from the Veda that this is because of the dharma of the king.
Just as, O King, all footprints produced by living beings are absorbed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too are all duties absorbed within the duties of a king.
Understand that all states are completely dissolved;
those who know the Dharma say that other dharmas have small support and yield small fruit.
The noble ones say that the duty of a kṣatriya— which has a great foundation and many auspicious forms— is superior to any other;
for all duties have the duty of a king as their primary principle.
All phenomena are protected;
all phenomena are seen within the duties of a king; and all branches of knowledge are taught within the duties of a king.
O King, among the duties of a king, total renunciation is paramount;
they say that among acts of renunciation, the ancient dharma is supreme.
O King, among the duties of a king, every form of exertion is required.
And they say that the ancient place of the King’s Duty (*rājadharma*) is this: if the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) were destroyed, the three Vedas would sink,
and all duties (*dharma*) would become subverted.
If the ancient royal duty of the Kṣatriya were abandoned, all the duties of the stages of life would vanish;
for all forms of renunciation are seen within the duties of kingship.
All initiations are declared within the duties of kings;
all yogas are declared within the duties of kings;
all worlds have entered into the duties of kings.
Therefore, O Ajātaśatru, there exists no dharma in the world more distinguished than the duty of kings;
all these actions, O best of the Bharatas, are contained within the *kṣatra* (the warrior class).
And the world of living beings remains established in the duty of the Kṣatriyas,
just as living beings, when slain according to their nature, serve to cause no further affliction for those who rely on dharma.
12,063.030c Thus, these people are devoid of the duties of kings; in every situation, they do not respect their own dharma.
12,064.001 Bhīṣma said:
O Pāṇḍava, the duties of the four stages of life, the duties of the various castes, and even those pertaining to the world-protectors are all established within the duty of the Kṣatriya;
all these duties, O best of the Bharatas, reside in the Kṣatriya.

Free from desire in the world of the living, they remain established in the duty of the warrior class (*kṣatra-dharma*). They elucidate through the scriptures that eternal state of being— the dharma of those dwelling in the stages of life (*āśrama*), which is imperceptible and possesses many doors.
Other disputants, through meritorious words, seek to establish worldly consensus; yet, being ignorant of the certainty of dharmas, they delight in other things that lack illustrative examples.
[The truth] is abundant in perceptible happiness, witnessed by oneself, and free from deception.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the Dharma that is for the welfare of all the world is established among the Kṣatriyas,

as well as among the Brāhmaṇas who are intent upon the stages of life (āśramas) and the duties of Dharma; just as in ancient times, the sacred tradition was recounted for the sake of the three other castes.

O Indra among kings, regarding the duties of royalty, that which is peerless in this world has been recounted to you through examples of virtuous conduct— just as [the account] was formerly told concerning the immensely powerful Viṣṇu, the Lord of all beings, the divine and sovereign Nārāyaṇa.

12,064.007e Very many heroic kings went forth for the administration of justice. 12,064.008a Having previously weighed each of their own deeds in their hermitages, the kings attended upon him, remaining firm in their adherence to authoritative examples.
The Sādhyas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins;
the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, and the hosts of Maruts—
these gods were created of old by the Primeval God.
And the perfected ones abide in the duty of the Kṣatriya;
here I shall explain to you the Dharma that determines the true purpose,
now that [the world] has become lawless and is reduced to a single path of violence toward the Dānavas.

O Indra among kings, there was once a powerful king named Māndhātṛ. In ancient times, that protector of the earth performed a sacrifice out of a desire to behold the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is without beginning, middle, or end.

O tiger among kings, that king Māndhātṛ touched with his head the feet of the supreme Viṣṇu during the sacrifice of the high-souled one. Then Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Vāsava, revealed himself to him.
Surrounded by those virtuous kings, he honored that Lord.
Between that assembly of monarchs and that high-souled one,
O you of great splendor, there occurred this great discourse concerning Viṣṇu.
Indra said:
"O best among the upholders of dharma, what do you desire? For what immeasurable being is it that you wish to see?"
He possesses infinite, immeasurable power and heroism toward sentient beings;
he is indeed Nārāyaṇa, the primordial god, the ancient one.
Even by me, that god of universal form cannot be [fully described].
Even Brahmā himself can behold him directly.
O King, whatever other desires reside in your heart,
I shall grant them to you, for you are a king among mortals.
Established in truth, devoted to dharma, with senses conquered,
he was a hero, firm, and delighted in love for the gods;
through his intelligence, devotion, and supreme faith, he was endowed with all virtues.
"Therefore, I shall grant you a boon as you desire.
Māndhātṛ said:
"O Blessed One, [I recognize you as] the primordial God, without a doubt."
Having propitiated him with my head bowed, I shall behold [the truth];
for, desiring dharma, I wish to abandon enjoyments and go to the forest— the path of the righteous cherished by the world.
Through this vast and immeasurable dharma of the Kṣatriyas,
worlds have been attained and his own glory established—
this very dharma which originated from the Primordial God.
"I do not know how to act as the elder of the world," [he said].
Indra replied:
"You should wander without an army and devoted to unrighteousness."
And being vigilant, you shall attain the supreme goal;
for the duty of the warrior class (kṣātra-dharma) originated from the Primordial God,
whereas all other duties are subsequent and subordinate to it.
For all other created things are finite, whereas these are infinite;
they are well-established and distinguished by the duty of the Kṣatriya.
Into this dharma all dharmas enter.
Therefore, they declare this to be the supreme dharma:
in ancient times, the gods and the seers of immeasurable luster were all protected by Viṣṇu through the duty of the Kṣatriya, after he had crushed his enemies by means of action.
For if that Blessed One,
the immeasurable possessor of all wealth, had not slain all his enemies, there would have been neither Brahmins nor the Creator of the worlds.
If that immeasurable one, the best of gods, had not existed in the past, there would be neither the True Dharma nor the Primordial Dharma, and he could not have conquered this earth by his prowess.
The four castes and the duties of the four stages of life—
all these would cease to exist due to the destruction of the Brahman;
for the eternal one has seen that all dharmas are manifold.
Furthermore, through the duty of the Kṣatriya, they have been set in motion again;
for in age after age, the original duties have been set in motion,
and they call the duty of the Kṣatriya the eldest in the world.
Sacrificing oneself, compassion for all beings,
knowledge of the world, and their liberation and protection;
the liberation of the despondent and the protection of the afflicted.
In the kṣatriya dharma of kings, there exists [this principle]:
those who have transgressed all bounds and are driven by lust and anger do not incur sin, provided they are afraid of the king.
And the rest, all endowed with righteousness, are of virtuous conduct and practice the noble Dharma;
they are to be protected like sons by kings according to the duty of their office.
All beings in the world move about without a doubt; the Kṣatriya is supreme among all dharmas, the eldest in the world, eternal,
perpetually reaching to the end of the imperishable, the imperishable itself, facing every direction.
Indra said: "One who possesses such prowess and is endowed with all virtues is the best among the Kṣatriyas; among all duties, this is the highest duty."
"You, who are noble lions among men, must protect [the people];
otherwise, in the event of their absence, there would be the destruction of all creatures.
[Therefore, perform] the consecration of the earth through the application of royal consecration."
A king should know that abstaining from begging, the protection of his subjects, compassion for all beings,
and the sacrifice of one's body in battle constitute the highest dharma.
Sages indeed declare that renunciation is supreme;
he who would cast off his body is the best of all. In the duties of kings, everything is eternally renounced.
These rulers of the earth are always directly perceived by you—
whether through great learning, service to their teachers,
or through the consolidation of others— to speak [the truth].
A Kṣatriya who is a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) and desires righteousness should always practice the duty of the single hermitage alone;
for when legal proceedings concerning common property have commenced.
By diligently avoiding both the pleasant and the unpleasant,
by establishing and protecting the four social orders, and through various spiritual disciplines and innate restraints; 12,065.005c.

They say that the duty of the stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*) consists of all efforts; yet the duty of the Kṣatriya is the foremost, being endowed with all virtues. Those castes who do not practice their own respective duties—
They speak of various dharmas incorrectly, regarding the eternal reality as being without boundaries and as having perished; indeed, they call those men who are like beasts.
Just as one leads another toward policy out of greed for wealth,
so too the duty of the Kṣatriya is superior to that stage of life [of the three Vedas] which is the goal of the Brāhmaṇas learned in the three Vedas.
And regarding this very stage of life (āśrama) which has been described for Brahmins,
they say that this is the foremost duty of a Brahmin;
performing any other [duty], he is to be slain like a Śūdra and like one who violates the sacred law.

O King, the duties of the four stages of life and the duties prescribed by the Vedas must be followed by the Brāhmaṇa; no one else may know them in any way. For one who behaves otherwise, that mode of livelihood is not ordained.
Dharma is manifested through action; he who acts like a dog is indeed like a dog.
A Brahmin who persists in improper conduct does not deserve respect;
for they know him to be untrustworthy if he does not apply himself to his duties.
These duties and all the social orders must be elevated by heroes;
this is the duty of Kṣatriyas.
Therefore, the duties of kings are the most excellent, and no others.
"Those whose primary quality is vigor and whose nature is heroic are my preferred ones," Māndhātṛ said.
"The Yavanas, Kirātas, Gāndhāras, Cīnas, Śabaras, and Barbaras— "
The Bāhlīkas, the Turuṣkas, and likewise the Pāñcālas are recorded; as well as the Śakas, Tuṣāras, Kahvas, Pahlavas, Andhras, and Madrakas;
the Oḍras, Pulindas, Ramaṭhas, Kācas, and all the Mlecchas from every quarter.
How shall the men born of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes, as well as the Vaiśyas and Śūdras,
all those dwelling within the realm, practice their duty?
And how shall all those who live like bandits be established by those such as I?
"I desire to hear this, O Blessed One; tell it to me.
For you, O Lord of the Gods, are a kinsman to us Kṣatriyas.
Indra said:
Indeed, service to one's mother and father must be performed by all dasyus;
likewise, service to teachers, gurus, and those dwelling in the stages of life (āśramas),
as well as service to the protectors of the earth, must be performed by all dasyus.
The performance of Vedic rites is indeed ordained as their duty;
likewise, they should offer sacrifices to the ancestors, dig wells, establish water-stations, provide resting places,
and bestow gifts upon the twice-born at the appropriate times.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, maintaining one's livelihood and inheritance, providing for one's sons and wife, purity, and freedom from malice— these,
as well as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for all sacrifices, must be given by one who desires prosperity.
"O sinless one, even all bandits must perform the highly esteemed *pākayajña* sacrifices.
O King, these and other such rites were ordained of old; they are the duties that must be performed here by everyone in the world."
Māndhātṛ said:
"In this world, men who are robbers are seen among all the social classes (varṇas),
even while existing within the outward signs of other [religious] orders and within all four stages of life (āśramas)."
Indra said: "O King, when the science of government has perished and the duty of kingship has been cast aside,
all living beings become utterly bewildered due to the wickedness of their rulers."

When this Kṛta Yuga has passed away, there will be innumerable monks and likewise those bearing sectarian marks, as well as various divisions among the stages of life (āśramas). Not hearing the excellent paths of the ancient laws, they shall fall away from them.
Driven by desire and anger, they will set out upon a wrong path; but when the wicked are turned back by the high-souled through the science of punishment,
then the supreme, eternal, and true Dharma does not waver.
He who disregards the king, who is the teacher of the next world,
finds that for him nothing given, nothing offered in sacrifice, and no ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) bears fruit anywhere.
He is the eternal lord of men, who has become a god.
The gods hold in high esteem a lord of men who desires righteousness;
for the blessed Lord Prajāpati, who created the entire world,
intended the Kṣatriya order for the sake of the engagement in and withdrawal from duties.
"For he who, with his intellect, remembers the course of the dharma that has been set in motion—he is to be honored and worshipped by me; in him the *kṣatra* is established.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Master surrounded by the hosts of Maruts, departed for his abode, the imperishable, supreme state.
O sinless one, when dharma had been set forth in this manner in ancient times, well-practiced—
What conscious man, possessed of great learning, would despise the kṣatra?
Those actions undertaken through injustice, as well as those withdrawn from it,
come to ruin in between, like those who are sightless upon a path.
"O tiger among men, conduct yourself in the very same way as when the wheel was first set in motion and the primordial refuge established; I recognize you, O sinless one.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, I have heard from my ancestors that the four stages of life (āśramas) for human beings have been described; explain their exposition to me as I ask you. Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, all dharmas here are known to you, O mighty-armed one, just as they are known to me and are esteemed by the virtuous. Yet,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, you ask me about that which resides within another sign."
"O best of those who uphold dharma, O lord of men, understand that dharma from me.
O son of Kuntī, O bull among men, all these things exist for those engaged in virtuous conduct and the duties of the four stages of life."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, for one who is free from desire and hatred, who governs by the science of polity, and who looks upon all beings with equanimity, there shall be the state of the mendicant order. He who understands the taking and giving away [of wealth], as well as restraint and favor, [attains this state].
For a hero who conducts himself as described, there shall be the stage of life of security (*kṣemāśramapada*).
O Pāṇḍava, for one who constantly honors those worthy of honor with a share of his possessions,
O Kaunteya, there shall be everywhere the stage of life of mendicancy (*bhaikṣyāśramapada*).
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for one who rescues kinsmen, relatives,
and friends who have fallen into distress, there shall be the state of the stage of initiation (dīkṣā-āśrama-pada).
[He attains] honor repeatedly among the leaders of the world and among the foremost of those bearing religious marks.
O Kaunteya,
for one who performs these daily rites— the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), and those pertaining to humans—
on a vast scale, O Pārtha, the state of the forest hermitage (*vanyāśramapada*) comes to be.
O King of kings, through the sharing of wealth with all beings, the honoring of guests, and the performance of sacrifices to the gods, one attains the state of the forest hermitage (vānaprastha),
O you of true valor who crushes enemy kingdoms for the sake of the righteous.
O tiger among men, for one who acts thus, there shall be the state of the forest hermitage (*vanyāśramapada*).
Through the protection of all beings and the safeguarding of his own kingdom,
the king’s various forms of consecration (*dīkṣā*) constitute the state of the forest hermitage.

Constant study of the Vedas, forbearance, reverence for the teacher, as well as service to the preceptor— this constitutes the state of the Brahma-āśrama for one who constantly recites his daily prayers and always worships the gods.
O tiger among men, through righteousness the hermitage of Dharma comes to be;
for that king whose resolve is fixed upon either death or protection,
the hermitage of Brahma comes to be in that gamble for life.

O Bhārata, for one who always follows the path that is straightforward and free from deceit toward all beings, there exists the state of the Brahma-āśrama. O Bhārata, this applies even among Brahmins living as forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) and those learned in the three Vedas (*traividya*).
O Bhārata, for one who bestows abundant wealth, his state shall be that of a forest hermitage; for him who shows compassion toward all beings and is devoted to kindness,
his state shall be the highest in every respect.

O Kauravya Yudhiṣṭhira, for one who shows compassion in every situation toward children and the elderly, there shall be a high station in every state of existence. O bull of the Kurus, one should provide protection to beings who have been oppressed by force.
O Kauravya, one should dwell in the householder’s life by providing refuge to those who seek it (12.066.015c),
by protecting all beings, both moving and stationary, in every way (12.066.016a),
and by always offering worship according to their merit (12.066.016c); thus should one dwell in the householder’s life.
O Pārtha, the restraint and favor shown toward one's senior and junior wives, brothers, sons, and grandsons— that is the austerity of the householder.
[Likewise is the service] toward virtuous persons worthy of worship who have realized the Self among their subjects.

O tiger among men, the protection [of others] constitutes the state of the householder’s stage of life (gṛhāśrama). O Bhārata, he who, while remaining in his own home, receives all the requirements of the other stages of life through his food— that, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is true householdership.
That man who stands firmly in the dharma as it was truly created by the Creator, O son of Kuntī, attains the unsurpassed fruit of all the stages of life (āśramas),
in which his virtues never perish.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, they say that even he who dwells in a hermitage is the best of men.
For by observing the proper measure of place, the measure of age, and likewise the measure of lineage,
one indeed dwells in all the stages of life, O Yudhiṣṭhira."

O son of Kuntī, tiger among men, by protecting the laws of the land as well as the laws of the family, a king becomes one who belongs to all the stages of life (āśrama). At the proper time, he should likewise provide for the prosperity of all beings and offer them gifts.

O tiger among men, one who honors the virtuous should dwell in the hermitage of the *sādhus*. Furthermore, O son of Kuntī, he who, though engaged in the tenfold duties, contemplates the Dharma, becomes a king of the entire world and a true inhabitant of the hermitage.
Those virtuous ones who are skilled in the Dharma and practice the Dharma in this world—

while they are protected within his realm, that king receives a fourth part as his share. But those men who do not protect human beings who delight in the Dharma and are devoted to the Dharma [are at fault].
O tiger among men, those kings take away the sin of those [who commit it];
and those who are the protectors and allies of the kings, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
they all likewise share in the portion of merit performed by others, O sinless one.

"For among all stages of life, they say that the householder's stage is the most resplendent and certain conclusion; it is the purifier, O tiger among men, which we ourselves attend to. Indeed, that man who treats all beings as he does himself—"

Having laid aside the rod and conquered anger, he attains happiness after death. A swift boat— arisen from Dharma, possessing the strength of living beings as its oars, having the bridge of Dharma as its rudder, and with renunciation as its wind for its course— will carry you across.

When every desire that resides in his heart has ceased from all things, then he becomes established in *sattva* and thereby attains Brahman. O lord of men, he is indeed perfectly serene through his disposition and through yoga.
O tiger among men, devoted to protection, you shall attain righteousness;
O sinless one, apply yourself to the effort of protecting the Brahmins who are devoted to the study of the Vedas and perform virtuous deeds, as well as all the world.

O Bhārata, the king who practices dharma while wandering in the forest and in hermitages obtains a hundredfold more merit than that through protection. O best of the Pāṇḍavas, this manifold dharma has thus been proclaimed to you.

"O Pāṇḍava, tiger among men, practice with one-pointed mind this eternal system seen by the ancients— the four stages of life (cāturāśramya) and the four social orders (cāturvarṇya). Devoted to its protection, you shall attain righteousness."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The four stages of life (āśramas) have been described here, as well as the four social orders (varṇas).
O Grandfather, tell me what is the most important duty for the kingdom."
Bhīṣma said:
This is the most essential duty for a kingdom: the consecration of a king.
For a kingdom that is without a lord and lacks strength is overcome by bandits.
In kingdoms without a king, righteousness does not endure; they devour one another, and thus, in every way, shame on the state of anarchy!
For the sacred tradition declares: "It is Indra whom one chooses when one appoints a king."
Just as Indra, so too is the king to be honored by one who desires prosperity.
It is a Vedic teaching that one should not dwell in kingdoms without a king;
for in kingdoms without a king, even Agni does not carry the sacrificial oblations.
If, however, a more powerful king seeking sovereignty should advance against kingdoms that are leaderless or whose kings have been slain,
he should go out to meet him and pay him honor; this is the well-advised course in such a case.
Indeed, there is nothing more evil than a state of lawlessness;
for if one were to perceive [the king] properly, all would be well.
For a powerful man, when provoked, might bring about total destruction.
He who, being weak, does not bow down shall become a partaker of great affliction;
a cow that is difficult to milk receives much distress,
but they do not trouble at all a cow that is easy to milk.
That which is not heated does not require further heating;
likewise, wood that is already bent by itself does not need to be bent again.
By this analogy, a wise man should yield to one who is more powerful.
He bows down to Indra, he bows down to the more powerful;
therefore, one who desires constant prosperity must always appoint a king. For those who live in a state of anarchy, there is no purpose for wealth nor any purpose for wives.
For in a kingless state, a wicked man delights in seizing the wealth of others;
yet when others plunder him, he then desires a king.
Even the wicked then never find security.
For two carry off the property of one, and many others carry off that of two;
a non-slave is made a slave, women are carried off by force,
and likewise the measure of goods is [falsely] weighed.
For this reason, the gods appointed protectors of creatures. If there were no king on earth to wield the rod of punishment,
the stronger would roast the weaker like fish upon a spit.
"We have heard that in former times, when the subjects were without a king, they perished, devouring one another like fish in the water devouring the smaller ones.
Then, having come together, they established agreements; so we have heard."
"He who is harsh in speech, a man of violence, one who commits adultery,
and he who would not give his own property—
such persons are to be avoided by us," [he said] for the sake of inspiring confidence among all social classes without distinction.
Having thus made that agreement, they did not abide by it;
then, together and afflicted by misery, they went to the Grandfather and said, "O Blessed One, we are powerless and perishing; point out a lord to us."
12,067.021 "He whom we may worship together and who may protect us"—
to them Manu assigned a boon, yet Manu did not approve of their request.
12,067.022 Manu said:
"I am afraid of cruel action, for ruling a kingdom is indeed extremely difficult,
especially among men who are constantly engaged in wrongful conduct.
Bhīṣma said:
The subjects said to him: "Do not fear; the sin shall go away through this act.
We shall give you fifty per centum of cattle, as well as gold, and a tenth part of grain to increase the treasury."
When maidens of beautiful form are to be given as a bride-price, and when marriages are being prepared,
those men who are foremost by virtue of their preeminent weapons and armor will follow you, just as the gods follow Mahendra.
O King, having gained such strength, you are invincible and majestic;
you shall maintain us all in happiness, just as Kubera does for the Nairṛtas. And whatever dharma the subjects shall practice when well-protected by their king—
"O King, that fourth dharma of yours shall remain centered in us;
cultivated by that great dharma through which happiness is attained,
protect us in every way, as Śatakratu protects the gods."
"Go forth quickly for victory, scorching like the sun;
shatter the pride of your enemies, and may Dharma always be victorious for us. Surrounded by a great army, that one of immense splendor went forth.
12,067.029c Endowed with a noble lineage, as if blazing with splendor,
12,067.030a seeing that majesty of his— like the gods beholding Mahendra— all were struck with awe and fixed their minds upon their own duty.
The *varṇas*, the *āśramas*, all the *mlecchas*, and all the *dasyus*—
then he traversed the earth like a rain-bearing cloud,
pacifying evils everywhere and enjoining them to their own duties.
Thus, whatever men on earth at any time should desire prosperity,
they should first appoint a king for the sake of showing favor to their subjects;
and they should always revere him with devotion, like disciples toward a teacher.
Just as subjects look upon the thousand-eyed king in their presence like a god,
so too does even a stranger hold one in high esteem when he is honored by his own kin here;
yet, one who is despised by his own kin is surely overcome by others.
The humiliation of a king by his enemies brings unhappiness to everyone. Therefore, they should provide the king with an umbrella, vehicles, garments, ornaments,
food, drinks, and dwellings.
Seats, beds, and all necessary utensils [should be provided].
One should protect oneself and remain invincible, speaking with a smile;
and when addressed by others, one should respond to those men with sweetness.
One should be grateful, firm in devotion, sharing with others, and a master of one's senses;
when looked at, one should look back gently, uprightly, and pleasantly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, what do the wise brahmins say is the divinity of the king, the lord of men? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
O Bhārata, of how Vasumanas questioned Bṛhaspati.
King Vasumanas by name, the ruler of Kosala and the best among the wise—

Having performed all the duties of a disciple toward Bṛhaspati, the knower of discipline, and having become his immediate successor as the sacrificial fee, he, being of perfected wisdom, bowed according to the prescribed rites and questioned the great ṛṣi Bṛhaspati.
Devoted to the welfare of all beings and seeking the benefit of his subjects, O lord of the people, he asked about the method for governing the kingdom, which has dharma as its root:
"By what do living beings prosper, and by what do they go to ruin?"
"By worshipping whom, O one of great wisdom, may they attain ultimate happiness?
O divine sage, explain this to me—a doubt concerning dharma, pleasure, and wealth.
Thus was he questioned by the great king of Kosala, who possessed immeasurable splendor.
Bṛhaspati, with an undistracted mind, recounted to him the honors shown by kings,
the discernment of sovereignty,
and the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*).
"O Great King, it is observed that dharma for the world has its root in the king.
It is only through fear of the king that subjects do not devour one another. For the king alone [restrains] the entire world when it is agitated and restless."
He pleases others through righteousness, and having pleased them, he shines resplendent.
For just as, O King, when the moon and the sun do not rise,
all beings would sink into blinding darkness, unable to see one another.
For just as fish in waterless places or birds in a cry-less wilderness might roam about at will, approaching one another again and again, and having mated,
might even transgress against each other despite their mutual suffering; so too [is this state].

Without a king, these subjects would surely perish in no time; there is no doubt in this. Just so, without a king, these people would be destroyed and sink into blinding darkness like cattle without a herdsman.
For the powerful would seize the possessions of the weak,
and they would kill those who resist, were the king not to protect them;
[they would take] vehicles, clothing, ornaments, and various kinds of jewels.
If the king did not protect, wicked men would seize [property] by force;
"this is mine"—such a sense of possession would not exist in this world.
There would be no wife, no son, no wealth, and no property.
If the king did not protect, universal chaos would prevail; indeed,
people would afflict or even harm their mother, father, the aged, the teacher, the guest, and the preceptor, were it not for the king’s protection.

Various kinds of weapons would fall in many ways upon those who practice righteousness, and unrighteousness would prevail if the king did not protect; there would be constant slaughter, imprisonment, and affliction for those who possess wealth.
If the king did not protect, people would no longer find a sense of ownership; this world would become as empty as space and fall prey to bandits,
and it would plunge into a terrible hell if the king did not protect.

If the king did not protect, cattle-rearing would not flourish, nor agriculture, nor trade; the Dharma would sink away, and the Triple Veda would no longer exist. Sacrifices performed according to rule with their proper sacrificial fees would not proceed.
12,068.022c There would be no marriages nor social assemblies if the king did not protect.
12,068.023a Bulls would not be driven about, nor would churning-vessels be stirred;
12,068.023c Cowherd settlements would go to ruin if the king did not protect.

If the king did not protect [them], everything would perish in an instant—terrified, with agitated hearts, crying out "Alas! Alas!", and deprived of consciousness. Year-long sacrificial sessions could not be maintained without fear from any quarter.
If the king did not protect [them],

ascetic Brahmins who have bathed in knowledge and bathed in austerity would not study the four Vedas according to rule with the prescribed sacrificial fees. If the king did not protect [them], they would not do so.
One hand would rob the other, and all embankments would break apart;
everyone would flee, afflicted by fear, if the king did not protect them. The people, struck down and slaughtered, would find no connection to righteousness.

If the king does not protect, the perpetrator, acting according to his own will, would go unpunished; lawlessness would prevail, and there would indeed be a confusion of the social orders (varṇasaṃkara). Famine would seize the kingdom if the king does not protect.

For with the king as their protector, men lie down at ease, having opened the doors of their houses according to their desire, secure on all sides and free from fear. No one endures verbal abuse, much less the seizing of one's hand.
If the king among men is a righteous protector,
then women, unaccompanied by men and adorned with all their ornaments, travel the road without fear when the lord of the earth provides protection.
When the protector of the earth provides protection, people resort only to righteousness and do not harm one another; they favor each other,
and the three social orders perform various great sacrifices.

When the protector of the earth provides protection, those who are disciplined study the scriptures. For this world has its root in the means of livelihood (vārtā) and is always sustained by the three Vedas;
all that proceeds correctly when the protector of the earth provides protection.
When the king takes up the most excellent burden and carries the subjects with the application of great power, then the world prospers;
for in his absence, there would be the destruction of all beings on every side.

If existence were to arise from existence, it would be eternal; who then would not revere him who bears the burden that brings happiness to all the world? Indeed, he who would conquer both worlds should remain devoted to what is pleasing and beneficial to the king.
If a person should even mentally contemplate evil toward him,
he will undoubtedly suffer distress in this world and fall into hell after death.
Therefore, a ruler must never be treated with contempt on the grounds that he is merely a human being.
For this great deity indeed abides in human form;
he who always assumes five forms according to the occasion—
becoming Agni, as well as Āditya, Mṛtyu, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
For when a king is treated with deceit, he then burns the wicked with his fierce splendor; at that time, the king becomes like fire.
When the protector of the earth perceives all beings through his spies...
When he departs after establishing security, he is then the Sun;
but when, filled with wrath, he destroys hundreds of impure men along with their sons, grandsons, and ministers, he then becomes the Ender (Antaka).
When he restrains all the unrighteous with harsh punishments and favors the righteous, he then becomes Yama.
But when he gratifies his benefactors with showers of wealth, [he becomes Varuṇa].
He seizes various jewels from those who have done him harm; he bestows prosperity upon some and takes it away from others.
At that time, O King, Vaiśravaṇa becomes the sovereign ruler of the world.

One who is skillful and unwearied in action, desiring righteous gain and free from malice toward the Lord, should not stand in opposition to him. For one who acts contrary to the king shall not attain happiness.
Whether he be a son, a brother, a friend, or even one as dear as oneself, the fire,
driven by the wind,
will leave nothing remaining; yet for one overcome by a king, no remnant whatsoever exists.
One should avoid from afar all things belonging to him that are to be protected;
a man should shrink from seizing the property of a king as he would from death.
By touching it, he perishes instantly, like a deer that touches a trap.
A wise man in this world should protect the king’s property as he would his own;
for those mindless ones who steal the wealth of a king fall for a long time into a vast, terrible, and bottomless hell.
"King, Bhoja, Virāṭ, Samrāṭ, Kṣatriya, Bhūpati, Nṛpa—
whom would one not wish to honor who is praised with such words?
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should be disciplined, self-conquered, and have his senses restrained."
An intelligent, mindful, and capable man should seek refuge with a lord of the earth who is grateful, wise, noble-minded, firm in devotion, self-controlled,
constant in righteousness, and established in his proper conduct; such a minister the king should honor.
A king should take refuge in one who possesses firm devotion, whose wisdom is cultivated, who knows the Dharma, whose senses are restrained,
who is heroic, whose actions are not mean, and who keeps base people at a distance;
for such a person makes the king bold.
The king nourishes the emaciated man. For one who has fallen into the hands of the king, whence can there be happiness?
But the king makes him who approaches him happy.
The king is the primary body of his subjects,
and the subjects are the incomparable body of the king;
without a king, lands do not exist.
Kings do not exist without their territories;
the king is the heart of his subjects, their weightiest support, their refuge, and their supreme happiness.
Relying upon whom, noble men conquer this world and the next; and the lord of men,
having likewise governed the earth, [attains his goal].
By means of self-restraint, truth, and friendship,
and having performed great sacrifices,
the highly illustrious one attains a honored station in the triple heaven.
Thus addressed by his preceptor, that best of kings, the heroic ruler of Kosala,
diligently undertook the protection of his subjects.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What specific task remains for a king?
How is the realm to be protected, and how are enemies to be guarded against? How should he employ spies, and how should he inspire confidence among the social classes?
"How [should one treat] servants, how wives, and how sons, O Bhārata?
Bhīṣma said:
"O great king, listen with full attention to the entire conduct of kings."

Whatever task must first be undertaken by a king, or by one of royal nature, the self must always be conquered by the monarch; only then may his enemies be conquered. How can a lord of men who has not conquered himself defeat his foes?
This much constitutes the conquest of the self: the restraint of the fivefold group.
A king who has conquered his senses is able to overcome his enemies.
O joy of the Kurus, he should station military outposts in fortresses and during times of peace.
In the city groves, in the royal gardens,
in all the assembly places, in the cities of the realm,
and in the center, O tiger among men, as well as in the king’s palace.
Then he should make his appointments with men who appear dull, blind, or deaf,
yet have been tested and proven wise, and capable of enduring hunger, thirst, heat, and fatigue—
among all his ministers and his three kinds of friends.
O Great King, being composed, one should direct one's intentions toward one's sons,
as well as toward the city, the countryside, and likewise toward neighboring kings;
for they should be directed in such a way that they do not know of one another.

O bull of the Bharata race, one should recognize spies sent by the enemy in marketplaces, pleasure grounds, assemblies, and among mendicants; likewise in groves, gardens, and in gatherings of learned men.
In houses, at crossroads, in assembly halls, and in dwellings—
thus should a wise man counteract the enemy's spies with his own spies.
O Pāṇḍava, everything that is countered by means of a spy is truly destroyed.
But when a king perceives himself to be inferior by his own judgment,
he should consult with his ministers and conclude a treaty with one who is more powerful. Wise Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Brāhmaṇas who are deeply learned [should be consulted].
When the science of government has been mastered, the ministers of the lord of the earth should first consult a Brāhmaṇa who knows the true meaning of the treatises on policy;
thereafter, the protector of the earth should question a Kṣatriya who is skilled in the principles of statecraft.
Furthermore, a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who are learned in the scriptures and act for one's benefit may do so;
or one who is unrecognized as being of low status may indeed form an alliance with another, whether out of a desire to obtain some specific object or because he is a discerning man acting in haste.
A king, protecting his kingdom according to dharma, should form alliances with those who are virtuous, highly energetic, knowers of dharma, and righteous.
A high-minded king, perceiving himself to be on the verge of being destroyed, [should act accordingly].

He should slay those who have previously done him harm and those who are hated by the world in every respect. A lord of the earth who is unable to benefit [an enemy] nor able to harm him, and whose nature is such that he cannot be uprooted— such a person should be ignored.

A wise and heroic king, possessing a healthy, well-nourished, and content army, should order an expedition against one who is unknown, who has no allies, who has no immediate neighbor, or who is distracted, negligent, and weak. (12.069.019–12.069.020)
Having first established the regulations for the journey,
as well as within the city, the inner apartments, the kingdom, and among all the officials,
even a king who is powerful would not be able to bring him under his control.
Inferior in strength and valor, he should cause him to waste away and dwell in exile;
he should afflict his kingdom with weapons, fire, poison, and fainting spells,
and incite disputes among his ministers and favorites.
A wise king who desires his kingdom must always avoid war. Bṛhaspati has declared that the acquisition of wealth should be achieved through three means:
by conciliation, by bestowing gifts, and by sowing dissension, O lord of men.

A wise man should indeed be content with whatever wealth he is able to obtain; O joy of the Kurus, one of immeasurable wisdom should likewise take a sixth part as tribute from his subjects for their very protection.
Whatever wealth, whether great or small, belongs to those who follow the tenfold dharma, he should not take it by force, for the sake of protecting the citizens; indeed,
the citizens are to be regarded as his own sons— of this there is no doubt.
And they should be shown due respect when legal proceedings are presented; moreover, the king should appoint a wise son who perceives all matters to preside over legal cases,
for the kingdom is firmly established therein.
In mines, salt-works, customs stations, ferries, and elephant forests,
the king should station his ministers or trusted and loyal men. By always wielding the rod of punishment justly, the king shall attain righteousness.
The king’s punishment, when always applied correctly according to the Dharma, is highly praised.
O Bhārata, a king should be wise, a knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, devoted to rigorous austerity, and constantly disposed toward charity and the performance of sacrifice.
All these qualities should always remain firm in a king.
But if there is a lapse in his performance of duty, O King, whence can there be heaven, and whence fame?
For when a king is oppressed by a more powerful king...

Then a wise lord of the earth should take refuge in a fortress; he should cause his subjects to enter those regions that are both well-guarded and difficult to assault. Having called upon his friends in three ways, he should prepare his strategic measures.
One should devise regulations for the purpose of creating dissension through the methods of conciliation and sowing discord.
One should station outposts on the roads and even cause villages to be abandoned;
furthermore, one should cause all those people to enter into subordinate towns (*śākhānagaraka*).
He should cause [the enemy] to enter those regions that are well-guarded and difficult to access;
and having repeatedly conciliated the wealthy and the leaders of the forces,
the lord of men himself should carry out the collection of grain.
If entry is impossible, one should burn [the enemy's property] intensely with fire.
Regarding the crops standing in the fields, one should incite the men of the enemy,
or else destroy their entire wealth by means of one's own army.
He should always cause bridges on rivers and roads to be destroyed; he should drain all water, and whatever cannot be drained, he should pollute.
By disputing over both present and future matters with his immediate neighbors regarding the land, [he should create discord].
When the time for an ally has arrived, even during a conflict with another in battle,
the king should cause the cutting off of the roots of forts on all sides;
and among all small trees, he should spare the sacred *caitya* trees.
One should likewise lop off the branches of trees that have grown large;
however, one must avoid under all circumstances even the falling of a leaf from sacred shrines (*caityas*).
These shrines are the abodes of the gods, as well as of *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and serpents (*bhogins*).
Of the *piśācas* and *pannagas*, as well as the *gandharvas* and *apsarases*,
and even of the fierce *bhūtas*— therefore, one should avoid them. For it is heard that the army of Saudāsa was destroyed by Nikumbha.
O King, in Vārāṇasī, Maheśvara Gaṇeśa shall properly cause ramparts to be built for Ākāśajanani,
and he shall fill the moats which are teeming with crocodiles and fish of Sthāṇu.
There should be straw-filled gates for the purpose of ventilation in the city;
their protection must be carried out with every effort, just like that of the other gates.
And at these gates, one should always install heavy mechanical devices.
He should cause *śataghnīs* to be mounted [on towers] and ensure they remain under his own control;
likewise, he should have timber brought in and cause wells to be dug.
Furthermore, those seeking water should have previously constructed wells thoroughly cleaned.
One should plaster even with mud houses that are thatched with grass;
and in the month of Caitra, one should remove the grass from the city beforehand out of fear of fire.
Furthermore, O lord of men, the king should have his meals cooked only at night.
Fire should not be kindled during the day inside the house, except for the *agnihotra* sacrifice. One should have houses constructed using stones or bricks as available,
or one may build them of clay, having first assessed the relative strength and suitability of the site.
The fire, being well-composed, should burn in the workshops of smiths and in houses of ill omen;
furthermore, having entered the dwellings, the consumer of oblations (Agni) must be duly controlled. And for him whose fire appears during the day, there shall be a heavy punishment.

Then, for the sake of protecting the city, O best of men, he should cause a proclamation to be made as follows: "Beggars, wheelmen, those intoxicated or insane, and actors must be sent outside; otherwise, they would indeed lead to trouble."
At crossroads, at sacred fords, in assembly halls, and in dwellings,
the king should everywhere issue injunctions according to the appropriate social class.
Furthermore, the lord of men should cause wide royal highways to be constructed.
He should assign water-stations and marketplaces according to their proper locations; likewise,
he should assign in every respect the treasuries, armories, granaries,
stables for horses, stables for elephants, and the military headquarters.

O Kauravya, O Yudhiṣṭhira, no one at all should ever see the moats, the gateways, or the narrow passages; this is a secret. Furthermore, a king oppressed by the forces of an enemy should make a store of provisions.

He should cause stores to be made of oil, honey, ghee, grain, and all kinds of medicinal herbs; as well as of charcoal, *kuśa* grass, *muñja* grass, *palāśa* leaves, *śara* reeds, fodder, fuel, and poisoned substances.
The lord of men should cause stores to be made of all types of weapons— spears, double-edged swords, javelins, and armor—
as well as collections of such items as all medicinal herbs, roots, and fruits.
He should especially assemble the four kinds of physicians; likewise, actors, dancers, wrestlers, and magicians should adorn this preeminent city and gladden everyone in every way.
From whomsoever suspicion might arise— whether from a servant, a counselor,
the citizens, or even the king himself— one should bring them under one's own control. O Indra among kings, once the task has been accomplished, one should honor them with stores of wealth.
O joy of the Kurus, having subdued the enemy through appropriate honor and various forms of conciliation, or having slain him,
the king becomes free from his debt, as it is shown in the scriptures.

"O descendant of Kuru, there are exactly seven things that must be protected by a king; learn them from me: himself, his ministers, the treasury, the army, his allies, as well as the countryside and the city."

This kingdom, consisting of seven constituents, must be protected with great effort. O tiger among men, he who understands the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*), the three aims (*trivarga*), and likewise the other triad, enjoys this earth.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn that which is called the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*):
namely, remaining seated after making peace, and marching forth after making peace;
remaining seated after declaring war, and marching forth after declaring war."
Likewise, the policy of double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*), as well as seeking refuge with others and with the enemy,
and also that which is called the "threefold group" (*trivarga*)— listen to these here with a focused mind,
O Yudhiṣṭhira; understand them!
O mighty-armed one, I shall speak of decline, stability, and growth, as well as another triad:
dharma, artha, and kāma; indeed, this is the eternal triad.

Mantra, power (*prabhāva*), and the Tantric enthusiasm (*utsāha*)—these are declared to be the three powers (*śakti-traya*). They are the supreme means for the attainment of the three aims of life (*trivarga*). Furthermore, the effect, the cause, and the agent have been fully described.
O Bhārata, one should know this to be even higher than the triple aggregate (trivarga), for,
O King, when all things perish, that triple aggregate remains eternal. Sattva, rajas, and tamas— this triad is traditionally held to be the fundamental cause.
Therefore, one who is utterly liberated is called a "liberated person" (*mukta-puruṣa*).
The complete destruction of all that is to be done (*kārya*) is designated as liberation (*mokṣa*). For this reason, the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*), the God of gods, is intent upon liberation.
The lord of men has declared the protection of the three aims for the sake of contentment;
therein the worldly course of the universe is eternally established. Therefore, virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*) should be pursued according to their proper time.
O tiger among men, those intent on prosperity must constantly practice the service of Dharma; for all activities whatsoever have their root in that.
Indeed, O protector of the earth, it is through Dharma that a king protects the world for a long time.
Any righteous king, even if he has met with misfortune,
continues to protect the earth for a long time, even if he is deprived of wealth and pleasure.
And on this point, two verses were sung by Aṅgiras himself:
"O son of Yādavī, may it be well with you; you ought to hear those two as well:
having performed all duties and properly protected the earth, and likewise having guarded the citizens, one prospers in happiness in the next world."
Of what use is asceticism to that king, and of what use are his sacrifices,
if his subjects are unprotected and deprived of righteousness?
Listen, O Yudhiṣṭhira, to these verses sung by Uśanas.
O King, that which is the root of the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) and of the three aims of life (*trivarga*),
the practice of Bhārgava and Aṅgiras, the sixteen-fold power, poison, illusions, destiny, and human effort— all these exist for the accomplishment of one's purpose.
Having reached a stronghold sloping toward the northeast,
the lord of the earth should take up that place which is fully provided with the three groups of the three aims (*trivarga*) and carry it away.
Having conquered six, five, ten, and eight [fortresses], the king [should do so].
Endowed with the three goals of life and the ten [virtues], one is not conquered even by the gods. One should not adopt the counsel of women or of foolish people—
those whose intellects are struck down by fate and who are devoid of the Vedas.
The king should not listen to them, for their intellects are turned away [from wisdom]. Kingdoms where women hold preeminence and which are abandoned by the learned,
being tormented by foolish ministers, wither away like drops of water.

The king should listen to those who are learned and renowned, those who are trustworthy in all undertakings, and those who have witnessed the course of action in battles; for he should rely upon destiny, human exertion, and the three goals of life.
By bowing down to the deities and the Brahmins, one shall become victorious.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Both the science of government (daṇḍanīti) and the king—these two together are [the pillars of sovereignty].
"O Grandfather, tell me this: for whom and by doing what is success achieved?
Bhīṣma said:
[I shall describe] the great majesty of the science of government (daṇḍanīti) through accomplished words accompanied by their reasons."
"Listen to me as I speak correctly here, O King, descendant of Bharata:
the science of government (daṇḍanīti), when properly applied by the ruler, restrains the four social orders from their respective duties and likewise restrains them from unrighteousness."

When the four castes abide in their respective duties, when there is no confusion of social boundaries, and when security is established through the administration of justice so that the subjects are free from fear from any quarter,
the three castes exert themselves according to the rule in the performance of the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, know that the happiness of gods and men is firmly established therein.
Whether time is the cause of the king, or the king is the cause of time—let there be no doubt in you: the king is the cause of time.
When the king conducts himself entirely and correctly according to the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*),
then the most excellent period known as the Kṛta Yuga prevails. In the Kṛta Yuga, righteousness (*dharma*) exists and unrighteousness (*adharma*) is not found anywhere.
The minds of all social classes indeed do not delight in unrighteousness;
the security and well-being of the subjects proceed accordingly— of this there is no doubt—
and even Vedic rituals become free from defects.
All the seasons become pleasant and free from affliction; the voices, complexions, and minds of men become serene. No diseases occur there, and no man is seen who is short-lived.
In this [place], women do not become widows, nor is anyone born cruel;
the earth yields crops without being ploughed, and likewise the medicinal herbs,
as well as the bark, leaves, fruits, and roots, become potent.
"No unrighteousness exists there; there is only righteousness alone.
Know these to be the qualities of the Kṛta age, O Yudhiṣṭhira, when the king follows three parts of the science of government (daṇḍanīti).
Having relinquished one-fourth part, the Tretā age then sets in.
One-fourth part of the inauspicious follows after three parts;
at that time, the earth yields crops without being ploughed, and so too do the medicinal herbs.
When the king abandons half [of his duty] and follows only half of the policy of statecraft, then that period known as Dvāpara begins; at that time,
two parts of inauspiciousness prevail.

When the lord of the earth completely abandons the science of government (daṇḍanīti) and oppresses his subjects through improper means, the earth yields only what is sown and becomes scant in fruit; at that time,
the Kali age enters.
In the Kali age, unrighteousness is predominant, while righteousness exists only in some places;
the minds of all the social classes (varṇas) have fallen away from their own duties. Śūdras live by begging for alms, and Brāhmaṇas live by performing service.
The loss of security and well-being occurs, and there is a confusion of the social orders (varṇasaṃkara). Furthermore, Vedic rituals become deficient in their efficacy;
likewise, all the seasons become unpleasant and fraught with disease.
The voices, complexions, and minds of human beings decline;
diseases arise there, and people die before their allotted lifespan has ended. Furthermore, women become widows here, and the offspring born are cruel.

In some places the rain-cloud pours down, and in some places the crops sprout; yet all essences go to ruin when the protector of the earth, though established in the science of punishment, does not properly protect his subjects.
The king is the creator of the Kṛta age, as well as of the Tretā and Dvāpara; he is the cause that brings about the fourth age. Because he brings about the Kṛta age, the king enjoys heaven eternally.
By initiating the Tretā age, a king enjoys heaven, though not eternally;
by initiating the Dvāpara age, he enjoys it according to his share;
but by initiating the Kali age, a king incurs excessive sin.
Then that evildoer dwells in hell for eternal years; submerged in the impurity of his subjects, he incurs infamy and sin whenever the king governs by prioritizing harsh punishment.

The security and well-being of the subjects proceed [only] when the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) is placed at the forefront; of this there is no doubt. A Kṣatriya who always understands this must properly protect his subjects, for they grant all desires both in this world and after death.
A wise Kṣatriya should seek to acquire what has not been obtained and protect what has been acquired;
O Bhārata, he should strive for what is unattained and guard what is already gained.

The science of government, when properly administered, is the boundary-maker for the world and the nurturer of the world; know, O bull of the Bharatas, that all beings exist within it, just as they do under a mother and a father.
This alone is the supreme dharma: that a king possesses the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*).
Therefore, O descendant of Kuru, protect your subjects righteously and with wisdom.
By conducting yourself in this manner and protecting your subjects, you shall conquer heaven, which is otherwise difficult to win.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of conduct, by what behavior may a lord of the earth, while living in this world,
obtain with ease those goals that result in happiness both here and after death?"
Bhīṣma said:
This is the group of thirty-six qualities, endowed with thirty-six attributes;
by performing these qualities while possessed of virtue, one shall attain excellence.
One should practice righteousness without bitterness, and one who is not an atheist should abandon attachment;
one should pursue wealth without cruelty, and one should pursue pleasure without arrogance. One should speak what is pleasant without being fawning, and one should be brave without being boastful.
A donor should not rain gifts upon the unworthy; he should be bold yet not harsh.

He should not form alliances with the ignoble, nor engage in conflict even with his kinsmen. He should not employ spies through those who are untrustworthy, and he should carry out his business without causing oppression.
One should speak of matters of substance, but not of the virtues of the wicked, nor of one's own.
One should not take from the virtuous, nor should one rely upon a base person.
One should not inflict punishment without investigation, nor should one disclose one's secret counsel.

He should not give [wealth] to the greedy, nor should he place his trust in those who have done him harm. Free from envy, he should protect his wives; the king should be pure and yet not lacking in vigor.
He should not indulge excessively in women, and he should eat what is wholesome, not what is unbeneficial.
Free from arrogance, he should honor those worthy of respect and serve his teachers without guile; he should worship the gods without hypocrisy and desire only blameless prosperity.
He should cultivate affection by abandoning deceit, and he should be skillful, yet not one who disregards the proper time.
One should offer consolation, yet not for the sake of sensual enjoyment; one should favor others, yet not treat them with contempt.
One should strike, but not without discernment; having slain enemies, one should leave no remnant.
One should not give way to anger without cause, nor should one be mild toward those who do harm.

"Conduct yourself thus while established in the kingdom, if you desire what is beneficial here; otherwise, the king incurs unsurpassed danger. Thus, he who follows all these qualities as they have been described,"
"Having experienced auspicious things here in this world, one is glorified in heaven after death.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard these words of the son of Śantanu..."
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, surrounded by the foremost of the Pāṇḍavas,
paid homage to his grandfather; and the wise king did exactly as he had been told.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me this: how may a king, while protecting his subjects, avoid being bound by mental anguish and not fall away from dharma?"
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, I shall declare to you in brief the settled principles of dharma;
for one could never reach the end of dharma through its detailed exposition."
You should provide shelter in your home to virtuous twice-born men who are established in dharma, learned in the Vedas, devoted to their vows, and honored;
having risen to meet them, you should clasp their feet and offer them salutations.
Then, together with your family priest, you should perform all the necessary duties;
having completed the religious rites and performed the auspicious ceremonies,
you should have the Brahmins recite benedictions for the attainment of wealth and victory.
Endowed with sincerity, O Bhārata, as well as fortitude and intelligence,
one should pursue wealth while avoiding desire and anger.
That king who pursues wealth while placing desire and anger at the forefront [fails].
That fool grasps neither righteousness nor worldly prosperity.
Do not employ those who are greedy and foolish in matters of pleasure or wealth; rather, you should appoint those who are free from greed and endowed with wisdom to all tasks.
For a fool appointed to matters of state, being unskilled in affairs and possessed by desire and hatred, oppresses the subjects through improper means—
by taking a sixth part as tribute, by customs duties, and by fines for offenders.

One should seek the acquisition of wealth through wages according to the principles of the treatises. Having caused the lawful tax to be paid always according to rule, the king, remaining vigilant, should provide for the security and prosperity of the entire kingdom.
Men take delight in one who is a protector, a giver, constant in righteousness, unwearied,
and free from desire and hatred. Do not seek the acquisition of wealth through unrighteous gain.
For him who is devoted to what is contrary to the scriptures, both dharma and artha become unstable. A king devoted to what is contrary to the scriptures does not achieve accumulation;
and all that wealth of his perishes in an improper place.
Rooted in greed, he brings about his own destruction by personally inflicting violence upon his subjects through taxes not sanctioned by the scriptures, out of delusion.
For he who, desiring milk, cuts off the udder of a cow, shall obtain no milk.
For just as one who cuts down a tree that has already borne fruit does not obtain fruit again,
so too a kingdom oppressed by improper means does not prosper. Yet, by taking [only] fodder and water, and through conciliation and discipline, [it may be sustained].
For he who attends upon a milch cow always obtains milk;
in this same way, one who enjoys the kingdom through proper means obtains its fruit.
Now, when the kingdom is enjoyed through proper means and well protected—
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it constantly produces incomparable growth of the treasury;
when well-protected by the king, the subjects yield grain and gold,
just as a satisfied mother constantly yields milk for her own children and others.
"O King, be like a gardener and not like a charcoal-burner;
thus disciplined, you will be able to enjoy and protect your kingdom for a long time. Even if there should be a depletion of your wealth due to an invasion by a hostile army,"
12,072.021c Now, if you should seek wealth from those who are not Brahmins by means of conciliation alone,
12,072.022a let your mind never waver upon seeing a Brahmin established in wealth, even in the most dire of circumstances— how much less so, O Bhārata, when you are prosperous?
"You should give wealth to them according to your ability and as is appropriate;
by consoling them and protecting them, you shall attain heaven, which is difficult to conquer.
Thus, by conducting yourself with righteousness, you shall protect your subjects."

"O joy of the Kurus, you shall attain a life that is auspicious, meritorious, and glorious. O Pāṇḍava Yudhiṣṭhira, protect your subjects through righteous conduct; thus engaged, you shall not be bound by mental anguish."
This indeed is the supreme duty: that the king protects his subjects. For among all beings, protection is the highest dharma and the highest compassion;
having attained happiness in this world and on the earth in the world beyond.
Thus, from those Brāhmaṇas who have transcended the mind, according to the prescribed rule,
