you shall— through your virtuous conduct— conquer heaven, which is difficult to win, for the sake of enjoyment.
Therefore, those who are experts in dharma consider this to be the supreme dharma:
that a king, intent on protection, exercises compassion toward all beings.
For whatever sin he commits in a single day by failing to protect his subjects from fear, [he must bear its consequence].
In twelve thousand seven hundred and twenty-eight years, a king reaches the end of that merit which he acquires in a single day by protecting his subjects according to dharma;
for ten thousand years, he enjoys its fruit in heaven.
When a king, while protecting living beings, does not perform his duty,

then that monarch shall not obtain one-fourth of the merit of his subjects. As many worlds as one who performs proper sacrifices, studies properly, and practices excellent austerities conquers— [so many shall he lose].
In a single moment, he attains them while protecting his subjects according to dharma.
O Kaunteya, by thus diligently upholding dharma,
you will obtain the fruit of merit in this world and shall not be bound by mental anguish.
And you shall obtain great glory in the heavenly world, O Pāṇḍava;
for such dharmas as these cannot possibly exist among those who are not kings.
Therefore, there is no one other than a king who may attain such a great fruit.
Having obtained a prosperous kingdom and protecting it according to dharma,
he gratified Indra with soma and his friends with objects of desire.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, he alone who would protect the virtuous and eliminate the wicked should be appointed by the monarch as the royal priest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What kind of brahmin is capable and competent to deliberate upon what ought and ought not to be done by kings? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
12,073.002c The dialogue between Purūravas, the son of Īla, and Mātariśvan.
12,073.003 Aila said:
12,073.003a From where indeed was the Brāhmaṇa born, and from where did the other three social orders arise?
"And why is he superior? O Vāyu, explain this to me.
Vāyu said:
"O best of kings, the Brāhmaṇa was created from the mouth of Brahmā."

The Kṣatriya was created from the two arms, and the Vaiśya is said to have come from the two thighs, O bull among men, for the purpose of serving the other three castes. But the fourth caste, the Śūdra, was subsequently fashioned from the two feet.
As soon as he was born, the Brāhmaṇa took birth over the earth as the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma. Whatever is seen here belongs entirely to the Brāhmaṇa.
O Prince,
he then created for this world a second caste, endowed with righteousness and praised, consisting of Kṣatriyas who bear the rod of punishment to protect the earth and guard the subjects.
"A Vaiśya, moreover, should support these three castes with wealth and grain;
for a Śūdra should serve them—this is the instruction of Brahmā.
Aila said:
"O Vāyu, tell me correctly: to whom would this earth rightfully belong, along with its wealth—a twice-born man or a kṣatriya? Vāyu replied:
All this that exists within the world belongs to the Brahmin:
wealth, grain, gold, women, jewels, vehicles,
auspicious objects, praised things, and whatever else exists.
Those wise ones skilled in dharma know that, in this world, by virtue of seniority of birth,
the Brāhmaṇa eats only his own, wears only his own, and gives away only his own;
for the twice-born Brāhmaṇa is indeed the elder and the most excellent among all social orders.

Just as a woman, in the absence of her husband, takes her brother-in-law as her husband, so does the earth, due to immediate proximity, take the Kshatriya as her lord. This is your primary rule; in times of distress, there may be another.
12,073.013c If you seek the supreme station in heaven through righteousness,
12,073.014a whoever might conquer the earth should offer it to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning and good conduct, who knows the Dharma, and who is devoted to austerity.
He who is contented with his own duty and does not become intent on wealth;
he who would lead the king by means of a fully perfected intellect—
he is indeed a Brahmin born in a noble family, one whose wisdom is cultivated and whose speech is disciplined.
By speaking eloquent speech, he leads the king toward the highest good. That king who practices the dharma pointed out by the Brahmin—
being desirous of hearing, free from egoism, and established in the vow of the Kṣatriya dharma— [attains prosperity].
For that long, the man of perfected wisdom remains established in fame;
the royal priest partakes in all of that merit. In this very same way, all subjects depend upon the king.
And when a highly learned Brāhmaṇa, one who is proficient in the science of statecraft, [is honored],
then those who abide by their own duty and conduct themselves rightly, being well-protected by the king, move through the kingdom free from fear of any kind, practicing that which is Dharma.
The king obtains a fourth share of that merit. Gods, humans, ancestors, Gandharvas, Uragas, and Rākṣasas all subsist upon sacrifice; indeed, there is no ritual activity in a kingless land.
By what is given from here, the deities and likewise the ancestors live;
the security and prosperity (*yogakṣema*) of this very dharma are established in the king. In shade, in water, and in the wind, one finds comfort when it is hot.
In fire, in clothing, and in the sun, he finds comfort when it is cold;
his mind delights in sound, touch, taste, form, and smell;
through all those enjoyments, being free from fear, he attains happiness.
He who is the giver of fearlessness alone obtains a very great fruit;
indeed, no gift equal to the gift of life is found in the three worlds. Indra is king, Yama is king, and likewise Dharma is king.
The king assumes various forms; by the king all this is sustained.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What kind of person, according to his caste, should be appointed as the king’s domestic priest?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what kind of domestic priest (purohita) should be appointed—
one who is fair-complexioned, or red, or even dark, provided he is free from disease and happy."
Free from anger, not fickle, and having his senses conquered in every respect.
Bhīṣma said:
A king should appoint as his domestic priest one who is learned and has heard much.

"O King, having immediately considered both dharma and artha— which are immeasurable and infinite— it is certain that for those kings who have a righteous priest (purohita) who knows dharma and is himself a soul of dharma,
there shall be the attainment of artha, kāma, and dharma."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn those verses sung by Uśanas:
'That king shall be like one who has consumed the remnants of a meal who has no domestic priest (purohita).
[He is prey] for Rākṣasas, Asuras, Piśācas, serpents, and birds.'"
He who has no domestic priest shall be slain by his enemies. Therefore, a twice-born man learned in the Atharva-veda should perform the office of the *brahmán* at all sacrifices.
Furthermore, one should have the king perform all his ritual duties according to the Atharva-veda.
He should constantly speak of censurable matters, great portents, and evils,
as well as of things associated with sacrifices and auspicious rites, and concerning the inner apartments,
during the king's approved occasions for song and dance.

The Vaiśvadeva offerings and other rites that ought to be performed must be carried out; at the junctions of the fortnights, the domestic priest should perform the Mahāśānti rite and a thousand Raudra oblations for the welfare and benefit of his king.
The king’s seven sinful stains, which the domestic priest encounters, are:
ministers who perform evil deeds, counselors who are indifferent, and the practice of theft among those who should attend to legal proceedings.
Punishing those who do not deserve punishment, failing to punish those who deserve it,
and inflicting violence outside of battle or sacrifice are called impurities. Furthermore,
the destruction of subjects by incompetent ministers is the seventh great impurity.

Through fierce oblations, great rites of pacification, and the ritual of the "butter-blanket" (*ghṛtakambala*), the domestic priest who knows the ordinances of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras shall indeed cast out the impurities. Having abandoned these seven great impurities, the king goes to heaven.

O Kauravya, O high-minded one, while he was thus engaged in the office of domestic priest (purohitya) and devoted to the protection of his subjects along with his ministers and chaplain, the divine Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the lord of the gods, spoke these verses: 12,074.002b@008_0023 Accompanied by his ministers and his family priest, he was intent on the protection of his subjects. 12,074.002b@008_0024 O Kauravya, O high-minded one, it was in this very capacity as a domestic priest that 12,074.002b@008_0025 the divine Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the lord of the gods, uttered these verses.

"O highly fortunate one, learn of those auspicious duties beneficial to the protectors of the earth; for the rites of kings have not been specified in the three locations— the Ṛgveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Yajurveda."

They were cursed by Yājñavalkya, who was intent on the welfare of sacrifices, by that most excellent among those most devoted to Brahman, with the approval of the powerful Brahmā. [He performed] rites for pacification, for nourishment, and for the destruction of those things undesirable.
One should avoid a Bahvṛca, a Sāmaga, and a Vājina. A Bahvṛca leads to the destruction of the kingdom; a Sāmaga, to the destruction of the king;
and the Adhvaryu, known as a Vājasaneyaka, is said to lead to the destruction of the army.
Among the non-Brahmin castes, one should always avoid the Vājasaneyaka mantras in rites for pacification, prosperity, and daily observances;
[these mantras] are in every way not contradictory to the Brahmin king.

"The four Vedas—these are the Brāhmaṇas, as well as those who know them. O Lord of the Earth, a Brāhmaṇa is the authority in the office of the domestic priest; one who merely provides protection from injury is not declared a Kṣatriya by birth."
Even one who stands outside the four castes is considered a Kṣatriya if he possesses those [qualities]. Their ritual duties are prescribed by the mantras of Bhārgava and Aṅgiras;
namely, both the sacrificial rites (*vaitāna*) and those domestic rites (*gṛhya*) that are traditionally taught.
For the three twice-born classes, all ritual acts are prescribed;
however, for those engaged in the duties of kingship, he should cause three types of rites to be performed for the sake of their welfare:
the pacifying (śāntika), the nourishing (pauṣṭika), and that which is for malevolent purposes (abhicāraṇa).
Those twice-born ones who perform sacrifices— such as the Agniṣṭoma and others— polluted by worldly activities and desiring no proper fruit,
will bring about the destruction of kings while serving as their domestic priests.

When performing sacrificial rites, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) may be from any of the [three] hostile classes; indeed, all members of the *brahman*, *kṣatriya*, and *vaiśya* castes are excluded from the office of domestic chaplain (*purohita*). In the absence of such [eligible persons], it is ordained that one from a foreign land may be appointed for royal duties.
The sage Yājñavalkya declared that it was exactly so and not otherwise;
he was one who had mastered his studies in the Vedas of the Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras lineages, was learned in the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga),
and was an expert in the ritual procedures of sacrifice as well as the rites for prosperity.
One who knows the rules for the eighteen types of pacifying rites (*śāntikarma*),
is free from all diseases, self-restrained, and has controlled senses; [he is not afflicted] by vitiligo, leprosy, consumption, emaciation, planetary influences, or epilepsy.

The king should not converse with those who are ill-omened, those afflicted by wind-disorders (*vātaduṣṭa*), or those standing at a distance; he should avoid a sick person, a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*),
and a domestic chaplain (*purohita*) who has never before served as a chaplain for anyone else.
The king should avoid all those whose patron (yājya) has died, or who has fallen from his status, or has become a wandering mendicant, or has been defeated in battle;
as well as one who was born under an unfavorable constellation, O lord of men.
A royal priest who is trained in the science of statecraft is superior for a king; one who understands the meaning of inauspicious omens and portents,
and who knows how to bring about the destruction of the enemy faction, is a superior royal priest.
In the absence of those [Vedic specialists], he should appoint Carakas and Adhvaryus; then,

he should appoint as domestic priests (purohitas) those who are experts in the Ṛgveda and Sāmaveda, those who have exerted themselves in the science of polity (nītiśāstra), and those skilled in the Atharvaveda.
For the mantras prescribed by the twice-born performers of Vedic sacrifices are indeed characterized by violence;
a wise man should not utter them, as they are contrary to the duty of a Kṣatriya. The subjects possess the qualities of the priest, and the priest possesses the qualities of the subjects.
And for those kings who possess such qualities, there is welfare in every respect.
Both increase their subjects— the former gods and the latter ancestors—
those two who stand firmly established in dharma, worthy of trust, and devoted to great austerity.
When the two are mutual friends, esteemed by one another, and of equal mind,
the subjects shall attain happiness through the honor accorded to both the Brahmin and the Kshatriya. Indeed, from the dishonor shown to those very two, the subjects will surely perish.
For the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are said to be the root of all duties.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Aila and Kaśyapa; listen to it, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
12,074.007 Aila said:
For when Brahman abandons Kshatra,
or when Kshatra abandons Brahman—
"Who among them follow after his strength? And who among them depart from his weakness? Kaśyapa replied:
The kingdom of the Kṣatriya becomes ruined where the Brahman and the Kṣatra are in conflict;
the Dasyus then share in that power which follows [the ruin].
In that state, the virtuous pass away;
for them, neither the bull nor the cow prospers;
the churning-vessel is not stirred, nor do they perform sacrifice.
Their sons do not study the Veda when the Kṣatriyas abandon the Brahman;
not even a bull ever thrives in their house.
Those Brahmins who abandon the Kṣatriyas do not study, nor do they perform sacrifices with their progeny; cast out, they become like Dasyus.
For these two are eternally joined in mutual support:
O twice-born ones, the Kṣatriya is indeed the source of the Brahmin, and the Brahmin is the source of the Kṣatriya;
both of them are eternally dependent upon one another.
They both attained great prosperity and stability. If their ancient alliance were to be broken,
then everything would indeed fall into utter confusion.
One seeking the further shore finds no raft here;
like a ship driven away in a deep abyss,
the fourfold order of society becomes utterly bewildered.
Then the subjects fall into a state of decay;
when the Brahma-tree is protected, it rains honey and gold,
but when it is not protected, it constantly rains tears and evil.
One who is not a practitioner of the holy life has fallen away from conduct;
when Brahmā desires protection within the Brahman,
the god rains there with wonderful showers.
There, unbearable [torments] constantly enter him who,
being wicked, has killed a woman or even a Brahmin,
and where he receives reproach in the assembly.
He does not fear even in the presence of the king;
yet from that, fear arises for the kṣatriya when sins are committed excessively by the wicked.
From that, this god Rudra is born.
Sinful people produce Rudra through their sins;
he then destroys all, both the virtuous and the wicked.
12,074.018 Aila said:
"From where does Rudra come, or what is Rudra like? Is it that one being is seen by beings as being slain?"
"O learned Kaśyapa, explain this to me: from what is this god Rudra born? Kaśyapa said:
Rudra is the self within the hearts of men;
he strikes down both one's own body and the bodies of others.
They say Rudra is like the violent gusts of wind.
"His form is like that of forest fires and clouds.
Aila said:
"Indeed, no one can obstruct the wind;"
Neither does the cloud rain, nor does the forest fire burn;
yet one so engaged is seen among men,
for by desire and hatred one is bound and released.
12,074.021 Kaśyapa said: Just as a blazing fire in a single house might swiftly consume an entire village;
"O God, he performs this delusion;
therefore, everyone is touched by merit and sin.
Aila said:
If punishment touches one who possesses merit,
since there is no distinction when sins are committed by the wicked,
for what reason would anyone perform a virtuous deed?
"For what reason would one not commit an evil deed?
Kaśyapa replied:
"Because of the failure to abandon those who commit evil, the innocent [are affected];"
The same punishment touches one because of association: "The wet is burned by the dry because of association;
therefore, one should not associate with evildoers in any way."
Aila said:
"The earth sustains both the virtuous and the wicked here;
the sun warms both the virtuous and the wicked here."
"The wind here blows upon both the good and the wicked;
likewise, the waters carry away both the good and the wicked.
Kaśyapa said:
In this way, O Prince, does one fare in this world, but not so in the next. After death, there is a vast difference between these two states.
Whoever indeed performs merit and whoever performs evil— for such a person there is the world of merit, honey-sweet, glowing with ghee,
a golden light, the navel of immortality.
There the celibate student rejoices after passing away;
there is neither death, nor old age, nor suffering there.
The world of the wicked is hell, devoid of light.
It is eternally painful and abounds in grief;
there, the doer of evil deeds laments for himself,
falling for many years without any support.
Due to mutual dissension between Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas,
the subjects enter into unbearable suffering. Knowing this, a wise man must certainly act here in this world.

The king shall consecrate as his domestic priest one who possesses manifold knowledge; such is the dharma ordained. For the Brāhmaṇa is declared to be the foremost of all in this world according to dharma.
For those who know the Dharma understand that the Brahmins were created first;
by virtue of his superior lineage, he has obtained everything that is excellent. Therefore, the Brahmin is to be honored and revered, and he is the one who should eat the first portion of the food.
Everything that is most excellent and most superior must, according to dharma, be offered to him. Indeed, this must certainly be done even by a powerful king;
for Brahman increases the Kṣatra, and from the Kṣatra, Brahman increases.
"Thus, the Brāhmaṇas should always be especially honored by the king.
The royal priest is the master of the king and of everyone else.
Bhīṣma said:
"For the security and prosperity of the kingdom is said to depend upon the king; yet the security and prosperity of the king himself depends upon the domestic priest.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Grandfather, you have described to me the power of the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas,
the influence of the domestic priest, and the characteristics of the family priest; now I wish to hear the definitive distinction between the Brahmin and the Kṣatriya.
For the Brahmin and the Kshatriya are the supreme cause of the entire world;
indeed, the security and prosperity of the kingdom depend entirely upon them. Furthermore, the Brahmin pacifies whatever unseen fear may afflict the subjects.
And that kingdom, seen by the king with his own two arms, prospers in happiness. In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between King Mucukunda and Vaiśravaṇa.
Having conquered this earth, Mucukunda, the lord of the earth,
desiring to test his own strength, marched against the lord of Alakā.
Then King Vaiśravaṇa unleashed the Rākṣasas.
Crushing his forces, those Nairṛtas advanced;
as his own army was being slaughtered, Mucukunda,
the subduer of enemies and lord of men, censured his learned domestic priest.
Then, having performed fierce austerities, Vasiṣṭha, the foremost knower of Brahman,
struck down the *rākṣasas* there and found a path as well.
Thereupon, King Vaiśravaṇa showed himself to Mucukunda.
While the armies were being slaughtered, he spoke these words:
"Indeed, former kings along with their domestic priests were more powerful than you,
yet they did not behave in the manner that you are behaving here."

Indeed, those lords of the earth, skilled in weapons and possessed of great strength, come and wait upon me, the master of pleasure and pain. If you possess the prowess of your arms, you ought to display it.

"Why do you act with such excessive arrogance on the strength of your Brahminhood? Then Mucukunda, enraged, replied to the Lord of Wealth with these words that were righteous, composed, and free from agitation:

This Brahman and Kṣatriya order was created by the Self-Existent One from a single source; yet, through their distinct distribution of power, they protect the world. The strength of austerity and sacred mantras is eternally established among the Brāhmaṇas.
The power of weapons and the strength of arms are eternally established among the Kṣatriyas;
by combining these two, the protection of subjects must be performed.
Yet, O Lord of Alakā, you reproach me as I am engaged in such a task.
Then Vaiśravaṇa said to the king and his domestic priest:
"O King, know this: I do not bestow a kingdom upon anyone unless it has been designated [for them], nor do I take away one that has been so designated."
"O hero, rule this entire earth given by me.
Thus addressed, King Mucukunda replied.
Mucukunda said:
"O King, I do not wish to enjoy a kingdom bestowed by you;
I desire to enjoy a kingdom earned through the prowess of my own arms.
Bhīṣma said:
Then King Vaiśravaṇa was struck with supreme wonder upon seeing Mucukunda standing unperturbed, firmly established in the duty of a kṣatriya. Thereafter,
that King Mucukunda ruled over the earth.
One who is devoted to the duties of the Kṣatriya, having properly acquired [his wealth] through the strength of his own arms—
such a king who knows Brahman and proceeds with Brahman at the forefront,
conquers the unconquered earth and attains great fame.
A Brāhmaṇa should always carry water, and a Kṣatriya should always carry weapons;
for upon these two depends everything that exists within the world—
fame, splendor, and the entire earth.
O King, he attains vast fame;
O Lord of Men, uphold the primary dharma,
as well as one-fourth of the dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me by what mode of conduct a protector of the earth causes his subjects to prosper and conquers the meritorious worlds."
12,076.002 Bhīṣma said: O Bhārata, a king should be disposed toward generosity and disposed toward sacrifice;
he should be devoted to fasting and austerity, and intent upon the protection of his subjects.

The king should always protect all his subjects in accordance with dharma; he should honor the righteous through exertion and vigilance. For when dharma is honored by the king, it is then honored everywhere.
Whatever the king practices, that indeed pleases his subjects. He should always have his rod of punishment raised against enemies like Death itself;
he should strike down all bandits from every side and should not show leniency toward anyone out of favoritism.
For whatever dharma people practice here while well-protected by the king,
O Bhārata, the king obtains a fourth part of that dharma—
whatever he studies, whatever he sacrifices, whatever he gives, and whatever he worships.
The king, protecting his subjects according to dharma, receives a fourth part of that [merit].
O Bhārata, whatever evil exists in the kingdom due to the king's failure to protect his subjects, the king incurs a fourth part of that sin.
"O protector of the earth, some say that all [evil] comes from action, while others are certain that it is more than half; even a cruel man who speaks falsehood incurs such sin.
Listen now, O King, to how a monarch may be liberated from such transgression."
If wealth stolen by thieves cannot be recovered,
it should be paid from his own treasury by one who is unable to subsist [otherwise]. Furthermore,
the property of Brahmins and the Brahmins themselves must always be protected by all social classes.

One must not remain in the realm of those who would do harm to the twice-born; for when the property of a Brahmin is protected, everything becomes protected. When their favor is secured, the king has fulfilled his duty.
Just as all beings depend on the rain-cloud and birds upon a great tree,
so do men depend upon that king who accomplishes all their aims;
for a king whose soul is devoted to desire and who is constantly of deceitful intellect [cannot fulfill these roles].
"Subjects cannot be protected by one who is cruel and excessively greedy.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I do not seek the pleasures of sovereignty; I do not desire the kingdom even for a moment."
"I desire sovereignty for the sake of Dharma, yet here Dharma is not found. Therefore, enough of this kingdom for me where Dharma does not exist;
out of a desire to practice Dharma, I shall go to the forest itself."
"There, in sacred forests, having laid aside the rod of punishment and conquered my senses, I shall practice dharma as a sage subsisting on roots and fruits.
Bhīṣma said:
"I know that intellect of yours, which is characterized solely by the quality of compassion.
Yet, it is not possible to serve a great being through pure compassion alone;
for you are gentle, self-controlled, exceedingly noble, and most righteous."

The world does not hold in high regard one who is impotent and devoid of a sense of duty toward righteousness. Observe the duties of kings inherited from your father and grandfather; this conduct which you wish to adopt is not the way of kings.
For you have not remained here adhering to a compassion mixed with despondency;
indeed, you have obtained the fruit of dharma born from the protection of your subjects.
Neither Pāṇḍu nor Kuntī ever sought such a blessing as this.
Vicitravīrya was righteous-souled, yet he was not a king of such varied prowess as you; nor was Śantanu, the protector of the earth who was honored by all the kṣatriyas,
endowed with such wisdom, my dear, as that which you exercise with your intellect.
"Your father always spoke of your heroism, strength, and courage; Kuntī entreated for your majesty, power, and generosity. Both Svāhā and Svadhā—the divine and the human—were ever present."

The ancestors and the gods always place their hopes in their sons. Whether it be this dharma or adharma— charity, study, sacrifice, and the protection of subjects— you were born with these at the very moment of your birth.
O son of Kuntī, for those who are yoked to their duty at the proper time and bear the burden placed upon them, even if they sink under its weight, their fame does not perish—
provided that they carry it forward unswervingly, restrained on all sides.
Because of the statement regarding faultless action, that success belongs to action alone;
no one here— whether a practitioner of dharma, a householder, a king, or even a celibate student— has ever wandered about without some degree of inevitable downfall.
Even a small deed that is predominantly virtuous is indeed a noble action; what is performed is better than what is left undone, for there is nothing worse than inaction.
This is especially true when one born of noble lineage and knowing the Dharma attains supreme sovereignty.
O King, at that time, security and prosperity lead only to well-being.
Having obtained a kingdom here, a righteous man should win over others through gifts, others by force, and others with truthful speech; thus he should encompass all from every side.
"For when physicians born of noble lineage, oppressed by the fear of lacking a livelihood,
obtain [wealth] from him and remain satisfied, what dharma could be greater than that?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What indeed is more conducive to heaven than this? What indeed is the highest joy than this? What indeed is the supreme sovereignty than this? Tell me, if you so deem it.
Bhīṣma said:
12,076.034 "He upon whom they are firmly established finds peace at that very moment;
he is the greatest conqueror of heaven for us—I tell you this as the truth. 12,076.035 Therefore, O best of the Kurus, you alone should be the one who takes pleasure in the welfare of the Kurus."
"Be a king, conquer heaven, protect the righteous, and slay the unrighteous. O dear one, let your friends, together with the virtuous, live depending on you—
just as all beings depend on the rain-cloud, or as birds depend on a tree laden with sweet fruit."
"May people live after you—you who are bold, heroic, a striker, compassionate, and a master of your senses; you who are affectionate and a generous sharer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"12,077.001 Some are engaged in their own duties, while others are likewise engaged in improper duties.
12,077.001c Tell me the distinction between those Brāhmaṇas, O Grandfather.
12,077.002 Bhīṣma said:
Endowed with the characteristics of knowledge and seeing the sacred tradition everywhere—
these Brāhmaṇas, O King, are proclaimed to be equal to Brahman. They are perfected as officiating priests and teachers, remaining steadfast in their respective duties.
O King, these [four] among the Brahmins are equal to gods; furthermore, O King,
the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the domestic chaplain (*purohita*), the minister (*mantrin*), the envoy (*dūta*), and the counselor on state affairs (*arthānuśāsaka*)—
these among the Brahmins are equal to Kshatriyas.
Those who rear cattle, sheep, buffaloes,
and mares for their livelihood are designated as Vaiśyas,
O Bhārata, as they desire power and seek material gain.
Those twice-born ones who delight in punishing and favoring others are known as Kṣatriyas.
O King, those among Brāhmaṇas who are horse-riders, elephant-riders, chariot-fighters, or foot-soldiers are indeed equal to Vaiśyas.
Whatever regions of the Mlecchas there may be that are inhabited by sinful men— a Brāhmaṇa who goes to those places becomes a Caṇḍāla both after death and in this world;
likewise, the lowest of the twice-born who officiates at sacrifices for Vrātyas, Mlecchas, and Śūdras [incurs the same fate].
Having incurred infamy in this world, he falls into hell for twenty-one cycles, alternating between the Mahāvṛnda and Samudra hells,
having brought about the ruin of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas through his folly.
For one *kalpa*, he is then born as a worm in various kinds of excrement—
among the *vrātyas*, the *mlecchas*, the *śūdras*, the thief, the outcast, and the impure;
in a wretched land, among the drinker of spirits, the slayer of a Brahmin, and the husband of a *vṛṣalī*.
One should never, under any circumstances, eat in the company of those who have not studied the Vedas, those who eat anywhere and everywhere,
those who kill children, women, or the elderly, nor with one’s mother, father, or teacher,
nor with one who betrays a friend, one who is ungrateful, or a killer of a cow.

A twice-born man should not employ mantras against one who has killed his son or against an enemy; this is declared by the eternal masters of mantra to be their failure. This applies even if the Brahmin is residing in a foreign land or has gone on a pilgrimage.

If a twice-born man, whether out of fear or having sought refuge, should recite the mantras while in an impure place devoid of cleanliness, he must do so being well-restrained and having become pure. Alternatively, one who is afflicted or intent on protecting the afflicted may likewise recite the mantra.
Even when employing [harsh words] toward those who are inferior, he is not considered a transgressor;
whether his actions are cruel or virtuous, or perhaps deceived by his own deeds,
the knower of reality avoids evil, being possessed of good character and restrained senses.
"O King, those who are devoid of [proper] birth and conduct, who are miserly, and who are Brahmins in name only (brahmabandhus)— these are equal to Śūdras among Brāhmaṇas. Indeed,
all those who are not learned in the Vedas (aśrotriya) and all those who have not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) are likewise so."

A righteous king should cause all of them to pay taxes and perform labor service. Those who summon [deities], those who subsist on temple offerings, those who sacrifice for villages, and those who sacrifice for constellations—
these are the *brāhmaṇa-caṇḍālas*, with the long-distance travelers as the fifth.
A king whose treasury is depleted may take tribute from these [people],
except for those equal to Brahmins and those who are like gods;
for it is a Vedic teaching that the king is the master of the wealth of non-Brahmins.
And whatever Brāhmaṇas may be engaged in improper occupations—
whether those already mentioned or those not yet mentioned— the king should cause them all to pay taxes.
However, those engaged in improper occupations must never, under any circumstances, be overlooked by the king.

They should be restrained and provided for with the desire to favor them through dharma. People who know the truth consider it the fault of the king himself if a twice-born man becomes a thief within his realm.

"O King, those who know the Dharma understand that even a thief who is a knower of the Vedas and a *snātaka* should be supported by the king through the provision of a livelihood. O scorcher of foes, if he does not turn back from his ways once a livelihood has been provided, [he should be punished]."
Then he, along with his kinsmen, should be banished from that country.
Sacrifice, sacred learning, freedom from backbiting, non-violence, honoring guests,
self-restraint, truthfulness, austerity, and charity— this is the characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharata race, over whose wealth does the king have power?
And by what conduct should he live? Tell me that, O Grandfather."
Bhīṣma said:
According to the Vedic tradition, the king is the master of the wealth of those who are not Brāhmaṇas;
and as for Brāhmaṇas, he is likewise the master of the wealth of any who are established in improper occupations.
"Brāhmaṇas who persist in improper occupations must never be overlooked by a king under any circumstances.
Thus do the virtuous recount the ancient precedent regarding kings:
"In whosever kingdom, O King, a twice-born man becomes a thief..."
"O King, they consider that sin to be the fault of the king alone;
because of that deed, they regard themselves as if they were accursed.
Therefore, all royal sages protected the Brahmins."
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
sung by the King of Kekaya while he was being carried away by a *rākṣasa*:
"A fierce *rākṣasa* seized the sovereign of the Kekayas."
"O King, he was devoted to the study of the Vedas and firm in his vows while living in the forest.
The king said:
"In my kingdom there is no thief, no miser, and no drinker of intoxicants."
You have not entered my domain unless you were one who has maintained the sacred fires, nor one who is uninitiated in sacrifice;

nor was there in my realm an unlearned Brāhmaṇa, nor one who observes no vows, nor one who does not drink the Soma, nor one who has not established the sacred fires. You have entered my domain only as such.
In my realm, no one performs sacrifices without giving the prescribed sacrificial fees; no one studies the Vedas without observing the vows. Enter my domain, O you who have entered it!
They study and teach, they sacrifice and officiate at sacrifices.
Established in the six duties, they give and receive; honored and sharing their wealth, they are gentle and truthful. These Brāhmaṇas remain steadfast in their own tasks—enter my inner self!
Those who are proficient in truth and dharma do not beg, but give;
they do not teach, yet they study; they do not perform sacrifices, nor do they act as officiating priests.
They protect the Brahmins and do not flee from battles.

"12,078.014c My kṣatriyas remain steadfast in their own duties; they have not entered into my domain. 12,078.015a They subsist by agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade without deceit; 12,078.015c they are vigilant, observant of ritual acts, firm in their vows, and speakers of truth."

Devoted to sharing, self-restraint, purity, and friendliness, my Vaiśyas remain established in their own duties; free from malice, they attend to the three other castes in accordance with the law. And so, O you who have entered my inner domain!
"O you who have entered my innermost heart, my Śūdras remain steadfast in their own duties.
I provide for the distribution of sustenance to all—the wretched, the helpless, the elderly, the weak, the sick, and women; O you who have entered my innermost heart."

"I shall not allow the interruption of any of the well-known religious traditions of my family, country, and so forth, according to the prescribed rules; do not enter into my heart. In my realm, ascetics are honored and protected."
Having shared [my wealth] with due honor, you have entered my inner heart. I do not eat without sharing, nor do I approach another's wife;
never playing for sport while acting independently, you have entered my inner heart.
One who is not a practitioner of celibacy does not possess the status of a monk, nor does a monk who is not celibate.
There is no sacrifice offered by one who is not a priest; do not enter into my inner heart. While I held the position of king, I have performed all the duties of kingship.
I have not deviated from the truth; do not enter my inner self! I do not despise the elders, nor the learned, nor the ascetics. While the kingdom sleeps, I remain awake; do not enter my inner self!
"I am one whose actions are pure in every respect; I have no fear of an evil rebirth.
Though I am a householder practicing the Dharma, do not harbor any ill will toward me. I am perfected in the study of the Vedas, an ascetic, and a knower of all duties."
"The illustrious lord of my entire kingdom is my priest.
Through generosity, I desire the divine worlds;
likewise, through truthfulness and the protection of the brahmins."
Through service I attend upon my elders;
I have no fear of the Rākṣasas.
In my kingdom there is no widow nor any Brahmin of base character.
I am neither a wretched Brahmin nor a thief, neither an adulterer nor a doer of evil deeds;
I have no fear of the Rākṣasas.
"There is not a space of even two fingers' breadth on my body that has not been pierced by weapons.
While fighting for the sake of dharma, you have entered into my very heart. My constant welfare lies in cows, brahmins, and sacrifice."
"People in the kingdom hope for [the end of] my rule; enter into my heart!
The Rākṣasa said:
"Due to the infidelity of women and the injustice of kings..."
Due to the sinful actions of the Brahmins, fear arises among the subjects:
drought, pestilence, disease, and constant terrors of hunger;
and in that land, there is always terrible conflict.
No fear whatsoever arises there from yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, or asuras, wherever brahmins are well-restrained; nor do gandharvas, apsarases, siddhas, pannagas, or reptiles cause fear.
Where women are devoted to their husbands, men do not seek to harm one another;
where Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are righteous,
there is no fear of irregular rains, nor famine, nor social upheaval.
Wherever there is a righteous protector of the earth, there is no defeat;
neither celestial nor human portents are seen there,
because you, in all circumstances, look only toward the Dharma.
"Therefore, O Kaikeya, go safely to your home; I am departing. For those, O Kekaya, for whom cows, Brahmins, and their subjects are protected, they have no fear of Rākṣasas, much less of humans."
Those men whose leaders are Brahmins, whose strength is the power of the Veda (*brahmabala*), and whose wives are fond of hospitality— they are indeed conquerors of heaven. Bhīṣma said:
Therefore, one should protect the twice-born, for when they are protected, they in turn protect [the king]. Through their blessings, the kingdom of kings prospers properly.
Therefore, a king must especially guard against those twice-born who persist in improper occupations.
Those who are to be restrained and those who are to be favored should be treated with impartiality for the sake of benefiting the subjects.
A king who conducts himself in this manner toward the people of both the city and the countryside experiences auspicious things in this world and attains the same world as Indra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, you have explained the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa in times of distress according to the duty of a Kṣatriya;
may he live by the duty of a Vaiśya in some way, or may he not?"
12,079.002 Bhīṣma said:
One who is incapable [of fulfilling] the duty of a Kṣatriya should live by the duty of a Vaiśya,
resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing when his livelihood is diminished due to misfortune.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, what commodities may a Brāhmaṇa sell while following the dharma of a Vaiśya without falling away from the heavenly worlds?"
Bhīṣma said: O Yudhiṣṭhira, [one should avoid] liquor, salt, sesame seeds, maned beasts, bulls, honey, meat, and prepared food.
In all circumstances, a Brāhmaṇa should avoid these;
by selling them, my dear, a Brāhmaṇa goes to hell.
The goat is Agni, the ram is Varuṇa, the horse is Sūrya, and the cow is Virāj.
A cow, a sacrifice, and Soma must never be sold under any circumstances.
The virtuous do not praise the bartering of cooked food for raw grain; O Bhārata, one may indeed exchange cooked food for raw grain for the purpose of obtaining a meal.
"We shall eat what is already prepared; may you prepare this [food] yourself.
Considering it thus and exchanging [the roles], there is never any unrighteousness. In this regard, I shall explain to you the ancient dharma."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn from me that which pertains to those engaged in legal proceedings:
"I give this to you; you must give that to him. When a matter proceeds according to what is agreeable, it is dharma; it does not proceed by force.
"In this manner, these ancient legal procedures were established for both the seers and others; this is undoubtedly virtuous.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"Then, dear one, when all subjects take up weapons and deviate from their own duties, the strength of the Kṣatriya wanes. When there is no king as a protector in the world, what then would be the ultimate refuge?"
"O Grandfather, explain this doubt of mine to me in detail.
Bhīṣma said:
"By means of charity, austerity, sacrifices, non-malice, and self-restraint..."
The social classes, headed by the Brahmins, should desire their own security.
Among them, those who possess the strength of the Vedas should rise up on all sides and increase the king’s power,
just as the deities increase the power of Mahendra.
For they say that for a king who is declining, the Brahman alone is the ultimate refuge;
therefore, one who understands should rise up by means of the power of the Brahman alone.
But when the victorious king establishes security within his kingdom, [he should act accordingly].
Then the social orders (varṇas) would engage in their own duties according to dharma.
But when lawlessness prevails and confusion is created by bandits,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, all the orders would not be at fault if they were armed in battle.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Now, if the Kṣatriyas should become hostile toward Brāhmaṇas on all sides, who would be the protector of those Brāhmaṇas? What is their duty, and what is their ultimate refuge?"
12,079.020 Bhīṣma said: At that time,
it must be restrained by means of austerity, celibacy, weapons, and strength,
as well as by both guilelessness and guile.

When the Kṣatriya power has grown excessively, especially toward the Brāhmaṇas, the Brāhmaṇa alone must be its restrainer; for the Kṣatriya is born from the Brāhmaṇa. Fire arose from water, the Kṣatriya from the Brāhmaṇa, and iron from stone.
The all-pervading energy of these three subsides within their own sources when iron strikes stone, when fire encounters water,
and when a Kṣatriya hates a Brāhmaṇa; then those three are extinguished.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the exalted, invincible splendors and powers of the Kṣatriyas are stilled within the Brahman,
once the power of the Brahman has become mild and the power of the Kṣatra has grown weak.
When all the castes have become corrupt in every respect toward the Brahmins,
what worlds await those who fight there, having renounced their own lives,
and protect the Brahmins?
Protecting the brahmins, as well as dharma and their very selves,
those high-minded and indignant men attain the worlds of merit;
for the taking up of weapons by all is desired for the sake of the brahmins.
Beyond the worlds of those who have performed excellent sacrifices and well-recited prayers, and beyond those of the ascetics,
those heroes who enter into fasting unto death or the sacred fire attain the supreme goal;
indeed, people know no other dharma than this self-sacrifice.

"Homage and blessings to those who offer their bodies as oblations, subduing the haters of Brahman; may we share the same world with them. Manu declared that those heroes are conquerors of the world of Brahmā and destined for heaven.

Just as those who have bathed at the final purificatory rite (*avabhṛtha*) of an Aśvamedha sacrifice become purified, so too do those slain by weapons in battle— both the evildoers and the well-doers— become pure. For indeed, both unrighteousness (*adharma*) and righteousness (*dharma*) [are transcended].
Due to the influence of place and time, such is the nature of place and time:
those who are friendly yet perform cruel deeds conquer the highest heaven;
those who are righteous yet commit sins go to the supreme goal.

A Brāhmaṇa incurs no fault by taking up arms on three occasions: when protecting himself, when defending others from bandits, and for the sake of self-preservation, to prevent the loss of caste, or in the defense of a fortress.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When the force of bandits has arisen for the sake of the Kṣatriyas amidst the confusion of the castes,
and when the social orders are utterly bewildered, if another powerful man should overcome them;
O best of kings, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra,
if he protects his subjects from bandits while upholding the rod of punishment according to dharma,
he may or may not perform his specific duties, and he may or may not be subject to restraint.
"One should not take up a weapon, except against one who is a kinsman of the kṣatriya class.
Bhīṣma said:
"He who is without a shore may become a shore; he who is without a boat may become a boat."
Whether he be a Śūdra or even someone else, he deserves honor in every way,
O King, by depending upon whom men may live in happiness;
for those who are without a protector, being oppressed by bandits, truly require protection.
They should honor him with affection, as if he were their own kinsman;
for one who constantly performs great deeds, O Kauravya, deserves high respect.
What use is there for a bull that does not carry a load, or for a cow that gives no milk?
What is the use of a barren wife? What is the use of a king who does not provide protection?
He is like an elephant made of wood, like a deer made of leather, like a cart without wheels on the road, or like a field of saline soil.
Thus, a king who does not protect, a Brahmin who does not study,
and a cloud that does not rain— all these are useless.
But he who constantly protects the virtuous and destroys the wicked [is truly effective].
"He alone should be made king, for by him all this is sustained.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, from what origins should the officiating priests (ṛtvij) arise, and what should be their character?"
"O Indra among kings, O best of speakers, tell me: what kind of person is he?
Bhīṣma said:
In former times, a specific ritual action was prescribed for the officiating priests."
Having first mastered the Vedic meters and the sacred learning of the twice-born—
those who are always single-mindedly devoted, steadfast, and never speakers of what is unpleasant; who are friends to one another, highly esteemed, and possessed of equal vision.
O Lord, those who possess compassion, truthfulness, non-violence, austerity, and straightforwardness;
who are free from malice and pride, and who possess modesty, forbearance, self-restraint, and tranquility—
it is with these very qualities that the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) should be endowed.
He in whom these qualities are seen is called a *purohita*:
one who is modest, firm in truth, self-controlled, and non-injurious toward living beings; one who is free from desire and hatred, and endowed with the three "whites."
"Non-violent and satisfied with knowledge, he is worthy of the seat of Brahman.
O dear one, all these great officiating priests (mahartvijas) are to be honored exactly as they are.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
This Vedic injunction which is prescribed regarding sacrificial fees—
that "this is to be given" and "that is to be given"— is not fixed in any single instance;
for this scripture does not concern wealth [in general], but rather the duty in times of distress according to what is not [ordinarily] taught.
This command of the scripture is formidable; it does not take one's capacity into account. "One should sacrifice, beginning with faith"—this is the Vedic revelation.
What indeed will faith accomplish for a sacrifice performed falsely?
Bhīṣma said:
No one attains greatness through contempt for the Vedas, nor through deceit, nor through illusion;
let not such a thought arise in you.
The sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), my dear, is a limb of the sacrifice and the nourishment of the Vedas.
Mantras devoid of sacrificial fees do not save one in any way whatsoever.
However, even a fee equal to a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) should be considered as no less than a minimum.
"O dear one, the three castes must certainly sacrifice according to the prescribed rule. 'Soma is the king of the Brāhmaṇas'—this is the Vedic revelation (śruti).
They desire to sell him [the Soma], yet a livelihood gained by improper means is not desired."
12,080.013e With that dharma purchased by him, the sacrifice is then extended. 12,080.014a Thus has it been declared according to dharma by the rishis who speak of dharma:
12,080.014c how a man, the sacrifice, and Soma may come to be established in righteous conduct.
"A man of unjust conduct belongs neither to another nor to himself.
"The body is the sacrificial vessels"—this is the Vedic revelation (śruti) that is heard. These [vessels] are properly prepared for the high-souled Brāhmaṇas.
"Austerity is superior even to sacrifice—this is the supreme Vedic revelation. O learned one, I shall explain that austerity to you; listen to it from me.
Non-violence, truthful speech, compassion, self-restraint, and kindness."
The wise know this to be austerity, not the mere emaciation of the body:
the denial of the authority of the Vedas, the transgression of the scriptures,
and a lack of stability in all matters— this indeed is the destruction of the self.
O Pārtha, learn now what the nature of the ordinance of the ten *hotṛ*s is:
consciousness is the sacrificial ladle, thought is the clarified butter, and supreme knowledge is the purifier;
freedom from deceit, freedom from crookedness, time, and place—these are the ten.
"Everything crooked is the path of death; straightforwardness is the path of Brahman. Such is the scope of knowledge; what will mere idle talk accomplish?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"Even a very small task is difficult for a single man to accomplish without assistance; how much more so a kingdom, O Grandfather? What kind of character and what kind of conduct should a king’s minister of affairs possess?"
"In what kind of person should a king place his trust, and in what kind of person should he not place his trust?
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, there are four kinds of friends for kings."

The friend who shares wealth is of two kinds: innate and acquired. The fifth type of friend is the righteous one; he belongs neither to one side nor to both, for he stands where righteousness lies, or else he remains neutral.
One should not reveal to another that matter which he would find unpleasant. O Bhārata, there is no inherent nature of friendship or enmity;
one becomes a friend through a benefit and an enemy through an injury.
For when a man desires death for another person,
he desires life for that same person once his own time has arrived;
thus kings, seeking victory, conduct themselves according to both dharma and adharma.
Of the four, the two middle ones are the best, yet the other two must always be suspected;
indeed, all must always be viewed with suspicion, for one's own affairs must be witnessed firsthand. A king must certainly never be negligent in protecting his friends.
For the worlds indeed despise a king who is negligent; the wicked man attains goodness, and the good man becomes cruel;
the enemy becomes a friend, and even a friend becomes corrupted.
A person whose mind is fickle—who could ever place trust in him?
Therefore, one should perform that primary task which is directly perceptible;
for absolute trust entirely destroys both dharma and worldly prosperity.
Lack of trust toward everyone is no different from death itself. Trusting in what is not timely leads to ruin;
for one who places trust in such a thing perishes, while the one who desires it lives.
Therefore, one should both place trust and remain suspicious of certain people;
this, my dear, is the course of policy and the eternal way to prosperity. One should consider: "Upon my death, this acquisition of wealth might fall to him."
Therefore, one should always be wary of such a person; the wise know him to be an enemy.
Even when water from one's own field flows into the field of another, the embankments of that other person should not be broken, even if he does not wish it.

Likewise, one who is terrified of [the enemy's] great power and desires its destruction—one should designate such a person as an enemy. Furthermore, one who is not satisfied by prosperity and becomes even more dejected in times of decline; one should recognize him as an enemy.
This is declared to be the characteristic of a supreme friend:
one whom one might think, "In my absence, he will cease to exist"—
in such a person one should place trust, just as one would in a father.

One should strengthen him with all one's power as he prospers; for he who constantly protects one from injury even in matters of duty and action— one should recognize such a person, who fears injury, as the highest mark of a friend.
Those who seek his downfall are considered his enemies. One who is constantly afraid of calamities and finds contentment only in prosperity—
such a friend is said to be equal to one's own self.
Endowed with beauty of form, complexion, and voice, patient, and free from envy; of noble birth and perfected in character—he should be your immediate successor.
Intelligent, possessed of a retentive memory, skillful, and by nature compassionate.
Whether honored or dishonored, he who is never corrupted at any time—
whether he be a sacrificial priest, a teacher, a friend, or one highly esteemed—
should dwell in your house as a minister, being held in the highest honor.
He shall know your supreme counsel and the nature of both material prosperity and dharma;
you should place as much trust in him as you would in a father. Neither two nor three [ministers] should be appointed, lest they should harbor mutual resentment toward one another.
12,081.025c From a single purpose alone, the diversity of beings always arises.
12,081.026a He who is preeminent in fame, and he who remains steadfast in his commitment;
12,081.026c he who does not hate those who are capable, and he who makes others capable.
He who would not abandon the Dharma out of desire, fear, greed, or anger—
one who is skillful and possesses sufficient eloquence— should be your immediate successor;
he must be brave, noble, learned, and proficient in practical action.
One who is of noble birth, endowed with virtuous conduct, patient, and free from envy—
such men should be appointed as ministers, established in all duties, honored, provided with shares of wealth, well-supported by allies, and properly maintained.
All these have been appointed to their respective duties;
engaged in great tasks, they bring about prosperity.
They perform their works, always emulating one another.
They carry out their affairs while conversing with one another;

therefore, you should always fear your kinsmen as if they were death itself, for a kinsman never tolerates the prosperity of a relative, just as a subordinate king cannot endure the wealth of a sovereign.

"O mighty-armed one, no one other than a kinsman rejoices at the destruction of one who is upright, mild, generous, modest, and truthful. Not being a kinsman is not particularly pleasant; therefore, one should never treat them with contempt."
Others indeed despise a man who has no kinsmen;
for one who is treated with contempt by other men, his kinsman alone is his refuge. A kinsman never tolerates the humiliation of a kinsman by others.
One perceives only oneself as being treated with contempt even by one's own kinsmen;
yet while virtues do exist in them, their lack of virtue is what is observed.
No one who is not a kinsman bestows favor, and no one who is not a kinsman shoots a poisoned arrow.
In the worlds of one's kinsmen, both the good and the bad are seen.
One should always honor and worship them through both word and deed;
one should do what is pleasing to them and never perform anything unpleasant.
One should always behave toward them as if trusting while remaining distrustful;
for neither fault nor virtue is seen in them when one is intimately involved with them. For a man who conducts himself in this way and remains vigilant, [there is no danger].

12,081.040c Enemies become completely appeased, and likewise they even become friends. 12,081.041a He who always conducts himself in this manner within the circle of kinsmen and relatives, 12,081.041c among friends and enemies alike, shall long endure in power and in fame.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In this way, when that circle of kinsmen and relatives is ungraspable, how is one's disposition toward friends and even enemies to be discerned?"
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Vāsudeva and the celestial sage Nārada.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Nārada, one who is not a friend does not deserve to know the supreme counsel;
nor does an unwise person, whether he be a friend or a wise man, provided he lacks self-control."
"O Nārada, relying on our friendship, I shall say something to you; O traveler to the third heaven, having considered my entire intellect, I ask you this:
I am indeed performing service for my kinsmen under the pretext of sovereignty."
"I am but a partial enjoyer of pleasures, yet I endure their harsh words;
like one desiring fire who rubs the kindling wood,
O divine sage, that ill-spoken speech burns my heart constantly."
"Strength resides eternally in Saṃkarṣaṇa, while gentleness resides in Gada. Pradyumna is superior to me in beauty; thus, O Nārada, I am without allies.
For the others are indeed highly fortunate, powerful, and difficult to overcome."
The Nāradas, Andhakas, and Vṛṣṇis were endowed with constant industry.
He who does not have them would surely not exist, yet he who has them faces great hardship;
restrained by both, I choose neither one.
"O great sage, for whom both Āhuka and Akrūra exist, what indeed could be more painful than that?
Or for whom neither of them exists, what indeed could be more painful than that?
Thus, O great sage, I am like the mother of two gamblers."
"I hope for victory for one and non-defeat for the second;
while I am thus distressed on both sides, O Nārada,
you ought to tell me what is for the welfare of my kinsmen as well as myself."
Nārada said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, calamities are of two kinds, O Vārṣṇeya: external and internal;
they arise either from one's own actions or from others."
This internal calamity of yours, born of your own actions and fraught with hardship,
has arisen from Akrūra and the Bhojas, for all these are his kinsmen. Indeed,
whether for the sake of wealth, or out of desire, or even through aversion, [they have acted].

The sovereignty you attained by yourself has now been bestowed upon another; it has taken root, gained renown, and found allies. It cannot be reclaimed by you, just as vomited food cannot be swallowed again.
"O Kṛṣṇa, the kingdom cannot be obtained by Babhru and Ugrasena by any means whatsoever, especially because of the fear of causing division among kinsmen— and this is particularly true for you.
Even if that goal were to be achieved through effort, it would require performing an exceedingly difficult task."
There may be great loss and expense, or there may even be total destruction. With a weapon that is not made of iron, yet soft and piercing to the heart,
pull out the tongues of them all, rubbing them one by one.
Vāsudeva said:
"O sage, how may I learn that weapon which is not made of iron and is yet mild,
by means of which I might extract their tongues after repeatedly wiping and stroking them?"
Nārada said:
The constant giving of food according to one's ability, forbearance, self-restraint, uprightness,
and honoring others as they deserve— this is a weapon not made of iron.
When your kinsmen desire to speak words that are both harsh and trivial,
you must pacify their hearts, their speech, and their minds with your own words.
No one who is not a great soul, no one lacking self-mastery, and no one without allies can achieve this.

He takes up a great burden; bear it, lifting it with your chest. Every ox indeed carries a heavy load on level ground, but when the path is difficult, only a noble bull carries a load that is otherwise hard to bear.
The destruction of assemblies comes from internal division; you are the leader of this assembly, O Keśava. Act in such a way that, having obtained you as its guide, this assembly does not perish.
There is no other means than wisdom and patience, and no other means than the restraint of the senses.
"A group does not remain with a wise man except through the renunciation of wealth.
O Kṛṣṇa, act in such a way that there may be prosperity, fame, long life, the exaltation of one's own side, auspiciousness, and the non-destruction of our kinsmen."
O Lord, there is nothing unknown to you regarding the future or the present,
concerning the application of the sixfold policy as well as the rules for marching and halting.
All the Mādhavas, Kukuras, Bhojas, and the Andhakas and Vṛṣṇis [are under your command].

O mighty-armed Mādhava, the worlds and those who are the lords of the worlds are attached to you; even the ṛṣis worship your intellect. You are the teacher of all beings; you know the coming and going [of all things].
"Having obtained you, O best of the Yadus, our kinsmen prosper in happiness.
Bhīṣma said:
"This is the first mode of conduct; hear the second, O Bhārata."

12,083.001c Any man whatsoever who might produce wealth for the king must be protected by the king. 12,083.002a Whether he be a paid servant or one who is not, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who reports that the royal treasury is being depleted or stolen by a minister [should be protected].
His secrets must be heard in private, and he must be protected from his ministers, O Bhārata;
for ministers, O Bhārata, most often strike down the one who would harm them. Those who plunder the royal treasury kill the very protector of the royal treasury.
When all these come together, they oppress him; unprotected, he perishes.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history of what the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya said to the King of Kosala.
When Kṣemadarśin had attained sovereignty over the Kośalas,
we have heard that the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya arrived;
he came having bound a crow in a cage, [intending to release it] within the realm of Kṣemadarśin.
Previously, intent and seeking worldly activity, I wandered about again and again, thinking:
"I am studying the science of crows; the crows foretell for me the future, the past, and that which is currently occurring."
Thus, wandering repeatedly throughout the kingdom with his men,
he inquired into the misconduct of all those appointed by the king; for he had come to know the entire disposition of that realm in every respect.
Having learned of all the transgressions committed by the king from here and there,
he took that very crow and went to see the king,
proclaiming his words: "I am omniscient," he, whose vows were strictly observed.
Having approached the decorated royal minister of Kosala, he said,
"By the word of a crow, it is known that you have done this in such-and-such a place;
both so-and-so and so-and-so know that the royal treasury has been stolen by you."
"This crow speaks thus; let him be pursued quickly.
He spoke likewise to others who were constantly stealing from the royal treasury, and it was never heard that anything he said was left unaccomplished anywhere.
O best of the Kurus, all the king’s officers, provoked by him,
bypassed him while he was sleeping at night and slaughtered a crow.
Seeing the crow pierced by an arrow within its cage, [they reported it].
In the forenoon, a Brāhmaṇa addressed these words to Kṣemadarśin:
"O King, I beg immunity from fear from you, the lord and master of life and wealth;
permitted by you, I shall speak words that are for your benefit."
He who, tormented for the sake of a friend, has gone forth with his whole being out of devotion—
should he speak while possessed by impatience, he robs you of your purpose;
for even when a man exerts his prowess, a great object may be lost through shame.

Like a charioteer wishing to awaken his horse, he spoke to his friend who was excessively overcome by anger; for one who understands the truth must forgive such a friend who, though acting out of passion, is intent on one's welfare.
"By a man who constantly desires sovereignty and wishes to prosper,
whatever you might say to me, O King,
how could I not endure it, since I am seeking my own welfare?"
"O Brāhmaṇa, acknowledge this; speak out if you so desire. For I shall carry out whatever words you tell me, O sage.
The sage said:
Having understood your policies, the calamities, and the dangers arising from your servants,
I have come into your presence out of devotion to explain my way of life.
Furthermore, this very fault of those who serve kings has already been declared by the teachers.
For this livelihood that is shared with kings is a path for those who have no other refuge; they say that association with kings is like association with venomous serpents,
for kings have many friends and likewise many enemies.

They say that those who serve a king must fear all of them; yet, O King, their fear may arise from even one of them in an instant. For it is not possible to maintain constant vigilance toward a sovereign.
One who desires prosperity must never, under any circumstances, allow for negligence;
for through negligence a king may stumble, and when he stumbles, there is no life. A king should be approached with the same caution as one would approach a blazing fire.
A person should always attend upon their lord— the master of life and wealth— with diligence, as if he were an enraged venomous serpent, thinking, "I am not [his equal].
He should remain wary of speaking ill, acting wickedly, or behaving improperly.
From improper sitting, from improper walking, from gestures, and from the movements of the limbs—
when propitiated, a king can indeed accomplish all purposes like a deity;
yet when enraged, he may consume everything root and branch like the fire Vaiśvānara.
"O King," Maya said, "it shall be so, and it is even now coming to pass;
furthermore, I shall accomplish this great purpose again and again. A minister such as I provides the aid of his intellect in times of adversity."
"O King, this crow has been dispatched by me for the purpose of bringing about your end. You are not to be blamed in this matter, nor are those to whom you are dear.
However, you should discern between what is beneficial and what is harmful; do not let your mind remain in ignorance."

"But those who dwell in your house solely intent on seizing [property], who desire the ruin of living beings— by such as these was I plotted against. Or rather, it is those who desire the kingdom immediately following your destruction."
"O King, by aiming through intermediaries they achieve success, and not otherwise.
Out of fear of them, O King, I shall go to another hermitage;
for by them, O Lord, an arrow aimed at me fell upon a crow."
"O King, by means of a stratagem, my crow was sent to the abode of Yama;
indeed, this was seen by me with the eye of long asceticism.
[It was like entering] a sea filled with many crocodiles, fish, and sharks, and teeming with tens of thousands of schools of *timiṃgila* monsters."
With this hook, like a crow, I have crossed over you, O river, which is filled with stumps,
stones, and thorns, teeming with tigers, lions, and elephants— difficult to approach and hard to enter, like a cave in the Himalayas.
A difficult passage consisting of darkness is traversed by fire, and that which consists of water by boats;
but the wise know of no means for descending into the fortress of a king. Your kingdom is a dense thicket, shrouded in the gloom of darkness.
"12,083.041c One cannot place trust here even by you, much less by me.
12,083.042a Therefore, this is not a favorable dwelling; for here, good and evil are equal.
12,083.042c For in this place, there is death for both the well-done and the ill-done—of this there is no doubt."
"By justice, there should be execution for evil deeds; how could there be death for a good deed?
It is not right to remain here for long; therefore, a wise man should depart with speed.
O King, there is a river named Sītā, in which even a raft sinks."
I consider this [world] to be like that—a snare that destroys all;
for you are like one who falls into honeyed wine, or like food mixed with poison. Your disposition is like that of the wicked, not like that of the virtuous.

O King, like a well surrounded by venomous serpents, where can one who is afflicted go when surrounded by the cycle of ritual actions? O King, you have been treated by me in the same way as a crow is struck down.
O King, just as a river with sweet water may have difficult fords, high banks, and be filled with *karīra* and cane reeds, yet remain full of sweet water— so too are you;
though surrounded by dogs, vultures, and jackals, you are indeed equal to a royal swan.
Just as a great thicket, relying upon a massive tree, grows to a great size,
it eventually envelops that very tree and continues to grow beyond it;
surely, a fierce forest fire, fueled by that very growth, consumes the wood.
For those ministers, O King, are indeed like that; purify them. Created by you alone, O King, and protected by you, they seek to kill what is dear to you out of contempt for you.
I have lived here in constant apprehension, guarding against negligence,
like a snake within a house or like a wife of a hero in her home; I have dwelt as a companion to the king, desiring to test his character.
"Is the king one who has conquered his senses? Are those within his inner circle subdued? Is the king dear to them, and are the subjects dear to the king?
O best of kings, I have come here desiring to know this about you."

O King, you are as pleasing to me as food is to one who is hungry; my ministers, however, are as distasteful to me as water is to one who has quenched his thirst. Indeed, they have brought this fault upon me simply because I act for your benefit.
There exists no other cause for this; of this I have no doubt.
For I have not wronged them, yet they have become as if possessed of faults.
Indeed, one must fear an enemy who is difficult to subdue, like a snake with a broken back.
The King said:
"O best of Brahmins, honored with abundant provisions and with great hospitality, please dwell further in my house."
"O Brahmin, those who do not wish for you shall not dwell in my house; indeed,
you yourself must determine what should be done immediately hereafter, so that punishment may be meted out to the evildoer and reward to the one who has acted rightly."
"Having thus considered this, O Blessed One, direct me toward that which is for my highest good.
The sage said:
"Do not point out these faults; weaken them one by one."
"Therefore, having ascertained the cause, kill each and every man. For when many share a single fault, they may crush even thorns;
the entire world is bound by wealth, and by wealth it is held in bondage."
"Human beings take pride in wealth; therefore, make that wealth shine forth. By means of one fault against another, incite them to act in opposition.
Having exposed his faults, he will cause him to seize that wealth."
O King, first employ conciliation toward some, and create mutual enmity through sowing dissension; thereafter, apply punishment.
Just as a wise man, concealing his true form with a wood-apple, [uses it to deceive].
"O King, destroy an impure minister by means of one who is likewise impure;
O King, I tell you this because of the fear that your secret counsel might be leaked.
As for us, we are known as Brahmins—those who wield mild punishment and are compassionate."
"I desire your welfare, as well as that of others, just as I do my own. O King, I declare myself to you: I am indeed your kinsman, a sage known by the name Kālakavṛkṣīya."

O King, when your father had passed away and his kingdom was in peril, he who was your father’s esteemed friend and true to his promise abandoned all desires and then practiced austerities for my sake.
Out of affection for you, I tell you this so that you may not fall into further delusion:
having obtained a kingdom by chance, and having seen both suffering and happiness, O King, how can you be negligent regarding a kingdom that depends entirely upon ministers?
12,083.065 Bhīṣma said: Then, once that bull among Brahmins had arrived, a great joy arose once again in the royal palace and in the household of the family priest.
Having brought the earth under a single umbrella for the illustrious Kausalya,
the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya performed supreme sacrifices.
Having heard those beneficial words, the King of Kosala governed the earth.
And so, O Bhārata, the king did exactly as he had been told by him.
Bhīṣma said:
"The virtuous are always restrained by modesty and are endowed with truthfulness and uprightness."
"Those who are capable of speaking correctly [on these matters] shall be your members of the assembly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord of the People, the members of the assembly, the allies, and the well-wishers..."
12,084.001d*0204_02 "O Grandfather, what should his attendants and ministers be like?

12,084.002a They should be exceedingly wealthy and exceedingly brave, as well as Brahmins of great learning, 12,084.002c well-contented, O son of Kuntī, and possessed of great energy in their duties."
O Bhārata, you should seek such companions in all calamities;
for one of noble birth, when constantly honored, does not conceal his power.
Whether he is pleased or displeased, oppressed or even robbed, [he remains steadfast].
For when one man is well-guarded, he indeed turns back the enemy most effectively.
Your attendants should be of noble birth, born in your own land, wise, handsome, highly learned, bold, and devoted to you.
Those of low birth, greedy, cruel, and shameless—

they would serve you, dear father, as long as their hands are still moist [with the offerings]. They would win over your loved ones with wealth, honor, respectful gifts, hospitality, and various luxuries.
Those whom you consider to be partakers of wealth should be partakers of happiness—
those who are unswerving in conduct, wise, of virtuous character, observers of their vows,
noble-minded, and speakers of truth; they would never abandon you, for they are ever-seeking of your welfare.
Those ignoble ones of dull intellect who do not understand the convention—
such should never be one's attendants or ministers;
one should loathe them and recognize them as those who have fallen from the convention.
One should not desire to abandon a group if one intends to join another; however, if a single individual is superior to many, one may certainly leave the group for his sake.
For this is the mark of superiority: that prowess is observed in him.
He who is preeminent in fame, he who abides by his commitment,
he who honors those who are capable, and he who does not compete with those unworthy of competition—
he shall never abandon dharma out of desire, fear, anger, or greed.
One who is free from pride, truthful in speech, capable, self-conquered, and honored by those worthy of honor— he,
having been tested under all circumstances, should be your companion in counsel.
He should be of noble birth, endowed with truthfulness, patient, skillful, and self-possessed.

O Pārtha, being brave, grateful, and truthful are the characteristics of one who seeks the highest good. When a man conducts himself in this way and possesses such discernment, his enemies become well-disposed toward him and even become his friends.
From this point forward, the king— self-controlled, wise, and desirous of prosperity— should examine the virtues and defects of his ministers through men who are trustworthy,
of noble birth, and natives of his own country.

By a man desiring prosperity and wishing to thrive, warriors who are unassailable, reliable, and thoroughly tested from all sides— whether they be hereditary troops, those bound by oath, or even others recruited as mercenaries— should be employed.

Those whose intellect is capable of discipline and whose nature is indeed auspicious— possessing brilliance, fortitude, patience, purity, devotion, stability, and constancy— who have had their virtues constantly tested, who are mature in character, and who are capable of bearing the burden; [such persons should be appointed].
And he should appoint as royal officials those who have passed the five tests of integrity,
who are eloquent, heroic, skilled in practical affairs, of noble birth, endowed with truthfulness, capable of discerning gestures, and free from harshness.
A king should always appoint as ministers those who know the proper place, time, and method, who desire the welfare of their master’s affairs, and who are ever intent upon all matters of state;
for one who lacks splendor and is not joyful never succeeds in his undertakings.
He inevitably creates doubts regarding all undertakings;
thus, a counselor who has heard little, even if he is of noble birth and devoted to virtue,
wealth, and pleasure, is not capable of examining counsel.
Likewise, even one who is unrefined, though he may be well-versed in the scriptures,
