becomes bewildered in matters requiring deliberation— like one who is sightless and without a leader.
Or rather, it is one whose resolve is unstable, even if he is intelligent and has mastered the traditional teachings.
Even one skilled in means is not able to carry out his work for long [if he lacks knowledge]; furthermore,
for a person of dull wit who has not heard the scriptures here, an investigation into specific details does not arise from mere conduct alone.
Trust is certainly not found in a minister who is disloyal;
therefore, one should never disclose secret counsel to one who lacks devotion,
for such a dishonest person, together with other ministers, would cause distress to the king.
Just as fire enters a tree through holes opened by the wind,
so too the master sometimes becomes enraged and casts one out from his position;
he may revile one with harsh words in his agitation, yet afterwards he becomes gracious again.
Those various [offenses] can be endured by a minister who is devoted;
yet the anger of ministers may become like the crash of a thunderbolt. But he who restrains them out of a desire to do what is pleasing to his master—
One should consult that man regarding matters of state who shares equally in both joy and sorrow.
However, even if he is devoted and endowed with other virtues,
one who is not upright does not deserve to hear the king's counsel, even if he is possessed of wisdom.
One who is allied with enemies and does not hold the citizens in high regard—
such a person, though appearing to be a friend, is unworthy of hearing the king's counsel.
So too is one who is ignorant, impure, arrogant, a servant of the enemy, and a boaster.
A friend who is angry and greedy does not deserve to hear counsel.
Even a newcomer who is devoted and highly learned may be honored and provided for, yet he does not deserve to hear counsel.
Even one whose father was formerly treated with injustice and subsequently honored and reinstated does not deserve to hear the counsel; likewise,
one who has been accused even once on account of some minor matter [is unfit].
One who possesses other such qualities does not deserve to hear the counsel.
However, one who is wise, intelligent, learned, a native of the land, pure,
and clean in all his actions— he deserves to hear the counsel.
One who is endowed with knowledge and discernment, who understands the nature of both himself and others,

and who is a friend as dear to the king as his own self— he is worthy to hear the secret counsel. One who is truthful in speech, perfected in character, profound, modest, and gentle [is likewise worthy].
One who has inherited [the lineage] from his father and grandfather deserves to hear the counsel;
one who is contented, esteemed, truthful, noble, and who hates sin; one who knows the counsel, knows the proper time, and is heroic—he deserves to hear the counsel.
O King, a secret counsel should be employed by one wishing to apply punishment against that person who is capable of bringing the entire world under his control through conciliation alone,
and upon whom the people of both city and countryside have placed their trust because of his righteousness.
A warrior who is also wise in policy deserves to hear counsel.
Therefore, ministers endowed with all these qualities, well-honored,
knowledgeable of the nature of things, at least three in number, and desiring great things, should be appointed.
Ministers should observe vulnerabilities within their own constituents as well as those of the enemy; for a king's kingdom prospers when its foundation is sound counsel.
An enemy should not perceive his vulnerability, yet he should pursue the enemy through the latter's weaknesses.
Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs, he should conceal his secrets and guard his own vulnerabilities;
for the wise ministers are the ones who grasp the counsel of the kingdom.
The king has counsel as his body, while other people are merely the limbs of that counsel.
For they declare that sovereignty has its root in resolve and its essence in counsel;
yet in this world, ministers follow their master for the sake of their livelihood.
Having subdued intoxication, anger, pride, and envy, he remains at peace.
He should constantly deliberate with ministers who have transcended the five obstacles;
having fixed his mind upon them, he should understand their various deliberations.
He should report his own conviction as well as that of others at the time of the subsequent mantra;
having approached one who knows dharma, artha, and kāma, he should question him.
When one who is disciplined has reached a definitive conclusion together with a preceptor, a Brahmin, regarding the supreme goal,
he should lead him along that path which is free from attachment.
"Those who know the definitive knowledge of the true meaning of counsel say that one should always deliberate in this manner; therefore,
you should always conduct yourself in this way."
A mantra capable of winning over the subjects:
there shall be no dwarfs, no hunchbacks, no emaciated ones, no lame,
no blind, no mentally dull, no women, and no eunuchs.
Neither here, nor sideways, nor in front, nor behind;
neither above nor below could anyone move about.
Having ascended to the empty window itself—
On a site that is open, bright, and free of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass (12.8),
having avoided defects of speech and body,
one should deliberate on the counsel regarding the task at the appropriate time.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Śakra.
Śakra said:
O Brahmin, what single thing, when practiced correctly by a man,
makes him an authority for all beings and brings him great fame?
Bṛhaspati said:
O Śakra, a man who practices conciliation with complete consistency becomes an authority for all beings and shall attain great fame.
O Śakra, this single word brings happiness to all the world.
By practicing it toward all beings, one becomes always beloved. For he who never speaks at all and whose face is constantly knit with a frown—
He who does not practice gentleness here becomes hateful to living beings; but for him who, having first observed [another], speaks first,
and who speaks with a smile, the world is well-disposed toward him.

For indeed, generosity everywhere that is not accompanied by gentle speech does not please living beings, just as food without seasoning. For even one who gives nothing to living beings, yet utters sweet words—

O Śakra, he brings this entire world under his control through conciliation; therefore, those who intend to employ punishment here should first apply conciliation. For it thus produces the desired result, and the people do not become agitated by him.
Indeed, there is never found anything equal to well-performed conciliation— gentle, smooth, and sweet— when it is properly practiced. Bhīṣma said:
"Thus addressed by his priest, Śakra performed everything exactly as instructed;
in the same way, O Kaunteya, you too should perform this correctly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Indra among kings, how indeed does a ruler protecting his subjects here specifically attain eternal fame in accordance with dharma? Bhīṣma said:
"By means of pure judicial procedure, one intent on protecting his subjects attains both dharma and fame; being pure, he gains both worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What kind of legal proceedings should a king conduct, and with whom should he conduct them?
O one of great wisdom, being thus questioned, you ought to explain this correctly. Furthermore, regarding those qualities previously mentioned in relation to a person—"
"For it is my conviction that these qualities do not exist in a single person.
Bhīṣma said:
"O man of great wisdom, it is exactly as you say, O intelligent one."
A man endowed with all these qualities and virtues is difficult to find;
however, in brief, such character is not difficult to attain here through effort.
But I shall tell you what kind of ministers you should appoint.
[He should appoint] four Brāhmaṇas who are learned, confident, virtuous, and pure;
eighteen or ten Kṣatriyas who are strong and armed with weapons;
and twenty-one Vaiśyas endowed with wealth.
He should employ three Śūdras who are disciplined, pure, and experienced in their former duties; and he should appoint a Sūta, a knower of the Purāṇas, endowed with the eight qualities,
fifty years of age, eloquent, and free from malice.
Endowed with intelligence and mindfulness, disciplined and possessing impartial vision,
capable in the affairs of those disputing over their interests, and free from greed regarding material wealth;
he must be utterly devoid of the seven most terrible vices.
In the midst of his eight ministers, the king should deliberate upon the counsel;
thereafter, he should dispatch it throughout the realm and cause it to be displayed to the people. By means of this legal procedure, those subjects must always be overseen by him.
Furthermore, you must not undertake any secret action that would undermine the state's affairs;
for if the state's business fails, that unrighteousness will afflict both you and them,
and your kingdom will flee like a flock of birds from a hawk.
Like a leaking boat shattered in the ocean,
so it is for a king who protects his subjects improperly through unrighteousness;
fear arises in his heart, and heaven is closed to him.
Now, O bull among men, if a king, a minister, or even a son, while appointed to the seat of justice, should protect [the people] contrary to dharma— though that very dharma is the root of heaven—
the protector of the earth goes to heaven together with his appointed ministers.
Those who serve the king and are authorized for official duties, yet fail to perform them properly,
go to the lower realms together with the monarch, having placed themselves first [in the line of transgression].
As for those who are forcibly oppressed by the powerful and speak much piteously, [the king must protect them].

The king, as the lord of the earth, should always be the protector of men who are without a protector. Therefore, when there is a conflict between two parties, the testimony of witnesses is the proper means of decision; however, a case that is without witnesses or where the parties are helpless must be investigated with particular care.
The king should inflict punishment upon the wicked in accordance with their offense;
he should terrify the wealthy with fines and the poor with death and imprisonment,
as well as by means of disciplinary measures and even blows against those of evil conduct.

He should protect the virtuous through conciliation and the distribution of gifts. For one who intends to commit the murder of a king, there shall be a diverse form of execution; as well as for a thief who makes a living by theft and for one who causes the intermixture of castes.
O lord of the people, for a king who inflicts punishment correctly and with due deliberation, there is no unrighteousness; rather, this is eternal dharma in this world.
However, that unwise man who inflicts punishment out of mere caprice [commits a sin].
12,086.023c He who is joined with infamy in this world shall, upon death, attain hell.

12,086.024a One should not inflict punishment upon others merely on the basis of hearsay from another; having investigated in accordance with the scriptures, one should either bind them or release them.
A king must never, under any circumstances, kill a messenger;
the slayer of a messenger shall enter hell along with his ministers. A king devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya [should treat] a messenger who speaks exactly as he was instructed.
If one should kill him, his ancestors would incur the sin of foeticide (bhrūṇahatyā).
A messenger should possess seven qualities: he should be of noble birth, endowed with good character, eloquent, skillful, pleasant-spoken, truthful in speech, and possessed of a retentive memory.
Endowed with these very same qualities, the door-keeper shall be his protector;
and the head-guard shall likewise be possessed of these same qualities.
One who knows the true principles of the treatises on Dharma and Artha shall be the minister of peace and war.
One who is wise, resolute, intelligent, and a keeper of secrets;
one who is of noble birth, endowed with truthfulness, and capable—such a minister is highly praised. One who possesses these very same qualities should likewise be the commander of the army.

One who understands the principles of military formations, machines, and weaponry, who is endowed with valor, who can endure rain, cold, heat, and wind, and who knows the vulnerabilities of the enemy—
such a person should inspire confidence in others, yet he himself should not place trust in anyone.
"O Indra among kings, trust even in one's own sons is not praised.
O sinless one, I have thus explained to you the true essence of the meaning of the scriptures;
mistrust toward rulers is said to be the supreme secret."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what kind of city a king ought to inhabit himself, whether one already built or one he has had constructed."
Bhīṣma said:
"O son of Kuntī, O Bhārata, wherever one must dwell together with one's sons, brothers, and kinsmen, it is proper there to inquire about security and means of livelihood."
Therefore, I shall describe to you specifically the construction of fortresses;
having heard this, it should be arranged accordingly and carried out with diligence. Having established the six kinds of fortresses, one should then settle the cities.
Whatever may be the preeminent excellence of all prosperity, or whatever abundance may arise— namely, the desert fort, the earth fort, the mountain fort,
as well as the human fort, the water fort, and the forest fort— these are the six.
A city that is well-fortified, provided with grain and weapons,
possessing strong walls and moats, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots,
where there are learned men, artisans, and well-stocked stores— [such a place should be established].

Where the people are righteous and established in the highest skill, where it abounds in powerful men, elephants, and horses, adorned with crossroads and marketplaces, where legal proceedings are well-known, and which is peaceful and free from fear from any quarter.
It was brilliantly radiant and resonant with sound, its dwellings highly praised; it was filled with brave and wealthy people, echoing with the chanting of the Vedas,
abounding in social gatherings and festivals, and where the deities were always worshipped.
A king whose ministers and forces are under his control should himself reside in that city. There he should increase the treasury, the army, his allies, and commerce;
and in both the city and the countryside, he should eliminate all evils.
One should diligently increase the stores of the treasury and the armory;
likewise, one should augment all accumulations, as well as machines, maces,
and clubs, along with wood, iron, chaff, charcoal, timber, horn, bone, and bamboo.
Marrow, fat, grease, honey, and the collection of medicinal herbs;
hemp, resin, grain, weapons, and arrows;
as well as leather, sinew, cane, muñja grass, balbaja grass, and bows.
The king must always take care to block wells and excellent reservoirs containing abundant water, as well as milk-yielding trees; likewise,
he should diligently honor his teachers, officiating priests, and domestic chaplains.
There were twelve thousand, eight hundred and seven great archers, master builders, astrologers, and physicians—
wise, intelligent, self-controlled, skillful, heroic, and deeply learned; men of noble birth, endowed with courage, and competent in all tasks.
The king should honor those who are righteous and restrain those who are unrighteous; he should diligently employ all social classes in their respective duties,
whether they be outsiders or insiders, including the people of both the city and the countryside.
Having thoroughly ascertained [the situation] through spies, he should then carry out his actions.
The king himself should personally attend to the spies, the secret counsel, the treasury, and especially the secret counsel; for everything is established upon these.
All that is intended by those who are neutral, enemies, and friends,
both in the city and in the countryside, must be known through the eye of spies;
thereafter, everything should be managed with vigilance and without negligence.
Constantly honoring devotees and subduing those who are hostile,
one should always perform sacrifices with rituals and give gifts without causing distress; one must protect the subjects and never perform a censurable act.
He should always provide for the welfare, security, and livelihood of the miserable, the helpless, the elderly, and widowed women; likewise,
he should ensure that clothing, vessels, and food are available in the hermitages at the appropriate times.
The king should always offer [these] with respect and without contempt; he should diligently entrust himself, all his affairs, and even his kingdom to the ascetic,
and remain forever humble before him.
A king should honor one who renounces all for the sake of others, who is born of noble lineage, and who is deeply learned; having seen such a person, he should provide him with beds, seats, and food.
Furthermore, in times of any calamity, the king should place his trust in him.
For even bandits place their trust in ascetics; therefore, one should deposit treasures with them and acquire wisdom from them. Yet, one should not serve them constantly, nor honor them excessively.
One [spy] should be employed within one's own kingdom, another in the kingdoms of others;
another should be employed in the forest regions, and yet another in the cities of neighboring vassals.
One should cause them to receive honors, formal rites, and shares of wealth.

Whether they reside in foreign kingdoms or in forest retreats, ascetics of firm vows should provide refuge as they would in their own territory; in any circumstance whatsoever, they should grant shelter according to the desire of a king seeking protection.
12,087.033 This brief enumeration of the characteristics has been proclaimed to you, such as the kind of city a king ought to inhabit himself. 12,088.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, O bull of the Bharatas, tell me— who am desirous of knowing it correctly— the protection of the kingdom and the consolidation of the realm. Bhīṣma said:
"I shall explain to you in full the protection of the kingdom and the proper consolidation of the realm;
indeed, I will declare all of this in truth—listen with a single-minded focus.
A lord of a village must be appointed, and likewise another for ten villages."
In this same manner, he should cause [the fines] for two hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand to be levied.
Whatever village offenses the headman (grāmika) fails to restrain within the village, he shall report them to the leader of ten (daśapā); and he, in turn, to the leader of twenty (viṃśatipā).
The *daśaka* (leader of ten) shall report them to the *daśin* (leader of ten); the *viṃśin* (leader of twenty), in turn, shall report to the leader of twenty;
and that leader of twenty shall report the entire conduct among the people of the countryside to the protector of a hundred villages.
The village headman (grāmika) shall enjoy those things that are fit for consumption by the villagers;
by him the leader of ten (daśapa) is to be maintained, and by him the leader of twenty (dviguṇādhipa). The leader of ten must be supported by the leader of twenty in the same manner.
The superintendent of a hundred villages, being duly honored, is entitled to enjoy one village from among those hundreds— a large one, O best of the Bharatas, teeming with prosperous people;
for there, O Bhārata, many resources of the king are dependent upon it.
The lord of a thousand villages is worthy to enjoy this excellent branch-city;
the provincial governor is prepared to provide for it with an abundance of grain and gold.
Likewise, whatever duties pertain to the village and whatever duties pertain to the district head, you yourself shall perform them.
Some minister who knows the Dharma should observe this vigilantly;
and in every city there should be one overseer of all affairs,
stationed in a high place, formidable in appearance like a planet among the stars.
He himself should always supervise them all;
or, some spy moving within the kingdoms should report their conduct—
those who are intent on killing, those with evil desires, those who seize the property of others, and the deceitful.

Those appointed as guardians of protection should protect these subjects from them. Having carefully considered the sale and purchase, the distance traveled, the food along with its incidental expenses, and the security of their goods, the king should cause taxes to be levied upon the merchants.
Having repeatedly examined the origin, the maintenance through gifts, and the craft itself,
he should cause artisans to pay taxes on their crafts.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, it is just that taxes levied by former kings were of various high and low rates.
The lord of the earth should act in such a way that [the people] do not decline;
having carefully considered both the fruit and the action, he should then ordain everything. No one should undertake any action without regard for its fruit.
Just as both the king and the producer would be sharers in the fruit of the work,
so too should taxes be levied by the king after due consideration.
Out of greed, he should not cut off his own root, nor that of others.
Having blocked the avenues of exertion, the king who displays affection [to his subjects] is respected;
people hate a king who is well-known for being excessively devouring. For one who is hated, how can there be welfare? One who is beloved obtains what is dear.
A king of undiminished intellect should milk his kingdom like a calf;
O Bhārata, a calf that has been nourished and has gained strength can endure the milking. But a calf that is milked too much, O Yudhiṣṭhira, does not perform its work.
For even a kingdom that has been over-milked does not perform great deeds. However,
that king who personally takes charge of and favors his kingdom,
living upon what it produces, obtains a very great reward.
For kings in this world gather stores for the sake of emergencies;
the kingdom itself should serve as the treasury, and that treasury should likewise be kept within the palace.
[One should protect] all the citizens and country-folk, as well as those who have sought refuge and their dependents.

One should show compassion to all those within one's reach according to one's ability; having sowed dissension among the external people, the middle group may be enjoyed with ease. In this way, the people—whether happy or suffering—will not become incensed.
But even before the collection of taxes has been announced again and again, he should assemble [his officials] within his own territory and demonstrate the danger facing the kingdom:
"This calamity has arisen; there is great fear from an enemy army."
Like the arrival of fruit upon a bamboo tree, it may not lead to my end;
yet these enemies, having risen up along with many bandits,
desire to oppress this kingdom solely for their own destruction.
"In this terrible calamity, when a dreadful fear has arrived,
I shall request your wealth for the sake of your protection;
and when the danger has passed, I shall restore everything to you."
The Nārāyaṇas will not restore what they have taken by force from here;
for if one first takes a wife, one's own property will surely perish by itself. Even if the accumulation of wealth is desired for the sake of sons and wife, [it must be done righteously].
I rejoice in your power, and I urge you as I would my own sons:
I shall favor you to the best of my ability, without causing oppression to the kingdom; and in times of calamity, you must bear the burden like excellent oxen.
"Nothing is more dear to you than wealth in any time of distress"—
with these sweet, gentle, and courteous words,
the man who knows the proper time should take up the yoke and let out his draft-animals.

Having carefully considered their movements, the maintenance of dependents, their expenditures, threats from cattle and villages, and their security and well-being, the king should cause taxes to be levied upon cattle-owners. For if neglected, cattle-owners would perish and become forest-dwellers.
Therefore, one should especially treat them with gentleness at first;
O Pārtha, one must constantly provide consolation, protection, gifts, and security for the cattle-owners, as well as shares of the produce and pleasant things.
The fruit [of this] should be constantly applied in every way toward those who possess cattle;
it causes the kingdom, commerce, and likewise agriculture to flourish. Therefore, a wise man should diligently cultivate affection among those who possess cattle.
"O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, being compassionate and vigilant while levying mild taxes,
security is easily maintained everywhere by those who possess cattle;
for there is no wealth whatsoever equal to this."
12,089.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O high-minded grandfather, when a king, though capable, should be desirous of wealth for his treasury, how should he proceed then? Tell me that.

12,089.002 Bhīṣma said: A king who seeks righteousness and is devoted to the welfare of his subjects should instruct them according to their place, according to the time, and also according to their strength.
In whatever way he considers it to be for their welfare and for his own,
in that manner the king should promote all righteous practices within the kingdom. He should milk the kingdom like honey, without destroying the bees.
One should milk the cow while having regard for her calf and should not bruise her teats. O lord of men, one should drain the kingdom gently, like a leech;
and one should carry off the subjects like a tigress carries her cub, thinking, "May I not fall [by harming them]."
Just as a porcupine-like rat constantly shakes its tracks,
so should one consume the kingdom through mild means;
by granting small amounts of gifts repeatedly, one should cause it to increase.
From that point, one should further and ever further increase the interest as desired;
like one taming draft animals, one should constantly increase the burden,
applying effort with gentleness at first, and gradually tightening the reins.
Once they have been scattered by the noose, those who were difficult to subdue will no longer be so;
with effort, they shall be made to enjoy their portion as is fitting.
Therefore, it is rare for a multitude of men to be available for every undertaking.
Having conciliated those who are the leaders, one should enjoy the rest of the people;
then, having sowed dissension among them so that they have conflicting desires for one another, one should enjoy them by means of conciliation alone, at ease and without effort.
One should not impose taxes upon them at an improper place or at an improper time;
rather, one should do so gradually, with gentleness, at the right time, and according to the prescribed rule.
I am declaring these as strategic means; I do not intend to speak of deceit.
By training them without skillful means, one provokes the horses to anger.
Likewise, taverns, brothels, courtesans,
actors, gamblers, and whoever else is of such a kind—

All these who are harmful to the kingdom must be restrained; for while remaining within the kingdom, they afflict even the virtuous subjects. No one should ever request anything from anyone except in times of distress.
"Thus was the established order of beings ordained by Manu in the past.
If all were not to live accordingly, and if they did not perform their duties here,
then all three worlds would undoubtedly cease to exist."
The king is the master in the matter of restraint; the scripture declares that he who does not restrain these [offenders] incurs a fourth part of their sin.
Just as he is the enjoyer of their sin, so too is he the enjoyer of their merit.
O lord of men, those who are wicked must always be restrained by the king;
for that king who does not restrain them incurs a fourth part of the evil committed [by them], while he likewise enjoys a fourth part of the merit performed [by them].
When these conditions converge in a single occasion, they bring about the destruction of prosperity.
What improper act would a man addicted to desire not commit?
[These include] liquor, meat, the property of others, as well as [the wives and wealth of others].

One who is under the sway of passion may take it for himself and likewise display the scripture; however, those who have no possessions and beg in times of distress should be given from the standpoint of Dharma by one who seeks to show compassion and mercy.
May there be no beggars in your kingdom, nor may there be many bandits; for these [bandits] are merely those who take what has been offered, not those who promote the welfare of living beings.
Those who show favor to all creatures and cause the subjects to prosper are the true benefactors.
"Let them all function within your kingdom; let there be no destroyers of living beings.
And those who are to be punished, O Great King, for the purpose of collecting wealth, you should cause them to perform labor, just like those who pay taxes."
A man should have agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, and whatever else is of a similar nature performed by many men who are workers;
for if a man himself practices agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, [he becomes exhausted].
If he incurs even the slightest suspicion, the king is thereby censured.
He should always honor the wealthy with vehicles, clothing, and food, and say to them: "Please favor me; these honors are shared by me."
O Bhārata, this is a great attribute of kings: the name "wealthy.
One who possesses wealth is the preeminent leader among all beings; of this there is no doubt.
Whether he be wise, brave, wealthy, or even righteous, it is the one with wealth who is truly so.
An ascetic who speaks the truth and possesses wisdom protects [the world].
Therefore, O King, be well-disposed toward all of these;
uphold truth, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, and compassion.
"In this way, O King, devoted to truth and integrity, you shall obtain both the army and the treasury, as well as allies and territory, provided you are endowed with friends and wealth.
Bhīṣma said:

In your kingdom, people shall not cut down trees that bear edible fruit; for the wise have declared that roots and fruits belong rightfully to the Brāhmaṇas. Other people may consume what remains after the Brāhmaṇas have taken their share.

No one else should ever take [property] by obstructing a Brāhmaṇa. O lord of men, if a learned Brāhmaṇa, emaciated by the lack of means of subsistence, should resort to renunciation, a livelihood must be provided for him along with his wife.
If he does not desist, he should be addressed in an assembly of Brahmins:
"In whom now shall this world establish its standard?
If he does not turn back from this point, he will undoubtedly do so [only] after being told further.
"O Kaunteya, this instruction must first be performed out of sight;
people say this, O Brahmin, but I do not believe it.
One should be invited with enjoyments, and only if one lacks a livelihood should one act thus."

Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the livelihoods of people in this world; furthermore, the triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā) exists for the higher purpose, for it nourishes all beings. Yet, while that [knowledge] is being pursued, there may be those who act as its adversaries.
For the sake of slaying those Dasyus here, Brahmā then created the Kṣatra.
"Slay your enemies, protect the subjects, and perform sacrifices with ritual offerings, O King! Fight in battle, becoming a hero, O delighter of the Kurus!"
That king who protects those who ought to be protected is the most noble of kings;
those who do not protect them have no purpose whatsoever.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the king must always learn from all the world.
Therefore, for this reason, a man should indeed support other men—protecting those within from those outside, and those outside from those within;
protecting outsiders from outsiders, and his own kin from their own kin; protect everyone at all times.

Protecting himself on all sides, the king should protect the earth; for wise men say that everything has its root in the self. "What is my vulnerability? What is my attachment? Or what remains unoverthrown? [he should thus reflect].
One should constantly reflect: "From where might a fault flow toward me? On the day past, they may or may not praise his conduct;
therefore, he should have secret and trusted spies roam throughout the earth.
Whether they praise my conduct as well-guided or not,
does my fame perhaps shine forth in the countryside and in the kingdom—
[the fame] of those who know dharma, who are steadfast, and who do not flee from battles?
Those who live within the kingdom and those who depend upon the king,
all the ministers, and all those who stand as intermediaries—
those who might praise you, or on the other hand, those who might censure you.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should cause all of them to be well-conducted;
for it is not possible, my dear, to please everyone exclusively. Among all beings, O Bhārata, there are friends, enemies, and neutrals."

Among those who possess equal strength of arm and likewise cultivate similar virtues, how could one person be superior so as to devour other men? For it is those who move who devour the immobile, and likewise, those with fangs devour those without fangs.
Like enraged venomous serpents attacking other snakes,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should always remain vigilant and exerted against these;
for they fall upon the heedless like Bhāruṇḍa birds.

I trust that the merchants in your kingdom, though oppressed by taxes, do not feel distressed as they purchase much with little, enduring the hardships of the wilderness. I trust that the farmers, though severely oppressed, do not abandon the kingdom.
12,090.023c Those who bear the yoke for kings support others as well;
12,090.024a By what is given from here, the gods and the hosts of ancestors live, 12,090.024c as do humans, serpents, *rakṣas* demons, birds, and beasts.
"O Bhārata, this is the conduct for the kingdom and the protection of the kingdom;
relying upon this very purpose, O Pāṇḍava, I shall speak further.
Bhīṣma said:
Those duties of the Kṣatriyas which Utathya, the best among the knowers of Brahman,
spoke with affection to Māndhātṛ, the son of Yuvanāśva—
just as that Utathya, the supreme knower of Brahman, instructed him.
"I shall explain all that to you in its entirety, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Utathya said:
"A king exists for the sake of dharma, and not for the sake of acting according to his own desires."
O Māndhātṛ, know this: the king is the protector of the world. Indeed, when a king practices righteousness, he goes to the state of divinity;
but if he does not practice righteousness, he goes to hell.
All beings abide in Dharma, and Dharma abides in the king. That king who governs rightly is a true king; he is the lord of the earth.
A king who is supremely righteous and prosperous is nevertheless called "sinful" [if he fails in his duty].
The gods fall into reproach and it is said that "there is no dharma. For those who abide in unrighteousness, the attainment of worldly success is observed;
therefore, the entire world follows after that very thing as a source of auspiciousness.
The practice of dharma is being cut off, and great unrighteousness prevails.
They say there is fear day and night when the wicked are not restrained. O dear one, according to the dharma of the virtuous, there is neither "this is mine" nor "this is not [mine]."
When evil is not restrained, no social order whatsoever can exist;
when the power of evil prevails among men, neither wife, nor cattle, nor field, nor dwelling can be seen.
The gods do not accept the worship, nor do the ancestors accept the *svadhā* offering;
indeed, guests are not honored when the wicked are not restrained. Furthermore, the twice-born who observe their vows no longer follow the Vedas.
When the wicked man is not restrained, the wise do not perform sacrifices;
O Great King, when the wicked man is not restrained, the minds of all men become as agitated as those of those condemned to death.
Having surveyed both worlds, the seers themselves created the king as a most great being, thinking, "This shall be Dharma.
They declare that he in whom Dharma shines forth is a king.
The gods know him as a *vṛṣala* in whom righteousness (*dharma*) has dissolved;
for the Blessed One, Dharma, is indeed the bull (*vṛṣan*), and he who acts contrary to it, the gods know as a *vṛṣala*. Therefore, one should not destroy righteousness.
When Dharma increases, all beings always increase;
when it diminishes, they perish. Therefore, one should cause Dharma to flourish.
For it is certain that Dharma flows from wealth, or rather, it is maintained by its preservation.
O lord of men, he is remembered as the one who establishes the boundary for forbidden acts.
For Dharma was created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the prosperity of all beings;
therefore, one should cause Dharma to increase for the purpose of showing favor to the subjects.
Therefore, O tiger among kings, it is traditionally held that dharma is supreme. He is a true king, a bull among men and a doer of good deeds,
who governs his subjects while disregarding desire and anger and upholding dharma alone.
O best of the Bharatas, dharma is the most conducive to the welfare of kings. The source of dharma is the Brahmins; therefore, one should always honor them.
And, O Māndhātṛ, one should fulfill the desires of the Brahmins without envy.
For when they act against his will, fear arises for the king;
his friends do not increase, and even they become enemies. Indeed, even enemies then become friends, and even friends become enemies.
When Bali, the son of Virocana, showed malice toward the Brahmins,
the radiant Goddess Śrī then departed from him;
having left him, she went to Pākaśāsana (Indra).
Then he later felt remorse upon seeing the splendor of Purandara. "O Lord, this is the fruit of malice and arrogance;
therefore, O Māndhātṛ, take heed, lest the scorching [consequence] abandon you."
"According to sacred tradition, O King, it is heard that a son named Darpa was born to Adharma by Śrī.
By him, O King, the gods, asuras, and many royal sages have been brought under his control on numerous occasions. Therefore, O ruler of the earth, take heed."

"Having conquered him, he becomes the king; being defeated by him, he becomes a slave. Therefore, O Māndhātṛ, conduct yourself in such a way that you do not practice unrighteousness joined with pride, if you wish to remain for a long time."

From one who is intoxicated, from one who is negligent, from a minor, and especially from one who is insane; from addiction to that [vice], from turning away [from duty], and from associating with harmful things; and especially from a minister who has been restrained, and from women.
One should be constantly vigilant against mountains, uneven terrain, difficult passes, elephants, horses, and reptiles; one should avoid wandering about at night,
and one should renounce excessive exertion, excessive pride, hypocrisy, and anger.
A king should not engage in sexual intercourse with women who are unknown to him, nor with eunuchs, nor with wanton women, nor with the wives of others, nor with maidens;
for in such families, sinful *rākṣasas* are born due to the confusion of castes.
When a king is negligent, these and others are born: those who are impotent, those with missing limbs, those with thick tongues, and those who are senseless.
Therefore, a king must especially conduct himself for the welfare of his subjects.
When a Kṣatriya becomes negligent, a great evil arises; unrighteousnesses come forth, causing the confusion of the people. In the heat there is cold, and in the cold no cold is found.

Drought and excessive rain, as well as disease, afflict the people; the constellations are eclipsed, and other terrible planets likewise appear. Furthermore, O King, many portents are seen here that bode the destruction of kings.
A king who does not protect himself and fails to protect his subjects sees his subjects diminish, and he perishes along with them.
For two take from one, and many others take from those two.

When maidens are violated, they say this is a blemish upon the king; among men, it does not remain with only one person [to bear]. When a king abandons righteousness and indulges in negligence, [the fault falls upon him].
Utathya said:
When the rain-cloud pours at the proper time and the king practices righteousness,
that prosperity which arises sustains the subjects in happiness.
Just as there is no washerman who does not know how to remove the dirt from clothes, nor how to cleanse those that are dyed,
so it is with the foremost of the twice-born, the Kṣatriyas, and the Vaiśyas.
Śūdras are established in various occupations among the four castes.
Agriculture is the duty of the Śūdra, trade of the Vaiśya, and the administration of justice of the King;
while celibacy, austerity, sacred mantras, and truthfulness belong to the twice-born.
Among them, he who knows how to cleanse the defects of character, just as one cleanses garments, is the father and is Prajāpati himself.
O bull of the Bharatas, [he is] the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages.
All royal duties and the king himself are said to constitute the Yuga;
likewise, the four castes, the Vedas, and the four stages of life—
all these indeed fall into confusion when the king becomes negligent.
The three sacred fires, the triple Veda, and the sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees—all these indeed falter when the king falters.
The king alone is the creator of beings; the king alone is their destroyer.
He who is righteous in soul shall be the creator, and he who is unrighteous in soul shall be the destroyer.
When a king becomes negligent, his wives, sons, kinsmen, and friends all gather together and grieve.

O King, when the ruler follows unrighteous conduct, the elephants, horses, cattle, camels, mules, and donkeys all perish. O Māndhātṛ, it is said that strength was created by the Creator for the sake of the weak.
That great being is weak, yet it is upon it that everything is established.
He who is a living being resorts to that being, as do those who are its progeny;
for when the king stands in unrighteousness, O King, everyone perishes.

For I consider the eye of a weak sage and that of a venomous serpent to be most difficult to withstand; therefore, do not attack one who is weak. My son, you should always recognize those who are weak as being never to be insulted.
"Let not those with weak eyes consume you along with your kinsmen;
for nothing at all grows again in a family scorched by the weak. It burns away everything down to the very roots—do not, therefore, approach the weak."
Indeed, weakness is better than strength, even that strength which is exceedingly powerful;
for nothing remains of strength when it is consumed by weakness. If one who is insulted, struck, or cried out against finds no protector, [he is truly lost].
A punishment inflicted there by a non-human being destroys the lord of men. My son, do not rely on strength, nor oppress the weak;
let not the eyes of the weak burn you up like fire consumes its own shelter.

The tears shed by those who weep while being falsely accused destroy the sons and livestock of those who have made such false accusations. If [the retribution] does not fall upon themselves, it falls upon their sons, or if not on their sons, then on their grandsons or great-grandsons.
For an evil deed committed does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow; but where a weak person, being struck down, finds no protector,
there a great and terrible punishment ordained by fate falls.
When the subjects of the realm, though disciplined, beg like Brahmins, such people destroy the king through the constant fault of begging. When there are many royal officials in the king’s realm—
When they act with injustice, that is a great sin for the king. When, though appointed, they conduct affairs out of passion or for the sake of wealth,
while people are piteously begging, that is indeed a great calamity for the king.
A great tree is born and it grows; all living beings take refuge in it. When that tree is cut down or burned;
When they practice the supreme Dharma in the kingdom, or proclaim the refinement that constitutes the virtues of a king, they become homeless, relying on that [Dharma].
By those very people, unrighteousness was practiced through delusion regarding dharma;
one should quickly abandon both merit and demerit where sinful men move about openly while being known.
When a king punishes men who do not deserve punishment, then strife overtakes the virtuous there, O protector of the earth;
that kingdom does not prosper.
That king who, having honored his minister according to his merit,
appoints him to both counsel and battle,
his kingdom prospers.
He enjoys the entire earth for a long time; moreover,
by observing and honoring both well-performed deeds and well-spoken words, the king attains unsurpassed merit.
When he eats after having shared [the food] and does not despise others,
and when he strikes down the strong and arrogant— he is said to fulfill the duty of a king.
For when he protects everyone through his speech, his body, and his actions, [he fulfills his duty].
Even for his own son, he would not tolerate [wrongdoing]; that is said to be the duty of a king.
When a king enjoys [the fruits of his rule] after having shared them with weak men, then they become strong; that is said to be the duty of a king.
When he protects the realms, when he drives away the bandits,
and when he is victorious in battle— that is said to be the duty (*dharma*) of a king. When one commits evil through action or through speech...

Even toward one who is dear, he would not tolerate [wrongdoing]; that is called the duty of a king. When a king protects those seeking refuge like his own sons and does not violate the boundaries of propriety, that is called the duty of a king.
When he performs sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees, endowed with faith and disregarding desire and hatred, that is said to be the duty of a king. Indeed,
when he wipes away the tears of the miserable, the helpless, and the aged, that too is his duty.
Producing joy among men, that is said to be the duty of a king; it increases his friends and likewise diminishes his enemies,
and he honors the virtuous— that is said to be the duty of a king.
He who maintains truth through his actions, constantly bestows land, and honors guests and dependents— he is said to possess the dharma of a king;
it is in him that both restraint and favor are firmly established.
In this world and indeed in the next, O King Māndhātṛ, the monarch obtains that fruit;
for King Yama is the supreme lord of the righteous,
restraining the vital breaths of beings, whereas one who does not restrain them is a sinner.
When one honors and does not insult the officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers, and treats them with proper respect,
that is said to be the duty of a king.
Yama restrains all beings indeed without distinction.
The king must act in accordance with him; his subjects must be governed according to the prescribed rules.
For the king is compared in every respect to the Thousand-eyed One (Indra).
O bull among men, whatever dharma he perceives, that indeed is dharma.
You should train with heedfulness in forbearance, wisdom, fortitude, and discernment;
always in the desire to know the true nature of beings, and in what is virtuous and what is not.
You should practice the gathering of all beings through generosity and sweet speech.
The people of both the city and the countryside must be protected like one's own offspring.
An incompetent king can never protect his subjects;
for sovereignty, my dear, is a truly immense burden and exceedingly difficult to perform.

A wise king who wields the rod of punishment, being brave and capable, is able to protect [his realm]; for it cannot be protected by one who lacks the rod, nor by one who is cowardly or lacking in intelligence.
[It requires those] who are handsome, born of noble lineage, skillful, devoted, and deeply learned.
Examine all the insights even of those dwelling in the hermitages of ascetics;
then you will truly know the supreme dharma of all beings. Whether in your own country or in a foreign land, your dharma shall not perish.
Dharma, artha, and kāma—of these, dharma alone should be supreme.
In this world and the next, one who knows dharma prospers in happiness. Honored men renounce even their wives and their very lives [for the sake of dharma].
The gathering of living beings, generosity, and sweet speech,
as well as heedfulness and purity, O dear one, bring about great prosperity. Therefore, O Māndhātṛ, never be negligent regarding these.

A king should be vigilant, observing the vulnerabilities of both himself and his enemies; he must not allow the enemy to see his own weak points, while he should pursue the enemy through their weaknesses.
This is the conduct of Vāsava, Yama, and Varuṇa.

And that which belongs to all the royal seers—do you too uphold it. Therefore, O Great King, practice the conduct followed by the royal seers; set out upon the divine path immediately, O bull among the Bharatas.
"O Bhārata, the gods, ṛṣis, ancestors, and gandharvas of immeasurable power proclaim the king who follows the conduct of dharma both in this world and after death. Bhīṣma said:

O Bhārata, having been thus addressed by Utathya, Māndhātā performed that without hesitation; acting alone, he attained the entire earth. You too, O lord of the earth, should act correctly in the same manner as King Māndhātā.
"By practicing dharma and protecting the earth, you shall attain a station in heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How should a righteous king conduct himself, desiring to remain established in dharma?"
"I ask you, O best of the Kurus, tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
This song, which reveals the reality of perceived objects, was sung by the wise Vāmadeva.
King Vasumān, the powerful and pure ruler of Kosala,
once questioned the illustrious great seer Vāmadeva.

"O Blessed One, instruct me in words endowed with both dharma and artha, by following which conduct I may remain established and not fall away from my own duty. To him spoke Vāmadeva, the ascetic and best among those who recite prayers.
Seated there, golden-hued like Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, he said:
"Follow dharma alone; nothing exists that is superior to dharma.
For kings established in dharma conquer this entire earth."
That lord of the earth who considers the supreme duty to be the accomplishment of his purpose,
and who makes his intellect true to reality, shines through righteousness. But that king who perceives unrighteousness and proceeds solely by force [does not shine].
Both the first and the middle [kings] have already departed swiftly from here. He who has wicked and most sinful ministers is a destroyer of dharma and deserves to be slain by the world;
together with his retinue, he perishes swiftly.
One who fails to carry out his duties, who acts according to his whims, and who is boastful,

perishes quickly even after having obtained the entire earth. On the other hand, one who does not take what belongs to others, who is free from malice, and has conquered his senses— [attains prosperity].
A wise king increases like the ocean with its streams; yet that lord of the earth should never think, "I am full," whether in terms of dharma, pleasure, wealth, wisdom, or even friends.
For upon all these indeed the course of worldly life is established;
hearing these, one obtains glory, fame, prosperity, and progeny.
Thus is he who is devoted to dharma and reflects upon the purpose of dharma.

Having carefully examined his objectives, he who undertakes them certainly attains greatness. For a king who is ungenerous, lacking in affection, and who oppresses his subjects with punishment, being violent by nature, perishes very quickly.
12,093.016 Now, if an unwise person commits an evil deed intentionally and does not perceive its consequence,
he is joined with infamy and, upon death, experiences hell.
12,093.017 But for one who honors [the recipient], who gives, who is pure, and who understands the essence [of the gift]—
Men seek to destroy their own calamity as if it were their own birth;
he who has no teacher in dharma and does not consult others,
being dependent on pleasure in the acquisition of wealth, does not enjoy greatness for long.
One who makes the guru preeminent in all matters of dharma, who personally investigates the meaning of those teachings,
and who holds dharma as the highest priority in the world, enjoys great rewards for a very long time.
Vāmadeva said:
Where one who is stronger imposes unrighteousness upon the weak,
those who follow that way of life and are born into that lineage come to imitate the king who has set such evil in motion.
A kingdom with undisciplined men perishes quickly. That very livelihood which men depend upon when he is established in his natural state,
even his own kin cannot endure from him when he is in a state of disorder.

Where a king of a violent nature does anything harsh, being contrary to the characteristics prescribed by the scriptures, he perishes very quickly. That Kṣatriya who does not follow the conduct practiced since time immemorial [is likewise lost].

He who, having captured an enemy who has performed his duty in battle, does not honor him out of malice— whether that enemy be conquered or unconquered— departs from the dharma of a Kṣatriya. He departs from the dharma of a Kṣatriya.

A capable king who is pleasant-faced should show compassion in times of distress; he becomes beloved by all beings and does not fall away from his prosperity. Even toward one who does him harm, he should act with even greater kindness.
He who acts kindly toward one who is unkind will soon become beloved. One should avoid false speech and perform kind deeds even when unasked;
this is the mark of a superior person, wherein prowess is observed.
He who is preeminent in fame, he who abides by the sacred law (*samaya*),
he who honors those who are capable, and he who does not compete with them;
he should not abandon the Dharma out of desire, nor out of agitation, nor out of hatred.
The wise man should conduct himself with sincerity alone and should not abandon the truth;
he should maintain self-restraint, righteousness, virtuous conduct, and the duty of a Kṣatriya that is beneficial to the subjects.
He should not feel shame when questioned, nor should he utter words that are overly haughty.
One should not hasten, nor should one be resentful; in this way, others are won over. One should not exult excessively in what is pleasant, nor be distressed by what is unpleasant.
One should not lose one's composure in times of financial hardship, keeping in mind the welfare of the subjects.
O lord of the earth, the king who always acts agreeably toward others on account of their virtues succeeds in his undertakings and is never abandoned by prosperity—
he who has desisted from what is disagreeable and conducts himself with what is pleasing.
A king should employ as his minister one who is devoted; for that indeed is the conduct of the virtuous in this world.
He should appoint to great tasks one whose senses are not scattered, who is wise, extremely loyal, pure, capable, and truly devoted.
In the same way, one who, though endowed with such qualities, does not show devotion to the lord,
and who is envious of his master's interests— such a person, being foolish, sensual, greedy, ignoble in conduct, and deceitful, one should not employ in any task.

If a king employs for a great task one who has not outgrown his base nature, who is violent, evil-minded, and lacking in learning; who abandons what he has acquired, is addicted to liquor, and is devoted to gambling, women, and hunting— that king is deprived of his prosperity.
But that king who protects himself and protects those who are worthy of protection,
his subjects flourish and he certainly attains great fortune. He should keep watch over all those who are lords of the earth, whoever they may be.
A king is not harmed by those friends who remain unrecognized;
yet, having done harm to one who is powerful, one should not feel secure thinking, "I am far away. For these [enemies] swoop down upon the negligent like hawks in their flight.

But one who is firmly rooted, pure in soul, and having recognized his own strength, should attack those who are weak, and not those who are more powerful. Having acquired the earth through prowess, he should protect his subjects with righteousness.
A king devoted to righteousness should meet his end in battle;
all this ends in death, for nothing here is free from suffering.
Therefore, a king established in dharma should protect his subjects according to dharma.

The administration of protection, warfare, the instruction of dharma, deliberation on counsel, and happiness in due season— by these five, the earth prospers. He whose [affairs] are guarded in these respects is a king, O best of kings.

A king who constantly attends to these [duties] enjoys this earth. It is not possible for one person alone to oversee all of these continuously; by appointing trustworthy men to these tasks, a king enjoys the earth for a long time.
People hold dear that man who is a giver, one who shares his wealth, who is endowed with gentleness, who is pure,
and who does not abandon human beings; whereas he who, having understood the supreme good, applies himself to that knowledge, [is likewise held in high esteem].
Having cast aside his own opinion, the world follows him;
he who does not tolerate the words of one seeking his welfare due to their opposition soon becomes dejected and listens to things that are contrary.

He who does not fully perceive an intellect characterized by non-vulgar conduct falls away from the duty of a Kṣatriya, whether toward those already conquered or those yet unconquered. He who abandons his principal ministers and favors those who are inferior is lost.
Indeed, having encountered deep calamity and being afflicted,
he who out of hatred does not respect kinsmen endowed with auspicious qualities finds no firm footing; being unstable himself and possessed of stubborn anger, prosperity does not abide near him.
Furthermore, he who brings even those endowed with excellent qualities— who are otherwise unpleasant to his heart—
under his control through what is dear to them, remains long-established in fame. He should not expend wealth at an improper time, nor should he ever be distressed by what is disagreeable.
One should not rejoice excessively over what is dear; one should apply oneself to the practice of maintaining health.
One should constantly reflect: "Which kings are devoted to me? Which have sought refuge out of fear? And which among them possess the faults of those who are neutral?"
One who has ever been powerful should never at any time place trust in the weak;
for these fall upon the heedless like *bhāruṇḍa* birds.
Even if a husband is endowed with all virtues and speaks kindly, [one should not trust him].
The evil-minded man seeks to do harm; therefore, one should indeed be wary of such people.
Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, declared this secret doctrine of kingship:
"One who is intent on victory over men slays even the most formidable enemies."
12,095.001 Vāmadeva said:
12,095.001a A lord of the earth should increase his victory without even fighting;
12,095.001c they say that victory achieved through war is the lowest kind, O lord of men.
Furthermore, one should not seek to acquire what has not yet been gained while one's own foundation remains too weak;
for the acquisition of territory is not prescribed for a king whose base is frail. He whose realm is prosperous, well-provided, and loyal to its king [is secure].
That king whose ministers are contented and well-nourished has firm roots; that lord of the earth, whose warriors are highly satisfied, conciliated, and established through thorough testing,
conquers the world even with a small army.
Wherever force is powerful, there conciliation is employed; the giving of gifts preceded by conciliation is praised as the root of sowing dissension.
When the king perceives that the efforts of these three [means] have become fruitless, [he should resort to force].
Having identified the vulnerability (*randhra*), one should then employ the staff [of punishment] without hesitation.
When one is overwhelmed by enemies who are more powerful, one should practice indifference; for the strength of the strong lies in their capacity to kill.
O Bhārata, when a ruler of the earth becomes weak,
one should employ indifference toward him in a manner that does not conflict with the four [other] means;
for that fifth means is the most powerful of all.
O Lord of Kosala, O knower of reality, having understood the true meaning of these verses sung by the descendant of Bhṛgu, you shall act according to that truth,
even if the Rākṣasa should be slain by a Piśāca anywhere at all.

In such a situation, equanimity must be maintained; let the strong be slain by the stronger. For a weak protector of the earth may uproot the enemy of his enemies, just as one removes a thorn stuck in the foot with a thorn held in the hand.
O Lord of the Earth, among deceitful ministers and barbarians,
this neglect is said to be the most powerful of all stratagems;
one may destroy iron with stone, and likewise stone with iron.
One should pacify barbarians with other barbarians, just as one might subdue bilva trees with other bilva trees;
for arrogant slaves as well, one should employ this very same method here,
along with the suppression of the Caṇḍāla and Mleccha castes by means of punishment.
One should act toward the deceitful and the ill-behaved exactly as they have previously spoken.
Other deceitful ministers, as well as corrupt Brahmins and the like—
who oppose the four aims of life— should be managed through the five expedients.
Those of the city and the countryside who are deeply devoted and well-honored by him—
these laborers of the realm, whether they are hostile toward the kingdom,
ill-behaved, or well-disciplined, all must be managed with diligent effort.
Even the Caṇḍālas and Mlecchas, heretics and those who act contrary to their duties, as well as the powerful, the hermitages, and likewise singers and dancers—
possessing wealth and abundant grain— that king was firmly rooted.

That king is firmly rooted whose kingdom these [brahmins] inhabit, for they cause the accumulation of grain and are assistants in the increase of revenue. When he considers his own power and time to be superior, [he should act].
Then the wise man should seek to acquire foreign lands and wealth.
For one who is not stingy regarding enjoyments, who is compassionate toward all beings,
and who protects himself while acting with diligence, his realm increases.

He who behaves falsely toward his own subjects while they are acting rightly carves away at himself, just as one hews down a forest with an axe. Indeed, enemies do not diminish for a king, even though he slays them constantly.
He who knows how to restrain anger finds no enemy. A wise person should not perform any action that is loathed by noble people;
rather, he should apply himself to whatever he considers to be auspicious.
Others do not despise him, nor does he himself suffer distress,
that king who, despite having duties remaining, desires to experience happiness—
this is the conduct of a lord of the earth who abides among men.
"Having completely conquered both worlds, he is firmly established in victory.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, having been thus addressed by Vāmadeva, the monarch performed all of that."
By acting in this manner, you too shall conquer these two worlds; of this there is no doubt.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Now, suppose a Kṣatriya desires to conquer another Kṣatriya in battle.
"What is his righteous victory? Being thus questioned, tell this to me.
Bhīṣma said:
"Whether with allies or without allies, having approached the kingdom, the lord of the earth..."
He should say: "I shall be your king, and I will always protect you.
Give me my lawful tribute; otherwise, what will you do to me? If they should choose him when he has arrived there, it would be well.

One should say, "We shall wage war; listen, may it be well with us. O lord of men, if those who are not Kṣatriyas should somehow oppose you, they must be restrained by all possible means, for they are engaged in improper conduct.
"Thinking another Kṣatriya to be powerless, he then seizes his weapon,
considering him utterly incapable even of providing protection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Now, O Grandfather, tell me this: if a Kṣatriya king should advance against another Kṣatriya, how should he be fought? Bhīṣma said:
"A Kṣatriya should not be fought in battle unless he is armored and clad in mail.
One should speak to another one-on-one: 'Cast it forth! I shall hurl it!
If he should come forth armored, then one must likewise be armored."
If he should come with an army, then one should challenge him with an army;
if he should fight with deceit, one should combat him with deceit;
but if he should fight according to dharma, one should repel him by dharma alone.

One should not attack a chariot-warrior with a horse; a chariot-warrior should prevail over a chariot-warrior. One must not strike one who is in distress, nor one who is terrified, nor one who has been defeated.
An arrow should not be smeared with poison, nor should it be barbed; such is the weapon of the wicked.
One should fight solely for the sake of victory; one should not become angry with one who does not intend to kill.
There is no single elephant that can withstand an elephant in battle, nor is there a single elephant that exists against another.
A foot soldier should not fight an elephant, nor should he strike a foot soldier with an elephant.
An elephant might sometimes fight another elephant, or a well-trained horse;
but one endowed with the power of divine weapons may fight at will at all times—
whether against an elephant, on the ground, on level terrain, or indeed by means of a chariot or a horse.
In the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa, the monkeys were indeed the foot soldiers;
so too, O King, were the illustrious Lakṣmaṇa and Vibhīṣaṇa.
And at the time of Rāvaṇa’s end, Rāghava [advanced] in the chariot of Indra.
He struck down the evil-doing Rāvaṇa of wicked conduct;
all this is ordained for one endowed with the power of divine weapons,
as has been seen by the ancients in the battles between the gods and the asuras.
But when there is mutual dissension among the virtuous, if one of them should fall into misfortune, he must not be struck down— whether he be wounded or childless— in any way whatsoever. [Likewise,
one who is] with broken weapons, whose horse has perished, whose bowstring is severed, or whose vehicle has been destroyed.

He should be treated in his own territory, or he should be sent back to his own home; even if he is free from wounds, he must be released—this is the eternal law. Therefore, one should fight according to righteousness; so said Manu, the son of Svayambhū.

Among the virtuous, dharma is eternal; one should abide by it and not let it perish. Indeed, that Kṣatriya who, though increasing in power, conquers through unrighteousness, is a sinful man living by deceit; he destroys himself by his own hand.
This is the conduct of the wicked: one should conquer evil with goodness;
death through righteousness is better than victory through sinful action.
O King, unrighteousness practiced does not bear fruit immediately, like a cow.
Just as fire follows along, burning both the roots and the branches of a tree,
so too the sinner, having acquired wealth through evil deeds, rejoices;
and as he prospers through theft, that sinner becomes further attached to sin.
Thinking that "there is no dharma" and as if mocking those who are pure,
he goes to his destruction because of his lack of faith;
bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, he considers himself immortal.
Like a great leather bag inflated [with air], he swells because of his own actions;
then, like a tree from the bank of a river, he is swept away root and all,
and people revile him as one would a jar shattered against a stone.
12,096.021e Therefore, a ruler of the earth should desire victory through righteousness alone.
12,097.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,097.001a A lord of the world should not seek to conquer the earth through unrighteousness.
Having achieved victory through unrighteousness, what king would approve of it? For a victory joined with unrighteousness is unstable and leads away from heaven;
it ruins both the king and the earth, O bull of the Bharatas.
One should not strike one whose armor is shattered, who says "I am yours," who stands with palms joined in reverence, or who has laid down his weapons;
nor should a ruler fight one who has been defeated by force.
One should let her pass for a year; born from that [union], she shall become [his] wife again.
A maiden won by valor should not be touched for less than a year.
In this very same way, it applies to all wealth and whatever else has been seized by force.

Wealth must not remain unproductive; the Brāhmaṇas should drink its milk, or they should employ oxen for labor, or else it should be forgiven at that time. A king should fight only with a king; such is the dharma ordained.
No one who is not a Kṣatriya should ever act as a king under any circumstances. If a Brāhmaṇa should happen to pass between two armies drawn up for battle,
desiring peace for both sides, then no fighting should take place.

He who would transgress against a Brāhmaṇa would break the eternal boundary. But if one who merely calls himself a Kṣatriya should overstep this boundary, he shall thereafter become unworthy of praise and unacceptable in the assembly.
A king desiring victory should not follow that course of conduct which involves the destruction of righteousness and the breaking of established boundaries;
for what gain could possibly exceed a victory obtained through righteousness?

Having suddenly subdued the subjects, he should quickly pacify them through conciliation and the granting of enjoyments; this is the supreme policy for kings. For when they are exploited unjustly, they become distressed within their own kingdom.
They would wait upon his enemies, biding their time for a flood of calamities; and they would quickly seize the opportunity for his downfall in times of distress,
O King, being thoroughly corrupted and longing for the monarch’s ruin from every side.
An enemy should not be utterly destroyed, nor should he be excessively mutilated in any way;
for a man who has been excessively maimed may even give up his life at some point. Indeed, an offender is satisfied even when treated with only a slight measure of punishment.
Even a mere pure life is highly esteemed by such a king as he whose realm is prosperous and well-provided, who is beloved by his subjects,
whose servants and ministers are contented, and whose foundation is firm.
He by whom the officiating priests, domestic chaplains, teachers, and others esteemed for their learning—
who are worthy of honor— are duly honored, is indeed called a conqueror of the worlds.
By this very conduct, the best of gods attained the earth.

Following the *Aindra-vijaya* [sacrifice], the kings indeed sought to conquer [all others]. Having conquered the king in battle, King Pratardana seized his city, with the exception of the land itself; furthermore, he constantly brought back the nectar-like medicinal herbs.

Divodāsa brought as sacrificial gifts twelve thousand and ninety-seven Agnihotra fires, the remnants of the sacred fires, and the vessels for the oblation; having thus performed his duty, he was subsequently troubled. Nābhāga gave away entire kingdoms along with their kings as his sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

Except for the property of a *śrotriya* and the property of an ascetic, O Bhārata— O Yudhiṣṭhira, the various modes of conduct among those ancient kings who knew the dharma were diverse; all of that is pleasing to me.
"Or rather, a lord of the earth who desires victory through the superiority of all branches of knowledge—
and who seeks his own prosperity neither through deceit nor through hypocrisy— [should act thus].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull among the Bharatas, there is no dharma more sinful than the dharma of the Kṣatriya. In marching forth and in battle, the king slays great multitudes of people.
Yet, it is by such action that the king conquers the worlds."
"O learned one, O bull among the Bharatas, speak to me who desires to know.
Bhīṣma said:
"By the restraint of the wicked and by the support of the virtuous..."
Through sacrifices and gifts, kings become pure and stainless.
Seeking victory, kings oppress living beings;
yet having attained victory, they in turn cause their subjects to prosper.
By the power of their gifts, sacrifices, and austerities, they cast off all evils;
through their benevolence toward living beings, their merit increases.
Just as a field-clearer, having once cleared the field, [reaps the harvest].
He destroys the undergrowth and the grain, yet the grain is not destroyed;
thus, while discharging weapons, he slays those who deserve death. This is his complete atonement, as he again brings beings into existence.

He who protects living beings from the loss of wealth, from slaughter, and from affliction, and who grants them life by shielding them from robbers, is a giver of wealth, a giver of happiness, and a sovereign ruler.
That king, having performed all sacrifices with the gift of fearlessness as his sacrificial fee, [attains the highest state].
Having experienced auspicious things here, he attains the same world as Indra.
He who, when a cause for the sake of a Brahmin arises, goes forth and fights—
having raised himself up as the sacrificial post— is a sacrifice of infinite dakṣiṇā.
Fearlessly scattering his enemies and likewise receiving their arrows,
the gods perceived nothing on earth superior to him;
for as many weapons as pierced his skin in battle, [so many were his].
He enjoys as many inexhaustible worlds that yield all desires as there were hairs on his body; no blood flows from his limbs where he was pierced,
for by that very blood he is liberated from all sins.
Those who endure the sufferings of being scorched by wounds know no greater austerity than that; so say those who understand the Dharma. Cowards and base men turn their backs in battle.
Seeking refuge with a hero, as living beings seek life from the rain-cloud,
people would act appropriately if a hero were to protect them equally in times of peace as well as in times of fear; yet that is not how it happens.
If, recognizing what has been done for them, they were always to pay him homage and act toward him with propriety and justice, that would not be so;
for among men who appear equal, a vast difference is observed.
In battle, at the edge of the ranks, when the war-cry is raised and the troops charge forward,
the hero falls facing the enemy, while the coward flees; by treading the path that leads away from heaven, he abandons his companions in the hour of peril.
"O dear one, may you never be born as those lowest of men who,
having abandoned their companions in battle, go home in safety; for the gods, led by Indra, bring misfortune upon them."

If there are Kṣatriyas who, by abandoning their companions, desire to save their own lives, they should be struck with wood or clods of earth, or burned with a fire of straw; or they should be killed like cattle— such is the fate of those who act in this manner.
It is unrighteous for a Kṣatriya to meet his death upon his bed,
emitting phlegm and bile while piteously lamenting,
and thus to reach his end with a body unwounded by weapons.
Those conversant with the past do not praise such an act for a Kṣatriya.
O dear one, death at home is not praised for Kṣatriyas;
for those who are heroic, it is unheroic, contrary to dharma, and wretched.
Groaning, "This is suffering! Alas, what misery! How wicked!
with his face distorted and his breath foul, he caused great sorrow among his ministers;
longing for those who are free from disease, he repeatedly desired even death.
A hero who is proud and full of self-confidence does not deserve such a death;
having caused carnage in battles while surrounded by his kinsmen,
a Kṣatriya deserves death when he is grievously wounded by sharp weapons.

For a hero, possessed by truth and wrath, fights most fiercely; he does not even perceive his own limbs being mangled by enemies. Having met his death in battle, which is praised and honored by the world—
Having attained the vast merit of his own duty (*svadharma*), he goes to the same world as Śakra. Every warrior who, having renounced everything and surrendered his life,
remains a hero without showing his back, attains residence in the same world as Indra.
Wherever a hero, surrounded by enemies, is slain,
he attains imperishable worlds, provided he does not yield to dejection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"12,099.001a What worlds await those heroes who, fighting, do not retreat?
12,099.001c Tell me that, O Grandfather, regarding their destination upon meeting death.
12,099.002 Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Ambarīṣa and Indra.
For Ambarīṣa, the son of Nābhāga, having gone to heaven— which is so difficult to attain— [continued to perform his duties].
He beheld his own lord, the commander-in-chief, staying in the world of the gods together with Śakra; he was seated upon a supreme, divine celestial chariot composed of all splendor,
traveling higher and higher.
Seeing the general named Sudeva, of noble intellect, ascending above and having reached the station of heroes, the king was amazed at Sudeva’s supernatural power and spoke to Vāsava.
Having ruled the entire earth bounded by the oceans according to the prescribed rites,
he applied himself to the four social orders according to the scriptures out of a desire for righteousness; he practiced rigorous celibacy and served the household of his preceptor.
Having studied the Vedas according to dharma and the entire science of statecraft, he honored guests with food and drink, the ancestors with *svadhā* offerings,
the seers with the vows of Vedic recitation, and the gods with unsurpassed sacrifices.
"O Vāsava, having remained established in the duty of a Kṣatriya according to the scriptures and according to the prescribed rules,
and while awaiting the enemy host, I conquered them in battle;
by the ripening of that merit, I have now come into your presence."
"O King of the Gods, this Sudeva was formerly my general; he was a warrior of tranquil soul. Why is it that he now rejoices in heaven, seated upon a celestial chariot as radiant as the sun?"
Śakra said:
"O Lord of the Earth, you have witnessed with your own eyes the deed performed by him, through which he has attained such sovereignty as is very difficult for all the gods to obtain."
O King, in former times, while you were rightly protecting the earth according to dharma,
all those enemies who acted as your adversaries were utterly defeated—
