namely Sandhāma, Vidhāma, and the mighty Sudhāma.
O lord of the earth, those three Rākṣasas, difficult to conquer in the world and intoxicated by battle,
were the sons of the Rākṣasa king Śataśṛṅga.
Then, at that auspicious time while you were performing your sacrifice, they arrived.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, he was performing the great sacrifice of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). Indeed,
three *rākṣasa*s arrived there for the purpose of creating obstacles for him,
leading a great army of *rākṣasa*s with a retinue of a hundred million.
Then all those subjects were taken captive by you;
all the subjects were overwhelmed, as were all your soldiers. And Sudeva, the commander of the army, was cast out by you.

12,099.010 Having heard those words of the ministers, he was excluded from all affairs. 12,099.011 Having again heard their deceitful speech, O Lord of the Earth, Sudeva was dispatched by you, accompanied by the entire army. 12,099.012 [He was sent] with all his troops.
O lord of men, for the sake of slaying the invincible Rākṣasas,
it is not desired that you return without first defeating the Rākṣasa army,
nor without having liberated Bandī.
Having heard those words, O King, Sudeva set out;
and he reached that region where the subjects had been taken captive. There he beheld a most formidable and vast army of Rākṣasas.
Seeing this, Sudeva, the commander of the army, reflected:
"This host cannot be conquered even by the gods and asuras led by Indra;
Ambarīṣa is not capable of destroying even a sixteenth part of them."
"How much more so am I such as this, endowed with the great power of celestial weapons? Then,
O King, he dispatched his entire army once again to where you were, O monarch, together with all your ministers and their stratagems.
Then, having sought refuge in Rudra, Mahādeva, the Lord of the world,
he praised the god whose banner is the bull and who dwells in the cremation ground.
Having offered praise, he took up a weapon and prepared to cut off his own head.
Out of compassion, the God of Gods seized his right hand along with the weapon; seeing this, he spoke as follows:
"Son, tell me, what reckless act do you intend to perform?"
Bowing his head to the earth, he said to Mahādeva:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, I am unable to conquer this army of Rākṣasas in battle; therefore, I shall give up my life."
"O Mahādeva, O Lord of the World, be the refuge for me who am distressed. You must not depart, O unconquered one," so said the Lord of the World.
"O Mahādeva, Ambarīṣa has been slandered along with his ministers."
Mahādeva spoke to Sudeva, who had fallen upon the earth,
his face cast downward; that Great-Souled One, desiring the welfare of all beings,
summoned Dhanurveda along with his attendants and his weapons.
Śaṅkara gave him a chariot crowded with elephants, serpents, and horses, adorned with divine weapons,
and that most illustrious chariot by which Tripura was destroyed;
he also gave him the bow Pināka, a sword, and the Raudra weapon.
With that [weapon], by which the three-eyed god slew all the asuras, Mahādeva struck them down;
and Mahādeva spoke to Sudeva, the commander of the army:
"O Sudeva, you shall be invincible upon this chariot even by the gods and asuras."
Deluded by illusion, you ought not to set foot upon the ground;
standing here, you shall forever conquer all the thirty gods and all the dānavas.
Neither the rākṣasas nor the piśācas are able to behold such a sight.
How could he have fought with you in a chariot that possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns? Having conquered all the Rākṣasas and effected the liberation of the captives,
and having slain them all in hand-to-hand combat, he has now been killed.
"O King, having encountered Vidhama, Vidhama has been struck down.
O Śakra, he did not perform sacrifices with the principal rites, nor were the twice-born gratified by him according to the rules; why then does he [afflict] me so excessively?"
Indra said:
"O dear one, for this Sudeva there was indeed a very great sacrifice of battle, as well as for any other man who fights."
"Every warrior who has donned his armor and been consecrated, having reached the front of the army, stands within the jurisdiction of the sacrifice of battle; this is the certain conclusion.
Ambarīṣa said:
"What are the oblations in this sacrifice here? What is the clarified butter, and what is the sacrificial fee?
And who are said to be the officiating priests here? Tell me that, O Śatakratu.
Indra said:

There, the elephants were the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and the horses were the *adhvaryu* priests; the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) consisted of supreme meats, and the blood served as the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Jackals, vultures, and crows were the members of the assembly (*sadasya*) at that long-duration sacrifice (*sattra*).

They drink the remnants of the clarified butter and consume the sacrificial oblation at the rite. Then, for that performer of the long sacrifice, the multitudes of spears and lances, the swords, javelins, and battle-axes— blazing, sharpened, and tempered— are his sacrificial ladles.
His great sacrificial ladle was an arrow— long as a bow drawn with force, sharp, capable of rending the bodies of enemies, straight, well-whetted, and yellowed;
it was sheathed in leopard skin and had a hilt fashioned from ivory.
In that battle, a sword held in the trunk of an elephant would serve as his sacrificial wooden sword (sphya).
With blazing, sharpened, and yellowed spears, javelins,
and battle-axes made of refined iron and tipped with sharp points, there shall be a shower of wealth [upon him].
Extensive as the number of moments, arising from noble birth and abundant—
whatever blood flows upon the earth in battle out of agitation,
that constitutes for him a full oblation to the Hotṛ priest, which is prosperous and grants all desires.
"For him at the head of the army from whom these words are heard—'Cut! Pierce!'—the chanters of Sāmans sing his funeral hymns in the abode of Yama.
They say that the front of the enemy's army is indeed his *havirdhāna* (sacrificial oblation-chamber)."
A collection of twelve thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine elephants, horses,
and armored men is prescribed for that sacrifice known as the Śyenacit fire-altar;
indeed, a headless torso (kabandha) arises therein when a thousand [enemies] have been slain.
That sacrificial post of that hero is said to be made of khadira wood and to have eight corners (12,099.024c).
When the *iḍā* has been invoked, the elephants, goaded by hooks, trumpet aloud (12,099.025a).
O King, with the sound of their slapping palms, they cry out like the *vaṣaṭ* call (12,099.025c).
In that battle, the drum is known as the Udgātṛ priest who chants the three Sāmans. He who, when the property of a Brahmin is being seized, casts off his dear body in battle—
having raised himself as the sacrificial post— is a sacrifice of infinite dakṣiṇā.
But that hero who, for the sake of his master, should display valor at the head of the army and not turn back out of fear— his worlds shall be just like mine,
with arms resembling iron clubs and swords shaped like dark blue moons.
The worlds of him whose altar is strewn with offerings are like my own;
and the worlds of him who, standing firm for victory, disregards all assistance as he plunges into the midst of the army are like my own.
This river has masses of *tomara* spears for its rafts, with drums for its frogs and tortoises;
it is difficult to cross, with the bones of heroes for its gravel, and flesh and blood for its mud. Swords and shields serve as its floats, while hair forms its moss and aquatic plants.
With horses, elephants, and chariots shattered, it formed a bridge;

with banners and standards for its reeds, it was a river whose current was the slain mounts. Filled to the brim with the water of blood, it was difficult for men who had reached the further shore to cross.
Filled with slain elephants and great crocodiles, carrying one to the next world and bringing ill omen;
having spears, swords, and banners for its banks, and vultures, herons, crows, and water-fowl for its rafts;
frequented by man-eaters, it brings terror to the timid.
The river flowing from the great sacrifice of warriors is known as his final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*).
For him whose altar is strewn with the heads of enemies—
upon the necks of horses and the backs of elephants— his worlds shall be just like mine.
The wise say that for him, the enemy's vanguard is the *patnīśālā* (the hall of the wives), his own army is the *havirdhāna* (the oblation-holding shed),
the warriors stationed in the center are the *sadas*, and the fire of the northern quarter is the *āgnīdhra*.
When the enemy host and its womenfolk are not far from all the worlds,
and when the battle array is formed on both sides with open space in front,
that space is his altar; likewise, in the sacrifice, the three Vedas are always the three sacred fires.
But that warrior who, turning back in terror, is slain by his enemies, goes to a bottomless hell; of this there is no doubt. He for whom a river is formed, overflowing with the torrent of his blood—
He who,
having killed a commander-in-chief, mounts his chariot, shall go to the supreme goal;
he is one who strides with the steps of Viṣṇu, a sacrifice equal to Bṛhaspati.
Whether it be the leader, or the authority, or whoever there may be who is honored—
if one seizes such a person alive, his worlds shall be just like mine. One should never grieve for a hero slain in battle.

For a slain hero is not to be mourned; he is glorified in the world of heaven. For those who desire to perform for him no funeral food, no water libation, no ritual bathing, nor even the rites of impurity—listen to me regarding the worlds that await him.
Twelve thousand, nine hundred and ninety-four thousand excellent Apsarases run in haste toward the hero slain in battle, thinking, "May he become my husband.
This indeed is austerity, merit, and eternal righteousness.

There are four who possess the four stages of life (āśramas) and do not flee in battle: one who is aged, one whose strength is spent, a woman, and a twice-born (dvija). Furthermore, one whose mouth is full of grass and one who says, "I am yours."
I [slew] Vṛtra, Bala, Pāka, Śatamāya, Virocana,
the irresistible Namuci, and Śambara of manifold illusions;
as well as Vipracitti the Daitya and all the sons of Danu.
"Having slain Prahrāda in battle, I then became the lord of the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"Having heard these words of Śakra and having accepted them,"
Ambarīṣa attained the perfection of his own twelve thousand nine hundred and fifty-nine warriors.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.

12,100.001c Hear, O Yudhiṣṭhira, how Pratardana and the King of Mithilā engaged in battle; 12,100.002a how Janaka of Mithilā, wearing his sacrificial thread in the midst of combat, 12,100.002c inspired his warriors with courage— learn that from me.
King Janaka of Mithilā, a high-souled knower of all principles, showed his own warriors both heaven and hell.
"Behold, these radiant worlds belong to those who are fearless; come, look! he said.
These [heavenly realms] are filled with Gandharva maidens and inexhaustible cows that grant all desires;
yet for those who flee, these hells stand before them,
along with eternal infamy and immediate downfall.

Seeing those enemies victorious, you should instead cultivate the resolve for renunciation; do not become subject to that bottomless hell. For the root of renunciation is the unsurpassed gateway to heaven for the brave.
Thus addressed by the king, O conqueror of enemy cities,
those warriors defeated their foes in battle, gladdening the lord of men. Therefore, one who possesses self-control should always stand at the forefront of the fray.

Elephants should be placed in the midst of chariot-warriors, cavalry behind the chariots, and armored infantry stationed in the intervals between the cavalry. A king who arranges his forces in this manner always conquers his enemies.
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, this must always be ordained:
all those who desire merit and are filled with great indignation at [the enemy's] conduct should agitate the enemy ranks in fair combat, like sea-monsters churning the ocean.
Having established mutual order, they should gladden those who are despondent;
he should protect the conquered land and not pursue too closely those who have been broken.
For those who return once more, having lost all hope for life, [the enemy becomes vulnerable].
"O King, the momentum [of those fleeing] is not easily endured; therefore, one should not pursue them too closely.
For heroes do not wish to strike those who are fleeing out of fear;
therefore, one should not carry out an excessive pursuit of those who are running away."
For the immobile are indeed the food of the mobile; the toothless are the food of those with fangs;
the handless are the food of those with hands; and the cowardly are the food of the hero.
Though they possess identical backs, bellies, hands, and feet;
The timid follow behind the brave;
therefore, afflicted by fear, they bow down repeatedly and wait upon the brave with palms joined in reverence.
This world always depends upon the arms of heroes like a son;
therefore, in all circumstances, a hero deserves honor.
Indeed, there is nothing superior to heroism to be found in the three worlds.
12,100.018 The hero protects everything; everything is established upon the hero.
12,101.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said: 12,101.001a O bull of the Bharatas, tell me how those seeking victory lead an army.
"Even if it involves slight oppression of dharma, tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"For some dharmas are established through truth, while others are established through logical justification."
Some, by virtue of their virtuous conduct, are likewise suitable [for this];
I shall explain the methods of practice that accomplish both material wealth and the Dharma. However, those who are lawless bandits become adversaries on the path.

To counteract these, I shall now declare the traditional wisdom; learn from me those means for the successful accomplishment of all tasks. O Bhārata, two kinds of intelligence are to be known: the straight and the crooked.
Knowing this, one should not serve a crooked person, and one should repel such a person when they approach.
For even enemies employ the method of sowing dissension against a king; therefore, a king who recognizes that deceit should repel it just as he would enemies.
The flanks of elephants, the skins of bulls and pythons, as well as quills, armor, and iron— these were considered their body protections;
their weapons were sharp and yellow, and their mail was yellow and red.
Let those banners and standards be dyed in various colors;
let there be double-edged spears, javelins, swords, and sharpened battle-axes,
as well as shields and shields of leather, prepared in great numbers.
The weapons have been mastered and the warriors have undergone their training;
the mobilization of the army is recommended during the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa,
for at that time the earth is rich with ripened crops and well-supplied with water.

O Bhārata, the season is neither too cold nor too hot; therefore, one should mobilize [the army] at that time, or during the calamities of the enemies. In these circumstances, the deployment of the army for the purpose of harassing the foe is highly recommended.
A path that has water and grass, which is level and easy to traverse, is praised;
for it has been made familiar by skilled scouts who range the forests,
and cannot be traversed by inexperienced forest-dwellers, just like a herd of deer.

Therefore, those seeking victory station at the front of all their armies a division of men who are capable, loyal, and of noble birth. A camp that possesses water, is difficult of access, and has open space on all sides is highly recommended.
Likewise, there should be a prevention of enemies who approach; however,
those people who are skilled in battle consider open space near a forest to be superior in its qualities due to the many varieties of advantages it offers.
In that situation, there should be the deployment of forces not too far away;
there should be the deployment of scouts and the concealment of foot soldiers, which serves as a refuge for the purpose of countering the enemy and dealing with calamities.
Keeping the Seven Sages behind them, they should fight like immovable mountains;
by this method, O King, one may even conquer those who are difficult to defeat.
Where the wind blows, where the sun shines, and where Śukra is, there victory lies.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, among these qualities, each preceding one is superior when they occur in combination.
Those who are skilled in warfare praise a terrain for horses that is free from mud, devoid of water, without boundaries, and without clods of earth."
A chariot ground that is level, waterless, and open is highly praised; one for elephant-warriors should have low trees, thick undergrowth, and be provided with water;
while a ground for infantry should have many obstacles, large trees, and be covered with cane and bamboo.
The earth, mountains, and groves are the proper ground for infantry;
O Bhārata, an army consisting largely of infantry is firm. An army consisting largely of chariots and horses is praised on clear days.
An army consisting largely of infantry and elephants is praised during the rainy season.

Having carefully enumerated these advantages, one should employ [the forces] according to the place and time. Thus reflecting, he who marches out, honored by the lunar day and the asterism, [attains success].
By employing his army correctly, he shall always achieve victory.
He must not strike those who are asleep, thirsty, exhausted, or scattered, nor during their withdrawal,
their march, their movement, or at the times of drinking and eating.

Having made external proposals that were overthrown, overturned, frustrated, and rendered insignificant— proposals that were well-concealed, yet initiated with great effort and tormented by their very presentation—
and having made them follow him into his own quarters; he sent out spies who moved about outside.
Those who follow at the gate that has come down through tradition, those who are attendants and gatekeepers, and whoever are the agile warriors;
those who break through the enemy ranks and those who cover up the broken ones.
They should share the same food and drink, and their wages should be doubled;
having ascertained their caste, lineage, and their most excellent and auspicious deeds,
they should be provided with double wages for the sake of protecting the body equally.
One should cause their wages to be set at three or four times [the standard rate].
Commanders of ten should be appointed, as well as commanders of a hundred;
one should appoint a brave and tireless man as the commander of a thousand among them.
Having assembled our principal leaders, we shall swear this oath:
"We shall not abandon one another in battle for the sake of victory. Let those among us who are cowards turn back right here.
12,101.030c They would not cause a breach while creating a rift when the tumult has arisen; 12,101.030d such men would neither create a rift nor carry out a slaughter in the encounter.
12,101.031a By fleeing in battle, one destroys oneself and one's own side.
In flight, there is the loss of wealth, death, infamy, and disgrace;
for the man who flees, there are unpleasant and unhappy words from one whose lips and teeth quiver and who has cast away all his weapons.
May it be so with our enemies— that they abandon their companions when life is in danger and flee while pursued by foes;
for those who turn their backs in battle are indeed the lowest of men.
They merely increase the ranks [of the enemy]; they are of no help either in the afterlife or in this world.
O dear one, enemies with joyful minds advance against the one who flees, while friends greet the victor with salutations and auspicious blessings.
O King, when enemies rejoice at one's misfortune,
I consider that grief to be more unbearable than even death. Know that prosperity is the root of dharma and of all happiness.
The coward goes to the enemy, while the hero attains her; desiring heaven, we, having renounced our lives in battle,
shall attain the state of the righteous whether we are victorious or slain.
Having thus sworn their oaths and utterly abandoned their lives,
those fearless heroes plunged into the enemy host. At the front would be the division of men armed with swords and shields.

The wagon-array should be at the rear, and likewise the women in the middle; this is for the purpose of resisting the enemy and for the concealment of the foot-soldiers, so that even those enemies who are greedy for plunder may be held in check by those stationed in the vanguard.
Those who were previously esteemed—endowed with courage and high-mindedness—should advance first; the other people shall follow them.
Furthermore, one must exert effort to inspire even those who are timid.
Or they may remain nearby, merely observing the enemy's divisions.

One should fight a small number of troops in a compact formation, but one may at will spread out a large number. When a small force is engaged with many, the array should be "needle-mouthed" (sūcīmukha).
Whether in the midst of battle or when rejoicing, whether it be true or false, one might raise one's arms and cry out, "They are broken! They are broken!
Our allies' forces have arrived; strike without fear!"
Making a terrifying roar, they should pursue [the enemy] shouting aloud;
they should sound war-cries (*kṣveḍā*), shouts of joy (*kilakilā*), conchs, saws, and cow-horns, as well as kettledrums, clay drums, small drums, and elephants.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Bhārata, O King, what is the character of those people, what is their exertion, and what is their appearance in battle? What is their armor, and what are their weapons? How should men be in combat?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this world, weapons and armor are fashioned exactly according to established practice;
it is precisely through such conduct that a person proceeds in their actions."
For the sake of seizing [the enemy], men likewise carry out such tasks:
the Gāndhāras and Sindhusauvīras, who fight with claws and spears,
and the very powerful Ābhīras— that army is capable of crossing over everything.
The Uśīnaras are indeed courageous and skilled in all weapons;
the Easterners are experts in fighting with elephants and are deceptive combatants.
Likewise are the Yavanas and Kāmbojas, as well as those who dwell around Mathurā.
These southerners, skilled in hand-to-hand combat and wielding swords and shields,
are everywhere born as heroes, beings of great essence and great strength; the people of Avanti are great heroes, and the Mālavas are experts in the fourfold army.
For even a single man may stand facing a thousand in battle; this is generally declared [to be the case]. Now listen to my characteristics:
they have mouths and eyes like those of lions and tigers, and they walk with the gait of lions and tigers.
Some had eyes like those of pigeons or kuṇḍalas; all were heroic and destructive.
Others had voices like deer, eyes like leopards, or eyes like bulls.
Some were eloquent, others were extremely fierce, wrathful, or possessed voices like those of kinnarīs.
Some had voices like thunderclouds and angry faces, while others made sounds like young camels; they had crooked noses and shanks, traveled great distances, and could leap far.
They were as thin as cats, hunched, with sparse hair and thin skin.
They are heroic yet fickle-minded, and thus difficult to overcome;
some have eyes like those of an iguana, while others are of gentle nature.
Those men who possess the gait and sound of horses are capable of reaching the further shore.
Well-knit, slender, broad-chested, and well-proportioned, they dance and rejoice at the sound of musical instruments and in the midst of quarrels;
their eyes are deep-set or protruding, tawny, and their faces are knit with frowns.
Likewise, all those heroes who were ready to cast off their bodies had eyes like those of a mongoose;
some had squinting eyes, others had prominent foreheads, and still others had fleshless jaws.
Their arms and fingers were crooked, they were emaciated, and their veins stood out prominently.
When the battle has arrived, they charge with extreme velocity;
like elephants in rut, they become difficult to approach.
Their hair-ends are blazing and disheveled, and their flanks, jaws, and faces are massive.
With elevated shoulders, broad necks, and massive calves, they were misshapen; some had upturned faces while others had beautiful necks, yet they were bent like birds,
with heads as large as balls and mouths like those of snakes or wildcats.
They possess fierce voices and are full of wrath, rushing into the clamor of battles; ignorant of dharma, arrogant, terrible, and displaying a cruel nature—
all these outcasts have surrendered their very selves and never retreat.
They should always be placed at the front of the army; they are slain, and they also slay.
These unrighteous men of broken conduct—truly, their defeat is justified. In this very way, they also frequently incite anger even against the king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull among men, what are the auspicious signs of victory for an army? I wish to know those things here."
Bhīṣma said:
O bull among men, I shall describe in their entirety all those auspicious forms that belong to a victorious army.
When impelled by time, fate first undergoes transformation within the human realm;
those who possess wisdom perceive this with the long eye of knowledge. And in this regard, those who know the truth [prescribe] the rules for expiation, as well as recitations and fire-oblations.
Performing auspicious rites, they even pacify all that is unfavorable. O Bhārata, in whichever army the warriors and the mounts have exalted spirits, one may declare certain victory for that side.
The winds blow following after her, and likewise do rainbows; the clouds follow her, as do the rays of the sun.
Jackals, cranes, and vultures all move in accordance with her from every side.
When they advance against the army, then there is unsurpassed success:
the fire is bright in luster, with upward-pointing rays, smokeless, and its flames turning to the right.
Auspicious fragrances and the smoke of oblations waft abroad; they say this is a sign of impending victory. There are deep-sounding and loud-voiced cries.
Where conchs and kettledrums resound and the combatants become irresistible,
they say this is the form of victory yet to come.
For those who have set out or are about to depart, deer seen on the left and behind are auspicious; for those wishing to strike, they say that deer on the right bring success.
But those who are in front ward off [the danger],
as auspicious-sounding birds cry out:
the swans, cranes, woodpeckers, and blue jays.
The warriors become joyful and full of courage;
they say this is the sign of victory to come. [This is seen] in their weapons, feathers, armor, and banners.
With the radiant complexions of the youths' faces and with the trumpeting elephants and neighing horses,
it was resplendent and difficult to look upon.
Those whose armies are obedient, free from arrogance, and established in mutual friendship overcome their enemies.
Those whose warriors practice purity— this they say is the form of victory yet to come.
Sounds, touches, and likewise scents circulate, pleasing to the mind.
Courage enters the warriors; that indeed is the gateway to victory.

For one who has already entered [the enemy's ranks], a favorable omen on the left is desired; for one about to enter, it is on the right. From behind, it accomplishes the objective; from the front, it forbids it.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, having assembled a great fourfold army,
you should first strive for his return through conciliation, and likewise through battle.
For that which is called war, O Bhārata, is the lowest form of victory."
"Whether victory in battle is due to chance or destiny— such was the deliberation.
Like a great torrent of water, or like herds of terrified deer,
the vast army, once broken, is most difficult to restrain."
"They are broken"—for this very reason, even the wise are shattered without cause.
This great army, possessing noble strength, resembles a herd of *ruru* deer;
they know one another, are filled with joy, have renounced their lives, and are firmly resolved.
Even fifty heroes crush the enemy host; or even five, six, or seven of noble birth, who are honored and firmly resolved, conquer their enemies here in this world.

A battle should not be undertaken by any means whatsoever if it can be avoided; among the methods of conciliation, sowing dissension, and bribery, war is said to be the last resort. For the mere approach of an army instills fear and afflicts the timid.
"Like from a blazing thunderbolt, where indeed will this fall?
Knowing that the assembly is about to advance,
the limbs of those warriors who then retreat, as well as those of the entire realm, tremble."
O King, the entire realm, including all things stationary and moving, is distressed;
the marrow of embodied beings, scorched by the heat of weapons, fails them.
Therefore, conciliation mixed with severity must be employed toward them again and again.

For when enemies are being oppressed, they resort to alliances in every way; therefore, one should dispatch spies for the purpose of creating dissension among those in the intermediate positions. An alliance with the king who is beyond that [the immediate enemy] is highly recommended.
For no other kind of affliction can be inflicted upon him as severe as being obstructed on all sides by an enemy; indeed,
forgiveness is the way of the virtuous, for constant intolerance is never right.
O Pārtha, understand the purpose of both forbearance and lack of forbearance:
the fame of a king who, having conquered his enemies, remains patient increases;
for even his enemies place their trust in him, despite his great offenses.
Śambara, however, thinks that patience is virtuous once one has emaciated oneself; yet,
when wood that has not been heated returns again to its original state,
the teachers do not praise this, nor is it a sound illustration.
They should be governed without causing distress and without destruction, like one's own sons.
A king who is harsh, O Yudhiṣṭhira, becomes hateful to all beings; they even despise him if he is too mild. Therefore, he should partake of both qualities.
O Bhārata, one who is about to strike should speak kindly; even while striking, he should do so with gentleness.
Having struck, he should feel compassion, as if grieving and as if weeping, saying these words beforehand: "It is not pleasing to me that he has been slain."
Though addressed by me again and again, you did not follow my words.
Alas, I desire life; such a man as you does not deserve death. Truly, men who do not flee from battle are very difficult to find.
"An unpleasant thing has been done by him who has slain this man in battle"—
speaking these words, he should honor his slayers while remaining in seclusion.
And as for what those offenders might do to the slayers, whether they have been killed or not...
Even raising his arm, he should cry out, desiring to win over the people;
acting thus with conciliation in all circumstances, the king who knows the dharma and is free from fear becomes beloved by all beings.
O Bhārata, all beings place their trust in him;
when one is trusted, he is able to enjoy whatever is presented according to his desire.
Therefore, a king should inspire confidence in all beings through sincerity.
"And he who desires to enjoy the earth must protect it on all sides.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, how [should one act] toward one who is mild, how toward one who is fierce, and how toward one who has a great following?"
"O Grandfather, tell me how a king should conduct himself toward an enemy.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having approached Bṛhaspati and saluted him with joined palms, Vāsava, the lord of the gods and slayer of enemy heroes, questioned him.
"O Brahmin, how may I act tirelessly toward those who are hostile? And how may I restrain them through skillful means without utterly exterminating them?
For when two armies clash, victory would be common to both."
"What must I do so that the blazing and majestic Śrī does not forsake me? Then, skilled in virtue, wealth, and pleasure, possessed of eloquence,
and knowing the ordinances of royal duty, he replied to Purandara.

One should never desire to restrain wrongdoers through quarreling; for resentment and intolerance are the ways of the foolish. One who desires the destruction of an enemy must not reveal his own vulnerability.
Restraining anger, strength, and indignation within his own self,
he should serve his enemy like a person of confidence, while remaining distrustful himself;
he should always speak what is pleasant and never do anything unpleasant.
One should desist from dry quarrels and avoid straining one's throat. Just as a skilled fowler, whose voice resembles that of birds,
brings those birds under his control, so too does the king who applies himself with skill.
"O Purandara, one should bring enemies under one's control and destroy them;
for one who constantly disregards his foes does not sleep in peace, O Vāsava. Such a wicked-souled person remains ever vigilant, like a fire that has broken out in a heap of rubbish."
O Lord, when a general victory has been achieved, one should not engage in a full-scale assault;

rather, having brought the enemy under control, one should inspire confidence and then deliver him into submission. One should bring them under control, but one should not suppress them with harsh and violent afflictions.
Just as one does not desire the depletion of a king’s sharp weapons, so too, O Śakra, one who understands resolve should be envious of the cause and envious of the fruit;
he should always conquer his enemies by means of their very faults, which appear in the form of virtues.
Having deliberated with his high-souled ministers who were skilled in counsel,
and while remaining indifferent even when treated with contempt— his heart unconquered—
he should then strike him at the right time, once the other's position has shifted even slightly.
And he should corrupt his army through trusted agents who act on his behalf;
knowing its beginning, middle, and end, he should investigate it in secret.
And knowing its strength according to its true measure, he should undermine his enemy's forces.
By means of sowing dissension, by bribery, and likewise by using medicines to create discord,
one should not, however, ever arrange a close association with enemies;
even after enduring them for a long time, one must surely destroy the adversaries.
Waiting for the right time, he should keep watch so that they may gain his confidence; O Lord of Śacī,
he should attend upon them and speak what is pleasing.

One should not strike one's enemies immediately; for victory seen without feverish haste is that which does not aggravate the existing wound nor create a new one. When the right time has arrived, one should strike; then it does not recur.
O Lord of the Gods, when a man desires to strike an enemy,
if the opportune moment should pass him by while he awaits that time,
that moment will be difficult for him to find again when he wishes to carry out his purpose.
Thus, by gathering those esteemed by the virtuous, one should surely conquer through vigor;
one should always accomplish things in due time and should not exert pressure before the [right] moment has arrived.
Having abandoned desire, anger, and likewise egoism, [one should act].

O Purandara, one who is disciplined should seek out the vulnerabilities of his enemies. O best of gods, O Śakra, mildness, punishment, laziness, negligence, and various forms of illusion overcome the undiscerning man.
Having destroyed these four and having countered his opponent's illusions,
he is then able to strike at his enemies without hesitation. Whenever it can be accomplished by a single means, one should employ that secret method.

Ministers keep secrets hidden from one another, yet they may also cause them to be divulged; or, considering something impossible, he should enter into an agreement with others. Against those who are unseen, he should employ the "brahma-punishment" (secret measures), and against those who are seen, the fourfold army.
The king should first employ sowing dissension, and likewise silent punishment; he should apply each at the appropriate time, as the occasion arises.
Furthermore, at the proper time, he should resort to prostration before a more powerful enemy.
One who is vigilant should seek the destruction of an enemy who is negligent,
even while that enemy is engaged in service through prostration, gifts, or speaking with sweet words; one should serve such an adversary but never cause him suspicion.
One should always avoid the haunts of those who are suspicious;
having harmed them, one should not place trust in them, for they remain watchful here, cast out.
Indeed, O best of gods, there is no task more difficult than this.
Just as there is sovereignty over those of various conducts, O Lord of the Immortals,
so too is the arising of those with various characters described.
One should strive by resorting to yoga, keeping both friends and enemies at bay.
People despise even one who is mild, yet they tremble before one who is harsh. Therefore, do not be too harsh, nor be too mild; be both harsh and mild.
Just as in a swift torrent where water overflows from all sides, [one must navigate with skill].
A king who is constantly negligent is undermined by his own subjects, just as a kingdom is ruined by one who is heedless.
O Purandara, one should not attack all enemies simultaneously; rather, one should employ conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force as the occasion demands.
Crushing them one by one, he should proceed skillfully against those who remain; even if capable, a wise king should not attack all at once,
especially when he possesses a vast army crowded with horses, elephants, and chariots.
When one considers that the sixfold army— abounding in infantry and machines and deeply loyal—
is facing a multiform increase [of the enemy] in an adverse manner, then,
having turned back, one should strike the bandits without hesitation.
Neither conciliation nor the secret application of force is praised; gentleness toward enemies is never conducive to one's journey.
There is neither the destruction of crops nor the act of mixing [grains].
Furthermore, there is no further deliberation regarding primordial nature (prakṛti),
nor are the various manifestations of illusion secondary;
likewise, evil arises from contact with the spies.
He should employ trustworthy men,
being fully engaged in both cities and provinces;
and the rulers of the earth should follow after their cities.
In those cities, they acquired all enjoyments here;
applying the established policy according to rule,
O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra.
Having bestowed secret wealth upon them,
having cut off their enjoyments and set aside their own [possessions],
and having declared, "They are wicked because of their own faults";
And they employ them in pure kingdoms,
likewise with others who are experts in the science of pleasure (*ratiśāstra*),
well-adorned, and who perceive according to the prescriptions of the treatises.
"By means of those well-trained and expert in the exposition of the commentaries,
you should ascertain the intentions of others.
Indra said:
"O best of the twice-born, what are the signs of a wicked person?
How may one recognize a wicked person? Being asked this, please tell it to me.
Bṛhaspati said:
He speaks of faults behind one's back and finds fault with one's good qualities;
when others are praising them, he remains silent or turns his face away.
For even in silence, there must be a reason for such behavior.
He betrays his trust by biting his lips and shaking his head; he speaks repeatedly, both in company and in solitude;
he changes his expression when not looked at, or fails to speak upon being seen.
He eats separately and does not share [the meal] today according to the prescribed rule;
his disposition is especially observable in matters of seating, bedding, and vehicles.
Suffering when one suffers and joy when one is dear to them—this much is the definition of a friend.

But that which is the opposite should be understood as the very characteristic of an enemy. O Lord of the Thirty-three, you should recognize these [characteristics] exactly as they have been described; for among men who are corrupted, their own nature is the most powerful.
"Thus, O best of gods, the cognition of the wicked has been described to you,
O Lord of the Immortals, after you have duly heard the true meaning of the scriptures.
Bhīṣma said:
Devoted to the destruction of his enemies, he made those words of Bṛhaspati come true; and in due time, that slayer of foes set out for victory.
And Purandara brought his enemies under his control.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"A righteous king, failing to attain his objectives and being oppressed by his ministers—"
"Having fallen away from both his treasury and his army, how should one who desires happiness conduct himself?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, this ancient history concerning Kṣemadarśin is recited."
I shall relate that to you; listen to it, Yudhiṣṭhira. We have heard that in former times, when Prince Kṣemadarśin’s strength was exhausted, the sage Kālakavṛkṣīya came to him.
Approaching him and clasping his feet, he who was beset by a dire calamity asked:
"O Brahmin, what should a man like me do, who is entitled to a share in wealth and strives for it again and again, yet fails to obtain a kingdom?"
"Except for death, except for theft, except for taking refuge with another,
and except for conduct that is base— explain that to me, O best of beings (12.105.005). [Tell me] also of one who is afflicted by disease, whether mental or otherwise (12.105.006)."
One who is learned, whose wisdom is perfected, and who is like you, would be a refuge.
For a man, having become disillusioned with desires and having restrained himself, prospers in happiness;
having abandoned both pleasure and grief, he attains wealth consisting of dispassion.
I grieve for those whose happiness is rooted in wealth; for my own vast riches have vanished like things seen in a dream.
Alas, they perform a difficult task indeed who renounce great wealth!
"Even though they are non-existent, we are unable to abandon them—
these who have reached such a state, wretched, afflicted, and fallen from prosperity.
O Brahmin, please instruct me regarding whatever other happiness exists here."
Thus addressed by the wise prince Kausalya,
the highly effulgent sage Kālakavṛkṣīya replied:
"O discerning one, this very resolve should have been formed by you long ago."
"All this—whatever exists as 'I' and 'mine'—is indeed impermanent. Whatever you think exists, know that all of it does not exist.
Thus, the wise man is not distressed, even when fallen into the most difficult calamity."
For that which has been and that which will be is certain not to exist;
thus, having known what is to be known, you shall be liberated from unrighteousness.
And whatever was in former aggregations, and whatever was in those even more ancient and further ones—

All that does not exist, and having known that very fact, who would grieve? Having been, one ceases to be; and having not been, one comes to be. Since there is no efficacy in grief, how could a man indulge in grief?
"O King, where indeed is your father today? Where indeed is your grandfather today?
You do not see them now, nor do they see you. Seeing the impermanence of yourself, why do you grieve for them?"
Understand this through your intellect: for you shall certainly cease to exist.
O King, both I and you—your enemies and your friends—will inevitably cease to be; indeed, everything shall cease to exist.
But those men who are twenty years old or thirty years old— all of them shall indeed die before even a hundred autumns have passed,
even if that man should be liberated from great wealth.
Thinking "this is not mine," one should do what is beneficial for oneself.
One should know that which has not yet come is "not mine";
one should know that which has passed away is "not mine."
Thinking that destiny is more powerful,
those wise ones say that such is the station of the virtuous:
even those who are not wealthy live, and they even rule kingdoms.

People endowed with intelligence and prowess who are equal to or superior to you do not grieve as you do; therefore, you too should not grieve. Are you perhaps not better than they, or at least equal to them in intelligence and prowess?
The prince said:
"O twice-born one, I consider that kingdom of mine to have been merely accidental;
indeed, all this is being carried away by great Time."
"As he was being carried away like a torrent, O one rich in asceticism, I perceived this fruit: that I shall subsist on whatever may be obtained. The sage said:

O Kausalya, just as you do not grieve over the future or the past due to your certain discernment of reality regarding all matters, so should you remain. Desire only those goals that are attainable, and never those that are unattainable.
"Experiencing only those things that have arisen in the present, do not grieve for what has not yet come.
O Kausalya, you shall find delight just as one who has obtained whatever wealth happens to be at hand. I hope that, though deprived of royal splendor, you do not grieve because of your pure nature."
Because of his former state, that evil-minded man of meager fortune constantly reviles the Creator; he cannot endure those who have obtained wealth,
and he considers other prosperous people to be undeserving of their success.

For this reason, O King, this suffering persists even more intensely for those who pride themselves on being men, yet are filled with excessive envy. I hope, O wise Lord of Kosala, that you are not such a miserly person.
Endure the prosperity of others, even if it does not exist within you;
for skillful people enjoy the fortune found elsewhere as well. Indeed, prosperity flows toward one even from an enemy.
Moreover, heroic men who practice dharma and know the duty of renunciation voluntarily abandon even their prosperity, sons,
and grandsons; this was practiced by Śubha in the lineage of Svāyambhuva and by Bharata as well.
"It is heard that a prosperous kingdom is strewn with various jewels;
likewise, other rulers have abandoned their highly flourishing kingdoms.
Having renounced their kingdoms, they all dwell in the forest, subsisting on wild fruits."
And those lords of the earth have reached the further shore of asceticism and the end of suffering; having seen that much is unstable, and through the means of seeking knowledge,
others likewise abandon this [body], considering it exceedingly difficult to attain.
But you, though appearing wise, are grieving piteously for objects that are undesirable, sought after [only by the ignorant], fleeting, and fraught with calamity;
desiring to understand that true wisdom, you yourself must renounce them.

12.105.037c Things that are harmful appear in the form of benefits, and things that are beneficial appear in the form of harms. 12.105.038a For indeed, for some, the loss of wealth occurs for the sake of true gain;
another, however, examines prosperity, thinking it to be an endless happiness.
Delighting in prosperity, someone may think there is no other good;
yet for one who strives in such a manner, his undertaking perishes. O Kausalya, when that which was desired and obtained with great difficulty is lost.

Then that man, his course broken, becomes disillusioned with that object; having realized that prosperity is impermanent, who would desire such prosperity? Some men of noble birth devote themselves to the Dharma.

Desiring happiness in the next world, they should become disenchanted with worldly life. Some men, devoted to the greed for wealth, even give up their lives; for such men do not consider life to have any purpose apart from wealth.
Behold their wretchedness; behold their lack of wisdom! Out of delusion, they have resorted to a thirst for wealth while life is transient.
For accumulation ends in destruction, and life ends in death.

In a union that ends in separation, who indeed would let his mind be led astray— whether it be wealth toward a man, O King, or a man toward wealth? Since one must inevitably abandon this, what wise person would grieve over it?
For calamity befalling another indeed brings satisfaction to a man;
because of that, he finds no peace, thinking, "It is not I [who am suffering].
Furthermore, the friends and wealth of others as well perish.
"Behold, O King, the calamity that awaits you through the intellect of men! Restrain,
control, and thoroughly subdue your senses, mind,
and speech regarding those things that are forbidden, unattainable, difficult to obtain, and harmful."
When things are diminished, when they have passed away, or when they are impossible to recover,
one like you— satisfied with wisdom, courageous, desiring little, steady, gentle, self-controlled, and firm in resolve— does not grieve.
One such as you, established in the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), does not fall into delusion.
You ought not, however, to seek the wretched livelihood of a skull-bearer (*kāpāla*);
it is a cruel way of life, most sinful, miserable, and fit only for a base man.
"Subsisting on roots and fruits, dwell alone in the great forest— restrained in speech, self-controlled, and endowed with compassion for all beings.
This is befitting of a wise man, like an elephant with tusks as long as plow-poles."
That one delights alone in the forest, and that one is content with even a little— just as a great lake, when agitated, becomes clear by itself,
so too does a man who has cultivated wisdom become serene through himself alone.

"O King, for one who has come to such a state as this— deprived of prosperity and lacking ministers and other resources, with destiny turned against him— I see only this as pure happiness. What do you consider to be the best course?"
The Sage said:
"Now, if you perceive even some measure of human prowess within yourself as a Kshatriya,
then, alas, I shall tell you the policy for the attainment of a kingdom."
"If you are able to carry this out and perform the action accordingly,
listen to everything in its entirety that I shall tell you in accordance with the truth. If you practice this action, you will attain great goals."
Whether it be a kingdom, or the counsel of a kingdom, or even great prosperity—if this pleases you, O King, speak again; I shall tell you more. The prince said:
"May the Blessed One speak of policy; I have approached you, O Lord.
May this meeting with you today not be in vain.
The sage said:
Abandoning arrogance, pride, anger, joy, and likewise fear,
serve your enemy by bowing down with palms joined in reverence;
gratify him with the highest purity and through your actions.

The King of Videha, true to his promise, ought to grant you a livelihood; you shall become an authority among all beings and attain a position of leadership. Thereafter, you will obtain energetic, pure, and disciplined companions.
Remaining steadfast in his own discipline, with self-restrained mind and conquered senses, he uplifts himself and brings peace to his subjects;
by that very same steadfastness and majesty, you have been honored.
Having established great authority over all beings and achieved a firm hold upon them,
and having then obtained the strength of allies and deliberated well upon counsel,
you should cause dissension among the enemies through their own kin and strike down the *bilva* with a *bilva*.
Or, having made an agreement with others, destroy his strength as well.
Those auspicious things which are unobtainable— women, garments,
beds, seats, vehicles, and costly houses— [should be seized].
Birds, species of wild animals, tastes, fragrances, and fruits—
upon these alone you should fix [the enemy's] attention, so that the adversary may perish of his own accord.
Whether he be one who must be restrained or one who deserves to be ignored, [you should act accordingly].

O tiger among kings, a wise man who desires his own welfare should never openly reveal his intentions toward an enemy if he wishes to maintain discipline. Dwell, therefore, within the domain of your supreme enemy, in a manner approved by the wise.
Associate with the worthless and useless friends of Śvetaka;
incite him to undertake great and difficult enterprises,
and let him come into conflict with powerful men regarding river-dams and obstructions.
"Expend his treasury for the sake of the pleasure of enjoyment— through costly gardens, couches,
and seats— and let praises of sacrifice and charity be recounted to him among the brahmins."
They will do what is pleasing to you, yet they will hunt you like wolves.
Without doubt, one of virtuous character attains the supreme goal;
such a king, O monarch, reaches the most meritorious station in heaven.
But when the treasury is exhausted, O King of Kosala, one falls under the power of enemies.
For one who is attached to both— dharma and indeed adharma—
the very root of his strength and wealth is cut off, and by that, his enemies rejoice.
Censure his human effort and extol his fate for him;
one who relies on fate will undoubtedly perish very quickly.
Perform the Viśvajit sacrifice for him so that he may be deprived of all his possessions.
Then let him go, his purpose unfulfilled and oppressed by the great multitude;
describe to him some shaven-headed man who knows the dharma of renunciation,
so that he might perhaps desire renunciation or go toward a state free from suffering.
By means of this perfected medicinal formulation that destroys all enemies,
cause harm to the elephants, horses, and men through artificial contrivances.
These and many other well-ascertained methods of deception exist.
"O prince, it is possible for one who is not a coward to endure this.
The prince said:
"O Brahmin, I do not wish to live by means of deceit or hypocrisy."
"I would not desire wealth joined with unrighteousness, even if it were very great;
O Blessed One, this was already renounced by me beforehand—
so that no one might suspect me, or so that everything might be for my welfare."
"Desiring to live in this world according to the dharma of compassion, I am not capable of doing this; this is not appropriate for me.
The sage said:
"O Kṣatriya, you have been born with this [nature] as you describe;
for you are endowed by nature and by intellect, O one of wondrous appearance.
For the sake of both of you—yourself and him—I shall strive."
"I shall indeed form with you an alliance that is eternal and unyielding.
For who would not make one such as you— a man born of noble lineage, compassionate, deeply learned, and skilled in the conduct of royal affairs— his minister?"

"You, who have renounced your kingdom and undergone the greatest hardship, yet desire to live as a kṣatriya through a life of compassion— O dear one, the King of Videha, true to his promise, will come to my house."
"He will undoubtedly do whatever I shall command him.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, having summoned the King of Videha, the sage spoke these words."
Born in a royal family, he is well-acquainted with my inner circle;
like a mirror, his soul is pure, like the autumnal moon. Having examined him on all sides, I see no fault in him whatsoever.
"Therefore, let there be peace between you both, so that you may have full confidence in me. O slayer of enemies, a kingdom cannot be governed without a minister;
a minister must indeed be brave and endowed with wisdom."
Behold the extent of the kingdom's peril arising from those two for the king! Nowhere in this world is there any other such fate for those whose souls are devoted to dharma.
This prince is self-disciplined and follows the path of the virtuous.

If this [kingdom], preceded by righteousness, is well-maintained by you and properly cultivated, it will seize great hosts of your enemies. Even if he should fight against you, that would be the duty of a kṣatriya.
Desiring to conquer you in battle for the ancestral station of your father and grandfather,
you too would have fought back, remaining steadfast in your vow to seek victory;
yet, O Vaideha, by my command, you have remained under my control even without fighting.
Therefore, look toward righteousness and abandon unrighteousness, which is improper. For you ought not to forsake your own duty out of desire or malice.
Victory is never constant, my dear, nor is defeat ever constant.
Therefore, one should feed others and one should eat with others;
for both victory and defeat are seen to reside within oneself alone.
O dear one, those who seek total destruction must fear the consequences of their own act of extermination.
Having been addressed thus, he replied with these words to that bull among brahmins,
after honoring him, treating him with hospitality, and showing respect to one worthy of worship—
just as a man of great wisdom would speak, and just as one of vast learning would speak.

"Just as one desiring his own welfare might speak that which is appropriate for both parties, so have I been addressed with these words; I shall do exactly as I was told. For this is the supreme good, and I have no hesitation in this matter."
Then the King of Videha, having summoned the King of Kosala, spoke these words: "I have conquered you by means of righteousness, policy, and even force;
yet, O best of kings, I have been conquered by you through the virtues of your own self."
Without disparaging yourself, may you conduct yourself as one who has already conquered.
I do not disregard your intellect, nor do I disregard your manliness; I do not disregard the thought "I shall conquer"—may you conduct yourself as one who has already conquered.
"O King, having been honored as is fitting, you shall go from my house to your own home.
Then, having honored that brahmin, the two of them departed for their homes with full confidence.
Thereupon, the King of Videha quickly led the King of Kosala into his palace.
He honored him, who was worthy of worship, with water for the feet, the arghya offering, and honey-mixture;
he gave him his daughter and various kinds of jewels. This is the supreme duty of kings: victory and defeat must both be endured.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O scorcher of foes, [tell me] the dharma, the conduct, the livelihood, and the fruits of the means of livelihood for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
The conduct of kings, the treasury, and the great means for generating the treasury; the increase in the qualities of ministers and the strengthening of the constituent elements of the state;
the application of the sixfold policy and likewise the leadership of the army.
The thorough recognition of the wicked and the characteristics of the non-wicked;

the collection of characteristics for those who are equal, inferior, or superior according to their respective strengths; and how one who is increasing in power should conduct oneself for the sake of satisfying the middling class.

And the conduct of one whose means of attraction have been exhausted has been duly proclaimed, O Bhārata, through this concise form of instruction and composition; likewise, the conduct of one who desires victory has been declared to you in the same manner.
"O best among the wise, O Bhārata, I wish to hear about the conduct of oligarchies (*gaṇas*), so that oligarchies may prosper and not fall into dissension,
and so that they may conquer their enemies and gain allies."
"For destruction is observed among groups to have its root in division;
it is my opinion that the concealment of counsel by many is a source of suffering.
O scorcher of foes, I wish to hear this in its entirety."
"And tell me, O King, how they may not be divided.
Bhīṣma said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, [I shall speak] concerning groups, clans, and kings."
"O lord of men, these two—greed and resentment—are the inflammers of enmity.
For one first chooses greed, and immediately thereafter resentment;
these two are joined by loss and expense, and they depend upon each other for their origin."

By means of spies, mantras, and the seizing of strength, through conciliation, bribery, and sowing dissension, and by employing strategies involving destruction, expenditure, and fear, they weaken one another.
In that regard, even groups that function through solidarity are divided by the use of bribery.
When divided, all become dispirited and fall under the power of their enemies out of fear.
Through division, groups perish; once divided, they are easily subverted by others. Therefore, groups should always strive for union.
For indeed, goals are accomplished through the power and human effort of a collective;
even outsiders show friendship toward those who act in concert.
Praising those advanced in knowledge, they serve one another.

Free from deceitful intentions, they prosper happily in every respect; by establishing righteous legal proceedings according to the scriptures and conducting them properly, these best of assemblies flourish.

Restraining their sons and brothers while always delighting in discipline, and supporting those who are disciplined, these best of assemblies flourish. They excel in the deployment of spies and secret counsel, as well as in the accumulation of treasuries.
O mighty-armed one, when they are ever-vigilant, the clans increase on all sides;
O King, by always honoring those who are wise, heroic, great archers, and firm in their manly exertion during tasks, the clans flourish.
Possessing wealth, being brave, skilled in weapons, and masters of the treatises,
they rescue their confederacies when those are bewildered in times of dire calamity.
Anger, sowing dissension, fear, punishment, harassment, restraint, and execution— [these are the means].
O best of the Bharatas, they immediately bring the hosts under the power of their enemies;
therefore, O King, those leaders of the hosts must be honored above all, for the course of worldly affairs depends largely upon them.
O crusher of enemies, O Bhārata, secrecy regarding counsel toward the leaders and the employment of spies are essential; the entire assembly ought not to hear the secret deliberations.
Rather, the leaders of the assembly should come together in private to accomplish what is for the welfare of the group.
When a group is divided, split, and dissatisfied,
its objectives fail and misfortunes arise;
this happens when they are at odds with one another while each pursues their own individual power.
The wise must apply restraint swiftly and primarily; for quarrels that arise within families, if neglected by the elders of the clan, O King, cause the division of the entire community.
Internal danger must be guarded against, while external danger is easier to guard against; danger arising from within immediately cuts away one's very root,
whether it be born of sudden anger, greed, or even delusion inherent in one's own nature.

When they do not speak to one another, that is a sign of impending defeat. Though all are equal by birth and likewise equal by lineage, they are not so in heroism, nor in intelligence, nor again in beauty or wealth.
"Because of internal division and through negligence, groups are brought low by their enemies;
therefore, they say that unity alone is the great refuge of groups.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

12.109.001a This path of dharma is great and has many branches, O Bhārata. 12.109.001c What among these duties is considered the most essential to perform? 12.109.002a What action do you consider to be the weightiest of all duties?
"So that this person may attain dharma both in this world and after death.
Bhīṣma said:
"The worship of mother, father, and teachers is highly esteemed by me."

12,109.003c A man who is devoted to this [duty] attains great worlds and great fame. 12,109.004a O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, whatever action these [elders], being highly honored, may recognize as right or contrary to dharma, that must be performed.

One should not prescribe another duty without being authorized by them; that which they authorize is the law—this is the settled conclusion. These three alone are the worlds, and these three alone are the stages of life (āśramas).
These indeed are the three Vedas; these indeed are the three sacred fires.
For the father is the Gārhapatya fire, and the mother is remembered as the Dakṣiṇa fire;
the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire—this triad of fires is most venerable.
By being vigilant regarding these three, you shall conquer the three worlds:
by serving your father, this world; by serving your mother, the next;
and by constant service to your teacher, the world of Brahmā.
"O Bhārata, conduct yourself correctly toward these three [goals] in the three worlds;
you shall obtain fame—may prosperity be yours—and dharma with its very great fruit.
Never should you transgress them, nor overeat, nor corrupt them."
One should always attend to these three; that indeed is the highest merit. O lord of men, you shall attain fame, virtue, renown, and the celestial worlds.
All the worlds are honored by him by whom these three are honored.
But for him by whom these are not respected, all his ritual acts are fruitless.
For him, O scorcher of foes, neither this world nor the next exists,
he by whom these three gurus are constantly dishonored.
Neither in this world nor in the next does his fame shine forth;
nor is any other auspicious merit for the hereafter proclaimed for him.
Yet, it is from them alone that I release all of that through my magical power (*kṛtyā*).
That [merit] of mine became a hundredfold and even a thousandfold;
therefore, O Yudhiṣ�ṭhira, the three worlds appear clearly to me. A single teacher of good conduct, however, surpasses ten Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*).

Ten teachers are equal to one sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*); ten sub-teachers are equal to one father; but a single mother outweighs even ten fathers, or even the entire earth, by virtue of her status as a teacher—there is no teacher equal to a mother.
"It is my conviction, O Bhārata, that the preceptor is weightier than both the father and the mother;
for while both the mother and father are instrumental in one's birth, it is they—
the father and the mother— who create this physical body."
That birth which is ordained by the teacher is divine; it is free from old age and death.
Indeed, a mother and a father are always inviolable, even if they have done one harm;
by doing so, one does not become defiled, nor do they defile him.
The gods, together with the seers, know those who strive for the sake of Dharma—
he who covers their ears with truth,
speaking the eternal law and bestowing immortality.
12.109.019c I consider him indeed to be both father and mother;
knowing what he has done for him, one should not bear him ill will.
12.109.020a Those who, having heard the sacred knowledge, do not respect their teacher...
Whether through thought or through action,
their sin is as grave as the murder of an embryo;
yet it does not yield for them the fruit of Brahman.
Just as they are to be cherished by their teachers,
so too are their teachers to be honored by them;
therefore, they should be worshipped and provided for with effort.
Those who desire the ancient dharma must honor their gurus. By that which pleases the ancestors, the Grandfather (Brahmā) is pleased;
by that which gratifies the mother, the earth is honored.
By that which one pleases the preceptor, by that the Brahman is honored.
Because he is [the source] both from the mother and from the father, the teacher is therefore most worthy of worship;
for by him the seers and the gods, together with the ancestors, are pleased.
When teachers are being honored, the teacher is therefore most worthy of honor.
For there is no conduct whatsoever by which a teacher may be treated with contempt;
neither mother nor father is such as the teacher is.
They do not deserve contempt, nor do they defile him;
for the gods, together with the ṛṣis, recognize that honor is due only to one's elders—
namely, the teacher, the father, and the mother.
Those who harbor malice toward them either in thought or in deed—
their sin is no different from that of killing an embryo; therefore, there is no other evildoer in the world greater than they.
That son born of his own body who does not support his aged father and mother, though he has been supported by them—
that indeed is a sin no different from the killing of an embryo.
Therefore, there is no other evildoer in the world than the betrayer of friends, the ungrateful, the slayer of women, and the slanderer;
we have never heard of atonement for these four.
All this has been created by way of extension;
whatever is to be done by a person in this world,
this is the highest good, and nothing else is superior to it.
Having followed all the teachings, this was said:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, how should a man who wishes to abide in dharma conduct himself?"
"O learned one, O bull among the Bharatas, speak to me who desires to know:
Truth and falsehood both stand encompassing the worlds.
O King, what should a man firm in dharma do regarding these two?"
"What indeed is truth? What is falsehood? What is the eternal dharma?
At what time should one speak the truth, and at what time should one speak falsehood?
Bhīṣma said:
Speaking the truth is virtuous; there is nothing superior to the truth.
O Bhārata, I shall tell you that which is very difficult to understand in this world of mortals:
there may be a case where the truth must not be spoken, and where a falsehood must be spoken.
Where falsehood may become truth, or truth may become falsehood—
in such a case where truth is not firmly established, the fool is bewildered. Having discerned truth and falsehood, one then becomes a knower of dharma.
Even a non-Aryan man, lacking wisdom and extremely cruel,
may attain very great merit, just as Balāka did from the killing of a blind creature.
And what is surprising in this, that a fool— though desiring dharma— is ignorant of what is truly dharma?
One may incur very great sin, just as Kauśika did at the Gaṅgā.
Such is this follow-up question, wherein dharma is extremely difficult to express; it is hard to determine through logic, yet one must resolve it here.
The proclamation of the Dharma was made for the sake of the power of all beings;
that which is joined with non-violence is the certainty of what constitutes Dharma. The proclamation of the Dharma was made for the sake of the non-violence of all beings.
Whatever is joined with non-violence is Dharma; this is the certainty.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, austerity, generosity, self-restraint, wisdom, lack of malice, lack of envy, lack of jealousy, and virtuous conduct—these indeed constitute Dharma.
O best of the Kurus, this eternal Dharma has been declared by the Supreme Lord, Brahmā, the god of gods; O King, a man who stands firm in this Dharma beholds auspicious things.
The Vedic dharma consists of killing, whereas non-violence is the ultimate dharma. They say that dharma is so called because it upholds; by dharma the subjects are upheld.
Whatever is endowed with the quality of upholding—that, they conclude, is dharma.
Where there may be benefit for beings who have fallen into great distress,
some say that this is the dharma of the Vedas, while other people say it is not;
yet we do not find fault with that, for everything is not prescribed [by the Vedas].

If there are those who, desiring to take by unjust means, ever seek wealth, one must not disclose that [wealth] to them; this is the settled rule of dharma. If liberation is attained without making a sound, one should not make a sound here in any way whatsoever.
One must certainly utter a cry, for others might suspect [the truth] from the lack of a cry; or even if there are others who would speak untruth, one should deliberate thus:
"In this case, it is better to speak an untruth than the truth"—this is what has been deliberated.
O King, one should indeed inflict punishment upon those who are incorrigible without hesitation;
when there is no perceived fault in a person's latent disposition, a falsehood spoken for that purpose may be better.
One is not released from the consequences of an association with thieves even by means of an oath.
In such a case, it is the established doctrine that it is better to speak a falsehood than the truth;
for by means of an oath, one is released from association with those who have committed evil.
And wealth must not be given to them under any circumstances, even if one is able to do so.
For wealth given to the wicked may even afflict the giver himself. It is better for those who, desiring to take [wealth] at the risk of their own bodies,
speak as witnesses somewhere for the sake of establishing the truth.
If one does not speak that which ought to be said there, all of them are speakers of falsehood.
Falsehood may be spoken in a life-threatening emergency and in marriage,
for the sake of protecting wealth, or for the purpose of dharma regarding others.
Desiring the Dharma for others, one should be humble as a seeker of the Dharma;
having given one's word, it must be fulfilled, even if the task is delayed until tomorrow or undertaken under pressure.
Whoever has fallen away from the covenant of Dharma and has resorted to unrighteousness [must be corrected].
He who has resorted to that path must be slain by means of deceit alone;
for he has always fallen away from the duties of his own order and has adopted a non-human way of life.
Being a rogue, he abandons his own duty and desires to subsist upon it [the wealth of others].
12.110.020c That wicked man who lives by deceit must be destroyed by every possible means.
12.110.021a "Wealth alone"—this is the firm resolve of all sinners here in this world;
for those who are unbearable, unfit to associate with, and have fallen through their own baseness.

Fallen from the realms of gods and humans, they are just like *pretas*; devoid of sacrifice and lacking in austerity, let there be no association with them. To deprive one of life is more painful than the seizure of wealth.
"This Dharma must be pleasing to you"—this should be said with great effort. "There is no such thing as Dharma for evildoers"—this is the certain conclusion.
Furthermore, he who would kill a Tathāgata is not defiled by sin.
One who kills what has already been killed by its own karma is himself merely being killed;
whoever should enter into an agreement with those whose intellects have been destroyed is just like a crow or a vulture— so too are those who live by deceit.
After the liberation from the body, they come to exist in these wombs. Whatever manner a man conducts himself toward another, he should be treated in that same manner; that is the law (*dharma*).
One who practices deceit should be met with deceit;
one who practices goodness should be met with goodness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that by which one may cross over the difficulties while beings are being afflicted here and there by various conditions. Bhīṣma said:

Those twice-born ones who abide in the prescribed hermitages according to the rules, with their selves restrained, cross over all difficulties. Those who do not mutter prayers out of hypocrisy, and whose livelihood is properly regulated, [attain success].
They restrain their senses and they cross over difficult places;
those who do not speak back when being addressed, who do not harm when harmed,
and who give but do not beg— they cross over difficult places.
Those who always provide hospitality to guests, those who are ever free from malice,
and those who are constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas— they cross over all difficulties.
And those who, being experts in dharma, maintain the proper conduct toward their mother and father, [cross over all difficulties].
Those who avoid sleeping during the day cross over all difficulties;
those who abide by their own wives— who conduct themselves with propriety— during every season,
and who are devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice, cross over all difficulties.
Those kings who, though shrouded by passion, do not lead away from their wealth out of greed,
and who protect their realms, cross over all difficulties.
And those who are heroes in battles, having cast aside the fear of death, [cross over all difficulties].
Those who desire victory through righteousness cross over all difficulties;
those who do no evil by deed, mind, or speech,
and who have laid aside the rod of punishment toward all living beings, they cross over all difficulties.

Those who speak the truth here even when the loss of life is imminent, and who have become authorities for all beings, cross over all difficulties. Those Brahmins who do not perform their private Vedic study during the periods forbidden for study [do not succeed].
Those who are constant in austerity, who have performed great penance,
whose actions are free from deceitful motives, whose speech is truthful and pleasant,
and whose wealth is used for righteous purposes— they cross over all difficulties.
Those who perform austerities while observing lifelong celibacy from their youth, and who have bathed after completing their studies, the Vedas, and their vows— they cross over all difficulties.
And those whose passion (*rajas*) has been stilled, and whose darkness (*tamas*) has been stilled—
Established in truth, those great-souled ones cross over all difficulties— those of whom no one is afraid and who themselves fear no one,
and for whom the world is as their own self; they cross over all difficulties.
Those virtuous bulls among men who do not burn with envy at the prosperity of others,
and who have desisted from vulgar food, cross over all difficulties.
They pay homage to all the gods and listen to all the teachings of the Dharma.
Those who are faithful and self-controlled cross over all difficulties.
Those who do not desire honor for themselves but honor others, and who, while being honored,
do not become conceited— they cross over all difficulties.

Those who, desiring offspring, perform ancestral rites on every lunar day with a perfectly pure mind, cross over all difficulties. Those who do not give way to anger and pacify those who are angry [attain the same].
They do not become angry with their servants and they overcome all difficulties— those men who here constantly abstain from honey and meat,
and from liquor from birth onwards, overcome all difficulties.
Those for whom food is for the sake of sustenance, sexual union for the sake of progeny,
and speech for the sake of truth— they cross over all difficulties.
[They worship] the Lord of all beings, the source and the dissolution of the world.
Those who are devotees of Nārāyaṇa cross over all difficulties.
This one, with eyes like red lotuses, clad in yellow garments, and mighty-armed—
he is your infallible (acyuta) kinsman, brother, friend, and relative.
He who, as the Lord of inconceivable self, Govinda, the Supreme Person, could by his will envelop all these worlds like a hide— this very one,
O bull among men, stands intent on the welfare and well-being of Jiṣṇu.
O King, Vaikuṇṭha, the invincible Puruṣottama, belongs to you;
