those who take refuge here in this Nārāyaṇa, Hari, with devotion,
cross over all difficulties— of this I have no doubt.
O Bhārata, those who have dedicated all their actions with their whole being to Kṛṣṇa, whose eyes are like lotus petals, cross over all difficulties;
he who was born of Aditi as the son of Kaśyapa for the sake of protecting the world.
Those who pay homage to the god Indra cross over all difficulties; those who pay homage to Brahmā, the creator of the worlds and the lord of the virtuous, cross over all difficulties;
and those who worship the god with sacrifices cross over all difficulties.
He whom Viṣṇu, Indra, Śambhu, and Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
praise with various hymns— the Great Lord, the God of gods—
those who constantly worship him cross over all difficulties.
Those who recite this *Durgātitaraṇa*, cause it to be heard,
and teach it to Brahmins, cross over all difficulties.
Thus, O sinless one, the summary of rites has been proclaimed by me to you.
By means of this, a person may cross over difficulties both in this world and in the next.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"There are those who are unkind yet appear kind, and those who are kind yet appear unkind."
"O dear one, how may we recognize such men as these?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn that dialogue between the tiger and the jackal. Long ago, in the glorious city of Purikā, there lived a king named Paurika,
a cruel and lowest of men who took delight in harming others.
When his lifespan was exhausted, he went to an undesired destination;
defiled by his former karma, he attained the state of a jackal. Recalling his previous birth, he fell into a state of supreme world-weariness.
He did not eat meat, even when it was offered by others; he was non-violent toward all beings, truthful in speech, and firm in his vows. And he took his food as desired from fallen fruits.

At times he subsisted on leaves, observing his restrictive vows; at other times, he lived restrainedly even on water alone. And his dwelling in the cremation ground became as acceptable to the jackals as it was to him.
Out of regard for his birthplace, he did not desire any other dwelling. Unable to endure his purity, all those born of the same lineage attempted to shake that resolve with words full of courtesy.
"Residing in the fierce forest of the ancestors (Pitṛvana), you wish to obtain purity? This is a contradiction for you, since you are a consumer of flesh;
or else, become equal to us, and we shall give you food."
"Eat, casting aside your purity; for that which is eaten truly belongs to you.
Hearing these words of theirs, he replied with a composed mind, using sweet, humble, reasoned, and gentle speech:
My lineage is rendered immeasurable by my birth and conduct;
yet, I shall strive for that deed by which my fame may spread. Let it be observed: even if my dwelling were in a cremation ground, my meditative concentration remains unshaken.

The self bears the fruit of one's actions; the stage of life (āśrama) is not the defining characteristic of dharma. If one were to kill a twice-born man while in a stage of life, or give a cow to someone who is not in a stage of life—would that not be a sin? Or would that gift be in vain?
"Sirs, out of total greed you are solely devoted to eating;
deluded, you do not perceive the faults that follow as a consequence. [This conduct] is censurable for creating distrust and corrupted by the loss of wealth."
"Therefore, I do not take pleasure in that way of life which is undesirable both here and in the hereafter.
Regarding him as pure and wise, the tiger of renowned prowess performed honors befitting himself and personally promoted him to the position of minister.
"O gentle one, you whose character is well known, go on your journey with me.
Let your desired enjoyments be provided and let abundant things to be avoided be set aside.
We declare to you that we are known as being fierce."
"By first acting gently toward those who would kill you, you shall attain what is for your own welfare.
Then, having honored those words of the high-souled king of beasts,
the jackal, bowing slightly, spoke these humble words.
"O King of Beasts, these words of yours regarding me are worthy of you:
that you seek companions who are pure and skilled in the matters of dharma and artha. For it is not possible to govern greatness without ministers."

O hero, one should strive to win over loyal allies who have not been brought together by a wicked minister who obstructs the body politic— men who are not at odds with one another, who desire victory, and who are free from greed.
"You should honor those wise and high-minded ones— who have transcended worldly attachments and are devoted to your welfare— as you would your teachers or your fathers,
O illustrious lord of beasts. But for my part, nothing else pleases me so much as my own contentment."
I do not desire pleasant enjoyments or sovereign power dependent upon you;
for my character will not harmonize with your old servants. They, being of a harsh disposition, will cause a rift between you and me.

You are a praiseworthy refuge even for other radiant beings; you are self-disciplined, highly fortunate, and not cruel even toward those who do evil. You are far-sighted, possessed of great energy, liberal in your aims, and endowed with great strength.

"You are skillful and one whose actions are never in vain, and you are adorned with all that is destined for you. Nevertheless, I am content with my own lot; this life of hardship has been undertaken because I am unacquainted with service and roam at will in the forest."
All the faults arising from the reproach of kings belong to those who dwell in dependence;
whereas forest life is free from attachment, fearless, and unrestrained.
Yet, for one summoned by a king, there remains a fear within the heart.
That [pleasure] does not abide for those contented ones living in the forest on roots and fruits;
whether it be water obtained without effort or delicious food accompanied by fear—
having reflected, I truly see that happiness wherein there is peace.
Servants have never been dismissed by kings for so many offenses as those servants who, having been defiled by their misdeeds, met their death.
If this task must be performed by me, O King of Beasts, and if you so intend;
"I desire that an agreement be made regarding how you should conduct yourself toward me:
my words must be honored by you, and you must listen to my beneficial advice; furthermore, the livelihood provided for you shall remain secure."
I shall never consult with those other ministers at any time;
for those who are skilled in policy and desirous of protecting me might speak falsely to me. Therefore, meeting with you alone in private, I shall tell you what is for your benefit.
And you must not ask me regarding the affairs of your kinsmen concerning what is beneficial or harmful; nor, after consulting with me, should you harm my ministers;
and when provoked, you must not inflict punishment upon those who belong to me.

"So be it," said that lord of beasts, honoring him; thus the jackal obtained the office of minister from his birth as a tiger. Seeing him so honored and engaged in his duties, [the other ministers were filled with envy].
Having formed a coalition, his former servants bore him constant malice again and again;
and those of evil intent, having conciliated and ushered in the jackal under the pretense of friendship, desired to lead him toward faults.
For otherwise, those who were formerly accustomed to seizing the property of others,
being restrained by the jackal, would be unable to take even the slightest wealth; thus,
they are enticed with stories while they long for an opportunity to rise up.
His mind was enticed by great wealth,
yet that man of great wisdom did not waver from his fortitude; then the enemies, having made a pact with him, remained intent on his destruction.
The meat that was prepared there for the lion,
which he desired, was indeed removed by them and placed in his own dwelling; they also explained for what purpose it had been stolen, by whom, and how it had been consecrated with mantras.
All that was known to him, and he endured it for the sake of his purpose. This agreement was made by him when he entered into the office of counselor:
"O King, you who desire friendship here must not harbor malice toward me."
Thus, for the sake of maintaining that mantra, it was disregarded.
Bhīṣma said:
"When the king of beasts, being hungry, had risen up to eat—"
When the food was being served, that meat was not to be seen;
the King of Beasts then commanded, "Let the thief be sought! And by spies, that meat was described to the Lord of Beasts.

Then, having heard the jackal’s insolence brought before him by his minister— who was learned yet proud of his own wisdom— the tiger-king became enraged; filled with indignation, he resolved upon the jackal’s execution.
Seeing that vulnerability of his, those former ministers said:
"He is intent upon the destruction of the livelihoods of all of us.
Having thus resolved, they then spoke in dispraise of his deeds.
And such is his conduct, yet it is protected by his popularity;
and as for what was previously heard by my lord, he is not like that at all. He is righteous in mere words, but cruel by nature.
For this wicked man is a hypocrite of the Dharma, one who adopts empty practices;
he has exerted himself in vows only for the sake of gain and for the sake of food.
If you have any doubt regarding this, we shall demonstrate it to you.
At that very moment, they brought that jackal’s flesh to him.
Knowing that the meat had been removed, the tiger, at their word, then commanded: "Let the jackal be killed!"
Having heard the tiger’s words, the mother of the tiger then approached to admonish the king of beasts with beneficial speech:
"My son, you must not accept this which is shrouded in a deceptive undertaking."
The pure person is defiled by impurities born from the friction of actions; no one endures an exaltation that brings about enmity,
for even against one who is pure and disciplined, blame alone is cast down.

Even for a sage dwelling in the forest who performs his own duties, three parties arise: friends, neutrals, and enemies. To the greedy, the pure are objects of hatred; to the cowardly, the energetic are objects of hatred.
To fools, the wise are objects of hatred; to the poor, the very wealthy;
to the unrighteous, the most virtuous; and to the deformed, those of beautiful form.
There are many who are wise yet greedy, and all of them live by means of deceit.

They might bring blame upon one who is blameless, even one with the intellect of Bṛhaspati. Furthermore, that meat which was taken from your empty house—you do not wish it given back; therefore, let this be reflected upon well.
Unreal things appear as if real, and real things appear as if unreal;
various phenomena are seen in this way, and therefore it is proper to investigate them. The sky appears as if it has a surface, and a firefly appears like a flame.
There is no floor in the sky, nor is there fire in a firefly;
therefore, even that which is perceived through direct observation ought to be examined. For one who makes things known only after having examined them does not later feel remorse.
"O son, it is not difficult for a lord to cause another to be slain;
rather, forbearance by those who possess power is praiseworthy and excellent in this world.
O son, you have established this man, renowned among his vassals, [in his position]."
A worthy recipient is found with great difficulty; therefore, let this friend of yours be maintained.
For he who perceives one who is pure as otherwise, because of the faults of others, perishes very quickly, having himself corrupted his ministers.
Then, from that host of enemies, a certain virtuous soul arrived from among the jackals;
he explained how this deception had been carried out. Thereupon, his character being recognized, he was honored and released.
Embraced affectionately again and again by the king of beasts, the jackal,
who was learned in the treatises on statecraft, took leave of the lion;
yet, consumed by that indignation, he desired to sit in fasting unto death.
There, with eyes overflowing with affection, the tiger—
most righteous in his conduct— restrained the jackal while honoring him in return. Beholding him, the jackal was overcome with agitation out of love.
Bowing down, he spoke these words with a voice choked with tears:
"I was honored by you before, but now I have been humiliated;
having been reduced to the status of another's servant, I am no longer worthy to dwell with you."
Those who are self-satisfied, those fallen from their positions, those degraded from honor,
those who have surrendered themselves, and those brought as captives by others;
those who are utterly destitute, greedy, cruel, and tormented by imprisonment.
Those who have been robbed of their wealth yet remain proud; those who have abandoned what they had acquired while craving more; those who are tormented and await a flood of calamities;
those who are hidden or those who are openly plotted against—all such people are dependent on others for their success.
"How will you place your trust in me again, or how shall I come to trust you once more, after I have been treated with contempt and then set aside?
Having accepted me as capable, having examined me, and having established me in office— "

Having broken the agreement you made, I have been insulted by you. One who was first proclaimed in the assembly as being virtuous must not speak of his own failings if he wishes to preserve his promise.
"And being thus treated with contempt here, how will you place your trust in me? For if there is no trust in you, I shall be filled with anxiety.
You will be suspicious and I shall be afraid, while our enemies will be looking for our vulnerabilities."
They are indeed unaffectionate and difficult to satisfy, and this task is full of deception; where there is first honor and then later dishonor,
the wise do not praise that which was honored and then dishonored.
That which is divided is joined together through suffering; that which is joined is separated through suffering.
But that affection which exists between one who is both divided and joined does not endure through mere attachment.
For indeed, it is only someone who is afraid of another—not out of regard for themselves—that is seen [to act thus].
For beings act out of regard for their own interests, and those who are affectionate are rare to find.
Knowing the minds of men is exceedingly difficult, for their hearts are ever-shifting; whether capable or incapable, one such person is found among hundreds.
"Without cause comes the rise of men, and without cause their downfall; likewise, through the lightness of intellect, they bring about good and evil fortune as well as greatness.
Having spoken such various words of conciliation, which were consistent with the principles of dharma and artha, [he addressed him].
Having appeased the king, the jackal departed for the forest. Disregarding the entreaties of that lord of beasts,
the wise jackal sat down to fast unto death and, casting off his body, went to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best among the upholders of dharma, tell me in truth all that which must be done by a king, and by doing what may he become happy."
Bhīṣma said:
"Behold, I shall declare to you; listen to the certain conclusion regarding what must be done. Hear how a king should act in this world, and what he must do to become happy."
But you must certainly not behave as we have heard this account;
listen, O Yudhiṣṭhira, to that great history of a camel.
There was a great camel who remembered his former births, born in the age of Prajāpati.

12,113.004c He performed very great austerities in the forest, firm in his vows. 12,113.005a At the conclusion of those austerities, the Lord became pleased; 12,113.005c thereupon, the Grandfather invited him to choose a boon.
The camel said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace may this neck of mine become long enough,
O Lord, to travel more than a hundred *yojanas* in order to graze."
12,113.007 Bhīṣma said:
Having been told "So be it" by that high-souled giver of boons,
and having obtained that most excellent boon, the camel went to his own forest.
Due to that boon, that evil-minded one practiced such indolence;
deluded by time, the wicked-souled one did not wish to go out to wander. Once, having thus stretched out his neck for a hundred yojanas—
He moved about with unwearied heart, and then a great wind arose.
Placing his head and neck within a cave, the animal remained there;
then a massive rain came, flooding the world.
Then the jackal, his limbs overcome by cold and afflicted by hunger and fatigue,
entered that cave quickly with his wife, distressed by the water. Seeing it, the meat-eater was indeed exceedingly overcome by hunger and exhaustion.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, he began to devour the camel’s neck. When that animal realized it was being eaten,
it, being deeply distressed, made a strenuous effort to contract its body.
As soon as the beast contracted its neck both upward and downward, it was devoured by that jackal together with his wife. Having then killed and eaten the camel, the jackal—
When the wind and rain had ceased, he emerged from the mouth of the cave.
Thus did that camel meet his death through his own wicked intellect;
behold how, through the gradual progression of indolence, a great calamity has come to pass.
You too, having abandoned this ritual procedure, should abide with your senses restrained through yoga;
for Manu declared that victory has its root in intelligence. O Bhārata, actions rooted in intelligence are the best, while those based on physical strength are mediocre.
Those who are inferior in their calves and inferior in bearing burdens [do not rule];
O sinless one, sovereignty remains with one who is skillful, whose senses are restrained, who listens to secret counsel, and who possesses good allies.
For the objectives of one who lacks companions never endure;
yet the objectives of one who acts with deliberation endure here, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
By one joined with allies, the entire earth can be ruled.

For this has been declared by the virtuous who know the ritual rules, O you whose majesty is equal to that of Mahendra; and it has also been spoken by me to you according to the vision of the scriptures.
"O King, conduct yourself here with diligence.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, having obtained a kingdom, a king who is weak—"
"How could one who lacks resources remain standing against an enemy who has grown exceedingly powerful?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
And [he related] the conversation between the rivers and the ocean, O Bhārata. The Ocean, the eternal abode of the enemies of the gods and lord of rivers,
questioned all the rivers regarding a doubt that had arisen within himself.
I see the shady trees here, along with their roots and branches, struck down by you who are full; yet there, I do not see the cane.
The cane is bodiless, of little substance, and grows on the riverbank—unlike you.
"Whether he was treated with contempt, or whether it was impossible [to deal with him], or whatever else he has done to you—
I wish to hear all of that, as well as the opinion of each and every one of you,
regarding how these riverbanks were breached and he was not brought under control."

Then the river Gaṅgā spoke these meaningful words in reply to the ocean, the lord of rivers— words that were reasoned and persuasive: "These mountains, who have made their sole abode here, remain each in its own place."
Then those mindless ones abandon that place because of its adverse nature;
just as the reed (*vetasa*) bends when it sees the oncoming force of the current, but others do not, so too,
once that force has passed by, he remains established, having regained his position.

Knowing the right time and knowing the proper occasion, the reed is always submissive and not stubborn; being compliant and not rigid, the reed does not suffer. Those who bend and rise again under the force of the wind and water—
Herbs, trees, and shrubs do not suffer defeat;
for he who does not first withstand the onset of a powerful, flourishing enemy intent on slaughter and destruction, perishes very quickly.
The wise man who, knowing the essence and non-essence, the strength and prowess of himself and his enemy, conducts himself accordingly, does not suffer defeat.
In this very same way, when a learned man perceives his enemy to be exceedingly powerful, [he should act with caution].
One should adopt the conduct of a reed; such is the characteristic of wisdom.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Bhārata, how should a wise man deal with one who is arrogant due to ignorance, or with one who is harsh toward the mild?
12,115.001c Being reviled in an assembly, O subduer of enemies, what should one do?
12,115.002 Bhīṣma said:
12,115.002a Listen, O protector of the earth, how this matter is traditionally recounted.
A man of pure mind always overcomes the small-minded person here in this world by not becoming angry when he is being reviled; thus, the patient one acquires the merit of the other’s good deeds,
while the one who does become angry indeed wipes away his own ill-deeds.
One should disregard that *ṭiṭṭibha* bird as it cries out like one who is ill;
having incurred the hatred of the world, he meets with fruitlessness. Thus he constantly boasts because of that sinful deed.
When this was said by me to a certain person esteemed in the assembly,
he stood there ashamed, withered, and like one dead,
having boasted of a deed unworthy of praise, devoid of shame.
Such a lowest of men should be ignored by one who is self-controlled;
whatever that person of small intellect may say, he should always endure it.
For what can an ordinary person do, whether praising or reviling?

Like a senseless crow crying out fruitlessly in the forest, if there were a practical application for the words of one who commits evil deeds, then those words alone would constitute his purpose; for there is no true purpose in one who merely intends to strike down another.
By his conduct and behavior, he proclaims his own impregnation to have been inverted,
like a peacock dancing and displaying its private parts. For him,
there is nothing in this world that is unspeakable, nor is there anything that he will not do.

A pure person should not engage in conversation with one whose actions are defiled. That man who speaks of virtues in one's presence but reviles them in one's absence is like a dog in this world; he has lost his way to the higher realms.
Whatever such a person gives or offers in sacrifice even for the sake of a hundred people,
he destroys that in an instant through backbiting in their absence.
Therefore, a wise man should immediately [avoid] such a person of sinful mind.
One should avoid what is shunned by the virtuous, just as one avoids the meat of a dog.
For a wicked soul who utters slander against a high-souled person reveals his own faults, just as a snake displays its raised hood.
He who wishes to retaliate against one who is merely performing his own duty is like a mindless donkey sinking into a heap of ashes in the dust;
he is an unappeased man-tiger.
One should abandon that man who is constantly intent on public scandal, roaring like a mad elephant,
as one would a most ferocious dog.
One who treads a path frequented by the undisciplined, devoid of self-restraint and modesty, wicked, ever devoted to the ways of enemies, and desiring one's ruin;
"Fie on that man of evil intent!"—
when you are thus addressed repeatedly by these [words], listen and do not become distressed in appearance.
Those of steady intellect indeed censure the union of the high with the low;
for one who is angry might strike with even five [arrows].
He may scatter dust or husks over him,
or, baring his teeth, he may terrify him;
for a fool, when enraged, is as good as dead.
That man who would endure the revilement inflicted by the most wicked of men in an assembly,
and who always recites this illustrative example as well;
He does not encounter any unpleasantness consisting of speech.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, I have this great doubt."
"O King, he must be cut down by you, for you are the sustainer of our lineage.
This, my dear father, is the manner of speech employed by men who are ill-behaved and evil-minded;
therefore, I inform you of this."

Whatever is beneficial for the administration of the kingdom and brings about the welfare of the family; whatever ensures security and prosperity both in the future and in the present; and whatever brings delight to sons and grandsons and causes the growth of the realm.
"Tell me what is beneficial for food, drink, and the body.
For how should a king— whether he has been consecrated, is established in his kingdom, is surrounded by friends, or is beset by enemies— delight his subjects?"

For he who delights in improper attachments, driven by the force of affection and passion, and who, lacking mastery over his senses, desires to associate with the wicked— of him, even all his servants born of noble lineage fall into a state of deficiency.
"And that king does not obtain wealth through the fruits of his servants' labor.
You, who are equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence, ought to explain these duties of kingship to me, for I stand in doubt regarding them which are so very difficult to attain."
"O tiger among men, you have been praised as one devoted to the welfare of our lineage;
so too has Vidura, who possesses keen wisdom and always speaks for our benefit.
Having heard from you words concerning the welfare of the family and the prosperity of the kingdom—"
"Like one satiated with the imperishable nectar of immortality, I shall sleep in peace.
What kind of servants, endowed with virtues, should stand in close attendance? With what sort of men, and from what lineage, should an expedition be undertaken?"
For a king who is alone and without servants cannot be a protector;
and all these people praise one of noble birth for this kingdom. Indeed, O Bhārata, it is not possible for a kingdom to be governed by one person alone.
"O dear one, O bull of the Bharatas, no goals whatsoever can be attained by one who lacks companions, nor can those already attained ever be protected. Bhīṣma said:
He whose entire body of servants is skilled in theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom, who seeks his welfare, is of noble birth, and is affectionate, enjoys the fruit of sovereignty.
He whose ministers are of noble birth, incorruptible, and have lived with him for a long time [enjoys the same].
The king has counselors who provide him with wisdom, who are experts in understanding relationships,
who provide for the future, and who are skilled in the knowledge of time;
not grieving over what is past, he enjoys the fruit of sovereignty.

He whose companions share equally in his sorrow and joy, who act with sincerity, and who are devoted to considering his welfare— he enjoys the fruit of sovereignty. He whose subjects in the neighboring territories are never distressed [enjoys the fruit of sovereignty].

He who is not mean-spirited and clings to the path of the righteous shall partake in the fruit of sovereignty. He whose treasury and record office are constantly maintained by trustworthy and contented people who increase the royal coffers is the best of kings.
A storehouse, when guarded by trustworthy men who are incapable of being led astray, intent on accumulation, worthy recipients, and free from greed, will become productive. Furthermore,
for that king in whose city legal proceedings result in the manifestation of the fruits of action, [the realm prospers].
He who is seen to follow Śaṅkha and Likhita shall partake in the fruit of dharma;
and that king who knows the duties of kingship, who maintains his subjects and embraces the group of six, enjoys the fruit of dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Bharatas, when a king has no companions born of noble lineage, should he employ those who are not of noble birth, or not?"
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history as an illustration in the world, which is always practiced by the virtuous.
This very same matter is consistent with what I heard in the penance grove from Rāma,
the son of Jamadagni, as it was spoken by the best of sages:
"In a certain great forest, uninhabited by humans..."

The seer subsisted on roots and fruits, disciplined and with senses restrained; devoted to initiation and self-restraint, he was peaceful, pure, and supremely dedicated to sacred study; his soul purified by fasting, he stood constantly upon the path of the righteous.
Upon perceiving the presence of that wise one as he sat there,
all the forest-dwelling creatures gathered near him:
lions, tigers, śarabhas, and even rutting great elephants.
Leopards, rhinoceroses, bears, and others of fearsome appearance—
all those blood-eaters— offered him inquiries after his well-being; they remained humble before that ṛṣi, acting for his pleasure like disciples.
Having offered their greetings of well-being, they all departed as they had come;
however, one domestic animal there—a dog—did not leave the great sage. Devoted and affectionate, he was constantly emaciated and weak from fasting.
Subsisting on a diet of fruits and roots, peaceful and appearing like a refined gentleman,
he approached the feet of that great sage who was seated there;
his disposition became intensely bound by affection, as if he were a human being.
Then a leopard of great prowess, a consumer of blood, approached— extremely enraged for the sake of the dog, cruel as Death the Ender himself—
laping his lips in thirst and intent on lashing his tail.
With his mouth wide open, overcome by hunger, and seeking that meat, he approached.
Seeing that cruel creature coming, O lord of men, the dog, desiring to live, spoke to the sage there; hear what he said, O high-minded one.
"O Blessed One, here my enemy, a leopard, wishes to kill me.
Through your grace, O Great Sage, may I have no fear of him.
Act accordingly, O mighty-armed one; you are omniscient, of this there is no doubt."
Having understood the cause of his fear, that sage— who knew the inner dispositions of beings,
who understood the cries of all creatures, and who was endowed with sovereign power—
spoke to him.
"You need have no fear of the tiger, nor of death from any quarter whatsoever. O son, this tiger shall become devoid of its feline form.
Bhīṣma said:
Then the dog was transformed into a leopard, possessing a form resembling refined gold;
with variegated limbs, quivering and joyful, he dwelt in the forest without fear.
Seeing him, that other leopard [thought] him beautiful and like himself.
Then, in an instant, he became unopposed to him.
Thereupon, a most fierce tiger, filled with hunger and with mouth wide open, approached—
licking its lips and eager for blood.
Seeing a tiger— fanged, forest-dwelling, and overcome by hunger—
the leopard went to the sage for refuge in order to protect its life.
Then, as the sage constantly cultivated an affection born of living together, [the tiger remained there].

12,117.019c That leopard was reduced to the state of a tiger by his enemies, who were far more powerful. 12,117.019e Then, O lord of the people, having seen him, that tiger did not attack him. 12,117.020a But that dog, having attained the state of a tiger, became a powerful eater of flesh.
At that time, he did not even harbor a desire for the enjoyment of roots and fruits,
just as the lord of beasts always longs for those dwelling in the forest;
in that very way, O Great King, he then became like a tiger.
A tiger, satiated by the slain deer, was sleeping at the base of the leaf-hut; then an elephant,
intoxicated like a rising cloud, came to that place—
tall, with temples exuding rut-fluid, marked with lotus-signs, and possessing a broad forehead.
With magnificent tusks, a massive body, and a roar as deep as a thundercloud— seeing that intoxicated elephant approaching, proud with rut,
the tiger, terrified by the fear of the beast, went to that seer for refuge.
Then that best of sages brought the tiger to the state of an elephant;
seeing him resembling a massive cloud, the elephant became terrified.
Then [he saw] clusters of lotuses and thickets of *śallakī* trees.
Filled with joy and adorned with the pollen of lotuses, he roamed about. While the elephant was thus sporting,
time passed day and night for that seer dwelling in his hermitage.

Then there arrived at that place a lion with a mane as red as saffron, a terrifying beast born in a mountain cave who was the destroyer of elephant herds. Seeing the lion approaching, the elephant was overwhelmed by fear of the lion.

Trembling and afflicted by fear, he sought refuge with the ṛṣi. Then, having been transformed into a lion by the sage, that lord of elephants no longer regarded the wild lion, for they were of the same species.
Having seen this, that wild lion, whose speech and strength were terrifying, ceased eating;
and that lion lived happily in that very forest within the hermitage. But other small animals dwelling in the penance grove did not [fear him].
They were seen constantly terrified by fear, longing for life. Once, by the turn of time, there appeared one who was a destroyer of all living beings—
powerful, feeding on blood, and a source of terror to various creatures.
The eight-legged śarabha, who moves upon its hind legs and roams the forest,
was coming to that hermitage of the sage to kill the lion. Seeing the śarabha approaching, the lion was overcome with intense fear.
Trembling and with palms joined in reverence, he sought refuge with the seer.
The sage, O subduer of enemies, transformed him into a Śarabha of superior strength.
Then that wild Śarabha stood before the sage’s Śarabha.
Seeing that exceedingly fierce and powerful [creature], he fled swiftly out of fear.
Thus, having been placed by the sage in the position of a *śarabha*,
he dwelt constantly by the side of the sage and attained the happiness associated with being a *śarabha*.

Then, terrified by the śarabha, O King, all the herds of deer fled in every direction from the forest, seeking to save their lives out of fear. The śarabha, too, was exceedingly delighted, for he was constantly devoted to the slaughter of living beings.

That eater of flesh did not desire the peaceful man who subsisted on fruits and roots. Then, driven by a powerful thirst for blood, that ungrateful creature born from a dog’s womb sought to kill the sage, Śarabha.
Then Śarabha, who had previously been a dog, reflected:
"It is solely by his power that I have attained this state of being a Śarabha, which is so difficult to obtain and strikes terror into all living beings— attained by him through mere words alone."
There are also other beings here who are terrified and afflicted by fear;
likewise, the herds of deer and flocks of birds live by taking refuge in the Sage.
To them as well, he occasionally bestows the state of being a *śarabha*.
In this world, he is the supreme among all beings, in whom strength is firmly established;
he might even at times bestow upon birds the power of Garuḍa,
provided he is pleased elsewhere and has taken recourse in compassion.
Being satisfied, he does not grant strength to any other being whatsoever;
therefore, I shall kill this brahmin very quickly.
There is no doubt that I am unable to remain here after the killing of the sage.
Then, having perceived him through the power of his asceticism with the eye of knowledge,
the highly wise sage recognized him and spoke to that dog. The sage said:
I am a sage named Agniprabha, born of the lineage of Bhṛgu.
With my mind, I can burn the entire world and yet sustain it. Excluding the gods, the entire world of moving and non-moving beings is under my control.

There are gods who, though filled with fear, do not abandon their own duty; I could consume with a mere word all those who have strayed from their own duty. How much more so you, whom I have brought to this healthy state of being a *śarabha*?
Cruel toward all beings, base, and indeed impure, you were a dog who attained the state of a leopard; the leopard became a tiger;
the tiger a rutting elephant; and the elephant attained the state of a lion.
That lion, endowed with exceeding strength, has once again become a śarabha;
yet, overcome by affection, I did not examine his lineage. Since you, O wicked one, desire to harm me, who am thus innocent!
Therefore, having entered your own womb, you shall indeed become a dog once again.
Previously, you were a dog, then a leopard, a tiger, an elephant, a lion, and likewise an eight-legged horse;
yet by your own inherent nature, you will become a dog once more.
Then, due to his hatred toward the sage, that evil-minded and foolish one was transformed into a dog;
however, having been cursed by the seer as a *śarabha*, he regained his own original form once more.
Bhīṣma said:
Having returned to his natural state as a dog, he fell into extreme wretchedness;
cursed with the sound "hum" by the seer, the sinful one was cast out from the penance grove.
Thus did the wise king, having recognized the dog's character and purity, [act].
Honesty, natural disposition, character, lineage, conduct, learning, self-control,
compassion, strength, valor, inner state, tranquility, and forbearance—
servants who are fit for particular roles should be stationed there, having been well-trained.
A protector of the earth ought not to appoint a servant without first examining him;
a king surrounded by men of low birth does not prosper in happiness. One born of noble family, when appointed by the king, always [conducts himself] through that very nobility of birth.
Even when being reviled for no fault, he does not set his mind on evil. But a man of low birth, who by nature has fallen away from the company of the virtuous,
having attained a sovereignty that is difficult to obtain, will turn into an enemy when reviled.
The crow, the dog, the one of low birth, the cat, and the serpent—just as these are, so too is a woman of low birth; they are all proclaimed to be equal.
The world-protectors, ever-anxious, look upon those born of low lineage as such.
Whether it be a woman or a man, character is the cause even in that regard. Even a woman who is of low birth, or a man who is of low birth,
may attain the status of noble lineage through the practice of non-violence, moral conduct, and righteousness.
Regarding dharma, O Great King, Bṛhaspati spoke these verses:
"Listen to them all, O Protector of the Earth, and you shall take them to heart:
[one who is] dark-skinned yet performs white deeds, who is self-controlled like an ascetic."

Even if he is a Caṇḍāla, the gods recognize him as a Brāhmaṇa if he stands firm in his conduct. If someone should cause the death of a wicked being for the welfare of the people and for the sake of the benefit of all beings, he is not a perpetrator of violence by that act.

For the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and for the protection of children and women, [he slew] the leopard, the śarabha, the lion, the tiger, and the elephant; as well as the buffalo, the wild boar, the pig, the dog, and the serpent.
He who harms those who do not protect the elderly and the sick is a knower of dharma;
whether he be a Brāhmaṇa of evil deeds or a Mleccha who is righteous and pure,
in that case the Mleccha would be superior, and not the Brāhmaṇa who commits evil.
Whether he be of low birth or of noble lineage, whatever man is possessed of virtuous character,
the king— having ascertained whether his nature is stable or unstable— being composed, should cause that virtuous man to perform the highest tasks.
The protector of the earth should employ a man of evil conduct in sinful deeds;
however, he should appoint one who is of noble birth, educated, wise, skilled in theoretical and practical knowledge,
who knows the true meaning of all the scriptures, patient, and likewise a native of the land.
One who is grateful, powerful, patient, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses; who is free from greed, content with what he has obtained, and desires to act as a friend to his master;
such a minister, who knows the proper place and time and is devoted to gathering all [resources], [should be appointed].
One who is honored, possessed of a disciplined mind, seeking the welfare [of others], and untiring; one who is skilled in conduct within his own domain, expert in peace and war,
a knower of the three aims of life for the king, and beloved by the people of both the city and the countryside.

He who knows the truth regarding the deployment of troops in trenches and arrays, who is skilled in inspiring the army with joy, who understands the reality of gestures and facial expressions, and who is expert in the conduct of military expeditions—
he divides a united host of kings and unites those who are divided.

A single elephant, when enraged in battle and properly urged on, can achieve much; yet who is capable of describing the splendor of one whose temples are moist with rut, whose eyes are slightly upturned, and whose broad cheeks are covered in perspiration?
Who is able to stand before an elephant that is charging with speed, with its trunk extended and its ears pricked,
as it roams through the ten directions?
Where that army was, there were elephants; where the king was, there were his elephants.
O King, those elephants, arrogant with rut, were like Victory incarnate—men who knew the true principles of elephant-training and were free from egoism.
Confident, skillful, self-controlled, powerful, and acting with propriety;
clean, surrounded by clean people, well-attired, and pleasant to behold;
a leader, skilled in policy, and endowed with sixty virtues.

He who appoints as a minister one who is free from arrogance, humble, capable, and gentle in speech; who is steadfast, mild, possessed of great power, and who acts in accordance with place and time— and who does not hold such a person in contempt.
His kingdom expands like the moonlight of the lord of planets.
A king endowed with these very qualities, learned in the scriptures, devoted to dharma, and intent on the protection of his subjects, is to be sought.

Steadfast, patient, pure, swift, knowing the right time and human effort; desirous of learning, possessed of what has been heard, a listener, and skilled in reasoning and refutation; intelligent, endowed with retentive memory, and one who establishes things according to the proper method.
Self-controlled, always speaking kindly, and patient even in adversity; one who personally undertakes the distribution of gifts, possesses excellent gates, and is pleasant to behold;
one who constantly extends a helping hand to the distressed, considers himself trustworthy, and delights in righteous conduct.
He does not speak of "I," he is free from the pairs of opposites, and he does nothing at random;
having performed his duty, he is the performer of unfailing deeds and is beloved by his servants. He gathers people to himself, yet remains humble, always possessing a serene countenance.

He was a giver, attentive to his servants, free from anger, and possessed of great magnanimity; he administered appropriate punishment rather than being without it, and he was an instructor in righteous deeds.
He always had spies as his eyes, observed the conduct of others, and was skilled in both dharma and artha.

A king should be sought who is endowed with hundreds of virtues; such a one should he be. And likewise, O lord of men, warriors should be sought who are possessed of every excellent quality. Good men must be sought out as allies for the maintenance of the kingdom.
A king who desires prosperity must not treat with contempt his warriors— those who are bold in battle, grateful, skilled in weapons,
conversant with the treatises on dharma, and accompanied by infantrymen.

This earth belongs to that king who increases his wealth and honor, who is skilled in the management of chariots, and who is proficient in the use of bows and missiles; it belongs to him who shows no contempt for his kinsmen and is ever free from deceit toward his servants.
He who possesses skill in the practice of benefiting others— that man shall possess this earth.
But he in whom laziness, sleep, vices, and excessive laughter are not found— his shall this earth remain for a very long time.
He who serves the elders, possesses great energy, and is indeed a protector of the social classes,
for whom the practice of dharma is constant— his is this earth for a very long time.
He who constantly follows the path of policy and maintains constant exertion [shall likewise possess it].
Not disregarding one's enemies—this is how this earth remains his for a very long time.
Both exertion and destiny, as well as the distinction between the two, were previously described by Manu; listen, for I shall speak of that very thing.

For Bṛhaspati, who knows the rules for both right and wrong policy, declared that exertion is indeed the strength of kings; therefore, O best of the Kurus, always remain one who perceives the vulnerabilities of enemies and provides assistance to friends.
Discerning the distinctions among his servants, he enjoys the fruit of sovereignty;
that king who is always intent on gathering all [resources],
who is industrious by nature, and rich in friends, is the best of kings.
"O Bhārata, with a thousand horses fit for heroic riders and a well-managed human force, it is possible to conquer the entire earth. Bhīṣma said:

That lord of men who appoints servants equal to dogs to their proper places in his affairs enjoys the fruit of sovereignty; for a dog, even if honored, does not become an authority by overstepping its own place.

A dog, having been removed from its own place, departs for another; likewise, servants who are endowed with noble birth and lineage and are established in their respective duties should be appointed by the wise, for it is not appropriate to employ them in an unsuitable position.
The king who assigns appropriate tasks to his servants enjoys the fruit of being endowed with the excellence of those servants;
like a śarabha in the place of a śarabha, he is as powerful as a lion among lions.
A tiger should be stationed like a tiger, and a leopard like a leopard;
likewise, servants should be assigned to corresponding tasks here according to the prescribed rule.
One who desires the fruits of action should not station servants in positions contrary to their nature.

That foolish king who, transgressing the proper standard, appoints subordinates in an improper manner does not win over his subjects. [Nor should he appoint] those who are childish, nor those who are base, nor those whose senses are unrestrained.
Men of noble birth should be stationed at the side of a king who desires his own welfare—
men who are virtuous, skillful, brave, wise, and free from envy;
men who are not mean-spirited, pure, and capable should serve as his attendants.

Submissive, devoted to their duty, patient, pure, naturally auspicious, and not disgraced in their respective positions— such should be the king’s outer attendants. Only persons who are truly like lions should constantly remain by the side of a lion-like king.
One who is not a lion, yet is accompanied by lions and acts like a lion, obtains the fruit [of a lion].
But he who is a lion surrounded by dogs, though devoted to the deeds and fruits of a lion,
is unable to enjoy the fruit of a lion when attended by dogs.
"O lord of men, with these heroes— wise, highly learned,
and of noble birth— it would be possible to conquer the entire earth.
No one who is unlearned, no one who is dishonest, no one who lacks knowledge, and no one who is not of great wealth [should be by one's side]."
O best among those who have servants, he should be gathered as a servant by the protectors of the earth. People devoted to their master's business proceed like arrows released from a bow;
one should employ conciliation toward those servants who are intent on the welfare of the king.
The treasury must be constantly guarded by kings with diligent effort;
for kings have their root in the treasury—therefore, become one who makes the treasury his foundation. And let your granary always be prosperous and well-stocked with grain.
May it always be well-bestowed upon the virtuous; be intent on wealth and grain.
May your servants be ever-disciplined and skilled in battle. Proficiency in the management of horses is desired here.
"O delighter of the Kurus, look after your kinsmen and relatives, be surrounded by friends and associates, and seek the welfare and interests of the citizens;
this is the final resolve and wisdom that I have declared to you."
"The dog, my dear, is an illustration for you; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, many modes of royal conduct have been described by you."
12.120.001c Those things previously ordained by the ancients who understood the purpose of the duties of kings—
12.120.002a That very same [teaching], seen by the ancients and approved by the virtuous, has been declared in detail.
12.120.002c O bull of the Bharatas, proclaim the essence of the duties of kings.
Bhīṣma said:
"The protection of all beings is considered the highest duty for a Kṣatriya.
Listen, O lord of the earth, to how that protection should be performed."
Just as the peacock displays its variegated plumage,
so should the king who knows the Dharma assume many different forms. He should manifest sharpness, crookedness, self-restraint, truthfulness, and even straightforwardness.
Remaining impartial and abiding in the quality of goodness (*sattva*), one thus attains happiness. One should assume that color and form which is beneficial for whatever purpose at hand;
for even a subtle matter does not fail for a king who possesses many forms.
He should always keep his counsel secret, like a mute peacock in autumn;
he should be gentle in speech, composed in demeanor, illustrious, and learned in the scriptures.
He should be vigilant at the gates of danger, as one would be at the outlets of a flowing stream.
Like mountain torrents of rain, he should take refuge with the twice-born who are perfected beings (*siddha*).
A king desiring wealth and pleasure should maintain his crest-lock like the banner of Dharma;
he should always have his rod of punishment raised and act with vigilance.
Having observed the income and expenditure in the world, like one leaping from tree to tree,
he should be pure among his own kin and cast away evil dispositions with his feet;
once his wings have grown, he should take flight and protect himself from impairment.

One should expose the faults of the sovereign and shake down the opposing factions, just as a peacock plucks flowers from the forests; one should serve under kings who are exalted, prosperous, and as stable as mountains.

One should resort to an unknown shadow and seek a secret place of refuge; like a peacock with its neck hidden during the rainy season, one should plunge into solitude at night and move about unobserved by women, possessing only the qualities of a peacock.
One should not cast off one's armor, but protect oneself by one's own effort; one should avoid entering enemy territories and falling into snares,
yet one should also harass that territory, for otherwise one may perish in the wilderness.
A man who constantly conducts himself according to this peacock-dharma shall slay those who are wrathful, highly venomous, crooked-moving, and harmful;
he shall not take refuge with those of childish plumage, but shall cause them to dwell in their proper abodes.
Like a peacock, he may at will indulge in pleasures as they arise;
yet he should gather wisdom from all quarters, just as a peacock gathers insects in the thickets. In this manner, like a peacock, the king should protect his own kingdom.
A wise person should employ a policy that brings about his own advancement:

self-restraint through intelligence, the penetration of the enemy's intentions through intelligence, and the attainment of personal virtues through intelligence; this is the instruction of the treatise.
One should further reassure [the opponent] with conciliation and observe one's own strength;
by examining oneself, one should deliberate upon one's intellect with the intellect.
A wise person, whose mind is intent on the application of conciliation, is a deliberator of what ought and ought not to be done.
A wise man should be of concealed intellect; when he ought to speak, he should speak accordingly.
Even if a clever man were Bṛhaspati himself regarding the discourse at hand, by means of his intelligence, he would return to his natural state like heated iron cast into water.
The lord of the earth should apply himself to all duties prescribed by the scriptures for both himself and others—
whether they concern the lowly, the cruel, the wise, the brave, or those skilled in worldly affairs.
One should employ others who are authorized by their words in their respective duties;
even without seeing them personally, one should direct all those engaged in appropriate tasks, just as a skilled lute-player follows the strings with his fingers.
Without violating the principles of dharma, one should act for the benefit of all; that king who thinks "this is mine" remains as immovable as a mountain.
Having resolved upon his duty, he should extend his long-reaching influence like the sun with its rays.

One should protect the Dharma alone, treating the pleasant and the unpleasant as equal. [One should appoint] those who know the Dharma, who speak gently, who are from noble families, native lands, and regions,
who are in the middle of their lives, faultless, devoted to the welfare [of others], and have conquered their senses.
The king should appoint those who are free from greed, well-trained, self-controlled, fully established in the duties of the law, and guardians of righteousness and wealth to oversee all affairs.
In this very manner, he should [ascertain] the origin and the course of all undertakings.
Diligent, well-satisfied, and supported by spies, he should carry out his duties; for one whose anger and joy are never in vain, who personally supervises his tasks,
and whose treasury is under his own direct control, the earth truly becomes a bearer of wealth.
He whose favor is manifest and whose punishment is also just according to the facts, who protects himself and protects his kingdom— that king is a knower of the dharma of kings.
He should constantly watch over his kingdom, as the rising sun watches over the cattle.
He should discern those who are mobile and those who are immobile; likewise, through his intelligence, he should not be distressed.
A king should accept wealth when it has come at the proper time, and he should not force wealth upon himself.
Day by day, the wise king should milk the earth like a cow.

Just as the six-legged bee gathers honey from flowers in due order, so should the king, having acquired wealth, make his accumulation. For that which remains after being protected is beneficial for both virtue (*dharma*) and pleasure (*kāma*).

A king who knows the treatises and possesses self-control should both accumulate wealth and disburse it. He should not despise even a small amount of wealth, nor should he underestimate his enemies. He should understand himself through his own intelligence and should never place his trust in those lacking wisdom.
Fortitude, skill, self-restraint, preeminent intelligence, steadfastness, heroism, awareness of place and time, and vigilance—
these lead to the increase of even a small or indeed a great [undertaking].
These eight are the fuel for wealth:
12,120.036a For a small fire grows when sprinkled with clarified butter,
and a single seed becomes many thousands.
Having observed that decline and rise are both vast,
a wise man should not despise even a small [enemy];
whether he be a child, one who is no longer a child, or an elder, whoever is an enemy [must be treated with caution].
Time shall slay the man who is ever heedless; another may seize his very roots. He who understands time is the most excellent among kings.
He would take away his fame and obstruct his dharma;
he would destroy his long-term vigor regarding wealth—
whether that enemy is hateful, weak, or strong.
Therefore, one who has restrained himself should never despise an enemy;
for both the destruction of the enemy and his own preservation,
as well as the two goals of dharma and pleasure, depend upon these two together.
Therefore, a wise man should form alliances with others;
for this reason, a king should rely upon one who possesses intelligence.
Blazing intelligence destroys even the powerful.
Strength, when protected by wisdom, increases; even a growing enemy is brought to ruin by wisdom. Action that follows after wisdom is what is praised.
For even a wise man who desires all objects of desire, when his body is debilitated and he is not overwhelmed by even a small amount of goodness (*sattva*),
seeks his own self through various means of acquisition.
For it fills the vessel of welfare to no small degree;
therefore, a king who has taken up arms against his enemies should seize the very root of their prosperity from every side.
Even when oppressed for a long time,
one who possesses knowledge, austerity, or abundant wealth should remain as steadfast as a flash of lightning.
All this is possible through resolve;
for Brahman dwells within those embodied beings who are intent upon it.
Therefore, one should know that resolve is all-powerful.
Where the wise and high-minded dwell,
where Śakra, Viṣṇu, and Sarasvatī reside,
and where all beings dwell eternally;
Therefore, a wise man should not despise the body;
one should always satisfy the greedy with gifts,
for the greedy never attains contentment with the wealth of others.
Every greedy person is intent on the enjoyment of the fruits of their actions; he who is destitute of wealth abandons both virtue and pleasure—
wealth, food, children, wife, and prosperity.
Every greedy person covets the possessions of others;
all faults arise here from greed.
Therefore, a king should not employ those who are greedy.
Upon seeing even a lowly person, one should urge that virtuous man [toward excellence]; thus,
O wise one, O Pāṇḍava, a minister who is both renowned and secret in his counsel destroys all the undertakings of enemies and accomplishes all goals consistent with righteousness.
O King, he is trustworthy, of noble birth, and capable of maintaining the kingdom.
Understand with your intellect these duties of a lord of men, as they have been declared in brief according to the prescribed rules.
Only that king who, having thoroughly investigated these [matters], applies them accordingly, is capable of protecting the earth.
If there is happiness born of improper conduct or arising from a lack of regulation, [it is not true sovereignty].
Various forms of violence are seen to be practiced;
for such a ruler of the earth, there is no destination,
nor is there the supreme happiness born of the kingdom.

Those who are distinguished by wealth, honored for their intelligence and character, endowed with virtues, whose prowess has been witnessed in battle, and who have been seen to be established in virtues— such men, O self-possessed one, will soon be found here.
Being mindful, one should strike down enemies after having formed an intention;
one should perceive various means through diverse courses of action,
and one should not apply the intellect to what is not a proper means.
A man who perceives only faults does not enjoy distinguished prosperity, vast fame, or wealth;
nor does he find joy in the engagement [in action] or likewise in its cessation.
Having discerned [the truth] among friends and having turned away from both sides,
the wise man should declare that very friend who bears the heavy burden as one truly affectionate.
I have thus declared these duties of kings to you;
apply your mind to the protection of men,
and you shall easily obtain the fruit of merit.
"For everything has its root in the supreme dharma of the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This eternal dharma of kings has been declared by the Grandfather."
The Lord is the great rod of punishment; everything is established upon the rod.
[It governs] the gods, the sages, the high-souled ancestors, the yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, and especially mortals.

"O Lord, you have stated that for all living beings in the world— even those dwelling among the animals— the rod of punishment, which is all-pervading and possessed of great power, is the highest good; thus,
everything moving and unmoving is subject to punishment."
The world, including the gods, asuras, and humans, is seen to be attached to it.
O bull of the Bharatas, I desire to know this in its true essence:
what is the rod? Of what nature is the rod? What is its form, and what is its ultimate goal?
Of what nature is it, of what kind is it, how many forms does it have, and how is it sovereign?
How does that Punishment (Daṇḍa) remain awake among living beings with an attentive mind?
And who is it that remains awake, protecting this world from beginning to end?
Who is known as the "foremost," and who is the other designated as the "staff"?
In what manner does the staff exist, and what is its intended course?
Bhīṣma said:
Listen, O descendant of Kuru, to what punishment is and how it is to be administered.
For that upon which everything depends is here called *daṇḍa* alone. O great king, the name of *dharma* is intended to be *vyavahāra*.
"How might there not be the disappearance of that [dharma] for one who is attentive in worldly affairs?"—
for this purpose, the very nature of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is intended.
Moreover, O King, this was proclaimed by Manu from the beginning in ancient times.

He who protects his subjects properly with a well-applied rod, treating the beloved and the unloved with impartiality— he is indeed Dharma alone. Furthermore, this very statement was already uttered by Manu in the past.
The birth [of Vyāsa] was told by Vasiṣṭha as the great word of Brahmā;
because this word was spoken previously, they know it as the *Prāgvacana* (the "Ancient Word"). And because it is an exposition of legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), it is here called the *Vyavahāra*.
From a well-guided rod of punishment, the three goals of life (trivarga) constantly proceed.
For the divine rod of punishment is supreme in form, like a fire with towering flames;
it is dark as the petal of a blue lotus, possessing four tusks and four arms.
With eight feet, one eye, spike-like ears, and hair standing erect;
with matted locks, two tongues, a copper-colored face, and clad in the skin of the king of beasts—
Danda, who is eternally difficult to restrain, always assumes this fierce form.
The sword, mace, bow, spear, trident, mallet, arrow,
club, axe, discus, javelin, staff, double-edged sword, and lance—
whatever weapons exist here in this world that are used for striking, [all these were present].
For punishment alone, possessing a physical form, moves through the world as the soul of all;
breaking, cutting, crushing, severing, splitting, and likewise tearing apart,
causing death and rushing forward— it is indeed punishment that moves about.
He is the sword, the cutter, the dharma, the one of sharp path, and the unassailable; he is the womb of prosperity, victory, the teacher, legal procedure, and the ever-watchful.
He is the scripture, the Brahminic mantra, the instructor, and the one who has attained the primordial word.
Dharmapāla, Akṣara, Deva, Satyaga, Nityaga, Graha,
Asaṅga, Rudratanaya, Manujyeṣṭha, and Śivaṃkara—
these, O Yudhiṣṭhira, are the names proclaimed for Daṇḍa.
For the Lord Viṣṇu is the staff, the sacrifice is the Lord Nārāyaṇa;
assuming his eternal, great form, he is called the Mahāpuruṣa. Lakṣmī, Nīti, and Sarasvatī are said to be the daughters of Brahmā.
The science of government is the sustainer of the world, for punishment indeed possesses many forms:
it is profit and loss, pleasure and pain, righteousness and unrighteousness, strength and weakness,
misfortune and good fortune, merit and demerit, and virtue and vice.
Desire and lack of desire, the season, the month, the night, the day, and the moment; lack of serenity and serenity, joy, anger, tranquility, and self-restraint;
destiny and human effort, liberation and bondage, fear and fearlessness.
Violence and non-violence, austerity, sacrifice, restraint, and then poison and its antidote;
the end, the beginning, and the middle, as well as the expansion of ritual acts; intoxication, negligence, pride, hypocrisy, fortitude, and right and wrong policy.
Incapacity and capacity, pride and its absence, expenditure and non-expenditure, discipline and renunciation, and the timely and the untimely, O Bhārata;
likewise, falsehood and ignorance, truth and faith, as well as lack of faith.
Impotence and resolve, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
sharpness and mildness, death, as well as arrival and non-arrival,
failure and success, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, and strength and weakness.
Envy and lack of envy, likewise dharma and adharma; shamelessness and modesty, as well as integrity and its opposite;
vigor, skill in action, eloquence, and the discernment of reality.
Thus, O Kauravya, is the manifold nature of punishment in this world.
If there were no punishment here, people would surely destroy one another;
it is through fear of punishment, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that they do not kill each other.

For when the subjects are protected day after day by the rod of punishment, O King, they cause the king to prosper in this world; therefore, the rod is the ultimate refuge. It quickly establishes order in this world, O lord of men.
Dharma established in truth resides within the Brahmins;
the twice-born, endowed with dharma, become possessed of the Vedas. From the Vedas sacrifice arose, and sacrifice gratifies the deities.
The gods, ever pleased, entrust [the world] to Indra;
and Śakra, bestowing food, shows favor to these creatures. For the life-breaths of all beings are eternally established upon food.

Therefore, creatures find their support, and the rod of punishment remains ever vigilant among them. With such a purpose, the rod has come to be the very essence of the Kṣatriya; well-established and imperishable, it remains eternally awake, protecting the subjects.
He is called by these eight names: Īśvara, Puruṣa, Prāṇa, Sattva, Vitta, Prajāpati, Bhūtātman, and Jīva.
Daṇḍa alone bestowed upon him both eternal sovereignty and dominion.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, strength joined with policy is always fivefold in nature:
lineage, physical prowess, wealth, ministers, and wisdom are declared to be these strengths;
there is also another strength, O Yudhiṣṭhira, consisting of the eight kinds of resources that can be acquired.
Elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, boats,
as well as porters and guides, and spies— this is known as the eightfold army.
Of this eightfold force, when properly deployed, there are the elephants and those who ride upon the elephants.
Horsemen, infantry, ministers, and poisoners; mendicants, judges, astrologers, and diviners;
the treasury, allies, grain, and all other implements.
That which is known here as the body of the state consists of seven constituent elements and eight limbs;
among these, the rod of punishment is indeed one limb, and it is the very source of power. For it must be maintained by the Kṣatriya through the diligent effort of the sovereign.

Punishment is meted out as an equalizing force; for punishment is this eternal principle. There is nothing more worthy of honor by kings than that which demonstrates righteousness, [ordained] by Brahmā for the protection of the world and for the establishment of one's own duty.

The cognition of the Vedic authority (*bhartṛpratyaya*) has arisen, as has another [type of] conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, that conventional usage which is observed to be accompanied by the characteristic of the cognition of the Vedic authority is said to have the Veda as its essence and to consist of the cognition of the Veda.
O tiger among men, there is the fundamental [punishment], as well as another declared in the scriptures;

and that punishment which has been described as characterized by the conviction of the master is to be understood as not residing in the king alone, but rather as having the conviction of the punishment itself.
Even that which is seen as being based on punishment is considered to consist of legal procedure;
and that which is considered legal procedure consists of the domain of the Vedas. That which has its origin in the Vedas is Dharma, which reveals the [true] qualities.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, this legal procedure (*vyavahāra*), which arises from the Dharma as its cause and is practiced by those who have perfected themselves according to the Dharma, is the protector of the subjects and was ordained by Brahmā. Possessing truth as its essence and increasing prosperity, it indeed sustains the three worlds.
That which is punishment is seen by us as the eternal legal procedure (*vyavahāra*); and that which is seen as legal procedure has been heard by us to be *dharma*.
That which is the Veda is indeed *dharma*, and that which is *dharma* is the path of the righteous (*satpatha*).
In the beginning, Brahmā was Prajāpati; he then became the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
For he is the creator of all the worlds—including the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas, as well as humans and uragas—and he is the maker of all beings.
Therefore, this worldly convention of ours is characterized by reliance upon a master;
for that reason, we have stated this illustration of conventional usage:
"The mother, the father, the brother, the wife, and likewise the domestic priest."
"There is no one who does not deserve punishment from kings if he does not abide by his own duty.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they also cite this ancient history."
In the land of Aṅga, there was a radiant king known as Vasuhoma.
Being ever-devoted to righteousness, that king, together with his wife,
performed great austerities and then went to Muñjapṛṣṭha, which is honored by hosts of celestial sages.
There, on a peak of the Himavat, on Mount Meru, the mountain of gold,
at the Muñjavaṭa where Rāma commanded the removal of his matted locks—
since that time, O Indra among kings, [the place has been frequented] by sages of rigid vows.
That region is called Muñjapṛṣṭha, and it is frequented by Rudra.
There, endowed with many qualities consisting of sacred learning,
he was honored by the Brāhmaṇas and became like a celestial seer (devarṣi).
Once, that noble-minded King Māndhātṛ, the subduer of enemies and honored friend of Śakra, approached Vasuhoma, the lord of men. Having drawn near to King Vasuhoma, Māndhātṛ—
Seeing him distinguished by his asceticism and humility, [the king] stood before him with reverence. Vasuhoma, for his part, offered the king a cow and the guest-offering (arghya),
and then inquired after the welfare of his eightfold kingdom.
O King, Vasuhoma asked him— who was following the path exactly as practiced by the virtuous of old— "What may I do for you?
Māndhātṛ, being exceedingly pleased, spoke to that best of kings.
O descendant of Kuru, Vasuhoma, who is possessed of great wisdom, was seated there.
"O King, you have studied the entire doctrine of Bṛhaspati;
likewise, O lord of men, the treatise of Uśanas is known to you."
I wish to hear that: how does punishment arise?
Or what is it that awakens first, and what is said to be supreme?
And how is it that punishment, residing among the Kṣatriyas, remains established in the present?
"Speak to me, O one of great wisdom; I shall give you the teacher’s fee.
Vasuhoma said:
"Listen, O King, to how the rod of punishment was created for the governance of the world."
For the sake of disciplining and protecting his progeny, the eternal self of Dharma,
the blessed Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, desired to perform a sacrifice;
indeed, we have heard that he did not see any officiating priest equal to himself.
That god bore the embryo upon his head for many series of years;
when a full thousand years had passed, that embryo fell from him as he sneezed.
O subduer of enemies, he was born as Prajāpati named Kṣupa.
O King, at that time, he served as the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) in the sacrifice of that high-souled one.
When that sacrificial session (*satra*) of Brahmā had commenced, O bull among kings,
Daṇḍa became invisible because his movements were characterized by a joyful appearance.
When he had vanished, there arose a confusion among living beings:

there was no longer any distinction between what should be done and what should not be done, nor between what was fit to be eaten and what was unfit; how could there be any distinction between what was drinkable and undrinkable?
For they began to harm one another, and where indeed was spiritual success to be found?
At that time, there was no distinction between those who were approachable and those who were not; indeed, what belonged to others and what belonged to oneself were regarded as equal.
They plundered one another like dogs fighting over meat; the strong struck down the weak, and all conduct became devoid of restraint.
Then the Grandfather, having worshipped the blessed and eternal Viṣṇu, the boon-granting god Mahādeva, spoke to him: "In this matter,
you ought indeed to show us pure compassion."
"This Viṣṇu is your companion for the protection of Dharma. For you indeed know all ordinances; you are the supreme refuge of all beings.
Let it be so ordained that no confusion may arise herein."
Then that Blessed One, the god of gods, Mahādeva— the supreme cause of the universe, who bears matted locks born of the trident— having meditated for a long time,
was accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Indra, as well as by all the gods and asuras.
For the sake of sustaining the world and for the destruction of worldly confusion,
that best of gods created by himself, through himself, the rod of punishment,
as well as the goddess Sarasvatī, the divine policy consisting of the practice of dharma.
She created that science of government (daṇḍanīti), which is renowned throughout the three worlds;
by means of it, punishment is constantly administered to evildoers. Indeed, because it leads (nayana) the punishment, it is called "the science of government" (daṇḍanīti) here on earth.
Then that Blessed One, the Lord who wields the trident, the Great God Maheśvara, having meditated for a long time,
created all the scriptures and all the means of valid knowledge in their entirety for the purpose of applying the science of government.
The four Vedas are the immutable sciences; their various conceptual divisions are the four Vedas themselves, along with Mīmāṃsā, the extensive system of Nyāya,
Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen sciences.
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
together with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, constitute the eighteen branches of knowledge. These eighteen are renowned as the compendia of Dharma.
Maheśvara has declared the detailed expansion (vyāsa) of these very sciences:
he stated three hundred scriptures (śāstra) and seventy tantras;
indeed, this expansion of the sciences was proclaimed by Mahādeva himself.
The *tantra* named Pāśupata, the renowned Pañcarātra,
the Yoga-śāstra, Sāṃkhya, and likewise the Lokāyata;
the *tantra* named Brahmatulā, and the science of logic (*tarkavidyā*) for the dwellers of heaven.
The inquiry into pleasure, pain, and the objects of knowledge, as well as the means of accomplishment (kāraka), are renowned;
likewise, the eight sciences of logic (tarka-vidyā) are declared to be the expansion of Nyāya. Furthermore, eighteen ancient compendiums of sacrifice (yajña-saṃhitā) are to be known.
The Purāṇas and the composed Saṃhitās are indeed to that same extent;
likewise, the Dharmaśāstras have the same purpose and not otherwise. The Purāṇas have a single purpose, and the Vedas are Saṃhitās with a single purpose.

The Lord Śaṅkara, the divine one, taught all the various treatises on logic (*tarka-śāstra*), as well as the sciences of time (*kāla-jñāna*) and the sixty-four branches of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), along with the *Āyurveda* and its supplements.
He spoke of the eternal science of government (*daṇḍanīti*) ending in eighteen branches, as well as the *gāndharva* [veda] and the *itihāsa* in its various extensive forms. Thus,
these are the sciences proclaimed by Śaṅkara, complete with words and meanings.
Furthermore, their detailed expansion consists of thousands of divisions;
together with the sages, gods, and gandharvas, it is practiced eternally in the world with its various conceptualizations and in full detail, as indeed is the Veda in every respect.
The four branches of knowledge are condensed, and they are remembered as the declarations of the Vedas;
he who has reached the further shore of these is said to have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Rudra, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Bṛhaspati have reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Śukra and Manu Svāyaṃbhuva, who knows the supreme dharma;
and Brahmā, the supreme god, who is always [honored] by all the gods and asuras; and Vyāsa, who has reached the further shore of the Vedas, through the grace of Śarva.
"O best of the Kurus, through the grace of Mādhava, Śaṅkara, and Brahmā, I am Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu;
and Yājñavalkya is likewise called a master of the Vedas in every respect."
In every eon, it is differentiated by highly fortunate seers who perceive the truth,
as well as by the sons of seers and the minor seers, and even by those of mixed lineage;
it has been conceptualized by Śiva, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu as well.

In the first eon, it was indeed divided again by the virtuous; even now, it is divided by the learned who exercise their discernment. According to the impressions of previous births, this Sarasvatī is manifested in many ways.
Again, that Blessed One, whose excellent weapon is the trident, having meditated for a long time,
appointed a lord for each of those various classes.
He made the thousand-eyed god the lord of the gods.
He also made Yama, the son of Vivasvat, the lord of the ancestors;
Kubera, the lord of wealth and of the Rākṣasas;
Meru, the lord of mountains; and the great ocean, the lord of rivers.
He appointed Varuṇa as the lord over the realm of the waters and the gods;
likewise, he made Mṛtyu the master of life-breaths and Hutāśana the lord of fiery splendors.
Furthermore, the Lord appointed Īśāna as the protector of the Rudras.
To the high-souled Mahādeva, the large-eyed and eternal one—
to him belong these eleven Rudras who have arisen from his own form;
that very Lord Śiva is the deity who assumes manifold forms.
He made Vasiṣṭha the lord of brahmins, Jātavedas the lord of the Vasus, Bhāskara the lord of radiant lights, and Niśākara the lord of the stars;
he made Aṃśumat the lord of plants and the most excellent lord of all beings.
He appointed the twelve-armed youth Skanda as king;
he made Kāla the lord of all, whose nature consists of destruction and discipline,
and who presides over death, the fourfold division of suffering and happiness.
The Lord is the master of all bodies, the king of kings, and the lord of wealth;
according to the sacred tradition (śruti), he is the wielder of the trident among all the Rudras.
