The Lord is consciousness, the agent, the Puruṣa, the cause, and Śiva.

Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Moon, the Sun, Śakra, and the gods along with their lineages—all these are indeed Śiva, whose nature is knowledge; he is the cause even of them. He creates and likewise devours [the world], just as this [universe] has become composed of darkness (tamas).
At that time, when the entire world was unperceived, there was indeed the one Maheśvara.
He gave that one Kṣupa, born after Brahmā,
as the preeminent lord of creatures and the foremost among all upholders of dharma.
Then, when that sacrifice had been performed according to the prescribed rites, Mahādeva,
having honored him, gave Daṇḍa— the protector of Dharma— to Viṣṇu;
Viṣṇu gave him to Aṅgiras, and Aṅgiras, the best of sages, [gave him to Kṣupa].
Indra gave it to Marīci, and Marīci gave it to Bhṛgu;
Bhṛgu then gave that staff, which is conjoined with dharma, to the ṛṣis.
The ṛṣis gave it to the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the world-protectors gave it to Kṣupa.
Kṣupa gave it to Manu, the son of Āditya;
and Śrāddhadeva gave it to his sons for the sake of the subtle purposes of dharma and artha. Indeed, Manu, the son of Sūrya, bestowed that which is essentially protective.

Punishment should be meted out after due deliberation according to the law, and not arbitrarily. Restraint through harsh speech, imprisonment, fines, banishment, mutilation of the body, or even execution must not be carried out for a trivial cause.
Various bodily afflictions, the abandonment of the body, and exile—this is the punishment administered in due order as he remains awake, protecting his subjects.
The blessed Indra remains awake; after Indra, the radiant Agni remains awake.
Varuṇa keeps watch over Agni, and Prajāpati keeps watch over Varuṇa; from Prajāpati, Dharma, whose essence is discipline, keeps watch.
And from Dharma comes the eternal Vyavasāya, the son of Brahmā.
From resolve, energy arises, guarding [the world];
from that energy come the medicinal herbs, and from the medicinal herbs, the mountains;
and from the mountains, sap arises, as well as from the qualities of sap.
The goddess Nirṛti is awake; even from the lights, Nirṛti is awake. The Vedas are the foundation of the lights; from them, the Lord Hayashiras is awake.
From him, the imperishable Lord Brahmā, the Grandfather, is awake.
The Lord Mahādeva Śiva is awake among the ancestors;
from Śiva come the Viśvedevas, and from the Viśvedevas likewise the Ṛṣis.
From the Ṛṣis comes the Lord Soma, and from Soma the eternal gods.
Understand that in this world, the Brahmins remain awake for the sake of the gods;
and from the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas protect the worlds according to dharma—
both the stationary and the moving, which are eternal, [derive their security] from the Kṣatriyas.
While creatures are awake in this world, the rod of punishment remains vigilant among them. Punishment is the condenser of all things; it is a sovereign power equal to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Time remains awake, O Bhārata, in the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
The Lord of all the worlds, Mahādeva, the Progenitor of creatures,
the God of gods, Śiva, Śarva— the Sovereign— remains ever awake;
he is Kapardin, Śaṅkara, Rudra, Bhava, Sthāṇu, and the Lord of Umā.
"Thus is this punishment proclaimed for the beginning, the middle, and likewise the end.
A king who knows the dharma should conduct himself according to justice by means of this.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus, O King, the man who hears this doctrine of Vasuhoma and,
having heard it, conducts himself correctly, shall attain all his desires.
Thus, O bull among men, I have explained to you everything concerning the rod of punishment.
O Bhārata, this controller of the entire world, which is governed by Dharma,
was heard by King Māndhātṛ, the sovereign, from Vasuhoma in ancient times;
likewise, I have also related this meritorious and celebrated narrative.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O father, I wish to hear the definitive conclusion regarding dharma, artha, and kāma;
for the entire course of worldly life is established upon these three."
"What are the roots of dharma, artha, and kāma, and what is the source of these three? How do they attach to one another, and how do they exist separately?
Bhīṣma said:
When they are well-disposed toward determining the purpose of the world’s constitution,
and when those three engage with the origins and structures of time,
then wealth (artha) is said to be the body rooted in dharma, and desire (kāma) is the fruit of wealth.
All those [desires] have their root in volition (*saṃkalpa*), and volition consists of sense objects (*viṣaya*). All sense objects, in their entirety, exist for the sake of providing sustenance.
This is the root of the three aims of life (*trivarga*); cessation [from them] is called liberation (*mokṣa*).
Dharma consists in the protection of the body; wealth is sought for the sake of dharma;
and desire here has pleasure as its fruit—all of these are characterized by passion (rajas).
One should pursue them when they are close at hand, yet one should not abandon them even in thought.
Freed from darkness, he who possesses the highest intelligence may, in a single moment, attain all things beginning with *dharma*, including those pertaining to desire and liberation; yet,
through intentional action, the desired result may or may not come to pass.

One thing may serve a purpose, while another is quite the opposite; one may lead to misfortune, or even after attaining a goal, it may elsewhere be a source of initial benefit. One should discern the true meaning here with intelligence, and not with a base intellect.
Malice is the stain of dharma; the concealment of wealth is the stain of profit; and desire, when pursued through one's own virtues, is the stain of joy.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history.

12,123.010 And the conversation between both Kāmada and Aṅgāriṣṭha. 12,123.011 Having saluted the seer Kāmada as he sat there, King Aṅgāriṣṭha, having observed the proper etiquette, then questioned him.
If a king, driven by the force of desire and delusion, commits a sin,
O Sage, what might there be for him when death is near to destroy that sin?
For one who, out of ignorance, practices here what is unrighteous as if it were righteous—
"And how could a king turn back one who is so renowned in the world?
Kāmandaka said:
"He who, having abandoned both dharma and artha, follows after desire alone—"
Through the abandonment of dharma and artha, he incurs the destruction of wisdom in this world.
Delusion is the destroyer of wisdom as well as the destroyer of dharma and artha;
from that, both nihilism and misconduct arise.
When the king does not restrain those of evil conduct who are corrupt,
the world trembles before him as if from a snake that has entered the house;
neither the subjects, nor the brahmins, nor the virtuous follow him.
Then he meets with destruction and likewise falls into a state of being slain.
Despised and humiliated, he lives a life of misery;
yet to live such a despised life would be a pure death.
Regarding this, the teachers say that the destruction of evil consists in studying the threefold knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), showing honor toward Brahmins,
being high-minded in the Dharma, and marrying into a noble family.
One should also serve Brahmins who are endowed with forbearance and possessed of wisdom;
one should recite prayers, be habituated to water, be pleasant-faced, and not intent on anything else. One should enter among those endowed with dharma, having indeed cast out the evildoers.
One should please others with sweet speech and also through one's actions;
one should always say "I am such-and-such," praising the virtues of others. For one whose conduct is thus free from malice will quickly become highly esteemed.
It shall pacify even sins and hardships; there is no doubt in this.
Whatever the gurus declare to be the supreme dharma, do that accordingly. For through the grace of the gurus, you will indeed attain the highest welfare.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of men, these people on earth always praise conduct as the very first thing in dharma; therefore, I have a great doubt."
"O best of the upholders of dharma, if that can be known by us,
I wish to hear all of it exactly as it is attained. O Bhārata, I wish to hear how this moral conduct (śīla) is acquired."
"O best among speakers, tell me what its characteristics are said to be.
Bhīṣma said:
"In the past, O giver of honor, Duryodhana here [spoke] to Dhṛtarāṣṭra..."

"O Great King, O Bhārata, listen to all that was told by me while I was performing penance after seeing your prosperity thus attained at Indraprastha, along with your brothers, and the mockery directed toward us in the assembly hall."
Having seen that assembly hall and its unsurpassed prosperity,
Duryodhana, while seated there, reported everything to his father.
And having heard those words of Duryodhana, Dhṛtarāṣṭra then—
He spoke these words to Duryodhana, who was accompanied by Karṇa:
"Why do you grieve, my son? I wish to hear the truth of it.
Having heard it, I shall console you, provided that you are right."
Just as you have attained great sovereignty, O conqueror of enemy cities,
so too do all your servants, brothers, friends, and kinsmen;
you clothe yourself in fine garments and eat meat with rice.
"Twelve thousand four hundred noble steeds carry you; why then do you grieve, my son?
Duryodhana said:
"There are ten thousand high-souled *snātaka* brahmins..."
In Yudhiṣṭhira’s residence, they ate from golden vessels;
and having seen that divine assembly hall, furnished with celestial flowers and fruits,
as well as horses speckled like partridges and various kinds of jewels.
"O giver of honor, seeing that auspicious and immense prosperity of the sons of Pāṇḍu, which is like that of Indra, I grieve for my enemies. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O dear son, O tiger among men, if you desire that same prosperity as Yudhiṣṭhira, or even something superior, become possessed of good character, my son;
for by means of good character, the three worlds can be conquered, without a doubt."
Indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in this world that cannot be accomplished by those possessed of virtuous conduct.
In one night Māndhātā attained it; in three days Janamejaya;
and in seven nights Nābhāga regained the earth.
"For all these kings were possessed of virtuous conduct and self-restraint;
therefore, the earth, won by their merits, came to them of her own accord.
Duryodhana said:
"How is that moral conduct attained? I wish to hear this, O Bhārata, by which moral conduct these [beings] quickly regained the earth.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history.
O Bhārata, in former times Nārada spoke concerning the power of character:
the kingdom of the high-souled Mahendra was seized by Prahrāda,
and by relying on his character, that Daitya brought the three worlds under his control.
Then Śakra, with palms joined in reverence, approached Bṛhaspati and said,
"O one of great wisdom, I desire to know what is most beneficial. Thereupon, Bṛhaspati imparted to him the supreme knowledge leading to the highest good.
O bull of the Kuru race, the Blessed One related this to the Lord of the Gods:
"Bṛhaspati declared that this much alone constitutes the highest good.
But Indra asked further, "Wherein might there be something superior?"
Bṛhaspati said:
"There is a great distinction, my dear, belonging to the high-souled Bhārgava;
go there once more, O Purandara—may prosperity be yours."
12,124.024 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Then that most illustrious one of supreme splendor, out of affection, further acquired knowledge concerning the Self from Bhārgava.
Having been thus permitted by that high-souled descendant of Bhrigu,
Śatakratu spoke again to Śukra, saying, "Is there yet further welfare to be gained?
But the descendant of Bhrigu, the knower of dharma, replied regarding the great-souled Prahlāda:

He possessed knowledge in particular, and because of that, he became joyful. Then, having assumed the form of a Brahmin and approached Prahrāda, the wise Indra, the subduer of Pāka, spoke: "I desire to know what is most beneficial."
Prahrāda, however, said to the brahmin, "O bull among the twice-born, there is no moment for me, as I am occupied with the sovereignty of the three worlds; therefore, I shall not instruct you.
The brahmin, in turn, spoke these words: "At what time might there be a moment?"
"Thereafter, I wish to be instructed in whatever other duties there may be.
Then King Prahrāda was pleased with the expounder of Brahman;
saying "So be it," he then imparted the essence of knowledge at an auspicious time.
The brahmin also performed the unsurpassed service toward his guru according to the proper rule, with his whole being, just as he desired in his mind.
And when asked by him many times, O subduer of enemies, [he replied: "How was it obtained?"
"O knower of dharma, tell me the reason for that sovereignty over the three worlds.
Prahlāda, O great king, spoke these words to the brahmin.
Prahlāda said:
"O best of the twice-born, I never feel resentment because I am a king.
O dear one, as they speak of the *kavyas*, I restrain them and carry out their commands. They speak with full confidence and always keep me under their control."
In the place of the seers, those teachers gather around me— who am devoted, desirous of hearing, free from malice,
righteous-souled, having conquered anger, self-restrained, and with senses controlled—
just as bees collect honey.
I, who have tasted the essences ground upon the tips of tongues, stand above my own kin as the moon stands above the stars.
This is the nectar on earth; this is the unsurpassed eye.
12,124.037c Having heard this *kavya* (offering to the ancestors) which proceeds from the mouth of a Brahmin...
12,124.038 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
12,124.038a "This much is the highest good," thus Prahrāda spoke to the teacher of Brahman.
Having been thus served by him, the lord of the Daityas then spoke these words:
"O best of the twice-born, I am well-pleased with your proper conduct toward your guru. Choose a boon—blessings be upon you—I shall grant it to you without a doubt."
"That is done," the twice-born one said to the lord of the Daityas;
but Prahlāda, being pleased, replied, "Let a boon be accepted.
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, if you are pleased with me and if you desire my welfare, I wish to attain your own character; this is the boon I seek. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:

Then the lord of the Daityas was both pleased and seized by a great fear, thinking that since the boon had been granted by the Brahmin, this man could not be one of insignificant power. "So be it," Prahrāda then said to him, filled with wonder.

Having offered the boon to the Brahmin, he became overcome with grief. When the boon had been granted and the Brahmin had departed, O great king, a profound anxiety arose within Prahrāda, and he could reach no certain conclusion.

As he was reflecting on this, O dear one, O you of great splendor, his energy— which had been like a shadow— then left his body in embodied form, O dear one. Prahrāda asked that large-bodied being, "Who are you?"
He replied: "Indeed, I am one who has abandoned my own nature; I shall depart with you.
O King, while that best of the twice-born remained there, I dwelt in that blameless place, having become his disciple and always remaining composed in mind toward you.
Having spoken thus, O Lord, that [being] vanished and entered into Śakra. When that splendor had departed, another being of similar form emerged from his body and asked, "Who are you?"
"Know me, O Prahrāda, to be Dharma, wherever that best of the twice-born is;
there I shall go, O Lord of Daityas, for where virtue is, there indeed am I.
Then another [being] appeared, O great king, as if blazing with splendor.
Emerging from the body of that great-souled Prahrāda, he who was possessed of great luster was asked, "Who are you? and he replied to him:
"O foremost of the lords of the Asuras, I am Truth; I shall follow Dharma here."
When that person had departed after following the Dharma, another person emerged from him. Being questioned by the high-souled one, he said:
"Know me, O Prahrāda, to be Conduct (Vṛtta), for I am indeed rooted in Truth."
When he had departed, the Great White One emerged from his body.
Being questioned, he said: "Know that my power is wherever conduct prevails.
Having spoken thus, O lord of men, he went to the place where that conduct was found.
Then a goddess composed of light emerged from his body.
The lord of the Daityas questioned her, and she replied, "I am Śrī.
He said, "O hero of true prowess, I have dwelt happily with you."
"Abandoned by you, I shall go to where the army is; for that is where I belong.
Then, fear arose within the high-souled Prahrāda, and he asked her again, "Where are you going, O dweller in the lotus?"
"For you, O Goddess, are devoted to truth and are the supreme sovereign of the world.
And who is that best of Brahmins? I wish to know the truth of this.
Śrī said:
That Śakra is now a celibate student who has been instructed by you;
O Lord, that sovereignty which you possessed over the three worlds has been taken away by him.
For by your virtue alone, O knower of dharma, all the worlds were conquered by you.

"O Lord, having understood that, Mahendra took away your virtue (śīla)—your righteousness, truthfulness, conduct, and even my own strength. O one of great wisdom, virtue is always the root; of this there is no doubt."
12,124.061 Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, Śrī departed, as did they all;
but Duryodhana spoke this once more to his father.
"O delighter of the Kurus, I wish to know the true essence of virtue (*śīla*),
and how that virtue is attained— tell me the means for that.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
The high-souled Prahrāda previously taught the means [to attain virtue];
now, O lord of men, hear in brief how that virtuous conduct is acquired:
by being free from malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech.
12,124.064c Favouring others and giving—this is praised as moral conduct (śīla).
12,124.065a Whatever human effort or action would not be beneficial to others, one should not perform it by any means, even if it were for oneself; or rather, one should feel shame for such a deed.
One should perform that action by which one may be praised in an assembly.
This conduct has been described in brief, O best of the Kurus.
Even if those lacking good conduct, O King, should occasionally attain prosperity—
"O dear one, they do not enjoy [their fruits] for long, and they fall along with their very roots.
Knowing this in its true essence, O son, become possessed of virtuous conduct (śīlavān),
if you desire, my dear, a prosperity far superior to that of Yudhiṣṭhira."
The assembly is won by one who possesses learning;
the assembly is won by one who possesses cattle.
The road is won by one who possesses a vehicle; everything is won by one who possesses virtue.
"Or even more than that, O Indra among kings; therefore, you must be virtuous.
Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of men, Dhṛtarāṣṭra spoke this to his son."
"O Kaunteya, perform this; from that you shall obtain the fruit thereof.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you have stated that character is the most important quality in a person."
"How did this hope arise?
Tell me that, O Grandfather; for this great doubt has arisen within me, and there is no one other than you, O conqueror of enemy cities, who can dispel it."
"O Lord, my grandfather had great hope for Suyodhana, thinking,
'When war arrives, he will do what is right.
A very great hope arises in every man."

When she was struck down, death followed inevitably and with great suffering. Thus, O King of kings, I am one whose hopes are shattered and whose intellect is corrupted by that evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra; behold my own foolishness.

"O King, I consider hope to be greater even than a mountain covered with trees, or even than the sky; indeed, it is immeasurable. And this hope, O best of the Kurus, is inconceivable and very difficult to attain."
"Because of its extreme rarity, I see nothing else more difficult to obtain than that.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate it to you; listen to that."
12,125.008c The history of Sumitra and Ṛṣabha has come to pass. 12,125.009a A royal sage named Sumitra, a descendant of the Haihaya lineage, went out on a hunt.
12,125.009c Having pierced a deer with a straight-knotted arrow, he pursued it.
Taking up the arrow, that deer of immeasurable prowess fled;
and the powerful king quickly pursued the deer from close behind.
Then, moving with great speed, the deer ran across both low ground and high ground.
In just a moment, O Indra among kings, he traveled along that level path.
Then, by virtue of his youth and innate strength, the king,
bearing his bow and sword, proceeded like a swan.
Having crossed over streams and rivers, as well as ponds and forests, he wandered through the woods,
passing by and repeatedly traversing them. But that deer, O King, having approached and repeatedly encountered the monarch, [continued its course].
Then, moving with great speed, he returned again;
struck by his many arrows, O king of kings, that forest-dweller approached him once more as if in play.
And again, O Indra among kings, the swift leader of the deer herd, exerting his speed, would repeatedly pass them by and then return to their presence;
at which point Sumitra, the crusher of enemies, discharged a terrible arrow that pierced his vital organs.

Taking up an excellent arrow, he discharged it from his bow. Then, at a distance of only two *gavyūtis*, the leader of the leaders of deer herds left the path of his arrow and stood there as if laughing.
When that flaming arrow had fallen upon the ground,
the deer entered the great forest, and the king likewise pursued it. Having entered the great forest, he then reached the hermitage of the ascetics.
Then the king reached that place and, being exhausted, sat down once more.
Seeing him then holding his bow, afflicted by fatigue and hungry,
the sages approached him and performed worship according to the prescribed rites.

Having accepted the worship offered by the sages, that lord of men questioned all the ascetics regarding their supreme increase in ascetic merit. Those whose wealth is penance, having received the words of the king, [responded].
The seers questioned that tiger among kings regarding their own purpose:
"For what reason, O auspicious-faced one, have you come to this grove of asceticism? Why do you travel on foot, O lord of men, equipped with a sword, a bow, and arrows?"
"O giver of honor, we wish to know this: from where have you come?
In what family were you born, and what is your name? Tell us.
Then, O bull among men, that king [spoke] to all those twice-born ones.
O Bhārata, he related everything according to the facts and described his service:
"Born in the lineage of the Haihayas, Sumitra, the delighter of friends,
wanders about slaying herds of deer with thousands of arrows."
"Protected by a great force, along with his ministers and the women of the harem,
the deer— pierced by my arrow and still carrying it— is fleeing. Having followed him as he ran, I have arrived at this forest by chance."
In your presence, I am one whose fortune is lost, whose hope is destroyed, and who am emaciated by fatigue.
What indeed could be more painful than this— that I, exhausted by toil,
with my hopes shattered and my auspicious marks vanished, have arrived at your hermitage?

O you whose wealth is asceticism, neither the loss of my royal insignia nor the loss of the city causes me such intense suffering as does the frustration of my hope. Neither the great mountain Himavat nor the vast ocean, the great reservoir of waters, [can provide such solace].
Just as the two worlds could not encompass the vastness between them,
so too have I not reached the end of the austerity that excels all hope;
for you, whose wealth is penance, are omniscient and know everything.
"O highly fortunate sirs, I shall therefore ask you about my doubt: Of these two—
a man who possesses hope, or even the intermediate space—
which appears to you as more preeminent in the world by virtue of its greatness?"
"I wish to hear this in its true essence: what is difficult to obtain here?
O you who are constant in austerity, if it is not a secret, do not delay in telling me here;
for I desire to hear nothing that is a secret, O bulls among the twice-born."
"If there should be any obstacle to your asceticism because of this, I shall desist from it;
or if there is some connection to the narrative regarding this question I have raised,
I wish to hear the full collection of reasons for it according to the truth."
"For you, O sirs, who are constant in austerity, should speak this with concentrated minds.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, among all those ṛṣis, the best of ṛṣis—"
Then the brahmin-sage named Ṛṣabha, as if smiling, said:
"O tiger among kings, O Lord, formerly while wandering through sacred fords,
I reached the divine hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa."
Where that beautiful Badarī is, as well as the celestial lake,
and where, O King, Aśvaśiras recites the eternal Vedas—
in that lake I formerly performed the libation according to the prescribed rites.
Then, after paying my respects to the ancestors and the deities, I went to that hermitage where the two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa were constantly dwelling. From there,
I went to a certain nearby hermitage for the purpose of staying.
Then, O mighty-armed one, I saw an ascetic coming toward me, named Tanu, a treasure-house of austerity, wearing rags and skins, emaciated, tall,
and exceedingly thin; his form, O great-armed one, was endowed with eight times the beauty of other men.
O royal seer, such emaciation as his has never been seen anywhere;
O Indra among kings, even his body was like that of a little finger,
and his neck, arms, feet, and hair were of wondrous appearance.
"O best of kings, his head was proportionate to his body, as were his ears and eyes; his speech and his movements were likewise ordinary.
Seeing that emaciated brahmin, I became afraid and deeply distressed."

Having prostrated at his feet, O bull among men, I stood before him with palms joined in reverence; having announced my name, my lineage, and my father, I sat down slowly upon the seat assigned by him.
Then, O great king, that best of the upholders of dharma spoke among the sages stories connected with righteousness and worldly purpose; while he was thus speaking,
the lotus-eyed king [listened].
Accompanied by his army and the women of the inner apartments, he set out on swift horses;
remembering his son lost in the forest, the wise father of Bhūridyumna— foremost among the Raghus and of great renown— was deeply distressed in mind.

"O King, in the past, while wandering through this forest, the monarch was driven by such hope, thinking, 'I shall see my son here; I shall see him. Yet that most righteous man is surely difficult for me to find."
"My only son has been lost in the great forest"—this was said by me repeatedly at that time.
"He is difficult for me to find, yet my hope is great. With my body overcome by that [hope], I am on the verge of death; of this there is no doubt.

Having heard this, the Blessed One, that slender sage, the best among the foremost of munis, stood for a moment with his head bowed, absorbed in meditation. Observing him thus lost in thought, the king became exceedingly dejected.
With a dejected soul, he spoke these words repeatedly, very softly and slowly:
"O brahmin-sage, what indeed is difficult to obtain, and what is the nature of hope?
May the Blessed One tell me this, provided it is not a secret from me."
O King, because of his own misfortune, that venerable great seer had previously been insulted by him while relying on a foolish mindset;
he was begging for a golden jar and bark garments.

Even though he had acted with contempt, the sage did not retaliate; consequently, that brahmin-seer became despondent and fell into despair. Having spoken thus, he then paid homage to that seer who is honored by the world.
Exhausted, that righteous-souled one sat down, O best of men, just as you have done. Then,
having brought water for the guest-offering and water for washing the feet, the great seer presented everything to the king according to the forest-dweller’s ritual.
Then all those sages, having surrounded that bull among men,
sat down placing him at their head, like the Seven Sages around Dhruva;
and there they questioned the unconquered king.
"This entire purpose is for the entry into the hermitage.
The king said:
"I am the king known as Vīradyumna, renowned in all directions."
I have come to the forest to search for my son Bhūridyumna, who has gone missing.
O foremost of Brahmins, he is my only son, and though he is but a child and sinless, he is not to be seen in this forest; therefore, I wander about searching for him.
12,126.029 Ṛṣabha said:
When these words had been spoken by the king, the sage remained there with his face cast down;
he became silent and did not reply to the monarch.
"For in the past, O Indra among kings, that brahmin was not highly honored by the king; thus, emaciated by hope, he undertook long austerities.
'I shall never again accept gifts from kings under any circumstances.'"
Thinking then, "This shall be so for the other castes as well," and resolving, "For hope stands waiting and makes the foolish man prattle;
I shall dispel it," he remained steadfast.
Vīradyumna, however, questioned that best of sages once more.
The king said:
"What is the cause of hope’s thinness, and what is difficult to obtain here on this earth?"
"May the Blessed One speak this, for you are a seer of dharma and artha.
Ṛṣabha said:
"Then, having recollected all of that, as if wishing to cause [them] to remember, he spoke."
Then the venerable brahmin, his body emaciated and thin, said to the king:
"O King, nothing is equal to the emaciation caused by hope, O monarch;
indeed, because it is so difficult to attain, I have sought after kings on its account."
The King said:
"O Brahmin, at your word, I have accepted both the emaciated and the non-emaciated;
and its rarity, O twice-born one, is like a Vedic statement."
"O one of great wisdom, a doubt has arisen in my heart; O best of beings, you ought to explain this to me in its true essence as I ask you.
What indeed could be more wretched than this? May the Blessed One tell me."
"O Brahmin, if it is not a secret to you in this world, what indeed is difficult to obtain?
The emaciated one replied:
"Even that which is difficult to obtain does not exist for one who seeks it and attains steadfastness."
O dear one, it is even more difficult to find someone who does not despise a petitioner, who,
having made a promise, assists another to the best of their ability and according to what is fitting;
that hope which is fixed upon all beings is weaker than I am.
That hope which is fixed upon the ungrateful, the cruel, and the lazy; that hope which is fixed upon those who do harm—that hope has become even thinner than I am.
A father with an only son, when that son is lost or likewise gone abroad...
O King, the hope of a woman who does not know when her labor will begin is even thinner than mine; likewise, the hope of old women for sons and the hope of wealthy men are both thinner than mine.
And having heard the appropriate conversations of maidens of marriageable age who were longing for husbands, she became even more emaciated than I was with hope.
Ṛṣabha said:
Having heard this, O King, that monarch,
together with the women of his inner apartments, touched the feet of that bull among the twice-born with his head and prostrated himself before him.
The king said:
"I propitiate you, O Blessed One; I desire union with your son.
O best of the twice-born, regarding that which has just been spoken by you, choose a boon, O Brahmin, whatever you desire, according to the prescribed rite."
Ṛṣabha said:
And the lotus-eyed king spoke these words to him:
"O Brahmin, what you have said is indeed true; there is nothing false in it."

Then the Blessed One, the slender one, the best among the upholders of dharma, laughed and quickly brought forth his son through his ascetic power and sacred learning. Having summoned that son and reproached the king, he spoke.
The best of those who uphold dharma revealed himself as Dharma;
and having shown himself, divine and wonderful to behold, he,
free from sin and devoid of anger, departed for the forest nearby.
"O King, this has been seen by me, and these words have been heard by me. Therefore, quickly cast away this hope that has become so exceedingly thin.
Bhīṣma said:
O great king, having been addressed thus there by the high-souled Ṛṣabha,
Sumitra then quickly cast off his even more slender hope.
In the same way, O son of Kuntī, you too, having heard these words of mine—
"Be firm, O King, like Himavat, the best of mountains.
For you are both the witness and the hearer here in matters of purposeful hardship;
having heard me, O Great King, you ought not to be distressed."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, as there is no satiety for me in hearing you speak, as if it were nectar, I remain unsatisfied even if this discourse were to come to an end."
"Therefore, O Grandfather, speak further of dharma alone;
for I do not reach satiety with dharma, as my curiosity regarding it is great.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Gautama and the high-souled Yama.
Having reached Mount Pāriyātra, there was the great hermitage of Gautama.
Listen to me regarding the time that Gautama dwelt there:
for sixty thousand years, that Gautama performed ascetic penance. That sage was engaged in fierce austerities and was purified by his asceticism.
Then Yama, the world-protector, approached that tiger among men;
he beheld the sage Gautama, the seer of great asceticism. Recognizing by his spiritual power that Yama had arrived, the Brahmarṣi—
Having approached with palms joined in reverence and being self-restrained, that ascetic [approached].
As soon as Dharmarāja saw that bull among men, he paid him homage and invited him according to dharma, saying, "What may be done for you?"
Gautama said:
"By doing what does one attain freedom from debt to one's mother and father?
And how does a man enjoy those auspicious worlds that are so difficult to attain?"
Yama said:
There is no other sacred ford, no other god, and no other dharma whatsoever that purifies a lord of the earth who is ignorant of man.

Therefore, having abandoned evil and established oneself in eternal devotion, one should worship [the Lord] through action, mind, and speech; thus one becomes free from debt. This applies to one who is constantly possessed of austerity and purity, and who delights in truth and dharma.
One should straightforwardly perform the worship of one’s mother and father day after day;
one should also sacrifice with many horse-sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. By this, a person attains worlds of wondrous appearance.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Bhārata, what is the course for a king who is abandoned by his friends, surrounded by many enemies, whose treasury is exhausted, and who is deprived of strength?
For one who has wicked ministers as companions, whose secret counsels are leaked on all sides,
who is being ousted from his kingdom and sees no other course,
and who is weak while being attacked by a stronger enemy’s army—
For one who crushes foreign kingdoms, who persists in conflict, who has not properly organized his own realm, and who disregards the requirements of place and time—
Reconciliation would be unattainable, or else there would be dissension due to excessive oppression;
or one’s life might be sacrificed for the sake of wealth—in such a case, what would be well-done?
Bhīṣma said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, you have asked about a most secret matter regarding dharma.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I am not able to speak of this dharma unless I am asked;
for dharma, O bull of the Bharatas, is subtler than mere words and even subtler than the intellect."
Having heard this and constantly attending to right conduct, one may at some point become virtuous;
yet, through action preceded by conscious intent, one may or may not become wealthy.
Such is this follow-up question; you should determine its meaning with your own intelligence.
"O Bhārata, listen to this method, rich in righteousness, for the sake of sustenance.
I do not desire such a dharma for its own sake as a cause of dharma;
rather, it is considered appropriate later on when one is able to take away the suffering of those who are wealthy."
Having reached a definitive conclusion regarding all states of existence,
for as often as a person constantly consults the scripture, so often does he understand it, and his discernment finds favor with him.
From lack of understanding, a lack of application arises in a person; for indeed, through lack of understanding, what is not yoga becomes yoga that brings about prosperity.
Listen to these words without doubt and without malice.

From the depletion of the king’s treasury alone arises the depletion of his army. A king should generate a treasury like one drawing water from waterless places; when the time arrives, he should provide support—this is the proper dharma in this matter.

Having obtained this dharma of skillful means practiced by people of old, O Bhārata, there is one dharma for those who are capable and another for times of distress. The treasury is said to be dharma, yet wisdom is more important than dharma.
Having attained the Dharma, a weak person does not find a righteous way of life,
because the acquisition of wealth is by no means certain;
therefore, even unrighteousness is heard of as having the characteristics of Dharma in times of distress.

The wise know that unrighteousness arises when [the king fails in his duty]; you are indeed perplexed as to what follows for a Kṣatriya. [Tell me] how his dharma may not decline and how he may not fall under the power of his enemies.
"That which ought to be done here," they say, "one should not let oneself perish. One who is despondent serves neither dharma, nor others, nor himself.
By every possible means one should seek to uplift oneself; this is the settled conclusion."

In this regard, O dear one, the conclusion of those who know the Dharma concerning the expertise in righteousness is that for the Kṣatriya, exertion is life and the strength of the arms is the source of livelihood; such is the sacred tradition. When his means of subsistence are blocked, what is there that a Kṣatriya ought not to take?
Except for the property of ascetics and the property of Brahmins, O Bhārata—
just as a Brahmin, when suffering, might officiate at a sacrifice for one for whom he should not officiate,
or eat food that is unfit to be eaten, so too is this [theft]; there is no doubt in this matter.
For one who is oppressed, what is not a door? Or for one who is held back, what is not a wrong path?
When one who is oppressed breaks forth through that which is no door, there follows a defeat by the entire world due to the depletion of his treasury and army.
The life of a mendicant is not prescribed for him, nor is the livelihood of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra.

His occupation should be that which follows immediately after his own *svadharma*, provided it does not depend on others; living by means of a secondary rule (*anukalpa*) when unable to follow the primary rule (*kalpa*).
When one has fallen into calamity, living by means that are contrary to the principles of righteousness—even this is seen among Brahmins when their livelihood is exhausted.
What doubt could there be regarding a Kṣatriya? This is always certain.
One may take from those who are superior; one should not come to ruin by any means.
They know the Kṣatriya to be both the slayer and the protector of subjects;
therefore, that kinsman of the ruling order must take what is required while protecting them.
"O King, for there is no livelihood here for anyone at all that does not involve injury,
even for a solitary sage dwelling in the forest.
It is impossible to live by adhering to the conduct prescribed by Śaṅkha and Likhita."
Especially for one who desires to protect his subjects, O best of the Kurus,
the king and the kingdom must always provide mutual protection during times of distress; this is the eternal dharma.
Just as a king protects his kingdom with floods of wealth during times of distress,
so too should the kingdom protect the king when he is in calamity. The treasury, the rod of punishment, the army, allies, and whatever else has been accumulated [should likewise be protected].
A king, even when his kingdom is overcome by famine, should not create a gap [in the sowing of seeds];
those who know the Dharma understand that seed must be procured along with food. In this regard, they cite the vision of Śambara, the master of great illusion.

"Fie on the life of that king in whose kingdom one perishes from lack of livelihood—even a mere outcaste who knows the words of Śibi! The treasury and the army are the root of a king; yet the treasury is the root of the army."
That is the root of all dharmas, for living beings have dharma as their root. Without oppressing others in this world, it is not possible to maintain a treasury, much less an army.
Therefore, even when one must oppress them for that purpose, one ought not to incur the fault.
Even that which is an improper act is performed for the sake of sacrifice during sacrificial rites;
for this reason, the king does not deserve to incur guilt. One thing serves the purpose of wealth, while another is its opposite.
Whether it be for the sake of what is not beneficial or even something else, all that indeed bears the mark of purpose.
Thus, with his intellect, the wise man should clearly perceive the determination of what ought to be done:
one thing exists for the sake of sacrifice, while another has no purpose within the sacrifice.
Everything else is solely for the sake of the purpose of the sacrifice; all that is a means for accomplishing the sacrifice.
In this regard, I shall state a simile that illuminates the true nature of dharma:
they cut down a sacrificial post for the sake of the sacrifice, and those who stand as obstacles therein [are likewise dealt with].
They surely cut down even those trees standing nearby;
and as they fall, they strike down other lords of the forest as well.
In this same way, those men who stand as obstacles in the path of a great treasury [meet their end].
"O scorcher of the foe, I see no success here without slaying them.
Both worlds are won through wealth—this one and the next; likewise, truth and the words of dharma exist for one who has wealth, for as there is nothing for the man without wealth."
By all possible means, one should acquire wealth for the purpose of performing sacrifices;
in this way, O Bhārata, there shall be no equal fault regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
These two [alternatives], O King, O Bhārata, are not possible in any way whatsoever.

Indeed, I do not see anywhere in the forests men who have increased their wealth. Whatever little wealth is seen here on this earth, people long for it, thinking, "May this be mine; may this be mine."
"O scorcher of foes, there is no dharma whatsoever equal to sovereignty. They praise dharma for kings as a means for dealing with calamities;
otherwise, some [attain their goal] through the act of giving, while other ascetics do so through austerity."
Others, by means of intelligence and skill, accumulate stores of wealth.
They say that one who has no wealth is weak; through wealth one becomes powerful.
Everything is attainable for the wealthy man; he who possesses a treasury overcomes all.
From the treasury [of the Vedas], both Dharma and Kāma, as well as this world and the next, are obtained;
therefore, one should seek that [treasure] through Dharma and never through Adharma.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and to Nara, the best of men...
Then one should utter the victory hymn to the goddess Sarasvatī.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Regarding] one who is impoverished, procrastinating, yet compassionate toward his kinsmen...
O Bhārata, for one whose citizens and the countryside are alienated, who possesses no store of wealth, whose chief ministers are suspicious, whose secret counsels have leaked,
and whose friends are not trusted, and whose ministers are divided on all sides—
"Tell me, what remains to be done for one who is weak and attacked by a stronger enemy's army, whose mind is overcome by calamity? Bhīṣma said:

If an external enemy should be one who desires victory, who is skilled in dharma and artha, and pure, one should quickly make peace with him, liberating those [allies] who were previously bound. But if the one desiring victory is unrighteous, powerful, and of evil resolve—

By means of his own confinement, he should effect a reconciliation with him; or, having abandoned the capital, he should overcome the calamity by other means. When that situation has ceased to exist, he, remaining alive, should recover his wealth once again.

But as for those calamities that can be overcome by mere renunciation—what person who knows the principles of wealth and dharma would sacrifice his own self further than that? One should guard against confinement; what compassion can there be for the wealth of a rival?
"But one's own self must never be surrendered by any means whatsoever, provided that it is possible [to avoid it].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When those within are provoked and those without are pressing hard..."
"When the treasury is exhausted and secret counsel has leaked, what task remains to be done?
Bhīṣma said:
"Either he should quickly desire peace, or he should quickly display fierce prowess."

The swift removal of the enemy's feet [from the field] is all that is required for success in this world; O Lord of the Earth, even with a small army, a king who is loyal, well-nourished, and joyful conquers the whole world.
Either slain he shall ascend to heaven, or victorious he shall dwell upon the earth;
by renouncing his life in battle, he attains the same world as Śakra. Having brought all the worlds under his sway, he may even attain a state of gentleness.
Through trust, one should practice discipline or even resolve to wear sandals;
or, if one wishes to depart, one should conciliate as desired. Having disguised one's identity with a friend, one should then personally take the initiative.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When the supreme dharma has declined, when all the world has transgressed its bounds,
and when every means of livelihood on earth has fallen into the hands of bandits;
"By what means, O Grandfather, should a Brāhmaṇa live when this most wretched time has arrived,
provided he does not abandon his sons and grandsons out of compassion?
Bhīṣma said:
Relying on the power of consciousness, one should live as a Tathāgata;
all this is for the sake of what is wholesome, and nothing at all is for the sake of what is unwholesome. He who takes away from the unwholesome and bestows upon the wholesome—
Making himself the bridge, he was indeed a knower of all dharmas. O King, though filled with great wrath, he remained established in his kingdom without provoking anger;
he would even take the wealth of a donor that had not been given, thinking, "This is mine."
He who, purified by the power of wisdom, conducts himself even among those who are censured— he who possesses right conduct and wisdom, the steadfast one— what can anyone say against him?
For those whose conduct is established upon the power of wisdom, nothing else is pleasing to them.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who are powerful increase in splendor.
Those who are mediocre adhere strictly to whatever treatise they have acquired without distinction, whereas the wise pursue what lies beyond it.
One should not cause suffering to officiating priests, family priests, and teachers who have been honored and duly worshipped; for by causing them suffering, one incurs sin.
This is the standard for the world, this is the eternal eye.
He should investigate it to that same extent; by that means, he shall determine whether it is right or wrong.
Even if many inhabitants of a village should speak to one another out of anger, the king should neither honor nor punish them on the basis of their words alone.

One must never utter slander, nor should it ever be heard under any circumstances; rather, one should simply cover one's ears or depart from that place elsewhere. Indeed, neither slander nor backbiting is the conduct of the virtuous.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, virtuous men among the virtuous speak only of virtues;
just as two well-trained, well-tamed draft-oxen, equally burdened and carrying their load well, bear the yoke, so indeed should a king conduct himself.
12.130.014 Just as there may be companions for one who travels, so too do others consider right conduct (*ācāra*) alone to be the most important characteristic of dharma.
12.130.015 Others, however, who are fond of the teachings of Śaṅkha and Likhita, do not accept this view.
Out of mildness or perhaps out of greed, they might speak such words as these:
"Even here they see the Vedic authority supporting the postponement of one who stands in an improper act;
for there exists no standard of proof anywhere that is equal to the Veda."
Even the gods punish the lowest of men who persists in improper action; for by acquiring wealth through deceit, one indeed falls away from dharma.
Yet, he is honored on all sides by the virtuous, who are the causes of the arising of prosperity.
That which one undertakes as dharma when authorized by the heart—that is dharma. He who knows dharma endowed with its four qualities is a knower of dharma;
for the track of dharma is as difficult to trace as that of a snake.
Just as a hunter might track the footprints of a wounded deer through the thicket by the trail of blood, so should one follow the path of dharma;
thus, O Acyuta, should the virtuous proceed along the disciplined path.
"Understand this to be the conduct of royal sages, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīṣma said:
"A king should generate a treasury from his own kingdom and from the kingdoms of others."
For from the treasury, O son of Kuntī, proceeds the dharma that is the root of sovereignty.
Therefore, one should generate the treasury by collecting [revenue] and protect it; having protected it, one should bestow favors. This is the eternal dharma.
A treasury is not produced by one who is merely pure in conduct, nor by one who is cruel;
adopting a middle course, one should carry out the accumulation of the treasury.
For how can there be a treasury for the weak? And how can there be strength for one without a treasury?
How can there be sovereignty for one who is weak? How can there be prosperity for one who lacks royal power?
The loss of prosperity resulting from high-handed conduct is just like death itself.
Therefore, a king should increase his treasury, his army, and his allies.
For men disregard a king whose treasury is depleted;
they are not satisfied with his meager resources and do not exert themselves for his sake. Indeed, it is because of his royal fortune that a king receives the highest honor.
She hides his sins, just as a garment conceals the private parts of a woman. People who were previously mistreated by him follow after his prosperity;
he finds them constantly, like wolves seeking to kill.

"O best of the Bharatas, how can such a king as this find happiness? One should indeed exert oneself and never grow weary, for exertion alone is manliness; even if one should break at an improper juncture, one should never bow down before anyone here."
One may even resort to the forest and dwell among bands of bandits;
however, one should never travel together with bandits who have overstepped the bounds of propriety.
O Bhārata, an army of bandits is easily found for those engaged in cruel deeds.

For everyone is indeed agitated by one who is utterly devoid of restraint; even bandits, who act without compassion, become apprehensive [of such a person]. Therefore, one should certainly establish the bounds of conduct that gladden the hearts of the people.
Even a small boundary established here in this world is honored;
yet people have resolved that neither this world nor the next exists. One who suspects fear in the nihilist is not capable of placing trust in him.

Just as the virtuous take what belongs to others, so do the bandits practice non-violence; living beings feel affection even for bandits who observe the bounds of propriety. Killing one who does not fight, violating another’s wife, and ingratitude—[these are the marks of the wicked].
The non-payment of debts to one who knows the Veda, as well as the total depletion [of resources],
the abduction of a woman, and standing among bandits— these are censured for a Dasyu.
Yet he remains a Dasyu even while avoiding these [other vices].
O Bhārata, those who do not act for his destruction,
but instead criticize him only partially, are certain not to succeed;
therefore, even when they have the power, enemies must leave something remaining.
One should not commit cruel deeds thinking, "I am powerful.
O dear one, those who leave a remnant see a remnant everywhere;
for those who act without leaving a remnant, there is constant fear arising from that very lack of remainder.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
here, those who know the past recite the words concerning the conclusion of ritual action.
For a discerning Kṣatriya, both dharma and artha are directly perceptible;
one must not allow them to be obscured by a hidden, procrastinating pursuit of dharma.
To claim that "unrighteousness is righteousness" is just like [confusing] the footprint of a wolf for that of a dog.
No one here has ever seen the fruits of merit or demerit;
one should simply desire to be powerful, for everything is under the control of the powerful.
In this world, the powerful man obtains prosperity, strength, and ministers.
For he who is not wealthy is fallen; that which is meager is but leavings.
Though much may be unwholesome, it protects nothing when one is strong against fear. Both of these, when presided over by truth, protect one from great danger.
I consider power to be superior to righteousness; from power, righteousness proceeds.
Righteousness is established upon power, just as all moving things rest upon the earth;
righteousness follows the will of power, just as smoke follows the wind.
In one who lacks power, righteousness is like a creeper clinging to a tree;
righteousness is subject to those who possess power, just as pleasure belongs to those who possess enjoyments.
There is nothing unattainable for the powerful; everything is pure for the powerful.
One of evil conduct whose strength is exhausted is brought under restraint; then the whole world trembles before him as if before a wolf. For being fallen and despised, he lives a life of misery.
Life is as cast aside as death itself;
when they say of him that he has been ruined by his evil conduct,
he suffers intensely, pierced by this arrow of words.
Regarding this, the teachers say that for the sake of liberation from evil,
one should devote oneself to the triple knowledge (trayī-vidyā) and likewise serve the twice-born; furthermore, one should propitiate them with sweet speech and through one's actions.
One should be high-minded and marry into a noble family;
one should speak thus, "I am such-and-such," while proclaiming the virtues of others;
one should recite prayers, be habituated to water, be gentle, and not talk excessively.

Having performed many difficult deeds, he should enter among the Brahmins and Kshatriyas, disregarding whatever various things are said by the world; for one whose conduct is thus free from evil will quickly become highly esteemed.
One may enjoy both comfort and wealth while protecting them through this conduct;
moreover, one should constantly bring back deer from the forest after killing them,
even from those [tribes] who would not accept gifts for fear that they are the food of bandits.
In this world he receives honor, and in the next world he gains great fruit.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history.
Just as a bandit who observes the bounds of propriety does not perish after death,
so too one who is an assailant yet wise, heroic, learned, and free from cruelty—
protecting imperishable dharma, devoted to the Veda, and honoring his teachers— does not perish.
Born of a Niṣāda woman by a Kṣatriya father, he was a follower of the duties of a Kṣatriya; known by the name Kāpavya, this Niṣāda attained perfection through his service as a hunter.
In the forest, during both the morning and evening, he would provoke herds of deer.
There was a hunter named Kāpālyasa, skilled in dharma,
knowledgeable in the proper methods, and an expert in the various species of wild animals and their watering holes;
he knew every part of the forest and always roamed the Pāriyātra mountains.
He was a knower of the dharma for all beings, one whose arrows were never in vain and whose weapons were firm;
he alone conquered armies numbering in the hundreds.
He honored his aged and blind parents in the great forest.
With honey, meat, roots, fruits, and various kinds of food,
he honored them and fed them,
attending to them with proper care while protecting the forest-dwelling Brahmins who had gone forth.
Having killed deer for them, he brought them to the great forest;
and as for those who would not accept them out of fear that they were food for bandits,
he would leave them in their houses and depart early in the morning.
Many thousands chose him for the leadership over those lawless *dasyu*s who act without compassion.
The *dasyu*s said:
"O wise one, knower of moments, places, and times, firm in character and armed,
become our leader and chief, esteemed by all of us. Whatever you shall say to us, we shall do exactly so."
"Protect us according to what is right, as a mother and as a father.
Kāpavya said:
"Do not slay a woman, nor one who is timid, nor a child, nor an ascetic."
One who is not fighting must not be slain, nor should women be seized by force.
Under no circumstances should a woman be killed by one engaged in battle among all living beings. One should always seek the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and one should fight for their sake.
One must not destroy the crops, nor should you create obstacles for the plowman.
For the ancestors, the gods, and the Brahmins will pronounce a curse upon one who prevents this.
Wherever the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the guests are honored...

Even among all living beings, a Brahmin indeed deserves liberation; one should show him honor even with one’s entire possessions. For if these [Brahmins] are provoked to anger against someone, they plot his ruin.
There is no one whatsoever in the three worlds who can be a protector for him who would insult Brahmins or seek their destruction;
his defeat is certain and inevitable, like the rising of the sun.
Seated right here, he awaits the fruit according to his power;
those who will not give to us, him he shall attack with his armies.
Punishment is ordained for the sake of discipline; it is certain that it is not for the sake of slaughter.

And for those who oppress the virtuous, their execution is ordained by law. For those who make their livelihood by obstructing the kingdom are measured out by that very act, just as maggots are produced from a corpse.
"Furthermore, those bandits who here abide by the treatises on dharma—
even though they are bandits— they would quickly attain success.
Bhīṣma said:
They all adopted that instruction of Kāpavya;
they all obtained their livelihoods and desisted from sinful deeds. By that action, Kāpavya attained great success.
Practicing what is beneficial for the virtuous and turning back wicked bandits,
he who constantly recites this account of Kāpya’s conduct shall never experience fear from wild creatures.
"He has no fear from mortals, nor from immortals in any way;
neither from the existent nor from the non-existent, O King, for he is the Lord of the Forests.
Bhīṣma said:
12.134.001 Here, those who know the past recite the verses sung by Brahmā concerning the path by which kings generate their treasury:
12.134.002 Wealth belonging to those devoted to sacrifice must not be taken away; it is indeed the property of the gods.
A Kṣatriya may rightfully seize the wealth of Dasyus and those who perform no religious rites.
O Bhārata, these subjects are both to be protected and to be consumed by Kṣatriyas;
for in this world, there is no second source of wealth for a Kṣatriya.
Whether that wealth of his be for the sake of power or indeed for the sake of sacrifice,
they cook only edible plants after having cut down those that are inedible.
Truly, he who does not honor the gods, the ancestors, nor mortals with an oblation—
Those who know the Vedas call that wealth "endless" (ānantikā).
O King, a righteous lord of the earth should take away such property;
for such wealth neither pleases the worlds nor fills the treasury, O Monarch.
He who takes from the wicked and bestows it upon the virtuous, making himself a bridge for them— I consider him alone to be a knower of Dharma;
in such a manner, and by whatever means possible, he shall conquer the worlds.
Some creatures born from sprouts possess articulate speech;
just as they come into being without [prior] desire, so too is the sacrifice extended.
It is just like gadflies and mosquitoes, and like gnats and ants.

That same mode of conduct applies to those who do not perform sacrifices; thus is dharma ordained. For just as dust, grass, and *ulapa* reeds arise spontaneously upon the earth, even so does dharma exist here—subtle and even more subtle.
Bhīṣma said:
Only two prosper in happiness—the one who provides for the future and the one who possesses presence of mind; the procrastinator perishes.
In this very context, listen attentively to this unsurpassed narrative concerning procrastination in determining what ought and ought not to be done:
in a pond that was not very deep, there were three fish who were friends.

In that place abounding in fish, O son of Kuntī, there lived three companions. Among those three aquatic creatures, one was a knower of the opportune moment, another was far-sighted, and the third was a procrastinator.
Once, fishermen drained that body of water from all sides through various openings into low-lying areas;
perceiving that the water was being depleted, they were struck by fear as the danger approached.
Then Dīrghadarśin spoke to those two friends:
"This calamity has arisen for all who dwell in the waters;
let us quickly go elsewhere while the path is not yet impassable."
"He who wards off future misfortune through wise policies does not fall into danger; may this please you both, let us depart.
But he who was dilatory there replied, "What is said is correct."
"But no haste should be made; such is my firm resolve.
Then, one who understood how to respond spoke to the far-sighted king:
"When the time arrives, nothing shall be lacking for me by way of what is right."
Thus addressed, the far-sighted and high-minded one departed;
he went by means of a single current to a deep reservoir of water. Then, having observed that reservoir of water with its flowing stream, [he entered].
The fishermen caught the fish by various means. While that reservoir was being stirred up and its water drained away, Dīrghasūtra, along with others, fell into their grasp there.
Seeing the net being cast for the fish,
the wise one entered among the others and swallowed it;
having swallowed that very net, he remained there just as he was.
But they all knew that those [fish] there were tied together.
Then, while the fish were being washed in clear water, he,
being quick-witted, released the rope and was swiftly set free.
But the procrastinating man, dull-witted, of inferior intellect,
and lacking discernment, meets his death like a fool whose senses are impaired.
Thus, he who through delusion does not perceive that the time has arrived is lost.
He perishes quickly, like a fish that procrastinates;
that man who, thinking "I am capable," does not perform what is beneficial at the outset, falls into danger, just like one who acts with hesitation.
The man who makes appropriate provision for the future attains great excellence, just like that far-sighted person;
for [time consists of] kalās, kāṣṭhās, muhūrtas, days, nāḍīs, kṣaṇas, and lavas.
Fortnights, months, seasons, and years are all equal;
the earth is said to be the "place," yet that time is not visible. And whatever is done according to the proper method for the sake of accomplishing a desired object is likewise [effective].

These two have been designated as the foremost by the seers in the treatises on dharma and artha, as well as in the treatises on liberation; they are desired by men as the lords of desire. One who acts with deliberation and is disciplined should properly bring them about.
One shall obtain the fruit through those two when the place and time are intended.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, you have stated that intelligence is the best in all circumstances."
"O best of the Bharatas, I wish to hear about that supreme wisdom— how it is yet to come, how it has arisen, how it is procrastinating,
and how it leads to destruction— so that a king, even when surrounded by enemies, shall not be deluded."
"O wise one, skilled in dharma and artha, and proficient in all treatises,
I ask you, O best of the Kurus: it behoves you to explain to me how a king who is beset by many enemies should conduct himself."
"I wish to hear all of this exactly as it occurred.
For even when a king is in a precarious position, many adversaries who have long been tormented by him strive together to overthrow that single individual."
"How can one who is weak and beset on all sides by those of great strength remain standing alone and without allies?
O bull of the Bharatas, how does one distinguish between a friend and an enemy?"
O King, how should one act in this situation regarding the interval between enemy and friend; when an enemy whose characteristics are well-known has attained the status of a friend,
what indeed should a man do, or by doing what would he become happy?
"With whom should one wage war, or with whom should one form an alliance? How should one who is weak conduct himself when situated among enemies?
This, O scorcher of foes, is indeed the most important of all political duties."
"There is no one who can speak of this, and even a listener is very difficult to find—
except for Bhīṣma, the son of Śantanu, who is true to his promise and has conquered his senses. Therefore, O mighty-armed one, seek it out and tell all of this to me."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this follow-up question of yours is worthy of you and brings forth virtue.
Listen to me, my son, O Bhārata, as I explain in its entirety the secret concerning times of distress."
An enemy becomes a friend, and even a friend may become hostile; for according to the requirements of circumstances, the course of affairs always follows that path.
Therefore, one should both place trust and engage in conflict as the situation demands.
Having understood the place and the time for determining what ought and ought not to be done, the wise who seek their own welfare must always resolve upon making peace;
even with enemies, one should make peace, O Bhārata, for life must be protected.
For that unwise man who never forms an alliance with his enemies,
O Bhārata, shall obtain no wealth whatsoever, nor even fruits. But he who makes peace with the enemy and opposes the friend [is truly wise].
Having perceived the application of purpose, one obtains a very great fruit.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between a cat and a mouse at a banyan tree.

In a certain great forest, there was a very large banyan tree, covered with a network of creepers and frequented by flocks of various birds; it possessed a massive trunk, resembled a cloud, and provided cool shade, being most delightful to the mind.
Near Vairantya grew a tree infested with predatory beasts;
at its base, having constructed a hundred-mouthed burrow,
a highly wise mouse named Palita lived.

Taking refuge in its branches, a cat named Lomaśa— who was a destroyer of birds and living creatures— used to dwell there happily before him. And a Caṇḍāla, who had made his dwelling at Vairantya, came there as well.
Every day, when the sun had set,
he would set that trap; having properly laid out snares made of sinew there, he would go home and sleep soundly until the night turned to dawn.

There, various kinds of wild animals were constantly being trapped at night. Once, however, a cat, though he was vigilant, was caught there. When that enemy, who was ever intent on doing him harm, had been bound, the highly wise [mouse]—
Knowing that it was the right time, Palita wandered about quite fearlessly. While he was roaming through that forest, moving with confidence and searching for food, he soon spotted some meat.
Having climbed that trap, he devoured that bait,
laughing in his mind at his captive rival standing above him; yet, while intent on the bait, he once looked up.
He beheld another terrible enemy approaching himself:
a restless mongoose named Harika, with copper-colored eyes, resembling a *śarapuṣpa* flower, and lying within a hole in the earth.
Attracted by the scent of that mouse, he approached in haste,
licking his mouth for the sake of food, standing on the ground with his face turned upward; meanwhile,
he saw another enemy perched on a branch, dwelling in a hollow.

There was an owl named Candraka, a sharp-beaked night-stalker; when he entered the territory of that mongoose, a great fear arose within him at that time, and this thought occurred to him: [The mongoose and the owl were then within range of one another. Then, having encountered that [danger], a very great fear arose in him.

In this most grievous calamity, when death has arrived and fear has arisen on all sides, how should one who desires his own welfare act? Thus obstructed on every side, he remained with an equal vision toward all things.
He became consumed by fear and made this supreme resolve:
"This calamity is fraught with total destruction, and life itself is but a hundredth part [of our time];
this peril has arrived, encompassing us on all sides with uncertainty."
For Nakula has already reached the ground; he might catch me. With the owl perched upon my head, the snake coiled below, and the cat bound by the snare—what should I do?
"O sinless one, do you possess the six royal qualities as well as the seven expedients?
For here, an owl remains while a cat stays within the range of his snare;
yet a wise man such as I ought not to fall into delusion."
"I shall exert effort for my life as long as I can restrain my breath;
for wise men endowed with intelligence and skilled in the treatises on policy do not fall into confusion when encountering calamity or when attaining great objectives."
At present, I see no other course for him here than that of a cat;
for this creature is in a precarious position, and a great task must be performed by me for his sake.
How indeed can he, who desires life, be left today when beset by three enemies?
Therefore, I shall indeed take refuge with this enemy, the cat;
relying upon the science of the kṣatriyas, I will consider what is for his benefit,
so that by means of my intelligence I may outwit this host of enemies.
"This man, my ultimate enemy, has fallen into extreme distress.
If it is possible through association to lead this fool to perceive his own self-interest,
he might perhaps, upon encountering calamity, enter into an alliance with me."

"Even the acceptance of an enemy who has taken up position against one who is stronger must be undertaken by one seeking life in difficult circumstances; so say the teachers. For a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend."
"For my life is now dependent upon my enemy, the cat.
Come, I shall explain to you the reason for my self-preservation;
perhaps even now this enemy may become wise through our association."
12,136.046d*0309_01 Thus the mouse reflected upon the enemy’s maneuvering. 12,136.047a Then, knowing the true nature of the course of affairs and discerning the proper times for peace and war,
12,136.047c the mouse spoke these words to the cat with a conciliatory preamble:
Out of friendship, I address you: do you still live, O cat?
For I desire your life, since our welfare is common to us both. Do not fear, gentle one; you shall live as before.

"I shall rescue you; indeed, for your sake, I would even give up my life. A certain effective means occurs to me here, by which liberation can be attained by you, just as prosperity was attained by me."
"Indeed, having reflected upon my own mind, I have seen this means:
for my sake and for yours, for our welfare is indeed common to us both.
For here stands that owl of evil intent, surrounded by mongooses."
"O cat, he does not dare to attack me; therefore, all is well with me for now.
This owl, chirping and with restless eyes, gazes at me as he perches upon the tip of a tree branch; because of him, I am greatly terrified."
"Friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; you are my companion in this dwelling, O wise one. I shall provide you with shelter, and you need have no fear of death.
For indeed, O cat, you are not able to sever these snares without me."
"I shall cut your snare, provided that you do not harm me.
You have taken refuge at the top of this tree, while I have taken refuge at its root. We have both lived here on this tree for a long time; indeed, this is known to you."
The wise do not praise those two whose minds are constantly anxious— the one who trusts in someone, and the one in whom no one trusts.
Therefore, let our affection increase, and let there be a true union between us.
The wise do not praise that which is past its time or devoid of purpose. Listen now to this meaningful reasoning as it truly is:
I desire your life, and you desire my life.
Someone crosses a very deep great river by means of a log; he carries that log across, and he is carried across by the log. Such will be our union, making it easy to cross over.
"I shall deliver you, and you shall deliver me.
Having spoken thus for their mutual benefit, Palita,
awaiting the proper time, waited expectantly, reflecting on the reasons that were both logical and acceptable.

Then, having heard his well-spoken words, which were reasoned and full of meaningful substance, the discerning cat, wise and eloquent, spoke these words in response: 12,136.063c–064a "The intelligent one, endowed with the power of speech, describing those words..."
Observing that final state [of the mouse], he honored him with gentle words alone.
Then Lomaśa the cat, whose teeth were sharp-pointed and whose eyes were like lapis lazuli gems,
looked slowly at the mouse and said:
"I rejoice, gentle one; may it be well with you, you who desire me to live. If you know what is beneficial, let it be done without hesitation.
For I am deeply in distress, and you are even more distressed than I."

"Let a reconciliation be made between the two who have offended; do not hesitate. Perform what is appropriate for the occasion so that the purpose of both of us may be accomplished. Once I am released from this hardship, your deed shall not go to waste."
"I have laid aside my pride; I am your devotee, your disciple, and likewise one who acts for your benefit.
I abide under your command and have come to you for refuge. When he had spoken thus, Palita [beheld] the cat brought under his control.
He spoke these beneficial words, which were well-composed in meaning and purposeful:
"What you have said is noble; this is not surprising for one such as you. However, listen to the course of action known to me for the sake of our welfare."
"I shall enter after you; I have great fear of the mongoose. Save me and do not kill me, for I am capable of rescuing you.
Protect me also from the owl, for that base creature seeks me out."
"I shall cut your bonds, my friend; I swear this to you by the truth.
Having heard those words—consistent, appropriate, and meaningful—Lomaśa looked up at Palita with joy and honored him with a welcome.
Having honored that Palita, the cat, remaining in a state of friendship, the wise one, being pleased, spoke to him quickly after reflecting well:
"Come quickly, may it be well with you; you are a friend as dear to me as my own life."
"O wise one, through your grace indeed I shall quickly regain my life.
Whatever can be done by me today while I am in such a state for your sake, command that; I shall do it. Let there be peace between us, O friend."
"Released from this doubt, along with your circle of friends and kinsmen,
I shall perform all actions that are both pleasing and beneficial to you.
O gentle one, may I too indeed be released from this calamity."
May I inspire joy in them and may I be able to repay them; for even one who returns a great favor does not equal the original benefactor, since the former acts only when a service has been rendered,
while the latter acts without any motive at all.
Having thus secured his own interest by making the cat believe it was for his sake, the mouse then entered with full confidence and went about its business perfectly at ease.
In this manner, that wise mouse was reassured by the cat.
The mouse slept trustingly on the chest of the cat, like a son with his father or a child with its mother.
Then, seeing the mouse nestled within the cat's limbs,
the mongoose and the owl departed for their homes, having lost all hope.
In that very same way, those two were deeply terrified and overcome with intense exhaustion; yet,
seeing their supreme affection for one another, they were struck with the greatest wonder—
those two who were powerful, wise, well-behaved, and worthy of honor.
Since they were unable to overcome them by force,
the owl and the mongoose, having seen that the cat and the mouse had formed an alliance for their own purposes, quickly departed for their respective dwellings.
But Palita, who knew the proper time and place, remained hidden within his limbs;
O King, desiring the right moment, he slowly and gradually cut the snares. Then the cat, distressed by his bonds, looked at the mouse.
Then, while he was cutting the snares and was not in a hurry, the cat, filled with haste,
began to urge on the grey-haired mouse who was so slow in severing the bonds.
"O gentle one, why do you not hasten? Why, having achieved your purpose, do you disregard me?
Cut these bonds, O slayer of enemies, before that dog-eater arrives! Thus addressed by him in such haste, the wise Palita replied:
To the cat, who was lacking in wisdom, he spoke these words for his own benefit:
"Be silent, gentle one; you need neither haste nor agitation. We alone here know the proper time, and the time shall not be let pass."
An undertaking begun at the wrong time does not lead to success;
that same undertaking, when begun at the right time, leads to great success. I would have cause for fear of you alone if I were released at an improper time.
"Therefore, wait for the right moment; why do you hasten, my friend?
Until I see the executioner approaching with weapon in hand, I shall cut your bonds once that common danger has arrived."
