At that moment, when you are released, you shall climb right onto the tree; for there will be nothing else for you to do but to live. Then, O Lomaśa, once he has passed away, you will be terrified and filled with fear.

"I shall enter the hole; you shall go to the branch. Thus addressed by the mouse for his own benefit, the high-minded cat—who was skilled in the essence of speech and desirous of life—spoke these words.
Then Lomaśa, hastening to perform his own duty and acting with perfect courtesy, spoke these words to the mouse Cirakārin:
"For virtuous men do not indeed perform the affairs of their friends with such affection."
"Just as you were liberated from distress by me acting with haste,
so too must you act for my benefit with haste. O one of great wisdom, exert yourself so that there may be well-being for both of us."
"Or perhaps, remembering our former enmity, you are merely biding your time. Behold, my life is clearly coming to an end due to my own evil deeds;
for whatever unpleasantness I previously committed out of ignorance,"

"You should not take that to heart; I beg your forgiveness, be gracious to me. To him who spoke thus, the wise mouse—learned in the scriptures and esteemed for his intelligence—then addressed these excellent words to the cat:
"O cat, I have heard you as you pursue your own interest; know that I too am pursuing my own interest. That friend who must be managed with fear, and that friend who is accompanied by danger—"
Therefore, one must act with great care, as if protecting one's hand from the mouth of a serpent.
He who does not protect himself after having made a treaty with a powerful foe finds that it leads to his ruin, like unwholesome food that has been consumed.

No one is anyone’s friend, and no one is anyone’s well-wisher; friends and enemies alike are bound together by self-interest. Just as wild elephants are captured by means of other elephants, so too are interests secured through further interests.
"For no one, once a task is completed, looks back at the doer;
therefore, one should cause all tasks to be performed with something remaining unfinished.
At that time, you too were filled with fear of the Divākīrtis.
He is not capable of seizing me; he is intent on flight. The multitude of threads has been severed, and only a single thread remains.
I shall cut that one as well quickly; be at ease, O Lomaśa.
While the two of them were thus conversing and likewise fallen into such distress,
that night came to an end, and fear entered Lomaśa.
Then, at the time of dawn, a deformed being, blackish-brown in hue, appeared.
With thick buttocks, disheveled hair, and a coarse appearance, surrounded by a pack of dogs;
with spike-like ears, a large mouth, gray hair, and a terrifying look—
there appeared a Caṇḍāla named Parigha, weapon in hand.
Seeing him, who resembled a messenger of Yama, the cat, his mind terrified, spoke in fear to Palita: "What will you do now?
And they both became utterly alarmed upon seeing that being of such terrible appearance.
In an instant, the mongoose and the owl then fell into despair,
for they were both strong and wise, and had formed an alliance; thus, it was impossible to overcome them by force through any stratagem.
Having seen that the cat and the mouse had formed an alliance for the sake of their purpose,
the owl and the mongoose quickly departed for their respective dwellings.
Then, that mouse cut the cord of the cat.
Then, having escaped, the cat rushed toward that very tree. Freed from that fear and released from his terrible enemy,
Palita entered a hole, while Lomaśa took refuge in a branch.
Then, taking up his club, the Caṇḍāla looked in every direction;
with his hopes shattered in an instant,
he departed from that place and went to his own abode, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then, having escaped from that danger and regained his life which is so difficult to obtain,
Lomaśa, standing at the top of the tree, spoke to Palita who remained in the hole:
"Without making any agreement whatsoever, I suddenly rushed upon you."
Do you not suspect me, who am grateful and have done what is beneficial? Having gained my confidence and having given me my life, why do you not approach me at this time of enjoying our friendship?
For he who, having first made friends, does not subsequently act accordingly— that evil-minded man does not find friends when faced with difficult calamities.
Therefore, O friend, I have been made your friend by you through your own capability.
"You ought to enjoy me, who have entered into friendship with you. Whatever friends I have and whatever kinsmen I have,
they will all honor you, just as disciples honor a beloved teacher."
And I shall honor you, along with your circle of friends and kinsmen—you who have restored my life; for what grateful person would not honor a giver of life?
May you be the master of both my body and my home.
"Be the instructor of all my affairs;
O wise one, be my minister and govern me like a father. You have no cause for fear from us; I swear it by my own life."
"In wisdom you are Uśanas himself; in strength we are your subordinates. For one joined with both your counsel and your power shall surely attain victory.
Thus addressed with these supreme conciliatory words by the cat, that mouse—
The knower of the supreme truth spoke these gentle words, beneficial for himself:
"O Lomaśa, everything that you have said has been heard by me.
Now listen as I speak what occurs to my mind."
Friends are to be recognized, and enemies are likewise to be understood;
this subtle distinction, esteemed by the wise, is observed in this world. For there are those who appear as friends but are enemies, and those who appear as enemies but are friends.
Their friends are gentle, yet their enemies are wrathful; though they are pacified, they do not understand, having fallen under the sway of passion and greed.
Though they are pacified, they do not understand, having fallen under the sway of passion and greed.
There is no such thing as an enemy by birth, nor does a friend exist by nature;
friends and enemies arise through the application of circumstances.
As long as one perceives their own self-interest in another while that person lives, so long will that person live for them.
He may be a friend to another only so long as no reversal occurs;
there is no such thing as stable friendship, nor is enmity constant. For friends and likewise enemies arise through the exigencies of self-interest.

A friend becomes an enemy after the passage of some time, and an enemy becomes a friend; for self-interest is indeed more powerful. He who trusts his friends and does not place undue trust in his enemies [is wise].
Without understanding the application of purpose, his life has become unstable.
He who, without understanding the application of purpose, sets his mind upon what is auspicious—
whether toward a friend or even an enemy— his own mind is likewise unstable.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place full trust even in the trustworthy. Danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots.
Indeed, through the pursuit of worldly interests, even father, mother, and sons are seen [to be treated as mere means].
Maternal uncles, nephews, as well as kinsmen and relatives—even parents will abandon a beloved son who has fallen from his status;
yet the world protects itself. Behold the essential strength of self-interest!

I consider him to be one whose intellect is rooted in deceit, who seeks without doubt to perform some action that will provide a means for his own comfort immediately following your liberation. You have been brought down from the banyan tree right here in this very dwelling.
Previously, due to my fickleness, I did not perceive the trap that had been set; being fickle myself, I do not exist [as a stable self], so how could it belong to others?
Therefore, a fickle person undoubtedly destroys all undertakings.
"He speaks sweetly to someone, saying, 'You are dear to me'; listen to me as I explain in detail how all that is a fabrication. One becomes dear for a reason, and one becomes hateful for a reason."
This world of living beings seeks only its own interests; no one is truly dear to another.
I do not recognize any disinterested affection here in this world, whether it be between two uterine brothers or between a husband and wife.

Even if brothers or a wife are angry due to some other cause, they are pleased by one's natural disposition; no other person is so easily pleased. One becomes dear through giving, and another through pleasant speech.
By means of mantras, fire-offerings, and recitations, another person is gratified for the sake of a specific purpose;
yet when that cause has arisen, there is no longer affection between us for any other reason,
and once the basis for that cause has perished, that affection ceases.
"What indeed do I consider to be that cause by which I am dear to you, other than for the sake of food? And even in that regard, we are wise.
"Time transforms the cause; self-interest follows it."
The wise man understands his own true interest, and the world follows the wise man.
But such a thing should not have been said by you to one who is learned and skilled in his own interest;
this motive of yours for your own benefit is ill-timed and inappropriate for one who is not in a precarious position.
Therefore, I shall not waver from my own interest, remaining firm in both peace and war;
for like the forms of clouds, things change moment by moment—
having been an enemy this very day, one may again become a friend this very day.
And again, see the fickleness of stratagems: my enemy is [here] this very day. Our friendship lasted only so long as there was a prior cause;
it has departed along with that very cause, constrained by time.
"For you are my ultimate enemy who, through expediency, has attained the state of a friend. That task having been accomplished, your true nature has returned to enmity.
Thus, I have understood these treatises in their true essence."
Tell me how I might enter the snare set by you;
for once I am released by your power and you likewise by mine,
when we have thus rendered mutual assistance, there shall be no further meeting between us.
"O gentle one, you have indeed achieved your purpose today, and likewise we have fulfilled our purpose. You have no further duty toward me other than to eat me;
I am the food and you are the eater. I am weak, and you are strong."
"No alliance exists between us when our forces are so unequal.
"I honor your wisdom, since immediately after my release, you surely seek food by means of this effortless stratagem; of this there is no doubt."
"You were bound solely for the purpose of being eaten, yet you were released and have now spread abroad with hunger.
Having deceived one who knows the scriptures, he will surely eat me today.
For I know that you are hungry, and it is now the time for your meal."
Thus, having deceived me, you seek me out again as food;
and as for your own wife and children whom you entrust to me— O friend, it is not right for you to perform service for me.
"Seeing me together with you, why would my beloved wife and those sons—who are affectionate toward you—not joyfully devour me? I shall not reunite with you; the reason for our meeting has passed."

"Remaining here, meditate upon Śiva for my sake, if you remember your past good deeds. What wise man would enter the domain of an enemy who has become his food— afflicted, hungry, and searching for prey?"
"May it be well with you; I shall depart, for I am afraid of you even from afar. I will not associate with you; be at peace, Lomaśa.
If you know what is right, then pursue that friendship."
Whether he is trusting or negligent, this very thing would have been done [by him]. For proximity with the powerful is never praised;
O wise one, one must always fear even a powerful person who appears peaceful.
"If you have need of me for some purpose, tell me what I may do for you;
I shall gladly give you everything, but never my own self. For the sake of one's self, one should abandon offspring, as well as kingdom, jewels, and wealth."

Even by relinquishing all one's possessions, one should protect oneself by means of the self. For we have heard it said that even when sovereignty, wealth, and jewels fall into the hands of an enemy, they may be seen to return to those who remain alive.
But the surrendering of oneself is not desired as one would that of wealth or jewels;
for the self must be protected above all else, even at the cost of wives and riches. For those who protect their own foundation and act only after thorough examination, [success is certain].
Calamities born of one's own faults do not befall men who correctly recognize their enemies— those who are weak yet powerful;
such a person is always suspicious of everyone, even while acting kindly toward them.

The intellect of those who are of noble birth, well-disposed, righteous, and great-souled— firmly resolved for its own true purpose— is never to be shaken. Thus was he clearly rebuked by his gray hair.
Feeling ashamed, the cat spoke these words to the mouse.
Lomaśa said:
"I swear by you that this is the truth; indeed, treachery toward a friend is censurable."
Friendship with the virtuous is formed in seven steps; how is it that you do not trust me?
I esteem your wisdom, you who are devoted to my welfare and have spoken the truth of the matter to me, even though your perspective was clouded by me.
"O virtuous one, you ought not to understand me otherwise in this matter;
my affection for you has arisen from the gift of life you bestowed upon me. I am a knower of dharma, a knower of virtues, and especially a knower of gratitude."
I am affectionate toward my friends, and especially so toward those such as you. Therefore, O virtuous one, since things have come to this pass, you ought not to drive me away.
For if I were driven away by you, I would give up my life along with all my kinsmen.
"The word 'fie' is indeed seen by the wise to be used toward high-minded men like me;
O knower of the truth of dharma, you ought not to suspect me of death. Thus was that mouse praised by the cat.
With a mind profound in its inner feeling, he spoke these words to the cat:
"You are a virtuous man, and I have heard your purpose; yet you are pleased with me but do not trust me. Neither through praises nor through floods of wealth can I ever be won over by you again."
For wise men do not come under the power of an enemy without cause, O friend. In this regard, listen to two verses composed by Uśanas:
"Having formed an alliance with a stronger power regarding a task common to both enemies,"
One who has accomplished his purpose should move about with composure and according to reason, yet he should not be overconfident.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place excessive trust even in the trustworthy. One should always inspire confidence in others, but one must never trust them.

Therefore, in all circumstances, one should protect one's own life; for wealth, progeny, and indeed everything exist only for one who lives. In brief, the supreme principle of the treatises on statecraft is considered to be mistrust.
Therefore, mistrust toward men is the most abundant benefit for oneself; for even the weak, when they do not trust, are not slain by their enemies,
whereas those who do trust are quickly killed, even if they are strong, by the weak.
"O cat, I must always protect myself from those like you;
you too must protect yourself from the Caṇḍāla, that outcaste of sinful birth. As he was speaking thus, [the cat] became seized with terror out of sheer fright.
Then the cat quickly fled with speed toward its own hole.
Thereupon, the wise Palita, who knew the true meaning of the scriptures, having proclaimed his own intellectual power, went to another hole.

Thus, by means of an intellect endowed with wisdom, even one who is weak can overcome those of great strength; by a single gray-haired man, many enemies were outwitted. Even with a capable enemy, a wise man should make peace.
The mouse and the cat were liberated through their mutual reliance;
thus, O protector of the earth, has this path of the duty of a Kṣatriya been shown by me in detail, but hear it again in brief.

Though they harbored mutual enmity, the two nevertheless displayed the highest affection; yet, each of them also had the intention to outwit the other. In that situation, the wise one succeeds in outwitting the other by relying fully on the power of his intellect.
Even through negligence, the wise man may be deceived by the foolish.
Therefore, though afraid, one should act as if fearless; though distrustful, one should act as if trusting. For he who is vigilant does not falter, and he who has faltered perishes.
"An alliance with an enemy at the right time, and war even with a friend at the right time— those who know the truth have declared this must always be done, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having reflected thus, O Great King, and having understood the meaning of the scriptures,"
One who is under attack should act with vigilance even before danger arises, behaving as if already afraid.
Like one who is afraid, he should take precautions and likewise establish a defensive alliance;
for it is from fear that the wisdom born of vigilant application arises.
O King, no fear exists for one who is already afraid when danger has not yet arrived;
however, for one who is fearless, a very great fear arises from overconfidence. Furthermore, under no circumstances should counsel be given to one who is thought to be excessively timid.
For through lack of discernment, one might fall into the power of those who see only their own advantage once something has been known;
therefore, though afraid, one should act as if unafraid, and though distrustful, as if trusting.
Having understood the gravity of one's duties, one should not practice any falsehood whatsoever.
"Thus has this history been proclaimed by me, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Having heard it in the midst of your friends, conduct yourself accordingly. And having acquired the highest intelligence, as well as the distinction between enemy and friend,"
He should determine the proper times for peace and war, as well as the means of liberation in times of distress.

Having made a treaty with a more powerful foe regarding a task common to both enemies, he should conduct his association with them through strategic means; yet, once his purpose is achieved, he should not place his trust in them.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this policy, which is not in conflict with the three aims of life— arise from this sacred learning and further delight your subjects. O Pāṇḍava, let your journey also be undertaken together with the Brāhmaṇas."
"O Bhārata, for the Brāhmaṇas are the supreme good both in heaven and here on earth. O Lord, they are knowers of dharma, ever grateful,
performers of auspicious deeds, and worthy of worship because of their ancient victories, O ruler of men."
"O King, sovereignty is the highest good; you shall obtain glory and fame, as well as the continuity of your lineage, in accordance with justice and due order.
O Bhārata, this [treatise on] peace and war belongs to both [of us]."
O King, having always reflected thus upon well-spoken words that produce excellence of intellect,
they should be practiced by a ruler within the circle of his enemies.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed one, you have stated that there is no trust to be placed in enemies. But how indeed should a king conduct himself if he were not to trust anyone at all?"
"O King, for a king, the greatest danger arises from misplaced trust. How indeed can a king who does not trust conquer his enemies, O ruler of the earth?
Cut through this doubt of mine; my mind is utterly bewildered."
Having heard this story of distrust, O Grandfather,
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen, O son of Kuntī, to what occurred in the house of Brahmadatta."

The conversation between Pūjanī and King Brahmadatta, O monarch. In Kāmpilya, there lived a bird named Pūjanī who resided within the inner apartments of Brahmadatta and had dwelt with him for a long time.
She understood the cries of all living beings, just like the jīvajīvaka bird;
though born among the animal kingdom, she was omniscient and knew all dharmas. There, she gave birth to a single son of great splendor.

And at that very same moment, a son was born to the king’s queen as well. Out of gratitude for the sake of those two, that celestial woman Pūjanī always went to the shore of the ocean and brought back two fruits.
For the sake of nourishing his own son and the prince as well,
he gave one fruit to his son and another to the prince—
each like the taste of nectar, increasing their strength and splendor.
Taking it again and again, she quickly gave it to them over and over;
there, by eating the fruits, the prince attained great growth.
Then that son of the king was carried on the hip by his nurse.
The boy, having approached out of childishness, saw that young bird;
and while still in the hands of his nurse, he played with that bird. Then, taking that bird which had been born together with him, he went into a secluded place.

12.137.010 Having killed him, O Indra among kings, he then went to the hand of his nurse. 12.137.011 Then, O King, that female bird arrived, carrying fruit; she saw her son slain upon the ground by that boy.
Seeing her son slain,
Pūjanī, her face filled with tears, wretched and tormented by grief, spoke these words while weeping:
"O Kṣatriya, there is no union, no affection, and no friendship."
In this world, people resort to a benefactor when they have a purpose, and once their goal is achieved, they abandon him.
One should place no trust in kṣatriyas, who cause harm to all;
even after doing them injury, they constantly offer empty conciliation.
Today I shall inflict a fitting vengeance upon this ungrateful, cruel, and utterly treacherous man— who grew up with me, shared my upbringing, and likewise shared my meals.
"Killing one who has come for refuge is indeed a threefold sin.
Having said this, Pūjanī pierced the eyes of the prince with her two feet; then, restored to health, she spoke these words.
Sin committed intentionally returns immediately;
for those who have performed a remedial act, neither their merit nor their demerit is destroyed. If some evil deed has been committed, it does not remain within that person [if a remedy is applied].
This [title] is applied to his sons, provided it does not extend to his grandsons or great-grandsons.
Having seen his son whose eyes had been taken away by Pūjanī, Brahmadatta,
considering it a retaliation for what had been done to him, spoke this to Pūjanī:
Brahmadatta said:
"Indeed, what was done by us has been countered by you; both of those acts have now reached an equality. Stay, O Pūjanī; do not go."
Pūjanī said:
"The wise do not praise that [conduct] of one who, having once committed an offense, lingers right there; rather, withdrawal from that situation is better."

O King, when conciliation is employed, one who has committed an act of enmity should not place trust in it; for the fool is quickly bound, as enmity does not truly subside. Among those who have harbored mutual hostility, the feud descends even to their sons and grandsons.
When sons and grandsons have perished, one goes to the next world. For all those who have harbored enmity, mistrust brings happiness;
one must never place absolute trust in a betrayer.

One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place full trust even in the trustworthy; for danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots. One may certainly inspire confidence in others, but one must never trust them.
Through lack of trust one kills others; through trust one is killed by others. The mother and father are the most excellent among kinsmen;
the wife is old age, while the son is merely the seed.
A brother with moistened hands is an enemy, while a friend is one who shares the experience of pleasure and pain alone;
for no reconciliation is possible between those who have harbored mutual enmity.

That purpose for which I dwelt here has now passed away. When a person who was previously an offender is honored with wealth and respect, his mind becomes distrustful; first, it forcibly strikes him with fear.

A man of integrity should abandon that dwelling where there was first honor and subsequently dishonor, having been both honored and then insulted. "I have lived in your house for a long time, unharmed."
"This enmity has arisen; remain at ease, for I am departing.
Brahmadatta said:
"One who indeed retaliates against that which was done [to him] does not thereby commit an offense."
"By this [debt], one becomes free from obligation; therefore, O Pūjanī, dwell here, do not go.
Pūjanī said:
"Friendship between that which has been done and the doer is never joined again."
The heart there knows both the deed and the doer.
Brahmādatta said:
"Friendship between the deed and the doer can indeed be joined once again."
The pacification of enmity has been observed; one does not incur further sin.
Pūjanī said:
One should not trust that enmity has ceased simply because one has been conciliated, thinking, "I have been appeased."

The fool is bound by trust; therefore, non-seeing is indeed better. Those who cannot be subdued by force, even with very sharp weapons, are restrained through conciliation, like elephants by female elephants.
Brahmadatta said:
"From living together, affection arises even toward those who bring one's life to an end,
and mutual trust develops just as it does between a dog-eater and his dog."
"Among those who have harbored mutual enmity, that enmity does not persist once it has become softened through living together; it remains no more than water resting upon a lotus leaf.
Pūjanī said:

Enmity arises from five sources, and the wise understand them: that caused by women, that arising from dwellings, that born of speech, and that produced by rivals or offenses. In such cases, the giver [of offense] must be struck down, especially by a Kṣatriya.
Having understood whether [the circumstances] are public or private, as well as the strength of the location and other factors,
one must not place trust even in a friend who has committed an act of enmity;
for enmity remains hidden, like fire concealed within wood.

O King, the fire of enmity is not extinguished by wealth, nor by harshness, nor by conciliation, nor by sacred learning; it is like the Aurva-fire in the ocean. Indeed, once the fire of enmity has been kindled, or an action born of transgression committed, [it cannot be quenched].

O King, it subsides without having burnt, for it does not cease except through the destruction of one of the two parties. Even toward one who has previously done harm, if he is honored with wealth and respect, there may be neither peace nor trust; action itself compels him by force.
"Neither have I ever done you any harm, nor have you ever done me any; previously I dwelt with you out of trust, but now I do not trust you. Brahmadatta said:
By time alone is a task performed, and likewise various activities;
by time alone they proceed—here, who offends whom?
For both birth and death indeed proceed equally.
And it is by Time alone that one is made to act, for it is because of Time that one lives.
Some are bound all at once, while others are not bound one by one; Time consumes all beings, just as fire consumes fuel upon reaching it.
"Neither I nor you are the authority over one another in this matter, O auspicious lady;
rather, it is Time that eternally ordains pleasure and pain for embodied beings. Therefore, dwell here with affection, unhindered, according to the proper time."
"Whatever was done [by you] has been forgiven by me; you too must forgive me, O Pūjanī.
Pūjanī said:
"If time is the authority for you, then no one should harbor enmity toward anyone else."
12,137.050 Why do kinsmen offer funeral honors when a kinsman has been slain?
12,137.051 Why did the gods and asuras in former times strike one another down?
If departure [from life], pleasure and pain, and existence and non-existence are all determined by time, [why these acts of violence]?
Why do physicians desire to administer medicine to the sick? If [the fruits] ripen in due time, what is the use of medicines?
Why is such great lamentation made by those fainting with grief?
12,137.053c If time is your authority, why does dharma exist among those who act?
12,137.054a Your son killed my child, and he was struck down by me;
12,137.054c immediately thereafter, O lord of the earth, I ought to be bound by you.
"Indeed, out of grief for my son, I have committed a sin against your offspring;
therefore, you must strike me accordingly, and hear the truth from me:
men desire birds either for food or for sport."
There is no third bond capable of enduring except for killing and imprisonment.
Some have resorted to the discipline of liberation out of fear of killing and imprisonment;
those who know the Dharma say that suffering arises from death and calamity.
Life is dear to everyone, and children are dear to everyone;
everyone trembles at suffering, and happiness is desired by all.
O Brahmadatta, old age is suffering, and the loss of wealth is suffering.
Suffering arises from dwelling with the disliked, and suffering is born from separation from the beloved;
there is suffering caused by the bonds of enmity, as well as that born of violence and that caused by women.
Thus, for people, suffering constantly alternates with happiness.
12.137.061a "There is no suffering in the suffering of others"—so indeed some of small intelligence have said.
12.137.061c He who has not experienced suffering himself speaks thus among the great multitude. 12.137.062a But he who grieves, afflicted by suffering, how could he venture to speak [otherwise]?
Though they be split apart or joined together, they cannot be overcome even by extremely sharp weapons;
yet they are subdued by conciliation, like elephants by female elephants. One who understands the nature of suffering treats others exactly as one treats oneself.

"O King, O subduer of enemies, that which has been done by me to you, and that which has been done by you to me— that cannot be wiped away even in hundreds of years. Since we have acted thus toward one another, no reconciliation is possible between us."
"By constantly remembering your son, a new enmity will surely arise.
He who wishes to establish affection while harboring a close-seated enmity finds no reconciliation, just as there is no joining of a broken earthen vessel."
Those learned in the treatises on statecraft have determined that mistrust leads to the arising of happiness.
Furthermore, in ancient times, Uśanas spoke these two verses to Prahrāda:
"Those who are enemies place their trust in truth, or even in what is other than truth."
Those who lack faith are slain like honey by dry grass;
for enmities within families are not appeased until the tenth generation,
provided that there remains a man in the lineage to recount them.

For kings conceal their enmities and offer conciliation, only to crush the opponent later like a full jar against a stone. O King, one should never trust anyone after having committed a wrong against them in this world.
For by betraying others through misplaced trust, one indeed experiences suffering.
Brahmadatta said:
"It is not out of a lack of trust that people do not accumulate wealth, nor do they strive for anything at all."
Constantly fearing one or the other, they become like the dead.
Pūjanī said:
"He whose feet here are wounded, yet who still crawls about on his feet..."
The feet of one who runs while remaining poorly concealed are injured; and for one who gazes against the wind with eyes that are already afflicted by pain,
a severe affliction of the eyes from the wind will certainly occur.

He who, out of delusion, takes to a wicked path and pursues it without knowing his own strength, finds that his life ends there. But the man who plows a field without understanding the season of the rains [perishes].

A crop that is deficient in human effort never reaches fruition again. And he who constantly consumes food that is bitter, astringent, or devoid of pleasant flavor, yet is wholesome, is fit for immortality.

If a man, out of greed, eats another meal after having consumed wholesome food, failing to recognize its transformation, that becomes the end of his life. Destiny and human effort exist in mutual dependence upon one another.
12,137.078c Those who are impotent worship the system of action belonging to the gods, which is characterized by high-pitched [effort].
12,137.079a One should perform action that is beneficial to oneself, whether it be harsh or mild;
12,137.079c But he who is devoid of action and possesses nothing is always swallowed by misfortunes.
Therefore, even when a matter is uncertain, one must certainly exert effort;
men should accomplish what is beneficial for themselves, even at the cost of sacrificing their entire possessions.
Learning, heroism, skill, strength, and patience as the fifth—these are the means.
The wise say that those by which men here maintain themselves are innate friends; they say that a dwelling, base metals, fields, a wife, and kinsmen—
these are acquired by a man everywhere.
The wise man delights everywhere and shines everywhere;
he does not frighten anyone, nor is he frightened himself. For the wealth of an intelligent person, even if it be very small, constantly increases.
One performs action through skill and stands firm through self-restraint. For men of small intelligence who are bound by affection for their homes,
a wicked wife devours their flesh, just as a female jackal devours the meat of a deer.

"Home, fields, friends, and one's own country"— others say this, and thus men sink down through a perversion of their intellect. One should flee from a diseased land that is afflicted by sickness and famine.
"Otherwise, he might go to live elsewhere or dwell there forever, constantly honored.
Therefore, O King, I shall go elsewhere to dwell; I do not venture to remain here. This [situation] has been rendered irreversible by your son."
One should avoid from afar a bad wife, a bad son, a bad king, a bad friend, a bad relative, and a bad country.
There is no trust in a bad friend; how can there be pleasure in a bad wife?
In a bad kingdom there is no peace; in a bad country one cannot subsist;
with a bad friend, whose affection is constantly unstable, there is no true companionship; and in a bad alliance, when wealth is lost, there is only humiliation.
She is a wife who speaks kindly; he is a son in whom there is joy;
that is a friend in whom there is trust; that is a country where one may live.
He is a king with stern commands in whose realm there is no oppression.
For there is no such bond for one who wishes to remain poor as that which exists when the king is virtuous and guided by righteousness—
[a bond consisting of] wife, country, friends, sons, relations, and kinsmen;
all this [is secured] under such a ruler.
When the king does not know the law and fails to exercise restraint, his subjects go to ruin.
The king is the root of the three goals of life; guarding them with vigilance, he should take a sixth part as tribute and employ that tribute for the sake of the people.
He who does not properly protect his subjects is a thief of the earth. That king who, having himself granted freedom from fear, does not act accordingly to uphold it, is likewise a thief.
Having perceived evil from all the world,
he whose mind is set on unrighteousness goes to hell.
But that king who, having granted protection from fear, always makes his word authoritative—
He who protects his subjects with righteousness should be known as the creator of all happiness.
Manu, the Lord of Creatures, declared that these seven qualities belong to a king: he is father, mother, teacher, protector, fire, Vaiśravaṇa, and Yama.
For the king who is compassionate toward his kingdom and his subjects is indeed their father; when he has been led astray by falsehood, a man goes to the animal realm.
He honors the distressed like a mother and provides them with refuge.
Like fire, he burns those who are undesired; by restraining them, he becomes Yama. Like Kubera, the granter of desires, he bestows wealth upon those who are dear to him.
He is a teacher through the instruction of dharma and a protector through his guardianship.
But that king who wins over the citizens and the people of the countryside with his virtues does not lose his kingdom, because he maintains the dharma of virtue. For,
by himself, he understands the affairs of the citizens and the people of the countryside.
That king rejoices happily both in this world and in the next; but he whose subjects are constantly anxious, oppressed by the burden of taxes, and ruined by calamities, goes to his own downfall.

The king whose subjects flourish like great lotuses in a lake shares in the fruit of all sacrifices and is glorified in this world. O King, conflict with one who is powerful is never praised in any way.
"For one who has entered into conflict with a stronger power, whence can there be a kingdom, and whence can there be happiness?
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus to King Brahmadatta, that female bird—

Having taken leave of the king, she then departed for her desired direction. This conversation between Brahmadatta and Pūjanī has been told by me to you, O best of the Bharatas; what else do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, O Grandfather, when dharma has been utterly depleted by the end of the age, and when the world is oppressed by bandits, how should one conduct oneself?"
Bhīṣma said:
"Behold, O Bhārata, I shall declare to you the policy for times of distress,
and how a ruler of the earth should conduct himself even by casting aside compassion when the occasion demands."
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Bharadvāja and King Śatruṃtapa.
There was a king named Śatruṃtapa, a great chariot-warrior among the Sauvīras.
Having approached Kaṇinka, he asked for a definitive determination of these matters:

"How does one desire to obtain what has not been obtained? By what means does what has been obtained increase? By what means should one protect what has increased, and how should one bestow what has been protected?"
To him, who had been asked for a definitive determination of the matter,
that Brahmin, having ascertained the point of the inquiry, spoke these reasoned words in reply:
"One should always have the rod of punishment uplifted and always display one's prowess."
One who is himself without flaw yet perceives flaws in others, pursuing their vulnerabilities,
causes people to tremble greatly when his rod of punishment is constantly raised.
Therefore, one should restrain all beings by means of that very rod alone.
In this very way, the wise who perceive reality offer their praise;
therefore, among those four [means], punishment is said to be the most important.
For when the foundation is cut off at the root, all those who depend upon it are destroyed.
For how indeed could the branches remain when the tree has had its root cut?
A wise man should first cut the very root of the opponent's position;
thereafter, he should cause all the allies and the entire faction to follow suit.
One should act with well-deliberated plans, great valor, skillful combat, and a strategic retreat when the time for such steps during calamities arrives; one should not hesitate.
One should be humble in speech alone, while remaining as sharp as a razor in one's heart.
One should speak with gentleness first and avoid both desire and anger.
Having made an alliance for a task involving rivals, one should not place trust in them;
once the objective has been achieved, the wise man should withdraw from there quickly.
One should conciliate an enemy who appears in the guise of a friend with peaceful words alone;
yet one should always remain wary of him, as if of a snake that has entered one's house. One should conciliate with reference to the past that person whose intellect one seeks to overcome.
One should speak with a future threat to the foolish, and with the present to the wise;
one who desires prosperity should speak with palms joined, with oaths, with conciliation, and by bowing the head,
as well as by shedding tears.
One should carry an enemy upon one's shoulder as long as the reversal of time has not yet come;
then, when that time has arrived, one should smash him like a jar against a stone.
O Indra among kings, it is better to blaze for even a moment like a firebrand of *tinduka* wood.

A man should not smoke for a long time like a flameless fire of chaff; one should not practice kindness toward an ungrateful person who lacks purpose. While it is possible to enjoy wealth when it is available, once one's purpose is achieved, such a person treats the benefactor with contempt.
Therefore, one should have all tasks performed with something remaining unfinished.
One should emulate that which is best among the following: the song of the cuckoo, the grunt of a boar, Mount Meru, an empty house, a venomous serpent, and a variegated painting.

Rising again and again, one should go constantly and with diligence to the houses of the enemy; one should inquire after their welfare, even if it be unwell. The indolent do not attain their goals, nor do the weak-willed, nor those who are overly proud.
Neither fearing public rumor nor constantly waiting for an opportunity,

one should ensure that an enemy does not discover one's own vulnerability, while discovering the vulnerability of the enemy; like a tortoise, one should withdraw one's limbs and guard one's own weak points.
One should contemplate one's goals like a heron, and exert prowess like a lion; one should snatch like a wolf, and dart away like a hare.
Drinking, dice, women, hunting, and song and instrumental music—these are [the vices].
One should pursue these with discernment, for attachment to them is fraught with danger. One should make a bow of grass, sleep like a deer,
be blind at the time for blindness, and even resort to deafness.
Having attained the proper place and time, the discerning man should exert his prowess;
for prowess that transcends the requirements of place and time becomes fruitless. Having carefully considered the right and wrong time, as well as one's own strength and weakness, [one should act].
Having ascertained each other’s strength, a king should likewise employ himself accordingly.
That king who does not restrain an enemy who has been subdued by force embraces his own death, just as a female mule conceives a fetus only to perish.
It may be in full bloom yet bear no fruit; it may bear fruit yet be difficult to climb. It may be unripe yet appear as if ripe, and never wither for anyone.
One should take what is to be taken and not give it away; one should speak pleasant words, even if they are meaningless.
One should make hope subject to time, and one should join that hope with obstacles.
One should explain the obstacle by means of its signs, and the sign by means of its cause. One should make preparations as if afraid, as long as the danger has not yet arrived.
Seeing that danger has arrived, one must strike fearlessly.
Without embarking upon uncertainty, a man does not behold prosperity;
but having embarked upon uncertainty, if he survives, he beholds it.

One should discern the future and cut off whatever danger has arisen; one should observe that which has occurred again through increase or decrease. One must avoid happiness whose time has already arrived.
And hope for future happiness is not the policy of the wise; he who, having made peace with an enemy, sleeps in trust,
is like one asleep on the top of a tree who awakens only after falling.
By whatever means possible here, whether mild or harsh, one should rescue one's own distressed self; once capable, one should practice righteousness.
One should cause all those who are enemies of one's enemies to be protected like sons.
One must also recognize one's own spies as well as those dispatched by enemies.
Spies should be carefully stationed for both oneself and the enemy;
one should cause heretics, ascetics, and others to enter the foreign kingdom.
Having discovered the enemy through spies who are unknown to heretics and others, he should bring him under his control.
[He should do so] in gardens, monasteries, water-stations, and dwellings; in taverns, brothels, sacred fords, and assembly halls.
Those who practice unrighteousness, the wicked, the spies of the world, and its thorns— once they have been identified, the king should restrain them or even put them to death.
One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one place full trust even in the trustworthy.

Fear follows one who has placed trust; therefore, one should not place trust without first investigating. Having gained the confidence of an enemy by means of a truthful motive, one should then strike him at the right time when his footing has shifted even slightly.

One should suspect even that which is not to be suspected, and one should always suspect those who are suspicious; for fear born from the suspicious cuts away everything, even to the very root. [One should not be deceived] by attentiveness, silence, saffron robes, matted hair, or antelope skins.
Having gained the trust of an enemy, one should spring upon him like a wolf;
whether it be a son, a brother, a father, or even a friend,
those who create obstacles to one's purpose must be slain by those seeking to increase their prosperity.
Even for a teacher who is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done,
and has set out upon a wrong path, punishment is the means of correction.
[One should show respect] toward someone by rising from one's seat, by salutation, and by the giving of gifts.
Like a bird with a sharp beak, he should strike with full force;
for without piercing the vital organs of others, without performing a terrible deed,
and without reflecting for a long time, a man does not behold prosperity.
Without killing [his prey], one does not attain supreme prosperity, just like a fisherman. There is no such thing as an enemy by birth, nor is there such a thing as a friend;
friends and enemies arise through the force of circumstances.

One should never release an enemy, even if he speaks piteous words; one should not feel pity in that situation, but should slay the one who has previously done harm. One should always strive to gather and favor others without being envious.
One who desires prosperity must exert effort even in subduing others. When about to strike, one should speak kindly; even after striking, one should speak even more kindly.
Even if one has severed the other's head, one should weep or even grieve for them.

One who desires prosperity should invite others with gentleness, honor, and forbearance; this is how one should act as a means of creating hope. One should not engage in groundless enmity, nor should one attempt to cross a river with one's bare arms.

The eating of a cow's horn is useless and detrimental to one's lifespan; the teeth are merely worn down, and no flavor is obtained. Regarding the three aims of life (*trivarga*), there are likewise three kinds of suffering and three types of consequences.
Having understood the consequences and the destruction [of the enemy], one should indeed avoid causing suffering.
A remnant of debt, a remnant of fire, and likewise a remnant of an enemy—
if not checked, even a small one will increase again and again.

A debt that continues to grow, enemies who have been humiliated, and diseases that are neglected all bring about severe misfortune. One should not perform actions improperly; one should always be vigilant.

For even a thorn, if poorly extracted, causes long-lasting distress. One should destroy a foreign kingdom by the slaughter of its people, by the spoiling of its roads, and by the destruction of its mines.
With the vision of a vulture, the stillness of a crane, the behavior of a dog, and the prowess of a lion; unagitated yet suspicious as a crow, one should conduct oneself like a serpent.
One should win over a hero with a respectful salutation and a coward by means of sowing dissension.

One should win over the greedy by bestowing wealth, and engage in conflict with equals; one should guard ministers against subversion by guild-leaders, through the conciliation of favorites, and even against their division or coalition.
People despise one who is mild and tremble before one who is sharp;
therefore, one should be sharp at the time for sharpness and mild at the time for mildness.
With mildness one destroys the very mild, and with mildness one destroys even the cruel.

There is nothing that cannot be accomplished by mildness; therefore, mildness is sharper than sharpness. He who is mild at the proper time and becomes stern at the proper time accomplishes his tasks and overcomes his enemies.
One who has come into conflict with a wise man should not trust, thinking, "I am far away.
For the arms of the intelligent man are long, with which he strikes back when he has been struck. One should not cross that [water] of which one cannot reach the further shore.
One should not take that which another might take back; one should not dig up that whose root one cannot uproot;
one should not strike him whose head one cannot strike off.
Thus has this been spoken, joined with deceit;
yet a man should not act in such a manner. But how could one listen to that which is instigated by another?
Therefore, seeking your welfare, I spoke those beneficial words exactly as they were;
having heard them, the Brahmin [addressed] the noble prince of Suvīra.
With undaunted resolve, he acted according to those words and,
together with his kinsmen, enjoyed radiant prosperity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When the supreme Dharma has declined, when that which transcends all worlds has been surpassed, when non-Dharma has been brought to the state of Dharma and Dharma has come to the state of non-Dharma,
when the boundaries have been shattered and the certainty of Dharma has been disturbed—
O lord of the people, when the world is oppressed by kings or even by thieves;
when all the stages of life have become confused and their duties are impaired;
and when, O Bhārata, people perceive danger arising from desire, delusion, and greed—
O King, when all people have become distrustful and are perpetually afraid,
when they are being struck down by deceit and are deceiving one another,
when the lands are set ablaze and the status of the Brahmins is oppressed.
When the rain-god does not send rain, when mutual dissension has arisen,
and when all the means of subsistence on earth have fallen into the hands of bandits—
by what means indeed should a Brāhmaṇa live when such a wretched time has arrived?
"O lord of men, wishing to transcend [the world] along with sons and grandsons, out of compassion,
tell me, O Grandfather: how should one conduct oneself in times of calamity,
and how should a king conduct himself when the world has fallen into impurity?"
"How may one not fall away from both material prosperity and righteousness, O scorcher of foes?
Bhīṣma said:
"O great king, security, well-being, and timely rains have their root in the king."
Among the subjects, there are indeed diseases, death, and fears;
the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages, O bull of the Bharatas—all these have their root in the king. Of this I have no doubt.
When that time has arrived which brings harm to living beings, one should then sustain life by relying on the power of discernment (vijñāna). In this regard, they cite this ancient history (itihāsa).
The dialogue between Viśvāmitra and a Caṇḍāla in a hamlet of outcasts;
formerly, at the junction of the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, O King, by the course of divine destiny,
there occurred a terrible twelve-year drought.
When the end of the age had arrived and the prosperity of living beings was waning— at the time of the departure of the Tretā-yuga and the onset of the Dvāpara-yuga—
the thousand-eyed Indra did not send rain, and Bṛhaspati became adverse.
Soma, his characteristic signs having vanished, took the southern path. At the end of the night, there was not even a dew-drop, much less rows of clouds;
the rivers, their floods of water diminished, had in some places become submerged within themselves.
The lakes, rivers, wells,
and springs appeared robbed of their luster due to the natural course of destiny; the reservoirs were dried up, and the assembly halls and water-stations had ceased their operations.

Sacrifices and Vedic recitations have ceased; the auspicious sounds of the *vaṣaṭ* call have vanished. Agriculture and cattle-rearing have been abandoned; buying and selling in the markets have stopped.
Social gatherings and customary observances have ceased; all great festivals have utterly perished.
Strewn with skeletons of bones, crowded with people crying out "Alas! Alas!", the cities were mostly deserted and the village dwellings burnt down;
in some places by thieves, in some by weapons, and in others by distressed kings.
Out of mutual fear, the land became mostly empty and deserted; its religious observances ceased, it was deprived of the elderly and children,
and it was bereft of cattle, goats, sheep, and buffalo— everyone fleeing one another.
With the Brahmins slain and the protectors killed, the stores of medicinal herbs destroyed,
and the earth then filled mostly with dark-complexioned beings,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the world became thus at that terrifying time when Dharma had declined.
Hunger-stricken mortals wandered about, devouring one another;
the seers, having abandoned their observances and forsaken their sacred fires and deities, completely deserted their hermitages and fled hither and thither.
Then the venerable great seer Viśvāmitra, being wise and without a fixed dwelling, was overcome by hunger and wandered in every direction,
having left behind his wife and sons in some assembly of people.
Regarding what may be eaten and what may not be eaten as equal, without a sacred fire and without a fixed dwelling, he once, while wandering about, came upon the abode of *śvapacas*—
cruel killers of living beings— in a certain part of the forest.
It was strewn with shattered jars, covered with dog skins,
and crowded with the broken bones of boars and donkeys, along with skulls and pots;
it was spread over with the clothes of the dead and adorned with discarded floral offerings.
The hermitage and its huts were marked with garlands of sloughed snake skins; it was filled with the frequent crowing of cocks and resounded with the braying of donkeys,
while women there quarreled with one another using harsh words.
Surrounded by temples bearing banners of owl feathers,
adorned with iron bells, and encircled by packs of dogs—
having entered that place, the great ṛṣi, the son of Gādhi, was overcome by hunger.
Devoted to the search for food, he applied himself with the utmost effort;
yet, though he begged everywhere, Kauśika did not find anywhere any meat, grain, roots, fruits, or anything else at all.
Realizing, "Alas, I have fallen into great distress," Kauśika fell to the ground from weakness in that settlement of Caṇḍālas;
and that sage reflected, "What indeed would be a meritorious deed for me?"
"O best of kings, thinking, 'How might death not be in vain?',
that sage saw a butchered piece of dog-meat spread out in the house of a *caṇḍāla*, O King, from one recently slain by a weapon."
He then reflected: "I must commit a theft from here;
for at present, no other means exists for the preservation of my life. In times of distress, theft is ordained even from those who are superior, equal, or inferior."
It is the settled rule that one should first take from the highest of the high; this is known as non-stealing. One should first take from an inferior person, and after that, from an equal.
Only in the absence of such [inferior or equal persons] may one take even from a superior and righteous person.
"Therefore, as I take this from those who dwell at the very edge of society, I see no fault in the act of theft; I shall seize this meat. Having established this resolve, the great sage Viśvāmitra—
In that place where he had fallen, O Bhārata, he fell asleep;
then, seeing that the night was deep and the settlement of Caṇḍālas was asleep,
the Blessed One rose quietly and entered the hut-monastery.
While still asleep, that Caṇḍāla— his eyes covered with phlegm,
his voice broken and harsh, and his appearance unpleasant— spoke:
"Who is rattling the loom while the Caṇḍāla settlement is asleep?"
"I am awake; I have not fallen asleep! You are slain!"—thus he spoke harshly.
"I am Viśvāmitra! he suddenly said to him, his fear having been instantly aroused and his heart trembling because of that deed.
"O long-lived one, I am Viśvāmitra; I have come here hungry.
Do not kill me, who possess a virtuous mind, if you perceive things correctly.
Having heard those words of the great seer of purified soul, the Caṇḍāla—
Startled from his bed, he then desired to rise up.
Shedding tears from both eyes and joining his palms in great reverence, he said to Kauśika at night: "O Brahmin, what is it that you intend to do?"
Viśvāmitra, however, spoke to Mātaṅga, consoling him:
"I am hungry and my life-breaths are departing; I shall take this dog's haunch.
My vital energies are failing and my memory is being lost through hunger."
"I am exceedingly thirsty,
weak, and deprived of consciousness; having lost all distinction between what is fit and unfit to be eaten, though I recognize my own duty, I shall eat the haunch of a dog."
"When I wandered for alms and could find nothing in your dwelling, I then set my mind on sin, thinking, 'I shall carry off the haunch of a dog.
When one is thirsty, he will drink even foul water; there is no shame for one who seeks food."
"12,139.050c Hunger corrupts righteousness here; I shall take this dog's haunch.
12,139.051a Agni is the mouth and the priest of the gods, the pervasive one with pure feet. 12,139.051c Just as he is the consumer of all things, O Brahmin, know me to be so according to dharma."
That Caṇḍāla said to him: "O great seer, listen to my words.
Having heard them, act accordingly so that you do not fall away from dharma.
O brahmin-seer, listen also to the dharma which I shall speak to you."
The wise declare the dog to be the lowest among animals;
even of that [dog], the lowest part of its body is the haunch of the thigh.
O Great Seer, this transformative act you have resolved upon is not right.

"Taking the property of a Caṇḍāla, especially that which is unfit to be eaten— O great sage, look instead for another virtuous means to sustain your life; do not let your asceticism be destroyed by greed for meat."
"For one who knows, a path not ordained must not be followed, nor should there be a confusion of dharma. Do not abandon dharma, for you are the supreme knower of dharma.
O King, bull of the Bharata race, having been addressed thus by Viśvāmitra, [the king] then...
Afflicted by hunger, the great sage replied once more:
"A very long time has passed for me while I have been running about without food,
and there is no means whatsoever for me to sustain my life."
By whatever specific means or by whatever action whatsoever, one who is sinking should sustain himself; once he is capable, he should practice dharma.
The dharma of Indra belongs to the Kṣatriyas, while that of Agni belongs to the Brāhmaṇas.

The fire of Brahman is my strength; out of hunger, I shall consume [the world] according to the law. Indeed, one should act in such a way that another may live without being oppressed; for life is better than death, and by living, one may attain dharma.

"Desiring life, I have resolved with full deliberation to consume even that which is unfit for food; may you grant me your permission for this. Living, I shall practice dharma and cast off all inauspicious things."
Just as the luminaries dispel great darkness through their ascetic powers and knowledge, [so too does he dispel sin].
The dog-cooker said:
"By eating this, you will not obtain any other life-force."
Neither long life nor the satisfaction of one who has attained immortality [is gained by this]; do not seek alms from others, let not your mind be set on this.
For a dog that eats dogs is indeed unfit to be eaten by the twice-born.
Viśvāmitra said:
"O Chāṇḍāla, in this famine no other meat is easily obtainable, nor is there any food, nor do I possess any wealth."
"Afflicted by hunger, without recourse, and hopeless, I consider these six flavors in this dog's flesh to be excellent. The dog-cooker said:
"O twice-born one, five five-nailed animals may indeed be eaten by those of the Brahmin and Kṣatriya castes:
the porcupine, the hedgehog, the monitor lizard, the hare, and the tortoise as the fifth.
If the scripture is authoritative for you, do not set your mind on what is forbidden to eat."
Viśvāmitra said:
"The asura Vātāpi was indeed devoured by the hungry Agastya;
I, having fallen into calamity and being distressed, shall eat this dog's haunch."
The dog-cooker said:
"Bring me some other alms; you ought not to do this. Surely this must not be done; take as much as you wish of the dog's haunch."
Viśvāmitra said:
"The learned are indeed the authority in matters of dharma; I follow their conduct. I consider this dog's haunch to be more pure and fit for consumption than even the eating of sacrificial meat."
The dog-cooker said:
"That which is practiced by the wicked is not the eternal dharma. One must certainly not imitate what is improper; do not commit a falsehood through deceit."
Viśvāmitra said:
"Being a seer, you ought not to commit a sin or an act of contempt.
I consider a dog and a deer to be equal; therefore, the haunch of a dog is fit to be eaten."
The dog-cooker said:
"That which was done for the sake of the brahmin by that seer who was entreated— by that [act], he has gained the right to eat [me]."
"That indeed is dharma wherein there is no evil;
for it must be protected by all possible means.
Viśvāmitra said:
This Brahmin is my friend and he is my very self;
he is dear to me and most worthy of worship in the world. Desiring to support him, I shall take this [wealth].
"I am not afraid of such cruel people," said the dog-cooker (śvapaca). "Men may indeed abandon their lives at will."
And there they do not provide remedies with things that are unfit for consumption;
O learned one, they obtain all their desires here. Therefore, remain at ease as you wish, even though accompanied by hunger.
Viśvāmitra said:
"In that case, there is indeed doubt regarding the state after death;
or rather, it is certain that actions perish."
But I, my mind set on the hope that "I shall live," protecting the root, will consume what is not to be consumed—
[thereby] [attaining] the merit of [eating only] roots, fruits, and leaves.
In that which is of the nature of delusion (*moha*), where it is like one's own food,
he is satisfied thinking that the intellect (*buddhi*) exists as something distinct;
yet through delusion, he perceives oneness, just as [one mistakes] a hide for an eye.
Just as the eye does not perceive the true nature of sound but sees form, so too is the eye;
even if I act out of doubt, it is just like that.
"I shall not become like you.
The dog-cooker said:
"It is my conviction that this suffering is a cause for falling [from one's status]."
"O wicked one, I am reproaching you because you are a Brahmin.
Viśvāmitra said:
"Cows continue to drink water even while the frogs are croaking."
"You have no authority regarding dharma; do not be one who praises yourself.
The dog-cooker said:
"O twice-born one, having become your friend, I instruct you, for I have compassion for you."
"Therefore, choose that which is better; do not, out of greed, devour a dog.
Viśvāmitra said:
"If you are my friend and desire my welfare, rescue me from this calamity."
"I know myself by my own nature; release me, for I am a dog.
The dog-cooker said:
"I do not dare to give her to you."
"I cannot ignore my own food being carried away. O Brahmin, both the giver and you, the receiver, would be smeared with our own impurity."
Viśvāmitra said:
"Having performed this sinful deed today, I shall live on while practicing great purification."
"Having purified my soul, I shall pursue dharma alone;
tell me truly which of these two is the weightier.
The dog-cooker said:
The self alone is indeed the witness in worldly affairs;
you yourself know what is wicked in this matter—
for who would respect dog-meat as fit for food?
"I believe there is nothing for him to avoid," Viśvāmitra said. "There is no fault in his taking or eating."
In this matter, one must always apply the principles of justice as exceptions [to the general rules]:
where there is no violence, nor even a trace of falsehood in speech, and no consumption of forbidden food, that act is not considered grave.
The dog-cooker said:
"If this is the reason for your eating,
then neither the Veda nor any other dharma is the cause for you."
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, I see no fault in eating what is not to be eaten, nor in [the eating of] that which you have described. Viśvāmitra said:
The consumption of this [meat] is not seen to be a sin;
the scriptural statement here that "one falls by drinking liquor" refers to those respective actions in their respective cases.
"One does not destroy one's duty by even a mere fraction.
The dog-cooker said:
"Whether from an improper place, from an inferior person, or from one who is contemptible;"
Even that wise man of virtuous conduct who regains his position after falling from it must indeed endure punishment.
12,139.088 Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, Mātaṅga then turned back toward Kauśika;
Viśvāmitra, having made up his mind, indeed took away the dog's haunch.
Then the great sage, seeking to save his life, accepted the five-limbed portion;
having offered it along with his wife, the great sage departed for the forest.
Thus his thought arose: "By this rite, I [shall offer] the haunch of dog-flesh."
Having first gratified the deities, I shall eat as I desire;
then, having established the fire according to the Brāhma ritual,
the sage himself cooked the sacrificial porridge (caru) according to the Aindrāgneya rite.

Then, O Bhārata, he commenced the rites for the gods and the ancestors, having invited Indra and the other deities to receive their respective portions according to the prescribed order. At that very time, Vāsava sent down rain.
Reviving all living beings, he caused the medicinal herbs to spring forth.
The venerable Viśvāmitra as well, his sins consumed by asceticism,
attained most wonderful perfection after a long period of time.
Having withdrawn that ritual action and without tasting that sacrificial oblation,
that best of the twice-born gratified both the gods and the ancestors.
Thus, a wise man of undepressed soul who desires to live, even when situated in calamity, [should act].
One who knows the means should rescue his distressed self by all possible means. Having established this understanding, one should always remain alive;
for while living, a man attains merit and beholds auspicious things.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, a wise man, having established his intellect in the determination of dharma and adharma, should conduct himself in this world with self-restraint.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"This which has been declared is terrible, as if unbelievable and untrue.
Does such a boundary of the Dasyus exist, which I must avoid? I am utterly bewildered and despondent; my dharma has been loosened."
"Though I reflect upon it from every side, I do not find any means of exertion.
Bhīṣma said:
"This instruction on dharma for you does not derive from mere scriptural tradition alone."

This is the entry into wisdom; it is the honey gathered by the poets. A king must acquire various forms of wisdom from here and there; for this worldly course does not proceed by means of a dharma consisting of only a single branch.
For kings who always practice righteousness, there arises an intelligence that generates success; know this to be my word, O Kauravya,
for it is through superior intelligence that kings seeking victory achieve triumph.
A king must apply the Dharma through his intelligence here and there;
the duty of kings is not ordained by a Dharma consisting of only a single branch.
How can there be wisdom for one who is weak? This has been declared previously.
One who knows not duality does not deserve to fall into doubt when faced with a twofold path.
O Bhārata, one should recognize the duality of the intellect even beforehand;
wisdom acts from the side, while the stream of passion flows away in all directions like a river.
When the Dharma is uttered, people understand it in various different ways:
some possess correct understanding, while others possess false understanding;
having realized that very truth as it truly is, they take up the knowledge of the virtuous.

Those who obstruct the dharma plunder the scriptures; out of a desire for profit, they proclaim the discordance of the sciences of wealth by asserting their uselessness. Desiring to live off their learning, they seek fame from all sides.
All those most wicked men, who are obstacles to Dharma—
being dull-witted and of immature intellect— do not know things as they truly are;
for they are always unskilled in the scriptures and remain unsettled in every respect.

Those who look for faults in the scriptures plunder the scriptures; thus their understanding of the sciences does not proceed correctly. Those who proclaim their own knowledge by means of disparaging the knowledge of others—

"O Bhārata, know those who possess speech as their weapon and the blade of their tongue, and who yield the fruit of knowledge like milk— know them to be like Rākṣasas, merchants of learning. Through such deceit, your entire understanding of dharma will be lost."
"We have heard that neither by speech nor by intellect is the word of Dharma [attained]," thus did Maghavan himself proclaim the knowledge of Bṛhaspati;
yet in this world, no word whatsoever is uttered without a cause.
Others determine their conduct according to the scriptures that have been well-disciplined;
yet some wise men here say that the course of worldly life is itself dharma. A learned man should not personally speculate upon the dharma prescribed by the virtuous.
O Bhārata, due to impatience, confusion regarding the scriptures, and lack of understanding,
the teaching of even a wise man goes unnoticed when spoken in a crowd. One is praised for one's speech only when it is delivered with an intellect that has mastered the traditional scriptures.
Because it arises from ignorance yet serves as the cause for knowledge, this speech is considered excellent;
it is indeed not refuted, nor is this treatise meaningless.
In ancient times, Uśanas spoke to the Daityas for the purpose of cutting through their doubts.
For knowledge that is inexpressible is indeed non-existent;
therefore, with its root cut away, whom do you intend to satisfy? Or rather, who would not accept this statement, which was formulated untruthfully?
For you were indeed created for fierce action, yet you do not consider it; O King,
look instead toward this royal policy by which another is liberated and for the sake of which one rejoices.
The goat, the horse, and the ruling power—these were made similar by Brahmā. Therefore, no undertaking succeeds for those who are not fierce.
But that fault which is incurred in killing one who should not be killed is remembered as being equal to the fault of not killing one who should be killed.
This indeed is the boundary which he must avoid:
therefore, a king should be stern and establish his subjects in their own duty;
for otherwise, they would roam about devouring one another like wolves.
He in whose kingdom hosts of robbers carry off the property of others, like crows snatching fish from the water, is indeed a disgrace to the Kṣatriya order.
Having appointed ministers of noble birth who are endowed with Vedic knowledge, [he should protect them].
"O King, rule the earth while protecting your subjects with righteousness.
This man, who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), who is devoted to silent recitation and burnt offerings,
and who is ever intent on bestowing blessings— this is the royal priest."
The king who accepts one of low birth and lacking in action,
being ignorant of the distinction between the two, is indeed a neuter among the kṣatriyas.
Neither severity nor leniency is praised here according to dharma.

One should not transgress either [of these two]: being fierce, become mild. This duty of a Kṣatriya is difficult, yet there is friendship established in you. You were created for fierce deeds; therefore, indeed, rule the kingdom.
"O King, do not be angry with anyone; conduct yourself in this very manner.
The constant restraint of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous—thus did the wise Śakra speak regarding times of distress, O bull of the Bharatas."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Is there perhaps a boundary for bandits which another might not transgress?
I ask you this, O best of the virtuous; tell me that, O Grandfather."
Bhīṣma said:
One should serve only those Brāhmaṇas who are advanced in learning, devoted to austerity, and rich in sacred knowledge, conduct, and virtuous behavior; for this is the supreme means of purification.
"May that same conduct which you maintain toward the deities be yours always toward the Brahmins.
For by angry Brahmins, O King, many deeds have been wrought;
through their favor one gains preeminent glory, but through their displeasure, the opposite."
For when pleased, O Brahmins, they are like nectar, but when enraged, they are like poison.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you who are possessed of great wisdom and are learned in all the scriptures..."
"Tell me that dharma which belongs to one who protects those who have come for refuge.
Bhīṣma said:
"O great king, there is a great dharma in the protection of those who have sought refuge."
"O best of the Bharatas, you are indeed worthy to ask this question.
O King, kings beginning with Nṛga, by protecting those who had come for refuge, O great monarch, attained supreme perfection."
"For it is heard that a pigeon, when an enemy came seeking refuge,
honored him according to the rule and invited him with his own flesh.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How was it, O Bhārata, that in former times a pigeon, having come for refuge to his enemy, fed him with his own flesh, and what destination did he attain? Bhīṣma said:"
"Listen, O King, to this divine narrative that destroys all sins—
the story of King Mucukunda as it was told by Bhārgava.
Long ago, O Pārtha, regarding this very matter, King Mucukunda..."
O bull of the Bharata race, bowing down, he questioned Bhārgava;
and to him, who was desirous of hearing, Bhārgava related this story:
how, O lord of men, perfection was attained by means of the pigeon.
"O mighty-armed King, listen attentively as I speak these words, which are joined with the certainty of Dharma and accompanied by considerations of pleasure and profit.
There was once a certain man of base conduct on earth, who was regarded as Death itself."
The wicked and terrible fowler wandered the earth,
his body black like a *kākolī* bird, coarse, and intent on evil; he was thin-waisted like a grain of barley, with a slender neck, short feet, and large jaws.
He has no friend at all, no relative, and no kinsman;
for he has been utterly abandoned by them because of that terrible deed. A man of sinful conduct must be shunned from afar by the wise.
How can one who harms himself be beneficial to another? Those cruel and evil-minded men who take the lives of living beings become like predatory beasts, causing terror to all creatures.
O lord of men, taking up a net and constantly killing birds in the forest, he would indeed sell those winged creatures. Thus did that evil-minded man continue his livelihood.
A very long time passed, yet he did not perceive any unrighteousness,
as he took constant delight with his wife as his companion; deluded by the power of destiny, no other way of life appealed to him.
Then, at one time while he was staying in the forest,
there arose a great and violent wind that seemed to strike down those trees;
the sky became crowded with clouds and adorned with circles of lightning.
In a mere moment, like the ocean covered by a vessel,
the earth was completely shrouded; and Śatakratu, filled with joy, inundated the world with masses of torrents of water in an instant.
Then, in that world tumultuous with torrents of rain, he wandered about, his senses lost; afflicted by the cold and with a deeply agitated inner self,
that bird-catcher could find neither low ground nor high ground anywhere in that entire forest.
Indeed, the path of that forest was filled with a flood of water; then,
birds struck by the force of the wind became hidden,
while deer, lions, and boars took refuge on the dry ground and remained there.
Terrified by that great wind and rain, those forest-dwellers,
afflicted by fear and hunger, wandered together through the forest.
But he, with his limbs struck by the cold, kept moving and did not stop.
He saw a female pigeon fallen on the ground, overwhelmed by the cold;
though he was himself distressed and evil-minded, upon seeing her, he cast her back into the cage. Even while overcome by his own suffering, he only caused further suffering for another.

Because he was evil-natured and a doer of evil, he committed only evil deeds. In the forest groves, he saw a lord of the woods as dark as a cloud, being served by flocks of birds seeking shade, shelter, and fruit.
He was created by the Creator like a virtuous man for the sake of helping others.
Then, in an instant, the sky became filled with clear stars,
like a great lake whose waters are strewn with blossoming white water-lilies.
Seeing the sky, rich with stars and resembling a white water-lily, and the cloudless firmament, the hunter, overwhelmed by the cold,
looked toward the quarters and the time of day, that evil-minded man.
"O Lord, since the village settlement is far from that region,
he resolved then to dwell for that night in that forest;
with palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words to the lord of the forest."
"I seek refuge in whatever deities reside here on this earth, O Bhārata. Having placed his head upon a stone and spread leaves upon the ground,
the bird-killer, overcome by great sorrow, then fell asleep.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O King, a bird with variegated plumage, dwelling there for a long time upon the branch of a tree together with its friends,"
His wife had gone out early in the morning to forage and did not return;
seeing that night had fallen, the bird was filled with distress.
A great wind and rain arose, yet my beloved did not come back.
What indeed could be the cause that she has not yet returned?
Might all be well with my beloved in the forest? For bereft of her, this home of mine is empty today.

Even if crowded on all sides by sons, grandsons, daughters-in-law, and servants, the home of a householder devoid of his wife is truly empty. They do not say that a house is a "home"; it is the wife who is called the home.
A house devoid of its mistress is considered to be like a wilderness.
If my beloved— with her eyes red at the corners, her limbs variegated, and her voice sweet—
does not come to me today, I have no need for life.
