She who does not eat while I have not eaten, and she who does not bathe while I have not bathed—she of virtuous vows; she who does not sit when I am standing, and she who lies down only when I have lain down;
she who becomes joyful when I am joyful, and she who is sorrowful when I am sorrowful.
When he was away she was dejected of face; when he was angry, she spoke sweet words. Devoted to the duty toward her husband, that virtuous woman was dearer to her than her own life.
For that ascetic woman knew me to be exhausted and afflicted by hunger.
He whose wife is devoted, beneficial, affectionate, and faithful to her husband— that man alone is truly blessed on earth;
for even at the foot of a tree, wherever his beloved stays, that is his home.
Even a palace, when deprived of her, is certainly like a wilderness. At times for dharma, artha, and kāma, a wife is a man’s companion;
and when he travels to foreign lands, she alone is his source of trust.
He whose wife is always devoted and likewise follows his will, and who possesses contentment even in the midst of wealth—for him, heaven is indeed right here on earth.
She is a true wife who is skillful in the home; she is a true wife who is faithful to her husband.
She is a wife who speaks kindly; she is a wife who is pleasing to the mind. She whose wife recognizes her virtues and follows her husband—she is indeed prosperity personified, and not merely wealth.
For it is taught that in this world, a wife is the supreme protector of a man;
she is his companion in the journey through life when he is without help in this world,
and likewise for one overcome by disease or constantly beset by hardship.
There is no medicine equal to a wife for a man who is afflicted;
there is no kinsman equal to a wife, and no refuge equal to a wife. There is no companion in this world equal to a wife for the accomplishment of dharma.
He who has no virtuous wife in his home who speaks kindly must go to the forest; for him, the house is just like the forest. Alas! Without fire, my mass of limbs is being consumed.
"That virtuous woman, devoted to her husband, was dearer to him than his own life. While that distressed brahmin was thus lamenting there,
his wife, who had been seized by the bird-killer, heard these words.
The female dove said:
"Oh, how exceedingly fortunate I am, whose beloved husband speaks thus of my virtues, whether they be real or not!"
One should not address as a "woman" her whose husband is not pleased;
when the husband is pleased, all the deities are pleased with women.
Even though this has fire as its witness, the husband is indeed the refuge of women.
"Like a creeper with its clusters of blossoms consumed by a forest fire,
may that woman be reduced to ashes whose husband is not pleased. Having thought thus, afflicted by grief, she then [addressed] her sorrowful husband.
Then the female pigeon, being cautious, spoke these words to the hunter:
"Ah, I shall tell you what is for your own welfare; having heard it, act accordingly. O beloved, especially protect those who have come to you for refuge."
"This fowler lies here, having taken refuge in your dwelling;
afflicted by cold and tormented by hunger, offer him hospitality. For whoever should kill a twice-born man or a cow, the mother of the world—"
The sin of one who would kill a refugee is equal to those [other sins]. Our livelihood, which is prescribed by the law of our birth as the practice of gathering pigeon-droppings,
is always rightly pursued by a self-possessed man such as yourself.
"But the householder who follows dharma according to his ability,
we have heard, attains imperishable worlds after death. You, O twice-born one, are now possessed of progeny and have sons as well."
Therefore, casting aside compassion for your own body and truly embracing dharma and worldly purpose,
offer him worship so that his mind may be pleased. O bird, do not feel any grief on my account.
"For the sake of maintaining your bodily existence, you shall take another wife"—
having spoken these words while standing in the salt-water pit, that ascetic female bird,
overcome with extreme grief, gazed upon her husband.
Having heard his wife’s words, which were consistent with righteousness and logic,
he was filled with great joy, though his eyes were clouded with tears;
and seeing that fowler, he [honored him] according to the rites prescribed by rule.
The bird honored the fowler with great care and said to him, "Welcome to you; tell me, what may I do for you?
You should not feel any distress, for you are staying in your own home."
"May your honor speak quickly: what shall I do? What do you desire?
I speak to you with affection, for you have come to us for refuge. Even toward an enemy who has come to one's house, hospitality is a duty."
Even when one comes to cut it down, a tree does not withdraw its shade; likewise,
one who has come for refuge must be received with hospitality with effort,
especially by a householder engaged in the five sacrifices.

But that householder who, out of delusion, does not perform the five sacrifices— for him, by the nature of dharma, neither this world nor the next exists. Therefore, speak with full confidence whatever you intend to say.
"I shall do all that; do not set your mind on grief. Having heard those words of the bird, the hunter said: "The cold indeed afflicts me; let protection against the frost be provided."
Thus addressed, the bird then carefully spread dry leaves upon the ground and quickly departed to fetch fire for the purpose of kindling it.
Having gone to a place where charcoal was being worked, he took some fire and returned.
Then, having kindled a fire upon dry leaves and made it blaze up brightly,
he said to him who had come for refuge:
"Heat your limbs with perfect confidence, free from fear on any side."
Thus addressed, the hunter said, "So be it," and warmed his limbs. When his life had returned through the fire,
he then spoke to the bird, overcome with great joy and with eyes agitated [with emotion].
"Having seen this bird, I desire food given by you according to the prescribed rite, for hunger indeed oppresses me. Having heard those words, that bird spoke these words in reply:
"I have no wealth with which I might satisfy your hunger;
for we forest-dwellers always live on what has been produced [by chance].
We possess no store of provisions, like sages in the forest."
Having spoken thus, his face then turned pale;
O best of the Bharatas, he became constantly absorbed in thought as to what indeed should be done, censuring his own conduct.
Having regained consciousness after a moment, that bird said to the bird-killer:
"I shall satisfy you; wait for a moment. Having spoken thus, he kindled a fire with dry leaves.
Filled with great joy, the pigeon spoke again:
"I have previously heard of the great dharma regarding the honoring of guests from the gods, the sages, and the high-souled ancestors."
"Show me your favor today; I tell you this truly.
My mind is indeed resolved upon honoring my guest.
Then that bird, true to his promise, as if laughing, spoke.
Having circumambulated that fire three times, O lord of the earth, he entered it.
Seeing that bird having entered the midst of the fire,
the hunter then reflected in his mind, "What is this that I have done?"
"Alas! For me, cruel and censurable as I am for my own deeds, a most great and terrible unrighteousness will surely come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
Thus did that hunter lament profusely in many ways.
12,142.044c Reproaching his own actions upon seeing the twice-born man who had thus come,
12,143.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,143.001a Then, beholding him, the hunter was overwhelmed with compassion.
Seeing the dove fallen into the fire, he spoke these words again:
"What a cruel deed has been done by me, a man of such little intelligence!
Indeed, as long as I live, this sin will remain forever in my heart."
Then, reproaching himself again and again, he said:
"Fie on me, the evil-minded one, always resolved upon deceit,
who, having abandoned virtuous action, am a fowler of birds!"
"Without a doubt, this is today the reprimand for my cruelty,
given by the high-souled pigeon as he gave his own flesh. Therefore,
having abandoned my wife and children, I shall give up my dear life."
"For the Dharma was indeed taught to me by the exceedingly virtuous pigeon.
From this day forward, I shall wither my own body, deprived of all enjoyments,
just as a small amount of water dries up in the summer heat."
Enduring hunger, thirst, and heat, emaciated and with my veins showing,
I shall practice various kinds of fasting for the sake of the world beyond. Oh, by the gift of this body, the honoring of guests has been demonstrated!
"Therefore, I shall practice Dharma, for Dharma is the supreme goal. Indeed, such is the Dharma as it has been seen by those most devoted to Dharma, O best of birds.
Having spoken thus and made his resolve, that hunter of fierce deeds—
Resorting to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*), he of firm vows set forth. Then, having bound those pigeons together with a staff, skewers, a net, and a cage, he released them.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, after the fowler had departed, the female pigeon spoke in her distress;
remembering her husband, she wept, overwhelmed by grief.

"O beloved, I do not recall ever having done anything displeasing to you. O sky-walker, every woman who is deprived of her husband becomes an object of pity for her kinsmen, even if she has many sons, however high-minded she may be."
I have always been cherished by you and consoled with great respect,
repeatedly with words that were sweet, affectionate, and most enchanting;
[and I have wandered] among the caves of mountains and at the waterfalls of rivers.

O beloved, I have been delighted by you among the lovely treetops; and while traveling through the sky, I have enjoyed happiness with you. O dear one, I have sported with you, yet now not a single thing of that remains for me.
For a father gives in limited measure, a mother gives in limited measure, and a son gives in limited measure;
who would not honor a husband, the giver of what is limitless?
There is no protector equal to a husband, nor is there any happiness equal to that of a husband.
Having surrendered all her wealth, she said: "A husband is indeed the refuge of a woman.
O Lord, I have no need for life here without you. What virtuous woman, even when deprived of her husband, would venture to live?"
Having lamented thus in many ways piteously, she, deeply afflicted and devoted to her husband, entered the blazing fire. Then she beheld her husband wearing variegated garments.
Seated upon a celestial chariot, being honored by great-souled doers of good deeds,
wearing variegated garlands and garments, adorned with every ornament,
and surrounded by hundreds of millions of celestial chariots belonging to those of meritorious fame.
And the male pigeon, seeing that beautiful female pigeon, was filled with great joy; he embraced her and said this:
"Oh, you have done well and auspiciously by following me!"
In a mere instant of suffering, she has thereby acquired happiness.
For as many hairs as there are on a human being— three hundred million and fifty million—
so long shall she dwell in heaven who follows her husband.
Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a serpent from its hole,
so too does she rescue her husband and rejoice together with him. Then, having ascended to heaven, the bird was reunited with his wife.
Honored by that deed, he took delight there with his wife.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, while those two were situated in their celestial chariot, the hunter indeed beheld them."
Seeing that couple, he reflected out of sorrow upon the supreme destination:
"By what kind of austerity here might I go to the highest state? Having thus resolved through his intellect, he prepared to depart.
12,145.003 Relying upon the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*), the fowler who lived by hunting birds remained motionless, subsisting on air alone, free from possessiveness, and desiring heaven.
12,145.004 Then he beheld a vast, heart-pleasing lake adorned with lotuses.
That auspicious lake, filled with cool water and crowded with various flocks of birds,
would satisfy even one afflicted by thirst upon seeing it— of this there is no doubt. Yet that hunter, O King, was exceedingly emaciated from fasting.
"Approach with joy this forest inhabited by beasts of prey," the hunter said, and having made this great resolve, he entered it. But as soon as he entered the forest, he was caught by thorns.

With his limbs mangled by thorns and his skin drenched in blood, he wandered through that desolate forest teeming with various wild beasts. Then, in that forest, a great wind blew among the massive trees.
From that friction, the great bearer of oblations arose;
the enraged fire, possessing a radiance equal to the fire at the end of an eon, consumed that forest thick with trees and crowded with creepers and branches.
Accompanied by sparks of fire tossed up by the wind and accompanied by flames,
it consumed that terrible forest teeming with beasts and birds.
Then, with a joyful heart, he [set about] for the sake of casting off his body.
Then the hunter rushed toward the fully grown fire; thereupon,
consumed by that fire, the hunter was cleansed of his sin and attained supreme perfection, O best of the Bharatas.
Then, freed from his feverish distress, he beheld himself established in heaven,
shining like Indra in the midst of Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Siddhas.
Thus indeed did the pigeon and the devoted female pigeon [attain their goal].
By virtue of their meritorious deeds, they have gone to heaven together with the hunter. Furthermore,
any woman who likewise follows her husband shines forth swiftly, established in heaven like that female dove.
Thus did this occur in the past concerning the high-souled hunter and the pigeon; such was the righteous destiny resulting from their meritorious deeds.
Whoever should constantly hear this, and whoever should recite it, [shall attain the highest state].
"O Yudhiṣṭhira,
best among the upholders of dharma, even for one who has committed an evil deed such as killing a cow, there may be atonement through this great dharma, provided he does not err even in thought."
There can be no atonement for one who would kill someone who has come for refuge.
O son, having heard this history which destroys evil,
one does not fall into an evil rebirth but goes to the heavenly world.
Those who come to one's house in distress are worthy of worship, as are those who have come for refuge.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Bharatas, what should he do who commits a sin unintentionally?"
"How can he be released from that sin? Tell me that.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
When the wise Indrota Śaunaka spoke thus to Janamejaya:
"There was once a king of great heroism, Janamejaya, the son of Parikṣit;
an unintentional act of Brahman-slaughter came upon that lord of the earth."
All the brahmins, together with the family priests, abandoned him;
that king, burning with grief day and night, went to the forest.
Having been forsaken by his subjects, he performed great acts of merit.
Burning with wrath, he performed excessive austerities;
for the sake of dispelling the sin of killing a Brahmin, that lord of men wandered over the entire earth, questioning many Brahmins in every land.

In this regard, I shall relate an ancient history that serves as an expansion of this dharma. Being consumed by his sinful deed, Janamejaya went to Indrota Śaunaka, who was firm in his vows and about to perform a sacrifice.
Having approached, he seized his feet and pressed them firmly. Then the highly wise one, filled with fear, rebuked him severely:
"O killer of a fetus, you who have committed a great sin, why have you come here?"
"What must you do with us? Do not touch me under any circumstances!
Go, go! Your presence here certainly does not please us.
Your scent is like that of blood, and your appearance is like that of a corpse."
Inauspicious yet appearing auspicious, though dead you wander as if alive;
with death within and an impure soul, you contemplate only evil.
You wake up, you sleep, you move about, and you live as if happy.
"O King, your life is in vain; you live a life of suffering. You were indeed created for evil, for the most base of deeds.
Desiring much that is auspicious, fathers long for sons."
"By means of asceticism, worship of the gods, salutations, and endurance,
behold this paternal lineage of yours fallen into hell because of you. All their hopes centered upon you have become utterly fruitless."
Those whom people honor obtain heaven, long life, fame, and happiness; your constant hatred toward those Brahmins is therefore futile. Having abandoned this world, you shall fall headlong downward.

For non-eternal and eternal years, you shall be devoured by vultures with black necks and iron beaks as a result of your sinful deed; having returned even from that state, you will go to a womb of sin.
"O King, as for what you think— that there is no hereafter, from where could it come?—
the messengers of Yama will remind you of this in the abode of Yama.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, Janamejaya replied to that sage:
"You reproach what is reproachable; you censure what is censurable.
You condemn me, who am worthy of condemnation; therefore, I seek to propitiate you."

12,147.002c For all this is my own doing; I burn as if placed within a fire. 12,147.003a Contemplating my own past deeds, my mind finds no joy. 12,147.003c Surely a terrible fear has now come upon me, even from Vaivasvata himself.
"But how shall I be able to live without extracting that dart? Having subdued all my rivalries, speak to me, O Śaunaka:
I shall once again become a wealthy provider for the kitchens of the Brahmins."
"Let there be a remnant of this lineage; let this family not perish.
For for us who have been cursed by a Brahmin, and who no longer obtain the Vedas or the understanding derived from the certainty of the Vedas, it is impossible for any remnant to remain."
Being deeply weary of it, I shall now speak further:
those devoid of dharma and devoid of sacred recitation will once again perish like [withered] plants,
and they will settle for the lowly life of outcasts like the Pulindas and Śabaras.

For those who do not perform sacrifices never reach that world by any means. O Brahmin Śaunaka, without even understanding my wisdom— as a truly wise man [would explain] to a child— look upon me as a father looks upon his sons.
Śaunaka said:
"What wonder is there that a wise man should indeed do much for the present?
Having thus become a learned man, he does not suffer on account of living beings."
Having ascended the palace of wisdom, he who is beyond sorrow looks upon grieving people;
like one standing on a mountain looking down at those on the ground, he observes them with wisdom.
Yet, he perceives nothing there, nor does he see any activities.
Whether you are despondent in spirit, out of sight, or censured by all virtuous men,
having understood the power and majesty of both the Veda and the Āgama,
perform here this great rite of pacification; may Brahmā be your refuge.
"That which is indeed pleasing to the Brāhmaṇas in the world beyond would not be disturbed, provided you repent for your sins and look toward righteousness. Janamejaya said:
"I am tormented by sin, yet I do not practice unrighteousness; O Śaunaka, I desire one who seeks prosperity and honors me. Śaunaka said:
"Having severed both arrogance and pride, O King, I desire your friendship.
Abide in the welfare of all beings and ever keep the Dharma in mind. It is not out of fear, nor out of wretchedness, nor out of greed that I invite you."
May the gods, together with the Brahmins, hear this true speech of mine:
I have no desire for anything at all, and I summon you to dharma while all beings cry out, "Alas! Shame!"
Those ignorant of dharma will speak against me, and people who are not my friends will speak likewise;
hearing those words, my true friends will be greatly distressed.
Only a few of great wisdom will fully recognize the necessity of this course of action.
"Know, O dear one, O descendant of Bharata, what has been done by me for the sake of the brahmins.
Act in such a way that they may obtain security through my efforts. And promise, O lord of men, that you will harbor no malice toward the brahmins."
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, neither by word, nor by thought, nor ever again by deed shall I be a hater of brahmins; I touch only your feet."
Śaunaka said:
"Therefore, I shall declare the dharma to you, whose mind has turned back [from worldly affairs],
for you are illustrious, possessed of great strength, contented, and one who regards righteousness."
"O King, having first appeared harsh, that which is most wonderful indeed brings beings under its influence through its own conduct;
for the world certainly determines the truth and falsehood of everything as a whole."
That you, having become such as you are, now perceive the Dharma—
having abandoned most excellent food and enjoyments and being established in austerity—
even this, O Janamejaya, is a marvel among living beings.
"If a donor should be weak, or a person rich in asceticism should be miserly,
they say that this is no wonder, for it does not lie far off. Indeed,
this entire state of wretchedness arises from a lack of foresight."
Therefore, it should be through discernment alone that there may be virtue in him;
O Lord of the Earth, sacrifice, charity, compassion, the Vedas, and truth—
these five are purifiers, and the sixth is well-practiced austerity.
O Janamejaya, that alone is the supreme purifier for kings;
by properly undertaking it, you shall attain the highest dharma. Visiting sacred places is remembered as the supreme purifier.
For they cite these verses sung by Yayāti:
"Whatever mortal should obtain life or live it again, he should perform sacrifice with single-minded devotion and, having renounced that, practice austerity."
They say Kurukṣetra is meritorious, and Pṛthūdaka on the Sarasvatī is likewise.
From Kurukṣetra one goes to the Sarasvatī,
and from the Sarasvatī to its sacred fords (*tīrthas*).
Having plunged into or drunk from there, one does not suffer such anxiety regarding death on the morrow.
You shall go to the great lakes Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Uttaramānasa,
and indeed Kāloda, having regained your life-span and your life once more.
Wandering along, you should frequent the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī;
devoted to the study of the Vedas, you should perform ritual ablutions at all sacred sites.
Among all purifying practices, he declared that the dharma of renunciation and the supreme state of saṃnyāsa are the highest.
Regarding this, they cite these verses composed by Satyavat:
"Just as the youth Satya was indeed neither meritorious nor a doer of evil, so too there is no suffering among all beings; how then could there be happiness?"
Thus, for those who are by nature subject to all forms of association and who generally cast off their lives when merit and demerit are laid bare,
I shall now tell you that which is indeed the most important of all duties for a king.
"By means of strength and through acts of distribution, conquer heaven and purify yourself. That man who possesses such power and vigor is the master of dharma;
for the sake of the happiness of the Brahmins, traverse this earth."
Just as you formerly cast them down, so now appease them.
O wise one, even if you are censured or abandoned in many ways, do not be angry, thinking, "I am not this [body]," for that is the vision of the Self.
Exerting yourself in your own duties, achieve the supreme, ultimate good. O scorcher of foes, one king may be like snow or fire in his severity, while another may be like a plow or a thunderbolt.
One should not think that [the self] is utterly non-existent, nor that it is incurable;
one should never entertain the thought "I am not" among the wicked.
One who is tormented by the performance of improper acts is released from a portion of their evil.
"‘This must not be done again’—by this one is released from the second [offense]. ‘I shall practice only the Dharma’—by this one is released from the third.
Being pure and frequenting sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one is released from the fourth."
A person desiring prosperity should approve of what is auspicious.
Those who associate with fragrant things become fragrant themselves;
those who associate with foul-smelling things become foul-smelling themselves.
One devoted to the practice of austerity is immediately liberated from sin; by tending the sacred fire for one year, even one accused of a grave offense is released;
and by tending the fire for three years, even a killer of an embryo is fully absolved.
Having traveled one hundred *yojanas*, the killer of an embryo is liberated;
by saving from death as many living beings of that same species as he would have naturally killed,
the killer of an embryo is liberated.

Or else, one may immerse oneself in water while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times; Manu has declared that this is equal to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) at the end of a horse sacrifice. It quickly dispels evil, and likewise, one receives honor.
Moreover, O King, even the elements become as if dull and mute toward him;
all the gods and asuras, having come together, questioned Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods.
O Great Seer, you know the fruit of dharma when it is performed,
as well as that which occurs otherwise in the hellish world of the wicked;
yet for whom both deeds are well-performed, [that person attains the highest state].
Which of those two would have the superior victory there?
Tell us, O Great Seer, the fruit of karma:
how does one of virtuous character dispel evil?
Bṛhaspati said:
"He who, having previously committed a sin unintentionally,
performs meritorious deeds intentionally,"
A person of virtuous character dispels that evil,
just as a soiled garment is cleansed by the application of alkaline salt;
having committed an evil deed, a man should not think, "I am not [that]."

One who is faithful and free from malice should indeed desire to perform what is auspicious. That man who, having committed a sin, turns toward what is auspicious, reveals his faults to the virtuous just as one reveals the holes in a garment.
Just as the sun, rising once more, dispels all darkness,
so too does one who practices what is auspicious dispel all evil.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus to King Janamejaya Indrota,
Śaunaka performed the horse sacrifice (vājimedha) for him according to the prescribed rites.
Thereupon, that king was cleansed of his impurity.
Endowed with splendor in the form of a blazing fire,
the subduer of his enemies entered his own kingdom,
like the full-bodied moon entering the heavens.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, has it ever been heard or even seen by you that a mortal man,
once dead, O King, could be restored to life again?"
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O King, it is heard that for those who do not abandon their exertion, even an objective that was once impossible may at some time be accomplished, however great it may be.
"Cut through this great doubt that remains within me; indeed, there is no one who can resolve it except for my grandfather Bhīṣma. Bhīṣma said:
"Listen, O Pārtha, to this ancient history as it occurred,
the dialogue between a vulture and a jackal that took place long ago in Vaidiśa.
A certain Brāhmaṇa had a son who was obtained with great difficulty, but who then died."
While still a mere child, Viśālākṣa was afflicted by an infant-seizing spirit (*bālagraha*).
Some people, distressed and overwhelmed with grief, took up the boy— who had not yet reached youth and who was indeed the very treasure of their family— and wept.
Then, taking up the dead child, they stood facing the cremation ground;
passing him from lap to lap, they wept upon the earth,
repeatedly lamenting those words he had spoken before.
Having cast that child upon the ground, they would not be able to depart;
at the sound of their weeping, a vulture approached and spoke these words:
"Leave this lone one in the world and go, without delay."
"Indeed, thousands upon thousands of men and thousands of women have been brought together here by Time; were they ever truly your kinsmen?
Behold the entire world governed by pleasure and pain."
Union and separation are perceived in alternation.
Those who go away taking others with them, and those who follow after the dead—
these living beings also depart according to the measure of their own lifespan.
Enough of staying in this cemetery, crowded with vultures and jackals, filled with skeletons, terrible, and terrifying to all living beings;
for no one who has succumbed to the law of time ever returns to life again.
Whether one is dear or whether one is hateful, such is the destiny of living beings. Indeed, everyone born in the world of mortals must die;
on the path ordained by the Ordainer (Kṛtānta), who can bring the dead back to life?
"When the world has turned toward its occupations and the sun is setting,
you must indeed depart for your own abode, casting aside your affection for your son.
Then, O King, having heard the words of the vulture, they began to wail aloud.

12,149.012 Your kinsmen approached, having abandoned their son upon the ground; 12,149.012d and they were all resolved, O Bhārata, regarding their departure. 12,149.013a Having thus made their decision, they then abandoned their own son.
Crying out here and there, "He is dead," they departed hopeless of seeing him,
their minds set on returning.
Despairing of his life, they ascended the path and stood there.
Then a jackal, whose color was like a crow or a cloud, emerged from its lair and said to those who were departing, "Truly, men are heartless!"
"O fools, this sun is still standing; show affection and do not fear!
The moment is multiform, and perhaps he may yet live.
You, however, having cast him upon the ground, are now bereft of love for your son."
"O pitiless ones, why do you depart after abandoning your son in the cremation ground? You have no affection for this child, who speaks so sweetly,
by whose mere words you would have been moved to favor."
Do you not see the affection that exists among beasts and birds? For them, there is no acquisition of fruit resulting from supporting their young;
yet among quadrupeds, birds, insects, and all living beings who are bound by affection, [this love persists].
Just as the sacrificial rites of sages are for those who have departed to the next world, so too,
for those whose delight is their sons, no benefit whatsoever is seen either in this world or in the next; yet they continue to support their offspring.

For those who do not see their beloved sons, grief does not persist; nor do those sons, once grown, ever nourish their parents. How can there be affection among humans, when such grief will surely arise?
"How will you go away, abandoning this son who shall perpetuate our lineage?
Weep for a long time and look upon him with affection for a long time; for such beloved things as these are indeed difficult to relinquish."
When one is exhausted, beset by calamities, or facing toward the cremation ground,
there is no one else who stands by where one's kinsmen stand. To everyone, life-breaths are dear, and everyone experiences affection.
Behold the kind of affection that even those in the animal realm possess for the virtuous! How could you abandon this one with eyes as long and tremulous as lotus petals and depart?
He is like a bridegroom newly wedded, bathed, garlanded, and adorned.
12,149.027 Bhīṣma said:
Having heard the words of the jackal as he lamented piteously,
all those men then turned back for the sake of the corpse.
The vulture said:
"Alas! Shame! Why do you, men of low spirit, turn back at the words of this cruel, small-minded, and base jackal?"
Devoid of the five elements, empty, and having reached the state of mere wood—why do you grieve for this motionless thing? Why do you not grieve for yourselves?
Indeed, practice intense austerity, by which you may be liberated from sin.

Everything is obtained through austerity; what will lamentation accomplish? Know that undesirable fortunes come along with their physical forms—those by which this world departs, having given rise to endless sorrow.
Wealth, cattle, gold, as well as jewels and gems,
and even offspring— these have austerity as their root and are obtained through the practice of austerity. Furthermore,
the experience of pleasure and pain among living beings is attained according to their past actions.
Taking [the fruits of] these, a living being is born to both sufferings and pleasures.
A son does not [suffer] by the karma of his father, nor does a father by the karma of his son;
they go by another path, having abandoned their good and evil deeds.
Practice righteousness with diligence and likewise turn away from unrighteousness;
conduct yourselves at the proper times toward the gods and the twice-born. Abandon grief and dejection, and turn away from attachment to your sons.
"Let him be abandoned here in the sky; therefore, return quickly.
Whatever auspicious deed or even what most terrible unrighteousness one performs, the doer alone experiences the fruit thereof—what indeed is the role of kinsmen in this?"
Having abandoned their dear kinsman here, relatives do not remain; casting off their affection, they depart with eyes clouded and filled with tears—
whether one be wise or foolish, wealthy or even destitute.
12.149.039c Everyone, endowed with both the auspicious and the inauspicious, comes under the power of time.
12.149.040a What will you achieve by grieving? Why do you mourn for one who is dead?
12.149.040c For Time is the master of all, and according to dharma, it regards all things with equanimity.
"Death enters those established in youth, the young, the old, and even those within the womb; such is this world.
The jackal said:
"Alas! Affection has been diminished here by this dull-witted vulture, even as you, overcome by love for your son, are mourning so intensely.
[Yet he speaks] with words that are balanced, properly employed, and full of humility."

"Accept all of this quickly; do not hesitate. Since you are going to the watery realm, cast off this affection so difficult to abandon—alas, because of the separation from your sons and the attendance upon that which is empty like the dead."
12,149.044c As they cried out, there was indeed intense suffering, like that of cows deprived of their calves. 12,149.045a Today I truly understand the sorrow of human beings upon the earth;
12,149.045c for seeing such piteous affection, tears have come to me as well.
Effort must indeed be constantly exerted; when it is performed, it succeeds through destiny. Destiny and human exertion are brought together by the final outcome.
One should always maintain perseverance, for how can there be happiness from despondency?

"Indeed, wealth is obtained through effort; why then do you go away so heartlessly? Having abandoned in the forest one who was sustained by your own flesh, whose body is half of yours, and who is the perpetuator of the lineage of your ancestors—where will you go?"
"Or else, when the sun has set and the time of twilight has arrived,
you shall either take the son away from here, or you shall remain right here."—
Śrī Bhīṣma.
"O King, having heard the words of the jackal, the vulture spoke;
I shall relate that to you—listen here with an attentive mind.
The vulture said:
"O humans, today it has been more than a thousand years since I was born,
yet I have never seen a dead person— whether female, male, or neuter— living again.
Some die in the womb, while others die as soon as they are born."
Some die while displaying their prowess, and others likewise while still in the prime of youth.
Fortunes here are transient, even for four-footed beasts and birds; the lifespan of both the mobile and the immobile stands at the very forefront [of all things].
Separated from their beloved wives and likewise filled with grief for their sons,
they go home daily, burning with sorrow;
[they endure] thousands of undesirable things as well as hundreds of desirable ones.

12,149.054c Having abandoned him here, the kinsmen have indeed departed, deeply afflicted by grief. 12,149.055a "Let this man be left behind—lusterless, empty, and reduced to the state of wood; 12,149.055c for his consciousness is attached to another body, while he merely attends to this corpse as if it were a log."
"O you whose life is now wandering, why do you not depart, casting aside these tears?
For this affection is indeed useless, and this attachment is likewise useless;
he neither hears with his ears nor sees with his eyes."

"Therefore, having abandoned him, go quickly indeed to your own homes. Addressed by me with words concerning the dharma of liberation— words that are reasoned, gentle, and purposeful— go swiftly each to your own respective dwellings."

12,149.059a By one endowed with wisdom and discernment, who brings about the perception of awakening, 12,149.059c let this harsh speech be proclaimed: "O humans, turn back! 12,149.059d Grief becomes twofold upon seeing and remembering his deeds."
Having heard these words, the men turned back;
then the jackal, having arrived quickly, saw him sleeping.
Having heard the vulture's speech, the jackal spoke these words:
The jackal said:
"How can you abandon this son, who possesses the luster of gold, is adorned with ornaments, and provides the funeral oblations for his ancestors, merely because of the words of a vulture?"
There is indeed no contradiction between affection and lamentation and weeping;
by abandoning this deceased one, there will certainly be grief.
It is heard that when the Śūdra Śambuka was killed, a Brahmin boy—

Having encountered the Dharma from Rāma, whose prowess is truth, he was restored to life; likewise, the son of the royal sage Śveta had reached the end of his allotted time, but on the following day, having been dead, he was brought back to life by that one who is ever devoted to Dharma.
"Perhaps some perfected being, a sage, or even a deity might show compassion for you who are wretched and weeping here. Bhīṣma said:

Having been addressed thus, they turned back, afflicted with grief and longing for their son; placing his head upon their laps, they wept most bitterly. At the sound of their wailing, a vulture approached and spoke these words.
The vulture said:
Drenched by the falling of tears and pained by the touch of hands,
he has been made to enter a long sleep through the agency of Dharmarāja.
For even one endowed with ascetic power is not spared by Time;
this city of the departed is the end of all attachments. Relatives always abandon thousands of children and the elderly here.
For 12,149 days and nights, they remain in suffering upon the earth. Enough of this persistence in surrounding yourself with grief;
for how can there be any hope of his life returning here today?
12.149.070a He will not regain life by the words of this jackal;
12.149.070c for one who is dead and has cast off the body, a body does not exist again.
12.149.071a Not indeed by the gift of a physical form, nor even by hundreds of jackals.
For even in hundreds of years, this child could not possibly be brought back to life—
even if Rudra, Kumāra, Brahmā, or Viṣṇu themselves were to grant him a boon, only then might this infant live.
Neither by the shedding of tears, nor by the taking of breaths, nor by long lamentation here will he return to life;
for I, the jackal, and you, his kinsmen, [are all alike].
12,149.074 "Having grasped both dharma and adharma here, we all proceed upon this path. If he should live again, I shall do as follows:
[I will avoid] what is unpleasant, harsh speech, malice toward others, and [adultery with] another's wife."
A wise person should avoid unrighteousness and falsehood from afar; instead,
they should diligently seek truth, righteousness, what is auspicious and just, great compassion for living beings, straightforwardness, and freedom from deceit.

For those who do not behold their mother, father, kinsmen, and friends while they are still living, there is a perversion of dharma. He who does not see with his eyes and does not move in any way at all—
"When his life comes to its final end, what will you do, weeping?
Bhīṣma said:
"Having been addressed thus, they abandoned that son on the ground, overwhelmed with grief."
Burning with affection for their son, the kinsmen departed for their homes.
The jackal said:
"This world of mortals is cruel, bringing destruction to all living beings."
There is separation from beloved kinsmen, and likewise, life is short;
there is much falsehood and untruth, as well as contentious speech and unpleasant words.
Beholding this renewed existence, which only increases suffering and grief—
This world of men does not please me for even a moment.
Alas! Shame! O humans, return at the word of the vulture;
you are as devoid of wisdom as those who are consumed by the grief for their sons.
"How can you go, casting aside your affection and the love for your son?
Having heard these words of the wicked vulture, who was devoid of self-restraint,
[they realized that] suffering follows happiness, and happiness follows suffering.
In this world joined with pleasure and pain, there is nothing here that is eternal.
Having laid down on the surface of the earth this child, endowed with beauty—
the source of grief for his family— where will you go, O fools, having abandoned your son?
Endowed with beauty and youth, shining as if with splendor—I see him alive in my mind; there is no doubt of this.
His destruction is unworthy, and you humans shall attain happiness.
For you who are consumed by the fire of grief for your son, even death today would be appropriate. Having endured this accumulation of suffering and having personally maintained your composure,
where will you go now, abandoning us like those of small intellect?
12,149.089 Bhīṣma said: Thus, acting in opposition to dharma and falsely coveting what was pleasing, he who dwelt constantly in the cremation ground then began to search for her during the night.
Then, by means of words like nectar, the jackal brought his kinsmen to a state of neutrality for the sake of his own purpose; thus they were stationed there.
The vulture said:
This region of the forest is crowded with hungry ghosts (preta), frequented by yakṣas and rākṣasas, and is dreadful; it resounds with the cries of owls,
is terrifying and most formidable, and possesses a luster like that of a dark blue cloud.
"Abandoning this corpse, perform the funeral rites while the sun has not yet set and while the quarters of the sky remain clear;
abandon him now and attend to the funeral rites."
The hawks cry out harshly, and the jackals howl dreadfully; the lions roar back in response as the sun goes down,
and the trees are stained by the blue smoke of the funeral pyres.
In the cremation ground, those embodied beings who subsist on nothing else rejoice;
all of them, possessing great prowess and being exceedingly cruel in this region,
will— deformed and meat-eaters— assail you.
"This region of the forest is far off, and there will be danger here;
let him be abandoned like a log of wood, and let the words of the jackal be endured. If the words of the jackal are fruitless and false,"
"Once you have lost your discernment, you will hear [this] and then all of you shall perish.
The jackal said:
"Stay here; there is no need to fear as long as the sun shines."
For so long, out of affection for his son, he remains here without despair;
and in this forest region, there is no fear from thieves, from the Virāṭas, or from kings, nor even from those whose intellects have been destroyed.
"Weep at your ease, full of confidence; look with affection as you please. In this formidable forest region, no fear shall come upon you.
This gentle forest area is the place where the ancestors met their end."
"Stay here as long as the sun remains; what is the use of these words of yours, which are like those of a flesh-eater?
If you, with your minds deluded, accept the fierce and impetuous words of the vulture, your son shall no longer exist."
Bhīṣma said:
While the sun had not yet set, the vulture said it had gone down; when it had actually set, the jackal said the same. Driven by hunger, those two spoke thus to the kinsmen of the deceased.
"O King, the vulture and the jackal were both skilled in their own duties;
exhausted by hunger and thirst, they prattled on, relying upon the scriptures. Between those two—the jackal and the bird—who were both learned in discernment,"
Indeed, by means of words like nectar, they stood still and moved about;
then, overcome by grief and dejection, they stood there weeping.
They were bewildered by the skillful artifice of those two who were expert in their own purpose.
While those two, both experts in the science of consciousness, were thus disputing,
Śaṅkara appeared before them as they stood with their kinsmen;
urged by the Goddess, the God’s eyes were moistened with compassion.
Then the wielder of the trident said to those men, "I am the granter of boons.
Standing bowed down and distressed, they replied with these words:
"We are all deprived of our only sons and are seekers of life."
"By granting life to our son, you ought to grant life to us.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, with his hand full of water,
bestowed life upon that prince for a full hundred years.

Likewise, the blessed Lord who wields the Pināka bow, devoted to the welfare of all beings, granted a boon to the jackal and the vulture that would destroy their hunger. Then, filled with joy at this blessing, they bowed down to that god.
O Lord, having accomplished their purpose, they then set out happily and joyfully,
through long-standing perseverance, firm resolve,
and by the grace of the God of gods, quickly attaining the fruit of their efforts.
Behold the union with the god and the resolve of our kinsmen;
for we have wiped away the tears of these wretched ones who are weeping.
Behold how, in a short time and through the pursuit of certainty, [this has been accomplished].

Having obtained grace from Śaṅkara, those who were suffering attained happiness; O best of the Bharatas, they became filled with wonder and joy through the restoration of their son by the grace of Śaṅkara.
Then, O King, having heard of that grief born of calamity, they hurriedly entered the city with joyful hearts, taking their son with them.
This wisdom has been shown for all people among the four social orders.
Having constantly heard this auspicious history, which is joined with dharma, artha, and mokṣa, a person rejoices both in this world and after death. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
An enemy who is powerful, constantly remaining nearby,
capable of both helping and harming, and prepared for action— yet who, through delusion, merely boasts and is actually insubstantial, weak, and insignificant; [one should treat him as such].
O Grandfather, having assailed you with unworthy words and relying on his own strength, how might a mortal man fare against him as he approaches,
exceedingly enraged and desiring to uproot us?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O best of the Bharatas, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Śalmali and Pavana.
Having reached the Himavat mountains, there stood a great lord of the forest,
grown over many series of years, possessed of branches, trunks, and foliage.
There, elephants in rut, afflicted by the heat and exhausted by fatigue, used to resort.
O mighty-armed one, there are those [forests] crowded with herds of boars, deer, tigers, and flocks of birds, where various other species of wild animals rest;
and there is a lord of the forest with dense shade, its circumference measuring a *nalva*.
Resounding with the cries of parrots and śārikā birds, and abounding in both fruit and flowers,
the sage Nārada once saw it and, filled with wonder, said:
"O Śālmali, you alone are blessed, for you are the beloved of the wind."

Caravans of merchants, as well as forest-dwelling ascetics traveling on their way, took up residence beneath that most excellent and beautiful tree. Having seen its vast branches and its trunks on all sides, they settled there.
O bull of the Bharatas, Nārada approached him and said:
"Aho! How delightful you are, and how enchanting you are!
O Shalmali, best of trees, we are always pleased with you."
"O dear one, birds, deer, and likewise elephants always dwell beneath you,
exceedingly joyful and beautiful. O great-branched one, your branches and your trunk are likewise vast."
"I do not see them broken by the wind in any way;
because of the presence of all dwellings and out of friendship, he protects them.
But why, my dear, is the wind so pleased with you, or is it perhaps a friend?"
12,150.010c By him, indeed, you are always protected in this forest; for it is certain that the wind—
12,150.011a blowing with great force, shakes trees both high and low from their very roots, 12,150.011c and the swift wind causes even the peaks of mountains to tremble.
The pure wind, blowing forth, surely dries up the netherworld (pātāla),
as well as the lakes, the rivers, and the oceans;
there is no doubt that the Wind-god would protect you out of friendship.
Therefore, you possess many branches, as well as leaves and flowers. And this appears beautiful in you, O lord of the forest,
that these birds, my dear, take delight in you with joy.

The sweet sound of these [birds], both individually and together, is heard as they call out most charmingly at the time when the flowers are in full bloom. Likewise, these joyful nāgas, who adorn their own herds and clans, [are present].
O *śalmali* tree, those afflicted by the heat find comfort upon reaching you;
likewise, you are graced by various species of wild animals,
and thus, O tree, you shine like Mount Meru with the dwellings of traveling caravans.

"O Śālmali, because of your kinship or perhaps your friendship with the Brahmins perfected in austerity, as well as with ascetics and recluses, I consider this very abode of yours to be equal to heaven itself; of this there is no doubt."
The all-pervading wind Bhīma constantly protects [the world];
O Śālmali, you have attained a state of supreme subordination to that wind,
because of which the Maruta always guards you, thinking, "I am yours."

"I do not see any tree or even any mountain on this earth that is so firm as not to be broken by the force of the wind; such is my thought. But you, O Śalmali, are surely protected at all times by various causes."
"By Vāyu, together with his retinue, you undoubtedly abide there.
Śālmali said:
"O Brahmin, Vāyu is neither my friend, nor my kinsman, nor my well-wisher."

"Even Parameṣṭhin does not possess such power as that by which the Wind-god protects me. For, O Nārada, though the terrible energy and strength of the Wind is great, he does not equal even an eighteenth part of my vital power."
The supreme wind was approaching, and it was forcibly restrained by me as it shattered trees, mountains, and whatever else there might be;
that very shatterer, though he himself is a destroyer, was broken by me many times.
"Therefore, O divine sage, I do not fear even the enraged Wind-god.
Nārada said:
"O Śālmali, your perspective is inverted; there is no doubt about this."
Indeed, there is no being anywhere whose strength is equal to the strength of the wind.
Indra, Yama, Vaiśravaṇa, and Varuṇa, the lord of the waters—
even they are not equal to the Maruts, let alone you, O Lord of the Forest.
Whatever living being here on earth moves, O Śalmali,
everywhere the blessed Vāyu is the lord who provides movement and life; he, properly extended, impels all living beings correctly.

12,150.030c Moving improperly and excessively, he acts with distortion among men. 12,150.031a Yet you do not honor such a wind, the best among all sustainers of beings, though he is worthy of worship; what else could this be but a deficiency of intellect?
"O evil-minded one, you are pithless; you speak much, yet in vain.
Enveloped by anger and other passions, O *śalmali* tree, you speak falsely.
My wrath has arisen because you have addressed me in such a manner."
I myself declare that you have spoken many harsh words against Vāyu.
[There are trees] such as sandalwood, spandana, śāla, sarala, devadāru,
reeds, and bindu, as well as others that are even more powerful.
But even by those self-controlled ones, O evil-minded one, the wind was not thus insulted;
for they know the strength of the wind as well as their own. Therefore, those best of trees indeed pay homage to the Wind.
"But you, out of delusion, do not know the infinite power of the wind.
Therefore, I shall go into the presence of Mātariśvan.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, O Indra among kings, Nārada, the best among the knowers of Brahman, related the entire speech of the *śālmali* tree to the Wind-god:
"On the slopes of the Himavat there is a certain *śālmali* tree that possesses a great retinue."
"O Vāyu, that tree with its massive roots and massive branches treats you with contempt.
It has addressed many words to you full of insults;
O Lord Vāyu, it is not proper for me to repeat those things to you."
"I know you, O Vāyu, as the best among all living beings;
you are most excellent and most formidable in anger, like Vaivasvata himself.
Having heard these words of Nārada, the Wind-god—
Approaching that *śalmali* tree, he spoke these words in anger:
"O *śalmali*, as for those words of contempt for me which you spoke to Nārada, I am Vāyu; I shall show you my own power and majesty."
"I do not fail to recognize you, O tree, for you are well known to me. The Lord Grandfather rested upon you during the creation of living beings;
it was solely because of his resting that this favor was bestowed upon you."

"O evil-minded one, O lowest of trees, you are protected by that [power] and not by your own prowess, since you despise me just as you would any other common person. Here I show myself, so that you may truly understand who I am."

Thus addressed, the Śālmali tree then spoke as if laughing: "O Wind, you who are enraged in this forest, show yourself by your own power! Let your anger be directed toward me; what will you do to me even if you are furious?"
"I do not fear you, O Wind, even though you are yourself a lord;
I am superior in strength to you, so I have no cause for fear of you. For those who are strong in wisdom are truly the most powerful."
"Those who possess only the strength of breath are not considered truly strong. When he had spoken thus, Pavana replied,
"I shall show you my power tomorrow," and then night arrived.
Then, having reflected in his mind upon the deed wrought by Vāta, and perceiving himself to be unequal to Mātariśvan, Śalmali realized:
"That which I said to Nārada regarding the Wind was false."
"For I am indeed powerless against the strength of the wind, for it is powerful;
the Wind-god is eternally mighty, just as Nārada has said. Indeed, I am weaker than other trees; of this there is no doubt."
"But there is no tree whatsoever equal to me in intelligence.
Therefore, by relying upon my intelligence, I shall free myself from the fear of the wind.
If the leafy trees in the forest were to act by relying upon that same intelligence,"
They would always remain unharmed by the enraged Wind; of this there is no doubt. These children here do not know how the Wind, when provoked to anger, might sweep them away, as I well know.
Then, having resolved this in his mind, the *śālmali* tree became agitated;
he himself then lopped off his branches, trunks, and twigs.
Having cast away his branches, leaves, and flowers, he remained there.
At dawn, the lord of the forest watched as the wind approached.
Then the wind, enraged and hissing, felling great trees,
came to that place where the *śālmali* tree stood.
Seeing that tree with its leaves fallen, its top branches dropped,
and its flowers scattered, Vāyu spoke these words to it with a smile:
"O Śalmali, with my own hand I have performed the complete stripping away of your branches out of anger, just as you did to me when you joyfully broke off the branches of the mudā-yuta tree."
"With its finest flowers and branches stripped away, and its sprouts and leaves withered, you have come here under the power of my prowess solely because of your own evil counsel.
Having heard these words of Vāyu, the Śālmali tree was then filled with shame.
12.151.025c Remembering those words that Nārada had spoken, he was consumed by remorse.
12.151.026a O tiger among kings, thus does a fool who, being weak, instigates enmity with one more powerful, suffer like the *śalmali* tree.
Therefore, one who is weak should not harbor enmity toward those who are stronger;
for he who cultivates enmity will surely grieve, just like the *śalmali* tree. Indeed, high-souled men do not manifest their resentment toward those who have done them harm.
O great king, they gradually displayed their strength.
A man of evil intellect should not harbor enmity toward one who lives by his intelligence;
for the intelligence of an intelligent person consumes its opponent like fire among tufts of cotton.
"O King, there is nothing equal to intelligence in a man;
likewise, O Indra among kings, one should consider that there is nothing equal to strength.
Therefore, one should be patient with the foolish, the dull-witted, and the deaf."
O Indra among kings, O slayer of enemies, that has been witnessed in you who are superior in strength; for even eleven and seven akṣauhiṇīs, O king of great splendor,
are not equal in force to the high-souled Arjuna.

Slain and broken were they by the illustrious Pāṇḍava, who moved through the battle relying on his strength, the son of Pākaśāsana. And those duties of kings and duties in times of distress were spoken to you, O Bhārata.
12,151.034c "In detail, O Great King, what more shall I tell you?
12,152.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
12,152.001a "What is the foundation of evil, from which evil proceeds?"
"I wish to know this in its true essence, O bull among the Bharatas.
Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of men, hear that which is the foundation of evil."
Greed alone is the great predator; from greed, evil proceeds. From this [greed] come both sin and unrighteousness, as well as unsurpassed suffering.
For this is indeed the root of deceit by which people become doers of evil.
From greed arises anger; from greed desire proceeds.
From greed come delusion, deceit, pride, arrogance, and malice toward others.
From it come intolerance, the abandonment of shame, the destruction of prosperity, and the decay of dharma.
Covetousness and the lack of wisdom— all these proceed from greed.
So too do injustice, improper reflection, actions performed through wrong occupations,
fraudulent sciences and the like, as well as pride in one's physical form and power.
Lack of trust in all beings, dishonesty toward all beings,
malice toward all beings, and impropriety toward all beings;
the seizing of others' property and the violation of others' wives.
The impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, and likewise the impulse of censure; the impulses of the genitals and the stomach, and the terrible impulse of death;
the powerful impulse of envy, and the impulse of falsehood which is so difficult to abandon.
The impulse of passion is difficult to restrain, and the impulse of the senses is hard to endure; likewise,
there are contempt, boastfulness, envy, evil, the performance of difficult deeds,
and the execution of all kinds of rash and improper acts.

Whether in birth, childhood, youth, or even old age, a human being does not abandon his own karma— that which does not decay even as he decays. O best of the Kurus, greed can never be satisfied by acquisition.
Like the ocean by rivers of ever-deep water,
he who does not exult at gains nor find satisfaction in desires,
and who is not [overpowered] by gods, gandharvas, asuras, or great serpents—
O King, it is known in its true essence by all classes of beings that greed,
along with delusion, must be conquered by one who has mastered the self;
likewise, hypocrisy, malice, slander, backbiting, and envy [must be abandoned].
O Kauravya, these qualities belong to those who are greedy and of undisciplined soul.
Though they may retain even the most extensive scriptures and possess great learning,
being capable of cutting through doubts, those of small intellect suffer here in this world.
Addicted to hatred and anger, excluded from the conduct of the virtuous, with razors within their mouths yet sweet of speech— like wells concealed by grass,
these base men who use the banner of Dharma as a pretext plunder the world.
Relying on the power of various causes, they create many different paths;
established in greed and ignorance, they destroy every path as the Dharma is being carried away by evil-souled men seized by greed.
Whatever transformation occurs, it proceeds from that very source:
pride, anger, intoxication, sleep, joy, grief, and excessive arrogance—
these, O Kauravya, are seen to arise precisely from those whose intellects are greedy.
Know these to be the unrefined, who are constantly possessed by greed; but you should inquire of the refined, whose vows are pure, whom I shall describe—
those in whom there is no fear for their livelihood and no fear of the next world.
They have no attachment to material things, nor to what is pleasant or unpleasant;
they for whom the conduct of the virtuous is dear, and in whom self-restraint is firmly established; for whom happiness and suffering are equal, and truth is their supreme refuge.
They were givers and not takers, and likewise possessed of compassion;
they were devoted to their ancestors, the gods, and guests, and were ever-diligent; they were benefactors to all, steadfast, and observers of all duties.
O Bhārata, those who are devoted to the welfare of all beings and who give everything that can be given cannot be shaken, for they have reached the further shore of the practice of dharma;
their conduct does not deviate from what was established of old by the virtuous.

Those who are neither fearful, nor fickle, nor violent, but remain established on the path of the righteous; those from whom non-violence is firmly rooted—such people should always be served by the virtuous.
Those who are free from desire and anger, devoid of possessiveness and egoism.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, attend upon those of excellent vows who are firm in their observances, and question them; for their dharma is not for the sake of cattle nor for the sake of fame,
but rather because such duties must necessarily be performed, as are the bodily functions."
In them there is no fear, no anger or fickleness, and no sorrow;
they do not carry the banner of righteousness as a pretense, nor do they harbor any secret motives. They are free from greed and delusion, and they are devoted to truth and uprightness.
O son of Kuntī, you should take delight in those among whom the mind is rendered free from weariness— those who do not rejoice in gains nor suffer in losses,
who are free from possessiveness and egoism, established in purity, and possessed of equal vision.
Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, O dear one, the agreeable and the disagreeable, death and life—
those of steady prowess for whom these are equal;
You should strive with diligence and vigilance to support those beings who possess the nature of Buddhas and abide in great majesty, by means of what is pleasant and agreeable to them.
"By fate all things become endowed with qualities,
just as auspicious and inauspicious utterances arise from speech.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, greed has been described as the foundation of all misfortunes. O dear one, I wish to hear about ignorance as well, according to its true nature.
Bhīṣma said:
He who commits evil out of ignorance and does not recognize his own transgression, and who hates those of virtuous conduct, incurs the censure of the world;
through ignorance he goes to hell, and likewise through ignorance he falls into a miserable rebirth.
Through ignorance one incurs affliction and likewise sinks into calamities.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[Tell me] the activity, the locus, the increase, and the decline and rise of ignorance.
"O King, I wish to hear in truth and according to reality the root, the application, the destination, the time, the cause, and the reason for this very thing;
for this suffering that is experienced here arises from ignorance."
Bhīṣma said: Passion, hatred, delusion, joy, sorrow, arrogance,
desire, anger, pride, drowsiness, and even laziness— these [are the afflictions].
Desire, hatred, as well as distress, being tormented by the prosperity of others,
and ignorance— these are specified as such, along with whatever actions are sinful.
The activity that proceeds from these, and those matters concerning prosperity and so forth about which you inquire, [are all rooted therein].
"Listen in detail to that, O mighty-armed lord of the people. Both of these, O Bhārata, yield equal fruits and possess equal faults;
know them both, O King, to be identical: ignorance and excessive greed."
Ignorance, born of greed, having increased, grows even further;
it reaches various states—attaining stability when there is stability, and decay when there is decay.
Greed is the root of great [suffering], and its course is indeed identical to that of Time itself.
Whether greed is cut off or not cut off, time alone is indeed the cause.
For from ignorance comes greed, and from greed comes ignorance;
likewise, all defects arise from greed. Therefore, one should abandon greed.
Janaka, Yuvanāśva, Vṛṣādarbhi, Prasenajit,
and other lords of men likewise attained heaven through the destruction of greed. Therefore, O best of the Kurus, abandon greed here within yourself before it becomes manifest.
"Having abandoned greed, you will enjoy happiness in this world and follow it even after death.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, for a Brāhmaṇa who has exerted himself in the study of the Vedas..."
"O you whose soul is dharma, what is said here to be the highest good for one who desires dharma?
Since there are many views in this world regarding what is the highest good, tell me that, O Grandfather, which you consider to be the highest good in this world and in the next."
"O Bhārata, this path of dharma is great and has many branches.
What among these dharmas is considered the most essential to be practiced?
[Tell me] in truth, O King, regarding this vast dharma with its many branches."
"O dear one, tell me without weariness all that which is the supreme root.
Bhīṣma said:
"Indeed, I shall tell you that by which you will attain the highest good."
Having drunk it like nectar, you, being wise, shall become satisfied with knowledge. The ordinances of dharma are manifold, each proclaimed by the great seers;
relying upon their respective insights, self-restraint is the supreme goal among them.

The elders who perceive the certain truth declare that self-restraint (*dama*) is the highest good; for a Brahmin especially, self-restraint is the eternal duty (*dharma*). For one who lacks self-restraint, the successful accomplishment of ritual acts is not properly attained.
Self-restraint surpasses charity, sacrifices, and sacred learning.
Self-restraint increases one's vital energy (*tejas*), and self-restraint is the supreme means of purification. Free from sin and endowed with vital energy, a man attains greatness.
12,154.010a We have heard of no other dharma in the worlds equal to self-restraint (dama). 12,154.010c For self-restraint is praised as supreme in the world by all who follow dharma.
12,154.011a And even after death, O lord of men, one attains the highest happiness.
For one endowed with self-restraint partakes in great dharma;
the self-controlled man sleeps in happiness and wakes in happiness;
he moves through the worlds in happiness, and his mind becomes serene.

An undisciplined person repeatedly encounters suffering and produces many other misfortunes born of his own faults. Among the four stages of life, they say that self-restraint alone is the supreme vow.
I shall describe its characteristics, the aggregate of which constitutes self-restraint (dama):
forbearance, fortitude, non-violence, equanimity, truthfulness,
uprightness, mastery over the senses, dexterity, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness.

Freedom from wretchedness, absence of agitation, contentment, pleasant speech, lack of desire to know others' faults, and freedom from envy— the combination of these constitutes self-restraint (*dama*),
O Kauravya, as well as reverence for teachers, compassion toward all beings, and absence of backbiting.
Gossip is false speech; one should avoid praise and blame.
Desire, anger, greed, pride, arrogance, boastfulness, delusion, envy, and contempt—being self-controlled, one does not indulge in these.
For a man who is blameless, free from desire, moderate in his wishes, and free from malice is like the ocean; he is never filled.
"I am in you, and you are in me; I am also in them."

Because of his connection with former associates, the self-controlled man does not indulge in these; likewise, he who does not resort to any worldly activities— whether pertaining to the village or the forest—
nor to blame or praise, is liberated.
Furthermore, for one who is friendly, endowed with virtue, possessed of good companions,
and liberated from various attachments, there is a great fruit after death.
One who is well-conducted, perfected in virtue, serene in soul, a knower of the self, and wise—
Having obtained honor in this world, he attains a happy rebirth. Whatever action is auspicious here and whatever is practiced by the virtuous—
that very dharma of the sage endowed with knowledge does not decline.
Having departed from home and established himself in the forest, endowed with knowledge and having conquered his senses,
one who lives thus awaiting his time is fit for becoming Brahman. He from whom all beings have no fear, and from whom all beings have no fear— [he is truly liberated].
For him who is liberated from the body, there is no fear from any quarter whatsoever.
He wears away his past actions and does not accumulate new ones;
equal toward all beings, he should move about with a disposition of friendliness.
Just as the path of birds in the sky or of aquatic creatures in the water cannot be seen, so too his path is not perceived; of this there is no doubt,
O King, for he who, having abandoned his home, pursues only liberation.
For him, worlds consisting of light are prepared for eternal years.
Having renounced all ritual actions, having renounced austerity according to rule,
having renounced various branches of knowledge, and indeed having renounced everything—
Not turning back from sense-objects, with a serene self, knowing the Self, and pure,
he receives honor in this world and attains heaven;
and that which is the station of the Grandfather (Brahmā), arising from the mass of Brahman.

That which is eternally concealed within the cave [of the heart] is attained through self-restraint. For the Buddha who delights in knowledge and is non-hostile toward all beings, there is no fear of returning to this world; how then could there be fear in the next world?
There is only one fault in self-restraint; a second does not exist:
that people consider one who is endowed with forgiveness to be weak. But, O man of great wisdom, this very fault possesses a most great virtue.
In the earth, vast worlds are indeed easily attained by one who is patient. O Bhārata, what need has the self-controlled man for a forest, and likewise, what need has the uncontrolled man?
For wherever a self-controlled man dwells, that is the forest and that is the hermitage.
12,154.037 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard these words of Bhīṣma, King Yudhiṣṭhira became as delighted as if he were satiated with nectar.
And once again he questioned Bhīṣma, the best among the upholders of dharma; O perpetuator of the Kuru race, he then told him everything concerning asceticism. Bhīṣma said:
12,155.001 All this, the wise declare, has its root in austerity (tapas). For a deluded person who has not practiced austerity does not obtain the fruit of his actions.
12,155.002 By austerity alone did the Lord Prajāpati create all this.
In the same way, the seers attained the Vedas through austerity;
for by means of austerity, practiced in due succession while subsisting on fruits, roots, and air,
those perfected ones, being well-composed, behold the three worlds through their ascetic power.

Medicines such as antidotes and the three refined branches of knowledge are indeed accomplished through austerity alone; for austerity is the root of all means of attainment. Whatever is difficult to obtain, difficult to learn, difficult to overcome, or difficult to endure—[all this is achieved through austerity].
All that can be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
A drinker of spirits, a thief of what is not given, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
a man is liberated from such sin by means of well-performed austerity alone.
12.155.007 For austerity, which manifests through various means and proceeds by various doors,
there is no austerity superior to abstention from food.
12.155.008 Non-violence, truthful speech, charity, and restraint of the senses—
"O Great King, for among these, there is no austerity superior to fasting.

There is nothing more difficult than giving, nor is there any stage of life (*āśrama*) higher than that of the mother. There is nothing superior to those who possess the three Vedas; renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is the highest austerity."
In this world, people guard their senses for the protection of wealth and grain;
therefore, for the sake of both material prosperity and dharma, there is no austerity superior to fasting.
The seers, the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and the best of beasts [all depend upon it].
And whatever other beings there are, both stationary and moving—
whether they be stationary beings or others that move—
all of them, being devoted to austerity, attain perfection through austerity.
Thus, by means of austerity, the gods attained greatness;
these desired divisions of rewards are always obtained through austerity. Indeed, even the status of a deity can certainly be attained through austerity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Brahmin-sages, the ancestors, and the gods praise truth as dharma.
O Grandfather, I wish to hear about truth; tell that to me."
"O King, what is the characteristic of truth, and how is it attained? What results from attaining truth, and how is it defined? Bhīṣma said:
The confusion of the duties of the four social orders is not praised;
O Bhārata, truth is the most unchanging among all classes.
Therefore, O Bhārata, truth is the most excellent among all classes.
Truth is always the dharma among the virtuous; truth is the eternal dharma. One should indeed bow to truth alone, for truth is the supreme goal.
Truth is dharma, austerity, and yoga; truth is the eternal Brahman.
Truth is declared to be the supreme sacrifice; everything is established upon truth.
Here, I shall duly describe the practices of truth in their proper sequence, as well as the characteristics of truth here in their correct order.
For truth is indeed attained; you ought to hear how that is so. O Bhārata, truth is of thirteen kinds throughout all the worlds, as are equanimity and self-restraint—of this there is no doubt.
O Indra among kings, non-avarice, forbearance, modesty, endurance, freedom from malice,
renunciation, meditation, nobility, constant steadfastness,
and non-violence— these are the thirteen forms of truth.
Truth is indeed imperishable, eternal, and likewise unchanging;
it is not in conflict with any dharma and is attained through yoga.
Furthermore, there is equanimity toward what is desired, what is undesired, and toward an enemy alike.
Having attained the destruction of desire and hatred, as well as the destruction of lust and anger,
self-restraint, lack of longing for others, constant fortitude, and indeed profundity—
fearlessness and the quelling of anger— are all acquired through knowledge.
The wise declare that non-avarice is generosity, and self-restraint is the practice of Dharma.
One who is constantly established in truth shall become free from envy. [One should understand] the lack of forbearance and forbearance, as well as what is pleasant and unpleasant in this world.
The virtuous person is patient toward all; the speaker of truth attains what is good. The modest person performs deeds of excellence and never boasts.
Always tranquil in speech and mind, such modesty is indeed obtained through righteousness (*dharma*).
For the sake of the Dharma and its purpose, one endures; this endurance is called *kṣānti*.
For the sake of gathering the world, however, it is attained through fortitude. Furthermore, freedom from envy is profundity; this is obtained through generosity.

The relinquishing of affection and likewise the relinquishing of sense objects—such relinquishment belongs to one who has abandoned passion and hatred, and not otherwise. It is said that meditation is freedom from deceit; this is attained through silence.

Nobility (*āryatā*) consists in one who, with diligent effort, performs auspicious action for living beings, remaining formless and free from passion. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is that by which one undergoes no transformation of state in pleasure or pain.

A wise man who desires his own welfare should always cultivate that [patience]. In every way, one should be patient and likewise devoted to truth; free from joy, fear, and anger, the learned man attains steadfastness.
Non-malice toward all beings in action, thought, and speech,
as well as benevolence and charity— this is the eternal dharma of the virtuous.
These thirteen forms are distinct, yet each has truth as its sole defining characteristic.
O Bhārata, they resort to truth alone in this world and cause it to increase. Indeed, O Bhārata, it is impossible to state the limit of the qualities of truth;
therefore, the Brahmins, together with the ancestors and the gods, praise truth.
There is no dharma higher than truth, and no sin greater than falsehood.
For truth is the foundation of dharma; therefore, one should not violate the truth. Indeed, from truth come both generosity and sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees.
Vows, the agnihotra sacrifice, the Vedas, and whatever other certainties of dharma there may be—
a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once placed upon a scale.
Indeed, truth outweighed even a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: O bull of the Bharatas, from what do anger and desire originate,
as well as grief, delusion, the desire to know, lethargy, and pride?
"12,157.002a Greed, stinginess, envy, censure, malice, and likewise compassion—
12,157.002c explain all of this to me exactly as it is, O one of great wisdom. 12,157.003 Bhīṣma said:
These thirteen are known as the exceedingly powerful enemies of living beings; indeed,
all these thirteen are considered the enemies of living beings,
O Great King, and they all attend upon men here in this world.
These are indeed known as the enemies of living beings who are possessed by greed. For these, ever-vigilant, drive away the heedless man;
like wolves, they seize and devour him as soon as they see one who is other than a man.
"From these proceeds suffering; from these proceeds evil"—
thus should a mortal always understand, O bull among the Bharatas,
