O best of men, the origin, the abiding place, and the destruction of these.
"Come now, I shall explain this to you; listen as I speak it to you. O Lord of the Earth, hear the origin of anger from the beginning, according to its true nature."
From greed, O King, anger arises; it is provoked by the faults of others. It subsides through forgiveness, and the illustrious one turns away from it.
Desire is born from mental construction; when indulged in, it increases.
When the wise man desists, then [envy] perishes immediately;
malice, anger, and greed are released from within. Through compassion for all beings, he turns away from world-weariness.
For the wise, [this doubt] departs through the perception of faults and through the knowledge of reality. For those of small intelligence perceive here that the scriptures are contradictory;
thus, a desire to know arises therein, which ceases upon the attainment of the knowledge of reality.
For that embodied being, sorrow arises from joy when it is separated from it;
when he realizes that [joy] is useless, it perishes immediately.
Delusion originates from ignorance and proceeds from the habitual practice of evil.
When one delights in the wise, then [that state] perishes immediately. The desire for death arises from anger, greed, and habitual practice;
it ceases through compassion for all beings and through world-weariness.

Through the abandonment of living beings, one becomes stingy and indulges in harmful things; however, O dear one, this is diminished by attending upon the virtuous. Likewise, pride arises in embodied beings from their lineage, knowledge, and power.
When these very things are understood, intoxication perishes instantly.
O Bhārata, envy arises from desire and from rivalry;
for other mortals, however, it is destroyed by wisdom.
O King, contempt arises from the confused and incoherent words of those who are excluded from the world and are full of hatred; it is pacified by indifference toward one who,
being powerful, inflicts harm that cannot be retaliated against.
Intense envy arises [from this], yet it ceases through compassion;
seeing those who are constantly miserable, pity is then born. Greed, which originates from ignorance, is always observed among living beings.
Seeing and knowing the instability of enjoyments, one turns away;
when one knows the culmination of the Dharma, then that compassion is stilled. They say these very [qualities] are conquered through tranquility, and thus there are thirteen.
"For all these thirteen faults of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra have been eternally conquered by you with your whole being, and you shall conquer them yet again.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, through the constant observation of the virtuous, I understand compassion; yet I do not understand the cruel, nor their deeds.
Just as men avoid thorns, a pit, and fire,"
In this way, men avoid a man who performs cruel deeds;
for a cruel man, O Bhārata, is always base both in this world and after death.
Therefore, O Kauravya, speak the definitive judgment regarding his dharma.
Bhīṣma said:
He who harbors secret desires, whose intentions are known through his actions, who reviles and is himself reviled, and who binds and is himself bound— [such a person is truly one with the world].
One who boasts of gifts received, one who is perverse, mean, dishonest, and deceitful; one who does not share, one who is proud, as well as one who is addicted to company and a boaster;
one who suspects everyone, one who is harsh, foolish, and likewise miserly.

Constantly praising his own lineage, he is ever hostile toward the stages of life (āśramas) and promotes their confusion; he constantly delights in violence, indifferent to the distinction between virtue and vice;
full of deceit, yet self-important, he is excessively greedy and a perpetrator of cruel deeds.
One who is of virtuous character and endowed with good qualities is perceived as "evil" by another;
through the inference of one's own character, such a person trusts no one.
Wherever there may be a fault in others, he reveals that which should be kept secret.
Even when the faults are identical, he would ruin [the other] for the sake of his own livelihood;
likewise, he considers even a benefactor to be a supreme deceiver,
and having given wealth at the proper time to a benefactor, he later feels regret.
Whether it be food to be chewed, food to be swallowed, food to be licked, or any other wholesome meal,
he who eats while others are looking on is known as a cruel man.
But he who, having first given the best portion to the Brahmins, eats together with his friends, is righteous.
Having departed this life, he attains heaven, and in this world, he enjoys infinity.
O best of the Bharatas, this cruel man has been described to you;
indeed, he must always be avoided by a man who desires prosperity.
Bhīṣma said:
One who has accomplished his purpose, one who intends to perform a sacrifice, one who has mastered all the Vedāntas,
or one who seeks wealth for the sake of his teacher, his father, or his wife, or even for the sake of Vedic study— [these may accept gifts].

"These indeed are seen to be the virtuous Brahmins who beg for the sake of dharma; to these, who possess no property of their own, gifts should be given according to the excellence of their knowledge.
But in other cases, O best of the Bharatas, that which is a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given."
For it is ordained that no food unprepared [for the sacrifice] should be placed outside the sacrificial altar for others; the king should bestow all kinds of jewels according to their merit,
as indeed the Brāhmaṇas and the sacrifices are accompanied by food and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
O King, those who vie with one another always perform sacrifices according to their respective qualities.
He whose provisions for three years are sufficient to maintain his dependents,
or even more than that, is worthy to drink the Soma.

If a sacrifice of a sacrificer should be deficient by even a single limb— especially in the case of a Brāhmaṇa while a righteous king is ruling— a Vaiśya who possesses many cattle but lacks the performance of sacrifices and does not drink Soma [should be made to perform it].
The king may take that wealth from his household for the sake of the sacrifice;
he may take whatever he desires from the property of a Śūdra from his house,
for there is no [independent] possession whatsoever belonging to a Śūdra in his home.
O Lord, if there is one who possesses a hundred cows but has not maintained the sacred fires, and another who possesses a thousand cows but has not performed sacrifices—
the king should, after having made a proclamation, constantly take [wealth] from the households of these two without hesitation. He should always take it from those who do not give.
For in this way, O King, the entire dharma of one who practices it shall be fulfilled.
Likewise, having fasted for six meals, at the time of the seventh meal,
one may take what is required for the next day from a person of low conduct who follows no prescribed rule.
Whether it comes from a threshing floor, a field, a house, or wherever else it may arise,
this must be reported to the king— whether he asks or does not ask.
A king who knows the Dharma should not impose a fine upon him in accordance with the law.
For it is through the folly of a Kṣatriya that a Brāhmaṇa suffers from hunger; having recognized his learning and character, one should provide him with a livelihood and protect him,
just as a father protects his own biological son.
One should always perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice at the end of each year;
it is the ancient dharma, free from alternative options, though it is merely proclaimed by those who discourse on dharma.
This was established by the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great ṛṣis.
In times of distress, those fearing death have created a substitute for the [sacred] marks. He who, though capable of following the primary rule, conducts himself according to a secondary rule—
no fruit pertaining to the next world exists for that person of evil intellect.

No man should inform the king against Brāhmaṇas; for one who reports them loses his own vigor, while one of great vigor finds even greater vigor in them. Therefore, the splendor of those who discourse on the Veda is always difficult for a king to withstand.
The one who is a thinker, a teacher, and an ordainer—the Brāhmaṇa—is called a god. One should not speak anything unwholesome to him, nor should one utter harsh speech.
A Kṣatriya overcomes his own misfortune through the strength of his arms.
A Vaiśya and a Śūdra [serve] through wealth; a twice-born man, indeed, through mantras and burnt offerings.
Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one ignorant of mantras, nor a child, nor likewise one who has not undergone the initiatory rites (asaṃskṛta) may be the attendant of the Agnihotra fire.

12,159.020 These fall into hell, as does he for whom they perform the sacrifice while offering oblations; therefore, the *hotṛ* priest should be skilled in the sacrificial rites and one who has mastered the Vedas.
12,159.021 Without having given the horse dedicated to Prajāpati as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), [one falls].
"He is called 'one who has not maintained the sacred fires' by those who perceive the Dharma.
One should perform other meritorious acts with faith and with senses subdued;
one should never, under any circumstances, sacrifice with sacrifices that lack sacrificial fees."
For a sacrifice without a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) destroys offspring, cattle, and heaven;
it cuts away one's senses, fame, renown, and lifespan.
Indeed, those who sit with a woman in her courses, and whoever are without the sacred fires, [are likewise excluded].
Those whose family lacks a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) are all subject to the laws of the *śūdra*.
A Brāhmaṇa who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* (low-caste woman) and lives in a village where water is drawn from a single well,
having resided there for twelve years, goes here to the state of a *śūdra*.
If a man supports an ignoble woman on his bed, or abandons one while supporting her, or considers himself no longer a Brahmin, he should sit behind some grass;
in this way, O King, he is purified— listen now to these words of mine.
Whatever sin a Brahmin commits by associating with one of black complexion for a single night,
he who observes the vow must wander about, subsisting only on standing and sitting.
One may pacify one's own sin within three years.
O King, a word spoken in jest does no harm, nor does one spoken toward women, nor at the time of marriage.
Neither for the sake of a teacher’s wealth nor for the sake of one's own life—
these five falsehoods they say are not sinful.
One who has faith should acquire auspicious knowledge even from a person of low status.

One may take even gold from an impure place; such is the established rule. One may take a jewel of a woman even from a base family, and one may drink nectar even from poison. For, according to the Dharma, women, jewels, and water are inherently pure.
For the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins, and in cases of the intermixture of castes,
a Vaiśya may indeed take up the bow for his own protection. [Likewise,
he may do so] in the event of drinking liquor, killing a Brāhmaṇa, or violating the bed of a Guru.
They consider these [offenses] to be indefinable and amounting to the end of life; this is the established doctrine.
Stealing gold, theft, association with outcastes, and mortal sin—likewise, consuming intoxicants while wandering about, as well as approaching women who should not be approached.
O Great King, through association with those who have fallen from their status, as well as by birth [from such],
one indeed becomes just like them before long;
by associating with a fallen person for a single year, one falls.

Not from officiating at sacrifices, teaching, or matrimonial alliance, but rather from sharing a vehicle, a seat, or food—these and other such things are to be avoided; this is the settled rule. By following the prescribed method, one shall remain free from addiction.
Food should not be offered obliquely during the rites for the deceased until [the funeral mound] has been cast down;
however, regarding these three aforementioned cases, one should not hesitate.
A righteous man may even abandon his ministers or his teachers for the sake of dharma.
One ought not to associate with those who do not perform penance. An evildoer destroys his sin through righteousness and austerity;
by calling a thief a "thief," one incurs as much sin as the thief himself.

By calling a non-thief a thief, one incurs double the sin; by calling a thief a non-thief, one incurs an equal amount of guilt. A girl who becomes defiled incurs a third part of the sin of killing a Brahmin.

But he who defiles her incurs the remainder of the sin. In this world, having merely threatened a Brāhmaṇa, the evil man remains for a hundred years without finding a firm footing; if he has actually touched him, his condition becomes even more grievous.
Indeed, having struck [another] in hell for a thousand years, he shall dwell there;
therefore, one should never even threaten [another], nor should one ever strike them down.
For as many particles of dust as the blood from a twice-born man's wound might collect—
For that many years, O King, he wanders in hell;
however, the killer of an embryo is purified by being struck down with a weapon in the midst of battle,
for he purifies himself by offering his own self as an oblation into the kindled fire.
A drinker of *surā*, having drunk hot *vāruṇī* liquor, is liberated from sin. When his body has been consumed by that [liquor] and he dies, he becomes pure after death;
thus the Brahmin attains the higher worlds, for he does not attain them otherwise.

Having violated the bed of his guru, that evil-souled man of sinful intent is purified by death after embracing a glowing iron image (sūrmī). Alternatively, having himself taken out his penis and testicles with his joined palms, he is purified.
Taking his stand in the southwest direction, he should fall [into the fire] moving straight forward;
or else, he may sacrifice his life for the sake of a Brahmin, by which he is purified;
or again, by performing the Aśvamedha or even the Gomedha sacrifice.

By means of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, one is indeed completely purified both in this world and after death. Likewise, for twelve years, the slayer of a Brahmin shall carry a skull-bowl and live as a mendicant, practicing celibacy and wandering as a sage while proclaiming his own deed.
Thus, one who is endowed with such austerity becomes a performer of the *savana* sacrifice even if he has killed a Brahmin;

likewise, he who approaches an unknown fetus or a woman of the Ātreya clan [becomes pure]. Indeed, the sin of killing a Brahmin is doubled in the case of the misfortune involving a woman of the Ātreya clan.
Restricting his food, observing celibacy, and practicing forgiveness, the drinker of *surā* should,
after three years, perform the *agniṣṭut* sacrifice. By giving away one thousand cows and one bull, he shall attain auspiciousness.
One should perform the six-fold penance for a Kṣatriya who has not been purified by initiation or consecration;
having killed a Vaiśya, however, one should give two years' worth of food and one hundred cows with a bull as the eleventh;
and having killed a Śūdra, one year's worth of food and eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh.
Having killed a dog, a barbarian, or a donkey, one should perform the very same vow as for a Śūdra. Having killed a cat, a blue jay, a frog, a crow, a vulture,
or a mouse, O King, the rule has been stated that the dharma is equal to that for killing a domestic animal, due to the taking of life.
Now I shall proclaim other penances in their proper sequence:

for lying on another's bed and for theft, one should perform the penance separately for one year; for the wife of a *śrotriya*, three years are prescribed, while for the wife of another man, two years are ordained.
Eating at the fourth time [of the day], he should be a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) observing his vows.
He should pass his time by alternating between standing and sitting, and three times a day he should rise and sip water.
By conducting himself in this very manner, O King, he is liberated from that sin.

In the same way, O Kauravya, he who fails to perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he who casts away the sacred fires, and he who abandons his father or mother without cause— such a person becomes an outcast; this is the settled rule regarding dharma.

"One should give food and clothing in abundance; this is the instruction. A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), having given to the twice-born, is liberated from sin—especially when his wife has been unfaithful and is kept under restraint."

Whatever penance is prescribed for men who commit adultery with the wives of others, that same vow the king should cause her to perform. If a woman, abandoning a superior man on her bed, seeks out one who is inferior,
the king should have her devoured by dogs in a crowded public place.
A wise man should have the male bound upon a red-hot iron bed;
he may even place logs there, so that the evildoer may be consumed by fire.
This, O Great King, is the punishment for women who transgress against their husbands.
For one who has been accused for twelve years, the penance for a wicked man shall be double.
For two years it is that same [penance]; for three years for one who associates with such people; and for four years, the wanderer (kucara) should subsist on alms, observing the vow of a sage.
The elder brother who is superseded, the younger brother who supersedes him, the woman by whom he is superseded,
and the one who takes her hand— all these are declared fallen according to dharma;
all of them must observe the same vow as the killer of a hero.
For the purification of such sin, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for a month or the Kṛcchra penance.

The younger brother who has married before his elder (the *parivettṛ*) shall give that daughter-in-law back to the elder (*parivitti*), provided he is permitted by the elder to marry again immediately thereafter.
By this, she and both of them obtain liberation from sin according to dharma.
Among non-human females, with the exception of cows, there is no fault in lack of rain [for conception].
They know that man to be the presiding consumer of animals.
Having put on a garment with the hair turned upward and taking an earthen vessel,
he should go for alms to seven houses, proclaiming his own deed. Eating only what is obtained there, he becomes purified after twelve days.
He should observe for a year that very vow which is prescribed for the *nirākṛti* offense;
such is the supreme expiation among human beings. Or, in the case of those addicted to taking what is not given, one should prescribe every form of gift-giving as the penance.
Among those who do not believe in the afterlife, they declare that the life-force consists of a single cow.
Having consumed the flesh, urine, or excrement of a dog, a pig, a human, a cock, or a donkey, one deserves a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).
Having smelled the breath of a Brāhmaṇa who drinks liquor, a Soma-drinker shall drink hot water for three days, drink hot milk for three days,
and having drunk hot ghee for three days, he shall subsist on air for three days.
12,159.072a Thus has this eternal penance been declared;
12,159.072c it arises specifically for a Brāhmaṇa through the knowledge of reality.
12,160.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
Then, finding an opportunity in the course of conversation, Nakula, who was skilled in sword-fighting,
spoke thus to his grandfather as he lay upon the bed of arrows:
"O Grandfather, there is a saying that the bow is the supreme weapon."
"But in my opinion, O knower of dharma, it is a well-sharpened sword alone [that is the means].
O King, when the bow is shattered and the horses are exhausted,
one is able to protect oneself effectively in battle with a sword."
Even against those bearing bows, as well as those wielding maces and spears,
a single hero armed with a sword is capable of resisting them.
In this matter, I have both doubt and great curiosity.
"O King, what indeed is the most excellent weapon among all weapons in battle?
How was the sword produced, for what purpose, and by whom?
And tell us, O Great-Grandfather, who was the first teacher of the sword?"
Having heard those words of the wise son of Mādrī—
words endowed with every skill, subtle, of variegated meaning, auspicious,
and articulated with perfect tone and phonetics— he then spoke this reply.
To the disciple of Droṇa who questioned him regarding the rules and methods of training,

Bhīṣma— who was fully accomplished in the science of instruction, knew all dharmas, and had reached the further shore of the science of archery— spoke from his bed of arrows to the high-souled Nakula.
"O son of Mādrī, listen to the truth regarding that which you ask. I have been awakened by you, like a mountain rich in minerals.
My dear one, in the past, all this was a single ocean of water."
There, amidst that which was motionless, devoid of space, with an indescribable surface,
enveloped in darkness, intangible, of unfathomable depth,
silent, and immeasurable, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) was born.
Like the unmanifest, beyond the *guṇas*, and devoid of the activity of karma, a lotus appeared; from that, the Grandfather was born.
That heroic one then created wind, fire, and the sun.
He created the sky above and the earth below, together with the region of Nirṛti;
he likewise created the atmosphere with the moon and stars, the constellations, and the planets;
and he created the years, days and nights, the seasons, as well as the *lava*s and *kṣaṇa*s.
Then, having established his body within the worlds, the blessed Grandfather procreated sons of supreme splendor:
the sage Marīci, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu.
Both Vasiṣṭha and Aṅgiras, as well as the lord Rudreśvara, [were present].
Likewise, Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, begot sixty daughters;
all those brahman-sages took them for the sake of progeny.
From them [proceeded] all beings: the gods, the hosts of ancestors,
as well as Gandharvas and Apsarases, various kinds of Rākṣasas, birds,
wild animals, fish, monkeys, and great serpents.

Others of various forms and strengths move upon the water and the earth; O dear one, thus was born the entire world, both stationary and moving— beings born from sprouts, born from sweat, born from eggs, and born from wombs.
Having created this evolution of beings, the Grandfather of all the worlds again established the eternal dharma recited in the Vedas;
the gods, together with their teachers and domestic priests, remained steadfast in that dharma.
The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, along with the Sādhyas, Maruts, and Aśvins;
Bhṛgu, Atri, and Aṅgiras, the Siddhas, and Kāśyapa whose wealth is asceticism;
Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Agastya, as well as Nārada and Parvata.
The Vālakhilya sages, the Prabhāsas, the Sikatas,
as well as the Ghṛtācas, Somavāyavyas, Vaikhānasas, Marīcipas,
the Akṛṣṭas, the Haṃsas, and the sages born from the fire.
The Vānaprasthas and the Pṛśnis remained established in the instruction of Brahmā;
but the lords of the Dānavas, having transgressed that command of the Grandfather and being possessed by anger and greed, brought about the decline of Dharma.
Hiraṇyakaśipu, Hiraṇyākṣa, Virocana,
Śambara, Vipracitti, Prahrāda, Namuci, and Bali—
these and many other Daityas and Dānavas together with their hosts [were there].
Having transgressed the bridge of dharma, those resolved upon unrighteousness took their pleasure;
"We are all of equal birth, just as the gods are,"—
adopting this as their rationale, they vied with the celestial sages.

O Bhārata, they showed neither kindness nor compassion toward living beings; having bypassed the three other means, they oppressed the subjects with punishment alone. Out of pride, those foremost of Asuras did not even enter into agreements with them.
Then indeed the blessed Lord Brahmā was attended by the Brahman-sages on the most delightful plateau of the Himavat,
which was strewn with clusters of lotuses and covered with heaps of jewels and pearls, extending for a hundred yojanas.
O son, on that excellent mountain with its forests of flowering trees,
Brahmā, the best of the gods, remained for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world. Then, at the end of a thousand years, the Lord prepared a sacrificial canopy.
It was performed according to the ritual prescribed by the Kalpa-sūtras as previously declared,
duly carried out by sages skilled in sacrifice who were experts in the performance of rites; it was overspread by the Maruts and illuminated by blazing fires.
Adorned with radiant golden sacrificial vessels and surrounded by hosts of gods, the sacrificial circle shone brightly;
likewise, it was graced by Brahman-sages serving as members of the assembly.
12,160.036c There, I have heard from the sages about a most terrible event.
12,160.037a Just as the moon rises into the stainless sky filled with stars, 12,160.037c so it is heard that a being then rose up, having rent asunder the fire.
Having the luster of the color of a blue lotus, with sharp fangs and a lean belly, he was tall,
difficult to behold, and possessed of exceeding brilliance;
and as he sprang up, the earth trembled.
There the great ocean, with its turbulent waves and whirlpools, was greatly agitated;
meteors fell as great portents, and trees shed their branches. All the quarters of the sky became gloomy, and an inauspicious wind blew.
Again and again, living beings were thus greatly distressed by fear.
Then, seeing that most tumultuous and wonderful event occurring,
the Grandfather spoke these words to the great seers, gods, and gandharvas:
"This which has been conceived by me is real; this is the powerful one named Asis (the Sword), for the protection of the world and for the slaughter of the enemies of the gods.
Then, casting off that form, he shone forth as a mere blade.
Stainless and with a sharp edge, it was raised like the Destroyer at the end of time.
Then Brahmā gave that blazing sword, which wards off unrighteousness, to Rudra, the blue-throated one whose banner bears the bull.
Then the blessed Lord Rudra, praised by the hosts of Brahman-sages,
that immeasurable soul, grasping his sword, assumed another form;
with four arms, though standing upon the earth, he touched the vault of heaven with his head.
With his gaze directed upward and his great *liṅga* manifest, he emitted flames from his mouth;
transforming himself in many ways, he displayed colors that were blue, pale-white, and red,
wearing a black antelope skin as a garment adorned with excellent golden stars.
One eye, resembling the sun, was upon his great forehead;
and his two stainless eyes, black and tawny, shone brilliantly.
Then the god Mahādeva, wielder of the trident and destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, appeared.
Grasping his sword, which resembled the sun at the end of time or a blazing fire,
and brandishing his triple-layered shield like a cloud charged with lightning,
he of great strength and prowess moved through various maneuvers.
O Bhārata, as he brandished his sword in the sky with the desire to bring an end to the Dānavas, the terrifying form of Rudra shone forth as he let out a roar and broke into a great laugh.
Seeing Rudra assuming that form, all the Dānavas, desiring to perform their fierce deeds, rushed toward him with joy;
they rained down stones as well as blazing torches.
With other terrible weapons, sharp-edged and iron-tipped,
that host of Dānavas— shaken by the power of Rudra’s sword and led by the infallible Acyuta— reeled and fell into a swoon.
Seeing him moving with such extreme speed, wielding his sword, and appearing so wondrous,
all the Asuras thought that single warrior was a thousand.
He continued cutting, piercing, crushing, slicing, tearing, and even violently crushing [his foes].
12,160.055c Rudra moved among the hosts of Daityas like a fire in dry grass.
12,160.056a Crushed by the force of his sword, with their arms, thighs, and chests severed,
12,160.056c and their heads cut off, those great Asuras fell upon the earth.
12,160.057a Other Dānavas, broken and oppressed by the blows of Rudra,
12,160.057c cried out to one another and fled in all directions.
12,160.058a Some entered the earth, and others likewise took refuge in the mountains.
Some went into the sky, while others entered the waters.
When that great and exceedingly fierce battle had taken place,
the earth then appeared terrifying, mired in blood.
O mighty-armed one,
the earth, drenched with blood and strewn with the massive, gore-soaked bodies of the Dānavas, then shone like a mountain covered with kiṃśuka trees.
Like a dark-complexioned woman intoxicated with passion, her garments wet with blood;
having slain the Dānavas and made the world preeminent in righteousness, that Rudra, the Auspicious One,
quickly abandoned his fierce form and assumed a benign appearance.
Then all the great ṛṣis and all the hosts of gods honored the God of gods with a victory of wondrous character. Thereupon,
the blessed Lord Rudra [beheld him] drenched in the blood of the Dānavas.
He gave the sword, the protector of Dharma, to Viṣṇu with due honor;
Viṣṇu gave it to Marīci, and the venerable Marīci gave that sword to the great ṛṣis, while the ṛṣis gave it to Vāsava.
Mahendra gave it to the world-protectors, and the world-protectors, O son, gave that broad-sword to Manu, the son of the Sun.
And they spoke thus to him, the first of men: "You are the lord of human beings."
"Protect the subjects with the sword that contains the essence of Dharma.
Those who have transgressed the bridge of Dharma— whether for the sake of subtle or gross matters—
should be protected by administering punishment according to the law, having distinguished the offense, and not according to one's own whim.
12.160.069a Punishment for harsh speech consists of a fine of abundant gold, 12.160.069c as well as mutilation of the body or execution, provided there is no minor cause [for such severity].
12.160.070a One should designate these forms— harsh speech and the rest— as belonging to the sword.
The measures of the sword are twelve thousand, sixteen thousand, and seven hundred and ten, due to the exceeding of its dimensions. Then, having empowered his own son as the sovereign of subjects,
Manu gave the sword to Kṣupa for the protection of the people.
From Kṣupa, Ikṣvāku received it; from Ikṣvāku, Purūravas; and from him, Āyu obtained it. From him, Nahuṣa received it on earth;
and from Nahuṣa, Yayāti; and from him, Pūru obtained it.
From him came Āmūrtarayasa; from him, O King, came Bhūmiśaya, who bestowed [the kingdom] upon Gaya;
and from Gaya, the king obtained it.
Bharata, the son of Duḥṣanta, also obtained the sword from Bhūmiśaya;
and from him, O King, the righteous Aiḍabiḍa likewise received it. And from Aiḍabiḍa, Dhundhumāra, the lord of men, obtained it.
From Dhundhumāra, Kāmboja obtained it, and from him Mucukunda received it;
from Mucukunda, Marutta, and from Marutta, Raivata; from Raivata, Yuvanāśva, and from Yuvanāśva, Raghu.
From him was born the powerful Hariṇāśva, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage; from Hariṇāśva, Śunaka obtained the sword, and from Śunaka,
the righteous-souled Uśīnara, as well as the Bhojas and the Yādavas.
Śibi received it from the Yadus, and Pratardana received it from Śibi; Aṣṭaka received it from Pratardana, and Ruśadaśva received it from Aṣṭaka;
Bharadvāja received it from Ruśadaśva, Droṇa from him, and Kṛpa from him.
Then, together with your brothers, you obtained the supreme sword.
The Kṛttikās are the lunar mansion of this sword, and Agni is its deity;
Rohiṇī is its lineage, and Rudra is its supreme preceptor.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, learn from me these eight secret names of the sword, by constantly reciting which one obtains victory:
Asis, Viśasana, Khaḍga, Tīkṣṇavartman, and Durāsada."
Śrīgarbha, Vijaya, and likewise Dharmapāla;
and the sword, the foremost of weapons, [was held] by the son of Mādravatī,
who had reached a firm conviction through the Purāṇa proclaimed by Maheśvara.
12,160.083 These names, indeed, were determined in the Purāṇa.
12,160.084 O subduer of enemies, Pṛthu produced the primordial bow;
by means of it, this earth was milked of very abundant crops.
"And according to the Dharma as it was in former times,
this earth was formerly protected by Vainya; therefore,
O son of Madri, you ought to accept this authority of the seers."
"12,160.085c Worship of the sword must always be performed by those skilled in battle.
12,160.086a Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, this first section has been explained to you in great detail: the origin and the application of the sword, exactly as they are."
12,160.087a Having heard this supreme method for the accomplishment of the sword (khaḍgasādhana) here in every respect, 12,160.087c a man attains fame and, after death, enjoys infinity.
12,161.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
When Bhīṣma had spoken thus and become silent, Yudhiṣṭhira,
taking the opportunity, questioned his brothers, with Vidura as the fifth,
regarding how the conduct of the world is properly established in virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
Among these, which is the heaviest, which is the middling, and which is the light?
Against what, indeed, should the self be restrained for the sake of conquering the three aims of life? O you who are contented, you ought to speak words of definitive truth as it truly is.
Then Vidura, who knew the truth regarding the course of affairs and was possessed of ready wit, spoke these words, recollecting the treatises on dharma:
"Extensive learning, austerity, renunciation, faith, the performance of sacrifice, and forgiveness— "

Purity of being, compassion, truthfulness, and self-restraint are the perfections of the self. Devote yourself to these alone; let not your mind waver. For these are the roots of dharma and artha, and this is the single path to well-being.
By dharma alone have the sages crossed over; by dharma the worlds are established.
By dharma the gods dwell in heaven, and in dharma is purpose (artha) contained. O King, dharma is the highest quality; artha is said to be intermediate.
The wise declare that desire is the youngest [of the senses];
therefore, one should be self-restrained and prioritize dharma.
Likewise, one should behave toward all living beings as one would toward oneself.
When he had finished speaking, Pārtha, who was skilled in the treatises on statecraft and knew the true meaning of speech, spoke these words without weariness:
"O King, this is the land of action; here, the means of livelihood (vārttā) is praised."
Agriculture, trade, cattle-rearing, and various crafts—
these constitute "wealth" (artha), and there is no deviation from this for all these activities.
According to the sacred tradition (śruti), neither dharma nor kāma can exist without wealth.

For one who is victorious and possesses wealth is able to practice the highest dharma and to pursue desire— that which is difficult for those of undisciplined soul to attain. According to the sacred tradition (*śruti*), both dharma and desire are branches of wealth (*artha*).
For when there is fulfillment through the accomplishment of one's purpose, both of these will come to pass: indeed,
beings of superior birth constantly attend upon a man who has achieved his goal,
just as all creatures attend upon Brahmā.
Wearing matted hair and deerskins, self-controlled, smeared with mud, and having conquered their senses,
some dwell apart as seekers of their own goals— shaven-headed and without possessions;
while others, clad in saffron robes, bearded, and well-restrained by modesty, [dwell likewise].

The wise, peaceful, and liberated from all possessions, are ever seekers of the true goal; they do not suffer on account of their actions. Among those seekers of the goal, some others are those who long for heaven.
Some follow their respective ancestral traditions, each established in their own path;
there are both believers and non-believers, all firmly restrained in supreme self-control.
Ignorance is characterized by darkness, whereas wisdom is luminosity.
"He who employs his servants with enjoyments and his enemies with punishments is truly wealthy.
This is my opinion, O best of the wise, stated exactly as it is. Now, however, listen to the words of these two eloquent speakers."
Then, immediately after, Nakula and Sahadeva, the two sons of Mādrī who were skilled in dharma and worldly affairs, spoke these further words:
"Whether sitting, lying down, walking about, or standing still,"
One should firmly establish the application of purpose even through various means, high and low.
When this [application] is well-perfected—being difficult to attain and most dear—one obtains all desires here in this very life; of this there is no doubt.

That purpose which is joined with dharma, and that dharma which is joined with purpose, are like honey mixed with nectar; therefore, these two are esteemed here. There is no desire for one who lacks purpose, and likewise, how can there be purpose for one who lacks dharma?
Therefore, the world is afraid of one who is excluded from dharma and artha.
Consequently, artha should be accomplished by one whose self is restrained and for whom dharma is paramount;
indeed, everything is possible when all beings have confidence in him.
One should first practice dharma, and likewise pursue artha in conjunction with dharma;
thereafter one should pursue kāma, for that is the fruit for one who has achieved artha.
Having spoken these words, those two sons of the Aśvins fell silent.
Then Bhīmasena proceeded to speak these words:
"One who lacks desire does not seek wealth; one who lacks desire does not wish for dharma;
even one who desires [other things] does not exist without desire. Therefore, desire is preeminent."
Rishis joined with desire are indeed absorbed in asceticism; subsisting on the fruits and roots of the *palāśa* tree, eating only air, and well-restrained,
others are devoted to the supplementary Vedic texts and have mastered their private recitation.
In the performance of *śrāddha* sacrifices and likewise in the giving and receiving of gifts,
merchants, farmers, cowherds, artisans, craftsmen,
and those who perform rites for the gods are engaged in their tasks according to their desire.

Others, possessed by desire, enter the ocean; for desire takes many forms, and everything is pervaded by desire. There has been nothing, there is nothing, and there will be nothing that exists apart from one whose soul is devoted to desire.
This is the essence, O Great King; here, Dharma and Artha are dependent upon it. Just as butter is [extracted] from curds, so is Kāma [derived] from Artha and Dharma.
Oil is better than oil-cake, and clarified butter is better than whey.
Desire is superior to virtue and wealth, just as flowers and fruit are superior to wood;
from desire happiness is born, like honey from flowers. Desire is the source of virtue and wealth, and it is also composed of them.
The Brahmins do not give their own food to other Brahmins without a motive;
they do not give wealth to the Brahmins without a motive;
nor do the various activities of the world occur without a motive.
Therefore, desire is seen as preceding the three goals of life [by means of women] who are beautifully attired, adorned,
intoxicated with passion, and sweet-spoken.
"Take your pleasure with women as you desire,
for desire, O King, strikes with speed.
This is my thought as I stand here in this assembly."
O Dharmaputra, let there be no hesitation in you;
having come together, let there be this supreme, compassionate speech, which is consistent with the virtuous and possesses unfailing essence.
Dharma, artha, and kāma should be pursued equally;
the man who pursues only one of them is base. For these three are always to be regarded without distinction.
They say that the middle [path] between the two is skillful; it is the best which, having divided time, is practiced while remaining devoted to the three aims of life.
The wise friend, anointed with the essence of sandalwood and adorned with various garlands and ornaments, then spoke these words concerning peace and war:
Having spoken thus, the younger Bhīma fell silent.
Then, after a moment, Dharmarāja, having reflected thoroughly upon their words, [spoke].
Smiling, he who was highly learned and the best among the upholders of dharma spoke these truthful words:
"Without doubt, those who have ascertained the treatises on dharma..."
All of you are well-acquainted with the authoritative scriptures; please listen to my words here as I seek to understand them, for I have heard that which is definitive.
12.161.041e But here, you must certainly listen with single-minded devotion even to these words as I speak them.
12.161.042a He who is indeed neither devoted to evil nor to merit;
A person who is free from defects, for whom a clod of earth and gold are equal, and who is neither attached to wealth, nor to dharma, nor to sensual pleasures—
he is liberated from the attainment of both suffering and happiness.
Beings are possessed of birth and death,
and are further accompanied by the transformations of old age;
moreover, they are repeatedly awakened by those various [conditions].
"They praise liberation, yet we do not know it; for one who is not bound by affection, those [defilements] do not exist"—
thus spoke the Blessed One, the Self-Existent.
The wise, intent upon nirvāṇa, declare this;
therefore, one should neither do what is pleasant nor what is unpleasant.
This is the primary principle, and not the doing of one's own will.
"I act exactly as I am appointed;
destiny appoints all beings. Know, all of you, that destiny is all-powerful."
One does not obtain through action that goal which is unattainable;
know that everything which is destined to be, shall be. For even one devoid of the three aims of life obtains his purpose.
Therefore, this secret has been spoken for the benefit of the world:
"Indeed, action alone is the cause of the fruit.
Thus, that supreme speech was pleasing to his mind;
Having then understood all of that with its profound reasons,
they cried out and rejoiced;
and they offered salutations with joined palms to the hero of the Kurus.
O King, having heard those words spoken by the son of Pṛthā— adorned with beautiful colors, syllables, and sounds; agreeable to the mind and free from the thorns of faulty speech— ;
Those lords of men indeed praised his speech;
and then the high-minded and heroic son of Dharma also praised them who were thus gratified.
Then again, he of undiminished courage questioned the son of the best of rivers regarding the dharma that follows from it,
for he was one who knew the definitive conclusions concerning dharma, artha, and kāma.
12,161.048f*0431_01 Yudhiṣṭhira, the protector of the Kuru lineage.
12,162.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
12,162.001a "O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O enhancer of the Kurus' fame!"
I shall pose a certain question; you ought to explain it to me:
What kind of men are gentle? With whom is supreme affection found? And who are those who are patient both in the future and in the present? Tell me that.

"For there is neither abundant wealth nor kinsmen and relatives there where friends abide; this is my conviction. Indeed, a friend who listens is hard to find, and a friend who provides what is beneficial is even harder to find."
"O best among the upholders of dharma, you ought to explain all of this.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, [I shall describe] those with whom one should form alliances and those with whom one should not, according to the truth."
Listen to me as I speak in its entirety, O Yudhiṣṭhira:
he who is greedy, cruel, abandoned by dharma, deceitful, and indeed treacherous; he who is base, of sinful conduct, suspicious of everyone, and likewise indolent.
One who is procrastinating, crooked, and difficult to deal with; one who violates the wife of his teacher;

one who abandons others in times of calamity; one who is evil-minded and shameless; one who perceives evil everywhere; an atheist who reviles the Vedas—[these are the characteristics of such a person].
He whose senses are scattered throughout the world, who wanders devoted to sensual desires,
is untruthful, hated by the world, unstable in his commitments, a slanderer, lacking wisdom, envious, and fixed in evil resolve.

One who is immoral, of undisciplined mind, cruel, and likewise a gambler; one who always seeks to exploit his friends for his own gain and is solely intent on wealth; and that dull-witted man who is not satisfied even when others carry their burdens to the best of their ability—[these are the types of men one should avoid].
O bull among men, he who always enjoys the friendship of a friend as if it were an enemy,
who becomes angry without cause and suddenly grows indifferent, and who quickly abandons his virtuous friends— that sinful man [is to be avoided].

O lord of men, a fool who, even when slighted or treated with ignorance, continues to serve his interests among friends while hating his true friends; one who is a friend in the guise of an enemy, looking askance and using seductive allurements— such a person is a foe.
He who would abandon such a man does not take pleasure even in what is auspicious:
one who drinks [intoxicants], who is hateful, cruel, pitiless, and harsh;
likewise, one who torments others, betrays friends, and delights in the slaughter of living beings.
An ungrateful person is the lowest in the world and should never, under any circumstances, be allied with.
One who seeks out vulnerabilities should not be allied with; now hear from me about those with whom one should ally.
They are those of noble birth, endowed with eloquence, and proficient in both theoretical knowledge and practical wisdom.
They were friends, wise, grateful, all-knowing, and free from sorrow; endowed with the quality of sweetness, devoted to truth, and masters of their senses;
they were constantly habituated to exertion, possessed sons, and were born of noble lineage.
Those who are handsome, endowed with virtues, free from greed, and have overcome fatigue; those who are devoid of well-known faults— such persons indeed should be accepted by the king,
O Lord, for the virtuous are satisfied by conduct that accords with their capacity.
They do not become angry at an improper time, nor do they lose their passion without cause; even when dispassionate, those who are skilled in worldly affairs do not grow wrathful even in their minds,
for they are devoted to the welfare of their friends even at the cost of afflicting themselves.
They do not turn away from their friends, like woolen cloth that has been dyed red;
nor do they reveal to their trusted friends the faults of wealth or young women, such as greed and delusion, for they are affectionate toward their kin.
Regarding clods of earth and gold as equal in value, possessing minds free from deceit toward friends,
they conduct themselves without pride, having renounced ornaments and wealth; always devoted to the interests of their master, they take care of their dependents.

The king who makes peace with such preeminent men finds his kingdom expand like the moonlight of the lord of the planets. They are constant in the sacred scriptures, have conquered anger, are powerful, and delight in battle.
Patient, endowed with the virtue of ethical conduct, and worthy of alliance—such are the best of men.
O King, a monarch who is devoid of a minister will have a short lifespan;
therefore, having recognized one who is of excellent character and widely learned as a minister, [one should appoint him].

One who desires his own happiness should employ that which produces merit; O sinless King, among those men whom I have described as being possessed of faults, the most base of all is the ungrateful betrayer of friends.
"12,162.026 That man of evil conduct must be abandoned by all; this is the settled conclusion.
12,162.027 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, I wish to hear the connection of these matters in detail."
"Tell me also of that one who is called a betrayer of friends and ungrateful.
Bhīṣma said:
"Indeed, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
O lord of men, regarding what occurred among the Mlecchas in the northern direction:
a Brahmin from the Middle Country, dark-limbed and devoid of Vedic knowledge,
beheld a village crowded with people and entered it in search of alms.
There lived a Dasyu named Dhana, who was knowledgeable in the distinctions of all social orders (*varṇas*),
devoted to the Brahmins, true to his word, and intent upon giving gifts.
Having approached his residence, [the sage] then begged for alms from him.
He gave that brahmin a shelter for his dwelling, alms for the rainy season, and a new, suitable garment;
he also gave him a woman of mature age who was then separated from her husband.

Having obtained all this from the bandit, O twice-born one, Gautama was then delighted in heart; and in that excellent house, O King, he took his pleasure with her. Furthermore, he rendered assistance to the bandit in matters concerning his family.
There he dwelt for many years in that prosperous abode of the Śabaras;
and Gautama applied himself with supreme effort to the art of archery.
Indeed, he constantly placed crooked-limbed birds everywhere within the range of his arrows.
O King, Gautama struck down [the enemy] just as a host of bandits would;
devoted to violence, devoid of compassion, and always intent on the slaughter of living beings,
Gautama attained equality with the bandits through his close association with them.
While he was thus living happily in that village of bandits,
many months passed as he continued killing numerous birds.
Then, on one occasion, another twice-born man arrived at that place.
Wearing matted hair and garments of bark and deerskin, devoted to sacred study and pure, he was humble, restrained in diet, devoted to Brahman, a master of the Vedas,
a fellow student from the same region, and a very dear friend of his.
He went to that village of bandits where Gautama was staying; seeking the houses of Brahmins and avoiding the food of Śūdras,
he wandered in every direction throughout the village crowded with bandit folk.
Then that best of the twice-born entered the house of Gautama;
and Gautama, having arrived, met him face to face.
He saw him with a bow in hand, bearing a load on his shoulder, and having committed an offense.
Seeing him— his limbs drenched in blood, having arrived at the door of the house,
resembling a man-eater, fallen and come to his end— the twice-born man recognized him, felt ashamed, and spoke these words:
"What is this that you do out of folly? For you are a brahmin born of noble lineage, renowned throughout the Middle Country; how have you come to such a state of banditry?
Remember those foremost of the twice-born, those celebrated masters who had reached the further shore of the Vedas."

O twice-born one, you who have been born into such a lineage as this—yet act as a disgrace to your family! Realize yourself by means of the self; remember truth, virtuous conduct, sacred learning, self-restraint, and compassion, and abandon this dwelling.
Dwelling in a wretched village, association with bad friends, passion for a bad wife, service to a base king, and indeed, affection for a false brahmin without cause— these are truly [to be avoided].
"Those who act thus are the most wicked.
Having been addressed in this way by that well-wishing friend at that time,
O King, he then replied with determination, as if in distress.
"I am destitute, O best of the twice-born, and I am not even a knower of the Vedas; know me, O most excellent of the twice-born, as one who has come here for the sake of a livelihood.
Yet, O brahmin-sage, by the mere sight of you, O twice-born one, I consider my purpose fulfilled."
"Tomorrow we shall go together; stay here for this night.
When Gautama had said, "So be it," that best of the twice-born went to sleep. That compassionate brahmin remained there, not touching anything at all.
Though hungry and being offered food, he did not take pleasure in eating.
Bhīṣma said:
When that night had passed and that best of the twice-born had departed,
Having departed, O Bhārata, Gautama went toward the ocean. There he saw merchants from the sea-coast standing on the road;
accompanied by that caravan, he set out toward the ocean.
O Great King, that caravan was then for the most part destroyed by an intoxicated elephant in a certain mountain cave.
O Brahmin, he (the merchant) somehow escaped from that caravan at that time.
Terrified and seeking to save his life, he fled toward the northern direction.
Having been deprived of everything— his caravan, his country, and his wealth— he ran alone through that forest like a *kiṃpuruṣa*.
Then, having reached the path leading toward the ocean,
he arrived at a vast and delightful forest filled with trees in full bloom.
It was adorned with mango groves that flowered throughout all seasons.
Resembling a region of the Nandana grove and frequented by yakṣas and kinnaras,
it was likewise adorned with forests of śāla, tāla, dhava, and aśvattha trees,
as well as with sandalwood trees of the finest kind.
On the delightful, auspicious, and fragrant mountain plateaus,
O best of the twice-born, birds of sweet song warble on all sides;
others there, known as Bhāruṇḍas, have faces like those of humans.

And other birds, such as the bhūliṅgas, were on all sides around the ocean. Hearing those exceedingly charming and most delightful warblings of the winged creatures, the brahmin Gautama proceeded along.
Then, in a most beautiful region covered with golden sand, level, variegated, and radiant like a portion of heaven,
he beheld a great banyan tree, endowed with splendor and perfectly circular in form.
Adorned with corresponding branches, it resembled a parasol;
its base was well-sprinkled with the water of excellent sandalwood,
graced with divine flowers, and glorious like the eternal abode of the Grandfather (Brahmā).

Seeing that unsurpassed place, beloved by sages— pure, resembling the abode of the gods, and surrounded by flowering trees— the son of Gautama was filled with joy; having approached it, he sat down beneath it.
O Kauravya, as Gautama sat there,
a pure and auspicious breeze blew, carrying the touch of flowers;
it gladdened all the limbs of Gautama at that time, O King.
But that brahmin, exhausted though he was, having been touched by the holy breeze,
attained comfort and fell asleep as the sun went to its setting. Then,
when the sun had gone down and the time of twilight had arrived, [the king departed].
From the world of Brahmā, the best of birds returned to his own abode;
he was known as Nāḍījaṅgha, the beloved friend of Brahmā,
the highly wise king of cranes, and the son of Kaśyapa.
Renowned as Rājadharmā, he was peerless on earth;
the glorious son of a celestial maiden, wise and possessing the splendor of the Lord of the Gods,
he was draped in refined gold and adorned with ornaments resembling the sun.
Adorned on all his limbs, blazing with splendor like the offspring of a god,
Gautama was struck with wonder upon seeing that twice-born man arrive;
yet, his soul overcome by hunger and thirst and seeking to do harm, he gazed at him.
Rājadharmā said:
"Welcome to you, O Brahmin! By good fortune you have arrived at my home;
the sun has set and this twilight has arrived."
"You have arrived at my abode as a beloved guest, O blameless one;
having been honored this evening, you shall depart tomorrow morning according to the prescribed rites.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard those sweet words, Gautama was then struck with wonder;
filled with curiosity, O King, he looked toward Rājadharmā.
Rājadharmā said:
"O, I am the son of Kaśyapa and my mother is Dākṣāyaṇī. You are a guest endowed with virtues; welcome to you, O bull among the twice-born.
Bhīṣma said:
Having offered him hospitality according to the rites prescribed by rule,
he prepared for him a divine seat made of *śāla* flowers.
[He described] the regions frequented by the Gaṅgā, which had been traversed by Bhagīratha’s chariot.
And he prepared for him those great fish that were swimming about—
both a brightly blazing fire and very plump fish;
Kāśyapa presented these to his guest, Gautama.
When that brahmin had finished eating and was pleased in spirit, the high-minded one fanned him with his two wings to dispel his fatigue. Then, as he sat there rested, he asked him about his lineage.
He replied, "I am Gautama," and spoke nothing else, O Brāhmaṇa.
To him he gave a divine bed made of *parṇa* leaves, scented with celestial flowers and rich in fragrance; there he indeed lay down in comfort.
Then, as Gautama was seated upon the couch, Bakarāja, the eloquent son of Kaśyapa, asked him: "What is the reason for your coming?
Thereupon Gautama said to him: "O high-minded one, I am poor."

"O Bhārata, desiring to go to the ocean for the sake of wealth, Kāśyapa spoke to him with pleasure: 'O best of the twice-born, you have accomplished your purpose; you shall return home with your wealth, so you need not feel anxious.'"
"For there are four ways of attaining one's goal, according to the doctrine of Bṛhaspati:
tradition, destiny, action, and friendship, O Lord. I have appeared before you as your friend, and my affection lies with you."
"I shall strive in such a way that you will become possessed of your goal.
Then, at the time of dawn, having inquired after his well-being, he said this:
"Go, gentle one, by this path; you shall have accomplished your purpose."

"Having gone three yojanas from here, there is a great lord of the Rākṣasas known as Virūpākṣa, who is my friend and possesses immense strength. O foremost of the twice-born, go to him, urged by my word."

"I shall grant you whatever desires you wish for; there is no doubt in this. Having been addressed thus, O King, Gautama set forth, his fatigue dispelled, eating at his pleasure fruits that were like nectar.

O great king, enjoying the forests of sandalwood, agallochum, cinnamon, and cardamom that line that path, he traveled swiftly. Then he reached the city named Meruvraja, which had gateways made of stone.
He reported that the city was surrounded by stone walls and ramparts, secured with stone engines and bolts, and that the gatekeepers had been informed by the command of Rājadharman;
thus he became known to that wise lord of the Rākṣasas.
O King, having been sent by his well-wishing friend who was pleased with him as a dear guest,
that lord of the Rākṣasas then spoke to his own servants, O Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Let Gautama be brought quickly from the city gate."

Then, from that excellent city, men dressed in white garments approached the city gate, addressing him as "Gautama. O great king, those servants of the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke thus to that twice-born man.
With hands covered and bodies clad in garments of bark, they approached Gautama with haste and agitation, saying: "Come, Gautama!
Hurry, come quickly; the King wishes to see you."
"The heroic lord of the Rākṣasas, known as Virūpākṣa, is indeed hastening to see you; therefore, let that be arranged quickly.
Thereupon, the brahmin, his fatigue dispelled by wonder, ran forth.
Gautama, beholding that splendor of the city, was filled with supreme wonder;
accompanied by those very men, the twice-born one then quickly hastened toward the king’s palace, desiring an audience with the lord of the rākṣasas.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, having been recognized by the king, he entered the excellent palace;
honored by the lord of the Rākṣasas, he sat down upon a preeminent seat.
When questioned by the king regarding his lineage, his school, his Vedic study, and his life as a student, he did not know even his own lineage; thus,
the twice-born man spoke nothing other than his lineage alone.
To one who was devoid of Vedic luster, who had ceased his private Vedic study,
and who knew only his lineage, the king asked about his residence:
"Where is your dwelling, O auspicious one, and what is the lineage of your Brahmin wife?"
"Tell me the truth; you need have no fear, rest as you please.
Gautama said:
"I was born in the Middle Country, but my dwelling is in the abode of the Śabaras."
"A Śūdra woman who was my remarried wife—this I tell you truly.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then the king reflected: 'How can this matter be resolved?'"
"How might I perform a virtuous deed? he reflected with this thought.
"This Brahmin is indeed a friend of that high-souled one from birth;
he has been sent here to my presence by that Kāśyapa."
"I shall do what is pleasing to him, for he has always relied upon me; he is my brother, my kinsman, my friend, and one who is dear to my heart.
Today, on the full moon of Kārttika, a thousand of the best of the twice-born shall dine at my house."
"In this matter, he is indeed a guest who must be fed, and I have wealth that ought to be given to him. Today is an auspicious day, and this guest has arrived;
since the wealth was already intended for him, what further deliberation is required?"
Then, O lord of the people, Virūpākṣa beheld those thousand learned and eminent brahmins who had arrived, well-adorned, having bathed, and wearing unwashed linen garments.
He received them as was fitting with rites prescribed by rule. By the command of the lord of the Rākṣasas,
O best of the Bharatas, seats were laid out for them upon the ground by the servants, covered with excellent carpets.
Honored by the king, those best of the twice-born sat down upon them; then the brahmins were worshipped according to the rules with sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water,
and the Viśvedevas, along with the ancestors and the sacrificial fires, were duly prepared.
Anointed with ointments, adorned with flowers, well-arranged, and highly honored,
they shone, O Great King, like the lords of the constellations.
Then there were pure and auspicious bowls made of Jāmbūnada gold, marked with diamonds.
He gave to the Brahmins excellent food filled with honey and ghee; likewise, on the full moon days of Āṣāḍha and Māgha, many twice-born men always received their desired, superior,
and honored meals.

Especially on the full moon day of Kārttika, he bestows gifts upon the twice-born at the end of autumn; such is the sacred tradition (śruti) regarding the full moon. He gives gold, silver, gems, and pearls.
Having scattered piles of jewels— diamonds, great treasures, beryl, skins, and rāṅkava wool— for the sake of the sacrificial fee, O Bhārata,
that highly illustrious Virūpākṣa then addressed the best of the twice-born.
"Take these jewels according to your enthusiasm and as you desire. O best of the twice-born, take those very vessels in which you have eaten and go to your own homes," so he said, O Bhārata.
When that high-souled lord of the Rākṣasas had spoken these words,
those bulls among brahmins took those jewels as they desired.
Then, they were all honored with those precious and auspicious jewels.
Then the brahmins, dressed in clean garments, became well-pleased.
Thereupon, O King, the lord of the rākṣasas, having indeed restrained the rākṣasas who had come from various directions, spoke these words again to those twice-born ones.
"O Brahmins, for one more day there is no fear for you here from any quarter;
rejoice yourselves against the Rākṣasas and depart as you please without delay.
Thereupon, all the throngs of Brahmins fled in every direction.
Gautama also, taking up a load of gold, hurried along;
carrying it with great difficulty, O hero, he arrived at the Nyagrodha tree. Exhausted, weary, and hungry, he sat down.
Then, O King, Rājadharmā, the best of birds, approached him;
affectionate toward his friend, he greeted Gautama with a welcome. With the flapping of the tips of his wings, the bird dispelled his exhaustion.
The wise one offered him worship and prepared a meal;
however, the evil-minded one, stripped of his feathers, lay upon that bed and burned with remorse.
Then, having reached an agreement, those two—the lord of birds and the best of brahmins—proceeded.
O Great King, they both sat down likewise beneath a vast *nyagrodha* tree.
Gautama, having eaten and being well-rested, reflected at night in the vicinity of that place. Thus did Gautama reflect then.
"This very great load of beautiful gold has been taken up by me out of greed and delusion; yet my journey is far,
and there is nothing on the road for me to eat to sustain my life."
"What must I do to sustain my life? he reflected. Then, O tiger among men, seeing nothing whatsoever to eat on the road, that ungrateful man thought this in his mind:
"This lord of cranes stands at my side with a heap of flesh;
having slain and seized him, I shall depart in haste.
Bhīṣma said:

Then, not far from him, a great flaming fire with the wind as its charioteer was stationed by the lord of birds for the sake of protection. And at that time, the king of cranes slept trustfully on his side.
But that wicked-souled ungrateful man, desiring to kill him, remained awake.
Then, with a blazing brand, he struck down the trusting one. Having killed him, he was filled with joy and saw no further consequence.

Having then made that man’s hair stand on end, he cooked him over the fire. O King, having eaten the cooked food, that ungrateful and sinful man departed in haste, as if his purpose were accomplished.

Taking that [child] and the gold, the twice-born one departed very swiftly. Then, O Bhārata, Virūpākṣa, reflecting that the son of Dākṣāyaṇī had not returned, was indeed tormented in his heart with grief.
Then, when another day had passed, Virūpākṣa said to his son:
"My son, I do not see Rājadharmā, the best of birds, today.
He always goes at the time of the morning twilight to pay homage to Brahmā."
Furthermore, that king of birds comes to see me;
not having seen me, that bird never goes home. For two nights, during both twilights, he did not come to my abode.
Therefore, my state is not purified; let that friend of mine be discovered. For he is devoid of Vedic study and destitute of spiritual luster;
I fear he has gone there, and that lowest of the twice-born might slay him.

But that Gautama of evil conduct and wicked intellect was noticed by me through his gestures; inactive yet cruel in appearance, he was like a base, black bandit. He has gone there, and because of him my mind is anxious.
"Son, go quickly from here to the residence of Rājadharman;
let it be known without delay whether that pure-souled one still lives. Having been thus addressed, he departed in haste accompanied by the Rākṣasas.
There he saw the skeleton of Rājadharman at the banyan tree;
weeping, the son of the wise lord of the Rākṣasas went with all his might in haste, indeed, to seize Gautama.
Then, not far from there, the Rākṣasas seized Gautama and the body of Rājadharman, which was stripped of its wings, bones, and feet. Taking them, the Rākṣasas then went swiftly to Meruvraja.
They showed the body of King Rājadharman,
as well as that ungrateful man, the evil-minded Gautama.
Upon seeing him, the king, together with his ministers and his domestic priest, wept.
A great cry of distress arose in his residence,
and the city, including its women and children, became distraught in mind.
Then the king said to his son, "Let this wicked man be put to death."
"O Rākṣasas, let all these [beings] sport at their pleasure with his flesh. This man of evil conduct, evil deeds, evil soul, and evil resolve must be slain by you; this is my opinion."
Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, those rākṣasas of terrible prowess did not wish to devour him, saying, "He is a man of evil deeds;
let this lowest of men be given today to the bandits."
"Thus spoke those night-rangers, O great king, to that lord of the Rākṣasas;
bowing their heads to the ground, they said to the sovereign of the hosts of Rakshasas:
'It does not behove you to grant us this sinful creature for our food.'"
"So be it," the lord of the *rākṣasas* said to those night-stalkers:
"O *rākṣasas*, let this ungrateful man be given to the bandits this very day!
When he had spoken thus, his servants, with pikes and mallets in their hands, [prepared to act].
Having cut that sinner into pieces, they then gave him to the bandits;
yet even the bandits did not wish to eat that evildoer,
for even flesh-eaters, O king of kings, do not consume one who is ungrateful.

O King, an expiation has been ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow; but for the ungrateful man, there is no expiation. A betrayer of friends, a cruel man, and an ungrateful man are the lowest of men.
Indeed, such [bodies] are not devoured by flesh-eaters, worms, or other [creatures].
Then, having seen Rājadharmā slain beneath the *nyagrodha* tree,
that *rākṣasa*, after weeping much and lamenting various things, [departed].
Overcome with rage, he set out indeed to seize Gautama;
the wicked Gautama was captured by the Rākṣasas, who were frantic with anger,
and the skeleton of the body of Rājadharman was likewise carried off.
And on the summit of Mount Meru, the Yātudhānas went;
those terrible ones, their eyes bloodshot with rage, were intent on the slaughter of Gautama. A skeleton was placed before King Rājadharman.
Seeing him, the king, along with his ministers and his retinue, became despondent. A great cry of distress arose in the palace of that high-souled one,
O King, when the son of Kāśyapa had been slain by the host of women.
The Rākṣasas said:
"And the king himself said to his son, 'This man is a sinner; let him be slain!
All of us, having gathered together, shall eat his flesh.'"
A doer of evil, one of sinful deeds, evil-natured, and established in wickedness—Virūpākṣa said:
"This evil-natured man, who is ungrateful, must indeed be slain; there is no doubt about this."
"I cannot bring myself to devour one who is ungrateful and a doer of evil deeds. Let this betrayer of friends, the lowest of men, be given to the slaves.
Bhīṣma said:
All the Dāsas were summoned, as well as other Yātudhānas;
yet they did not wish to devour that ungrateful man, O Supreme Person.
Then, O Great King, by force they fell to the ground with their heads.
"You ought not to inflict this sinful punishment upon one who has become so obstinate for the sake of wealth.
Let the Yātudhānas told by the king—'Let this evildoer be executed, let him be eaten, or let him be abandoned; let him be removed from my sight'—carry it out."
Then those enraged servants, with spears and swords in their hands,
hacked him into pieces and, having mutilated him, gave him to the flesh-eaters.
But even the flesh-eaters, O king of kings, did not wish to consume his flesh.

For even carnivorous beasts do not devour those who are dead and ungrateful. An expiation has been ordained by the virtuous for one who steals the property of a Brahmin, for a thief, for a killer of a Brahmin, and for one who violates the teacher’s bed; but for the ungrateful, there is no expiation.
Flesh-eating creatures and worms indeed never consume one who betrays a friend, the ungrateful, the cruel, and the lowest of men. Bhīṣma said:
Then the Rākṣasa had a funeral pyre prepared for the lord of the cranes,
adorned with many jewels, perfumes, and garments. There, O King, the powerful one set fire to the king of the cranes.
The lord of the Rākṣasas performed the funeral rites according to the prescribed rules.
At that time, the auspicious goddess Surabhi, the daughter of Dakṣa,
appeared above him, yielding her milk.
O sinless one, foam mixed with milk then fell from her mouth;
it fell upon that funeral pyre of Rājadharman. Thereupon, O sinless one, the king of cranes was restored to life by it.
Having flown up, the lord of the *bakas* joined Virūpākṣa.
Then the king of the gods approached the city of Virūpākṣa and said this to Virūpākṣa: "By good fortune, he lives!"
Indra then caused that ancient Virūpākṣa to hear how,
in former times, a curse had been pronounced by Brahmā upon Rājadharman:
"O King, when the lord of the Baka birds does not approach Brahmā..."
Then, out of anger, the Grandfather spoke this to the lord of the cranes:
"Since that fool, that lowest of cranes, has not come to my assembly,
therefore that evil-minded one shall soon meet his death."
Then, at his word, Baka was indeed slain by Gautama;
yet, sprinkled with nectar by that very same one, he was restored to life.
Thereupon Rājadharmā, having prostrated before Purandara, spoke.
"O Purandara, if your mind is inclined toward showing me favor,
then restore my very dear friend Gautama to life.
Having understood his words, O bull among men, Vāsava [acted].

Having restored him to life, O King, the lord of the *bakas* then gave that Gautama back to his friend, along with all his goods and utensils; having approached his well-wisher, he embraced him, filled with the highest affection.
Then the king of cranes, Rājadharmā, having dismissed that evildoer along with his wealth, entered his own abode;
and that crane then departed for the assembly of Brahmā as was appropriate.

Then Brahmā, seeing Baka— who was devoted to dharma— arrived at his own assembly hall, honored that high-souled being with the rites of hospitality. And Gautama, having returned once more to that dwelling of the Śabaras, [proceeded].
He begot upon a Śūdra woman sons who were doers of evil deeds;
and then a very great curse was pronounced upon him by the hosts of gods,
because he had finally begotten sons in the womb of his remarried wife.
"O Lord, this ungrateful man shall fall into a great hell"—
this was everything that Nārada told me in the past, O Bhārata; and having recalled that very great narrative, O bull among men, [I have related it].
I too have described everything to you exactly as it is.
Where is the fame of an ungrateful person? Where is his standing? Where is his happiness?
For an ungrateful person is not to be trusted; there is no atonement for ingratitude.
A man, especially, must not commit treachery against a friend;
one who betrays a friend falls into a terrible and endless hell.
O sinless one, one should always be grateful and desirous of the welfare of friends.
From a friend truth arises; from a friend strength arises.
One may enjoy pleasures through a friend, and by means of a friend one is delivered from calamities.
A wise person should honor a friend with the highest marks of respect.
Bhīṣma said:
The king, being composed, had the learned man consecrated according to the rites for royalty and caused that twice-born one to be cremated with many perfumes.
At the word of that god Indra, Bakarāja was here; sprinkled with nectar by him, the crane was restored to life. Then Rājadharmā spoke to that thousand-eyed subduer of enemies.
"O Gautama, where is that brahmin? Let my dear friend be released!
Having understood his words, Kauśika, the best of the gods, took leave of Gautama and, being pleased yet eager to depart, set out.
The gentle Rājadharmā, having been recognized, departed for his own abode; meanwhile,
the cruel Gautama, that betrayer of friends and lowest of men, was released and went then to the dwelling of the Śabaras with all his goods and utensils.
There, he was born in the body of a Śabara woman, which resembled a hell;
such was the great curse released there by the hosts of gods.
Thereupon, the powerful king of birds was consumed by the king of the Rākṣasas.
Beside the funeral pyre stood the milch-cow Surabhi, who restored him to life;
O sinless one, a bubble of foam, no more than a drop of milk, fell from her mouth and was carried by the wind to that pyre of Rājadharman.
Then the king of the gods arrived at the city of Virūpākṣa. Virūpākṣa, too, went out to meet the king of the gods who had arrived, saying, "O god, this is the son of Kāśyapa; let my brother live!"
But Kauśika, being repeatedly pleased, spoke thus once more:
"O Rājadharmā, because you have never come to see this assembly of mine, you have been addressed by Brahmā with words of wrath."

"Therefore, you shall become Baka, a man of virtuous character and a knower of ancient lore. Once, a performer of evil deeds— a Brahmin living among the Śabaras, ungrateful, and the husband of a low-caste woman— will come to your dwelling."
"When you have destroyed [your enemies], then liberation will be yours," he said to him;
therefore, he went to the world of Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. But that evil-doer, a defiler of his lineage, fell into hell.
Having heard these great words spoken by Nārada in the midst of the assembly,
I too have described them to you exactly as they are, O Indra among kings—
concerning the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise one who has fallen from his vow.
O King, expiation has been ordained for all [sins], but there is no expiation for an ungrateful person.
Where is the fame of the ungrateful? Where is his standing? Where is his happiness?
For the ungrateful man is not to be trusted; indeed, there is no expiation for the ungrateful.
A man, especially, must not commit treachery against a friend;
one who betrays a friend falls into a terrible hell. O sinless one, one should always be grateful and maintain a spirit of friendship.
Everything originates from a friend; a friend is remembered as a source of prosperity. Between the acquisition of wealth and the acquisition of a friend, the acquisition of a friend is superior.
For wealth is easily obtained through a friend, but it is fitting to strive for a friend.

A friend who is beloved and affectionate, and the fruit that is the reward for the virtuous— a wise man should honor such a person with hospitality accompanied by his own kinsmen. Dark as a rain cloud, with a mass of matted hair bound together and tawny in hue...
Tall and staff-bearing, clad in the skin of a black antelope,
purifying the worlds in person, may the preeminent sage,
the son of Parāśara, manifest his form on the sacred festival days.

With that very life-force, he who was sinful and eager to return to his own country cursed him, saying: "May this one be born from the body of a Śabara woman. Thus, that sinner begot sons in the womb of a remarried woman (punarbhū).
"Therefore, let that Brāhmaṇa who killed Baka in the house, a bond of sin,
be bound tightly with terrible nooses made of serpent-skin.
Then Virūpākṣa, having heard these words, honored them.
And Śakra went with him to the side of Brahmā;
Gautama reached hell because of that connection, as did Baka;
and the king of the Rākṣasas was filled with distress due to the gift of wealth.

Having heard these words spoken by the high-souled Bhīṣma, Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, was always pleased in mind. [He reflected: "The wise should abandon a sinner who is ungrateful and shameless."

"A betrayer of friends, a charcoal-brand to his own lineage, an evildoer, the lowest of men—this sinner has been described by me to you as the foremost among those who uphold dharma. He is indeed a betrayer of friends and ungrateful. What more do you wish to hear?"
12,167.024 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having then heard these words spoken by the high-souled Bhīṣma,
Yudhiṣṭhira became joyful in mind, O Janamejaya.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
as well as to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory" (Jaya). [One should meditate on] Viṣṇu, clad in white garments, moon-colored, and four-armed.
