One should meditate on the one with a serene countenance for the pacification of all obstacles.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The auspicious duties concerning the duties of kings have been spoken by the Grandfather."
"O King, you ought to declare the supreme dharma of those belonging to the various stages of life (āśramas).
Bhīṣma said:
Dharma is ordained for all [stages]; austerity has heaven as its goal and truth as its fruit."

In this Dharma which has many doors, no action is ever fruitless. O best of the Bharatas, whatever specific discipline one adopts as one's own settled conclusion, it is that alone which one truly understands, and nothing else.

To whatever extent one examines the worldly system as being devoid of essence, to that same extent detachment arises therein; of this there is no doubt. Such, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is the world determined to be, fraught with many defects.
"A wise man should indeed strive for the sake of his own liberation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When wealth is lost, or when a wife, a son, or a father has died—"
"Tell me that wisdom, O Grandfather, by which one may dispel grief.
Bhīṣma said:
"When wealth is lost, or when a wife, a son, or a father has died..."
"Alas, what suffering!"— meditating thus, one should perform the rites for the alleviation of grief.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
as a certain Brahmin once spoke these words to Senajit:
Seeing the king tormented by grief for his son, overwhelmed by sorrow, and dejected in countenance, the brahmin spoke these words:
"Why indeed are you so deluded? You yourself are the one to be pitied; why do you mourn for another?"
When even you, grieving for us, shall go to that destination as one who is to be pitied—
then you, I, and all others who attend upon you, O King,
shall all go there from whence we have come.
Senajit said: "O Brahmin, what is your wisdom? What is your austerity? O one rich in penance, what is your meditative absorption?
What is your knowledge, or what is your learning, by having attained which you do not despair?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
I grieve for this Self who dwells within my heart, who rejoices when sinking down and suffers when there is a reversal of pleasure and pain.
Behold all beings everywhere entangled in suffering—superior, inferior, and middling—due to their various actions here in this world.
I am alone; no one belongs to me, nor do I belong to anyone else.
I do not see anyone whom I do not see as my own;
this self of mine is not mine, nor is the entire earth mine.
With the realization that "as it is for me, so it is for others," I have no distress.
Having attained this understanding, I neither rejoice nor do I grieve;
for just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart,
such is the meeting of living beings.
In this way, one should not form attachment toward sons, grandsons, kinsmen, or relatives, for separation from them is certain.
Having come into view from the unseen, they have once again gone back beyond sight.
He does not know you, nor do you know him; being who you are, for whom do you grieve?
Suffering arises from the affliction of craving, and pleasure arises from the affliction of suffering;
from pleasure, suffering is born—thus it happens again and again.
12,168.018e After happiness comes suffering; after suffering comes happiness.
12,168.018f*0460_01 Happiness and suffering revolve for human beings like a wheel.
12,168.019a Having fallen from happiness into suffering, you shall again attain happiness.
One does not experience suffering eternally, nor does one experience happiness eternally.
The body alone is the locus of happiness,
and the body is also the locus of suffering.
Whatever action the embodied being performs with the body, by that very means he experiences its result;
for both life and the body are born together from the moment of birth.

Both increase together, and both perish together. People whose sense-objects are possessed by various kinds of bonds of affection sink down without having achieved their purpose, like embankments of sand in the water.

Like sesame seeds pressed by oil-pressers, everything is crushed within the wheel of rebirth by the force of affection; just as one is overcome by sesame-crushers, so too is a man, out of regard for his wife, oppressed by afflictions born of ignorance and accumulates unwholesome karma.
A single person incurs afflictions both in this world and in the next;
all human beings, attached to their children, wives, and families,
are submerged in the ocean of the mire of grief like aged wild elephants.
O Lord, upon the loss of sons, the loss of wealth, or even the loss of kinsmen and relatives,
one encounters immense suffering comparable to a forest fire;
all this— happiness and sorrow, existence and non-existence— is dependent upon destiny.
Whether one is without friends or has friends, whether one has enemies or possesses allies,
whether one is endowed with wisdom or devoid of wisdom— it is by destiny that one obtains happiness. Friends are not sufficient for happiness, nor are enemies sufficient for suffering.
Wisdom is not sufficient for worldly objects, nor is wealth sufficient for pleasures;
intelligence does not lead to the acquisition of riches, nor does dullness lead to poverty.
Only the wise man understands the nature of the world’s cyclical course, and no one else.
Whether one is intelligent or foolish, brave or timid, dull-witted or wise,
weak or strong, happiness attends that which is its rightful portion—
just as a cow belongs to the calf, the cowherd, the owner, and the thief alike.

"Whosoever drinks the milk from that cow, it is certain that the cow belongs to him. Those who are the most foolish in the world and those who have gone beyond the intellect—those men prosper in happiness; the person situated between them suffers."
The wise take delight in extremes; they do not find delight in the middle.
They say that reaching an extreme is happiness, while that which lies between the two extremes is suffering. The dull-witted man sleeps happily, unconcerned with his own past deeds.
Enveloped by a great cloak of ignorance, as if by a woolen blanket,
those who have attained the bliss of wisdom— transcending dualities and free from envy—
are never at all troubled by either gain or loss.
Now, those who have not attained wisdom and have transcended delusion rejoice excessively and likewise undergo great distress;
the deluded are constantly delighted, like the hosts of gods in heaven.
Enveloped by great arrogance, they are deprived of their senses.
Laziness leads to happiness that ends in suffering, while skillfulness leads to happiness that arises from prosperity; for success and fortune dwell together with the diligent, not with the lazy.

Whether it be happiness or suffering, whether it be hateful or dear, one should accept whatever comes with an unconquered heart. There are thousands of occasions for grief and hundreds of occasions for joy.
Day after day, these afflictions enter the fool, but not the wise man;
sorrow does not touch that person who is intelligent, possessed of perfected wisdom, attentive, free from envy, self-controlled, and has conquered his senses.
Having established this understanding, the wise man should move about with his mind guarded;
for one who knows the paths of light and darkness, the departure of gods and asuras,
and the rising and setting [of the sun], sorrow is not able to touch him.
Whatever cause there may be for grief, or fear, or even suffering, or from whatever root arises exhaustion— one should abandon even a single part of that.
Whatever among sensual desires one abandons, by that much one is filled with happiness.
A man who follows after desires perishes along with those desires. Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there is in heaven—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the destruction of craving.
Karma performed in a previous body, whether auspicious or inauspicious,
attends the wise, the foolish, and the brave, according to what was done.
In this very same way, indeed, these things— both pleasant and unpleasant— [follow one].
Suffering and happiness revolve among living beings.
Therefore, having established such an understanding, one endowed with virtue should live happily;
one should hold all desires in contempt and cast behind oneself all attachments.
This matured death, consisting of the mind, resides within the heart;
it is called "anger" by the wise, dwelling in the bodies of embodied beings.
When it withdraws all desires from every side, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
Then that light of the self and the self itself become serene within the self alone. Whenever even the slightest thing is conceived as "mine," all of that then results in suffering.
When he fears nothing and when nothing fears him,
when he neither desires nor hates, then he attains Brahman.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, as well as sorrow and joy, fear and fearlessness, [he becomes one with Brahman].

Having abandoned both the pleasant and the unpleasant, you will become one whose self is perfectly tranquil. When the wise man commits no evil toward any living beings through action, thought, or speech, he then attains Brahman.
"That which is difficult for the foolish to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
that disease which ends only with life— happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving.
O King, here the verses sung by Piṅgalā are heard.
Just as she obtained the eternal Dharma even in a time of distress—
when the courtesan Piṅgalā was separated from her lover at their rendezvous—
she then, having fallen into hardship, established a tranquil state of mind.
Piṅgalā said:
"For a long time I, though mad, dwelt with my lover who was not mad; though that delightful one was present and real, I did not recognize him before."
I shall shut up this little house with one pillar and nine doors;
for who here would think, "This is my beloved," when seeing a lover approaching? These rogues, who take on forms at will, are actually hell incarnate, though they appear as objects of desire.
They shall not deceive me again; I am awakened, I am vigilant.
Even misfortune becomes fortune through fate or by what was done in the past.
Fully awakened and free from outward form, I am no longer one whose senses are unsubdued today.
Free from desire, one sleeps in happiness; freedom from desire is the supreme happiness. For by turning hope into hopelessness, Piṅgalā indeed sleeps in peace.
Bhīṣma said:
By these and other reasoned arguments thus spoken by the Brahmin,
King Senajit was consoled and rejoiced happily.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When this time has passed away, which brings about the destruction of all beings, what is the highest good that one should attain? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between a father and his son; listen to that, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O Pārtha, it concerns a certain twice-born man who was indeed devoted to the study of the Vedas.

He had an intelligent son named Medhāvin by name. That son, who was skilled in the meaning of the *mokṣadharma* and discerning regarding the true nature of the world, spoke to his father, who was devoted to the practice of Vedic study.
"O father, what indeed should a wise man do when he knows that the lifespan of human beings quickly slips away? O father, tell me this according to the truth."
"By what means may I practice the Dharma in due succession?
His father said:
"O son, having studied the Vedas through the life of a student (brahmacarya)..."
Desiring sons for the sake of purifying his ancestors, he should establish the sacred fires according to rule and perform sacrifices; then,
having entered the forest, he should desire to become a sage.
The son said:
"When the world is thus struck down and surrounded on all sides, and while these unerring weapons are falling, why do you speak like one who is composed?"
Pitṛ said:
"How is the world assailed? By whom is it surrounded?
What things fall here that are never in vain? Why do you seem to terrify me?"
The son said:
The world is assailed by death and surrounded by old age;
these days and nights fall away—surely, why do you not wake up?
The nights pass and come again, never failing;
when I know this— that death does not wait—
how can I remain waiting, moving about as if covered by a net?
When night after night has passed and life becomes ever shorter,
who then could find happiness, like a fish in shallow water? From the very first night that the embryo dwells within its mother’s womb...
On that very night, one who turns back from death sets out;
when that night has passed, if one does not perform even a single virtuous deed,
the wise should know that very day to be barren.
While his desires remain unfulfilled, death approaches the man—
like a she-wolf seizing a ram— as he wanders with his mind elsewhere, picking at blades of young grass. Death comes and carries him away.
Do this very day what is for your welfare; let not this time pass you by. For death indeed drags one away while tasks remain unaccomplished.
One should do tomorrow’s work today, and the afternoon’s task in the forenoon.
For death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished; death is certain for all embodied beings, while life is indeed without cause.
For who knows whose army of death will descend upon them this very day?
Death does not come to summon the Lord of the World when he desires to take him away; rather, while one is still unawakened, death seizes him, just as a fisherman catches fish.
Therefore, one should be devoted to the Dharma while still young, for life is without certainty.
When dharma is practiced, there is fame in this world and indeed happiness after death.
For one who is possessed by delusion and strives for the sake of son and wife,
whether he performs what ought to be done or what ought not to be done, he provides nourishment for them.
Death seizes and carries away that man who is intoxicated by sons and cattle, whose mind is deeply attached, like a great flood sweeping away a sleeping tiger.
It takes him while he is still alone, gathering objects of desire and remaining unsatisfied.

Like a tiger seizing its prey, death seizes and departs; while one thinks, "This has been done, this is to be done, and this other is half-finished," Death brings under its control the person thus attached to the pleasures of worldly striving.
Death carries away the one who has not yet reaped the fruit of the deeds he has performed, who is attached to the fruits of his actions, and who is clinging to fields, shops, and houses—
whether he be weak or strong, brave or timid, dull-witted or wise.
Death departs, taking away one who has not attained any of their desired goals.
Death brings under his power those men whose minds are fixed on "this shall be mine" and "that shall be mine," while their desires remain unfulfilled.
Death, old age, disease, and suffering arising from manifold causes— since these are ever-attached to the body, why do you remain as if you were healthy?
For as soon as an embodied being is born, the Ender follows him for his destruction, and old age follows as well.
12.169.022c These beings, both stationary and moving, are pursued by these two [pairs]. 12.169.023a Indeed, that delight which one finds living in a village is the very house of death;
12.169.023c "The forest is the stall of the gods"—so says the sacred tradition (śruti).
This attachment to living in a village is a binding rope;
having severed it, those of good deeds depart, while those of evil deeds cannot sever it.
For he who does not harm living beings through the causes of mind, speech, or body [is liberated].
One is not bound by actions that deprive others of their livelihood; no one can ever repel the approaching army of Death,
except through truth that must never be abandoned, for immortality is rooted in truth.

Therefore, one whose conduct is devoted to the vow of truth, who is intent on the yoga of truth, who delights in truth, who is impartial and self-controlled— by truth alone shall he conquer Death. Both immortality and death are established within the body.
Through delusion one encounters death; through truth one attains immortality.
For I am non-violent, seeking truth, and cast out from desire and anger;
equanimous in pain and pleasure, secure, I shall leave death behind like an immortal.

Devoted to the sacrifice of peace, self-controlled, and established in the sacrifice of Brahman, I shall become a sage who performs the sacrifice of speech, mind, and action during the northern solstice. For how could one such as I perform sacrifices involving animals that are characterized by violence?

Even a wise man who performs sacrifices for the sake of sovereignty like a Piśāca, though he be learned, is limited by their finite results. However, he whose speech and mind are always perfectly restrained,
and who possesses austerity, renunciation, and yoga— he indeed shall attain everything.
There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no strength equal to knowledge.
There is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation. Born of the self by the self alone, one is established in the self, even if childless.
"I shall exist in the Self alone; my offspring do not deliver me.
There is no wealth for a brahmin such as this: namely, solitude, equanimity, and truthfulness."
Stability in virtue, laying aside the rod [of punishment], uprightness,
and withdrawal from various activities— what use have you for wealth or even for kinsmen?
O Brahmin, what use have you for wives when you yourself shall die?
Seek the Self that has entered the cave;
where have your grandfather and your father gone?
12,169.037 Bhīṣma said:
O King, having heard these words of his son, the father acted accordingly;
in the same manner, you too should conduct yourself, being devoted to truth and righteousness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, for those who possess wealth and those who are without it, yet both live independently, what is the nature of their attainment of happiness and suffering, and how does it come about?"
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
sung by Śamyāka when he had been released and had attained peace.
Long ago, a certain brahmin who had adopted renunciation told me this:
"A human being born here in this world from the very moment of birth is indeed afflicted by a bad wife, by ragged clothing, and by hunger."
Various kinds of sufferings and pleasures arise;
if one were to lead him toward either of those two paths,
he would not rejoice upon attaining pleasure, nor would he be distressed upon encountering suffering.

Indeed, you do not pursue that which is better for yourself, nor that which you truly seek; for even if you are free from desire, by always shouldering the burden and wandering about with nothing at all, you will experience true happiness.
One who possesses nothing sleeps in happiness and indeed rises in happiness. Possessionlessness is a bliss in this world—wholesome, auspicious, and free from ailment;
it is without enemies, difficult for others to attain, yet easily attained by the virtuous.
12,170.009a For one who possesses nothing, who is pure, and who has been born completely [free from defilements],
12,170.009c while surveying the three worlds, I perceive no equal. 12,170.010a I have weighed both the state of possessing nothing and sovereignty upon a scale.

Poverty exceeds even sovereignty in its excellence; this is a very great distinction between the state of possessing nothing and the state of ruling a kingdom. For one who possesses wealth is constantly anxious, as if standing within the jaws of death.
Neither fire, nor the sun, nor death, nor robbers have power over him who is liberated from the loss of wealth and free from expectations. Indeed,
he always moves according to his will and sleeps upon no bed.
The gods praise one who uses his arm as a pillow and who is thus tranquil. A wealthy man possessed by anger and greed loses his discernment;
he glances askance, his mouth becomes parched, and his face is contorted with a frown.
"His lower lip is bitten and he speaks harshly in anger;
who would wish to look upon him, even if he wishes to give away the earth? For constant association with prosperity deludes one who lacks discernment."
She captivates his heart, as the wind disperses an autumn cloud.
Then, possessed by pride in his beauty and pride in his wealth, he thinks:
"I am of noble birth, I am perfected; I am no mere mortal."
12.170.017e By these causes, his mind becomes overwhelmed by three things. 12.170.018a With his mind thus overwhelmed, he abandons the enjoyments accumulated by his ancestors;
12.170.018c being utterly destitute, he considers the seizing of others' property to be right.
Kings restrain that man who has transgressed the bounds of propriety and seizes here and there from all sides, just as hunters strike down a greedy deer with arrows.
In this way, these various sufferings befall a human being in this world.
Various [afflictions] arise, born from the contact of the limbs;
one should apply the remedy for those supreme sufferings through the intellect,
having fully understood the worldly condition of the constant being joined with the inconstant.
"Without renouncing, one does not attain happiness; without renouncing, one does not find the supreme state.
Without renouncing, one does not sleep free from fear; having renounced everything, be happy.
Thus was this described by the brahmin in Hastināpura.
In former times, Śamyāka gave even his own body to me; therefore, renunciation is considered the highest virtue.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If one who exerts himself in various undertakings should fail to acquire wealth..."
"And being overcome by thirst for wealth, what could one do to obtain happiness?
Bhīṣma said:
"Equanimity toward all things, lack of exertion, and truthful speech, O Bhārata."
The man who possesses both world-weariness and the desire for no further knowledge is a happy man.
The elders say that these very five states lead to tranquility;
this is both heaven and dharma, and the unsurpassed happiness of the virtuous.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
listen, O Yudhiṣṭhira, to that which was sung by Maṅki out of world-weariness. Striving for wealth again and again, Maṅki found his efforts repeatedly frustrated.
With a certain remainder of wealth, he had purchased a pair of young oxen. Those two well-trained oxen, having been let loose for training,
suddenly rushed straight toward the camel as it sat in their midst.
When those two had arrived, the camel, unable to endure it,
rose up and, tossing those two young bulls aside, fled with great speed.
As those two young bulls were being carried away by that tormenting camel, they cried out.
Seeing the two of them dying, Maṅki then said this:
"Even by one who is skillful, wealth cannot be acquired through effort if it is not destined;
even for one who is disciplined, endowed with faith, and correctly pursues his endeavors."
"Though I have previously acted rightly and performed my duties despite being beset by misfortunes, behold this calamity of fate that has befallen me through the turn of events!
Though I repeatedly raise my two young ones, it moves as if along a rugged path."
Like a jackal seizing its prey by chance through a sudden stroke,
[I have seized you] as you were running along a wrong path while I was also running along a wrong path;
two jewels hang from you, my dear young calves.
For this destiny alone is pure; therefore, there is no such thing as human effort at all.
Or, even if that which is called human effort should occasionally arise, when it is thoroughly investigated, it too is found to rest solely upon destiny.
Therefore, one who desires happiness must cultivate world-weariness in this very life.
One who is weary of the world sleeps in peace, free from hope for the attainment of worldly aims.
"Ah! Shuka has spoken most excellently for one who seeks liberation in every respect."
Departing from Janaka’s abode for the great forest—
between one who might obtain all desires and one who renounces them entirely,
the renunciation of all desires is superior to their attainment.
No one has ever reached the end of all things that desire to be known. The thirst for both the body and life increases in the dull-witted man.
Turn away from the desire to know; become tranquil, having grown weary of the world, my friend.
"O body, you have been humiliated by me many times and yet you do not feel weary;
if I am not to be destroyed by you, and if you truly take such pleasure with me,
then do not bind me to this vain greed for wealth, O seeker of riches!"
Again and again, the wealth you have accumulated has been lost to you. O fool, O seeker of riches, when will you be liberated from this craving for wealth?
You are an obstacle to all that is auspicious, a refuge for evil.
"Alas! How great is my foolishness, that I have been your plaything! O pitiless one, you constantly yoke me to all manner of afflictions.
Has a man never before fallen into the state of servitude to others?"
Neither those of the past nor those of the future have ever reached the end of desires.
Having abandoned all undertakings, I am awakened; I am awake. Surely, O Desire, your heart is firm, made of the essence of a diamond.
That it does not shatter into a hundred pieces, though possessed by hundreds of calamities—
O Desire, I renounce both you and whatever else is dear to you. Seeking happiness for you, I find happiness within myself.

"O Desire, I know your root: you are born, it is said, from mental construction (saṃkalpa). I shall no longer construct you; thus, you shall cease to exist along with your very root. The pursuit of wealth is not pleasant, and once obtained, anxiety becomes even greater."

The loss of what has been gained is like death; whether one gains it or not, what indeed could be more painful than for one who, having departed, does not obtain it? And yet, one is not satisfied with what has been gained, but seeks even more.
The object of one's craving is indeed as sweet as the water of the Gaṅgā;
but this is merely my own delusion—wake up and abandon it!
As for this collection of elements that has taken refuge in my body:

"Let him go from here as he pleases, or let him dwell as he finds comfort; I have no affection for you here, who follow after desire and greed. Therefore, having abandoned all of you, I take refuge in truth alone."
Beholding all beings within my own body and mind,
fixing my intellect on yoga, my being on sacred learning, and my mind on Brahman,
I shall wander at ease, unattached, happy, and free from ailment throughout the worlds.
"O Desire, so that you may never again direct me toward such sufferings,
for when I am driven away by you, no other path is found for me;
indeed, you are always the source of thirst, sorrow, and exhaustion."

I consider the loss of wealth to be a greater sorrow than anything else; for kinsmen and friends indeed hold one in contempt who has fallen from his fortune. Indeed, the evils resulting from thousands of such insults are more painful than poverty itself.
Even that fraction of happiness found in wealth is produced by sufferings.
Robbers first strike down the man who possesses wealth;
they afflict him with various punishments and constantly cause him agitation.
It was only after a long time that I realized the craving for sensory objects is suffering.
Whatever object of desire you grasp, you pursue that very thing alone.
You are ignorant of reality, childish, difficult to satisfy, insatiable, and like a fire.
"You do not know what is easily obtained, nor do you know what is difficult to obtain.
Like the netherworld (pātāla), impossible to fill, you wish to yoke me with sorrows. O Kāma, I cannot be ensnared by you again today."
Having encountered despondency through the accidental loss of my wealth,
and having attained supreme tranquility, I no longer think of desires today. I endure these extreme sufferings here, for I was not wise enough to realize [their futility] before.
"Defeated by the loss of my wealth, I lie here with all my limbs free from fever. O Desire, I abandon you, casting aside all the movements of the mind;
O Desire, you shall no longer find pleasure with me, like a bull led by a nose-rope."
I shall endure those who are intolerant, and I shall not cause harm even when harmed. Though spoken to with hatred, I shall speak kindly, disregarding that which is unpleasant.
Always content, with my senses at ease, I shall subsist on whatever is obtained.

"I shall not fulfill your desires, for you are an enemy to my very self. Know that I have come to you for refuge— renunciation, liberation, contentment, peace, truth, self-restraint, forgiveness, and compassion toward all beings."
"Therefore, let desire, greed, thirst,
and even miserliness abandon me, for I am now established in goodness (*sattva*). Having cast off desire, greed, anger, and harshness,"
Today, having fallen under the sway of greed, I shall experience suffering as one who lacks self-mastery.
Whatever one renounces among sensual desires, by that much is one filled with happiness;
he who is perpetually under the sway of desire encounters only suffering.

Having cast aside desires, a person shakes off whatever passion there may be; the suffering born of desire and anger, as well as shamelessness and discontent, he shakes off. Having entered into Brahman, I am like one who has entered a cool lake in the heat of summer.
I am stilled, I have attained final nirvana, and I abide in absolute bliss. Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving.
"Having slain desire— the seventh [enemy]— as one would slay a most formidable foe,
and having reached the indestructible city of Brahman, may I be happy like a king. Having established his mind upon this thought, Maṅki fell into a state of world-weariness.
Having renounced all desires and attained the great bliss of Brahman,
Maṅki indeed achieved immortality by subduing his senses;
he cut the root of desire and thereby obtained supreme happiness.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history;
O King, hear the song sung in the past on this very matter by the high-souled Janaka, the King of Videha, while he was attaining tranquility.
"Infinite indeed is my wealth, though I possess nothing at all;
even when Mithilā is ablaze, nothing of mine is burned.
In this very context, they cite these verses of Bodhya:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, awaken to that which has been set forth for the sake of world-weariness (*nirveda*).
King Nahuṣa questioned the self-controlled sage Bodhya,
who had attained peace through world-weariness, was tranquil, and was satiated with wisdom."
"O one of great wisdom, teach me the instruction regarding tranquility. Contemplating what kind of understanding do you wander about peaceful and liberated?
Bodhya replied:
I act according to instruction; I do not instruct anyone here.
I shall describe its characteristic; let that be reflected upon by oneself. Piṅgalā, the osprey, the serpent, and the search for deer in the forest.
The arrow-maker and the young girl—these six are my gurus.
Bhīṣma said:
Hope is powerful and painful; freedom from hope is the supreme happiness.
Having turned hope into despair, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace,
seeing the osprey with its prey being killed by those without prey;
through the renunciation of its prey, the osprey prospers in happiness.
The building of a house leads only to suffering and never to happiness;
a snake, having entered a dwelling made by another, prospers in comfort.
Sages live happily, relying on the practice of begging for alms.
Like birds that do not harm living beings,
a certain arrow-maker, his mind entirely fixed on his arrows,
did not even notice a king passing by his side.
"Among many there is constant strife; between two, rivalry is certain. I shall wander alone, like the maiden Śaṅkhaka.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of conduct, by what behavior should one wander the earth free from sorrow?
And by doing what in this world does a man attain the supreme goal?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Prahrāda and the sage Ājagara:
[it concerns] a certain Brahmin wandering about, healthy in mind and free from ailment.
12,172.003c The wise Prahrāda, esteemed by the learned, questioned him:

12,172.004a "Established in yourself, capable, gentle, self-controlled, free from desire, and without malice; 12,172.004c eloquent, highly regarded in the world, and wise, you move about like a child."
You do not crave gain, nor do you grieve over losses;
O Brahmin, like one who is eternally contented, you hold nothing in contempt. You remain as if unperturbed even while living beings are being carried away by the current.
In matters of dharma, pleasure, and wealth, you appear as if immovable like a mountain peak.
You do not pursue dharma or wealth, nor do you dwell in pleasure;
disregarding the objects of the senses, you move about like one who is liberated, acting as a witness.
"O Sage, what is your wisdom, or what is your learning, and what is your conduct?
O Brahmin, tell me quickly what you consider to be the highest good in this world. Thus questioned, that wise man, who understood the ordinances of worldly dharma, [replied].
He spoke in gentle words, which were not in vain, to Prahrāda:
"O Prahrāda, seeing the birth of beings without a [fixed] cause,
as well as their decline, growth, and destruction, I neither rejoice nor am I distressed."
Seeing that all activities proceed solely from their own inherent nature (svabhāva),
and that all things are devoted to that very nature, I am not distressed by anything at all,
O Prahrāda, as I observe that all unions end in separation.
He did not direct his mind toward any accumulations, knowing them to end in destruction; for one who perceives that all beings are finite and composed of the qualities (guṇas),
and who knows their origin and dissolution, what duty remains to be done?
O Lord of Asuras, I perceive the end of even those born in water through the process of succession— of great bodies and minute ones alike in the great ocean,
and of all beings, both mobile and immobile.
O best of Dānavas, I clearly perceive death from every side for all earthly beings, as well as for those who move through the air— the birds—
even for the powerful, death arises according to its own time.
"I perceive the luminaries in the sky, both small and great, moving about and falling down at their appointed times;
thus do I behold all beings incessantly pursued by death."
Knowing all things in their commonality, having accomplished what was to be done, I sleep in happiness.
Even if a very large morsel is obtained by chance, I eat it;
yet again, I lie down without eating for even many days.
Food flows toward me at times—abundant and of many qualities;
at other times it is of few qualities and meager; and at other times it does not even come at all.
Sometimes I eat grains, and sometimes I swallow oil-cake.
I eat rice and meats, as well as various other foods, both high and low.
Sometimes I sleep on a couch, and at other times I sleep even upon the ground; yet at times, a bed in a palace is provided for me.
I wear rags, hempen cloth, linen, and skins;
yet at other times, I wear garments of great value. I do not, however, by chance partake of any pleasurable enjoyment that has not been acquired through righteous means.
I reject this [worldly state], for I do not pursue that which is so difficult to attain—
the immovable, undecaying, auspicious, sorrowless, pure, incomparable state established in the minds of the wise.
This vow of the python, which is unloved and not practiced by the foolish, I, pure, observe with an unwavering mind,
never falling from my own duty.
Having limited my wandering through saṃsāra, knowing the higher and the lower,
free from fear, impurity, greed, and delusion,
I practice this pure vow of the python.
Food, drink, and edibles whose fruits are not fixed,
prepared according to rule with due regard for place and time, which gladden the heart and have never been tasted by the miserly;
I practice this pure vow of the python;
[I observe] people who, overcome by craving for "this" and "that," despair because they have not attained wealth.
Having carefully reflected with a mind intent on reality,
I, pure, practice this vow of the python;
having observed the manifold ways for the sake of worldly ends, [I have turned away from them].
Compassionate toward the noble and the ignoble alike who take refuge here,
I— self-possessed, tranquil, and delighting in peace—
practice this pure vow of the python.
Having observed in accordance with reality that pleasure and pain, misfortune and the gain of wealth, joy and sorrow, death and life, are all determined by destiny;
I practice this pure vow of the python,
free from fear, passion, delusion, and pride;
endowed with fortitude, intelligence, and wisdom, I am profoundly tranquil.
Having observed those who enjoy the fruits that come to them of their own accord,
I practice this pure vow of the python,
naturally remaining without fixed sleep or seat.
Endowed with self-restraint, vows, truth, and purity,
free from the accumulation of fruits, and joyful,
I practice this pure vow of the python.

Having perceived that the mind— which has approached objects of pleasure through the pursuit of worldly aims— is thirsty and unsteady, one whose intellect has attained [insight] and who is established in the Self strives to restrain it.
I practice this pure vow of the python;
neither my heart nor my mind yearns for the unattainability of pleasant happiness and for impermanence.
Observing both of these, as it were,
I practice this pure vow of the python,
having attained a gain of wealth that is otherwise difficult to find.
Endowed with fortitude, intelligence, wisdom, and prowess,
and practiced by wise men capable of discernment,
I, pure in conduct, observe this vow of the python.
Much indeed has been said by the wise poets who seek to spread their own fame; here and there, they have spoken of this and that particular matter.

Having closely observed that [truth] which is profound due to the various doctrines of our own and others, and which has been departed from by foolish men here who have each followed their own separate paths through mere reasoning; 12,172.036a.
"Unsettled and with no further shore due to endless faults, I wander among men, having subdued my anger and thirst.
Bhīṣma said:
The high-souled one who, having subdued passion, would here observe this vow of the Ajagara conduct—
free from fear, anger, greed, and delusion;
He indeed shall dwell happily in this state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, in this world, is it kin, action, wealth, or wisdom [that brings happiness]?"
"What would be the foundation of a man? Being asked this, tell it to me.
Bhīṣma said:
"Wisdom is the foundation of all beings; wisdom is considered the supreme attainment."

Wisdom is the highest good in the world; wisdom is considered by the virtuous to be heaven itself. For it was through wisdom that Bali attained his goal even when his sovereignty had perished, as did Prahrāda, Namuci, and Maṅki; what, then, could be superior to it?

In this regard, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Indra and Kāśyapa; listen to that, O Yudhiṣṭhira. A certain Vaiśya, my dear, [approached] the seer Kāśyapa, who was firm in his vows.
The illustrious and arrogant one caused the ascetic to fall from his chariot.
Stricken and fallen, he spoke in anger, casting away all hope for himself: "I shall die here; for one who possesses no wealth, there is no purpose in living."
12.173.007 While he was sitting there, about to die— silent and unconscious—
Indra, in the form of a jackal, spoke to him as his mind was filled with anger:
12.173.008 "All beings everywhere desire birth in a human womb."
Everyone indeed rejoices in the status of a Brahmin within the human condition. You are a human, you are a Brahmin, and you are a learned master of the Vedas, O Kāśyapa;
having attained this which is so very difficult to obtain, you wish to die because of some fault.
"Truly, the sacred tradition is true when it says that all gains are accompanied by pride;
for out of greed you consider yourself one whose form ought to be satisfied.
Oh, how successful are those who possess hands in this world!"

"O Brahmin, we have a longing for hands just as you have for wealth; indeed, there is no gain whatsoever superior to the acquisition of hands. Because we lack hands, O Brahmin, we cannot even pull out thorns."
We do not even scratch the various creatures biting our limbs; yet those whose hands possess ten fingers, like those of the gods,
pull out the worms from their bodies as they bite and scratch them.
They provide protection against snow, rain, and heat;
they enjoy clothing, food, comfortable beds, and shelter from the wind.
Having taken possession of cattle in this world, they consume them and make them work.
By many means, they indeed bring others under their own control.
Those who are truly tongueless, wretched, of little strength, and handless endure those sufferings; by good fortune, O Sage, you are not like them.
"By good fortune, you are indeed not a jackal, nor a worm, nor a mouse;
nor a serpent, nor a frog, nor anyone else born of a sinful womb.
Even with this much gain, O Kāśyapa, you ought to be content."
How much more so for you, who are the supreme among all beings and the best of brahmins?
These worms are devouring me;
yet, because I lack hands, I have no power to extract them—behold this, my condition!
Thinking, "This is an improper act," I did not abandon my own self,
lest I fall into another womb even more wretched than this;
for among the wombs of sinful beings, it is that of a jackal into which I have entered.
There are many other more wretched states of existence than these;
some are happier by their very birth, while others are intensely miserable. I do not see anyone anywhere in this world who possesses absolute happiness.
For human beings, having attained wealth, desire sovereignty immediately thereafter;
from sovereignty they desire divinity, and from divinity even the state of Indra. Even if you were to become wealthy, you would be neither a king nor a deity.
Even having attained divinity and the status of Indra, you would not be satisfied if that were the case;
for there is no satisfaction in the acquisition of what is dear, and thirst is not quenched by water—
it blazes up even more, like a fire with fuel.

Indeed, sorrow exists in you, and likewise joy exists in you; both happiness and suffering exist as well—what cause for lamentation is there in that? Having thus severed all desires and all actions, [one remains steadfast].
Restrain the collection of the senses at their root, as one would birds in a cage.
Nowhere does the cutting off of a second head exist, nor the [severing] of a third hand; that which does not exist brings no fear.
Indeed, desire never arises in one who does not know the taste;
it arises from touch, or from sight, or even from hearing.
Do you not remember the *vāruṇī* wine and the *laṭvāka* birds?
There is nothing anywhere to be eaten that surpasses those two.
And as for whatever other foods and delicacies exist in distant places, O Kāśyapa,
since you have never before eaten them, there is simply no memory of them.
Not eating, not touching, and indeed not even looking [at it]—
this discipline for a man, I believe, is undoubtedly superior. Those who possess hands, those endowed with wealth, and those who are powerful— of this there is no doubt.
12,173.032c Humans are reduced to servitude by other humans;
12,173.033a They are tormented again and again with slaughter, imprisonment, and afflictions. 12,173.033c Yet even they take pleasure, rejoice, and laugh.
Others, strong of arm, learned, and high-minded,
yet follow a loathsome, miserable, and sinful way of life;
and they are even capable of pursuing another livelihood.
That which is ordained by one's own karma must indeed come to pass in that way. Neither a Pulkasa nor a Caṇḍāla desires to abandon himself;
being dissatisfied with his own birth, behold what kind of illusion it is!
"Seeing men who are withered, paralyzed on one side, and afflicted by disease, you are fully complete in your own nature; you have obtained your gain, O Kāśyapa!
If, O Brāhmaṇa, your body is free from distress and free from ailment."
With all your limbs intact and not censured by anyone in the worlds for any truthful accusation that would deprive you of your status,
arise for the sake of dharma, O brahmin-sage; you ought not to abandon yourself.
"O Brahmin, if you hear this and have faith in my words,
you shall obtain the primary fruit of the dharma declared in the Vedas. Diligently maintain your private Vedic study and the consecration of the sacred fires."
"Be truthful, self-controlled, and generous; do not compete with anyone.
How could those who are devoted to their own Vedic study and engaged in performing sacrifices for themselves or for others ever grieve, or even contemplate anything unwholesome?"
Desiring to dwell [there], may they attain great happiness; moreover, having been born under auspicious stars, at excellent sacred sites, and at favorable moments,
they strive according to their capacity for sacrifice, charity, and procreation.
Under inauspicious lunar mansions, others— born at evil crossings and evil moments—
fall into an asuric womb, devoid of the fruits of sacrifice.
I was once a self-styled scholar, a rationalist who reviled the Vedas.
Devoted to the useless science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*),
he was a proponent of causal arguments who spoke with reason in assemblies;
indeed, he was one who reviled and spoke abusively toward the twice-born during the Vedic sacrifices (*brahmayajña*).
"O twice-born one, this attainment of the state of a jackal is the fruit of my being an atheist, doubting everything, a fool who fancies himself a scholar.
Could such a thing ever happen even after hundreds of days and nights?"
If I, as a jackal, should again obtain a human birth,
may I be contented and vigilant, devoted to sacrifice, charity, and austerity; may I indeed become a knower of what is to be known, and likewise one who avoids what is to be avoided.
Then that sage Kāśyapa rose up and said to him:
"Oh, how skillful you are! How wise! Thus amazed, the brahmin gazed at him with an eye made long by knowledge.
He beheld Indra, the god of the gods and lord of Śacī; then Kāśyapa paid homage to the one whose vehicle is green horses. Having been granted permission by him, he then entered his own hermitage.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Grandfather,
if there is anything given, sacrificed, or likewise austerity performed,
as well as service rendered to one's elders, tell me of that."
"O best of kings, know that as it is here, so it is there.
Listen now to how evildoers act in this world.
Bhīṣma said:

When one is joined with what is disadvantageous to oneself, the mind enters into evil; having performed a defiled deed, one is placed in great suffering. From famine to famine, from affliction to affliction, and from fear to fear.
The poor who commit evil deeds go from death to further death;
those who have faith, who are self-controlled, wealthy, and performers of auspicious deeds go from festival to festival, from heaven to heaven, and from happiness to happiness.
In places difficult due to predatory beasts and wild elephants, and amidst fears of snakes and thieves, atheists proceed by groping with their hands; what can be more [ridiculous] than this?
Those who are devoted to the gods and guests, generous, and fond of the virtuous—
They have set out upon the secure path of those who possess self-mastery, which is held in the right hand.
Like shriveled grain among crops, or like gnats among birds—
such are those among men for whom dharma is not the motive.
Fate runs after one even as he runs very swiftly;
it lies down with him as he lies down, according to whatever has been done by each person. It stands by one who stands, and follows one who goes.

Whatever action one performs, it follows that doer like a shadow. Whatever specific deed was previously accumulated by a person, in whatever manner and to whatever extent, that very thing he inevitably experiences, for it was ordained by himself.
Time drags away this entire multitude of beings from every side— beings who are distracted by the fruits of their own actions and protected by the laws of destiny—
just as flowers and fruits fall without being prompted.
Just as one's own time does not pass by, so too does previously performed karma;
honor and dishonor, gain and loss, decline and rise— having come forth, they recur again and again at the end of their appointed course.
Suffering is ordained by oneself; happiness is ordained by oneself.
Beginning from the bed of the womb, one experiences the fruits of actions performed in previous bodies.
Whether as a child, a youth, or an old man, whatever good or evil one does—
In each and every state, in birth after birth, he experiences [the results];
just as a calf finds its mother among thousands of cows,
so does the karma performed in the past follow after the doer.

Just as a garment that is first soiled becomes clean later through cleansing, so too even an evil deed is purified later by meritorious action. Through austerity the body is refined; through austerity one attains greatness.
For those purified by fasts, there is long-lasting and infinite happiness. Through the practice of austerity for a long time in the forest of penance,
the desires of those whose sins have been shaken off by dharma are fully realized.
Just as the track of birds in the sky or of fish in the water cannot be seen, so too is the path of those who possess knowledge. Enough with these other censures and recounted transgressions.
"What is skillful, appropriate, and beneficial for oneself should be done.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"From what was this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, created?"
"O Grandfather, tell me this: at the time of dissolution, to what does it go?
By whom was this world created—with its oceans, its sky, its mountains, its clouds, its earth, its fire, and its wind?"
How were the elements created, and how did the divisions of the social orders arise?
What is their purity and impurity, and likewise, what are their dharma and adharma? Of what nature is the life-principle (*jīva*) of living beings, and where do those who have died go?
"May your lordship recount to us everything concerning the passage from this world to that world.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
12,175.005c This excellent [teaching] was spoken by Bhṛgu to Bharadvāja, who questioned him.
12,175.006a Having seen the great seer Bhṛgu seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, blazing as if with vital energy (ojas), 12,175.006c Bharadvāja addressed him.
By whom was this world created— along with its oceans, its sky, its mountains, its clouds,
its earth, its fire, and its wind? How were the living beings produced, and how did the distinctions between the social orders arise?
How do purity and impurity belong to them, and likewise, how do dharma and adharma? What is the nature of the life-force (jīva) for those who live, and where do those who have died go?
May your lordship explain all of this to us regarding both this world and the next.
12,175.010a Thus questioned by Bharadvāja regarding his doubt, 12,175.010c that Blessed One, the great seer who resembles Brahmā, then told him everything. 12,175.010d Bhṛgu said:

Of him who is named Nārāyaṇa, who is immutable, whose nature is the Imperishable, who is unmanifest, immeasurable, and withdrawn from primordial matter— such indeed is that God; and he created Puruṣa in two ways.
Bhṛgu said:
Nārāyaṇa is the embodiment of the universe, the eternal inner self;
he is the unchanging, imperishable, unmanifest, untainted, all-pervading Lord.

Eternal and beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he is inaccessible even to the senses. Desiring to create, that Lord emitted from a thousandth part [of himself] a Puruṣa known as Mānasa, who had been heard of before by the great seers (*maharṣi*).
The God who is without beginning or end, likewise indivisible, ageless, and immortal; he is renowned as the Unmanifest (avyakta), eternal, imperishable, and immutable—
from whom all beings are created, and in whom they are born and die.
First, that God created the one known by the name Mahat;
then the Lord Mahat created Ahaṃkāra, and he,
the sovereign sustainer of all beings, created that which is celebrated as Ākāśa.
From space arose water; from water, fire and wind. From the conjunction of fire and wind, the earth then came into being.
Then, a divine lotus consisting of light was created by the Self-born One.
From that lotus arose Brahmā, a treasure-trove consisting of the Vedas,
known as Ahaṃkāra, the creator of the self of all beings; indeed, Brahmā is possessed of great splendor, and these are the five elements.
The mountains are known as his bones; the fat and flesh are the earth;
the oceans are his blood, and space is likewise his belly;
the wind is his breath, fire is his heat, and the rivers are his veins.
Agni and Soma are his renowned eyes, the moon and the sun;
the sky above is his head, the earth his feet, and the quarters of space his arms. Indeed, because of his infinity, he is difficult to perceive even by the Siddhas; of this there is no doubt.
That very Blessed One, Viṣṇu, is renowned as Ananta;
abiding as the self within all beings, he is difficult to be known by those of unrefined soul. He is indeed the creator of the ego-principle for the sake of the existence of all beings.
"From whom the universe originated—this is what I have been asked by you here.
Bharadvāja said:
"Of the sky, of the directions, of the earth, and of the wind..."
"What are the measurements here? Cut through my doubt regarding the facts.
Bhṛgu said:
"This sky is infinite, frequented by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas."
Delightful and filled with various dwellings, its end cannot be found;
above it, and even below, the moon and sun are not seen.
There, the gods are self-luminous, radiant, and possess the brilliance of fire.
Even they, though possessed of celebrated prowess, do not see the end of the sky;
know this from me, O giver of honor, that it is because of its inaccessibility and its infinity.
And above, ever higher, there are those who blaze with their own inherent radiance.
This space is obstructed and immeasurable even for the gods.
At the end of the earth lies the ocean, and at the end of the ocean, darkness is said to be. They say that at the end of darkness is water, and at the end of water is fire itself.
At the end of the netherworld (rasātala) is water; at the end of the water is the lord of serpents;
at the end of that is space again; and at the end of space is water once more. Such is the limit of the Blessed One and the measure of the waters.

Difficult to discern even for the gods, it arises from fire, wind, and water. The colors of fire, wind, water, and the surface of the earth are indeed like the sky; they are distinguished only by the vision of reality.
And the sages recite in various scriptures how the measurement was established for the three worlds and the ocean;
yet who could state a measurement for that which is invisible and inaccessible?

When the movement of the *siddhas* and the deities is limited, then the name "Ananta" (the Infinite) is known as a secondary designation for that high-souled Mānasa, whose very name corresponds to his nature.
But when that divine form wanes and increases again—
who else could know it, even if there were another such as he?
Then, from Puṣkara, the omniscient Lord was manifested in embodied form.
"Brahmā, consisting of dharma, was the first and unsurpassed Prajāpati.
Bharadvāja said:
"If he was born from Puṣkara, then Puṣkara must be the eldest."
"You have spoken of Brahmā as the first-born; this is indeed a source of doubt for me.
Bhr̥gu said:
"That which was the mental form here has attained the state of Brahmā."
For the purpose of providing a seat for him, the earth is called a lotus; Mount Meru is its raised pericarp, towering into the sky. Standing in its center, the Lord of the world creates the worlds.
Bharadvāja said:
"O best of the twice-born, tell me how that Lord Brahmā, situated in the midst of Meru, creates the various emanations of progeny."
"12,176.001d*0485_01 How did Brahmā, stationed in the midst of Meru, create progeny?
12,176.001d*0485_02 Tell all this to me as it truly is, for I am asking you.
12,176.002 Bhṛgu said:
With his mind, Mānasa created the various emanations of progeny. For the sake of nourishing all beings, water was first created;
it is that by which the vital breaths of all beings increase and by which creatures flourish.
Those who are abandoned perish; therefore, all this is pervaded by him.
The earth, the mountains, the clouds, and whatever else possesses form—all that is to be known as belonging to Varuṇa; yet the waters were once again solidified.
Bharadvāja said:
"How was the water produced, and how were fire and wind?
And how was the earth created? In this regard, I have a great doubt."
Bhṛgu said:
"O Brahman, formerly, in the Brahma-kalpa, at a gathering of the celestial rishis,
a doubt concerning the origin of the worlds arose among those high-souled ones."

Relying on meditation and maintaining silence, those twice-born ones remained motionless for a hundred divine years, abstaining from food and subsisting only on air. The voice of Dharma reached the ears of them all.
There, the divine Sarasvatī emerged from the expanse of the sky.
Formerly, the atmosphere had been motionless and silent, like a mountain;
with the moon, sun, and wind vanished, it appeared as if fast asleep.
Then water arose, like a further darkness within darkness;
and from that pressure of water, the wind rose up. It was as if a vessel without cracks appeared to be entirely silent.
And as that [space] is being filled with water, the wind makes a sound;
likewise, when the end of space is completely obstructed by water,
the wind pierces the surface of the ocean and rises up with a roar.
This very wind, born from the agitation of the ocean, moves about;
having reached its station in space, it finds no rest.
In that friction between wind and water, he of blazing splendor and great power [arises].
A fire with upward-pointing flames appears, making the sky free from darkness; joined with the wind, that fire causes water to rise from the void.
Through its union with the wind, that fire attains a state of density.
That other moisture which falls into the sky and remains there,
having attained a state of condensation, becomes earth.
This applies likewise to all fluids, all fragrances, all moistures, and living beings.
"Earth is to be known here as the womb, from which everything is produced.
Bharadvāja said:
"These are those five elements which Brahmā created in the past."
By those things designated as the great elements (mahābhūta), these worlds are enveloped. When that one of great intelligence created thousands of beings,
how is it that the state of being a "great element" (bhūtatva) applies only to five?
Bhṛgu said:
"The great sound of infinite beings proceeds from their coming into existence;
therefore, this term 'great element' (mahābhūta) is applied to them."
Movement is wind, the void is space, heat is fire, liquidity is water,
and the solid mass here is earth; thus, the body is composed of these five elements and consists of both the stationary and the moving.
12,177.005 Hearing, smell, taste, touch, and sight are designated as the sense organs.
12,177.006 Bharadvāja said:
If mobile and immobile beings are composed of the five elements, [how is it so?]
The five elements are not seen in the bodies of stationary beings; in reality, they are not perceived within the bodies of trees, which lack heat, lack movement, and are solid.

They do not hear, they do not see, they do not experience smell or taste, nor do they perceive touch; how then can they be composed of the five elements? Because they lack liquidity, lack fire, lack earth, and lack air.
Because space is immeasurable, trees possess no material substance.
Bhṛgu said:
"Even for dense trees, there is space; of this there is no doubt."
In these [trees], the manifestation of flowers and fruits is constantly perceived;
yet, when they are withered by heat, their leaves, bark, fruit, and even their flowers fade away. Since they do not wither in the cold, it follows that touch does not exist here [in the tree].
By the crashing of wind, fire, and thunderbolts, their fruits and flowers are shattered;
since sound is perceived by the ear, trees therefore hear. A creeper winds itself around a tree and moves toward it from every side.
For there is no path for that which is unseen; therefore, trees see.
Likewise, through merits and demerits, as well as by various fragrances and incenses, they remain free from disease and in bloom; therefore, trees smell.
Through its feet it drinks water, and there is even the appearance of diseases;
because it counteracts diseases, the sense of taste exists in the tree.
Just as one might draw up water upward through the mouth by means of a lotus-stalk, [so does the tree draw up moisture].
Likewise, joined with the vital wind (*pavana*), the tree drinks through its feet;
because it experiences pleasure and pain, and because it grows back when cut,
I perceive that trees possess life— their lack of consciousness does not exist.
By that [fire], the water is taken up; it digests the fire and wind. From the transformation of food, moisture and growth arise.
And in the bodies of all mobile beings, there are five constituent elements (dhātus).
They are distinguished individually by those through which the body moves:
skin, flesh, likewise bones, marrow, and sinew as the fifth;
thus is that which consists of earth enumerated here in the body.
Radiance, fire, as well as anger, the eye, and likewise heat—fire also causes decay; these are the five fires within embodied beings.
Furthermore, the ear, the nose, the mouth, the heart, and the stomach [are the five fires].
From space, these five elements [arise] within the bodies of living beings:
phlegm, bile, sweat, fat, and blood. Thus, water always exists in five ways within the bodies of living beings.
By means of *prāṇa*, the living being is led forth; likewise, by means of *vyāna*, it exerts itself. *Apāna* moves downward, while *samāna* is situated in the heart.
By means of *udāna*, one breathes out, and through its differentiation, one speaks.
"These five winds thus cause the embodied being to move here in this world.
Possessing a body, one perceives the quality of smell from the earth and taste from the waters;
one sees light with the eyes and perceives touch through the wind."
Smell, touch, taste, form, and sound are known here as the qualities (guṇas).
And likewise, one possessing a body hears sound through space (ākāśa).
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the qualities of the elements (bhūtas).
I shall describe in detail the qualities of that fragrance: it may be pleasant or unpleasant, sweet or pungent;
it may be diffusive, concentrated, oily, dry, or clear.
Thus, the detailed classification of the ninefold earthly fragrance should be known.
Sound, touch, form, and taste are recorded as the qualities of water.
Now I shall speak of the knowledge of taste; listen to me as I recite it.
12.177.030a Taste has been declared by the wise of celebrated soul to be of many kinds: 12.177.030c sweet, salty, bitter, astringent, sour, and likewise pungent.
12.177.030e This sixfold expansion of taste is remembered as being composed of water.
Sound, touch, and form—light is said to possess these three qualities.
Light perceives forms, and form is remembered as being manifold:
short, long, thick, square, minute, and circular.

White, black, red, blue, yellow, and likewise ruddy—thus it is remembered that the nature of light has a twelvefold expansion. Sound and touch are to be known as its qualities; thus wind is said to possess two qualities.
The quality of wind is touch, and touch is said to be of many kinds:
hard, sticky, smooth, slimy, soft, and harsh;
hot, cold, pleasant, painful, oily, and clear.
Likewise, rough, soft, smooth, light, and even heavy—thus the twelvefold quality of wind is described.
Among these, space has a single quality; it is traditionally known as sound alone.
I shall explain in detail the various natures of that sound:
the peaceful, the terrible, and the deluded, as well as those not born of competition;
likewise, the *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, and *pañcama*.
Dhaivata is also to be known, as well as Niṣāda;
this sevenfold quality, characterized by space (ākāśa), is thus declared to exist everywhere, even in drums and other instruments, through the three musical scales.

Whatever sound is heard—whether of clay drums, kettledrums, or conchs; whether the roar of thunder or the rattling of a chariot; or any sound whatsoever, whether from a sentient being or an insentient object—it is proclaimed that all these fall within this very domain.
Thus, sound arises from space in many such forms.
They say that sound is born of space together with these qualities of wind; when unobstructed, it is perceived, but it is not known when it arrives in a discordant manner.
And those elements are constantly nourished by those very elements;
water, fire, and wind are ever awake within embodied beings. These are the root of the body, and having pervaded it, they remain here as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Bharadvāja said:
How does the bodily fire come to exist by depending upon the earthly element? And how does the wind circulate through the specific spaces [of the body]?
Bhṛgu said:
"O sinless Brahmin, I shall describe to you the course of the wind—
how the powerful vital air (anila) impels the bodies of living beings."
Agni, however, rests upon the head, protecting the body;
and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), existing both in the head and in Agni, performs its functions.
He is the living being, the self of all creatures, that eternal Puruṣa.
Mind, intellect, ego, the elements, and the objects of the senses— thus,
in this world, he is everywhere protected by the *prāṇa* (outgoing breath), while from behind he is supported by the *samāna* (equalizing breath) as each relies upon its own respective course.
Resting upon the base of the bladder, the anus, and the digestive fire,
the *apāna* wind circulates, carrying both urine and feces.
It is that single force which operates within these three— effort, action, and strength.
Those who are learned in the inner self call that *udāna*;
likewise, the wind situated in all the joints is taught as *vyāna* within the bodies of men.
The fire within the bodily constituents is spread throughout, impelled by the *samāna* wind;
it remains active, maintaining the fluids, the tissues, and the humors. Situated between the *apāna* and *prāṇa* breaths, it is concentrated within both the *prāṇa* and *apāna*.
Endowed with its own foundation and well-established, the digestive fire (pāvaka) properly digests [the food].
For the mouth is connected to the anus, and at its end lies that which is known as the rectum (guda);
from that [central channel], all the channels of embodied beings arise.
From the convergence of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), a convergence (*saṃnipāta*) is produced;
it should be known as heat and fire, which digests the food of embodied beings. Carrying the force of the fire, the *prāṇa* is struck back at the end of the rectum.
Having ascended upward, it again throws the fire upward. The receptacle of digested food (*pakvāśaya*) is below the navel, while the receptacle of undigested food (*āmāśaya*) is situated above it.
In the center of the navel, all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are concentrated within the body.
All these channels, ten in number, extend from the heart— sideways, upwards, and downwards— and, impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), they carry the essences of food. This, moreover,
is the path of yogis, by which they go to that supreme state.
Having conquered fatigue and mastered their postures, the wise ones place the self in the crown of the head.
Thus, when the prāṇa and apāna breaths of all embodied beings are regulated,
the fire remains eternally established therein, as if carefully contained within a vessel.
Bharadvāja said:
"If it is the wind that breathes and the wind alone that moves,
and if it is the wind that sighs and speaks, then the living soul (jīva) is purposeless."
If the state of heat belongs to fire, and it is cooked by fire, and if fire itself undergoes decay, then the *jīva* is purposeless;
for when a living being is dying, the *jīva* is not perceived at all.
The wind itself abandons him, and his state of warmth perishes.
If the living soul were like the wind, or if there were a union with the wind,
it would be visible like a circle of air and would depart along with the hosts of Maruts.
If there is an obstruction by wind, or if, because of that, it perishes—
just as a vessel of water other than the great ocean [would dry up] due to being separated from it—
one might as well pour water into a well or place a lamp in a fire.

Just as that which is cast in quickly perishes, so too does this perish; both of those perish in that same way, for the life-force consists of wind and fire. Indeed, in this body which is common to the five elements, whence is there life?
12,179.007c Because of the abandonment of any one of these four, there is no longer a collection [of the elements]:
12,179.008a For water perishes from lack of food; wind perishes from the suppression of breath;
12,179.008c space perishes from the breaking of the internal cavities; and fire perishes from the absence of fuel.

The earth itself is shattered by the afflictions of disease and wounds; for when any one of these is afflicted, the aggregate dissolves into five parts. When that has reached its dissolution into the five elements, what does the living soul pursue?
What does the living soul perceive, or what does it hear, or what does it say:
"This cow shall deliver me when I am situated in the next world"?
When a creature dies after having given [the cow], whom will that cow deliver?
When the cow, the recipient, and the giver are all equal, they go to dissolution right here; how then can there be a reunion for them?
For one who has been consumed by birds or fallen from a mountain peak, [there is no such reunion].
And once consumed by fire, how can there be a return to life? If the root of a severed tree does not sprout again, yet its seeds continue to propagate, where will this deceased person go once more?
"That which was created in the beginning as mere seed continues to revolve;
those who have died perish again and again, yet from seed, seed proceeds.
Bhṛgu said:
There is no destruction of living beings, nor of what has been given or done.
The living being passes into another body, while the physical frame alone dissolves. The living being does not reside within the body; therefore, when that [body] is destroyed, it does not perish.
Just as fire is not destroyed when the fuel has been consumed,
Bhāradvāja said:
"If, in that same manner, there is no destruction of that [self] for the fire..."
At the end of the fuel's consumption, that fire is no longer perceived; I know only that it perishes when the fire is extinguished and without fuel—
its destination, its measure, or its configuration being nowhere seen.
Bhṛgu said:
"The destruction of the individual soul and of the fire with its fuel never occurs;
at the conclusion of the consumption of the fuel, the fire, though still present, is simply not seen."
For, because it has entered into space and is without support, it is difficult to grasp;
likewise, upon the abandonment of the body, the living soul remains like space.
Due to its extreme subtlety, it is not perceived, just as light [is not seen when it enters the eye]—of this there is no doubt.
For it is fire that sustains the vital breaths; let it be understood that this is the living soul. Indeed, fire is maintained by the wind; it perishes when the out-breath is suppressed.
When that fire of the body has perished, the body becomes insentient.
When fallen, it returns to the state of earth, for the earth is its destination; indeed,
for all things mobile as well as immobile,
the wind reaches the ether, and the light follows after it.
Among those three, one is identical and two are established upon the earth:
where there is space, there is wind; and where there is wind, there is fire. Those [elements] should be known as formless, while water and earth are likewise possessed of form.
Bharadvāja said:
"O sinless one, if fire, wind, earth, space, and water are present within embodied beings, what are the characteristics of the *jīva* therein? Please explain this to me."
In this body of living beings— which consists of five elements, delights in the five [objects], is joined with the five consciousnesses,
and is a mass of flesh and blood, a collection of fat, sinews, and bones— I wish to know what kind of soul (*jīva*) it possesses.
When the body is being dissected, the *jīva* is not perceived at all.
If the body, composed of the five elements, were devoid of a *jīva*,
who would experience that pain— the physical and mental suffering?
The living soul hears what is spoken with its two ears, yet it does not hear it when the mind is distracted, O Great Seer; therefore, the living soul is purposeless.
It perceives everything that is visible by means of the eye joined with the mind.
For when the mind is agitated, one does not see even while seeing.
Furthermore, fallen under the power of sleep, one neither sees, nor speaks, nor hears, nor smells; nor does one perceive touch or taste.
"Who is it that rejoices and who is it that becomes angry? Who grieves and who trembles with fear? Who desires, meditates, hates, or utters speech?
Bhṛgu said:
There is nothing here common to the five [elements]; the inner self alone sustains the body. It perceives odors, tastes, and hearing.
Tactility, form, and whatever other qualities there are— displaying these five qualities within that which consists of the five elements—
that is the inner self (antarātmā) pervading all limbs.
Therein, that [consciousness] experiences both sufferings and pleasures;
however, due to separation from it, the body does not experience them.
When there is neither form, nor touch, nor the state of heat in the fire, [the body remains insentient].

Then, when the bodily fire has been extinguished, he perishes after abandoning the body. All this is indeed composed of water; water is the physical form of embodied beings. Therein resides the mental self, Brahmā, the creator of the worlds within all living creatures.

The Self (ātman) is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) when joined with the qualities of primordial nature (prākṛtaguṇa); but when liberated from those very same qualities, it is designated as the Supreme Self (paramātman). Know that Self to be the essence of the welfare of all worlds.
Know that he who is situated within that body like a drop of water on a lotus leaf is the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field), eternally characterized by the welfare of the world.
Know these— *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*— to be the qualities (*guṇas*) of the individual soul (*jīva*).
One should know the *jīva* as a quality of the self, and the self as belonging to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). They say that consciousness is a quality of the *jīva*;
it acts and causes everything else to act.
Beyond that, they speak of the Knower of the Field,
who set the seven worlds in motion;
for there is no destruction of the living being when the body is divided.
"The ignorant say this falsely: 'He is dead'; for the living soul departs enveloped by another body;
the dissolution of the body is merely its fifth state."
Thus, hidden and concealed, he moves within all beings;
however, he is perceived by those who see reality through a subtle and supreme intellect.
The wise man, constantly applying himself during the first and last watches of the night, [perceives him].
Eating light food, with a purified self, one perceives the Self within the self. Indeed, by the serenity of the mind, having abandoned both auspicious and inauspicious karma,
one who is serene in self abides in the Self and enjoys imperishable bliss.
"The mental fire within bodies is designated as the *jīva*.
This is the creation of Prajāpati, according to the determination of the elements and the self.
Bhr̥gu said:

In the beginning, Brahmā Prajāpati created only the Brāhmaṇas, produced from his own splendor, possessing a radiance equal to the sun and fire. Then he created truth, righteousness, austerity, and the eternal Veda.
The Lord ordained both proper conduct and purity for the sake of heaven;
[as did] the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, daityas, asuras, and great serpents,
as well as the yakṣas, rākṣasas, nāgas, piśācas, and likewise human beings.
O best of the twice-born, he created Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras,
as well as other groups of the various classes of beings.
The color of the Brāhmaṇas is white, while that of the Kṣatriyas is red.
The color of Vaiśyas is yellow, and that of Śūdras is black.
Bharadvāja said:
"If the castes of the fourfold order are distinguished by their color..."
Indeed, a mixture of castes is seen among all the social orders.
Desire, anger, fear, greed, grief, anxiety, hunger, and fatigue prevail over all of us; why then is the caste system distinguished?
Sweat, urine, feces, phlegm, bile, and blood—the body of all beings exudes these; why then is their complexion differentiated?
There are innumerable species of both mobile and immobile beings.
"How can there be a determination of caste among those of such diverse colors?
Bhṛgu replied:
"There is no distinction between castes; this entire world is Brahman."

Indeed, those who were previously created by Brahmā attained the status of the *varṇas* through their actions. Those twice-born ones who were fond of sensual enjoyments, fierce, wrathful, and prone to violence, having abandoned their own duty (*svadharma*) and possessing red limbs, attained the state of the Kṣatriya.
Having established their livelihood among cattle, those who subsist on agriculture have become yellowish;
they do not follow their own dharma and have indeed fallen to the state of Vaiśyas.
Fond of violence and falsehood, greedy, and subsisting by all manner of occupations—these are they.
12,181.013c Those twice-born who have fallen away from purity have become Śūdras.
12,181.014a Thus, by these various actions, the twice-born have entered other castes;
yet, their dharma and the performance of sacrifice are never prohibited for them.

These are indeed the four castes for whom the Brahmic Sarasvatī was ordained by Brahmā in the past; however, through greed, they have fallen into ignorance. For those Brāhmaṇas who remain established in the system of dharma, their ascetic merit does not perish.
