Those who constantly uphold the Veda, as well as the vows and restraints— those ignorant ones who do not know this Veda created in the beginning,
for them there are indeed various other castes here and there.
Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Pretas, and various Mleccha tribes—
whose knowledge and discernment have perished, whose conduct and actions follow their own whims— the subjects [will be] consecrated by the Brāhmaṇas and firm in their resolve toward their own duties.
Others are created by the ṛṣis through their own ascetic power (tapas), and still others by superior beings. Originating from the Primordial God, rooted in Brahman, imperishable and undecaying—
that creation is known as the "Mānasī" (mental), devoted to the system of Dharma.
Bharadvāja said:
"O best of the twice-born, by what does one become a Brāhmaṇa, or a Kṣatriya?
O Brahmin-sage, best among speakers, tell me how one becomes a Vaiśya or a Śūdra."
Bhṛgu said:
But he who has been purified by the purificatory rites beginning with the birth-ceremony, who is pure,
perfected in the study of the Vedas, and established in the six duties;
One who is firmly established in purity and right conduct, who eats only the remains of the meal, who is dear to his guru,
who is constant in his vows, and who is devoted to truth— he indeed is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Truth, charity, self-restraint, freedom from malice, kindness, forgiveness, and compassion— [these are his qualities].
He in whom austerity is observed is remembered as a Brāhmaṇa.
He who follows the duties born of the Kṣatra, is devoted to the study of the Vedas,
and delights in giving and receiving [gifts] is indeed called a Kṣatriya.

He who constantly and purely engages in agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade, and is perfected in the study of the Vedas, is designated as a Vaiśya. One who always delights in eating all kinds of food, performs all types of labor, and is impure— [is a Śūdra].

One who has abandoned the Vedas and is devoid of proper conduct is indeed remembered as a Śūdra. This characteristic may be found in a Śūdra, yet it does not exist in a twice-born man. Indeed, such a person is no longer a Śūdra, nor is he a Brāhmaṇa.
By every possible means, one must restrain greed and anger;
this is to be known as purifying, as is self-restraint. Indeed, these two must be warded off with all one's being, for they arise for the purpose of destroying one’s welfare.

One should always protect one's ascetic merit from anger, one's prosperity from envy, one's knowledge from honor and dishonor, and one's self from negligence. He whose undertakings in this world are all free from the bonds of desire—
He for whom everything is sacrificed in renunciation is a true renouncer and he is wise;

non-violent toward all beings, he should conduct himself with a disposition of universal friendliness. One should not place trust where there is no reliability, but one should fix the mind upon that which is reliable.
Having renounced all possessions, one should become a master of the senses through wisdom; one should abide in that state free from sorrow, which is fearless both in this world and the next.
By means of a sage who is constant in austerity, self-controlled, and of restrained mind, [one attains this].
One who desires to conquer the unconquered should remain unattached amidst attachments. Whatever is grasped by the senses is established as the manifest (*vyakta*);
that which is beyond the senses and graspable only through its marks (*liṅga*) is to be known as the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
One should restrain the mind in the vital breath (prāṇa), and one should fix the vital breath in Brahman. Through Nirvāṇa alone one becomes extinguished; one should not think of anything at all.
Indeed, the Brahmin attains that bliss which is Brahman through this very means.
"Constantly endowed with purity, likewise possessed of proper conduct,
and compassionate toward all beings— this is the characteristic of the twice-born.
Bhṛgu said:
Truth is Brahman, truth is austerity; truth creates all beings. By truth the world is sustained; by truth one goes to heaven.
Untruth is the form of darkness; by darkness, indeed, one is led downward.
Those seized by darkness do not see the light, as they are enveloped in gloom. They say that heaven is light and hell is indeed darkness;
both of these are attained by the inhabitants of the world through truth and falsehood.
In this world, such a mode of existence consists of both truth and falsehood;
it comprises righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, as well as suffering and happiness.
Among these, that which is truth is righteousness; that which is righteousness is light; and that which is light is happiness.
In this regard, that which is false is unrighteousness (*adharma*); that which is unrighteousness is darkness (*tamas*); and that which is darkness is suffering (*duḥkha*). Here it is said:
[one is afflicted] by physical and mental sufferings, and even by pleasures that result in unhappiness.
12,183.006A Thus it is stated.
The discerning, clearly perceiving the creation of the world, are not deluded;
therein, the wise person should strive for liberation from suffering,
for the happiness of living beings in this world and the next is indeed impermanent.

Just as the moonlight of the moon seized by Rāhu does not shine, so too the happiness of beings overwhelmed by darkness falls away. Indeed, that happiness is said to be of two kinds: physical and mental.
Indeed, in this world and in the next, all undertakings and activities are said to be for the sake of happiness;

for there is no fruit of the three aims of life (trivarga) more distinguished than this. This very desirable excellence of qualities is the undertaking of dharma and artha; it is their cause, and its arising has happiness as its purpose.
Bharadvāja said:

"As for what you have stated—that women are the supreme among pleasures—we do not accept that. For this particular excellence is not unattainable by these sages who abide in greatness, nor do they desire it."
12,183.010C And it is heard that the Blessed One Brahmā, the creator of the three worlds, remains alone as the Lord;
12,183.010D as a celibate student, he does not apply himself to the pleasures of desire.
12,183.010E Moreover, the Blessed One Viśveśvara, the Lord of Umā, brought Kāma to rest by turning him into the bodiless one (Anaṅga) when he was about to approach.
12,183.010F Therefore we say that although this was not accepted by the Great Beings, it is not because it is a particularly distinguished quality; I do not believe this of the Blessed One.

12,183.010G For the Blessed One has said that women are the supreme among pleasures. 12,183.010H Furthermore, there is a worldly proverb concerning the two-fold arising of results: "From good deeds, happiness is obtained; from evil deeds, suffering."
12,183.010 Let this be said here.
12,183.011 Bhṛgu said:
12,183.011 Indeed, from falsehood darkness has arisen; those seized by darkness follow only unrighteousness, not righteousness.
Enveloped by anger, greed, delusion, pride, falsehood, and the like, they indeed obtain no happiness in this world nor in the next;
they are overwhelmed by the afflictions of various multitudes of diseases,
and they are tormented by the distresses of execution, imprisonment, illness, and the like, as well as by the sufferings caused by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion.

12,183.011E They are tormented by terrifying physical sufferings caused by fierce winds, excessive heat, and extreme cold; 12,183.011F they are overwhelmed by mental sorrows caused by the loss and separation from kinsmen and wealth, as well as by others caused by old age and death. 12,183.012A But he who is not touched by these physical and mental sufferings experiences happiness.
And these defects do not manifest in heaven;
indeed, there in heaven the breeze is exceedingly pleasant, and likewise the fragrance is sweet-smelling.
There is no hunger, thirst, or fatigue; there is neither old age nor evil.
In heaven there is only constant happiness, whereas here [in this world] there is both happiness and suffering. They say that in hell there is only suffering, but the Supreme State is equal [to all].

The earth is the progenitor of all beings, and women are of that same nature; the male is Prajāpati, and they know his seed to be composed of splendor. Thus was this creation of the worlds ordained by Brahmā in ancient times.
"12,183.016c Living beings revolve, enveloped by their respective karmas.
12,184.001 Bharadvāja said:
"12,184.001a What do they say is the fruit of giving, of dharma, and of conduct?"
"From well-performed austerity, from the study of sacred texts, and from oblations—Bhṛgu said: 'Sin is pacified by oblation; in the study of sacred texts, there is supreme peace.'"
They say that through giving one obtains enjoyments, and through austerity one may attain everything.
They declare that giving is of two kinds: for the sake of the next world and for this very world. Whatever is given to the virtuous stands to one's credit in the hereafter.
"That gift which is given to those who are unworthy is enjoyed here [in this world];
whatever kind of gift is given, such is the fruit obtained.
Bharadvāja said:
"What is the practice of dharma for whom, or what is the characteristic of dharma?
Furthermore, how many kinds of dharma are there? You ought to explain that.
Bhṛgu said:
Those wise ones who are intent upon practicing their own dharma attain the fruit of that dharma; he who acts otherwise is deluded. Bharadvāja said:
"Regarding this system of the four stages of life (āśrama) ordained of old by the Brahmanical seers—
please tell me here what the specific duties (ācāra) are for each of them.
Bhṛgu said:
12,184.008A Previously, while performing what is beneficial for the world, the Blessed One, for the sake of protecting the Dharma, designated four stages of life (āśrama).
12,184.008B Among them, they first cite the residence in the teacher’s house (gurukula-vāsa) as the very first stage of life.

12,184.008C Here, one who has been properly prepared through purification, sacraments, discipline, and observances, with a self-subdued mind, [worships] the two twilights, the sun, fire, and the deities.
Having attended upon [the teacher] and abandoned drowsiness and laziness, with his inner self purified by saluting the guru, practicing the Vedas, and listening to them;

having performed ablutions at the three periods of the day; being constant in celibacy, tending the sacred fire, and serving the guru; with his inner self dedicated to offering all things such as alms-food to him; and not being contrary to the performance of the instructions given by the guru, he should be intent upon the study of the Veda obtained through the guru’s grace.
But that twice-born man who, having fully propitiated his guru, obtains the Veda—for him there is the attainment of the fruit of heaven, and his heart’s desire is fulfilled.
On this point there is a verse:
*For him there is the attainment of the fruit of heaven, and his heart’s desire is accomplished.*
12,184.010A They indeed call the householder’s life the second stage of life (āśrama). 12,184.010B We shall fully explain all its characteristics of proper conduct.
12,184.010C For those who have returned [from their teachers], who have taken wives, and who seek the fruit of practicing dharma together, the householder’s stage of life is prescribed.

12.184.010D For the attainment of virtue, wealth, and pleasure is the means of accomplishing the three goals of life; therefore, having acquired riches through irreproachable action— whether by means of wealth obtained through excellence in Vedic study, or that produced by Brahman-sages, or that found within the heart of mountains, or wealth obtained through the favor of the gods resulting from the practice of sacrificial offerings and observances— a householder should carry out the duties of the householder's state.
12,184.010F For they declare that this is indeed the root of all stages of life (*āśrama*).

Whether they be students dwelling in the teacher’s house (*gurukula*), wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), or others who perform the duties of vows and observances according to their resolve—it is from this very source that their alms, offerings, and distributions proceed. 12,184.011A As for forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), it is generally said that these virtuous men, who perceive what is right and wholesome, are devoted to Vedic study; they go to sacred fords (*tīrtha*) for the purpose of visiting various regions.
They wander the earth [performing] rising to meet them,

saluting them, speaking words free from malice, showing a pleasant countenance, offering seats, beds, and food according to one's ability, and honoring them; yet, the guest from whom one turns away with hopes frustrated [reaps the consequences].
And on this point there is a verse:
"Having given his misdeeds to him, he departs taking away [the other's] merit.
Moreover, in this world, the deities are gratified by sacrificial rites; the ancestors by the offering of funeral oblations; and the sages by the study, hearing, and retention of the Vedas.
By procreating offspring, one is called a *prajāpati*;
one should speak words that are affectionate toward all beings and pleasant to the ear.
On this subject, there are two verses: [Verse 1] [Verse 2]

Slander, injury, and harshness are censured here; contempt, egoism, and hypocrisy are likewise condemned. Non-violence, truthfulness, and freedom from anger constitute the austerity belonging to all stages of life.

Moreover, in this [stage], there is the attainment of garlands, ornaments, garments, ointments, perfumes, and objects of enjoyment; the experience of dancing, singing, instrumental music, pleasant sounds, and delightful sights; the enjoyment of various kinds of food—whether chewed, eaten, drunk, licked, or sucked; contentment with one’s own wife for recreation; and the attainment of sensual pleasure.
For him who constantly finds fulfillment in the virtues of the three aims of life within the householder stage (gṛhāśrama), [this is the case].
Having experienced pleasures here, he shall attain the destination of the virtuous. For that householder who subsists by gleaning grains, who is devoted to the practice of his own duty,
and who has renounced the pursuit of sensual pleasure, heaven is not difficult to attain.
Bhṛgu said: Indeed,

those who have retired to the forest (vānaprasthas), following the dharma of the sages, wander about performing austerities at sacred fords, rivers, and springs in well-secluded forests teeming with deer, buffalo, boars, sṛmara antelopes, and elephants.

Having abandoned the clothing, food, and enjoyments of the village, they subsist on a varied and restricted diet of wild herbs, roots, fruits, and leaves; they remain standing or seated, sleeping on the earth, stones, sand, gravel, pebbles, ashes, or dust; their bodies are covered with *kāśa* grass, *kuśa* grass, skins, or bark; they wear their hair, beards, nails, and body hair; they perform ritual ablutions at fixed times and carry out the offerings and oblations at the prescribed hours; and they find rest only through the gathering of sacrificial wood, *kuśa* grass, and flowers, and through the performance of oblations and cleansing rites.

With their entire skin cracked and scorched by cold, heat, and wind, their flesh and blood drained away through the performance of dharma prescribed by various rules and yogic practices, they become mere skin and bone; yet, devoted to fortitude, they sustain their bodies through the application of spiritual strength.
He who, being self-restrained, should practice this conduct ordained by the Brahman-sages—
He shall burn away his defects like fire and conquer worlds that are difficult to conquer.
Furthermore, the conduct of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) is as follows:
having abandoned attachment to fire, wealth, wife, and possessions, and having shaken off the bonds of affection for themselves, they go forth into homelessness.

Regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal; with intellects unattached to undertakings directed toward the three aims of life; behaving with equanimity toward enemies, friends, and neutrals; not harming through speech, mind, or action any living beings—whether stationary, born from a womb, born from an egg, born from sweat, or born from a sprout; homeless and wandering among mountains, riverbanks, the roots of trees, and temples of deities, they may enter a city for the sake of shelter.

Having entered a village or a city for five nights, they should stay for one night in the village; and for the mere purpose of sustaining life, they should approach the houses of twice-born men of unconfused conduct, receiving alms that have fallen into their bowls and are unsolicited, being free from desire, anger, pride, delusion, greed, miserliness, hypocrisy, slander, arrogance, and violence.
The sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings— regarding this,
there is a verse:
"No fear arises for him from any living being anywhere."
Having established the *agnihotra* within his own body,
he offers the bodily fire into his own mouth with oblations obtained through the practice of begging for alms.
He who practices the stage of liberation as prescribed, pure and endowed with a well-resolved intellect, transcends the worlds of the funeral pyres.
"Like a flame without fuel, he is utterly tranquil;
that twice-born man takes refuge in the world of Brahman.
Bharadvāja said:
"A world beyond this world is heard of, yet it is not perceived. I desire to know that; you ought to speak of it.
Bhṛgu said:
On the northern side of the Himavat, auspicious and endowed with every excellence, there is a world said to be holy, secure, desirable,
and supreme. For there dwell those whose actions are free from evil, pure, and utterly stainless.
Free from greed and delusion, men there are free from affliction;
that region is like heaven, for auspicious qualities are said to exist there. Death prevails only at the proper time, and diseases do not touch them.
There was no lust for the wives of others, as people were devoted to their own spouses; there was no mutual killing there, nor was there greed for possessions, nor was there any sense of wonder.
There was no dharma based on secrecy, nor did any doubt ever arise.
In that place, the fruit of what has been done is perceived directly:
some possess beds, vehicles, and seats, dwelling in palaces and mansions; they are provided with all objects of desire and adorned with golden ornaments.
For some, however, only the mere maintenance of life is possible;
some maintain their lives through great exertion.
In this world, some men are devoted to dharma, while others are deceitful.
Some are happy and some are miserable; some are poor and others are wealthy.
In this world, exhaustion, fear, delusion, and intense hunger arise, as well as greed for wealth on the part of men, by which even the wise are bewildered.
In this world, there are many kinds of reflections regarding the actions of dharma and adharma;
the wise man who understands both of these is not defiled by evil.
Deceit with fraud, theft, slander, and malice—these are the ways of the wicked.
For harming others, violence, slander, and likewise falsehood—
whosoever indulges in these, his austerity (tapas) is diminished;
but the wise man who does not practice these, his austerity increases.

This world is the field of action; having performed good and evil deeds here, one attains happiness through good deeds and the opposite through evil deeds. Here, in the past, were Prajāpati, the gods, and likewise the hosts of sages.
Having performed their desired austerities and being purified by sacrifice, they have taken refuge in the world of Brahmā.
That northern region of the earth is most meritorious and auspicious;
indeed, those people who perform meritorious deeds in this world are born there.
Others, performing improper deeds, are born among the animal species;
likewise, others, their lifespans exhausted, perish upon the surface of the earth.
Devoted to devouring one another, they are possessed by greed and delusion.
They revolve right here; they do not go to the northern direction—
those wise ones who serve their gurus, self-restrained and living as celibate students (brahmacārins),
know the path of all the worlds.
"Thus has this dharma, created by Brahmā, been declared by me in brief. For he who truly knows the dharma and adharma of the world is wise.
Bhīṣma said:
O King, having been addressed thus by Bhṛgu, the powerful Bharadvāja,
whose soul was devoted to the highest dharma, was filled with wonder and honored Bhṛgu in return.
"O King, this origin of the world has been fully proclaimed to you."
"O one of great wisdom, I have heard this in its entirety; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O sinless father, tell me the rule for conduct as it is being proclaimed by you."
"I wish to hear this, O knower of dharma, for you are considered by me to be omniscient.
Bhīṣma said:
"Those of evil conduct, wicked deeds, poor understanding, and who delight in rashness—"

For those who are not virtuous are indeed well-known, while the virtuous are characterized by their conduct. Those men who do not void excrement or urine on the royal highway, amidst cows, or in the midst of grain are auspicious.

Those who do not perform [these acts] in the fire-sanctuary or on the riverbank are virtuous. Having performed the necessary purification and the libation to the deities, they declare this to be the dharma for men; having sipped water, one should cross the river.
One should always worship the sun and not sleep at sunrise;

reciting prayers at dawn and dusk, one should stand during both the morning and evening *saṃdhyā* rites. Having five parts still moist from bathing, one should eat facing the east while observing silence.
One should not disparage various kinds of food, and one may eat whether it is sweet or not sweet.
One should not rise with wet hands, nor should one sleep at night with wet feet.
This is the definition of proper conduct as proclaimed by the divine sage Nārada.
One should always circumambulate clockwise a bull that desires purity, a cow-pen belonging to the gods, a crossroads, a righteous Brāhmaṇa,
all guests, servants, and one's own kinsmen.
Eating in common with one's dependents is praised for a man;
eating in the evening and in the morning is the meal ordained by the gods for human beings.
Eating in between these times is not seen [in the scriptures]; thus, one should remain as if fasting.
Offering oblations at the time of the *homa*, likewise approaching his wife during her fertile period, and avoiding other women, the wise man should remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
The remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal are nectar; they are fashioned by the Mother as her own heart.

A person should attend to truth; the virtuous attend to truth. But that man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails, is constantly impure, and is as fickle as a thorn—such a one does not find a long life in this world.
One who has desisted from eating meat should not eat meat consecrated by a *yajus* mantra;
one should not eat meat killed for no purpose and should avoid meat from the back of an animal.
Whether in one's own country or in a foreign land, one should never let a guest go hungry.
Having obtained the fruit of actions performed for specific desires, one should offer it to one's teachers. One should give a seat to the teachers and perform salutation;
by honoring the teachers, one becomes endowed with long life, fame, and prosperity.
One should not look at the rising sun, nor at another man’s wife when she is naked;
one should engage in sexual intercourse with one’s own wife during her season in accordance with dharma, and keep it secret.
The heart is the essence of sacred fords, and the heart is the purity of the pure.

All purification performed by the noble ones and the touching of children [are required]. At every sight, one should always utter a greeting of "Are you well? In the evening and in the morning, salutation to the Brahmins is prescribed.
In a cow-pen, in the midst of cows, on the path of ritual action for Brahmins,
during Vedic study, and while eating, one should raise the right hand;
likewise, one should perform the worship of Brahmins morning and evening according to the prescribed rule.
Among merchandise, the finest goods are excellent; among agricultural pursuits, the cultivation of barley is praised.
Among crops, it is highly beneficial, and likewise, among cattle, the draught-ox is the most useful.
There is always abundance in food, and likewise, satisfaction in drink.

One should say "well-cooked" when addressing rice-porridge (*pāyasa*), barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), or rice-and-pulse mixture (*kṛsara*). When it is time for shaving, or upon sneezing, bathing, or eating,
as well as for all those who are ill, one should offer words of blessing for their longevity.
One should not urinate facing the sun, nor look at one's own excrement. One should avoid sharing a bed with one's son or wife, as well as eating together with them.
One should avoid addressing elders by their personal name or using the term "thou" (tvam) toward them.
There is no fault in [the conduct] of both inferiors and equals;

however, the heart of those whose conduct is wicked reveals its corruption. Those who conceal their deeds after having acted with prior knowledge perish when they are brought before the great assembly.
Those of little learning conceal the evil they have committed intentionally;
men do not see it, but the dwellers of the third heaven do.
For when evil is done by means of evil, it follows after that very evil.
Dharma, when covered by Dharma, follows only Dharma;
Dharma performed by one who acts according to Dharma follows the doer.
An evil deed does not manifest itself immediately, like a debt with its burdens.
When it is being ripened, the evil deed returns to the doer;
the fool does not remember the evil he has committed here, yet as he turns away [from life], it goes back to the doer.
Just as Rāhu approaches the moon,
so too does evil karma approach the ignorant man.
Wealth that has been accumulated with hope but is not enjoyed here in this world at the proper time— [is lost].

The wise do not praise that [life] which does not await death; the sages say that the mind is the dharma of all beings. Therefore, one should practice what is auspicious toward all beings with one's mind.
One should practice the Dharma alone; there is no companionship in the Dharma. Having attained the path by oneself, what can a companion do?
The gods are the source of humans, and for the gods, there is immortality in heaven.
"12,186.032c After death, happiness resulting from dharma is eternally enjoyed by them. 12,187.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
12,187.001a "Regarding this which is called 'the supreme self' (adhyātma), which is contemplated here by man—"
"O Grandfather, tell me that which is internal and from whence this arises;
from what has this entire universe—the world of the moving and the unmoving—been created? And at the time of dissolution, into what does it enter? You ought to explain this to me here."
Bhīṣma said:
O Pārtha, since you ask me this regarding the supreme self (adhyātma),
I shall explain it to you, my dear, as that which is most conducive to welfare and happiness.
The teachers have fully demonstrated this [treatise], which is joined with the accounts of creation and dissolution;
by knowing which, a person in this world finds joy and happiness,
there shall be the immediate attainment of results, and it is beneficial for all living beings.

O King, having thus enveloped the stainless Self which remains established in this way, darkness shines eternally within it, just as the moon [shines] in that [darkness]. Knowing this, one whose sins have been destroyed is fit for becoming Brahman.
Just as darkness constitutes the limit of those things that serve as the covering for eggs,
so too earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—
these great elements (mahābhūtas) are the source and the place of dissolution for all beings.

Then those great elements, once created, go back again and again to that very place, just as the waves of the ocean [return to it]. And just as a tortoise extends its limbs and then withdraws them again, so does he.
In the same way, the Self of beings, having created the elements, withdraws them again.
O bull of the Bharatas, that collection of qualities within the body is constantly dissolving and emerging once more.
That which, being absent, one neither hears nor sees nor shines forth,
and that upon which [the self] depends and from which it arises— that is called "internal" (adhyātma).
At that time, that knowledge, known as having a single form, is endowed with manifold wisdom.
That speech would not be consistent with reality if it were devoid of the essence of things; indeed, from space itself, truly great qualities arise within those worthy of sacrifice.
Thus, all this—both the stationary and the moving—is composed of that very essence.
At the time of dissolution, it returns to that [source], and from there it is emitted again. Having created [them] within the great elements, the Self of beings (bhūtātman) withdraws them once more.
The Creator of beings has established these five great elements within all beings.
The individual soul (jīva) indeed perceives that inequality among them:
sound, the ear, and the bodily cavities—these three are born from the womb of space (ākāśa);
while skin, touch, movement, and speech—this quartet belongs to wind (vāyu).
Form, the eye, and likewise digestion—these three are said to be fire.
Taste, moisture, and the tongue—these three are remembered as the qualities of water.
Odor, the nose, and the body—these three are the qualities of earth.
There are exactly five great elements (mahābhūta), and the sixth is said to be the mind (manas).
O Bhārata, the sense organs and the mind are its [the body's] consciousnesses;
they say that the intellect (buddhi) is the seventh, while the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the eighth.
The eye is for seeing alone; the mind creates doubt;

the intellect is for determination; and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) stands like a witness. The intellect, presided over by the power of consciousness (cicchakti), is renowned as "sentience" (cetana).
Immediately following volition, the living being perceives that [object] and it is observed; when it is seen neither abandoning nor emitting the body,
there would be the perception of consciousness in that [body], or else darkness covers it.
That which is above the soles of the feet, and that which one perceives below and above—
know that by this alone all this internal space is pervaded. And here, within the person, the sense organs are to be understood in their entirety.

Know that darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva) are the states dependent upon that [Self]. Having understood this with his intellect— the coming and going of all beings— and having observed it gradually, a man attains supreme peace.
The intellect leads the qualities; the intellect likewise leads all the senses, with the mind as the sixth. In the absence of the intellect, where would the qualities be?
That by which one conceives of an object is the mind.

Thus, all this—both the stationary and the moving—is composed of that alone; it dissolves and arises from it, and is therefore designated as such. That by which one sees is called the eye, and that by which one hears is called the ear.
One smells with the nose; one knows taste with the tongue;
one touches sensations with the skin; and the intellect undergoes modification repeatedly. That by which one conceives of some object is the mind.
For the bases of the intellect are fivefold, each having a distinct object;
those which they call the five sense-faculties, the invisible one presides over them. Presided over by the Puruṣa, the intellect operates within the three states of being.
Sometimes one finds joy, sometimes one grieves;
sometimes one dwells in neither pleasure nor pain. Thus, in the minds of men, [these feelings] abide in three states.
This intellect, whose nature is existence, does not transcend these three states of being, just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, does not overstep its great shore despite its waves.
When the intellect has transcended these states, it abides in the state of the mind.
For when *rajas* is active, it follows that state;
indeed, it always causes all the sense organs to manifest.
Joy is *sattva*, sorrow is *rajas*, and delusion is *tamas*—these are the three.
Whatever entities exist in this world, they all fall within these three:
goodness (*sattva*), intelligence (*buddhi*), and the state of darkness (*tamas*). Through the conjunction with joy, [goodness] proceeds.
Thus, O Bhārata, the entire course of intelligence has been explained to you.
All the sense faculties must be conquered by the wise man;
for *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* always reside within living beings,
and the threefold experience is seen among all creatures.
O Bhārata, it is of three kinds: characterized by *sattva*, by *rajas*, and by *tamas*.
The quality of *sattva* is experienced as pleasure; the quality of *rajas* is experienced as pain;
and when joined with the quality of *tamas*, they become non-functional in worldly affairs.

In that regard, whatever is associated with joy, whether in the body or in the mind, one should then observe that as the state of sattva. Furthermore, that which is associated with suffering and causes dissatisfaction for oneself—
One should reflect upon that which has set in as "rajas" without becoming agitated.
Furthermore, that which is joined with delusion, which is as if unmanifest, inconceivable, and unknowable— one should understand that to be "tamas."
Exultation, joy, bliss, happiness, and tranquility of mind—
these qualities of *sattva* arise in some way or another.
Dissatisfaction, distress, grief, greed, and likewise intolerance— [these are the qualities of *rajas*].
These signs of *rajas* are seen through both causes and non-causes:
self-conceit, delusion, negligence, sleep, and lassitude;
thus various qualities of *tamas* manifest in some way.

He whose mind— which wanders far, travels in many directions, and consists of longing and doubt— is well-restrained, is happy both in this world and after death. Behold this subtle difference between the *sattva* (the field) and the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).

One indeed creates the qualities, while the other does not create the qualities. Just as a gnat and a fig are always joined together, so too is their union, being distinct from one another yet mutually connected.
These two are distinct by nature, yet they are always conjoined;
just as a fish and water are conjoined, so too are these two.
The qualities do not know the Self, but the Self knows the qualities in every respect.
The witness of the qualities always considers himself their creator;
yet, through the senses— seven including the intellect— which are inactive and devoid of consciousness, the Supreme Self acts like a lamp for the purpose of illumination.
For the *sattva* creates the qualities (*guṇas*), while the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field) observes them. This union between the *sattva* and the *kṣetrajña* is constant;
yet there is no substratum whatsoever for either the *sattva* or the *kṣetrajña*.
The mind creates the *sattva*, but never indeed the *guṇas*. When one properly restrains their rays by means of the mind,
then one's self shines forth like a lamp burning within a jar.
The sage who, having abandoned worldly action, is constantly delighted in the Self and has become the self of all beings—he shall go to the supreme goal.
Just as a water-dwelling bird, though smeared by water, is not defiled; so too is he.
In this very way, one whose wisdom is perfected moves among living beings;
a man should dwell with his own intelligence, knowing that this is the very nature of things,
neither grieving nor exulting, and acting free from envy.

By means of the perfection of its own nature, it eternally creates the qualities (guṇas) that are already fully established; just as a spider is the creator [of its web], so should the qualities be understood as being like threads. Once destroyed, they do not return, nor is their cessation perceived.
The imperceptible is established through inference based on that which is perceptible.
Thus some determine it; others say it is cessation. Having thoroughly considered both of these, one should reach a conclusion according to one's own understanding.
Thus, having released this firm knot of the heart consisting of the fragmentation of the intellect, one should dwell in happiness; with doubts severed, one should not grieve.
Just as men who are defiled attain purification upon reaching a full river, so too does one attain purity by crossing over the river of worldly existence.
Having plunged into this knowledge, O wise one, know it to be thus:
for just as one who knows the further shore of a great river does not suffer while crossing, so the knower of reality does not suffer once the fruit is known; indeed, he has crossed over.

Thus those who know this supreme knowledge of isolation regarding the inner self— having understood all this and having gradually observed through their intellect the coming and going of all beings, a person thereafter attains the highest peace.
He for whom the threefold aim of life is understood from the very beginning—that man of Prāgjyotiṣa is liberated.
Having investigated with a disciplined mind, the seer of reality remains free from longing. Yet the Self cannot be perceived through the senses individually.

When these [senses], which are difficult for those of unrefined self to conquer, are released here and there, one who understands this becomes awakened; what other characteristic of an awakened one could there be? For he accepts [objects] and conceals them, yet appears otherwise.
That which they call "not creeping" is obstructed everywhere;
just as fire that is not brightened by smoke cannot cause the sun to move,
one observes this state [of stability] when the Lord of the Dhiṣṇyas is pleased.

Because it is exceedingly distant and subtle, its departure does not manifest; having entered that which is called "hearing" (śruta), the wise, without [further] accepting anything composed of consciousness (cinmaya), realize it and consider their task accomplished.
Therefore, fear does not exist for the wise,
which would be a very great fear for the ignorant; for there is no higher goal for anyone.
For when a virtue exists, they proclaim its incomparability:
that which one performs without prior intention,
and that which dispels what was done in the past.
Neither of those two is unpleasant to him; how then could that which he performs here produce what is pleasant? People find fault with one who grieves for a world that is itself afflicted.
That [state] produces for him everywhere in this world a state where people are crying out in affliction; see how they grieve over that very same thing in many ways.
"There, behold those who are skillful and do not grieve,
who always know both of those states.
Bhīṣma said:
"Come now, O Pārtha, I shall declare to you the fourfold yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga),
knowing which the supreme ṛṣis attain eternal perfection. Just as meditation is properly practiced, so do the yogins perform it."
The great seers, satisfied by knowledge and with their minds set upon nirvāṇa,
do not return again, O Pārtha, being liberated from the defects of saṃsāra; having exhausted the defect of birth, they are established in their own true nature.
Free from dualities, eternally established in purity, liberated and ever-reliant; unattached, free from dispute, and bringing peace to the mind—
one should fix the one-pointed mind there, absorbed in the study of the sacred word.
Having withdrawn the collection of the senses and sitting like a log of wood, the sage should not perceive sound with the ear, nor should he feel touch with the skin;
he should not recognize form with the eye, nor likewise tastes with the tongue.
The knower of yoga should abandon all fragrances through meditation;
the energetic one should not desire these things that agitate the group of five.
Then, having concentrated the group of five upon the mind, the wise man [proceeds].
The wise man should compose his wandering mind— which roams without support through the five gates, flickering and unstable— together with the five sense faculties,
within the interior of the mind upon the path of prior meditation.
When he draws together the senses and the mind as one,
this is the first path of meditation described by me; immediately thereafter, his mind, with the six senses restrained, becomes concentrated upon that.
It will quiver and be utterly agitated, like lightning in a cloud;
just as a drop of water on a leaf is unsteady and moves in every direction,
even so does his mind become upon the path of meditation.
For a brief moment, it remains concentrated on the path of meditation;
yet again, the mind wanders onto the path of the wind and becomes like the wind itself. One who is free from despondency, free from afflictions, free from sloth, and free from envy—
The knower of the yoga of meditation should again concentrate the mind through meditation.
As the sage concentrates, there arise, at the very beginning of the first meditation, investigation (*vitarka*), analysis (*vicāra*), and discernment (*viveka*).
Even when his mind is afflicted by distress, he should practice meditative concentration;
the sage should not fall into despondency, but should instead act for his own welfare. Just as heaps of dust, ashes, and dried cow dung are piled up, so too [should he accumulate merit].
If sprinkled with water all at once, they do not undergo thorough soaking;
just as dry powder that is somewhat oily would gradually and slowly absorb it all until it is thoroughly soaked.

In this very way, one should gradually cultivate the collection of the senses; by withdrawing them step by step, they will become perfectly stilled. So too, O Bhārata, the mind and the group of five [senses] will subside of their own accord.
Having first attained the path of meditation, one attains peace through constant yoga.
That happiness which comes to one whose self is thus restrained is achieved neither by human effort nor by any destiny whatsoever.
Endowed with that happiness, he shall delight in the practice of meditation;
for in this way, yogis proceed to that Nirvana which is free from all affliction.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
The duties of the four stages of life have been told to you, as well as the duties of kings;
and many various histories based on diverse subjects have been heard from you, O high-minded one, along with narratives endowed with righteousness.
"But I have a certain doubt; you ought to explain it to me. O Bhārata, I wish to hear about the attainment of fruit by those who recite [prayers].
What fruit is said to belong to those who recite, and where do those who recite abide?"
O sinless one, you ought to tell me the entire procedure for *japa*. What is this that is called "the reciter" (*jāpaka*)? Is it the practice of Sāṃkhya, Yoga, or ritual action?
Is it the very procedure of sacrifice, or what is this that is termed *japya*?
"Tell me all this, for in my opinion you are omniscient.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The ancient account of Yama and the Brahmin Kāla;
the Sāṃkhya and Yoga as taught by the sages who perceive liberation; and the dispute between Ikṣvāku and Mṛtyu concerning the cause of dharma.
In the Vedānta, renunciation alone prevails regarding the practice of recitation;
peace arises from the realization of the Vedic teachings through abiding in Brahman.
Both of these paths are relied upon, yet they are not truly relied upon.

O King, as it is heard in tradition, the reason for this shall now be explained. O ruler of men, this auspicious procedure for the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*), which has been ordained in due order, should be understood as having a support (*sālambana*).
In this regard as well, concentration of mind and mastery over the senses are prescribed;
truthfulness, the practice of tending the sacred fire, and dwelling in solitude; meditation, austerity, self-restraint, forbearance, freedom from envy, and moderation in eating.

Withdrawal from sense objects, moderation in speech, and likewise tranquility—this is the dharma of active engagement; now hear that of withdrawal. Learn how the karma of one who recites prayers and observes the vow of celibacy comes to cease.
There is neither recitation nor meditation, neither desire nor aversion or joy;
for that, O tiger among kings, is indeed to be well-comprehended through yoga. Constantly performing the recitation, one who truly practices the vow of celibacy—
With the mind focused on that meaning, the reciter proceeds toward the Supreme;
for it is through the manner in which the recitation is heard that one truly becomes a reciter. It is held that the Sāvitrī is supreme when joined with the *saṃhitā* and the *praṇava*.
Whatever else is appropriate, pure, and established by the Vedas and Smṛtis—
all this one should avoid entirely, exactly as described,
having reached the threefold path that is manifest, unmanifest, and without support.
Seated upon a heap of *kuśa* grass, with *kuśa* in his hand and his hair bound with *kuśa*,
he was likewise covered in rags and concealed by *kuśa* in that place;
there he should pay homage to the sense objects and should not dwell upon them.
Having established equanimity of the mind, fixing the mind upon the mind itself,
he meditates on that Brahman with his intellect while reciting the beneficial *saṃhitā*; or else, established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he indeed renounces even that.
Relying on the power of the *saṃhitā*, he generates meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) therein;
pure in soul through austerity, self-controlled, and free from hatred and desire,
the accomplished man should then mutter his chosen mantra, beginning with the *praṇava*.
Upon whatever [object] the mind has fallen, one should fix it there—
whether in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), in a mantra, or in the *saṃhitā* according to the rule.
Free from passion and delusion, beyond the pairs of opposites, he neither grieves nor clings.
He is not the agent of things that should not be done, nor of things that must be done; such is his state.
He should not direct the mind anywhere through the application of egoism. He is neither intent on grasping at a self, nor is he contemptuous, nor is he inactive.

Devoted to the practice of meditation, disciplined, possessed of meditative concentration, and firm in his resolve regarding meditation, he gives rise to *samādhi* within that meditation and gradually abandons even that.
Indeed, in that state, having accomplished the relinquishing of everything, he is happy.

Free from desire, he relinquishes his life-breaths and takes recourse in the body of Brahmā. Having become supportless through mindfulness, he possesses meditative concentration for the sake of death;
having traversed all the worlds in succession, he indeed attains the Supreme.
Alternatively, if he does not desire to dwell there among the company of Brahmā, then,
established on the path, he transcends and is never born anywhere again;
having maintained the realization of the Self, he becomes peaceful and free from affliction.
One attains the self, which is immortal, stainless, and pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The attainment of the highest goal among those who recite prayers has been described here."
"Is this their only destination, or do they go to another as well?
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen attentively, O King, O Lord, to the destination of those who recite [the sacred texts]."
O bull among men, just as they go to many hells,
so too does that reciter who does not practice what was previously taught;
he who performs only a portion of the rite goes to hell.
One who acts out of contempt, neither finding satisfaction nor feeling remorse—such a reciter goes to hell; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, all those who act out of egoism are destined for hell.
A person who treats others with contempt will go to hell.
And he who, being deluded, performs recitation preceded by covetousness— indeed,
he goes to that very hell upon which he fixes his covetousness.
12,190.007ab Then, having become engaged in [the pursuit of] sovereignty, that reciter becomes attached to it.
12,190.007cd That itself is his hell; he is not liberated from it. 12,190.008ab Deluded therein, the reciter performs the recitation out of passion.
Wherever his passion falls, there he is reborn; the one of evil intellect and unrefined wisdom remains in a wavering mind. He follows a wavering course and goes to hell.
The foolish reciter of mantras, lacking cultivated wisdom, falls into delusion. Through that delusion he goes to hell, and having gone there, he grieves.
Clinging firmly to the thought "I am doing it," the reciter mutters his mantra.
"Neither complete nor joined [with the fruit], he goes to hell.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That which is the supreme signless, unmanifest, and abiding in Brahman—"
"Why would a practitioner who has become truly existent enter a body?
Bhīṣma said:
"Many hells are proclaimed to result from poor understanding."
The practice of recitation is praised, yet these faults are inherent in its nature.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Describe to me: what kind of reciter goes to hell?"
"Indeed, curiosity has arisen in me; you ought to explain that.
Bhīṣma said:
"You have been born as a portion of Dharma; by your very nature, you are most righteous."
O sinless one, listen attentively to these words which have their foundation rooted in Dharma:
those abodes of the gods, who are the supreme self,
possess various structures and colors, as well as various forms and fruits.
Divine celestial chariots that move at will, as well as assembly halls,
O King, various pleasure gardens, and lotus-pools of pure water belong to the four world-protectors, as well as to Śukra and Bṛhaspati.
Of the Maruts, the Viśvedevas, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins;
of the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and likewise other dwellers of heaven—
these indeed, my dear, are the hells relative to the station of the Supreme Self.
It is fearless and signless, and not obscured by the fear of afflictions;
it is liberated from two, liberated from three, and liberated from eight as well as three;
it is devoid of the four characteristics and free from the four causes.

Free from exultation, free from joy, free from sorrow, and devoid of fatigue—there time ripens its effects; indeed, time is not the master there. O King, he is the master of time and likewise the lord of heaven.
This indeed is the station of Brahmā for the high-souled reciter;
meditating there upon the Supreme Self with perfect concentration,
O best of kings, he shall attain union with Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having attained the state of absolute selfhood and gone there, one does not grieve. Such is that supreme station, and those hells are likewise.
These hells have all been described to you exactly as they are.
"In this world, all those designated as hells are inferior states compared to that supreme abode.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of beings, [tell me] regarding Time, Death, Yama, and the Brāhmaṇa."
"The dispute was previously mentioned; you ought to explain that.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
Listen to me as I relate what occurred between Ikṣvāku, the son of the Sun, and the brahmin,
as well as what transpired with Kāla and Mṛtyu; and hear how their conversation took place and the location where it occurred.

For this very reason, there was here a certain Brahmin named Kauśika Paippalādi, who was endowed with the discourse on Dharma; he was a reciter, a follower of the path of Dharma, possessed of great fame, learned in the six Vedāṅgas, and of great wisdom.

He possessed direct intuitive knowledge of the six Vedāṅgas as well as the Vedas; he was thoroughly proficient in them and took refuge at the foot of the Himālayas. Restrained in conduct, he performed the final Brahmanic austerity while reciting the *Saṃhitā*.
Thus, a thousand years passed for him in strict observance of his vows. Then, the Goddess appeared to him in person and said, "I am pleased.
Yet, while silently repeating his prayers, he did not say anything at all to her.
Out of compassion for him, the Goddess was then pleased;
the Mother of the Vedas then honored that recitation of his.
Consisting of eight syllables, it was joined with four syllables during the drinking of Soma.
Consisting of twenty-four syllables and joined with the seed-syllable of the world,
the righteous-souled one, having completed his recitation, rose and fell at the feet of the Goddess with his head, and spoke these words:
"By good fortune, O Goddess, you are pleased and have come into my sight. If indeed you are pleased, may my mind find delight in my recitation.
Sāvitrī said:
"O brahmin-sage, what do you seek? What desired thing shall I do for you? Speak, O best among those who recite prayers; all that shall be yours. Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed by the goddess, that brahmin, who was conversant with dharma,
replied: "O auspicious one, may my desire for this recitation increase again and again,
and may my mental concentration grow day by day."
"So be it," the goddess then replied sweetly. And desiring to do what was pleasing to him, the goddess spoke this further:
"You shall not go to hell, where those bulls among the twice-born have gone."
"You shall go to the station of Brahmā, which is causeless and beyond reproach.
I shall accomplish that for which I have been requested by you here; perform your recitations with self-restraint and one-pointed mind, and Dharma will come to you."
"Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Yama shall indeed come into your presence;
and there shall be a dispute between you and them concerning dharma.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lady departed for her own abode.
Then the Brahmin remained engaged in silent recitation for a hundred divine years,
ever self-controlled, having conquered anger, true to his word, and free from malice.
When that observance of the wise Brahmin was completed, [the gods appeared].
Then Dharma himself, being pleased, revealed himself to that twice-born man.
Dharma said:
"O twice-born one, behold me, Dharma; I have come to see you."
Listen now to me regarding the fruit of that recitation which you have obtained:
all the worlds, both divine and human, have been conquered by you;
O virtuous one, having transcended all the hells of the gods, you shall go forth.
"O sage, give up your life; go to the worlds you desire. By casting off your own body, you shall then attain those worlds.
The brahmin said:
"O Dharma, you have indeed fulfilled your duty toward the worlds; now depart as you please. O Lord, I shall not cast off this body, which is the locus of much suffering and pleasure.
O Great-minded One, having made your mind firm, abandon the body."
"What connection do you have with this? How will you fall into delusion? Dharma said:
"O bull among sages, your body must inevitably be abandoned."
"O Brahmin, ascend to heaven; or what else pleases you, O sinless one?
The Brahmin said:
"O Lord, I do not desire residence in heaven without my body."
"Go, O Dharma! I have no faith in going to heaven without my own self. Dharma said: "Enough of fixing your mind on the body; abandon the body and be happy."
"Go to the worlds free from passion, where having gone you shall not grieve.
The Brahmin said:
"O illustrious one, I rejoice in my recitation; what need have I for those eternal worlds?"
"O Lord, must I go to heaven with my physical body or not? O best of sages, such is your delight in this undertaking.
Dharma said:
"O twice-born one, if you do not wish to abandon this body, behold indeed: Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Yama have approached you. Bhīṣma said:
Then, O Lord, the triad consisting of Vaivasvata, Kāla,
and Mṛtyu approached that highly fortunate Brāhmaṇa and said this:
"Of this well-performed austerity and likewise of his well-conducted life..."
"Your attainment of the fruit is most excellent; I am Yama, and I address you.
You have duly obtained the supreme fruit of this recitation. It is time for you to ascend to heaven; I, Time, have come to you."
"O knower of dharma, know me to be Death himself, come here in person,
impelled by Time, O brahmin, to lead you away from this place this very day.
The brahmin said:
"Welcome to the son of the Sun, to Kāla, the great-souled one, to Mṛtyu, and to Dharma! What service may I perform for you?
Bhīṣma said:
Having offered them the guest-water and water for the feet in that assembly, he, being exceedingly pleased, said to them: "What may I do for you according to my power?
You are intent on your own affairs and are the cause of distress to others."
"O most excellent ones, you who share the common nature of the world, for what purpose do you speak thus?
Dharma replied:
"We too, with undistracted minds, act in accordance with the command of the Creator."
Bhīṣma said:
"Driven on and running indeed, devoted to their share of ritual action,
at that very time they arrived on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords."
Ikṣvāku went there, O Lord, to where they had gathered. Having honored and bowed down to all those royal sages,
that best of kings inquired after the welfare of everyone.
Then, having offered him a seat as well as water for his feet and the guest-offering, the brahmin, after exchanging greetings of welfare, spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O Great King; tell me whatever you desire here."
"What may I do here according to my own power? May you tell me that.
The King said:
"I am a king, and you are a Brahmin established in the six duties."
"I shall give you some wealth; tell me what you desire.
The brahmin said:
"O King, brahmins are of two kinds, and dharma is likewise remembered as being twofold."

"O lord of men, there are those who follow the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtta*) and those who follow the path of withdrawal (*nivṛtta*); I have withdrawn from accepting gifts. Bestow your gifts upon those who are engaged in worldly activity.
I do not accept them; what sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) or what gift may I give to you?"
"O best of kings, tell me: what shall I accomplish through my ascetic power? The king said:
"I am a Kṣatriya; I do not know how to utter the word 'give' anywhere."
"O best of the twice-born, we say this: 'Grant us battle!
The brahmin said:
'O King, you are satisfied with your own duty; likewise, we too are satisfied.'"
"There is no superior to one another; therefore, do whatever you desire.
The king said:
"You previously declared, 'I shall give according to my own power.'"
"O twice-born one, I entreat you: let the fruit of this recitation be given to me.
The Brahmin said:
"You boast that my speech always begs for battle."
"And why do you ask for battle with me again?
The king said:
"Brahmins are said to have speech as their thunderbolt; Kṣatriyas live by the strength of their arms."
"O Brahmin, this intense verbal battle between you and me is now underway.
The Brahmin said:
"That very same vow remains mine even today; what may be given by my own power?"
"Speak, O Indra among kings; since I possess the means, I shall give it to you without delay.
The king said:
"That which was to be chanted by you for a full hundred years while performing your recitation—"
"12,192.047c If you are desirous of giving, then bestow upon me that fruit which has been obtained.
12,192.048 The Brahmin said:
12,192.048a Let the supreme fruit of that which I have recited be accepted by you."
"Or rather, you shall obtain half of its fruit without hesitation;
or else, O King, if you desire it all here, you may obtain the entire fruit of my recitation as you wish."
The King said:
"All has been done; may it be well with you. You have recited that which was requested by me.
May it be auspicious for you; I shall now depart. Now, tell me, what is its fruit?"
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not know the attainment of fruit from what has been given, recited, or muttered by me;
this Dharma, Time, Yama, and Death are my witnesses."
The King said:
"What will the fruit of this dharma do for me, since it is unknown?
You speak of the fruit of dharma, yet you do not tell me the fruit of that which is performed through recitation."
"Let that fruit be attained by the Brahmin; I do not desire it with any doubt.
The Brahmin said:
"I shall not take back what has been spoken by another; the fruit has already been given by me through my word."
"O royal sage, the word is authoritative for both me and you:
'The portion falls but once; a daughter is given but once;
"I give"—this is said but once. These three things happen only once."
"O tiger among kings, no specific intention was ever previously formed by me regarding this recitation; how then shall I know the fruit of this recitation?
You said, 'Give it,' and likewise I said, 'I give it.'"
"I shall not defile my speech; protect the truth and remain steadfast.
If you do not act upon these words of mine as I speak them now, O King, a great unrighteousness will accrue to you through your falsehood."
"O subduer of enemies, it is not proper for you to speak falsely;
likewise, I too am unable to speak more than the truth. Furthermore, I previously promised without hesitation, 'I shall give.'"
Therefore, accept it without hesitation, if you are established in truth.
For having come here, O King, you asked me for the fruit of my recitation; accept that which is granted by me, and remain firm in truth as well.

For one devoted to falsehood, O King, there is neither this world nor the next, nor can he deliver his ancestors; how much less his descendants? Indeed, neither sacrifices, nor Vedic study, nor gifts, nor religious observances can deliver him.
O bull among men, truth in the world beyond is indeed such that all the austerities you have performed and those austerities you shall perform for hundreds and thousands of years do not excel it.
Truth is the single-syllabled Brahman; truth is the single-syllabled austerity. Truth is the single-syllabled sacrifice; truth is the single-syllabled sacred revelation.
Truth awakens within the Vedas; the fruit of truth is remembered as supreme.
From truth arises dharma and self-restraint; everything is established upon truth.
Truth is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; truth is the sacrifice as well as its ritual procedure. Vows and religious observances are truth, and the syllable *oṃ* is indeed truth itself.
The birth of living beings is truth, and their very continuity is truth. By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun gives heat.
By truth the fire burns, and heaven is established upon truth.
Truth is sacrifice, austerity, the Vedas, the chants, the mantras, and Sarasvatī.
We have heard it said that when Dharma and Truth were placed upon a scale, they held the balance equally; however, since Truth held its side down, it was found to be the weightier of the two.
Where there is dharma, there is truth; everything prospers through truth.
O King, why do you wish to perform an untruthful act? Fix your mind firmly on truth, O King, and do not commit falsehood.

"Why do you perform this inauspicious act of speaking a falsehood by saying 'give'? O King, if you do not accept the fruit of my recitation that has been given, you shall wander through the worlds, fallen away from your own duties."
"He who, having made a promise, does not wish to fulfill it, and he who, having requested something, does not desire it—both of these are liars; you ought not to act falsely.
The King said:
"O twice-born one, it is said that the duty of a Kṣatriya is to fight and to protect;
Kṣatriyas are declared to be givers. How then could I accept [this gift] from you?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O King, I did not entreat you, nor did I come to your house;
having come here and made my request, why do you no longer accept it? Dharma said:
"Let there be no dispute between you two; know that I have come for the sake of dharma.
Let the twice-born be endowed with the fruits of giving, and the king with the fruit of truth.
Thus spoke Heaven.
"O Indra among kings, know me to be Heaven itself, come here in person.
Let there be no dispute between you two; you both shall have equal rewards.
The king said:
"I have accomplished my purpose regarding heaven; go to heaven as you please.
If the brahmin wishes to give, let him accept wealth from me.
The brahmin said:
"If in my youth I extended my hand out of ignorance,
I now attend to the dharma characterized by renunciation while reciting the *saṃhitā*.
O King, why do you entice me, a Brahmin who has long since desisted from worldly life?"
"O King, I shall perform my own duty; I do not desire any fruit from you. I am devoted to austerity and the study of the Vedas, and I have desisted from accepting gifts.
The king said:
"O Brahmin, if the supreme fruit of your recitation has been bestowed upon you,
let whatever fruit we both possess here be shared between us.
For the twice-born are intent on receiving gifts, while those born of royal lineage are givers."
"O Brahmin, if this merit has been heard by you, let its fruit be ours together. Or, if there is not to be a shared enjoyment, then receive my fruit;
accept the merit performed by me if you have favor toward me."
Bhīṣma said:
Then two men of distorted appearance arrived, dressed in rags; grasping one another and entwining themselves, they spoke these words.
"You do not owe me," said one; "I do owe you," said the other. "We have this dispute here, and this king is the judge.
I am telling the truth: you do not owe me."
"You speak untruth here; I hold this debt from you.
Both of them, being greatly distressed, said this to the king:
"Let it be investigated so that neither of us may be censured here."
Virūpa said:
"O tiger among men, O lord of the earth, I maintain here the fruit of the deformed cow;
yet the deformed one does not accept it from me as I give it."
Vikṛta said:
"O lord of men, this deformed man owes me nothing;
he speaks falsely to you, O lord of men, for his appearance is deceptive."
The king said:
"Virūpa, tell me what you are carrying for him;
having heard it, I shall act accordingly—this is the resolve of my mind."
Virūpa said:
"Listen attentively, O King, as I relate this in its entirety, O bull among men, concerning this deformed royal sage."
"O sinless royal sage, in former times this auspicious cow was given by you for the sake of attaining merit to a brahmin devoted to austerity and Vedic study.
O King, having approached her, I have now requested this fruit from her."
And it was given to me by Vikṛta with a perfectly pure inner self;
thereafter, I performed meritorious deeds for the purification of my soul,
having purchased two tawny cows that were affectionate toward their calves and yielded much milk.
"O King,

those [gifts] which were bestowed by me for the sake of my livelihood according to the rules and according to my faith— that, O Lord, I now take back here today and bestow upon you with double the fruit."
"O tiger among men, regarding this one woman, who is pure and who here is at fault?
O King, we two have come here disputing thus; settle our dispute and establish for us what is dharma and what is adharma."
“If he does not wish to give me a gift such as has indeed been given by him, may you, O Lord, remaining firm in this matter, establish him on the right path. The king said:
"Why do you not accept this debt that is being offered to you today?
Accept it without delay, exactly as it has been authorized for you.
Thus spoke Vikṛta.
When he said, "Let it be given," I likewise replied, "I give. He said, "He does not owe this to me; let him go wherever he wishes.
The king said:
"While he is giving, you do not accept; this seems improper to me. Indeed, in my view, you deserve punishment for this—of this there is no doubt.
Thus spoke Vikṛta.
"O royal sage, this was given to him by me; how then could I take it back?
Granted, there has been an offense on my part here; O Lord, command what punishment I should receive.
Virūpa said:
"If you will not take what is being given by me by any means,
this king, who instructs in righteousness, will restrain you.
Thus spoke Vikṛta.
"How can I take back today that which was given by me here when it was requested? You may go; I grant you permission.
The brahmin said:
"O King, you have heard this which was spoken by these two; take that which was promised by me to you without hesitation. The king said:
"This very great task we have undertaken is as deep as a cavern.
How will this firm resolve of the reciter come to pass?
If I do not accept what has been offered by the Brahmin,"
"How may I indeed not be stained by this great fault today?
Bhīṣma said:
"And that royal sage said to them, 'Having accomplished your task, you two shall depart.'"
Now that I have encountered you here, let not the duty of a king become false;
this is the settled conclusion: the specific duty of kings must be preserved.
Furthermore, the exceedingly weighty duty of a Brahmin has entered into me, who am lacking in self-control.
The Brahmin said:
"Take it; I shall hold it for you, for I have heard what was requested by you. O King, if you will not accept it, I shall curse you—of this there is no doubt."
The king said:
"Fie on the duty of kingship,
for which the determination of this matter here is such that I must accept wealth for this purpose so that it may be equal!"
"O Brahmin, this hand is extended for the first time as a pledge; whatever you hold from me, let that now be returned.
The Brahmin said:
"Whatever merit has been acquired by me through reciting the *Saṃhitā*,
accept all of that, if there is anything at all here belonging to me.
The king said:
"O best of the twice-born, this water has fallen upon my hand;
let it be equal [to the gift], let it be offered together, and may you indeed accept it.
Virūpa said:

"Know us to be desire and anger; we have caused you to act thus, O best of the twice-born, desiring to test the thoughts arising from your minds. As for what you said regarding our meeting, the worlds of you and of this [other] are indeed equal."

He does not retain anything [of his own]; rather, this inquiry has been made on your behalf. Time, Dharma, Death, as well as Desire and Anger—you two and all these—have been rubbed against one another upon the touchstone while you were looking on.
Above all is the abode of Brahmā, whose birth is unmanifest;
yours is an incomparable station, free from duality and pure in essence. Let us all go there, as shall we to our respective worlds.

"Go to the worlds won by your own deeds, wherever you desire. Then Dharma, Yama, and the others spoke these words to the king and the twice-born: "That which is known as the head of us all is remembered as the world of Brahmā."
"For you two are stationed there; indeed, we have been conquered by you both. Your desire has been fulfilled; therefore, grant that which is desired without hesitation.
Bhīṣma said:

I have fully proclaimed to you the attainment of fruits by those who recite [the mantra], as well as the destination, the station, and the worlds won by the reciter. One who studies the *saṃhitā* goes to Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Or else he approaches fire, or even enters the sun;
if he finds delight there through his fiery nature,
being deluded by passion, he takes on their qualities.
In this same way, when [the self] resides within the body of the moon, the wind, earth, or space,
it dwells there with passion, practicing their respective qualities. But if it becomes dispassionate toward them, it then proceeds to a state of uncertainty.
Desiring the supreme and imperishable, he enters into that very state once again;
having attained the immortal from the immortal, he becomes cooled, free from self-identity,
become Brahman, beyond dualities, happy, peaceful, and free from affliction.
The station of Brahmā, from which there is no return, known as the single imperishable— free from suffering, undecaying, and peaceful— that station he attains.
It is devoid of the four characteristics, as well as the six and the sixteen.
Having transcended the person, he attains the ether;
then, if his nature is characterized by passion, he presides over everything. Whatever he desires, that too he attains through the mind.
Or rather, he beholds all the worlds situated in hell;
free from desire and liberated from everything, he rejoices there in happiness. Such, O Great King, is the destiny of the reciter.
"All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What did those two do next after that had been spoken by him?"
"O Grandfather, tell me: was it a Brahmin or a king?
Or did those two go there as you have described? What conversation took place between them, or what did they do there?"
Bhīṣma said:
Having thus promised "So be it," O Lord, and having honored Dharma,
as well as Yama, Kāla, Mṛtyu, and Svarga, each according to their merit;
Having honored with his head all those other eminent brahmins who had previously assembled there, he spoke these words to the king:
"O royal sage, endowed with this fruit, go forth to attain merit."
"Permitted by you, I shall indeed recite [the mantra] once more.
O mighty one, lord of the people, a boon was previously granted to me by the Goddess:
'Your faith shall always remain firm as you recite.'"
The King said:
"If, O Brahmin, your success in chanting is thus fruitless and your faith is likewise, then go with me and obtain the fruit of your recitation."
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"A very great effort has been made here in the presence of everyone;
now let us two go together toward our destination, for we both possess equal merit."
Bhīṣma said:
Having learned of their resolve there, the Lord of the Thirty-three gods approached them together with the deities and likewise with the world-protectors.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts; the great luminaries, the rivers, the mountains, the oceans, and various sacred fords (tīrthas);
the ascetic penances, the rules of ritual union, the Vedas, the chanted interjections (stobhas), and Sarasvatī.
Nārada and Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā and Hūhū,
as well as Tumburu and others,
along with the Gandharva Citrasena accompanied by his retinue of attendants.
The Nāgas, the Siddhas, and the Munis; the God of gods, Prajāpati;
and the Lord of gods, the imperishable Brahmā, who consists of the Vedas, arrived;
and the inconceivable god Viṣṇu, with a thousand heads, also came together.
O Lord, kettledrums and musical instruments resounded in the sky;
divine showers of flowers fell there upon those great-souled ones,
and throngs of Apsarases danced here and there on every side.
Then the embodied Heaven spoke these words to the brahmin:
"O highly fortunate one, you have attained perfection; and you too, O King, are likewise perfected. Then, O King, those two together, according to the prescribed ritual, [honored one another].
Both of them performed the withdrawal from the sense objects;
likewise, they established the prāṇa, apāna, udāna, samāna,
and vyāna breaths within the mind, and thus, having fixed those [breaths] in the mind, they placed the mind in the vital breaths.

With their bodies rendered motionless, they fixed their steady gaze and composed minds upon the tip of the nose, the area between the eyebrows, and the *kuṇḍalī*— gradually holding them there with the mind.
Having thus mastered his posture and fixed his self within his head,
he then tore open the region of the palate of that high-souled Brāhmaṇa;
thereupon, a great flame of light ascended to the third heaven.
Then a great cry of "Alas! Alas! arose in all directions. That light, while being praised, then entered Brahmā.
Then the Grandfather said to that splendor, "Welcome."
O lord of the people, having risen to meet the Puruṣa who was a span in height,
he spoke yet another sweet word:
"There is no doubt that for practitioners of yoga, the fruit is equal to that of those who recite prayers."
The fruit of yoga from these [practices] is, first of all, the direct perception [of the truth];

however, for those who recite [the mantra], the distinguished result is the attainment of meditative absorption (samādhi) through rising up [in reverence]. Having said, "Dwell within me," he then awakened him once more.
Then a brahmin, free from all distress, entered his mouth;
and by this same method, the king likewise entered the blessed Grandfather,
just as that tiger among the twice-born had done.
Then the gods, having saluted the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū), spoke:
"This effort is for the sake of the reciter; it is for his sake that we have come. Having been honored by you equally, these two shall receive equal fruit."
"Today, indeed, a most great fruit has been seen from the practitioner of yoga and the reciter of mantras;
having transcended all worlds, these two shall go wherever they desire.
Brahmā said:
Whoever recites the *Mahāsmṛti* as well as the auspicious *Anusmṛti*, those two shall also go to my world by this very method.
And whoever should be devoted to Yoga, he too [shall do so]; of this there is no doubt.
By this rite, at the end of the body's life, one shall attain my worlds. Depart; I shall accomplish the respective stations for the sake of success.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, that god then vanished right there.
Then, having taken leave of him, the gods went each to his own abode.
And all those high-souled ones, having honored Dharma there, indeed departed.

O King, they all followed behind him with highly delighted minds. This fruit of those who recite [the sacred texts], as well as their destiny, has been proclaimed exactly as it was heard, O Great King; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what is the fruit of the yoga of knowledge, of the Vedas, and of religious observances; and how is the self of all beings to be known?"
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between Manu Prajāpati and the great seer Bṛhaspati.
In ancient times, Bṛhaspati— the great seer who is the foremost among the hosts of celestial rishis— asked this ancient question of Prajāpati, the most excellent being upon the earth.
Then the disciple, having bowed to his teacher, asked:
"For what reason has the ritual of mantras been set forth,
and what fruit do the Brahmins proclaim resides in knowledge?"
"O Blessed One, please explain to me correctly that which has not been revealed by the words of mantras—
that [truth] known by those who are experts in the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*), traditional scriptures (*āgama*), and mantras."
Whatever great fruit is attained through numerous sacrifices and the gift of excellent cows—
what will that be, how will it come to pass, and where will it abide?
The earth, those born of the earth, the wind, the atmosphere, aquatic creatures, water, and heaven—
indeed, from whom the dwellers of heaven were produced;
Therefore, O Blessed One, let that ancient knowledge be told to me, for from whatever knowledge a man seeks it, his activity proceeds toward that very end.
Nor do I know the supreme Purāṇa;
how indeed could I engage in falsehood?
I [know] the collections of Ṛks, Sāmans, and Yajus.
