Having studied the Vedic hymns, the movements of the stars, Nirukta, grammar along with ritual manuals, and phonetics, I still do not know the true nature of beings.
May your lordship explain all of this to me:
whatever fruit exists in knowledge or in action,
expressed through both general terms and specific qualifications.
May your lordship first explain this to me:
how the embodied soul falls away from the body, and how it again enters a new body.
Manu said:
Whatever is dear to one is called happiness; that very thing, when undesired, they declare to be suffering.
"May what is desired be mine and the opposite not be mine;
for this purpose the ritual procedure of action was undertaken,
so that neither the desired nor the undesired should affect me."
For this purpose, the method of knowledge has been set forth: those whose nature is desire engage in ritual actions through the Veda;
one who is liberated from these shall attain the Supreme.
A man seeking happiness, engaged in various paths of action, does not go beyond [this world].
Bṛhaspati said:
The desired and the undesired, as well as pleasure and pain—
Manu said—
that [state] accompanied by aspiration is restrained by one's actions.
Separated from these, he entered the Supreme;
for his sake, the ritual of action was set in motion,
being kindled by the self and other actions.
The radiant one, seeking happiness, has applied himself to the Dharma;
for that which is beyond the path of action is indeed supreme,
free from longing, and necessarily dedicated to the Brahman.
Creatures are created through both mind and action;
these two are the true paths favored by the world.
Having observed that action is both eternal and finite, [one should understand its nature].
The renunciation of the mind is the cause, and there is no other;
it is like the eye acting as a guide by its own nature for one whose self was enveloped in darkness at the end of the night.
But knowledge, when joined with the quality of discernment (*vijñāna*),
perceives impure karma as something to be avoided—
like snakes, the tips of *kuśa* grass, or a well.
Knowing this, wise men avoid it;
out of ignorance, the deluded fall therein.
Behold how the fruit of knowledge is distinguished!
But when the entire mantra is employed according to the rule, as well as the sacrifices as prescribed and their sacrificial fees,
the giving of food and the concentration of the mind [are likewise required].
They say that the fruit of action consists of five elements (12,194.016a);
the Vedas say that action consists of the qualities (guṇas);
therefore, the mantras are [the source], for action is rooted in the mantras.
The ritual act, the object to be performed, and the mental realization are the means; the embodied soul is the enjoyer of the fruit,
just as there are meritorious sounds, forms, and tastes.
Tactile sensations and fragrances that are likewise auspicious— by these,
a man becomes a lord who has attained his proper station;
this fruit is accomplished in the world of karma.
Whatever action one performs with the body, being joined with the body, one experiences that very result;
the body alone is the abode of pleasure.
The body is also the locus of suffering.
Whatever action one performs by means of speech,
one experiences all of that through speech alone.
Whatever action the mind performs, it experiences that very thing while remaining situated in the mind; thus,
one who seeks results [experiences] the multitude of actions according to their qualities.
Established in the fruit of action, he acts;
in whatever way he is thus associated with the qualities (guṇas),
he experiences the fruit of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
Just as a fish rushes toward the current,
so does previously performed karma approach one; he rejoices in what is auspicious, but in what is ill-done, he suffers.
The supreme embodied being is indeed not satisfied by that from which this entire world is produced;
knowing that [reality], those possessed of self-control transcend it.
That which has not been revealed by the words of mantras—
listen to me as I describe that supreme reality,
which is devoid of various tastes and diverse fragrances.
Soundless, intangible, and formless,
ungraspable, unmanifest, and colorless, he created that which is one, yet fivefold, for the sake of living beings.
It is neither female, nor male, nor neuter;
it is neither being, nor non-being, nor both being and non-being—
that which the men who know Brahman perceive.
"Know that syllable to be 'akṣara' because it does not perish.
Manu said:
"From the syllable comes space; from that, wind; from wind, light; and from that, water."
The world was produced from water; in the world, the world is born.
These [beings], having entered into water with their bodies, [proceed] from water to fire, to wind, and to the intermediate space.
Those who are not destined to exist turn back from eating;
those who are destined to exist attain the Supreme.
It is neither hot nor cold, neither soft nor sharp.
It is neither sour, nor astringent, nor sweet, nor bitter;
it possesses neither sound nor smell,
nor does it possess form— that is the supreme intrinsic nature.
The body perceives touch, the tongue taste,
the nose smells, and the ears sounds;
the eye perceives forms, and there is nothing beyond that.
People who do not know the inner self seize [upon objects],
having withdrawn the tongue from flavors,
the nose from odors, and the ear from sounds.
From touch it perceives the body, but from the quality of form it sees the eye;
beyond that, it beholds its own true nature.
For, having grasped that from which it acts and that which it does, [it perceives].
That in which one initiates that activity,
that in which it occurs, that by which it is done, and he who is the agent— these they call the cause and the means.
That which is victorious, effective, and all-pervading; that which is praised in the world like a mantra; that which is the cause of all and acts for the ultimate goal;
That cause is the effect; whatever is other than this [is not].
Just as a certain man, by means of his good deeds, obtains both the auspicious and the inauspicious without contradiction.
Thus, within bodies— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
this knowledge is bound by the results of one's own actions,
just as a lamp is set ablaze before one.
Just as a lamp, while shining, makes another thing visible, so too here the trees of the five sense-faculties,
though ignited by knowledge, remain dependent upon others.
Just as a king has many ministers who, when appointed, each declare their own distinct authority,
so too do the five [elements] exist within bodies.
That supreme portion of knowledge belongs to them alone,
just as the flames belong to fire, the speed to the wind,
the rays to the sun, and the waters to the rivers.
They go and they come while being stretched out;
in that same way are the bodies of embodied beings.
And just as someone, having taken up an axe—
Just as one might not see smoke or fire within the wood,
so too, having cut through the body, the belly, the hands, and the feet, they do not perceive anything other than that.
Just as one might see smoke and fire by rubbing together those very pieces of wood through application,
so too does the man of excellent intellect [perceive] through the equalization of the senses.
The wise man perceives his own supreme nature, just as one sees one's own limb fallen upon the earth,
or perceives something other than oneself within a dream.
Endowed with the ears and other senses, cheerful-minded and possessed of keen intellect,
he thus departs from one subtle body (liṅga) to another subtle body through the conjunctions of birth,
growth, and decay.
That supreme embodied being is not [perceived] by this sign; rather,
another sign goes unobserved due to its connection with rebirth.
The self does not see form with the eye,
nor does it undergo any contact whatsoever;
nor does it accomplish any purpose by means of them.
They do not see him, but he sees them,
just as one perceives a certain form born of heat from a blazing lamp.
It does not possess any internal quality of form;
in that very way, its form is seen,
just as a person [is seen] after casting off the body.
Having cast off the body among the great elements, it enters another invisible body; then,
depending upon that [new] support, it assumes a form.
The embodied soul enters from all sides into space, wind, fire, water, and the earth;
these various supports, engaged in their respective functions, [sustain it].
The five [faculties] beginning with hearing rely upon the qualities:
12.195.020a Hearing arises from space, and likewise the nose from earth;
form consists of fire, as does digestion.
Sweat is said to have its source in water, as is the essence (rasa); and touch is a quality produced by that which has the nature of wind. These five reside within the great elements.
The objects of the five senses likewise follow the senses;
all these follow the mind,
and the mind follows the intellect, while the intellect follows its own inherent nature.
Whatever pure or impure karma he has performed,
that very thing he receives back within his own body;
high and low states follow after the mind.
Like leeches moving with the current in a stream,
it moves as it enters the range of vision;
though subtle, it appears as if it were a large form.
One perceives one's own form and likewise perceives another form; thus it enters the path of the intellect.
Manu said:
When the qualities that were previously assisted by the senses have long since been attained,
and those very senses are subsequently impaired, [he remembers them].
That supreme nature, which consists of the form of consciousness,
does not perceive all sense-objects simultaneously in their entirety at one and the same time.
That wise one moves according to his power;
therefore, he alone is the supreme embodied being.
Rajas, tamas, and sattva as the third—these are [his qualities].
That Supreme Self moves through manifold qualities of knowledge,
yet it is not bound by them; rather, it binds the universe,
and here it does not follow after those qualities.
In this way, the embodied one enters the senses,
just as the wind enters the fire situated within the fuel;
it does not perceive its own form with the eye.
One does not perceive contact as the sense organ nor the sense object; there is no sign of hearing in the act of hearing.
When one perceives the Tathāgata in that way, that [perception] perishes.
The ear and the other senses do not perceive their own respective selves by themselves;
the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is all-knowing and all-seeing, perceives them—
just as one cannot see the far side of the Himalayas or the back of the moon.
It has never been seen before by human beings, yet it does not exist for that reason alone;
in the same way, this subtle Self of beings, consisting of knowledge,
has never been seen before with the eyes, yet it does not exist for that reason alone.
Just as one who sees the mark [of the hare] in the moon does not find it in the world, so too,
whether "it exists" or "it does not exist," that is not the ultimate resort;
for the wise, because of its formlessness, perceive the one who possesses form in the rising and setting [of phenomena].
Those who have attained that state perceive the course of the sun through their intellect;
likewise, by means of the lamp of wisdom, the highly discerning desire to bring the object of knowledge— which though situated at a distance— near to themselves, being united with gnosis.
Indeed, no purpose whatsoever is accomplished by means that are not skillful;
just as those who live by the water catch fish with nets of thread,
and just as deer are captured by means of deer and birds by means of birds.
Just as elephants are perceived by elephants, so too is that which is to be known grasped through knowledge;
for it is an illustration that only a snake perceives the feet of a snake.
In the same way, one perceives through knowledge that which abides within forms by means of those very forms.
Just as the senses themselves are not able to perceive the senses,
even so, in this world, the higher intellect does not perceive the Supreme by means of the intellect.
For just as the moon is not seen on the new moon day because it lacks a visible mark, [so too is the Self].
And yet its destruction does not occur; know the embodied soul to be just like that. For the moon, its orb diminished on the new-moon day, does not shine;
in the same way, the embodied soul, when separated from its form, is no longer perceived.
Just as the moon shines again upon reaching another mansion,
so too the embodied soul shines again upon reaching another subtle body (liṅga).
Furthermore, its birth, growth, and decay are perceived through direct observation.
That, however, is the manifestation of the moon, not of that embodied being;
for just as he is perceived through birth, growth, and decay,
so too does the moon itself exist in embodied form on the new moon day.
Just as darkness is seen neither approaching nor leaving the moon,
so too, behold the embodied soul as it emits and approaches;
for just as that darkness is perceived when conjoined with the moon and the sun.
In the same way, the embodied soul (śarīrin) is perceived only when conjoined with a body;
just as Rāhu is not perceived when released from the moon and sun,
so too the embodied soul is not perceived when released from the body.
"Just as the moon, having gone [to conjunction], is united with the constellations on the new-moon day,
even so one who is released from the body is united with the fruits of his actions.
Manu said:
Just as this manifest body lies here while the conscious being moves about in a dream,
so too, when consciousness is joined with the senses, there arise existence and non-existence after death.
Just as one sees a form with the eye when the water is clear, so it is.
In the same way, one whose sense faculties are clear perceives the object of knowledge through wisdom. Just as one does not perceive a form when those [faculties] are agitated,
so too, when the sense faculties are disturbed, one does not perceive the object of knowledge through wisdom.
Lack of wisdom is produced by ignorance; through lack of wisdom, the mind becomes corrupted.
When the mind is corrupted, the five mental faculties become thoroughly corrupted.
One who is satisfied with ignorance and immersed in sense objects is not seen [to attain liberation].

But even without seeing [the truth], one whose self is purified turns away from sense objects. In this world, the cutting off of thirst does not occur for a person due to impurity; rather, thirst ceases only when evil has come to its end.
With a mind burning with internal evil and subject to the fluctuations of the auspicious and inauspicious, he is not born again;
for he has no attachment to sense objects and does not rely on the eternal.
Even while desiring something else with the mind, one does not attain the Supreme;
knowledge arises for men through the destruction of evil karma,
and then one beholds the Self within the self, as if in the surface of a mirror.
One who has the senses unrestrained is miserable; one who has them restrained is happy.
Therefore, one should restrain the self from the objects of the senses by means of the self.
The mind precedes the senses, and the intellect is superior to that.
Knowledge is superior to the intellect (*buddhi*), and that which is beyond is superior to knowledge.
Knowledge has issued forth from the unmanifest (*avyakta*); from that comes the intellect, and from that, the mind (*manas*).
The mind, when joined with the ears and other senses, correctly perceives sound and the other objects of sense.
He who abandons those [objects], beginning with sound, as well as all manifested forms,
and withdraws his outstretched senses like a tortoise,
relinquishes the multitude of material shapes; having abandoned them, he partakes of the immortal.
Just as when the sun rises it emits a circle of rays,
its circle is visible but the sun itself is not seen;
in the same way, the body is perceived, but the supreme Self is always invisible.
For that which is swallowed is constantly vomited forth; one should always know the *udgītha*.
In childhood, through the yoga of the two chariots, the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) is attained. That very [knowledge] reaches its setting, and he restrains it within the self.
The radiant inner self, having entered the body, takes up the essence of all beings through the rays of the senses;
having reached the five qualities of the senses, it returns and goes to its setting.
Though he may be deprived of his circle of light, he does not cease to exist by that much;
being led again and again along the path prepared by his own actions,
this self-possessed man attains the abundant fruit of his deeds and the Dharma.

The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied soul who abstains from food, with the exception of the taste for them; even that taste turns away from him when he has seen the Supreme. When the intellect, freed from the qualities of action, abides in the mind, [then it attains liberation].

Then it attains Brahman, having gone to dissolution right there— Brahman which is intangible, unheard, tasteless, unseen, odorless, and beyond discursive thought; [the self] enters that supreme Being.
From the unmanifest, knowledge emanated; from that, the intellect (*buddhi*); from that, the mind (*manas*).
The intellect emanates from the Self and is called the unmanifest knowledge.
Therefore, it is known as the intellect by those who know that [reality], and from that, the mind is said to have proceeded.

Therefore, the five forms are said to be preceded by the mind; higher than that is the intellect (*buddhi*), and knowledge is remembered as higher than that. Subtler than that is the self (*ātman*), and there is nothing higher than that.
The senses perceive these objects in every way through the mind;
the forms are submerged in the mind, but the mind transcends the intellect (*mati*). The intellect, in turn, transcends knowledge (*jñāna*), and knowledge reaches the Supreme.

The accomplishment of the mind is through the senses; the mind does not perceive the intellect (*buddhi*). The intellect does not perceive the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); rather, it is the Subtle One (*sūkṣma*) who perceives these.
Manu said:
When physical or mental suffering has arisen,
one should not dwell upon that against which no effort can be made;
this non-dwelling upon it is the medicine for suffering.
For when it is reflected upon, it subsides, yet it arises again;
one should destroy mental suffering through wisdom and physical suffering through medicines. This is the power of discernment; it does not reach the level of the foolish.
Youth, beauty, life, and the accumulation of wealth are impermanent;
health and dwelling with loved ones—the wise man should not be attached to these. One ought not to grieve alone over suffering that affects the entire country.
One should not grieve, but should instead take remedial action if one perceives a means of recovery.
There is no doubt that in this life, suffering is far more abundant than happiness;
and for one who is attached to the objects of the senses, death is unpleasant due to delusion.
The man who abandons both suffering and pleasure attains the absolute Brahman; those wise ones do not grieve. For wealth leads to suffering, and there is no happiness in its preservation.
They are attained with difficulty; one should not worry about their destruction.

Know that knowledge arises from the object of knowledge, and that the mind is an attribute of knowledge. When joined with the instrument of wisdom (*prajñā*), from that, the intellect (*buddhi*) proceeds.
When the intellect, endowed with its qualities, abides in the mind, then Brahman is realized through the meditative absorption of yoga.
This very intellect, though possessed of qualities, moves only among the qualities.
When one attains that primordial meditation which is free from qualities— like water flowing down from the peak of a mountain—
then Brahman becomes manifest, just as gold is revealed when tested on a touchstone.

But the mind, having carried away the intellect which perceives the objects of the senses, does not directly behold the qualities; it is the indicator of that which is devoid of qualities. Having restrained all these doors, one should remain established in the mind.
Having achieved one-pointedness of mind, he attains that supreme state.
Just as the great elements cease when their qualities are exhausted, so too the intellect, having withdrawn the senses, abides in the mind.

When that intellect, endowed with the quality of resolve, abides within the mind moving inward, then the mind becomes perfected. When the mind, possessed of qualities, is united with the qualities of those who possess them, it attains the quality of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Then, having abandoned all qualities (*guṇa*), one attains the qualityless (*nirguṇa*). There is no comparable illustration for the realization of the unmanifest (*avyakta*) in this world;
since there is no footprint to be set down there, who could reach that domain?
Through austerity, inference, virtues, birth, and sacred learning— with a purified inner self— one should seek to lead oneself toward that Supreme Brahman;
for one devoid of virtue follows after that path only outwardly.
Due to the absence of qualities and by its very nature, it is inconceivable and commensurate with the object of knowledge.
Through the absence of qualities one attains Brahman; through the presence of qualities one turns away from it.
The intellect, spreading out through the qualities, is like fire amidst fuel.
Just as the five senses are liberated by their respective functions,
so too is that supreme Brahman liberated, transcending primordial nature (prakṛti).
In this way, all embodied beings arise from primordial nature.
They turn back, and upon that cessation, they do not undergo creation again.
Puruṣa, Prakṛti, intellect, the specific objects, the senses, ego, and self-consciousness— these constitute what is known as the aggregate of the elements.
The first manifestation proceeds from Pradhāna;
the second determines the manifestation of pairs through the non-specific.
From dharma arises that which is superior, and likewise from adharma arises that which is inferior.
"One possessed of passion returns to *prakṛti*; one free from passion becomes possessed of knowledge.
Manu said:
"I consider that very thing to be impossible to describe in full detail."
Just as a thing cannot be understood according to its outward appearance,
and just as one does not know the core essence as it actually exists,
so too is this consciousness within the body like the luster of another's body.

Without the body there is no shadow, nor does the body exist without that shadow; in the same way, here in this world, there is no functioning of primordial nature (prakṛti) without the Spirit (puruṣa), nor does the Spirit exist without primordial nature.
This [Spirit] does not exist without the Supreme, nor does the Supreme exist without this.
"He was severed by the individual self (jīvātman), and this [severing] was indeed performed by the supreme self (parātman).
Some understand it thus, while others say it is untrue. O learned one, both views are held by me as being consistent with the cause of liberation.
Even that deer, with senses restrained, is seen by those who are liberated;
indeed, he is not visible to everyone, for he flashes like lightning. He is visible even to a Brahmin in meditative absorption—how much more so then [to others]?
The supreme, pure Fire exists as the witness;
therefore, this Śruti is eternal, and for that reason, he is considered the one Supreme. No purpose is aimed at by the activity of that Great-Souled One.
One should consider it thus: "May it be so"; for in that way, by the Great-Souled One, truth is always [established] through various forms of distinction, like the diversity of states of existence.
Its distinction has been fully explained, for such a distinction indeed exists.
Thus, O wise one, know the imperishable Supreme Self,
who is associated with various designations according to the specific qualities [of His manifestations];
He is the Lord of all, the embodiment of all, and the impeller of all.
He who is the soul of all, possessed of all powers, the cause of all causes,
common to all, and worshipped by all great souls—
he is renowned as Vāsudeva; by knowing him, one attains immortality.
When those five [senses], along with the mind, are liberated from the five [objects],

Just as [the soul] is attached through its own actions to pearls, corals, earthenware, and silver;

By whichever body this [person] performs whatever action,

In this way, the intellect follows after action, perceiving the inner self.
Desire arises preceded by knowledge; intention is preceded by desire;
action is preceded by intention; and from that, action is the root of the fruit.

One should know that the fruit has action as its essence, and likewise, action has the object of knowledge as its essence. One should know that the object of knowledge has knowledge as its essence, and knowledge has both being and non-being as its essence.
Thus is Brahman intended; it is differentiated through analytical enumeration.

At the end of the exhaustion of cognitions, fruits, objects of knowledge, and likewise of actions, there arises that divine fruit: knowledge established in the object of knowledge. For yogis who are disciplined perceive that which is truly great and supreme.

The ignorant do not perceive it, for their intellects are fixed upon the qualities (guṇas) that reside within the self. Here, the form of water is greater than the form of earth; light is greater than water, and wind is greater than light.
From the wind comes the great ether; beyond that is the mind. Greater than the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*); greater than the intellect, time (*kāla*) is remembered as the greatest.
Beyond time is the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, to whom this entire world belongs.
Neither beginning, nor middle, nor end exists for that deity.
Because it is without beginning, without middle, and without end, it is imperishable. It transcends all sufferings, for suffering is said to have an end.
That is declared to be the supreme Brahman; that is remembered as the supreme abode. Having gone there, they are liberated from the domain of time and have attained liberation.
Yet, by means of these qualities, they shine forth, for beyond that lies the quality-less (nirguṇa).
Dharma, characterized by cessation, likewise leads to infinity.
The *ṛg*, *yajus*, and *sāman* verses, dependent upon the body, proceed from the tips of the tongues; they are accomplished through effort and are subject to destruction.
And Brahman is not thus accepted as having its origin dependent upon a body;
that Brahman is not to be accomplished through effort, it has no beginning or middle, nor does it have an end.
Likewise, it is said to be the beginning of the Ṛg-verses, the Sāman-chants, and the Yajus-formulas.
An end is observed among things that have a beginning, yet no beginning is recorded for Brahman.
Because it is without beginning and without end, it is infinite and immutable;
and because it is immutable, it is free from dualities, and due to the absence of dualities, it is therefore supreme.
12.199.020 Because of the unseen, because of lack of means, and because of the intentionality of action,
mortals do not perceive that by which they go to the Supreme. 12.199.021 And because of attachment to sense-objects and because of the vision of the eternal.
Desiring something else with the mind, one does not attain the Supreme. When people here perceive the qualities (guṇas), other persons desire them;

We know them with a subtle mind, yet we are unable to express them in words.
For the mind is to be grasped by the mind, and vision by vision;
having purified the intellect with knowledge, and likewise the mind with the intellect,

Deprived of intellect and failing in mental resolve,
one who is thus devoid of aspiration falls into the state of the qualities (guṇas); for here, even while being enticed, it abandons the Supreme.
Like the wind fanning a fire situated within its fuel,
the mind is always engaged in the acquisition of qualities and the separation from them, through both the higher and lower intellects.
Engaged in this very manner in the acquisition of qualities, he attains the body of Brahman—
a person whose self is unmanifest and whose actions are unmanifest.
For at the time of death he goes to the unmanifest state; indeed, this one, whose form is action, exists through those very sense organs as they either develop or decay.

so indeed does that Sage here become free from all distinctions;

The future destiny of those who have performed good deeds, the supreme goal,
the self-existent one, the inexhaustible source of all power,
that which is eternal, immortal, and imperishable state;
Having reflected upon that tranquility, one attains immortality.

These are the twelve Ādityas, born from the self of Kaśyapa. And Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins.
These two are the sons of Mārtāṇḍa, the eighth Prajāpati;
and the illustrious Viśvarūpa of great fame is the son of Tvaṣṭṛ,
as well as Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Virūpākṣa, and Raivata.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Tryambaka, Sureśvara,
Sāvitra, Jayanta, Pinākin, and Aparājita—
these eleven Rudras, the lords of the three worlds, have been described.
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, Anala,
the highly fortunate Pratyūṣa, and Sāvitra is remembered as the eighth;
these eight highly fortunate Vasus were proclaimed previously.

These gods of such a kind belong to Manu Prajāpati himself; they and the ancient gods (suras) are remembered as the two classes of Pitṛs. Others, however, delight in virtue and beauty, while others likewise belong to the Siddhas and Sādhyas.
The Ṛbhus and the Maruts are indeed the hosts of gods who are their instigators.
Thus these Viśvedevas and the two Aśvins have been enumerated.
The Ādityas are their Kṣatriyas, while the Maruts are likewise their Vaiśyas.
The Aśvins are considered Śūdras who were absorbed in fierce asceticism;
however, the divine Aṅgirasas are remembered as Brāhmaṇas—this is the settled conclusion. Thus has the fourfold caste system of all the gods been proclaimed.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should indeed recite these names of the gods,
is liberated from all sin, whether born of oneself or committed by another.
[These are] Yavakrīta, Raibhya, Arvāvasu, and Parāvasu.
Auśija Kakṣīvat and Nala, the sons of Aṅgiras; Kaṇva, the son of the seer Medhātithi, and likewise Barhiṣad— these,
O dear one, are the creators of the three worlds, as well as the Seven Seers of the east.
Unmucha and Vimucha, the powerful Svastyātreya, Pramuca, Idhmavāha, and the blessed Dṛḍhavrata,
as well as the majestic Agastya, the son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
These Brahman-sages dwell eternally in the southern direction:
Ruṣadgu, Kavaṣa, Dhaumya, the heroic Parivyādha,
and the great ṛṣis Ekata, Dvita, and Trita.
The venerable son of Atri and likewise the lord Sarasvata—
these nine high-souled ones occupy the western direction. Also Ātreya, Vasiṣṭha, and the great ṛṣi Kaśyapa.
Gautama, along with Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Kauśika,
as well as the venerable Jamadagni, son of the high-souled Ṛcīka— these seven have taken refuge in the northern direction.
12,201.033 These high-souled ones of fierce splendor, who are the creators of the worlds, have all been proclaimed as witnesses for each of the directions.
12,201.034 Thus these great souls are stationed individually in every direction.
By reciting their names, one is liberated from all sins.
In whichever direction these [deities] reside, by taking refuge in that direction,
one is released from all evils and shall return home in safety.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O you whose prowess is truth in battle,
I desire to hear in its entirety about Kṛṣṇa, the imperishable Lord."
"O bull of the Bharatas, tell me everything according to the truth: what is his immense splendor and what was his ancient deed?
How did Hari assume a form belonging to the animal kingdom?"
"By what performance of duty [is this attained]? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"In former times, having gone out on a hunt, I stayed at the hermitage of Mārkaṇḍeya."
There I saw hosts of sages seated by the thousands;
then they offered me the guest-offering of honey-mixture (*madhuparka*),
and having accepted that honor, I greeted the seers in return.
12,202.006a This story was told there by the great seer Kaśyapa; 12,202.006c listen now with a focused mind to that divine tale which gladdens the heart.
12,202.006d For the Blessed Viṣṇu is Dharma himself, the Boar who assumes the form of sacrifice.

The entire world is composed of that [Brahman], and the Self is the master of all. In ancient times, indeed, hundreds of great Asuras, such as Naraka and others, who were the leaders of the Dānavas, were filled with anger and greed and intoxicated by their own power.
In the same way, many other Dānavas, intoxicated by war,
could not endure that unsurpassed prosperity of the gods;
Naraka and others, who were most terrible, took refuge with Hiraṇyākṣa.
Then they made a supreme effort to subdue the gods;
for a million years he subsisted on air alone.
Then the exceedingly fierce Hiraṇyākṣa obtained [boons] from the Grandfather, the God.
O King, being oppressed by the Dānavas in hundreds and thousands of ways— both inconceivable and incomparable— the gods and celestial sages found no peace, fleeing here and there.
The dwellers of heaven beheld the earth appearing distressed,
overrun by Dānavas of terrible form and great strength—
oppressed by their weight, dragged down, suffering, and sinking away.
Having seized the goddess Earth, she then dwelt in the netherworld (pātāla). Consequently, the entire triple world, including all its collections of medicinal herbs,
became entirely devoid of Vedic study and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* on every side.
Then the terrified Adityas spoke thus to Brahmā:
"O Brahman, how shall we be able to withstand the oppression by the Dānavas?
O Blessed One, this Earth has been seized by Hiraṇyākṣa."
"We shall not be able to enter there, for it is a fortress of water.
To them, the Blessed Lord Brahmā said:
"Let the sage Agastya, who possesses great splendor, be propitiated; he will immediately drink up that water."
Having said, "So be it," those gods, filled with joy, spoke to the sage:
"O brahmin-sage, protect the worlds; bring this water to its end.
Having said, "So be it," the Blessed One, whose splendor was like the fire of cosmic destruction, [proceeded].
Meditating, he drank the mass of water-eating creatures along with the water itself in an instant. When the ocean had been dried up, the gods,
led by the sages, prostrated before Brahmā and said, "The water has been dried up by the sage."
"Tell us further, O Lord, what shall we do?
To them the Self-Existent One said this: "The ordinance for this has been ordained by me;
they are intoxicated by their boon, by their strength, and by pride."
The deluded ones will not recognize Viṣṇu, whose form is unmanifest—
the god in the form of a boar, who is invincible even by the immortals.
For he shall go with speed to where those lowest of Dānavas are.
"Terrible beings dwelling by the thousands within the depths of the earth shall be pacified upon hearing this. Hearing this, the best of the gods rejoiced.
Then Viṣṇu, possessed of great splendor, assumed the form of a boar.
Having entered the interior of the earth, he went toward the sons of Diti.
And seeing that superhuman being together with all the Daityas,
they all suddenly stood their ground by force, deluded by Time.
And all of them, having rushed forward together, seized the boar at once;
enraged, they dragged that boar from every side—
the lords of the Dānavas, who possessed massive bodies, great heroism, and were exalted by their strength.
O Lord, they were unable to do anything at all to him then;
consequently, those lords of the Dānavas were struck with amazement out of fear,
and by the thousands they considered themselves to have fallen into peril.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, that Lord, the God of gods, whose self is yoga and who has yoga as his charioteer, having resorted to yoga,
let out a great roar, agitating the Daityas and Dānavas.
By that resounding roar, all the worlds and all the ten directions were made to vibrate;
by the sound of that clamor, the worlds fell into great agitation,
and all the quarters, with the gods led by Śakra, became bewildered.
Then the entire world, both mobile and immobile, became utterly motionless, bewildered by that roar. Thereupon,
all those Dānavas were terrified by that sound.
12,202.024c They fell down, deprived of life, utterly bewildered by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
12,202.024d Seeing the gods terrified, Brahmā, the Grandfather, said:
"This Blessed Lord, the Master of Yoga, has assumed the form of a boar."
Roaring there, he approaches; do not fear, O best of gods!
Having spoken thus, Brahmā, the Grandfather, then paid homage to Viṣṇu for the sake of liberation, as did the deities and the sages.
Then Hari, endowed with great splendor, having greeted Brahmā,
and like a boar, tore apart with his hooves the enemies of the gods who had gone to the netherworld (rasātala), along with their heaps of flesh, fat, and bones.
By that great sound, he is remembered as Sanātana;
he is Padmanābha, the Great Yogin, the Teacher of Beings, and the Sovereign of Creatures.
Then all the hosts of gods addressed the Grandfather.
Having gone there, they spoke to that Great-Souled One, the Lord of the World:
"O God, what kind of sound is this? O All-pervading One, we do not understand it.
Who is he, or to whom does this sound belong, by which the world has been thrown into such agitation?"
Both the gods and the Dānavas were bewildered by his splendor. In that interval, Viṣṇu assumed the form of a boar and arose as Mahādeva, being praised by the great ṛṣis.
The Grandfather said:
A divine battle took place between those two great-souled ones,
Hiraṇyākṣa and Viṣṇu, which caused the agitation of the entire universe.
And Hari slew Hiraṇyākṣa as he had gone beneath the earth.
Having heard that, the highly effulgent Brahmā spoke sweetly.
The Grandfather said:
Having slain the lords of the Dānavas, he of massive form and great strength— this god, the great yogin, the self of all beings, the creator of beings,
the lord of all creatures, the yogin, the source, and likewise the self of the self.
"Be steadfast! This is Kṛṣṇa, the destroyer of all sins.
Having performed this most excellent deed that was impossible [for others], he of immeasurable splendor, the highly fortunate and immensely radiant one, has returned to his own self."
Padmanābha, the great yogin, the self of all beings, the creator of beings— O best of gods, you should feel no distress, no fear, nor any grief;
this is the cosmic law, its very power, and Time, the bringer of dissolution.
While supporting these twelve thousand, two hundred, and three worlds, this Great-Souled One released a roar.
For he alone is the highly fortunate one, honored by all the worlds— the Infallible, the Lotus-Eyed, from whom all beings originate.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, you ought to tell me once again in truth the majesty of the high-souled Keśava."
"O Bhārata, even though I see and hear him, I am not yet satiated.
Bhīṣma said:
"O mighty-armed one, since it is thus regarding Kṛṣṇa, therefore tell this to me."
O King, listen to this Vaiṣṇava narrative which destroys all sins;
it is that which Nārada told me in the past, and which I shall now relate to you.
Formerly, the celestial sage Nārada said: "I shall indeed come to know the true nature of Hari."
Having thus reflected in his mind, he meditated upon the eternal Brahman for a hundred divine years on the auspicious and divine Himālaya,
remaining without breath, abstaining from food, with self-restrained soul and conquered senses.
Then, from the sky, a divine, external, and incorporeal voice, with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud, addressed that preeminent sage:
"O best of supreme sages, for what purpose have you entered this meditative absorption?"
"I shall give you knowledge; choose from me either that or the Dharma.
Having heard this, the sage reflected, his mind overcome with agitation, and after considering what it might mean, he spoke these further words in reply.
Why have you broken your vehicle today, while standing upon it and addressing me with these words? Indeed,
no other form of yours is seen.
"You are presided over by such a one as this.
He spoke again to that sage: "I am Ananta, the most vast.
The deluded do not know me; only the wise truly know me."
The illustrious sage, bowing down with humility, replied to him:
"I wish to know you; tell me the truth of who you are.
Having heard those words of his, the Lord of the World spoke to Nārada.
"Know me through knowledge; you do not have the power to know me otherwise.
Nārada said:
"But of what kind is that knowledge by which I may know your form?"
The World-Protector said:
"O Infinite One, if you are disposed to show me favor, tell me that which is free from conceptual construction, vast, and its [summit]."
That knowledge is distant, auspicious, and supreme; by means of that, O Sage, you know the means [of attainment].
For this [knowledge] stands here as unobstructed, pure, while the other is false.
"O best of sages, all this has been told to you in brief.
Nārada said:
"O Teacher of the World, tell me that very truth which belongs to you."
“I wish to know you, O Imperishable One; what is your true nature?
Then the Blessed One, laughing, spoke with a voice as deep as a thundercloud: “The Lord of all beings replied: ‘I have neither mouth nor ears.’”
“O Sage, there is neither nose nor tongue, nor sight, nor skin;
how then shall I speak of myself, for I am likewise bodiless? Having understood that, the sage, overcome with wonder, bowed to him and said:
"How is it that you, being pleased with me, previously told me, 'I am infinite, I am the greatest, I am capable'?
To him, the Blessed One spoke again: "Indeed, you also possess the senses."
"O Nārada, if you are able, speak of yourself to him;
O sage, so that the Self may become known to you just as it is known to you. And since you know me, you are the sole means for us both."
Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, the God, said nothing further.
Nārada, too, smiling yet distressed, wondered, "Where has that Lord gone?
And for a long time the sage remained there with his mind bewildered.
The Blessed One said to me: "I am the god Ananta, the most vast. [I asked: "Because of that, who among all is called 'Ananta' or the 'most vast'?
What indeed is this earth called 'Ananta,' for it is surely vast?"

"In that [place] where all beings know they have dissolved from here and there—that young woman I shall question; surely she has spoken to me. Having thus reached this conclusion within himself, that illustrious sage—
Having descended to the surface of the earth and prostrated himself, he spoke this:
"O Vasundharā, you are wonderful, you are blessed, and you are vast.
O beautiful one, I wish to know here what kind of being you truly are."
Having heard that, the goddess Dharaṇī, smiling, spoke these words:
"O Brahmin, I am neither Bṛhatī nor Anantā, O best of beings.
Tell me of that which is my cause, the one whose nature is fragrance."
Then the Sage, having prostrated himself before that Reality, spoke these words:
"You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast. I desire to know you; O Imperishable One, what is your true nature?"
Then that one whose nature is fragrance replied in turn to the sage:
"Water is indeed a cause greater than I.
Having gone to the ocean and prostrated himself, the sage spoke as follows:
"You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast. O Imperishable One, I desire to know what you are like.
Having heard that, the ocean, lord of rivers, spoke to the sage:
"In this matter, ask me about the cause, which is the essence of taste and exceedingly vast.
O knower, O best of sages, you should then ask about that which is even vaster than that. Then the sage, having examined that reality of water according to its proper application, [proceeded].
Having bowed to the one whose self is water, the sage established in the water-element said:
"You are wonderful, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast. I wish to hear from you, O Imperishable One: what is your true nature?"
Then that one, whose essence is flavor, spoke again and again to the sage:
"Ask the fire, who is the form of splendor, about my cause as well.
O Brahmin, O best of beings, I am neither greater nor infinite."
Then, having prostrated before Agni, the sage, his mind filled with wonder,
spoke to him who is the soul of sacrifice, the great abode, and the one honored by all beings:
"You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast."
“I wish to know you, O Imperishable One; what is your true nature? Then the Blessed One, the Sage Sviṣṭakṛt, smiling, said to the Muni:
“O Brahmin, I am not the greater, nor am I infinite, O best of beings.”

"O best of sages, ask me the cause of my form. Then, having entered that well-known [form] by means of the sequence of yoga, Nārada, the foremost of speakers, bowed to the one whose self is form and said:
"You are wonderful, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast.
I wish to know who you are, O Imperishable One—what is your true nature? Having smiled, the one whose essence is form replied to that sage.

"O Brahmin, O best of sages, Vāyu is my cause; ask him, for he is more glorious, infinite, and possesses greater strength than I. Having been thus addressed, that blessed and best of sages bowed to Māruta and spoke.
You are one perfected in yoga, a great yogi who has reached the further shore of knowledge and discernment. You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast.
I desire to know you: what is your nature, O Imperishable One?
Then Vāyu spoke to Nārada, the best of sages:
"O Blessed One, ask me today about my nature as touch;
for he is more vast than I, glorious, and likewise infinite."
Then, having heard his words, he [the Wind] spoke to him whose nature is touch:
"You are wonderful, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast.
I desire to know you; what kind of being are you, O Imperishable One?"
Having heard those words of his, the one whose nature is touch (the Wind) said to the sage:
"O Brahmin, O best of beings, I am neither the greatest nor am I infinite;
for me, space itself is greater."
"Ask him, O tiger among sages, who is all-pervading and immutable.
Having heard those words, the illustrious Nārada, skilled in speech,
approached the ether, bowed with palms joined in reverence, and spoke.
"You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast. O Imperishable One, I wish to know what you truly are. To that best of sages, Ākāśa replied with a smile:
"O Brahmin, I am not the greater one; indeed, sound is my instrument. Ask him, O tiger among sages, for he is truly greater than I.
Then, having entered the ether, he who is the self of sound spoke.
Combined with vowels and consonants, adorned with various causes,
it is called the Veda— the supreme secret, the imperishable cause of the Vedas. You are marvelous, you are blessed, for you are infinite and most vast.
"I wish to hear from you, O Imperishable One, what kind of being you are.
The Soul of the Vedas replied thus to Nārada, the bull among sages:
"With me acting as the cause, the Grandfather [Brahmā] is the knower of all."
O great sage, I abide within the sphere of Brahmā’s intellect;
therefore, the lotus-born one of great intelligence is greater than I. O tiger among sages, ask him about the cause of all causes.
Then, having gone to the world of Brahmā, Nārada [beheld] that Great-Souled One being served by the foremost of sages, by the world-protectors, by the hosts of Maruts,
by the oceans, by the rivers, and by the principles of existence together with the mountains.

[He saw] Brahmā, the Lord of the World, the Supreme beyond the supreme, being worshipped by Gandharvas, Apsarases, and hosts of luminaries, as well as by the Munīśvaras through Vedic hymns, *stomas*, *grahas*, and *stobhas*.
Having bowed with joined palms and a humble posture to Hiraṇyagarbha, the Lord of the Universe, who is adorned with four faces, that bull among sages spoke to him:
"You are a marvel, you are blessed, for you are Ananta, the most vast."

"I wish to know you, O Imperishable One; what is your true nature? Having heard this, the Blessed Brahmā, the Grandfather of all the worlds, smiling, spoke these words to the sage who was seeking to destroy the very root of karma.
“O Brahmin, I am neither greater nor infinite, O best of beings;
there is one who is greater than me, the lord of all worlds. He dwells in the family of the cowherd Nanda, surrounded by the cowherd boys.”
The protector of all the worlds, he remains established in the guise of a cowherd;
and assuming my own form, he performs the creation of the universe.
Established in his sovereign power, the glorious one constantly destroys and protects.
Viṣṇu, whose form is his own true nature, that Hari is my cause. Ask him, O tiger among sages; he is Ananta, the most vast.
Then the blessed great sage descended from the world of Brahmā.
In the family of Nanda the cowherd, they beheld this Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of the Universe,
intent on childhood play, adorned with a herd of calves,
and having just finished feeding them, binding them while his face was grey with dust.
Surrounded on all sides by those plunging [into the water], laughing, and dancing,
as well as by hand-clappers and flute-players,
the venerable sage Nārada bowed down and spoke to him.

"You are marvelous, you are blessed, indeed infinite and most vast; you are the knower and you are imperishable—I wish to know what kind [of being] you are. Then the Blessed One, smiling, replied to Nārada.
There is nothing higher than me; everything is established in me. There is nothing else greater than me; I alone am the greatest. And I, who existed before space, have told this very thing to you.
No person knows me; my illusory power (*māyā*) is difficult to overcome.
But the yogis, endowed with unswerving devotion, know me. You are dear to me, you are my devotee; behold my true nature!
I grant you that knowledge by which you shall perceive reality,
as well as to my other devotees whose souls are devoted to yoga;
I grant them divine knowledge, and by means of it, they go to my abode.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, Kṛṣṇa Hari went to the house of Nanda the cowherd.
This, O King, has been narrated to you—the unsurpassed reality of Viṣṇu.
"O best of beings, worship this large-eyed one while muttering 'Kṛṣṇa.
He deludes both me and you; he hears what is uttered by me. O mighty-armed one, that righteous-souled one protects his devotees and not otherwise."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O master of all scriptures,
what should be chanted at the time of departure by those seeking liberation who contemplate the ultimate truth?"
"What should one recollect, O best of the Kurus, when death has arrived?
Bhīṣma said:
One would attain supreme perfection; I wish to hear this according to the truth."

O sinless one, you have asked a question that is appropriate, beneficial, and subtle. Listen attentively, O King, to what was heard by Nārada in the past concerning Him who bears the Śrīvatsa mark, the seed of the universe, the infinite witness of the world.
In ancient times, Nārada questioned the god Nārāyaṇa:
"They call you the imperishable, the supreme Brahman, devoid of qualities, beyond darkness,
the object of knowledge, the highest abode, and the source of the lotus-born Brahmā."

O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, how are you to be meditated upon by devoted practitioners who have conquered their senses and desire liberation? What should be chanted, and what should a human being chant daily upon rising at dawn?
"How should one who is constantly engaged in yoga meditate? Tell me the eternal truth.
Having heard what Nārada had spoken, the Lord of the gods himself, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the powerful master and granter of boons, replied to Nārada.
Come now, I shall declare to you this divine recollection (*anusmṛti*),
by the study of which one attains my own state at the time of departure,
O Nārada, having placed the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and having paid homage to me.
Having become one-pointed and disciplined, he should utter this mantra:
"Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva.
Thus addressed, Nārada spoke, standing with palms joined in reverence and bowing low.
I take refuge with palms joined in reverence in Viṣṇu, the Lord of all gods, the soul of all, the sovereign Hari;
the unmanifest, eternal deity, the source, the Supreme Person, the imperishable,
the highest state.
I take refuge in the ancient, eternal, and imperishable source, the witness of the world; in the lotus-eyed Lord who is compassionate toward his devotees,
the protector of the world, the thousand-eyed, the marvelous, the supreme state.
I have taken refuge in the Blessed One, the Lord of the past, the future, and the present;
the creator of all worlds, the infinite one whose face is turned everywhere;
I take refuge in Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, the true and infallible.

I take refuge in that one who is the Golden Womb (*hiraṇyagarbha*), the immortal, the Womb of the Earth, and higher than the highest; the Lord of lords, without beginning or end, possessing the splendor of the sun,
the thousand-headed Puruṣa, the great seer (*maharṣi*) who contemplates the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
I take refuge in the subtle, immovable, and most excellent one who bestows fearlessness— Nārāyaṇa, the ancient seer, whose self is yoga, the eternal,
the stable Lord who is the foundation of all principles.
May that Lord Viṣṇu, the master of all beings, by whom all this is pervaded, the teacher of the moving and the unmoving, be gracious to me;
from whom the eternal Brahmā, whose source is the lotus, is born.
May that Viṣṇu, the source of Brahman, the soul of the universe, be gracious to me— He who, when the dissolution of the past has arrived and all things moving and stationary have perished,
remains while Brahmā and the others have dissolved and the world, both high and low, has been destroyed.

And when the dissolution of all beings has occurred and the world has been absorbed, the Great One, the unconditioned Soul of the Universe, remains alone; may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me. [He who is worshipped] with four, with four, with two, and indeed with five.
And he who is again invoked by these two— may that Viṣṇu be gracious to me!
Parjanya, Earth, the harvest, Time, Dharma, action and non-action—
he who is the mine of all virtues, may that tawny Vāsudeva be gracious to me!

May that Viṣṇu be gracious to me, who inflames the splendors of Agni, Soma, the Sun, and the stars, as well as those of Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and the yogis; O Abode of Yoga, salutations to You, the Abode of All, the Giver of Boons!
O Yajñagarbha, O Hiraṇyāṅga, O you who are the essence of the five sacrifices, homage be to you!
O four-formed one, supreme abode, dwelling place of Lakṣmī, most highly honored; O Vāsudeva, abode of all, creator of primordial matter, homage be to you!
The unborn, free from disease, the pathless one who possesses all forms;
O cutter-away, knower of the five times, salutations to you, O ocean of knowledge! From the unmanifest the manifest was born; he who is beyond the unmanifest is the Imperishable.
I have gone for refuge to Him than whom there is nothing higher;
to Him who is neither Pradhāna nor Mahat, who is the conscious and unborn Puruṣa;
I have gone for refuge to Him who is superior to these two.

I have gone for refuge to that Lord whom Brahmā, Īśāna, and the others constantly contemplate, yet do not attain certainty regarding. These great-souled ones, who have conquered their senses and are devoted to knowledge and meditation, [seek him].
Having reached whom they do not return, to Him I have gone for refuge.
The All-pervading One stands supporting the entire world with but a single fraction of Himself. Ungraspable and eternally devoid of qualities, to Him I have gone for refuge.
May that Great-Souled One, who consists of the splendor of the moon, the sun, and fire, and whose radiance is composed of stars,
who is born in the heavens— may he be gracious. He is the source of the qualities yet devoid of qualities, the primordial, the possessor of Lakṣmī, the conscious, and the unborn.
May that subtle, omnipresent yogin, that Great Soul, be gracious.
The unmanifest presiding lord, inconceivable, beyond both being and non-being— Established in the supreme, may that Great Soul, who enjoys it, be gracious.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) experiences Prakṛti through fivefold means by means of five gates.
May that Great-Souled One, who experiences the Great Principle (mahat) and the qualities (guṇas), be propitiated.
The Moon resides in the midst of the Sun, and she who resides in its midst—
May that Great-Souled One, whose radiance transcends all beings and external things, be gracious.
Homage to You, who are everywhere, O All, whose eyes, heads, and mouths are on every side! Homage be to You, the changeless one, the witness, the eternal abode of the field (kṣetra).
O you who transcend the senses, homage to you! You are not measured by manifest signs.
Those who do not recognize you wander through the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
[But those] who are completely liberated from desire and anger, and freed from passion and hatred, [attain you].
Those who honor and revere [the Lord] understand this, but the twice-born followers of Māra do not.
For those who are solitary, free from dualities, and perform actions without desire— their karma burnt away by the fire of knowledge— they enter into you with firm resolve.
Formless yet residing within the body, equal in all embodied beings—
devotees, liberated from merit and sin, indeed enter into You.
The unmanifest, intellect, ego, mind, the elements, and the senses.
Those qualities are in you, and you are in them; yet you are not in them, nor are they in you.
Those who understand this oneness, otherness, and manifoldness go to the Supreme. You are equal toward all beings; there is nothing hateful to you, nor anything dear.
With devotion, and with no other thought in mind, I long for equality.
This entire world of moving and non-moving beings, this fourfold collection of creatures,
is woven upon you alone, like clusters of gems on a thread.
You are the creator and the enjoyer, the immutable one; though not the reality, you are designated as the reality. You are the non-agent, the cause, the immovable, abiding separately within the self.
There is no union for me with the elements, for I transcend the qualities and the true nature of the elements.

I have no connection with the three qualities (*guṇas*) through either egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) or the intellect (*buddhi*). I have neither merit (*dharma*) nor demerit (*adharma*), nor any undertaking, nor rebirth.
O All-pervading One, I have taken refuge in you for the sake of liberation from old age and death.
Never again shall there be for me a coming together with sense-objects or even with the sense-faculties. Let my sense of smell go to the earth; let my sense of taste go to the water.
Let visible form go to fire, and let touch go to the wind.
Let the ear go to space, and let the mind, which is subject to transformation, likewise depart;
let the sense organs also return to their respective sources,
and let the earth go to water, water to fire, and fire to air.
May the wind enter into space, and may the mind likewise enter into space alone;
may the mind, which deludes all embodied beings, enter into the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*);
from that, the ego-sense enters into the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect, O Acyuta, enters into the Unmanifest (*avyakta*).
"When Pradhāna has returned to its primordial nature and the equilibrium of the *guṇas* is established, may I be separated from all instruments, qualities, and elements;
O God, I long for Your supreme, absolute state."

May there be oneness with you; may I not be born again. With my intellect fixed on you, my life-breaths gone to you, devoted to you, and having you as my supreme goal, I shall remember you alone when death has arrived.
May the diseases committed by me in previous bodies enter into me;
may painful afflictions torment me, so that my debt may be discharged. You have been meditated upon, O Lord of Gods; may there be no further birth for me.
"Therefore I say: 'May my karmic debts not arise;
may all diseases accumulated in the past not afflict me.
The Blessed One said:
Free from debt, I desire to go to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. I belong to that Blessed One, and He is my eternal [belonging].
I do not perish for Him, nor does He perish for me.

Having restrained the organs of action and the five organs of perception— these ten organs— one should dissolve the mind into the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the ego-sense into the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect into the Self (*ātman*).
With the senses of the intellect restrained, one should see; by means of the intellect, one should realize that which is higher than the highest.
"This is mine," [one thinks]; I am his, by whom all this is pervaded.
Having joined oneself with the Self, one should remember the Supreme Self.
Then, having realized that which is beyond the intellect, one attains no further rebirth.
And whoever, when death has arrived, should thus recollect me—
even if they are of sinful conduct— they go to the supreme goal.

Oṃ! Homage to that Blessed One, the Supreme Self of embodied beings, to Nārāyaṇa, the eternal one who is the sole object of devotion for his devotees. With a well-composed mind, one should recite this divine Vaiṣṇava *anusmṛti*.
Whether sleeping or waking, one should recite it and practice it wherever one may be;
especially on the full moon day, the new moon day, and the twelfth lunar day,
one should cause those who have faith, and especially my devotees, to hear it.
If one performs the acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity while relying on the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
one obtains their fruit, but that leads to rebirth. Even while worshipping the ancestors and the gods, reciting, offering oblations, and giving sacrificial portions (*bali*).
He who remembers me as a blazing fire attains the supreme goal. Sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the means of purification for embodied beings;
therefore, one should perform sacrifice, charity, and austerity, free from desire for rewards.

O Nārada, even for an outcaste, the world shall be imperishable if he, being my devotee and endowed with faith, should simply utter the name "Namo. How much more so for those practitioners who worship me according to the prescribed rites?
Those who possess faith, whose selves are restrained, and who take refuge in me—they come to me.
Actions in this world have a beginning and an end, but my devotee does not experience their end.
Therefore, O divine sage, meditate upon me alone constantly and without weariness.
Then you shall attain perfection; indeed, you shall behold my own state.
And whoever should give knowledge for the sake of one who is ignorant, providing instruction in the Dharma—that fruit is not equal to the merit of one who might give the entire earth.
Therefore, one should give to the virtuous that which removes the fear of birth and bondage.
By giving in this manner, O best of men, one attains spiritual welfare and valor,
even more than one who might perform a thousand times a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Bhīṣma said:
"He does not attain that station which is attained by my devotees.
Thus was I questioned in the past by that celestial sage Nārada."
O you of excellent vows, that which Śambhu spoke at that time has been told to you;
you too, becoming single-minded, should meditate upon that which is to be known, which transcends the qualities (guṇas). Worship the imperishable Supreme Self with your whole being.
Having heard these divine words uttered by Nārāyaṇa, Nārada became possessed of extreme devotion to the Lord and attained a state of exclusive dedication;
for ten years, he remained devoted to no other than the divine seer Nārāyaṇa.
By reciting this indeed, one attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. What need has he for many mantras who possesses devotion to Janārdana?
The mantra "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" is the accomplisher of all goals.
Having studied this supreme secret recollection, one attains definitive wisdom;
having abandoned all sufferings and released oneself from distress.
Wandering this earth, free from passion,
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Furthermore, among the gods, asuras, and humans, or even among the foremost of sages..."
"Who among the wise truly understands that reality of Viṣṇu as it has been described? Tell me all this, for I am not yet satiated with the truth.
Bhīṣma said:
O best of the Bharatas, it proceeds thus; it is my conviction that you are omniscient.
O King, O best of monarchs, why have I been reminded by you of what occurred to me in the past, regarding my former conversation with Garuḍa?

Formerly, O Bhārata, having undertaken ascetic penance with Vāsudeva as my supreme refuge, I remained seated on an island in the Gaṅgā for ten years, meditating upon, praising, bowing down to, and sacrificing to him alone.
And that goddess, my mother, the purifier of the world, was seated near me for my protection, O Acyuta. At that time, there appeared the wonderful, glorious Lord, who consists of all the Vedas.
Suparṇa, the best of those who fly, resembling Mount Meru and Mandara,
arrived— pure in soul and of great renown— to behold the Gaṅgā.
When that high-souled one had arrived, I went out to meet him as was required.

Having prostrated according to the rule, he stood with palms joined in reverence. That illustrious god, having greeted the highly blessed Jāhnavī and being honored by her in return, sat down upon a seat.
Then, in the course of our conversation, I spoke these words to him:
"O knower of the Vedas, O you of great heroism, O Vainateya of mighty strength,
you who constantly endure Hari, Nārāyaṇa, Hṛṣīkeśa!"
"You know how to speak of Janārdana as he truly is.
Garuḍa said:
"O best of beings, you ought to tell me, too, of his true nature."
"Listen, Bhīṣma, according to the proper method, as to how in the past many excellent sages and perfected ones dwelling on Mount Mānasottara [spoke] to you here."
Those of great wisdom, who are devoted to Vāsudeva, questioned me:
"O Lord of Birds, you know that supreme state of Vāsudeva;
there is no one equal to you, nor even anyone as dear to him."
Having heard their words, I prostrated before the Great Hari and spoke of everything as it had occurred regarding myself and Nārāyaṇa:
"Listen, O tigers among sages! In former times, I carried off the Soma."
As I was flying through the sky, I indeed heard these words there:
"Excellent, excellent, O mighty-armed one! I am pleased by the sight of you. Choose a boon from me now, O lord of birds, Garuḍa."
"O knower of the essence of devotion, I speak these supreme words to you"—thus spoke Dhruva there; and the Blessed One replied to me once more:
"I am a seer of great power; neither you nor anyone else knows me."
And that fool, having heard this and becoming arrogant, showed me contempt.
In the midst of the hosts of gods, I spoke these words:
"O Sage, choose a boon from me first; only then shall I grant it."
"O best of sages,
because the illustrious Lord, the glorious one marked with the Śrīvatsa,
beholds you today, [I grant this: O Lord of Birds, always become my vehicle."
"O Lord of Birds, I choose this very boon from you today.
Seeing him thus established in selflessness, she said, "So be it.
For I desire to conquer Viṣṇu, the master of illusion, by means of my own illusory power.
"O best of supreme sages, I choose this boon from you today:
I shall remain above you; grant me this boon. "So be it," laughed the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, and he said.
"And you alone, O Lord of Birds, shall always be my banner;
O King of Birds, may your station remain forever above me. Having spoken thus, the Blessed Lord, the bearer of the conch, discus, and mace, [departed].
The glorious one with a thousand feet, resembling a thousand suns;
the Great Puruṣa with a thousand heads and a thousand eyes;
the inconceivable, all-pervading lord with a thousand crowns and a thousand faces.
With divine rows of various ornaments resembling garlands of lightning,
Hari was seen in some places with four arms, in others as an inconceivable mass of light, and in others seated upon his shoulder.
12,202.033d@017C_0059 Thus, while I was victorious, the god vanished right there. 12,202.033d@017C_0060 Then, filled with wonder after having accomplished that unsurpassed task,
12,202.033d@017C_0061 O lords of sages, having released his mother, I [departed] together with him.
"This one is inconceivable; who was it that spoke to me before?
What is the nature of that Blessed One?"—thinking thus, I remained there, and immediately after, the God of gods took his place upon my shoulder.
Carrying me, O lotus-eyed one, I beheld that wonder; helpless under his influence, wherever he desired, my heart was filled with amazement as I wondered, "What is this?"
Carrying everything within the waters, I went forth once again;
I was praised by the highly fortunate gods led by Indra, and by those beginning with Brahmā who live for an eon,
and I was individually honored by each of them.
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, on a divine and auspicious ground made of jewels,
is the abode named Vaikarṇa belonging to that high-souled Hari;
it is celestial, full of splendor, glorious, and inconceivable even to the immortals.
Adorned on all sides with pillars made of fire and wind, arranged in various forms, and embellished with radiant gold,
it was divine, endowed with light, and graced by song and instrumental music.
There I heard a sound, yet I did not see a corporeal being;
neither on the ground nor elsewhere around my feet was anyone present. Trembling, I stood there with my hands joined in reverence.

Then Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the guardians of the world, the sages headed by Sanandana, and others who subsist on the Supreme, along with the most excellent of the gods and gandharvas, arrived there at the gate of the assembly hall.
Then, placing Brahmā before them with their palms joined in reverence,
Mahāviṣṇu appeared as if manifested, being awakened by the spray from the Ocean of Milk in that interval.
I behold Śeṣa, richly adorned with a garland of a thousand hoods, remaining in his unmanifest state within the sky; upon him stands Janārdana.
He is seen with long, rounded, and symmetrical coils, radiant with armlets and bracelets.
Endowed with four arms,
clothed in yellow garments, resplendent with the Kaustubha gem,
and possessed of a chest occupied by Lakṣmī.
With his eyes slightly opened, he, the cause of all causes,
shone above the Ocean of Milk like a supreme dark cloud;
no one spoke, no one said anything, and no one uttered a word.
"Let there be no sound from Brahmā down to a blade of grass!"— thus incensed,
those hosts of various beings stood with their eyes narrowed by frowning brows.
Then the inconceivable and glorious Hari, having looked toward the Grandfather (Brahmā), [spoke].
Having performed [these rites], he set out from there with a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
Then, saying to me, "Go," he addressed me as "Garuḍa. Thereupon, I prostrated before him and stood with palms joined in reverence.
Having said to me, "Come," he departed for the northern route;
with an exceedingly gentle manner, he appeared as if he were walking away.
For ten thousand, a hundred thousand, a million, and likewise ten million [yojanas], I followed him.
"Though I fly incessantly for leagues in every direction, am I not indeed devoted to you? I stand here; please govern us. "Come, Garuḍa! Mādhava spoke thus once more.
Then, as I was falling further through the sky,
I arrived at that terrible place, which was enveloped by hundreds of millions [of beings],
where there were mountain-like creatures resembling masses of darkness.
Seeing the lotuses as if they were all identical, I stood there in fear.
Then a terrible servant seized me with his hand— me who was a hundred *yojanas* long— and flung me from there like a clod of earth.
Having transcended that darkness, as well as the waters and the sky,
I then heard the sounds of the syllable *huṃ*— resembling the crash of thunderbolts—
at the root of my ears, as I was surrounded by spirits.
"Then, O Lord of the gods, O lotus-eyed one, save me!"—thus I spoke there. Then Viṣṇu said to me:
"A certain terrifying being has thrown me into the mouth of a hollow."
In an instant, I beheld a fire and a circle of wind;
having gazed upon it as if it were space itself, I approached, desiring to cast myself down. There, overcome with suffering, I remained crying out in lamentation.
In an instant, indeed, the terrible and wrathful Supreme Self,
seeing me, cast [me] down along with the king of his own faction; he who was as fearsome as a thousand suns [belonged to] the lineage of Garuḍa.
Then, having seen me standing there— though I was very weak and had been there for but a short time—
they were filled with wonder, thinking, "Ah, a bird has arrived! Having seen me, they said, "I see the one whose banner is Garuḍa there."

Twelve thousand two hundred and twenty-three. [He is] twelve thousand yojanas in extent, possessing the splendor of a thousand suns, and mounted upon a thousand Garuḍas; those Garuḍas are possessed of great strength.
O Lord, this most wonderful being, by his physical form, is born of our own lineage.
"Whose life-force is so slight and whose body so small—what bird is this that has come here?
Having heard that, my pride vanished; I was struck with fear and filled with shame.
Then, being personally awakened and deeply agitated, I listened once more.
"Come, Garuḍa!"— at these words, I then mounted my vehicle.
Having traveled a further hundred yojanas,
I then beheld there indeed Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
There too, the Blessed One Madhusūdana spoke aloud, "Come again," to another there who was the grandfather of a hundred koṭis;
then I beheld that imperishable one of noble lineage and immeasurable proportions.
Resembling *kapittha* fruits and shaped like eggs, they were gathered together;
there the glorious Hari stood and split open one egg. Indeed, having seized me as the Great Being (*mahad-bhūta*), he cast me back again.
In their midst, I beheld the seven oceans, as well as Brahmā and the gods, according to their respective positions, as well as my mother and my own family;
for thus was it experienced by me while desiring to seek the ultimate truth.
"O best of sages, behold me indeed as being like a palanquin (śibikā)," O Bhīṣma,
thus did I speak to the Brahmins in the past;
O most excellent one, I have related all that to you exactly as it happened.

Yogis behold Him by perceiving that supreme knowledge, Hari; otherwise, this Supreme Person cannot be reached. That Great Hari can be attained only through exclusive devotion and the realization of knowledge.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, the blessed Lord Suparṇa, the king of birds,
took leave of my mother and vanished right there.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, Vāsudeva—the soul of all and the creator of the primary cause—is easily attained through knowledge and devotion; it is not otherwise. This is my conviction.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, O Bhārata, tell me of that supreme yoga which leads to liberation.
I wish to know it in its true essence, O best among speakers. Furthermore, for the sake of remaining established in the true nature of knowledge, I speak to you."
"O best of beings, therefore please explain that which is called Vāsudeva, for it is inconceivable.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
12,203.002c A dialogue concerning liberation between a disciple and his teacher: 12,203.003a A certain man [approached] a Brāhmaṇa seated there, a preceptor and the best of sages,
12,203.003b*0559_01 a great-souled mass of splendor, true to his word, and one who had conquered his senses.
A disciple of supreme intelligence, seeking the highest good and well-composed,
stood with his palms joined in reverence after clasping the teacher’s feet and said:
"O Blessed One, if you are indeed pleased with my service,"
I have a certain great doubt; you ought to explain it to me:
from whence am I and from whence are you? Tell me truly that which is supreme. And how is it, O best of the twice-born, that all beings are equal?

Those who act rightly turn back from [suffering], while those who act perversely experience decline and rise. O learned one, you ought to explain in accordance with reality all that which is stated in the Vedas, as well as that which is worldly and pervasive.
The Teacher said:
"Listen, O disciple of great wisdom, to this supreme secret of Brahman,
which is the inner self of all beings and the treasure of all the scriptures."
Vāsudeva is all this; he is the mouth of the universal Brahman. The Blessed Lord sports like a child with his toys.
Truth, charity, sacrifice, forbearance, self-restraint, and uprightness [are his].

Listen to me as I relate this history concerning that very Brahman, the eternal Viṣṇu, whom those who know the Vedas recognize as the Puruṣa, the unmanifest, and the everlasting creator of creation and dissolution; listen to me regarding this Vārṣṇeya, who is that Brahman.
A Brāhmaṇa should have it proclaimed by Brāhmaṇas, a Rājanya likewise by Kṣatriyas,
a Vaiśya by Vaiśyas, and the high-minded Śūdra by Śūdras—
the majesty of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor.
O auspicious one, you are worthy; hear from me that which is supreme concerning the descendant of Vṛṣṇi:
that which is Acyuta, the highest, eternal, devoid of marks, and stainless; that which is Nirvāṇa, the immortal, and glorious—that is the supreme station of Viṣṇu.
In this world, giving—which is distinct and differentiated like existence—is a cause of merit;
yet that other person (the Puruṣa) is never attached to it. Pradhāna, presided over by the Puruṣa, is the eternal cause, Brahman.
The nature of Time, being agitated by the powerful Viṣṇu in his form as Rūpa,
indeed creates various beings part by part;
having seen that which is not the ultimate reality, the Puruṣa proceeds, becoming a witness.
Having entered that [state], according to its application, being both non-different and possessing differentiated characteristics,
the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra)— which is without beginning or end and has existence and non-existence as its own characteristic—
revolves like a wheel within all beings throughout the three worlds.
That which they call the imperishable, unmanifest, immortal, and eternal Brahman— Keśava, that tiger among men and bull among beings—
is indeed that inconceivable Imperishable which appears in diverse forms.
