Behold Time, which is called *kāla*, which is never hot nor excessively cold;
these qualities do not exist within it, yet from it all proceeds. This cool season has arrived, and likewise the summer as well.
Indeed, all beings will say regarding the rising of the sun:
"They come and they return; that is the time, a mass of qualities.
And it is not [perceived] by one who remains in their natural state, constantly joined with time.
Through its qualities, Nature (prakṛti), presided over by the Spirit (puruṣa), eternally brings forth enjoyment, aversion, and that which is skilled in the knowledge of reality;
likewise, it produces the ancestors, the gods, the seers, as well as the yakṣas and dānavas.
The supreme, imperishable Lord creates the Nāgas, Asuras, and humans;
likewise, he creates the Vedic scriptures and the eternal laws of the world.
Having returned to primordial nature at the time of dissolution, the Lord brings them forth again at the beginning of the age.

Just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle according to the time, so too do those very same signs appear during the days and nights of Brahmā. Furthermore,
whatever is destined to occur at any time through the conjunction of the ages, that comes to pass.
That specific knowledge arises which is produced from the performance of worldly affairs;
this is declared to be *śruti*, because it serves as the cause for that purpose. Indeed, because they were not established by the rules of the *āmnāya*, the Vedas have become hidden.
At the end of the eon, indeed, all beings and various scriptures perish;
yet, due to the destruction of all sentient beings, they are remembered as eternal through the soul (jīvātman). They exist perpetually within another cosmic egg.
At the end of the age, the great seers, authorized by the Self-born One, recovered through ascetic penance the Vedas along with the Itihāsas that had disappeared;
by the command of Brahmā, these Brahmins became the sustainers of the world's order.
The venerable Bṛhaspati, the knower of the Vedas, proclaimed the Vedāṅgas;
Bhārgava proclaimed the science of polity (nītiśāstra) for the welfare of the world;
Nārada proclaimed the Gāndharva Veda; and Bharadvāja proclaimed the science of archery.

Gārgya [taught] the conduct of divine sages; Kṛṣṇātreya, medical science; and Gautama truly knows the system of logic in its entirety. Furthermore, the all-pervading one, who knows the Vedas and knows Brahman, [knows] the Vedānta and the yoga of action.
Dvaipāyana mastered the science of arts (*śilpaśāstra*), while Bhṛgu likewise [mastered] many systems of logic (*nyāyatantra*) propounded by various disputants;
that which is declared through reasoning, scripture, and the conduct of the virtuous is what is to be honored.
That supreme Brahman, which is without beginning, is not known by the gods nor by the seers;
the Lord Dhātṛ, the Master Nārāyaṇa alone, knows it.
From Nārāyaṇa [proceed] the hosts of seers, as well as the principal gods and asuras.
I shall declare to you that supreme medicine for suffering, which was obtained by me from the seer Dvaipāyana— the ancient royal sages [have declared it].
Nature (*prakṛti*) always gives birth to the state presided over by the Person (*puruṣa*).
12,203.023c Therefore, the entire world revolves, joined with its causes;
12,203.024a Just as from one lamp thousands of other lamps proceed, 12,203.024c so too does primordial nature (prakṛti) create; because it is infinite, it is never diminished.
Intellect, born from the unmanifest and characterized by action, gives birth to the ego (ahaṃkāra). From the ego arises space, and from space arises wind;
from wind comes fire, from that water, and from water indeed the earth emerges.
There are eight root-natures; the world is situated within them.
From these arise the five organs of perception, the five organs of action, the five objects of the senses, and the mind as the sixteenth, which belongs to the realm of transformation.
The ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose are the five sense organs;
likewise, the feet, the anus, the generative organ, the hands, and speech are the organs of action.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are their respective objects.

The pervasive mind (*citta*) is to be known as the all-pervading mental faculty (*manas*) among those [faculties]. The ten sense organs and their objects are said to be the sources of conjunction; and when there is the union with existence and non-existence, it is designated as the "mind" (*manas*).

The intellect (*buddhi*) has the quality of determination; the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is characterized by self-conceit. In the union with the body, it is not the seed, because it is the activator of the seeds of karma.
Furthermore, this tongue is for the cognition of taste, and likewise, speech is for articulation.
One should know these sixteen deities individually: all the various sense organs, as well as the mind in its distributed state;
they attend upon the knower who dwells within bodies as their presiding agent.
In the same way, the tongue has the quality of soma; smell is the quality of earth;
the ear has the quality of sound, and the eye likewise has the quality of fire;
one should know that touch is the quality of air at all times among all beings.
They say that the mind has the quality of *sattva*, and likewise that *sattva* is born from the Unmanifest.
It abides as the self within all beings; therefore, the wise man should understand this. These states sustain the entire world, including all that is moving and stationary.
12,203.034c They have taken refuge in the stainless God, whom they call the supreme state.
12,203.035a Pervading this holy city with nine gates, which is endowed with these states of being, the Great Self dwells; therefore, he is called Puruṣa.
He is undecaying and immortal, possessing the instruction on both the manifest and the unmanifest;
he is all-pervading, endowed with qualities, subtle, and the substratum of the qualities of all beings—
just as a lamp is luminous by nature, whether it be small or great.
One should know that the Puruṣa, whose nature is consciousness, exists thus within all living beings.
He is the one who experiences what is to be known here; he hears and he sees.
This body is merely his instrument; he is the agent of all actions.
Just as fire residing within wood is not seen when the wood is split apart,
so too the Self, though dwelling within the body, is perceived here only through yoga. For just as fire is seen by churning the wood with the proper means, [so is the Self perceived].
In the very same way, the self residing within the body is perceived here through yoga alone;
just as waters are joined together in rivers, just as rays of light are concentrated in the sun,
and just as they proceed in a continuous stream, so too do the bodies of embodied beings.
Just as the self, joined with the five senses, departs from the body during the state of dreaming, so too is it perceived here;
it is first pervaded by karma, and by karma it is reborn.
One is led elsewhere by one's own powerful karma. I shall now fully explain how that being, born of its own actions, leaves one body and attains another.
The Teacher said:
"The four classes of beings, both stationary and moving,
are said to have their origin in the Unmanifest and their dissolution in the Unmanifest."
One should know that the mind has the unmanifest as its dissolution and has the self of the unmanifest as its essence.
Just as a great tree contained within the seed-pod of an ashvattha tree is seen to have fully emerged once it has developed, so too does manifestation arise from the unmanifest.
The intellect, born from the unmanifest, likewise follows after the Self;
the mind follows it, just as iron moves toward a magnet when it is in close proximity— both being devoid of consciousness.
Just as entities produced from their own inherent nature (svabhāva) and other such things are so,
likewise entities produced from the Unmanifest (avyakta) possess the characteristics of having an agent as their cause;
being insentient, they are brought about through a sentient cause that intends them.
There was no earth, no ether, no heaven, no beings, no sages, and no gods or asuras;
there was nothing else except the Living One (jīva), yet they did not reach him in his unified state.
He is all-pervading by virtue of his universal nature, the cause of the mind, and possessed of its characteristics.
This characteristic of the cause has been described as the activity of ignorance;
for when joined with its causes, it brings about the collection of effects,
by which this great wheel, without beginning or end, revolves.
By which the existence of intrinsic nature is established, being caused and possessing a cause;
thus, relying upon the Supreme Person (puruṣa), the expansion of primordial matter (prakṛti) has the Unmanifest as its navel, the Manifest as its end, and is circumscribed by transformation.
The wheel, presided over by the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), revolves with steady, smooth axles. Because of its smoothness, the entire world is crushed within this wheel like sesame seeds,
being overwhelmed by enjoyments born of ignorance, just as sesame seeds are crushed by oil-pressers.
For when this [body] is stilled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), its protection occurs through non-opposition; he who dwells within the arrows of the body is pure, inconceivable, and eternal,
causing them to revolve as they move.
Accompanied by the wheel of time, he moves along,
constantly deluding all beings and having attained the speed of that wheel; yet,
due to the presence of the substance of oiliness, there is no attachment to material objects.
Just as when a wheel is pressed like sesame seeds and crushed by the pressure of a machine,
and while it is being operated from the outside, so too does the karma arising from the wise man perform action out of thirst, through the grasping of egoism.
In the conjunction of cause and effect, that cause has been established;
and having heard that unsurpassed knowledge of reality, the disciple understands that the effect does not transcend the cause, nor does the cause transcend the effect.
In the accomplishment of tasks, time becomes the causal factor;
the primary elements and their transformations, joined with causes and presided over by the Puruṣa, always proceed in mutual interaction.

Driven by the qualities of passion and darkness (*rajas* and *tamas*), and impelled by the power of causes, one who has fallen away follows after the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) just as dust is driven by the wind;
yet that state is not touched by those qualities, nor are they touched by that Great-Souled One.

Just as the wind may be both dusty and dustless, so should the wise man understand the distinction between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Being thus disciplined through practice, he shall not return to *prakṛti* again.
The Blessed One, the Seer, cut through this arisen doubt:
"One should examine news that is consistent with established signs,
just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again."
"Likewise, the self is not bound again by the afflictions once they have been burnt away by knowledge.
The Teacher said:
"How this dharma characterized by worldly activity comes about—"
For those whose conviction rests solely on the Vedas, no other reality is pleasing. Those who are learned in the Vedas and established in what is declared therein are difficult to find;
therefore, they seek here a well-praised path that serves a practical purpose.
They do not understand the true nature of the Veda, which is established upon the path of knowledge;
yet this conduct is irreproachable because it is practiced by the virtuous.
This is one kind of wisdom, while that by which one attains the supreme goal is another.

One who possesses a body takes up all forms of possession out of delusion, joined with states such as desire and anger that are characterized by passion and darkness. Therefore, one who desires the maintenance of the body should not perform impure acts.
By creating an opening for karma, one shall not attain auspicious worlds. Just as gold mixed with iron does not shine when smelted,
so too knowledge that has not matured its so-called "impurities" (kaṣāya) does not manifest.
Some have attained the qualities of the self and are liberated from the bond of the wheel; others, however, are joined with the pairs of suffering and are thus devoted to suffering,
being born again and again in accordance with their own past actions.
Those whose inner faculties are always deluded and possessed by anger, greed, and pride— just as a shadow previously did not exist through eternity,
so too do the wise understand that the qualities (guṇas) alone are to be contemplated as "coming to be" and "passing away."
But he who, out of delusion, practices unrighteousness while following after desire and greed,
having stepped onto the path of dharma, perishes along with his followers;
failing to attain immovable knowledge, he of restless mind goes toward what is unstable.
Therefore, one should not be carried away by passion toward objects such as those that provoke lust;
for anger, joy, and despondency arise from one another.
Virtues are to be cultivated, yet anger and joy, pleasure and pain, and the pleasant and unpleasant are all produced in mutual succession.
The all-knowing one should likewise conquer pairs of opposites such as these.
Within this body composed of the five elements and characterized by the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
whom does he praise, or at whom does he cry out, and what indeed would he say?
12,205.010a Fools fall into attachment toward touch, form, taste, and the like;

12,205.010c through lack of discernment, they do not understand that these are qualities born of the earth-element (pārthiva). 12,205.011a Just as a shelter made of clay is plastered with clay itself, so too [is this body].
Just as this earthly body is smeared with various modifications of clay—
honey, oil, milk, clarified butter, meats, salt, molasses,
grains, fruits, roots, and modifications of clay along with water— so too is it [subject to change].
Just as one traveling through a wilderness should not indulge in longing,
but rather take food out of exhaustion even if it is tasteless, for it serves to sustain him; so too, while traversing the wilderness of saṃsāra, one should be intent upon exertion.

For the sake of sustenance, one should eat food just as a sick person takes medicine. If one makes use of objects of the senses for the sake of maintenance along the path of saṃsāra— just as a deer, while being pursued by predators on its trail, consumes [grass] for the sake of survival— [then that is permissible].

One should not go [there] out of a desire for enjoyments, for then one falls upon a wrong path; therefore, established on the path that is free from suffering, one should keep it in mind. Indeed, there are many trees there with various leaves and fruits.
The sages are indeed its enjoyers; therefore, the forest is even more excellent than that.
[It is known] through inferences as well as through scriptures, and by fame and valor, and by truth, purity, straightforwardness, renunciation, fame, and valor.
Through patience, fortitude, intelligence, the mind, and indeed through austerity,
one who desires peace and possesses a noble soul should dwell among all beings according to their conduct and in due order, while restraining the senses.
Deluded by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*,
living beings indeed revolve incessantly like a wheel due to ignorance;
therefore, one should thoroughly examine the defects born of ignorance.

One should constantly abandon the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), which originates from ignorance. Know that the great elements, the sense-faculties, and the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—these are the roots of the body; therefore, they are not the Blessed One.
I shall explain by means of skillful methods that death which is difficult to overcome. The entire triple world, together with its lord, is established upon the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
Just as time here inevitably displays the seasonal qualities, so too does it manifest [the fruits of action].
In the same way, one should know that egoism (ahaṃkāra) is the instigator of the elements among all beings. One should know that tamas is delusive, black, and born of ignorance;
from it arises the Great Principle (mahat), produced by the qualities of primordial nature (prakṛti), and from that, egoism.
Furthermore, after the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the collection of elements (bhūtagrāma) is declared; [these arise] from the qualities (guṇa) of the Unmanifest (avyakta). Now, understand those qualities:
all three qualities are bound up with pleasure and pain.

Now learn of those qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*: delusion born of joy, pleasure, freedom from doubt, fortitude, and mindfulness—know these to be the qualities of *sattva*; and now these [others] to be of *rajas* and *tamas*.
Discontent, intolerance, lack of fortitude, and insatiability regarding sense objects—these are indeed the qualities of *rajas*. Now hear those that are *tāmasa*:
delusion, drowsiness, suffering, sleep, laziness, and heedlessness.
Dejection and procrastination— this is declared to be the quality of *tamas*.
Desire, anger, negligence, greed, delusion, fear, fatigue,
dejection, grief, discontent, pride, arrogance, and ignobility [are likewise its marks].
Having thus examined the relative weight and lightness of such faults as these,
one should reflect upon each one as it resides within oneself in its continuous succession.
That in which this world is established, and from which the emergence of true knowledge occurs— [that one should examine].
One should constantly perceive the ego-sense as being superior to all beings. While perceiving it thus, he then, by means of his own subtle intellect,
sees that very form which is utterly pure by its own nature.
The disciple said:
Which faults are abandoned by the mind? Which are weakened by the intellect? Which return again and again? And which are as fruitless as delusion?
"O Wise One, regarding whom should a learned man deliberate with his intellect by means of reasons concerning their strength and weakness?
O Lord, explain all of this so that I may understand it;
O Knower, speak this with certainty to me, who am desirous of hearing."
Because of its tranquility, because of the future limit, and because of its commencement from one side—
thus have the wise declared the cause to be explained here.
The Teacher said:
The degree of respect for the qualities depends on the strength or weakness of their causes. When the defects have been severed at the root, the purified self is liberated;
it destroys whatever has arisen, just as fire consumes iron.

One whose self is unpurified perishes through innate defects born of passion (*rājasa*); likewise, one who has not disciplined the self perishes through innate defects born of passion. Passionate action and even that born of darkness (*tāmasa*) arise from the performance of impure deeds.

Relying on his own intellect alone, the twice-born should pacify his being; and with a pure self established in wisdom, he should abandon both these [desires] through the mind. All that is the seed for embodied beings, and it is the same for everyone who possesses a self.
Therefore, one who possesses self-mastery should avoid both *rajas* and *tamas*;
when liberated from *rajas* and *tamas*, *sattva* attains purity. One should always avoid foods that are *rājasa* and *tāmasa*.
They return again to the state of Brahmā, remaining as immovable as mountains, no longer subject to delusion.
Or rather, they might utter the sacrificial formulas (*yajus*) of the flesh-eaters as if reciting mantras;
that very [formula] is the cause for non-appropriation and for the observance of pure dharma.
Through *rajas*, one may accomplish even those tasks joined with righteousness (*dharma*),
as well as those joined with material gain (*artha*) to an extreme degree, and one indulges in all objects of desire (*kāma*).
Through *tamas*, one indulges in things joined with greed and those born of anger.
Delighting in violence and sport, and possessed of sloth and sleep, he remains established in *sattva*;
relying upon it, he perceives pure, *sāttvika* states. That embodied being becomes stainless, glorious, pure, and endowed with knowledge.
The Teacher said:
"O bull among men, delusion is produced by *rajas*, and by *tamas* as well;
anger, greed, fear, and pride—by purifying oneself from these, one becomes pure."
They enter Viṣṇu, the supreme, the Supreme Self, the imperishable and undecaying God, whose form is unmanifest, the best of deities;
yet those whose limbs are scorched by his *māyā*, who have fallen away from knowledge, and who are devoid of hope [enter him as well].
Due to the delusion of their knowledge, human beings indeed proceed toward desire;
from desire, human beings then attain anger, as well as greed and delusion;
from pride and arrogance they reach egoism, and from egoism, then ritual actions arise.
Through actions there arises attachment, and from attachment follows grief;
through the undertaking of pleasure and pain, moments are created for birth after birth.
From birth comes dwelling in the womb, which originates from semen and blood.
Turbid with the moisture of excrement, urine, and blood,
one who is overcome by thirst is bound by these very things and wallows within them;
likewise, situated in the pit of hell, one is ensnared by the ropes of craving.
With his body driven by merit and evil, he is born like a worm;
bitten by mosquitoes and bedbugs, he is likewise afflicted by various forms of slaughter.
Overwhelmed by manifold diseases, he somehow reaches youth.

The tortoise casts itself back again, and the rope seeks its own mouth; likewise, one who follows the power of birth and karma seizes a woman and goes to hell. The suffering caused by the pursuit of cities and fields is impossible to describe.
Who there is indeed a reviler who is cooked intensely in hell?
One should not transgress old age; one should undertake action there again.
After the Blessed One has been praised, what shall I tell you further?

One should understand that women there carry the stream of saṃsāra; by their very nature they are the field (kṣetra), while men are characterized as the knower of the field (kṣetrajña). Therefore, wise men should especially transcend them.
For these spells of terrible form delude those who lack discernment;
the eternal form of the senses is concealed within passion (*rajas*).
Therefore, living beings are born from that seed which consists of thirst and attachment.
Just as one would cast off worms born from one's own body that are not recognized as oneself,
so too should one cast off those worms recognized as sons who are not born from oneself. Indeed,
living beings are born from semen, from vital fluids, and from affection.

Whether by their own nature or through the application of karma, the wise man should remain indifferent toward them. Rajas is overturned into tamas, and sattva is situated within tamas; ignorance—characterized by the intellect (buddhi) and ego (ahaṃkāra)—is the locus of knowledge.
They call that the seed of embodied beings; that seed is known as the *jīva*. Through action joined with time, it causes the revolution of *saṃsāra*.
Just as this [self], possessing a body as it were, sports with the mind in a dream.
By means of qualities that have karma as their womb, the embodied being enters that womb;
whatever sense organ is impelled by karma acting as the seed,
that is born from the ego through a mind joined with passion.
From attachment to sound, the ear arises for this one of cultivated self;
from attachment to touch, the skin arises for this one of cultivated self;
likewise, from attachment to form, the eye arises, and the nose from the desire for odors.
From the attachment to tastes, the tongue arises for one whose self is cultivated;
likewise, from tactile sensations, the wind arises, which depends upon the prāṇa and apāna breaths. Along with vyāna, udāna, and samāna, these five sustain the body.

Enveloped by Brahmā, a man is born with limbs produced by his past actions; he is beset by physical and mental sufferings that have suffering at their beginning and end, and suffering in their midst. One should know that suffering arises from grasping and increases through self-conceit.
Through renunciation of these, cessation occurs; one who knows cessation is liberated.
Both the origin and the dissolution of the senses reside in passion alone.
Having examined this, the wise man should conduct himself accordingly, with the eye of the scriptures.
The organs of knowledge do not approach the objects of the senses for one who is free from thirst;
and through known causes, the embodied soul does not deserve a body again.
The Teacher said:
In this regard, I shall declare the means according to the eye of the scriptures;
by practicing through that knowledge, the wise man shall attain the supreme goal.
Among all beings indeed, the person (puruṣa) is said to be the best.
They say that among men, the twice-born are superior; among the twice-born, those who recite the mantras;

they are distinguished above all beings, being omniscient and all-seeing—these Brāhmaṇas who know the true essence of the Vedas and have reached certainty regarding the course of the meaning of reality.
Just as one who is sightless encounters hardships alone upon a journey, so it is in this world for one devoid of knowledge; therefore, those who possess knowledge are superior.
Those who desire dharma practice various religious duties according to the scriptures.
But these qualities—
purity of speech, body, and mind, forbearance, truthfulness, fortitude, and mindfulness—
are not known as "qualities" by those who know dharma among all duties unless they are accompanied by a commonality of purpose.
That which is known as *brahmacarya* is the very form of Brahman;
it is superior to all beings, and by means of it, people attain the supreme goal.
It is devoid of the union of sexual organs and free from the touch of the body.
Hearing with the ear and seeing with the eye,
touching with the skin and smelling with the nose—
whatever tasting there is with the tongue, that too has been abandoned.
Through discernment and resolve, one who practices stainless celibacy and maintains right conduct attains the world of Brahmā; one of middling conduct attains the gods;
and the foremost of the twice-born, though following the lowest mode of life, becomes a wise man.
The practice of celibacy is extremely difficult; hear from me the means for it.
A twice-born man should restrain his mind when it is set in motion or becomes agitated.
One should not listen to stories about women, nor should one look at them when they are naked.

If, through seeing them at some time, passion should enter a weak man, he should perform the *kṛcchra* penance when desire arises; he should enter the water three times during the day. And if [passion] occurs in a dream, he should mentally recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times while submerged.
In this way, the wise man, with a mind endowed with knowledge and constant application, should burn away the evil that has entered within and consists of passion (rajas)—
just as one would [burn] a corpse joined with impurities, even when bound by seamless fetters.

In the same way, one should know that the self residing within the body is bound by the body; just as one does not wish to look at a vessel filled with impurities and covered with a foul mass of phlegm, how could one proceed to touch such a vessel?

This vessel of a body, filled with impurities and covered externally by perspiration, is loathsome to men and women; to the wise, it is considered a hell. Just as a leaking jar continuously discharges whatever solid matter is contained within it.
Just as water situated within [a vessel] leaks out, so too does the water in the bodies of embodied beings leak away—phlegm, tears, urine, filth, feces, and semen;
it is merely an exudation from a mass of phlegm. O mind, abandon this attachment to the body.

The nutrient fluids (rasas) satisfy the wind, bile, phlegm, blood, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, marrow, and the network of vessels in human beings. One should know that there are ten arteries here which convey the qualities of the five sense organs.
From these, thousands of other subtle vessels branch out.
In this way, these rivers of channels, carrying the essence, nourish the ocean of the body at the proper time, just as rivers nourish the great sea.
And in the center of the heart, there is one vessel that carries the *manas*;
it releases the semen produced by mental resolve from all the limbs of men. For its vessels extend throughout all the limbs.
Carrying the quality of fire (taijasa), they reach the two eyes;
just as butter hidden within milk is churned out by churning-sticks,
so too is the semen churned out by the churning-sticks born of the body's volitions.
Even in a dream, just as passion born of mental volition approaches him,
the mind-carrying channels discharge his semen from the body without physical contact;
the venerable great seer Atri knows the origin of that semen.
It has three seeds and Indra as its deity; therefore it is called *indriya*.

Those who indeed know the course of the semen (*śukra*), which causes the confusion of beings, and who are free from passion and have burnt away their defects—they shall not undergo rebirth in a body.

Having attained equilibrium of the qualities by means of the mind alone, one who impels the bodily functions and the vital breaths at the time of death is liberated. Knowledge shall arise from the mind; the mind itself expands [into that knowledge].
Luminous, stainless, and divine, this state is perfected here for the great-souled ones.
Therefore, one should perform sinless action so as not to obstruct that [attainment];
having abandoned passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas) in this world, one shall not fall into the state of a lower animal.
Knowledge acquired in youth becomes weakened by old age;
when the intellect has matured through time, it attains mental strength.
It is the same with regard to sons, wives, kinsmen, relations, and friends.
Overwhelmed by diseases and other afflictions, he grasps at desire in his heart;
wandering here and there, he finds not even the slightest bit of happiness. Having fallen into manifold suffering, he subsequently resorts to world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Having relied upon the tree of knowledge, one subsequently enjoys extinction (*nirvṛti*).
Having traversed the path that is so difficult to travel— the bond of the qualities (*guṇa*)—
when one perceives [the truth], then, having transcended the defects (*doṣa*), one enjoys the deathless (*amṛta*).
The Teacher said:
"Living beings who are attached to the objects of the senses, which end in misery, come to grief;
but those great-souled ones who are unattached attain the supreme goal."
Seeing this world constantly afflicted by birth, death, old age, suffering, diseases, and mental exhaustion, the wise person should strive for liberation;
being pure in speech, mind, and body, they should remain free from egoism.
Tranquil and possessed of wisdom, the monk should wander happily, free from all dependencies.
Women are the snares for those seeking liberation; their form is the ensnarer. Even while perceiving it as difficult to grasp, one who is deluded then thinks it desirable.
Thus beholding the self as it is meditated upon among kinsmen,
I know it to exist in a state of differentiation through its lack of true reality;
or rather, one may perceive the attachment of the mind out of compassion for living beings.
In this regard as well, one should maintain equanimity, knowing that the world is the fruit of karma:
whatever action was performed previously, whether auspicious or evil, that is what one experiences.
Therefore, one should perform auspicious deeds through speech, thought, and physical action.
Non-violence, truthful speech, and straightforwardness toward all beings,
as well as patience and vigilance— he who possesses these shall be happy.
That Brahman, stainless and supreme to the world, cannot be attained by means of the senses.
Self-luminous, ungraspable, causeless, and immovable,
it abides in the form of lightning, established within the flow of discriminative knowledge; it is seen from the *vaikārika* [sattva] like a stream of honey in red chalk.

He who knows this supreme Dharma, which brings happiness to all beings and provides an escape from suffering, is a knower of reality and shall be happy. Therefore, one should hold the mind, composed through the intellect, upon all beings.

One should not harbor ill-will, nor should one covet, nor should one think of improper or unreal things. Through the application of restraint in speech, that which is agreeable proceeds— whether for one desiring to speak virtuous words or for one contemplating the subtle Dharma.
One should speak words that are true, non-injurious, and free from slander; words devoid of guile, not harsh, not cruel, and free from backbiting.
Such speech should be spoken sparingly and with an undistracted mind.
For if one who is awakened by speech should speak out of passion or dispassion,
then through an intellect that is not restrained and with a mind [driven] by passion (rajas), one engages in tamasic action by means of the instruments (karaṇa) composed of rajas.
Having encountered suffering in this world, he is reborn in hell;
therefore, one should practice self-restraint through mind, speech, and body.
For it is just as if a scattered load of sheep were being driven by bandits.
Having understood that the direction is contrary, as the ignorant do regarding *saṃsāra*,
one who has entered the path of *saṃsāra* should avoid it in its contrary form. And just as one would cast off those very bandits and go toward an auspicious direction, so too [should one proceed].
Likewise, having abandoned actions characterized by passion and darkness, one shall attain happiness;
indeed, free from doubt and devoid of desire, liberated from all possessions, wandering in solitude, eating lightly, practicing austerity, and with senses restrained.
One whose afflictions have been burnt away by knowledge, who delights in spiritual practice, and who possesses self-mastery,
attains that supreme state with a mind free from movement. One who is steadfast and self-possessed should undoubtedly restrain the intellect.
One should restrain the mind with the intellect, and the objects of the senses with the mind by means of the self;
having fixed the mind there upon the Supreme Self so that it becomes motionless,
Brahman is revealed to one who is intent on the practice of yoga.
Know this to be absolute certainty: the abiding of all things within one another. They perceive the particularities as being of the nature of the cause, devoid of [independent] distinction.
Or rather, the Lord does not abide therein in that Supreme Self.

The one whose essence is yoga, having mastered the future reality, should undertake the Yoga-tantra. For him who has subdued his senses and keeps the mind under control, those deities appear; delighted, they approach that Lord.
With a mind fully absorbed in them, one shines forth like Brahman;
when all these have departed, one becomes fit for the state of Brahman. Alternatively, if [the mind] does not proceed [toward that goal], one should apply oneself through the methods of yoga.
Whatever is necessary for the practice of this Tantra-system to function as its application, that he should perform.
He should consume, in rotation, broken grains, oil-cakes, boiled sour gruel, vegetables, barley-meal, as well as roots, fruits, and alms-food.

One should examine and then follow a diet that is regulated, appropriate to the place and time, and characterized by *sattva*; one should not obstruct what has already begun to function, but should kindle it gradually, like a fire.
Then, kindled by knowledge, knowledge shines forth like the sun.
Ignorance, which has knowledge as its support, presides over the three worlds;
yet knowledge, when followed by higher discernment (*vijñāna*), is drawn away from ignorance.
Because of their separateness and their conjunction, one who is free from envy knows the eternal. Knowing the liberation of these two, he who is devoid of passion is released;
having transcended age and conquered old age and death, he attains the eternal Brahman.
One attains that nectar which is imperishable and immutable.
The Teacher said:
"By one who desires to practice stainless celibacy at all times,"
Sleep should be abandoned by every means by one who observes the faults of dreaming;
for in a dream, the embodied soul is overcome by *rajas* and *tamas*,
and having lost its memory, it wanders as if it had entered another body.
12,209.003a From the practice of knowledge, one who is awake [remains so] immediately for the sake of inquiry;
12,209.003c but through attachment to discernment (*vijñāna*), one remains perpetually awake at all times.
12,209.004a Here it is asked: what indeed is this state that, as it were, possesses objects within a dream?
12,209.004c With his senses dissolved, the embodied soul exists as if possessing a body.
12,209.005a Regarding this, it is said that Hari, the Lord of Yoga, knows this exactly as it is;
12,209.005c likewise, the great seers describe this matter in accordance with its true meaning.
The wise say that sleep arises from the exhaustion of the sense-faculties and is all-pervading. They say that the sense-faculties consist of that [sleep], and thus they indeed go along with it.
Regarding this, some say that the triad [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep] is eternal; if you say this is untrue, it is not so.

While existing in the first [state], he always perceives a triad; however, having approached the other two, he does not cognize them in any way whatsoever. For when he has entered the state of dreaming, he cognizes it as "dream" alone.
That triad, too, is inconsistent with reason and is characterized by delusion;
when one is liberated from the threefold self, then, being freed from what is unreal, one knows.
Because the mind has dissolved, they call that very state the illustrative example.

Just as the mental resolve of one whose mind is distracted by worldly affairs— even while awake— is like the sovereignty of one's desires in a dream, so too does the soul of one possessed by desire obtain those [experiences] throughout countless cycles of rebirth.
That Supreme Person knows everything that has entered the mind;
he knows whatever action of the qualities (guṇas) is present,
and all beings proclaim each thing according as the mind is conditioned.
Then, qualities belonging to the *rajas* and *tamas* modes follow him,
or those of the *sattva* mode according to their application, as the fruits arise in immediate succession.
Thereafter, he perceives [the humors] as disconnected, with wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*kapha*) predominating.
They say that even this [mind] is difficult to follow when it is affected by states arising from *rajas* and *tamas*. Whatever the mind conceives through the clear senses,
the vision of the mind beholds that very thing even in a dream when [the waking state] has ceased.

The mind, all-pervading and unimpeded, exists within all beings. Having taken recourse to the body, it dwells in the mental gateway that is hidden within the mind. That which is both being and non-being, the unmanifest—this is the illustration of how it sleeps therein.
Transcending all manifest distinctions, that which is perceived is pure consciousness alone. The wise know it to be the internal quality (adhyātmaguṇa) abiding as the self of all beings.
And whoever would desire the divine quality through the mind by means of volition—

One should know him through the power of the self, for all deities reside within the self. Thus, endowed with ascetic power, that embodied being is like the sun beyond darkness; through asceticism, he is Maheśvara, the source of the three worlds.

For austerity is presided over by the gods, while the darkness that destroys austerity belongs to the asuras. This, which is guarded by both gods and asuras, they call the characteristic of knowledge.
They know sattva, rajas, and tamas to be the qualities of the gods and the asuras.
One should know that *sattva* possesses divine qualities, while the other two qualities belong to the asuras.
*Sattva*, the mind (*manas*), and likewise the intellect (*buddhi*) are designated as "the gods. For one is indeed enveloped by these; therefore, knowing this supreme truth...
Through the mental fluctuation of sleep, the virtuous enter [into the state] like the world; established in their own nature, their essence hidden and free from impurities,
those things described as the beginning of night are considered the impurities of the worlds.

Devoid of those [senses], that pure city, existing both internally and externally, is eternally composed of bliss; having become that, one should pursue the Supreme. Thus has been declared this exceedingly stainless practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
That supreme state called Viṣṇu is free from all bonds;
inconceivable and marvelous in the world, it is realized through knowledge.
That Brahman is the supreme object of knowledge, immortal, luminous, and imperishable.
Those whose selves are purified know this and attain the supreme goal. This much can be explained through reasoning by one who possesses the eye of knowledge;
or else, the unmanifest Brahman can be known through the withdrawal of the senses.
The Teacher said:
"He does not know the supreme dharma who does not know the fourfold [truth], namely,
the manifest, the unmanifest, and that reality which was attained by the Great Seer."
One should know that the manifest is the mouth of death, while the unmanifest is the immortal state.
The seer Nārāyaṇa declared that dharma is characterized by active engagement;
within this very [unmanifest] is situated the entire threefold world, including all things mobile and immobile.
Prajāpati then declared that the dharma characterized by cessation is the unmanifest, eternal Brahman; whereas the dharma characterized by activity leads to rebirth,
while cessation is the supreme goal.
The sage who is devoted to cessation attains that supreme goal—
he who is eternally intent on the reality of knowledge and who discerns between the auspicious and the inauspicious.
Thus, both of these— the unmanifest and the person— are to be understood in this way.
But whatever else may exist that is greater than both the unmanifest and the person—
that distinction a wise man should observe with particular care;
for both of these are without beginning or end, and both are likewise without marks.
Both are eternal, subtler than the subtlest, and greater than the great. This is the commonality of both; thus, there is another [aspect] which is their distinction:
[their existence] by nature as having the quality of creation and likewise possessing the threefold *sattva*.
One should know that the characteristics of the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field) are the opposite of this:

it is the witness of both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations, and is devoid of the qualities (*guṇa*). They call the *jīva* (the individual soul), however, the agent who is enveloped by the qualities.
That by which they know the ungraspable is knowledge, and it is armored by that;
armored by that very thing, one is eternally such that no quality can overcome them.
These two persons are ungraspable because they are without marks and are not joined together.
The production characterized by conjunction, born of action,
is perceived through those instruments produced by action; whatever the agent performs with them is designated by verbal names such as "Who am I?", "This one," or "That one."

The ignorant one, perpetually obscured, thinks, "This body is mine. Just as one who possesses a crown is covered by three garments, so too is this embodied being covered by the qualities of goodness (*sattva*), passion (*rajas*), and darkness (*tamas*).
When that person knows the object of difference as non-different, then he, being the Supreme Self, indeed becomes stainless. Furthermore,
in the practice of action known as "difference," much is condensed in certain places.
Among the Vasus, Rudras, Gaṇas, and others, he exists through his own experience as enjoyment;
thus this supreme being is established in various forms,
appearing first in a condensed state and later abiding in a single form.
Therefore, these four things accumulated by these causes must be known;
for one who possesses this correct understanding will not be deluded at the time of death,
just as the wind and the sun shall attain their respective natures.
Desiring to attain divine glory, pure in speech and mind, one should perform stainless austerity through severe bodily restraints;
for the three worlds are pervaded by austerity, which exists within as a radiant light.
Both the sun and the moon shine in the sky through their ascetic power (*tapas*). Furthermore, that which is an equality of righteousness (*dharma*) is again proclaimed as *tapas*.
In this world, prowess is known as *tapas*, and knowledge is proclaimed as *tapas*.

That action which destroys passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*) is the specific characteristic of austerity (*tapas*). Indeed, this triad has been declared; for it is by means of this that the moon shines here once again, illuminating with its own radiance.
In the conjunction of the sun, whatever junction occurs, all austerity (*tapas*) is set ablaze.
Celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) are called bodily austerity (*śārīra-tapas*). Restraint of speech and mind and equanimity are called mental austerity (*mānasa-tapas*).
Food obtained from twice-born men who are knowledgeable in the rules is especially distinguished;
by such restraint in eating, his passion-born sin is destroyed,
and his senses turn away from their objects with a lack of attachment.

Therefore, one should take only as much as is necessary for the purpose at hand. At the time of death, due to the advanced age, one should perform [the rites] gradually while remaining free from distress.
Thus, with a disciplined mind, that knowledge is attained.

And by means of passion (*rajas*), this embodied soul, possessing a body, moves about like a sound; yet, with his intellect unobstructed by worldly duties and established in *prakṛti* through dispassion (*vairāgya*),
he is liberated from the end of the body due to vigilance until the body's final end.
The constant emission of beings is joined with causes, and their dissolution is likewise;
yet, in the case of an emission dependent on another, one does not transcend what is determined.
Those whose wisdom concerns the origin and end of existence remain in error.
12.210.023 Supporting their bodies through fortitude, with minds withdrawn by means of the intellect,

they worship those [subtle elements] even as they dissolve from their locations because of their subtlety. 12.210.024 And all that, according to the traditional scriptures, is not truly understood by the intellect.
Some whose selves are cultivated remain until the end of the body, being without support; some, disciplined by *dhāraṇā*, worship pure existence;
others practice upon the supreme God, the Imperishable designated as lightning.
For at the time of death, those who have drawn near [to the goal] and whose sins have been burnt away by austerity—
all these great-souled ones go to the supreme destination. One should observe their subtle distinction with the eye of the scriptures.

One should know the body to be supreme, liberated, and free from possessions; it is distinct from the intermediate space, with the mind fixed in concentration. Those whose minds are united with knowledge are liberated from the world of mortals.
Having become Brahman and free from passion, they then go to the supreme goal.
Thus, those people who know the Vedas declare this to be the singular path of dharma; by practicing it according to their knowledge, all go to the supreme goal.
Those in whom arises unshakable knowledge free from all taints go to the highest worlds, becoming purified according to their strength—
[those who worship] the divine Lord Viṣṇu, the unborn, known as the Unmanifest.

Those who are pure, satisfied with knowledge, and free from desire, proceed by means of their true being; having realized Hari abiding within themselves, those imperishable ones do not return. Having attained that supreme station, they rejoice in the eternal and immutable.
This much is this consciousness; it both exists and does not exist.
The entire world, bound by craving, revolves like a wheel.
Just as this lotus fiber, situated within the stalk, extends throughout it from all sides.
The thread of craving, without beginning or end, is always present within the body;
just as a weaver moves the thread through the cloth with a needle,
so too is the thread of saṃsāra bound together by the needle of craving.
Having gathered form from here and there, he will bring it forth;
he who correctly understands modification, primordial nature, and the eternal Puruṣa, becomes free from craving and is liberated.
The blessed seer Nārāyaṇa proclaimed this immortal [teaching], for the sake of compassion toward all beings and for the welfare of the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what conduct did Janaka, the lord of Mithilā, who knew the proper way of life and understood dharma, attain liberation after renouncing human enjoyments? Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
by which conduct the knower of conduct attained great happiness. Janaka Janadeva was the lord of men in Mithilā.
He was constantly engaged in reflecting upon the duties pertaining to the afterlife.
A hundred teachers, proponents of various heretical doctrines, lived perpetually in his house, demonstrating their diverse systems of dharma.
Regarding their determination concerning the state after death and rebirth,
he remained for the most part rooted in scripture and was not satisfied with the true nature of the self.
Therein was a great sage named Pañcaśikha, the son of Kapila.
Wandering across the entire earth, he eventually reached Mithilā.
Having thoroughly mastered the meaning of all the dharmas of renunciation through the definitive realization of the knowledge of reality, he was free from dualities and his doubts were destroyed.
They say that he whom the sages call the one who descended among men out of desire— seeking eternal and ultimate happiness so difficult to attain—
is the supreme seer Kapila, whom the followers of Sāṃkhya call Prajāpati.
I believe that he himself causes wonder by means of that form—
[the form] of the first disciple of Āsuri, whom they call Cirajīvin (Long-lived),
who performs a sacrificial session at Pañcasrotas for a thousand years.
Approaching him as he sat there within that great circle of the Kapilas,
[he was] one who was proficient in the five streams, an expert in the Pañcarātra,
known as the "Five-knower," the "Five-doer," the "Five-attribute," and the "Five-crested" (Pañcaśikha).
Teaching that the unmanifest is the state of the Supreme Person,
the sage, having attained perfection through the *iṣṭi-sattra* sacrifice and further through austerity,
came to understand the manifestation of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), for he possessed divine vision.
"That single-syllable Brahman which is seen in manifold forms— tell me that, O best of the twice-born, for you know it in its true essence.
Thus questioned, Pañcaśikha’s hair stood on end with joy.
Having attained the state of a seer, Āsuri entered that assembly of Brahmins devoted to Baudhāyana and realized that imperishable [truth].
His disciple was Pañcaśikha, who had been nourished by human milk.
There was once a certain housewife, a Brāhmaṇī named Kapilā.
Having become her son, he drank from the breasts of that woman;
thereafter, he obtained the name Kāpileya and attained a resolute intellect.

The Blessed One told me this concerning the origin of Kāpileya; his status as Kāpileya and his unsurpassed omniscience [were explained]. Kapila, having recognized that which is common to all—the unsurpassed knowledge of dharma—[attained it].
O King, having approached a hundred teachers, the wise sage Pañcaśikha confounded them with logical arguments; desiring to refute them all, he made known their many fallacious reasons.
But Janaka, deeply attached [to him] upon seeing the son of Kapila,
abandoned his hundred teachers and followed after him. To that most excellent man, who had bowed according to dharma, he [spoke].
He spoke of that supreme liberation which is prescribed as Sāṃkhya;
for, having spoken of weariness with birth, he spoke of weariness with action;
and having spoken of weariness with action, he spoke of universal weariness.
That for the sake of which there is attachment to actions and the arising of the fruits of actions— that is unreliable, futile, perishable, unstable, and transient;
for its destruction is visible, evident to the eyes, and witnessed by the world.

Even one who asserts that there exists something beyond the *āgama* is defeated; for the non-self (*anātman*) is indeed death to the self, and affliction consisting of old age is death. To imagine the self [as the non-self] out of delusion—that is considered an incorrect supreme view.
12,211.024a Even if such a thing exists that is not possible in the world, 12,211.024c this king considers himself thus: "I am ageless and immortal.
12,211.025a Furthermore, the notions of "it exists" and "it does not exist" apply only when that defining characteristic is absent.
Based upon what could one declare the determination of the course of worldly life?

For direct perception is the root of both these—logical reasoning (*kṛtānta*) and traditional lore (*aitihya*). Indeed, there is no scripture (*āgama*) or logical reasoning that is not itself directly perceived.
In whatever inference there may be, whether it be something produced or even something cultivated,
the soul is held by the materialists (nāstika) to be distinct from the body—
just as [the scent of] semen, the seed of a banyan tree, or the infusion of ghee during cooking.
Recollection of past lives, the magnet, the sun-gem, subsisting on water,
the transcendence of the elements after death, supplication to the deities,
and the cessation of karma at death— these are established as authoritative means of knowledge.
But there are no such causes as these which are established in form;
for a commonality between the immortal and the mortal is not possible.
Some, moreover, say that rebirth results from ignorance, karma, and volitional activities.
Greed and delusion are the causes, as well as the indulgence in the faults;
for they say that ignorance is the field, and likewise, performed action is the seed. Craving is the moisture that generates them; this is their rebirth.

When that mind, subject to death, has been dissolved and consumed, another body is born from one another; they call that the destruction of the being (*sattva*). When it is different in form, in birth, in learning, and in purpose—
12,211.034c How could there be a connection such as "he is in this" when there is no conjunction [of self]?
12,211.035a And if this were so, what joy would there be in the power of giving, knowledge, and austerity,
12,211.035c if one person were to undergo all the actions performed by another?
For when this [body] here on earth is afflicted with suffering by others who are common folk—
whether they be happy or miserable— the determination of its nature remains visible;
for even if they were to strike that body with clubs, it would arise once more.
There is a distinct knowledge, other than that by which this [world] is not perceived;
the seasons, the year, the lunar days, cold and heat, and the pleasant and unpleasant—
such is the dissolution of beings, through which they perceive these things as having passed away.
For one enveloped by old age or destroyed by death,
that which was previously weak becomes even weaker, as if the house itself is falling apart;
[so too do] the sense-faculties, the mind, the vital air, the blood, the flesh, and the bones.
In due order they perish and return to their own constituent elements; yet the maintenance of worldly life, the attainment of the fruits of the dharma of giving,
the purpose of Vedic words, and worldly conventions all persist.
Thus, when one reflects correctly, there are many such reasons [for doubt]:
"This exists," "that exists"—one cannot arrive at any certain conclusion.
While they are thus deliberating and rushing here and there toward various [theories], [the truth remains hidden].

In some places the intellect settles, and there it decays like a tree. Thus all living beings are afflicted by gains and losses, dragged about by scriptures just as elephants are led by their mahouts.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it increases all the more.
So too are wealth and those things that bring extreme pleasure.
Desiring these many things free of cost,
they have fallen into even greater suffering;
having abandoned the bait, they go under the power of death.
For one who is subject to destruction and whose life is unstable,
what is the use of kinsmen and the company of friends, since he must depart, leaving everything behind?
Having gone for a moment, it does not return;
for earth, space, water, fire, and wind always sustain the body.
Having observed this, how could there be any delight?
For in that which is subject to destruction, no peace is found.
This is a statement free from ulterior motives and devoid of guile.
Having beheld that which is supremely free from affliction and personally realized by himself,
the king was struck with wonder and proceeded once more to question him thus.
Bhīṣma said:
Janaka, the lord of men, having been instructed by the supreme ṛṣi,
questioned him once again regarding existence and non-existence in the life hereafter.
12,211.048d@018_0003 O Blessed One, if this perception occurs for someone after death,
12,211.048d@018_0004 then, such being the case, what will ignorance or knowledge accomplish?
12,211.048d@018_0005 This [self] is established precisely through dispute, just as the sensation [of pain] establishes the cause.
Pañcaśikha said:
"For consciousness exists here, as does the causal basis residing in the mind;
this is established through scripture alone, for the Vedic revelation states that it is self-established."
They function separately from one another, for they do not exist in their activities without depending [on each other]. For the conscious parts therein maintain their own forms;
thus, they rely upon that Self, which is both innate nature and the fruit of human action.
Depending upon that, embodied beings bound by their physical frames come into existence.
Its knowledge consists of the qualities and its recognition is not through signs as it is with sound;
they call each of those [qualities] an illustration within the elements, beginning with earth.
This self exists as distinct, yet it is present everywhere;
likewise, the Śruti declares that the Supreme Self alone resides within this body.
It is like space, wind, heat, moisture, and that which belongs to the earth.
Just as [the three qualities] proceed in a threefold manner, so is that Puruṣa traditionally described.
Just as [something] is hidden within milk, so too is the Great-Souled One pervading [all].
Because he was previously devoid of the connection with sovereignty, for this reason he is not "possessed of a remainder" (śeṣavān).
Sound, time, action, and the body—these are but conceptualizations of me alone. This nature of mine is composed of that [consciousness], yet it appears as the form of *māyā* with its divisions;
though it bears various names, it is supremely pure, free from conceptual construction, and the highest Self.

The gods reside within the *liṅga* and other such forms; such is the knowledge of the god. For this [reality], called *nāda*, consists of consciousness (*cinmaya*); it is sound, the great mind, and it possesses movement. Like a phoneme, it connects with words.
Indeed, they possess no body, nor do they have any further space [for rebirth].
They are declared to be "unmarried," yet all of them are corrupters of the Dharma.
Consciousness does not perceive the consequences; through knowledge, one attains that which is certain and imperishable.
For those by whom the self is always conceived through various distinctions and conceptualizations,
there are indeed many proponents of the self who hold it to be something other than primordial nature (prakṛti). Indeed, for them,
no contradiction is established regarding the existence of the self.

And at other times, they were considered outsiders to the Vedas because they held different views. For their denial of the [reality of] difference—whether it be of a single or manifold nature—is what constitutes their deviation.
Therefore, know that the heart of the Veda is non-dual.
This world proceeds in all its affairs because of the unseen power (adṛṣṭa) derived from the Vedas;
from that, the various Smṛtis have arisen along with the Itihāsas.
That which cannot be accomplished is not Brahman, nor does it have a beginning, a middle, or an end.
The senses together with the elements, the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the mind,

as well as the self (*ātman*) which is supremely pure— he is declared to be the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa*). Furthermore, this [world] is characterized by origination, whereas the other two are its opposite.
He who knows Prakṛti as eternal, and likewise that [nature] of the Self,
burns away what is called karma, like a fire arisen from a forest conflagration;
being pure and supreme as mere consciousness, he abides within all forms.
Like space, stainless, and endowed with various powers;
heating all beings, situated in the midst of the luminaries—he dwells in suffering yet is himself free from suffering; the wise man, knowing this, is not defiled.
Just as that [person] eats, so does the bee eat the honey;
in this same way, this Great Self does not perceive the non-Self.
"You are of such a nature"—when one has studied well, the Supreme is understood through this.
"There, the wise are awakened by the virtuous;
yet no one indeed says 'of the wise' (budhasya). Listen to me accordingly:
having not fallen into grief for him, you [should remain so], for you are thieves of the scriptures."
"Those who are divided destroy the world; indeed, they say that even kinsmen slay one another here.
Such is the task of that all-pervading Creator, this Great-Souled One.
Those great-souled ones forgive it, being free from all dualities."
If one approaches the Great-Souled One in a manner other than this,
what sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self?
Through association with him, even one who is pure becomes impure.
Just as the body and so forth are both impure and pure through knowledge,
the visible is not seen, and what is seen is not the visible at all; established as transcending the three times, it exists eternally in the form of knowledge.
Thus those possessed by passion, delusion, and pride do not practice correctly;
these evil-minded ones, who stand outside the Veda, are partakers of suffering in saṃsāra.
Those whose knowledge conforms to the scriptures become endowed with wisdom.
Through the intellect, that which is grasped by the intellect becomes like the nature of the Self once it is realized;

there is no doubt that they do not go beyond the blinding darkness—of this there is no uncertainty. Having performed the obligatory and occasional rites and having attained the destruction of sin, [they proceed].
Those of pure being, great-souled, whose stains have been shaken off by knowledge,
move about unattached like the wind; or else they wander through saṃsāra, yet they are not joined with the afflictions arising from the sense of "I."
Having gathered knowledge from here and there, they indeed investigate it;
endowed with such knowledge, that person of great intelligence destroys darkness like the sun.
Thus, having examined the self as being possessed of manifold sufferings...
The body is submerged in the mud and filth, yet it is stainless in the ultimate sense;
one who possesses the Supreme Self should liberate that very [body] from all suffering. Endowed with the vow of celibacy, he remains excluded from all attachments.
One who eats light food and whose self is purified attains supreme *nirvāṇa*.
The sense faculties, the mind, the vital air (*vāyu*), the blood, the flesh,
and the bone perish in succession and return to their own constituent elements (*dhātu*).

If the effect follows from its cause and yet that [cause] perishes, how can there be a sign for that which is signless? That is certainly false. Indeed, there are no causes whatsoever that exist as material forms.
A commonality between the immortal and the mortal is not possible,
just as it is observed in the world that a person born from sweat cannot produce offspring through a woman.
Through the recollection of what has been performed, the Supreme Person, who is accessible through the Veda, is realized.
The Veda, which follows direct perception, is not accepted as being caused by [human] authors.
Just as a branch is indeed connected to the branch of a tree, so too is the Supreme Self perceived through Śruti; He, moreover, is without marks (aliṅga).
That Brahman is to be established by means other than [inferential] marks (*aliṅgasādhya*); there are many reasons for this:
the maintenance of worldly life, the attainment of the fruits of the duty of giving, the words of the Veda for that purpose, and worldly linguistic conventions.
12,211.048d@018_0092 Thus, there are many such reasons for these [views] when one reflects correctly.

12,211.048d@018_0093 "This exists" or "that exists"—nothing at all is perceived [as real]. 12,211.048d@018_0094 While they are thus deliberating and chasing after this and that, [the truth remains hidden].
The intellect settles upon something here and there, and there it withers away like a tree.
Thus all living beings are tormented by gains and losses,
dragged about by scriptures just as elephants are led by elephant-drivers.
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, like a fire fed with clarified butter, it only increases all the more.
This is likewise true for wealth, which brings about extreme suffering.
Many others, withered and parched, though desiring [happiness], have fallen into even greater suffering; having abandoned happiness, they go under the power of death.
For one who is subject to destruction and whose life is unstable, what is the use of kinsmen or the holding of secret counsels,
since he must depart, leaving everything behind?
Having gone in a single moment, it does not return;
for space, earth, water, fire,
and wind always sustain the body.
"Beholding this, how could there be any delight? For there is no activity belonging to this which is subject to destruction.
Bhīṣma said:
"This statement, free from substrate, devoid of deception, supremely free from affliction, and personally realized—
having observed this, the king was struck with wonder."
12,211.048d He proceeded once more to question him.
12,212.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,212.001a Janaka Janadeva, having been instructed by the supreme ṛṣi, [spoke].
He questioned him once more regarding existence and non-existence in the life hereafter:
"O Blessed One, if some person possesses a consciousness after death,
then in that case, what will ignorance or knowledge effect?"
"O best of the twice-born, behold this: everything would result in annihilation. Whether one is heedful or heedless, what difference will it make?
For there is no association with the elements, nor is there any association with those things that are subject to destruction."
"By what method could a definitive conclusion be reached here in truth?
For [the mind] is shrouded in darkness, as if bewildered and distressed.
Then, calming him once more with his words, the seer Pañcaśikha spoke:
There is no finality in annihilation here, nor is there a finality in existence.
For this collection of body, sense-faculties, and mind proceeds in its activities, both separately and by depending upon one another.
The elements—space, wind, fire, water, and earth—constitute this five-branched body.
They exist by their own inherent nature and are separated by their own inherent nature.
Space, wind, heat, moisture, and that which belongs to the earth;

This collection of the five [elements] is the body; it is manifold. That which is denoted by the word "I" among the twice-born, which possesses a distinguished form of intellect, is eternal and beyond the scope of speech; thus shall it be known.
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and likewise ignorance—this is said to be the threefold knowledge. Knowledge, heat, and wind—this is the threefold collection of karma.
The sense faculties, the objects of the sense faculties, intrinsic nature, volition, and the mind.

In this [state], the prāṇa and apāna breaths, as well as the modifications and the constituent elements (dhātus), have emerged. Likewise, the vital breaths and the like, as well as the objects of touch, do not encounter obstruction.
That supreme Person shall consist of pure consciousness alone, and everything shall be dependent upon his son.
Hearing, touch, the tongue, sight, and likewise the nose—
these five sense-faculties are qualities preceded by the mind.
Therein, associated with consciousness, the threefold feeling is constant.
That which they call pleasure and pain, and likewise neither-pain-nor-pleasure;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—
these five objects of the embodied self, possessing six qualities, exist until death for the sake of accomplishing knowledge.
In them [reside] the relinquishing of karma and the determination of the meaning of all principles.
They call that the supreme, pure, and imperishable Great Intellect (*mahat*),
the Lord who stands beyond the realm of passion (*rajas*).
Through dispassion toward that [world], the mind— which is ever-moving within the quality of passion— ceases from it.
When that [mind] is serene, one should perceive this collection of qualities as merely a gathering of attributes for one who views it as such by way of its own nature.
Through incorrect views, suffering is endless and does not subside;
therefore, a wise and intelligent person should not become attached to these. And that which is seen as "not-self" is also [seen] as "neither I nor mine."
Upon what basis does this continuous succession of suffering proceed?
In that regard, "Right Mind" (*samyag-manas*) is the unsurpassed treatise on renunciation;
listen to it as it is being spoken for the sake of your liberation.

Indeed, for all those who are constantly ill-behaved, even the performance of all prescribed actions is considered to be merely renunciation; it results in affliction and brings about suffering. However, ritual acts pertain to the renunciation of material objects, while vows pertain to the renunciation of enjoyments.

The application of austerity lies in the renunciation of pleasure; the culmination lies in the renunciation of everything. This non-dual path for the total renunciation of all things has been shown for the abandonment of suffering, for otherwise there would be a miserable state.
He lies, liberated from the fears of old age and death,
when merit is exhausted and evil has departed,
and when the foundation consisting of the motive for asceticism has vanished.
Just as space is without marks in its fruit;
having spoken of the five organs of perception with the mind as the sixth in relation to the intellect,
I shall now speak of the five organs of action with the mind as the sixth.

The two hands are to be known as the organ of action; likewise, the two feet are the organ of locomotion. The penis is the organ for procreation and pleasure, while the anus is the organ for excretion.
But they know speech to be for the purpose of specific sounds, possessing a fivefold range of movement.
Thus, one should release these eleven by means of the intellect into the mind.
The two ears, sound, and the consciousness—these three are involved in the act of hearing.
Likewise for touch, likewise for form, and similarly for taste and smell.

The eye, form, and likewise the mind—these three are included in seeing. The nose, odor, and likewise the mind—these three are included in smelling. The skin, touch, and likewise the mind—these three are included in touching.
The tongue, taste, and likewise the mind—these three constitute the collection of tasting.
Thus, these five triads are the qualities for the perception thereof;
by means of each, a threefold state arises in succession.
These three are the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa*.
Among them, the threefold sensations arise, which are the means for all [experiences]:
exultation, affection, bliss, happiness, and tranquility of mind.
Whether from no cause or from some cause, the quality of *sattva* arises from the mind.
Dissatisfaction, distress, grief, greed, and intolerance—
these are the marks of *rajas*, seen whether through a specific cause or without one.
Lack of discernment, as well as delusion, negligence, sleep,
and lassitude— various qualities of darkness (tamas) manifest in some way or another.
Among these, whatever is associated with pleasure may arise either in the body or in the mind.
One should regard that as a state of *sattva* which proceeds in such a way;
however, that which is joined with distress and is unpleasant to the self,
one should consider that to be the activity of *rajas*.
Now, that which is associated with delusion (moha), whether it occurs in the body or in the mind—
unthinkable and unknowable— one should understand that to be darkness (tamas).
For that element (bhūta) has the ear as its locus, and sound is dependent upon the ear.
Neither both [sound and its cognition] nor the cognition of the other [object] exist within the cognition of sound.
In this same way, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these, along with the mind (*manas*), [are engaged] with touch, form, taste, and smell.

The simultaneous occurrence of one's own functions resides within these ten; know that the mind is the eleventh, and the intellect (buddhi) is the twelfth. When these do not occur simultaneously, there is no destruction resulting from darkness (tamas).
When these exist simultaneously, that is worldly conventional usage. Even after having cast aside the senses and having previously seen what was heard through scripture,
one who reflects does not wander about, being endowed with only three qualities.
When the mind, which is unstable and characterized by rapid fluctuations, is struck by darkness (tamas) and brings about cessation at the [wrong] time, they call that happiness born of tamas.
Whatever [happiness] is connected with scriptural tradition but does not lead to complete tranquility—
Then, even there, one takes up darkness as if it were manifest reality;
thus this quality, conditioned by its own karma,
is reckoned to function correctly for some, or not to function at all for others.
This state of "I" indeed does not rest elsewhere;
he whose state is firm and constant is truly wise, as is the other. Likewise, the nature of the body is eternally firm within all beings.
By this very inference, dharma should be abandoned; for in such a way [is it understood]:
through knowledge a living being is liberated, and one whose soul is dharma becomes possessed of knowledge. The world is sustained by dharma; everything is established upon dharma.
Dharma alone generates all goals and is the cause of everything. Indeed, nothing at all is seen in the world that serves every purpose;
therefore, when the renunciation of everything has been performed, the Supreme Self becomes pleased.

From the manifest, the unmanifest, incomparable [principle] revolves within the worlds. Thus do those who contemplate the inner self call this "the field" (kṣetra), a collection [of elements]. That state which is situated in the mind is indeed called the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña).
This being so, how could there be annihilation or permanence? For all beings exist by way of their own nature through causal conditions.
Just as rivers flowing into the ocean abandon their individual forms and names, so it is with these beings.

And they do not maintain their own identity; such is the destruction of sentient beings. This being so, how could there be any notion of "re-existence" after death, when the living soul is completely intermingled and is perceived only in the midst [of the elements]?
But he who understands this wisdom of liberation and seeks the Self with vigilance is not smeared by the undesirable fruits of his actions.
Like a lotus leaf sprinkled with water,
he was released from many firm bonds,
even those caused by his offspring and by the gods.
For when he abandons both pleasure and pain,
he is then liberated and, free from all marks (aliṅga), attains the supreme goal through the auspicious means of the authority of the Vedas and the traditional scriptures.
He lies having transcended the fear of old age and death,
when merit is exhausted and evil has departed,
and when the fruit arising from those causes has perished.
12,212.046c Thus, having taken their stand in that which is stainless, space-like, and signless, those who are unattached behold the Great One.
12,212.047a Just as a spider moving about [spins its web];

While he was reflecting thus in secret, Suvarcalā said to him:
"O father of great wisdom, give me to one who is not blind, not to one who is blind.
The father replied:
"O wise sage, always remember this request of mine;
O child, it seems to me that what you have requested today cannot be granted,
for a transformation has arisen within me— both blindness and non-blindness."
Suvarcalā said:

"If there exists such a husband who knows the Vedas, he shall support me. Bring here those twice-born men to whom you think I should be given.
Bhīṣma said:

O King, many sages arrived at the hermitage of Devala.
Having honored the sages and the young sons of sages according to the proper rule, and having worshipped them there according to the prescribed rites, the great father spoke to his daughter:
