"O blessed lady, among these who are perfected in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, of noble birth, and esteemed for their virtuous conduct— whichever of them you desire as a husband of great vows,
choose that prince today; O auspicious one, I shall give him to you."
Having said, "So be it," the auspicious and illustrious lady, who resembled molten gold and was endowed with all the marks of excellence,
then spoke these words after bowing down to the ascetics and beholding the assemblies of Brahmins.
“If there is a Brahmin in this assembly who, though blind, is not blind [to the truth], he shall be my chosen husband.
Hearing this, the sages there looked at one another; yet those highly blessed Brahmins said nothing, for they considered her to be ignorant of the Vedas.

Then, at one time, there was a learned man devoted to Brahman, skilled in logic,

Śvetaketu, renowned as one who knows the distinctions of the self, who honors his father, and who is an ocean of virtues, having heard this account with reverence,
quickly arrived there for the sake of the maiden, accompanied by Devala.
Having seen Śvetaketu, the son of Uddālaka, who was observing a great vow,
Devala honored him according to the prescribed rites and addressed him:

"Choose this man of great wisdom, who has mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
Having heard that, the maiden looked up at the son of the *ṛṣi* in anger.
The brahmin-sage said to her, "O blessed lady, here I am, come to you."
"I am blind; indeed, I have always considered this to be the truth. Know me to be one with wide eyes and free from doubt.
Choose me, O lady of beautiful hips; I shall worship you, O blameless one."
By which one constantly sees this, or hears, or touches;
by which one constantly smells, speaks, or again tastes this; by which one perceives reality, or by which one understands once more—[that is the Self].
For this eye does not exist; he is indeed called one blind by nature, through whom this [world] proceeds— seeing, hearing, and even touching,
as well as smelling and tasting— by means of that eye.
"I do not possess that; therefore, O auspicious lady, choose me today as one who is blind.
Out of regard for the world's view, I perform here the obligatory and occasional rites and so forth, yet from the perspective of the Self, I am eternally untainted by all of that."
Established, full, and peaceful, I am free from the notion of cause and effect;
crossing over death through ignorance and that immortality through knowledge,
I dwell here without envy, beholding only what has come to pass.
Bhīṣma said:

Then Suvarcalā, having seen him, spoke to that best of the twice-born.
"O wise one, you have been chosen by my mind; you are the one who shall complete what remains for me, my father. Choose me as your father; this is the sequence of Vedic injunctions.
Having understood her intention, Devala, the best of sages, became her father.
Having honored Śvetaketu in that same manner as Uddālaka had done,
he gave his daughter to him in the presence of the sages, preceded by the offering of water.
Indeed, they recite there concerning him, having beheld that Śvetaketu:
Hari, the abode within the lotus of the heart and the self of all beings,
that Madhusūdana exists here in the form of Śvetaketu;
may the divine Mādhava be pleased, as well as this wife of mine, my daughter.
"I shall bestow upon you this auspicious maiden as your partner in dharma.
Having spoken thus, Devala, the bull among sages, gave her to him;
and the highly illustrious Śvetaketu accepted that maiden.
Having taken her hand according to the rule and performed the rites here according to the ordinance,
and having completed the unsurpassed marriage ritual for the sages,
that wise man, dwelling in the householder’s life, spoke thus to his wife:
"And whatever has been declared in the Vedas, all that do, O beautiful one;
together with me, according to what is right, as my partner in dharma. I am established in the very state of being 'I', and you likewise."
Therefore, you should perform actions, and after that, I too shall perform them; with the realization that "this is not mine" and by abiding in the fire of knowledge,
you should subsequently reduce those actions to ashes.
"You must act in this way at all times so that I am not rendered unfortunate by you.
Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do;
therefore, for the sake of the world's accomplishment, as well as for your own accomplishment, you must act accordingly."
Having spoken thus, that man of great wisdom, the sole vessel of all knowledge,
having begotten sons through her and having gratified the deities with sacrifices,
remained eternally devoted to the yoga of the Self, free from dualities and devoid of possessions.
Having obtained that worthy wife, like the intellect and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña),
the wife and the husband likewise reached another world; acting as witnesses in this world, they moved about filled with joy.

Then, on one occasion, Suvarcalā questioned her husband Śvetaketu: "Who are you here? Tell me that, O best of the twice-born. To her, the eloquent and blessed one replied: "Without a doubt, you already know who I am."
"Having addressed me as 'O best of the twice-born,' whom else do you wish to question?
She said to that high-souled one, "I am asking him who dwells within my heart.
Having heard that, he replied to her, "O beautiful woman, he will not speak."

If you conceive of yourself as being endowed with a name and a lineage, that is false; for while the lineage exists, there remains the bondage of the body. This notion of "I" is likewise firmly established within you.
"You too am I, and I am everything; thus it proceeds. This is not indeed the ultimate truth—why do you ask about this?
Then, laughing, that joyful wife who practices dharma spoke to her husband.
O King, smiling at that time, she then spoke these words:
"O Brahman-sage, what is the use of this manifold conflict? Through your various ritual acts, you have always been one whose knowledge has perished."
Śvetaketu said:

Whatever the best person practices, that very thing other people do."

By this, this world proceeds and will become confused; when the Dharma is thus confused, the social classes (varṇas) fall into intermixture. And once intermixture has set in, the "law of the fish" prevails.

and Śvetaketu replied:

for that which consists of a reversal of phonemes produced by a *parivādinī* (lute) should be understood as "word" (*śabda*), while its inflection (*nipāta*) is called the "meaning" (*artha*).
Suvarcalā said:
"Is there indeed a relationship between word and meaning, or is there not? Śvetaketu replied:
Tell me that according to the truth: if it is indeed the object itself that resides in the place of the word,
and if there is no connection whatsoever between the word and its object—
Suvarcalā said:
"You know that water exists in the lotus-leaf just as it does elsewhere;
for the existence of a word is based on its actual referent, and its existence cannot be otherwise.
Śvetaketu said:

Suvarcalā said:
Words characterized by qualities do not apply to the supreme, inconceivable [reality].
I am dark-complexioned in every limb, and you are likewise so;
therefore, O best of sages, tell me this according to the truth, if it be so.
Śvetaketu said:
"For just as the nature of a clay pot is considered to be that same [clay] nature,

"That I am you" or "this is that"—such is the name of conceptual construction (*saṃkalpa*) regarding others.

Hence, O timid one, they turn away from it entirely with the mind.

With the skin, one indeed touches the wind situated in space again and again;

The host of stars, the year, and even the sky are no longer seen; moreover, the space of space is determined to be the true form. For these [categories] are merely conceptualized for that purpose, and Viṣṇu alone is the ultimate reality.

All this has come forth from Him; everything is established in Him.
Just as both a large jar and a small one are supported by the earth, so too there is neither woman, nor man, nor even a neuter.

That is pure, absolute knowledge alone; everything is established within it. The elders, whose minds are concentrated on the sacred revelation, praise self-restraint alone for all social classes, and especially for the Brāhmaṇa. For one who lacks self-restraint, the successful accomplishment of ritual acts is not properly attained.
Action, austerity, and the Vedas—all are established in self-restraint (*dama*). Self-restraint increases one's vital energy; self-restraint is said to be a means of purification.
Free from sin and fearless, the self-controlled man attains the Great.

The self-controlled man sleeps in peace and awakens in peace; he moves through the world in happiness, and his mind remains serene. Splendor is maintained through self-restraint; that which is fierce does not attain it.
He constantly perceives many enemies within himself as distinct from his own self;
there is always fear of those who are unrestrained, just as living beings fear carnivorous beasts. To restrain them, the Self-Existent One created the king.
In all stages of life, self-restraint (dama) alone is preeminent;
for by means of it, Dharma is protected, since they are the very bridges of Dharma. Furthermore, whatever fruit exists in that Dharma is said to be even greater in one who is self-controlled.
I shall describe their characteristics, the accumulation of which constitutes self-restraint (dama):
freedom from miserliness, absence of agitation, contentment, faithfulness,
freedom from anger, constant uprightness, lack of excessive speech, and absence of pride.
Worship of the guru, freedom from malice, compassion toward all beings, and absence of backbiting;
the avoidance of idle gossip, falsehood, praise, and blame; and desiring what is virtuous without coveting—by these one gains the confidence of men.
Free from enmity, easy to approach, impartial toward blame and praise, well-conducted, endowed with virtuous character, serene in soul, self-possessed, and wise— the learned man,
having received honor in this world, indeed goes to heaven after death.
Having attained that which is difficult for all beings to reach, he rejoices in happiness;
devoted to the welfare of all beings, he does not indeed despise people out of pride. Unshakeable like a great lake, satisfied by wisdom, he remains serene.

He grants fearlessness to all beings, for from him there is fearlessness for all; he is to be saluted by all beings, being self-controlled and possessed of knowledge. He does not exult in great gain, nor does he grieve in calamity.
He who possesses limited wisdom yet is self-controlled is called a twice-born man.
Endowed with sacred learning through his actions and practicing the auspicious conduct of the virtuous,
he who is ever joined with self-restraint enjoys a great reward.
Absence of malice, forbearance, tranquility, contentment, pleasant speech, truthfulness, generosity, and lack of exertion— this is not the path of the evil-minded; rather,
it is characterized by desire, anger, greed, envy for others, and boastfulness.
Deceit, arrogance, and pride—this is not the path of the great-souled ones.
Discontent, falsehood, and delusion—this is the path of the evil-minded.
Having brought desire and anger under control, one should be a celibate student with senses conquered.
Exerting himself in fierce austerity, that Brahmin of rigid vows,

Bhīṣma said:
Those who, while performing their duties, observe the vows prescribed in the Vedas;
those who eat while observing the vows prescribed in the Vedas but have fallen away from them, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
and those Brāhmaṇas who, having undertaken the purity of their vows, eat at any time—[these are the ones who attain the fruit].
That food, having become nectar, enters the sacrificer.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ordinary people say that this fasting is penance."
"O great king, is this austerity, or what else might constitute austerity?
Bhīṣma said:
"People consider that fasting for a month or a fortnight constitutes austerity."
That which involves injury to one's own body is not austerity; that is not considered austerity by the virtuous. Renunciation and humility alone are taught as the highest austerity.
One should always be as if fasting and always remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).

A Brahmin should always be a sage and should always worship the deities; O Bhārata, he who desires dharma should be a householder, yet always refrain from sleep and always abstain from meat, and he should always recite purifying prayers.
One should always be an eater of nectar (*amṛta*) and never an eater of poison;
one should always be an eater of remnants (*vighasa*) and always fond of guests.
One should always be full of faith and a worshiper of the gods and the twice-born.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How may one be a perpetual faster? How may one become a celibate student? And how may one be an eater of *vighasa* and always fond of guests?"
Bhīṣma said:
He who does not eat at all, between the morning meal and likewise the evening meal, would be as one who is perpetually fasting.
A Brahmin who approaches his wife only during her season remains a celibate student; that man who always speaks the truth and is constantly devoted to knowledge,
and who does not eat meat not intended for sacrifice, is indeed a non-eater of meat.
Know this, O Yudhiṣṭhira: he who is constant in giving, who is pure, who does not sleep by day,
and who always eats only after his dependents and guests have eaten—
he eats nothing but nectar in its entirety.
That twice-born man who never eats while others have not yet eaten,
and who does not eat without first giving food to guests— he is beloved by guests. He who does not eat without first offering food to the deities is a deity himself.
By that fasting, heaven is indeed conquered by him; for he who eats what remains after [offering] to the deities, the ancestors, the dependents, and the guests,
is called an eater of *vighasa*.
For them, indeed, are infinite worlds in the abode of Brahmā;
attended by Apsarases, those denizens of heaven move about.
Together with the deities and the ancestors, they enjoy [those realms].
They rejoice with their sons and grandsons, and their destination is unsurpassed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, some say there are two ways in this world, three ways, or many ways."
There is no means of cognition, nor is anything else perceived; that Brahman is indeed not [an object of perception].
There are various kinds of scriptures and diverse types of logical arguments.
Bhīṣma said:
"Upon what basis do I stand? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Great-souled men, each devoted to their own respective fields, are authoritative in their scriptures;
they conduct themselves as scholars in the world—what is a man of learning (*vidvān*) and who is a scholar (*paṇḍita*)?"

Without knowing the true nature of all things, one may act according to one's own preference. Regarding this matter, there is an ancient historical account (itihāsa) concerning the sages of purified souls, which involves a great dispute.
Seated on the slopes of the Himavat were the sages of rigid vows;
that assembled host consisted of six thousand sages.
Among them, some held the universe to be eternal, while others maintained it to be with a Lord or without a Lord.
There is no primordial cause; this entire world is not thus.

By this [view], other Brahmins [hold one position], while others hold that it is inherent nature (*svabhāva*), others that it is action (*karman*), and others that it is human effort (*pauruṣa*), destiny (*daiva*), or indeed that which consists of inherent nature and the rest.
O King, endowed with hundreds of diverse arguments and propounding various treatises,
the Brahmins sought to defeat one another through their own inherent nature;
from that, a root [of dispute] arose, joined by proponents and opponents.
And because of the striking of the alms-bowl and staff, and the [striking] of the bark-garments, deerskins, and clothes,
some of those best of the twice-born were overcome with anger; then others, having become pacified,
all said to Vasiṣṭha, "Tell us the eternal truth."
“I do not know,” that lord replied to them, O best of Brahmins.
Then all those Brahmins together spoke to the seer Nārada:
“Tell us, O highly blessed one, for you are a knower of reality.”
"O twice-born ones, I do not know where we have come together; indeed, where are we going?
Thus the Blessed One spoke to them, and then he said to those twice-born ones:
"Who in this world is wise, free from delusion, and possesses the wonderful nectar of immortality?"
And those incorporeal Brahmins heard that speech;
having gone to the armored twice-born ones, they said, "Ask him, and he will tell you.
Then a certain most excellent and best of the twice-born spoke to him.
Vibhāṇḍaka, whose mass of Vedic knowledge is adorned—
who are you, sir, that you do not appear amidst the distinctions of meaning while yet uttering words?
Then the Blessed One said this to Sanatkuṃāra:
“O great sage, know me; you are wise, for I am the ancient seer (*ṛṣi*), eternally of one form.”
That which those who know the Vedas call the imperishable,
that very thing this Great-Souled One spoke of again; tell me, O Pārtha, he spoke of that which is established in its own nature.
"O bull among sages, today you alone [know] the true nature of reality; or rather, what else could it be?
Then he spoke these most profound words of reply:
For the Great-Souled One, the primordial, is bodiless;
O Sage, he has neither ears nor mouth,
nor does he have hands or feet, for his essence is not composed of limbs.
Having spoken thus to the sages and looked at them,
the wise one, having reflected within his mind, said to himself:
"O seer, why do you speak these words?"
There was no one there who could think of it, nor was there anyone who knew it; for the best of the twice-born had not heard of that reply,
and so they looked toward the sky, laughing here and there.
Thinking it a marvel, those best of sages, together with their attendants, went to the great golden mountain which resembled Sanatkumāra;
having ascended that mountain, they beheld him as he was absorbed in meditation.
[They beheld] the divine Kumāra, the Arhat, who had transcended the Vedas;
then, when a full year had passed, O king of kings, the twice-born stood bowing down before the great sage Sanatkumāra, who had returned to his natural state.
To those who had arrived, the Blessed One, whose stains were shaken off by knowledge, said:
"O hosts of sages, I have understood that incorporeal speech. O bulls among sages, ask today whatever you desire to be done."
With palms joined in reverence, they spoke to that great sage,
the best of the twice-born, a treasury of knowledge and perfectly pure:
"How may we [attain] that most excellent treasury of knowledge?"
"O Youth, we shall worship the one of universal form;
be gracious to us, O Blessed One, [granting] a fragment of knowledge for the sake of the happiness of those who have reached the state of honey."
"O Great Sage, regarding that state which is of universal form—
tell me, O Lord of great majesty, what is there and where is it? For that Blessed One, the Great-Souled One, is devoid of those [qualities]."
Listen to that which belongs to the one who is unattached and knows the truth; and indeed,
throughout many thousands of eons,
he possesses a serene nature through his auspicious command.
O best of the twice-born, just as that bodiless one previously spoke to you, so too was that speech uttered as truth; yet you did not understand it. Listen now to the supreme reason for this.
How is this understood?
Because a specific transformation through cooking is observed day after day.
By that, one mixes everything together; just as there is a visible example for all in the circle [of the eye],
so it exists for those with vision.
In knowledge, one perceives the true nature [of things],
just like a reflection within a mirror;
that very [knowledge] is everything.
The wise one neither fears nor wanders;
not being involved in the thought "Where am I?", "Whose am I not?", or "By what [means]?", he understands. He is pervasive throughout the ages.
That which exists separately is not the ultimate reality (*aparamārtha*),
just as the wind, though being one, is stirred in many ways.
Or it is the distinction of the basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*),
or that which has [such] a basis;
as in the case of a twice-born, a deer, and a tiger, respectively.
In a human being,
the wind residing in the veins is divided; yet that wind is one, and so too is this Self, which is distinct from the Supreme Self.
It appears as if it were so; thus the self alone moves.
Seeing everything, the self neither hears, nor smells, nor speaks.
Ten rays surrounded that Great-Souled One on all sides,
following that Lord just as they emerge from and follow the sun; day after day, they set toward the west and rise again from the directions.
Both of them did not cry out; likewise, know that they were embodied beings.
O best of Brahmins, when he fell, know that one was intent on eating while the other was intent on running.
One remained above, and the other stood below.
Having reached that supreme state, it should be known as the golden abode;
for by means of the self, one perceives that lamp of the self within the self, that person who is the self. Having previously accumulated [merit], he moves about like a bee, hovering repeatedly.
He who knows [it] as if with pride is neither deluded nor diminished;
no one sees him with the eye,
but with the heart and the intellect one beholds his form.
Neither white nor black is that supreme reality,
dwelling in the cave of the heart and held in the hand of the Goddess of Knowledge;
it does not even exist within the likeness of a Brahmin, so how much less in others?
But that best of the twice-born who, as a sacrificer, performs the sacrifice with the mantra—
neither virtuous nor non-virtuous, transcending dualities and free from envy—
he, whose self is immortal and who is satiated by knowledge, sleeps in happiness; of this there is no doubt.
In this way, the Lord creates this world through his illusory power (*māyā*);
yet, with his nature obscured, he does not know himself to be the cause.
He alone is the meditator, the seer, the thinker, the knower, and the observer of what is seen.
"Who, being wise, [could fully describe] the Supreme Self, the infinite creator of the worlds? O bulls among sages, go now; I have told you as much as was possible for me to speak.
Bhīṣma said:
Having thus prostrated before Sanatkumāra, who has arisen from the ocean of knowledge, those best of Brahmins, having beheld him, returned once more to Ruci. Therefore,
O son of Kuntī, you too should be devoted to the yoga of knowledge.
O Great King, knowledge alone is the destroyer of all suffering;
it was fashioned of old as a protection for men who are gathered within this great mass of misery.
By the ancient person, the high-souled seer, that was certainly [spoken] by the foremost of great sages.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
[That was spoken] by the foremost of great sages; that is certain.
"What is this that they call 'austerity' (tapas)? What is proclaimed as austerity? Is it fasting, or something else, or perhaps the practice of the Vedas?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, tell me what constitutes austerity (*tapas*) according to the scriptures.
Those whose wealth is austerity consider fasting for fortnights, months, and so forth to be austerity;
others who have mastered the Vedas consider the Vedic vows and other such observances to be austerity."
Some say that the complete study of the Vedas is the truth, while others say it is the practice of conduct as prescribed; all have reached the state of austerity through their vows.
That which is the ordinance of self-knowledge is proclaimed to be the highest austerity.

Renunciation, austerity, and likewise tranquility; austerity is the restraint of the senses, and celibacy is declared to be austerity—thus have the twice-born spoken. That wise man who always observes fasts should remain perpetually a celibate student.
The sage who is always wise, eats only the remains of the meal, and is free from envy;
he who is constantly fond of guests is said to have attained the infinite. Therefore, he who never eats between meals is one who fasts perpetually and observes the great vow.
He who approaches his wife according to the seasons is thus declared [righteous], and he who eats the remains of a meal is remembered by the wise as one who eats *vighasa*.
He who eats what remains after the servants have been fed, as well as the remnants of a sacrifice, eats *amṛta*.
In this way, the practice of austerity is eternally described as being joined with various purposes.
For whose worlds are indeed boundless? They are all established in the vow of truth.
Those who declare that [the world] is composed of karma are remembered as the twice-born Brāhmaṇas;
honored by hosts of Apsarases, they delight in divine enjoyments.
Those who, being firmly resolved, declare that the word "austerity" (tapas) has knowledge as its essence— O best of kings, they have indeed attained the true nature of the inner self.
This which you asked, O tiger among kings, has been explained to you.
Furthermore, various perceptions arise according to the objects themselves.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, kings are once again dependent upon the sovereign."
And there are thousands of other various names as well—
counterparts to these that are hidden and have set.
Behold indeed that all this, everywhere, is firmly rooted in primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Bhīṣma said:
Therefore, O King, let it be for men according to their inclination and as they have come to it. In this matter, O King Yudhiṣṭhira, hear an ancient account.

O learned one, that which Suvarcalā— the daughter of Devala, adorned with all auspicious marks, a maiden named Suvarcalā whose consciousness was purified by yoga— spoke in the assembly of Brāhmaṇas; [that I shall relate].
"By what cause was she born free from dualities and with her doubts destroyed?
She, intent on seeking a boon, spoke to her father, the Brahmin:
"O highly wise one, having beheld this one with beautiful eyes, give me to the blind man."
The father said:
"O sage, my child, it was indeed this very thing that I have constantly requested of you.
But today, O child, it no longer seems possible for you to request it."
"Whether there is blindness or lack of blindness—such a doubt arises within me.
The maiden said:
"O large-eyed one, you speak these words like a madwoman, my daughter."
"I do not speak to you today out of madness or delusion; I tell you this with full awareness. Know that such a person exists in the world who, being a knower of the Vedas, honors me.
O best of the twice-born, whatever gifts you think to give me here, [accept them]."
"O highly fortunate one, bring others; for among them I shall see him.
Having said "So be it," the brahmin dispatched his disciples.
Those best of the twice-born, having witnessed the power of the seer and that of the maiden, [acted accordingly].
"O King, many sages arrived at Devala’s hermitage.
Having honored them upon their arrival, the great father said to his daughter:
'If you desire a husband, O blessed one, choose that brahmin yourself.'"
Having said, "So be it," the auspicious lady, whose face resembled molten gold and whose waist was as slender as a hand, spoke these words, O ascetics:
"If there is a Brahmin who is esteemed, even if he is blind, he shall be my chosen husband."
The highly fortunate sages did not offer any reply, nor did they respond; and the maiden remained there in her father’s house, O Bhārata,
while Śvetaketu, the brother-in-law of Kahāla, was a supreme knower of dharma.
Having heard this, O lord of the earth, Brahmā then arrived and said to the maiden:
"O blessed lady, I am that twice-born man whom you previously mentioned as having returned.
Suvarcalā said:
"Know me to have wide eyes; I am blind, so choose me! "How is it that you have wide eyes, or how is it that you are sightless?
The twice-born one said:

"Speak later, O learned one; I shall examine you, O best of the twice-born. You must explain, with their underlying causes, the corresponding names that have been concealed and have set in relation to sound, touch, form, taste, and smell."

My mind does not engage with them, for they are not directly perceived by me; I am merely a beholder, and therefore no movement [of agency] exists therein. By means of that [faculty], O fair-hipped one, one sees, speaks, and likewise touches.
"It is constantly tasted, smelled, heard, and likewise perceived;
that eye exists within me by which one sees clearly. O blessed lady, I am indeed one with good eyesight; ask me, or what shall I tell you?"
"In this regard, there is nothing unknown to me; for I am a knower of the ultimate truth.
Having thus become purified, she bowed down to the great sage Śvetaketu and honored him; and he, in turn, accepted her as his wife.

O King, O highly wise one, a maiden endowed with dispassion obtained such a supreme husband; therefore, O King, the purpose [of each] is distinct. This has been told to you, O King; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, whatever action there is in this world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, it surely yokes a person to the experience of its fruit."
"Is the person indeed the agent of that [action], or is it not? This is my doubt.
O Grandfather, I wish to hear this from you according to the truth.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Prahrāda and Indra.
[It concerns one who is] unattached, cleansed of evil, born of noble lineage, and deeply learned.
Free from arrogance and free from egoism, established in purity (*sattva*) and devoted to his vow; equal toward blame and praise, self-controlled, dwelling in empty dwellings;
he has understood the origin and the passing away of all beings, both moving and unmoving.
Neither feeling anger nor rejoicing toward things unpleasant or pleasant,
seeing with equanimity both gold and a clod of earth,
the steadfast one possesses certain conviction regarding the knowledge of the supreme good for the self.
He who knows the high and the low among beings, the omniscient one of equal vision,
who has entered with his heart into Govinda, the unmanifest Self, Vāsudeva, the Great Soul, the one who brings about the welfare of all beings.

Śakra [approached] Prahlāda, the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu, who was seated in a secluded place with his senses restrained, a devotee of the Lord, eternally dedicated to Nārāyaṇa, and meditating upon the Supreme Self.
Desiring to understand her wisdom, he approached her and said this:
"Whatever qualities there may be by which a man is esteemed among men in this world,
we perceive all those qualities to be inseparable from you."
Now, your intellect here appears to be the same as that of childish people;
while considering yourself [wise], what do you regard as the highest good in this world?
Bound by fetters, fallen from your station, and come under the power of your enemies.

"O Prahrāda, though deprived of fortune, you do not grieve over that which is worthy of grief. O son of Diti, is this because of your attainment of wisdom, or perhaps because of your fortitude? For you appear composed even while beholding your own calamity."
Thus urged by him, the steadfast one, whose resolve was firm,
spoke with gentle words, describing his own wisdom:
"He who does not understand the engagement and the withdrawal of living beings..."
Arrogance may arise from ignorance, but for one who perceives [reality], there is no arrogance.
It is the profound essence of all beings, the object of meditation, eternal and ancient,
ungraspable, incomparable, possessing all forms, and higher than the highest.
All that has arisen from the veil proceeds from that; behold, even I am composed of that, characterized by various marks. He indeed protects the world, the creator, designated as Viṣṇu.

When [the time] has arrived, the Lord of the Gods (*sureśvara*) shows [himself] once more. All entities (*bhāva*) and non-entities (*tathābhāva*) proceed from their own nature (*svabhāva*) and likewise cease; thus, no purpose for a person (*puruṣārtha*) exists.
In the absence of a human purpose, there is no agent whatsoever;
yet, for one who acts by himself, pride might arise here in this world.
But he who considers himself the agent of both the good and the evil—
It is my opinion that his wisdom is flawed, for he does not know his own true nature.
If a person were the creator,
then surely his undertakings would succeed for the sake of his own welfare, and he would never suffer defeat.
For even when people exert themselves, the occurrence of the undesired and the non-occurrence of the desired are observed;
how, then, can there be any human purpose (puruṣārtha) derived from that? Indeed, the manifestation of the undesired and the concealment of the desired [are seen].
We observe that for some, this occurs effortlessly by their very nature; some who possess excellent intelligence are seen to assume a form that is unattractive,
seeking the acquisition of wealth from those who are ugly and of little wit.
When all qualities, whether auspicious or inauspicious, enter [into experience] impelled by their own inherent nature (svabhāva), what cause for pride can there be therein?
It is my firm conviction that all this arises from inherent nature alone.
Wisdom established in the self does not exist for me; it is otherwise than that.
However, I consider the connection between actions and their results—whether auspicious or inauspicious—to be born of karma here.
I shall speak of the entire domain of actions; listen to that.
Just as a crow, while cawing, might somehow indicate the presence of boiled rice,
so too all actions are merely the characteristic of inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
He who knows only the transformations does not know the supreme primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

Arrogance may arise from his youth, but for one who perceives [reality], there is no arrogance. When one has reached certainty regarding all things that exist by their very nature, what can pride or conceit do?
I know the entire ordinance of dharma and the impermanence of all beings;
therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve, for all this indeed has an end.
Free from "mine-ness," free from egoism, free from desire, and released from bonds—
Established in myself and free from distraction, I behold the origin and dissolution of all beings;
for one whose wisdom is perfected, who is self-controlled, free from thirst, and devoid of desire,
there is no more exertion, O Śakra, as he perceives through the knowledge of the world.
In both the primal nature and its transformations, I have neither affection nor aversion;
I see no hater who today would claim me as his own.
Neither upward, nor downward, nor across, nor anywhere else, O Śakra, do I desire anything.
12,215.032c Neither in consciousness, nor in the object of consciousness, nor in ignorance is there any peace.
12,215.033 Śakra said:
12,215.033a By what is this wisdom obtained, and by what is tranquility attained?
"O Prahrāda, tell me correctly that means as I ask you.
Prahrāda said:
"By means of straightforwardness, vigilance, serenity, and self-possession,"
O Śakra, by serving one’s elders, a person attains greatness.
One obtains wisdom through one’s own nature and attains peace through one’s own nature.
Whatever you perceive at all, all that arises from nature alone.
Having heard [the teaching] from the mouth of the Guru, the ascetic no longer perceives any distinction; then,
having mentally contemplated the meaning of the words, he beholds the Self as one who has attained the realization of discernment.
12,215.035d@021_0004 Out of fear, he becomes dispassionate toward that [world] and seeks the Supreme Lord.
12,215.035d@021_0005 He seeks Him as the protector from all sufferings, just as one seeks happiness.
12,215.035d@021_0006 He associates with the virtuous; indeed, the virtuous lead to happiness.
Having learned the path from the presence of the virtuous through its characteristic marks,
one who is liberated from all attachments reaches the Supreme Self; for the dharma performed out of desire for sense objects is full of passion and brings fear.
By that [negligence], a person again gradually incurs a loss of dharma;
he becomes devoid of devotion toward the Supreme Self, O Acyuta, and even toward the speaker [of the scripture]. Yet, once liberated, he certainly does not lose his station.
He would always find delight in what is defective and find delight in cyclic existence;
because of his constant lack of discernment, his very self is not realized.
He becomes one of mad conduct and proceeds in this manner;
his impurity increases constantly and is not pacified by any means. And for him who is thus attached to sense objects, the desire for liberation does not arise.
Absorbed in fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), he indeed praises worldly qualities;
filled with pride and arrogance, he does not listen to the scriptures at all,
nor does he recognize that enjoyment is established by its own nature.
The assumption of the form of consciousness is indeed the supreme, immutable reality. Yet,
having entered various wombs and being whirled about by one's own actions,
one who is possessed by great delusion does not recognize the further shore.
Having attained discipline through reliance on a teacher,
he accumulates it further and further within those favorable dharmas;
for this reason, O slayer of Bala and Vṛtra, he is known as "Ācārya."
By that very certainty, there is true existence in future births and so forth;
the mass of cotton-like accumulated karma is cast away by the wind of knowledge.
Thus, one whose conduct is disciplined brings about the cessation of saṃsāra.

O Śakra, that which constantly cuts off favorable conduct like a sword, and by which one has fallen into this state and does not attain freedom from craving— this is known as the "internal" [craving]; one should completely avoid such equanimity.
First, he is pursued by that very action performed [in the past];
second, he encounters the application of dreams through action. Endowed with these factors, he stands manifest before his eyes.
This fourth state, called deep sleep, is not possessed of any veils.

By worshipping and offering oblations to that Lord according to worldly practice, one becomes self-controlled; through the yoga of exertion within the Self, he becomes actionless, higher than the highest.

One recognizes that [world] as the extent of the Supreme Self; this is the Māyā of the Paramātman. Just as the state of fire arises from a spark—which is of the same nature as the fire—so too does that which consists of consciousness arise from the intellect (buddhi) through its apparent commonality.
Thus, for ignorant children, the notion of a self is conceived otherwise.
Even regarding that which is to be accomplished and is called "unsubstantial," how could there be friends, enemies, and so forth?
In the absence of those, O Lord of the Gods, grief and other such states do not arise.
"Understand this, O Blessed One: one should pursue equanimity.
This is declared to be the means; do not go astray, O Lord of Gods. Through knowledge one perceives action; for the wise, it does not lead to further involvement."
As long as that which has been commenced here for him does not come to rest, so long he indeed departs at its conclusion; such is my conviction regarding the wise man.
Whatever I shall declare to be his designator, from that this [state] shall always arise.
And by each respective state, one perceives misfortune therein;
just as this speech resides in various locations such as the palate,
so too do objects residing in the intellect always reside within the intellect itself.
He who is liberated from all particular volitions,
the supreme among the supreme, the Great Self—
he is celebrated by those who know the end of the three Vedas.
Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Lord, exists eternally as no quality whatsoever among castes,
worlds, or distinguishing attributes;
he is the Great-Souled Vāsudeva who dwells within all things.
He bestows upon everyone the form of action corresponding to their qualities, in its entirety;
yet His form does not stand within the range of vision.
No one sees him with the eye; rather,
with devotion and fortitude, he whose self is composed beholds here his true nature as pure consciousness.
"Those things they speak of, the Blessed One gave them to me; he himself, that high-souled Maghavan, [gave] the remainder.
Know this, O Śakra, to be my means."
"Therefore, the world never exists for me.
Bhīṣma said:
Having been addressed thus by the lord of the Daityas, Śakra was filled with wonder.

Then, O King, being filled with joy, he honored those words. Having thus paid homage to the lord of the Daityas, the sovereign and lord of the three worlds took leave of the king of the Asuras and departed for his own abode.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that wisdom by which a protector of the earth, deprived of his fortune and crushed by the rod of Time, may wander the world."
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Vāsava and Bali, the son of Virocana.
Having approached his grandfather and prostrated with palms joined in reverence,
Vāsava, having conquered all the Asuras, questioned Bali:
"For whom, while giving away wealth, does it never diminish?"
"O Brahmin, I do not find that *bali* offering; tell me of that *bali*.
For it was he who set toward his setting, and he who illumined the quarters;
it was he who, unwearied, poured down rain according to the proper seasons."
"O Brahmin, I do not find that *bali*; tell me of that *bali*.
He is Vāyu and he is Varuṇa; he is Ravi and he is Candramas. He is Agni who heats all beings, and he also becomes the Earth."
"I do not find that *bali* offering, O Brahman; tell me of that *bali*.
Brahmā said:
"O Maghavan, it is not right for you to ask this."
"When questioned, one should not speak a falsehood; therefore, I shall tell you of Bali.
Whether among camels, cows, donkeys, or even horses, he will become the most excellent being in an empty house, O Lord of Śacī."
Śakra said: "O Brahman, if I were to encounter a powerful man in an empty house, whether I should kill him or not— O Brahman, instruct me on that."
Brahmā said:
"O Śakra, do not harm Bali; Bali does not deserve death.
Rather, O Śakra, O Vāsava, you should question him regarding the principles of justice, if you so desire."
12,216.011 Bhīṣma said:
Having been thus addressed by the Blessed One, Mahendra then traversed the earth, mounted upon the shoulder of Airāvata and endowed with splendor.
Then he saw Bali, disguised in the form of an ass,
dwelling in an empty house just as the Blessed One had described.
Śakra said:
"O Dānava, having entered the womb of a donkey, you are now a consumer of chaff.
This is your lowest birth; do you grieve for it, or do you not grieve?
Alas, I behold what was never seen before: one who has fallen under the power of his enemies."
Deprived of fortune and friends, and fallen from his strength and prowess—
he who formerly, surrounded by thousands of vehicles and kinsmen,
scorched all the worlds, would come toward us without hesitation.
The Daityas, with you at their head, remained under your command;
indeed, during your sovereignty, the earth yielded crops without being ploughed.
Is it that you grieve for this present calamity of yours, or do you not grieve?
When you stood upon the eastern shore of the ocean,
licking your lips while distributing wealth among your kinsmen, what was your state of mind then?
When thousands of celestial maidens danced for you in unison— what was your thought at that time?
For many series of years, that monastery has shone with splendor.
All [the trees] were garlanded with lotuses, all possessed the luster of gold.
O Lord of the Dānavas, how is it that your mind is the same today as it was then?
Your parasol was exceedingly large, made of gold and adorned with jewels,
beneath which sixty thousand Gandharvas danced in seven groups. Your sacrificial post was immense, made entirely of gold, and worthy of worship.
When you gave away ten thousand times ten thousand cows, O Daitya, what was your thought at that time? What was your mindset when you subsequently gave away a thousand more,
as you traveled about performing sacrifices across the entire earth?
"O Lord of Asuras, what was in your heart then when you departed by the rite of throwing the *śamyā*?
I do not see your golden pitcher, nor your parasol, nor your fan;
and I do not see the garland bestowed upon you by Brahmā."
Bhīṣma said:
Then Bali, having heard what was uttered by Vāsava— deep with pride— and having laughed, spoke to the king of the gods.
"O Lord of the hosts of gods, how great is your folly here! This painful speech of yours, O King of the Devas, is unbecoming.
Bali said:
"You do not see the golden pitcher, nor the parasol, nor the fan;
you will not even see the garland given to me by Brahmadatta, O Vāsava.
You ask about my jewels, yet they have been placed within a cave."
"When my time comes, then you shall see those things.
You do not know, O Lord, that perfection exists in the form of auspicious limbs and beautiful features;
in due time it shall come to all, for no one bypasses this, O Vāsava."

But this is not worthy of you, either in terms of your fame or your lineage, that you, having attained all your goals, should wish to boast to me who have failed to achieve mine. For those who are wise do not grieve in times of suffering, nor do they exult in times of prosperity.
Those who have perfected their wisdom, who are satisfied with knowledge, patient, virtuous, and wise—
O Purandara, you alone boast with a vulgar intellect;
when you become like me, then you will not speak thus.
"O King, why do you not realize this through the delusion of the intoxication of power? You will realize it in time, O King, when you are joined with downfall.
Bhīṣma said:

But Śakra, laughing once more, spoke these words to him as he sighed like a serpent, O Bhārata, while he was surrounded by his kinsmen and a thousand chariots: "Since you, surrounded by your kinsmen and a thousand chariots..."

Scorching all the worlds, he will come toward us without hesitation; seeing this most piteous condition of yourself and your army, abandoned by kinsmen and friends, do you grieve or do you not grieve?
Having previously attained incomparable joy and having established the worlds under your own control,
do you now grieve over this downfall, or do you not grieve?
Bali said:

"O King of the Gods, casting aside pride and conceit, listen to me. I have previously practiced great sincerity toward you; [now hear of] the inevitable turn of time and the transformation of one's own state."
Having perceived this world’s greatness—
and the impermanence of my own passage through time—
I do not grieve, O Śakra, for all of this indeed has an end.
"O Lord of the Immortals, these bodies of living beings are finite;
therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve, for this [death] is not my fault.
Indeed, life and the body are born together after passing away."
Both increase together, and both perish together.
Having encountered such a state as this, being entirely without autonomy,
if I understand it thus, what cause for distress could there be for one who knows?
The destruction of beings is their end, just as the ocean is the end of rivers.
O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, men who understand this correctly do not fall into delusion;
but those who do not understand it thus are devoted to passion and delusion.
Having encountered hardship, those whose intelligence perishes sink into despair.
For when a person gains intelligence, he casts off all evil; being free from evil, he attains purity, and established in purity, he becomes serene.
But those who turn back from there, being born again and again,
are miserable and tormented, impelled by misfortunes; for them,
the attainment of wealth and loss, as well as life and death, are all alike.

I neither hate nor desire the fruit of pleasure or pain. For the man who kills anyone who has already been killed is himself truly slain; both he who kills and he who is killed lack true understanding.
"O Maghavan, whoever acts like a man after having killed and conquered, is indeed a non-doer; for it is the Doer alone who performs that act.
For who in this world brings about both the destruction and the origin of all things?"
For that which was done has been done by action itself, and there is yet another agent for that as well.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—beings have these as their source; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Whether one possesses great knowledge or little knowledge, whether one is strong or weak, whether one is handsome or ugly, and whether one is fortunate or unfortunate—
Time, profound in its own splendor, takes away everything.
When he has fallen under the power of time, what grief can there be for me, who understands this?
One merely burns after that which is already burnt, and strikes down that which is already struck down;
one perishes after that which is already lost, and a man obtains only that which was destined to be obtained.
No island is seen for him, much less a further shore or a near shore; even as I reflect upon it, I do not perceive the end of this divine ordinance,
were Time not to destroy all beings while I am looking on.
O Lord of Śacī, let there be joy, pride, and even anger within me; yet,
knowing me to be one who eats only chaff while in a secluded house,
you revile me after having assigned me the form of a donkey.
If I so desired, I could indeed transform myself into many forms, terrifying to behold, upon seeing which you yourself would flee from me.
Time takes away everything; Time bestows everything.
"O Śakra, do not exert your human prowess against everything that is sustained by Time.
O Purandara, when I am enraged, all shall tremble;
indeed, all the inhabitants of heaven will flee along with you."
"I understand, O Śakra, the eternal dharma of this world.
You too should regard it in this way; do not fall into self-amazement. For power and majesty are never established in the self alone."
"Your mind is still that of a youth, O Maghavan, just as it was in the past. Behold this; attain a resolute understanding.
The gods, humans, ancestors, Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas—"
"Twelve thousand, two hundred and seventeen point two nine—[all] were under my control; you know all that, O Vāsava.
Let there be homage even to that quarter in which Bali, the son of Virocana, resides.
Thus did they approach me, deluded by pride and envy.
"O Lord of Śacī, I do not grieve for that, nor for my own fall from status;
such is my settled resolve, and I abide under the authority of the Teacher.
For one may see [others] born in noble families, handsome and powerful."
"O Śakra,
one who is born of a low family, deluded, and ill-fated is seen living happily together with his ministers; for it must indeed be so according to destiny."
O Śakra, a woman who is auspicious and endowed with beauty is seen to be unfortunate; O Śakra, one who lacks auspicious marks and is deformed is seen to be fortunate.
This was not done by us, O Śakra, nor was this done by you, O Śakra.
Whether you have come to such a state, O wielder of the thunderbolt, or whether we ourselves have come to such a state,
it is neither your karma nor that of others— how could it be mine, O Śatakratu?
Whether there is prosperity or even adversity, that is determined solely by the turn of time.
I see you standing there as the radiant King of the Gods,
glorious and effulgent, roaring above me.
And this would indeed be so, were it not for Time, which stands having seized hold of me.
Today, I could strike you down with my fist even if you were armed with a thunderbolt;
yet this is not the time for valor—this is the time for forbearance that has arrived.
Time establishes everything, and likewise, Time ripens all things.
If Time has come for me, the powerful lord of the Dānavas,
who am roaring and scorching [my enemies], to whom else will it not come?
For [it shall come] to all twelve of you, the high-souled Ādityas.
"O King of the Gods, the splendors of them all have been taken away by me alone.
O Vāsava, I alone carry the waters and I release them;
I heat the three worlds and I alone cause the lightning to flash."
"I protected, I plundered, I gave, and I took; I restrained and I controlled—I am the lord and master over the worlds.
But today, O Lord of the Immortals, that sovereignty of mine has ceased."
"Submerged as I am in the army of Time, nothing at all appears clear to me.
Neither I am the doer, nor are you, nor is anyone else the doer, O Lord of Śacī. For the worlds are enjoyed in turn by chance, O Śakra."

Those who know the Vedas say that this [universe] has months and half-months for its dwelling, is encompassed by days and nights, has the seasons for its doors, and has the rainy season for its mouth.
Some people, through their wisdom, say that all this is to be contemplated.
The five years of the embodied beings are impermanent; the sixth is seen [only] rarely.
I shall investigate these five thoughts in five ways, yet even at that time, O slayer of Vṛtra, I do not perceive them.
They say that Brahman is profound, dense, and great, like a vast ocean of water; it is without beginning or end, imperishable, and supreme.
Although it is itself without marks, it enters as a mark within all beings.
Those men who perceive reality consider him to be indeed eternal;
yet they think there has been a reversal of states for living beings. For this [world] could not be traversed, since he is beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
For if you do not follow the course of all living beings, where will you go? That which cannot be abandoned by one who runs, nor lost by one who stands still—
that the five senses do not perceive in any of their five ways.
Some call him Agni, and some call him Prajāpati; others [call him] the seasons, the months, the fortnights, as well as the days and the moments (kṣaṇas);
and still others [call him] the forenoon, the afternoon, and the midday.
They say that even for a single moment, he who is one appears as many; know him to be Time, under whose control all this exists. O Vāsava, many thousands of Indras have already passed away.
O Lord of Śacī, just as you are endowed with strength and heroism,
even you— Śakra, the king of the gods, possessed of exceeding power and fierce in might—
Kāla, when his time arrives, will bring to rest through his great prowess.
"O Śakra, remain steadfast against him who seizes all this;
he cannot be overcome by me, nor by you, nor by those of old.
Having attained that unsurpassed royal splendor which you now perceive..."
"It is false that she remains with me; for she does not abide in one place alone. Indeed, she has remained with thousands of Indras who are far superior to you.
O Lord of the Gods, fickle as she is, she has abandoned me and gone to you."
"Do not act thus again, Śakra; you ought to become tranquil.
Even having reached such a state, she will soon abandon you and go to another, impelled by time, O Śakra, O performer of a hundred sacrifices; let there be no pride in you."
"Forgive me; know that this is the arrival of the proper time, O Lord of Gods! Why are you so shameless, O King of Devas, that you boast thus?
You are the sovereign of all asuras and the one who strikes fear into all the gods."
"Who could know the path by which he, having conquered the world of Brahmā, has come?
Bhīṣma said:
"Then Śatakratu beheld the blazing [splendor] of the high-souled Bala."
Seeing Śrī, who possessed her own form, emerging from his body at that time,
the illustrious Lord Pākaśāsana,
Vāsava, his eyes wide with wonder, questioned Bali.
"O Bali, who is this woman who has departed from you— radiant,
wearing a crest-jewel, adorned with armlets, and shining with her own splendor?
Bali said:
"I do not know whether she belongs to the Asuras, nor to the gods, nor to humans. You yourself must question her, or do as you wish, O Vāsava.
Śakra said:
"Who are you, radiant and wearing a crest, who have come away from Bali?
O lady of pure smiles, tell your name to me, for I do not know it. Who are you that stand here like an illusion, blazing with your own splendor?"
"O lady with beautiful brows, having abandoned the lord of the Daityas, tell me that truthfully. Śrī said:
"Virocana did not know me, nor did Bali, the son of Virocana, know me."
"They call me Duḥsaha, and they know me as Vidhitsā;
O Vāsava, they call me Bhūti, Lakṣmī, and Śrī. You do not know me, Śakra, nor do all the gods know me."
Śakra said:
"Is this for my sake, or rather for the sake of Bali?
For you are greedy for his virtues; what, then, is Bali's lack of merit?"
"O Duḥsaha, though I have dwelt with him for a long time, I shall now abandon him.
Śrī said:
"Neither the Creator nor the Ordainer can dispose of me in any way whatsoever."
"O Śakra, time indeed has its turn; do not disregard him, O Śakra.
Śakra said:
"How was Bali abandoned by you, or for what reason, O Śikhaṇḍin?"
"And how may you not abandon me? Tell me that, O lady of pure smiles. Śrī said:
"I am established in truth, in charity, in vows, and indeed in austerity."
In prowess and in righteousness, Bali was then surpassed by him;
for though he had always been devoted to Brahmanas, truthful, and self-controlled,
he now began to show malice toward the Brahmanas and touched clarified butter while still impure from eating.
Having formerly been devoted to sacrifice, this deluded soul, oppressed by time, said to the worlds, "Sacrifice unto me alone. Therefore,
O Śakra, O Vāsava, having been cast out from there, I shall dwell in you.
"I am to be sustained by one who is vigilant, through austerity and prowess.
Śakra said:
"Is there among gods, humans, or any living beings whatsoever a man..."
"O you whose abode is the lotus, who alone would be able to withstand you?
Śrī replied:
"Neither a god, nor a gandharva, nor an asura, nor a rākṣasa."
"O Purandara, is there anyone at all who is capable of withstanding me alone?
Śakra said:
"O auspicious one, tell me how you might always remain dependent upon me."
"I shall carry out your word; you ought to speak the truth.
Śrī said:
"O Lord of the Gods, listen to how I shall abide eternally within you."
"Divide me into four parts according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas.
Śakra said:
"I shall indeed place you [in these parts] according to my power and according to my strength."

"O Lakṣmī, may there never be any transgression on my part toward you. Among men, it is the earth alone that supports all beings and brings them into existence; it is my conviction that she is capable of enduring even your foot."
Śrī said:
"This is my one foot that has been set down, which is established upon the earth;
therefore, O Śakra, place my second foot well-settled."
Śakra said:
"The waters alone, flowing among men, are their attendants;
let them endure your foot, for the waters are capable of enduring it."
Śrī said:
"This foot of mine has been placed down, which is established here in the waters;
therefore, O Śakra, place my third foot well-settled."
Śakra said:
"O Agni, that third foot of yours, in which the gods and the sacrifices, and in which the Vedas are established, you shall hold it firmly."
Śrī said:
"O Śakra, this foot of mine which was placed here and established in the fire— therefore, make my fourth foot well-established."
Śakra said:
"Those who are indeed virtuous among men, devoted to Brahman, and speakers of truth—let them endure a quarter [of the sin]; the virtuous are capable of enduring."
Śrī said:
"This is my foot that has been placed here, which is established among the virtuous.
O Śakra, maintain me who am thus distributed among all beings."
Śakra said: "O you who,
having first purified the ground, satisfy the beings with water and offer sacrifices in the fire— for them, you shall be unfailing."
Those yogins who, through well-colored ritual acts, are endowed with causes and concentrated,
being possessed of knowledge, rejoice when they have obtained what they desired;
for you, O Bhūta, were indeed deposited here by me while you were still present.
"May he who would strike [this] down be my enemy; let them thus hear my words.
Bhīṣma said:
"So be it," she replied, and having fallen [from her state], she was honored by all the worlds.
That goddess, whose abode is the lotus, protected Vāsava.
Then King Bali, having been abandoned by Śrī, spoke to the Daityas:
"As long as he blazes in the eastern quarter, so long indeed shall he rule the southern quarter."
At that very same time, the sun likewise reaches the west and the north;
and when the sun sets at midday,
then there shall be another battle between the gods and asuras, and you shall be my victor.
"When the sun, standing in a single place, shall scorch all the worlds,
then, O Śatakratu, I shall be the victor over you in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Śakra said:

"I have been commanded by Brahmā that you are not to be slain; therefore, O Bala, I do not release the thunderbolt upon your head. Go wherever you wish, O Lord of Daityas; may it be well with you, O Great Asura."
The sun has never stood still in the midst of its course;
for its law was established long ago by the Self-Existent One. It revolves eternally, heating all creatures with truth.
His course consists of six months, the northern and likewise the southern,
by which the Sun traverses the worlds, emitting cold and heat.
Bhīṣma said:

O Bhārata, having been addressed thus by Indra, Bali, the lord of the Daityas, departed for the southern direction, while Purandara went toward the north. This is the song sung by Bali, characterized by the absence of egoism.
Having heard these words, the thousand-eyed one then ascended into the sky.
Bhīṣma said:
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me, what is the highest good for one who is submerged in calamities? O mighty-armed one, speak further to me regarding that which leads to stability.
In this very regard, they cite this ancient history."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, Purandara spoke thus to Śatakratu regarding his conversation with Namuci,
as he sat bereft of fortune like the unshakeable ocean,
knowing the origin and end of all beings.
Bound by nooses, fallen from your station, and come under the power of your enemies, you are bereft of your splendor, O Namuci; do you grieve, or do you not grieve? Namuci said:
Nothing is gained by grief, and the body is only tormented;
enemies rejoice, and there is no help to be found in sorrow. Therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve, for all this indeed has an end.
O Lord of the Gods, through affliction one’s beauty and even one’s dharma perish;
through affliction one’s prosperity perishes,
and through affliction one’s life-span perishes.
Having indeed subdued that suffering born of dejection which has arisen,
one who understands what is auspicious should meditate with a mind that is pleasant and favorable.
For in whatever way a person directs the mind toward what is auspicious, [in that same way does his mind become established].
At that very moment, all his goals become favorable; there is no doubt about this.
There is one Teacher, there is no second Teacher;
the Teacher instructs the person even as they lie within the womb.
Instructed by him, I carry out my duty just as I have been directed, like water flowing down a slope;
thus perceiving both existence and non-existence, I recognize what is most important.
I know what is beneficial, yet I do not perform it; fulfilling the hopes of my well-wishing friends,
I carry out the task just as I have been appointed.
In whatever manner he is destined to obtain, in that very manner he obtains;
in whatever manner it is destined to come to be, in that very manner it comes to be. Wherever the Creator joins him again and again, there he enters as an embryo.
He dwells right there and there, not where he himself desires; one whose constant disposition is, "This state has come upon me; this is what must happen to me," shall never be deluded.
Among those who are being struck down by various means, no assailant is found;
yet this is suffering: that one thinks, "I am the hater," or "I am the doer.
[This applies even to] the seers, the gods, and the great asuras.
What calamities do not befall those in this world who are aged in the three Vedas and are sages in the forest? Yet,
those who know both the higher and the lower are not thrown into confusion.
The wise man neither becomes angry nor does he cling;
he neither desponds nor exults, and he does not grieve in times of financial hardship or calamity.
He stands by his nature as immovable as the Himalayas;
neither does supreme success in his aims cause him joy,
nor does calamity at the proper time cause him delusion.
He who experiences pleasure, pain, and likewise that which is intermediate, is a man who bears the burden. Whatever state a person may encounter, [he should remain steadfast].
One should take delight in that [state] without being tormented;
thus one should drive away from the body the mind-born fever, which has grown so great and causes such distress.
Having entered that assembly, that council, those members of the court,
the wise man who does not feel fear of the assembly, having plunged into the true nature of dharma;
He who accepts this is a man who bears the burden.
The actions of the wise are difficult to follow;
indeed, the wise do not lose their way even at a time of delusion.
Even when fallen from his position, Gautama did not lose his composure;
for even after encountering such a dire calamity, the old man— neither by the power of mantras, nor by heroism, nor by wisdom, nor by human effort— remained steadfast.
Neither by virtue, nor by conduct, nor likewise by the attainment of wealth,
does a mortal obtain what is unobtainable; what lamentation can there be in that regard,
since the Ordainers ordained this for one born into such a state?
I shall experience that very thing; what can death do to me?
One obtains only those things that are to be obtained, one goes only to those places that are to be gone to, and one encounters only those sorrows and joys that are destined to be encountered.
The man who, having understood this in its entirety, is not deluded, is skilled amidst pleasures and pains; he is indeed the lord of all wealth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O protector of the earth, when a man encounters misfortune or hardship— whether it be the loss of kinsmen or even the loss of his kingdom— what indeed is best for him? For you, O bull of the Bharatas, are our supreme counselor in this world."
"I ask this of you; you ought to tell me that here.
Bhīṣma said:
For one who is separated from sons, wife, pleasures, and wealth..."
O King, in times of great calamity and hardship, fortitude brings about the highest good. For one endowed with steadfastness, the body does not waste away;
freedom from sorrow bestows happiness and maintains supreme health.
They become submissive through fortitude, whether it be toward a king or not; of this there is no doubt.
One who possesses fortitude attains prosperity, and through fortitude, righteousness increases.
Furthermore, from the health of his body, he recovers his prosperity once more.
"O dear one, that king whose men abide in a state of sattvic conduct possesses stability, fortitude, and perseverance in his undertakings.
In this very regard, they cite this ancient history."

12,220.006c Again, O Yudhiṣṭhira, regarding the dialogue between Bali and Vāsava: 12,220.007a When the war between the gods and the Asuras had occurred, resulting in the destruction of the Daityas and Dānavas,
12,220.007c and when the worlds had been traversed by Viṣṇu, while Śatakratu was the king of the gods.
While the gods were being worshipped, while the fourfold social order was established,
while the three worlds were flourishing and the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) was filled with joy,
[he was accompanied] by the Rudras, the Vasus, the Ādityas, the two Aśvins, and also by the Ṛṣis.
Surrounded by Gandharvas, lords of serpents, Siddhas, and others, the Lord Śakra mounted Airāvata,
the king of elephants— four-tusked, well-tamed, and endowed with splendor—
and traversed the three worlds.
Once, on the shore of the ocean in a certain mountain cave,
the wielder of the thunderbolt (Vajrin) beheld Bali, the son of Virocana, and approached him;
he saw him seated upon the head of Airāvata, surrounded by hosts of gods.

Seeing Bali standing there fearless and unchanging, the lord of the Daityas felt neither grief nor agitation; then, mounted upon his preeminent elephant, Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, spoke thus: 12,220.012c The lord of the Daityas neither grieved nor trembled at the sight of Indra, the lord of the gods.
12,220.013a Seeing Bali standing there, established in equanimity and free from fear, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, mounted on his best of elephants, spoke as follows.
O Daitya, you do not waver because of your heroism, or perhaps because of your service to the elders,
or due to being purified by asceticism; for in every respect, this is extremely difficult to achieve—
having been brought under the power of enemies and deprived of your unsurpassed position.
"Vairocana, relying on what do you not grieve when you ought to grieve?
Having attained preeminence among your own kin and having enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures,
tell me, why do you not grieve now that your strength and kingdom have been taken away?"
Having formerly been the lord in the station of your father and grandfather,
why do you not grieve today upon seeing that very position seized by your rivals?
Bound by the nooses of Varuṇa and struck by the thunderbolt—
"Your wife has been taken away and your wealth has been seized; tell me, why do you not grieve?

That you do not grieve despite being stripped of fortune and deprived of power is difficult to achieve. For who else, upon the loss of sovereignty over the three worlds, would dare to continue living?"
Having heard him speak these and other harsh words with contempt, Bali, the son of Virocana, remained unperturbed and spoke calmly:
"O Śakra, now that I have been thoroughly subdued by you, what is the use of your boasting?"
"O Purandara, I see you standing there brandishing the thunderbolt.
Previously you were powerless; how have you somehow come to possess power? Who else but you would be capable of uttering such cruel words?"
But that man who, though capable, shows mercy to an enemy fallen into his power—
a hero who has come within his grasp— him indeed they know as a true man;
for in battles between two contending parties, the outcome is indeed uncertain.
One attains victory, and the other indeed meets with defeat.
O bull among gods, let it not be your thought that this is my inherent nature; for I am the Lord of all beings, conquered by you through your prowess and strength.
"O Śakra, this was not done by us; O Śakra, this was not done by you.
That you have come to such a state, O wielder of the thunderbolt, or that we have come to such a state—just as I am today, so were you, and just as you are, so shall we be."
"Do not think, 'I have committed an evil deed.
For a person experiences pleasure and pain in alternation.
You attained the status of Śakra through the natural course of time, O Śakra, and not by means of [meritorious] action."
Time leads me away at its appointed time, and this very Time leads you away as well. Therefore, I am not as I was today, nor are you as you were;
for there is no longer service to mother and father, nor the worship of the gods.
No other conduct of virtue brings happiness to a man;
neither learning, nor austerity, nor charity, nor friends, nor kinsmen are able to protect a person afflicted by Time.
Indeed, even with hundreds of obstacles, men are unable to thwart a non-returner (anāgāmin),
unless they possess the power of wisdom;
for those who are being struck down by such successive calamities, no protector is found.
But this, O Śakra, is suffering: that one thinks, "I am the doer.
If the doer were truly the master of his action, he would never be made to act;
but because the doer is made to act, therefore even the doer is not independent.
"In time I conquered you, and in time I have been conquered by you. Time is the destination for all who go; Time impels all creatures.
O Indra, you do not perceive this because you speak with a vulgar intellect."
Some hold you in high esteem, considering that you have attained preeminence through your own deeds.
How could one such as I, knowing the ways of the world, grieve or become bewildered when struck by time during the turmoil of worldly affairs?
For one who is perpetually overwhelmed by time— whether it be myself or someone like me—
the intellect sinks when encountering calamity, like a shattered boat.
Both I, you, and whoever else shall become lords of the gods [are likewise subject to this].
"O Śakra, all of them shall follow the path traveled by hundreds of Indras;
even you, so difficult to overcome and blazing with supreme splendor,
Time shall carry away when the time has ripened, just as it carried me away."

12,220.041a Many thousands of Indras belonging to the Daityas have passed away in age after age through time; for time is indeed difficult to overcome. 12,220.042a But having obtained this station, you consider yourself to be great.
The god who is the source of all beings, like the eternal Brahmā—
this immovable station is not the infinite abode of anyone else;
yet you, with your childish intellect, think, "This is mine."
"You place your trust in what is untrustworthy and consider the impermanent to be permanent.
O Lord of the Gods, your soul is thus perpetually overcome by time. Out of delusion, you desire royal splendor, thinking, 'This is mine.'"
This [fortune] is considered stable neither for you, nor for us, nor for others;
having passed over many others, it has rested with you for the time being.
O Vāsava, this fickle thing, having remained with you for a certain period of time, will depart.
Like a cow leaving a watering hole, she will go elsewhere;
for there have been kings whom I am unable to count,
and O Purandara, there will be many others besides you.
This earth, with its trees, herbs, and jewels, along with its rivers, mountains,
and mines— those by whom this world was formerly enjoyed, I no longer see them now:
Pṛthu, Aila, Maya, Bhauma, Naraka, and likewise Śambara.
Aśvagrīva, Puloman, Svarbhānu, Amitadhvaja, Prahrāda, Namuci, Dakṣa, Vipracitti, Virocana,
Hrīniṣedha, Suhotra, Bhūrihā, Puṣpavān, and Vṛṣa.
Satyeṣu, Ṛṣabha, Rāhu, Kapilāśva, Virūpaka,
Bāṇa, Kārtasvara, Vahni, Viśvadaṃṣṭra, and Nairṛta; Ritthā, Huttha, Vīratāmra, Varāhāśva, Ruci, and Prabhu.
Viśvajit, Pratiśauri, Vṛṣāṇḍa, Viṣkara, Madhu,
Hiraṇyakaśipu, and the Dānava Kaiṭabha,
as well as the Daityas known as the Kālakhañjas— all of them together with the Nairṛtas.
These and many others— those who were former and even more ancient lords of the Daityas and lords of the Dānavas, as well as others whom we have heard of—
many former lords of the Daityas have departed from this earth after abandoning it.

All have been struck down by Time, for Time is indeed most powerful. You alone are not the performer of a hundred sacrifices (*śatakratu*); all were devoted to dharma, and all were constant performers of sacrificial sessions.
All were wanderers of the intermediate space; all were warriors who fought face-to-face.
All were endowed with firm physiques, and all had arms like iron clubs.
All possessed a hundred illusions, and all could travel wherever they desired.
12,220.058c Having encountered battle, none of them were ever heard to have been defeated.
12,220.059a All were devoted to the vow of truth; all were enjoyers of their desires.
12,220.059c All were devoted to the Vedic vows; and all were deeply learned in the scriptures.
All those lords attained sovereign power unitedly,
yet never before had there been such intoxication with power among those high-souled ones.
All were givers according to what was right, and all were free from envy.
12,220.061c All of them, in all beings, attained [their end] as was fitting;
12,220.062a All the sons of Dakṣāyaṇī, the offspring of Prajāpati, possessed of great strength,
12,220.062c Blazing and scorching, were withdrawn by Time.

And when you have enjoyed this earth and must eventually abandon it again, O Śakra, you will not be able to restrain your own grief. Renounce your desire for the enjoyment of pleasures; renounce this pride born of prosperity.
"In this way, you will endure the grief when your own kingdom is lost.
Do not grieve in a time for sorrow, and do not rejoice in a time for joy. Abandoning the past and the future, conduct yourself according to the present."
"If Time has come for me, who have always been disciplined and unwearied, then forgive me; O Indra, it will approach you before long.
O Lord of the Gods, you seem to threaten me here with your words as if to wound me."
While I am restrained, you surely think highly of yourself.
Time first approached me and only afterwards pursues you;
therefore you roar, O Lord of the Gods, for I have already been struck down by Time.
"Who indeed in this world is able to stand before me when I am enraged in battle? Time alone is powerful and has arrived; for that reason you remain standing, O Vāsava.
That end of the thousand years must now be fulfilled."

12,220.070c Since all my limbs are unwell and my vital energy is destroyed, 12,220.071a I have fallen from the station of Indra; you are now the established Indra in heaven. In this most variegated world of living beings, you are to be worshipped due to the revolution of time.
"What indeed have you done today to become Indra, and what indeed have we done to fall from our position?
Time is the creator and the destroyer; everything else is not the cause. Loss and destruction, sovereignty, pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence—all these are wrought by time."
12.220.073c Having obtained such [a state], a wise man should neither exult excessively nor be distressed.
12.220.074a "For you alone, O Indra, know us, and I know you, O Vāsava;
why do you boast to me while I am bound by Time, O shameless one?"
For you yourself know what my prowess was in former times; my valor displayed in battles is sufficient evidence of that.
Even the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Sādhyas, and the Vasus—along with them—[could not withstand me].

All the Maruts and the lord of Śacī have been utterly defeated by me. You yourself, O Śakra, know what happened during the encounter between the gods and the asuras; all the assembled deities were shattered by my might in battle.
12,220.078a Mountains, along with their forests and forest-dwellers, 12,220.078c and those terrible peaks with their jagged summits, have been repeatedly hurled by me at your head in battle.
12,220.079a What indeed can be done by me, since Time is insurmountable?
"Indeed, I do not lack the power to slay you with my fist, even if you were armed with the thunderbolt;
yet this is not the time for valor, but the time for forbearance that has arrived.
Therefore, O Śakra, though you are most difficult to endure, I tolerate you."
