"O Śakra, when the time has matured and you are enveloped by the fire of Time, surely bound by the noose of Time, you boast in vain. This is that dark-hued Person, whom the world cannot transcend."
12,220.082c The fierce one stands binding me, as if a beast with a rope.
12,220.083a Gain and loss, pleasure and pain, desire and anger, existence and non-existence,
12,220.083c Killing, bondage, and liberation— all are obtained through Time.
"I am not the agent, nor are you the agent; rather, he who is the eternal Lord is the agent.
It is this Time that ripens me, like fruit that has come to maturity upon a tree. Whatever actions a man performs, by those very deeds he is joined with happiness in due time."
12,220.085c Again performing those very same [actions], one is joined with sufferings in the course of time.
12,220.086a And one who knows the nature of time, when touched by time, ought not to grieve.
12,220.086c Therefore, O Śakra, I do not grieve; there is no help to be found in grief.
"For when grief does not remove the calamity of those who grieve, there is no efficacy in grieving; therefore, I do not grieve today.
Thus addressed, the thousand-eyed Lord Pākaśāsana [replied].
Withdrawing his fury, Śatakratu spoke thus:
"Seeing my arm raised with the thunderbolt and the nooses of Varuṇa,
whose mind here would not tremble— even that of Death himself when he desires to slay?"
Your intellect, which perceives reality, remains unshaken and steadfast;
speaking thus, you do not waver, O you of true prowess. For what embodied being indeed places trust in objects or in the body?
12,220.091c Seeing the world set forth on its course, no one in this world dares to act [against it].
12,220.092a I too know this world to be exactly thus— non-eternal— 12,220.092c placed within the terrible, secret, ever-moving, and imperishable fire of Time.
And there is no escape here for anyone touched by time,
whether they be subtle or great beings undergoing their ripening; for one who is powerless and heedless, the elements are constantly cooking him.
One who has not turned back from time does not escape when its destruction arrives. While beings are heedless, Time remains vigilant among them;
though one strives, no one has ever been seen to transcend it.

The ancient and eternal Dharma is equal toward all living beings; it cannot be avoided by Time, nor can it be transgressed. [Time measures] days and nights, months, moments (kṣaṇas), units of time (kāṣṭhās), divisions (kalās), and instants (lavas).
Time gathers us in, just as a moneylender collects his interest.
Time, having arrived, carries one away who says, "I will do this today, I will do that tomorrow," just as the current of a river sweeps away a raft.
"Just now he was seen by me; how has he died?"—such lamentations are heard from men as they are carried away by time. Wealth, enjoyments, status, and even sovereignty perish in this way.
All is impermanent and unstable; indeed, perseverance is difficult to achieve. The life of those in the world of the living is led away by time as it arrives.
One should not even think in one's mind, "I am happy," as if it were permanent.
Elevations end in falls, and existence resides only within non-existence.
Your intellect, which perceives reality, remains unshaken and immovable;
you do not even conceive in your mind that "I existed in the past."
As this world is being overcome by powerful Time and brought to maturity,
you do not realize that you are being cast down— neither as the eldest nor as the youngest—
amidst envy, pride, greed, desire, anger, and fear.
The world, attached to longing, delusion, and pride, becomes utterly bewildered;
but you, O wise one, who know the true nature of existence and are endowed with knowledge and austerity,
perceive Time as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of your hand.
12,220.105a You know the truth of the movement of time and are proficient in all the scriptures;
12,220.105c O son of Virocana, you have perfected your self and are envied by those who possess wisdom.
12,220.106a For I believe that this entire world has been encompassed by your intellect.
Dwelling liberated in every respect, you do not become attached anywhere. For neither passion nor darkness touches you, whose senses are conquered;
you attend to a self that is free from worldly delight and devoid of the fever of distress.
Seeing you— a friend to all beings, free from enmity, and peaceful in mind— compassion has arisen in me for you. O Buddha, I do not wish to kill one such as you while he is in captivity.

Compassion is the supreme dharma, and such is your benevolence. By the turning of time, these nooses of Varuṇa shall be released from you. Due to the misconduct of living beings, may it be well with you, O great asura.
When a daughter-in-law will employ her aged mother-in-law in menial service,
and when a son, out of delusion, will command his father to perform manual labor;
when Śūdras will cause Brāhmaṇas to wash their feet— [then the end of the age has come].

And Śūdras will fearlessly take Brāhmaṇa women as their wives; even Brāhmaṇas and Śūdras alike will employ them for the sake of sensual enjoyment. And when men shall cast their seed into those who are not of their own kind, [the end of the age has come].
When there is a confusion of castes through the use of bronze vessels and offerings made in inferior containers,
and when the entire fourfold order of society has become lawless,
then each one of your nooses shall be released in succession.
"You have no fear from us; observe your agreement. Be happy, free from affliction, healthy in mind, and without disease.
Having spoken thus to him, the Blessed One Śatakratu—
Having conquered all the asuras, the lord of the gods returned, mounted upon his royal elephant;
he rejoiced with great joy and became the sole sovereign.
The great seers immediately praised Vṛṣākapi,
the lord of all that moves and is stationary;
the dispeller of cold swiftly carried the sacrificial oblation upward.
Thus the nectar was offered to the Lord by the best of the twice-born who had arrived from all directions; praised by them,
the Lord, blazing with splendor, was freed from his anger.
With a tranquil mind and filled with joy, Vāsava reached his own abode, Triviṣṭapa, and rejoiced.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, O Grandfather, tell me the preliminary signs of a man who is destined for success, as well as those of one who is destined for defeat. Bhīṣma said:

The mind alone proclaims for a man his former appearances, as well as those yet to come— may you be blessed— and likewise those that will not come to pass. In this regard, they cite this ancient history.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn from me that conversation between Śrī and Śakra. Having attained equality with the ṛṣis dwelling in the world of Brahmā through the fruition of great asceticism, he beheld both the higher and lower worlds.
Possessing immeasurable and radiant splendor, his sins stilled and his ascetic power great,
Nārada wandered at will through the three worlds. Once, having risen in the morning, he desired to touch the pure water.
He went to the Gaṅgā, which flows from the gate of Dhruva, and descended into it;
beholding that Gaṅgā, which originates from the foot of Meru and has fallen from the foot of Nārāyaṇa,
he approached that place with a joyful heart.
Having reached Gaṅgādvīpa, which is filled with divine beings, possesses fine golden sands, and is adorned with various trees.
Adorned with rows of *sāla*, *tāla*, *aśvakarṇa*, and sandalwood trees, and filled with various flowers and *haṃsa* and *kāraṇḍava* birds,
he reached the riverbank, bathed, and offered libations to the deities.
The righteous-souled one recited his prayers with a radiant absorption in that state.
Then the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of Śambara and Pāka,
arrived at the bank of that river frequented by divine sages.
Having bathed and restrained their minds, the two of them, having performed their prayers,
sat down together upon reaching the riverbank, which was covered with fine golden sand.
There they recounted stories told by divine seers and celebrated for their meritorious deeds.
Those two, whose minds were pure and joyful, engaged in conversation;
composed and focused, they spoke of events from former times that had long passed. Then, the sun rose, preceded by its web of rays.
Beholding the full orb of the moon, the two of them rose and stood waiting;
delighting with joy in a secluded and auspicious place,
they beheld the rising of the sun in the sky.
A light was seen in the sky, filled with blazing flames and adorned by a multitude of stars; rising up on all sides, it possessed a radiance equal to the rising sun, like another sun.
Equal to the brilliance of the sun and possessing a radiance like that of the sun,
O Bhārata, it was seen approaching them;
it was the Vaiṣṇava station, which follows the path of Suparṇa and the sun.
Shining with incomparable splendor, illuminating the three worlds, he blazed forth.
Seeing him, those two valiant ones stood before him with palms joined in reverence,
gazing in turn at that divine and wondrous celestial chariot.
At that time, she was there— truthful, beloved, the darling of the world, supremely auspicious,
the nurse of the world, delightful, the mother of the world, and imperishable—
honored by celestial nymphs of divine and beautiful splendor.
They beheld Śrī, who resembled the vast radiance of the sun, like a great flame; she was adorned with ornaments resembling the stars, wearing a garland of star-like clusters,
and stood visibly upon a lotus like the goddess Padmā herself.

Descending from the top of her celestial chariot, that peerless woman approached Śakra, the lord of the three worlds, and the seer Nārada. Followed by Nārada, Maghavan himself came forward to meet her.

With palms joined in reverence, O King, that all-knowing lord of the gods, having introduced himself to the goddess by his own self, performed incomparable worship for her and spoke these words to Śrī: 12,221.016c With palms joined in reverence, the goddess [was addressed]; having introduced himself to her by his own self, 12,221.017a he, the omniscient one, also performed incomparable worship for her;
and the king of the gods, O King, spoke these words to Śrī.
"Who are you, O lady of lovely smiles, and for what purpose have you arrived?
From where have you come, O fair-browed one, and where must you go, O auspicious lady? Śrī replied:
In the three worlds, among all beings— both stationary and moving— who possess merit, they strive with their supreme self, desiring my own nature. Thus,
I was indeed born from a lotus awakened by the rays of the sun.
For the prosperity of all beings, I am Padmā, Śrī, and she who wears a garland of lotuses. O slayer of Bala, I am Lakṣmī, I am Bhūti, and I am Śrī;
I am faith, intelligence, humility, victory, and stability.
I am fortitude, I am success, I am splendor and prosperity;
I am *svāhā* and *svadhā*, as well as praise, destiny, and action—
present at the forefronts of the armies and upon the banners of victorious kings.

O slayer of Bala, I always dwell with that lord of men who is a hero appearing victorious, who never retreats in battles, and who resides in realms and cities where the people are virtuous in their conduct.
In one who is constant in dharma, possessed of great wisdom, devoted to Brahman, truthful in speech, humble, and of a generous disposition— I always dwell within him;
likewise in one who is ever intent on non-violence, whose words are true, and whose senses are restrained.
"Formerly, I dwelt among the Asuras, bound by the laws of truth; but having perceived them to be perverted, I have chosen to dwell with you. Śakra said:
"O lady of beautiful countenance, how did you dwell among the Daityas of such conduct? And having seen what here, have you come, leaving behind the Daityas and Dānavas?
Śrī replied:
I am indeed devoted to those beings who abide by their own duty, who are unshakable through fortitude,
and who delight in the path to heaven;
[I am devoted] to giving, study, sacrifice, worship, and the honoring of gurus and deities.
Service to the Brahmins and guests was constantly performed by them;
their houses were well-swept, they had conquered their wives, and they maintained the sacred fires.
They were devoted to serving their gurus, self-controlled, venerators of the Veda, and speakers of truth.
Faithful, having conquered anger, characterized by generosity and free from envy,
they have supported their sons, ministers, and wives, and are indeed devoid of jealousy; though not easily provoked, they never at any time covet one another's possessions.
The wise are never distressed by the prosperity of others;
they are givers, gatherers of friends, noble, and compassionate. They possess great serenity, are upright, firm in devotion, and have conquered their senses.
Their servants and ministers were contented, grateful, and pleasant of speech; they bestowed honors and wealth according to merit, were restrained by a sense of shame, and were firm in their vows.
Constantly on festival days, they bathed well, were anointed with unguents, and were beautifully adorned.
Devoted to fasting and austerity, they were renowned exponents of the Veda; the sun never rose while they were still asleep, nor did they ever go to bed before dawn.
At night, they always strictly avoided curd and barley meal.
In the early morning, those pure and celibate ones looked upon the clarified butter;
they beheld auspicious objects and also honored the Brahmins. For the dharma of those who always give is constant, as is the dharma of those who never accept gifts.
May he always approve the inheritance and the distribution of wealth for those who sleep half the night and do not sleep during the day,
as well as for the miserable, the helpless, the aged, the weak, the sick,
and women.
Time has passed for those who abide in happiness and on the path of Dharma.
They constantly offer consolation to those who are dejected, terrified, anxious, afflicted by fear, tormented by disease, robbed of their wealth, and distressed by calamity.

They followed only the Dharma and did not harm one another; they were cooperative in their duties and served their teachers and elders. They also worshipped the ancestors, the gods, and guests in the prescribed manner.
Devoted to truth and austerity, they always eat only what remains;
many do not eat sumptuous food, nor do they go to the wives of others.
They behaved toward all living beings with compassion as they would toward themselves.
They never took pleasure in the emission of the senses at any time— not in open space, nor among livestock, nor in an improper place, nor on sacred festival days.
Furthermore, they were constantly devoted to charity, as well as to skillfulness and straightforwardness at all times.
O Lord, they possessed energy free from egoism, supreme benevolence, and forgiveness;
truthfulness, charity, austerity, purity, compassion, and gentle speech;
and they harbored no malice toward their friends—all these qualities were present in them.
Sleep, lassitude, lack of affection, envy, lack of foresight,
discontent, despondency, and lack of desire did not enter them.
Formerly, I dwelt among the Dānavas who possessed such qualities.
Having undertaken the creation of beings, [I observed] not just one, but many reversals of the ages.
Then, due to that reversal of time and the consequent transformation of their qualities,
I saw that Dharma had vanished from those whose souls were under the sway of desire and anger.
While those elders among the members of the assembly were telling truthful stories, the younger men—
inferior in virtue— laughed at them and showed contempt for all the elders who had approached and sat down together with the youths.
They no longer honored him with rising or salutation as they had before; even while their father was still alive, the sons acted according to their own power,
assuming the role of servants to an enemy and proclaiming it without shame.
Thus, those who attained great wealth through censurable actions that deviated from dharma felt a longing for such things;
and while they spoke aloud at night, the fire there burned low.
Sons addressed their fathers, and wives addressed their husbands;
they did not greet their mothers, fathers, elders, teachers, guests,
or gurus as they were wont to do, nor did they care for their children as they had previously done.
Without giving alms or the sacrificial offering (bali), they eat food themselves;
without having performed sacrifices or distributed portions to the ancestors, gods, guests, and teachers,
their cooks likewise pay no heed to purity.

In thought, deed, and word, their food was consumed without restraint; while the children looked on, they ate the offerings, deluded by folly. Of them there would be one male slave, and likewise two female slaves.
Some Dānavas possessed three cows, while others possessed four;
some had six horses, seven elephants, and others five buffaloes.
They never, even for a night, refrained from curds and barley-meal.
Within ten days, the senseless ones consume the milk of cows;
they do not practice milking in due order, but instead feed upon the calves' own milk. They constantly strike and revile their helpless and wretched wives.
Moreover, Brahmins nourished by the food of Śūdras become shameless;
the housewife does not look after the mixed grains;
and men play with cats, cocks, and dogs.
In the houses of those evil-minded ones, there were thorny trees, as well as *niṣpāva* creepers and sacrificial trees that were to be cut down.
Constantly delighting in bathing at wells, they engage in sexual intercourse on sacred festival days; they eat sesame seeds at night and lie down anointed with oil;
they dwell in the shade and at the roots of *vibhītaka* and *karañja* trees.
Deluded, they will wear the *karavīra* flower;
deluded, they will eat lotus seeds and smell flowers.
Thus, the Daityas, deluded by Time, shall never again enjoy [these things].
Those people, his eternal enemies, reviled the praise of Viṣṇu. There was no smoke from burnt offerings there, nor likewise the sound of the Vedas;
and sacrifices were no longer performed as before in every household.
The succession of disciple and teacher no longer existed; fathers were [taught] by their own sons. Having abandoned Viṣṇu, the Lord of the gods who is devoted to Brahman, they resorted to heresy.
Deprived of offerings to the gods and ancestors, and bereft of knowledge and study, they [fell away].

Those who delight in consuming the property of the gods, as well as those who delight in the property of Brahmā, [shall dwell there]. All the abodes of the gods shall be entirely devoid of hymns and auspicious rites;
the grains shall be scattered about, serving as food for crows and mice.
The milk remained uncovered, and those who had partaken of the remnants touched the clarified butter;
the hoe, the basket, and the vessel were scattered about, and the wife of the household did not even look at any of the utensils or articles.

They did not repair the destruction of their walls and houses; for these women were base, lacking in refinement, devoted only to nourishing their bellies, fallen from purity and proper conduct, shameless, and deprived of true enjoyment.
Furthermore, there were women there who, with both hands, were scratching their heads;
they were situated within the lattice-windows of the houses like artificial husbands placed between their mothers-in-law and fathers-in-law.
Shameless women, though possessing the marks of noble lineage, gaze [lustfully];
they do not respect the livestock they have bound with fodder and water,
as they themselves eat their own food while the children look on.
Likewise, the Dānavas ate all their servants,
and they cooked milk-rice, rice-and-pulse mixtures, meat, cakes,
and fried pastries for their own sake; they consumed meat that was not prepared according to rule.
They all used to sleep after sunrise and rise before dawn;
quarrels broke out there in every house, day and night.
Furthermore, the ignoble ones there would sit around and wait upon those who were noble.
Those established in hermitages who were engaged in improper acts hated one another; intermixture of castes occurred, and purity no longer existed.
Even those Brahmins who were knowers of the Vedas and those who were clearly ignorant of the Ṛgveda [fell into confusion].
Without any distinction between honor and dishonor,
those maidservants attended to his gestures, ornaments, dress, gait, posture, and glances,
following a practice characteristic of wicked people.
Women in male attire and men wearing female dress attained supreme delight in their play, amorous dalliances, and diversions.
They enjoyed the gifts bestowed by their powerful ancestors upon those who were worthy.
12,221.068c Out of atheism, they did not turn back even when opportunities for gain arose; 12,221.069a When a friend was entreated by a friend regarding some matter of doubtful outcome,
they would destroy that wealth for their own sake, even by as much as the tip of a hair.

Those who delighted in taking the property of others were seen engaging in trade and commerce among the noble castes; even Śūdras became rich in asceticism. Some studied the Vedas without observing vows, while others observed vows in vain.
A certain disciple who would not obey his teacher, and a teacher who was merely a companion to his disciples;
likewise, both father and mother, exhausted as if their festivities had ended,
being old and lacking authority, beg for food from their sons.

There, wise men learned in the Vedas, who were like the ocean in depth, became addicted to agriculture and other such pursuits; the fools consumed the *śrāddha* offerings. Day after day, there was the asking of questions, the making of arrangements, and the performance of errands.
The teachers, dispatched as disciples to him, likewise performed their duties;
and the daughter-in-law, in the presence of her mother-in-law and father-in-law, instructed the servants.
And she summoned her husband and spoke to him, giving him counsel.
Even though the father guarded his son’s mind with great effort, they divided [the property] out of agitation and lived in such a state of misery;
wealth was lost through fire, by thieves, or seized by kings.
Seeing them, even those esteemed as friends laughed out of malice;
they were ungrateful, atheistic, wicked, violators of their teachers' wives,
devoted to eating forbidden food, devoid of moral boundaries, and shorn of their luster.
All the sons, having abandoned their parents, followed after their fathers-in-law;
likewise, they spoke thus: "I have been born through my own karma. While they were practicing such conduct in this state of perversion, [the world fell into ruin].
"O Lord of the Gods, it is my resolve that I shall not dwell among the Dānavas.
O Lord of Śacī, welcome me as I have come to you of my own accord.
O Lord of the Devas, once honored by you, the gods will place me at their head."
"Wherever I am, there shall my beloved ones—those distinguished by me and surrendered to me—dwell; seven goddesses with me as the eighth shall abide with me in eightfold form.
They are Āśā, Śraddhā, Dhṛti, Kānti, Vijiti, Sannati, and Kṣamā."
"O Pākaśāsana, the eighth mode of conduct among these is the foremost.
Having abandoned the Asuras, both they and I have come to your realm; we shall dwell among the gods, whose inner selves are established in dharma."
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken these words, both Nārada, the sage of the three worlds, and Vāsava, the slayer of Vṛtra, rejoiced exceedingly at the goddess.
Then, in the abodes of the gods, the wind, the friend of fire, began to blow—
possessing a pleasant fragrance, a comfortable touch, and bringing delight to all the senses. And for the most part, the thirty gods remained in that pure and consecrated place.
Desirous of beholding Maghavan seated together with Lakṣmī,
the thousand-eyed one, endowed with Śrī and accompanied by his friend, the celestial ṛṣi, then reached heaven.
12,221.087c The bull among the gods, highly honored, went to the assembly hall of the deities in a chariot yoked with bay horses;
12,221.088a Then Nārada perceived the gesture of the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Reflecting in his mind upon the goddess Śrī,
he whose prowess was witnessed by the gods announced her arrival there with auspiciousness and great supernatural power.
Then the radiant sky rained down nectar upon the abode of the Self-born Grandfather;
and drums, though unstruck, resounded.
The quarters of the sky shone with such clarity that Vāsava sent rain upon the crops according to the season,
and no one at all swerved from the path of dharma.
The earth was adorned with many mines of jewels,
and the inhabitants of the world rejoiced in its resounding glory; the men were devoted to their duties and possessed of great fame.
Men, gods, kinnaras, yakṣas, and rākṣasas— abiding on the auspicious path of those who perform meritorious deeds— shone forth,
prosperous, happy, and renowned.
Never did a flower fall out of season, much less its fruit, even from a tree shaken by the wind; and the cows yielded milk at will and were like wish-fulfilling cows.
No harsh word was uttered by anyone.
This worship, together with all the wish-granting [trees],
along with Śrī and the deities headed by Śakra—
Those groups of Brahmins who recite this in assembly,
having their desires fulfilled, attain prosperity—
O best of the Kurus, that which was impelled by you.
This supreme exposition on existence and non-existence has been fully proclaimed by me today;
having examined the truth, you ought to accept it.
Remembering Hari, who transcends the range of the intellect and the senses, who is the abode of all within his own domain, and who removes great sins— those people [attain liberation].
Having recollected and fully worshipped [Him], their sins were shaken off;
they were constantly restrained by restraints and observances,
and they beheld the true nature of Viṣṇu.
By following the path of the gods, those who immerse themselves in the yoga of liberation attain the supreme state;
even so, O Indra among kings, one who is constantly devoted to recitation and fire-offerings [attains the same].

Constantly devoted to Vāsudeva and dedicated to knowledge and meditation, always delighting in the duty of charity, do you protect the subjects. [Protect those] who are constantly devoted to Vāsudeva and dedicated to knowledge and meditation.
"You should honor them with distinction and constantly attend upon them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What should be their character, what their conduct, what their knowledge, and what their ultimate goal?"
One attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme, eternal, and beyond primordial nature.
Bhīṣma said:
One who is disciplined in the duties of liberation, moderate in diet, and has conquered the senses—
He attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme, eternal, and beyond primordial nature (prakṛti).
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Jaigīṣavya and Asita.

O Indra among kings, listen duly to that which occurred during the interval of Mahādeva and likewise during the interval of the Goddess; it bestows knowledge and destroys sin. [It concerns] Jaigīṣavya, the highly wise one, who has mastered the traditional teachings of the Dharmas.
Asita Devala said to him who neither became angry nor rejoiced:
"You do not feel pleasure when being praised, nor do you become angry when being reviled.
What is this wisdom of yours? From where does it come? And what is its ultimate goal?"

Thus questioned by him, that great ascetic spoke to him these great words— unambiguous, pure, and full of profound meaning: "That which is the goal, that which is the supreme state, and that which is the peace of those who perform meritorious deeds."
I shall fully declare that to you, O twice-born one, concerning which you indeed ask me:
one who is always equal toward those who revile and those who praise, O Devala,
and who conceals both their agreements and their good deeds.
Those who have been addressed do not wish to speak to one intent on their harm;
indeed, the wise do not desire to strike back at their assailant. They do not grieve for what has not yet come to pass, but act when the time is right.
They do not grieve for those who have passed away, nor do they claim them as their own.
And when those worthy of honor arrive, O Devala, those capable ones who have undertaken their vows provide for their needs according to their desire and their means.
Those of perfected knowledge, possessed of great wisdom, having conquered anger and subdued their senses,
do not offend anyone in thought, deed, or word. Free from envy, they never cause harm to one another at any time.
The wise are never distressed by the prosperity of others;
they do not excessively speak of the blame or praise of another,
nor are they ever altered by such blame or praise.
Those who are completely tranquil in every way and devoted to the welfare of all beings—
neither angry nor elated, and never offending anyone—
they wander at their ease, having untied the knots of the heart.
Those mortals who act in this way live happily at all times— those who have no kinsmen and are not the kinsmen of others; those who have no enemies and are not the enemies of anyone.
O best of the twice-born, those who know the Dharma follow the Dharma alone;
for those who have fallen away from this path both rejoice and tremble with fear.
Having established myself upon that path, whom should I envy, and in what manner?
Whether being censured or praised, for what reason should I feel elated? Whatever path men desire, they pursue it;
neither censure nor praise will cause my decline or my increase.

The knower of reality should be as satisfied with contempt as if it were nectar; the wise man should always shrink from honor as if it were poison. One who is disregarded sleeps happily both in this world and in the next.
He who treats [this] with contempt is bound, though he may be liberated from all sins.
And those wise men who seek the supreme goal—
by relying upon this vow, those people prosper in happiness.
Having gathered together all sacrifices from every quarter, one who has conquered the senses attains the station of Brahman, which is supreme and eternal beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Neither the gods, nor the *gandharvas*, nor the *piśācas*, nor the *rākṣasas* [can reach it].
They descend upon the state of one who has attained the supreme goal. Having heard these words of that sage, Devala likewise became his disciple, dependent upon him and liberated from all dualities.
Now, O King, listen with attention to another ancient account concerning the wise Jaigīṣavya— one who is endowed with all knowledge,
whom they call the Lord of all worlds and who is honored by all the worlds.
He who possesses eight forms and is the form of the universe, adorned with his desired alliances;
having attained whom, people do not despair, do not grieve, and do not tremble;
whose inherent power is this entire world, both moving and unmoving.
That god, the Supreme Lord, whose self is all-pervading, moves and abides there. To the northeast of Mount Meru, in a place adorned with every kind of jewel,
inconceivable and stainless, and filled with flowers of every season—
It is eternally adorned with trees stirred by divine breezes;
it is frequented by various hosts of beings and is honored by all the gods.
There, the hosts of Vidyādharas and the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases [dwell].
The world-protectors, the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the lakes;
the Vālakhilya sages, the sacrifices, and those called *stobhas*;
as well as the lords of creatures—all these paid homage to the God.
There, the illustrious Rudra Mahādeva, whose banner bears the bull and whose eyes are the moon, the sun, and fire, dwells together with the goddess Umā.
Having thus beheld the god there, the goddess Dhātrī Vibhāvarī [approached].
12,222.024d@024_0021 Umā, the goddess, filled with humility, questioned the Supreme Lord:
12,222.024d@024_0022 "O Blessed One, what is *artha*, and what is the power of *artha*? Tell me, for I am seeking this.
12,222.024d@024_0023 Thus questioned by her, the god Maheśvara spoke.
I am the object of purpose, and you are the power of that purpose; I am the enjoyer, and you are indeed the object of enjoyment.
Know this, O illustrious one: you are *prakṛti* (primordial nature), for I am the Supreme.
I am Viṣṇu, I am Brahmā, and likewise, I am the sacrifice itself.
"O weak one, there is no difference between us in the ultimate sense; nevertheless, we perceive a distinction in you. Why, then, do you question me?
Having been addressed thus, she then said: 'Tell me more about these two.'"
"O Mahādeva, I know you as the Supreme; 'Salutation' (namaḥ) alone," said the passionate woman.
Standing in that interval was the wise great sage Jaigīṣavya, who, in the form of a Vasu, smilingly spoke, making the sound "Artha" (the Goal).
"Another superior [element] exists apart from us, the mass of earth; the *apara-śakti* is merged within it, having been expanded and accumulated through specific forms such as rings and the like.
Having heard these words, the Goddess asked in anger, "Who is this?"
"Having broken this statement of Śaṃkara today," he said.
Hearing that, the wise and great sage departed for his own hermitage; the learned one, endowed with the sovereign power of yoga, left his place for the company of the gods in heaven.
Then, having laughed, the Blessed One Hara, the remover of all sins,
the great sage Jaigīṣavya of tranquil soul, spoke to the Goddess:
"This great sage here is my devotee, my friend, and my disciple."
Having said, "I am known as Jaigīṣavya," he departed, O auspicious lady.
Upon hearing that, she became enraged and thought, "He has indeed acted improperly;
O Lord, I have been disfigured by him, and likewise by the sage."
"O Lord of Gods, I did not hear that [teaching] when it was received in the midst of those ignorant of it.
Having heard this, the Blessed One, Mahādeva, the wielder of the Pināka bow, said:
"That sage, a yogi free from all expectations, remains established by taking refuge in me."

"Free from dualities, ever wise, and established in the nature of equanimity—therefore, O Goddess, forgive him; he must be protected by you. Thus addressed, that goddess spoke to the high-souled sage.
"O Destroyer of Death, I wish to see the state of hopelessness.
Having said "So be it," the Lord, the Master of the World, mounted his bull with haste while being praised by hosts of gods and gandharvas.
Where that great sage dwells— his self unaging, immortal, and pure—
there the highly illustrious sage, wandering at that time for the sake of clothing his body, gathered [materials] here and there with hosts of heroes.
Having gone out to meet Mahādeva and honored him as was fitting,
he once again sewed his tattered garment with needle and thread as before.
The Blessed Lord Śambhu said to him, "O Sage, what shall I give to you?"
"Choose from me, Jaigīṣavya, everything that you desire.
But not looking up at the God of gods, the great sage said,
"O Lord whose banner is the bull, I see nothing unattained from you."

"I have achieved my purpose and am fulfilled; since you have what needs to be done, you may depart. Laughing, Śarva spoke to him again: "Choose a boon from me; indeed, an unsurpassed boon must certainly be granted by me."
Jaigīṣavya said to him, "This must be heard by you from me:
O Mahādeva, as one follows the thread along the needle, [so it is with this].
Then the Blessed One, Śaṅkara, laughed and looked toward Gaurī."
Rejoicing and honored by all the gods, he departed for his own abode.
This has been told to you, O King, concerning that which you asked.
Those self-existent ones are eternally free from the pairs of opposites and are yogis in every respect.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who indeed on earth is that man who is beloved by all the world, who is cheered by all living beings, and who is endowed with every virtue?"
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, O bull of the Bharatas, since you ask,
I shall relate to you the conversation between Ugrasena and Keśava concerning Nārada."
Ugrasena said:
"Behold, the world is intent upon the praise of Nārada; I consider him to be endowed with all virtues. Tell me about him as I ask you."
Vāsudeva said:
"O lord of the Kukuras, listen as I speak of those whom I consider [worthy],
by hearing which your mind shall become pure and attain the state of supreme sovereignty."
O lord of men, I have briefly described the virtuous qualities of Nārada. He possesses no egoism born of his conduct that would lead to the destruction of his body;
because his learning and conduct are inseparable, he is honored everywhere.
Lack of contentment, anger, fickleness, and fear—these do not exist in Nārada. He is not dilatory and is courageous; therefore, he is honored everywhere.
Nārada is truly an ascetic, and there is no transgression in his speech.
Whether out of desire or out of greed, he is therefore honored everywhere.
Knowing the true principle of the internal discipline, patient, capable, with senses conquered,
upright, and truthful— therefore he is honored everywhere.

By virtue of his splendor, fame, intelligence, policy, and discipline, as well as by his birth and asceticism, he was aged; therefore, he was honored everywhere. He was pleasant in character, possessed of excellent enjoyments, provided with fine food, respectful, and pure.
He is eloquent and free from envy; therefore, he is honored everywhere.
He performs what is auspicious with great vigor, and no evil is found in him.
He does not take pleasure in the wealth of others; therefore, he is honored everywhere.
Through the Vedic revelations and sacred narratives, he seeks to master the true meanings;
being patient and free from contempt, he is therefore honored everywhere. Indeed, because of his equanimity, there is no one who is dear to him nor anyone who is disliked in any way whatsoever.
Speaking agreeably to the mind, he is therefore honored everywhere.
Being learned, a narrator of wonderful tales, wise, untiring, and free from deceit;
being undepressed, free from anger, and without greed—he is therefore honored everywhere.
Never before has he had a conflict regarding wealth, dharma, or pleasure;
his faults have been utterly eradicated, and therefore he is honored everywhere. He is firm in devotion, blameless in character, learned, and free from cruelty.
Free from the defect of delusion, he is therefore honored everywhere; unattached to all attachments, yet appearing as if his soul were attached;
free from prolonged doubt and eloquent in speech, he is therefore honored everywhere.
His concentration is not for the sake of pride, nor does he ever praise himself; free from envy and firm in speech, he is therefore honored everywhere,
never disparaging the various conducts of the world or even its inherent nature.
Skilled in the science of association, he is therefore honored everywhere.
He does not find fault with any traditional teaching, nor does he live off his own ascetic power.
His time is never spent in vain, and his self is under control; therefore, he is honored everywhere.
Having exerted effort and perfected his wisdom, yet not satiated with meditative concentration,
remaining steadfast in his observances and vigilant, he is therefore honored everywhere;
modest, disciplined, and easy to lead, he is guided by others toward the highest good.
He does not betray the secrets of others, and for that reason he is honored everywhere.
He does not rejoice in gains, nor is he distressed by losses;
with steady intellect and unattached soul, he is therefore honored everywhere.
"Who would not do what is pleasing to one who is endowed with all virtues, skillful, pure, undaunted, knowledgeable of the proper time, and an expert in policy?
Having spoken thus and praised him, Ugrasena departed from the palace.
Kṛṣṇa was seated thus in solitude upon a couch adorned with jewels.
Once, the venerable great sage entered there;
having honored him according to the prescribed rule, Janārdana remained silent.
Perceiving Keśava to be as if distressed, he spoke these words:
"O Keśava, O Janārdana, what is this dejection of yours?
Śrī Vāsudeva said:
"O Govinda, you ought to explain to me this which has never happened before:
today no one who is not my dear friend deserves to know my supreme misfortune, whether he be unwise or wise, and whether he be self-controlled or lacking self-control."
As such, you are a friend, a wise man, and one who has conquered his own self; you ought to listen.
You ought to hear that sorrow which dwells in my heart. Out of a desire for sovereignty, I am even performing servitude toward my kinsmen.
"His kinsmen, relatives, and friends constantly hate him in their anger;
likewise, even divine enjoyments were separately bestowed upon them by me.
Nārada said:
"Nevertheless, those who hate me continue to exist among one another. Having polished and wiped it repeatedly with a weapon not made of iron,
the Blessed One said:
"Pull out their tongues, so that they shall not speak further.
O best of sages, how may I obtain a weapon that is not made of iron?
Nārada said:
"Tell me that truthfully, by which means their tongues may be pulled out. Cast into their mouths cows, gold, garments, jewels, and whatever great wealth there is—
this weapon of theirs is not made of iron."

This weapon has indeed been described as being for one's friends, relatives, allies, teachers, and kinsmen; therefore, cut again and again with it their bestowals of sovereignty upon you and their praiseworthy words.
Bhīṣma said:
"Recognizing you as capable, those men speak thus.
Then the Blessed One, having laughed and honored the great sage, [spoke].
Thus did he of great splendor act, impelled by the words of the sage.
Such is the power of Nārada, the best of sages and a Brahman-seer. O best of kings, that which you asked me has now been told.
"Engaged in the welfare of all beings and devoted to the dharma of truth,
those who are skilled in knowledge and discernment attain the state of being beloved by the world.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Kaurava, I wish to hear about the beginning and end of all beings,
their meditation, their actions, and likewise the time and the lifespan in each age;
as well as the reality of the world in its entirety, and the coming and going of beings."

From where do creation and destruction proceed? What is the differentiator, and what is the reality of differentiation? Likewise, what is the opinion of others, and what indeed is the threefold state, O Grandfather?
"O best of virtuous men, if your mind is inclined toward showing us favor here, I ask this of you; may you explain it to me. For having previously heard the supreme words spoken by Bhṛgu,"

From that [instruction] of the brahmin-seer Bharadvāja, my supreme intellect has arisen—most righteous and established in a divine state. Therefore, I ask you further; you ought to explain that to me.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history (itihāsa) which the blessed Vyāsa sang to his son when he questioned him.

Having studied all the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches and Upaniṣads, Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, seeking the lifelong practice of asceticism out of his perception of the subtleties of dharma, approached Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.
He asked about this doubt, having severed his uncertainty regarding dharma and artha; [he asked] about the creator of the multitude of beings, certainty in the knowledge of time,
wisdom, Brahman, and yoga, and how this world consists of the cow.
But when this [fourth] arrives within the triad, then how indeed could there be a distinction? For how could there be a fourth without defining characteristics;
and what would this entity be that appears as distinct within the interval between knowledge and the object of knowledge?
"You ought to explain that knowledge, as well as their characteristics and their creator, and what the duty of a Brahmin is. To him,
his father spoke all of that as he was questioned by his son.
The wise one, the omniscient knower of all phenomena, who knows both the past and the future— O true son, as you ask me, I shall declare this to you exactly as it is.
Listen with focused attention to how this world has come to be.
Having known both that which begins with the effect and ends with the cause, and that which begins with the cause and ends with the effect— that knowledge, which is true, supreme, and auspicious,
is celebrated as Brahman; indeed, the wise perceive it as such.

In the beginning, there was the wondrous Brahman, a being composed of splendor and the cause of all beings; those who know it call that the Pradhāna. They know that Great Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas, to be the Prakṛti belonging to Viṣṇu.

That which is thus without beginning or end, unmanifest, undecaying, and eternal; inconceivable and unknowable, that was the first modification of Brahman. That indeed is designated as Pradhāna, consisting of the three subtle [principles] and having the nature of the three qualities (guṇas).

The great [Principle], established in its own state, possesses the quality of perfect yoga; yet when agitated by desire, its nature—which consists of the three powers—is causal in essence. It is eternally dependent and joined with a presiding controller.
Having entered into that which is called her own nature, she assumes a form of delusion; she has arrived for the sake of the enjoyment of this various living being,
just as a fragrance causes agitation by its mere presence.
In that same way, the mind is remembered as being higher than the entirety [of the elements];
having created it and entered into it, He, remaining therein, caused agitation.
The Great Principle (mahat) is threefold: characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa).
Emerging from the principle of Pradhāna, it is known as the Great (Mahat) because of its greatness.
The principle of Mahat, having emerged, completely enveloped the principle of Pradhāna. Overpowered by Time, that [Mahat] is a portion of the Supreme Self.

And that very one is sung of as the Person of immeasurable self; he is known as the Great One, and the Veda indeed calls him Pradhāna. He consists of threefold nature: the Sāttvika, the Rājasa, and the Tāmasa.
This threefold ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) was born from the principle of the Great One (mahattattva). This tamasic ego-sense is designated as "the source of the elements" (bhūtādi);
because it is the origin of the elements, this tamasic ego is known as the "red serpent."

That *bhūtādi*, undergoing transformation, then emitted the remaining subtle element (*tanmātra*); it produced the subtle element of sound, which is space characterized by sound. Space, characterized by sound, enveloped the subtle element of sound.
Being compressed by that, he emitted the mere quality of touch;
that [quality] became space (ākāśa), and the mere quality of sound enveloped the mere quality of touch. By being compressed by that, he emitted wind—so says the sacred tradition (śruti).
Then the wind, which consists of the subtle element of touch alone, enveloped the subtle element of form;
being thus compressed by it, it emitted fire—so says the Śruti. Then the subtle element of form, having emitted the fire, enveloped it.
Being pressed by that, he emitted the mere essence of taste;
the light residing in the mere form enveloped the mere essence of taste.
Being pressed by that, he emitted water—so says the sacred tradition.

The subtle element of taste (*rasa-tanmātra*), consisting of the essence of taste, further enveloped the subtle element of taste; being compressed by that, it then emitted the subtle element of smell (*gandha-tanmātra*),
which likewise enveloped the water-pot [the subtle element of taste].

Being thus compressed by that [sound], it emitted solidity; from that, born from the subtle element of smell (gandha-tanmātra), the earth was produced. All this is indeed composed of water, yet the waters solidified once again.

These elements—earth and the others—have indeed arisen; such is the Vedic revelation. The wise consider that the very form of these elements is their food, and that within each of them lies a subtle essence (*tanmātra*); thus they are known as *tanmātras*.
They say the ten sense organs are taijasa, while the ten deities are vaikārika;
here, the eleventh, the mind, is also recorded as being a vaikārika deity. Time is their upholder, existing in various distinct forms.
The Supreme Self and the Elemental Self exist through the differentiation of the qualities (*guṇas*);
though one alone, divided threefold, He performs various activities.
As Brahmā, He creates beings; as the imperishable Nārāyaṇa, He protects them.
Rudra, whose form is the universe, is Time (Kāla), the knower of action;
even Time is composed of that [Rudra], inconceivable, eternal, and consisting of the three qualities (guṇas). Unmanifest and inconceivable, he exists with distinct characteristics.
However, this [universe], though divided by the nature of time, is heard to be non-different [from Brahman];
for that which is without beginning or end, unborn, divine, undecaying, firm, and immutable,
inconceivable and unknowable, existed as Brahman in the beginning.
Fifteen *nimeṣas* make one *kāṣṭhā*,
and one should count thirty *kāṣṭhās* as one *kalā*;
thirty *kalās* likewise constitute one *muhūrta*.
The tenth part of a *kalā* would be one-twelfth [of a day];
thirty *muhūrtas* constitute a day and a night— such is the calculation set forth by the sages.
A month is said to consist of thirty nights and days;
twelve months are declared to be a year.
They say that a year consists of two solstices (ayana).
The sun divides day and night for the human world;
for living beings, night is for sleep and day is for the performance of actions.
A month is a night and a day for the ancestors; furthermore, their division is as follows:
the dark fortnight is the day for the performance of ritual acts, and the bright fortnight is the night for sleep.
A year is a night and a day for the gods; furthermore, their division is as follows: [the winter solstice is the day and the summer solstice is the night].
There, twelve thousand years constitute the northern course (udagayana), and the night would be the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana).
Having calculated the number of those days and nights previously described as pertaining to the world of the gods, I shall now declare the total duration of a year in the day and night of Brahmā.
I shall declare to you, in due order, the number of years at the beginning of those ages:
the Kṛta, the Tretā Yuga, as well as the Dvāpara and the Kali.
They say that the Kṛta Yuga consists of four thousand years.
Its morning twilight and its evening twilight are each of that same duration;
in the other three ages, along with their respective twilights and twilight-portions,
the thousands and hundreds decrease by one.
These sustain the eternal and ancient worlds;
this, O dear one, is known as the eternal Brahman by those who know Brahman. In the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete in its four quarters, as was Truth.
No acquisition whatsoever proceeds for him through unrighteousness (*adharma*). In others, however, dharma is diminished by one quarter through their conduct;
truth, purity, longevity, and dharma likewise depart quarter by quarter.
Through theft, falsehood, and deceit, unrighteousness increases.
In the Kṛta age, people are free from disease, achieve all their goals, and have a lifespan of four hundred years;
in the Tretā and subsequent ages, their lifespan decreases by one quarter in each.
We have heard that the declarations of the Vedas diminish with each successive age,
as do lifespans, blessings, and the very fruits of the Veda itself.
The duties in the Kṛta age are of one kind, and those in the Tretā and Dvāpara ages are different.
In the Kali age, other duties are performed according to one's capacity, as it were.
Austerity is supreme in the Kṛta age; knowledge is highest in the Tretā;
they say sacrifice alone is the duty in the Dvāpara; and charity alone in the Kali age.
The wise know this period of twelve thousand [years] as what is called a *yuga*.
A thousand such cycles is said to be a single day of Brahmā; his night is of equal duration. At the beginning of that day, the Lord creates the universe.
Having entered the inner self at the time of dissolution and slept, he awakens at the end;
those people who know that the day of Brahmā lasts for a thousand yugas,
and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas, are the ones who truly understand day and night.
Awakened at the end of the night, Brahmā undergoes transformation;
he creates the Great Being (mahad-bhūta), and from that arises the mind (manas) whose nature is manifest. This Brahmā is composed of splendor and is the seed from which this entire world proceeds.
From each single element, the two-fold world of the stationary and the moving arises.
At the beginning of the day, having awakened, he creates the universe through his creative knowledge (*vidyā*).
First of all, he creates the great element, the mind (*manas*), which is characterized by rapid manifestation.
Overpowering all that is luminous here, he emitted the seven mental sons;
the mind, impelled by the desire to create, brings forth its own creation— far-reaching, manifold in its course, and characterized by longing and doubt.

From that, space (ākāśa) is born; sound is considered its quality. From space, undergoing transformation, arises the pure and powerful wind (vāyu), which carries all fragrances; touch is considered its quality.

From the transforming wind, light—dispeller of darkness—is born; it is radiant and is said to have the quality of form (*rūpa*). From the transforming light, the waters arise, whose essence is taste (*rasa*).
From water, earth arises with the quality of fragrance; this is said to be the prior creation.

The qualities of each preceding element are acquired by each subsequent one. Whichever element possesses a specific number of constituent parts, it is traditionally held to possess that many qualities.

If some, through lack of skill, should perceive fragrance in water and say it is there, one should know that it belongs to earth alone, which has taken refuge in both water and air. These seven persons, however, possess diverse powers individually.
Unable to create living beings without coming together from all sides,
they met and took refuge in one another, that Great-Souled One;
thus, having obtained a support for their bodies, he is called Puruṣa.
From this nourishment, the body becomes embodied and composed of sixteen constituents. The great elements enter it along with karma,
having taken up all beings for the sake of practicing austerity.
They call that very Great Being the original creator, Prajāpati.
He indeed creates all beings; he alone is the supreme Puruṣa. As the unborn, he generates Brahmā, the celestial seers, the ancestors, and human beings.
The worlds, rivers, oceans, directions, mountains, and trees; humans, kinnaras, and rākṣasas; birds, domestic animals, wild beasts, and serpents;
both the imperishable and the perishable—the duality of the stationary and the moving.
Whatever actions they performed in a previous creation, those very same actions they undertake again and again as they are created anew—
whether violent or non-violent, gentle or cruel, righteous or unrighteous, truthful or false.
Therefore, whatever the Creator (dhātṛ) intends, that is what pleases him.
The diversity among the great elements, the objects of the senses, and material forms, as well as the specific application of all beings, the Creator alone ordains.
Some people who understand action say that human effort is the cause; other Brahmins say it is destiny, while those who contemplate the elements say it is inherent nature.
Human effort, action, destiny, and the manifestation of results all arise from inherent nature.
These three are inseparable, yet some do not perceive their lack of distinction.
Thus it is that the elements create the world—both as "it is so" and "it is not so.
Those established in action speak of inequality, while those established in *sattva* perceive with equanimity.
Austerity is the supreme good for a living being; its roots are self-restraint and tranquility.
By means of that, one obtains all those desires which one wishes for in the mind.
Through austerity, one attains that by which he creates the world of beings.
Having become that, he becomes the lord of all beings.
The seers studied the Vedas day and night through austerity;
the speech, without beginning or end and eternal, was emitted by the Self-existent One.
In the beginning, there was the divine Veda, from which all activities proceed;
the names of the ṛṣis, the creations found within the Vedas,
the manifold forms of beings, and the setting in motion of karmic actions.
In the beginning, that Lord creates from the very words of the Veda the names of the seers and those creations which appear in the Vedas;
at the end of each night, he bestows upon those who are born exactly those same things.
The distinctions of names—known as austerity, action, and sacrifice—are worldly accomplishments;

however, self-perfection (*ātmasiddhi*) is proclaimed in the Vedas through ten successive stages. That which has been declared in the Vedic discourses is profound, being perceived by those with Vedic vision.
At their respective ends, this is observed according to the proper sequence of application:
this state of separation, joined with the pairs of opposites, arises from karma;
yet once the realization of the Self is attained, it generally loses its power.
Two Brahmas are to be known: the Śabdabrahman and that which is the Supreme Brahma. One who is proficient in the Śabdabrahman attains the Supreme Brahma.
Sacrifices involving physical undertakings belong to the Kṣatriyas, while the Havis-sacrifices belong to the Vaiśyas.
Śūdras have the sacrifice of service, while the twice-born have the sacrifice of austerity;
such is the rule for these sacrifices in the Tretā Yuga, but not in the Kṛta Yuga. In the Dvāpara, sacrifices fall into disorder, and likewise in the Kali Yuga.

In the Tretā age, those mortals of great power— who were not distinct in their essential nature from the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas— perceived desired prosperity as something separate through their ascetic penances, and thus they appeared as a unified whole.
They are the restrainers of all things, both stationary and moving. Indeed, in the Tretā age, these sacrifices and the social orders were unified;
however, due to the contraction of the lifespan, they become divided in the Dvāpara age.

In the Kali age, the Vedas in their entirety are neither seen nor even perceived; together with the sacrifices, they utterly perish, leaving only the mere remnants of the bridges of dharma. That dharma which was clearly manifest among the Brāhmaṇas in the Kṛta age—

Established among those who possess self-control, asceticism, and sacred learning, the declarations of the Vedas— though abiding in their own dharma— are modified according to the dharma of each successive age, following the conjunction of unrighteous vows with each yuga.
Just as all beings, both moving and stationary, become more numerous through rain during the monsoon season, so too do dharmas arise in each successive age;
just as the various signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle.
Those very same things are seen likewise during the day and night of Brahmā;
thus has the diversity of time, which is without beginning or end,
been described to you previously— that which procreates and devours all creatures.
Yama, the restrainer, establishes the place for the maintenance of beings;
by their very nature, they exist in abundance, joined with pairs of opposites.
Emanation, time, action, the Vedas, the agent, the object, the act, and the fruit [are all established].
"O son, everything that you asked me has indeed been told to you.
Now I shall describe the withdrawal [of the senses] at the beginning of the night when the day has passed—
how the Lord performs this most subtle internalization of the universe."
In the sky, the seven suns, like crested fires, burn with their radiance;
at that time, this entire world is set ablaze, filled with those flames.
Vyāsa said:
Whatever beings exist on earth, both moving and stationary, they first dissolve and return to the state of earth. Then,
when all things, both stationary and moving, have likewise dissolved, [the earth dissolves].
The earth is seen to be without wood and devoid of grass, appearing like the back of a tortoise.
When the waters take up the quality of smell from the earth,
the earth, its scent having been taken away, is then prepared for dissolution.
Then the waters arise, surging with waves and making a great roar;
filling this entire world, they remain still and flow. O dear one, when light takes up even the qualities of the waters, [it prevails].
Then the waters, having assumed their qualities, cease within the light;
when the crests of the flames conceal the sun situated in their midst,
this entire sky blazes forth, filled with those very rays.
When the wind seizes even the quality of light, its form,
then the light subsides and the great wind blows violently.
Then, having reached the root of its own origin, the wind [remains].
It vibrates below, above, and across the ten directions;
when space swallows even the quality of wind— touch—
it is then that wind subsides, and space remains resounding.
Formless, without taste or touch, without smell, and not possessing material form,
it resounds through all the worlds yet remains itself without sounding.
The mind makes manifest sound, which is the quality of space.
And when he too devours [the mind], it becomes tranquil during the reabsorption (*pratisaṃcara*). That reabsorption of the manifest and unmanifest mind is the state of Brahman.
Then, having entered the quality of the self (*ātman*), the moon devours the mind.

When the mind has ceased its activity, it abides within the internal moon. After a long period of time, volition brings that [moon] under its control; volition swallows the mind, and that is the unsurpassed knowledge.
"Time swallows consciousness; Time is power—so says the sacred tradition.
But the wise man brings that power under his own control, for he makes Time itself subject to him.
Then, the wise man internalizes that very sound of space within his own self."

That is the unmanifest, the supreme Brahman; it is eternal and unsurpassed. Thus all beings are indeed merged back into Brahman. This has been correctly proclaimed exactly as it is; of this there is no doubt.
Having perceived that which is to be awakened as consisting of knowledge, by yogins who are supreme selves,
so too do expansion and contraction occur again and again for Brahmā in the unmanifest—
at the beginning of the thousand yugas of his day, and likewise at the beginning of his night.
Vyāsa said:
I have thus described to you that which is ordained for the multitude of living beings;
now I shall declare to you, who ask, what the duty of a Brāhmaṇa is.

From the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) onwards, his performance of rites accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should continue until his formal return (*samāvartana*) from the teacher who has mastered the Vedas;
having studied all the Vedas while remaining devoted to service for his guru.

Having become free from his debts to his teachers and being conversant with the sacrifices, he should perform the *samāvartana* ceremony; then, permitted by his teacher, he should duly observe one of the four stages of life (*āśrama*) until the liberation of his body.
Whether by procreating offspring and taking a wife, or again by practicing celibacy, or by living in the forest in the presence of a guru, or again by following the duty of an ascetic—
the householder alone is said to be the root of all four [stages of life].
There, indeed, one whose impurities have been cooked away and who is self-controlled succeeds in every respect;
possessing progeny, learned in the Vedas, and having performed sacrifices, he is liberated from the three divine debts and thereafter,
purified by his deeds, proceeds to the other stages of life.
One should dwell in whatever field of knowledge on earth is most meritorious; one should strive therein to attain authority and supreme fame,
whether through very great austerity or by reaching the further shore of the sciences.
Through sacrifice or through gifts to the Brahmins, one’s fame increases;
for as long as one’s glorious renown persists in this world,
for that long does a person enjoy the infinite worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds.

He should teach, he should study, he should officiate at sacrifices for others, and he should perform sacrifices himself; he should not accept gifts in vain, nor should he give them away under any circumstances—
even if he receives great wealth from a patron, from a pupil, or even through a daughter.

If [a guest] should arrive, one should sacrifice for him, give to him, and under no circumstances should one eat alone. For one who dwells in the home, there is no other sacred ford than the act of receiving [gifts] for the sake of the gods, sages, ancestors, and teachers, or for the aged, the sick, and those who are hungry.
To those who have disappeared from view yet are tormented by distress and who desire to survive according to their strength,
one should give goods even beyond one's own capacity, even if they have been prepared for others;
for there is nothing whatsoever that should not be given to those worthy ones who are appropriate recipients.
They know that even the horse Uccaiḥśravas is to be bestowed upon the virtuous;
having given it away, he went to the worlds praised by the gods, beginning with that of Brahmā. Having thus conciliated him, Kāvya—true to his promise and of great vows—[departed].

Having saved the life of a brahmin with his own life-breaths, he ascended to heaven. And Rantideva, the son of Saṃkṛti, having offered cool and warm water to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, is glorified upon the surface of the celestial realm.
Having given various kinds of wealth to the two Arhats, Candramas and Damaya, that wise lord of the earth, Ātreya, went to the infinite worlds.
Śibi Auśīnara gave his limbs and his own beloved biological son.
Having dedicated himself for the sake of a Brahmin, Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, departed from here to the vault of heaven; by giving his own eyes to a Brahmin,
he enjoys incomparable fame both in this world and the next.
Having given a divine, golden umbrella of supreme splendor, adorned with polished ribs, Devāvṛdha ascended to heaven along with his entire kingdom.
Likewise, Sāṃkṛti of the Atri lineage [bestowed] the attributeless Brahman upon his disciples.
Having instructed him, the one of great splendor departed for the unsurpassed worlds. After giving cows to the Brahmins, the powerful Ambarīṣa,
together with his kingdom, ascended to heaven— ten and one *arbudas* of them.
Sāvitrī gave up her two divine earrings and Janamejaya his own body for the sake of a Brahmin; having thus sacrificed themselves, they both went to the highest world.
Vṛṣādarbhi, Yuvanāśva, and others likewise gave away all their jewels and their beloved wives.
Having given a beautiful dwelling, he departed for that world;
Nimi gave his kingdom to the Brahmins, the son of Jamadagni gave the earth, and Gaya likewise gave the earth with its cities.
And when the rain-god did not send down rain, Vasiṣṭha repeatedly restored all living beings to life, just as Prajāpati restores his progeny;
likewise, Marutta was the son of Karaṃdhama, a king.
Having given his daughter to Aṅgiras, he quickly ascended to heaven.
And Brahmadatta, the king of the Pañcālas and the best among the wise,
having given the treasure Śaṅkha to the foremost of the twice-born, attained the celestial worlds.
King Mitrasaha, having given his beloved Madayantī to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, ascended to heaven along with her;
and the illustrious royal sage Sahasrajit likewise gave up his cherished life.

Having renounced everything for the sake of a brahmin, King Śatadyumna went to the unsurpassed worlds; having given a golden mansion filled with all objects of desire to Mudgala, that lord of the earth departed for heaven.
The powerful Śālvarāja, known by the name Dyutimat,
having given his kingdom to Ṛcīka, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
And the royal seer Madirāśva, having given away his slender-waisted daughter, [went to those same realms].
Hiraṇyahasta went to the worlds praised by the gods;
and the lordly royal seer Lomapāda, having given his daughter Śāntā to Ṛśyaśṛṅga, was united with all abundant objects of desire.
Having given a hundred thousand cows along with their calves, King Prasenajit,
endowed with great splendor, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
These and many others likewise [attained success] through gift-giving and austerity.
Those high-souled ones, disciplined in spirit and having conquered their senses, have gone to heaven;
their fame is firmly established for as long as the earth shall endure,
for it was through acts of charity, sacrifice, and the procreation of offspring that they attained the celestial realm.
Vyāsa said:
One should examine the knowledge of the three Vedas as declared in the Vedas and their auxiliary branches—
namely, according to the syllables and letters of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, Yajurveda, and likewise the Atharvaveda.
The Blessed One abides established in these six duties. For those who are skilled in the Vedic doctrines and proficient in the knowledge of the inner self—
those beings of great fortune— they perceive both the origin and the dissolution [of all things].

Thus he should conduct himself according to dharma and act like those who are refined; indeed, the twice-born man should seek his livelihood without causing obstruction to living beings. Having acquired knowledge from the virtuous, he is refined and expert in the sacred scriptures.
Performing his duties in this world according to his own dharma and remaining true to his promise,
that twice-born householder abides in these six activities; moreover,
full of faith, he should constantly perform the five sacrifices.
Possessed of fortitude, vigilant, self-controlled, knowing the Dharma, and having mastery over himself; free from joy, fear, and anger—a Brāhmaṇa such as this does not perish.
Giving, study, sacrifice, austerity, modesty, uprightness, and self-restraint—these are his duties.
By these [practices], one increases one's vital energy (*tejas*) and casts off evil;
being cleansed of sin, wise, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses,
and having brought desire and anger under control, one should seek to lead oneself to the state of Brahman.
One should honor the fires and the Brahmins, and one should bow down to the deities;
one should avoid harsh speech and injury associated with unrighteousness.
This is prescribed as the ancient mode of conduct for a Brahmin.
Performing actions through the acquisition of knowledge, one succeeds in those very actions.
The wise man crosses the terrible river— difficult to traverse, with the five senses as its waters, greed as its banks, and anger as its mud— which is otherwise unassailable.
That which is puffed up by desire and anger, and perpetually deluded,
is constantly carried away by the natural current of the world through a great, irresistible force ordained by fate.
It was filled with the great waters of Kāla, with a continuous downpour of rain-swirls, with months as its waves and seasons as its current, with fortnights as its foam-grass and blades of grass,
and with the twinkling of eyes as its froth and days and nights as its velocity.
By means of the terrible snare of desire, by the raft of Vedic sacrifices, by the island of Dharma for all beings, by the roar of wealth and pleasure,
by the banks of the stairs of Truth, and by the river that carries away the tree of violence.
By means of the flood of the river of the age (*yuga-hradaugha*) and by becoming as one with Brahman,
the beings created by the Creator are dragged to the abode of Yama;
the wise and steadfast ones cross over this by means of that which consists of wisdom (*prajñāmaya*).
For what can those who lack a raft do, being witless? Indeed, it is fitting that the wise man should cross over, and no other person;
for the wise man perceives virtues and faults from afar in all circumstances.

One who is of a doubting nature, whose soul is possessed by desire, whose mind is wavering, and who is of little intelligence—being unwise, he certainly does not cross over; for he who merely sits still does not go forward.
Indeed, like one without a raft, he encounters great calamity as he is carried away by the current.
For one seized by the crocodile of sensual desire, even knowledge is no raft.
Therefore, a wise person should strive for the sake of emerging;
this is his emergence: that he becomes a true brahmin.
Born into a family of triple purity, free from the three doubts, and performing the three duties—one should remain like one emerging from the water; one should cross over by means of wisdom.
For he who is refined, self-controlled, disciplined, and has perfected his self—
For the wise man, success follows immediately both in this world and in the next.
A householder should dwell among them without anger and without malice;
he should constantly perform the five sacrifices and offer oblations, eating only the remains of the meal.

One should conduct oneself according to the behavior of the virtuous and perform actions as the learned do. Without obstructing the path of dharma, one should seek a livelihood that is beyond reproach.
One who knows the truth of the Vedic revelation and its understanding, who follows the conduct of the learned, is truly discerning.
Performing his duties according to his own dharma, he remains untainted by the fruits of his actions.
Being active in ritual, full of faith, generous, wise, and free from malice,
and knowing the distinction between dharma and adharma, he crosses over everything that is difficult to cross.
Possessed of fortitude, vigilant, self-controlled, knowing the Dharma, and having mastery over the self— he who is free from joy, fear, and anger, such a Brāhmaṇa does not perish.
This is ordained as the ancient way of life for a Brāhmaṇa.
Performing actions with the wealth of knowledge, one succeeds everywhere.
For the undiscerning person here, desiring what is righteous, performs what is unrighteous;
and he performs what appears to be unrighteous while grieving as if it were righteousness.
Thinking "I am performing dharma," one performs adharma;
and desiring adharma, one performs dharma.
The fool, not understanding both types of action, acts thus.
That embodied being is born and also dies.
Vyāsa said:
Now, if one should find this pleasing, one might likewise harbor malice in the mind.
Emerging and submerging, the man of knowledge should possess a raft;
by means of rafts fashioned through wisdom, the steadfast carry the ignorant across.
The ignorant cannot, in any way, carry others across, nor even themselves.

The sage whose defects have been severed, disciplined in yoga, should practice the twelve yogas; he who is fearless regarding means and ends should pursue the ten objects that bring happiness through action,
being wise and possessing insight through both his eyes and his mind.
One who desires supreme knowledge should restrain speech and mind with the intellect;
one who desires peace for the self should restrain the self with knowledge. Even if a man were extremely cruel, he would be [liberated] if he is a witness to these.
Whether he be a knower of all the Vedas, or one who has neither studied nor recited them; whether he be a righteous performer of sacrifices, or the worst of evildoers;
whether he be a tiger among men, or one who bears the mark of impotence.
He indeed crosses over the great and difficult ocean of old age and death;
for by thus applying himself even to a single [verse] through this yoga,
one who seeks to know it indeed transcends the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman).
The Dharma is its seat, modesty its fender, and skillful means with their opposites its pole-axle;
the downward breath is its axle-pin, the upward breath its yoke, wisdom its life-span, and the vital principle its binding lash.
Consciousness is its beautiful seat-cushion, and right conduct is its beautiful rim.
Carrying sight and touch, carrying smell and hearing,

with wisdom as its axle-pin, the goad for all the faculties, and knowledge as its charioteer— this steadfast chariot is presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), preceded by faith and self-restraint.
Following the path of renunciation, secure, abiding in purity, and having meditation as its range—
this divine chariot, joined with the individual soul (jīva), shines resplendent in the world of Brahman.
Now, for one who is hastening and desiring to yoke this chariot:
I shall describe the method for one whose mind desires to go to the Imperishable (akṣara) swiftly. He who, restraining his speech, practices the seven complete concentrations (dhāraṇās),
as well as the other secondary concentrations (pradhāraṇās) behind and on the sides— [attains his goal].
One gradually attains the sovereignty over the earth, as well as that of wind, space, and water; likewise, the sovereignty of light, of the ego (ahaṃkāra), and of the intellect (buddhi);
and finally, one attains the sovereignty of the unmanifest (avyakta) in due order.
He who possesses these strides likewise applies himself through yoga.
Then, for him who is joined in yoga and beholds perfection within himself, [the Self],
being churned forth due to its subtlety, reveals these forms.
Just as a subtle wisp of winter smoke pervades the sky, so too does the first form of one liberated from the body manifest. Then, upon the cessation of that smoke, the second form is perceived.
One perceives there, within that very self, a form like water in the sky;
and when the water has passed away, the form of fire shines forth; and when that too has ceased, it is regarded as being like yellow cloth.
Furthermore, even the subtle form belonging to the wind-element manifests there;
when that has ceased, the form of space manifests.
And its form shines forth with a color like that of wool;
then, having attained a white state, the Unborn [soul] reaches even the subtle realm of Vāyu.
When that has ceased, the form of his intellect shines forth.
The non-white [state] is the subtlety of the mind, which is indeed the unmanifest Brahman.
Listen now to me regarding the various fruits that arise even when these are born:
for one born with sovereignty over the earth, the desired creation is ordained.
Like Prajāpati, he is unshakeable as he creates beings from his own body;
likewise, with a mere finger, thumb, hand, or foot,
he alone causes the earth to tremble— this is known as the quality of wind.
Having become like space, he perishes in space due to his similarity in nature;
yet he is perceived by his color and drinks from the reservoirs out of desire.
Furthermore, his form is not seen by means of its brilliance, nor does it thus subside.
