When the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) is conquered, these five [senses] become subject to its control; and when the six [faculties] are conquered within the self and the intellect (buddhi), one then attains mastery. Indeed, faultless intuitive insight (pratibhā) then approaches him in its entirety.

In the same way, the manifest self attains the unmanifest state from which the world emerges and comes to be designated as "manifest. In this regard, listen to my detailed explanation concerning that which consists of the unmanifest.
Likewise, first learn from me the enumeration consisting of the manifest;
twenty-five principles are equal and identical on both sides. Listen now to me regarding the distinctions therein, both in Yoga and in Sāṃkhya.
That which is said to be manifest is that which is born, grows,
decays, and dies, being endowed with these four characteristics;
that which is the opposite of this is declared to be unmanifest.
In the Vedas and in the established doctrines, two selves have been proclaimed. Furthermore, they describe another fourfold set arising from the four characteristics:
the manifest, that which is born from the unmanifest, the enlightened, and its opposite.
Both "sattva" and "kṣetrajña" have been shown here;
in the Vedas, two selves are described as being attached to sense objects.
For the Sāṃkhyas, the withdrawal from sense objects is the defining characteristic of perfection.
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, and with doubts severed,
he neither becomes angry nor feels hatred, nor does he utter untruthful words. Even when reviled or struck, he meditates with friendliness and not with ill-will.
He who restrains the three— speech, action, and mind— is equal toward all beings and advances toward Brahman. Established in mere sustenance, he neither desires nor lacks desire.
Free from greed, undisturbed, self-controlled, neither acting for his own sake nor rejecting anything; his senses are not distracted, and his desires are not over-extended;
he is intent on the welfare of all beings, friendly, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal.
The wise one who regards the pleasant and unpleasant as equal, who views blame and self-praise as equal,
who has no longing for any desires, who is firm in the holy life (*brahmacarya*),
and who is non-violent toward all beings— such a follower of *sāṃkhya* is liberated.

Now learn from me the causes by which they are liberated from yoga: he who transcends the sovereignty of yoga and passes beyond it is liberated. Thus has this wisdom born of existence been declared to you; of this there is no doubt.
Thus one becomes free from dualities and attains Brahman.
Vyāsa said:
Then the wise man, having taken hold of the raft of knowledge, abides in peace.
"Emerging and submerging, one should take refuge in knowledge alone.
Śuka said:
"What is that knowledge, or what is that wisdom, by which one transcends duality?"
"Indeed, dharma is characterized by both worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and renunciation (*nivṛtti*).
Vyāsa said: "But he who, being insentient, perceives existence as devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),"
And furthermore, one who is liberated from causes nourishes all things through wisdom.
But those for whom intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is considered the sole cause,
having winnowed away the chaff of straw, obtain nothing at all.
And those of small intelligence who, relying upon this position,
conduct themselves while regarding inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause, do not attain the highest good.
For inherent nature, born of delusion, action, and the mind, leads indeed to destruction.
This is the definition of these two: intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*).
For activities such as agriculture, the harvesting of crops, and the construction of vehicles, seats, and houses have been devised by those possessed of wisdom.
Regarding pleasure gardens, houses, diseases, and the absence of disease, those who are wise are the true expounders, acting in accordance with the knowledge of the learned.
Wisdom unites one with meaningful goals; through wisdom, one attains the highest good.

Kings who possess equal characteristics enjoy their sovereignty through wisdom. Indeed, the distinction between this world and the next among living beings is perceived only through knowledge. O dear one, for all created things, knowledge is the supreme goal; by means of knowledge alone is it attained.

The birth of all various beings is fourfold; one should observe it as being from the womb, from an egg, from a sprout, and from sweat. One should observe that mobile beings are superior to immobile ones.
For it is logical that the activity of two distinct things should differ;
they say that bipeds and many-footed beings are both mobile,
yet even among the many-footed, bipeds are superior.

They say that bipeds are of two kinds: those belonging to the earth and others. Those belonging to the earth are distinguished, for they consume these foods. They say that those belonging to the earth are also of two kinds: the middling and the superior.
The intermediate [knowledges] are distinguished because they sustain the characteristics of their respective classes;
the intermediate ones are said to be twofold: those consisting of knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and those other than them.
Those consisting of knowledge of phenomena are distinguished because they sustain what is to be done and what is not to be done.

They say that there are two kinds of knowers of Dharma: those who know the Vedas and others. Those who know the Vedas are distinguished, for the Veda is established within them. They say that there are two kinds of knowers of the Vedas: those who expound them and others.
The preceptors are distinguished by their retention of all dharmas; for it is through them that the Vedas— along with the sacrifices, the ritual manuals, and the fruits of all religious acts—
are known to have issued forth.
They say that there are two kinds of teachers: those who know the Self and others.
Those who know the Self are superior because they comprehend both birth and non-birth. Indeed, he who knows these two aspects of dharma is all-knowing and a knower of all dharmas.
He is a renouncer, one whose resolve is truth, he is patient, and he is a lord; for the gods know him as a Brahmin who is established in the knowledge of Dharma,
proficient in the Śabdabrahman, and has reached a firm certainty regarding the Supreme.
We bow to those gods and those twice-born ones, dear son, who know that which is within and that which is without, as well as that which pertains to sacrifice and the presiding deities;
upon them this entire world of beings and the whole universe is established.
There is nothing whatsoever equal to their state of majesty. Having completely transcended beginning, end, and action, they are the self-existent lords of all fourfold beings.
Vyāsa said:
This is the most ancient mode of life prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa;
indeed, it is only the man of knowledge who succeeds in all undertakings while performing his duties.
If there were no such doubt regarding the determination of action— namely,
whether this nature is action or rather knowledge—
then there would be a desire to know it here, provided that knowledge pertains to the person.
I shall describe it through birth and perception; listen to that. Some men say that human effort is the cause in actions; some praise destiny, and other people [praise] inherent nature.
Human effort, destiny, and the nature of the ripening of fruits—these three are distinct, yet some regard them as non-distinct.
It is thus, yet not thus; both, yet neither.
Those established in action speak with partiality; those established in being see with equanimity. In the Tretā and Dvāpara ages, as well as among those born in the Kali age, there is doubt.
This is the rule for dharmas in the Tretā Yuga, not in the Kṛta Yuga.
In the Kṛta Yuga, ascetics were tranquil and established in goodness (sattva);
they all perceived no difference among the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas,
and having seen desire and hatred as distinct [from the self], they practiced austerity.
Endowed with the dharma of austerity, constant in penance, and firmly resolute,
he obtains through that all the desires which he wishes for in his mind.
By means of austerity, he attains that state by becoming which he creates the world.
Having become that, he then becomes the sovereign lord of all beings;
this has been declared in the Vedic discourses as something profound by those who perceive the Vedas,
yet in the Upanishads it is made manifest and perceived through the sequential application of yoga.

Sacrifices involving physical exertion are prescribed for the Kṣatriya; sacrifices of oblations are recorded for the Vaiśya; Śūdras have sacrifices of service, and the twice-born have sacrifices of silent recitation (japa).
Indeed, a twice-born man becomes one who has fulfilled his duty through the study of the Vedas (svādhyāya).

Whether he performs other rites or does not perform them, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa. At the beginning of the Tretā age, the Vedas, sacrifices, and the system of castes and stages of life were complete;
however, due to the contraction of the lifespan, these are divided during the Dvāpara age.
In the Dvāpara age, the Vedas fall into disorder, and likewise in the Kali age they are seen and yet not seen again and again at the end of the Kali;
and their own duties perish there, oppressed by unrighteousness.

Whatever essences belong to cattle, to the earth, to the waters, and to the plants; whatever Vedas have been obscured by unrighteousness, as well as the duties of the Vedas and the stages of life (āśramas);
and all beings, both mobile and immobile, who abide in their own dharma—all these undergo transformation.
Just as rain pours down upon all earthly beings,
so do the Vedas manifest their various limbs in every age;
thus has the diversity of time been unfolded, which is without beginning or end.

That has been described by me previously, from which beings come and to which they go. Dhātṛ is the source of origin for these beings, and Yama is their restrainer. Created in pairs, they proceed by their own inherent nature in great abundance.
Creation, time, fortitude, the Vedas, the agent, the action, the performance, and the fruit—
this, O dear one, which you asked me, has been told to you.
Bhīṣma said:
Having been thus addressed, and having praised this instruction of the supreme ṛṣi which is connected with the meaning of the dharma of liberation, Śuka proceeded to ask this:
Śuka said:

"How does one who possesses offspring, is learned in the Vedas, has performed sacrifices, is aged, wise, and free from malice— how does such a person attain the Brahman that is yet to come and beyond traditional authority?
"By means of austerity, celibacy, total renunciation, and intelligence..."
Whether it be in Sāṃkhya or in Yoga, please explain this to me as I have asked: by what means do men attain one-pointed concentration of both the mind and the senses? You ought to explain that to me.
Vyāsa said:
No one attains perfection anywhere except through knowledge and austerity, except through the restraint of the senses,
and except through the renunciation of everything.

All the great elements were the first creation of the Self-existent; they are most abundantly established within embodied beings in the multitude of living creatures. It is taught that the body comes from earth, the essence from water, and the two eyes from light.
Vāyu is the support of the prāṇa and apāna breaths; Ākāśa resides in the cavities of embodied beings.
Viṣṇu is in their stride, Śakra is in their strength, and Agni is in the stomach, digesting what has been eaten.
The quarters of the sky are in the ears as hearing, and Sarasvatī is speech in the tongue.
The ears, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these are declared to be the organs of perception, the gateways for the accomplishment of food.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth [are their respective objects].
The senses indeed display their respective objects to the mind;
the mind yokes the senses, which are under its control, just as a charioteer yokes his horses;
and the inner self (bhūtātman), residing in the heart, always yokes the mind as well.

Likewise, among all these senses, the mind is their lord; it is likewise the self of beings in both their restraint and their release. The senses, the objects of the senses, inherent nature, consciousness, and the mind [are thus established].
The prāṇa, apāna, and the individual soul (jīva) are eternally present within the bodies of embodied beings.
There is no substratum for the *sattva*; the word "quality" (*guṇa*) does not apply to consciousness.
For *sattva* indeed creates radiance, but it never creates qualities.

Thus, the wise and learned sage, with his mind, beholds the seventeenth [principle] within himself, surrounded by the sixteen qualities in the body. For this is not visible to the eye, nor indeed to all the senses.
When the mind is thoroughly illuminated, the Great Self shines forth. Devoid of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, it is imperishable;
bodiless within its own body, one should behold it as being without senses.

He who perceives the Unmanifest residing within the bodies of manifest mortals as the immortal— having departed this life, he is fit for becoming Brahman. [One should look upon] a Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and noble birth, a cow, an elephant, ...
The wise look with an equal eye upon a dog and even a dog-eater;
for that one Great Self dwells in all beings, both moving and stationary, by whom all this is pervaded.

When the self of all beings sees the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, then that self of beings attains Brahman. As far as the Self extends within oneself, so far does the Self extend within the Supreme Self.

He who knows this constantly is fit for immortality. Even the gods are bewildered regarding the path of that trackless one who has become the self of all beings and is devoted to the welfare of all beings, as they seek his footprints.

Just as the movement of birds in the sky or of aquatic creatures in the water cannot be seen, even so [the movement] of that great-souled one cannot be perceived. Time ripens all beings within itself, by means of itself.
But no one here knows that time in which [all] is cooked;
it is neither above, nor across, nor below, nor again in any other direction.
It is never grasped by the senses or even by the intellect.
No one receives anything from anywhere in the middle;
all these worlds are contained within [the Self], and there is nothing external to them.
Just as an arrow released from a bowstring reaches its mark, so too does one who has attained the thousandfold [Self].
One would not reach the end of this cause, even if one possessed the speed of thought. There is nothing subtler than that which is subtle, and nothing grosser than it.
Its hands and feet extend everywhere; its eyes, heads, and faces are on all sides.
Possessing ears everywhere in the world, it stands pervading all things.
That very same [Self] is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great;
though it dwells eternally within all beings, it is not perceived.
The imperishable and the perishable—this is the twofold nature of the self.
The perishable exists in all beings, while the divine is the immortal imperishable.
Having entered the city of nine gates, the *haṃsa* (the individual soul) is indeed restrained and self-controlled.
The Lord of all beings, both stationary and moving,

is called the "Swan" (haṃsa) by those who see the further shore, because he is unborn and because he takes recourse in the nine transformations consisting of loss, destruction, and modification of bodies.

That which is spoken by the *haṃsa* and is indeed the imperishable (*akṣara*), that is the immutable (*kūṭastha*) syllable. Having attained that imperishable through knowledge, the wise man abandons both life and birth.
Vyāsa said:
O virtuous son, since you have asked me here according to the facts and in accordance with reality,
I have proclaimed this which is joined with the logic of Sāṃkhya;
now listen as I shall describe to you the entire practice of Yoga in its entirety.
The oneness of the intellect and the mind, as well as that of all the senses with the self— O dear one, for one who meditates, this is the unsurpassed knowledge.
This [knowledge] is attained by one who is tranquil, self-controlled, and devoted to the practice of the inner self.
The Buddha, who delights in the self and performs pure deeds, must realize that which is to be realized; having utterly severed the five defects of yoga known by the wise—
namely, desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth.
One conquers anger through tranquility and desire by abandoning purposeful thought; by cultivating the quality of purity (*sattva*), the wise man should strive to eliminate sleep.
One should guard the genitals and the stomach with fortitude, and the hands and feet with the eyes.
One should abandon fear through vigilance regarding the eyes, ears, and mind, and greed through the service of the wise;
thus, one should constantly and untiringly conquer these defects of yoga.
One should honor the sacred fires and the Brahmins, and bow down to the deities.
One should avoid angry speech, as well as speech associated with violence, and instead follow what is agreeable to the mind.
For the Veda is composed of radiant energy, pure, and its essence is this entire universe.
From a single being, two types of beings—stationary and moving—arose. [These qualities are:
meditation, study, charity, truthfulness, modesty, uprightness, forbearance, purity, purification of food, and restraint of the senses.
By these, one's spiritual luster increases and evil is cast away;
all one's goals are accomplished and higher knowledge proceeds. Remaining equanimous toward all beings, one lives with whatever is obtained or not obtained.
Having shaken off evil, radiant, moderate in diet, and with senses conquered,
one who has brought desire and anger under control should seek to lead [the self] to the state of Brahman;
being composed and having achieved one-pointedness of mind and the senses.
During the first and last watches of the night, one should hold the mind within oneself. For this living being with five senses, if even a single sense-faculty has a flaw,
wisdom flows away from him like water from the foot of a leather water-skin.

The knower of yoga should first withdraw the mind, just as a fisherman draws in small fish; then the ear, then the eye, the tongue, and the nose. Having restrained these, the ascetic should establish them within the mind.

In that same way, having cast aside all volitional thoughts, one should indeed fix the mind upon the Self. Having unified the five [senses] through knowledge, the ascetic should establish them within the mind.
When these, with the mind as the sixth, abide within the Self, [then the yogi is established].
When they become tranquil through steadfast composure, then Brahman shines forth;
like a smokeless fire with blazing flames, or like the radiant sun,
or like the lightning-fire in the sky, one beholds the Self by means of the self.
And all of that is seen there, because it pervades everywhere. The high-souled Brahmins who are wise, steadfast, possessed of great insight, and devoted to the welfare of all beings— these see it.
Practicing in this manner for such a limited time, one whose vows are firmly resolved,
sitting alone in seclusion, shall indeed attain identity with the Imperishable.
Confusion, dizziness, and whirling sensations may occur in the smelling, hearing, and seeing.
Marvelous phenomena regarding taste and touch, cold and heat, and the forms of wind— having encountered such flashes of intuition and obstacles through the power of yoga,
the knower of reality should disregard them and turn back by means of his own self alone.
The disciplined sage, being self-restrained, should practice yoga at the three times of day;
he should apply himself to it on a mountain peak, at a shrine, or at the tops of trees,
having fully controlled the collection of his senses, like a cowherd watching over his cattle with his mind fixed on the vessel.

With one-pointed mind, one should constantly reflect and not agitate the mind from its yoga. By whatever means it is possible to restrain the flickering mind, one should, being disciplined, practice that very method and never deviate from it.
He should approach for the purpose of dwelling in empty mountain caves, temples of deities, and empty houses with one-pointed mind;
he should not become attached to others through speech, action, or even thought.

Maintaining equanimity and being restrained in food, one should remain the same whether obtaining or not obtaining [alms]. Whether someone should praise him or disparage him, he should remain equal toward both; he should not dwell upon either the auspicious or the inauspicious.
One should not rejoice in gains, nor dwell upon losses;
being equal toward all beings, one possesses the same nature as the wind.
Thus it is for the virtuous one who has realized the self in all things and perceives equality everywhere.
For one who is constantly disciplined for six months, he transcends the Brahman of sound.
Seeing living beings afflicted by pain, and regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal,
one who is devoted to this path shall not turn back, being free from delusion.
Even one of low caste, or a woman desiring dharma,
should also proceed by this path to the supreme goal—
the unborn, ancient, undecaying, and eternal.
Whatever a steadfast man perceives with his senses—
that which is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great—
the self-possessed man, disciplined in yoga, beholds that by means of the self.
Having reflected upon this speech of the high-souled great seer as it was truly spoken, and having observed it with the mind, one should proceed toward identity with the Supreme Lord.
"Whatever destiny for beings the wise attain," Śuka said:
"Regarding this Vedic statement, 'Perform action' and 'Renounce it'— "
"To which direction do they go by means of knowledge, and to which do they go by means of action?
I truly wish to hear this; may your lordship explain it to me.
For these two exist in mutual opposition and contradiction."
12,233.003 Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, the son of Parāśara replied this to his son:
"I shall explain these two—the perishable and the imperishable—which consist of action and knowledge."
"Listen with a single-minded focus, my son, to that direction which they go by means of knowledge and that which they reach through action; for this distinction is indeed profound.
It is said that 'Dharma exists,' yet one might say right here that it does not exist."
"Then this [path] would be suitable for me, being consistent with that side.
Now, there are these two paths upon which the Vedas are established:
dharma characterized by worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and that well-expounded [dharma] consisting of renunciation (*nivṛtti*)."
A living being is bound by action, but is liberated by knowledge;
therefore, ascetics who see the further shore do not perform action. After death, one is born through action as a corporeal being composed of sixteen elements.
Through knowledge, one is born eternally as the imperishable, for one's nature is indeed imperishable.
But some men of very little intelligence praise action; by means of that, they worship while taking delight in a multitude of bodies.
But those who have attained supreme understanding and perceive the subtleties of Dharma do not praise action, just as one drinking from a river does not praise a well.
Through action one obtains its fruit: pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence.
By means of knowledge, one attains that state where, having gone, one does not grieve;
where, having gone, one does not die; where, having gone, one is not born;
where, having gone, one does not decay; and where, having gone, one does not increase.
Where that supreme Brahman resides—unmanifest, undecaying, and eternal; unimpeded, effortless, immortal, and inseparable;
where one is not afflicted by the pairs of opposites, nor by mental action.
For 12,233.014c years, they were everywhere friendly and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
12,233.015a Know, my dear, that one Puruṣa consists of knowledge, while another consists of action;
he exists like the moon on the new-moon day, remaining by means of a subtle digit.
That person consists of knowledge, eternal, and has wisdom as its essential quality;
this very thing proclaimed by the Seer is inferred in detail,
like seeing the newly risen moon or a curved thread in the sky.

"Know him, my dear, to be embodied, consisting of the eleven transformations, sustained by a collection of *kalās*, and composed of the qualities of action (*karma-guṇa*). For the fire that resides within him is ever present, like [fire] placed within a cooking pot."
Know that Self to be eternally conquered through renunciation;
know that Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) to be eternally conquered through renunciation, upon whom the deity rests like a drop of water on a lotus leaf.

Know that darkness (tamas), passion (rajas), and goodness (sattva) are these qualities of the individual soul (jīva). One should know the individual soul to be a quality of the self (ātman), and the self to belong to the Supreme Self (paramātman).
They say that consciousness is a quality of the individual soul.
He stirs and causes all to stir;
those who know the field speak of him as such—
he who set the seven worlds in motion.
Śuka said:

That creation which begins from the perishable (kṣara), as well as the senses endowed with qualities, and that auspicious meditation upon the Self for the purpose of the manifestation of intellect and sovereign power— [all this has been described].
Furthermore, I desire that you describe in detail the virtuous conduct in this world— the conduct based on right livelihood— by which the righteous proceed.
For in the Veda, both the injunction "perform action" and the injunction "renounce action" have been spoken.
"How may I understand this? You ought to explain it to me.
O knower of the truth of the world's course, I am purified by the instruction of my teacher;
having formed this resolve, I shall cast off my body with a detached mind and without distress."
Vyāsa said:
This very mode of life was ordained of old by Brahmā himself;
it has been practiced by the ancient virtuous ones, the supreme ṛṣis.
"By means of celibacy, the supreme seers indeed conquer the worlds. Seek the highest good for yourself within your own heart and mind.
Even while living in the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, and performing vast ascetic penance,"
Wandering among sacred sites and non-violent toward living beings,
when he has reached the time for it, he who subsists on alms in the hermitage of a forest-dweller— where the smoke has ceased and the pestle is laid aside— is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
Free from praise and free from salutation, having abandoned both the auspicious and the inauspicious, wander alone in the forest, sustained by whatever food you may obtain.
Śuka said:
"If this statement of the Veda contradicts worldly discourse, then when both the authoritative and the non-authoritative are in conflict, how can there be the status of a scripture?
I wish to hear this; may the Blessed One explain it to me."
"How does this proceed without contradicting the laws of karma?
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, the son of Gandhavatī replied to his son as follows.
The Ṛṣi honored those words of his son of immeasurable splendor:
"Whether one is a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
all who act according to what has been taught attain the supreme goal."
He who should practice these stages of life according to the rule,
free from desire and hatred, is glorified in the hereafter. For this four-stepped ladder is firmly established upon Brahman.
Relying upon this ladder, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
For a fourth part of his life, a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin), free from malice and skilled in the meaning of dharma, should dwell with his teacher or with the teacher’s son.
One who desires prosperity should study under a teacher with diligence beyond the ordinary;
he should be dexterous and not a detractor, and when summoned, he should attend upon his teacher. In the teacher’s house, he should go to bed later and rise earlier.

Whatever task must be performed by a disciple or even by a servant, having completed all of that as if it were already done, he should stand by his side— a servant who performs everything and is skilled in all labors.
Pure, skillful, and endowed with good qualities, he should speak without haste, like an arrow.
With his senses subdued and composed, he should gaze upon his teacher with steady eyes.
He should not eat while the teacher has not eaten, nor drink while the teacher has not drunk.
One should not remain standing when [the other] is sitting, nor should one sleep while they are not asleep. With both hands turned palm-upward, one should gently touch their feet;
one should press the right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand.

Having saluted his teacher, he should say: "Venerable sir, please teach me. He should say: "Venerable sir, I shall do this; and this has already been done by me. O Brahman, I shall also do whatever you tell me again."
Having thus obtained permission for everything and having offered his wealth to the teacher, he should perform [the rites];
and having performed all that, it must be reported to the teacher once again.
Furthermore, those fragrances or flavors which the religious student (*brahmacārī*) does not partake in—

"Having completed his studies, he should serve them; this is the settled rule in the sacred laws (dharma). Whatever specific observances have been prescribed in detail for the religious student (brahmacārin), he should observe them all and remain inseparable from his teacher."
Having thus offered pleasure to his guru according to his ability,
a disciple should conduct himself in this manner through his actions in each successive stage of life (āśrama).
When a quarter of his life has passed, he should do so by means of Vedic study, vows, and fasting.
Having given the sacrificial fee to the teacher according to the rule, he should perform the *samāvartana* ceremony; then,
being united with a wife obtained through righteous means, he should duly establish the sacred fires and spend the second quarter of his life as a householder observing the vows of a married man.
Vyāsa said:
During the second portion of his life, a householder should live at home,
having obtained a wife through righteous means and having established the sacred fires, being firm in his vows.

Four modes of livelihood for householders have been prescribed by the sages: first, the one who possesses a granary of grain; immediately after, the one who possesses a jar of grain; then the one who does not store for more than a day; and finally, the one who adopts the "pigeon" mode of subsistence.
Among them, each succeeding one is superior according to dharma and is the greatest conqueror of the worlds. One performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth is established in the *brahmasattra*.
12,235.004e Here, they declare the great vows of the householder.
12,235.005a One should not cook food for one's own sake, nor should one kill animals in vain;
whether living or non-living, [an object] deserves consecration with a *yajus* formula.
He should never sleep during the day, nor during the first or last watches of the night;
he should not eat at improper times, nor summon his wife for intercourse outside of her season.
No Brahmin should dwell in his house without being honored, even if that Brahmin is fasting.

Likewise, his guests who convey the *havya* and *kavya* offerings must always be honored— those who have bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), who have mastered the Vedas,
who live according to their own duty, and who are self-controlled, observant of ritual acts, and devoted to austerity.
For them, offerings to the gods (havya) and to the ancestors (kavya) are prescribed for the purpose of honoring; however,
these do not apply to one who travels with donkeys, one who is ignorant of his own duty,
one who has abandoned the Agnihotra fire, or a teacher who acts falsely.
In this matter, a distribution of food must be provided here for all beings;

likewise, the householder should give to those who do not cook for themselves. He should always be one who eats the remains of the meal (vighasa), and he should always be one whose food is nectar (amṛta).
The remnant of a sacrifice is *amṛta*; such food is equal to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
But he who eats the remnant of what has been served to dependents is called a consumer of *vighasa*.
*Vighasa* is the remnant of what is served to dependents, while the remnant of a sacrifice is *amṛta*.
Devoted to his own wife, self-controlled, free from envy, and having conquered his senses;

together with the officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers; with maternal uncles, guests, and dependents; with the elderly, children, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives, and blood-brothers.
One should not engage in disputes with one’s mother and father, sisters, brother, son, wife, daughter, or group of servants. By avoiding these quarrels, one is liberated from all sins.
By conquering these, one undoubtedly conquers all the worlds:
the teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods.
Sisters reside in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen in the realm of the Viśvedevas; relatives and friends in the cardinal directions; maternal uncles and mothers on the earth;
and the aged, children, the sick, and the emaciated are the powerful ones in the sky.
An eldest brother is equal to a father; a wife and son are one’s own body;
a group of servants is one’s own shadow; and a daughter is the ultimate object of pity.
Therefore, when reviled by these, one should always endure it without distress.
The wise man, devoted to the duties of a householder, constant in dharma, and having conquered fatigue, should perform actions neither bound by worldly gain nor for the sake of mere ritual duty.
There are three modes of conduct for the householder; among them, the highest good is the supreme one.
In that same way, they spoke of the system of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*).
All those rules that have been declared must be performed by one who desires prosperity,
whether he follows the practice of keeping grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*), the gleaning of ears (*uñchaśila*), or the "pigeon-like" mode of life (*kāpotī*).
In whatever kingdom these Arhats dwell, that realm prospers;
it purifies ten ancestors before and ten descendants after, including the grandfathers.
He who, free from distress, conducts himself according to these modes of life for householders, [attains this merit].
He shall attain a destination befitting those who wander the worlds of the *cakracaras*,
or else this destination is ordained for those whose senses are restrained;
the heavenly world is beneficial for householders of noble mind.
12,235.025c Heaven, joined with celestial chariots and seen in the Vedas, is beautifully blossomed.
12,235.026a In the heavenly world, this is the established state for householders of restrained soul; 12,235.026c for it is by this path ordained by Brahmā that one is liberated.
Having reached the second stage in due order, one is glorified in the heavenly world. Beyond this, they speak of the third, most exalted stage of life for those who cast off the body.
"Listen to this supreme [teaching] for the forest-dwellers and householders who have purified their bodies.
Bhīṣma said:
12,236.001a That mode of life for householders which has been declared as ordained for the wise, 12,236.001c and that which was spoken immediately after it— learn that, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
12,236.001d as it was formerly told by Vyāsa to his high-souled son.
Having gradually shaken off this third mode of life,
which is the highest for those dwelling in the forest hermitage who are weary from their vows of ritual union—
listen, O Pārtha, may you be blessed, to [the state] of those whose very selves are the refuge of all worlds.
[This is] for those who act with foresight and dwell in meritorious regions.
Vyāsa said:
When a householder perceives his own wrinkles and grey hair, [he should retire].
The offspring of one's offspring itself should likewise resort to the forest;
for the third part of his life, he should dwell in the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*).
There, as a sacrificer, he should tend those very same sacred fires and worship the gods who dwell in heaven.
Restrained, restricted in diet, eating only at every sixth mealtime, and remaining vigilant— this is the *agnihotra*, those cows, and all the constituent parts of the sacrifice;
namely, rice and barley grown without cultivation, wild grains, and the remnants of offerings.
One should present sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) in these five types of sacrifices;
even in the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vānaprasthāśrama*), these four modes of subsistence are prescribed.
Some [forest-dwellers] are those who wash their provisions immediately, while others store enough for a month.
Some store provisions for one year, while others store for twelve years,
for the sake of honoring guests and for the successful accomplishment of sacrificial rites. During the rainy season they dwell under the open sky, and in the winter they take refuge in water.
In the summer, they practice the penance of the five fires, always restricting their food;
they roll about on the ground or stand even on their tiptoes. They pass their time in standing and sitting postures, and they bathe at the three daily libations.
Some use their teeth as mortars, while others grind with stones; some drink boiled barley-gruel only once during the bright fortnight,
and others drink it only during the dark fortnight, eating according to this sequence.
Some, firm in their vows, subsist on roots, some on fruits, and others on flowers;
following the Vaikhānasa doctrine, they live according to the prescribed rule.
These and various other initiations belong to those wise men.
The fourth duty, pertaining to the Upaniṣads, is remembered as common to all;
from that, the other two—the forest-dweller and the householder—proceed.
In this very age, O dear one, it was established by the Brahmins who perceive all things.
Agastya, the seven sages (Saptarṣis), Madhucchandas, Aghamarṣaṇa, Sāṃkṛti, Sudiva, Taṇḍi, Yavānnas, Kṛtaśrama,
Ahovīrya, Kāvya, Tāṇḍya, Medhātithi, and Budha.
Śala, Vāka, Nirvāka, Śūnyapāla, and Kṛtaśrama—
learned in such dharmas as these, they thereafter ascended to heaven. O dear one, likewise did the Yāyāvara clans, who had direct perception of dharma.
There were sages of fierce austerity who perceived the subtleties of Dharma;
and immeasurable, blameless Brahmins had taken refuge in the forest—
Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, and others such as the Sikatas.
Through their deeds, they are free from worldly joy; constant in the Dharma and having conquered their senses, they have all taken refuge in the forest as those who perceive the Dharma directly.
Without the stars and invincible, these hosts of luminaries appear [like them].
Worn out by old age and afflicted by disease,

when a fourth part of his life remains, he should abandon the stage of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha-āśrama*) after performing the *sadyaskārā* sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee (*sarvavedasadakṣiṇā*).

He is a sacrificer of the self, delighting in the self, sporting in the self, and taking refuge in the self. Having internalized the sacred fires within himself and having renounced all possessions, he should always perform here the Sadyaskra sacrifices and the Iṣṭi offerings.

For one who always performs sacrifices, the sacrifice to the self ceases from the external sacrifice. One should properly worship the three fires within the self alone for the sake of liberation of the self.
From the vital breaths, one should offer the *yajus* oblations and consume the five or six portions without disparaging them.
Then, having shaved off his hair, body hair, and nails, the sage who has become a forest-dweller (vānaprastha) immediately goes from one stage of life to the next, purified by his deeds.
That twice-born man who departs for the wandering life after granting fearlessness to all beings—
Twelve thousand, two hundred and thirty-six, and twenty-seven worlds consisting of light belong to him, and after death he enjoys infinity.
One who is well-conducted, whose behavior is virtuous, and whose impurities have been removed, has nothing further to strive for, neither in this world nor in the next.
Free from anger and delusion, having abandoned both alliance and conflict,
a man who knows himself should remain like one indifferent; he should not be distressed even when restraints have taken hold within him.
For one who sacrifices to the Self, whose prowess lies in the mantras of the oblations from the sūtras of his own scripture, there will be movement according to his desire;
of this there is no doubt for one devoted to dharma and whose senses are subdued.

Beyond that, hear now of the fourth and supreme stage of life (āśrama), which is most excellent, endowed with preeminent virtues, transcending the three [preceding stages], and declared to be the highest.
As this supreme refuge is being proclaimed,
Śuka said:
"And likewise, remaining here in the stage of life of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha)..."
"One who desires the supreme state should indeed strive for the Self according to one's ability.
Vyāsa said:
"Having obtained the purificatory rites through these two stages of life, thereafter [one proceeds] further."

Listen here with a one-pointed mind to that which is the task for the sake of the ultimate goal: having ripened the defilements (*kaṣāya*) through the three stages of the ranks (*śreṇī*), one should go forth into the supreme state— the unsurpassed life of a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).
Therefore, having practiced in this manner, you should conduct yourself accordingly; listen further:
for the sake of attaining perfection, one should always wander alone without companions.
He who wanders alone, perceiving the truth, neither abandons nor is abandoned.

He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling, resorting to a village only for the sake of food. He should not provide for the morrow, being a sage endowed with pure intent; eating lightly, his diet restricted, he should consume food only once a day.
An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, solitude,
and equanimity toward all beings— this much is the characteristic of a monk.
Into him words enter like stones dropped into a well.
They do not return to the speaker; he shall dwell in the stage of absolute liberation (*kaivalyāśrama*).
He should never see nor hear anything that is unfit to be spoken of by anyone, and especially regarding Brahmins, he should never speak [such things] under any circumstances.

One should always speak only that which is wholesome for a brahmin; one should remain silent when there is censure, thereby applying a remedy to oneself. For by him alone, the sky is always made as if full.
The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa by whom that which is crowded with people is made empty;
the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa who is clothed in whatever [garment], fed on whatever [food], and sleeps wherever he may be.
The gods know him as a Brahmin who is afraid of a crowd as of a snake, of satiety as of hell, and of women as of a corpse;
he who neither becomes angry nor rejoices when honored or dishonored.
The gods know him as a true brahmin who grants fearlessness to all beings.
He should not rejoice in death, nor should he rejoice in life;
he should simply await his time, just as a servant awaits his master’s command.
One whose mind is unassailed and likewise whose speech is unassailed,
being liberated from all evils— what fear can there be for one who has no enemies? Since he grants fearlessness to all beings, he receives fearlessness from all beings.
For one who has been liberated from the body, there is no fear whatsoever from any quarter.
Just as the footprints of all other creatures that walk upon the earth are encompassed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too are all classes of footprints contained within the footprint of the elephant.
Thus, everything pertaining to dharma and artha is contained within non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
He who practices non-violence dwells eternally as one who is immortal.
One who is non-violent, equanimous, truthful, steadfast, and has his senses restrained—

He who is a refuge for all beings attains the unsurpassed goal. Thus, for the wise man who is satisfied with wisdom and free from fear, death is not a state that transcends him; rather, he transcends death.
The gods know him to be a *brāhmaṇa* who is liberated from all attachments, who stands like space, who is without possessions, who wanders alone, and who is tranquil;
he whose life is for the sake of *dharma*, and whose *dharma* is solely for the sake of dispassion.
The gods know him as a brāhmaṇa who spends his days and nights for the sake of merit;
they know him as a brāhmaṇa who is free from desire, free from worldly undertakings, free from ritual salutations, and free from praise— whose karma is exhausted and who is himself undecaying.
All beings delight in happiness;
all tremble violently at suffering.
For them, [the king] feels weariness born from the arousal of fear.
For one who has faith should not perform [worldly] actions;
for the gift of the assurance of fearlessness to all beings surpasses all other gifts here in this world.
He who first casts off his sharp body attains infinite fearlessness for all creatures;
with mouth upturned, he offers the oblation.
The navel of the world and the foundation of the universe— Vaiśvānara has entered into every limb and every member of that [body], as well as all that is done and all that is yet to be done.
That which is situated in the heart, measuring a span— into that the self-sacrificer offers the vital breaths. His *agnihotra* sacrifice is thus offered, established within the self.

Being honored in all the worlds,
those capable gods go to the realm of the well-done;
they [know] the Vedas, that which is to be known, and the entire ritual procedure.
Furthermore, he who thoroughly understands etymology and the ultimate truth— all of it— within the self of the body;
for him the gods always yearn.
Unattached to the earth and immeasurable in heaven,
he who is golden, the egg-born within the cosmic egg,
the winged bird in the intermediate space;

He who knows the revolving, undecaying transformation within the self that is the object of experience— [a wheel] with six rims, twelve spokes, and excellent joints, [and which possesses] blazing rays.
In whose mouth this entire universe revolves— that wheel of time is placed in the secret cave.
He who is the serene composure of the world, its very body.
He attains all the worlds here;
in that [fire] offered, he satisfies the gods here,
and they, being satisfied, satisfy his mouth.
Consisting of splendor, eternal-bodied, and ancient,
he attains infinite, fearless worlds;
from him living beings never tremble.
He is never afraid of living beings;
he is beyond reproach and does not reproach others;
such a man indeed is a Brahmin who beholds the Supreme Self.
With delusion subdued and impurity removed,
he who seeks no worldly gain neither in this world nor in the next, is free from anger and delusion, regarding a clod of earth and gold as equal.
With sorrow abandoned, free from both alliance and conflict, beyond blame and praise, and indifferent to the pleasant and unpleasant—
this mendicant wanders like one who is neutral.
Vyāsa said:
The modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti) surround the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña);
they do not know him, but he knows them as well.
With these senses, of which the mind is the sixth, he performs his work here,
just as a charioteer controls with firm and well-tamed supreme horses.
For the objects of the senses are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects of the senses.
Higher than the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*); higher than the intellect is the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*).

Higher than the Great is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*); higher than the Unmanifest is the Immortal (*amṛta*). There is nothing higher than the Immortal; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal.
Thus, the Self hidden within all beings does not shine forth;
however, it is seen by those who perceive reality through a subtle and supreme intellect.
Having dissolved the senses, with the mind as the sixth, into the inner self by means of the intellect, [one perceives it].
Not contemplating the many things to be thought about— the sense organs and the objects of the senses—
and having brought the mind to the cessation of meditation through the perfection of knowledge,
one who is no longer a master [of the senses] and whose self is tranquil then attains the immortal state.
But one who has not mastered all the senses and whose mindfulness is wavering,
that mortal, by surrendering himself, encounters death.
Having abandoned all volitions, however, he should fix his mind upon pure being (*sattva*).
Having caused the mind to enter into the *sattva* [quality], one then becomes Kālañjara.
Through the clarity of the mind, the ascetic indeed abandons both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
with a tranquil self, abiding in the Self, he enjoys infinite bliss.
The characteristic of serenity is like one who, being satisfied, sleeps happily;
or like a lamp burning in a windless place that does not flicker.
Thus, during the first and last watches of the night, one should yoke the self by means of the self.
One whose self is purified by the food of living beings perceives the Self within the self.
This secret of all the Vedas— neither based on tradition nor on scriptural transmission,
but a teaching to be realized through one's own self— is this instruction for my son.
In all the discourses on dharma and in all the discourses on truth, whatever wealth there was— ten thousand of these *ṛks* have been churned out like nectar,
just as butter is extracted from curds and fire from wood.
In this very way, the knowledge of the wise has been extracted for the sake of a son.

This scripture, which is an instruction for a son, should be spoken to those who have completed their Vedic studies (snātaka). This [instruction] must not be given to one who is not tranquil, nor to one who is not self-controlled, nor to one who does not practice austerity.

It should not be spoken to one who does not know the Veda, nor to one who has not followed [the teacher], nor to one who is envious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who does not act as instructed,
nor to one consumed by the science of logic, nor likewise to a slanderer.
This secret dharma should be spoken for one who is praiseworthy, tranquil, and an ascetic; for a beloved son and for a devoted disciple, but never to anyone else under any circumstances.

Even if a man were to give this entire earth filled with jewels, the knower of reality would consider that very [knowledge] to be superior to it. Therefore, that which pertains to the inner self (*adhyātma*) is more secret than secrets and transcends the human condition.
That which has been perceived by the great seers and is sung in the Vedāntas—
that very thing I shall fully declare to you, concerning which you question me, and that supreme matter which dwells within your mind.
And wherever you have any doubt, listen; here I am before you. O son, what more indeed shall I tell you?
Śuka said:
"O Blessed One, O best of sages, please explain to me once again in detail here the nature of the *adhyātma* (the supreme self) and how this *adhyātma* exists."
Vyāsa said:
"O dear one, that which pertains to the self (adhyātma) which exists here for a person—that I shall fully declare to you; listen to this exposition of it."
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—
these are the great elements (mahābhūtāni) of all beings, like the waves of the ocean.
Just as a tortoise extends its limbs here and then withdraws them again, [so does he manifest and dissolve these worlds].
In the same way, the great elements transform within the younger ones;
thus, all this—both the stationary and the moving—is composed of those [elements] alone. Therefore, it is described as such, both at the time of creation and at the time of dissolution.
"The Creator of beings fashioned the five great elements within all beings,
O dear one, according to whatever inequality he perceived in each.
Śuka said:"
"How could one perceive that which [the Creator] has placed within bodies?
How could one perceive the senses and those various qualities?
Vyāsa said:

I shall explain this vision to you here exactly as it is; listen with one-pointed attention to its reality, according to its true nature and just as it is. Sound, the sense of hearing, and the bodily cavities—these three originate from space.
Vital breath, movement, and touch—these three are the qualities of wind (vāyu). Form, the eye, and digestion—light (jyotis) is thus established as being threefold.
Taste, the sense of taste, and moisture—these three are the qualities of water (ambhas).
The object of smell, the sense of smell, and the body—these three are the qualities of earth.
The ear, the skin, the eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth:
this much is the collection of sense organs explained as consisting of the five elements.
Touch is said to belong to wind, taste to water, and form to light;
sound has its origin in space, and smell is recorded as the quality of earth. Mind, intellect, and the internal state—these three are born from the Self.
They do not transcend the qualities (guṇas), yet they are considered superior to the qualities. In a person, there are five senses; the mind is said to be the sixth;
the intellect (buddhi) is called the seventh; and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is the eighth.
The eye is for perception alone; the mind creates doubt;
the intellect is for determination; and the Knower of the Field is called the witness. Rajas, tamas, and sattva—these three are born from their own source.
One should perceive that [the Self] is equal toward all beings and their qualities.
Just as a tortoise here extends its limbs and then withdraws them,
even so the intellect (buddhi), having projected the collection of the senses, withdraws them.
Whatever one perceives above the soles of the feet and below the crown of the head,
the highest intellect (buddhi) operates solely within this sphere of activity. The intellect leads the qualities (guṇas), and the intellect likewise leads the senses.
When the intellect (*buddhi*) is absent, how can there be qualities for all the senses, with the mind as the sixth?
Whatever one perceives within oneself that is joined with joy,
tranquil and utterly pure— that one should understand to be *sattva*.

Whatever is associated with distress, whether in the body or the mind, that is the passion (*rajas*) which incites activity; it is constantly captivating for embodied beings. One should observe therein that passion has indeed set in.
But that which is joined with delusion, whose object is the unmanifest, which is beyond reasoning and unknowable— that should be understood as *tamas*.
Exultation, joy, bliss, equanimity, and a state of mental composure are [the marks of *sattva*].
Whether it occurs spontaneously or for some specific cause, the quality of *sattva* prevails.
Arrogance, falsehood, greed, delusion, and intolerance—
these are the marks of *rajas*, which manifest whether there is a cause or no cause.
Likewise, delusion, negligence, lassitude, and unawakened sleep arise in some way; these are to be known as the qualities of *tamas*.
Vyāsa said:
The mind projects existence; the intellect is determinative; the heart knows what is pleasant and unpleasant—this is the threefold impulse to action.
For the objects of the senses are superior to the senses, and the mind is superior to the objects.
Higher than the mind is the intellect (*buddhi*), and higher than the intellect is held to be the self (*ātman*).
The intellect is the self of a human being; the intellect alone constitutes the very essence of the self.
When it undergoes a modification of state, it then becomes the mind (*manas*).
Due to the distinctness of the senses, the intellect (*buddhi*) undergoes modification in subtle ways:
when hearing, it becomes the ear; when touching, it is called the sense of touch;
when seeing, it becomes the eye; and when tasting, it becomes the sense of taste.

When smelling, it becomes the sense of smell; the intellect is modified separately. They call these the "senses," and the invisible one presides over them. Abiding in the person, the intellect functions within three states.
Sometimes one finds joy, and sometimes one grieves; at times here, one is joined neither with pleasure nor with pain. This very nature of existence transcends these three states of being.
Just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, possesses great tides amidst its waves,
so too when it desires something, that [desire] becomes the mind.
One should indeed contemplate these various bases through the intellect as distinct entities.

The senses alone are the objects to be purified; they must be conquered entirely and in their proper sequence. For whatever [sense] is not brought under control, the intellect, failing to achieve its distinction, remains fixed upon the objective world within the mind.
When *rajas* is active, it follows after *sattva* as well.
Whatever states of being exist, they all proceed within these three [guṇas],
moving in accordance with their purpose like spokes on the rim of a chariot wheel.
A person should employ the senses, which are the highest forms of intelligence, for the purpose of illumination—
emerging according to their proper application, yet remaining indifferent and spontaneous. Knowing that this world is of such a nature, the wise man is not deluded.
Neither grieving nor exulting, always free from envy— for the Self cannot be seen by means of the senses whose domain is desire,
which operate toward what is improper, being difficult to restrain for those of undisciplined soul.
But when one properly restrains their rays with the mind,
then the Self shines forth like a lamp burning within a jar,
just as for all beings when darkness has departed.
All this becomes manifest; let it be understood in this way:
just as a water-dwelling bird is not smeared while moving through the water, so too the yogi whose self is liberated is not smeared by the defects of the qualities (*guṇas*).

In this very way, one of perfected wisdom, while moving among sense objects, is not defiled by faults in any way whatsoever, remaining unattached to all things. Having abandoned previously performed karma, his delight is always in the Self.
For one who has become the self of all beings and does not cling to the paths of the *guṇas*,
the *sattva*-self never produces the *guṇas*;
nor do the *guṇas* know the self, but the self knows the *guṇas* at all times.
He is the observer of the qualities (guṇas) and their creator exactly as they are. Know this to be the distinction between the subtle sattva and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña).
One creates the qualities, while the other does not create the qualities.
Though these two are distinct by nature, they are always conjoined;
just as a fish is distinct from water yet remains conjoined with it, so too are these two. And just as a gnat and a fig tree are likewise conjoined together.
"Just as the blade of grass exists both separately and together within the Muñja grass,
even so these two exist together, each established within the other.
Vyāsa said:

The *sattva* (the material principle) emits the qualities (*guṇas*), while the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) presides over them; the Lord remains indifferent toward all the qualities as they undergo transformation.
All this, by which he emits these qualities, is joined with its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*).
Just as a spider emits its thread, it projects qualities like a strand of fiber;
once destroyed, they do not return, and their active manifestation is no longer perceived. That which is beyond perception is established through inference based on what is directly perceived.
In this way some resolve [upon action], while others resolve upon cessation;
having carefully weighed both of these, one should decide according to one's own understanding.
By this very method, one becomes a great being dwelling in the womb.
Having attained that which is eternal and without beginning or end, a man may wander about;
the divine chariot, joined with victory, is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Then, having quickly approached it, he who desires to yoke the chariot in this manner—
I shall describe the method for one whose mind is intent on reaching the *akṣara* (the Imperishable) swiftly:
[one should proceed] by way of the seven *yodhāyanas* in their entirety, or otherwise from another direction; others follow behind and at the sides, as far as the expansion of its mouth extends.
One gradually attains the sovereignty over the earth, as well as that of wind, space, and water; then the sovereignty of light, of ego-consciousness, and of the intellect,
and finally the sovereignty of the unmanifest.
And for one who possesses these [qualities] through such disciplined yoga, there arises for that practitioner, as he beholds the method within himself, a vision of the Self.
When being churned, the subtle self manifests these forms:
just as wintry smoke subtly pervades the sky,
so too does that former form manifest for one who has been liberated from the body.
Then, upon the cessation of smoke, there is a second vision of form:
one perceives space as if it were the form of water right there within oneself; and when that too passes away, the form of fire shines forth.
When that has ceased, even the subtle form belonging to the wind-element manifests there; likewise, O Unborn One, a yellow-colored form also appears.
When that has ceased, the form of space manifests.

That which is to be inferred is the form of the *savarṇa*; its own form shines forth therein. When that has ceased, the form of his intellect (*buddhi*) shines forth—extremely pure for the Brahmin whose mind is perfectly concentrated upon the unmanifest.
Listen now to the various fruits that arise even from these births:
for one born with the sovereignty of kings, this creative power is ordained;
like Prajāpati, unshakable, he creates offspring from his own body.
It is perceived by its color in the waters, yet it does not drink from reservoirs; furthermore,
when one bathes,
its form is burned away by his splendor and likewise extinguished.
With a thumb and forefinger, like the bursting of a bladder, they cause the earth to tremble; this is known as occurring through the loss of their qualities.
Having become like space, they are not seen in space because they have attained the nature of gold.
Upon the conquest of the ego, those five will come under one's control; moreover,
when the six are firmly established within the self, the intellect indeed attains its full power.
For this entire [universe], arising from the faultless source, proceeds forth;
in that same way, the manifest attains the unmanifest. From which the world emerges and comes to be designated as "the manifest."
In that regard, listen to my detailed explanation concerning the unmanifest (avyakta),
and likewise first understand from me the explanation concerning the manifest (vyakta).
The twenty-five principles (tattvas) are equal and identical in both cases.
Likewise, hear from me the distinctions regarding Yoga and Sāṃkhya as well: that which is born, exists,
lives, and dies— being endowed with these four characteristics— is said to be entirely futile.
That which is contrary to this is declared to be the Unmanifest (avyakta). Furthermore, two evil-natured beings are mentioned even in the established doctrines (siddhānta) among the gods;
they are the fourfold class of living beings characterized by four marks, which is designated as the fourfold aim of life (caturvarga).
The manifest and that which is born from the unmanifest, as well as the intellect and what is other than that—

this pair consisting of the *sattva* (the field) and the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field)— is the vision of the unmanifest. Furthermore, two selves shine forth among the gods and within the objects of the senses.

The withdrawal from sense objects, along with the light that is the mark of spiritual accomplishment; being free from "mine-ness," free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, and with doubts severed;
neither becoming angry nor feeling hatred—these are your words regarding the true Self.
Even when reviled or struck, he meditates on loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and not on what is unwholesome; he turns back the three types of violence— of speech, mind, and body—
and being equal toward all beings, he transcends even Brahmā.
Established in mere sustenance, he desires nothing, nor does he desire not;
free from greed, self-controlled, he is neither of good form nor of no form.
His senses, mind, vital breaths, and intellect do not belong to him who is the witness of all.

Neither becoming angry nor rejoicing, always free from envy— having thus transcended the firm knot of the heart composed of the thoughts of the intellect, one should dwell in happiness, free from grief and with doubts severed.

Just as men who have fallen from the earth might suffer when plunging into a full river, know that the ignorant are likewise submerged in this world. But the wise man does not suffer; knowing the truth, he moves upon dry land.
Thus, he who finds the Self as the absolute knowledge of the self—
having understood this and having carefully observed the entire coming and going of all beings, a man gradually attains supreme peace.
This indeed is the true capacity of birth for a Brahmin, especially:
self-knowledge and tranquility; that is sufficient for his ultimate goal.
Having understood this, one becomes enlightened; what other characteristic of an enlightened one could there be?
Having realized this, the wise, having accomplished what was to be done, are liberated. For those who know, there is no great fear—
that which would be a very great fear for the ignorant.
For there is no higher goal for anyone than that which is eternal for the wise man; people, however,
find fault with the world that is afflicted by suffering.
And beholding each of those very things, one grieves. Behold there those who are skillful and do not grieve— they who understand both that which is done and that which is left undone.
Whatever one does without prior intention, and whatever previously done one now dispels—
both of these are neither pleasant nor unpleasant.
That produces for him [the result] as he performs it here.
Śuka said:
There is no dharma whatsoever in this world superior to that dharma.
"Tell me that which is superior to all dharmas.
Vyāsa said:
"I shall fully declare to you the ancient dharma praised by the seers."
Listen now with one-pointed mind to that which is superior to all dharmas:
having restrained with effort the turbulent senses that tend to rush outward in every direction, as a father restrains his young children, by means of the intellect.
The one-pointed concentration of the mind and the senses is indeed the supreme austerity;
it is superior to all dharmas, and that is called the highest dharma. Having unified all those [faculties], with the mind as the sixth, through wisdom—
One should remain as if satisfied within oneself, not thinking of the many things that ought to be thought about.
When the senses have withdrawn from their objects and abide in their own abode,
then you shall, by means of the self, behold the supreme, eternal Self.
The great-souled Brahmins who are wise behold him as the self of all, the Great Soul, like a smokeless fire;
he is like a great tree with many branches, endowed with flowers and fruit.
The self does not recognize its own nature, wondering, "Where is my flower? Where is my fruit?
In this same way, the self does not know, "Whither shall I go? From whence indeed have I come?
For there exists another inner self here who perceives everything.
With the blazing lamp of knowledge, one perceives the self by means of the self. Having seen the self by means of the self, become selfless and all-knowing;
liberated from all evils like a snake that has cast off its skin.
Having attained supreme understanding here, free from sin and devoid of fever,
one crosses the terrible river that flows toward all worlds, which possesses the five senses as its crocodiles and the volitions of the mind as its banks.

This foremost of rivers has greed and delusion for its grassy cover, desire and anger for its reptiles, truth as its bathing-ghats, and falsehood for its turbulence; it has wrath for its mud. Originating from the Unmanifest, it flows swiftly and is difficult to cross for those who have not disciplined their selves.
O dear one, cross over with your intellect this river, which is infested with the crocodiles of desire;
it flows toward the ocean of saṃsāra, is difficult to traverse due to the depths of the womb,
arises from one's own birth, has the tongue for its whirlpools, and is hard to approach.
That which those of perfected wisdom, the steadfast, and the wise cross over—
having crossed it, you, being liberated on all sides, purified in soul, a knower of the Self, and pure,
shall attain the state of Brahman by relying upon the highest intelligence.
Having crossed over all afflictions, with a serene self and free from stain,
observe the beings on the lower stages as one standing upon a mountain;
remaining neither angry nor elated, you should likewise be of a non-cruel mind.

Then you shall behold the origin and dissolution of all beings. Thus indeed, O best among the upholders of dharma, the wise sages who perceive the truth have considered this dharma to be superior to all other dharmas.

Having understood this instruction for my sons concerning the imperishable Self, it should be spoken to one who is self-controlled, who seeks his own welfare, and who follows [the path]. This knowledge of the Self is secret, the greatest of all secrets, and sublime.
"O dear one, that which I spoke directly, with my own self as witness—
that this is neither female, nor male, nor even neuter;
it is Brahman, devoid of suffering and pleasure, the essence of the past, the future, and the present."
Having known this, neither man nor woman shall undergo rebirth;
this path is prescribed for the sake of attaining non-becoming (abhava).
Just as all doctrines are held [to be true], yet they are not exactly so.
"O son, these things have been recounted by me— those that exist and those that do not.
[This was told] by a son endowed with affection and virtue, possessed of the qualities of a true son."
"Indeed, being asked this by one who is affectionate and seeking his welfare,
one should speak here that which was said regarding the son.
Vyāsa said:
He should not pursue fragrances, flavors, or pleasure;
he should not seek out various ornaments;
nor should he desire honor, renown, or fame.
This indeed is the conduct of a seeing Brāhmaṇa:
even if one should study all the Vedas, being obedient and observant of the vow of celibacy— yet by the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, and the Sāman-chants alone, he is not thereby a Brāhmaṇa.
To all beings he is like a kinsman; he is all-knowing and a knower of all the Vedas. He never dies without desire, nor is he not a Brāhmaṇa because of that.
Having performed various *iṣṭi* sacrifices and *kratu* rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, he attains [the highest state].
One never attains the state of Brahman by any means through covetousness.
When one does not fear, when others do not fear him, when one neither desires nor hates— then one attains Brahman.
When one does not harbor evil intent toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then one attains Brahman. The bond of desire alone is the only bond here; there is no other bond.

For one who is liberated from the bonds of desire is fit for becoming Brahman. Being freed from desire like the moon emerging from a grey cloud, the wise man, free from passion and awaiting his time, conducts himself with fortitude.
Just as waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immovability,
so he is one who desires [the fulfillment of] desires, but is not one who hankers after desires.
That embodied soul indeed goes from this world to heaven;
likewise, he into whom all desires enter attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Truth is the secret essence of the Veda; self-restraint is the secret essence of truth; generosity is the secret essence of self-restraint; austerity is the secret essence of generosity;
renunciation is the secret essence of austerity; and happiness is the secret essence of renunciation.

Heaven is the secret foundation of happiness; tranquility is the secret foundation of heaven. You desire that state of being which is characterized by supreme peace through contentment—a state that dries up both grief and mental distress along with craving.
Free from sorrow, free from possessiveness, peaceful, serene in soul, and the best among those who know the Self— he,
endowed with these six characteristics, shall return once more,
accompanied by six wise and highly skilled ministers who are possessed of the qualities of goodness.
Those who know the Self both after death and while remaining here, they know it truly as that which is uncreated,
indestructible, natural, and unadorned;
such a person of perfected wisdom enjoys the imperishable bliss of the inner self.
Having made the mind free from movement and having established it firmly in every respect,
that satisfaction which one attains cannot be achieved otherwise. By this one is satisfied even without eating, and by this one is contented even without wealth.
By means of that [subtle essence], one who is without attachment sustains his strength; he who knows that is a knower of the Veda.
For that disciplined Brāhmaṇa who remains with the doors of his senses well-guarded and closed, reflecting within himself, is said to delight in the Self.
Composed in the supreme reality, with desire extinguished and firmly established,
he follows after bliss from every side, just like the lunar body.
For the sage who does not partake in the specific elements or the qualities, [there is this state].

Suffering is dispelled by happiness, just as darkness is dispelled by the sun. Old age and death do not find that Brahmin who has transcended karma, who has transcended the destruction of the qualities (guṇas), and who is no longer attached to sense objects.
When he is liberated from all sides and remains equanimous,
staying within the body, he transcends the senses and the objects of the senses;
having reached the supreme cause, he has passed beyond the state of being an effect.
"There is no returning for one who has attained that which is beyond the supreme.
Vyāsa said:
"One who desires to know liberation, having practiced both material prosperity and dharma, [transcends] the pairs of opposites."
A disciple should first be made to hear this great [teaching] by a virtuous teacher:
space, wind, light, water, and earth as the fifth;
existence and non-existence, and time—[these reside] within all beings in these five.
Space is the inner self; the sense organ of hearing consists of that [space]. One who knows the rules of the treatises on form should know that sound is its quality.
The foot [of the Veda] is the nature of wind, and the prāṇa and apāna breaths consist of that [wind].
One should know that the sense organ is touch, and likewise, tactile sensation consists of that [earth]. From it comes digestion and manifestation; light is the eye, and it consists of that [fire].
One should know its quality to be form, whose nature is characterized by darkness (*tamas*).
Moisture, subtlety, and oiliness—these are taught to be the nature of water. Blood, marrow, and whatever else one might know to be oily are composed of that [water].
The faculty of taste, the tongue, and the sense of taste are considered to be qualities of water.
The earth element consists of the aggregate [of the body]: the bones, teeth, and nails;
the beard, body hair, and head hair; the veins, sinews, and skin;
as well as the sense organ known as smell, which is designated as the nose.

And this odor, which is the object of the sense organ, should be known as consisting of earth. Among the subsequent elements, all qualities exist; and among all [preceding] ones, the subsequent qualities are present. The sages know the continuity of the five collections of elements.
Of these, the mind is the ninth, while the intellect (buddhi) is recorded as the tenth;
the inner self (antarātman) is said to be the eleventh, transcending all. The intellect has the nature of determination, while the mind has the nature of conceptualization.
Through inference from karma, that living being known as the "field" (kṣetra) is to be understood.
The wise man who perceives all things as pervaded by all these states, including time as the eighth, remains undefiled and does not follow delusion.
Vyāsa said:
Those whose minds are fixed on the scriptures perceive, by means of the actions prescribed in the scriptures, the embodied soul as a subtle being indeed liberated from the body.
Just as rays of light move together,
appearing to go, stay,
and so forth, so too those liberated from bodies wander through the worlds.
In the same way, a being of great power perceives a reflection of another being, just as the heat of the sun is perceived in the waters. (12.245.3)
Those who know reality, whose senses are restrained and who abide in purity, perceive those subtle beings— freed from the body— by means of their own essential nature;
they are perceived by all, whether sleeping or waking, as the object of one's own contemplation of the self.
For those yogis who have abandoned the passion born of action through the resolution of the duality of the primary constituents (guṇas),
the self consisting of sattva remains perpetually under their control— just as it is by day, so it is by night; and just as it is by night, so it is by day.

Among them, the self of beings (bhūtātman) is eternally impermanent; it is constantly accompanied by the seven subtle qualities, is mobile, and is free from old age and death. Overpowered by the mind and the intellect, it perceives its own body as well as the bodies of others.
Even in dreams, this cognizer experiences pleasure and pain;
