there too one encounters suffering, and there too one encounters pleasure.
Yet even there, having committed acts of anger and greed, one meets with calamity.
He becomes delighted even upon obtaining great wealth;
he performs meritorious deeds therein and perceives them as if he were awake. Even while entering the state of the womb, he remains enveloped in great heat.

Having dwelt in the womb for ten months, he does not decay like food. Those who are possessed by *tamas* and *rajas* do not perceive him— the one who consists of supreme splendor, the self of all beings— though he resides within the heart amidst the physical forms.
Devoted to the yoga of the scriptures and desiring to preserve their own self,
they [perceive] those things which are breathless, formless, and even like a thunderbolt,
amidst the four distinct duties of the stages of life that have been created.
12,245.013 Śāṇḍilya has declared that this very yoga in meditative absorption is tranquility.
12,245.014 Having understood the seven subtle principles and Maheśvara with his six limbs,
one who is established in the application of the primary matter (pradhāna) attains the supreme Brahman.
Vyāsa said:
In the heart stands the wondrous tree of desire, born from an accumulation of delusion; its great trunk is anger and pride, and it is entwined by the longing for sensory experience.
Ignorance is its root, and negligence is its irrigation;
it has malice for its leaves and is nourished by the essence of past misdeeds.
It has delusion and anxiety for its trunk, grief for its branches, and is terrifying to behold.
Enveloped by deluding and thirst-inducing creepers,
greedy people desiring fruit wait upon that great tree; bound by the snares of exertion, they strive to encircle it for its fruits.
He who, having brought those snares under his control, pulls down that tree,
has reached the end of the two sufferings by striving against them both. For the one of unrefined wisdom causes the tree to grow back through his very distress.

It destroys that very [defilement] from which it arose, like a poison that has been swallowed by a sick man. By means of equanimity— which takes the form of renunciation and vigilance— that root of the root of residual attachment is forcibly uprooted with the supreme sword.

He who thus understands that desire is merely a dragging down—indeed, a slaughter of the science of desire—he transcends all sufferings. They say the body is a city; the intellect is held to be its mistress.
Therein, the intellect’s faculty residing within the body is called the mind (*manas*), which contemplates objects;
the senses are the citizens, while the supreme creative power is their sovereign.
Therein lie two harsh defects: namely, darkness (*tamas*) and passion (*rajas*).
That purpose for which the citizens, together with the lord of the city, subsist—

that very purpose two defects subsist upon by means other than the proper gate. In this regard, the intellect is indeed invincible, while the mind is said to possess a nature similar [to the intellect].

The citizens were also terrified in their minds, and their stability was likewise shaken. That purpose for which the intellect exerts itself does not fail; however, for one who is deprived of the counsel of the citizens, that purpose gradually collapses.
For whatever purpose the mind dwells separately, that [object] causes it to become exhausted. When the mind becomes solitary and separated from the intellect (buddhi),
then the empty rajas remains enveloped therein.
That mind, having come into contact with *rajas*, forms a friendship with it;
taking that person along, it delivers them over to *rajas*.
Bhīṣma said:

"O sinless son, listen once more to the enumeration of the qualities of the elements as they issued from the mouth of Dvaipāyana, out of his supreme praise. Resembling a blazing fire, the Blessed One spoke them to Dhūmravarca."
12,247.002c Therefore, my son, I shall further provide an illustration.
12,247.003a The stability, extensiveness, hardness, and productive nature of the earth;
12,247.003c its odor, heaviness, power, cohesion, steadfastness, and fortitude.
The coldness of water is its taste, its moisture, its fluidity, its unctuousness, and its gentleness; likewise, the tongue is its exuding quality, as is the flowing of the waters on earth.
The invincibility of fire is its brilliance, its heat, its capacity for cooking, and its illumination.
Purity, passion, lightness, sharpness, and tenthly, upward movement;
irregularity, touch, the locus of speech, and independence belong to wind.
Strength, speed, delusion, activity, and the performance of action are its manifestations.
Sound is the quality of space (*ākāśa*), as well as its pervasiveness and porosity;
it is without support, without a basis, unmanifest, and immutable;
it possesses non-obstructiveness, the state of being an element (*bhūtatva*), and various modifications.
Five hundred qualities are said to be produced from the nature of the five elements:
mobility, birth, manifestation, emission, imagination,
patience, existence, non-existence, and speed— these are indeed the nine qualities of the mind.
The discrimination between the desirable and the undesirable, resolve, concentration, doubt, and comprehension— these are the five qualities here associated with the intellect (*buddhi*).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

How is it that the intellect (*buddhi*) possesses five qualities, and how is it that the five sense organs possess qualities? Are these [qualities] produced from those [elements], or do they belong to their own nature or even to the Self (*ātman*)? O Grandfather, explain all of this to me, for you possess subtle knowledge.
Bhīṣma said:
They say there are sixty qualities of the elements,
which are distinct from the elements themselves and eternally attached to them.
"O son, those things that are attached to the elements and produced from syllables are not said here to be eternal. O son, what has been spoken is fashioned by thought."
Indeed, you shall here soon attain the entirety of the true nature of reality as it is; through the power of that which has become, may your mind become tranquil.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"These lords of the earth who lie here upon the surface of the ground—
these mighty warriors, indeed, have lost their life-force in the midst of the army."
Each one of them possessed formidable strength, equal to ten thousand elephants;
yet these have been slain in battle by men of equal splendor and might. Never before have I seen anyone among living beings who could be their slayer in combat.
Endowed with prowess and possessed of splendor and strength,
O one of great wisdom, these now lie here with their life-breaths departed;
thus the word "dead" is applied to those whose lives have gone.
"12,248.005a These kings who have died were for the most part of terrible prowess.
12,248.005c A doubt has arisen in me regarding this: from where does the designation 'dead' come?
12,248.006a Whose is death? From what does death arise? By what means do living beings here meet their death?"
"O one who resembles an immortal, tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"In former times, O dear one, in the Kṛta age, there was a king named Avikampaka."
Having fallen under the power of the enemy with his mounts exhausted in battle,
his son named Hari— who was equal to Nārāyaṇa in strength—
was slain there in the conflict along with his army and his followers.

That king, fallen under the power of his enemies and overwhelmed with grief for his son, while wandering at will intent on performing rites of pacification, beheld Nārada upon the earth. The lord of men related everything to him exactly as it had happened.
"The capture by enemies in battle and likewise the death of his son.
Having heard those words of his, Nārada, whose wealth is asceticism,
then related this narrative which dispels the grief for a son.
"O King, listen now to this very extensive narrative,
exactly as it occurred and as it was heard by me, O lord of the earth.
Having created living beings, the Grandfather of great splendor [proceeded] with the creation of progeny."
12,248.013c The creatures, having become exceedingly numerous and very old, could no longer endure it.
12,248.014a For there was not the slightest space anywhere among the living beings, O Acyuta; 12,248.014c the three worlds became, O King, as if swollen and breathless.
O lord of the earth, a thought regarding universal dissolution arose within him;
yet, as he reflected, he could not find the cause or reason for such a dissolution.
O great king, from his wrath, fire burst forth from the pores of his skin.
O King, by that [fire], the Grandfather burned all the directions;
then, O King, the fire born from the Lord’s wrath consumed heaven, earth, the sky, and the entire world with its mobile and immobile beings.
There, all beings— both mobile and immobile— were consumed by fire when the Great-Grandfather became enraged with a surge of great wrath.
Then there appeared Śiva, the one with tawny matted hair, the motionless Sthāṇu, the Lord of the Vedas and sacrifices.
The god, the slayer of enemy heroes, spoke for refuge to Brahmā. When Sthāṇu had approached out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures,
the boon-granting god, blazing as it were, then addressed Śiva.
"Today I shall fulfill whatever desire you wish; in my view, you are worthy of a boon.
For I shall do what is pleasing to you, O Śambhu, whatever dwells within your heart.
Sthāṇu said:
"O Lord, know that this activity of mine is for the purpose of creating progeny. These beings were created by you; do not be angry with them, O Grandfather.
O God, by the fire of your splendor, all creatures are being consumed on every side."
"Seeing them, compassion arose in me; O Lord of the World, do not be angry with them.
Prajāpati said:
"I am not angry, nor is it my desire that you should not become progeny."

"For the sake of lightening the earth, its dissolution is therefore desired. For this goddess, always oppressed by the burden, has urged me toward its withdrawal, O Mahādeva; she is sinking into the waters because of her weight."
"When, despite reflecting deeply with my intellect,
I could not find a means for the destruction of these aged women, anger took possession of me," Sthāṇu said.
"Be gracious unto the end of this dissolution; do not be angry, O Lord of the Thirty-three.
Do not destroy the creatures, both the stationary and the moving, nor all the ponds, nor any grass or shrubs."
The fourfold collection of beings, both stationary and moving—this entire world has been reduced to ashes and overwhelmed. Be gracious, O holy Lord; this is the boon I have chosen.
"Once these creatures have perished, they will not return by any means whatsoever.
Therefore, let this energy be withdrawn by your own power;
consider another means out of a desire for the welfare of all beings."
"O scorcher of the foe, so that all these creatures might turn back [from destruction], and so that the progeny, with their offspring diminished, might not go toward non-existence,
they should therefore be led into the power of death by means of successive methods."
O Unborn One, having conceived of me as your son through your ascetic power,
I have been appointed by you to the office of the presiding deity over these worlds, O Lord. For this entire world, both mobile and immobile, has its origin in you, O Lord of the Universe.
"O Mahādeva, having propitiated you, I beg for those beings who are subject to rebirth.
Nārada said:
"But having heard these words of Sthāṇu, the God, whose speech and mind were restrained—"
He restrained that energy within his own self once more by means of his inner soul.
Then, having withdrawn the fire, the Blessed Lord, honored by the worlds,
the Sovereign, ordained both the path of worldly activity and the path of withdrawal.
As that high-souled one was then withdrawing that fire born of his wrath, a woman emerged from all the pores of his body;
she was dark-complexioned, wearing crimson garments, with red eyes and red palms and soles.
Adorned with divine earrings and decorated with celestial ornaments,
she emerged from the apertures of his body and took refuge in the southern direction;
then both those gods, the lords of the universe, beheld the maiden.
Then the God, the Lord and origin of the worlds, summoned her and said,
"O Death, O protector of the earth, slay these creatures;
for you were conceived by me in anger with the intent of universal destruction."
Therefore, withdraw all creatures, both the ignorant and the wise; O beautiful lady, withdraw the creatures without distinction,
for by my command you shall attain the highest good.
Thus addressed, that goddess Mṛtyu, garlanded with lotuses,
became sorrowful and, as a young woman, shed profuse tears.
O lord of men, he [Yama] caught those tears with both his hands.
For the sake of the welfare of human beings, she entreated him once again.
Nārada said:
Having suppressed her grief, that woman of exceedingly long eyes—
Then, bowing like a creeper with palms joined in reverence, she said:
"O best of speakers, how could a woman such as I, created by you,
be born with such fierce deeds that she becomes a source of terror to all living beings?"
I am afraid of unrighteousness; prescribe for me a righteous task. O Lord, look upon me, who am terrified, with an auspicious eye.
May I not carry off innocent children, the elderly, and those in the prime of youth.
O Lord of living beings, obeisance to you; be gracious toward me.
O God, I am afraid that they will harbor ill-will toward their beloved sons, friends, brothers, mothers, and even fathers once they have died.
The burning of the tears of the wretched would consume me for eternal years;
terrified of them, I have come to you for refuge,
O Lord, for those who perform evil deeds go to the abode of Yama at the end.
"O Giver of Boons, I seek to propitiate you; O Lord, grant me your favor. O Grandfather of the Worlds, I desire this wish from you:
O Lord of the Gods, through your grace, I wish to perform ascetic penance."
12,250.009 Pitāmaha said:
"O Mṛtyu, you were created by me for the purpose of destroying living beings;
indeed, you were conceived by me in anger with the intent of universal destruction."
"Go, withdraw all these creatures, and do not hesitate.
This must certainly come to pass; it cannot be otherwise. O sinless one of faultless limbs, let my word be carried out exactly as spoken."
12,250.011 Nārada said:
O mighty-armed conqueror of enemy cities, having been addressed thus, Death remained silent and stood bowed, gazing up at the Blessed One.
Though she was addressed again and again in this manner, that noble lady remained silent as if her life-force had departed; then the god, the Lord of the lords of gods,
Brahmā, being self-possessed, became truly gracious in his own person.
Smiling, the Lord of the World gazed upon all the worlds. When that invincible Blessed One had turned away from his anger,
we have heard that the maiden departed from his presence.
Having departed then without promising to bring about the destruction of creatures,
O Indra among kings, Mṛtyu approached Dhenuka as if in great haste.
There, that goddess performed supreme and difficult penance.
She remained standing on one foot for twelve thousand, five hundred, and sixteen *koṭis* of years.
While she was thus performing that most difficult ascetic penance there,
the highly resplendent Brahmā spoke these words once again.
"O Death, act according to my word! But disregarding that,
O dear one, she quickly stood once more on a single foot for seven other days,
and then for six, five, and two padmas, O giver of honor.
Furthermore, O dear one, she wandered with the deer for ten thousand padmas; and for another twenty thousand years, O best of men, O high-minded one, she subsisted on air alone.
Then, O King, having gone from there, she observed the highest vow of silence.
O King, for eight thousand and one hundred years she remained within the waters.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, that maiden went to the Kauśikī river,
where she again practiced her religious observances, subsisting on air and water alone.
Then the highly fortunate lady went to the Gaṅgā and to Meru alone;
she stood there motionless like a piece of wood, desiring the welfare of all beings.
Then she went to the summit of the Himavat, where the gods had performed their sacrifice.
There, O king of kings, he stood upon another *nikharva* [of years] with his thumb, and he diligently gratified the Grandfather (Brahmā). Then,
the source and dissolution of the worlds spoke to him there:
"12,250.024c What is this that is happening, my daughter? Let my word be done.
12,250.025a Then Death spoke again to the blessed Grandfather: 12,250.025c 'I shall not carry away the subjects, O Lord; I beseech you once more.'"
To her, who was terrified by the fear of unrighteousness and was thus entreating him once more, the God of gods then spoke these words after restraining her:
"O auspicious Mṛtyu, there shall be no unrighteousness for you; restrain these subjects."
"O blessed lady, nothing whatsoever that has been spoken by me shall ever become false here;
eternal Dharma itself shall enter into you right now,
and both I and the gods are always devoted to your welfare."
"I grant you this other wish as well, desired by your mind:
beings afflicted by disease shall not afflict you with harm.
And among men, you shall become a man in form."

Among women she takes the form of a woman, and among those of the third gender, she becomes a neuter. Thus addressed, O Great King, she spoke with palms joined in reverence to that high-souled, imperishable Lord of Gods, saying, "No."
Then the God said to her: "O Mṛtyu, gather in human beings. No unrighteousness shall be yours; I shall so ordain it, O auspicious one.
For you, O beautiful lady, are vigilant, disciplined, and were born first."
"Instructed and faultless, therefore do as I advise you:
those teardrops which I saw falling,
which were held by my hands before me."
These diseases of terrible form will afflict human beings when their time has come, O Death;
you shall be the ender of all living creatures at the time of their passing.
You should employ desire and anger together;
in this way, immeasurable dharma will come to you, and you,
maintaining equanimity, shall not incur unrighteousness.
"If you will protect the Dharma in this way as has been taught, and will not immerse yourself in unrighteousness,
then you may take pleasure in the desire that has come to you."
"Then, having joined them together, withdraw all living beings here.
At that time, out of fear of the curse, she who was designated by the name Mṛtyu said to him, "So be it."
Furthermore, at the time of death, [Death] seizes the vital breaths of living beings and,
having rendered them deluded by means of desire and anger, he slays them.
Those tears which fall from the eyes of dying men are the very diseases of Death.
That by which the bodies of humans are afflicted,
and indeed that which afflicts all living beings at the end of their lives— for this reason, do not grieve, but understand it with your intellect.
All the gods, at the end of the life-breaths of living beings, having gone forth and passed away, return in that very same way;
even so do all human beings at the end of their life-breaths.
Having gone forth and returned like a god, O lion among kings,
he is the wind— terrible, of fearsome roar, and of great power—
the very life-breath of all living beings.
The various modes of existence for embodied beings arise from the difference in their bodies;
therefore, Vāyu is distinguished as the God of gods.
All other gods are distinguished only by the designation of "mortal."
All mortals are distinguished by the designation "deity" (12,250.040c).
Therefore, O lion among kings, do not grieve for your son;
having attained heaven, your son indeed rejoices.
Thus, Death, created by the God, duly withdraws living beings when their time has come;
and the diseases are her very tears.
"Destroying living beings here when the time has arrived.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"All these men, indeed, are full of doubt regarding dharma."
"What is this *dharma*, and from whence does *dharma* arise? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Is this *dharma* for the sake of benefit in this world, or is it for the sake of benefit in the next world, or is *dharma* for the sake of both? Tell me that, O Grandfather."
Bhīṣma said:
Right conduct, the Smṛtis, and the Vedas—these three are the characteristics of dharma;
the wise say that the fourth characteristic of dharma is worldly purpose (artha).
For even when actions have been performed, they are distinguished as superior or inferior;
the regulation of dharma has been established here solely for the sake of maintaining the course of the world,
resulting in happiness in both this life and the next.
Failing to obtain the subtle Dharma, the evil person becomes addicted to evil.
And those who have committed evil are not released from their sins even in times of distress. When one speaks no evil, one becomes a knower of the Dharma.

The culmination of dharma is one's own conduct; relying upon that alone, you shall awaken. When a thief, possessed by unrighteousness, seizes wealth, and a robber takes pleasure in carrying off the property of others in a kingless land—
When others carry away his wealth, he then desires a king; then he envies those who are indeed content with their own riches. Fearless and pure, he approaches the royal gate without hesitation.
Indeed, one perceives no misconduct whatsoever within one's inner self;
speaking the truth is excellent, for there is nothing superior to the truth. Everything is sustained by the truth; everything is established upon the truth.
Even those who are fierce evildoers, having each individually made a solemn vow, proceed with non-malice and without deception, relying upon that [truth].
If they were to harbor mutual lack of fortitude, they would undoubtedly perish.
"It is the eternal law that another's wealth must not be taken," so they believe; yet the powerful maintain that this law was established by the weak,
and it is only when their own power is constrained by destiny that they find such a rule pleasing.
For those who possess great strength are not necessarily happy;
therefore, you must never, under any circumstances, set your mind upon dishonesty. For such a person, there is no fear from the wicked, nor from thieves, nor from the king.
Doing nothing for anyone, one should dwell pure and fearless;
a thief suspects everyone, like a wild animal that has entered a village,
and he perceives his own manifold committed sins as being elsewhere.
Joyful, pure, and always fearless, he approaches from all sides;
for he perceives no misconduct whatsoever in himself or in others. "One must give"—this is the Dharma taught by those devoted to the welfare of living beings.
Those possessed of great wealth consider that [misery] to have been brought about by the wretched; yet when their own destitution becomes fixed, it is precisely this that they find pleasing.
For those who possess abundant wealth do not remain so forever, nor even those who are happy.

Whatever action a person does not desire to be done to himself by others, knowing it to be unpleasant to himself, he should not do that to others. How can one who would be the paramour of another’s wife be fit to say anything at all?
If another were to do that to him, it would not be forgiven; such is my view.
How could one who desires to live himself cause another to be slain? Whatever one desires for oneself, one should consider that for another as well.
One should share one's surplus enjoyments with others who possess nothing;
for this reason, the Creator ordained the practice of usury.
However, it should be conducted in such a manner that the gods may remain satisfied in that agreement.
Moreover, if stability in righteousness is maintained even at the time of gaining wealth,
the wise say that everything is acceptable when it is consistent with what is dear to dharma. Behold this summary of characteristics regarding dharma and adharma, O Yudhiṣṭhira.

"O best of the Kurus, this supreme conduct of the virtuous— which was ordained of old by the Creator for the sake of maintaining the world, which is fixed upon the subtle meaning of dharma, and which is declared to be the very characteristic of dharma— has been described to you."
Therefore, you should never, under any circumstances, set your mind upon dishonesty.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The subtle and virtuous definition of dharma has been well explained by you."
"I possess a certain intuition; let me express it through inference.
The many questions that were in my heart have been answered by you. O King, I shall now state another, not as if from a quarrel."
For these [scriptures] lead one forward, create [results], and cause one to cross over;
yet, O Bhārata, Dharma cannot be understood merely through rote recitation.
The Dharma for one established in prosperity is different from that for one in adversity.
"How can calamities be known through recitation?
Good conduct is considered *dharma*, yet the virtuous are defined by their conduct.
How can what is achievable or unachievable be known, for good conduct has no fixed characteristics?"
An ordinary person practicing unrighteousness may appear in the form of righteousness, while someone extraordinary practicing righteousness may appear in the form of unrighteousness; furthermore,
its authoritative measure has indeed been pointed out by those learned in the scriptures.
"We have heard that the teachings of the Vedas diminish with each successive age:
the duties in the Kṛta age are of one kind, others in the Tretā, and still others in the Dvāpara;
the duties in the Kali age are different, as if performed according to one's capacity."
"The statement of the sacred tradition (āmnāya) is true"—this is for the sake of maintaining worldly order. From the sacred traditions, the Vedas have issued forth in all directions;
if all of them are indeed authoritative, then that [authority] does not exist.
When both the authoritative and the non-authoritative are contradicted, how can there be the status of a scripture?
When Dharma is being carried away by powerful and evil-minded men,
whatever established form is altered, that too perishes.
We know this, or perhaps we do not; it may be possible to know, or perhaps it is not.
It is subtler than the edge of a razor and greater even than a mountain.
At first, it appears like a city of the Gandharvas.
Though investigated by the wise, it again goes out of sight;
like watering-troughs near cattle, or like an irrigation channel in a field, O Bhārata,
even the eternal Dharma, though remembered, is no longer seen when it has fallen into decay.
Some follow out of desire, others out of exhaustion, and still others for various other reasons;
indeed, many others who are not virtuous engage in empty conduct. Yet that which is true dharma quickly dissolves among the wicked.
Others call them madmen and even mock them;
for the great masses have turned away from them and have taken refuge in the duties of kingship.
Indeed, no single mode of conduct is seen that is beneficial to all.
By that very same [cause], another arises; that, in turn, obstructs yet another.
And again, by chance, it is seen to be identical in form. By that very same [cause] through which one arises, it also obstructs others.
One should observe the lack of uniformity in the practices of all people;
for the Dharma was proclaimed by the sages of old as having been established long ago,
and through that ancient practice, the eternal order is maintained.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the words of Tulādhāra concerning dharma, in conversation with Jājali.
In the forest, there was a certain forest-dwelling twice-born man named Jājali;
having gone to the vicinity of the ocean, that great ascetic practiced austerities. Restrained and moderate in diet, he wore rags, skins, and matted hair.
Covered in the mud of impurities, that wise sage remained so for many groups of years.
Once, O lord of the earth, that highly effulgent brahmin seer, dwelling within the waters, traveled through the worlds at the speed of thought while observing them.
Once, while in the midst of the water, that sage,
having gazed upon the earth extending to the ends of the ocean with its groves and forests, reflected:
"In this world of mobile and immobile beings, there is no one equal to me."
"May he who is other than I go from the waters into the sky," he said. Then, while being watched by the *rākṣasas*, he spoke thus in the midst of the water.
And the *piśācas* said to him, "You ought not to speak in this manner."
"Tulādhāra, the merchant of great renown in Vārāṇasī, who follows the dharma of a trader—
even he would not speak in such a manner as you do, O best of the twice-born.
When he was thus addressed by the beings, Jājali, of great asceticism, replied:
"May I see that wise and illustrious Tulādhāra"—
to the ṛṣi speaking thus, the rākṣasas, having lifted him out from the ocean,
said: "Go, O best of the twice-born, by taking this path."
Thus addressed by the beings, Jājali then departed dejected in mind;
having reached Tulādhāra in Vārāṇasī, he spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What meritorious deed was performed by Jājali in the past, O dear one, by which he attained supreme perfection? You ought to explain that to us.
Bhīṣma said:
Endowed with exceedingly fierce asceticism,
that great ascetic indeed became devoted to bathing in the river morning and evening;
that twice-born one properly tended the sacred fires and was supremely dedicated to the private recitation of the Vedas.
Jājali, who was well-versed in the rules for forest-dwellers and blazing with spiritual luster,
remained steadfast in truth and austerity, yet he did not perceive any higher dharma;
during the rains he slept under the open sky, and in the winter he took refuge in the water.
Enduring wind and sun in the summer, he did not find even a modicum of comfort;
he experienced various painful beds and rolled about upon the ground.
Then, on one occasion during the rainy season, that sage took his stand in the open air.
From the atmosphere, he repeatedly received the water upon his head;
then, O Lord, his matted locks became soaked and matted together.
His matted locks became soaked and matted together as he was drenched, O Lord.
Constantly dwelling in the forest, soiled and covered in dirt,
that great ascetic once remained without food, subsisting only on air;
he stood as motionless as a log of wood and never wavered at any time.
O Bhārata, while he remained motionless like a pillar,
O King, two *kuliṅga* birds built a nest upon his head.
That compassionate brahmin-sage watched over that couple.
While that great ascetic remained motionless like a pillar, constructing a nest there among his matted locks with blades of grass and fibers,
the two of them, becoming completely confident, then dwelt there in comfort.
Then, when the rainy season had passed and the autumn time had arrived,
O King, those two sky-dwellers, deluded by desire through their trust [in one another], deposited their eggs there upon his head according to the ritual prescribed by Prajāpati.
That radiant brahmin, firm in his vows, perceived them;
and having perceived them, the highly energetic Jājali did not stir at all.
With his mind always fixed on dharma, he never took pleasure in adharma.
Day after day they would come there, O Lord, and dwelling upon his head, those two remained there, greatly delighted and comforted. Then,
from the well-nourished eggs, young birds were born.
They grew right there, yet Jājali did not move;
guarding the eggs of the sparrows, he of firm vows remained exactly as he was— righteous-souled, motionless, and composed in meditation.
Then, in the course of time, those birds grew their wings;
and the sage perceived that the young birds had developed their pinions.
Then, on one occasion, while observing those birds there, he who was firm in his vows—
Then that best of the wise became supremely delighted;
seeing them thus fully grown, he attained great joy.
The two birds dwelt there fearlessly together with their offspring.
Every evening, the brahmin Jājali saw those birds— whose wings were now fully grown— fly away and return once more; though they came again and went away continuously, Jājali did not tremble.
Though abandoned by his mother and father, Jājali did not waver. Then, O King, having gone out to forage during the day,
those birds returned there again in the evening for the purpose of dwelling.
Once, after flying away for five days,
the birds returned on the sixth day, yet Jājali did not tremble;
and in this manner, they all departed again for many more days.
When those birds, having gained their strength, did not return—
once, after flying away for as long as a month, O King, they did not come back at all— then Jājali departed from that place.
Then, when they had dissolved away, Jājali was filled with wonder;
he formed the thought, "I have attained perfection," and pride took possession of him.
Having seen the birds thus departed, he who was firm in his vows—
Having been honored, he felt deeply gratified and highly esteemed.
Then, having sipped water from the river and offered libations to the sacrificial fire,
that man of great asceticism approached the rising sun.
Having honored the sparrows upon his head, Jājali, the best among those who recite prayers,
slapped his arms in the air, exclaiming, "Indeed, I have attained Dharma! Then a voice arose in the sky, which Jājali heard.
"O Jājali, you are indeed not equal to Tulādhāra in terms of righteousness.
O highly wise one, Tulādhāra is established in Vārāṇasī;
even he would not speak in the manner that you speak, O twice-born one."
Overcome by indignation and desiring to see Tulādhāra,
O King, he wandered the earth as a sage who makes his home wherever evening finds him.
After a long time, he arrived at the city of Vārāṇasī.
He saw Tulādhāra selling various wares; and upon seeing that Brahmin approaching, the merchant,
filled with great joy, rose up and honored him with a welcome.
Tulādhāra said:
"O Brahmin, it is known to me that you have indeed arrived; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the twice-born, listen to the words that I shall speak."
"Having resorted to the coastal marshlands of the ocean, you performed great austerities;
yet formerly, you had no knowledge whatsoever of the nature of dharma.
Therefore, O Brahmin, when you had attained perfection through your penance, birds—"
"O twice-born one, they were quickly born upon your head and were nurtured by you;
when their wings had grown and they flew away here and there,
you then considered dharma to have its origin in the sparrow."
"O best of the twice-born, you heard my voice from the sky directed toward me;
overcome by indignation, you have therefore arrived here.
O best of the twice-born, tell me what pleasing thing I may do for you."
12,254.001 Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed at that time by the wise Tulādhāra,
the intelligent Jājali, the best among those who recite prayers, spoke these words.
"O merchant, while you were selling all kinds of juices, all kinds of perfumes,
trees, medicinal herbs, and their roots and fruits,
you attained a definitive realization. From where did this come to you?"
"O you of great intelligence, explain all of this to me in its entirety.
Thus addressed by the illustrious Brāhmaṇa,
the Vaiśya Tulādhāra, who knew the true essence of dharma and its purpose, spoke of the subtle points of dharma.
O King, at that time Jñānatṛpta spoke to Jājali, who was performing arduous penance:
"O Jājali, I know the eternal Dharma along with its secret mysteries—
that ancient Dharma which people know as being friendly and beneficial to all beings."
That mode of life which is characterized by non-injury toward living beings, or at least by minimal injury, is the supreme dharma; it is by this that I live, O Jājali.
This shelter has been constructed by me from limited pieces of wood and grass.
O brahmin-sage, having purchased lac, *padmaka*, *tuṅga*, various perfumes, and many different juices— excluding liquor— I sell them back from the hands of others without any deceit.
He who is always a friend to all and is devoted to the welfare of all through deed, thought, and speech— he knows dharma, O Jājali.
I neither praise nor do I revile the actions of others.
O brahmin seer, like the sky, beholding the diversity of the world, I neither conform nor resist; I harbor no hatred and have no desire. I am equal toward all beings; behold my vow, O Jājali.
"Free from the desirable and the undesirable, and cast off by affection and attachment,
my scale remains equal toward all beings, O Jājali;
know me thus, O Jājali, as one who is the same for the whole world."
O best among the wise, you for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal;
to me who beholds you, you are like those blind, deaf, and insane men who are always intent only on breathing, their doors closed even by the gods.

Just as the elderly, the sick, and the emaciated are free from desire for sense-objects, so too has my desire for wealth, pleasure, and enjoyments vanished. When one does not fear this world, and when this world does not fear him—

When he neither desires nor hates, then the twice-born truly attains perfection. When he does not harbor sinful intent toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then he becomes one with Brahman.

There is nothing that has been, nor will there be anything, nor is there any dharma whatsoever that is not a source of fear for all living beings; he who is free from such fear attains the state of fearlessness. For everyone in the world trembles before him, as if from the jaws of death.

Through harshness of speech and cruelty in punishment, he incurs great fear. We follow the conduct of those high-souled elders who possess sons and grandsons, who live according to the law, and who are non-violent.
The eternal Dharma has been lost, obscured by the delusion of false conduct;
by that [delusion], even a learned man, an ascetic, or one who is powerful is led astray.
O Jājali, through right conduct a wise man quickly attains Dharma.
Thus, one who is self-controlled and free from malice should wander among the virtuous;
just as a piece of wood being carried along here in a river by chance might happen to meet with another piece of wood by mere accident.
There, other materials— grass, wood, and dried cow dung— are gathered from here and there, sometimes even without prior consideration;
in this very manner, this custom has arisen from various sources.

O Sage, because he never causes any living being to tremble in any way whatsoever, he always attains fearlessness toward all beings. O learned one, because the entire world trembles before him as if before a wolf—
Just as all aquatic creatures reach the shore when crying out,
so too does he who has companions and wealth— whether fortunate or otherwise— reach his goal;
therefore, the wise indeed proclaim this very truth in their treatises.
Those who possess little inner resolve, yet are eloquent and have reached complete certainty for the sake of fame—
by means of austerities, sacrifices, gifts, and words based on wisdom—
they obtain whatever fruit one enjoys here in this world through the gift of fearlessness.

In this world, he who bestows the gift of fearlessness upon all beings, having performed all sacrifices, attains the gift of fearlessness himself. There is no dharma whatsoever superior to non-violence toward living beings.
O great sage, he from whom no living being is ever agitated in any way whatsoever attains fearlessness from all beings;
whereas the world is agitated by him, as if by a snake that has entered its home.
He does not attain dharma in this world or in the next—
he who has become the self of all beings and perceives all beings correctly;
even the gods are bewildered regarding the path of that trackless one who seeks the footprints [of the truth].
They say that the gift of fearlessness to all beings is the highest of all gifts;
I tell you this truth, so believe it, O Jājali.
Having been fortunate, he becomes unfortunate once again.
Seeing the failure of ritual acts, people always feel revulsion;
for here, O Jājali, there is no dharma, even the subtlest, that exists without a cause.
Indeed, the proclamation of dharma in this world has been made solely for the sake of the welfare of beings, both past and future.

Because of its subtlety, it cannot be discerned, as it is deeply concealed; yet, perceiving other internal behaviors, one comes to understand it. And those who castrate [the bull], and those who pierce the nostrils—
They carry heavy burdens, bind them, and subdue them; having killed living beings, they devour them—how is it that you do not censure this? Humans indeed enjoy other humans as their slaves.
By means of killing, binding, and opposition, they make [them] work day and night.
You yourself know what suffering there is in killing and beating;
in all beings possessing the five senses, every deity dwells.
The sun, the moon, the wind, Brahmā, the vital breath, Kratu, and Yama—
having sold these living beings, what consideration can there be for those who are dead?
The goat is Agni, the ram is Varuṇa, the horse is Sūrya, and the earth is Virāj.
The cow and the calf are indeed Soma; this cannot be accomplished by selling them.
O Brahmin, what [value is there] in oil, in ghee, in honey, in water, or in medicinal herbs?
[One should instead give] animals raised in comfort in a region free from gadflies and mosquitoes.
Knowing them to be dear to their mothers, men nevertheless trample upon them in many ways and lead them to regions full of biting gadflies and sharp *kuśa* grass, as well as to places of much mud.
Some draft animals, oppressed by the burden, collapse through such improper treatment.
I do not consider even the killing of an embryo to be worse than that deed. People consider agriculture to be a virtuous thing, yet that livelihood is truly cruel;
for the iron-tipped wood strikes both the earth and those who dwell within it.
"O Jājali, look likewise at these oxen yoked [to the cart].
'Aghnyā' is the name for cows; who would dare to kill them? Pṛṣadhra committed a great misdeed, as if he were slaughtering cows."
"O Nahuṣa, the ṛṣis and ascetics have indeed informed you of this:
'You have slain the cow, your mother, and the bull Prajāpati;
O Nahuṣa, you have committed an act that should not be done, and we shall suffer fear because of your deed.'"
Those highly blessed ṛṣis, O Jājali, cast down one hundred and one diseases upon all living beings among the progeny;
yet they said of Nahuṣa, the killer of the embryo, "We shall not offer oblations for you."
Having spoken thus, all those high-souled sages, ascetics, and tranquil ones who perceive the truth of reality, swiftly replied:
"O Jājali, such inauspicious and terrible practices as these exist here."
But because it is practiced by the solitary, you do not perceive it, O skillful one.

One should seek dharma through its underlying cause; one should not merely follow the conduct of the world. Listen also to this, O Jājali: regarding both him who would strike me and him who praises me.
"Those two would be equal to me, for I have neither the pleasant nor the unpleasant.
Wise men praise such a dharma as this;
it is endowed with logical consistency and is practiced by ascetics."
[He was] constantly characterized by those of virtuous conduct and distinguished by his skill.
Jājali said:
"Just as Dharma has been set in motion by you, who hold the scales."
He will block the gateway to heaven and the livelihood of living beings. For from agriculture food arises, and from that you too live;
O merchant, mortals live by means of livestock and medicinal herbs.
"From this sacrifice proceeds even atheism, which you yourself are speaking of; for this world could not subsist if it were to abandon its very means of livelihood.
Tuladhara said:
"O Jājali, I shall explain the [proper] way of life; O Brāhmaṇa, I am not an atheist.
Nor do I revile sacrifice, yet one who truly understands sacrifice is very difficult to find. Homage to the sacrifice of the Brāhmaṇas and to those people who are knowers of sacrifice."

"O Brahmin, having abandoned their own Vedic sacrifices, the Brahmins have here adopted the sacrificial rites of the Kṣatriyas— rites set in motion by greedy men devoted to wealth, who are atheists and who,
failing to understand the declarations of the Vedas, propagate a falsehood that merely has the appearance of truth."
"This must be given, this must be given"—thus one never desires to reach the end [of giving]. Know, O Jājali, that this is indeed the Dharma set in motion by the gods.
For this other state is unstable; such is not our understanding.
From this, O Jājali, theft and forbidden acts arise.
That alone is a well-performed oblation by which the deities are satisfied—
namely, through prostration, the sacrificial offering, Vedic study, and likewise medicinal herbs.
Indeed, the worship of the deities should be performed according to the instructions of the scriptures.
From the sacrificial offerings and charitable works of the unrighteous, offspring of a wicked nature are born;
from the greedy, the greedy are born, and from the even-minded, the even-minded are born.
Just as the sacrificer and the officiating priests [are sustained], so too are the subjects;
from sacrifice, offspring arise like pure water from the sky.
O Brahmin, the oblation cast into the fire reaches the sun.
From the sun rain is born; from rain comes food, and from that, living beings.
Therefore, by performing it well, the ancients obtained all their desires;
the earth yielded crops without being ploughed, and plants grew through mere blessings.
They perceive no fruit whatsoever in sacrifices, nor in their own selves. Those who, suspecting some reward from sacrifice, might perform it in any way at all,
are born as wicked, deceitful, and greedy men whose sole purpose is wealth.

That man who, by means of an improper measure, would perform an evil act against one who is innocent, shall go to the worlds of evildoers because of his unwholesome karma; O best of the twice-born, such a person is always evil-minded and lacks wisdom in this world.

The Brahmin who understands both that "this must be done" and that which is to be done as "not to be done," abides in Brahman alone in this world and does not return again to the state of duty. Furthermore,
we have heard from tradition that even a defective action is superior [to inaction].
There was no injury to any living being, and there was restraint regarding the acquisition of fruits;

all people performed sacrifices of truth and sacrifices of self-control, were free from greed, and were satisfied with themselves. They renounced what they had acquired and were entirely devoid of envy.
Those who know the truth of the field and the knower of the field, being firmly established in their own sacrifice and studying the Veda of Brahman, satisfy even the immortals.
For the entire host of deities and all that is divine is centered in Brahman and rests upon the Brāhmaṇas.

When one is satisfied, the gods are satisfied; when one has attained contentment, O Jājali, they too are satisfied. Just as one who is satiated with all flavors does not crave anything further, so for one satisfied by wisdom, there is eternal contentment that gives rise to happiness.
Delighting in the Dharma and finding happiness in the Dharma, they were thus entirely resolute;
seeking with wisdom, they thought, "There is more for us in reality.
Some, possessing knowledge and discernment, desired to cross to the further shore.

That place is exceedingly meritorious and always endowed with the merit of its noble origin; having gone there, they do not grieve, they do not fall away, and they do not suffer. Indeed, those who are characterized by sattva attain that abode of Brahmā in this world.
They do not desire heaven, nor do they sacrifice with wealth for the sake of fame;
they follow the path of the virtuous according to their strength through non-violence.
They know the lords of the forest, the medicinal herbs, and fruits and roots.
Nor did those greedy officiating priests, seeking wealth, perform sacrifices for them;
rather, the twice-born performed the sacrifice again, acting for their own sake,
once their duties were completed, out of a desire to favor the subjects.
Therefore, those greedy officiating priests cause inauspicious men to perform sacrifices.
"They would surely lead all creatures to heaven through the practice of their own duty"—
this is the view that occurs to my mind, O Jājali, as being consistent everywhere.
O bull among the twice-born, O great sage, those wise ones who always employ these [mantras] in sacrifice travel by that path leading to the gods;
for one there is a return, but for the wise there is no return.
Both of them, O Jājali, travel by the path of the gods;
their oxen yoke themselves and carry the burden,
and the cows milk themselves through the perfection of their mental resolve.
Taking the sacrificial posts themselves, they perform sacrifices with abundant fees. Only one whose self is thus purified is fit to immolate a cow;
O Brahmin, those who are not such as these should sacrifice with herbs.
Placing the renunciation of intellect at the forefront, I shall describe such a one to you:
the gods know him as a *brāhmaṇa* who is free from desire, free from undertaking, free from salutation, and free from praise; who is undecaying, yet whose karma has been exhausted.
O Jājali, what destination does one go to who neither causes [the Vedas] to be heard, nor performs sacrifice, nor gives to the Brāhmaṇas,
yet desires the way of life of a householder? But by making this [the cow] his deity, how may he attain the fruit of sacrifice?
Jājali said:
"We have never heard the truth from the sages;
O merchant, I ask you about this difficult matter."
The seers of old and those before them did not look back upon this; they do not establish him beyond this point.
In this very "ford of the self," even the beasts would not find happiness.
"O merchant, by what action of one's own might one obtain happiness?
Tell me that, O man of great wisdom; I have indeed full faith in you.
Tulādhāra said:
Whether they be sacrifices or non-sacrifices, those do not merit the title of *makha* (sacrifice) anywhere;
yet the cow itself becomes a *makha* through its clarified butter, milk, curds, especially the full-oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*),
and even through its hair, horns, and hooves.
And by employing this ritual procedure, he makes his wife [participate] as well;
for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is said to be the pure essence of all animals. All rivers are Sarasvatīs, and all mountains are meritorious.

"O Jājali, the self alone is the sacred ford; do not become a guest of various regions. O Jājali, practicing such duties as these here, one who seeks dharma through external causes does not attain the auspicious worlds."
Bhīṣma said:
Tulādhāra praises such duties as these—
those which are endowed with logical justification and are constantly practiced by the virtuous.
Tulādhāra said:
"Whether this path has been followed by the virtuous or by the wicked, let it be clearly demonstrated; then you will truly understand how it is."
"These many birds are indeed wandering all around;
hawks and other species have been born upon your head. O Great Brahmin, call them out as they enter from here and there."
"Behold these birds clinging to his hands, feet, and indeed to his entire body; they honor their father because they have been honored by you.
Without doubt, O Jājali, you are the father; call out to your sons."
12,256.005 Bhīṣma said: Then, summoned by that Jājali, the birds uttered divine speech, indeed, by the command of Dharma.
Action performed through non-violence and other virtues bears fruit both in this world and the next;
yet rivalry, O Brahmin, destroys it, and once destroyed, that rivalry slays the man himself. Sacrifice cannot protect one whose faith has been diminished by speech and mind.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite these verses sung by Brahmā:
"The gods considered the mind of one who is pure but lacks faith, and that of one who has faith but is impure, to be equal in the performance of a sacrifice."
"Having deliberated upon both— the miserly Vedic scholar and the generous usurer— the gods declared their food to be equal.
Prajāpati said to them, 'This has been made unequal!'"
The food of a generous man is purified by faith; that of another is destroyed by a lack of faith.
The food of a generous man is fit to be eaten, but not that of a miser nor that of a usurer.
Only one who lacks faith is unworthy to offer oblations to the gods.
Those who know the Dharma understand that one must not eat the food of such a person.
Lack of faith is the supreme evil; faith is the deliverer from evil. One who possesses faith casts off evil just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
The cessation of ritual acts, accompanied by faith, is superior to all purifiers.
He who has turned away from the faults of conduct and possesses faith is truly purified;
what need has he for austerity, what need for ritual observance, or what need for self-discipline?
"This person consists of faith; whatever his faith is, that he truly is.
Thus has dharma been declared by the virtuous who perceive the true meaning of dharma. Desiring to know this, we have approached you because of our vision for dharma.
"Abandon your rivalry, O man of great wisdom; then you shall attain that which is supreme.
O merchant Jājali, one who possesses faith, who is full of conviction, who adheres to the duties here, and who remains established in his own path—he is indeed superior."
Thus was this matter of great significance spoken by Tulādhāra;
he was properly instructed, and the eternal Dharma was declared. Having heard these words of that man of renowned prowess, that twice-born one—
O Kaunteya, Tulādhāra attained peace itself. Then, after a short time, both he and Tulādhāra, being possessed of great wisdom, went to heaven and dwelt there at their pleasure.
Having each returned to their own respective abodes won by the fruits of their own karma—
those who were equal, faithful, self-controlled, and pure-minded,
performing what they considered to be sacrifice— sacrifice was never withheld from them.
O King, Śraddhā is indeed the goddess of the *sattva* quality; she is the daughter of the Sun. She is Sāvitrī, the Progenitress, and likewise the one who inspires confidence in living beings.
O Bhārata, Śraddhā protects that which is increased by speech and that which is increased by the mind.
"By this teaching through similes, what more do you wish to hear?
Bhīṣma said:

Out of compassion for his subjects, King Vicakṣuṇa sang this song:

"May there be well-being for the cows in all worlds"— this etymological explanation was thus provided; for when violence had begun to prevail,
this benediction was devised [as a remedy] by men who were deluded, atheistic, and devoid of established moral boundaries.
By those of doubting mind and unrefined nature, violence has indeed been proclaimed;
yet Manu, whose soul was dharma, declared that non-violence prevails in all actions. Driven by desire and passion, men slaughter animals outside the sacrificial altar.

Therefore, the subtle Dharma must be understood through the means of valid cognition by one who possesses discernment; for non-violence alone is considered superior to all other dharmas. Having fasted, having become self-restrained, and having abandoned the Vedic scriptures composed by the seers—
Those who claim that "proper conduct" consists of improper conduct are wretched people motivated by the desire for rewards.
If men were to eat meat in vain under the pretext of sacrifices, trees, or sacrificial posts, this would not be praised as dharma.

Meat, honey, wine, fish, fermented liquor, and rice mixed with sesame—this has been introduced by rogues; it is not ordained in the Vedas. This practice of gluttony was set in motion out of desire, delusion, and greed.

In all sacrifices, the Brahmins recognize Viṣṇu alone; his worship is likewise prescribed with milk-rice and flowers. Furthermore, those trees designated as fit for sacrifice in the Vedas [are to be used].
And whatever else is to be done, if it is performed with purity and well-prepared by those of great being and pure intent, all of that is indeed worthy of the gods.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The body and even calamities contend with one who does not practice violence. How will the maintenance of the body succeed for one who is free from all exertion?
Bhīṣma said:
12,257.013a So that the body may not waste away and so that it may not fall under the power of death,

"How should one examine a task—whether quickly or after a long time?
In every way, regarding this difficult matter at hand, you are our supreme preceptor.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history concerning what formerly occurred in the lineage of Aṅgiras regarding Cirakārin:
"O Cirakārin, may it be well with you; may it be well with you, O Cirakārin!"
For the wise man who acts with deliberation does not err in his deeds. The son of Gautama was named Cirakārin because of his great wisdom;
indeed, being discerning, he would undertake all tasks only after long reflection.
Reflecting long upon his purposes, staying awake for a long time, and sleeping for a long time,
he is called "Slow-Acting" (*cirakārī*) because of his success in accomplishing tasks only after a long delay. Furthermore, the dull-witted man is likewise called "Indolent" (*alasa*).
By a person of superficial intellect and lacking foresight,
when some transgression occurred,
the father— having bypassed his other sons— spoke in anger: "Kill this mother of yours."
Having spoken thus, that brahmin Gautama, the best among those who practice austerities,
the highly fortunate one, went straight to the forest without further reflection.
Having said "So be it" after a long time, Cirakārika remained as he was by his very nature.
Reflecting for a long time due to his habit of acting with deliberation, he pondered at length:
"How can I carry out my father's command, yet not kill my mother? How can I avoid sinking like a wicked man into this deception of dharma?"
Obedience to one’s father is the highest duty, and the protection of one’s mother is one’s own inherent duty;
likewise, the state of being a son entails a lack of independence—how could these not cause me pain? For who, having killed both his mother and a woman, could ever be happy?
Who, having shown contempt for his father, could attain a firm standing? Disregarding one's father is improper; honoring him and protecting one's mother are both appropriate.
How can I not transgress these two duties, which are both consistent with righteousness and patience?
"For a father places himself within his wife, thinking, 'May I be born again.
This is for the sake of maintaining the lineage, conduct, family name, and the clan.
Thus, I am that very self, brought forth once more by my father into the state of a son."
"How might my consciousness not exist?"— thus he awakened to its origin within himself.

What his father had said during the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and what he had said during the preparatory rite (*upakarman*) was sufficient confirmation for his certainty regarding his father’s gravity.
The teacher is the foremost and supreme dharma, for he is beneficial through nourishment and instruction. Whatever the father says is dharma; this is well-established even in the Vedas.
The son is merely a source of joy to the father, but the father indeed possesses everything belonging to the son.
12,258.017c The body and other such things are to be given, yet the father alone bestows them.
12,258.018a Therefore, the word of the father must be carried out; it should not be questioned in any way whatsoever.
12,258.018c Even those who have committed sins are purified by acting according to the word of the father.
In matters of wealth, fortune, procreation, and as a guide for all the world; likewise, in union with a husband and at the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*),
the father is heaven, the father is dharma, and the father is the supreme austerity.
When the father is pleased, all the deities are pleased;
those blessings which the father pronounces attend that man. When the father rejoices, it is the atonement for all sins.

A flower is released from its bond; a fruit is released from its stalk. Yet even while suffering through affection for his son, a father does not relinquish that affection. This, then, is the reflection upon a son’s reverence for his father.
For I shall consider my father’s station to be inferior; I shall think of my mother.
Indeed, this aggregate composed of the five elements that exists within me in its mortal state—of this, my mother is the cause, just as the fire-drill is the cause of fire.

The mother is the fire-drill for men’s bodies; she is the relief for everyone who suffers. Upon finding a mother, one has a protector; in her absence, one is without protection. One does not grieve, nor does old age overcome him.
Even one who is destitute of fortune, if he addresses his mother at home as "Mother," that man,
though filled with anxiety, shall surely attain joy himself,
provided he has taken refuge with his mother and is surrounded by sons and grandsons.
Even at the end of a hundred years, he may behave like a two-year-old child;
whether he is capable or incapable, emaciated or otherwise,
the mother alone protects her son— no other nourisher exists according to the natural law.

Then he becomes old when he becomes afflicted with suffering; then the world is empty for him when he is separated from his mother. There is no shade equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother.

There is no protection equal to a mother; there is no well equal to a mother. She is called a *dhātrī* because she sustains one in her womb, a *jananī* because she gives birth, an *ambā* because she nourishes the limbs, and a *vīrasū* because she gives birth to heroes.
Because she nurtured him while he was an infant, the mother is called *śuśrū* (the nourisher). A conscious man whose head is not hollow would surely slay her immediately after his body [is born].
Indeed, that agreement which was made between husband and wife regarding the union of their lives—
Only the mother or the father knows him; the true reality resides in the mother.
The mother knows his lineage, and the mother knows whose son he is.
Through the mere act of nourishing, the mother feels affection and love for her offspring, whereas the father’s concern is for his progeny.
If men, having themselves performed the joining of hands and entered into the common practice of dharma, should cast off their wives, those women do not deserve to be cast off;
for it is from supporting her that a husband is called "bhartṛ," and from protecting her that he is called "pati."
But when this quality ceases, he is neither a sustainer nor a husband;
thus, the woman does not commit an offense, for it is the man alone who commits an offense,
and by transgressing, the man alone incurs great guilt.

For a woman, the husband is indeed remembered as the supreme lord and the highest deity; he gave her his own self as her supreme counterpart. Because she does not fail in any duty, women do not commit offenses.
For that instruction which was spoken for the satisfaction of a woman's sexual desire—by clearly recalling it, there is clearly unrighteousness; of this there is no doubt.
[This applies even] to one as long as she is a woman, or a mother, or one who stands in a position of superior respect.
Even animals, though lacking discernment, know her to be inviolable;
they recognize her as the father of the gods gathered together in one place,
and out of affection for both mortals and deities, she approaches as their mother.

As he was thus reflecting, a great deal of time passed by due to his habit of acting with deliberation; then his father, the highly wise Gautama Medhātithi, who was established in asceticism, arrived.
Having reflected for that length of time upon the transgression committed by his wife,
he spoke, tormented by grief and shedding profuse tears;
through the clarity of his learning and fortitude, he was overcome with remorse.
Purandara, the lord of the three worlds, arrived at my hermitage;
assuming the form of a Brahmin and adhering to the vow of hospitality,
he was welcomed with a greeting and comforted with kind words.
He was duly presented with water for his hands and feet by her;
he was told, "I am dependent on another," and he replied, "I shall act with prudence.
Furthermore, since this misfortune has arisen, there is no transgression on the part of the woman.
"Thus, neither the woman, nor I, nor the traveler, nor the Lord of the Thirty-three gods has offended against Dharma; rather, it is negligence that offends.
They say that calamity is born of envy, and for that reason, those whose semen is drawn upward [the *ūrdhvaretas*] are [free from it]."
But I, provoked by envy, am submerged in an ocean of evil deeds;
having slain a virtuous woman who was disciplined because of her addiction,
and my wife who was to be supported— who indeed shall deliver me?
"In the meantime, the noble-minded Cirakārin was indeed commanded by me;
if today Cirakārin were present, he would save me from this sin.
O Cirakārin, may it be well with you! May it be well with you, O Cirakārin!"

"12,258.051c If you are indeed one who acts after long deliberation today, then you are truly Cirakārika. 12,258.052a Save me and my mother, as well as the ascetic merit I have earned; 12,258.052c and save yourself from sins—be a Cirakārika today!"

Your innate habit of acting with long deliberation, due to your long-standing wisdom, has caused us both such mental anguish that it would not have been so from an unproductive result. May that [habit] of yours now bear fruit; become, this day, a "Cirikāraka" (one who acts after long deliberation)!

Long has he been longed for by his mother, and long has he been borne within her womb. O Cirakārika, make your habit of acting slowly bear fruit! For one who delays out of distress sleeps for a long time once restrained.
"O Cirakārin, considering the long-standing suffering of us both,"—
thus did that great seer Gautama, O King, being then afflicted with grief,
behold his son Cirakārin standing near him.
But Cirakārin, seeing his father, was deeply distressed;
casting aside his weapon, he then began to propitiate him by prostrating with his head at his feet. Gautama, however, seeing his son fallen upon the ground with his head bowed, [spoke].
And his wife, though formless, attained supreme joy;
for that high-souled one did not bring about any union with her as his wife while he remained in the solitary hermitage, and his son likewise remained composed.
One should strike [the enemy] without reproach while the son stands with weapon in hand; having questioned him who is disciplined, one should then resolve upon one's own duties.
And there arose a realization in her mind upon seeing the son prostrate at his father’s feet.
"Out of fear, he restrains his fickleness in taking up weapons.
Then, after his father had praised him for a long time, smelled the crown of his head for a long time, and embraced him with both arms for a long time, he was addressed: "Live long!"
Thus Gautama, filled with joy and delight, having congratulated his son, spoke these words:
"O Cirakārika, may prosperity be yours; act slowly and be one who deliberates long."
"Since you have delayed so long, I have been deeply distressed for a long time," said the wise Gautama, the best of sages, reciting these verses concerning those who act with deliberation,
based on the enumeration of their virtues: "In those who act slowly and steadfastly, there lies a reliance upon the manifestation of excellence."
One should form a friendship slowly and abandon what has been done slowly;
for a friendship formed slowly deserves to be maintained for a long time.
[This applies] regarding passion, pride, arrogance, malice, and sinful deeds.
When an unpleasant task must be performed, one who acts slowly is praised—
toward kinsmen, friends, servants, and women;
when offenses are unmanifest, one who acts slowly is praised.
Thus, O Bhārata, Gautama was pleased with his son for that deed, O Kauravya, because of that very quality of acting with deliberation. Therefore,
a man should always deliberate upon all matters before acting.
Having made a decision after a long time, one does not suffer for long;
one harbors anger for a long time and carries out an action for a long time. No action that causes remorse ever arises.
One should attend upon the elderly for a long time; having sat near them for a long time, one should honor them.
One should practice the dharmas for a long time and pursue their investigation for a long time.
Having sat near the learned for a long time and having attended upon the disciplined for a long time, [one attains wisdom].
Having long disciplined himself, he remains for a long time free from contempt;
even when another speaks words endowed with righteousness,
he should inquire for a long time and speak for a long time, and thus he is not humiliated for a long time.
Having spent many years in that hermitage performing great austerities,
that brahmin, together with his son, then ascended to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How may a king protect his subjects without causing them any distress? I ask you this, O best of the virtuous; tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Dyumatsena and King Satyavat. We have heard that Satyavat spoke what had not yet been spoken.
When men are being led away to execution by the command of their father himself,
dharma becomes adharma, and adharma becomes dharma;
that killing should indeed be considered dharma— this cannot be so.
12,259.005 Dyumatsena said:
12,259.005a "If non-killing were indeed the dharma, what dharma could ever exist?
12,259.005c If bandits were not slain, Satyavat, there would be a confusion of social orders."
"In the Kali age, the notion 'this is mine' would no longer prevail, and the course of worldly life itself would cease to exist; if you know otherwise, then tell us.
Satyavat said:
All three castes indeed must be made subject to the authority of the Brāhmaṇas;
for those bound by the fetters of dharma, transgression will be minimal. Whosoever among them should commit a transgression, that twice-born man should certainly report it.

"If he does not listen to me," the king should resolve thus regarding him; that which is prescribed in the treatises according to the unerring truth must be carried out, and not otherwise— nor should there be execution without having duly examined the actions in accordance with the science of polity.
A king indeed slays either the Dasyus or even many who are innocent;
when a man is killed, his wife, mother, father, and son are also slain.
Therefore, when an offense has been committed by another, the king should deliberate with perfect care.
Even an unvirtuous man may at times acquire good character;
likewise, from the virtuous, offspring that are not beautiful may be born from those who are unvirtuous.
One must not strike at the root [of the lineage], for this is not the eternal dharma.
Furthermore, indeed, atonement is prescribed even without execution— through causing terror, imprisonment, and disfigurement; they are to be afflicted by these punishments,
not by the infliction of capital punishment.
When those seeking refuge approach your priest, saying, "O Brahmin, we shall never again commit a sin," then they are worthy of release; such is the royal ordinance.
A shaven-headed Brahmin carrying a staff and an antelope skin deserves clothing.
For repeated offenses, those who are increasingly grave deserve progressively heavier punishments; they do not deserve such treatment as they did for the first offense.
Dyumatsena said:
"In whatever way the subjects can be restrained within the bounds of agreement,
that is declared to be dharma as long as it is not transgressed."
But if they were not being oppressed, everything would surely have perished;
for in former times and even earlier,
people were easy to govern— gentle, devoted primarily to truth, with little malice and little anger.
In former times there was only the punishment of reproach, and after that, the punishment of verbal censure.
There was also the punishment of seizure; today, however, the punishment of death prevails.
Yet even by means of execution, other people cannot be restrained.
"He is neither a plunderer of men nor of the gods," so says the sacred tradition;
he is not [the plunderer] of Gandharvas or the ancestors; for here in this world, no one belongs to anyone else.
He takes the lotus from the cremation ground and even the deity from the Piśāca.
12,259.022c He who would make a compact with those ignorant ones whose intellects are destroyed—
12,259.023 Satyavān said:
12,259.023a "If you are unable to protect those virtuous ones through non-violence..."
"Bring an end to this by obtaining some being, whether past or future.
Dyumatsena said:
"Kings perform supreme austerity for the sake of maintaining the course of the world."
They feel shame before such as those [virtuous ones], and they conduct themselves accordingly;
even when threatened, the doers of good do not kill evildoers out of desire. It is primarily through their own goodness that kings govern their subjects.
In this way, the world follows the conduct of those who are superior;
for human beings always follow the behavior of their elders. He who, without having composed himself, seeks to compose others—
Men laugh at one who, under the influence of pride and delusion, would do anything improper toward the king regarding his sensory objects;
such a person must be restrained by every possible means so that he turns away from evil.

First, one who restrains evil deeds must restrain oneself; one should punish even close kinsmen with severe penalties. Indeed, where a wrongdoer is not punished, he does not experience great suffering.

"Evil deeds increase there, and righteousness surely declines. Thus did that learned Brāhmaṇa, whose nature was compassion, instruct; and thus, O dear one, have I been instructed by my ancestors and grandfathers of old.
By those who comforted him most intensely out of compassion,
as well as by those following the primary rule, the king enjoyed [the earth] in the Kṛta age; likewise, he may proceed in the Tretā age with even a quarter less of dharma.
In the Dvāpara age, however, it exists with two feet, and in the next age, the Tretā, with one foot; likewise, when the Kali age has arrived due to the wicked conduct of kings,
by the specific nature of that time, there remains only a sixteenth part of Dharma.
Now, if there should be a confusion regarding the first ritual procedure,
one should prescribe the penance after specifying the lifespan, the capacity, and the time,
so that for the sake of truth, one may not lose the great fruit of dharma in this world.
For the sake of compassion toward all beings, Svāyambhuva Manu declared this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Renunciation that does not conflict with the welfare of living beings brings about the sixfold excellence."
"O Grandfather, tell me that which is the dharma common to both;
for between the dharma of the householder and the dharma of renunciation, both of which lead to similar goals, which indeed is superior, O Grandfather?"
Bhīṣma said:
Both dharmas, O highly fortunate one, are exceedingly difficult to practice;
both yield great fruits, my dear, and both have been practiced by the virtuous.
"12,260.004a Here I shall explain to you the authority of both of them;
12,260.004c listen with a one-pointed mind, O Pārtha, so that your doubts regarding dharma and artha may be severed.
12,260.005a In this regard, they also cite this ancient history."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn from me that dialogue between Kapila and the cow. For we have heard that in ancient times, Nahuṣa, observing the eternal and constant Vedic tradition, seized the cow of Tvaṣṭṛ.

Then Kapila, noble-minded, established in purity, devoted to his vow, possessed of knowledge, and restricted in diet, beheld her as she was thus engaged. Having attained supreme wisdom, he reached a state of steadfastness free from all fear.
"12,260.008c 'I remember truth as something lax,' so he said once regarding the Vedas.
12,260.009a The seer Syūmaraśmi, having approached that cow who was a renunciant, said to her:
12,260.009c 'Oho! If the Vedas are considered [the authority], by whom are other dharmas considered [authoritative]?"

12,260.010a For those who are ascetic, steadfast, and whose eyes are the wisdom of the Vedas, 12,260.010c indeed consider everything uttered by one who has realized the Self to be the word of a seer (ārṣa).
12,260.011a Of him who is thus free from thirst, free from fever, and free from desire—
"What intention could there be in the Vedas for one who is entirely devoid of all undertakings?
Kapila said:
"I do not revile the Vedas, nor do I ever intend to do so."
We have heard that the duties of those in the various stages of life (āśramas), though distinct, lead to a single goal:
the renunciant indeed attains it, the forest-dweller attains it,
and both the householder and the student attain it as well.
For four eternal paths leading to the gods are considered to exist;
among them, the superiority or inferiority, as well as the relative strength or weakness, has been declared in terms of their fruits.
Having understood this, one should undertake all goals—such is the Vedic teaching.
Elsewhere, another definitive scriptural tradition is heard stating, "One should not undertake [action].
For while there is no fault in non-undertaking, there is a supreme lack of fault in undertaking;
thus, for a scripture established in this way, the relative strength and weakness [of its injunctions] is difficult to discern.
"If there is anything here that is considered superior to non-violence (ahiṃsā) as a matter of direct perception,
apart from the teachings of the traditional scriptures (āgama), tell me that if you see it.
Syūmaraśmi said:
"The one who desires heaven should sacrifice"—thus the Śruti is constantly heard. For having first conceived of the fruit, the sacrifice is then extended.
[There are] the goat, the horse, the ram, the cow, and those which are the flocks of birds.
"Village and forest plants are the food of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," so says the Śruti. Likewise, food is indeed offered day after day, both evening and morning;
and cattle as well as grain are limbs of the sacrifice—so says the Śruti.
Prajāpati fashioned these together with the sacrifice; by means of that sacrifice, the Lord Prajāpati worshipped the gods. All those living beings, moving about one another, were seven times seven.
The cow, the goat, the human, the sheep, the horse, the mule, and the donkey—
these seven are declared by the wise to be domestic animals.
Likewise, lions, tigers, boars, buffaloes, and elephants [are wild].
The buffalo and the monkey are likewise remembered as the seven wild animals;
