they say that all these, when dedicated in sacrifices, are designated as "supreme. This very practice was authorized by those of old and even those before them.
What learned man would ever fail to examine his own power? Animals, humans, trees, and medicinal herbs alike all desire heaven; yet heaven is not attained without sacrifice.
Herbs, animals, trees, creepers, clarified butter, milk, curd,
the oblation, the earth, the quarters, faith, and time— these are the twelve.
The *ṛg*-verses, the *yajus*-formulas, the *sāman*-chants, and the sacrificer as the sixteenth.
Agni is to be known as the master of the house; he is said to consist of seventeen parts.

These are the limbs of the sacrifice, for the Śruti declares that the sacrifice has its root in the sacrifice itself. [It is performed] with clarified butter, milk, curd, dung, and curdled milk, as well as with the skin.
The cow indeed contributes to the sacrifice by means of her hairs, her horns, and her feet;
in this way, everything that is prescribed for her, each part individually,
together with the officiating priests and the sacrificial fees, carries out the sacrifice.
12,260.028 Having combined all these, they indeed accomplish the sacrifice;

12,260.029 for they were created for the sake of sacrifice, just as it is heard in the sacred revelation (śruti). In this same way, men of former and even more ancient times engaged in [the practice].
For he does not harm, he undertakes [the rite] without malice, and he bears no ill will toward anything;
he who performs sacrifice with the thought "sacrifice must be performed," desiring no fruit for himself—
without doubt, these are indeed the limbs of sacrifice as they have been described.
12,260.031c Those who are joined with the prescribed rule save one another by means of that rule.
12,260.032a I behold the traditional teaching of the seers (*ārṣa-āmnāya*) in which the Vedas are established;
12,260.032c the wise perceive it through following the insight of a Brahmin.
Sacrifice originates from the Brāhmaṇas, and it is indeed offered to the Brāhmaṇas. The entire world follows sacrifice, and sacrifice always follows the world.
"Oṃ" is the source of the Veda; likewise are "Namaḥ," "Svāhā," "Svadhā," and "Vaṣaṭ."
"Those for whom these [rites] are performed, even if accomplished only according to their capacity—
of them it is known that there is no fear of the next world in the three realms; thus do the Vedas, the Siddhas, and the supreme Ṛṣis declare here."

In whom all these— the *ṛg* verses, the *yajus* formulas, the *sāman* chants, and the ritual exclamations (*stobhas*)— as enjoined by the injunctions, exist even externally, he indeed is a twice-born man.
O twice-born one, whatever occurs at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) and whatever occurs when the *soma* has been pressed;
Whatever is known by others through great sacrifices, the Blessed One knows that by himself.
Therefore, O Brahmin, one should perform sacrifices and officiate at them without hesitation;
for one who sacrifices according to the heavenly rites obtains the great fruit of heaven after death.
"There is no world for those who do not perform sacrifices, nor is there a world beyond; this is the certain conclusion.
Furthermore, those who know the declarations of the Vedas hold both of these to be authoritative.
Then Kapila said:
Perceiving only this much, the ascetics who travel the path proceed;
for them, there is no transgression whatsoever in any of the worlds.
Free from dualities, free from salutations, and released from the bonds of hope, they are the wise.
Freed from all evils, they move about pure and stainless; having made their resolve for liberation, renunciation,
and wisdom, they are devoted to Brahman, have become one with Brahman, and have made their abode in Brahman alone.
"Free from sorrow and with their passion destroyed, their worlds are eternal. Having attained that supreme goal, what purpose would there be in the householder's life?
Syūmaraśmi said:
If this is the supreme goal, if this is the supreme path,
no other stage of life (āśrama) proceeds without depending upon the householder;
just as all living beings live by depending upon their mother.
In this way, the other stages of life depend upon the householder.
It is the householder alone who performs sacrifice; it is the householder who practices austerity. Whatever moves has its root in the householder’s stage of life.

"O Sage, all living beings have indeed come forth from procreation; furthermore, procreation is not found in any other way whatsoever. O twice-born one, those plants which exist outside [the womb] as well as those many that grow in the forest [arise thus]."
Since no living being whatsoever exists outside of plants,
whose words could be true that there is no liberation from the household? [Such words belong only] to those who lack faith, who lack wisdom, and who are devoid of subtle insight.
For those who are hopeless, listless, exhausted, and tormented by their own deeds,
the cessation of toil is seen by the wise as that which is called "renunciation" (pravrajyā).
For it is indeed the cause of the three worlds, the eternal and fixed boundary.
The venerable one called a Brāhmaṇa is honored from birth onwards;
for even before the rite of conception, sacred mantras are applied to the twice-born. They are employed in matters of trust as well as in matters of distrust, without a doubt.
Furthermore, when the cremation has been completed and [the bones] have been collected, there is the feeding from the vessel,
the gift of cows or other animals, and the immersion of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) in water.
The ancestors are traditionally known as the *arciṣmantas*, the *barhiṣadas*, and the *kravyādas*.
"Even for one who has died, the mantras authorize [the rites], and the mantras are the cause.
While the Vedas thus cry out, how can there be liberation for anyone? For mortals remain indebted toward their ancestors, the gods, and the twice-born."
This is the talk of idle scholars who are bereft of prosperity;
it is a lack of understanding of the Vedic teachings, appearing like truth though it is falsehood.
Indeed, one is neither carried away nor dragged down by sins.
The Brahmin who sacrifices according to the Vedic scriptures—
his sacrifice ascends together with the sacrificial animals; once fully gratified, it in turn satisfies him with all his desires.
A person does not attain the Great through contempt for the Vedas, nor through deceit, nor through illusion; rather, one attains Brahman and finds Brahman within Brahman. Kapila said:
The Darśa and Paurṇamāsa sacrifices, the Agnihotra of the wise,
and the Cāturmāsya rites— these constitute the eternal sacrifice among them. Free from ritual undertakings, steadfast, pure, and devoted to Brahman, they abide therein.
Seeking immortality, they satisfy the gods with the Brahman itself.
For one who has become the self of all beings and perceives all beings as himself,
even the gods are bewildered on his path as they seek the footprints of the trackless one.
This person has four gates and four faces;
censure approaches him from four directions: from his two arms, from his speech, from his belly, and from his generative organ.
One should desire to be their gatekeeper at the door;
one should not play with dice, nor should one take the wealth of others,
nor should one accept cooked food from one who is not of a proper birth.
The wise man, even when provoked to anger, should not strike back; thus his hands and feet are well-guarded. He should not seek to revile others, nor should he speak untruth.
One should not engage in slander or idle gossip;
being devoted to truth, moderate in speech, and vigilant,
one's gateway of speech is thus well-guarded.
One should not be a non-eater, nor should one be a glutton;
free from greed, one should be accepted by the virtuous.
One should take food here only for the sake of sustenance.
In this way, his protection of the gateway to the stomach shall be secured:
one should not consort with the wife of a hero,
nor should one summon a woman for intercourse outside her season.
For he should maintain the vow of a wife within himself;
thus there shall be protection for the gateway of his generative organ.
For that wise man whose gates are all well-guarded, [his senses remain under control].
The generative organ, the belly, the arms, and speech as the fourth—these indeed constitute the twice-born.
For one whose gates are unguarded, all these functions become utterly futile. What need has he for austerity, what need for sacrifice, or what need for the self?
The gods know him as a Brahmin who wears no upper garment, sleeps on the bare ground, uses his arm as a pillow, and remains tranquil;
he is the sage who delights in solitude while all others delight in pairs.
The gods know him as a Brahmin who does not dwell upon others;
he by whom all this is understood— both the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikṛti*), and who knows the destinies of all beings— the gods know him as a Brahmin.
He who grants fearlessness to all beings and from whom all beings receive fearlessness—
he who has become the self of all beings, him the gods know as a Brāhmaṇa. They do not acknowledge any fruit of ritual action apart from the Vedas.
Having authorized all of that, they find something else to be fruitless;
yet they perceive actions that are fruitful, productive of results, and certain, as well as those that are deficient and uncertain.
"Moreover, the qualities here are very difficult to understand, and even when understood, they are very difficult to practice;
you perceive that even when performed, they have an end.
Syūmaraśmi said:
"How is the authority of the Vedas established, and how is renunciation fruitful? O Blessed One, explain to me clearly both of these paths.
Kapila said:
"Those of you who stand on the path of the righteous see this directly here. But what is there that is directly perceived which you worship?
Syūmaraśmi said:
"O Brahmin, I am Syūmaraśmi; I have come here for the sake of inquiry. Desiring my own welfare, I spoke out of sincerity and not from a desire for debate.
May the Blessed One explain this terrible doubt to me."
"O you who stand upon the path of the virtuous, seeing directly here before you,
what is it that you worship as most perceptible in this world—
apart from the treatises on logic and according to the traditional scriptures?"
The Vedic doctrine is indeed *āgama*, as are the treatises on logic (*tarkaśāstra*);
one should practice according to *āgama*, for in that regard *āgama* is established. And accomplishment, which takes the form of direct perception, is seen to arise from the certainty of *āgama*.
"For like a boat tied to another boat, being carried along by the current, how, O Brahmin, will it carry those of evil intellect across?
May the Blessed One explain this; I have approached you as a student—teach me, sir!"

There is no one at all who is truly renounced, nor contented, nor free from sorrow, nor free from affliction; nor is there anyone who seeks solitude, nor one who has turned away from the world, nor one who has not turned away.
And you, too, rejoice and grieve just as we do.
The objects of the senses are common to you and to all living beings;
likewise, among the activities of the four castes and the four stages of life,
what is the faultless certainty for those who rely upon a single [truth]?
Kapila said:
Whatever scripture one practices in all activities,
wherever its application lies, there one finds freedom from affliction.
One who follows knowledge purifies all knowledge;
however, that mode of conduct which deviates from knowledge destroys living beings.
You, sirs, are eternally possessed of knowledge and are entirely free from worldly attachments.
For indeed, some person at some time attains a state of oneness;

yet certain people, having not understood the scripture according to its true nature, fall under the sway of egoism due to being overcome by desire and hatred, relying instead on the strength of mere debate.
Not understanding the scriptures as they truly are, these robbers of the scriptures—
thieves of Brahman, devoid of spiritual effort, immature in intellect,
and inauspicious— perceive only defects and do not inquire after virtues.
For those whose bodies are composed of darkness, darkness alone is their ultimate resort. Whatever a living being’s innate nature may be, he remains subject to the power of that nature;
for him there arise aversion, desire, anger, hypocrisy, falsehood, and pride.
The qualities born of nature perpetually revolve;
perceiving this with their intellect, ascetics devoted to self-restraint, desiring the supreme goal, should renounce both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
"Since he is different from him by nature, by birth, by name, and by purpose,
how could there be an inseparable connection such that one could say, 'He is in this'?
Syūmaraśmi said:
"O Brahmin, all of this has been proclaimed by me according to the scriptures;
for indeed, no activities proceed without understanding the meaning of the scriptures.
Whatever conduct is righteous—that is the entirety of the scripture; such is the sacred tradition."
"That which is unjust and contrary to the scriptures—this is what is heard in the sacred revelation (śruti).
It is certain that there is no activity whatsoever apart from the scriptures;
whatever is other than the declarations of the Veda is 'non-scriptural' (aśāstra)—so says the revelation."
Many who consider themselves wise perceive that which deviates from the treatises;
others do not see the faults of the treatises, both in this world and in the next. Furthermore, the objects of the senses are the same for you as they are for all living beings.
Thus, among the activities of the four castes and the four stages of life,
as they are being determined in every direction,
those whose wisdom is destroyed by ignorance— those of deficient wisdom, shrouded in darkness— [fail to perceive].
But it is possible for one who is liberated, who has fully accomplished his task,
who speaks of the infinite, who is capable, and who has conquered his own self, to wander in all directions while relying upon nothing more than a mere morsel of food.

Relying on the doctrines of the Vedas, he speaks of the existence of liberation; yet he has departed from the science of logic and is censured by the whole world. But this is a difficult task for one who remains dependent upon a household.
Giving, study, sacrifice, procreation, and uprightness—
if even after performing all this, there is no liberation for anyone,
then shame on the doer and the deed; this labor is useless.
"There would be atheism and a turning away from the Vedas;
O Blessed One, I desire to hear directly about the infinity of this [ātman].
Speak the truth to me, O Brahmin; I have approached you as a disciple—teach me, sir!"
"12,261.061c Just as liberation is known to you, so do I desire to learn it.
12,262.001 Kapila said:
12,262.001a The Vedas are the authority for the worlds; the Vedas are not to be cast aside."
Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound (śabdabrahman) and that which is the Supreme Brahman.
One who is proficient in the Brahman of Sound attains the Supreme Brahman. This body performs what the Veda performs as its form.

For a Brāhmaṇa whose body has been purified becomes a worthy recipient. I shall tell you that which leads to infinity through action— [an act] that is without scripture, without tradition, yet perceptible and witnessed by the world.

Those who perform sacrifices with the thought "this is dharma" alone, free from desire for rewards, who have renounced what they have acquired, who are without greed, and who are devoid of pity and envy—
for them, this is indeed the path regarding wealth: its distribution at sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Never dependent on sinful deeds arising from the source of karma,
they are perfected through the resolve of their own minds and possess certainty in pure knowledge;
they are free from anger, free from malice, and devoid of egoism and envy.
Established in knowledge, pure in the three ways, and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
they were for the most part householders who did not deviate from their own duties;
and likewise, the kings and the Brahmins were similarly engaged according to the prescribed rule.
For they were equanimous, endowed with uprightness, contented, and firm in their knowledge;
they had direct perception of dharma, were pure, and had faith in both the higher and the lower.
Having previously cultivated their selves, they had practiced their vows according to the rule.
Even in times of hardship and in difficult circumstances, they practiced their duty while remaining closely united.
For those who practiced their duty in unison, there was formerly nothing but happiness;
for them, there was never at any time anything that required to be ordained as an expiation.
For those who abide in truth and righteousness are considered most invincible;
they do not compromise on even a fraction [of their duty], nor do they resort to any subterfuge regarding dharma in the end.
Together, they practice that very first course of conduct which is the primary rule.
For those established in this state, no expiation exists;
the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that expiation arises only for one of weak soul. Since such were the ancient Brahmins who carried out the sacrifices, [there is no need for it].
Those who are aged in the three Vedas, pure, possessed of good conduct, and renowned— wise men who, performing sacrifices day after day, are free from the bonds of desire;
for them, the sacrifices, the Vedas, and their ritual acts are performed according to the traditional scriptures.
Their arrivals were at the proper time and their intentions were according to their vows; free from desire and anger, naturally firm in soul,
upright, constant in tranquility, they remained steadfast in their own duties.
"12,262.015e Our eternal Vedic revelation declares that everything was indeed infinite.
12,262.016a For those of undepressed spirit, whose conduct and deeds were difficult to perform,
and who were restrained by their own karmas, austerity reached a state of extreme intensity."
That wonderful, ancient, eternal, and constant conduct of the virtuous,
which has been indicated in the teachings for those unable to practice even a portion of it—
this conduct in times of no distress consists of vigilance and non-defeat.
Among all those castes, there was no transgression whatsoever;
those bulls among men relied solely upon the Dharma with its four feet. Having duly attained that, the virtuous proceed to the supreme goal.

Some, having departed from their very homes, have taken refuge in the forest; others, remaining dependent on home, are celibate students (*brahmacārin*). The Brahmins know this fourfold stage of life (*āśrama*) to be Dharma.
The station of Brahman is infinity; this is the certain conclusion regarding those called Brāhmaṇas.
Therefore, these ancient Brāhmaṇas who practiced dharma are seen in the heavens as the twice-born, having become luminous bodies.

"Like the many hosts of stars upon their celestial stations, they have attained infinity through contentment; such is the Vedic teaching. Yet, if such as these should return again to the cycle of existence within the various wombs,"

They are never stained by evil deeds arising from the source of karma. Only one who is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), devoted to service and firm in resolve, being thus disciplined, may be a true Brahmin; any other would be a mere Brahmin in name.

"Karma alone, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is said to belong to a person. Thus, for those whose passions have been ripened away through infinite sacred learning, everything becomes infinite; such is our eternal tradition."
For those whose thirst has departed, who are cleansed and pure in soul,
the fourth duty— that which pertains to the Upaniṣads— is recorded as common to all. It is constantly practiced by perfected Brahmins who have restrained their selves.
Rooted in contentment, characterized by renunciation, and said to have knowledge as its foundation,
this eternal and ancient dharma of the ascetic leads to liberation;
it is practiced according to one's strength, whether in common with others or in solitude.
For one who goes on and on toward security, the weak person perishes here;
seeking the station of Brahman, the pure one is liberated from saṃsāra.
Syūmaraśmi said:
Among those who enjoy [pleasures], those who give gifts, those who perform sacrifices, and those who study;
or among those who rely on renunciation with means acquired through dharma—
which of these attains the highest heaven after death?
"O Brahmin, explain this to me as it truly is, for I ask you.
Kapila said:
"All acquisitions are auspicious, as are all prosperities that arise from one's qualities."
"But you have not attained the happiness of renunciation; you see this yourself.
Syūmaraśmi said:
"You are indeed established in knowledge, while householders are resolved upon action."
It is said that in the final consummation of all the stages of life (āśrama), there is unity;
and regarding both unity and diversity, no other distinction is declared.
May the Blessed One explain this to me correctly and according to the proper method.
Kapila said:

"Ritual actions lead to the maturation of the body, but knowledge is the supreme goal. When the impurities have been matured and cast out by emetics, one does not remain within the perception of tastes."
Compassion, forgiveness, tranquility, non-violence, truth, uprightness,
freedom from malice, absence of pride, modesty, endurance, and likewise self-restraint—
these are the paths of Brahman; by means of these, one attains that which is supreme.
Knowing this, one should understand with the mind the determination regarding action—
that goal which the Brahmins, who are entirely tranquil, pure, and certain in their knowledge,
and who are contented, attain; that they call the supreme goal.

Having known the Vedas, that which is to be known, and how they exist in their true state, one is called a knower of the Vedas; anyone other than such a person is merely a reciter of the wind. Those who know the Vedas know all, for everything is established in the Veda.
For in the Veda lies the foundation of everything—of both what exists and what does not exist.
This indeed is the foundation of all that exists and does not exist;
it is the end and the middle for one who understands the real and the unreal.

The renunciation of everything is indeed established as tranquility (*śama*); contentment is here the auspicious state established in liberation (*apavarga*). Righteousness (*ṛta*) and truth (*satya*) are known and are that which is to be known.
The Self of all is both the moving and the stationary;
it is all happiness, that which is auspicious and supreme;
it is Brahman, the unmanifest, the source, and the imperishable.
Luster, forbearance, peace, health, and auspiciousness—
such is the eternal and constant ether (*vyoman*).
It is apprehended by the eye of the intellect through these words.
"Salutation to that Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, the Vedas proclaim dharma, artha, and kāma."
"Whose gain is superior in this matter? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
In the past, Kuṇḍadhāra kindly rendered assistance to a devotee out of affection.
A certain destitute Brāhmaṇa, desiring righteousness, looked toward it;
then, seeking wealth for the sake of performing a sacrifice, he performed severe austerities.

Having then made this resolution, he worshipped the deities with devotion; yet, even after worshipping the deities, he did not obtain wealth. Thereupon, he fell into reflection once more: "Which deity indeed is that?"
"If it would quickly grant me favor, being unclouded by human limitations," he thought.
Then, with a gentle form, he beheld a follower of the gods standing nearby, the cloud-bearer Kuṇḍadhāra.
Upon merely seeing that great-souled one, devotion arose within him:
"He will bestow the highest good upon me, for his form is indeed such;
he is in close proximity to the God and is not surrounded by other men."
"He will give me abundant wealth very quickly.
Then that twice-born man worshipped him with incenses, perfumes, various garlands, and diverse offerings.
Then, after a short time, the cloud-god was pleased and spoke these words, fixed upon doing him a favor:
"To the slayer of a Brahmin, to the drinker of liquor, to a thief, and likewise to one who has broken his vow— "
Expiation has been ordained by the virtuous for all [sins], but there is no expiation for the ungrateful. Unrighteousness is known as the son of Hope, and Anger is the son of Envy;
Greed is the son of Deceit, but the ungrateful man does not deserve offspring.
Then that brahmin, lying upon kusha grass at that time, beheld all living beings in a dream through the power of Kuṇḍadhāra;
he was purified by tranquility, austerity, and devotion.
On the night of the twelfth day, the pure-souled Brāhmaṇa beheld a vision:
he saw Maṇibhadra, the highly effulgent deity of the gods, standing there as a great-souled being giving instructions, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
There, the gods bestow kingdoms and wealth upon those who have begun with auspicious deeds, while they cut them off from their inauspicious ones. Then,
while the yakṣas were looking on, the immensely radiant Kuṇḍadhāra—
Having rushed out, O bull of the Bharata race, he fell upon the ground before the gods.
Then, at the word of the gods, the highly illustrious Maṇibhadra spoke to Kuṇḍadhāra, who was prostrate on the earth: "What is desired?"
Kuṇḍadhāra said:
"If the gods are pleased with me, then this Brahmin is my devotee;
I desire to bestow some favor upon him that shall result in happiness."
12,263.020 Bhīṣma said: Then Maṇibhadra spoke these words again to the immensely radiant Kuṇḍadhāra, at the very command of the gods.
"Arise, arise! May it be well with you; your task is accomplished, so be happy.
If this Brahmin seeks wealth, let wealth be given to him—whatever wealth this Brahmin, your friend, requests."
"By the command of the gods, I shall grant him an incalculable [span of life]. But Kuṇḍadhāra, having reflected upon the instability and impermanence of human existence,
set his mind upon asceticism for the sake of that illustrious Brāhmaṇa.
Kuṇḍadhāra said:
"O giver of wealth, I do not beg for riches from you for the sake of this Brāhmaṇa;
rather, I desire that a favor be bestowed upon me, who am your devotee."

I do not desire the earth filled with jewels, nor even a great accumulation of wealth for my devotee; rather, let him be righteous. Let his intellect delight in dharma, and let him live by dharma alone.
"Let him be one for whom Dharma is paramount; this is my intended favor.
Maṇibhadra said:
"When sovereignty is the fruit of Dharma, as well as various pleasures..."
"Let him eat only fruits, free from physical suffering.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then the highly illustrious Kuṇḍadhāra [did] that very thing many times over."
He practiced dharma with such intensity that the deities were gratified by him.
Maṇibhadra said:
"All those deities, as well as this twice-born man, are pleased."
"This righteous-souled one shall come into being, and his mind shall be fixed upon dharma.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the cloud was pleased, having accomplished its purpose."
O subduer of enemies, that brahmin was tormented by greed for the kingdom;
yet, having obtained from others a boon desired by his heart and difficult for others to attain,
that best of the twice-born then beheld fine garments of bark-cloth.
Having approached from the side with his hands joined in reverence, he then fell into despondency.
The brahmin said:
"This man does not recognize a good deed; who else indeed will recognize what has been done?"
"I shall go to the forest; it is better for me to live according to dharma.
Bhīṣma said:
"Out of world-weariness and through the grace of the deities, that best of the twice-born..."
Having entered the great forest, that twice-born man then undertook severe asceticism; subsisting on fruits and roots remaining from his offerings to the gods and guests,
O great king, he developed a deep delight in dharma.
Having abandoned all roots and fruits, the twice-born one subsisted on leaves; having abandoned leaves, that best of the twice-born then subsisted on water;
and thereafter, for many groups of years, he lived on air alone.
Yet his vital breath did not diminish, which was like a marvel;
for him who had faith in dharma and was engaged in fierce austerity,
after a long time, divine vision arose.

The thought occurred to him: "If I were to give great wealth, or even my kingdom, to one who is satisfied with me, I would undoubtedly be ruined. I am not pleased with anyone at all; let my word not be false."
Then, with a joyful countenance, he once again began his ascetic penance. And having attained perfection, he further reflected upon that which he had reached:
"If I am indeed pleased, I shall grant the kingdom to whomeversoever."
"Within a short time he shall become king; my word shall not be false. O Bhārata, Kuṇḍadhāra appeared before him in person, impelled by friendship because of the Brahmin’s ascetic power and yoga.

Having met with him, O King, that brahmin then performed worship according to the prescribed rites; he was filled with wonder at Kuṇḍadhāra. Then Kuṇḍadhāra said, "You possess a supreme, divine vision."
"O Brahmin, behold the destiny of kings and observe the worlds with your eye! Then, with his divine vision, that Brahmin saw from afar thousands of kings who had sunk into hell."
Kuṇḍadhāra said:
"If, after honoring me with devotion, you were to encounter suffering,
what would have been accomplished by me for you, and what favor would have been bestowed upon you?"
"Behold, behold once more! How could a man desire objects of sense-pleasure? For the gateway to heaven is indeed blocked, especially among human beings.
Bhīṣma said:
Then he saw Desire, Anger, Greed, Fear, and Arrogance,
as well as Sleep, Drowsiness, and Indolence, standing there surrounding men.
Kuṇḍadhāra said:
By these [beings], the worlds are thoroughly obstructed, and the gods have cause for fear of humans.
Likewise, at the command of the gods, they create obstacles in every way. No one becomes righteous without being authorized by the gods.
"By means of your ascetic power, you are capable of granting me a kingdom and riches.
Bhīṣma said:
Thereupon, the Brahmin prostrated with his head before the bearer of the waters.
The righteous-souled one said to him: "A great favor has been done for me.
Since you previously showed me displeasure due to the persistence of desire and greed, not recognizing my affection, you ought to forgive me for that."
Having said, "I have indeed forgiven you," Kuṇḍadhāra embraced that bull among the twice-born with his arms and vanished right there.
Thereafter, the brahmin wandered through all these worlds.
12,263.052c Through the grace of Kuṇḍadhāra, he was formerly endowed with ascetic power;

12,263.053a [he attained] the ability to travel through the air, as well as the fulfillment of his intended purposes; 12,263.053c [these came] from dharma, from power, and likewise from yoga, as well as the supreme goal itself.
The deities, the Brahmins, the virtuous, the Yakṣas, and the human Cāraṇas—
here in this world, they honor those who are righteous, not those who are wealthy nor those who are lustful;
for the gods are well-pleased with you because your mind is devoted to Dharma.
"In wealth there is but a small fraction of happiness, but in dharma there is supreme happiness.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, among the many sacrifices and austerities which have a single purpose,"
"How can a sacrifice be properly performed for the sake of dharma and not for the sake of pleasure?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you what was proclaimed by Nārada."
Regarding the ancient account of a Brahmin who lived by the practice of *uñcha* for the sake of sacrifice: in the preeminent kingdom of Vidarbha, which was supreme in righteousness,
there lived a certain twice-born sage who lived by *uñcha* and performed a sacrifice within a sacrifice.
There, Śyāmāka grain was their food, and the sun-plant *suvarcalā* was their companion; even bitter and tasteless herbs attained sweetness through her ascetic power.
Having approached the earth in the forest, she remained there without harming any living being.
"O scorcher of foes, even a sacrifice for the sake of heaven may be performed with roots and fruits. His wife, purified by vows and emaciated, a dweller of the lotus-ponds,
was brought to the status of sacrificial consort and follows him in truth."

Terrified by the curse, she did not follow her own nature; and for her, who was unwilling, garments made of the withered feathers of peacocks were prepared there at the sacrifice, following the path of the *hotṛ* priest.
Śukra was born again, though he was ignorant of dharma because of his malice;
in that forest, there was a deer living nearby who was his companion, and with its words it spoke the truth: "A wicked deed has been committed by you."
"If this sacrifice is deficient in its mantra-components and thus becomes deformed,
O sir, cast me into the *hotṛ* fire and go to heaven without weariness.
Thereupon, Sāvitrī herself directly addressed him regarding the sacrifice.
"Even when invited, I would not kill a fellow-dweller. Having been addressed thus, she turned back and entered the sacrificial fire,
desiring to see what misdeed had occurred in the sacrifice down in the netherworld (rasātala).
But she, with palms joined in reverence, again entreated the deer with truth: "Embraced by truth, you have been commanded to depart.
Thereupon, that deer went eight steps and then turned back.
"O Truth, it is well; kill me! Being slain, I shall go to a good destination.
Behold, indeed, with the divine vision granted by me, the celestial Apsarases and the variegated aerial chariots of the high-souled Gandharvas."

Then, having seen that most beautiful creature with eyes fixed in longing, he envisioned dwelling in heaven through the act of killing the deer. But that Dharma, having become a deer, had lived for many years in the forest.
He provided an atonement for that act, for it was not part of the sacrificial ritual.
However, because of that disposition of his—his mind being intent on harming the deer—his great ascetic merit was utterly destroyed; therefore, violence is not fit for sacrifice.
Then the Blessed Dharma himself performed that sacrifice for him. Through his asceticism, he attained supreme composure regarding his wife.
For non-violence is the entirety of dharma; violence is not established in a true sacrifice.
"I shall tell you the truth regarding that dharma which belongs to those who speak the truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How does one become a sinful soul, and how does one perform dharma?"
"By what does one attain world-weariness, and by what does one go to liberation?
Bhīṣma said:
"All dharmas are known to you; you ask this for the sake of establishing [others in them]."
Listen to the account of liberation along with detachment, and of sin and merit from their very root.
For it is for the sake of discerning these five that desire first arises;
having encountered them, O bull of the Bharatas, either passion or aversion is born.
Then, for that purpose, one strives and undertakes action once again;
one desires to practice the enjoyment of desired forms and scents.
From that, passion arises, and immediately after that, hatred.
From that, greed arises, and immediately after it, delusion.
For one who is overcome by greed and delusion, and possessed of passion and hatred, the intellect does not turn toward the Dharma; rather, he practices Dharma through hypocrisy.
When one practices dharma through deceit, even the pursuit of wealth through deceit becomes pleasing.
O joy of the Kurus, when riches are being acquired through deceit,
one fixes the mind upon that very path and thereafter desires to commit sin.
O Bhārata, even when being restrained by friends and by the wise,
he speaks a reply that is connected with logic and consistent with the rules;
yet his threefold unrighteousness, born of passion and delusion, continues to increase.
One who thinks of evil, speaks of it, and acts upon it— of that person who has set out upon unrighteousness, the virtuous perceive the faults;
yet those of similar character form friendships with such evildoers.
Such a person does not find happiness here in this world, much less in the next.
Thus is the nature of the evil-minded one; now hear from me concerning the righteous one—how that person of virtuous dharma attains what is wholesome.
Through wholesome dharma alone, one attains a desirable rebirth—
he who, by means of wisdom, perceives these faults beforehand;
skilled in the nature of pleasure and pain, he also attends upon the virtuous.

Through his virtuous conduct and through practice, his wisdom increases; he delights in the Dharma and lives by the Dharma alone. Then, with wealth acquired through righteousness, he sets his mind upon it.

He waters the very root of that [virtue] wherein he perceives qualities; thus he becomes righteous and obtains auspicious friends. Through the acquisition of such friends and wealth, he rejoices both in this world and after death.

O Bhārata, a living being attains mastery over sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; the wise know this to be the fruit of dharma. Having obtained that fruit of dharma, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one is not yet satisfied.
O Kaunteya, for those established in dharma amidst all activities involving enjoyments,
one who is never satisfied takes up disillusionment through the eye of knowledge.
When one whose eye is wisdom perceives only the defect in desire, [one attains detachment].
Then he becomes dispassionate toward desires and does not abandon the Dharma;
seeing that the world is subject to decay, he strives for total renunciation.
Thereafter, he exerts himself for liberation through the proper means, and not by what is not a means.
Gradually one attains detachment and abandons evil action;
one becomes righteous in soul and attains supreme liberation.
This, my dear, which you asked of me, has been told to you.
O Bhārata, [one understands] evil, dharma, as well as liberation and detachment;
therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, you should engage in dharma under all circumstances. For those established in dharma, O son of Kuntī, there is eternal success.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you have stated that liberation is attained through means and not without means;
O Bhārata, I wish to hear about those means according to the proper method."
Bhīṣma said:
"O one of great wisdom, this subtle insight is indeed worthy of you,
that you always seek all goals through skillful means, O sinless one."
O sinless one, the cognition that arises regarding the making of a jar does not exist once the jar has been produced;
likewise, among the means for attaining dharma, there is no other cause for dharmas themselves.
The path that leads to the eastern ocean does not go to the western one.
For there is but one path to liberation; hear that from me in detail:
One should eradicate anger through forgiveness, and desire by abandoning formative volitions (*saṃkalpa*). By cultivating the quality of purity (*sattva*), the wise man ought to destroy sleep.
One should guard against fear through heedfulness, and [guard] the breath through the practice of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
One should turn back desire, hatred, and passion through fortitude.
Through constant practice, one should turn back delusion, confusion, and the whirlpool [of worldly existence].
The knower of reality dispels both sleep and mental dullness through the practice of knowledge; likewise, he overcomes afflictions and diseases by eating wholesome, digested, and moderate food;
he subdues greed and delusion through contentment, and the objects of the senses through the vision of reality.
Through compassion one may conquer unrighteousness, and through equanimity one may conquer righteousness;
through the future one may conquer hope, and by abandoning attachment one may conquer wealth.
And through the contemplation of impermanence, the wise man conquers affection, and through yoga he conquers hunger.
One should conquer self-conceit through compassion, and craving through contentment;
one should conquer sloth through exertion, and discursive thought through certainty;
one should conquer excessive talk through silence, and fear through courage.
One should restrain speech and mind with the intellect; one should restrain that intellect with the eye of knowledge.
One should restrain knowledge with the Great Self (mahān ātmā); one should restrain that Self through the peace of the self.
One should restrain knowledge by the awakening of the Self, and restrain the Self by the Self.
This must be understood by one who is tranquil and pure in action,
having completely severed the five defects of yoga which the wise have identified:
desire, anger, greed, fear, and sleep as the fifth.
Having abandoned those [worldly things], one should practice these means of yoga:
meditation, study, charity, truthfulness, modesty, straightforwardness, forbearance,
purity, cleanliness of food, and restraint of the senses.
By these, his splendor increases and he destroys evil;
his intentions are fulfilled and higher knowledge arises. Shaken free from sin, radiant, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses—
Having brought desire and anger under control, one should seek to lead oneself to the state of Brahman.
Freedom from delusion, lack of attachment, the abandonment of desire and anger, absence of dejection, lack of arrogance, freedom from agitation, and steadfastness— [these are the means].
"This path to liberation is indeed serene, stainless, and pure;
likewise, it consists of the restraint of speech, body, and mind from desire. Otherwise, it is not so.
Bhīṣma said:
In this very context, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between Nārada and Asita Devala:
"Having perceived that the aged Devala was seated, [Nārada], the best among the wise— "
Nārada questioned him thoroughly regarding the origin and dissolution of beings:
"O Brahmin, from where has this entire universe, both mobile and immobile, been created?
And unto whom does it go at the time of dissolution? May you explain that to me."
Asita said:
"Those from whom Time, impelled by the disposition of beings, creates all creatures—
the thinkers of beings call them the five great elements."
Impelled by the Self, Time creates beings from them;
he who would say there is anything beyond these would undoubtedly speak what is non-existent. Know, O Nārada, that these five are eternal, immovable, and constant.
He is a mass of great splendor, with Time as his sixth constituent by nature; water, space, earth, wind, and fire—
there is no doubt that the Unmanifested (Asiddhi) is superior even to these elements.
Neither by birth nor by logic can one say with certainty that something is non-existent; yet you know those who have come into being—these six who constitute the heaps:
the five elements, time, and the two states of existence and non-existence alone.
The eight elements of beings are eternal, governing both their emergence and their dissolution. From non-existence they arise within those very things that have been brought into being,
and even when a creature has perished, it becomes fivefold once again from those same elements.
His body consists of earth; his sense of hearing is born from space (*ākāśa*);
the sun is his eye; the Asura Vāyu is his breath; and blood indeed arises from water.
His eyes, nose, ears, skin, and tongue as the fifth [constitute his faculties].
The wise know the cognitions of the objects of the senses to be the senses themselves.
Know that seeing, hearing, smelling, touching, and likewise tasting—
these five qualities [arise] through their occurrence in the five [senses] in five ways.
Form, odor, taste, touch, and sound—these are their qualities;
these five are perceived in five ways by the five sense organs.
Form, odor, taste, touch, and sound—these indeed are their qualities.
The senses do not perceive; rather, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) perceives by means of them.

The mind (citta) is superior to the aggregate of the senses, and the intellect (manas) is superior to that. The higher intellect (buddhi) is superior to the mind, and the Knower of the Field is superior to the intellect.
First, a living being perceives objects individually through the senses;
having reflected upon them with the mind, he then determines them with the intellect—
he who determines all objects perceived by the senses [is the intellect].
The mind, the collection of the senses, the intellect, and likewise the eighth, the manas—
those who contemplate the inner self call these the eight organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*).
The hands, the feet, the anus, the organ of generation, and the mouth as the fifth [are the organs of action].
Listen now to the organs of action as they are enumerated:
the mouth is called an organ for the purposes of speaking and eating;
likewise, the feet are the organ of locomotion, and the hands are the instruments for performing actions.
The anus and the generative organ are two organs whose functions are identical, both serving the purpose of emission—namely, the emission of feces and the emission of sexual desire.
Strength is the sixth; these six [organs] have been correctly described by speech in accordance with the tradition.

I have enumerated all the qualities of knowledge, activity, and the senses. When there is a cessation from the exhaustion of the senses' own functions due to the withdrawal of the senses, then indeed a person sleeps.
If the mind does not cease even when the senses have ceased,
and it continues to experience objects, one should know that to be the state of dreaming. Furthermore,
those states that are characterized by goodness (sāttvika), as well as those of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), [are likewise to be understood].
They praise those engaged in action who are characterized by *sattva*, as well as others; joy,
the success of actions, right understanding, and the supreme goal—
these are the signs of one characterized by *sattva*, according to the tradition of the Smṛti.
Among living beings, those who have thus adopted this method are of one kind;
for these two states, there is a constant desire for the direct perception of both.
The sense organs, the objects of the senses, and the qualities are recorded as seventeen.
Among them, the eighteenth is the embodied one who is eternal within the body.
Alternatively, all those qualities of embodied beings exist together with the body;
for when separated from that [body], they no longer possess a body.
Alternatively, this body composed of the five elements is a combination;
there are twenty qualities belonging to embodied beings— namely, one, ten, and eight—
along with heat, making this aggregate of the five elements a collection of twenty.
The Great One, together with the vital wind (vāyu), sustains this body. When he is joined with these states of being, there is a sign for the dissolution of the body;
just as something arises, so too does it go to the state of the five elements (pañcatva).

At the end of the destruction of merit and demerit, impelled by merit and demerit, he enters a body produced by karma in due course; for having repeatedly abandoned one body, he proceeds to another body, having made it his refuge.
Urged on by Time, the owner of the field moves from one dilapidated house to another;
therein, the wise, whose resolve is firm, feel no remorse,
whereas the wretched people who pride themselves on their kinship do feel remorse.
For this [self] belongs to no one, nor does anyone belong to it;
indeed, it exists eternally as a single entity, experiencing pleasure and pain within the body.
A living being is never born, nor does it ever perish.
Having experienced this body, he sometimes attains the supreme goal;
exhausting the body composed of merit and demerit through the depletion of his accumulated karma,
the embodied soul, once his body is worn away, attains the state of Brahman.
And for the sake of destroying merit and demerit, the knowledge of Sāṃkhya is prescribed;
for when those are destroyed, they behold his supreme state in the nature of Brahman.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Brothers, fathers, sons, kinsmen, and friends alike have been slain by us— cruel and evil-minded as we are— for the sake of wealth.
O Grandfather, how may one overcome this thirst that arises from wealth?"
"For we have committed this evil, driven by craving.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
12,268.003c A song was sung by the King of Videha in response to the inquiry of Māṇḍavya:
12,268.004a "Oh, how very happily I live, I who possess nothing at all! 12,268.004c Even when Mithilā is in flames, nothing of mine is burned."
Indeed, for those who truly understand suffering, even abundant riches are a source of great pain;
yet when they are lacking, they constantly delude the undiscerning.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there may be—
These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the destruction of craving;
just as the horn of a cow grows as it grows in age,
so too does craving grow as wealth increases.
Whenever even a slight thing is imagined as "mine," that very thing leads to torment when it is subsequently lost. One should not pursue desires; indeed, delight in desires is suffering.
Having obtained wealth, one should employ it for righteous purposes and abandon desire;
the wise man should act toward all beings as if he were tiger-skin meat [fearing their consumption].
Having accomplished his purpose and purified his soul, he indeed renounces everything together.

Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, sorrow and joy, the pleasant and the unpleasant, and having completely relinquished fear and fearlessness, he is perfectly tranquil and free from affliction—
that which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, and which does not age even as one ages.
For one who abandons that thirst which is a disease ending only with life, there is happiness; beholding his own conduct as pure as the moon and free from ailment,
the righteous-souled one attains fame both here and after death, according to his pleasure.
12,268.014a Having heard those words of the king, the twice-born man became joyful.
12,268.014c And having honored that speech, Māṇḍavya took recourse in liberation.
12,269.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Of what character, of what conduct, possessing what knowledge,
and having what as his ultimate goal does one attain the station of Brahman, which is beyond primordial nature and eternal?
Bhīṣma said:
One who is devoted to the duties of liberation, moderate in diet, and has conquered the senses,
attains the supreme station, which is eternal and beyond primordial nature. In this regard,
they also cite this ancient history.
Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, to that which was sung by Hārīta in the past:
"Having departed from his own home, the sage should remain equanimous toward gain and loss; even when objects of desire are presented, he should wander as a mendicant, free from attachment."

One should not find fault with another through the eye, the mind, or speech; one should never utter words of censure, whether in the presence or absence of the person. One should not harm any living beings, but should conduct oneself according to the path of universal friendliness.
Having attained this life, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone.
One should endure harsh words and never, under any circumstances, take offense. When provoked to anger, one should speak kindly; when reviled, one should speak words of goodwill.
One should not perform circumambulation, whether clockwise or counter-clockwise, in the middle of a village.

Without having fallen into the practice of begging for alms, one should not go where one has been previously invited. Even if violated or well-guarded, one should certainly not speak unpleasant words.
He should be gentle, not harsh, confident, and free from anger. When the smoke has ceased, the pestle is laid aside, the embers are extinguished, the people have finished their meal,
and the passing of bowls has ended, the sage should indeed seek alms.
One who is indifferent toward obtaining even a small portion of wealth as a follower of his purpose should not be distressed by failure to obtain it,
nor should success in obtaining it cause him joy. He should not desire common gains, nor should he enjoy them when they are highly honored.
One such as he should indeed loathe gains obtained through honor;
he should neither criticize defects in food nor praise its virtues. He should always honor a secluded place for his bed and seat.
Having gone to a deserted dwelling, the foot of a tree, a forest, or a cave,
he should lead an unknown life and then settle elsewhere.
He should remain equanimous toward favor and opposition, immovable and steadfast.
He should not be attached to either good or evil deeds;
he should be eternally content, well-satisfied, with a serene face and senses; devoted to meditation and silent recitation, observing silence, and having fully taken recourse to dispassion.

Beholding this world-creation to be unstable and composed of the elements, and seeing that the destiny of beings is likewise elemental, he remains free from desire and views all with equanimity; subsisting on both the digested and the undigested,
he finds delight in the Self, his mind is perfectly tranquil, his diet is light, and he is free from affliction.
The ascetic should indeed subdue these impulses: the impulse of speech, the impulse of anger in the mind, the impulse of the desire for knowledge, and the impulses of the stomach and the genitals.
Neither blame nor praise should wound his heart;
he should remain neutral, equal toward both praise and blame. This is the supreme purification in the stage of life of the wandering mendicant.
High-souled, firm in his vows, self-controlled, and entirely independent, he follows an unprecedented path; gentle, homeless, and composed,
he should never associate with either forest-dwellers or householders.
One should seek that which is desired by those who do not yet know it, nor should joy take possession of him.
For those who understand, this is liberation; for those who do not understand, it is mere toil.
Hārīta declared this entire vehicle of liberation for the wise.
"He who departs from his home after granting fearlessness to all beings attains worlds consisting of splendor; thus, he is fit for infinity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Fortunate, fortunate!"— thus do all people speak of us. O best of the Kurus, there is no man more miserable than we who have encountered such suffering despite being honored by the world.
"O Grandfather, even though we have attained birth among humans by the grace of the gods,
when shall we perform that renunciation which is known as liberation from suffering? O best of the Kurus, the maintenance of these bodies is itself suffering."
O Great-Grandfather, those sages of firm vows, being liberated from the seventeen causal factors, the five sense objects, and the eight qualities, do not undergo rebirth.
"When shall we become such, O scorcher of foes, having abandoned the kingdom?
Bhīṣma said:
"There is nothing infinite, O great king; everything falls within the scope of enumeration."
Rebirth is also reckoned as non-existent; nothing here is immovable.
Nor is anything actually gone, O King, for this fault does not follow [from our position]. O knower of dharma, through exertion alone you shall go in due time.
O King, this embodied soul is the constant master of merit and demerit;
yet it is also obstructed by the darkness arising from those very same sources,
just as the wind [is obscured] by collyrium or again by the dust of red arsenic.
Having entered [the body], it is seen taking on that color, coloring the directions;
likewise, the embodied self, colored by the fruits of its actions and enveloped by darkness,
assumes a pale hue and wanders through various bodies.
For when a living being dispels the darkness born of ignorance through knowledge, then the eternal Brahman shines forth;
the sages declare that this is accomplished without effort.
Those who are liberated should be venerated by you and by the world together with the gods;
therefore, the assemblies of great seers do not cease their activity.
O King, listen with a single-minded focus to this matter sung of old:
how the Daitya Vṛtra acted when he had fallen from his sovereignty, having been defeated,
rendered helpless, and deprived of his kingdom, O Bhārata.
"Relying solely on his intelligence and remaining free from grief in the midst of his enemies,
Uśanas once spoke these words to Vṛtra when he had lost his sovereignty:
'O Dānava, do you feel no distress today, having been defeated?'"
Vṛtra said:
"Having understood through truth and austerity that there is indeed a total destruction [of all things],
I neither grieve nor rejoice at the coming and going of living beings."
Impelled by time, living beings sink helplessly into hell;
the wise declare that all these divine realms are clearly perceived.
But having exhausted that calculated period of time, they are impelled by time once again.

With a remainder of time still to run, living beings arise again and again; having passed through thousands of animal births and even into hell, these helpless souls emerge, bound by the fetters of time.
Thus have I seen living beings wandering in saṃsāra;
"as is the action, so is the fruit"—this is the teaching of the scriptures.
They go among the animals, to hell, to the human state, and even to the divine realm.
Having previously experienced pleasure and pain, as well as the liked and the disliked,
all the world falls under the power of the laws of destiny;
indeed, all beings always travel the path already traversed.
12,270.023 Bhīṣma said:
To him who was speaking of that which is calculated by the reckoning of time and devoted to the creation and maintenance of the world,
the blessed Uśanas replied.
"Why, O dear one, do you utter such terrible and wicked ravings?
Vṛtra said:
"This is evident to you as well as to other wise men."
"Formerly, greedy for victory, I performed great austerities;
taking away the fragrances of beings and their various essences as well,
I grew by my own splendor, having indeed traversed the three worlds."
Enveloped by garlands of flames and moving through the air,
I was invincible to all beings and forever free from fear;
yet that sovereignty, attained through asceticism, has been lost due to my own actions.
"O Blessed One, having established myself in fortitude, I do not grieve because of that which occurred in the past when I fought with the high-souled Mahendra;
thereafter, I beheld the Blessed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Sovereign."
Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣa, Viṣṇu, Śukla, Ananta, Sanātana, he with hair like muñja grass, with a golden beard, the grandfather of all beings—
surely there remains yet a residue of his ascetic power for me.
"O Brahman, I wish to ask you about the fruit of action: in which caste is great sovereignty established,
and how does that supreme sovereignty again come to an end?"
12,270.032 Why do living beings live, or rather, why do they continue to exist? Or what supreme fruit, having attained which, does the soul remain eternal?
12,270.033 By what action, or by what knowledge, can this be achieved?
"O Brahmarṣi, you ought to explain to me how that fruit may be obtained. Being thus addressed, O lion among kings, listen to what that sage then replied.
"O bull among men, listen with an undistracted mind along with your sisters to what I am about to say.
Thus spoke Uśanas.
"Salutations to that Blessed Lord, the omnipotent God,
O dear one, for whom the surface of the earth together with the sky is within the reach of his arms;
and whose head, O best of Dānavas, is the infinite abode."
"I shall proclaim to you the supreme majesty of that Viṣṇu.
Bhīṣma said:
While the two of them were thus conversing, the great sage arrived.
The righteous Sanatkumāra, for the purpose of cutting through his doubts,
was honored by the lord of the Asuras as well as by the sage Uśanas;
O King, that bull among sages sat down upon a costly seat.
To him, the highly wise one, as he sat there, Uśanas spoke these words:
"Proclaim to this lord of the Dānavas the supreme majesty of Viṣṇu.
Then Sanatkumāra, having heard that, spoke these meaningful words.
[He spoke] this account endowed with the majesty of Viṣṇu to the wise lord of the Dānavas:
"Listen, O Daitya, to all this supreme majesty of Viṣṇu;
know, O scorcher of enemies, that the entire world is situated in Viṣṇu."
O mighty-armed one, he creates this multitude of beings, both moving and unmoving;
at the appointed time he withdraws them, and at the appointed time he emits them again. In him they go to their dissolution, and from him they likewise come forth.
This cannot be attained through generosity, nor indeed through austerity or sacrifice;
it can only be achieved through the restraint of the senses. Established in the mind, one remains so through action both externally and internally.
He purifies himself through his intellect and attains infinity in the hereafter;
just as a goldsmith indeed purifies silver in the fire many times with great effort exerted by himself.
In the same way, the living soul is purified by hundreds of births through even a small amount of action;
yet, it may also be purified within a single birth through great effort. Just as one might effortlessly wipe away a little dust from one's own body, so too is the soul cleansed.

Just as the removal of defects requires great effort, so too does the perception of the subtle; yet, just as sesame or mustard seeds scented with even a small amount of garland do not relinquish their own fragrance, such is the vision of the subtle.
Just as that very [garment], being repeatedly perfumed with many garlands,
relinquishes its own scent and comes to abide in the scent of the garlands; even so,
one who is joined with hundreds of births through qualities alone becomes attached to those very things.
By means of the intellect, a fault is indeed removed through effort born of practice.
O Dānava, listen now to how beings, colored by their own actions— whether attached or detached— attain various specific results according to those deeds.
O Lord, I shall explain to you in due order how they proceed and upon what they rest; listen here with a focused mind.
The glorious Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa is without beginning or end.

He indeed creates all beings, both the stationary and the moving; he is the perishable and the imperishable within all beings. Having the eleven transformations as his essence, he drinks up the world with his rays.
Know his two feet to be the earth and his head to be the very heavens;
his arms, O Daitya, are the quarters of space, and his hearing is the ether.
His sun is composed of splendor, and his mind is established in the moon.
O best of Dānavas, his intellect is eternally established in knowledge, and his essence flows as water. The planets are situated between his eyebrows,
the circle of constellations in his two eyes, and the earth at his feet.

Know Him to be the Lord who has become all things, the origin of all, and the Supreme. Know that the earth, along with the netherworlds (pātāla), and the solar orb at His feet, as well as passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and goodness (sattva), are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
O dear one, they know him to be the mouth of the *āśramas* and the fruit of action;
he alone is the supreme, imperishable fruit of inaction as well. The Vedic meters are his body hairs, and the Imperishable is his speech.
The Dharma, which has many bases and many aspects, is established in the heart;
that Dharma is supreme Brahman, it is austerity, and it is both the existent and the non-existent.
It is endowed with the Vedas, the scriptures, and the sacred texts, and it is the sacrifice performed by the sixteen officiating priests.
Pitāmaha and Viṣṇu, the two Aśvins and Purandara, Mitra and Varuṇa, Yama and likewise Dhanada—
though they appear as distinct entities, they are perceived as one within him.
"Know, O Lord of Daityas, that this entire world is under the control of a single God. Though He exists in manifold forms, this scripture declares His oneness;
when a person perceives Him through knowledge, then true being (sattva) is revealed."
There are thousands of millions of cycles of dissolution and expansion;
living beings remain, and others continue to move about;
such is the measure of the creation of progeny.
O Daitya, there are many thousands of ponds;
those ponds are one yojana in width and one krośa in depth.
All of them are five hundred *yojanas* in length;
each is increased by one *yojana*.
One might cast water from a pond with the tip of a hair; [yet it would not diminish].
Know that at the end of those [ages], there is a single emission (creation) and likewise a single withdrawal (dissolution) of all beings, occurring once during the day and never a second time.
The six colors of living beings are the supreme measure:
black, smoky, and blue are its middle state; red, moreover, is more tolerable and brings happiness.
It is turmeric-colored, very pleasant, and white;
but that which is supremely white, stainless, and free from sorrow—
having transcended fatigue, O Lord of Dānavas— it attains perfection.
Having passed through thousands of births from wombs, O Daitya, the individual soul attains perfection;
and such is the destination which the Lord has declared.
Having gone there, he spoke only of auspicious visions:
"O Lord of Asuras, the destiny of living beings is determined by their caste (varṇa), and likewise, caste is determined by time."
O Daitya, one hundred and fourteen thousand [yojanas] here is the supreme limit for the quality of the living soul;
O Daitya, one who is excessively attached falls even from hell.
From there, he revolves further and further;
know that their ascent has already been accomplished,
as well as their station and their departure.
The destination of one of black complexion is lowly;
he sinks into hell while being cooked there,
and likewise his state is among the miserable realms.
They say that after wandering for many hundreds of thousands of emanations of beings,
one subsequently attains a green complexion.
And he dwells there without mastery,
his self enveloped in darkness at the end of the eon;
yet when he is indeed endowed with the quality of *sattva*, [he attains liberation].
Dispelling darkness by means of his own intellect,
he assumes a reddish hue and becomes blue;
thus he revolves in the world of men.
There, while being afflicted by the bonds born of his own karma, he undergoes the very process of withdrawal and emission;
thereafter, he attains a yellowish (hāridra) complexion.
When hundreds of cycles of dissolution and emanation have passed—
specifically 12,271,041— he, being yellow in color, remains wandering through thousands of emanations of living beings.
O Daitya, he was not released from hell for ten thousand other thousands of years;
his states of rebirth lasted for five thousand more.
Know him to be liberated from hell and from all other possible states of existence, as well as from the four types of destructions.
He dwells constantly in the world of the gods; falling from there, he attains human status. He undergoes eight hundred cycles of dissolution and manifestation.
Abiding among mortals, he attains immortality;
yet, through the power of time, he falls from that state and remains upon the dark ground, subject to all suffering.
O hero among the Asuras, I shall explain to you how this world of living beings attains success:
he [the Creator] has fashioned seven hundred divine arrays.
Red, yellow, and likewise white—
having resorted to this white one, he moves through the junction;
[he traverses] those eight other most worshipful worlds.
And those eight hundred and sixty [verses] which were contrary to the minds of the greatly effulgent ones;
that which is the supreme goal of the white color—
O one of great power, three [doors] are indeed blocked;
he dwells as one who lacks mastery over the withdrawal and expansion of the world, over that which is undesirable, and over four others.
The supreme goal of the sixth caste is attained by one who is perfected, distinguished, and free from fatigue; among them,
the powerless dwells in the seventy-seventh [state].

Having returned from that state after a hundred cycles of withdrawal and manifestation, with a remainder of time remaining— specifically 12,271,048 years— he then enters the human world and attains the status of a great man.
Therefore, having withdrawn from that, he gradually stood at the forefront of the creation of beings;
and seven times did he traverse the worlds.
Having undertaken his journey by means of both withdrawal and expansion,
he remains in the world of the perfected ones (siddhaloka), having brought about seven cycles of dissolution and calamities.
Thereupon, he goes to the imperishable and infinite abode of the god Viṣṇu, as well as that of Brahmā,
Śeṣa, and Nara.
At the time of universal dissolution, when their bodies have been completely consumed by fire, all creatures indeed always go to Brahmā, the supreme Lord Viṣṇu.
And all the hosts of gods, whose nature is activity—
even those immortals from the world of Brahmā—
they too [perceive] the emission of creatures along with the remaining time.
Living beings remember only their own respective places;
at the end, those men who are equal in all calamities go to that state where nothing remains.
But those who have fallen from the world of the Siddhas in due order,
their living beings go to that destination in the same sequence, possessing the power, dress, and form of those higher ones.
They return to their own course by way of reversal (12.271.054a).
As long as he remains with his meal yet unfinished,
so too do the subjects and the two queens remain pure.
At that time, having restrained this form of the five senses, he whose nature is purified among them attains that supreme,
pure state.
Constantly discerning with a pure mind,
he then attains the imperishable state of Brahman;
indeed, he reaches that which is eternal and difficult to attain.
"O you of undiminished courage, I have thus described to you here this strength of Nārāyaṇa.
Vṛtra said:
Thus that divine Blessed One spoke,
Sanatkumāra, speaking with sweet words:
"Since things have come to pass thus, I have no grief whatsoever."
And I truly perceive these words of yours; having heard your speech, O being of undaunted spirit,
I am today cleansed of stain and likewise freed from sin.
"O Blessed One,
O Great Seer, this wheel of the infinitely radiant one has been set in motion; it belongs to Viṣṇu, the infinite and eternal, and possesses boundless power."
He is the abode in whom all creations have proceeded;
he is indeed the Great-Souled One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama);
in him this entire universe is established.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, O son of Kuntī, Vṛtra cast off his life-breaths;
having thus united himself [with the Supreme], he attained the highest station.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, this is that very Lord, the divine Janārdana,
who in former times recounted [this] to Sanatkumāra for the sake of Vṛtra."
Bhīṣma said:
Abiding in the root by means of his own infinite splendor, that Blessed One,
established therein and possessed of great austerity, creates those various states of being.
Know that this Keśava, the infallible, constitutes one half of a fourth part of him;
know that Brahmā, the Great-Souled One, constitutes another half of a fourth part of him. With this remaining half of a fourth part, this wise one sustains the three worlds.
But he who stands below, remaining stable until the end of the kalpa—
that Lord of exceeding strength, that Prabhū— lies within the waters;
as the Creator of tranquil soul, he moves through those eternal worlds.
The infinite one makes all things non-empty;
as Sanatkumāra, he wanders through the worlds;
and as Aniruddha, that Great-Souled One creates.
"All this diverse world is situated within that.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of the supreme truth, I believe Vṛtra perceived his own destiny."
Therefore, O Grandfather, he who is auspicious is happy and does not grieve;
being pure and born of a pure lineage, such a Sādhya, O sinless one, does not return from that state,
having been liberated from rebirth as an animal and from hell, O Grandfather.

O King, one who exists in a yellow or red state perceives only the horizontal [animal realm], being enveloped by tamasic actions. But we, having fallen into great distress, are stained red in this miserable and joyless face of calamity.
"What destination shall we attain—a blue one, or a black, or the lowest of all?
Bhīṣma said:
"The Pāṇḍavas are endowed with pure lineage and are firm in their vows."
Having sported in the worlds of the gods for 12,271.068 years, you shall return again to human status;
and having returned at the proper time, you will experience the creation of progeny with ease, and after enjoying pleasures among the gods, you shall come back once more.
"You shall go happily to the rank of the perfected ones;
let there be no fear for you, for you are all pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O dear one, oh, how righteous was Vṛtra of immeasurable splendor! For his knowledge was incomparable, and his devotion to Viṣṇu was likewise. This [nature] of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor, O dear one, is difficult to comprehend."
"O tiger among kings, how did he come to know that state?
For I have faith in what you have said, O Acyuta;
yet, because of my perception of the unmanifest, a further thought has arisen in me."
"How was Vṛtra slain by Śakra, O bull of the Bharatas—
he who was most righteous, devoted to Viṣṇu, and a knower of reality according to the sequence of the stages?
Tell me this, O bull of the Bharatas, as I ask you to resolve my doubt."
"O tiger among kings, tell us how Vṛtra was defeated by Śakra,
and how that battle took place; relate it in detail, O Grandfather,
for my curiosity is great, O mighty-armed one."
12,272.007 Bhīṣma said: In ancient times, Indra indeed set forth on his chariot together with the hosts of gods;
then he beheld Vṛtra standing before him, resembling a mountain.
O subduer of enemies, it rises five hundred yojanas high, and its width is three hundred and three yojanas. Beholding such a form as that, which is invincible even by the three worlds—
The gods were terrified by Vṛtra and found no peace;
but then, O King, Śakra’s thighs suddenly became paralyzed with fear upon seeing that supreme form of Vṛtra.

Then, as that battle was about to commence, there arose the sound of shouting and the resonance of musical instruments from all the gods and asuras. Then, O descendant of Kuru, Vṛtra beheld Śakra standing before him.

Neither agitation, nor any fear, nor any sense of reliance arose [in them]. Then there occurred a battle between Śakra, the lord of the gods, and the great-souled Vṛtra, which caused terror to the three worlds.
With swords, sharp-edged spears, spikes, javelins, lances, and mallets;
with various kinds of rocks and loud-sounding bows;
and with various divine weapons as well as fire-brands.

Then, with the armies of the gods and asuras, everything became completely agitated. Led by the Grandfather (Brahmā), all the hosts of gods as well as the highly fortunate sages came there to witness that battle.

O great king, O bull of the Bharata race, the Siddhas and the Gandharvas, together with the Apsarases, met in their most excellent celestial chariots. Then Vṛtra, the best among the upholders of dharma, covered the sky.
With a shower of stones, he completely covered Devendra from the mountain.
Then the hosts of gods, enraged, warded off that shower of stones sent forth by Vṛtra from all sides with showers of weapons in the battle.
O tiger among the Kurus, Vṛtra, possessed of great illusion and great strength,
completely bewildered the lord of the gods with his illusory warfare. Then, afflicted by Vṛtra, Śatakratu fell into a state of confusion.
There, Vasiṣṭha awakened him with the *rathaṃtara* [sāman].
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Indra, lord of the gods, you are the best of deities, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods."
"Endowed with the power of the three worlds, O Śakra, why do you despair? Here are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, the lords of the universe;
here is the blessed god Soma, and all the supreme ṛṣis."
Seeing you so deeply distressed, they said, "May it be well with you; may victory be yours!
"O Śakra, do not fall into despondency like some other inferior being.
O Lord of the Gods, set your mind on noble battle and slay the enemy."
This three-eyed Teacher of the World, the Blessed One who is honored by all the worlds, gazes upon you; O Lord of the Gods, abandon your delusion! And here are the celestial sages, led by Bṛhaspati.
"O Śakra, with this divine hymn they indeed praise you for victory.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus was he being exhorted by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha."
The strength of Vāsava, who possesses supreme splendor, became exceedingly great.
Then, having applied his intellect, the blessed Lord Pākaśāsana,
endowed with great yoga, dispelled that illusion.
Then the illustrious son of Aṅgiras and those supreme ṛṣis,
having witnessed the prowess of Vṛtra, approached Maheśvara and spoke for the sake of destroying Vṛtra and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

Then the splendor of the Blessed One, the Lord of the World, having become a fever, entered Vṛtra, the most fierce and best of Daityas. And the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, worshipped by all the worlds, [also entered him].
Devoted to the protection of the world, he took up the thunderbolt of Indra.
Then the wise Bṛhaspati, the highly effulgent Vasiṣṭha, and all the supreme ṛṣis approached Śatakratu.
Having approached Vāsava, the giver of boons who is honored by the worlds, they spoke with one-pointed minds: "O Lord, slay Vṛtra!
Maheśvara said:
"O Śakra, this Vṛtra is great, surrounded by a vast army;
he is the soul of all, omnipresent, possessed of many illusions, and renowned. Therefore, this best of Asuras is difficult to conquer even for the three worlds."
"Resorting to yoga, slay him; do not despise him, O Lord of the Gods.
For he has performed this austerity for the sake of power, O Sovereign of the Immortals, and Brahmā granted him a boon after sixty thousand years."
O Lord of the Gods, the greatness of the yogis, their mastery over great illusion, as well as their great strength and supreme splendor—
this very energy of mine indeed enters into you, O Vāsava.
"Kill this Dānava Vṛtra with your thunderbolt in that very same way.
Śakra said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace [I shall slay] the son of Diti, who is so difficult to approach."
"O bull among the gods, while you look on, I shall strike him down with my thunderbolt.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, as that Daitya, the great Asura, was being possessed by the fever..."
