A great roar of joy arose from the deities and the sages. Then, kettledrums and conchs of immense sound, as well as drums and ḍiṇḍimas, were sounded by the thousands.
A great loss of memory occurred among all the Asuras, and a powerful destruction of their wisdom took place in an instant. Then,
perceiving that they were thus possessed, the sages and the gods likewise [acted].
Praising Śakra, the Lord, they likewise urged him forward. Indeed,
at the time of battle, the form of the high-souled Śakra as he stood upon his chariot while being praised by the ṛṣis was exceedingly difficult to behold.
Bhīṣma said:
O great king, listen to me regarding those signs that appeared throughout Vṛtra’s body when he was possessed by fever.
His mouth blazed, becoming terrible, and he underwent extreme paleness;
there was a great trembling of his limbs and a heavy panting of breath.
O King, there was intense horripilation and a deep sighing.
O Bhārata, from his mouth there issued forth a most dreadful and highly terrifying jackal that appeared inauspicious; that was his own memory (smṛti). Blazing meteors also fell flaming at his side.
Vultures, herons, and crows let out most dreadful cries;
exulting above Vṛtra, they circled around like a wheel.
Then, having mounted that chariot which had been strengthened for the battle by the gods, [he advanced].
Śakra, with his hand raised holding a thunderbolt, gazed at that Daitya.
Then that great Asura let out a superhuman roar and,
O King of kings, yawned, seized as he was by a violent fever.
Then, as he was yawning, Śakra released his thunderbolt.
That thunderbolt, possessed of immense splendor and resembling the fire of universal destruction,
swiftly struck down the massive-bodied Daitya Vṛtra.

Then, O bull of the Bharatas, upon seeing Vṛtra slain, a roar arose once more from all sides among the gods. Having killed Vṛtra, the illustrious and highly renowned Lord, the enemy of the Dānavas, [prevailed].

With the thunderbolt joined by Viṣṇu, he entered heaven itself. Then, O descendant of Kuru, from Vṛtra’s body there issued forth the most terrible Brahman-murder— fierce and bringing fear to the worlds.
O Bhārata, she had formidable fangs, was terrifying, deformed, and dark-brown; her hair was disheveled, her eyes were ghastly, and,
O bull of the Bharatas, she wore a garland of skulls and was emaciated.
O knower of dharma, drenched in blood and clad in garments of rags,
O king of kings, she emerged with such a terrifying form and then,
O best of the Bharatas, began to search for the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Then, after some time had passed, O joy of the Kurus, the slayer of Vṛtra set out toward heaven, desiring the welfare of the worlds.
But seeing Śakra of great splendor emerging from the lotus stalks, [the sages spoke].
He seized the Lord of the Gods by the neck, and she then became firmly attached to him.
Indeed, when that fear arising from the slaughter of a Brahmin had arisen,
he remained for many series of years within the stalks of a lotus.
Having pursued him with effort, O Kauravya, he was indeed seized by that Brahmahatyā and then became motionless. Śakra made a supreme effort to drive her away.
And Devendra was unable to cast off that Brahman-slaughter; indeed,
O bull of the Bharatas, while still seized by it,
he approached the Grandfather and honored him with his head bowed low.
O best of the Bharatas, when he learned that Śakra had been seized by the sin of killing the foremost of the twice-born,
Brahmā then reflected upon it;
O mighty-armed one, the Grandfather then spoke to that personified Brahman-slaughter.
Then, O Bhārata, consoling him as it were with a sweet voice, she said:
"O beautiful lady, let this lord of the thirty gods be released; do what is pleasing to me.
Tell me, what shall I do for you today? What desire do you wish for here?"
Brahmahatyā said:
"O God, worshipped by the three worlds, when you, the creator of the three worlds, are pleased, I consider my purpose here already accomplished; however, please ordain a dwelling for me."
"O Lord, this boundary has been established by you, who desire the protection of the world;
indeed, a very great ordinance has been set forth by you.
O Knower of Dharma, O Lord of all the worlds, O Master, when you are pleased,"
"I shall depart from Śakra; please provide me with a dwelling place.
Bhīṣma said:
"The Grandfather then said 'So be it' to that Brahmahatyā."
Through a skillful means, he dispelled Śakra’s sin of killing a Brahmin. Then, the high-souled self-existent one meditated upon Agni;
having approached Brahmā, Agni then spoke these words.
"O Blessed One, O God, O Subduer of Enemies, I have arrived in your presence.
O God, you ought to tell me what must be done by me.
Brahmā said:
"I shall divide this sin of Brahman-slaughter into many parts;
for the sake of Śakra's liberation today, accept from me one-fourth.
Agni said:
"O Brahman, O Lord, please reflect upon this: what indeed is the end of my liberation?
O one honored by the worlds, I wish to know this according to its true nature.
Brahmā said:
O Agni, that man who, shrouded in darkness, having encountered you blazing before him, should not himself worship you with seeds, herbs,
and juices— he shall quickly go to her and dwell right there.
"O Havyavāha, may the sin of Brahman-slaughter depart from you, and may the fever of your mind pass away.
Bhīṣma said:
Having been addressed thus, the consumer of sacrificial offerings (Agni) accepted those words.
"O Lord, it was thus that it came to pass for the Grandfather, O Blessed One. Then,
having summoned the trees, herbs, and grasses, the Grandfather,
O Great King, began to speak regarding this matter."
"This great and terrifying sin of Brahman-slaughter has come upon me from Vṛtra.
O Puruhūta, you all must accept a fourth part of it.
Then he spoke the same truth regarding trees, herbs, and grasses.
O King, [the gods], distressed like fire, spoke this to Brahmā:
"O Grandfather of the worlds, what is the end for us regarding the sin of killing a Brahmin?
You ought not to slay us again when we have already been struck down by our own nature."
"O God, we constantly endure cold, rain driven by the wind, as well as cutting and piercing; likewise,
today, by your command, we shall endure this sin of killing a Brahmin."
"O Lord of the Three Worlds, we shall seize those who contemplate liberation.
Brahmā said:
"But when a sacred festival day has arrived, whoever performs cutting or piercing [of the body]..."
"Whatever a man shall do out of delusion, she will follow after him.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O trees, herbs, and grasses, having been thus addressed by that high-souled one,"
Having worshipped Brahmā, he quickly departed as he had come.
Then, O Bhārata, the god who is the Grandfather of the worlds summoned the Apsarases and spoke to them in sweet words, as if consoling them.
"O beautiful women, this Brahman-slaughter has come down from Indra;
indeed, as I have told you, accept one-fourth of its portion.
The Apsarases said:
"O Lord of Gods, by your command, for us who have resolved to seize [the nectar], consider our liberation according to the agreement, O Grandfather. Brahmā said:
"Whoever indeed engages in sexual intercourse with women during their menses, her [curse] shall swiftly fall upon him; let the fever of your minds depart.
Bhīṣma said:
"Very well," said the hosts of Apsarases with joyful minds;
then, O bull of the Bharatas, having reached their own abodes, they rejoiced.
Thereafter, the god who created the three worlds, possessed of great ascetic power, once again—
He meditated upon the waters, and once meditated upon, they arrived. Having all come together before Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
O King, they bowed down to the Grandfather and spoke these words:
"O God, O subduer of enemies, we have arrived here in your presence at your command, O Lord of Gods. O All-pervading One, give us your orders.
Brahmā said:
"This great terror, the murder of a Brahmin, has followed Indra from Vṛtra; you all must accept a fourth part of it.
The Waters said:

"Let it be so, O Lord of the World, just as you tell us, O Master. You ought to consider our liberation according to the agreement. For you, O Lord of Gods, are the supreme teacher of the entire world."
"What other grace could there be that would rescue us from this distress?
Brahmā said:
"The man who, being deluded in intellect, considers [the gods] to be insignificant—"
"12,273.052c He will discharge phlegm, urine, and excrement upon you;
12,273.053a she will go to him quickly and dwell right there.
12,273.053c In this way your liberation shall come to pass—I tell you this as the truth."
12,273.054 Bhīṣma said: Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having released the lord of the gods, the Brahman-slaughter departed for the place she had been assigned, by the command of the god.
Thus, O lord of men, did Śakra incur the sin of killing a Brahmin;
having obtained the permission of the Grandfather (Brahmā), he prepared for the horse sacrifice.
For it is heard, O great king, that this [sin] was indeed incurred by Vāsava.
O lord of the earth, having thereby attained purification from the slaughter of a Brahmin through the horse sacrifice,
and having acquired sovereign glory while slaying his enemies by the thousands,
the divine Vāsava experienced incomparable joy.
O Pārtha, from the blood of Vṛtra were born the khukhuṇḍas;
they are not to be eaten by the twice-born who have been consecrated or by those whose wealth is their asceticism.
Therefore, in every circumstance, you too must do what is pleasing to these twice-born.
"For these, O joy of the Kurus, are indeed renowned as gods upon the surface of the earth.
Thus, O descendant of Kuru, was the great Asura Vṛtra slain by Śakra of immeasurable splendor through subtlety of intellect and the employment of strategic means.

In this way, O Kauravya, you too shall become unconquered upon the earth, just like the god Śatakratu, the slayer of enemies. And those who [recite] this divine story of Śakra at every change of the lunar fortnights...
"Those who shall recite this in the midst of the assembly of Brahmins shall not incur any sin.
Thus, my dear son, I have related to you this great and most wonderful deed of Śakra concerning Vṛtra. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O master of all the śāstras,
a desire to speak arises within me solely because of the slaying of Vṛtra."
"O lord of men, you have told me that Vṛtra was deluded by fever and slain here by Vāsava with the thunderbolt, O sinless one.
But how, O highly wise one, did this fever come into being, and from where did it originate?"
"O Lord, I desire to hear in detail about the origin of fever.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen, O King, to the origin of fever here, which is renowned throughout the world."
I shall describe its extent and its very nature, O Bhārata. Formerly, O great king, there was a peak of Meru renowned throughout the three worlds,
named Jyotiṣka, belonging to Savitṛ, and adorned with every kind of jewel.
O Bhārata, it was immeasurable and invincible in all the worlds;
by its own splendor, it stood covering the radiance of the sun.
There, upon a mountain slope adorned with gold and minerals, the god [resided].
He sat there, shining resplendently like a couch;
and the daughter of the King of Mountains stood constantly by his side, radiant.
Likewise, the high-souled gods and the Vasus of great prowess were present.
Likewise, the two high-souled Aśvins, the best of physicians;
and King Vaiśravaṇa,
the glorious lord of the Yakṣas, who dwells on Kailāsa and is surrounded by Guhyakas.
Both the treasures Śaṅkha and Padma, together with supreme supernatural power,
waited upon the Great-souled One, as did the great poet Uśanas and the great seers headed by Sanatkumāra.
The celestial sages, headed by Aṅgiras, as well as others; the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, and likewise Nārada and Parvata;
and multitudes of hosts of Apsarases arrived there in great numbers.
A pure, auspicious, and pleasant wind blew, carrying various fragrances. Great trees were laden with flowers and possessed blossoms of every season.
Likewise, the Vidyādharas, Siddhas, and those whose wealth is asceticism [were present].
O Bhārata, they sat in attendance upon Mahādeva Paśupati;
and then, O great king, there were beings assuming various forms,
as well as most fierce Rākṣasas and Piśācas of great strength.
Assuming many forms, joyful, and with various weapons raised,
the attendants of the god stood there, resembling fire.
And the blessed Nandin remained there by the god's command.
Grasping his blazing trident, which was radiant with its own splendor,
Gaṅgā— the best of rivers, born from the waters of all sacred fords—
waited upon that god in embodied form, O joy of the Kurus.
Thus, while being worshipped there by the celestial sages and the highly fortunate gods, the Blessed One, Mahādeva, remained present. Then,
after some time, there was a progenitor named Dakṣa.
Following the previously mentioned procedure, he prepared for the sacrifice.
Then, all the gods, led by Śakra, having assembled, resolved to go to his sacrifice.

Accompanied by their blazing celestial chariots, which possessed the radiance of fire, those great-souled ones departed for Gaṅgādvāra with the permission of the god; such is the sacred tradition. Then, seeing the deities set forth, the daughter of the King of Mountains [spoke].
The virtuous lady spoke these words to her husband, the god Paśupati:
"O Blessed One, where indeed are these gods going, led by Śakra?
Tell me the truth, O knower of reality; this doubt of mine is great."
Maheśvara said:
"O highly fortunate lady, there is an excellent lord of creatures named Dakṣa who is performing a horse sacrifice; the dwellers of heaven are going there."
Umā said:
"O highly fortunate one, for what reason do you not attend this sacrifice?
By what prohibition is your going prevented?"
Maheśvara said:
"O highly fortunate one, all this has been performed by the gods themselves;
no share was assigned for me in any of the sacrifices."
"O lady of excellent complexion, by virtue of the path attained through my previous means,
the gods do not grant me a share of the sacrifice according to dharma.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, you are preeminent among all beings in power and superior in virtues;
you are invincible and unassailable by virtue of your splendor, fame, and majesty.
O highly fortunate one, by this portion assigned to you through your prohibition—"
"O sinless one, extreme suffering has arisen within me, and I am trembling.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus to her husband, the god Paśupati, that goddess—
O King, she became silent, her heart burning with grief. Then, having understood the queen’s intention and what she desired in her heart,
he commanded Nandin, saying, "Stay here."
Then, having summoned his power of yoga, the Lord of all lords of yoga,
the god of gods who wields the Pināka bow and possesses great splendor, suddenly caused that sacrifice to be destroyed by his terrible followers.
Some released cries, while others broke into laughter;
others, O King, scattered fire there with their blood.
Some, with distorted faces, uprooted sacrificial posts and wandered about.
Others likewise devoured the attendants with their mouths;
then, O King, that sacrifice, being slaughtered on all sides,
assumed the form of a deer and fled into the sky.
Perceiving that sacrifice proceeding in such a manner,
the Lord took up his bow and arrow and pursued it;
then, from the wrath of that Lord of the Gods, who possesses immeasurable splendor—
A terrible drop of sweat emerged from his forehead;
as soon as that drop of sweat fell upon the earth, a vast fire appeared, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction.
And there, O bull among men, a man was then born—
short in stature, with exceedingly red eyes, a tawny beard, and terrifying;
with hair standing erect and limbs covered in excessive hair, he was like a hawk or an owl.
Fierce, dark-complexioned, and likewise clad in red garments,
that great being consumed that sacrifice like fire consumes dry grass;
he roamed everywhere among the gods and likewise rushed toward the sages.
Then all the gods fled in fear toward the ten directions. O lord of the people, as that being roamed about there, O King, bull of the Bharatas, the earth trembled violently.
When a world-terrifying cry of "Alas! Alas!
had arisen, and perceiving the entire world to have fallen into such a state of lamentation, the Lord Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke, pointing out Mahādeva.
"O Lord, all the gods will surely grant you a share as well;
O Sovereign of all the gods, let this withdrawal be performed by you.
For here are all these deities and the sages, O scorcher of foes."
"O Mahādeva, because of your wrath, they did not attain peace.
And this person who has been born from your sweat, O best of the gods,
shall wander through the worlds in the name of Jvara (Fever), O knower of dharma."

"O Lord, the entire earth is not capable of sustaining this splendor when it has become unified; let him be created in many forms. Thus addressed by Brahmā, the God [Śiva] was also assigned his portion.
"12,274.047c To the Blessed One, Brahmā of immeasurable splendor, he replied, 'So be it.
12,274.048a And the wielder of the Pināka bow experienced supreme joy, smiling;
12,274.048c and then Bhava received his share exactly as prescribed by Brahmā."
Then the Knower of all Dharmas emitted the fever in many forms for the sake of the peace of all beings; hear that also, my son. The headache of the Nāgas became bitumen from the mountains.
One should know that *nīlikā* is among the waters and the sloughed skin among serpents;
it is the hoof-disease of cattle and the saline soil upon the surface of the earth. Furthermore, O knower of dharma, it is that which obstructs the vision of animals.
Then, for horses, there is the affliction of the vital organs (*randhra*); for peacocks, the bursting of their crests;
and for cuckoos, eye disease—this fever has been proclaimed by the Great-Souled One. Furthermore, for all lotuses, it is the breaking of the bile (*pitta*); thus we have heard.
For all parrots as well, O knower of dharma, hiccup is said to be fever; among tigers, O knower of dharma, exhaustion is here called fever;
but among humans, O knower of dharma, this is renowned by the name "fever."
Entering a man at death, at birth, and likewise in the interval between,
this is the splendor of Maheśvara, the most terrible fever by name;
it is the Lord who is to be saluted and honored by all living beings.

For Vṛtra, the best among the upholders of dharma, having been possessed by this [power], yawned; then Śakra hurled his thunderbolt at him. Having entered Vṛtra, O Bhārata, the thunderbolt tore him asunder.
Torn apart by the thunderbolt, that great yogin, the mighty asura,
went to the supreme abode of Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor;
for by his devotion to Viṣṇu, this entire world had previously been pervaded by him.
"And because he was slain in battle, he attained the station of Viṣṇu.
Thus, my son, I have related to you in detail this account concerning the great fever that took refuge in Vṛtra; what else shall I tell you?"
The man who, with a mind free from dejection and always well-composed, recites this account of the origin of fever,
shall be liberated from disease, happy, and filled with joy.
He shall obtain his desires exactly as he wishes.
Janamejaya said:
How did it come about for Dakṣa, the son of Pracetas, during the Vaivasvata interval?
O Brahmin, the horse sacrifice of Prajāpati came to ruin because the Lord,
the soul of all, became enraged, perceiving it to have been caused by the goddess’s anger.
How was that sacrifice restored by Dakṣa through his grace?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"I wish to know this; tell it to me exactly as it happened.
Long ago, on the ridge of the Himavat, Dakṣa indeed performed a sacrifice."
In the auspicious region of Gaṅgādvāra, frequented by sages and perfected beings, crowded with Gandharvas and Apsarases, and covered with various trees and creepers,
Dakṣa— the best among the sustainers of sacrifice— was surrounded by hosts of ṛṣis.
Those who dwell on earth, in the intermediate space, and those who inhabit the heavenly world—
all of them, including the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas, stood before Prajāpati with their palms joined in reverence.
The Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, as well as Tumburu and Nārada; Viśvāvasu and Viśvasena, along with the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Sādhyas, together with the hosts of Maruts.
All of them, together with Indra, arrived as partakers of the sacrifice—
the *ūṣmapas*, the *somapas*, the *dhūmapas*, and the *ājyapas*—
as well as the *ṛṣis* and the *pitṛs*, who came along with Brahmā.
These and many others— the fourfold host of beings, namely those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and those born from sprouting—
all have been summoned and addressed, as have all the gods together with their wives.
Seated upon their celestial chariots, they shone like blazing fires.
Seeing them, Dadhīci, overcome with indignation, spoke these words:
"This is neither a sacrifice nor a righteous act where Rudra is not worshipped."
"12,274.060d@028_0025 Having indeed fallen into slaughter and bondage, what indeed is this reversal of time?
12,274.060d@028_0026 Why, out of delusion, do they not see that destruction is at hand? 12,274.060d@028_0027 They do not perceive the terrible danger that has arrived during this great sacrifice."
Having spoken thus, that great yogi beheld with his eye of meditation Mahādeva and the auspicious Goddess who grants boons,
as well as the high-souled Nārada standing near the Goddess.
Having reached the supreme satisfaction, the knower of yoga concluded thus:
"All of them are of one mind, since the Lord was not invited.
Departing from that place, Dadhīci spoke these words.
By honoring those who are not worthy of honor, and by failing to honor those who are worthy of honor,
a human being constantly incurs a sin equal to the three great crimes (tripātaka). Never before have I spoken an untruth, nor shall I ever speak one at any time.
"Among the deities and the seers, I speak the truth: I have come before the Lord of Creatures, the Creator, the Master of the World. Dakṣa said:
"Behold, indeed, the Lord who is the non-enjoyer of the sacrifice among all [the gods].
We have many Rudras with tridents in their hands and matted hair.
Dadhīci said:
"Though I have reached the eleventh stage, I do not know Maheśvara. This is a common failing of all those by whom the Lord has not been invited [to the sacrifice].
Just as I see no other deity superior to Śaṅkara," so he said.
Dakṣa said:
"In this way, this vast sacrifice of Dakṣa shall not take place.
[He spoke] these words to the Lord of Sacrifice in a golden vessel.
"I offer this entire oblation, purified by ritual and mantra, as a portion for Viṣṇu, the incomparable one.
The Goddess said:
He is the Lord, the All-pervading, and the one worthy of oblations;
what gift, restraint,
or austerity could I perform today by which he might become my husband?
"May the inconceivable Blessed One receive a share," Vaiśampāyana said;
"or perhaps half of that share, or even a third."
To his wife, who was speaking thus and was agitated, the Blessed One, appearing joyful, said:
"O Goddess, O lady of slender waist and limbs, you do not know me."
"What indeed is appropriate for me, who am the Lord of Sacrifice?
For I know this, O large-eyed one;
the wicked, being devoid of meditation, do not understand."
Today, through your delusion, the three worlds, including the gods with Indra, are utterly bewildered;
yet the reciters praise me at the sacrifice.
The chanters of the *sāman* sing the *rathaṃtara* to me;
the Brahmins worship me in the *brahmasattra*.
The Goddess said:
"Even those who are but simple folk, O Blessed One, prepare their portions for me in the assembly of women. The Blessed One said:
"He praises himself and even becomes arrogant; of this there is no doubt.
"I do not praise myself, O Queen of the Gods; behold me, O slender-waisted one!
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O lady of excellent hips, O woman of beautiful complexion, I shall create [a being] for your sake"—
having spoken thus to his wife Umā, who was dearer to him than his own life,
the Blessed One created from his mouth a terrifying and exhilarating being.
"Destroy the sacrifice of Dakṣa," Maheśvara said to him. Then, with a single lion effortlessly released from that mouth,
the sacrifice of Dakṣa was indeed destroyed for the sake of dispelling the Goddess’s wrath.
And Mahākālī, the most formidable and sovereign goddess, out of wrath,
together with her followers, stood as a witness to his own deeds; then, perceiving the will of the God, she bowed her head in reverence.
Equal to himself in valor, endowed with strength and beauty,
that very Lord Krodha is likewise endowed with a corresponding form;
he possesses infinite strength and heroism, and infinite power and manliness.

Known as Vīrabhadra, the dispeller of the Goddess’s wrath, he created from his pores the lords of the Gaṇas named Raumāḥ. These fierce Gaṇas were followers of Rudra, possessing the heroism and prowess of Rudra.
Then, for the sake of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice, they fell swiftly from there—
by the hundreds and thousands— with terrifying forms and massive bodies,
as if filling the sky with their shouts of "kilakila."
Terrified by that great sound, the inhabitants of heaven there were struck with fear;
the mountains crumbled and the earth trembled. The winds whirled about and the abode of Varuṇa was agitated.
The sacrificial fires do not blaze at all, nor does the sun shine;
the planets do not appear, nor the lunar mansions, nor the moon;
the sages do not shine, nor the gods, nor human beings.
Thus, when everything has become shrouded in darkness, those who have been insulted burn with rage; others strike out fiercely, uproot sacrificial posts,
crush some, and likewise trample others down.
They rush and run about with the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought;
the sacrificial vessels and divine ornaments are pulverized,
appearing like stars falling from the vault of heaven as they shatter apart.
Heaps of divine foods, drinks, and delicacies, resembling mountains;
then rivers of milk are seen, with mud made of ghee and milk-rice; divine waters of whey, with sands of candied sugar and granulated sugar.
These delightful streams of molasses carry the six flavors;
there are various meats of high and low quality, diverse kinds of foods, divine drinks, and all things to be licked and sucked.
With various mouths, they devour, plunder, and seize;
these great-bodied ones, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, are filled with Rudra’s wrath. Agitating the hosts of gods, they strike terror on all sides.

They played with distorted forms and threw the celestial women about; Bhadrakālī swiftly consumed that sacrifice on all sides, even though it had been diligently protected by all the gods through Rudra’s wrath.
He let out a terrible roar that struck fear into all living beings;
having indeed severed the head of the sacrifice, he roared and rejoiced.
Then the gods, headed by Brahmā, as well as Dakṣa the progenitor of creatures, [were filled with awe].
Vīrabhadra said:
"They all spoke with palms joined in reverence, saying, 'Tell us, who are you? [He replied:
'I am neither Rudra, nor the Goddess; I have not come here to eat.'"

Perceiving that this was caused by the goddess’s wrath, the Lord, who is the soul of all, became enraged. O best of Brahmins, know that I have arrived here neither to see you nor out of curiosity, but for the purpose of destroying your sacrifice.

The one known as Vīrabhadra emerged from the wrath of Rudra; she who is to be known as Bhadrakālī emerged from the wrath of the Goddess. Sent by the God of gods, they have both arrived here at the conclusion of the sacrifice.
"O best of Brahmins, go for refuge to the God of gods, the Lord of Umā.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Even the anger of the God is a boon; it is not so from any other source."
Having heard the words of Vīrabhadra, Dakṣa, the best among the upholders of dharma,
prostrated himself before Maheśvara and gratified him with a hymn of praise:
"I take refuge in the Lord Īśāna, who is eternal, constant, and imperishable."
To Mahādeva, the Great-Souled One, the Lord of the entire universe—
at the sacrifice of the Prajāpati Dakṣa— with well-prepared ritual materials,
all the deities and the sages whose wealth is asceticism were invited.
There, the god Viśvakarman, the Great Lord, was not invited;
there the enraged Mahādevī dispatched her hosts. When the sacrificial enclosure was set ablaze and the twice-born had fled, [she acted].
When the fierce, blazing, and great-souled [Rudra] had overtaken the host of stars,
his attendants, their hearts pierced by spears, were moaning;
sacrificial posts, dug in and then uprooted, were cast about here and there.
With vultures greedy for flesh flying up and falling down,
shaken by the wind of their wings and resounding with the cries of hundreds of jackals;
and with hosts of yakṣas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
Having restrained his inhalation and exhalation with effort through the opening of his mouth,
and having surveyed the vision everywhere, the conqueror of enemies,
the lord of the gods of gods, suddenly rose from the fire-pit.
Possessing the splendor of a thousand suns and resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, he smiled and spoke these words: "Tell me, what shall I do for you?
Then, after the preceptor of the gods had recited the chapter on sacrifices, [Bhīṣma said: "Then..."
Having joined his palms in *añjali*, Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, spoke to that god—
fearful, apprehensive, and trembling, with tears in his face and eyes:
"If the Blessed One is pleased, and if I am dear to you..."
If I am worthy of favor, or if a boon is to be granted to me:
whatever sacrificial materials were burnt, eaten, drunk, chewed, or wasted; and whatever was ground into powder or cast away—all that effort for the sacrifice [may be restored].
"Accumulated over a long period of time and with great effort, let that not become false for me; I choose this boon. "So be it," said the Blessed One, Hara, the destroyer of Bhaga's eyes.
The overseer of dharma, Virūpākṣa, the three-eyed god, the lord of creatures—
having knelt upon the earth and received a boon from Bhava, Dakṣa departed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
With eight thousand names he praised the one whose banner bears the bull.
With those very names by which Dakṣa, the god and lord of creatures, offered praise—
Bhīṣma said:

"O dear one, you ought to speak to me; O sinless one, I have the desire to hear. Listen, O Bhārata, to the secret and manifest names of the God of gods, whose deeds are wondrous, and who observes hidden vows."
Dakṣa said:
"Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods;
O paralyzer of the power of Indra, worshipped by gods and dānavas."
O thousand-eyed one, O Virūpākṣa, O three-eyed one, O beloved lord of the Yakṣas!
You whose hands and feet extend everywhere, whose eyes, heads, and mouths are on all sides;
you who possess ears everywhere in the world, you stand encompassing all.
O Śaṅkukarṇa, Mahākarṇa, Kumbhakarṇa, you whose abode is the ocean!
O Gajendrakarṇa, Gokarṇa, Pāṇikarṇa, homage be to you!
O Śatodara, Śatāvarta, Śatajihva, Śatānana!
The singers of the *gāyatrī* sing of you; the chanters of hymns worship you as the hymn.
They regard you, the Brahman, the Lord of a hundred powers, as being like the exalted sky.
For you, O Great-Formed One, whose form is the universe, are like the ocean and the firmament.
Indeed, all the deities dwell within this [body] like cattle in a cow-pen. Within your body, I behold Soma, Agni, the Lord of Waters,
Āditya, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Bṛhaspati.

Homage to Bhava, to Śarva, to Rudra, and to the Giver of Boons— the Lord who is the cause, the effect, the action, and the instrument; who is likewise the origin and the dissolution of both the non-existent and the existent.

Salutations indeed to the Lord of beasts, and salutations to the slayer of Andhaka; Salutations to the one with three matted locks, to the three-headed one, to him who holds the excellent trident in his hand;
Salutations indeed to Tryambaka, to the three-eyed one, and to the destroyer of Tripura.
Homage to the fierce one, to the shaven-headed one, to the egg-born one, and to the bearer of the cosmic egg;

homage indeed to the wielder of the staff, to the one with symmetrical ears, and to the one with a shaven head and a staff; homage to the one with upward-pointing fangs and hair, to the white one, and to the one who is expansive.

Homage indeed to the deep-red one, to the smoke-colored one, and to the blue-necked one; homage be to the peerless one, to the multiform one, and to Śiva; to Sūrya, to him who wears a garland of suns, and to him whose banner and flag are the sun.
Homage to the Lord of the Destroyers, whose shoulders are like those of a bull, who wields the bow; homage to the subduer of enemies, to the Punisher, and to him who wears garments of bark;
homage to the Golden Embryo and to him whose armor is gold.
Homage to the one whose crest is made of gold, homage to the Lord of Gold!
Homage to the praised, to the praiseworthy, and indeed homage to the one being praised! Homage to the All, to the consumer of all, and to the inner self of all beings!
Homage to Hotṛ and to Mantra, who possesses white banners and flags;
homage to Nābha and to Nābhya, and homage to Kaṭakaṭa;
let there be homage to Kṛśanāsa, to Kṛśāṅga, and to Kṛśa.
Homage to the one who is thrilled and the one who is exultant, and to the one who shouts "kilakila"!
Homage be to the one lying down, to the one who has lain down, and to the one who has risen; to the one standing, to the one running, to the shaven-headed one, and to the one with matted hair!
Homage to the one whose nature is dancing, who plays wind instruments with his mouth; homage to the one greedy for offerings of food, who is skilled in song and instrumental music;
homage to the eldest, to the most excellent, and to the subduer of strength.

Salutations eternally to Kālanātha, to Kalya, to Kṣaya, and to Upakṣaya; salutations to him whose laughter is like the sound of a terrifying drum, and who maintains formidable vows; salutations to the Fierce One, and let there be salutations to the Ten-Armed One.
Homage to the one who holds a skull in his hand and who is fond of the ashes of the funeral pyre;
homage to the terrifying one, the formidable one, who maintains fearsome vows; homage to the one with a distorted face, with a sword-like tongue, and with fangs.

Salutations to the one who craves cooked and raw meat, and to the one fond of the lute made of gourd; salutations to the Bull, to the one who bestows virility, to the Bull among cattle, and to the Bull itself;
salutations to Kaṭaṅkaṭa, to the Fierce One, and to Pacapaca.
Homage to the most excellent, the supreme, and the bestower of boons;
homage to him who possesses choice garlands, perfumes, and garments, the giver of boons beyond the best.
Homage to him who is both attached and detached, the meditative one wearing a rosary of beads.

Salutations to the one who is both united and divided, to the shadow and to the heat; salutations to the one who is neither terrible nor of terrible form, and to the one who is more terrible than the most terrible; salutations to Śiva, the peaceful, and salutations to the most profoundly peaceful.
Homage, again and again, to the one-footed, many-eyed, and single-headed one.
Homage to the humble, to the greedy, and to him who delights in sharing. Homage to Pañcāla, to the white-bodied one, and to Śamaśama.
Homage to Caṇḍikaghaṇṭa, to Ghaṇṭā, Aghaṇṭa, and Ghaṇṭin; To Sahasraśataghaṇṭa and to him who is fond of garlands of bells; Homage to Prāṇaghaṇṭa, to Gandha, and to Kalakala.
Homage to the one who has reached the further shore of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*, and to the one who is fond of the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ*;
Homage always to Śamaśama, whose dwelling is in mountains and trees;
To the one who is the embryo, the flesh, and the jackal, and to Tāraka and Tara.
Homage to the sacrifice, to the sacrificer, to the oblation offered, and to the oblation fully poured;

homage to the carrier of the sacrifice, to the self-controlled, to the one who undergoes austerity, and to the one who performs austerity; homage to the shore, to the one dwelling on the shore, and homage to the Lord of all shores.
Salutations to the giver of food, to the lord of food, and likewise to the eater of food;
salutations to the thousand-headed one and to the thousand-footed one; salutations to the one who raises the trident a thousandfold and to the thousand-eyed one.

Homage to him who has the color of the rising sun and who assumes the form of a child; homage to the protector of children as his attendants and to him whose playthings are children. Homage to the aged one, to the greedy one, to the agitated one, and to the agitator.
Salutations indeed to the one whose hair is marked by waves, to the one with hair like *muñja* grass;

salutations to the one who is pleased by the six ears, and to the one devoted to the three-fold duties; salutations to the one who duly ordains the distinct duties for those of the various castes and stages of life.
Homage to Ghuṣya and to Ghoṣa, and homage to Kalakala;
To the one with white and tawny eyes, and to the one with black and red eyes;
To the breaker of vital breaths, to Daṇḍa, to Sphoṭana, and to Kṛśa.

Salutations to the one who speaks and explains the four goals of life—dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa; to the foremost of the Sāṃkhya, the originator of Sāṃkhya-yoga; salutations to the one who is the path, the non-path, and the chariot at the crossroads.
To you who have a black antelope skin as an upper garment, who wear a serpent as a sacred thread,
O Īśāna, mass of thunderbolts, golden-haired one, homage be to you!
To the three-eyed lord of Ambikā, the manifest and unmanifest, homage be to you!

O Kāma, O giver of desires, O destroyer of desires, O you who move among the satisfied and the unsatisfied! O All, O giver of all, O destroyer of all, O you whose hue is like the twilight—homage be to you! O you of great strength, O you of mighty arms, O you of great being, O you of great splendor!
Homage be to you, Mahākāla, who resembles a mass of great clouds; to you with thick, matted hair and aged limbs, who wear bark garments and deerskins;
to you with matted locks blazing like the sun and fire, clothed in bark and deerskin.
O you who resemble a thousand suns, ever devoted to austerity, homage be to you! O Unmādana, Śatāvarta, you whose hair is moistened by the waters of the Gaṅgā,
O Candrāvarta, Yugāvarta, Meghāvarta, homage be to you!
You are food and the eater of food, the giver of food and indeed the enjoyer of food;
you are the creator of food and its digester, the consumer of what is digested, the wind, and the fire.
You are those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from sweat, and likewise those born from a sprout.
O Lord of the gods of gods, you alone are the fourfold collection of beings;
you are the creator of all that is moving and unmoving, and likewise the one who withdraws it.
Those who know Brahman call you Brahman, O best among the knowers of Brahman.

The wise who discourse upon Brahman declare you to be the supreme source of the mind, the ether, the wind, and the treasury of lights; likewise, they call you the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the syllable *Oṃ*.
You are *hāyi-hāyi*, *huvāhāyi*, *hāvuhāyi*, and so on, uttered repeatedly.
O Best of Gods, the chanters of the Sāman and the exponents of Brahman sing of you;
you are composed of the Yajus, composed of the Ṛk, and likewise composed of oblations.
Indeed, you are recited through the hymns of the collections of Vedas and Upaniṣads.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those of lower castes—you alone are they; you are the masses of clouds, the lightning, the thunder, and the roar;
you are the year, the seasons, the month, and even half a month.
You are the Yugas, the Nimeṣas, the Kāṣṭhās, the constellations, the planets, and the Kalās;
you are the pre-eminent peak of trees and the summits of mountains;
you are the tiger among beasts, Tārkṣya among birds, and Ananta among serpents.
Among the oceans, you are indeed the Ocean of Milk; among machines, you are the bow;
among weapons, you are the thunderbolt; and among vows, you are truth alone.
You alone are hatred and desire, passion and delusion, as well as forgiveness and intolerance.

Resolve, fortitude, greed, desire and anger, victory and defeat—you are the wielder of the mace, you are the bearer of the arrow and the bow, as well as the one with the skull-topped staff and the rattle-drum.
You are the cutter, the piercer, the striker, the leader, the thinker, and the father; thus you are regarded.
Dharma, artha, and even kāma are endowed with the ten characteristics;
so too are the Gaṅgā, the oceans, rivers, ponds, and lakes;
as well as creepers, climbing plants, grasses, herbs, domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds.
He is the commencement of substances, actions, and qualities; he bestows time, flowers, and fruits.
He is the beginning and the end of the gods, as well as the Gāyatrī and the syllable Oṃ.
He is green, red, blue, black, crimson, and likewise ruddy.
Kadru, Kapila, Kapota, and likewise Mecaka;
Avarṇa, Suvarṇa, Varṇakāra, and indeed Anaupama;
Suvarṇanāman, and likewise Suvarṇapriya.
You are Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Kubera, and Agni; you are Upaplava, Citrabhānu, Svarbhānu, and Bhānu;
you are the oblation, the priest, the material for sacrifice, the act of sacrificing, and likewise the Lord.

The *Trisauparṇa*, the *Brahma-yajus*, the *Śatarudriya* among the *Yajus* hymns, the *Pavitra* among purifiers, and the most auspicious of all auspicious things; as well as the *Girika*, the *Hiṇḍuka*, the *Vṛkṣa*, the *Jīva*, and the *Pudgala*.
Prāṇa, sattva, rajas, and tamas, as well as vigilance;
prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna;
and opening and closing of the eyes, sneezing, and yawning.
With eyes reddish within, large-mouthed, and large-bellied;
with pure body hair, a golden beard, and hair standing erect; ever-moving and restless;
he is a knower of the principles of song and instrumental music, and is fond of singing and playing instruments.
The fish that moves in the water, caught in the net, the one without parts, the playful sound, and strife;
the untimely, the excessive time, the evil season, and Time itself;
Death, the razor, the ritual act, the winged one, and the destroyer of those without wings.
Meghakāla, Mahādaṃṣṭra, Saṃvartaka, Balāhaka;
Ghaṇṭa, Aghaṇṭa, Ghaṭī, Ghaṇṭī, Carucelī, Milīmilī;
and among the Brahmakāyika fires, Daṇḍī, Muṇḍa, and Tridaṇḍadhṛk.
He who is the four yugas, the four Vedas, and the originator of the fourfold priestly offices; he who is the leader of the four stages of life and the creator of the four castes;
he who is always fond of dice, the rogue, the presiding officer of the hosts, and the lord of the hosts.
Wearing red garlands and garments, Giriśa is beloved by Girikā;
he is Śilpika, the best among artisans, and the originator of all crafts. He is Bhaganetrāṅkuśa, Caṇḍa, and the destroyer of Pūṣan’s teeth.
Svāhā, Svadhā, Vaṣaṭkāra, Namaskāra, salutation, salutation;
he whose vow is secret, whose austerity is secret, the Savior, consisting of salvation;
the Ordainer, the Disposer, the Uniter, the Arranger, the Sustainer, the Unassailable.
Brahmā; austerity and truth; celibacy and uprightness;
the soul of all beings, the creator of beings, the being who is the source of the past, the future, and the present;
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svar, and Dhruva; the self-controlled Maheśvara.
He is the initiated and the uninitiated, the patient and the difficult-to-tame destroyer of the untamed;
he is the whirlpool of the moon, the turner of the age, the dissolution and the one who sets it in motion;
he is desire, the drop, the subtle, and the gross; he is fond of garlands of *karṇikāra* flowers.
Nandīmukha, Bhīmamukha, Sumukha, Durmukha, Amukha,
Caturmukha, Bahumukha, and likewise Agnimukha in battles;
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śakuni, Mahoragapati, and Virāṭ.
Adharmahā, Mahāpārśva, Daṇḍadhāra, Raṇapriya,
Gonarda, Gopratāra, Govṛṣeśvaravāhana,
Trailokyagoptṛ, Govinda, Gomārga, and Amārga.
The most excellent, the steadfast, the pillar-like, the motionless, and indeed the trembling; the irresistible, the unbearable, the unendurable, the insurmountable;
the invincible, the unshakable, the venomous, the unconquerable, and the Victor.
The hare-marked moon, the subduer, the bearer of cold, heat, hunger, old age, and mental anguish; he who is both mental and physical affliction, the destroyer of disease, and disease itself;
the hunter of the sacrificial deer for me, and the arrival and departure of all maladies.
Śikhaṇḍin, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, whose abode is the lotus forest; Daṇḍadhāra, Tryambaka, Ugradaṇḍa, and Aṇḍanāśana;
you are the drinker of poison and fire, the best of gods, the drinker of Soma, and the Lord of the Maruts.
O Lord of the World, God of gods, Lord of the Gaṇas, you are the drinker of nectar;
you are likewise the drinker of poison and fire, the drinker of death, the drinker of milk, and the drinker of Soma.
You alone are the foremost drinker of those from whom honey flows, and the drinker of the clarified butter of the Tuṣitas.
You alone are the golden-seeded Puruṣa;
you are woman, you are man, and you are neuter;
you are the child, the youth, the elder, and the one with decayed teeth.
You are the enemy of the lord of serpents, the creator of the universe, and the most excellent;
you possess arms on all sides, you are radiant, and you have faces everywhere. You are the moon and the sun, the heart, and the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Sarasvatī is the strength of speech, and the supreme wind is the agent of the opening and closing of the eyes throughout day and night;
neither Brahmā, nor Govinda, nor those ancient seers possess such power.

O Śiva, those forms of yours that are extremely subtle, which are capable of knowing your majesty exactly as it is— those do not come within my sight. Save me always and protect me, as a father protects his own biological son.
Protect me, protect me! I am worthy of your protection, O sinless one; homage be unto you!
The Blessed One is compassionate toward his devotees, and I am forever devoted to you—he who, difficult to behold, stands enveloping many thousands of men.
He stands alone at the edge of the ocean; may he be my protector forever.
To him, the soul of yoga, whom those who are sleepless, whose breath is conquered, who abide in purity, and who perceive with equanimity, behold as light while practicing yoga—to him I bow.

Salutations to that one who is Rudra himself, who always possesses matted locks, carries a staff, and has a pot-bellied body; who bears a water-pot and a quiver. In whose hair are the clouds, and in whose every joint are the rivers.

Salutations to Him whose belly contains the four oceans; salutations to that Soul of Water. When the end of the age has arrived, He who, having consumed all beings, lies within the midst of the waters—to that Sleeper in the Waters, I take refuge.
May he who, having entered the mouth of Rāhu, drinks the Soma at night, and who,
becoming Svarbhānu, swallows the sun— he shall protect me;
and those embryos that have fallen [into the womb] and wait upon their respective portions.
Salutation to them! Svadhā! Svāhā! May they attain it and rejoice.
Those persons the size of a thumb who reside within the bodies of all embodied beings—may they protect me always and may they constantly nourish me.
Salutations forever to those who, dwelling within the body, do not weep, yet cause embodied beings to weep; who gladden others, yet do not themselves rejoice;
and who abide in rivers, oceans, mountains, and caves.
At the roots of trees, in cow-pens, and in the depths of the wilderness; at crossroads, on carriage-roads, in squares, and on riverbanks;
in the stables for elephants, horses, and chariots, and in ruined gardens and dwellings.
And those who are within the five elements, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions;
those situated between the moon and the sun, and those within the rays of the moon and the sun; those who have gone to the subterranean realm (rasātala), and those who have reached the highest state.

Homage to them, homage to them, homage to them be evermore! To those Rudras for whom there is no number, no measure, and no form—homage to those of incalculable qualities; let there be homage to them forever.
Since you are the creator of all beings, the lord of all beings, Hara,
and the inner self within all beings, for that reason you were not invited; indeed,
it is you alone who are worshipped with sacrifices accompanied by various sacrificial fees.
"You alone are the creator of everything; for that reason, you were not invited. Or perhaps, O Lord, I have been deluded by your subtle *māyā*.
For this reason as well, you were not invited."
"Be gracious to me; may it be well with you, for my being is fixed upon you. O Lord, my heart is in you, my intellect is in you, and my mind is in you.
Having thus praised Mahādeva, Prajāpati ceased speaking.
The Blessed One, also being well-pleased, spoke again to Dakṣa:
"I am thoroughly satisfied with this hymn of yours, O Dakṣa of noble vows.
What need is there for much speaking here? You shall remain in my presence."
"O Prajāpati, by my grace, you shall partake in the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices. Then Bhava,
the lord of the three worlds, spoke these words to him.
The master of speech uttered these words, which were comforting and perfectly measured:
"O Dakṣa, O Dakṣa, you must not harbor anger toward this obstacle;
I am the one who takes away your sacrifice—this has been seen since ancient times."
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, I grant you another boon; accept it.

With a serene countenance, listen now with a one-pointed mind. Having extracted [this knowledge] from the Vedas along with their six ancillaries, and from Sāṃkhya and Yoga through reasoned application—
This penance was well-performed, vast, and difficult to practice even for gods and dānavas;
it was unprecedented, auspicious in every way, facing all directions, imperishable,
lasting ten days for twelve years, secret, and beyond the reproach of the ignorant.

O Dakṣa, this Pāśupata vow— which is superior to the stages of life (āśrama), which is sometimes contrary to and sometimes equal to the duties (dharma) performed by those in the various castes (varṇa), and which has reached its ultimate conclusion— was established by me in the past through yoga.
"The abundant fruit of that which has been rightly practiced belongs to him. May that be yours, O fortunate one; let the fever of your mind be cast aside.
Having spoken thus, Mahādeva, whose banner is the bull, together with his consort, [departed].
He of immeasurable prowess attained invisibility from Dakṣa. Whoever recites or hears this hymn proclaimed by Dakṣa shall encounter no inauspiciousness and shall attain a long life.
Just as the Blessed Lord Śiva is the most excellent among all the gods,
so too is this hymn the most excellent among hymns, equal to the Veda.
It is [to be recited] by those desiring fame, kingdom, happiness, sovereignty, desire, purpose, and wealth.
Those desiring knowledge should listen with effort, establishing themselves in devotion.
One who is diseased, suffering, wretched, seized by thieves, afflicted by fear,
or engaged in royal service is liberated from great danger.
By this very body, one shall attain equality with the Gaṇas;
endowed with splendor and fame, one becomes stainless. Neither Rākṣasas nor Piśācas, nor Bhūtas nor Vināyakas [can harm such a one].
In that house where this hymn is recited, obstacles shall not arise.
And whatever woman, devoted to him and practicing celibacy, should hear it,
she becomes as worthy of honor as a deity among both her father’s and her mother’s kin.
Whoever should hear this entire hymn or recite it with a concentrated mind,
all his actions will constantly attain success—
whatever has been conceived by the mind and whatever has been proclaimed by speech.
Everything is accomplished for one through the recitation of this hymn to the God together with Guha,
to the Goddess, and to Nandīśvara—
having performed a well-prepared offering with self-restraint and religious observance.
Then, being disciplined, one should quickly grasp the names in their proper sequence;
that person obtains his desired goals, as well as pleasures and enjoyments. Upon death, he attains heaven and is not born among the animals.
"Thus spoke the blessed Lord Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara.
O best among the upholders of dharma, this meritorious and righteous tale has been told;
what else shall I relate here? You should tell me that."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Living beings always fear sorrow, suffering, and death.
O Grandfather, tell me how both of these may not befall me."
Bhīṣma said:
In this very connection, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Nārada and Samaṅga.
Nārada said:
You seem to bow with your very chest and to swim with your arms;
with a mind always exceedingly joyful, you appear as if free from sorrow.
"I do not perceive even the slightest agitation in you here;
you behave like one who is eternally satisfied, composed, and yet acting like a child.
Saṃgaṅga said:

O giver of honor, everything that has been, is, and will be among all beings—I know their true nature; therefore, I am not despondent. Furthermore, I know the methods of undertaking actions and the resulting emergence of their fruits.
Since there are such diverse fruits in this world, I am not at all despondent. O Nārada, some are bottomless and without support, yet others possess movement;
some are blind and dull-witted, yet they live—look at us as well, we too are living!
By that very [means] ordained, the dwellers of heaven live with unimpaired limbs;
both the strong and the weak [live thus]. In the same way, honor us.
Those who possess thousands live, and likewise those who possess hundreds live.
"Others live on vegetables alone; behold us also living thus.
O Nārada, what would not be possible for us through righteousness or through action, such that we might never grieve?"
When pleasures or pains, being subject to the power of destiny (kṛtānta), do not overwhelm him,
and for whom men proclaim wisdom— [he is a steadfast man].
For the clarity of the faculties has its root in wisdom.
When the faculties are deluded, they become bewildered and grieve;
for one whose faculties are deluded, there is no attainment of wisdom.
The pride of the deluded is itself merely delusion;
for the deluded, neither this world nor the next exists.
Indeed, sufferings do not persist forever.
Or rather, the constant attainment of happiness— which is of the nature of existence and ever-evolving—
a person like me would never experience such feverish distress.
One should not cling to desired enjoyments or to pleasure,
nor should one dwell upon suffering that has arrived.
Being concentrated, one should not covet the possessions of others.
One should not rejoice in future gain,
nor should one exult even at the acquisition of vast wealth;
likewise, one should certainly not despair at the loss of wealth.
Neither kinsmen, nor wealth, nor noble lineage; neither sacred learning, nor secret mantras, nor prowess—
none of these are able to protect one from suffering.
Those who are not established in virtue do not attain peace in the next world. For one who is undisciplined, there is no wisdom; without discipline, there is no happiness.
Both steadfastness and the abandonment of suffering lead to our well-being.
For what is dear produces joy, and joy increases arrogance; arrogance leads only to hell, therefore I renounce it. These—sorrow, fear, and arrogance—are the delusions regarding pleasure and pain.
I see you as a witness in this world because of the movements of this body;
having abandoned wealth and desire, free from sorrow and free from fever,
and having cast off thirst and delusion, I wander this earth.

"O Brahmin, having performed great and inexhaustible austerity, I know this: there is no fear at all— neither from death, nor from unrighteousness, nor from greed, nor from anything else— either in this world or in the next, as if one had drunk the nectar of immortality."
"Because of that, O Nārada, [the truth] has been attained; grief does not afflict me.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For one who does not know the reality of the scriptures and whose mind is constantly filled with doubt..."
"O Grandfather, tell me what is beneficial for one who has not yet formed a firm resolve.
Bhīṣma said:
"Constant reverence for one's teacher and attendance upon the elderly."
The hearing of the sciences is said to be the immutable highest good.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Gālava and the celestial seer Nārada.
To Nārada, who possessed divine luster, who had returned to his own hermitage— a brahmin free from delusion and fatigue, satisfied with knowledge, having conquered his senses,
self-controlled, and desiring the highest good— Gālava spoke.
Whatever qualities a man may possess that are esteemed among people in this world,
I perceive all those qualities to be inseparable from you.
You, being such as you are, ought to dispel our doubt.
Unconfused, [you speak] to those long-confused who do not know the true nature of the world;
for such is the engagement in knowledge for one who discerns what ought and ought not to be done.
You ought to tell us that which we cannot determine as our duty.
"O Blessed One, all the hermitages display various modes of conduct;
they have run in different directions, each saying, 'This is the highest good,' or 'That is the highest good. Seeing them thus divided, and seeing those who delight in their respective scriptures,"
We do not find the highest good for those who are satisfied with their own respective treatises;
if there were but a single treatise, then the highest good would be manifest.
However, because there are many treatises, the highest good has been further concealed.
"For this reason, the highest good appears to me as a dense thicket.
May the Blessed One explain it to me; I have approached you as a disciple, O Lord, please teach me.
Nārada said:
"O dear one, there are four hermitages, each established according to its own purpose.
O Gālava, you should visit them all, taking refuge in each one in turn. For you must go from here to those various hermitages."
Behold the various descriptions of forms and qualities, set forth individually;
they lead one surely to that which is intended.
Thus, seeing straight on, one correctly perceives the supreme goal of the stages of life (āśramas).
That which is the highest good is truly free from doubt;
the wise say that the welfare [of others], the favoring of friends, the subduing of enemies, and the pursuit of the three goals of life constitute the highest good.

Abstaining from evil deeds, constant cultivation of virtuous conduct, and proper behavior toward the righteous— this is undoubtedly the highest good. Gentleness toward all beings and straightforwardness in one's dealings [are likewise essential].
Speech that is indeed sweet is declared to be this, and there is no doubt that it leads to welfare;
sharing with the gods, the ancestors, and even toward guests,
as well as not abandoning one's dependents— this, too, is undoubtedly conducive to welfare.

Speaking the truth is excellent, yet the knowledge of truth is difficult to attain; that which is ultimately beneficial to all beings—that, I declare, is truth. Furthermore, there is the renunciation of egoism and the restraint of attachment.
Contentment and solitary conduct are said to be the immutable highest good (śreyas). Likewise,
the study of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (vedāṅgas) according to dharma, as well as the desire to know the objects of knowledge— this, without doubt, is the highest good.

O scorcher of foes, one who seeks the highest good should not indulge excessively in sound, form, taste, touch, and smell in their pure forms. One should avoid wandering at night, sleeping during the day, laziness, backbiting, and intoxication.
One who seeks the highest good should avoid both excessive application and lack of application. One should not seek excellence in one's own actions by censuring others;
rather, one should seek distinction from the common folk through one's own virtues alone.

For the most part, men who are devoid of virtue and full of self-conceit disparage other virtuous people because of their own lack of merit; moreover, when they are not spoken to by the great, they imagine themselves to be superior.
Proud of themselves according to their own estimation, they spoke of no one else’s faults while describing their own virtues; yet the wise man, endowed with excellence, surely attains great fame.
"A pure and fragrant scent of flowers wafts through the air," they said;
"and likewise, the sun shines stainless in the sky without a word being spoken.
Such were the words and others like them, uttered with discernment.
Those who do not speak of themselves shine with glory in the world;
a fool does not blaze in this world merely by praising himself. Moreover, even one who is hidden in a pit shines if he is possessed of true learning.

Even a word spoken loudly fades away; yet even a well-spoken word shines forth in the worlds, however softly it may be uttered. The speech of the foolish and the arrogant is abundant, yet it is devoid of essence.
The inner self reveals itself like the sun revealing its form by day;
for this reason, people seek various kinds of wisdom,
for the attainment of wisdom appears to me as the highest goal for all beings.
One should not speak to anyone unless asked, nor to one who asks improperly;

even if possessed of knowledge and being intelligent, one should conduct oneself among the world like one who is dull-witted. Then, one should seek a dwelling among virtuous people who are ever devoted to dharma.
Among men who are generous and devoted to their own duties,
one who seeks his own welfare should never, under any circumstances, make his dwelling where there is a transgression of the dharma of the four castes.
Even though he is free from worldly undertakings here, subsisting on whatever he happens to obtain,
he shall attain pure merit among the meritorious and evil among the evil;
just as one experiences the touch of water, fire, or the moon.

In this way we perceive the touch of both sin and merit; not perceiving the objective sphere of food, those who subsist on remnants eat. Know that one who eats the objects of food is experiencing the sphere of karmic actions.

A self-possessed man should abandon that country where one who asks improperly is told the Dharma of Brahman by those who do not study it; for a well-behaved Brahmin, even if he is of poor conduct, is better than a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.

Who, having abandoned a wicked cow, would milk a well-behaved she-ass? Even the word of a learned Śūdra who is devoted to all the scriptures is not to be accepted, just like an oblation licked by a dog.
Who would abandon that place where the conduct between pupil and teacher is perfectly harmonious, where they are endowed with the scriptures as they truly are,
and where even those dwelling in the sky would surely speak of the faults of the wise?
Who that is wise would dwell there, where people are indeed intent on self-adulation,
and where the bridges of dharma have mostly been swept away by the greedy?
Who would not abandon such a region, which is like a mountain peak ablaze with fire?
Where people may practice dharma without hesitation and free from envy,
there one should move about and dwell among those virtuous men of meritorious character. But where men would practice dharma for the sake of material gain, [one should not].

One should never dwell among those people, for they are evildoers who live by sinful deeds, seeking only their own livelihood; one should flee from them swiftly, as if from a dwelling infested with snakes.
Whatever action would cause one to lie upon a bed of misery as a result of its consequences,
that should not be done from the very beginning by one who desires his own well-being—
wherein both the king and the king’s immediate officials [are involved].
A self-possessed king should abandon that kingdom where householders eat before [the guests];
however, he should dwell in that kingdom where *śrotriyas*— who are constant in dharma and eternal— eat first, being engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching.

Where the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and *vaṣaṭ* are properly performed and proceed incessantly, there one should dwell without hesitation. One should observe those things that are impure here, as well as Brahmins emaciated by their lack of livelihood.
One should abandon that kingdom as one would avoid meat placed near a predator;
where men, being well-disposed, give even unasked,
there a self-possessed man may dwell with a tranquil mind, as if his purpose were already accomplished.

One should move about and dwell among virtuous and holy men where punishment is meted out to the undisciplined and honor is shown to those who have cultivated the self; but not among those who are afflicted by passion, the unsubdued, the ill-behaved, or the wicked.
When there is the imposition of very severe punishment upon the undisciplined and the greedy,
where the king— ever devoted to dharma and the master of desires— having cast aside his own passions, dwells in his kingdom without hesitation; there indeed the kingdom is well-served.
For kings of such character quickly unite all those dwelling within their realm with prosperity when prosperity presents itself.
O dear one, this which is beneficial has been declared by me to you as you questioned me.
Indeed, it is not possible for one’s own welfare to be measured by material prosperity.
For one who conducts oneself in this way, with a disciplined mind, it will become clearly evident that the greater good in this world arises primarily through austerity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How indeed should a king such as I wander the earth once liberated?
With what constant qualities is he endowed so that he is released from the snare of attachment?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history told by Ariṣṭanemi to Sagara when he questioned him.
Sagara said:
"O Brahmin, what is the supreme good by performing which one enjoys happiness in this world?
How may one neither grieve nor be agitated? This I wish to know."
12,277.004 Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Tārkṣya, who was proficient in all the scriptures,
having understood that supreme excellence, spoke these virtuous words.
The happiness of liberation in this world is not understood by the world,
which is attached to children and cattle and preoccupied with wealth and grain;
one whose intellect is thus attached and whose self is unpeaceful cannot be cured.
The fool, bound by the snare of affection, is not fit for liberation.
I shall describe to you here those snares born of affection; listen to them from me.
They can be severed by one who possesses wisdom and uses his ears as an instrument.
Having honored your sons in due time and established them in youth,

and knowing them to be capable of maintaining themselves in life, wander at ease as one who is liberated. [Leave behind] your aged wife, who has borne you sons, who was cherished by you, and who is devoted to her children.
Having understood this, and having kept the welfare of others in view, you should renounce at the proper time;
whether with offspring or without offspring, wander at ease, liberated,
after having duly experienced the objects of the senses through the senses.
Having satisfied your curiosity regarding those matters, wander at ease and remain equanimous toward gains obtained through chance.
This much has been proclaimed by me to you in brief.

I shall speak further at length on the subject of liberation; listen to that. Men who are liberated and free from fear move about in this world in happiness; men whose minds are attached perish—of this there is no doubt.
Likewise, there are those who hoard food, such as insects and ants;
in this world, those who are unattached are happy, while those who are attached are destined for destruction. One whose mind is set on liberation should not harbor anxiety regarding one's own kin.
"How will these [beings] exist without me?"— thus one thinks;
yet a living being is born by itself, it grows by itself alone,
and likewise, it encounters pleasure, pain, and death by itself alone.
In this world, food, clothing, and even the support provided by mother and father are obtained through one's own past actions; nothing exists that was not performed previously.
All beings have been ordained their respective sustenance by the Creator upon the earth.
In this world, beings run about hither and thither, protected by their own past actions.
For one who is himself like a lump of clay, always dependent on others, and lacking a firm self,
what reason is there to nourish or protect his own kin?
For when death strikes down one's own kin even as you look on,
despite great effort being exerted, you must realize this for yourself;
and even while they are still living, [you must provide] for their maintenance and protection.
If you abandon [this body] before it is completed, you will die later;
and once dead, you will not recognize your own kin in any way—
whether they are happy or suffering— surely this must be understood by yourself.

Whether you are dead or alive, if people indeed enjoy [the fruits of their actions], they surely act only after realizing what is their own doing; thus, one should work for one's own welfare. Understanding this, who in this world can be certain as to whose [belongings] are whose?
Direct your mind toward liberation and listen further:
that embodied being who has conquered hunger, thirst, and other such states,
as well as anger, greed, and delusion, is a man of strength and is truly liberated.
That man who, through delusion, does not become intoxicated by gambling, drinking, women, and hunting— he is truly liberated at all times,
day after day and night after night.
He who is weary of the thought "this must be enjoyed" is said to possess the perception of defects.
He who, being ever-yoked, perceives his own self as well as women as already liberated again and again, is truly liberated in accordance with reality.

He who understands in truth the origin and destruction of beings, as well as their activities, is indeed liberated in this world. [One should maintain] a single measure of grain for every thousand loads, and likewise for the sake of travel, even among millions.
He who sees a couch situated within a palace is liberated. He who sees the world struck by death and oppressed by diseases, as well as emaciated by lack of livelihood, is liberated.
He who sees [the world] and remains happy and contented, yet is not distressed when he does not see it;
and he who is satisfied even with little—he is indeed liberated in this world. And he who perceives that "Agni and Soma are all this"—[he too is liberated].
He is not touched by extraordinary phenomena; he is indeed liberated.
That embodied being for whom a couch-bed and the ground are equal, and for whom fine rice and coarse food are the same—he is indeed liberated.
He for whom linen, grass-cloth, silk, bark-garments,
wool, and skin are all equal is indeed liberated.
And he who perceives the world as arisen from the five elements [is likewise liberated].
And so he conducts himself; having seen this, he is indeed liberated in this world— He for whom pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat,
desire and aversion, fear and agitation are the same— he is in every respect truly liberated.
Having seen this body as an accumulation of blood, urine, feces, and humors (doṣas), and as being full of defects, one is liberated from the onset of wrinkles and graying hair,
as well as emaciation and discoloration.
He who perceives the state of hunchbackedness through old age is liberated; likewise, he who perceives the destruction of virility by time, the cessation of sight,
deafness, and the failing of the vital breaths is liberated.
He who perceives that the ṛṣis have likewise departed, and that the gods and asuras have likewise departed,
from this world to the world beyond— he is liberated. Thousands of lords of the earth have been endowed with various such powers.
Knowing that those who have departed have abandoned the earth, one is liberated.
He who perceives that worldly objects are difficult to obtain, while afflictions are easy to encounter,
and that there is indeed suffering for the sake of one's family— he is liberated.
Seeing the defects of offspring and the very deficiency of people for the most part in the world, who would not hold liberation in high esteem?
That man who, awakened by both scripture and the world, perceives everything—
Human existence is entirely as insubstantial as a hollow reed; he who realizes this is truly liberated.
Having heard these words of mine, may you conduct yourself like one who is liberated, even while remaining in the householder’s life, provided your resolve for liberation remains firm and undaunted.
Having heard those words of his, that lord of the earth,
who was endowed with the virtues born of liberation, protected his subjects.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, this curiosity has always remained in my heart;
therefore, O grandfather of the Kurus, I wish to hear about it from you:
how is it that the celestial seer Uśanas Kāvya, the highly intelligent one, [is always present]?"
Doing what was pleasing to the Asuras and delighting in what was displeasing to the Suras,
why did he increase the splendor of those of immeasurable power? Furthermore,
the Dānavas were eternally bound in enmity with the foremost of the Suras.

And how did Uśanas, who possesses the splendor of an immortal, attain the state of Śukra? How did he attain such prosperity? Tell me all of this. And why does that radiant one not travel through the middle of the sky?
"I wish to know this in its entirety, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to all this exactly as it is."
O sinless one, according to my own understanding and as I have previously heard it,
this sage— the descendant of Bhṛgu— is truthful and firm in his vows;
he acts for the benefit of the Asuras due to a compassionate motive.
Then Indra, King Dhanada, and he who is the lord of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas— the powerful master of the treasury and likewise the sovereign of the world—
the great sage, perfected in yoga, entered his very self.
Having restrained the god Dhanapati through yoga, he took away his wealth.
When his wealth was thus taken, the Giver of Wealth found no peace;
filled with resentment and agitation, he approached the best of the gods.
Then he announced it to Śiva of immeasurable splendor—
the best of gods, Rudra, the gentle one who possesses many forms.
Kubera said:
"By Uśanas, whose nature is yoga, my wealth was seized after he had obstructed me;
having made his way through yoga, that one of great asceticism departed.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard this, O King, the great yogin Maheśvara became enraged;
with bloodshot eyes, he stood there grasping his trident, his supreme weapon, and cried out, "Where is he? Where is he?"
12,278.014c Uśanas, having learned from afar what he intended to do, shone forth. 12,278.015a Having perceived that anger of the great-souled one,
the powerful master knew his departure, his arrival, and his location.
Having meditated upon the high-souled Maheśvara with fierce austerity,
Uśanas, whose self was perfected through yoga, appeared upon the tip of the trident;
his true form was then recognized by the archer who had attained perfection through penance.
Having perceived the trident, the Lord of Gods bent it with his hand. Then,
with the trident thus bent by his hand of immeasurable splendor,
the Lord, whose weapon is fierce, called that trident "Pināka."
Having entered the hand of Maheśvara,
that lord Uśanas was seen by the Lord of Umā within the palm; then,
opening his mouth, the Bull-bannered One slowly cast him back into his hand.
Having entered the stomach of Maheśvara, the lord Uśanas,
that high-souled descendant of Bhṛgu, roamed about there.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"For what purpose, O King, did Uśanas wander within the belly of that wise god of gods, and what did he of great luster do there? Bhīṣma said:
O King, in former times that one of great vows remained within the water like a motionless pillar for millions and billions of years;
having performed difficult austerities, he rose up from the great lake.
Then Brahmā, the god beyond gods, approached him;
he inquired after his increase in ascetic power and his eternal well-being,
and the bull-bannered Lord replied, "My penance has been well-performed."
Through that union, Śaṅkara, the great-minded one whose nature is inconceivable and who is always devoted to truth and righteousness, beheld prosperity;
that great yogi was enriched by both ascetic power and wealth.
O great king, that heroic one shone resplendent throughout the three worlds.
Then the wielder of the Pināka bow, whose soul is absorbed in yoga, entered into the state of meditative concentration; and Uśanas, becoming greatly agitated, hid himself within his belly.

And the great yogi, remaining right there, praised the god while longing for liberation; however, he was struck down by the deity's splendor. Then the great sage Uśanas, staying within the belly, spoke.
"O subduer of enemies, show me favor! he said again and again.
To him, Mahādeva replied, "Go; seek deliverance through your penis. Thus spoke the bull among the gods, having blocked all the streams.
Not seeing a door and being enclosed on all sides, the sage wandered about, burning with heat here and there; having emerged through his penis,
he attained the state of semen.
Because of that task, the great sage did not come from the midst of the sky;
rather, he remained established among the gods and performed the office of domestic priest for the Daityas in order to increase their splendor.
Then, seeing him who had emerged as if blazing with splendor,
Bhava, overcome by rage, stood with his trident raised in hand;
the Goddess restrained her husband, Paśupati, who was thus enraged.
When Śaṅkara was thus restrained by the Goddess, he attained the status of her son.
The Goddess said:
"He must not be harmed by you; he has become my son."
"Indeed, no one who has emerged from the womb of a goddess meets with destruction.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then he became pleased with the goddess and, smiling, spoke these words."

"Let him go as he pleases," O King, [the god said] again and again. Then, having bowed down to the boon-granting god and likewise to the goddess Umā, the wise and great sage Uśanas attained his desired destination.
12,278.038a This has been told to you, O dear one, regarding the great-souled Bhārgava; 12,278.038c his life-story, O best of the Bharatas, which you asked me about.
12,279.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O mighty-armed one, tell me what is superior to this;
