O Grandfather, I am not satiated by your words, which are like nectar.
O best of men, what auspicious deed must a person perform?"
"Tell me that by which one attains the highest good both here and after death.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you what was done in former times by the highly illustrious [king]."
King Janaka questioned the high-souled Parāśara:
"What is the highest good for all beings in this world and in the next?
Please tell me that which ought to be practiced."
Then that sage, endowed with ascetic power and knowing the ordinances of all duties, being intent on showing favor to the king, spoke these words:
"Dharma alone, when practiced, leads to the highest good in this world and in the next."
Indeed, there is nothing higher than that, as the wise have declared.
Having practiced righteousness, a person is glorified in the heavenly world. O best of kings, for embodied beings, the rule of action consists of righteousness.
In that [state], those who are true ascetics perform their own duties here;
for, O dear one, a fourfold way of life is ordained for the world,
wherein mortals abide, and that proceeds from desire.
Having performed deeds both well-done and ill-done through various sequences,
there are manifold destinies for beings who are divided into five classes.
Just as a vessel is cast from gold or even silver, so too is one's state determined.
In this way, a living being is infused [into a new state], following the power of its prior karma.
Nothing whatsoever is born from what is not a seed; without having acted, one does not prosper in happiness.
Having reached the dissolution of the body, a man who has performed good deeds finds happiness.
"O dear one, I do not perceive destiny; there is no accomplishment through destiny. For the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas have attained their perfection through their own inherent nature (svabhāva).
After death, people never remember the actions performed in their previous births."
Indeed, regarding the attainment of its fruit, his action is fourfold;
and sound, which rests upon the Vedas, has been established as the basis for worldly conduct. O dear one, this is for the sake of calming the mind; it is not merely the instruction of the elders.
O King, whatever kind of action one performs in four ways— by sight, by mind, by speech,
and by deed— one encounters a corresponding result; and that action, O King, bears fruit both continuously and intermittently.
Whether it be auspicious or evil, there is no destruction of it.
O dear one, a good deed sometimes remains as if immovable,
even while one is sinking in *saṃsāra*, until one is liberated from suffering.
Then, having brought about the destruction of suffering, one experiences the fruit of well-performed deeds;
know, O lord of men, that upon the exhaustion of those well-performed deeds, the fruit of ill-performed deeds follows.
Self-restraint, forgiveness, fortitude, energy, contentment, and truthfulness—these are its qualities.
Modesty, non-violence, freedom from addiction, and skillfulness—these bring about happiness. A living being cannot remain indifferent toward either evil deeds or good deeds;
therefore, the wise person should always strive for the concentration of the mind.
This person does not experience the merit or the evil deeds of another;
whatever kind of action one performs, that is what one encounters.
Having taken up both pleasure and pain, a person proceeds by means of something other [than himself].
O King, all people are joined with others by means other than themselves;
therefore, a man should not personally do that which he would find fault with in others.
For he who is envious and acts in such a manner incurs only ridicule.
A cowardly warrior, a Brahmin who eats all things,
a Vaiśya lacking effort, and a low-caste man who is indolent; a learned man of bad character, one devoid of conduct, and a man of noble birth [who lacks these virtues].

A Brahmin fallen from truth, a corrupt woman, one who is lustful yet claims to be liberated, one who cooks for his own sake, a fool who speaks, and a kingdom bereft of a king— [these are like the aforementioned]. 12,279.025a.
"O King, all these go to a state of lamentation;
so too does he who is improper and devoid of affection toward his subjects.
Parāśara said:
Having mounted the chariot of his desires, with the objects of the senses as its horses,
the man who proceeds by means of the reins produced from knowledge is wise.
For one devoid of livelihood, service is recommended when performed with a focused mind.
12.280.002c Those who have emerged from the hands of the twice-born are not, however, equal to one another.
12.280.003a Having obtained this life, which is so difficult to attain, O Lord of the People, a man should not let it slip away;
he should strive for excellence through meritorious deeds.
Even one who has fallen away from his caste deserves honor,
provided he does not, having attained a state of respectability, engage in the actions of a *rājasa* nature.
A man attains elevation in caste through meritorious deeds.
For having failed to obtain that which is difficult to attain, one might indeed destroy oneself through sinful action. For sin committed through ignorance can be cast off by austerity alone;
for a sinful deed committed by oneself bears fruit as sin itself.
Therefore, one should not practice evil action that results in the arising of suffering;
even if an action has great fruit, if it is followed by evil,
a wise person should not practice it, just as a pure person avoids a foul pool.
"What bitter suffering do I perceive as the fruit of evil karma? For when one has fallen back into wrongdoing, one's own self does not shine forth;
and such is the case for that fool in whom no sense of remorse arises here."
Even for such a person, a very great torment arises when setting out on the journey.
A cloth that is free from stains is cleansed, but not one that is already stained black;
understand from me, O lord of men, that evil is likewise [difficult to purify] despite one's efforts.
But the man who, having himself committed a sin, subsequently performs virtuous deeds and undertakes penance, experiences the results of both separately. Indeed,
non-violence removes the injury committed through ignorance.

"Brāhmaṇas [are purified] by the injunctions of the scriptures," so say the exponents of Brahman. Likewise, "even his intentional misdeed is removed by [the performance of] the Hiṃsā sacrifice," so say the Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas and know the treatises on Dharma.
I, for my part, behold whatever action is performed that is endowed with virtue, manifest, and unaccompanied by sin—
just as subtle actions bear fruit here exactly as they are.
When those actions are performed here with intelligence joined to the mind,
even a deed that is habitually fierce yields little fruit,
O knower of dharma, if it was done without prior conscious intent.
Whatever deeds have been performed by the gods and likewise by the sages— a righteous soul should not practice them, nor should he disparage them even after hearing of them;
rather, O King, having reflected with his mind and having understood his own capacity.
He who performs auspicious action indeed beholds prosperity. Just as water placed in a new earthen pot diminishes,
so too does that which is not new reach a state permeated by happiness.
Just as water poured into water that already contains water attains increase within that very water,
so too, O King, are those actions here which are joined with intelligence.
Even those most meritorious [deeds] are not equal to these when they are deficient here; a king must conquer those who are armed and arrogant,
and he must provide proper protection for his subjects.
Agni is to be worshipped even with many sacrifices;
however, at the end or in the middle [of life], one should dwell having taken refuge in the forest.
A man endowed with self-control and characterized by righteousness—
One should regard all beings as oneself;
one should honor those who are superior according to one's own ability.
O lord of men, through truth and virtuous conduct, one finds happiness.
Parāśara said:
Who benefits whom, and who bestows anything upon whom? This living being performs every action by himself solely for his own sake.
One should avoid one who has abandoned respect and is devoid of affection—
even a uterine brother, let alone any other ordinary person.
For both giving and receiving are equal when performed between those who are distinguished and by those who are distinguished.

The gift bestowed upon a twice-born man is more meritorious than those two. Wealth acquired by the social orders through righteous means and increased only by righteous means must be protected with diligent effort for the sake of *dharma*; this is the settled conclusion.

One who seeks righteousness should not acquire wealth through cruel deeds; one should perform all duties according to one's ability and should not hanker after prosperity. For water, when purified, is cool, yet it may be heated by fire.
By giving according to his ability to a guest afflicted by hunger, one enjoys the fruit [of that act]. Through Rantideva, the high-souled one, success was attained in the worlds;
he honored the sages with fruits, leaves, and roots.
With those very fruits and leaves, he gratified Māṭhara;
from him, even Śaibya, the lord of the earth, attained the supreme station.
[He offered] to the gods, guests, servants, ancestors, and likewise to himself.
A mortal is born burdened by debt; therefore, he should attain freedom from that debt:

toward the great seers through the private study of the Vedas, toward the gods through the performance of sacrifice, toward the ancestors through the offering of *śrāddha*, and toward men through respectful hospitality.
By preserving the remnants of speech and by protecting himself as well as his circle of servants, he should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for even those who are destitute of wealth can achieve complete success through diligent effort.
Having offered oblations correctly into the sacrificial fire, the sages attained perfection;
the son of Ṛcīka became the son of Viśvāmitra after that illustrious one had praised the gods who partake in the sacrifice with Ṛg-verses.
Uśanas attained the state of Śukra through the grace of the God of gods;
having praised the Goddess, he rejoices in the sky, enveloped in splendor.
So too do Asita, Devala, as well as Nārada and Parvata.
Kakṣīvat, Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Tāṇḍya, and likewise Aṃśumat;
Vasiṣṭha, Jamadagni, Viśvāmitra, and Atri;
Bharadvāja, Hariśmaśru, Kuṇḍadhāra, and Śrutaśravas.
12.281.017 These great seers, being composed, praised Viṣṇu with *ṛg* verses; through their austerity and by the grace of that wise one, they attained perfection.
12.281.018 Even those who were unworthy attained worthiness, for they were virtuous and praised him alone.
One should not seek prosperity here by performing a censurable act.

Those gains which are obtained through righteousness are true; those obtained through unrighteousness—fie upon them! One should indeed never abandon eternal dharma in this world out of a desire for wealth.
For that righteous soul who has established the sacred fires is the highest among the performers of merit.
O Lord of kings, all the Vedas, O Master, reside within the three fires. And that Brahmin who has established the fires is one whose ritual actions never fail.
It is better indeed not to maintain the sacred fires than to perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice without performing the required duties.
O tiger among men, the fire, one's own self, the mother, the father who begot one, and likewise the preceptor— all these must be served according to their respective natures.

That man who, having abandoned pride, serves the elders; who, though learned, looks upon others with the humility of a eunuch out of a spirit of affection; who is not lacking in skill, is endowed with righteousness, and is not arrogant—[he attains success].
In this world, the noble one is indeed honored by the virtuous.
Parāśara said:
For one who is lower than the [other] three castes, subsistence from their presence is excellent.

12.282.001c Offered out of affection, it is declared that [a gift] always makes even those who are most righteous [unrighteous]. 12.282.002a If a Śūdra has no fixed means of livelihood inherited from his father and grandfather, 12.282.002c he should not seek a livelihood from others; rather, he should employ himself in service.
Association with the virtuous who perceive the Dharma is always auspicious in all circumstances, never so with the wicked; this is my conviction.
Just as an object on the Mountain of Sunrise shines by its proximity [to the sun].
In the same way, even one of low caste shines through association with the virtuous.
For just as a white cloth is made to take on whatever color it is dyed with,
know from me that this is how it is.
Therefore, you should take delight in virtues and never in faults;
for the life of mortals here is impermanent and ever-shifting. Whether abiding in happiness or in sorrow, the wise man [should remain thus].

He who accumulates only auspicious deeds beholds prosperity here in this world. A wise person should not practice an action that is devoid of Dharma, even if it yields great fruit; such an act is not said to be beneficial in this world.

Whatever action, though consistent with righteousness, may result in only a small reward, that should be performed without hesitation, for such an act brings about ultimate happiness. A king who, having seized thousands of cows, gives them away while failing to protect his subjects [incurs great sin].
That king who is a thief partakes only in the fruit of his reputation.
In the beginning, the Self-Existent One created Dhātṛ, who is honored by the world;
Dhātṛ created a single son, devoted to the sustenance of all creatures.
Having honored him, the Vaiśya should make it exceedingly prosperous;
it must be protected by the Kṣatriyas and utilized by the twice-born who are straightforward,
free from guile and anger, and who offer oblations to the gods and ancestors.

Śūdras must perform the sweeping; in this way, dharma does not perish. When dharma is not destroyed, the subjects become happy. O Indra among kings, through their happiness, the deities rejoice in heaven.
Therefore, that king who protects is honored for his righteousness; as is the Brahmin who studies, the Vaiśya who is devoted to acquisition,
and the Śūdra who constantly serves with his senses restrained.
Otherwise, O lord of men, one falls away from one's own duty (*svadharma*).
Even kārṣāpaṇas, when prescribed as an offering despite causing pain to one's life-force, yield great fruit;
how much more so other gifts given by righteous means, even by the thousands?

O lord of men, he who always gives to the twice-born with due honor, whatever it may be, enjoys a corresponding and powerful fruit. They say that what is given with joy after having approached the recipient is meritorious and highly praised.
The wise say that what is given when one is entreated is middling;
likewise, that which is given with contempt or even without faith,
the truth-telling sages call the lowest gift.

A man who is always sinking while transgressing through various [sins] should exert such effort that he may be liberated from this peril. A Brahmin shines through self-restraint, but a Kṣatriya through victory.
The Vaiśya [shines] by wealth, while the Śūdra always shines through skillfulness. Parāśara said: For a Brāhmaṇa, [wealth] comes from receiving gifts; for a Kṣatriya, it is won by weapons.
Wealth acquired by a Vaiśya through lawful means, and that acquired by a Śūdra through service—
even if it be very small— is praised when used for the sake of dharma, as it yields great fruit. A Śūdra is said to be the perpetual servant of the three other castes.

A twice-born man does not fall by following the dharma of a Kṣatriya or the dharma of a Vaiśya; however, when he performs the work of a Śūdra, then indeed the twice-born falls. [Likewise, he does not fall by] trade, cattle-rearing, or living by the arts.
When no means of livelihood arises even for a Śūdra, these are prescribed for him: appearing on the stage, living by his physical beauty,
subsisting on liquor and meat, and the sale of iron and leather.

One who has not previously practiced it must not perform an action censured in the world; however, for one who has practiced it before, the Śruti declares that abandoning it constitutes a great merit.
When a man who has attained perfection in the world commits a sinful act, [he does so only under the influence of passion].
One whose mind is overwhelmed by intoxication is said to be incapable of grasping that [truth].
Indeed, it is heard in the Purāṇas that in ancient times there were subjects governed by the punishment of mere reproach—
self-controlled, preeminent in righteousness, and followers of justice and dharma.
"O King, in this world, dharma alone is always praised among men;
for those men on earth who have increased in dharma cultivate only virtuous qualities.
But the Asuras, O dear one, could not endure that dharma, O lord of people."
Increasing gradually, they entered into those creatures.
Pride arose among them, destroying the dharma of the people. Then, from that pride, anger was born once again within them.

Then, O King, as they were overcome by anger, their conduct was devoid of shame; modesty itself perished, and from that, delusion arose. Then, enveloped by delusion, they could no longer see things as they had before.
They lived at their pleasure, free from mutual oppression;
yet, having encountered them, that rod of punishment became purposeless. Consequently, they proceeded, showing contempt for both the gods and the brahmins.
At that very time, the gods went for refuge to Śiva, the best of gods, the hero of many forms and lord of the hosts; by him,
those sky-dwellers were cast down to the earth along with their cities.
With a single arrow, whose splendor was augmented by the gods, he pierced all three;
their leader was Bhīma of terrible prowess,
who caused fear even to the deities, yet he was slain by the wielder of the trident.
When he was slain, the men then returned to their own true nature;
the Vedas and the Śāstras indeed began to flow once more just as before. Then they consecrated Vāsava in the sovereignty of the gods in heaven.

The Seven Sages were appointed to wield the rod of punishment over men. After the Seven Sages, there was a king named Vipṛthu; thereafter, various Kṣatriya kings arose, each ruling over their own respective territories.
Those born in great families and those who were virtuous in former times— even for them,
the Asura nature does not depart from their hearts. Therefore, by that very disposition and its lingering attachment, the kings [were overcome].

Those of terrible prowess devoted themselves exclusively to the deeds of the Asuras; they established themselves in those very practices and continue to instill them in others. Even today, those men who are most foolish continue to follow them.
Therefore, O King, having reflected according to the scriptures, I say to you:
one should perform actions for the attainment of perfection and should abandon those whose nature is violence.
A wise man should not seek wealth through the mixing of castes.
Abandoning justice for the sake of mere profit— that is not said to be auspicious.
Therefore, you, being such a self-controlled Kṣatriya who cherishes your kinsmen,
must protect your subjects, servants, and sons according to your own duty.
The union with the desirable and the undesirable, as well as enmity and friendship,
revolve through many thousands of births;
therefore, you should take delight in virtues and never in faults.
For he who is devoid of virtue and is evil-minded is said to be his own enemy.
O great king, among human beings, both dharma and adharma prevail;
they do not exist in the same way among other creatures here that are devoid of human nature.
A wise man of virtuous character, whether active or inactive,
should always move through the world as its very self, never harming living beings;
for when his mind becomes free from mental agitation, he truly attains that state.
"Then there is no falsehood, and he attains auspiciousness.
Parāśara said:
"O dear one, this rule of dharma for the householder has been proclaimed."

I shall now declare the rules for austerity; listen to me as I speak them. For generally, O best of men, a sense of "mine-ness" arises in the householder through attachments born of the qualities of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas).
"Households, cattle, fields, and wealth,
as well as wives, sons, and servants, indeed belong to a man here in this world by depending upon him.
Thus it is for one who is active and constantly observes [these things]."

For passion and hatred increase in one who does not perceive impermanence. And when a man is overcome by passion and hatred, O lord of men, he follows after the power of material things, and there arises in him what is called delight born of delusion.
Having achieved his purpose through enjoyment, he becomes entirely devoted to pleasure;
he perceives no gain other than sensual pleasure apart from sexual delight.
Then, his soul overcome by greed, he increases his circle of people through attachment.
Desiring the welfare of that person, he seeks to accomplish his purpose here for the sake of his prosperity;
yet, though knowing it to be an improper act, that man pursues it for the sake of his own interest,
his soul overwhelmed by affection for his child, and he suffers remorse when that [prosperity] perishes.
Then, filled with pride and seeking to protect himself from defeat,
he acts with the thought, "By this means I shall become a possessor of enjoyments," and for that reason he perishes. For austerity, when joined with wisdom, is the eternal vision of Brahman.
For men who seek auspicious deeds while abandoning pleasure, O King, despondency arises from the destruction of the objects of affection, from the loss of wealth,
and from the torment of mental and physical ailments.
"From world-weariness comes self-awakening; from awakening comes the vision of the scriptures.
O King, from seeing the meaning of the scriptures, one perceives only austerity. For rare, O lord of men, is the man who possesses such discernment."

He who, when his beloved pleasures have perished, resolves to practice austerity— O dear one, such austerity is ordained even for the lowly man; it leads the one with conquered senses and self-restraint along the path to heaven.

In the beginning, the powerful Prajāpati created living beings through austerity, O King; at various places, he remained devoted to his vows, undertaking various observances. [From him were born] the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, as well as the Agnis, Aśvins, and Maruts.
The Viśvedevas, as well as the Sādhyas, the ancestors, and the hosts of Maruts;
the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and other denizens of heaven; those perfected by asceticism, O dear one, and all others who dwell in the celestial realm.
Those Brāhmaṇas who were created by Brahmā at the beginning through austerity in ancient times, they wander about nourishing the earth as well as heaven; likewise,
there are kings in the world of mortals and others who are householders.
They are seen in great families; all that is the fruit of asceticism.
So too are garments of silk, auspicious ornaments, vehicles, seats, and carriages—all that is the fruit of asceticism.
Thousands of beautiful women who are pleasing to the mind,
as well as dwellings upon the rooftops of palaces— all this is the fruit of asceticism; likewise, there are excellent beds and various kinds of foods.
All desired things come to pass for those who have performed their duties.
O scorcher of foes, there is nothing unattainable by means of austerity in these three worlds;
however, the renunciation of enjoyments is the fruit for those who have not performed such deeds.
Whether happy or even suffering, a man should abandon greed,
O best of kings, by reflecting upon the scripture with his mind and through his intelligence. Discontent leads only to unhappiness, and from greed arises the delusion of the senses.
Then his wisdom perishes, like knowledge deprived of practice.
When one's wisdom is lost, then one does not perceive the right course. Therefore, when the destruction of happiness has arrived, a man should perform fierce austerity.
That which is desired is called happiness; that which is loathed is said here to be suffering. Behold the kind of fruit that results from austerity performed or left unperformed:
those who practice it constantly behold auspicious things and enjoy the objects of the senses.
Having performed stainless austerity, they attain manifest glory;
yet one who seeks fruits, having abandoned the path of the righteous, encounters unpleasant things, insults, and manifold suffering, becoming devoted to the objects of the senses.
Doubt arises in him regarding dharma, austerity, and charity;
having committed only evil deeds, he goes to hell. O best of men, whether he is abiding in happiness or even in suffering, [he remains thus].

That man who does not deviate from his own duty is one whose eye is the scripture. For it is taught, O Lord of the People, that the pleasure derived from the contact of touch lasts no longer than the flight of an arrow;
the same applies to taste, sight, smell, and hearing.
Then, from the exhaustion of that [merit], there arises for him an intense sensation,
because of which the wise praise liberation as the unsurpassed happiness. Thereafter, he acts for the sake of the fruit, and the higher qualities come into being.

By constant adherence to the practice of dharma, one does not fall away from the goals of desire and wealth. Householders should always enjoy those objects of sense that come to them without effort; yet it is my view that one's own duty (svadharma) must be pursued with diligent effort.

When a human action performed by those who are proud, born of noble lineage, and whose eyes are always fixed on the meaning of the scriptures— yet who are devoid of righteous deeds and whose self-restraint stems from incapacity— comes to naught, [then one should know the time has come].
In this world, no other duty exists for them except austerity.
A householder, however, should with his whole being resolve upon action;
O King, he should practice his own dharma with skill for the sake of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean,
so do all those in the various stages of life find their resting place in the householder.
Janaka said:
"O Great Sage, by what cause is the specific coloration of complexions produced?
I wish to hear this; tell me, O best among speakers. For there is a Vedic tradition stating that the offspring who is born is indeed that very same person."
"How is it that one born from a Brāhmaṇa has attained such a distinction?
Parāśara said:
"It is even so, O Great King; he by whom one is born is indeed that very person."
Through the diminution of ascetic merit (*tapas*), however, one falls into the state of being defined by birth (*jāti*).
From a good field and a good seed, a meritorious birth arises;
from the deficiency of either one of these, an inferior being is born.

Those who know the Dharma understand that as Prajāpati was creating the worlds, [beings] were born from his mouth, his two arms, his two thighs, and his two feet. O dear one, those born from the mouth are Brāhmaṇas, and those born from the arms are the Kṣatriyas.

O King, those born from the thighs are the wealthy, while those born from the feet are the servants; O bull among men, the origin of these four castes alone is thus established. Any others who are in excess of these are indeed known as those born of intermixture (*saṃkara*).
O lord of men, the Kṣatra-born, the Ambaṣṭhas, the Ugras, and likewise the Vaidehakas;
the Śvapākas, Pulkasas, Stenas, Niṣādas, Sūtas, Māgadhas,
Āyogavas, Karaṇas, Vrātyas, and Caṇḍālas.
12,285.009c These are born from one another among the four social classes (varṇas).
12,285.010 Janaka said:
12,285.010a Since they are all born from the one Brahman, how is there diversity in terms of lineage (gotra)?
"O best of sages, there are indeed many lineages here in this world;
how is it that sages born here and there returned to their own source?
Others were born from the womb of a Śūdra, and likewise others from a non-womb."
Parāśara said:
"O King, this should not be accepted as being possible for one of inferior birth;
for the high-souled ones, whose selves are purified by austerity, their origin is through ascetic power."

O King, having procreated sons here and there, the sages established their status as ṛṣis once again through their own ascetic power. My grandfather and Ṛśyaśṛṅga, the son of Kaśyapa, were likewise [established] in former times.
Vaṭa, Tāṇḍya, Kṛpa, Kakṣīvān, Kamaṭha, and others;
Yavakrīta, O King, and Droṇa, the best among speakers; Āyu, Mataṅga, Datta, Drupada, and Matsya as well.
O Vaideha, these have returned to their own original nature through the power of asceticism;
for they are established in the knowledge of the Vedas, in self-restraint, and in austerity.
O King, the four primary lineages (mūlagotrāṇi) have thus arisen.
O King, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Bhṛgu—
other lineages arose from their actions;
these names and their acceptance by the virtuous came about through ascetic power.
Janaka said:
"O Blessed One, please tell me the specific duties of the social classes, as well as their common duties; for you are indeed skilled in all matters."
Parāśara said:
O King, receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and likewise teaching—these are the specific duties of Brahmins; for Kṣatriyas, the beautiful duty is protection.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of the Vaiśyas;
and service to the twice-born is the duty of the Śūdras, O lord of men. These specific duties of the social orders have been proclaimed, O King.
"O dear one, listen to me in detail regarding those qualities that are common [to all]:
compassion, non-violence, vigilance, sharing with others, performing ancestral rites, hospitality toward guests, truthfulness, and freedom from anger."
Contentment with one's own wife, purity, constant freedom from malice, self-knowledge, and forbearance— these, O King, are the common duties for all.
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the three twice-born castes.
12,285.025c Herein, O best of bipeds, they have authority over their respective duties. 12,285.026a The three castes, O King, fall if they persist in improper occupations;
12,285.026c but they rise again by adhering here to their own duties according to their true nature.
Nor is there a certainty that a Śūdra falls [from his status],
nor that he is unworthy of the sacraments (saṃskāra) in this world; yet he does not attain the dharma set forth in the revealed scriptures (śruti).
Nor has there been any prohibition against him regarding the Dharma; O Great King, those twice-born who are endowed with sacred learning declare that a Śūdra may be a Vaidehaka.
"For I behold you, O lord of men, as the god Viṣṇu, the preeminent one of the universe and of the world;
those who, desiring to uplift the lowly, follow the conduct of the virtuous."
They do not incur fault when performing rites for prosperity, provided they exclude the sacred mantras. For in whatever measure other people adopt virtuous conduct,
in that same measure they attain happiness and rest in peace both in this world and after death.
Janaka said:
"O great sage, what is it that defiles this person—is it action or birth?
A doubt has arisen in me; you ought to explain this to me."
12,285.032 Parāśara said:
12,285.032a Without doubt, O Great King, both are causes of defect; 12,285.032c namely, both action and birth. But hear now the distinction between them.
One who is corrupted by both birth and action practices evil deeds;
yet that man who, though corrupted by birth, does not commit sin is a true person.
One should condemn the action that treats a man who is preeminent by birth as if he were despicable.
"12,285.034c That action defiles him; therefore, such action is not auspicious.
12,285.035 Janaka said:
12,285.035a "O best of the twice-born, which actions in this world are righteous?"
"Indeed, beings are never harmed here while these [rites] are being performed.
Parāśara said:
"Listen to me in this matter, O Great King, concerning that which you ask of me."
Those non-violent actions which always protect a man—
having renounced the sacred fires and sitting in meditation, they behold [the truth], freed from all feverish distress,
having ascended the path of dharma that leads to the supreme good in due order.
Humble, endowed with discipline, constant in self-restraint, and firm in their vows,
they go to the undecaying state, freed from all karma.
All castes [attain this] through the proper performance of their duties.
O King, having performed [these deeds], having spoken words of truth,
and having abandoned cruel unrighteousness in the world of the living,
they go to heaven; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Parāśara said:
"In this world, fathers, friends, teachers, and women are never truly devoid of merit."
O King, they are devoted to no other, speak kindly, are beneficial, and likewise submissive;
for human beings, the father is the supreme deity.
They say the father is superior to the mother;
they say the attainment of knowledge is supreme;
those who have conquered the objects of the senses attain the highest state.
On the field of battle, where the bed of arrows is like a fire,
the prince, having met his death, is consumed by it and proceeds to those worlds that are very difficult even for the immortals to attain.
He enjoys the fruit of heaven at his pleasure:
one who is exhausted, terrified, deprived of weapons, weeping, turned away from the fight, or lacking in equipment.
O King, one should not harm a sick man who is pleading for help, nor children or the elderly; however,
one may strike those who are well-equipped with their gear, prepared for battle, and have reached a state of equality [with the enemy].
A king may pass over a son of a Kṣatriya in battle; it is the settled rule that in this world, death at the hands of an equal or a superior is better,
whereas death at the hands of one who is inferior or a coward is censured for kings.

O lord of men, for one who is wicked, of evil conduct, and base, death at the hands of another wicked person is declared to lead to hell; this is the certainty. O King, no one can save one who has fallen under the power of destiny.
Even when one's lifespan has a remainder, someone may nonetheless shorten it; therefore,
one should desist from actions performed here with affection that are violent in nature,
for one should not desire to take another's life for the sake of one's own longevity.
For all householders who desire their own destruction,
O dear one, death upon the sandbanks while performing sacred rites is auspicious;
when life has reached its end, they attain the state of the five elements.
That does not arise without a cause; it is brought about by causes.
Likewise, the body comes to be from that by which the body is produced. This one has gone along a path, and this one has arrived from house to house.
Therein, no second cause whatsoever exists;
that body, joined with the embodied beings, abides among those elements that constitute liberation.
It is a mass of veins, sinews, and bones, crowded with loathsome and impure things.
The wise who contemplate the inner self say that the body extends to the skin as the meeting point of the elements, the senses,
and the qualities; yet even when exhausted of its qualities, the body remains subject to mortality.

Abandoned by the embodied soul, motionless and devoid of consciousness, it then sinks into the earth as the constituent elements return to their primordial nature. Impelled by the application of karma, it is born again here and there.
O Vaideha, this body dies here or there;
yet another nature is observed, namely the discharge of karma.
However, O King, this [soul] is not born again for some time.
The elemental self wanders about like a great cloud in the sky;
O King, it is born again here upon reaching a new abode, O monarch. For the Self is superior to the mind, and the mind is superior to the senses.
"O King, among the two kinds of beings, the mobile are supreme;
likewise, among the mobile, bipeds are considered supreme;
and among bipeds, the twice-born are indeed remembered as supreme."
O Indra among kings, even among the twice-born, those possessed of wisdom are considered superior;
among the wise, those who have awakened to the Self; and among those awakened to the Self, those who are free from pride.
It is a settled certainty that death follows birth for all men.

For living beings pursue actions that have an end, according to their qualities. O King, he who meets his death when the sun has reached its northern course, under an auspicious lunar mansion and at a holy moment, is a doer of meritorious deeds.
Having afflicted people with suffering and having overwhelmed them with evil deeds,
and having performed actions here according to his own power through an extraordinary death—
such as by poison, hanging, burning, at the hands of bandits, or likewise by execution— [he falls].
The killing of fanged animals and beasts is called a natural act; those who perform meritorious deeds are not bound by these [acts], nor by those arising from intentional design,
nor by many other such natural acts.
"O King, the vital breaths of those who perform meritorious deeds depart upward and find their foundation there;
those of middling merit depart from the middle, and those of evil deeds depart downward.
There is but one enemy, and no second enemy exists."
O King, ignorance is equal to a man's [greatest enemy], shrouded by which he, being impelled,
performs terrible and most cruel deeds.
O Prince, he for whom there is the study of the Vedas and the Dharma for the sake of awakening, and who honors the elders, is indeed one whose goals are achieved through effort.

One who has studied the Vedas, practiced asceticism as a celibate student, and here on earth offered the five sacrifices according to his ability, departs [from this world] when pierced by the arrow of wisdom.
A man desiring dharma should go to the forest after having secured his welfare and established his own lineage; even when deprived of enjoyments, he should not let himself sink into despair.
"O dear one, even in the state of a *caṇḍāla*, human birth is difficult to obtain in every respect.
For this is the primary womb, O Lord of the World, having attained which one is indeed able to save oneself through actions characterized by auspiciousness."
"O Lord, how may we not fall away from this womb? Men perform dharma by perceiving the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*),
having indeed attained this human birth which is so difficult to obtain in this world."

He who despises the Dharma and is possessed by desire is surely deceived. But he who, O dear one, looks upon all beings with eyes preceded by affection, as long as the flame does not perish, sees them as being like lamps.
By means of conciliation, the granting of gifts, and kind speech,
as well as by becoming one who shares equally in both sorrow and joy, he is honored in the next world.
Generosity, renunciation, and a beautiful form [arise] from the waters;
Furthermore, one's body must indeed be purified by austerity at Sarasvatī, Naimiṣa, and Puṣkara,
as well as at whatever other holy places exist upon the earth.
For those whose vital breaths depart within their homes,
it is prescribed that they be carried out by means of a vehicle to the cremation ground.
Indeed, through purity and according to the prescribed rule, there is cremation;
as well as the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, nourishment rites, performing sacrifices for oneself, officiating at sacrifices for others, giving gifts, and the practice of meritorious deeds.
Whatever is praiseworthy regarding the paternal estate, a man who performs all such acts for his own sake by his power—
O lord of men, [these include] the treatises on dharma, the Vedas, and the six auxiliary sciences.
"These [rites] are prescribed for the sake of the highest good for a man of unblemished action.
Bhīṣma said:
"All this has indeed been declared by the great-souled sage."
12,286.041c O lord of men, in ancient times, for the sake of the highest good, [he spoke] to the King of Videha.
12,287.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,287.001a Janaka, the ruler of Mithilā, questioned him once again.
[He asked] Parāśara, the high-souled one who possesses the highest certainty regarding dharma:
"O Brahmin, what is the highest good? What is the ultimate goal? What, once done, does not perish?
Having gone where does one not return? Tell me that, O great sage."
Parāśara said:
Non-attachment is the root of the highest good; knowledge is the supreme goal of knowledge.
Merit gained through performed austerity does not perish, just as seed sown in a fertile field does not go to waste.
When one has severed the noose made of unrighteousness and takes delight in righteousness,
and when one has bestowed the gift of fearlessness, then one shall attain perfection. He who gives thousands of cows and hundreds of horses—
The gift of fearlessness toward all beings surpasses all other gifts.
A wise man, even while living in the midst of sensory objects, does not truly dwell there;
whereas one of evil intellect dwells even among wicked sensory objects.
Unrighteousness does not cling to the wise man, just as water does not adhere to a lotus leaf;
however, excessive sin clings to the unwise, like lac to wood.
Unrighteousness does not release its perpetrator without regard for the cause.
The agent indeed attains all that at the proper time;

those who have perfected their selves do not falter, for they perceive through self-realization. Indeed, he who is heedless and does not wake up regarding the organs of perception and action [is lost].
One whose soul is attached to the auspicious and the inauspicious incurs very great fear;
but he who is always free from passion, who has conquered anger, and who is perfectly composed— even while remaining amidst sense objects— is not joined with evil.
When bound within its boundaries, the bridge of dharma does not collapse;
like a well-nourished stream, its accumulation becomes abundant.
Just as a pure gem absorbs the light that falls upon it through concentration, so too does it gather virtue.
O tiger among kings, in this way Yoga proceeds:
just as here, through contact with flowers, the quality of sesame seeds individually attains an exceeding sweetness.
Just as the quality of *sattva* manifests according to its basis among men on earth whose selves are purified,
so too [the sage] abandons his wife and does not strive for worldly riches.
When a man’s mind is set upon the celestial realm— with its chariots drawn by noble steeds and its various activities—
his intellect then turns away from worldly objects.
The man whose intellect is attached to sense-objects never awakens to his own welfare; he possesses a mind that follows after all worldly states of being.
Like a fish drawn in by the lure of a king,
the mortal world, though possessed of a collective body and mutually dependent,
sinks like a boat in the water, as hollow as the core of a plantain tree.
The time for dharma for a person is not fixed,
nor does death wait for a person; indeed,
the performance of dharma is always auspicious.
When a person approaches the mouth of death,
just as a blind man moves about in his own house by means of practice alone,
so does the wise man go to that destination with a disciplined mind.
Death is said to be inherent in birth, and birth indeed depends upon death. One who is ignorant of the dharmas of liberation wanders like a wheel, bound.
Just as a lotus stalk quickly sheds the mud that clings to it, so does the wise man cast off worldly existence.
In this way, the self of a person here is completely liberated by means of the mind;
the mind leads the self, and it directs it toward [the goal]. When it becomes disciplined, then one sees that Supreme.
But he who, while engaged in the welfare of others, considers his own interest to be primary,
being attached to the objects of the senses, falls away from his own true purpose.
[He experiences] rebirth as a lower creature or an animal, or even the supreme state in heaven.
The self of both the wise man and the other attains [its state] here through its own deeds. Just as a liquid is poured into a baked earthen vessel,
so too does the body, when heated by austerity, enjoy its objects.
He who indulges in sense objects will undoubtedly not enjoy [liberation];
whereas he who renounces enjoyments is truly intent upon enjoyment [of the Self].
For he is shrouded in mist, devoted solely to his genitals and belly.
Like one born blind, he whose self is obscured does not perceive the path.
Just as a merchant indeed obtains wealth according to his merit from the ocean,
so too is the destiny of a living being in the ocean of mortals determined by their karma and knowledge.
In this world consisting of day and night, Death, moving about in the form of old age,
devours all beings as a serpent swallows the wind.
Once born, a living being encounters the very actions that it has performed itself.
No one here obtains anything, whether pleasant or unpleasant, that has not been performed by themselves;
whether lying down, walking, sitting, or engaged in the objects of the senses,
auspicious and inauspicious deeds always follow a person.
For once one has reached the other shore, one does not resolve to cross back again;
indeed, a downfall into the great ocean is rarely seen for such a person.
Just as a boat laden with a heavy burden [is held] by a rope in the great waters, so it is.
In this way, through mental application, the mind indeed draws the body toward itself;
just as other rivers are woven together around the ocean,
so too is primordial nature (prakṛti) always interwoven with yoga.

Men whose minds are attached by various snares of worldly affection perish while remaining in their natural state, like a house of sand in water. For the embodied soul who dwells in the house of the body, which is a sacred bathing place for purification—
For one who has set out upon the path of wisdom, there is happiness both in this world and the next.
Elaborations are joined with afflictions, whereas brevity brings happiness.
All elaborations are for the sake of others; they know renunciation to be one's own true benefit.
The circle of friends is born of one's own intentions; kinsmen are bound by self-interest; wives, servants, and sons pursue their own ends.
Neither mother nor father gives anything to anyone else.
A living being, whose provisions for the journey are generosity, experiences the fruit of its own karma.
Mother, son, father, brother, wife, and likewise friends—
these are placed upon the squares of the board like pieces on a dice-board.
All actions performed in the past, whether auspicious or inauspicious, follow a living being. Having recognized that the fruit of action has arrived, [one should act accordingly].
The inner self thus impels the intellect;
relying upon resolve, he who finds companions—
no undertaking of his ever fails.
Prosperity never abandons one who is single-minded, disciplined, heroic, steadfast, and wise— just as rays never leave the sun—
provided he possesses faith, perseverance, skillful means, wonder, and intelligence.

Whatever undertaking a man of blameless soul begins does not fail. Every living being necessarily encounters for itself all its own past deeds, both auspicious and inauspicious, as well as both types of karma that were previously performed by it, from the very moment of conception.
Death is unavoidable and moves with equal force, severed only by time;
it brings one to the end of their work like a saw made of iron-reddened stone reducing wood to powder,
[reducing] the expansion of one's own self-made nature to its true essence.
For every person obtains a noble lineage and an accumulation of abundant wealth according to their past deeds,
through their own performed actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
12,287.045 Bhīṣma said: O King, having been addressed thus by the wise man according to the truth, Janaka—
the best among those who know dharma— attained supreme joy upon hearing it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, the learned men in this world praise truth, forgiveness, self-restraint, and wisdom; what is your opinion on this?"
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall relate to you an ancient history, the conversation here between the Sādhyas and a swan."
Then, having become a golden swan, the unborn and eternal Prajāpati traversed the three worlds and approached the Sādhyas. The Sādhyas said:
"O Śakuni, we are indeed the Sādhyas, the gods; we address you.
We ask you about the dharma of liberation, for you are surely a knower of liberation. You have been heard of by us as a learned man, wise in speech."
"O bird, the word 'well done' falls upon you.
O twice-born one, what do you consider to be most excellent?
O high-souled one, in what does your mind find delight?"
"O best of birds, therefore command us in that one task which you consider the most excellent among all duties,
by performing which a man is indeed freed from all bonds."
"O lord of birds, he shall be liberated quickly here.
The swan said:
"O drinkers of nectar, I hear that this is the task to be done."
Austerity, self-restraint, truthfulness, and the protection of the self—
having untied all the knots of the heart,
one should bring both the pleasant and the unpleasant under one's own control.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor a speaker of cruel words;
one should not take from another what belongs to an inferior person.
One should speak that speech by which another might be agitated.
One should not utter that harsh speech which leads to a world of sin;
for word-arrows fly forth from the mouth,
struck by which one grieves day and night.
These [arrows] fall upon the vital spots of another;
a wise person should not discharge them at others. If another should strike him with the arrows of harsh speech;
One should strike back violently, yet in this world, forbearance alone must be practiced.
He who endures when being provoked to anger truly takes away the merit of his adversary.
He who, through self-restraint, subdues the blazing anger born of insults and offenses—remaining pure-minded, joyful, and free from envy;

He indeed takes on the merit of others:
when reviled, I say nothing;
I always endure even when being struck.

For the noble ones say that this is the best: forbearance, as well as truth, uprightness, and compassion. Truth is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of the Veda, and self-restraint is the secret essence of truth.
Liberation is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of self-restraint (*dama*); this is the instruction for all things:
[the subduing] of the impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, the impulse of anger, the impulse of the desire to know, and the impulses of the belly and the genitals.
I consider him truly a Brahmin and a sage who can endure these surging impulses;
he who is free from anger is indeed superior to those who are angry.
Likewise, one who endures is superior to one who does not;
a human is indeed superior to a non-human;
and similarly, one who possesses knowledge is preeminent over one who lacks it.
When reviled, one should not revile in return; for the anger of one who endures it consumes the abuser and secures for himself the merit of his good deeds.
He who, when addressed harshly, speaks neither bitterness nor pleasant words;
But he who, when struck, does not strike back out of fortitude,
and who does not desire evil for his assailant—
for him the gods always long.
One should indeed forgive one who is worse, as well as one who is better or equal. Even when insulted, struck, or reviled, one will thus attain perfection.
Always do I wait upon the noble ones with humility.
I have no desire to know [the world], nor do I harbor any anger; I do not approach others with a longing for gain,
nor do I ever proceed by any crooked way.
"I, being cursed, do not curse anything in return;
for I know that self-restraint is the gateway to immortality here.
This secret Brahman, I declare this to you."
For there is nothing indeed superior to a human being;
being liberated from evils like the moon from clouds,
the wise man, free from passion and awaiting his time, attains perfection through fortitude.
He who indeed becomes worthy of worship by all,
like a noble pillar at the point of sprinkling,
to whom they speak words of high praise;

He whose self is restrained indeed goes to the gods. (12.288.23a) Those who investigate faults desire to speak of the lack of virtue in these men more than they desire to speak of their auspicious qualities. (12.288.23c)
He whose speech and mind are guarded and always properly restrained—he shall obtain all this:
the Vedas, austerity, and renunciation. Through the abuse and insults of the ignorant, the wise man prospers.
Therefore, one should not exalt another, nor should one harm oneself;
a twice-born man should indeed be as satisfied with contempt as if it were nectar.
For he who is held in contempt sleeps in peace, while he who holds others in contempt perishes.
Whatever one who is angry sacrifices, whatever he gives, or whatever austerity he performs or oblation he offers— Vaivasvata seizes all of that from him.
The exertion of one who is prone to anger is in vain.
O best of immortals, he whose four gates are well-guarded knows the Dharma: the genitals, the stomach, the hands, and speech as the fourth.

Constantly practicing truth, self-restraint, uprightness, and compassion, as well as fortitude and endurance, he remained devoted to the study of the Vedas and was free from longing for the possessions of others.
One who is devoted to solitude shall attain an upward course;
yet, though I followed all these [virtues] like a calf following its four teats,
I have never anywhere found anything more purifying than truth.
I shall declare it to men, returning from among the gods:
truth is the ladder to heaven, like a boat for crossing from this shore to the other.
According to the kind of people one dwells with and according to those whom one serves—
Whatever a person desires to become, such he becomes;
whether he serves the virtuous or the wicked,
the ascetic or even the thief.
Just as a garment takes on the color of the dye,
so too does he come under their influence.
The gods always converse with the virtuous.
They do not go to see the human realm;
for the wind is incomparable, indeed it has no equal,
and he who knows it understands the manifold variety of the objective world.

When the inner person within the heart remains untainted, the gods are indeed pleased by that very person who stands upon the path of the virtuous. Those who are always devoted solely to the genitals and the belly—
Knowing them to be free from faults— [yet] being thieves and always harsh in speech—
the gods avoid them from afar.

The gods are certainly not to be propitiated by one who is deficient in strength, nor by one who eats all things or performs evil deeds; rather, they are pleased with those men who are devoted to truth and are grateful.
Those who delight in the Dharma share it with them.
They say that silence is better than speech;
one should speak the truth—that is the second [best].
To speak the truth is the third utterance;
to speak what is pleasant is the fourth utterance.
The Sādhyas said:
"By what is this world enveloped? By what does it not shine? Why does one abandon friends? And why does one not go to heaven?
The Swan said:
The world is shrouded by ignorance; it does not shine because of stinginess. Through greed one abandons friends; through attachment one does not go to heaven.
The Sādhyas said:
Who among the Brahmins is the one who rejoices alone? Who is the one who dwells in contentment with many? And who is the one who, though weak, is strong?
"Who indeed does not fall into their quarreling?
The swan replied:
"One wise man among the Brahmins finds delight [in solitude];"
The wise man alone dwells in contentment among many; the wise man alone is strong, even if he is weak;
the wise man does not involve himself in their quarrels.
The Sādhyas said:
What constitutes the divinity of the Brāhmaṇas, and what is called their goodness? What is their lack of goodness, and what is considered their human nature?
The Haṃsa said:
Their study of the Vedas is called divinity; their observance of vows is called goodness. Slander is called lack of goodness, and death is called the human state.
12,288.045 Bhīṣma said:
12,288.045 Having spoken thus, the Lord, the boon-granting God, eternal and immutable,
ascended to heaven together with the hosts of Sādhyas and the gods.
This [dialogue], which brings fame, longevity, and sons, and leads certainly to heaven,
was revealed by the supreme, immutable God of gods. This excellent dialogue of the Sādhyas has thus been proclaimed.
"The field (kṣetra) is indeed the womb of actions; true being is said to be truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O father, you ought to tell me the distinction between Sāṃkhya and Yoga."
"O Omniscient One, O best of the Kurus, everything is indeed known to you.
Bhīṣma said:
"The Sāṃkhya followers praise Sāṃkhya, and the twice-born practitioners of Yoga praise Yoga."

"O crusher of enemies, those who argue for the primacy of causal factors do so indeed to exalt their own position. 'How can one who is not the Lord be liberated?'— thus do the wise practitioners of Yoga rightly declare the primacy of causal factors."
The twice-born followers of Sāṃkhya declare this to be the correct cause:
that he who, having understood all destinies in this world, becomes dispassionate toward sense objects,
will clearly be liberated after the body falls, and not otherwise.

12,289.005c This, indeed, the highly wise call the Sāṃkhya, the vision of liberation. 12,289.006a One’s own position should be accepted when it is logical and its speech is beneficial; 12,289.006c for the opinion of the learned should be accepted by those like you who are esteemed by the learned.
The Yoga systems have perception as their means of proof, while the Sāṃkhya systems rely on the determination of the scriptures;
both these doctrines, my dear Yudhiṣṭhira, are truths according to me. Both these doctrines are recognized as valid knowledge by the learned, O King.
When they have practiced according to the scriptures, they shall both attain the supreme goal. O sinless one, their purity is equal, as is their application of compassion toward all beings;
their observance of vows is equal, yet their philosophical vision is not the same.
But the correct perception of those two applies to the subtle state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, if the vow, purity, and compassion here are equal [for both],"
"Why is their vision not equal? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"Attachment, delusion, as well as affection, desire, and anger alone—"
By severing these five defects from the very beginning through yoga, practitioners attain that state;
just as large fish with unblinking eyes, having broken through the net, reach the water again, so too do those free from defilement reach that goal through yoga.
Just as powerful deer, having broken through the snare,
reach the stainless path freed from all bonds,
even so, O King, those endowed with strength [break] the bonds born of greed.

Having severed the bonds, the stainless yogis proceed upon the supreme path to auspiciousness. O King, just as weak deer and others perish in snares, so too do they perish without the power of yoga; of this there is no doubt.

O son of Kuntī, O Indra among kings, those who are weak in strength reach their end just like fish caught in a net; so too do those whose yoga is very feeble. And just as small birds, O subduer of enemies, having encountered a net, [meet their destruction].
There, those who are attached perish, while those endowed with strength are liberated.
O scorcher of foes, likewise, yogins bound by the fetters born of karma—
those who are weak indeed perish, while those endowed with strength are liberated.

"Just as a small and weak fire, O King, is extinguished when overwhelmed by thick fuel, so too is yoga, O Lord, when it is weak. But when that very same fire, O King, has regained its strength once more..."
Just as a fire joined with the wind would quickly burn even the entire earth,
so too a yogi who has gained power, blazing with splendor and great strength,
can dry up the entire world like the sun at the time of the end.
Just as a weak man, O King, is carried away by a current,
so too is a yogin lacking in strength helplessly carried away by the objects of the senses.
And just as an elephant checks that very same current, [so should the yogin restrain the senses].
In the same way, having obtained the power of yoga, one arrays oneself amidst many sense objects;
and those masters of yoga, endowed with the power of yoga, enter— though they are not subject to them— the lords of creatures, the seers, the gods, and the great elements, O Pārtha.
Neither Yama, nor the Terrible End-maker, nor Death of fearsome prowess,
O King, has power over one of immeasurable splendor who possesses yoga;
for such a one can manifest many thousands of selves, O bull of the Bharatas.

Having acquired strength through yoga, he should traverse the earth with all those [powers]; he should enjoy sense-objects and then again perform fierce austerity. And he should withdraw them once more, O Pārtha, just as the sun withdraws its qualities of light.
"O King, for one who possesses strength, it is undoubtedly appropriate that he has the power to effect liberation from bondage;
these powers in yoga have been described by me, O lord of the people."

O Lord, for the sake of illustration, I shall speak again to you of subtle matters regarding the concentration of the self and the practice of *dhāraṇā*. O bull among the Bharatas, hear from me these subtle illustrations.

Just as a vigilant archer, being fully concentrated, hits the target, so too the yogi who is properly disciplined attains liberation without a doubt. Just as one might fix the mind immovably upon a vessel filled with oil, [so should one remain steady].
Just as a man with a focused mind might ascend a staircase,
O King, so too this yoga, having yoked the self,
makes the self stainless and visible like the sun.
And just as a concentrated helmsman, O son of Kuntī,
may swiftly lead a ship upon the great ocean to its port, O King— so too does the knower of reality, having applied himself through yoga to the concentration of the self.
O King, having abandoned this body, he reaches that place which is difficult to attain.
And just as a charioteer, being well-composed, having yoked excellent horses,
swiftly leads the archer to his desired destination, O bull among men.

In the same way, O King, the yogin who is concentrated in the *dhāraṇās* quickly attains the supreme station, like an arrow released from its mark. And the yogin who, having absorbed the self within the Self, remains immovable—
Like one who slays fish, he destroys his evil and attains the ageless state. O you of immeasurable prowess,
[this occurs] at the navel, the throat, the head, the heart, the chest, and the sides,
as well as in seeing, touching, and smelling.
O lord of the people, that yogi who, concentrated in the great vow, properly unites the subtle self with the Self within these stations,
quickly— possessing stainless wisdom— burns away both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
"By resorting to the supreme yoga, one is liberated if one so desires.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, by consuming what kinds of food and by conquering what [senses], does one attain this?"
"A yogin attains power; you ought to explain that.
Bhīṣma said:
"One who is intent on eating grains and consuming oil-cake..."
By abstaining from unctuous substances, the yogi intent on practice shall attain strength. O subduer of enemies, by eating dry barley-gruel for a long period of time,
the yogi who delights in solitude and has purified his soul shall attain strength.
Moving through fortnights, months, and various seasons, as well as through caves,
the yogi who drinks water mixed with milk shall attain strength,
O lord of men, even for an entire month without interruption.
Having fasted properly, the yogi of purified soul shall attain strength;
likewise, having conquered desire and anger, as well as cold, heat, and rain,
fear, sleep, breath, virility, and the objects of the senses.

O King, O best of monarchs, these great-souled ones, by means of their own self, illuminate the subtle Self— overcoming discontent, the terrible thirst that is so difficult to conquer, all tactile sensations, and lethargy, which is likewise hard to subdue.
Free from passion and possessed of great wisdom through the perfection of meditation and study—
this path of the discerning Brahmins is considered difficult to traverse;
for no one, O bull of the Bharatas, proceeds along it with ease.
Just as someone might enter a terrible forest, teeming with many snakes and reptiles, full of chasms, devoid of water, difficult to traverse, and thick with thorns—
a wilderness consisting mostly of desolate wilds where the trees have been consumed by forest fires.
Just as a young man might safely traverse a path infested with robbers,
so too, O twice-born one, any who, having entered the path of yoga,
should abandon it in safety, is known to be full of many faults.
O lord of the earth, it is easy to stand upon the sharpened edges of razors,
but it is difficult for those of unrefined soul to remain steady in the concentrations of yoga. O dear one, when these concentrations fail, they lead to an inauspicious state.

O King, just as boats without a helmsman [cannot carry] men across the ocean, so it is for those who lack a leader. But he, O son of Kuntī, who abides in the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) according to the rule,
abandons death, birth, suffering, and pleasure.

This supreme yoga, perfected through various scriptures and proclaimed among yogis, is that which is entirely established and certain among the twice-born. For that Great Brahman is supreme, O high-souled one.
Brahmā, the Lord, and Viṣṇu the giver of boons;
Bhava, Dharma, and the six-faced one;
and the six sons of Brahmā of great majesty.
And the terrible, great darkness, and passion (rajas),
and pure goodness (sattva), and the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti),
and the goddess Siddhi, the wife of Varuṇa;
All splendor and great fortitude,
the stainless lord of the stars together with its constellations,
and all the gods, serpents, and ancestors—
All the mountains and the terrible oceans, all the rivers along with their forests and clouds,
the nāgas, the trees, the hosts of yakṣas, and the quarters of space;
Having attained union with hosts of gandharvas, men, and women, the great-souled yogi,
being liberated, enters [the supreme state] before long.
And this auspicious discourse, O King,
which has been engaged upon the god of great heroism and wisdom— he, having surpassed all mortals through his yogic powers;
The Great-Souled One, whose self is Nārāyaṇa, performs [this].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, this [dharma] approved by the learned has been correctly described by you."
The path of yoga has been explained here according to the rule by one desiring the welfare of his disciple;
now, however, please declare in its entirety the method of Sāṃkhya to me who asks,
for all that knowledge which exists in the three worlds is indeed known to you.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen to me regarding this pure doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas who have realized the Self— a teaching ordained by the wise and lordly ascetics, such as Kapila and others.

O bull among men, in whom no delusions whatsoever are seen, in whom there are many virtues and the absolute absence of faults— he, O King, having reckoned through knowledge that the objects of the senses are full of defects, [attains liberation].
Having understood all the human realms that are difficult to conquer, as well as the realms of the piśācas; having understood the realms of the rākṣasas and likewise the realms of the yakṣas;
and having understood the realms of the uragas and likewise the realms of the gandharvas.
O King, having known the realms of the ancestors who wander among the animals, having known the realms of the Suparṇas as well as the realms of the Maruts,
and having known the realms of the royal sages as well as the realms of the brahmin sages—
Having understood the domains of the Asuras as well as those of the Vaiśvadevas; having understood the domains of the divine seers (devarṣis) and even the lords of yogas;
and likewise the domains of the lords of creatures (prajeśas) and the domains of Brahmā.
O best among speakers, having understood in truth the ultimate duration of life in this world, and having understood the supreme reality of happiness,
[you know] the suffering that arises when the time comes for those who fall, being seekers of sense-objects.
The suffering of those falling into the animal realm and that of those falling into hell,
O Bhārata— the entire merits of heaven and all its defects,
as well as the defects found in Vedic discourse and whatever merits belong to the Vedas.

O King, whatever faults there are in the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) and whatever virtues there are in that yoga; O King, whatever faults there are in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and likewise whatever virtues there are;
and whatever faults and virtues there are in the others, O Bhārata—[all these have been declared].
Having calculated the enumeration and considered Sāṃkhya to be superior in its qualities—
having understood *sattva* to possess ten qualities, *rajas* likewise nine qualities,
*tamas* eight qualities, and *buddhi* seven qualities— (he attained liberation).
Having known space as having six qualities, and likewise the mind as having five;
having known the intellect as having four qualities, and the great *tamas* as having three;
and having known *rajas* as having two qualities, and *sattva* again as having one quality.
Having understood the path in its true essence, as well as the vision at the time of dissolution,
those endowed with knowledge and realization, refined by auspicious causes,
attain the auspicious liberation— the subtle, supreme ether in this world.
The eye is joined with form, and the nose with the quality of odor;
likewise, the ear is attached to sound, and the tongue to the qualities of taste.
The body is similarly attached to touch, and the wind is supported in space.
Delusion is attached to darkness, greed is rooted in objects of sense; Viṣṇu is in movement, Śakra is in strength, and likewise Agni is attached to the digestive cavity.
The Goddess is attached to the waters, and the waters are supported by fire.
Fire is attached to air, and air is supported by space; space is joined with the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle is supported by the intellect (buddhi);
the intellect is attached to darkness (tamas), and darkness is supported by passion (rajas).
Passion (*rajas*) is attached to goodness (*sattva*), and goodness is likewise attached to the self (*ātman*).
The self is attached to the Lord, the god Nārāyaṇa;
and the god is attached to liberation (*mokṣa*), yet liberation is attached to nothing at all.
Having understood that the body is joined with the sentient being and enveloped by the sixteen qualities,
and having understood both its inherent nature and consciousness as they reside within the body,
one perceives the single Self as standing in the middle, in whom no evil exists.
O King, having understood the second activity of those who seek sense-objects— namely,
that all the senses and their objects are dependent upon the self— and having understood, according to the sacred scriptures, the extreme difficulty of attaining liberation;

Having truly understood the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna breaths, as well as the downward-moving wind (avāka) and the upward-flowing wind (pravaha), and likewise the remaining seven winds in their sevenfold manner according to the rule; 12,290.026c–12,290.027c.
O scorcher of foes, having known the Lords of Creatures (Prajāpatis), the seers (ṛṣis), and very many excellent paths; having known the many Seven Seers (Saptarṣis) and royal seers (rājarṣis);
and other great celestial seers (surarṣis) and great seers (maharṣis) who resemble the sun.
O King, having learned after a long time that those who had fallen from their sovereignty were lost, and having heard, O Ruler of the Earth, of the destruction of great multitudes of beings,
and having understood, O Monarch, the evil destiny of those who perform sinful deeds;

The suffering of those fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river in the abode of Yama, as well as the impure transmigrations through various wombs, and dwelling within the foul womb— a vessel of blood and water— [are all experienced].

In this impure city with nine gates, filled with phlegm, urine, and excrement of pungent odor, a mass of semen and blood, bound together by marrow and sinews, and strewn with hundreds of veins; (12,290.032c–12,290.033)
O King, having understood himself to be afflicted, as well as the various types of yoga belonging to tamasic beings whose souls are shrouded by what is pleasant,
and that which is contemptible for sattvic beings, O bull of the Bharatas—
This was censured by the great ones, the Sāṃkhyas who have realized the Self;
likewise, having seen the terrible eclipses of the moon and its brilliance, the falling of the stars, and the revolution of the constellations.
O King, having understood the miserable separation of pairs,
and having seen the inauspicious mutual devouring of living beings;
and having recognized the delusion of childhood and the inauspicious decay of the body.
When passion and delusion have arisen, some being may take refuge in [the path];
yet among thousands of men, only a rare one takes recourse in the resolve for liberation,
having understood the extreme rarity of liberation through the sacred scriptures.
O King, having again understood the lack of regard for things not yet obtained, the indifference toward those already obtained, and the inherent wickedness of sense objects;
and having seen, O son of Kuntī, the impure bodies of those whose life-breaths have departed.
O Bhārata, having understood the suffering of living beings dwelling in various families,
and having known the most dreadful fate of those who have fallen— namely, the wicked-minded Brāhmaṇas addicted to drinking liquor— and having understood the destination of those who slay Brāhmaṇas.

12,290.042 Having understood the inauspicious destiny of those who are attached to the wives of their preceptors, [know that] those men, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who do not behave properly toward their mothers, 12,290.043 and who do not conduct themselves rightly toward all beings, including the gods, [fall from their status].
Having understood through that knowledge the destiny of those who perform unwholesome deeds,
and having discerned the various destinies of those born in the animal realm,
he likewise [understood] the diverse declarations of the Vedas and the cycles of the seasons.
Having observed the waning of years and likewise the passing away of months, having seen the disappearance of fortnights as well as the exhaustion of days,
and having likewise witnessed directly the waning and waxing of the moon;
Having observed the increase of the oceans and likewise their subsequent decrease; having seen the decline of wealth and its subsequent growth once again;
and having observed the dissolution of unions, especially that of the Yugas.
Having seen the destruction of the mountains and likewise the destruction of the rivers,
having seen the destruction of the social classes (varṇas) and their repeated end in decay,
and having seen old age, death, birth, and indeed all sufferings;
Having understood the defects of the body and their suffering in accordance with reality,
and having correctly comprehended the frailty of the body, O Bhārata,
and having recognized all the defects of the self residing within the self;

Having likewise perceived the foul odors arising from his own body— such as urine, phlegm, excrement, and other loathsome things born of sweat— Yudhiṣṭhira said: 12,290.051c Having likewise perceived the foul odors arising from his own body, 12,290.051d such as urine, phlegm, excrement, and other loathsome things born of sweat, 12,290.052 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O you of immeasurable prowess, what defects arising from your own body do you perceive?
You ought to explain this entire doubt of mine according to the truth.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Lord, O slayer of enemies, listen to those five defects in the body which the wise Sāṃkhya followers of Kapila, who know the path, proclaim:
desire, anger, fear, sleep, and the fifth is said to be breath."

12,290.054 These defects are seen in the bodies of all embodied beings. 12,290.055 One cuts off anger through forgiveness, desire by abandoning mental construction (*saṃkalpa*), sleep by cultivating goodness (*sattva*), and likewise fear through vigilance.
O King, by means of moderate diet, they cut off the fifth breath;
having understood virtues through hundreds of virtues, faults through hundreds of faults,
and diverse causes through hundreds of diverse causes, they have realized them according to reality.

Having seen this world—which is like the foam upon the waters, enveloped by hundreds of Viṣṇu’s illusions; which resembles a wall of the mind, lacking even the slightest essence, and being useless; which is like a pit of darkness, resembling rain-drops and bubbles—[he became disenchanted].
12,290.058c It is prone to destruction, inferior to happiness, and follows destruction, leading to non-existence;
12,290.058e it is like a helpless elephant sunk in the mud, submerged in passion and darkness.
12,290.059a O King, the highly wise followers of Sāṃkhya, having abandoned the body produced by progeny...
O King, by means of the pervasive and great Sāṃkhya consisting of knowledge and the knowable,
one [overcomes] inauspicious odors born of rajas, as well as similar ones born of tamas,
and auspicious odors born of sattva, all of which are produced by touch and reside in the body.
O Bhārata, having swiftly cut through [this] with the weapon of knowledge and the staff of austerity,
one then crosses the terrible river whose waters are suffering, which has anxiety and grief for its great deeps, disease and death for its great crocodiles, and great fear for its great serpents.

O subduer of enemies, O King, they cross over this ocean by means of wisdom— a sea whose tortoise is darkness, whose fish are passion, whose mire is affection, whose difficult pass is old age, whose island is touch, which is unfathomable due to karma, yet has truth as its shore and is established in firm vows.
Violence is a great river with swift and mighty currents, a vast mine of manifold flavors;
