it is a great jewel of diverse pleasures, yet a wind that fans the fever of suffering. It has the great whirlpools of grief and craving, and the great elephants of acute diseases.
O subduer of enemies, it was a mass of piled-up bones with phlegm for its foam;
it was a terrifying mine of pearls in the form of gifts, with blood-pools for its coral;
it resounded with the noise of laughter and shouts, and was exceedingly difficult to cross due to various forms of ignorance.
[It is] a salt-water ocean of weeping tears, devoted to the abandonment of attachments;
it is the flood of worlds from birth onwards, with sons and kinsmen as its ports,
bounded by non-violence and truth, and possessing the great waves of the sacrifice of life.

O Bhārata, perfected sages cross the ocean of the *vaḍavāmukha*— which has the attainment of the Vedānta for its island, the compassion for all beings for its depth, and liberation as its difficult-to-reach shore— by means of the yoga of knowledge.
Having crossed over birth, which is difficult to transcend, they enter the stainless sky.
Then, O King, the sun carries those virtuous followers of Sāṃkhya by means of its rays; entering them like a lotus fiber, it carries them away as it moves through the spheres of sense-objects.
There, O Bhārata, the wind Pravaha receives those ascetics who are free from passion, perfected, endowed with vigor, and whose wealth is their austerity—
subtle, cool, fragrant, and pleasant to the touch, O Bhārata.
O son of Kuntī, he who goes to the auspicious worlds as the foremost of the seven Maruts carries them to the highest goal of the sky;
O Lord of the World, the sky carries him to the highest goal of the *rajas* realm.

O Indra among kings, darkness carries one to the supreme state of passion; O Indra among kings, passion carries one to the supreme state of goodness. O pure-souled one, goodness carries one to the supreme Lord Nārāyaṇa.
The pure-souled Lord bears the Supreme Self by means of his own self. Having attained the Supreme Self, those who are stainless— the abode of that being—
are fit for immortality and do not return, O Lord.
"O Pārtha, that is the supreme goal of the great-souled ones who are free from the pairs of opposites,
who delight in truth and uprightness, and who possess compassion for all beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O sinless one, having attained that supreme station, do those of steadfast vows remember the Blessed One from birth until death, or do they not? You ought to tell me what is the truth in this matter exactly as it is."
"O Kaurava, apart from you, I ought not to ask any other human being.
This is a great defect regarding liberation, concerning those sages who have attained perfection— if even they, as supreme ascetics, remain attached to that very same state of consciousness."
"O King, I perceive the supreme Dharma as characterized by worldly activity;
for what indeed could be more painful than being submerged in the knowledge of the Supreme?
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, you have asked a most difficult question according to the proper method.
Even for the Buddhas, there is confusion regarding this question, O bull of the Bharatas. Listen now correctly to the supreme truth concerning this as it is uttered by me."
And where the supreme intellect of the high-souled followers of Kapila resides,
O King, even the senses perceive their own body as belonging to the embodied one;
they are the instruments of the self, and it is he who, being subtle, perceives through them.
Deprived of the self, they are like wood or a wall;
they perish without a doubt, like froth in the great ocean,
O scorcher of enemies, when the embodied being is asleep along with the senses.
Subtle, he moves everywhere like the wind in the sky;
O Lord, he perceives according to the proper order and experiences touches,
becoming aware of everything here just as before, O Bhārata.
12,290.085a All the sense organs here, in their respective places according to rule,
12,290.085c dissolve away due to their lack of autonomy, like snakes whose venom has been neutralized.
12,290.086a But of all the sense organs, in all respects, within their own locations—
Having ascended, the Self moves through subtle states of existence; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, O Bhārata, it experiences all the qualities of *sattva*, the qualities of *rajas*, all the qualities of *tamas*, and the qualities of the intellect.
O righteous-souled one, likewise the qualities of the mind and the qualities of space; again, the qualities of wind and the qualities of fire;
as well as the qualities of water, O Pārtha, and even the qualities of earth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having pervaded the field-knower (kṣetrajña) with all its attributes,
that Self (ātman) departs along with the field-knower and its auspicious and inauspicious actions,
as do the senses, O Lord, like disciples following their great-souled teacher.
Having transcended even primordial nature (*prakṛti*), he goes to the imperishable Self—
the supreme Nārāyaṇa, free from dualities and beyond nature—
liberated from merits and sins, having entered that state which is free from ailment.
O Bhārata, one does not turn back from the supreme Self, which is devoid of qualities (aguṇa). But here, O dear one, O Bhārata, the mind and the senses remain;
they return at the proper time, carrying out the instructions of the teacher.

O son of Kuntī, it is possible for one who seeks virtue, who is disciplined, and who possesses the knowledge of yoga and liberation, to attain peace in a short time. O King, the highly wise followers of Sāṃkhya likewise go to the supreme goal.
"O son of Kuntī, there is no knowledge equal to this knowledge.
Let there be no doubt in you regarding this; Sāṃkhya is considered the supreme knowledge. It is the imperishable, the constant, the unmanifest, the primordial, eternal Brahman."
That which those whose nature is tranquility describe as being without beginning, middle, or end; free from dualities; the agent; eternal; immutably fixed;
and indeed permanent—that from which all the transformations of creation and dissolution proceed.
That which the supreme ṛṣis proclaim in the scriptures, and what all the Brahmins, the gods, and those people who know the Āgamas declare—
that is the supreme deity devoted to Brahman, the infinite, the transcendent, and the infallible.
Seeking him, those Brahmins whose intellects are fixed on his qualities speak of him;
likewise do the properly disciplined Yogins and the Sāṃkhyas of immeasurable vision.
O son of Kuntī, the sacred tradition declares that for him who is formless, the Sāṃkhya system is his very form.
"O bull of the Bharatas, they say that his [the king's] authority is indeed based on these marks of recognition.
O lord of the earth, there are two kinds of beings here on this earth:
those designated as mobile and those designated as immobile; of these, the mobile are superior."
O King, that great knowledge which exists among the great ones—
in the Vedas, in the Sāṃkhya systems, and likewise in Yoga—
and whatever various ancient lore has been seen;
O King, all that is found in the Sāṃkhya,
whatever is seen in the great Itihāsas, and whatever is in the treatises on statecraft (Arthaśāstra) favored by the learned— [all that has been gathered here].
Whatever knowledge exists here in this world, O Great-Souled One, all that is contained within the Sāṃkhya system; it is the great [system],
wherein tranquility is seen and supreme strength is found.
Knowledge is subtle and has been explained exactly as it is (12.290.105c);
likewise, O King, subtle austerities and the means to happiness have been duly prescribed in the Sāṃkhya.
For by the opposite of that, O Pārtha, the followers of Sāṃkhya go perpetually to the gods with ease; and having moved among them,
they then achieve their purpose.
They descend again upon self-restrained Brahmins,
O Pārtha; and having abandoned the body, the followers of Sāṃkhya enter liberation, just as the dwellers of heaven enter the celestial realm.
O King, those twice-born ones take even greater delight in that highly precious Sāṃkhya system favored by the wise;
indeed, no downward migration is ever seen for them.
The path of speech is not for evildoers, nor is it the dwelling place of the ignorant; yet those twice-born ones,
O King, who are devoted to this knowledge, are indeed such.
The great-souled one, O King, [taught] the vast, supreme, and ancient Sāṃkhya—
a stainless, noble, and beautiful great ocean—
and the entirety of the Sāṃkhya system.
Nārāyaṇa sustains this immeasurable [universe].
O god among men, I have declared to you this truth:
Nārāyaṇa is this ancient universe.
At the time of creation, he brings forth creation;
and at the time of dissolution, he consumes it again,
having withdrawn everything and established it within his own body.
Having performed [this], the inner self of the world lies upon the waters.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is that which is called the "imperishable" (akṣara), from which one does not return again?

And what is that which is called the perishable (*kṣara*), from which one returns again? O slayer of enemies, O mighty-armed descendant of Kuru, I desire to understand the manifestation of the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable in their true nature.
"For you, O Brahmin, are called a treasury of knowledge by those who have mastered the Vedas,
by the highly fortunate ṛṣis, and by the great-souled ascetics. Only a few days remain for you while the sun is in its southern course."
"When the blessed sun has turned back, you shall go to the supreme goal. Once you have departed, from whom shall we hear what is beneficial?
You are the lamp of the Kuru lineage; you shine by means of the wealth of knowledge."
"O bestower of honor to the Kuru lineage, I desire to hear this from you;
O Indra among kings, I am not satiated here while hearing such nectar.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history,
the conversation between Vasiṣṭha and Karāla Janaka.
[It concerns] Vasiṣṭha, the most excellent among sages, seated and radiant as the sun.

King Janaka, having saluted Maitrāvaruṇi as he sat there with palms joined in reverence, asked him about the supreme knowledge that leads to the highest good— the ultimate expertise in the inner self and the definitive understanding of the course of the inner self.
In the past, King Karālajanaka questioned the best of sages with words that were well-articulated, humble, sweet,
and refined: "O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the supreme, eternal Brahman."
Because from that place the wise do not undergo return;
and that which is called the Perishable (*kṣara*), wherein this world dissolves; and that which is proclaimed the Imperishable (*akṣara*), auspicious, secure, and free from affliction.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Listen, O protector of the earth, to how this world decays,
and how it does not decay through the power of its former merit and the duration of time."

Know that twelve thousand *yugas* constitute a *kalpa*, and four times that is a day of Brahmā. A hundred such *kalpas* passed constitutes a single day of Brahmā, O King; his night is of equal duration, at the end of which he awakens.
The self-born Śambhu, whose nature is formless, creates the first-born great being, the infinite in action and possessed of form; he is the Lord,
the imperishable light, characterized by the powers of atomization, levitation, and attainment.
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands encompassing all.
This Lord Hiraṇyagarbha is remembered as the intellect (buddhi).
In the systems of yoga he is called "The Great One" (*Mahān*) and also "Viriñca";
in the Sāṃkhya scripture, he who possesses many forms is recited by various names;
he is known as the one of manifold appearance, the soul of the universe, and the Single Syllable (*Ekākṣara*).
By whom the entire triple world, though consisting of many natures, was pervaded by his own self;
likewise, because of his manifold forms, he is remembered as Viśvarūpa (the Universal Form).
Having indeed undergone transformation, he creates himself by means of himself.

The one of great splendor [created] Ahaṃkāra, the Prajāpati who is characterized by egoism. They call that the "creation of knowledge" (vidyā-sarga), which arose as the manifest from the unmanifest; and they also call the Great One (Mahat) and Ahaṃkāra the "creation of ignorance" (avidyā-sarga).
Non-vidyā and vidyā have both arisen from the same source;
they are known as ignorance and knowledge by those who contemplate the meaning of the Vedas and the scriptures.
Know, O King, that the third creation is the creation of the elements from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra).
Know that among the elements associated with ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), the fourth is the modified (*vaikṛta*).
Likewise [there are]: wind, light, space, water, and earth;
as well as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
"Know, O Indra among kings, that this group of ten which has thus arisen simultaneously is undoubtedly the fifth meaningful creation, consisting of the elements.
[The five organs of perception are] the ear, the skin, the two eyes, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth."
Speech, the hands, the feet, the anus, and likewise the generative organ— these,
O King, are the organs of perception as well as the organs of action,
which have arisen here simultaneously with the mind.
This twenty-fourfold reality exists within all forms;
having known it, the Brahmins who perceive the truth do not grieve. This has been fully described as the body among all embodied beings in the three worlds.
O best of men, it should be known that [this applies] among gods,
humans, and dānavas, along with yakṣas, bhūtas, and gandharvas, together with kinnaras and mahoragas, as well as cāraṇas and piśācas, and indeed among divine ṛṣis and niśācaras.
In a place filled with gadflies, insects, and mosquitoes, with putrid worms and mice;
with dogs, outcastes, bamboo-workers, as well as Caṇḍālas and Pulkasas;
and likewise with elephants, horses, donkeys, tigers, trees, and even cattle.
Indeed, whether it be with elephants and horses, or with tigers, bears, and cattle—
whatever possesses a physical form, this is the illustration for all of it. It is certain that [this power exists] in water, on earth, and likewise in space, and nowhere else.
"We have heard that there is a station for embodied beings;
however, O dear one, everything known as the manifest (vyakta) wastes away entirely day after day. Therefore, the self of beings (bhūtātman) is remembered as 'the perishable' (kṣara)."
This is called the Imperishable (*akṣara*), whereas this world is said to perish;
they say the world is of the nature of delusion, being unmanifest yet designated as manifest. And Mahat is likewise eternal and the first-born; such is the illustration of that which perishes.
12,291.036c This has been told to you, O Great King, from which one does not return again.

12,291.037a Viṣṇu is the twenty-fifth, beyond the principles (nistattva), yet designated as a principle (tattvasaṃjñaka). 12,291.037c Because he is the refuge of all principles, the wise call him "the Principle" (Tattva).
Whatever manifest [entity] he created that was formless, he presides over it through his own form. For the twenty-fourth principle is manifest, while the twenty-fifth is formless;
he alone, possessing self-mastery, dwells within the heart in all forms.

Conscious and eternal, possessing all forms yet himself formless, he who is beyond creation and dissolution abides eternally within the sphere of that which is subject to creation and dissolution; though devoid of qualities, he is designated by the name of "qualities."
Thus this Great Self, skilled in creation and dissolution,

undergoing transformation and possessing the primary nature (prakṛti), being devoid of wisdom, conceives of itself through its association with darkness, goodness, and passion within various wombs here in this world.
12,291.042c Because of a lack of awakening and from associating with unawakened people, 12,291.043a one who is essentially of the nature of dwelling together [with them] thinks, "I am not another.
12,291.043c Having said, "I am he; I am he," one indeed turns back following after the qualities (guṇas).
Through *tamas* one encounters various *tāmasa* states;
through *rajas*, *rājasa* states; and by resorting to *sattva*, *sāttvika* states.
These three forms are indeed white, red, and black.
Know that all these forms are indeed derived from primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Those characterized by *tamas* go to hell; likewise, those characterized by *rajas* go to the world of humans.
Those characterized by *sattva*, partaking of happiness, go to the world of the gods.
Through exclusive evil one attains the state of an animal;
through a mixture of merit and evil, the human state; and through merit alone, the gods.
Thus do the wise describe the perishable realm of the Unmanifest.
This twenty-fifth [principle], which proceeds from knowledge alone—
Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, due to a lack of awakening, one follows after that which is unawakened.
From one body, it likewise attains thousands of bodies;
it is born among thousands of animal wombs and sometimes even among the gods, through conjunction with the *guṇas*, until the exhaustion of those *guṇas*.
From the human state one goes to heaven, and from heaven back to the human state;
from the human state one reaches the abode of hell for eternity.
Just as the silkworm binds itself within its own cocoon, so does one bind oneself.
Just as a thread is constantly joined with strands of yarn, so this one who is without qualities is joined with qualities;
though free from dualities, he encounters pairs of opposites within various wombs here in this world—
whether in headache, eye disease, toothache, or throat obstruction.
In cases of dropsy, hemorrhoids, fever, glandular swellings, and cholera;
in leucoderma, skin diseases, burns from fire, as well as in ringworm and epilepsy;
and whatever other dual disorders (dvaṃdva) exist among embodied beings arising from the primary elements (prākṛta).
Various [states] arise, and he conceives an attachment to them— sometimes among thousands of animal births, and even among the gods;
through such conceit, he likewise conceives an attachment to his own good deeds.
Wearing but a single garment, poorly clad, and likewise always sleeping on the ground;
sleeping like a frog, as well as remaining in the *vīrāsana* posture; wearing rags (*cīra*), sleeping in the open air, and standing [without sitting].
He slept upon beds of bricks and likewise upon beds of thorns; he lay upon a bed of ashes, slept on the bare ground, smeared himself with [dust],
and rested in the posture of a hero (*vīrasthāna*), in water, in mud, and upon wooden planks.
Seeking fruit among various kinds of beds, he was yet without fruit;
wearing a girdle of *muñja* grass, naked, or clad in linen, black antelope skin,
or garments of hemp and bark, he was covered with a tiger skin.
Some were clad in lion skins, and likewise some wore silk garments;
some wore wooden planks as clothing, and others wore garments of thorns; some wore clothes made of insects, and likewise some wore rags from a dust-heap.
The unintelligent person covets many other garments,
various foods, and diverse jewels; [he knows] eating with only one garment as an undergarment and eating only once a day.
Eating at the fourth and eighth meal-times, as well as eating only at the sixth meal-time; eating only every six nights, and likewise eating only every eight days;
eating once every seven nights or ten days, and even eating only every twelve days.
One who fasts for a month, one who subsists on roots, and likewise one who subsists on fruits; one who feeds on air, one who drinks water, one who eats oil-cake, and one who eats cow dung;
one who consumes cow urine, and one who eats vegetables and flowers.
Subsisting on *śaivala* moss and likewise maintaining himself with mouthfuls of water (*ācāma*),
and subsisting on withered leaves and scattered fruits,
he undergoes various kinds of ascetic hardships (*kṛcchra*) out of a desire for happiness.

He performs various *cāndrāyaṇa* penances according to the rules and assumes diverse outward marks (*liṅga*). He resorts to the path of the four stages of life (*cāturāśramya*) and even takes on the specific characteristics of those stages. Furthermore, he frequents heretics as well as mountain caves.
Secluded shadows of rocks and likewise mountain springs; secluded sandbanks and secluded forests;
sacred abodes of the gods and secluded lakes.
And there were secluded mountain caves resembling houses,
where various recitations, various vows,
diverse observances, and manifold austerities were practiced.
He established sacrifices of various forms and likewise various ritual injunctions;
he established the paths of trade, as well as the duties of the twice-born, the kṣatriyas, the vaiśyas, and the śūdras;
and he ordained gifts of various kinds even for the poor, the blind, and the wretched.
Through a lack of awakening, he thus conceives of the three qualities—
sattva, rajas, and tamas— as well as dharma, artha, and kāma; indeed,
the self, by means of primordial nature (prakṛti), differentiates itself in this manner.
The utterances *svadhā* and *vaṣaṭ*, the utterance *svāhā* and acts of salutation; officiating at sacrifices, teaching, giving gifts, and likewise receiving them;
as well as sacrificing and studying, and whatever else there may be.
"In birth, death, conflict, and likewise even in slaughter—
all this, consisting of the auspicious and the inauspicious, they call the path of action (kriyāpatha).
The Goddess Prakṛti performs it, as does the Great Dissolution itself."
At the end of the day, having withdrawn these qualities, he alone remains;
like the sun withdrawing its web of rays at that time,
he thus repeatedly regards everything as his own for the sake of sport.

Manifesting these various qualities of his own form that are dear to the heart, thus performing the acts of creation and dissolution, he is attached to the path of action and non-action; he consists of the three qualities, yet transcends the three qualities.
Endowed with the path of action and non-action, one likewise conceives it to be so;
O Lord, by its very nature this entire world is blinded,
pervaded in manifold ways by passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*).
"Thus these pairs of opposites constantly beset me;
they arise from me alone and they afflict me.
"O lord of men, all these must be overcome."

Indeed, due to a lack of understanding, he thinks: "These meritorious deeds must be enjoyed by me once I have gone to the world of the gods," and "I shall experience here itself the arising of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious actions."
One should perform only that which leads to happiness; having performed it once, may there be happiness for me.
One who seeks happiness should abandon suffering, which is the opposite of happiness. May there be happiness for me until the very end, in birth after birth.
"And there will be endless suffering for me here even because of what has been done;
for human existence is great suffering, as is sinking into hell. And from hell, in time, I shall return again to the human state."
From the state of humanity one goes to the state of divinity, and from the state of divinity back again to the human state; from the state of humanity one enters hell in turn.
Thus, through such succession, I shall encounter suffering and then happiness once more.

He who always knows that the selfless one is indeed enveloped by the qualities of the self, is reborn among gods, humans, and even in hell. Constantly shrouded by the sense of "mine-ness," he revolves right there.
Throughout thousands of millions of creations, within forms that end in death,
he alone who performs such action— consisting of the fruits of good and evil—
experiences that very fruit, embodied, throughout the three worlds.
Prakṛti performs action, consisting of the fruits of both good and evil; and Prakṛti, moving at will through the three worlds, experiences that [fruit]—
whether in the animal realm, in human status, or likewise in the world of the gods.
One should know that these three states are indeed natural (*prākṛta*).
They say that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is without marks (*aliṅga*), yet we infer it by means of its marks (*liṅga*);
likewise, one perceives the mark of the Puruṣa through inference.
Having reached another subtle body (*liṅga*), which is a natural and unblemished form,
it presides over the openings of the wounds [the sense organs] and conceives of actions within itself.
These include all the five organs of hearing and so forth, as well as the five organs of action.
Speech and the other faculties proceed among the qualities (guṇas) together with the qualities themselves.
One who performs these [actions] might think, "These are mine," and likewise, "These are my senses. Yet, being devoid of senses, one should realize: "I am without wounds; I am not wounded."
He who is signless perceives himself as having signs; he who is beyond time perceives himself as having time;

he who is non-existence perceives himself as existence; he who is not reality perceives himself as reality; he who is immortal perceives himself as mortal; he who is immovable perceives himself as moving.

The fieldless one [regards] the self as the field; the non-creator [regards] the self as the creation; the passionless one [regards] the self as passion; the one without motion [regards] the self as motion;
the non-existent one [regards] the self as existence; and the fearless one [regards] the self as fear.
The non-agent regards himself as the agent; the seedless regards himself as the seed of the self; the imperishable regards himself as perishable—thus does one lacking wisdom imagine. Vasiṣṭha said:
Thus, due to a lack of awakening and from associating with ignorant people,
one undergoes thousands of millions of creations that end in downfall;
from one state to thousands of states, one goes until death.
In the animal realm, in the human state, and likewise in the world of the gods,
this unintelligent one dissolves thousands of times there like the moon [into its phases], because he lacks awakening.
The fifteen digits (kalās) are the womb; that is recited as "the abode.
Know this to be eternal: Soma is the sixteenth digit. From that digit, the unintelligent one is born incessantly, again and again.
They consume his essence, yet it is born ever again.
That subtle sixteenth digit should be understood as Soma;
though it is not consumed by the gods, it sustains the gods.
Having thus exhausted that [ignorance], O best of kings, one is indeed born;
for that is seen to be his *prakṛti*, and liberation is said to arise from its destruction.
Thus, this body, designated as the "unmanifest," consists of sixteen parts.
Thinking "this is mine," one revolves right there;
likewise, the twenty-fifth principle (the self) remains so due to its lack of awakening,
even though it is stainless, pure, and frequents the pure wind.

O King, even one who is impure becomes pure in soul when associated with such a person; likewise, even a wise man may fall into a state of ignorance through the service of the unwise. In the same way, O best of monarchs, one who is not awakened should be understood [in this manner].
"By serving the *prakṛti* consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), one becomes *prākṛta*.
Karālajanaka said:
'This relationship between these two, the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable (*kṣara*), is thus desired.'"
"O Blessed One, the relationship between a woman and a man is said to be just like that.
For without a man here, a woman does not conceive a fetus;
likewise, without a woman, a man cannot bring forth a form."
Through mutual connection and by resorting to each other’s qualities,
this brings about form in all wombs;
through mutual union for the sake of pleasure and by resorting to each other’s qualities.
In the season, the form is produced; I shall state the illustration of that.
Whatever qualities belong to the father here, and likewise whatever qualities belong to the mother—O twice-born one, we know that the bone, the sinew, and the marrow are derived from the father.
"We have heard that skin, flesh, and blood are indeed born of the mother;
thus it is recited in the Vedic scriptures, O best of the twice-born. Whatever authority is declared in the Vedas and whatever is recited in the Śāstras [is to be accepted]."
"The authority of the Vedic scriptures is eternal authority.
Thus, O Blessed One, I perceive that *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are eternally bound; therefore, the dharma of liberation does not exist."

Alternatively, give me some illustration of what has been done immediately [beforehand]; tell that to me in its true nature, for you are a witness in every respect. We also, desiring liberation, long for that which is free from suffering.
"Bodyless, undecaying, divine, beyond the senses, and without a lord.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"This which has been stated by you is the illustration from the Vedic scriptures."

"It is exactly as you say; for you do not grasp this matter in the way it truly is. O Lord of Men, although you maintain the texts of both the Vedas and the Śāstras, you are not one who knows the true reality (*tattva*) of those texts as it actually is."
For he who is intent on memorizing the texts of the Vedas and the Shastras,
yet does not know the true meaning of those texts, his memorization is in vain;
he merely carries a burden, for he does not understand the meaning of that text.
But for one who knows the true reality of both the text and its meaning, the acquisition of the text is not in vain;
and when questioned regarding the meaning of the text, such a person is worthy to speak,
so that through the realization of the truth, he finds its purpose.
But as for one who, possessing only a coarse intellect, might speak of the meaning of the text in assemblies—
how could that person of dull understanding explain the text with certainty? And even if he were to reach a conclusion, being of a flawed nature, he would not state it according to reality.
Since even a self-possessed person may fall into a state of being subject to derision,
therefore listen, O Indra among kings, to how this is observed according to the truth among the high-souled followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
That which the practitioners of Yoga perceive is followed by the followers of Sāṃkhya. He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one is wise.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew—
"O dear one, what you have said here is indeed based on sensory perception:
that from substance arises substance, and likewise from sense organ arises sense organ;
that one obtains a body from a body, and just so, a seed from a seed."
The subtle measures residing within the subtle body increase through the nourishment of their seeds.
How can there be qualities for this embodied being who is devoid of senses, devoid of seeds, and devoid of material substance, since the Great Self (mahātman) is by nature without qualities?
Qualities arise from qualities and dissolve back into them;
thus, qualities are born from primordial nature (prakṛti) and yet do not truly exist.
Skin, flesh, blood, fat, bile, marrow, bone, and sinew—
Know that these eight are indeed the primary (prākṛta) qualities of Śukra. Both male and non-male—the threefold gender—is remembered as primary.
That which is neither male nor non-male is designated as "possessing gender" (liṅgin).

12.293.037a Nature is without marks, yet it is perceived through its own-born marks; 12.293.037c just as the seasons, though formless, are constantly perceived through their flowers and fruits. 12.293.038a Even so, that which is without marks is indeed perceived by means of inference.
O dear one, the twenty-fifth principle, whose nature is not fixed within the [material] signs,
is without beginning or end, infinite, all-seeing, and free from affliction;
yet, due solely to the presence of ego-consciousness (*abhimāna*), that which is devoid of qualities (*aguṇa*) is said to possess qualities (*guṇa*).
Qualities belong to one who possesses qualities; how can there be qualities for one who is devoid of qualities?
Therefore, those people who perceive qualities understand it thus.
But when he identifies with all the qualities derived from primordial matter (prakṛti), [he becomes bound].

Then that virtuous one perceives through supreme insight that which the Sāṃkhyas and Yogins everywhere declare to be beyond the intellect— the Greatly Wise One who is awakening, by virtue of having abandoned the non-awakened state.
Then, they say that the unawakened and unmanifest one is the Lord endowed with qualities (saguṇa),
while the eternal Lord devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) is the presiding controller alone;
thus do the wise speak of the twenty-five principles consisting of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the qualities.
Skilled in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, those seekers of the Supreme awaken; when they have awakened, being afraid of worldly conditions and rebirth, they awaken to that which is being awakened— the Unmanifest—
and then lead it to equanimity.
O subduer of enemies, this is the correct illustration of right and wrong perception, explained separately for the awakened and the unawakened;
this has been spoken by each other as the illustration of the perishable and the imperishable.
They say that oneness is the imperishable (*akṣara*), while multiplicity is called the perishable (*kṣara*).
When this [soul] proceeds correctly, it culminates in the twenty-five [principles];
for it, oneness is vision, and multiplicity is non-vision.
This is the distinct illustration of both reality (*tattva*) and non-reality (*nistattva*).
The wise declare that the twenty-fifth principle is reality,
while they say the supreme illustration of the twenty-fifth is non-reality.
The square of the group, the conduct, the principle, and from that principle, the eternal.
Karālajanaka said:
"O best of sages, you have spoken of this as both manifoldness and unity."
O sinless one, I perceive this illustration of these two— the unawakened and the awakened— as well as that of one who is currently awakening; yet,
due to my dull intellect, I do not see this reality clearly, of this there is no doubt.

O sinless one, although you have stated the reason for the distinction between the imperishable and the perishable, even that has, as it were, vanished from my mind due to the instability of my intellect.
Therefore, I wish to hear this teaching on the vision of multiplicity and unity.
O Blessed One, [I wish to know] the Buddha and the non-Buddha, and that which is awakening in reality; knowledge and ignorance, the imperishable and the perishable;
and Sāṃkhya and Yoga in their entirety—both separately and as not separate.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"Indeed, O Great King, I shall explain to you that which you ask; listen to me as I describe the practice of yoga in its distinct details."
The practice of yoga for practitioners is meditation alone, which is the supreme power.
Those who know the Vedas say that this meditation is of two kinds:
one-pointedness of mind and likewise breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is both with attributes (*saguṇa*) and without attributes (*nirguṇa*), as is the case for the mind. O lord of men, one should not practice it during the three times of urination, defecation, and eating; at all other times, one should apply oneself to it with devotion.
Having withdrawn the senses from the objects of the senses by means of the mind, the sage— whether by means of ten,
twelve, or even twenty-four [stages]—
should then, being wise, impel his self with those exhortations.
That which remains undecaying, as described by the wise;
we have heard it taught that the Self must be constantly known by them— this is the firm conclusion that for one whose mind is not deficient, the substance [of the Self] exists, and not otherwise.
Freed from all attachments, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses,
one should fix the mind upon the Self during both the first and the last parts of the night,
O Lord of Mithilā, having steadied the entire collection of the senses by means of the mind.
Having made the mind steady by means of the intellect, one should be as motionless as a stone;
one should be as unshakable as a pillar and as immovable as a mountain.
Then the wise, who know the rules of practice, declare that one is "yoked" (in samādhi).
He does not hear, nor does he smell; he does not taste, nor does he see;
he does not perceive touch, nor does his mind form conceptualizations.
He does not conceive anything, nor is he conscious of anything, remaining like a piece of wood.
Then the wise say that he has attained his true nature and is disciplined; like a lamp burning in a windless place, so does he appear—
motionless, steady, and rising upward, without attaining a horizontal course.
Then one should perceive that [Self] by seeing which it is described as the "inner self" (antarātman) residing in the heart; O dear one, it should be known as the Knower by those like me.
It is like a smokeless fire with seven flames, or like the sun endowed with its rays.
Like lightning in the sky, so is the Self perceived within the self;
it is that which the great-souled, steadfast, and wise Brahmins— those established in the source of Brahman— behold as the unborn, immortal essence.
They say that very same thing is subtler than the subtle and greater than the great;
though it stands eternally within all beings, it is not seen.
By means of the substance of the intellect and with the lamp of the mind, the creator of the world may be perceived.
Standing on the far shore of the great darkness, O dear one, he who is himself beyond darkness is called the Dispeller of Darkness by those who know reality and have mastered the Vedas;
he is stainless, free from darkness, without marks, and designated as the Unmarked.
For I consider this to be the yoga of all yogas, the very definition of yoga.
Seeing thus, they perceive the supreme, undecaying Self. This much of the vision of yoga has been declared to you by me according to the truth.
I shall proclaim the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, which is a demonstration of enumeration. Those who discourse on primordial nature (*prakṛti*) say that the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) is the supreme nature.
From that, O best of kings, the second principle, the Great One (*mahat*), was produced.
We have heard that ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) is the third [evolute] of the Great One (*mahat*). Those who follow the Sāṃkhya philosophy say that the five elements arise from ego-consciousness.
These, then, are the eight primary natures (*prakṛti*), and there are also sixteen transformations (*vikāra*).
The five specific qualities (*viśeṣas*) and likewise the five sense organs—
this much alone, the wise say, is the enumeration of the principles (*tattvas*). Those who know the rules and ordinances of Sāṃkhya are eternally devoted to the path of Sāṃkhya.
For whatever is born from something, that very thing is dissolved back into it.
The elements are created by the Inner Self in direct order, and they are dissolved in reverse order;
they are born in direct order and dissolved in reverse order.
The qualities are constantly within the qualities, like the waves of the ocean.
O best of kings, such is the extent of the creation and dissolution of *prakṛti*:
its state of unity during dissolution, and its multiplicity when it brings forth creation.
In this very same way, O Indra among kings, it should be understood by those who contemplate the objects of knowledge:
that the Unmanifest is the presiding controller; and for this [Unmanifest] as well, there is this illustration—namely, unity and multiplicity according to the true nature of Prakṛti.
Its unity exists at the time of dissolution, and its multiplicity arises from the process of manifestation. The Self, through manifold means, brings forth the creative *prakṛti*.
And the Great Self, the twenty-fifth principle, presides over that field (*kṣetra*).
"O Indra among kings, he is called the 'presider' (adhiṣṭhātṛ) by the best of ascetics.
We have heard that he is the presider because of his presiding over the fields (kṣetra). Furthermore, because he knows the unmanifest field, he is called the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña)."

It is said that the Puruṣa lies within the unmanifest city; the field (kṣetra) is one thing, and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is said to be another. The field is called the unmanifest, while the knower is indeed the twenty-fifth principle.
Knowledge is indeed one thing, and the object of knowledge is said to be another.
Knowledge is called the Unmanifest, while the object of knowledge is the twenty-fifth principle. The Unmanifest is called the Field (kṣetra), as well as Sattva and likewise the Lord (īśvara).
That twenty-fifth principle is without a lord and is not the ultimate reality;
such is the Sāṃkhya philosophy, a system of enumeration. It indeed establishes the Sāṃkhya and explains primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having enumerated the principles (tattvas) as twenty-four according to their true nature,
the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the twenty-fifth principle, together with primordial matter (prakṛti), is beyond the principles (nistattva).
This twenty-fifth principle is known as the unawakened self when it is still in the process of awakening.
But when one realizes the Self, then one becomes solitary.
This much has been spoken to you in truth regarding perfect vision;
those who understand this indeed attain equanimity.

This is the correct illustration: direct perception of *prakṛti* is likewise [the means of knowing] these principles of the *guṇas*; yet there is another who is devoid of the *guṇas*. For those who exist in this way, there is no further return.
Because it is of the nature of the imperishable, it exists as mutually undecaying.
Those who perceive with a single-mindedness do not see them correctly; O subduer of enemies, they return again and again to the unmanifest.
Knowing all this, they shall become manifest through the awakening of the All, and they will abide under the control of the Manifest.
It has been said that "all" is the Unmanifest; the twenty-fifth principle is not the All.
"For those who truly know him, no fear exists.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"O best of kings, this much of the Sāṃkhya philosophy has been declared to you."

"Now, however, learn from me about knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) in their proper order. They say that ignorance is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), which indeed possesses the nature of creation and dissolution; whereas knowledge is the twenty-fifth principle, which is free from creation and dissolution."

Understand now, in due order, that very ignorance which exists between them, O dear one, according to the illustration of this Sāṃkhya system as taught by the seers. Knowledge is said to be the faculty of the senses of cognition in relation to all the organs of action.
"Likewise, we have heard that the specific objects of the sense organs are the *viśeṣas*. The wise say that the mind (*manas*) is the knowledge of those *viśeṣas*,
and they declare that the five elements are the knowledge of the mind."

The ego (ahaṃkāra) is indeed the source of the five elements; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, O Lord of Men, the intellect (buddhi) is the source of the ego. The unmanifest (avyakta) is the source of the intellect, the supreme lord of all principles.
"O best of men, knowledge is to be known, and the supreme method is traditionally taught.
They say that the twenty-fifth principle is indeed the knowledge beyond the unmanifest;
O King, it is said that the 'all' is the object of knowledge for all knowledge."
Knowledge is said to be the unmanifest, while that which is to be known is indeed the twenty-fifth principle.
Likewise, knowledge is the unmanifest, and the knower is the twenty-fifth. I have explained this to you specifically according to the true nature of knowledge and ignorance.

Now listen to me as I explain what has been said regarding both the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable (*kṣara*). Both of these have been called perishable, and both of these have also been called imperishable;
I shall, however, declare the reason why they are so designated according to their true nature.
Both of these are considered to be without beginning or end, and both are regarded as lords.

Those who contemplate knowledge declare that both of these possess the designation of "reality" (tattva). Because it possesses the nature of creation and dissolution, they call the unmanifest (avyakta) the imperishable (akṣara).
This very [Prakṛti], undergoing transformation again and again for the sake of the creation of the qualities (guṇas),
gives rise to the mutual production of the qualities beginning with Mahat.
Because it presides over them, they call this the twenty-fifth principle, the Field (kṣetra).

But when that web of qualities is withdrawn into the unmanifest Self, then the twenty-fifth principle dissolves along with those qualities. The qualities dissolve into the qualities; at that time, there remains only one primordial nature (prakṛti).
O dear one, when even the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is completely dissolved into that field,

then Nature (prakṛti), which is designated by the qualities (guṇas), attains the state of the Imperishable (akṣara); and it attains the state of being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva), O Vaideha, because of its ceasing to operate within the qualities.

In this very way, when the knowledge of the field (*kṣetra*) has perished, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed devoid of qualities by nature; thus have we heard. But when he becomes subject to decay, then he possesses qualities.
But when he recognizes the nature of *prakṛti* as well as the qualitylessness of the self,
then he becomes pure through the complete relinquishing of *prakṛti*. When the wise man realizes, "I am one, and this [nature] is another," [he attains purity].
Then this [soul] attains a state of otherness and does not enter into a state of mixture; for even by its very nature, O King of kings, it is seen to be unmixed and distinct.
But when one feels revulsion toward that net of qualities which is derived from primordial matter (prakṛti), [one attains liberation].
When one sees another vision while seeing, then, seeing, one should not be distressed, thinking:
"What have I done that for so long I have followed this person,
just as a fish follows the net out of ignorance?"

Indeed, through delusion, I have followed from one person to another, just as a fish here follows along [the current] due to its perception of water. Just as a fish, through ignorance, does not perceive itself as distinct from the water.
In that same way, out of ignorance, I perceive myself as being distinct [from the Self].
Fie upon me, the unawakened, who out of delusion have again followed after one person after another, sinking into this [cycle of existence].
"He here shall be my kinsman; with him there shall be liberation.
Having attained equality and oneness, whatever he is, such am I.
I perceive equality here; indeed, I am just like him."
For this one is indeed stainless and manifest, while I am such as I am; I,
who through the delusion of ignorance have proceeded with a lack of knowledge, now stand for this duration of time free from attachment, whereas I was previously possessed by attachment.
"Under her influence, I have remained in this state for so long that I did not realize it.
How could I dwell with her among those who are high, middling, and low? And how could I live here together with one who is so utterly base?"
"Because I was unaware of her nature, I am now departing; let me now remain firm.
I shall not go to dwell with her, for this is a deception of time. Indeed, I have been deceived by her, who, though changeless herself, causes change in others."

This is not her fault; rather, this is my own fault, since I remained attached here while she stood with her face turned away. Therefore, though formless, I have come to abide within these many-formed bodies.
Though formless, the self has assumed form and is assailed by the sense of "mine.
Due to its subjection to *prakṛti*, it is led through various wombs here in this world.
What has been done by that which is truly free from "mine" through this sense of "mine" in those various births?
Wandering through these wombs with a mind whose true perception is lost, I have no need for this [body] which is fashioned by egoism; it is she who,
having divided herself into many forms, repeatedly joins me to this state.

12,295.036 Now I am this Buddha, free from "mine-ness" and free from egoism. 12,295.037 This sense of "mine," which is eternally constituted by egoism, I shall cast off; having abandoned it, I shall take refuge in that which is free from affliction.
"I shall attain equality with this [twenty-fifth principle], not with this mindless one;
it is fitting for me to be with him, not to have oneness with her.
Thus, through supreme awakening, the twenty-fifth [principle] became enlightened.
One should ascertain the imperishable state by abandoning the perishable,
the unmanifest which possesses the attributes of the manifest, and likewise that which has qualities as well as that which is without qualities;
having first perceived that which is without qualities, O King of Mithilā, one becomes like that.
This illustration concerning the imperishable and the perishable has been declared by me here for you,
endowed with knowledge, according to the illustrations found in the scriptures—
free from doubt, subtle, fully awakened, and likewise stainless.
I shall speak to you further; listen to that as it was heard by me. Sāṃkhya and Yoga have been declared by me according to the exposition of two scriptures;
for whatever scripture is spoken of by the Sāṃkhyas, that is indeed the vision of Yoga.
O lord of the earth, the knowledge of the Sāṃkhyas, which brings about awakening,
is clearly expounded therein out of a desire for the welfare of their disciples; indeed,
learned people call that scripture "The Great" (Bṛhat).
And in this treatise on yoga, there is curd again and again, and curds again;
O lord of men, one sees no principle beyond the twenty-fifth.
However, that which is supreme among the Sāṃkhyas has been described therein exactly as it is.
They say that, according to the teaching of yoga, there is the unawakened Buddha, the one awakening in reality, and the one who is both awakening and awakened. Vasiṣṭha said:
Now hear about this unawakened, unmanifest process of the *guṇas*.
For she sustains the *guṇas*, and likewise creates and withdraws them. O lord of men, she undergoes these transformations here eternally for the sake of sport.
Having made itself manifold, it perceives those very forms;
though perceiving this transformation in such a way, it does not perceive [itself]. And because of the awakening to the unmanifest, they also call it "the one being awakened."
But the unmanifest is never perceived, whether it possesses qualities or is devoid of them;
indeed, they say that this [unmanifest] is always unawakened. Yet, if one should perceive the unmanifest, it is truly this twenty-fifth principle.
"He who is awakening becomes characterized by attachment," so says the Śruti.
By this [state], they call the unmanifest and imperishable "the unawakened. And because of the awakening of the unmanifest, they likewise call it "the awakening one."
He does not perceive the Great-Souled One, the twenty-fifth;
nor does he perceive the twenty-sixth—the stainless, awakened, immeasurable, and eternal.
Yet, he constantly perceives both the twenty-fifth and the twenty-fourth.
For those two of great splendor are both pervaded by the seen and the unseen; yet,
O dear one, that Brahman alone does not perceive the Unmanifest,
nor does the twenty-fifth principle perceive the twenty-fourth.

When, while awakening to the Self, he thinks "I am another," then he becomes possessed of *prakṛti*, his vision being unmanifest. But when he perceives the supreme intellect (*buddhi*), which is pure and stainless—
O tiger among kings, at that time, as the twenty-sixth [principle], he attains the state of Buddhahood.
Then he abandons the unmanifest (avyakta), which is subject to creation and dissolution; being devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), he knows Prakṛti, which is endowed with qualities and insentient.
Then, through the vision of the Unmanifest, he becomes one whose nature is pure dharma;
having united with the Absolute (Kevala), being liberated, he shall attain the Self.
This they call the Reality (Tattva)—the reality beyond all realities, ageless and immortal.
O giver of honor, because it rests upon the principles (*tattva*), this [unmanifest] appears to possess principles;
however, the wise declare that there are twenty-five principles. Yet, O dear one, this [supreme self] does not possess principles; rather, this intelligent being is beyond all principles.
12,296.015c For this one quickly releases the reality that is the characteristic of a Buddha.
12,296.016a The wise one, being grasped as "I am the twenty-sixth," who is ageless and immortal,
12,296.016c through his power alone, undoubtedly attains equality.
Though awakening by means of the awakened twenty-sixth principle, one who is still being awakened is not yet wise;
this is called "diversity" according to the teachings and illustrations of the Sāṃkhya. This refers to the twenty-fivefold aggregate when it is conjoined with the conscious principle.
When one does not perceive with the intellect that which is to be perceived, one indeed attains oneness;
O King of Mithilā, the perceiver becomes equal to the unawakened. Though his nature is free from attachment, O lord of men, he becomes subject to attachment.
Having attained the unattached Self, they know the twenty-sixth to be unborn. When the all-pervading Lord awakens to this, he abandons the unmanifest;
through the awakening of the twenty-sixth, the twenty-fourfold [principles] become unfathomable.
O sinless one, this has been declared by you according to the teachings of the scriptures as the unawakened, the awakening,
and the awakened in their true nature; thus should the diversity and unity [of beings] be perceived through the vision of the treatises.
Just as there is distinctness between a gnat and a fig, so too is there distinctness between these two;
just as a fish is [distinct] from water, so too is distinctness perceived.
In this very way, the multiplicity and unity of these two are to be understood.

This is called liberation, conjoined with the knowledge of the Unmanifest. They say that this [Self], which exists within these bodies as the twenty-fifth principle, must be liberated from the domain of the Unmanifest.
This very person is liberated in this way and not otherwise; such is the certainty.
Having indeed come together with another, he becomes possessed of the qualities of another.
That wise one possesses pure qualities through his union with the Pure One and the Awakened One.
O bull among men, having united with one who is liberated in nature, one becomes liberated; likewise, having united with one whose nature is discipline, one becomes disciplined in nature;
and so too, having united here with one who possesses liberation, one becomes liberated.
He becomes pure in action and indeed pure himself, possessing immeasurable radiance; he becomes a stainless soul by uniting with one who is stainless,
and likewise a solitary soul by uniting with that which is solitary.
And one who is independent attains independence through that which is independent.
This much has been told by me to you,
O Great King— the truth, according to the reality of things as they are.
O King,
for a person devoted to the Vedas, there is no [need for] accepting wealth through lack of envy, nor for the eternal, pure, and primordial Brahman.
This supreme teaching, which brings about awakening, should be given by you to one who desires to know it— an instruction for the sake of enlightenment to one who is bowed in devotion.
This should not be given to one who is false to his own self,
nor to the deceitful, the impotent, or the crooked-minded;
nor to one who inflicts injury upon others through the knowledge of the learned.
Understand this: this should be given by you to one who is endowed with faith, endowed with virtue,
and always refrains from slandering others.
To the one of pure yoga, to the wise,
to the active, to the patient, to the benefactor, to the one of secluded conduct, and to the lover of ritual injunctions;
To one who is free from dispute, possessed of great learning,
discerning, and incapable of enduring what is harmful— to one capable of self-restraint and tranquility among embodied beings.
This should not be given to one who is most deficient in these qualities;
they call this the supreme, pure Brahman.
What is done for such a person will not unite him with the highest good.
Even if one were to give this entire earth filled with jewels to a teacher of the Dharma,
one should not give this [instruction] to one who lacks vows.
"O lord of men, this supreme gift should undoubtedly be given by you to one who has conquered his senses.
O Karāla, let there be no fear whatsoever in you."
Today you have heard this supreme Brahman as it was truly spoken by you— supremely purifying,
free from sorrow, and without beginning or middle.
O King, having perceived that birth and death are bottomless,
and that [the state beyond them] is free from disease, devoid of fear, and auspicious,
abandon all delusion this very day.
O lord of men, having understood this true meaning of knowledge,
this was indeed obtained long ago from the eternal Dharaṇyagarbha as he spoke it.
Having propitiated with effort that one of fierce splendor,
just as you have today [propitiated] the eternal Brahman,
O lord of men, I have been questioned by you just as [I am now].
Thus have I spoken this to you today,
O lord of men; likewise, I have obtained from Brahmā that great, ancient knowledge of those who know liberation.
Bhīṣma said:
"O great king, this has been declared as the Supreme Brahman, from which one does not return again, according to the instruction of the Great Seers regarding the twenty-fifth principle."
Having attained supreme knowledge, one returns no more; yet, though perceiving [the truth], one who is not awakened does not realize it in its true essence, being subject to old age and death.
This which I have declared to you is the supreme among all forms of knowledge, leading to the highest good.
O King, having heard this in its true essence from the celestial sage Hiraṇyagarbha, it was told by the high-souled seer Vasiṣṭha;
and from Vasiṣṭha, O tiger among sages, Nārada obtained this.
This eternal Brahman has been made known to me by Nārada. Do not grieve, O lord of the Kauravas, having heard of this supreme state;
for one who knows both the perishable and the imperishable through this, no fear exists.
O King, fear exists for him who does not know this; and because of his ignorance, the deluded soul, repeatedly encountering calamities,
undergoes thousands of births ending in death after he has passed away.
Thus one experiences the world of the gods, as well as the realms of animals and humans;
yet, if in time one is purified from that ocean of ignorance,
having crossed over this fathomless abyss, one attains the supreme excellence.
The terrible ocean of ignorance is indeed said to be unmanifest and bottomless,
O Bhārata, wherein living beings sink day after day;
yet you have emerged from that unfathomable, unmanifest, and eternal state.
"Therefore, O King, you shall be free from passion (*virajas*) and free from darkness (*vitamaska*).
Bhīṣma said:
"Once, while wandering on a hunt in a lonely place, a certain son of Janaka..."
In the forest, he beheld the lord of brahmins, the ṛṣi who upholds the lineage of Bhṛgu. Sitting near him as he sat, and bowing his head to the sage,
Vasumān, having subsequently received his permission, asked this.

"O Blessed One, what might be the highest good for a man— both here and after death— who dwells in this impermanent body and remains under the sway of desire? Thus was the great-souled one of immense asceticism questioned with due honor.
Then he spoke these words to him, which are conducive to his welfare:
"If you desire things that are not disagreeable to the mind both here and after death, then,
with your senses restrained, desist from doing anything harmful to living beings."
Dharma is beneficial to virtuous men, and Dharma alone is the refuge of the virtuous.
From Dharma, O dear one, the three worlds, including all things moving and unmoving, have proceeded. O seeker of sweet pleasures, why do you not attain freedom from thirst for desires?
"O evil-minded one, you see the honey, but you do not see the precipice.
Just as one who desires the fruit of knowledge must cultivate familiarity with that knowledge,
so too must one who desires the fruit of Dharma cultivate familiarity with that Dharma."
For one who is unrighteous yet desires the Dharma, pure action is difficult to perform;
but for one who is righteous and desires the Dharma, even difficult action is easy to perform. He who dwells among the pleasures of the village while in the forest is just like a villager.

Like a forest-dweller who enjoys the happiness of the forest even while living in a village, remain composed and place your faith in the qualities of mind, speech, and action; having carefully weighed the merits and demerits of both withdrawal from worldly activity and engagement in it.
One should constantly give much to virtuous persons without malice;

what is requested should be given with ritual purity and self-restraint, honoring it according to the place and time. One should bestow upon a worthy recipient that which has been acquired through auspicious means.

Having cast off anger and given a gift, one should neither regret it nor boast of it. A twice-born man who knows the Veda— compassionate, pure, self-controlled, truthful in speech, established in uprightness, and purified by both lineage and conduct— is a worthy recipient.
In this world, a woman who is honored and has only one husband is considered a source of noble birth;
a learned man who knows the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and performs the six duties is called a worthy recipient.
That very same act may be dharma for one man and adharma for another, depending on the individual.
Depending on the specific nature of the vessel and having regard for the place and time,
just as a man might wipe away a small amount of dust from his body with ease,
so too is the removal of great sin accomplished through immense effort.
Just as clarified butter becomes a wholesome medicine for one who has been properly purged,
so too does the dharma pertaining to the afterlife bring happiness to one whose defects have been removed. Indeed, the mind operates toward all beings in both auspicious and inauspicious ways.
Having drawn [the mind] away from unwholesome things, one should cause it to enter only into wholesome ones.
A wise person should diligently destroy mental suffering by serving the elderly, bodily suffering with medicines, and verbal suffering through the recitation of mantras.
Honor everything that is being done by everyone everywhere;
wherever you have passion for your own duty, let that duty be performed according to your desire.
O you of unsteady self, abide in steadfastness; O you of evil intellect, become wise.
"O you who are not tranquil, become tranquil; O you who are not wise, act as if you were wise. Prosperity can be attained through energy accompanied by skillful means;
for both in this world and after death, supreme fortitude is its root."
The royal sage Mahābhiṣa,

namely Yayāti, fell from heaven because of his lack of fortitude once his merit was exhausted; yet, by means of fortitude and through service to ascetics, the righteous, and the wise, he regained the worlds.

"You shall attain vast wisdom and likewise achieve the highest good. Thus questioned by the king, the son of Janaka, that brahmin in the forest explained in its entirety the supreme dharma of the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama).
But he, endowed with a virtuous nature, having heard those words spoken by the sage,
turned his mind away from desire and fixed his intellect upon dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
That which is liberated from dharma and adharma, liberated from all dependence,
liberated from birth and death, and liberated from merit and demerit—
that which is auspicious, eternal, fearless, eternally imperishable, and undecaying.
"You ought to tell me that which is pure, eternal, and free from exertion.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
O Bhārata, [this is] the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Janaka.
The highly illustrious King Janaka Daivarāti, the best among those skilled in questioning, questioned Yājñavalkya, the most excellent of sages, regarding a certain question.
"O Brahman-sage, how many sense organs are there, and how many primal natures (prakṛtis) are traditionally taught?
What is the Unmanifest, and what is the Supreme Brahman; and what is even beyond that? Furthermore, [tell me] of its origin, its dissolution, and likewise the calculation of time."
O best of Brahmins, you ought to speak for me, who desires your grace. Out of ignorance I have questioned you, for you are a treasure-house consisting of knowledge.
Therefore, I wish to hear all of this without any doubt.
12,298.008 Yājñavalkya said: "Listen, O protector of the earth, to that which you ask concerning the supreme knowledge of the yogas and, in particular, of the Sāṃkhyas."
"There is nothing unknown to you, yet you wish to question me;
when asked, one must speak—this is the eternal law. Eight primary natures (prakṛtis) have been declared, as well as sixteen transformations (vikāras)."
Then, those who contemplate the supreme self declare that there are seven manifest principles: the Unmanifest, the Great One (Mahat), and likewise the Ego (Ahaṃkāra),
as well as earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
These eight are the primary constituents (prakṛtis); now hear from me also about the transformations (vikāras):
the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth;
and likewise sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
Speech, hands, feet, the anus, and likewise the genitals— these,
O King of kings, are the specific distinctions within the five great elements; and these,
O Maithila, are the organs of perception along with their respective objects.
Those who contemplate the course of the internal self declare that the mind is the sixteenth [element],
as do you and other learned men who are experts in the understanding of reality.
And from the unmanifest, O King, the Great Self (mahān ātmā) arises.

The wise call this first creation "the primary" (*prādhānika*). And from the Great One (*mahat*), O lord of men, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) arises; they call this the second creation, which is known as being of the nature of intellect (*buddhi*).
From ego (ahaṃkāra) arose the mind (manas), which consists of the qualities of the elements;
this is called the third creation, the creation of ego. But from the mind, O lord of men, the great elements (mahābhūtas) were produced.
O King, the great elements were produced from the mind; this is called the fourth creation, the mental one. Sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell—
Those who contemplate the elements call the fifth creation the "elemental" (bhautika).
The ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose as the fifth—
these they call the sixth creation, which is known to consist of manifold thoughts.
O Lord of Men, the collection of sense organs arises below;
they call this the seventh creation, known as that which pertains to the senses.
Likewise, O Lord of Men, there arises the upward-streaming and the horizontal-streaming [creations].
The wise call this the eighth creation, known as Ārjavaka;
then, O lord of men, the Tiryak-srotas and Adhaḥ-srotas are produced—
the wise call this the ninth creation, known as Ārjavaka.

O lord of men, these nine creations and the principles (tattvas) have been declared as twenty-four according to the scriptures and by way of illustration. Beyond this, O great king, is the reality of these qualities (guṇas).
"Learn from me the calculation of time as proclaimed by the great-souled ones.
Yājñavalkya said:
"O best of men, learn from me the calculation of time regarding the Unmanifest."
Ten thousand kalpas doubled is said to be his day;
his night is of equal duration. Upon awakening, O lord of men, he first creates the medicinal herbs, the sustenance for all embodied beings.
Then he created Brahmā, who arose from the golden egg;
we have heard that he is the embodiment of all beings.
Having dwelt within the egg for a year, the great sage emerged.
Prajāpati assigned half to the entire earth and half to the sky;
O King, this is recited in the Vedas: "Of heaven and earth. Between those two fragments, the Lord created the intermediate space.

And the calculation of this [day] by those who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas is as follows: ten thousand kalpas less one-quarter is said to be his day; those who contemplate the supreme self declare his night to be of equal duration.
The great seer first created from his body the seer Ahaṃkāra, who is a divine being, as well as four other sons; likewise,
there were the seven ancient great seers and the four Manus.

"O best of kings, those who are known as the Pitṛs are indeed heard to be the Pitṛs themselves. The gods are the sons of the Pitṛs, and by the gods the worlds—both moving and unmoving—are pervaded, O best of men; thus have we heard."
Parameṣṭhin, however, as the ego (ahaṃkāra), created the fivefold elements:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
They say that for him, too, this was the third night as he performed his work here.
Five thousand kalpas are said to constitute a single day;
sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth— these,
O king of kings, are the specific qualities within the five great elements.
O King, those beings who are possessed day after day by these [spirits] desire one another, yet they delight in each other's welfare;
likewise, they hold one another in high regard while competing with one another.
Being slain by one another through their captivating qualities, though they are immutable,
they revolve right here, entering the wombs of animals;
for three thousand kalpas, this is said to be their day.
O lord of men, night is of this same duration as the mind.
O king of kings, the mind moves through all that is experienced by the senses;
yet the senses do not see, for it is the mind alone that sees here.
The eye sees forms, but not by means of the eye; rather, it is by means of the mind.
When the mind is distracted, the eye does not see even while looking.
In this same way, all the sense faculties are said to "see."
When the mind has ceased, O King, the cessation of the senses occurs;
but when the senses have ceased, the cessation of the mind does not occur.
In this way, one should discern that the senses are subordinate to the mind.
"For the mind is said to be the lord of all the senses;
into it all beings here enter, O you of great fame.
Yājñavalkya said:
The number of creations of the principles (tattvas) and likewise the number of time-cycles have been declared by me in their proper sequence; now hear from me also concerning the dissolution,
how he withdraws living beings and creates them again and again.
Brahmā, who is without beginning or end, eternal and indeed imperishable,
having perceived the end of the day, remained in a state of sleep during the night;
then the Blessed One, the Unmanifest, impelled the conscious Person (Nara).
Then the Sun, whose rays are hundreds of thousands, being impelled by the Unmanifest,
divided himself twelvefold like a blazing fire and swiftly consumed the fourfold host of creatures with his splendor.
O lord of men, the beings born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat,
and those born from sprouts— all that is stationary and moving— perished in a mere twinkling of an eye;
then the earth became level on all sides, like the back of a tortoise.
Having burned the world, he of immeasurable power then quickly fills the entire earth with mighty waters on all sides; thereafter,
having encountered the fire of time, those waters go to their destruction.

O Indra among kings, when the waters have perished, a great fire blazes intensely. That immeasurable and exceedingly powerful Vibhāvasu, blazing forth, is the heat of all beings and possesses seven flames; he then appears directly.
The powerful and mighty wind, possessing eightfold nature and immeasurable vital breath, devoured [all] as it moved transversely, upwards, and downwards. Then,
space itself swallowed that formidable and irresistible one by its own power.
The mind devours the space that resounds even beyond it;

the mind devours all, for it is the universal self, the ego (ahaṃkāra), the Lord of Creatures (prajāpati). The Great Self (mahān ātmā) devours the ego, being the knower of the past, the present, and the future.
Even that incomparable Self, the universe, Śambhu, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati),
the imperishable light, the sovereign (Īśāna) who possesses the powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), and attainment (prāpti),
has hands and feet extending everywhere, and eyes, heads, and faces on every side.

Possessing ears everywhere in the world, he stands pervading all things. The high-souled Lord, the size of a thumb-joint, dwells in the hearts of all beings; indeed, that infinite master devours the entire universe.
Then everything became imperishable, undecaying, and without flaw;
likewise, [he is] the sinless creator of beings past and future, and of men. O Indra among kings, this dissolution has thus been explained to you exactly as it is.
"Listen to [the exposition of] the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva).
Yājñavalkya said:
"The Brahmins who perceive the truth say that the feet are the internal."
The organ of excretion is the *adhyātma*, they say those who see the meaning according to reality;
its *adhibhūta* is the act of voiding, and Mitra is the *adhidaivata* therein.
"The generative organ is the internal self," they say, according to the teaching of Yoga; likewise, pleasure is the external element, and Prajāpati is the deity.
"The two hands are the internal self," they say, according to the teaching of Sāṃkhya.
The object of action (*adhibhūta*) is that which is to be done, while Indra is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*) therein.
They say that speech (*vāk*) is the internal self (*adhyātma*), according to the illustration of the revealed scripture;
the object of action is that which is to be spoken, while Agni is the presiding deity therein.

12.301.006a "The eye is the internal [self]," they say, according to the illustration of the revealed scripture (śruti). 12.301.006c Form (rūpa) is the elemental substrate (adhibhūta) therein, while the sun is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) there.
12.301.007a "The ear is the internal [self]," they say, according to the illustration of the revealed scripture.
The exponents of the Sāṃkhya system declare that the ears are the internal (adhyātma);
sound is the corresponding element there (adhibhūta), and the quarters of space are the presiding deity there (adhidaivata).
According to the teaching that reveals reality as it is, they say that the tongue is the internal.
Taste is the *adhibhūta*, while water is the *adhidaivata* therein.
They say that the sense of smell is the *adhyātma*, according to the indications of the revealed scripture (*śruti*). Odor is the *adhibhūta*, while earth is the *adhidaivata*.
Those proficient in the knowledge of reality declare that the skin is the *adhyātma* (the internal self);
touch is the *adhibhūta* (the elemental correlate), while the wind is the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity).
According to the evidence of the revealed scriptures, they declare that the mind is the *adhyātma*.
The object of thought (*mantavya*) is the *adhibhūta*, while the moon is the *adhidaivata*. They say that the ego-principle (*ahaṃkārika*) is the *adhyātma* according to the vision of reality;
self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is the *adhibhūta*, and Bhava is the *adhidaivata* therein.

12.301.013 "Intellect is the internal self," they say, according to the teachings of the Vedas; that which is to be known is the external object, while the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the presiding deity therein. 12.301.013 Yogins of subtle vision declare that the mind is the internal self.
They call the Caitya mountain *adhibhūta*, and Rudra is the *adhidaivata* there.
O King, this manifestation of yours has been described by you in detail—
by one who knows reality, according to its true nature, in the beginning, the middle, and the end.
Prakṛti transforms the qualities (guṇas) at her own will and by her own desire,
O Great King, for the sake of sport, in hundreds and thousands of ways.
Just as mortals produce thousands of lamps from a single lamp.
In this way, primordial nature (prakṛti) transforms the many qualities of the person (puruṣa): goodness (sattva), abundance of bliss, joy, luminosity,
happiness, purity, health, contentment, and faithfulness.
Freedom from wretchedness, absence of agitation, forbearance, fortitude, non-violence,
equanimity, truthfulness, freedom from debt, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness;
purity, straightforwardness, proper conduct, lack of greed, and composure of heart.
Not boasting of the separation from the desired or the undesired that one has brought about, showing favor through giving, acting for the sake of others without desire for reward,
and compassion toward all beings— these are recorded as the qualities of *sattva*.
The aggregate of the qualities of *rajas* constitutes form within the embodiment of sovereignty: excessive greed, lack of compassion, indulgence in pleasure and pain,
delight in slandering others, and the pursuit of disputes.
Egoism, lack of respect, anxiety, the cultivation of enmity, remorse, deprivation, loss of shame, dishonesty,
as well as divisiveness, harshness, lust, anger, and intoxication— these are [the qualities of tamas].
Arrogance, hatred, and excessive speech—these are declared to be the qualities of *rajas*.
Now, listen as I describe the collection of those belonging to *tamas*:
delusion, lack of clarity, *tāmisra*, and that which is known as *andhatāmisra*.
Death is called *andhatāmisra*, and *tāmisra* is said to be anger.
Here, the characteristics of *tamas* are a craving for foods,
an insatiability regarding meals, and likewise a lack of satisfaction with drinks.
Delight in perfumes and garments, in monasteries, beds, and seats; delight in sleeping by day, in disputes, and indeed in various forms of negligence;
and, out of ignorance, placing one's trust in dancing, instrumental music, and singing.
Aversion toward specific qualities—these indeed are the *tāmasa* attributes.
Thus, this seventeenfold aggregate is designated as the Unmanifest (*avyakta*). It is joined here with all the objects of the senses, both manifest (*vyakta*) and unmanifest (*avyakta*).
This group, consisting of the manifest and the unmanifest, is called the "twenty-five.
