When joined with all of these, one is designated as "Puruṣa" (the Spirit).
Yājñavalkya said:
O best of men, these three qualities of Pradhāna always remain inseparable from the entire universe;
the Blessed One, whose form is unmanifest, exists in a hundredfold and thousandfold manner.

In a hundred ways, a thousand ways, and likewise a hundred-thousand ways, and even by the millions, he makes himself manifold from his own self. For one characterized by *sattva*, there is the highest station; for one characterized by *rajas*, there is the middle station in this world.
Those who contemplate the supreme self say that the lowest station belongs to one characterized by darkness (tāmasa). Through merit alone in this world, one attains an upward destiny;
through a mixture of merit and sin, one attains human status; and through unrighteousness, one attains a downward destiny.
Now hear from me, in truth, the pairs among these three, as well as their conjunction— of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Indeed,
*rajas* is seen to be associated with *sattva*, and likewise *tamas* with *rajas*.

Likewise, from darkness (tamas) one attains goodness (sattva), and from goodness, the unmanifest (avyakta). From the unmanifest, one attains goodness, and from goodness, indeed the manifest (vyakta). One who is united with the unmanifest and goodness shall attain the world of the gods.
Endowed with *rajas* and *sattva*, one is reborn among human beings;
joined with *rajas* and *tamas*, one is born in the wombs of animals; and when joined with *rajas*, *tamas*, and *sattva*, one attains the human state.
They say that the place of the wise, who are free from merit and sin,
is eternal, immutable, imperishable, and fearless;
it is the supreme birthplace of the knowers, a station that is without wound and undecaying.
That which is beyond the senses, seedless, and the dispeller of the darkness of birth and death; that supreme state abiding in the unmanifest—O lord of men, this is what I have been asked by you.
Indeed, when it abides in its own nature, it is designated as "the Stationary" (tasthuḥ).
"And this [Pradhāna], O King, is considered unconscious and abiding in its own nature;
presided over by Him (the Puruṣa), it indeed creates and also destroys.
Janaka said:
O great sage, both of these are indeed without beginning or end;
they are formless, immovable, unshakable, and without flaw.
O tiger among sages, both are ungraspable; how then is one of them insentient?
12,302.014c Thus, one who possesses consciousness is called the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field).
12,302.015a For you, O chief of Brahmins, worship the dharma of liberation in its entirety.
12,302.015c I wish to hear the dharma of liberation in its fullness, according to its true nature.
Tell me of existence and isolation, as well as non-existence; tell me of the deities who indeed reside within the body,
and likewise of the point of departure for the embodied one when they are separated from it.
"O twice-born one, tell me truly what station one attains through time; likewise, explain the knowledge of Sāṃkhya in its essence, as well as Yoga separately.
O best of beings, you ought to speak also of the signs of death (ariṣṭas) according to their true nature."
"All this is known to you, like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of your hand.
Yājñavalkya said:
"O dear one, O lord of the people, it is not possible to attribute qualities to that which is devoid of qualities."
"Understand from me, according to the truth, both the one possessed of qualities and the one devoid of qualities.
For those great-souled sages who perceive reality declare that one is indeed 'possessed of qualities' by virtue of qualities, and likewise 'devoid of qualities' when lacking them."
The unmanifested, whose nature consists of the *guṇas*, revolves toward the *guṇas* themselves;
it employs them alone, for by its very nature it is ignorant. But the unmanifested does not know, whereas the *puruṣa* is by nature the knower.
"He constantly conceives the pride that 'there is nothing superior to me. For this reason, this Unmanifest is insentient;
because it is eternal and imperishable, whereas the perishable [elements] are otherwise in their true nature."
When, through ignorance, it repeatedly brings about the creation of the qualities (guṇas),

and when it does not know itself, it is then called the "Unmanifest" (avyakta) here. Furthermore, because it is the agent of the principles (tattvas), it is likewise called the "possessor of the nature of the principles" (tattvadharmī).

Because he is the agent of the wombs, he is likewise called the one possessing the nature of the womb; because he is the agent of the primary elements (*prakṛti*), he is likewise the possessor of the nature of the primary elements;
and because he is the agent of the seeds, he is likewise called the possessor of the nature of the seed.
Because it gives birth to the qualities (guṇas), it likewise possesses the nature of procreation;
because it is the agent of dissolutions, it likewise possesses the nature of dissolution;
and because it is the agent of productions, it likewise possesses the nature of origination.
Because it is the seed, because it is the primal nature (*prakṛti*), and likewise because it is the place of dissolution;
because it is indifferent, because it is other, and because of pure self-conceit— thus do the pure ascetics, freed from the fever of the internal self, reflect.
"The unmanifest is both impermanent and eternal; indeed, we have heard this.
They say that the oneness of the unmanifest and likewise the multiplicity of the Puruṣa belong to those who are compassionate toward all beings and established solely in knowledge."
That other person is unmanifest, unstable, yet designated as stable;
for it arises from this just as the *iṣīkā* reed arises from the *muñja* grass.
And yet, due to its connection with the *muñja*, the *iṣīkā* does not perceive itself as the agent.
One should know that the mosquito is one thing and the fig tree another;
yet the mosquito is not smeared by its contact with the fig tree.
Likewise, the fish is considered to be one thing and the water another.
A fish is not smeared in every way by contact with water;
for fire is one thing and the cooking pot is another—know this always, O sir! Indeed, that fire is not smeared by contact with the pot.
The lotus is indeed one thing here, and the water is likewise known to be another;
the lotus is not smeared by contact with the water.
Such is their constant cohabitation and separation.
Ordinary people do not perceive him as he truly is, nor do they see him as eternal;
those who perceive him otherwise do not possess correct vision,
and they clearly enter the terrible hell again and again.
12,303.020a This supreme Sāṃkhya philosophy has been fully enumerated to you.

12,303.020c For it is by means of such complete enumeration that the followers of Sāṃkhya attain isolation (kaivalya). 12,303.021a But for those others who are skilled in the principles (tattva), this is the illustrative exposition.
12,303.021c Hereafter, I shall proclaim the exposition of the yogas as well.
12,304.001 Yājñavalkya said:
12,304.001a The knowledge of Sāṃkhya has been declared by me; now learn from me the knowledge of Yoga.
O best of kings, according to what has been heard and seen in truth:
there is no knowledge equal to Sāṃkhya, and there is no power equal to Yoga. Both of these are practiced as one, and both are traditionally held to be eternal.
But those men who, being devoted to limited intellect, perceive [the self] as distinct and separate— O King, we, however, perceive it as one alone through certainty.
That very thing which the followers of Yoga perceive is likewise seen by the followers of Sāṃkhya.
"He who perceives Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one is a knower of reality.
Know, O scorcher of foes, that there are other Yogas with Rudra as their chief;
by means of those very [powers], they roam through the ten directions even in this body."
For as long as the dissolution lasts, O dear one, wandering through the worlds at ease by means of subtle yoga endowed with eightfold qualities and having renounced [all attachments], O sinless one—
the wise declare that in the Vedas, yoga is characterized by these eightfold qualities.
O best of kings, they say that the subtle [state] possesses eight qualities, and not otherwise; however,

they declare the practice of yoga with qualities (*saguṇa*) to be twice as effective, while the yoga without qualities (*nirguṇa*) is the supreme among yogas, according to the indications of the scriptures.
12,304.008d*0774_01 Hereafter, O King, I shall explain breath control (prāṇāyāma),
12,304.009a as well as the concentration (dhāraṇā) of the mind and breath control, O King;
12,304.009b*0775_01 the one-pointedness of the mind and likewise breath control.

For breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is with attributes (*saguṇa*), whereas the fixing of the mind (*dhāraṇā*) is without attributes (*nirguṇa*). O best of the Maithilas, wherever one might be seen releasing the vital breaths, an excess of wind (*vāta*) certainly occurs; therefore, one should not practice it there.
In the first watch of the night, twelve exhortations are prescribed;
having slept during the middle [watch], there are likewise twelve exhortations in the final watch.
Thus, by one who is tranquil, self-controlled, and devoted to solitude—
The Buddha, who delights in the self, should undoubtedly yoke the self;
having cast aside the fivefold defects of the five sense-faculties— namely,
sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell.
O King of Mithilā, having withdrawn his creative intuition (*pratibhā*) and liberation,
and having indeed concentrated the entire aggregate of the senses within the mind,
he likewise established the mind in the ego (*ahaṃkāra*), O lord of men.
Likewise, one should dissolve the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) into the intellect (*buddhi*), and the intellect into primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Having thus performed this sequential enumeration, one should then meditate upon that which is free from passion,
stainless, eternal, infinite, pure, and without blemish.

One should observe, O Great King, the characteristics of one who is disciplined: the Puruṣa who stands firm as a being, indivisible, undecaying, and immortal; eternal and indeed immutable; the Lord and the imperishable Brahman.
The characteristic of serenity is like one who, being satisfied, sleeps in comfort;
or like a lamp filled with oil that burns in a windless place with a steady, upward-pointing flame— thus do the wise describe one who is disciplined.

Just as a stone struck by drops of rain rising from the clouds cannot be moved, such is the characteristic of one who is thus disciplined. [He remains unmoved] by the sounds of conchs and drums, and by various songs and musical instruments.

One who is disciplined should not tremble even when these [senses] are active; this is the illustration for one who is concentrated. It is like a man holding a vessel full of oil with both hands, ascending a flight of stairs while terrified and being threatened by those with swords in their hands.
With his self restrained out of fear of them, he should not let even a drop fall from the vessel; likewise for one who is ascending, with a one-pointed mind,
because of the steadiness and immobility of his senses.
One should observe the characteristics of a sage who is thus disciplined:
being disciplined, he perceives that Brahman which is supreme and immutable,
situated in the midst of great darkness, resembling a blazing fire.
By this alone, O King, one goes forth after abandoning the body which is without a witness, after a long period of time; such is the eternal Vedic revelation.
For this indeed is the yoga of yogis; what other characteristic of yoga could there be?
Having realized that, indeed, the wise consider their purpose fulfilled.
Yājñavalkya said:
Listen attentively, O King, to how [the soul] likewise departs.
For one who ascends by means of the feet, the station of Viṣṇu is declared;
by means of the shanks, however, one shall attain the Vasu deities—so we have heard; and by means of the knees, one shall attain the highly fortunate Sādhyas.
Departing through the anus, one attains the station of Mitra;
through the perineum, the earth; through the thighs, Prajāpati;
through the sides, the Maruts and the gods; and through the nostrils, the Moon.
They say that through his two arms he attains Indra, and through his chest, Rudra;
through his neck, O best of sages, he attains Nara, the unsurpassed;
and through his mouth he attains the Viśvedevas, while through his ears he attains the quarters of space.
Through the sense of smell he attains the bearer of fragrance (Vāyu), through the two eyes the Sun himself;
through the eyebrows the two divine Aśvins, and then through the forehead the Pitṛs.
Through the head he likewise attains the all-pervading Brahmā, the first-born of the gods.
O Lord of Mithilā, these points of departure have been declared;
now I shall describe the omens of death as ordained by the wise,
which may occur for embodied beings when their separation from life is imminent within a year.
Those who have never before seen the star Arundhatī,
as well as those who see Dhruva, the full moon, or a lamp as appearing broken on the right side— they too have but one year of life remaining.
O King, those who do not see their own reflection in the eyes of others—
appearing as a shadow-form of themselves— have but one year of life remaining.
Likewise, those with excessive luster or excessive wisdom, as well as those lacking wisdom or luster, [share this same fate].
The transformation of one's natural constitution is a sign of death within six months. One who disregards the deities and comes into conflict with Brahmins,
and whose complexion becomes dark or swarthy, has the signs of death within six months.
Just as one sees a hole in a wheel with a broken hub when looking at the moon,
so too does a man who smells the stench of a corpse even while encountering something fragrant become subject to death within seven nights.

But one who stays in a temple of the gods shall meet death within six nights. The drooping of the ears and nose, discoloration of the teeth and eyes, loss of consciousness, and loss of body heat are the signs of immediate death.
O lord of men, if one’s left eye should suddenly water,
or if smoke should issue from the head, these are signs of immediate death. Having recognized these many omens of death, a self-possessed man [should act accordingly].
Day and night, one should unite oneself with the Supreme Self,
awaiting that time which will come for each individual. If death is not yet desired, one should wish to remain and perform this practice.
Concentrated in mind, one should maintain all fragrances and tastes;
for by means of that supreme inner self, one conquers death. And having understood this very concentration along with Sāṃkhya, O bull among men.
And by means of yoga, with his inner self devoted to that [goal], he shall conquer death;
having attained the entire imperishable, unborn, auspicious, and undecaying state, he shall go to the eternal,
immovable station that is difficult to reach for those of unrefined soul.
Yājñavalkya said:
"O lord of men, you have asked me about that supreme state which resides in the unmanifest.
O King, listen with focused attention to this most secret answer."
O Lord of Mithilā, while I was practicing here according to the rishi’s rule with humble devotion, the *yajus* mantras were obtained by me from the Sun;
and through great austerity, the most fervent deity was served by me.
O sinless one, I was then addressed by the gracious Lord Sūrya:
"Choose a boon, O brahmin-sage, whatever you desire, however difficult it may be to obtain. With a joyful heart, I shall grant it to you, for my favor is indeed hard to attain."
Then, having bowed my head, I said to that best of heat-givers:
"The Yajus formulas have not been used; I desire to know them quickly.
Thereupon the Blessed One said to me: "O twice-born one, I shall impart them to you."
"Sarasvatī, having become speech, shall enter your body here. Then the Blessed One said to me, "Open your mouth. Thereupon I opened my mouth, and Sarasvatī entered it.
Then, O sinless one, being scorched by the heat, I entered the water out of ignorance and resentment toward the high-souled Bhāskara. That great sage named Vaiśampāyana was my maternal uncle.
"Let that which was studied by you from me be released," he said. Tormented by that indignation toward my high-souled maternal uncle,
I was then addressed by the blessed Sun as I was burning with grief.
"Endure this burning for a moment; thereafter you shall become cool.
And seeing me cooled, the Blessed One, the Maker of Light, said:
'O twice-born one, the Veda, along with its supplements, its appendices, and its commentaries, shall be established within you.'"
"O bull among the twice-born, you shall compose the entire Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa;
at its conclusion, your mind will be directed toward non-rebirth,
and you shall attain that desired state sought after by the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga."
Having spoken thus much, the Blessed One set toward the setting [mountain].
Then, having heard those words uttered after the god Vibhāvasu had departed,
I returned home and, filled with joy, meditated upon Sarasvatī.
Then the goddess Sarasvatī, adorned with vowels and consonants, began her most auspicious speech, beginning it with the syllable *oṃ*. Thereafter,
I offered the ritual water of honor (*arghya*) to Sarasvatī according to the prescribed rules.
Seated before the most excellent of those who radiate heat, with him as his sole refuge,
he then composed, with supreme joy, the entire Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa along with its secret doctrines, its compendium, and its supplements.
Having completed their studies, those one hundred excellent disciples [were employed] for the purpose of causing displeasure to my high-souled maternal uncle along with his own disciples; then,
together with my disciples, I was like the sun with its rays.
"O great king, the sacrifice of your high-souled father was seized;
even as Devala looked on, I took half of it away during the conflict with my maternal uncle over the sacrificial fee for the Vedas."
"O sinless one, Sumantu, Paila, Jaimini,
your father, and other sages likewise authorized me; thus,
O blameless one, I obtained fifteen *yajus* mantras from Arka."
In that very same way, the Purāṇa was mastered through the bristling of his body hairs;
likewise, the Purāṇa was also thoroughly grasped through the horripilation [caused by the Goddess]. Taking this as the seed and also the Goddess Sarasvatī herself, [he composed it].
O lord of men, it was by the power of the Sun that I was impelled to compose the *Śatapatha* Veda; it has been brought to completion for me,
and that path has been established exactly as I desired.
The entire and complete [teaching], along with its compendium, was authorized for the disciples;
and all the disciples, being pure, departed filled with supreme joy. These fifteen branches of knowledge were revealed by Bhāskara.
Having established [the fire] according to my desire, I reflected upon that which is to be known:
"What here is the truth pertaining to Brahman, and what is the unsurpassed object of knowledge?
While I was reflecting there, a Gandharva approached and questioned me.
Then, O King, Viśvāvasu, who was skilled in the knowledge of the Vedāntas,
having asked twenty-four questions concerning the Veda, O Ruler of the Earth,
asked a twenty-fifth question regarding the science of inquiry (anvīkṣikī).
O tiger among men, [he knows] the All and the Non-all, as well as the Horse and the Non-horse, Mitra and Varuṇa, and likewise Puruṣa and Prakṛti.

Knowledge and the object of knowledge, likewise the ignorant and the wise; one who performs penance and one who does not perform penance; "the sun-eater" and "the sun"—as well as ignorance and knowledge; the knowable and the unknowable, O King, and likewise the immovable and the movable.
"12,306.029c This unprecedented, inexhaustible, yet exhaustible question is unsurpassed.
12,306.030a Then, O King, I spoke to the king, that best of Gandharvas, who had asked this excellent and meaningful question in due order."
"Wait for a moment while I reflect upon this.
"Very well," the Gandharva replied, and he remained silent.
Thereupon, I further called upon the goddess Sarasvatī.

O King, that question of mine has been extracted from my mind like clarified butter from curds. Therein, O dear one, having perceived the supreme science of inquiry (*anvīkṣikī*), I churn with my mind both the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) and the remaining portion.
"O tiger among kings, this fourth knowledge concerning the hereafter has been proclaimed by me to you, established upon the twenty-fifth principle. Then, O King, King Viśvāvasu was addressed by me."

Listen to that which you have asked us here as a question: regarding this "the All" and "the Non-all" that you inquire of me, O Lord of Gandharvas— the All should be known as the Unmanifest, supreme, and the source of fear for all that has been and is yet to be.
Because he is the agent of the qualities (*guṇa*), he is threefold; likewise, because he is devoid of parts, he is not the universe (*aviśva*).
In the same way, the horse is a pair; thus it is observed. They call the Unmanifested (*avyakta*) "Prakṛti," and the one devoid of qualities "Puruṣa."
In the same way, one should regard Mitra as the Puruṣa and Varuṇa as Prakṛti.
They say that knowledge is Prakṛti, while the object of knowledge is indeed partless (niṣkala). Therefore, the Puruṣa is called both ignorant and knowing, yet he is said to be partless.
12,306.040a Who is said to be *tapas* (heat) and who is said to be *atapā* (without heat)? Who is that which is called the *puruṣa*?

12,306.040c They say that *prakṛti* is *tapas*, while the partless (*niṣkala*) is remembered as *atapā*. 12,306.040d The Sun is called the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), but that which is beyond the Sun is the partless.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) should be known as *prakṛti*, while knowledge (*vidyā*) is said to be the *puruṣa*.
One should know that which possesses the sun (*sūryā*) as *prakṛti*; that which lacks the sun (*asūryā*) is remembered as being fruitless.
One should know *vidyā* as the *puruṣa*, and *avidyā* as the supreme *prakṛti*.

In the same way, the unmanifest (avyakta) is said to be unknowable, while the Puruṣa is called knowable. You have also spoken of that which is "moving and unmoving"; listen to my explanation of that as well.
They declare Prakṛti to be the moving cause of both dissolution and creation.
The Puruṣa is traditionally held to be the unmoving agent of both projection and creation;
both are unborn and without progeny, and both are likewise imperishable.
Those who have reached certainty regarding the course of the supreme self declare that both are unborn and eternal.
Because it is imperishable in its procreative power, they call it the unborn (*aja*) and the undecaying (*avyaya*);
they call the Puruṣa imperishable, for no decay is found in him.
Because its qualities (*guṇa*) are subject to decay, the wise call Prakṛti perishable, but because of his agency (*kartṛtva*), they call the Puruṣa imperishable.

This is your fourth science, the *ānvīkṣikī*, which pertains to the hereafter. Having made knowledge one's wealth through constant ritual action, all the Vedas are traditionally held, O Viśvāvasu, to be the vision of absolute truth.

O best of Gandharvas, those who do not know the meaning of the Vedas— that which is to be known— even if they study the five Vedas along with their limbs and sub-limbs, are born and die in that [place] from which they have fallen.
He who carries the burden of the Vedas but does not know that which is to be known through the Vedas is indeed a bearer of the weight of the Vedas,
O best of Gandharvas; for he who, seeking ghee, would churn the milk of a she-donkey,
would find only excrement there, and neither cream nor ghee.
Likewise, one who knows the Veda does not perceive that which is to be known as either "knowable" or "unknowable";
he is considered merely a person of deluded intellect, carrying the burden of knowledge. These two must always be perceived with an inner self devoted to that [reality].
12,306.051c So that birth and death may not occur for him again and again;
12,306.052a having reflected upon this constant cycle of birth and death, he abandoned this triple Veda and took his stand in the imperishable Dharma that is not subject to decay in this world.
But when, O Kāśyapa, he perceives [the truth] completely day after day,
then, having become isolated (kevalībhūta), he beholds the twenty-sixth.
One is eternal and unmanifest, while the other is the twenty-fifth.
The virtuous perceive that one [Self] as two; therefore,
they do not recognize this imperishable Twenty-fifth [Principle],
even though the practitioners of Yoga and the followers of Sāṃkhya, seeking the Supreme, are terrified by the fear of birth and death.
Viśvāvasu said:
"O best of Brahmins, regarding this twenty-fifth principle which has been described to you,
you ought to tell me whether it is so or not so."
I have heard [this] from Jaigīṣavya, Asita, and Devala;
from the brahmin-sage Parāśara, the wise Vārṣagaṇya;
and from the mendicant Pañcaśikha, as well as from Kapila and Śuka.
Of Gautama, Arṣṭiṣeṇa, and the high-souled Garga;
of Nārada and Asura, as well as the wise Pulastya;
and then of Sanatkumāra and the high-souled Śukra.
I have already heard from my father Kaśyapa,
and subsequently from the wise Rudra Viśvarūpa, concerning the gods,
the ancestors, and the Daityas, from here and there.
"12,306.061c 'I have attained all this that is to be known, which they indeed call eternal.
12,306.062a 'Therefore, O Brahmin, I wish to hear that with your wisdom; for you are the foremost of those learned in the scriptures, eloquent and possessed of supreme intelligence.'"

"Nothing is unknown to you; you are remembered as a treasury of the Vedas (*śruti*). O Brahmin, this is proclaimed in the world of the gods and in the world of the ancestors, and even the great seers who have reached the world of Brahmā speak thus."
And the Sun, the lord of all that gives heat, constantly speaks to you:
"O Brahmin Yājñavalkya, you have attained the entire knowledge of Sāṃkhya,
as well as the knowledge of Yoga in its particular details."
"You have undoubtedly awakened to the understanding of all that is moving and unmoving. I wish to hear that knowledge, which is like the cream extracted from clarified butter.
Yājñavalkya said:
"O best of Gandharvas, I consider you to be one who holds all knowledge in its entirety. And since you wish to question me, O King, listen to this as it has been heard by me:
the twenty-fifth principle perceives the primordial nature (prakṛti) even though it is itself unperceiving."

But the Gandharva does not perceive the twenty-fifth principle (the Puruṣa). Because of this lack of awakening, those who know the truth through Sāṃkhya and Yoga call it *pradhāna*, according to the teachings of the Śruti.
O sinless one, another likewise sees both that which is seeing and that which is not seeing;
the twenty-sixth perceives the twenty-fifth and the twenty-fourth,
yet he who perceives this does not perceive it while he is perceiving.
The twenty-fifth [principle] should consider: "There is nothing else superior to me.
Nor is the twenty-fourth [principle] graspable by men who possess insight and vision.
Like a fish follows the water, it moves along with its movement.
Just as a fish awakens, so too does this [being] awaken;
through constant dwelling together, it becomes possessed of affection and always filled with pride. It sinks away when it does not perceive its oneness with Time.
For one who is enveloped by the sense of "mine" emerges from Time;
but when the twice-born man realizes, "I am one, and this [world] is another," then,
having become isolated (*kevalībhūta*), he beholds the Twenty-sixth.
"O King, one is inferior and another is the twenty-fifth;
because they abide therein, the virtuous perceive them as being truly one.
Therefore, they do not take delight in this imperishable twenty-fifth."

Frightened by the fear of birth and death, O Kāśyapa, the practitioners of Yoga and Sāṃkhya— pure and devoted to that as their supreme goal— behold the Twenty-sixth. When he has become isolated (kevalībhūta), he beholds the Twenty-sixth.

Then that all-knowing wise man does not undergo rebirth. Thus, O sinless one, I have described to you according to reality— the unawakened, the awakening, and the awakened— based on the evidence of the Vedas.
"Behold, behold, O Kāśyapa! He who perceives security and reality—
both the absolute and the non-absolute, the primordial, and that which is beyond the twenty-five," said Viśvāvasu.
"O sir, what you have spoken is indeed true and auspicious;
it is correct, secure, and divine, exactly as it is. May there be eternal and inexhaustible well-being for you."
"Salutations to you, who are always endowed with wisdom through your intellect.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Having spoken thus, he departed for heaven."
Shining indeed with a glorious appearance,
the high-souled one, satisfied and greeting me with supreme contentment, performed a circumambulation of me.
O lord of men, he indeed showed that very vision to Brahmā and the other sky-dwellers on earth, as well as to those who dwell below.
Those who have indeed resorted to the path that is truly secure and peaceful—
namely, all the Sāṃkhyas who delight in the dharma of Sāṃkhya, and likewise the Yogins who delight in the dharma of Yoga.
And those other men who desire liberation—
for them this vision is seen through knowledge;
from knowledge, liberation arises for persons.
"It is not through ignorance that they speak thus, O Lord of Men;
therefore, knowledge should be sought according to reality,
by which one may liberate oneself from birth and death."
Having repeatedly obtained knowledge from a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra of low birth,
one who possesses faith must always maintain faith in it.
Birth and death do not enter one who possesses faith.
All castes are Brahmins and born of Brahman;
all constantly utter Brahman.
I declare this truth, this scripture, with the realization that it is Brahman;
for this entire universe is all Brahman.
From his mouth, the Brāhmaṇas were produced.
From the two arms, the Kṣatriyas were indeed produced;
from the navel, the Vaiśyas; and from the feet, the Śūdras.
All the social classes (varṇas) are to be understood in no other way than this.
"O King, through ignorance they resort to the womb of action; just as they go toward various states of non-existence,
so too do those of the castes who lack knowledge fall."
From terrible ignorance arises the material web of birth;
therefore, knowledge must be sought everywhere.
I have told you that this [knowledge] resides in all things.
Brahmā remained, as did the other who had remained; the best of the twice-born say that eternal liberation belongs to him. That which was asked by you has been taught by me.
Knowing this as it truly is, O King, be free from sorrow; go to the further shore of this matter.
This has been correctly explained; may there be constant well-being for you here.
12,306.091 Bhīṣma said:
12,306.091a Having been thus instructed by the wise Yājñavalkya,
12,306.091c the king, the lord of Mithilā, was then filled with joy.
When that best of sages had departed after being circumambulated,
King Daivarāti, who was seated there as a knower of liberation,
touched ten million cows and likewise ten million pieces of gold.
Then he gave one handful of jewels to the Brahmins;
and having thus established his son in the kingdom of Videha,
the lord of Mithilā lived while practicing the dharma of an ascetic.
Studying the knowledge of Sāṃkhya and the entire Yoga-śāstra in its entirety,
O Indra among kings, he censured both dharma and adharma as merely material (prākṛta),
regarding them as eternal, absolute, and infinite.

O king of men, he reflected constantly that merit and demerit, virtue and vice, truth and falsehood, as well as birth and death, are all merely the activity of the unmanifest Brahman; such is the nature of Prakṛti, O lord of men.

The practitioners of Yoga and Sāṃkhya, who have established their definitions according to their own scriptures, behold that Brahman which is beyond the highest; for it stands apart, free from both the desired and the undesired.
The wise call it eternal; therefore, being pure, become pure.
Whatever is given, whatever one receives, and whatever gift one approves of— consider that all this is done by the Unmanifest; do not think otherwise,
O best of men, regarding both what one gives and what one accepts.
One gives the unmanifest itself and receives that very same unmanifest;
for the self is indeed the self’s own, being one and the same. Who else could be superior to you? Always think in this way; do not contemplate otherwise.
He by whom the Unmanifest— both with qualities and again without qualities— is not known,
by that unwise man must holy fords and sacrifices be resorted to,
O joy of the Kurus; neither by Vedic studies, nor by austerities, nor by sacrifices [is liberation attained].
O Lord of the Earth, having known the Unmanifest (avyakta), one attains its state;
likewise, one attains the station of the Great One (mahat) and that which consists of the ego (ahaṃkāra); and beyond the ego, one may also attain those higher stations.
But those devoted to the scriptures who know that which is eternal and beyond the unmanifest— freed from birth and death, and distinct from both being and non-being—
this [knowledge] was obtained by me previously from Janaka.
O King, he too obtained that distinguished knowledge from Yājñavalkya; for sacrifices are not like that,
for one crosses over the difficult passage by means of knowledge, not by sacrifices.
"O King,
those who possess knowledge do not say that birth and death are conducive to prosperity through sacrifices, austerities, observances, and vows."
Having reached heaven, they fall back to earth;
therefore, worship that which is supreme, great, pure,
auspicious, liberation, stainless, and holy.
"O King, one who knows the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) performs the sacrifice of knowledge;
by worshipping that reality, you will indeed become a seer (ṛṣi). At that time, he then imparted the Upaniṣad."
For in former times, Yājñavalkya taught King Janaka that which is reckoned as eternal and immutable; he attains that auspicious, deathless state free from sorrow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, having attained great sovereignty or wealth,
or even having obtained a long life, how might one transcend death?"
"By means of great austerity, or by ritual action, or by sacred learning,
or by the application of elixirs— by what means do one does not encounter old age and death?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation here between the mendicant Pañcaśikha and Janaka.
King Janaka of Videha [approached] the great seer, the most learned in the Vedas.
He questioned Pañcaśikha, whose doubts regarding the meaning of the Dharma had been severed:
"O Blessed One, by what conduct might one transcend old age and death— by austerity, or by wisdom, or by action, or by sacred learning?"
Thus addressed, he who knew what lies beyond replied to the King of Videha:
"There is no turning back for these two, nor is there any way to avoid their course.
For days do not return, nor months, nor again the nights."
This very person, though unstable, enters upon this path that is eternal;
he is the destruction of all beings, who is constantly carried away like a current. He is being swept along and submerged in the boatless ocean of time.
In this great sea whose crocodiles are old age and death, no one ever arrives [safe].
No one shall belong to him, nor does he belong to anyone. This meeting on the road with wives and other kinsmen is merely a temporary encounter.
12,307.009e For this eternal dwelling together has never been attained by anyone before.
12,307.010a They are cast away here and there, groaning again and again; 12,307.010c for those born and born again by time are like masses of clouds driven by the wind.
For old age and death are devourers of living beings like two wolves;
they prey upon the strong and the weak alike, the small and the great as well. Such is the nature of these beings, who are eternally subject to instability.
How could one rejoice when beings are born, and how could one burn with grief when they have died?
From where have I come, who am I, and where shall I go? To whom do I belong?
In what do I abide, where will I be, and for what reason do you grieve for me?
If you have truly renounced both yourself and [your possessions], what is the use of this [external act]?
For there is no one who sees heaven, nor likewise hell. Nevertheless, without transgressing the sacred scriptures, one should indeed give gifts and perform sacrifices.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O best of the Kuru rājarṣis, who has attained discipline through wisdom without abandoning the life of a householder? Tell me the true essence of liberation.
"Tell me, O Grandfather, how this self is renounced, who it is that has renounced the self, and what that supreme state of liberation is. Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Janaka and Sulabhā. Long ago, there was a certain king who sought the fruit of renunciation.
There was a king of Mithilā named Janaka, renowned as Dharmadhvaja.
He was thoroughly versed in the Vedas, the treatises on liberation, and his own [lineage’s] scriptures; having mastered his senses, he ruled this earth.
O Lord of Men, having heard of that virtuous conduct of that wise knower of the Vedas, other men in the worlds longed for it. Then, in that age of Dharma, they practiced the dharma of yoga.
A female mendicant named Sulabhā wandered alone over the entire earth. As she traveled throughout this world, O Lord of Mithilā,
she heard from various places the discourse on liberation being expounded by ascetics bearing the triple staff (tridaṇḍins).

Having heard that extremely subtle discourse, she became filled with doubt as to whether it was true or not; indeed, a longing arose within her to behold Janaka. Then, through the power of yoga, she cast off her former form.
Assuming another peerless form of faultless limbs,
the lotus-eyed woman of beautiful brows, moving with the swift speed of light weapons, traveled to the city of the Videhas in the mere twinkling of an eye.
Having reached the beautiful city of Mithilā, which was crowded with prosperous people,
she beheld the Lord of Mithilā under the pretext of wandering for alms. The king, having observed her supreme delicacy as well as her form, [was struck by it].
"Who is she? Whose is she? And from where has she come? he thought, overcome with wonder.
Then, having offered her a welcome and assigned her an excellent seat, he honored her by washing her feet and satisfied her with choice food.

Then, having eaten and being pleased, the female mendicant, amidst those who were experts in all forms of discourse, questioned the king who was surrounded by his ministers: "Is he liberated in matters of dharma, or not? she asked, still harboring doubt.
O Lord of the Earth, those skilled in yoga entered his being with their own being;
joining the rays of her two eyes with the rays of his two eyes,
she bound him, who was about to exert himself, with the bonds of yoga.
King Janaka, too, smiling and distinguishing her disposition,
that best of kings received her disposition with his own disposition.
Let this dialogue between them be heard in this single location.
"Where has this conduct of the Blessed One been performed—she who is liberated from the umbrella and other royal insignia, and free even from the triple staff? And where will she go?
Whose is she, and from whence does she come? Thus the lord of the earth questioned her.
In matters of learning, age, and lineage, true character cannot be discerned;
therefore, one’s reply regarding these points should be made when meeting with the virtuous.
Know me to be entirely liberated from all particularities, such as the [royal] umbrella and other such emblems.
"I wish to honor you, for you are considered by me worthy of respect.
Listen also to that [teacher] from whom this specific knowledge was previously obtained by me— one who has no other proponent regarding liberation."
"I am the highly esteemed disciple of the aged and great-souled mendicant Pañcaśikha, who belongs to the Pārāśarya lineage;
likewise, [I am proficient] in the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, in Yoga, and in the science of statecraft."
Having traversed this threefold path of liberation and severed all doubt,
he wandered here according to the path seen in the scriptures;
formerly, he dwelt happily with me for the four months of the rainy season.

By that foremost of the Sāṃkhya teachers, who had clearly perceived the truth in its essential nature, I was instructed in the threefold path to liberation, yet I was not moved from my royal duty. Thus,
I [adopted] that entire threefold mode of conduct associated with liberation.
Free from passion, I wander alone, established in the supreme state. Furthermore, detachment is the highest method for this liberation;
and it is through knowledge alone that detachment arises, by which one is liberated.
Through knowledge one exerts effort, and through effort the Great is attained;
that Great leads to liberation from the pairs of opposites—that is the perfection which transcends old age. This supreme wisdom has been attained by me, and with it, freedom from duality.

Just as a field that has been softened and saturated with water produces a sprout, so too does karma produce rebirth for men who have not yet dispelled delusion, even while they act here with freedom from attachment.
Just as a seed that has been scorched, whether in a potsherd or elsewhere, does not sprout even when it encounters the conditions for a shoot because it is no longer a viable seed— so too,
O sinless one, whatever action is performed by a mind whose latent impressions (*vāsanā*) have been exhausted [does not lead to rebirth].
Just as a burnt seed no longer produces a sprout,
so too by that Blessed One, the monk Śikhin,
has my knowledge been rendered seedless; it shall not arise again toward sense objects.

He does not become attached to anything— neither to what is harmful nor to worldly possessions— and he finds no delight in these things because of the futility of passion and hatred. And as for one who might sprinkle my right arm with sandalwood paste...
Whether one carves the left side of this [body] or the right, both are equal to me.
Happy am I, having attained my goal, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same;
free from attachment, I abide in the kingdom, distinguished among other triple-staffed ascetics.
For threefold is the final goal in liberation, as seen by the great seers of old:
namely, supramundane knowledge and the total renunciation of actions.
Some people, who are experts in the treatises on liberation, declare that the final goal is knowledge alone.
Likewise, other ascetics of subtle vision are devoted to action;
having abandoned both of these— knowledge and action alone—
this third state was proclaimed by that Great-Souled One.
In self-restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*), in hatred, desire, and possessiveness,
in pride and hypocrisy, as well as in affection— they are just like householders.
If liberation exists through the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) and other such signs by means of some knowledge, [then it must be the same for all].
12,308.042c How could it not be so in the case of parasols and other such things, when the cause for their appropriation is the same?
12,308.043a For whatever purpose a person has here in this world, by whatever means,
12,308.043c he takes hold of that very object, everyone in regard to his own respective possession.
But he who, seeing the defects in the householder’s life, proceeds to another stage of life—
even while abandoning some attachments and grasping others— is not truly liberated from attachment. For his sovereignty remains equal, consisting as it does of both restraint and favor.
12,308.045c By what cause are royal sages, mendicants, and teachers liberated?
12,308.046a Now, even though they possess sovereignty through truth, are those who abide in the supreme state liberated by knowledge alone, or are they not liberated?
Wearing saffron robes, shaving the head, the triple staff, and the water-pot—
these external signs are, in my view, not sufficient for liberation.
Even if these signs are present, it is knowledge alone that is the cause here.

12,308.048c For the sake of liberation from suffering here, the mere mark (liṅga) is useless. 12,308.049a Or rather, having observed the alleviation of suffering, the mind is fixed upon the mark; 12,308.049c why then is that same commonality of purpose not perceived in things such as umbrellas?
In the state of nothingness there is no liberation; in the state of having something there is no bondage.
Whether in the state of having something or in the other, a living being is liberated through knowledge. Therefore, regarding virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as the possession of a kingdom—
Know that I stand upon a ground free from bondage within these very places of confinement.
The snare consisting of royal power and sovereignty, bound by the attachment to the objects of affection,
has been severed here by me with the sword of renunciation, sharpened on the whetstone of liberation.
"Thus situated, I am liberated; yet you have conceived an attachment toward me, O mendicant. For your appearance is not what it seems; listen as I tell you this:
your delicacy, your beauty, your preeminent form, and likewise your youth—"

12,308.054c There is doubt whether all these [signs] together constitute a restriction; 12,308.055a and as for this conduct of yours, which is inconsistent with this outward mark: "Has he been liberated, or not?"—thus my possession has been provoked.
Even for one who is liberated, there is no triple staff (tridaṇḍaka) when joined with desire;
yet this [staff] is not being guarded by you, nor is there any concealment for one who is truly liberated. Furthermore, listen to the transgression you have committed by taking refuge in my side.
"Since you have by your very nature taken possession of my former domain,
by whom was your entry made into my kingdom and likewise into my city?
Or by whose instigation have you entered my heart?"
"You are a Brāhmaṇī, the foremost among the best of castes, while I am indeed a Kṣatriya. There can be no union between us; do not cause a confusion of castes.
You abide in the dharmas of liberation, whereas I am in the stage of the householder."
And this second confusion of life-stages (*āśrama-saṃkara*) is also very grievous for you:
you did not know that she was of the same lineage as yourself, nor did you know me. As you have entered into one of the same lineage, this is your third confusion of lineage (*gotra-saṃkara*).
"12,308.062a Now, if your husband is alive, even though he is away on a journey somewhere,

12,308.062c you are unapproachable as another man's wife— this is the fourth confusion of dharma. 12,308.063a Yet, out of regard for what ought to be done, you are resolving upon these improper acts."
Whether you are possessed by ignorance or by false knowledge,
or perhaps you are acting independently due to some fault of your own,
whatever learning you may have acquired has all been rendered useless.
This third sign of a corrupted woman, which obstructs the touch of true affection, has been observed and proclaimed; it must be declared.
Your intention, O seeker of victory, was not directed toward me alone, but was fixed upon winning [the contest].
"You wish to conquer this entire assembly of mine;
for in that very way, you again direct your own view toward the refutation of my position and the promotion of your own."

Deluded by the power of your own arrogance born of resentment, you once again discharge the weapon of yoga, which is like poison and nectar combined in one. For when both a man and a woman desire each other, their union is like nectar.
And for one who is not attached, even non-attainment is a fault here comparable to poison. Do not touch it; know this well and uphold your own scripture.
For you have made this inquiry of me as to whether I am liberated or not.
12,308.070e All this has been concealed from me; you ought not to hide it.
12,308.071a Whether it be for your own sake, O lord of the earth, or for the sake of another, 12,308.071c being thus disguised by a ruse, you ought not to conceal it from me.

One should never approach a king with falsehood, nor a twice-born man under any circumstances, nor a woman endowed with feminine virtues; for these, when approached falsely, will destroy one. Indeed, the power of kings is sovereignty, while the power of those who know the Veda is the Veda itself.
Beauty, youth, and charm are the unsurpassed strength of women. Therefore, those who desire their own welfare should approach these women with sincerity; for insincerity leads only to ruin.
"Therefore, you ought to speak truthfully regarding your birth, learning, conduct, disposition, nature, and the purpose for your arrival.
Thus [he spoke] with these unpleasant words, which were improper and inconsistent.
Though rejected by the lord of men, Sulabhā did not waver; when the king had finished speaking, the beautiful Sulabhā then proceeded to speak words even more charming.
Free from the nine defects of speech and the nine defects of intellect, it is endowed with meaning that is appropriate and possesses eighteen qualities:
subtlety, enumeration, both sequences, and a conclusion accompanied by its purpose.

"O King, these five categories of meaning are called a sentence. Listen now to the excellent definition of each of these meanings— subtlety and the rest— as they are further analyzed through words and sentences."

Knowledge operates according to the distinctions among the objects of knowledge; therein, the intellect that excels is designated as "subtlety" (*saukṣmya*). It is the precise measurement of both defects and virtues, categorized individually.

With a certain purpose in mind, that [arrangement] should be understood as *saṃkhyā* (enumeration). When that which one intends to say— whether it be "this first" or "this later"— is expressed according to its sequential order, those who know the nature of speech call that *vākya* (sentence) the application of sequence (*kramayoga*).
Having made a specific promise regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,
that which is declared at the conclusion of the statement as "this is that" is called a *vinirṇaya* (final determination).
Where an excellence arises amidst the sufferings born of desire and aversion— [that is the state of liberation].
12,308.085c O King, that which is the conduct therein is intended as the purpose.
12,308.086a These aforementioned qualities, beginning with subtlety, O lord of men,
12,308.086c being united toward a single goal— listen now to my statement.
I shall speak to you the supreme [teaching], which has a coherent meaning, an indivisible meaning, and is neither deficient nor redundant; it is neither harsh nor ambiguous,
and it is not bound by heavy syllables, nor is it turned away from the face [of truth].
It was not false, nor opposed to the three aims of life (trivarga), nor was it unrefined;
it was neither deficient, nor harsh-sounding, nor expressed in a disjointed order; it was not fragmentary, nor merely a secondary alternative, nor without cause or reason.
"O King, out of desire, anger, fear, greed, wretchedness, or even ignobility— I shall not speak at all, whether out of shame, compassion, or pride—
provided that the speaker, the listener, and the speech itself are all complete."
When there is a desire to speak, that object shines forth equally [to both parties]. But when a speaker, while having something to say, disregards the listener—
whether speaking for his own sake or for the sake of another— then his speech does not take root.

Now, when a person sets aside his own interest and speaks for the sake of another, suspicion arises regarding him; even that speech is considered flawed. But the speaker who declares the welfare of both parties without contradiction—
O King, that speaker—and no other—is for the sake of both the listener and himself. Therefore, this speech is meaningful and endowed with excellence;
O King, you ought to listen with an undistracted mind and one-pointed attention.
"O King, you have questioned me, asking 'Who are you? Whose are you? From where do you come? Listen now with an undivided mind to these words that constitute my reply:
Just as lac and wood, or dust and drops of water..."
O King, in this world, the birth of living beings occurs through these closely joined elements:
sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, as well as the five sense organs.
The self is distinct from these ten; yet they are joined together like lac and wood.
And it is this the certain conclusion: there is no impulse whatsoever for these [senses].
Here, the cognition of each one does not exist within itself, nor likewise in another. The eye does not know its own state as an eye; the ear does not operate within itself.
In the same way, they do not exist in mutual deviation;
though closely joined, they do not arise [as a single entity], just as water and dust here [in this world].
They depend upon other external qualities; hear from me about those as well.
In the act of seeing, three factors are the causes: the visible form, the eye, and light.
Just as it is here, so too are there causes for other instances of knowledge and its objects.
Within that interval between knowledge and the object, there is another quality called the mind.
By means of which he deliberates upon what is right and wrong for the sake of reaching a certainty; furthermore,
the twelfth quality there is known as intellect (*buddhi*),
by which one determines among those objects of cognition that are preceded by doubt.
Now, in that twelfth [category], there is another quality called *sattva* (being),
by which a living being is inferred as having great *sattva* or little *sattva*. Furthermore,
the fourteenth quality therein is also called *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).
"By that [wisdom] through which one thinks 'this is mine,' yet does not think it so—
O King, this is remembered as the fifteenth quality therein.
That which is the totality of the collection of distinct parts is here called *sāmagrya*."
Furthermore, there is another quality therein, the sixteenth, called "conglomeration" (saṃghāta), upon which rest these two qualities:
generic form (ākṛti) and individual manifestation (vyakti).
[Therein also reside] pleasure and pain, old age and death, gain and loss, and the pleasant and the unpleasant.
Thus, this nineteenth is known as the "Coupling of Pairs" (dvaṃdvayoga).
Beyond the nineteenth is another quality called Time (kāla).
Know that by means of these twenty [qualities], there is the origin and dissolution of all beings.

This aggregate consists of twenty parts: the five great elements, the two qualities consisting of the conjunctions of existence and non-existence, and the other two qualities which are illuminating. Thus, there are twenty-seven qualities that have been traditionally taught.

Method (*vidhi*), semen (*śukra*), and strength (*bala*)— these three are the supreme qualities. When these twenty-one and ten parts are reckoned together and exist in their entirety therein, that is known as the body.
Some maintain that the unmanifest (avyakta) is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of these constituent parts (kalā);
likewise, another person of gross vision perceives them as manifest (vyakta). Whether they be unmanifest or manifest, whether they be twofold or fourfold—
Those who contemplate the inner self perceive the primordial nature (*prakṛti*) of all beings.
This very nature is unmanifest (*avyakta*), yet it has attained manifestation through its constituent parts (*kalā*).
O Indra among kings, both I and you, as well as all other embodied beings, [are derived from it].
The stages beginning with the deposition of the drop (*bindu*), which arise from the union of semen and blood,
and by whose very occurrence the stage called the *kalala* is produced;
from the *kalala* arises the *arbuda*, and from the *arbuda* arises the *peśī*.
From the *peśī*, however, the limbs are produced, and from the limbs come the nails and body hair.
O King of Mithilā, when the ninth month is complete for a living being that has been conceived,
it is thus that the creature becomes fully formed in the ninth month, O King of Mithilā.

From that, the state of name and form arises, distinguished by gender as either female or male. As soon as that form is born— with its copper-colored nails and fingers— it undergoes the stage of childhood, and its [original] form is no longer perceived.
From childhood one reaches youth, and from youth, old age;
by this sequential order, each preceding stage is not attained [simultaneously].
There is a distinct differentiation of various parts at every single moment.
It exists within all beings, yet it is not perceived because of its subtlety. O King, neither their dissolution nor their origin is observed;
in every successive state, its movement is like the flickering of a lamp’s flame.
Even for one of such power, who runs like a noble steed, there is no end to the constant coming and going of all the world; from where does it come, or from where does it not?
To whom does this belong, or to whom does it not belong? From whence is this known, or from whence is it not?
What connection can there be here for living beings even with their own constituent parts?
Just as fire arises from the sun, from a gem, and from plants,
so too do living beings arise from the collection of various elements.
Just as you perceive the self by means of the self within the self,
why do you not likewise perceive the self by means of the self in another? This is so if you have resolved upon the equality between yourself and others.
"Then, why do you ask me, 'Who are you? Whose are you? for what purpose?

O King of Mithilā, for one who is liberated from the dualities of 'this should be mine' and 'this should not be mine,' what is the use of such words as 'Who are you?', 'Whose are you?', or 'From where do you come?'"
O protector of the earth, what mark of liberation can there be for one who has acted toward the enemy, the friend, and the neutral party, regarding victory, peace, and war,
yet here in this world does not clearly understand the three aims of life (trivarga) manifested in seven ways within his actions?

What mark of liberation is there in one who is attached to the three aims of life? What mark of liberation is there in one whose eye is not equal toward the beloved and the unbeloved, or toward the weak and the powerful?
O King, that pride you may feel regarding your liberation while you are not yet liberated must be restrained by your friends with medicines, as one would treat a person who has lost his senses.
O subduer of enemies, you should observe each and every station where attachment resides.

One should perceive [the self] by means of the self within the self; what characteristic of liberation could there be in that? Listen to me regarding these other subtle points concerning liberation—those bases of attachment which proceed through four factors.
He who rules this entire earth under a single umbrella is indeed but one king, and he dwells in but a single city; and within that city,
there is but one house which he occupies.
Even if one shares a single bed in the house at night where [the deity] dwells,
half of that person's bed is occupied by her first;
therefore, one is joined with this very fruit through such association.
In this very way, regarding enjoyments such as food and clothing,
and regarding limited virtues in matters of restraint and favor,
the king is always dependent on others; yet even for these small things, he becomes deeply entangled.
In the application of peace and war, how can there be independence for a king?
In matters of women, play, and recreation, he is always dependent; and in counsel within the assembly of ministers, how indeed could there be independence?

But when he commands others, then his independence is said to consist in this: that, though established in each respective quality (*guṇa*), he is made to act against his will. One who desires to sleep does not obtain sleep because of people seeking to have work done.
Even when permitted to lie upon his bed, he is awakened against his will while asleep;
"Bathe! Touch! Drink! Eat! Offer oblations into the fires!
Sacrifice!"—thus, rendered powerless, he is made to act by others with the commands, "Speak! and "Listen!"
Men constantly approached him again and again to beg,
yet he, a guardian of wealth, did not dare to give to the multitude;
for by giving, his treasury would have been depleted, and by not giving, he would have incurred enmity.
In an instant, faults that produce dispassion arise within him.
He suspects wise men, heroes, and likewise the wealthy—even those in his own presence. Fear arises in the king even where there is no fear, toward those whom he constantly attends upon.
And when those whom I have mentioned, O King, become corrupt, then fear of them arises for him; behold what kind of thing it is.
Everyone is a king in his own house; everyone is a householder in his own house.
Exercising both restraint and favor, he is equal to other kings, O Janaka.
For sons, wives, one’s own self, the treasury, friends, and accumulated wealth—
these are indeed common to others as well, through various causes of their own.
"The country is ruined, the city is burned, the chief elephant is dead"—
though these things are common to all the world, one suffers through false cognition. Not yet freed from mental sufferings arising from desire, hatred, and what is dear, [one remains bound].
Afflicted by diseases such as headaches and other calamities,
and struck by various pairs of opposites, he remains suspicious on all sides and passes his nights counting them while presiding over a kingdom full of enemies.

That [kingdom] brings very little happiness and is exceedingly full of suffering; it is devoid of essence, resembling a fire blazing through grass, and like a bubble on the surface of foam. Who would undertake sovereignty, once having attained tranquility?
"O King, as for this city and kingdom which you think, 'This is mine,' and your army, treasury, and ministers— to whom do these belong, or to whom do they not?
"The king possesses friends, ministers, city, kingdom, punishment, and treasury."

"O King, the collection of the seven constituent parts is called sovereignty (*rājya*). Of this sevenfold sovereignty, which stands like a triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) with its parts joined by mutual qualities,
which is superior to another in terms of its quality?"
For at various times, this or that constituent part is distinguished; whichever limb accomplishes a particular task is considered preeminent for that purpose.
Furthermore, O best of kings, there is the sevenfold aggregate, as well as three others.

This group of ten, having come together, enjoys the kingdom like a king himself. And that king who possesses great energy and is devoted to the duty of a Kshatriya should be satisfied with a tenth part; others, however, [should be satisfied] by those who are less than ten.

There is no king who is not common [to his people], nor is there a kingdom without a king. If there is no kingdom, whence can there be dharma? If there is no dharma, whence can there be the Supreme? Even that which is the supreme dharma here—the purifier of both the king and the kingdom—[depends upon them].
"He for whom the earth is the sacrificial fee— that horse sacrifice does not exist.
"O King of Mithilā, I am capable of recounting these deeds and the sorrows of sovereignty by the hundreds, or even by the thousands."
"I have no attachment to my own body; how much less, then, to the possession of another? You ought not to speak such words to me, who am thus liberated.
Surely you have heard the entirety of the doctrine of liberation from Pañcaśikha."
12,308.163c Accompanied by means, accompanied by secret doctrines, accompanied by implements, and possessed of resolve;
12,308.164a for you, who are free from attachment and stand having overcome the bonds— O King, how can there be attachment again toward specific things such as parasols and the like?
"I think what you have heard has not been heard, or perhaps what was heard was heard falsely;
or else, you have heard something else that merely resembles what is heard. Nevertheless, you remain established in these worldly designations."
Bound by both attachment and confinement, you are merely an ordinary man to me. For this entry into you that I have made was through my own essential nature (*sattva*);
what harm was done to you therein, if you are liberated from everything?
"For this is the rule among the duties of ascetics: dwelling in solitude.
And since I am dwelling in solitude, what of whom have I offended, O sinless one? Not with my hands, nor with my arms, nor with my feet or thighs."
"O lord of men, I do not touch you with any other part of my body. One born of a great lineage, possessed of modesty and foresight,
should not speak such words— whether true or false, whether done in private or in public."
"These Brahmins are gurus, as are these ministers, who are the highest of gurus; and you, moreover, are their guru. Thus, there is mutual respect among one another.
Therefore, having considered this, you must examine what should and should not be said."
"O Maithila, this union between a woman and a man must not be spoken of by you in public; just as water resting upon a lotus leaf remains there without touching it, so shall I dwell within you."
"Or even if you perceive some touch from me, though I am one who does not touch—
how has that knowledge been rendered seedless here by that mendicant?
He has fallen away from the life of a householder, yet he has not attained liberation, which is so difficult to know."
And you abide in the interval between both as one who teaches the doctrine of liberation.
For when there is the union of existence and non-existence for one who is liberated and one who is liberated, or for a knower regarding unity and diversity, no confusion of castes arises.
Regarding the distinctness of the castes and stages of life, for one who perceives the reality of the object as being non-distinct,
knowing that "one is not other than the other," nothing proceeds as something other than another. Just as the bowl is in the hand, the milk is in the bowl, and the flies are in the milk.
Through the connection of the supported and the support, we are distinct from our support;
yet, the state of being milk does not reside in the vessel, nor do flies reside in the milk.
These entities resort to their own [natural] support, and not to a support provided by another.
Since the stages of life (āśramas) are distinct and likewise the castes (varṇas) are different,
and because they are mutually separate, how can there be a mixture of castes for you?
I am not of the highest caste by birth, nor am I a Vaiśya, nor indeed a low-caste woman.
"O King, I am of the same caste as you, born of pure lineage and unblemished.
You have surely heard of the royal sage named Pradhāna;
know that I am Sulabhā, born into his family."
Mount Droṇa, Mount Śataśṛṅga, and Mount Vakradvāra—
these were piled by Maghavan together with my ancestors during their sacrificial sessions.
Born into that lineage, yet deprived of a husband such as myself, [I am here].
Disciplined in the teachings of liberation, I wander alone, observing the vow of a sage.
I am not disguised by a shroud of hypocrisy, nor do I covet the property of others. I do not cause the confusion of dharma; I am firm in my vows regarding my own duty.

O lord of men, I am not unsteady in my own promise, nor do I speak without due reflection; nor have I come into your presence without careful consideration. Having heard that your mind is resolved upon liberation, I, seeking what is beneficial, have come here.
I have come here for the purpose of inquiring into both your liberation and this [state] of yours.
I do not speak thus out of partiality toward my own side or against the other side; for one who is liberated is not being liberated, and one who is already peaceful does not need to become peaceful.
"Just as a monk might dwell for a single night in an empty house from of old,
even so shall I dwell this night within this body of yours.
Thus honored by you with the gift of a seat and with the hospitality of speech,"

"O King of Mithilā, having slept well, found a secure refuge, and being pleased, I shall depart tomorrow. Having heard these words, which were both reasoned and meaningful, the king could think of nothing further beyond them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull among the Bharatas, [tell me] the certainty regarding the principles of the unmanifest and the manifest.
Bhīṣma said:
O descendant of Kuru, you ought to tell us what the deeds of the unborn god are.
In this regard, they cite this dialogue between a teacher and a disciple.
Āsuri said:

O Blessed One of immeasurable wisdom, you ought to explain to me in accordance with the facts the liberation from all suffering for both Kapila and the lord of the Asuras, as well as the definitive determination of the principles of the unmanifest and the manifest, which is the certainty of the intellect.
What is manifest? What is unmanifest? What is more manifest than the manifest? How many principles (*tattva*) are there?
What among the principles is the first, what is the middle, and what is internal (*adhyātma*), elemental (*adhibhūta*), and divine (*adhidaivata*)?

What indeed is the attainment of heaven? How many creations are there? What has been, what will be, and what is to come? What is knowledge, what is the object of knowledge, and who is the knower? What is awakened, what is unawakened, and what is awakening?
"How many joints are there? How many streams? How many wombs of karma? What is unity? What is diversity? What is cohabitation and separation? What is knowledge and ignorance? Thus [he asked].
Kapila said:

Regarding what you have asked—what is the manifest (*vyakta*) and what is the unmanifest (*avyakta*)—we reply: it is the unmanifest. The unmanifest is that which is ungraspable, inconceivable, and immeasurable.

The unmanifest is perceived through its manifestations. Just as the seasons, though formless, are perceived through their flowers and fruits, so too is the unmanifest perceived through its qualities (*guṇas*).
It moves eastward, westward, upward, downward, and across.
And because the existent (*sat*) cannot be grasped, it is formless (*sākṛti*).
Of that which is unmanifest (*avyakta*), there are *tamas*, *rajas*, and *sattva*; that is the Pradhāna, the supreme reality, the field (*kṣetra*).
"Water, nectar, fearlessness, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the imperishable (*akṣara*), the unborn (*aja*), the living soul (*jīva*)"—these and others are names of the unmanifest. Thus it is said:
"The unmanifest is the great grasper of those things whose nature is that of seeds; it is insentient."
From that, the Lord was born as the single-fold quality; that is the manifest reality (tattva).
This is the unmanifest (avyakta), whose nature consists of procreation, maintenance, and withdrawal; [it is] water in its capacity for maintenance and procreation.
In the acquisition of virtues, its nature is always supreme vigilance toward that single cause and effect.
Furthermore, regarding what was asked—"What is the manifest?"—we reply:
that which was previously called "Asura" is indeed the manifest.

From the unmanifest (avyakta) is born the Lord (īśvara), which, abiding in the qualities (guṇas) of the unawakened, is designated as "Puruṣa" and is called "Mahat," as well as "Buddhi," "Dhṛti," "Sattā," "Smṛti," "Mati," "Medhā," and "Vyavasāya."
They speak of such things as "samādhi" and "attainment" as manifest synonyms.
Thus it is said:
"Success depends upon the great, and because there is great doubt."
For the sake of the manifestation of offspring and for the sake of supreme longing,
he— due to his orientation toward the upward stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and because of his own lack of awakening— produces the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*),
which is more unmanifest than the unmanifest (*avyaktāvyaktatara*).
Regarding what was asked— namely, "What is the more manifest and unmanifest?"— we reply: that which is called the "more manifest and unmanifest" is the third principle, designated as the Puruṣa.
Thus, the origin of each of these two— Viriñci and Vairiñca— is as follows:
Viriñci consists of egoism (*abhimāna*),
non-discrimination (*aviveka*), envy (*īrṣyā*), desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), greed (*lobha*), pride (*darpa*), delusion (*moha*), and the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*).
These are the synonyms for *ahaṃkāra*. Thus it is said:
"The Lord, as the *ahaṃkartṛ* (the 'I-maker'), created the universe. They know this third person to be characterized by the quality of self-conceit (*abhimāna*).
From the *ahaṃkāra*, he simultaneously produced the five great elements characterized by sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
These very [elements] are what perceive; thus it is said. The wise person who understands the creation of the elements from the *ahaṃkāra*...

Having transcended that great conceit, he becomes firmly established. Furthermore, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) among living beings is likewise said to be of a dissimilar nature. Again, for the purpose of being the cause of objects, it is known by the name "mind" (*manas*).
From the *vikhara* [state], one simultaneously produces the *vaikhara* [speech] together with the sense faculties:
namely, the ear, nose, eye, tongue, and skin;
these perceive sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
"12,308.191d@029A_0051" thus they speak of the five sense-faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*). The teachers say this: [the faculties are] speech, the hands, and so forth.
The feet, the anus, and the organ of generation—these five are the specific organs of action (*karmendriya*).
The sun, the two Aśvins, and the stars—these they call the synonymous names for the sense-faculties (*indriya*). Thus...
He said:

"Having thus produced the elements from the ego (ahaṃkāra) through the Great One (mahat) and the Self (ātman), one then understands the state of the manifest (vaikharatva); thereafter, the manifest consists of the objects of the senses."
Then, having understood the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) as residing within the realm of transformation (vikāra),
a person attains great sovereignty as long as the moon and stars endure.
Kapila said:
As for what was asked— "How many principles (tattvas) are there?"— these have already been previously stated by me;
thus he spoke.
He who correctly understands these principles as they have been explained will not be defiled by evil; he is liberated from all impurity.
Furthermore, regarding what was asked—namely, "What is the first and the middle among the principles?"—we reply: this [first principle] is the beginning.

It has been stated that the twenty-three principles (tattvas), beginning with intellect (buddhi) and ending with the specific objects (viśeṣa), constitute the middle [category] and are to be known; thus he spoke. To the question "By what means? it is said here:

Devadatta, Yajñadatta, Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, Caṇḍāla, Pulkasa, and so forth—these, beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with the particularities (*viśeṣa*), are to be known, reflected upon, and understood;
they have been thus described. This constitutes the first and the middle [categories].
From this, the origination of the principles occurs,
and herein they are dissolved;
thus say some teachers.
This aggregate of the body, characterized by the notion of "I," is manifest in the three worlds;
it is presided over by the unmanifest and the subtle.
12,308.191d@029A_0071 The vision of yoga for embodied beings known as Devadatta; however,
for those who do not see the Buddha-person, [it is different].

Regarding the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), the teachers say that there is one who is distinct from both the conscious (*buddhamāna*) and the unconscious (*apratibuddha*), who is indifferent (*upekṣaka*), pure (*śuci*), and free from error (*avyabhra*). And thus he says:
"But one who knows the twenty-four principles abides in the unmanifest (*avyakta*)."
"One who knows the twenty-five principles transcends even the unmanifest.
Kapila said:
"As for what was asked—'What is the inner self (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata)?'—we shall explain. First, the inner self:"
We shall explain the *adhibhūta* and *adhidaivata* with respect to the Asura.
Internally (*adhyātma*), the feet are the object to be traversed; Viṣṇu is the *adhibhūta*, and he is the *adhidaivata*.
The anus is the internal; emission is the elemental; Mitra is the presiding deity.
Pleasure is the internal; experience is the elemental; Prajāpati is the presiding deity. The hands are the internal; that which is to be done is the elemental; Indra is the presiding deity.

Speech is the internal self; that which is to be spoken is the elemental sphere; fire is the divine sphere. The nose is the internal self; that which is to be smelled is the elemental sphere; earth is the divine sphere.

The ear is the internal self; that which is to be heard is the elemental sphere; space is the divine sphere. The eye is the internal self; that which is to be seen is the elemental sphere; the sun is the divine sphere.
The tongue is the internal self, taste is the objective element, and water is the presiding deity.
The skin is the internal self,
the tangible is the objective element, and wind is the presiding deity.

The mind (*manas*) is the internal; that which is to be thought of (*mantavya*) is the external element; the moon is the presiding deity. Egoity (*ahaṃkāra*) is the internal; self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is the external element.
Viriñca is the presiding deity;
the intellect (*buddhi*) is the internal self (*adhyātma*), that which is to be known (*boddhavya*) is the elemental object (*adhibhūta*), and Puruṣa is the presiding deity.
Thus far, the internal self, the elemental object, and the presiding deity are to be understood in all cases.
He said:
"Whether toward a brahmin, a king, an insect, a dog-cooker, a dog, an elephant, a gnat, a mosquito, or a bird, one should be equal."
Through the union of the Unmanifest and the Puruṣa, the intellect (buddhi) arises within the self;
by that [intellect], this entire triple world, including all things moving and stationary, is pervaded. He who knows this triad—as pure, as distinct, and as indifferent—[attains liberation].
Free from passion and free from darkness, stainless, auspicious, and immutable;
liberated from doubt and confusion, devoid of sense faculties and without a lord;
without sprouts and without seed, one shall attain that eternal state.
