Regarding what was asked— "What indeed is the creation and dissolution?"— we reply as follows: Just as the four classes of beings— the viviparous, the oviparous, the moisture-born, and the soil-born— are [consumed] by the fire of time, which is produced from the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) and possesses many hundreds of thousands of rays.
Being consumed by fire, they dissolve into the earth;
having taken up its fragrance,
the earth, resembling the back of a tortoise, dissolves into the waters.
All that water became [fire];
even fire took up the water,
and it then became composed of fire.
He also takes up fire; that fire becomes wind. That wind blows upward, downward, and across;
thus it has become wind.
It became the wind; it even took up the ether.
That very ether became the resonance.
That ether dissolved into the mind.
The mind [is dissolved] into the ego, the ego into the Great Principle (mahat), and the Great Principle into the Unmanifest;
this is what constitutes dissolution. This dissolution, which ends with the Unmanifest, is called the "Great Dissolution" (mahāpralaya).
When all possessions have perished, that [state] becomes incomparable darkness;
it is ungraspable, indivisible,
impenetrable, inconceivable, beginningless, unthinkable, without support, without location, imperishable, unborn, and eternal.
Thus he spoke:
"He who understands in truth the extent of this creation and dissolution crosses over this inauspicious state and attains auspicious infinity."
Kapila said: Thus [ends the section].
As for what was asked regarding Āsuri—namely, how many types of creations, both primary (*prākṛta*) and secondary (*vaikṛta*), there are—[it is as follows:]
there are nine creations, both primary (prākṛta) and secondary (vaikṛta).
From the Unmanifest (avyakta), the Great One (mahat)...
It arises;
they call that the creation of knowledge (vidyā-sarga).
And from the Great One (mahat), the ego (ahaṃkāra) arises.
From the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) arises the creation of the five elements; from the elements arise the transformations,
because [they constitute] the entire world.
"This very splendor has its origin and its dissolution. Thus he spoke:
"He who knows the origin, the destruction, and the middle state of beings and of the self, and who knows both knowledge and ignorance—he is to be called 'Bhagavān'."
Regarding what was asked—“What is past, what is present, and what is future?”—we reply to this:
The past, the present, and the future are the three worlds and time within the realm of the Asuras;
that Great-Souled One is the present of both the past and the future.

He spoke thus: "Time is the creator of those things that bring about [other] creators, as well as their benefactor and their destroyer; it is the Lord (Īśvara), the fashioner of the past, the present, and the future."
Whoever understands this and proceeds accordingly is liberated from suffering.
From what kind of suffering?
From birth, old age, death, ignorance, deafness, blindness, being humpbacked, having deficient or redundant limbs, killing, bondage, disfigurement, anxiety, disease, and so forth.
Kapila said:
"And by many others...
Regarding what was asked, namely, "What is knowledge?", we shall now explain.
Knowledge (*jñāna*) is wisdom (*prajñā*) in the case of an asura.
That by which one understands what is to be understood is intelligence (*buddhi*). What, then, is that which is to be understood? To this it is said:
That which is to be understood is twofold, produced by the desirable and the undesirable.
For example: this is righteous (dharmya), this is unrighteous (adharmya).
This is to be spoken; this is not to be spoken.
This is to be done; this is not to be done.
This is to be grasped; this is not to be grasped.
This is approachable, this is unapproachable; this is fit to be heard, this is unfit to be heard;
this is visible, this is invisible.
This is edible, this is inedible;
this is fit to be eaten, this is unfit to be eaten; this is drinkable, this is undrinkable; this...
This is to be licked, this is not to be licked;
this is to be sucked, this is not to be sucked.
And from where do these [distinctions] persist?
Where do they dissolve?
To whom do they belong? Or to whom do they not belong?
To this it is replied: these abide in the unmanifest;
they are indeed the unmanifest.
They dissolve.
Regarding the question of whether these belong to the unmanifest (avyakta) or to the person (puruṣa), he says:
if [they arise] from the unmanifest...
These remain and dissolve back into the unmanifest itself.
By what cause, then, is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) now affected by the pairs of opposites produced by desirable and undesirable things?
Why does he conceive such pride? He says: "These pairs of opposites belong to me; I am theirs;
they abide in me, and they are utterly absorbed in me alone. Thus he speaks.
These qualities proceed from primordial nature;
enveloped by darkness, this ignorant person possesses perverted vision and falsely conceives, "I am the doer."
When this [person] conceives the thought, "These [elements] abide in the unmanifest; they are the unmanifest," he is not even capable of bending a blade of grass.
"These [elements] dissolve back into the Unmanifest; they are not mine. Then, through his connection with discernment (*vijñāna*), he becomes detached. Thus it is said:
"Nature (*prakṛti*) is like a bridge, the qualities (*guṇa*) are like water, and the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrī*) is like a fish."
Just as a fish moves about in water that has been stirred by its own nature,

so it is held that *prakṛti* creates the qualities (*guṇas*) through the operation of its own nature. That Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), who is wise and supreme beyond *prakṛti*, does not move among those who are ignorant.
As for what was also asked, "What is the knowable?"—
to this we reply:
the so-called knowable is the Puruṣa within the Asura.
"Thus he said: 'There are twenty-five principles (tattvas):
the unmanifest (avyakta), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṃkāra), and the five great elements (mahābhūtas);
and they say there are the five specific objects (viśeṣas), making eleven manifestors.'"
There are exactly eleven faculties; this much is designated as the "knowable.
Indeed, the five groups of five should be understood according to reality. Having known these twenty-five principles according to reality, [one attains liberation].
The pure person, freed from the [three] groups [of qualities], does not grieve;
knowing the twenty-five principles, he remains content in whatever stage of life he may be. He who knows the three triads within the pure Self merges into that very Self.
Regarding the question, "What are those three triplets? we reply:
the first is *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
the second is the producer (*utpādaka*), the sustainer (*anugrāhaka*), and the concealer (*tirobhāvaka*).
The Awakened One (*buddha*), the Unawakened One (*apratibuddha*), and the One Being Awakened (*budhyamāna*)— this is the third.
Thus, these three constitute three groups.
Thus he spoke:
"A person who understands the three groups of three as they truly are,
being completely liberated through action, mind, and speech, does not grieve."
Effect, cause, and agency—these are the qualities of the threefold group (trivarga).
What are the qualities?
They are the mere qualities, the definition of quality, and the constituent parts of quality.

The qualities are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Among these, the characteristics of *sattva* alone are: the vision of reality, the destruction of fear, a state of being established in one's own nature, clarity of the senses, and sleeping and waking in happiness.
Passionateness, envy, recklessness,
being tormented by misfortune, and awakening from nightmares— these are the qualities of *rajas*.
Delusion and being overcome by sleep are the qualities of *tamas*.

Hatred toward the Dharma, excessive delight in improper actions, and the loss of mindfulness— these are the constituents of darkness (*tamas*). Having worshipped the functioning of the qualities (*guṇavṛtta*), one who dwells amidst all beings is overcome by darkness.
He sleeps; purified of existence, he awakens. Immediately upon awakening from the dream, Kapila said:
"Thus [he knows] the constituent parts;
the wise one who understands them in this way is liberated from everything.
As for what was asked—"Who is the knower?"—to that we reply:
The Knower is called the *asura*, the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*);

he is the seer, pure, indifferent, the triad of knowledge, and superior to both the awakening and the unawakened. Having known him as partless and free from affliction, one is liberated from this suffering; thus it is said.
He said: "Indeed,
by knowing the stainless, pure, and unblemished [Self] beyond the twenty-five principles,
a person does not grieve, according to the teachings and demonstrations of the Sāṃkhya."
As for what was asked—namely, "What is the unawakened? What is the awakening?"—to this we reply: that which is called "unawakened" is the unmanifest (*avyakta*) within the *asura*;
that which is "awakening" is situated within the intellect (*buddhi*).
Apart from these two, he has spoken thus of that which is equanimous, pure, knowing,
and cloudless. Having understood the state of being beyond and within— that of the awakened one who is selfless and of the unawakened— one shall attain the fruitfulness of knowledge.
"But those who might understand it thus, according to the indications of the scripture," Kapila said, "among them,
O Asura, there was a threefold failure regarding the scripture."
Regarding what was asked—how many *parvan*s there are—it is said here:
there are five *parvan*s, namely:
*tamas*, *moha*, *mahāmoha*, *tāmisra*, and *andhatāmisra*.
"Tamas" refers specifically to ignorance;
"moha" refers specifically to indolence.
"Great delusion" (mahāmoha) refers specifically to sensual desire (kāma).
Why is that?
"Even for the great gods, dānavas, and maharṣis,
there arises a great delusion here"; by this,
he refers specifically to *tāmisra* as anger (*krodha*).
The term *andhatāmisra* refers specifically to despair;
and despair is death.
Furthermore, that [death] occurs for one who is unawakened.
Why?
Because one who, out of delusion, perceives "I am established in the *sattva*" sees, upon the destruction of that *sattva*, the destruction of the eternal *kṣetrajña*.
There, at one and the same time,
he encounters the blinding darkness of despair and thinks,
"I am going to die."
I am immortal because of my impermanence and because of my lack of cognition; yet, when death and birth reside within one's own body,
one clings to what is designated as another's body.

"I am yours," "you are mine," "I am the mother of my mother," "I am the son of my father"— in such ways he speaks regarding the objects of affection. Constantly bound by suffering, being cast into various states of birth, [he thinks], "May there be happiness for me."
Struck by all the dualities beginning with "this is my suffering," touched by egoism, possessed by envy, desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, arrogance, and intoxication, and afflicted by craving,
[he acts] in accordance with the inclinations of the sense faculties.
Because it is extremely difficult [to understand], one whose mind is fixed, performing only wholesome or unwholesome karma, will certainly be reborn among the stationary beings, in the hells,
or in the animal realm for hundreds of billions of infinite thousands of years due to a single lack of realization.
For thus it has been said:
He who, being ignorant, does not perceive each of these terrible joints [of time],
is bound by the nooses of death, possessed as he is by joy and sorrow. But he who is awakened, whose self is undepressed, and who has known the truth according to reality—
"One who has attained certainty through knowledge is liberated from the snares of death" (12,308.191d@029B_0138).
And as for what was also asked: "How many streams are there? (12,308.191d@029B_0139–12,308.191d@029B_0140).
To this we reply: there are five currents—
the primary current, the horizontal current, the upward current, the downward current, and [the transverse current].
Kapila said:
"And there is the stream of grace. As for what was asked, "How many are the sources of action? [the answer follows].
To this we reply:
there are five wombs of action (karmayoni),
namely, steadfastness (dhṛti), faith (śraddhā), happiness (sukha), the desire to know (vividiṣā), and the lack of desire to know (avividiṣā).
In this context, "steadfastness" (*dhṛti*) is the source of action. One who guards steadfastness by means of the threefold action arising from speech, mind, and body— thus it is said.

He who guards his promise in speech, in action, and in resolve— being established in that and firm in that promise, this is the specific characteristic of fortitude (*dhṛti*). Faith (*śraddhā*) is the source of action.

But he who practices faith [thinks]: "I shall attain the highest good through freedom from malice, self-restraint, and the like; through union with higher knowledge, celibacy, residence in the family of the teacher, the stages of the householder, the forest-dweller, giving, study, receiving gifts, and the recitation of mantras; and by means of the lunar mansions and religious observances."
"Perform your duties in this manner," he said. "Chastity, freedom from malice, charity, study, austerity,
performing sacrifices, and officiating at sacrifices— these are recorded as the characteristics of faith."
Happiness indeed has its source in karma;
he who desires happiness and is devoted to expiation practices it with supreme effort.

For example, it is said that truth, desire, anger, objects of the senses, cattle, Brahmins, and ritual action— these, as well as the *sāvitrī* and other various sciences (*vidyā*) belonging to the *anuloma* castes, lead many to the world of Brahmā. Thus he spoke.
But for one who exerts effort through ritual action (*karman*), knowledge (*vidyā*),

and austerity (*tapas*), that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and austerity itself shall be a characteristic for the sake of happiness. "The desire to know" (*vividiṣā*) is indeed the source of ritual action.
There is a desire to know everything; and one who longs for a distinction in learning investigates the scriptures, asking: "Where is perception? Where is non-perception? Thus he speaks:
"He who, having fully understood all this, indeed undertakes action."

This very desire to know (*vividiṣā*), when practiced as the source of action (*karmayoni*), is called "the absence of the desire to know" (*avividiṣā*); it is entirely a state of not wishing to know.
"Turning away from all actions"— thus he said: "He who,
having fully understood all this, turns away from actions— this is indeed that state called 'the desire to know' (avividiṣā), wherein the source of action has been brought to an end."
As for what was asked— whether there is unity or plurality—
we reply: Unity is that state,
O Asura, in which this *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) clings to existence (*sattva*), as well as to the manifest and the unmanifest.
Because it is not yet awakened, that unity is designated as such;
whereas what is called "multiplicity" is that which is traditionally held to evolve from this unmanifested existence.
This diversity is taught because of their awakened state.
Thus, for these four types of persons—the elemental, the egoic, the personal-spiritual, and the unmanifest—there is both unity and diversity by virtue of their *sattva*. So it has been said.

The unintelligent person who does not perceive this much—the distinction and the unity—is bound by all fetters; through non-attachment, one is liberated. As for what was asked: "What is meant by dwelling together or dwelling apart? [it is as follows:]

To this we reply: that which this *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) identifies with the *asura* called "Co-dwelling" (*sahavāsa*)— namely, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) due to its lack of awakening— is designated as "co-dwelling."

That which is called "departure" (vivāsa) is when this [being] returns from its dwelling in the unmanifest state back to the manifest; because it has awakened, this is designated as "departure. Thus, for those who are unawakened and attached to sense-objects—consisting of the elements, the ego-principle, the Great Principle (mahat), and the Unmanifest—this [occurs].
The cohabitation and separation of the four persons together with *sattva* [is established] because of their distinctness. And thus it is said:
"He who, though wise, does not perceive both separation and cohabitation..."
"Bound by association with sentient beings, he is not liberated from saṃsāra," so said Kapila.
As for what was asked regarding "what is knowledge and what is ignorance," we reply: ignorance is indeed the Asura.
This threefold knowledge regarding rebirth consists of that which is desirable, undesirable, and neither;
it belongs to the Asuras. However, the knowledge of *anvīkṣikī* (critical inquiry) regarding that which is beyond the desirable and undesirable pertains to non-rebirth.
She who grants fearlessness to all beings,
who is intent upon illuminating all worlds and awakening through all-encompassing knowledge,
and who has taught for the sake of liberation from all suffering— having approached such a teacher, [one attains it] through the vision of things as they truly are.
Thus he spoke:
"A wise person should not desire anything—above, below, or across;
for a human being does not find happiness through knowledge when ignorance persists."

From the state of humanity one goes to the state of divinity, and from the state of divinity back to humanity; thus he wanders incessantly, having fallen under the power of ignorance. But he who, having cast aside ignorance and awakened to the goal of knowledge, [proceeds further].

He who neither rejoices in knowledge nor hates ignorance is wise. Having understood and realized the bliss in both the further shore and the near shore, the enlightened one is liberated from the succession of bodies and attains immortality beyond the body.
Āsuri said:
"Venerable One, what is wholesome and what is unwholesome? What is with parts and what is without parts? What is total destruction? And what is pure and what is impure?"

"What is permanent and what is impermanent? What is absolute and what is non-absolute? What is beyond the beyond? What is visible and what is invisible? What is eternal and what is non-eternal? What is distinct and what is non-distinct? What is yoga and what is non-yoga?"—regarding these matters, doubt arises in me because they are not perceptible.
"This is directly perceived by the Blessed One;
therefore, may the Blessed One deign to repeat it for my benefit in accordance with the Dharma.
Thus spoke Kapila.
Regarding what was asked by Āsuri, "What is wholesome and what is unwholesome?",
we reply: that which is called "wholesome" (kuśala) is the state of having realized the true nature of things as it is, according to all the Vedas, all the treatises, and all the sciences.
12,308.191d@029B_0209 That which is called unwholesome (*akuśala*) is the state of all [beings] not having realized reality as it truly is (*yāthātathya*).
12,308.191d@029B_0210 They say that this wholesome and unwholesome karma constitutes a sentient being (*sattva*); indeed, these [two] are rooted in the sentient being.
The wholesome and unwholesome, having become sentient beings, go to their dissolution as sentient beings alone. Furthermore, one abandons the undifferentiated state of being a sentient being;
and this root of wholesome and unwholesome action is entirely [abandoned] within the state of being a sentient being.
Thus it was said:
"Threefold action is known to be performed by the body, fourfold by speech,
and likewise threefold by the mind— whether wholesome or unwholesome."
As for what was also asked— "What is the *varga* and what is the non-*varga*?"—
to this we reply:
that which is called *varga*, O Asura, is as follows.
The person consists of twenty-five principles (*tattva*):
the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great one (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*), the five specific objects (*viśeṣa*), and the eleven sense organs (*indriya*).

That is the group. From this square (varga), which is 12,308.191, the liberated one (apavarga)—the kṣetrajña, pure and indifferent, beyond both the awakened and the unawakened—has emerged. Thus he spoke.

Beyond the twenty-five is the Manifest; beyond that is the Ego (ahaṃkāra). Beyond the Ego is the Intellect (buddhi); beyond the Intellect is the Great Self (mahān ātmā). Beyond the Great is the Unmanifest (avyakta); beyond the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
"Knowing the higher and the lower among the principles of reality, one attains the unborn and unsurpassed.
Thus spoke Kapila.
Regarding what was also asked, "What is total destruction?"—
to this we reply:
total destruction (kṛtsnakṣaya) refers to [the destruction] of the asuras.
The Puruṣa consists of twenty-five principles (tattvas):

the unmanifest (avyakta), the Great One (mahat), the intellect (buddhi), the ego (ahaṃkāra), the five great elements (mahābhūtas), the five specific objects (viśeṣas), and the eleven sense organs (indriyas). These are to be known by the Puruṣa.
They arise from themselves; therefore, the principles [tattvas] are not mine, nor are they in me, nor am I in them, nor are all of them in every respect. Thus he spoke.

One endowed with right vision attains the total destruction [of defilements], whereas one who delights in wrong vision does not attain total destruction. As for what was also asked: "What is pure and what is impure?"
To this we reply: that which is called "pure" is the *kṣetrajña*, the seer who is a mere witness, superior to both the waking and the non-waking states.
One who knows the twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśatitattva) reflects upon what is to be reflected upon, perceives what is to be perceived, speaks what is to be spoken, and acts what is to be done.
Thus one acts because of being unawakened to the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
By the awakened Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), everything is seen:
all scriptures, all dualities, all forms of knowledge—heat and non-heat, purity and impurity.

By this path, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) who possesses impure qualities attains purity. By the wrong path, however, even after performing very extensive austerities, one sinks into *saṃsāra* alone due to a lack of awakening, because of the authority of knowledge, analogy, and scripture. Thus he said:
Even upon seeing a perfectly pure person, he considers him to be impure;
having undergone extensive asceticism, he remains established in the cycle of existence.
Kapila said:
12,308.191d@029B_0244 Thus it is said.
12,308.191d@029B_0245 Furthermore, as to what was asked—“Is it permanent or impermanent?”—to this we reply: It is permanent.
O Asura, the unmanifest is impermanent;
modifications are impermanent;
they declare the unmanifest to be impermanent.
Because modifications possess the nature of arising and ceasing,
they likewise declare the presiding agent to be impermanent;
because he is the agent who presides over the modifications.
For this very reason, because both of these are eternal, he has said that the *kṣetrajña* is eternal;
[he spoke thus] regarding the awakened one who is selfless, in contrast to those who are being awakened and those who are unawakened.
But having understood the eternal and the non-eternal, one shall not undergo birth again.
As for what was asked— namely, "What is the 'exclusive' (kevala) and the 'non-exclusive' (akevala)?"—
to this we reply:
The *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) alone is absolute (*kevala*), supreme, unconditioned by nature (*aprakṛti*), and changeless (*avikāra*).
Because it is presided over by the qualities of nature and its transformations, it is non-absolute (*akevala*).
The teachers [refer to] the person who is established in the Buddhi and is awakening.
For if he were to awaken, thinking "I am not these modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti)," he would be solitary and distinct [from them].

It would be so. However, when this [Self], presiding over these modifications of nature (*prakṛti-vikāra*), conceives the notion "these modifications of nature are mine" and "I am theirs," then, because it presides over the modifications of nature, it would not be absolute (*akevala*). Thus he said.

When, being awakened, he presides over the modifications by means of his intellect, then, together with the qualities (*guṇas*), he becomes subject to creation and dissolution. But when he perceives himself as distinct from the modifications, thinking "I am other [than them]," [he is liberated].
Then, having transcended the transformations, one shall attain the supreme unmanifest.
Kapila said:
thus [he spoke].
As for what was asked, "What is beyond the supreme?",
we reply:
that which is called "beyond the supreme" belongs to the Asuras.

The organs of action are superior to the organs of cognition; the mind is superior to the organs of cognition; the specific objects are superior to the mind; the gross elements are superior to the specific objects; the ego-sense is superior to the gross elements; the intellect is superior to the ego-sense;
the Great Principle (Mahat) is superior to the intellect; and the Unmanifest is superior to the Great Principle.
This very [state] becomes higher than the highest for the Asura;
this is the lower. But the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is other than these, characterized by neither creation nor dissolution.
The unmanifest (avyakta) and the person (puruṣa) possess the characteristics of neither creation nor dissolution; they are the non-awakened and the awakening one.
However, it is not merely because of being the awakening and the non-awakened that [this distinction holds].
The Buddha spoke thus:
"By understanding the unawakened and the awakening, and by knowing the higher and the lower regarding the selfless Buddha, one shall not undergo birth again."
12,308.191d@029B_0273 Thus, by perceiving through these two—the awakened and the unawakened—another who is truly awakened, one does not grieve.
12,308.191d@029B_0275 As for what was asked, "What did you see, and what did you not see?"
To this we reply:
Because it is without beginning or end and because it is an object of apprehension, the unmanifest (avyakta) belongs to the Asuras and is eternal.
It is impermanent because its intrinsic nature consists of the qualities of producing,
maintaining, and grasping; and other teachers likewise [describe] the presiding agent by means of this very [same principle].
By this reason, they describe [the self] as eternal;
yet the Blessed One, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), possesses the nature of a seed.
He is distinct from both primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*), and his nature is pure and liberated. Thus he spoke.
"The seer sees the one who sees and also sees the one who does not see;
because those two do not see, the seer does not see the one who sees and the one who does not see.
Thus [it is said].
As for what was asked, "What is distinct?"—
to this we reply:
that which is called "distinct" (*vyatirikta*) is, in fact, non-existent (*asur*).
The twenty-fifth principle is the person, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Just as a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf does not adhere to it because of their distinctness, so too is the field [distinct] from the knower of the field.
Just as the reed-stalk drawn out from the *muñja* grass does not enter back into it because it is distinct, so too is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) distinct from the field (*kṣetra*).
Just as a fish does not move along when the water moves because it is distinct, so too is the knower of the field distinct from the field.
Just as a gnat on an udumbara fruit, once the udumbara is broken, does not cling to it again because of their difference, so too is the field and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
Just as a tree falling from its bank leaves that bank behind because of their difference, so too [is the relationship between the field and the knower of the field].
The field and the knower of the field:
just as a bird, when flying up from a tree, leaves that tree behind because it is distinct from it, so too does the knower of the field leave the field.
Why? Because of their difference.
All things are thus different: the bank is one thing, the tree is another.
The gnat is one thing and the udumbara tree another;
the fish is one thing and the water another;
the muñja grass is one thing and the iṣīkā reed another.
The water is one thing and the lotus leaf another;
likewise, the field is one thing and the Knower of the Field is another— the Puruṣa, the twenty-fifth principle.
Kapila said:
"And there is another, distinct from this, called the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field).
As for what was asked, 'Is there separation or non-separation?'"
To this we reply: "Non-separation" (aviyoga), O Asura, means that no disjunction occurs between the object and the subject because of a lack of awakening.
"Separation" (viyoga), O Asura, means that the Puruṣa is unattached to the twenty-five principles and does not think "I am."
Not conceiving the thought "these others and these [others] are mine," one becomes free from attachment;
knowing the twenty-five principles, one becomes the Supreme Self and immortal.
Kapila said:
Released from that continuum of reality (tattva-saṃtāna), he attains equality with the Supreme.
Thus, O Āsuri, one who is unawakened perceives the Manifest as something other than the Supreme Person;
because of their distinct natures, the Unmanifest possesses the qualities of the Field (kṣetra-dharma), whereas the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) does not possess the qualities of the Field.

The unmanifest, characterized by the nature of a seed, is the field-knower (kṣetrajña) who is devoid of the nature of a seed; the unmanifest, characterized by the nature of emanation, is the field-knower who is devoid of the nature of emanation.
The unmanifest has the nature of *prakṛti*;
the *kṣetrajña* does not have the nature of *prakṛti*.
The unmanifest has the nature of the *guṇas*; [the *kṣetrajña*] does not have the nature of the *guṇas*.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
The unmanifest (avyakta) possesses impure qualities (avimaladharma), whereas the Knower of the Field possesses pure qualities (vimaladharma).
The unmanifest possesses the qualities of non-intelligence (abuddhidharma).
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has the nature of intelligence;
the Unmanifest has the nature of impurity, while the Knower of the Field has the nature of purity.
The Unmanifest has the nature of being unliberated, while the Knower of the Field has the nature of being liberated.

The *kṣetrajña* is unmanifest with respect to non-discriminated phenomena (*aviviktadharma*), yet it is the *kṣetrajña* that possesses discriminated phenomena (*viviktadharma*). The *kṣetrajña* is unmanifest with respect to unwholesome phenomena (*akuśaladharma*), yet it is the *kṣetrajña* that possesses wholesome phenomena (*kuśaladharma*).

The unmanifest has the quality of being insentient; the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) has the quality of seeing. The unmanifest has the quality of being unconscious; [the Knower of the Field] has the quality of consciousness.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is characterized by non-separation; the Unmanifest (avyakta) is characterized by separation. The Knower of the Field is characterized by non-liberation; the Unmanifest is characterized by liberation.
The knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is the one who possesses the nature of liberation. Furthermore, the knower of the field is the seer, and that which is to be seen is the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

The hearer is the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and that which is to be heard is the Unmanifest (avyakta). The thinker is the Knower of the Field, and that which is to be thought is the Unmanifest. The perceiver is the Knower of the Field, and that which is to be perceived is the Unmanifest.
In this very way, O Asura, the unmanifest is one thing and the Puruṣa is another; such is the twenty-fifth principle.
Kapila said:
"The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is distinct from this [unmanifest] and is another."
Having understood this thus through the intellect of an *āsura* (asuric) nature— one that is free from dualities, free from salutations, free from the utterances of *svāhā* and *svadhā*,
and free from egoism— one perceives the pure Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) by means of one who is free from dualities, peerless, pure, non-covetous, non-violent,
subsisting on whatever is obtained, and who has cast off desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and arrogance, and is self-possessed.
By one who perceives all beings, who possesses right view, who is self-restrained,
peaceful, and self-controlled; by one who dwells in empty houses, on riverbanks, at the roots of trees, in hollows of trees, in heaps of chaff, in sheds, or in huts—
anywhere at all— subsisting with food and clothing only for the sake of sustenance.
A monk who lies down should perform his own duty;
having conquered obstacles through mindfulness,
he should accomplish the task of yoga through application.
That meditation is of two kinds: namely, that consisting of breath control (prāṇāyāma),
which is fourfold and characterized by qualities (saguṇa), and that which is mental and devoid of qualities (aguṇa).

Just as the ear withdraws from things to be heard, the nose from things to be smelled, the eye from forms, the skin from tangibles, the tongue from tastes, the mind from objects of thought, the ego-sense from acts of conceit, and the intellect from objects of cognition; so too [does he withdraw].
Having restrained each of these deities of the collection of senses from their respective sense-objects by means of their own [mastery], he causes them to turn back;
he causes them to dissolve, as it were, into mental volitions like water-born creatures returning to the water.
He withdraws his mind from the senses,
and likewise withdraws it from mental volitions; having thus withdrawn it, the Great-Souled One directs his ritual intention upward.
The great sacrifices and the primary elements,
as well as the specific secondary elements, having distinguished the great self and the sacrifices within the Great Self,
pursue the manifest.

In that state, one who has transcended becomes secure; therefore, this [state] is disclosed. And from that, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) becomes unobstructed, free from dualities, without a second, pure, liberated, eternal, and solitary.
This is the end, this is liberation, this is the final goal, this is the state of actionlessness;
it has been taught exactly as it is by former teachers through the process of initiation.
Such is the instruction. On this point there is a verse:
"Just as a dream might occur to one who is awake, so it may be enveloped by darkness."
Kapila said:
"Liberation belongs to one who knows the distinction; however, he who is ignorant shall be born again.
Thus far, O Asura, has meditation been described."
Furthermore, an enumeration has been stated:
"These twenty-four principles are the cause. Regarding this, we say: that which is present in the intellect (*buddhi*) is being perceived.

The teachers maintain that this [Puruṣa] alone is pure because of his lack of awakening; they do not consider any other person to be devoid of qualities. But who is this one designated as the "presiding agent" (adhiṣṭhātṛ), distinct from the transformations of primordial nature (prakṛti) and yet incapable of remediation?

He has declared that this Puruṣa is distinct from that which is designated as both the primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikāra), being unmanifest (avyakta), pure, absolute, partless, unborn, and secure;
by him [is supported] this prolific mother along with her offspring, who clings to the world as her refuge.
He by whom men situated in the womb are always known through his intellect as if he were a Buddha,
who is the supreme seer, devoid of qualities, the fourth state beyond knowledge, and imperishable— he who,
being thus wise and liberated, conducts himself here, is superior to the womb.
"This enumeration has been described according to the vision of reality as a means for awakening those who have not yet understood," said Kapila.

Having extracted the nectar from the eight branches of knowledge—the Asura Vedas consisting of the five limbs along with the histories—I have described this Sāṃkhya knowledge; this much is to be known:
the twenty-five principles.
This should not be imparted to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who does not offer all his possessions,
nor to one who has not resided [as a student] for a year;
for it is the supreme knowledge— so say the seers.

"They shall know that which is to be known as proclaimed in the Vedas"— this they do not understand, being possessed by demonic nature and constantly defiled, having set out on a different path through the utterances of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *oṃ*, and *vaṣaṭ*.
There are infinite thousands of millions of sages who, by virtue of actions performed that are either desirable or undesirable,
as well as gods, dānavas, asuras, piśācas, bhūtas, rākṣasas, vidyādharas, gandharvas, yakṣas, nāgas, kiṃnaras, and others—
these various classes of beings who have resorted to the path of ignorance, rely solely upon ignorance; they are born.

Due to their repeated lack of knowledge, they are reborn many times over in the states of stationary beings, hells, and animal wombs for many hundreds of thousands of millions of years. By some rare chance, someone might even develop a sense of dharma;
how much less could there be a sense of liberation?
Desiring happiness through liberation itself, they strive only to avert disagreeable suffering;
yet, seeing nothing other than the three worlds as the source of existence, they fall headlong into the very depths of those three worlds, which they mistakenly perceive as the means of escape.
In the same way, even among the worldly views of the Asuras, the authority of the Veda is supreme.
Yet these [views] also serve only to set one upon the cycle of suffering in saṃsāra. Why is this so?
Because sacrifice is for the sake of the Veda’s meaning, heaven is for the sake of sacrifice, and happiness for the sake of heaven; thus, that which is desired is merely a locus of delusion.
Birth originates from delusion;
that birth, which has pleasure and pain as its cause, originates from delusion. In the very same way, death also [originates from delusion].
And that too has suffering as its cause;
therefore, this collection of mantras is the mutual cause of suffering.
Therefore, those who delight in tranquility and desire to cross the flood of the ocean of suffering abandon all the Vedas and apply themselves to the treatises on tranquility;
through the practice of those, [they attain their goal].
And they effect the severance of suffering and the path [to it] according to the teaching; they abide as one within their own self, having become cooled and attained the deathless. Thus he said.
Through the study of those teachings, the stream of suffering is turned back;
when the stream of suffering is utterly severed,
there is peace for the final end of suffering in this very life.
This very primordial knowledge was realized by me, the Asura, at the very moment of my birth;
therein the Lord Viriñca appeared within.
He cried out seven times,
yet no one gave him any reply.
Bhīṣma said:

Then, having bestowed [this knowledge], you, O Blessed One, have once again engaged in creation; thus you have withdrawn from it. This very supreme knowledge was taught with the highest reverence by the venerable Kapila, the supreme seer and teacher, to Āsuri.
The Blessed One [taught] the treatise to Āsuri;
Āsuri to Pañcaśikha; Pañcaśikha to Kātyāyana;
Kātyāyana to Gautama; Gautama to Gārgya; Gārgya to Āvaṭyāyana; and Āvaṭyāyana to the sages.
This supreme knowledge was obtained from the sages by the blessed Vyāsa through his extensive exposition; likewise, it was attained by me from him, and now it has been received by you from me.
Therefore, my dear, one should cause those Brahmins of firm vows to hear this.
[He saw] Kṣatriyas who were performers of sacrifices and devoted to the protection of their subjects; Vaiśyas, O tiger among kings, who had taken a vow to offer hospitality to all guests;
and Śūdras, intent on service and dedicated to the welfare of all living beings.

Even if there were three castes who are indeed entitled to participate in the sacrifice, the Śruti declares that for Śūdras, ritual action is seen to be performed "without mantras. This statement of the author of the Sūtras is, therefore, the word of the author of the Veda itself.
"We have heard that the authors of the treatises likewise proclaim this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"While living beings are suffering in the ocean of birth and death..."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that by attaining which one does not encounter suffering.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada;
the blessed Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, possessed of great fame; and his three elder brothers, who were exponents of the Veda, are here described.

Sanaka, Sanandana, and the third, Sanātana— according to sacred tradition, they were all enlightened as soon as they were born. And the fourth among them was that Blessed One, the most excellent of yogis.
The great seers indeed speak of him as Sanatkumāra;
the sage Vasiṣṭha is remembered as the fifth, born of Hiranyagarbha;
and the sixth is the blessed Sthāṇu, the immeasurable soul who bears the trident.
Then others were born from the fire during the sacrifice of Varuṇa;
indeed, there were the mind-born sons of the Self-existent One, headed by Marīci. Bhṛgu was the younger brother of Marīci, and likewise Aṅgiras was the son of Bhṛgu.
Then Atri was the younger brother of Aṅgiras; likewise, Pulastya was the younger brother of Atri.
The learned Pulaha, of incomparable splendor, was the younger brother of Pulastya. Indeed, these [sages] of immeasurable power are recited by the wise as the sons born of Brahmā.
O Great King, while performing this creation, the great primordial teacher— the Lord, the All-pervading One, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds, possessed of infinite glory—
[created] those who were embodied, immortalized, and endowed with splendor and supreme austerity.
There, Sanaka and the other two—these three—attained the supreme state;
having reached the total destruction [of the body], they were liberated from the bondage of form.
But the powerful Sanatkumāra, a knower of yoga, remained established in yoga.

He wandered through the three worlds with supreme sovereignty. And the highly illustrious Rudra attained eightfold yoga; he alone, O King, O best of monarchs, attained that subtle eightfold state, and no others.

"O dear one, all those headed by Marīci were appointed for the purpose of creation alone, O tiger among kings; hear from me about their creation. In the Purāṇas, this is established as the conclusion: that there are seven Brahmās."
They are declared in all the Vedas and in the Khilas, of this there is no doubt;
in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, this is the ancient Śruti. Those who have reached the further shore of the Vedānta say that she is called Varadā (the Giver of Boons).

"O dear one, they call these the fathers and the sons; O great king, there are seven classes, both embodied and likewise unembodied. And regarding the fathers, O lord of kings, the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that the gods are their sons."
12,308.191d@029C_0037 "These worlds are pervaded by the gods"— thus indeed have we heard.
12,308.191d@029C_0038 From Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, and likewise from Devasthāna,
12,308.191d@029C_0039 And from Devala and from Kāśyapa, O best of men, this was heard by me.
From Gautama, from Kauṇḍinya, and likewise from Bhāradvāja;
from Mārkaṇḍeya, and similarly from the seer Devatamāt;
and by my father as well, O king of kings, this was spoken at the time of the śrāddha ceremony.
O Indra among kings, this is the supreme secret of Brahman, the Supreme Self.
Beyond this, O Bhārata, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
listen to me with one-pointed mind and with faith, being fully attentive.
[This is] the dialogue between Svāyambhuva and the wise Nārada.
The blessed Sanatkumāra, having kindled a lamp with his splendor,
became the size of a thumb and wandered about as a great sage.
Once, O Great King, that best of men met on the summit of Mount Meru with the sage Nārada, a proponent of Brahman,
as they both sought to know one another’s views regarding the nature of Brahman.
O dear one, those two who have attained the portion of Brahmā are contemplators of the ultimate reality;
the wise one is the best among the wise, the intelligent one is more intelligent than others, the learned one is the best among the learned, and the mindful one is more mindful than others.

To Sanatkumāra, the knower of fields, the best among those who know the fields; the knower of knowledge, the most excellent among those who know knowledge; the knower of worlds, the best among those who know the worlds; and the knower of the self, the most excellent among those who know the self—to that Blessed One, the subduer of enemies and knower of reality.
Skilled in the meaning of all the Vedas and proficient in all the Śāstras, he who knew Sāṃkhya and Yoga as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of his hand—
Nārada, O best of men, then questioned that high-minded one.
O great sage, I wish to hear in accordance with reality the origin and the dissolution of the twenty-three principles, including the Unmanifest (avyakta),
as well as their internal (adhyātma), elemental (adhibhūta), and divine (adhidaiva) correspondences.
Sanatkumāra said:
"You ought to speak of the calculations of time and the creations.
Listen attentively to the nine creations in their proper sequence."
O best of sages, likewise [I shall explain] the measurement of time for the principles (tattvas),
as well as the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva) aspects,
along with the calculation of time and the entire process of creation, O great sage.

The creation performed by one characterized by darkness is designated as "tāmasa" by the twice-born who know Brahman and who are constant contemplators of the supreme self; wise men declare these to be its synonymous names.
I shall declare those to you; listen here with a single-minded focus.
They are Mahārṇava, Arṇava, Salila, and likewise Guṇa;
the Vedas, austerity, sacrifice, and Dharma, the blessed and all-pervading Lord.

"O Brahman-sage, these names— Prāṇa, Saṃvartaka fire, Vyoman, and likewise Kāla— are indeed proclaimed by me, O best of the twice-born, according to the authority of the scriptures as names of the Lord who possesses a body."
O subduer of enemies, those Brahmins who perceive the truth declare that a thousand cycles of four yugas constitute a thousand kalpas;
indeed, ten thousand such kalpas form the great night of the Unmanifest.
In this very way, the followers of Yoga and the Sāṃkhyas declare it according to the truth. Having slept through the night, the Blessed One then awoke at the end of the night.
O dear one, having spent the day happily, the Lord, the Sovereign, brought forth creation.
The universal self, Hiraṇyagarbha, born from the egg and born from the waters, the sage,
the sinless and all-pervading creator of the past, present, and future, the embodied Great Soul, the universe itself, Śambhu, the Self-born.

They possess the powers of atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), and attainment (prāpti), and are the supreme lords of all luminaries. Those who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas declare that his night is likewise five thousand kalpas, and his day is of exactly the same duration.
Brahmā does not create the evolution of the *tāmasa* [aspect] in its successive order;
rather, he creates the imperishable *ahaṃkāra*, the Supreme Lord (*parameṣṭhin*). Indeed, the worlds are pervaded by *ahaṃkāra* and that which is produced from *ahaṃkāra*.
Possessed by this, all beings— gods, sages, dānavas, humans, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras— sink into the ocean of the unmanifest, surging up,
sinking down, and moving upward, downward, and across.

They say that for him as well, while he performs the third watch of the night, there are three thousand kalpas; his day is exactly of the same duration. And the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra) indeed creates the five great elements.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth— these,
the twice-born say, are the five constituent principles (guṇatattva) of these [elements]: namely,
sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell.
Delighting in these qualities, they do not rise up, like elephants stuck in the mud; having lost their self-mastery, they remain attached in the ocean of the unmanifest.
Indeed, for those who perform this fourth creation here, [this is the case].
Twelve thousand three hundred and eight years and one hundred and ninety-one days constitute a day and night;
this fifth creation is known as Ananta. According to the evidence of the revealed scriptures, there are eleven sense organs.
O dear one, the mind, having entered the process of creation, pervades this entire world. No other elements are as powerful as the mind;
indeed, the twice-born say that its creation is the sixth.
A day indeed consists of a thousand kalpas, and the night is of the same duration. The Brahmins know the seventh creation to be that of the upward-streaming (ūrdhvasrotas),
while the eighth is the downward-streaming (adhaḥsrotas), and the ninth is recorded as the transverse-streaming (tiryaksrotas).
O great sage, these nine creations and the principles (tattvas),
O sinless one, have been declared to be twenty-four, as well as the calculations of time;
and likewise, O great sage, the dissolution and the origin of the unmanifest (avyakta).
I shall proclaim another truth: who is the lord of whom, as well as their respective *adhyātma*, *adhibhūta*, and *adhidaiva*. Sanatkumāra said:
Learn from me exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen:
regarding the downward-flowing creation and likewise the crosswise-flowing creation—
one should know the Lord (Īśvara) through these two, and likewise through the upward-flowing creation.

The Lord of the five organs of action is said to be the object of the intellect; furthermore, the mind is called the lord of the organs of perception. They say that the five elements, together with their qualities, are the lords of the mind.
One should know Brahmā Parameṣṭhin as the lord of all beings; for you are indeed skilled in the highest duties. Even the fire of time, your own day, consumes the world with its rays.
Then all beings, both stationary and moving, were reduced to a state of "Alas!
Alas! and consumed; they were indeed driven back to their own source of birth.
The earth, resembling the back of a tortoise, was stripped of its grass and thorns.
Then, burnt by the fire of time (*kālāgni*), the world was devoid of trees and even grass;
the world dissolved into the world, and the world dissolved into the waters. Then, with its fragrance lost and becoming subtle, it became water alone.
Then, by the network of rays from the sun, the water is absorbed;
at that time, O best of Brahmins, that which consists of water dissolves into the sun. Then fire consumes the beings situated in the intermediate space.
Then they declare that the sky becomes like fire;
indeed, the great wind destroys it as it thus flashes forth,
for the radiant sun takes it up with great force and speed.
When space swallows even the quality of wind, which is touch, then wind perishes; but space remains, resounding. At that time, the mind indeed takes up that sound, its resonance.
Deprived of the quality of sound, he indeed remains formless;
yet, O dear one, he then experiences space, which has the quarters as its essence. When the nature of space has dissolved, he increases as the essence of volition (*saṃkalpa*).
By its own power, the mind indeed takes up the self consisting of volition;
then, O best of sages, the ego grasps the mind,
and when the mind has perished, the ego becomes the Great One (mahat).
Then the Great Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), assumes the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
But when self-conceit (abhimāna) has perished, the Great Brahmā shines forth. At that time, he is born as the primordial form within the forms of the three worlds.
By him, who seeks the qualities of creation, this entire universe was fashioned;
even the Lord of Waters took form, consisting of the nature of resolute effort. The Blessed Brahmā, the consumer, is manifest as the unmanifest without a doubt.
This dissolution and its passing away have been described by me to you;

now hear concerning the internal (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaiva). Space is the first element; the ear is the internal; sound is the elemental; and the quarters are the presiding deity.

Wind is the second element; internally it is the skin, externally it is touch, and its presiding deity is lightning. Light is the third element; internally it is the eye, externally it is form, and its presiding deity is the sun.
Water is the fourth element; the internal organ is the tongue, the external element is taste, and Soma is the presiding deity.
Earth is the fifth element; the internal organ is the sense of smell.
The fragrance is the presiding element (*adhibhūta*), and the wind is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). These four have been described as consisting of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*).

From this point forward, we shall describe the threefold rule of the faculties (*indriya*). The feet are the internal (*adhyātma*); that which is to be traversed is the objective element (*adhibhūta*); and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*).
The hands are the internal self;
their external correlate is action, and Indra is the presiding deity.
The anus is the internal self; its external correlate is excretion.
Mitra would be the presiding deity;
the lap is the internal self, and bliss is the elemental correlate;
Prajāpati would be the presiding deity.

Speech is the internal self (*adhyātma*); that which is to be spoken is the external object (*adhibhūta*); fire (*agni*) is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). Mind is the internal self; that which is to be thought is the external object; the moon (*candramas*) is the presiding deity. Ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is the internal self; the sense of "I" (*abhimāna*) is the external object; Viriñca is the presiding deity.
Intellect (*buddhi*) would be the internal, resolve (*vyavasāya*) the elemental, and Brahmā the divine. In this way, the Blessed Unmanifest repeatedly creates and repeatedly withdraws the worlds.
Why? For the sake of sport (*krīḍārtham*).

Just as the sun casts forth its web of rays and withdraws them again, and just as a mass of clouds arises from the atmosphere accompanied by thunder and rumbling, and then dissolves back into that very place; so too is it with the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

In this way, the unmanifest creates and withdraws the qualities (*guṇas*). Just as a network of waves, rising and falling, emerges from the ocean and subsides back into it, so too does the unmanifest create the worlds.
And he withdraws them;
just as a tortoise extends its limbs out of desire and then draws them back in again, so the Unmanifest extends the worlds and swallows them up.

The Blessed One, the twenty-fifth, is conscious and pure. Presided over by him, primordial nature (prakṛti) becomes conscious. He is eternal, co-existent with the dharmas, and while the Blessed Unmanifested One is active, the Blessed Supreme Primordial Nature is inactive.
Nārada said:
"The *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field) is atomic and secure.
If primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is insentient and yet brings about consciousness when presided over by a conscious being, why is there no liberation?"
For those like you who desire the mind, the practitioners of Yoga and Sāṃkhya indeed teach a "twenty-fifth" [principle] as the mind;
yet they teach that which is incorrect.
And because of that deception, it conforms to the present nature as ten thousand types of co-arising dharmas; thus, from conforming [to it],...
And we consider that [the mind] is "consciousness" because it possesses presiding power and because it is minute;
and for this reason, the fault indeed remains. For example, it is like someone who, possessing a companion, travels a long distance.
For one who is unattached and possesses the scriptures,
there is no purpose in going; yet if he does go, even he is attached.
The fish and the water are indeed co-existent;
thus, according to the word of the Blessed One,
are *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*.
"If a fish follows along with flowing water, is it not indeed attached?
Sanatkumāra said:
"The fish remains unattached; what is the use of its following the mode of the water's flow?"
"O divine seer, they describe the non-attachment of a person in that state; for the Blessed One, who is devoid of qualities, there is no attachment to that which possesses qualities."
Regarding this, the wise recite these verses;
listen to them as they provide synonymous expressions for a single meaning:
"The person is eternally established by nature, and not by means of a self."
He possesses conceit; therefore it is called attachment. Consciousness belongs eternally to the person, not to time nor to the self. He possesses conceit; therefore it is called attachment.
For the person (puruṣa) is eternally the seer of the mind, but not of the self (ātman). Because of that [mind], he has the conceit (abhimāna); therefore, it is called attachment (āsaṅga).
For the person is eternally the knower of the Veda, but not of the self.
He develops conceit; therefore it is called attachment. For the person is always the knower of the field, but not of himself;
he develops conceit; therefore it is called attachment.
For the person is eternally the agent of another and not of himself;
because he possesses conceit regarding that [agency], it is therefore called attachment (*āsaṅga*).
O celestial sage, they describe this very attachment in relation to the person.
For the Blessed One is pure;
they declare the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) to be impure by nature. For he who is attached becomes possessed of attachment.
Regarding the term "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*): he who perceives the self, which is indeed unattached, as being attached is called ignorant by the wise here.
For him who is seized by ignorance and is being submerged hundreds of thousands of millions of times in the ocean of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), [this state continues].
A very great conjunction of suffering occurs,
just as for a caravan of merchants seeking wealth who have set out upon the ocean and whose ship has entered the belly of the sea, even though they have performed their penance.
Being torn apart here and there by fierce winds and being shattered by pure waves, the people, crying out "Alas! Alas!", would perish;
and hundreds would have their desires unfulfilled.
Having seized the rafts,
they hang on to them as the rafts bob up and down, one after another.
In this way, the ignorant person rises and sinks;
yet, just as someone rising and sinking therein might reach the further shore, he is then liberated from that calamity— the jaws of death.
Nārada said:

O Blessed One, when primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is indestructible, indivisible, unburnable, inconceivable, infinite, unfashionable, and without beginning, middle, or end, the person (*puruṣa*) likewise possesses these very same qualities.
"How then do they describe the impermanent *prakṛti* as eternal, while the *puruṣa* is eternal? Sanatkumāra said:

"O divine sage, you have spoken correctly. For both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*) are indeed indestructible, indivisible, unburnable, inconceivable, infinite, unfathomable, and without beginning or middle."
Because it possesses agency, they declare *prakṛti* to be impermanent; because it lacks agency, the *puruṣa* is eternal. If [it were] *prakṛti*...
One should cultivate virtues and know oneself as both a person and [the self];
furthermore, there is the state of being free from passion regarding the permanent and the impermanent,
as well as his freedom from the pairs of opposites.
But when one thinks, "This alone shall be mine; there is nothing else superior to me," one attains the state of permanence.
Regarding this, they cite these verses:

Indeed, both are formless and both are undecaying; they are known by the great-souled ones as the subject and the object, O great sage. The Puruṣa is eternally the subject, while Prakṛti is traditionally held to be the object.
For as the experts in the scriptures have explained the case of the gnat and the fig tree:
Nature, being insentient, does not perceive that it is being enjoyed;
whereas the Puruṣa perceives it, and he who enjoys is that which is enjoyed.
"O twice-born one, the qualities beginning with the Great One (mahat) are the object of enjoyment, while Prakṛti is the enjoyer.
Those who understand this distinction consider the enjoyer to be its Lord. O best of the twice-born, lordship arises from mastery over Prakṛti."

Because it lacks sovereignty, they declare that the *puruṣa* possesses no lordship; yet, O Great Sage, because of its pervasiveness, the *puruṣa* indeed possesses omnipresence. Because it exists in states of duality, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is likewise impermanent.
The Puruṣa here is declared to be free from dualities, devoid of qualities, and eternal;
O twice-born one, Prakṛti is impermanent because of its association with action and instruments,
whereas the Puruṣa is said to be eternal because he is devoid of action and instruments.
Thus do the ascetics, offering praise, acknowledge the Puruṣa as the Sattva,
the Field (kṣetra), the Supreme, the Maker of the Cave, the Maker of the Moving Wound, the Night-walker, the Treasure, Intellect, Mindfulness, and Fortitude;
these are synonyms for Prakṛti.
Furthermore, [he perceives] the past, the present, and the future;
he observes that this triad of qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—is *prakṛti*.
Then he perceives that which is beyond the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the imperishable, the auspicious, consisting of security, pure, cloudless, and stainless.
"Immaculate, immovable, undecaying, unformed, shoreless, and non-becoming"—
non-becoming, non-leading,
and non-coming are distinct; these are synonyms for the *puruṣa*.
In this regard, may you behold the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is liberation, free from sorrow and free from delusion—
[attained] through the overcoming of deception, attachment, and transformation.
From compassion, which is contrary [to cruelty], they perceive non-covetousness, which is without refuge, fearless, and indivisible.
Just as the separation and coexistence of a gnat and a fig tree are entirely different in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), even so are the separation and coexistence of knowledge and ignorance.
Knowledge is indeed one thing, and ignorance is another.

The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) will abandon primordial nature (prakṛti), yet primordial nature does not abandon the Knower of the Field. The Knower of the Field perceives primordial nature, yet primordial nature does not perceive the Knower of the Field.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) perceives primordial nature (prakṛti), yet primordial nature does not perceive the Knower of the Field;
the Knower of the Field beholds primordial nature.
Furthermore, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) does not perceive the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
O divine seer, they perceive this as "living together while being apart," which is the vision of their distinctness.
May you perceive that Knower as unattached within the person;
regarding this, they cite a verse:
The followers of Yoga and Sāṃkhya rightly declare that there is nothing whatsoever beyond the twenty-five principles; yet,
if one views this reality otherwise, [it is not so].
"But we perceive duality only through the command of the Guru"—
this is the view of Yoga.
Regarding this, the Sāṃkhyas have sung:
There is a verse:
The Seer sees the one who sees, and he also sees the one who does not see. Because those two do not see, the Seer does not see the one who sees and the one who does not see.

Nature is the field, and there is another who is the knower of the field; the twenty-sixth [principle], the knower of the field, observes it. Neither that which consists of the twenty-five nor nature perceives the supreme knower of the field.

O divine sage, that which has been attained by me through many births is now [realized]. For those who see thus, there is indeed auspiciousness both in this world and the next; of this there is no doubt.
I declare that supreme birth is happiness, but I do not know of any other death.
Cease from this conflict of intellects; you are supremely pure, so worship as one free from possessiveness.
This unstable body, composed of the primary elements, is indeed besieged by many enemies. If you conquer this body alone, surely all your enemies are conquered.
By following that supreme and most pure path proclaimed by the sages and seers, they have attained liberation.
O celestial sage, this was taught by me to those who have taken refuge [in me]: to the great asura Hiraṇyanābha,
to Śiva, to Namuci, to Nārada, to Prahlāda, to Vṛtra, to Virocana,
to Bali, to Marīci, and to Pulastya and Pulaha.

In the same way, it was spoken by me for Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśyapa; for Śukra, Indra, and Bṛhaspati, the best of the Aṅgirases; and likewise for Viśvāvasu, along with the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
This Brahman is to be seen as equal everywhere—
in Brahmins, in Indra, in a dog, in a worm, and in flies, gadflies, and mosquitoes— with perfect equanimity.

Furthermore, from observation we see that the dharma of liberation exists for everyone. This state is free from agitation, dispels the darkness of birth and death, is tranquil, has transcended [the world], and is firmly established.
Bhīṣma said:
"Free from fever.
Having heard this, Nārada, the best of sages and a great ascetic, [proceeded].
Filled with supreme joy, he bowed his head to his teacher,
circumambulated him, and departed for his own home;
the Blessed One, too, vanished from that very spot instantly.
Bhīṣma said:
Saṃyamana, the lord of Kāśī, questioned the sage who had gone to Avimukta regarding knowledge and realization. Saṃyamana said:
From whom has this scripture come? Who creates this entire universe, and who withdraws it all?
And who, presiding over the universe, remains like fire within wood?
And who perceives both the universe and the non-universe as eternally so? O tiger among sages, who are those two whom I revere?
How many principles (tattvas) are there for the Blessed One, the Soul of the Universe, the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors?
Furthermore, according to the teachings seen in the scriptures, what is the *havya* (offering to the gods) and what is the *kavya* (offering to the ancestors)?

And who is born from the *sattva*? Therefore, who is the one skilled in that reality (*tattva*)? Who is said to be the beginning of that reality, and likewise, who is the beginning of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)?
O best of sages, why do the elements (*bhūtādi*) and likewise the modifications (*vikārādi*) repeatedly take up and then cast off [the body],
both with respect to the internal self (*adhyātma*), the objective world (*adhibhūta*), and likewise the divine realm (*adhidaiva*)?
"O Blessed One, this liberation which resides within bodies—
along with consciousness, the ten [faculties], and likewise the Upaniṣads, O Sage— is present in you in its entirety, as is the science of Yoga."
O best of sages, you know the ancient and eternal [Veda] according to your understanding; O knower of the Vedas, the four Vedas with their limbs (aṅgas) and sub-limbs (upāṅgas) abide within you,
as does all this knowledge, both in its textual form and its meaning.
For that which is to be known has indeed been known by you, like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of the hand.
We have heard this concerning the Blessed One: "He is the knower of the high and the low. Therefore, I question you, who are devoted to the welfare of all beings.

"O God, O best of ascetics, this is beyond our perception, yet it is directly manifest to you; we consider this in our minds, O Lord. Therefore, by means of your inexhaustible and imperishable grace..."

O sinless Sage, you ought to unite me with that body which is eternal, immeasurable, immovable, and immortal, and which is liberated from birth and death; for that body of mine is, in every respect, a false knot.
"O Blessed One, I have come for this very purpose: to be bound eternally.
O subduer of enemies, having renounced the kingdom of Kāśī, I have come to you, O Blessed One;
I wish to hear this exactly as it is, according to the truth."
O Blessed One, O Great Sage of immeasurable intellect, you ought to speak for the sake of my peace regarding this matter concerning me, your disciple who remains humble;
for my mind indeed yearns to hear the ultimate truth, the supreme refuge.
Pañcaśikha said:
"O tiger among kings, listen to all this without doubt— it is the destroyer of sin, the supreme nectar, and the ultimate refuge of purifiers."
"And you, O best of the people of Kāśī, are the one who has fully realized all this knowledge. Because he enters into (*viśana*) the universe (*viśva*), they call him Viṣṇu, O best of men;
and they likewise proclaim that the worlds are indeed the universe itself, O lord of men."
Because it does not enter even into the worlds, they know it as "Non-All" (*aviśva*).

From the perspective of the scriptures, they say that this very [state] is of such a nature; O best of men, those devoted to the realization of reality call these two "The All" (*viśva*) and "The Non-All" (*aviśva*).
O tiger among men, this is the truth regarding human beings, of which there is no doubt.
Indeed, they say that all three of these are immortal and eternal;
our sacred tradition (śruti) declares that they are eternally distinct and pure.
O King, they are unborn and formless, indeed unshakable and immutable; they are ungraspable, beyond reasoning, and likewise immortal,
O sinless one, and they are without beginning or end and likewise without form.
They are indeed indestructible, immortal, and truly incapable of being burned;
they are devoid of qualities, yet conscious, and possessors of vision, O lord of men—
just as this has been stated by the teachers, so it is without doubt.
O best of kings, all these qualities indeed reside in these three.
I shall declare the truth to you, according to the vision of the Teacher:
that among them, one is possessed of qualities and likewise devoid of consciousness.
And it is recited, O Great King, that "the Unmanifest" (pradhāna) is perceived;

indeed, the mental application (vidhāna) toward the causal condition (pratyaya) and the affliction (upasarga) is intended as the mind. "The Unmanifest" is its name; the nature of these two is thus described.
"O Indra among kings, we have heard it said that he wanders [through births];
I shall explain that to you, so listen to those nine from me.
Four of them are natural (prākṛta), while five are indeed modified (vaikṛta)."
First, the Manifest arises from the Unmanifest; it is called the beginning of manifestation. Those who contemplate the inner self call this the very origin of the vital breaths.
And those learned in the Vedas call its name "the Great" (Mahat).
"O King, some call it *buddhi*, while others call it *viriñci*. Indeed, O lord of men, from this [source] the creation of Viriñci arises.
From Viriñci, O tiger among kings, the creation of Viriñci is said to proceed."

Each one indeed arises from Viriñca, for they are known to have originated from Vairiñca. O Great King, these creations are what we hear from scripture as "knowledge" (vidyā) and "ignorance" (avidyā).
O Lord of Men, the five elements are derived from Vairiñca; they belong to Viriñca.
"O Great King, without a doubt, they arise from the *ahaṃkāra*:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth;
and the five specific elements, O descendant of Kāśi, arise simultaneously."
Vairiñca, however, being desirous of sense-objects, was born among the five elements;
he is designated as "Mind" (manas), and likewise, from the Vaikharī [speech], the Vaikhara [sound] arises.
O King of kings, there are likewise the organs of perception (buddhīndriya) and the organs of action (karmendriya).
"O dear one, those who have reached certainty regarding the supreme self say that the wise man creates the four primary creations and the five secondary creations simultaneously;
you and others, O Indra among kings, are likewise experts in the wisdom of reality."
The horizontal creation, the primary [creation], the upward, and the downward flow, as well as the fifth, the grace— know these nine, O King,
to be the ninefold creation according to the teaching of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.

O sinless one, this enumeration of the principles has been recounted by me to you in due order; it has been described according to that from which each principle arose and its subsequent development. Indeed, they say that the mind arises from the *vikāra* (evolutes), and from the three [qualities] arise the five groups.
But they say that the five elements, beginning with earth, are indeed the *vikhara*;
and the Brahmins who perceive the truth call Viriñca the first of the vital breaths— namely, prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna.
"O best of kings, regarding the twenty-three manifest principles (*tattva*),
they say that the first is the unmanifest (*avyakta*), according to the evidence of the scriptures. Pañcaśikha said:
"Indeed,
this collection of forms among all embodied beings in the three worlds bears a resemblance to the unmanifest Prajāpati Viriñca."
"The Unmanifest is said to be the source of the Manifest," so says our scripture regarding the one of universal form (viśvarūpa).
O Great King, that eternal one of universal form is to be known through the self (adhyātma), through the elements (adhibhūta), and likewise through the divine (adhidaiva).
I shall declare this according to reality; listen to it, O lord of men. The ear is the internal self (adhyātma); sound is the external element (adhibhūta); space is the presiding deity (adhidaivata).
The skin is the internal self...
Tactile sensation is the *adhibhūta*; Vāyu is the *adhidaivata*. Speech is the *adhyātma*; that which is to be spoken is the *adhibhūta*; Agni is the *adhidaivata*.
The nose is the internal; odor is the external element; the earth is the presiding deity.

The feet are the internal; that which is to be traversed is the external element; Viṣṇu is the presiding deity. The hands are the internal; that which is to be done is the external element; Indra is the presiding deity.
The anus is the internal;
its external correlate is excretion, and its presiding deity is Mitra.
The generative organ is the internal; its external correlate is sexual pleasure.

Prajāpati is the deity with respect to the divine; the mind is the self with respect to the self; that which is to be thought of is the elemental being; and the moon is the deity with respect to the divine.

The ego (ahaṃkāra) is the internal self (adhyātma), self-conceit (abhimāna) is the elemental (adhibhūta), and Viriñca is the presiding deity (adhidaivata). Intellect (buddhi) is the internal self, that which is to be known (boddhavya) is the elemental, and Puruṣa is the presiding deity. All this—the internal self, the elemental, and the presiding deity—must be fully understood.
O best of Brahmins, this [attitude] should be applied toward all beings without malice— toward dogs, insects, moths, gnats, and mosquitoes;
indeed,
it should be applied even toward one's own self and its characteristics, which are unmanifest, great-souled, and distinct from those derived from ego-consciousness, the elements, and transformation.
And we shall explain the knowledge of time to people.
This very [knowledge] is taught in hundreds of thousands of ways as five hundred [units],
which constitute five days and nights for five men.
In that regard, the teachers will state that for one [day], the unmanifest is prohibited; for the four [principles] beginning with the Great One (*mahat*),
they will state eighty hundred thousand cycles during a day and night.

It is declared that for one who follows the Pradhāna, forty hundred thousand cycles [of time] constitute a day and night. It is declared that for the Mahat, [the same duration constitutes] a day and night.
Ten thousand cycles of the person composed of ego (āhaṃkārika) and the material elements (bhautika) constitute a day and night;
this is taught.
Furthermore, a cycle of the mind (manas) of the transformative person (vaikārika) constitutes a four-yuga period.
12,308.191d@029D_0118 These constitute fifty hundred thousand cycles of the day and night of the Unmanifest (avyakta), which is not distinct [from the totality].
12,308.191d@029D_0119 From these, one should constantly perceive the knowledge of time.
Regarding this knowledge of time, [it pertains] to this Unmanifest, which is insentient.

"Knowledge and discernment"— thus they see the one whose nature is the seed (bījadharmī), [and] those whose nature is the seed, those whose nature is non-procreation, those whose nature is not-primal-matter, and those whose nature is dissolution, as well as those whose nature is dissolution.
Saṃyamana said:

"O Blessed One, just as fire, while abiding within hundreds of thousands of millions of pieces of wood, would indeed always possess the same nature as that [wood] because of its location therein; even so, this [Self], while abiding within hundreds of thousands of millions of fields, possesses the same nature as those because of its location therein."

He should always be a companion in dharma. For if his companionship in dharma were with that which is undesirable, he, while engaging in both the desirable and the undesirable, would not conform to his true nature.
For the sake of the manifestation of qualities, let there be the manifestation of qualities;
and as for that state of conforming to one's own nature which would belong to one who persists [in existence],
let it be so.
For one does not become attached to that which is pursued by undesirable qualities; rather, his own nature is what is desired, and he conforms to those very qualities.
This is because of that attachment and because of that following.
And because it abides in that [permanent entity], we perceive the impermanent as permanent;
we shall explain that this is merely due to its cause.
Someone might come together with a possessor of qualities and their qualities;
and having come together, he would perform the function of cause and effect.
And when that possessor of qualities (guṇin) thus engages with the desirable and the undesirable, the quality (guṇa) follows after it because of its abiding therein.
