[Objection: But does not that [quality] also become like the desirable and the undesirable because of its abiding therein?
For if this existence were distinct from the desirable and the undesirable, it would not possess the quality of being desirable or undesirable; yet,
because its state of being desirable or undesirable is accepted by that [self] through which it follows after and clings to them,
we observe that, due to this clinging and following, it becomes the agent of what is to be done and what is not to be done.
Because he is the agent of both what is to be done and what is not to be done, he becomes the possessor of the desirable and the undesirable.
As for the statement that "he is neither the desirable nor the undesirable," that is false;
this *kṣetrajña* possesses qualities (*guṇa*).
One who lacks qualities is not [an agent].
If this [self] were devoid of qualities, it would not conform to its substrate, the nature that operates toward the desirable and the undesirable.
We observe that those [qualities] are subsequently described because of the dual nature of duality. That would be untenable, for there is no state of being distinct in that which is non-distinct;
rather, behold the state of being dual in that which possesses duality.
"O Teacher, behold the non-isolation of that which is isolated.
Pañcaśikha said:
"The impermanence of the eternal, the non-isolation of the isolated, and its lack of independence."

"O Saṃyamana, as for what was said by you— that we do not accept this [position] of his in that way— it is precisely oneness (*ekatva*) that has been taught by you there, which is not desired [by us].
[We] know conjunction (*saṃyoga*) to be eternal."

We shall now explain in detail the qualities and the withdrawal of those qualities, which are repeatedly emitted and withdrawn. For example, there are four classes of living beings: the viviparous, the oviparous, the soil-born, and the sweat-born.
Being burned by the fire of time (*kālāgni*), which is the ego-principle (*ahaṅkāra*) of immeasurable power and majesty and possesses the brilliance of a hundred thousand suns,
they fall to the ground, reeling and helpless. Then, the earth, deprived of those beings, becomes naked.
The earth became pure, level, and resembling the back of a tortoise;
the waters then enjoyed that earth, the mother of the world, which had become thus.
The earth would perish and become water alone;
the sun draws up that water with its rays.
Due to the total destruction of the waters, the blazing fire [consumes] those moving in the atmosphere.
Having consumed the primary elements, fire takes up water;
and the wind takes up fire.
When fire has perished, the wind itself becomes fire.
Then, having withdrawn the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) of all living beings, the wind becomes space (*ākāśa*);
space becomes the mind (*manas*); the mind becomes the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); and the ego-sense [becomes the unmanifest].
The Great Sun is so called because he brings forth light.

Having unified all the worlds of all the suns throughout the entire universe, he stands alone in the midst of the great darkness for its destruction; even that [darkness] he withdraws into the Unmanifest.

This dissolution lasting five days and nights is called the "great dissolution" (*mahāpralaya*). From the great dissolutions, that [universe] becomes one, with all its possessions destroyed; the water, which was to be destroyed by the Lord of the entire network of forms, becomes one with form.
This [sacrificial offering] is both *havya* (for the gods) and *kavya* (for the ancestors); by virtue of the context, it is called *kavya*.
It is termed *havya* because of its being carried (*haraṇāt*).

This very thing, though possessing qualities or being devoid of qualities, is called "possessing qualities" (*guṇin*) due to the application of qualities and because it acts as the agent of those qualities.
It is said by the wise that [the Lord] repeatedly creates the qualities (guṇas) solely for the sake of play; and another [being], due to lack of awakening, [is bound].
"May I alone exist and there be no other"—

if he were to perceive this [desire], thinking "there is another who is my superior," he would not create; and because of his indifference toward creation and dissolution, there would be no origination.

12,308.191d@029D_0165 As it was asked: "O Saṃyamana, who creates this entire universe and who withdraws it all? 12,308.191d@029D_0166 And as it was further asked: "And who, like fire in wood, remains presiding over the universe?
12,308.191d@029D_0167 [The answer is: The twenty-fifth principle is distinct from the other—the unmanifest and the twenty-three principles—being the twenty-fourth.

The seer of what is to be seen, the hearer of what is to be heard, the thinker of what is to be thought, the knower of what is to be known, or the presiding controller—by him presided over, primordial nature (prakṛti) gathers together and displays its qualities. One should perceive that the insentient [nature] is not [insentient], and that the one possessed of qualities is not [possessed of qualities] by means of the sentient and qualityless [Self]; thus one perceives, not otherwise.

By the pure [it becomes] impure; by the eternal, non-eternal; by the absolute, non-absolute; by that which has the nature of creation, that which has the nature of non-creation; by that which has the nature of non-perception, that which has the nature of perception; by that which has the nature of the field, because of the perception of the field. Why?
Because of their distinctness.
For you, it is not accepted that there is multiplicity for one who attains a state of separation from this [Self].
This view—that there is identity between *prakṛti* and the *kṣetrajña*—is a vision born of non-comprehension; it is the vision of the ignorant.
For the wise do not perceive it thus; they see the identity of the seer and the seen. Behold!
One who sees by means of divine power is a seer of a different kind;
why?
Because of the teaching of the scriptures.
Because he does not understand the vision of the scriptures, he is called "unwise" by the wise;
yet this knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is indeed wise.
One perceives the qualities (guṇas), such as intellect and the rest, as they emerge from primordial nature (prakṛti);
and that [nature] is the object to be known.
However, primordial nature does not likewise perceive the qualities or the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña).
Because of a lack of understanding.

For if they were to understand it thus, then either primordial nature (*prakṛti*) or the qualities (*guṇas*) would be the Buddha, or they would be of the same nature as the Buddha. They would [become so].
And they: the Buddha awakens to that; because he has awakened to it, primordial nature conceives the pride [thinking], "I alone am this, and no other."
One clings to what is desired for one's offspring: sacrificing and officiating at sacrifices, studying and teaching, giving and receiving;

[the distinction between] what is fit and unfit to be eaten, what is fit and unfit to be drunk, what is fit and unfit to be spoken; as well as going and contracting, extending, the pleasant and unpleasant, and what is fit and unfit to be approached.
Due to a lack of understanding, one produces qualities such as the auspicious and the inauspicious, as well as the acquisition of sound, touch, form, taste, smell, and so forth; thus,
primordial nature (prakṛti) is experienced through the state of duality.
Thus, a state of multiplicity would accrue to this *kṣetrajña*; and for this one who is free from dualities yet remains active,
as he perceives, there would arise the defect produced by the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
"I reject this;
I perceive this"—
yet it does not see, it speaks, it conceives, or it perceives.
And it is because of ego-grasping (*ahaṃkāra*). For if one were to conceive of [an object] as "I" or cling to it,
one would be thus awakened [to its nature].
It would follow that [the self] possesses power because of its persistence;

and because of possessing power, it would follow that it is distinct [from the body]. For if this [self] were indifferent to both the desirable and the undesirable, how could it be the agent of what is desirable and undesirable?
There would be a fault;
however, because it is free from duality and because it is non-adhesive,
there would be its state of transcendence.
And you have these two verses on this point:
"Just as the lotus is not defiled by the impurity of the mud,
so the Absolute (kevala) is not defiled by the impurity of the Unmanifest (avyakta)."
Just as there is a state of separateness between mud and a lotus growing from it,
so too, because of its coexistence, its non-existence [in the absence of the other] is traditionally taught.
Thus, O Saṃyamana, this distinctness belongs to that which is distinct.
"Because it is non-simultaneous, and because of its non-simultaneity; because it is other, and because of its otherness, it is without reality.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
Those people of true insight consider that which is more utterly vanished than the vanishing— terrible, bottomless, and unmanifest—
to be the contrary of anything else; whereas those who are ignorant do not perceive oneness through the practice of austerity.
Because they are essentially one with the manifest ultimate, they are born and they die;
though their nature is eternally free from dualities, they are nonetheless subject to dualities by those whose nature is dualistic.
And because they are impermanent, O Great King, they abide in duality.
O King, those who lack faith in the teaching and are characterized by dualism sink into this mouth of Time; yet, for those whose nature is to grasp the Unmanifest, liberation arises from non-dualism.
Pañcaśikha said:
"O Saṃyamana, by being liberated from this [bondage], there would be liberation; through non-liberation, however, there is rebirth.
Thus it is for another as well—one who possesses the nature of the unmanifest is likewise without qualities, while one who possesses the nature of the manifest has qualities."

The immovable is distinct from that which possesses the nature of movement; the unchanging is distinct from that which possesses the nature of change; the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) is distinct from that which possesses the nature of the Field (*kṣetra*);
the liberated is distinct from the unliberated; the stainless is distinct from the unstained; the pure is distinct from the impure; union is distinct from non-union;
and liberation is distinct from non-liberation.

Thus, like a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is eternally unattached because of its abiding therein— just as the relationship between a gnat and an udumbara fruit, or between a fish and water, is evident through their coexistence; in this way, the distinctness of this Knower of the Field is established.
That [is the state] of one who is being awakened—
of one who sees yet does not see, of one who sees with the cognition of not seeing, of one who is unawakened, of one who is conscious and unconscious,
of one who is both exclusive and non-exclusive, of one who is eternal and non-eternal, and of one who possesses knowledge and ignorance.
Thus, O sir,
for this one who is unknown and unmanifest, the requisite is that which brings freedom from sorrow out of sorrow,
and freedom from delusion out of delusion.
From the stable, the more stable;
from the cloud, the cloudless; from the wound, the unscarred; from the calamity, the calamity-free; from the boundary, the boundless;
from the city, the non-city—and yet it is taught that this very [state] is the "city-ness" (*puratva*) which pierces through the city.
From light, darkness;
from time, non-time; from fear, fearlessness; from auspiciousness, inauspiciousness;
and through omnipotence, even non-omnipotence—thus indeed for one who observes this, who perceives the oneness of this unmanifest and uninhabited [reality], it is the supreme observation.
Because of their diversity, that which is secure may become insecure; from that which is insecure and unmanifested, [other states] arise. And there are verses on this matter:
One should not perceive the secure as being constantly insecure.
But another is secure; however, one does not perceive him at all—
whether he be the twenty-sixth or the twenty-fifth, O King—
thus say those who know the rule regarding the Unmanifest.
O King, this twenty-fifth principle, which is the knower of the supreme [self], thinks "I am such a one";
yet it is through the awakening of the Awakened One that he is correctly understood.
This one moves, yet he is not moving; you, however, are not moving.
Thus the awakened one, being absolute through the absolute, would be manifest, as well as characterized by both consciousness and non-consciousness.
For one who is free from duality yet whose nature consists of duality, there would be no state of being; there would be no pure power,
and through the awakening of purity, impurity would then arise.
This one alone becomes the absolute Kevala, having attained that which is eternal, stainless, and perfectly pure, which sets in motion the qualities of the true nature of the three worlds.
O Saṃyamana, they teach that the awakening to the twenty-sixth occurs for one who is awakened to the pure twenty-fifth, which is the knower;
[they teach this] regarding the knower as distinct from that which is being known.
The state of being distinct is established:
"I am not anyone belonging to her; she is not anyone belonging to me; I belong to the Twenty-sixth [Tattva]; and there is oneness between me and him."
Regarding this, there is a verse:
The wise say that one who is equal, having seen the equal, is pure; for they have cast aside the darkness and perceive the conscious principle as supreme beyond the unmanifest.
Thus it is said.
This very great reality (*mahat tattva*), having been attained by the Blessed One, the Buddha, the supreme seer (*paramarṣi*), the supreme teacher (*paramaguru*),
and by my teacher Kapila and my teacher Asuri over many hundreds of births, has now been attained by me.
[This state] was obtained from Kapila through the total destruction [of defilements].
In the same way, having likewise attained the status of being one of ten disciples, it was acquired by me from the Blessed One Āsuri over the course of many hundreds of births.
And from me it was obtained by Kātyāyana;
from Kātyāyana it was obtained by Gautama; and from Gautama...
It was attained by Gārgya.
Thus, this supreme reality of the goal of immortality, which brings about the total destruction [of defilements], has been attained through a lineage by many teachers;
it is stainless and pure knowledge.

Having cast aside that which is bottomless, insentient, non-isolated, and unmanifest, one perceives the eternally conscious, isolated, awakened knowledge— the twenty-sixth principle— by means of the awakened twenty-fifth.
On this matter, there are these verses:
"This has been described for my son at Vārāṇasī by the king playing there, at my command."
To one who asks about the knowledge of reality, one should stand with palms joined;
as he asks, one should explain it both according to the text and its meaning— this is indeed declared as the formidable "Sixteen Questions."
O King, having understood these twenty-six [principles] called "Beyond Reality," and having bowed my head to the feet of that child with great joy, I stood near him.
Having traveled on foot and attained the entire truth,
I indeed received the supreme nectar from Sanatkumāra;
it was taught to me by Sanatkumāra.
This great Brahman has been heard by you today exactly as it is; having attained this great question and its meaning, become free from sorrow.
May you regard them as equal— whether it be Brahmā,
Indra, Sthāṇu, or a mosquito;
whether it be a winged insect, a worm, a dog, or an outcaste.
O Lion among Men, for all things exist everywhere;
he of little intelligence who perceives them otherwise,
O King, shall find his end in the unmanifest.
Indeed, not perceiving the true nature of every sentient being,
the unintelligent person constantly encounters suffering;
yet that suffering does not truly belong to him, for he himself undergoes it.
Having fallen into a state of distorted perception through delusion,
O King, go now to your own great city of Vārāṇasī quickly by means of horse and chariot.
This much is the supreme secret;
I have declared it all to you for your complete benefit.
You are now a man of knowledge, no longer one whose intellect is unawakened.
For your intellect is superior, O lion among kings;
you have awakened to that which is foremost, supreme, and most pure—
the Twenty-sixth, which is beyond the Twenty-fifth.
The supreme among men is not born again from the twenty-fifth principle. Wherever he may dwell, one who understands the three aims of life shall become pure;
for the twenty-fifth principle is likewise pure, as is the twenty-sixth.
"When you realize this, then you shall become pure.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"In former times, King Yudhiṣṭhira, with a disciplined inner self..."
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he questioned Dvaipāyana, the best of sages,
together with all his brothers— men of noble mind, auspicious, seated upon the earth, humble, and possessed of supreme energy.
The Blessed One is the all-knowing and all-seeing one among all beings,
renowned throughout the three worlds for his righteousness and self-restraint; O best of sages, we desire to hear that auspicious [account] from you.

"Tell us the discourse spoken by the Blessed One, which destroys all sins, if we are all considered worthy of the Blessed One's favor. Speak, O best among the truthful; we are attentive and shall listen."
Thus addressed with great courtesy by Yudhiṣṭhira, whose very soul is truth and who speaks the truth, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, having been honored, spoke:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O man of great wisdom, O enhancer of the Kuru lineage!"
O Kaunteya, you and your brothers desire to hear this auspicious narrative;
having heard it, O Pārtha, victory for men and the accomplishment of their goals will not be difficult to attain in this world.
This narrative, which brings peace, prosperity, and protection, and destroys all evil dreams,
possesses a divine form and is recounted even by the gods.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history.
O hero, O King, that which was attained in former times during the Kṛta Yuga by the high-souled Agastya— the great ṛṣi born from a jar,
the illustrious son of Mitra and Varuṇa, the powerful one of exceeding asceticism— was acquired by him in his youth.
And in that holy hermitage, O King, bull of the Bharatas, that man of meritorious deeds and great asceticism remained for twelve years,
alone in his own dwelling, observing a vow as vast as the cloudless sky.
When Mitra and Varuṇa, whose natures were virtuous, had gone to heaven,
on the northern shore of Puṣkara there is a mountain named Bhāskara, which is saluted by all the gods and possesses a splendor like the sun through its own radiance.

From there, O King, flows the great river Puṇyasrotas, known by the names Varadā and Vitamā, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas; on that excellent mountain stands the hermitage of his ancestors, where he was born.
Adorned with trees endowed with meritorious flowers and fruits,
the youth performs alone for twelve years an austerity such as was never before performed,
O child, by other divine ascetics rich in penance.
Neither by Īśvara, nor by Indra, Yama, or Varuṇa could he be shaken;
with his arms perpetually raised, the sage stood facing the sun as it shone,
his face turned upward, unsupported, self-conquered, and like the wind.
Unobstructed, without support, self-restrained, with senses conquered,
free from dualities, without egoism, without expectation, and having no desire for anything whatsoever,
he practiced austerities like a piece of wood, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Blissful, free from distress, steadfast, withdrawn from everything, and equanimous— toward him who has thus attained perfection, whose mind is noble and pure,
the sun always shines, scorching him intensely.
O Bhārata, he indeed increased through righteousness in that land of great merit.
Then, O Kaunteya, bull of the Bharatas, after some time,
there were eighty-eight thousand ascetics of meritorious deeds.
Having circumambulated the earth in due order,
including its mountains, forest regions, rivers, streams, and oceans,
Dvaipāyana said:
In various places there were those of great merit who longed for sacred pilgrimage sites. In the meantime, O Pārtha, that great assembly of sages,
having circumambulated the earth, proceeded toward the Mountain of the Sun.
Having then performed a circumambulation of that holy, preeminent mountain, they approached the sacred mountain river for the sake of performing ablutions at its *tīrtha*s. There,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, were eighty-eight thousand [sages].
Having plunged into that water, O King, the sages became overjoyed. Some bathed as they pleased; some performed ritual ablutions there;
and some gratified the ancestors and the gods with the holy water.
Some there were sporting about, while others, rich in asceticism, were chanting prayers; some were contemplating the supreme self (*adhyātma*), while others were studying the Vedas;
and others heard discourses being delivered by other ascetics rich in penance.

Others indeed practiced meditation, while others sat in that manner; thus, O tiger among men, that river which increases merit and dispels darkness shone with those seers who were perfected through their wealth of asceticism.
In the meantime, O Pārtha, Purandara, the king of the gods,
having placed the Grandfather at his head, arrived there together with the gods,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, at that river in its secluded spot where all deceit had vanished.
Then Puṣkaraja spoke to the lord of the gods, the subduer of enemies,
having perceived that the assembly of sages had developed a longing for the Dharma:
"O Puraṃdara, O mighty-armed one, you ought to listen in every way."
O best of immortals, since passion for dharma has arisen in these seers,
O Lord of the Gods, at this very moment egoism will prevail among them all; it will lead them away from heaven, without a doubt.
"O Lord of the foremost gods, you, being righteous-souled, ought to depart from this place;
it is not fitting for you to behold this.
Then, having heard those words from the Grandfather, the King of the Gods [responded].
O best of the Bharatas, O subduer of enemies, he departed together with the gods.
When Śakra, the lord of the gods, had gone forth preceded by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
the eighty-eight thousand [sages] attained supreme joy.
They danced, sang, and even laughed; free from deceit, those others sported in that holy water. And in a secluded spot stood the highly wise Nārada, who was fond of quarreling.
Taking up the *tantrīyuktaka*, the Sage studied the Vedas. Then, O son of Kuntī, descendant of Bharata, Saṃvarta also rose from the water and,
filled with great joy, spoke to all those sages.
"O twice-born ones, let all you sages hear these words of mine. O best of munis, if it pleases you all, let it be done.
O brahmins, I am one of fierce asceticism, and you likewise are as well."
No other person is equal to me in power and likewise in righteousness;
I do not see any strength of asceticism whatsoever that could in any way match the power of Yama’s long-practiced self-restraint and discipline.
Having heard those words of Saṃvarta, that entire circle of sages fell under the sway of egoism and applauded his speech. Then,
O son of Kuntī, all those sages, having become filled with self-conceit—
Then, O great king, those sages of immeasurable power, having disregarded one another,
were honored by the entire assembly of ṛṣis; thereupon Bhr̥gu spoke these words to Saṃvarta with due respect.
"O you who are firm in your vows, there is no doubt that what you have said is exactly so.
Therefore, we ought to behold the power of your asceticism in its entirety. O sages, firm in your vows, please listen for a moment to my words."
"I am pure, I am the best, I possess fierce ascetic power;
I am the foremost"— O you whose wealth is penance, as for this which you prattle again and again out of egoism, what is the meaning of it?
"We wish to see here the fruit of dharma manifested before our eyes;
for there is no austerity found among all beings that is beyond doubt. Having touched the water, let us then return."
Behold the great fruit of the Dharma well-practiced! Gather together and show that penance which was performed by whom, and in what manner, according to its tenfold nature.
Then, having heard those words of Bhṛgu, that entire assembly of sages,
placing the speech of Bhṛgu before them, said "So be it" to the great seers.
But all those great seers, having fallen into egoism through anger—

12,308.191d They proceeded to touch the waters of that holy river, Vitamā. 12,308.191d Having touched the auspicious water there in Vitamā, O great king, those who had fallen away from their ascetic practices then performed their silent recitations (*japa*).
Then that sky was filled by all those best of sages,
O best of men, as they undoubtedly displayed the power of their asceticism;
one of them, having entered the atmosphere, blazed forth with pure heat.
Likewise, other twice-born ones who had attained heaven were purified by the Apsarases;
others were honored even by the Guhyakas with showers of flowers.
Some, entering the sky, performed divine feats.

O subduer of enemies, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as they looked at one another there and laughed, a great roar arose from them out of joy. O bull of the Bharata race, having seen each other’s strength, they [praised] the power of Dharma.

O Lord, O tiger among the Kurus, while they were thus conversing on the bank of the river, Nārada, perceiving that lapse in the dharma of those great-souled ones, struck the one appointed to the lute.
Then all those sages, O slayer of enemies, desiring to go to the sky as they had done before, were indeed unable to proceed;
for there were eighty-eight thousand sages of purified souls.
O King, being unable to proceed, they then looked at one another;
cast out, devoid of energy, and hopeless regarding their departure,
O illustrious one, they remained right there like birds whose wings have fallen away.
Having spoken thus, the great seers looked at one another, saying, "What is this? What indeed is this? while others cried out, "Alas!
How tragic! As they gazed about, miserable and deprived of their senses, they were lost in heaven.
Overcome by great egoism, they have been cast down upon the earth;
having fallen under the sway of delusion, all of them are deprived of their senses and perceive nothing of either dharma or the path to liberation.
When all those birds had fallen from the sky as if dejected in mind,
Nārada then spoke these words to them out of joy:
"O you who stand in delusion, why do you look on while desiring to go to the vault of heaven?"
This virtue is difficult to find again for you whose righteousness has perished.
Through great egoism, the eternal dharma has been destroyed. This being the case, I do not see how we may go to heaven as before.
"All of you are now like sages who are wingless birds, because of that transgression of dharma contemplated by that evil-minded one. You have all become hopeless regarding your departure."
Dvaipāyana said:
"Perform your religious duties with diligence on the auspicious and holy bank of the river.
Having heard those words of his, the sages became dejected in heart.
Then, bowing down before that Nārada, the best of sages, they said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, how may the vault of heaven be occupied by those like us once again, so that there shall be no confusion of dharma?"
Having heard their words, Nārada spoke again; having entered into meditation for a moment and attained auspicious yoga, he said:
"O sages, you must recognize the terrible power of ego."
What indeed can be hoped for by one who has performed sinful deeds?
Alas, this great fruit of ignoble and evil action is being obtained! For such a fault as this is what is called "egoism" (*ahaṃkāra*) by the great seers.
Where is that fruit of the asceticism practiced for thousands of years?
Where has that sacrifice performed in the past vanished, and where indeed is the self-restraint and discipline?
To what place has the fruit of those who, with arms upraised and tranquil, have gone?
For what purpose were the gods, the ancestors, and those whose wealth is asceticism worshipped?
O Brahmins, where indeed has the fruit of that supreme austerity gone? These duties must be performed by you once again, just as they were before.
This being the case, I do not see a way for you to go to the triple heaven;
because of the power of egoism, your path is rendered uncertain. I, however, shall indeed follow you by means of my own karma alone.
For this reason, he conceived such doubt within himself:
"This river Pravarasrotas has auspicious and meritorious waters;
yet, if there is no movement through the sky, how can dharma be practiced here?"
Subsisting on air, taking no food, self-restrained and with senses conquered,
you ought to practice the Dharma here with great composure;
for even by Vāsava, the high-souled lord of the gods, [this was practiced] here.

The fierce Dharma, well-practiced and free from deceit, is situated above the city. Here, in ancient times, the god and the goddess Rudra performed a very great austerity for thousands of divine years according to the prescribed rite.

Even by the high-souled Viṣṇu, having reached this best of rivers and touched its auspicious waters, the destruction of his difficult-to-overcome [sins] was attained. O knowers of dharma, such is the power of this river; of this there is no doubt.
"Having performed meritorious deeds here in this world, you shall then go to an auspicious destination.
When they were all dejected and had fallen into extreme misery,
Nārada spoke to those high-souled ones.
Abandoning this wretchedness that brings all undertakings to ruin,
you should all listen with a disciplined inner self; and whatever I shall say must be carried out by you as the means to accomplish your task.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, if you will cast aside pride in every way and, with humility and self-restraint, carry out these words of mine today,
then for this moment this sky shall return to its former state."
"If you all carry out my words exactly as spoken, at this very moment the defilement of everyone shall go to destruction. Never before have I spoken an untruth; I am a sage, O you of firm vows."
"Listen well to my words, O you whose wealth is asceticism: I am Nārada. Since you have abandoned pride, both dharma and heaven shall be yours. Accept my words for a moment, all of you."

The words of friends, which always convey the true nature of things and are consistent with righteousness, should always be accepted without hesitation. Accept this beneficial advice of mine; by doing so, you shall duly attain your welfare in this world.
"I shall relate this to you all properly among the virtuous;
having heard it and discerning what is appropriate for endurance, you shall do whatever is beneficial.
Dvaipāyana said:
"You shall go to your respective places, eternal and everlasting.
O King, having heard his words, all those best of sages then became filled with joy, their eyes wide with delight.
Then Bhrigu, having become purified, spoke these beautiful words in wonder to that celestial seer Nārada, the best of men:
"O Brahmin, what indeed was that deity, or was it a vow, or perhaps a religious observance?"
"O best of sky-goers, by performing what may we attain the vault of heaven?
O divine sage, it is not at all surprising that you hold such a view;
for you speak thus, O righteous one, out of compassion for us."
"Therefore, speak words that are beneficial; this sin has been wiped away.
O Brahmin, what rule must we observe again?
For all of us, these sages, O best of munis," [are here].
With palms joined in reverence and bowed low to propitiate you, O Holy One;
and having heard those words of Bhṛgu, whose soul is dharma,
that highly illustrious great sage looked upon those ṛṣis with their palms joined in reverence.
Then, laughing at those words, Nārada, the best of sages, spoke these words to all who were seated there: "Behold! I shall tell you; let everyone listen."

This boy, born of Mitra and Varuṇa, named Agastya, whose nature is righteousness, has undertaken austerities upon this excellent mountain for the sake of heaven and his own welfare— conduct that is both appropriate and favorable.
In steadfastness, asceticism, righteousness, and self-restraint,
there is no one equal to him, even among all of you.
[I seek] that boy of fierce austerity, whose soul is devoted to dharma and who is beyond reproach.
"O sages, approach him, restraining your own pride. If you abandon pride, delusion, and mere arrogance, approach that youth; you shall go [to him] as you did before."
For he, resplendent like the sun, practices austerities on Bhāskara, the best of mountains, firm in his vows for the sake of the world’s welfare;
there is no one equal to him in brilliance, in righteousness, or in self-restraint.
"12,308.191d@029E_0230 All of you should attend upon that bull among sages, the giver of boons.
12,308.191d@029E_0231 Then, having heard the words of the high-souled Nārada,
12,308.191d@029E_0232 they all, with joyful minds, resolved to follow his command."

Having said "So be it" to Nārada and having circumambulated him, O hero, they all departed with serene minds for the Bhāskara mountain. They [ascended] that sacred, preeminent mountain, where trees bear fruit in all seasons.
Having ascended it, those of restrained self gazed all around;
for that righteous-souled one, pure and performing fierce austerities, moves higher and higher than the king of mountains, like the radiant sun.
O destroyer of enemies, seeing him, all the sages were struck with wonder; they could not comprehend that which had been spoken by Nārada. Then all those best of sages approached that boy.
Eighty-eight thousand [sages], disciplined and self-controlled, all spoke with one voice; there, Bhrigu,
firm in his vows and blazing with his own splendor, addressed that high-souled being.

O Agastya, best among the virtuous, you who are ever devoted to well-performed vows, O knower of dharma, son of the foremost of sages, you ought to hear my words. We have been deluded by the ego born of divine creation.
Having abandoned self-restraint through passion and being deluded by worldly attachment,
we desire, by your grace, to go to a desired and auspicious state. Be the refuge for all of us who have been consumed by egoism and the like.

Having liberated these eighty-eight thousand people from their defilements through this supreme Dharma, O Great Sage, best of sages, you shall eternally attain the worlds by virtue of this merit of giving.
"Save yourself, your ancestors, and the world of the living. We have all approached you with devotion for the sake of heaven;
by your splendor, may we deliver these eighty-eight thousand."
"We have all come here desiring heaven; with hope, we seek from you the auspicious state. O knower of dharma, act according to the purpose for which the sages have arrived here."
Dvaipāyana said:
"You ought to protect those who have come to you for refuge by means of your own splendor.
Having seen those hosts of sages who had come to him for refuge, Agastya [acted].
With a joyful countenance, he [beheld] them all with palms joined in reverence; having approached them all with humility and honored them in return,
that best of sages spoke these words to them all with hands folded in salutation.
"May there be a most welcome arrival for you all, virtuous ones, here in every respect.
For now, this hermitage of the sages is your own. Then, that twice-born man performed the rites of hospitality toward them as they deserved.
Having sat down according to the prescribed rule and remaining bowed with humility,
Agastya then addressed them all with palms joined in reverence:
"Homage be equally to all of you, O Blessed Ones."
"I am your son, or rather, your virtuous disciple," I said, bowing low. "What power do I, a mere child and a sage whose deeds are yet unaccomplished,
have to grant you fearlessness or lead you to heaven?"
For this duty to be performed by the Sage is indeed only something very slight.
Having heard that "this is called Dharma," I have become somewhat observant of restraints;
but from where comes Dharma? From where comes merit? From where comes generosity? And from where comes self-control?
By which means may I bestow the Dharma upon you who desire heaven? Be gracious; you ought not to harbor anger toward me. I do not value myself so highly that I would not grant you fearlessness.
Having heard these words of that high-souled sage, they then formed the very same resolve to depart, free from all hesitation; thereupon,
Agastya, firm in his vows, suddenly spoke to them.
Then the boy, his heart full of joy, bowed his head with palms joined in reverence toward the eighty-eight thousand seers of purified souls, and spoke these words to them all.
"None of you, the hosts of sages, should depart from here for now;
I shall grant your request for heaven if I am able. You shall go as before, provided that righteousness prevails."

"Wait for a moment, until I have performed my ritual ablutions. Having gone quickly to the holy Vitamā river, that self-controlled seer performed his ablutions according to the prescribed rites and then returned.
Then, standing with his face turned northward and his hands joined in reverence, the wise one, with a joyful mind, spoke while stationed facing the eastern direction:
"If there is any merit whatsoever, or if the deities have been well-worshipped..."
"May these eighty-eight thousand go as they did before;
may the station of heaven be eternal for all these great-souled ones,
by my truth, my austerity, my self-restraint, and my discipline."
O bull of the Bharata race, at the conclusion of these words,
eighty-eight thousand sages of meritorious deeds ascended to heaven, rejoicing as they had done before.
Immediately thereafter, the words "Excellent! Excellent! were heard there.
"Excellent, O son! You are a good son to your friend, you who are firm in your vows. Excellent, O best among the virtuous! Excellent, O foremost among the truthful!"
Excellent is this gift of yours, a source of merit; excellent too is your devotion to the Brahmins.
By your grace, we have all reached the vault of heaven in an instant, just as before. Oh, how inexhaustible is your generosity!
The drums resounded in heaven: "O, how great is the fruit of giving!
O Great Sage, the three worlds proclaimed the excellence of that gift;
the gods, the great serpents, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, the siddhas, and the cāraṇas [all rejoiced].

They showered Agastya, the best of men, with rains of flowers; likewise, the Gandharvas, with the sound of songs and various musical instruments, proclaimed, "Oh, what a gift! and truly honored Agastya.
Ūrvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Śyāmā, Kālī,
as well as Rāmā, Yojanagandhā, and Gandhakālī—
these excellent Apsarases danced for Agastya, O bull of the Bharatas.
"O giver of honor! A hundred times they proclaim, 'Ah, what a gift!'—
the gods, Gandharvas, and Pannagas, exceedingly joyful and delighted,
then raised a great shout in praise of Agastya."

Facing toward heaven, they stood and exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! Then they said, "Surely his gift is firm; indeed, those three worlds [belong] to him. Clouds bearing divine flowers appeared from all sides.
Showers of flowers rained down toward the hermitage of Agastya. Thus, O Great King, did Dvaipāyana speak those words of praise for Agastya.
"O bull of the Bharatas, the cry 'Aho! A gift! resounded everywhere;
indeed, while that Brahman-sage was thus proclaiming his gift, Nārada beheld that supreme wonder and marvel."
Rising from that Vitamātīra, that bull among sages,
filled with great joy, ascended Mount Bhāskara. Having climbed it, O one of great wisdom, he beheld the young sage Bālaka.
Seeing that child Agastya, the best of sages, sitting there unchanging and endowed with great fortitude— resembling an immortal— the celestial seer Nārada joyfully offered him his congratulations.
"O knower of dharma, O best of sages, may you prosper by good fortune for the sake of Dhruva!
O great sage who desires the welfare of others, you have conquered the worlds after reaching the vault of heaven with eighty-eight thousand [followers]."
This great gift, which brings such great prosperity, has been attained by you;
it was not attained even by the gods led by Indra, nor by the sages—
that which you have today obtained, O one of great wisdom, as a mere child.
"O knower of dharma, O best of sages, these celestial worlds have been won by you for Dhruva,
who desires the welfare of all the worlds;
indeed, you must practice dharma extensively and without doubt."
"In this age, you shall be remembered as the one preeminent sage among the ancients by virtue of your qualities;
O one of great wisdom, you will become firm, eternal, and undecaying. Having heard those words of the high-souled Nārada, [he replied].
Having saluted him according to custom, he spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, it was solely out of childishness that I, having somehow been prompted by those high-souled ones, spoke today regarding the ascetic power I have acquired."

"O Nārada, at my word, all those high-souled ones have suddenly gone to the vault of heaven; for that merit has been fully earned by them. Having heard Agastya’s words, O bull of the Bharata race, Nārada—
Extremely pleased, he spoke these words in honor of him:
"O Agastya, what do you consider yourself to be? O one of great wisdom, by your great righteousness, the worlds have long been conquered by you."
In former times, you alone were a sage named Vṛṣabha by name;
O observer of great vows, when a yuga of ten million years existed,
there was [a period] called Divyasaṃkalpaka in the previous Kalpa, during the Kṛta Yuga.
When Viṣṇu, together with the lotus-born Brahmā, resolved upon the islands, the oceans, the mountains, and the forests,
even then you yourself were born from the waters, O Lord.
Just as Brahmā arose from the lotus and as fire arises from water,
so too are you, O knower of dharma, self-born and born from the waters;
for thus did the boon-granting one, born from the lotus, declare.
"O one of great wisdom, your entire previous birth consisted of ascetic penance. Agastya said: "That is not what should be known by you; let your own birth be understood."
"O Blessed One, let it be as you have said; by good fortune those sages have departed.
By good fortune, O Blessed One, the word uttered by you has not been in vain, but has proven true.
I consider this to have been brought about by my own egoism, and it could not have been otherwise for me."
Vyāsa said:
"O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, O highly wise one, I do not recall ever having spoken an untruth; listen now to this most wonderful thing."
O best of men, having heard this, one's defilement shall perish;
no evil dream shall occur, and sin shall have no power. It is eternally auspicious and blessed, and it shall result in sons and grandsons.
"O Great King, there shall be freedom from disease even in the world of the living.
I shall relate this to you; O son of Kuntī, listen to me.
It is that which was attained in the past by Agastya over the course of twelve years."
Once, O Great King, that high-souled one born from a jar—
having completed a great fast,
being restrained by his vows, pure, bathed, and having successfully maintained his observances— sat down at its conclusion.
Then, indeed, that one of great asceticism suddenly leapt up;
he went into the sky like one borne aloft by the wind,
following the path frequented by the Siddhas and traversed by gods and Gandharvas.
Having reached the intermediate space, which was crowded with *siddhas* and *cāraṇas* and frequented by *vidyādharas*, the Blessed One said, "What indeed? What is this?
Having traversed the seventh path of the wind, that one of great austerity—
He then ascended into the sky, borne aloft as if by the wind;
he beheld all ten directions, stainless and pure, traversed by gods and gandharvas and frequented by the siddhas, O best of kings.
Beholding everywhere the celestial palaces of the gods, the mountains, and the forests, as well as the yakṣas of great majesty,
and the divine abodes and mansions of the deities.
He beheld here and there a city of the Gandharvas,
as well as the delightful earth consisting of seven islands, adorned with many mountains,
filled with towns and dwellings, and graced by the four oceans.

O bull of the Bharata race, O King, O descendant of Bharata, Agastya beheld with his divine eye the beautiful earth, as well as the deities. Then, having entered the sky, he traversed the path of the seven winds.
"O King, bull of the Bharatas, Agastya is being led away by Dharma.
He beholds the sky ablaze, filled without interval with flames and rays of light,
shrouded in the darkness of smoke, resembling a forest on fire."
Seeing him, Agastya, the one born from a jar, was then distressed;
agitated by the thought, "What is this?", he halted his established course.
Then, a deity in human form suddenly approached.
He stood by the side of Agastya with palms joined in reverence; having approached him with humility, he spoke,
while Agastya remained ever self-restrained and pure in mind.
"I am a Brahmin, O illustrious one; how have you come through the sky?
Having seen this blazing light, I am filled with apprehension; let it be told clearly, for since you possess a physical body, I do not know what kind of being you are."
"O Lord, I am distressed because of that; therefore, be gracious and speak to me. O King, when the sage had thus questioned that deity, the deity, having honored his words, then spoke these words.
"O Agastya, I recognize you as a most righteous ṛṣi;
because you have attained [this state] with your physical body, I have come before you.
Indeed, O observer of vows, this entire sky is now nothing but fire."

Therefore, it is called *jyotiṣa* (astronomy/astronomy) for a specific reason; of this there is no doubt. For the thousand-rayed Sun, the maker of day, constantly heats these luminaries—the stars, the constellations (*nakṣatras*), and likewise the planets.

"O you who are firm in your vows, that which you see here in the form of fire is heaven; therein dwells the one of great splendor, the burner, the purifier. Therein is the great, radiant consumer of oblations, who wanders through the three worlds."

O Brahmin, Agni himself resides there; therefore, this sky is ablaze. At that time, the gods along with the hosts of sages approach him who dwells therein—the highly fortunate consumer of oblations, the granter of boons, and self-luminous.

12,308.191d@029E_0424 Madhusūdana, who is honored by all the gods, approaches the boon-granting God stationed here for the sake of the peace of the deities. 12,308.191d@029E_0425 Stationed here, Brahmā and the world of the gods were created by the deities.
The mountains, the oceans, the islands, and likewise the rivers—
this is that first abode of Agni, honored by the three worlds,
which you beheld blazing and became apprehensive upon seeing it, O best of the twice-born.
"Therefore, O Sage, enter this without hesitation; do not be distressed.
This sky, though radiant, is not [hot] for one whose soul is devoted to Dharma, but is as cool as the wind.
Having heard those words of the deity, he who was firm in his vows—

Having honored that [instruction], the sage entered the sky without confusion. Beholding the gods and the hosts of ṛṣis stationed there, he proceeded while being gazed upon and honored by them as well.
That great-splendored one entered that sky, cool as snow,
which was crowded with deities like a pool filled with lotuses;
and standing there, he beheld the celestial chariots of the gods.
The one of great splendor beheld in that celestial fire-altar flags with their banners, palaces, and archways; he also saw Gandharvas and throngs of Apsarases dancing there in the sky.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O descendant of Kuru, how did Śuka, the son of Vyāsa, attain detachment in former times? I wish to hear this, for my curiosity is great."
"O descendant of Kuru, you ought to explain the certainty regarding the principles of the unmanifest and the manifest— the certainty of the intellect— and what the creative act of the unborn God is.
Bhīṣma said:
Having taught his son the entire Veda (*svādhyāya*), his father instructed him as he lived according to the natural and excellent conduct, free from fear from any quarter:
"O son, practice righteousness (*dharma*), for both cold and heat are exceedingly sharp."
Always conquer hunger, thirst, and the vital breath, having mastered your senses. Diligently observe truth, straightforwardness, freedom from anger, lack of envy, self-restraint, austerity,
non-violence, and compassion in accordance with the prescribed rules.

Abide in truth, delight in dharma, and abandon all crookedness. Maintain the journey of your life by means of what remains after serving the gods and guests. For this body is like a vessel of foam, and the living soul within it is as transient as a bird.
"O son, how can you sleep when dwelling with loved ones is impermanent? While your enemies are vigilant, awake,
ever-ready, and seeking an opening, you, a fool, do not perceive it."
While the years are being counted, while life is thus wasting away, and while one's lifespan is diminishing— why do you not rise and run?
People strive for worldly things that merely increase flesh and blood.
Those who are deeply atheistic and utterly negligent regarding matters pertaining to the next world— those men possessed by delusion of intellect who harbor malice toward Dharma—
even a follower of theirs is afflicted when they travel upon a wrong path.

But those who are contented, well-restrained, devoted to truth and the scriptures, and have ascended the path of dharma— serve them and question them; having understood the opinion of those elders who perceive the dharma.
12,309.012c Restrain with supreme intelligence the mind that has indeed gone astray.
12,309.013a Thinking with a mind focused only on the present, "tomorrow is far off," they are fearless;
12,309.013c devouring all things, those of distracted mind do not perceive the field of action.
Climbing the ladder of Dharma, ascend little by little;
you do not realize that you are binding yourself like a silkworm,
like an atheist who has broken the bounds of conduct and is as unstable as a collapsing riverbank.
Confidently cast aside to your left the man who is as arrogant as a bamboo reed.
Having fashioned a boat made of fortitude, cross over the difficult straits of birth— the river whose waters are the five senses, and which carries desire, anger, and death.
When the world is struck by death and tormented by old age,
and while these [arrows] fall unfailingly, cross over by means of the vehicle of Dharma. For death seeks out its prey whether one is standing or lying down.
Why do you find peace when you have been suddenly destroyed by death? While he is still gathering [wealth] and remains unsated with desires,
Death seizes him and departs, just as a she-wolf seizes a lamb.
Gradually built up into a great flame consisting of the intellect of Dharma,
let this lamp be held with effort when one must enter into the darkness. For it may happen that, falling through the multitude of bodies, one might eventually find oneself here among humans.

A living being attains the status of a Brahmin; therefore, my son, protect it. For this body of a Brahmin is not born for the sake of sensual pleasure, but for the sake of austerity and hardship in this world, and for incomparable happiness after death.
The status of a Brahmin is attained through many austerities;
having obtained it, one must not treat it with contempt as if it were a mere wager.
One should be constantly devoted to Vedic study, austerity, and self-restraint.
Seeking security and devoted to the wholesome, always exert yourself!
This one has unmanifested nature as his origin, the arts as his body; he is a subtle self, with moments and instants for his joints and the blink of an eye for his hair.
With its mouth like that of a sacrificial fire, with eyes of equal strength— white and black—
the horse of human life gallops away, its body of flesh;
seeing it spread forth, incessant and of fierce speed.
If your eye is not led by others as you go here constantly without regard [for worldly things],
then let your mind be fixed upon the Dharma after having heard it thoroughly.
But those whose conduct is driven by wavering desire for worldly things,
who constantly cry out due to their association with the undesirable,
suffer with bodies overwhelmed by painful sensations.
Though he has been greatly influenced by many latent tendencies toward unrighteousness,
the king, who is always devoted to dharma and a protector of virtue,
beholds and bestows worlds upon those who have performed good deeds.
It bestows upon him many kinds of happiness that have not yet been attained and are blameless, even as he wanders;
[there are] terrifying dogs and birds with iron beaks.

And flocks of vultures and herons, twelve thousand three hundred and nine with twenty-eight thousand eight hundred and eighty-nine more, drink the blood of men in the carnage, disregarding the words of their elders as they tear apart the deceased.
He who breaks these ten-fold boundaries established here by the Self-Existent through the power of his mind dwells in great misery in the realm of the ancestors.
That wicked man who, being excessively greedy and a speaker of pleasant falsehoods, delights constantly in deceit and trickery, plunges into the forest [of hell].
Having caused suffering through deposits, that evildoer goes to the supreme hell and experiences intense misery;
he enters the great river Vaitaraṇī, which is scorching hot.
With his body pierced by the forest of sword-leaves,
he lies fallen in the forest of axes;
and, intensely tormented, he dwells in the great hell.

12,309.032a You boast of great strides, yet you do not look toward the ultimate goal; 12,309.032c for a long time you have failed to realize that the bringer of death has arrived. 12,309.033a For those who must depart, why do you sit idle? A great danger has arisen!

This [world] is exceedingly turbulent and terrible; let provision be made for happiness, lest you, having died, be led away by the command of Death to the presence of Yama. Therefore, exert yourself toward uprightness in order to avoid that [fate].

"Before the Lord Yama, who knows no sorrow, carries you away along with your roots and kinsmen, your life here shall be taken; there is no one who can ward him off. Before the wind that precedes Yama blows, [you must depart]."
Before you are led away all alone, perform what is necessary for the hereafter;
before the end-maker, the wind that causes shuddering, blows upon you;
and before the quarters of the sky whirl about you at the onset of great terror.

"O son, your memory will be completely obstructed here before long as you proceed in agitation; therefore, maintain the highest meditative concentration regarding what has been done and what remains to be done,
both auspicious and inauspicious, which are often corrupted by the karma of negligence."

Remembering this, do not suffer; deposit the treasure within yourself alone. Before old age makes your body frail and decrepit—before that which robs strength, limbs, and beauty—deposit the treasure within yourself alone.
Before the Ender shatters your body with the arrows of disease,
and before life is forcibly brought to its end, practice great austerity. Before the terrifying wolves that range within the human body appear, [act now].
They rush from all sides; strive in the practice of virtue!
Before you behold the darkness alone, hasten indeed! Before you gaze upon golden mountains on the mountain peak.

In former times, bad associations and enemies disguised as friends used to distract you from your vision; therefore, my son, strive for that which is supreme. That wealth of which there is no fear from kings or from thieves—[strive for that].
Acquire that wealth which does not leave one even when dead;
for in that state, there is no mutual sharing of one's own deeds,
and whatever is one's own separate property, that alone one enjoys there.
"O son, give away only that by which one may live in the next world;
acquire for yourself that wealth which is imperishable and certain. As long as the barley-gruel of the great multitude has not yet been cooked,"
While the barley-gruel is still uncooked, you must depart in haste;
neither mother nor father, nor kinsmen, nor beloved friends will follow after you as you go alone into this perilous strait.

Whatever action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— one has performed entirely by oneself, that alone becomes one's dowry as one goes to the next world. Accumulations of gold and jewels are gathered only through [the weight of] one's own good and evil deeds.
When that body perishes, there are no executors of one's deeds for him who has gone to the next world;
for men in this world, there is no witness equal to oneself regarding the actions performed or left undone.
When one departs for the next world, the human body becomes empty;
behold this with the eye of wisdom, for it is seen everywhere.
Here in this world, the three—fire, sun, and wind—are dependent upon the body.
These very ones, who perceive the dharma, become his witnesses.
Just as [the sun] shines upon all things at all times, touching everything without exception, whether in open or secret conduct, protect your own dharma alone.
In that place, which is beset by many obstacles and guarded by hideous and fierce beings, one must protect one's own karma alone; for it is one's own karma that goes there.
There, one does not share with others through the mediation of their respective karmas.
12,309.057c Just as it was performed, that very fruit born of one's own karma is experienced.

12,309.058a Just as the hosts of Apsarases, together with the great seers, enjoy the fruit of happiness, 12,309.058c so too do they obtain [it] through their karma, traveling at will in celestial chariots.
Just as here, whatever merit has been performed by those who are free from sin and have disciplined their selves,
so do human beings of pure birth attain that;
they reach the same world as Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, and Śatakratu.
12,309.060c Those who proceed by means of the bridges of the householder’s dharma attain the supreme goal.
12,309.061a We are able to proclaim this in thousands and many ways; 12,309.061c yet, without the Lord, there is no way to dispel the delusion of the unawakened mind.
Twelve thousand three hundred and nine years, six months, and two days have passed; you are certainly twenty-five years old.
Accumulate a store of merit, for your youth is passing away. Before the Ender (Death) can make heedlessness his mouthpiece, you must practice self-restraint.
12,309.063c As it was grasped, so it has arisen; hasten to protect the Dharma!
12,309.064a When you yourself shall go behind and you yourself shall go before, 12,309.064c as you thus proceed upon that path, what need is there for self or for another?
That which belongs to those who travel alone when they depart for the next world—
deposit that great treasure for the sake of future security amidst dangers;
for the Lord, being unattached, carries away one's kinsmen along with their very roots and branches.
"For him there are no obstructors; therefore, establish a store of merit.
O son, this illustration has been approved by me for you here;
it has been described according to my own observation and inference—act upon it."
He who, by his own action, bestows wealth upon anyone at all,
is joined with but a single virtue born of the absence of delusion and ignorance. May your learning be effective as you perform auspicious deeds.
That alone is the true vision there—grateful and consistent with one's purpose. This attachment to living in a village is a binding rope;
having severed it, the virtuous depart, while the wicked do not sever it.
"What use have you for wealth, what use for kinsmen,
or what use for sons, my son, since you must die? Seek the Self that has entered the cave."
Where have all those grandfathers of yours gone?
One should perform tomorrow's task today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or not.
For who knows this? Into whose army of death shall one enter today?
Having followed the deceased as far as the edge of the cremation ground, the kinsmen and friends here turn back, having cast the man into the fire.
"Confidently place to your left those who are nihilists, devoid of compassion, and established in sinful thoughts, as you strive tirelessly for the supreme goal.
Thus, when the world is struck down and oppressed by Time,"
Relying upon great fortitude, practice the Dharma with your whole being. Now, that man who correctly understands this means of vision,
having properly performed the Dharma here, prospers in happiness in the world beyond.
For those who understand that there is no death at the dissolution of the body,
nor any destruction when the path is well-guarded,
he who increases his righteousness is indeed wise.
He who indeed falls away from the Dharma becomes deluded;
when two paths of action have been undertaken, the agent receives the fruit of his own deed according to the rule.
One of base conduct falls into hell;
one who has reached the further shore of dharma goes to the third heaven. Having attained this human state, which is difficult to obtain, it serves as a staircase to heaven.
In this way, one should compose oneself so that one does not fall away again;
for him whose mind does not stray from the path leading to heaven,
they call him a man of meritorious deeds, beyond the grief of friends and kinsmen.
For one whose intellect is not impaired and who relies upon certainties,
there is no great fear once a place has been secured in heaven—
for those who were born in the forests of asceticism and met their end right there.
The merit of those who do not understand the enjoyment of desires is very small;
however, for one who renounces enjoyments and practices austerity with the body,
there is nothing that cannot be attained by him— this result is highly esteemed by me.
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives—those yet to come and those already past—to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong?
I am alone; no one belongs to me, nor do I belong to anyone.
I do not see that which I do not see, nor him who does not see me. You have no concern for them, nor do they have any concern for you. They have gone because of their own deeds, and you too shall go.
In this world, even a stranger acts as a kinsman to those who possess wealth;
but for the poor, even their own kin vanish while they are still alive. Out of regard for his wife, a man accumulates unwholesome karma.
12,309.087c Then one encounters suffering both in the next world and likewise in this one.
12,309.088a Behold indeed the world of living beings as full of vulnerabilities due to their own karma.
12,309.088c Therefore, my son, act accordingly upon everything that has been fully explained.
Having clearly perceived this, one who desires the world beyond should enter that land of action and practice virtuous deeds,
by means of the revolving cycle known as months and seasons.
Time forcibly ripens all beings with the fire of the sun, using day and night as its fuel, while the fruits resulting from one's own actions serve as the witness.
What is the use of wealth that one neither gives nor enjoys?
What is the use of strength by which one does not subdue enemies?
What is the use of sacred learning by which one does not practice righteousness?
"What is the use of a self that has not conquered the senses and lacks self-control?
Having heard these beneficial words spoken by Dvaipāyana,
Śuka departed, leaving behind his father, the guide to liberation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me how the righteous Śuka, a man of great asceticism, was born to Vyāsa,
and how he attained supreme perfection."
And upon whom did Vyāsa, whose wealth is asceticism, beget Śuka?
For we do not know the mother of this great-souled one, nor his foremost birth. And how did his mind, while he was still a child, come to be intent upon subtle knowledge?

"O one of great splendor, I wish to hear this in detail, for there is no one else in this world, nor indeed a second person here, [who possesses such knowledge]. For I am not yet satiated by hearing this supreme nectar."
"O Grandfather, tell me truly and in due order about the majesty, the self-discipline, and the wisdom of Śuka. Bhīṣma said:
"Neither by years, nor by grey hair, nor by wealth, nor by kinsmen did the seers establish dharma; he among us who is learned in the Vedas is great.
All this about which you ask me, O Pāṇḍava, has its root in austerity."

When one restrains those senses, it becomes asceticism (*tapas*); it is not otherwise. Through attachment to the senses, a person undoubtedly incurs fault; but by fully restraining them, a human being attains perfection (*siddhi*).
"O dear one, the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices is not equal to even a sixteenth part of the fruit of yoga.
In this regard, I shall describe to you the fruit of birth and yoga as it truly is."
And [he told of] Śuka’s supreme state, which is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.
Long ago, it is said, on a peak of Mount Meru filled with groves of *karṇikāra* trees,
Mahādeva sported, surrounded by his formidable hosts of spirits.
In ancient times, the goddess who is the daughter of the King of Mountains was also present there;
it was there that the lord Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana performed divine austerities,
having entered into himself through yoga and being devoted to the dharma of yoga.

12,310.013c Bearing this in mind, O best of the Kurus, he performed austerities for the sake of a son. 12,310.014a "O Lord, may there be a son for me who is equal in prowess to Fire, Earth, Water, Wind, and Space," he said.
Then, by means of this resolve— which is difficult for those of unrefined self to attain— he,
established in supreme austerity, chose the Lord of the Gods as his boon. For it is said that the Lord subsisted on air alone for a hundred years.
He propitiated Mahādeva, the multiform Lord of Umā.
There, all the Brahman-sages as well as the celestial-sages,
the world-protectors, and the Sādhyas together with the Vasus [propitiated] the Lord of the World.
The Ādityas and the Rudras, the Sun and the Moon, the Maruts and the Mārutas, as well as the oceans and the rivers;
the two Aśvins, the divine Gandharvas, and likewise Nārada and Parvata.
The Gandharva Viśvāvasu, the Siddhas, and the hosts of Apsarases were there;
and Rudra Mahādeva, wearing a beautiful garland made of Karṇikāra flowers, shone like the moon amidst its moonlight.
In that divine and delightful forest, crowded with gods and celestial sages,
the seer remained established in supreme yoga, intent upon obtaining a son;
yet his complexion did not fade, nor did any exhaustion arise.
That appeared like a marvel even to the three worlds. And the matted locks of that one of immeasurable splendor, who was absorbed in yoga, were seen blazing with energy like the crests of fire.
The venerable Mārkaṇḍeya indeed related this to me;
he always recounted here to me the deeds of the gods. Even today, these [powers] of Kṛṣṇa are illuminated by that asceticism.
"O dear one, the matted locks of that high-souled one shine with the color of fire.
O Bhārata, by such asceticism and through his devotion,
Maheśvara, with a gracious soul, formed a resolution in his mind.
Then Mahādeva, accompanied by Ambikā, revealed himself to him;
and the Blessed Lord Tryambaka, as if smiling, said to him:
"O Dvaipāyana, such a son as this shall be born to you."
"Just as fire, as wind, as earth, as water,
and as space, so shall his great son become pure. He will share their nature, possess their intellect, have their self, and take refuge in them."
"Enveloping the three worlds with his splendor, he shall attain absolute glory.
Bhīṣma said:
"Having obtained that supreme boon from the god, the son of Satyavatī—"
Then, taking hold of the fire-drill (araṇī) with the desire to produce fire, he churned it.
Then, O King, the venerable seer beheld an Apsaras named Ghṛtācī, who was bearing a supreme form by her own splendor.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, upon suddenly seeing the Apsaras in that forest, the venerable sage Vyāsa was instantly deluded by desire. And she,
having then caused Vyāsa’s mind to be agitated by passion, [acted accordingly].
Having become a female parrot, O great king, Ghṛtācī approached him.
Seeing that Apsaras disguised in another form,
he was overcome by passion arising from his body, which pervaded all his limbs.
But though that sage Vyāsa restrained his heart with great fortitude, he was unable to control his mind which had already spread abroad;
for he had been captivated by the beauty of Ghṛtācī due to the power of destiny.
As that sage was striving with great effort, desiring to kindle a fire,
his semen suddenly fell into the fire-drill itself.
Yet that best of the twice-born remained with a mind free from doubt, exactly as it was.

The Brahman-sage churned the fire-drill, O King, and from it Śuka was born. While the seed was being churned, Śuka— the great ascetic, supreme seer, and master of yoga— was born from the womb of the fire-drill.
Just as the kindled fire shines at a sacrifice while receiving the oblation,
even so was Śuka born, blazing as it were with splendor;
O Kauravya, he bore his father’s unsurpassed form and complexion.
Then, his soul purified, he shone like a smokeless fire blazing;
O lord of men, Gaṅgā, the best of rivers, having approached Meru’s summit in her own embodied form,
bathed him with her water.

And from the intermediate space, O descendant of Kuru, a staff and a black antelope skin fell to the earth, O lord of kings, for the sake of the high-souled Śuka. The Gandharvas sang repeatedly and the hosts of Apsaras danced.
Celestial drums of great sound resounded,
and the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, as well as Tumburu and Nārada,
and the Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū, praised the one born from Śuka.
There, the world-protectors, headed by Śakra, had assembled,
as did the gods, the celestial seers, and the Brahman-seers as well;
and there the wind rained down all kinds of divine flowers.
The entire world, both moving and stationary, became filled with joy.
Then the high-souled and most radiant one, together with the goddess,
personally and with affection performed the birth rites for the son of the sage according to the prescribed ritual as soon as he was born.
To him, Śakra, the lord of the gods, out of affection gave a divine water-pot of wondrous appearance, as well as celestial garments, O Lord;
and there were thousands of swans, cranes, and saras cranes.
O Bhārata, parrots and blue jays moved clockwise around him. Then the highly effulgent son of Araṇi, having obtained his divine birth,
remained right there— wise, observant of vows, and composed in mind.
O great king, as soon as he was born, the Vedas, along with their secret portions and compendiums, appeared before him just as they had appeared before his father. He,
however, chose Bṛhaspati, who was an expert in the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and their commentaries.
O Great King, constantly reflecting upon the Dharma alone,
he studied all the Vedas together with their secret Upanishads and their compendiums,
as well as the Itihāsas and the treatises on statecraft in their entirety, O Lord.
Having given the teacher’s fee to his preceptor, the great sage, having completed his studies,
being a celibate student and composed in mind, undertook fierce austerities;
for even in his childhood, he was a man of great ascetic power among the gods and the seers.

He is one to be consulted and honored for his knowledge and asceticism; yet, O lord of men, the mind of this man, who perceives the dharma of liberation, finds no delight in the three stages of life rooted in the householder state.
12,312.001 Bhīṣma said:
Reflecting upon liberation, Śuka approached his father; desiring the highest good and endowed with humility, he saluted his preceptor and spoke.
"O Blessed One, skilled in the dharmas of liberation, please explain this to me, O Lord, so that supreme peace may arise in my mind. Having heard his son's words, the supreme ṛṣi spoke to him.
"Study liberation, my son, as well as the various duties (dharmas).
At his father's command, Śuka, the best among the knowers of Brahman,
mastered the entire Yoga-śāstra and the system of Kapila, O Bhārata.
When Vyāsa perceived that his son was endowed with Brahmanic splendor, possessed valor equal to that of Brahmā, and was proficient in the science of liberation,
he then said to him, "Go to Janaka, the lord of Mithilā."

He will explain to you the means to liberation in its entirety and in detail. By his father’s command, he went to King Janaka of Mithilā to inquire about the ultimate limit of dharma and the supreme goal of liberation.
And he was told by the human: "Go by the path of men without being amazed;
you must certainly not travel through the air by means of supernatural power.
You should proceed with straightforwardness alone, not by a path that seeks after pleasure."
One should not seek out specific distinctions, for such distinctions lead to complications. You must not harbor pride toward that lord of men when he is the one to be honored;
rather, you should remain under his control, and he will sever your doubt.
"That king is skilled in dharma and proficient in the treatises on liberation;
he is worthy of my sacrifice, and whatever he says should be done without hesitation.
Thus addressed, that righteous sage departed for Mithilā.
Capable of traversing with his feet the earth together with its oceans through the air,
he passed over mountains, crossed rivers and lakes,
as well as various forests teeming with many beasts of prey and wild animals.
Having passed through Meru and the two regions of Hari, as well as the region of Haimavata,
in due order, he reached the land of Bhārata. Beholding various countries inhabited by Cīnas and Hūṇas, he proceeded onward.
The great sage arrived in this land of Āryāvarta,
having obeyed his father’s command and reflecting upon that very purpose; moving through the sky like a bird, he traversed the road as if gliding through the air.
Beholding delightful ports and prosperous cities,
as well as various kinds of jewels, Śuka did not see them; likewise, he saw beautiful gardens and sacred shrines.
Having traversed the road and passed by many sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
he reached Videha in no long time;
it was protected by the high-souled Dharmarāja Janaka.
There he saw many villages providing abundant food and drink, prosperous hamlets and cowherd settlements crowded with many herds of cattle,
and flourishing lands rich in rice and barley, frequented by swans and cranes.
Adorned with hundreds of glorious lotus ponds,
he passed through the Videha country, which was inhabited by prosperous people,
and reached the delightful and magnificent grove of Mithilā.
Seeing that place crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and thronged with men and women, Acyuta passed through it as if he did not see it at all;
bearing that burden with his mind, he reflected only upon that very purpose.
Delighting in the self and with a tranquil soul, he reached Mithilā. Having arrived at its gate, he was stopped by the gatekeepers;
remaining there, absorbed in meditation, he entered once he was recognized as one who was liberated.

Having reached the royal highway crowded with prosperous people, and having arrived at the king’s palace, he entered it without hesitation. There, too, the gatekeepers barred his way with harsh words.
In that same manner, Śuka remained there free from anger; though tormented by the heat and the journey, and afflicted by hunger, thirst,
and fatigue, he did not faint, nor did he grow weary, nor did he move away from the heat.
Among those gatekeepers, one was filled with sorrow;
seeing Śuka standing there like the sun reached its zenith,
he honored him according to custom and saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
Then he was ushered into the second courtyard of the royal palace.
Seated there, O dear one, Śuka reflected only upon liberation;
that man of great splendor looked with equal vision upon both shade and sunlight.
After a mere moment, the king’s minister approached him with palms joined in reverence and led him into the third courtyard of the royal palace. There,
connected to the inner apartments, was a great grove resembling Caitraratha.
Having shown Śuka that excellent forest, delightful with flowering trees and featuring well-distributed water-gardens,
the minister led Śuka into the supreme pleasure grove.
Having assigned a seat for the Arhat, he then departed once more.
[There stood] young women of lovely appearance and beautiful hips,
dressed in fine red garments and adorned with ornaments of refined gold.

Skilled in conversation and chatter, proficient in dance and song, they spoke with a smile and were equal to the *apsarases* in beauty; they were skilled in the arts of love, perceptive of inner feelings, and experts in all matters.
More than fifty thousand courtesans rushed forward;
having offered water for the feet and other gifts, and having honored him with supreme worship, they gratified him with excellent food appropriate to the time and place.
O dear one, O Bhārata, after he had finished eating, they showed him that most beautiful grove of the inner apartments, one by one;
and while playing, laughing, and singing, those women [showed] the parrot.
Then all those who knew his nature attended upon that noble-souled one;
but the pure-souled Āraṇeya— free from the three doubts, performer of the three duties,
with senses under control and anger conquered— neither rejoiced nor was he provoked to anger.

To him those supreme women offered a celestial bed and seat, worthy of the best, adorned with jewels, and spread with exquisite coverings. Having performed the washing of his feet and observed the twilight devotions, Śuka—
He sat down upon the holy seat, reflecting upon that very matter;
having devoted himself to meditation there during the first watch of the night,
the Lord took sleep at midnight according to the proper rule.
Then, having risen after a moment and immediately performed his purification,
the wise and infallible son of Kṛṣṇa, surrounded by women, devoted himself once more to meditation for the remainder of that day according to this rite.
And he spent that night in the royal palace, O Bhārata.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O Bhārata, King Janaka, together with his ministers, [deliberated].
Placing the family priest at the head, along with all the women of the inner apartments,
and bringing forward the seat as well as various jewels,
