he approached the son of his guru, carrying the respectful offering (*arghya*) upon his head.
Taking that seat— which was adorned with many jewels,
spread with a magnificent carpet, auspicious on all sides, and endowed with supernatural power—
the king, having touched it with his hand as it was held by the domestic priest, [prepared to sit].
He gave that most highly honored [gift] to Śuka, the son of his preceptor. Having seated the son of Kṛṣṇa there, he honored him according to the scriptures;
first offering water for the feet, he then presented the guest-offering (arghya) and a cow.

And he accepted that worship, accompanied by mantras, according to the prescribed rule. Having accepted that worship from Janaka, the best of the twice-born, having granted leave regarding the cow and having shown honor to the king, [he departed].
The one of great splendor, Śuka, inquired after the king’s inexhaustible welfare and his health, O Indra among kings, along with that of his followers. Then,
having been granted permission by him, he sat down together with his attendants.
The king, a noble being of high lineage, with palms joined in reverence upon the ground,
having inquired after the welfare and well-being of the son of Vyāsa,
that monarch asked: "What is the purpose of your visit?"
Śuka said:
"May you be blessed! My father told me that the king of Videha, the famous Janaka, is an expert in the meaning of the dharma of liberation and is my sacrificial priest."
"Go there quickly if you have any doubt in your heart;
whether regarding worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) or renunciation (*nivṛtti*), he will sever that doubt for you.
It is by my father’s command that I have come here to question you."
O best among the upholders of dharma, you ought to tell me this correctly:
what is the duty of a brahmin here, and what is the nature of the goal of liberation? How is liberation to be achieved—through knowledge or through austerity?
Janaka said:
"Listen to what must be done by a Brahmin here from birth onwards:
once the initiation ceremony has been performed, my dear, he should be devoted to the Vedas."

O Lord, through austerity, service to his guru, and celibacy, he became free from debt to the gods and the ancestors, being devoid of malice. Having studied the Vedas with self-restraint and having bestowed the sacrificial fee, he remained disciplined.
Then, having obtained permission, the twice-born man should indeed perform the *samāvartana* rite. Having returned home, he should dwell in the householder stage with his wife, self-restrained,
free from malice, acting according to the rule, and likewise maintaining the sacred fires.
Having produced sons and grandsons, he should dwell in the forest hermitage,

honoring those very same fires according to the scriptures and being fond of guests. That knower of dharma, having properly internalized the fires within himself while in the forest, [should proceed].
Free from dualities and with a self devoid of passion, one should dwell in the stage of the Brahma-ashrama.
Śuka said:
When knowledge and realization have arisen, eternal and manifest within the heart—
"12,313.020c Must one necessarily dwell in hermitages and forests? 12,313.021a This I ask of you; you ought to explain it to me.
12,313.021c Speak to me according to the true meaning of the Vedas, O lord of men."
Janaka said:
Without knowledge and realized wisdom (jñāna-vijñāna), there can be no attainment of liberation;
and without a connection with a guru, the attainment of knowledge is not possible.
The teacher is its boatman, and knowledge is said here to be the boat.
Having gained realization and accomplished his purpose, he who has crossed over should abandon both.
This is for the non-cessation of the worlds and for the non-cessation of actions.
The dharma practiced by the ancients, consisting of the discourse on the four stages of life (āśramas),
is attained here as liberation after performing good and evil deeds through action across many births according to this sequential method.
Through these causes brought about over many births in the various wombs of saṃsāra,
the pure-souled one indeed attains liberation in the first stage of life. Having attained that, for the wise man who is liberated and has seen the goal, [there is no further rebirth].

Among the three stages of life (āśramas), what indeed could be the goal for one who seeks the supreme? One should constantly avoid the defects of passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa), and, established upon the path of goodness (sāttvika), one should perceive the Self by means of the self.

Perceiving the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, one is not defiled, just as an aquatic creature is not wetted by water. Like a bird that rises above the water, one attains infinity in the hereafter.
Having abandoned the body, liberated, free from the pairs of opposites, and attained tranquility—
listen here, O dear one, to the verses sung of old by King Yayāti,
which are preserved by the twice-born who are experts in the scriptures on liberation.

The light is within the self and not elsewhere; it is indeed fixed right there. And it is possible for one with a well-composed mind to see that by oneself. He from whom another does not fear, and who does not fear another—[he is liberated].
He who neither desires nor hates then attains Brahman;
when he does not harbor any evil intent toward any living being through action, mind, or speech, then he attains Brahman.
Having disciplined the self through austerity, having cast off delusive envy,
and having abandoned desire and greed, one then attains the state of Brahman. When [one perceives] non-dissolution in all beings, whether in what is audible or visible, [then one attains that state].
When one becomes equanimous and free from the pairs of opposites, one then attains Brahman— when one views praise and blame with perfect equality,
as well as gold and iron, and likewise pleasure and pain.
Cold and heat, likewise profit and loss, the pleasant and the unpleasant,
life and death— even these, one then attains to Brahman.
Just as a tortoise here extends its limbs and then withdraws them again, so does the Self manifest and then dissolve.
In this way, the senses must be restrained by the mind by the monk;
just as a house enveloped in darkness is seen by means of a lamp,
so too can the Self be perceived by means of the lamp of wisdom.

"O best among the wise, I perceive all this within you; whatever else is to be known, you know that in its true essence. O Brahman-sage, you are well-known to me as one who has reached the very end of all objects of knowledge."
"O Great Sage, by the grace of my preceptor, by your own instruction, and through his very grace,
this divine knowledge has appeared within me; therefore, you are known to me."
Your wisdom is superior, your state is superior,
and your sovereignty is superior; yet you do not perceive this,
whether due to childishness, doubt, or perhaps from the fear born of a lack of liberation.
Even when consciousness has arisen,
one who has severed his doubts through those like me does not attain that state by means of mere pure resolve;
rather, having untied the knots of the heart, he attains that state.

And you, O Brahmin, having produced discernment, being firm in intellect and free from greed, attain that supreme state through resolute effort; for you there is no distinction between pleasure and pain, nor is there any longing.
No longing arises for dance or song, nor does passion take hold;
you have no attachment to kinsmen, and there is no fear in you regarding dangers.
O illustrious one, I see you as one for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are equal.

Both I and other wise men behold you established upon that supreme path which is imperishable and free from suffering— that fruit which belongs here to a Brahmin, and that which constitutes the very essence of liberation.
"O Brahmin, you indeed abide in that; what else do you ask?
Bhīṣma said:
"Having heard these words, he who had perfected his soul and reached firm resolve—"
Abiding in the self by means of the self, and having seen the self by means of the self, he—
his task accomplished, happy, and tranquil— departed silently toward the north. Resorting to yoga, he proceeded contentedly toward the northern quarter.
At that very time, the celestial sage Nārada,
sharing the nature of the wind, set out toward the Śaiśira mountain to behold the Himavat, which is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
It was crowded with throngs of *apsarases* and resounded with the sound of singing;
it was likewise filled with hosts of *kiṃnaras* and *bhṛṅgarājas*,
as well as *madgus*, *khañjarīṭas*, and various *jīvajīvaka* birds.
It resounded with the cries of hundreds of peacocks of variegated plumage,
with flocks of joyful royal swans, and likewise with cuckoos; and Garuḍa, the king of birds, always frequented it.
The four world-protectors and the gods, together with the hosts of sages,
always assemble there out of a desire for the welfare of the world;
it is there that the high-souled Viṣṇu performed austerities for the sake of obtaining a son.
And at that very spot where, in his childhood, the prince cast down the dwellers of heaven—
having indeed disregarded the three worlds— he laid his spear upon the surface of the earth; there Skanda, casting it down, then spoke these words to the world.
"O Brahmins, let him who is superior to me, for whom [the gods] are more dear,
or who is a second person devoted to Brahman (brahmiṣṭha) and possessed of prowess in the three worlds—
let him lift up this spear, or at least shake it."

Upon hearing that, the worlds were distressed, wondering, "Who shall lift her up? Then the Blessed Viṣṇu beheld the entire host of gods, their senses and minds agitated, along with the Asuras and Rākṣasas, all cast down.
Reflecting, "What indeed would be the right thing to do here?
he could not endure that insult and glared at the son of Agni. Then, that pure-souled one, laughing, [seized] the blazing spear.
Puruṣottama shook it with his left hand. As the spear was being shaken by the powerful Viṣṇu at that time,
the entire earth, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, trembled.
Although he was capable of lifting it up, the Lord did not lift it, but merely shook it,
protecting Skanda from being insulted;
having shaken it, the Blessed One spoke this to Prahrāda:
"Behold the prowess of the prince; no one else could have accomplished this. Unable to endure those words and determined to lift it up, he seized that spear of his, yet he could not even shake it.
Having uttered a great roar, he fainted upon the mountain peak; overwhelmed,
the son of Hiraṇyakaśipu fell to the ground,
having gone toward the northern direction on the side of that king of mountains.
O dear one, the invincible bull-bannered god constantly performed austerities there;
his hermitage was surrounded by a blazing fire,
and it was named Ādityabandhana, unassailable by those of undisciplined souls.
Neither yakṣas, rākṣasas, nor dānavas are able to go there;
it is ten yojanas in width and enveloped in flames of fire.
There the blessed and powerful Pāvaka himself resides.
Pacifying all obstacles for the wise Mahādeva,
who stood upon one foot for a thousand divine years,
Mahādeva remained there firm in his vow, causing distress to the gods.
Taking his stand in the eastern direction on a secluded mountain slope of the wise king of mountains, Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and a man of great asceticism,
taught the Vedas to his disciples.
Surrounded by these disciples— the highly fortunate Sumantu, Vaiśampāyana, the immensely wise Jaimini, and the ascetic Paila— Vyāsa, of great austerity, remained seated.
There, the pure-souled son of Aṛaṇi, like the sun in the sky, beheld his father’s most excellent and holy hermitage. Then Vyāsa saw it surrounded, glowing like a blazing fire.
He beheld his son approaching, possessing a radiance equal to the sun,
moving without clinging to trees, mountains, or uneven terrain—
the high-souled one, joined in yoga like an arrow released from a bowstring.
Having approached, the son of Araṇī grasped his father’s feet; the great sage also greeted them according to their pleasure. Then he reported everything in its entirety to his father.
With a joyful heart, Śuka related his conversation with King Janaka; meanwhile,
the powerful Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and great sage, continued teaching his disciples and his son in this manner as he dwelt upon the slopes of the Himalayas.
Then, on one occasion, his disciples stood surrounding him—
men perfected in the study of the Vedas, tranquil in soul, with senses subdued,
who had attained mastery in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches, and were great ascetics.
Then those disciples, with palms joined in reverence, said to their teacher Vyāsa:
"We have been endowed with great prosperity and have increased in fame;
now we desire one favor to be granted by our teacher."
Having heard these words of theirs, the Brahmarṣi said to them:
"O dear ones, let that which is your beloved task be told to me.
Hearing these words of their preceptor, those disciples were delighted in their hearts.

Once again, O King, with palms joined in reverence and bowing their heads to their preceptor, those twelve thousand three hundred and fourteen [pupils] spoke these excellent words together: "If our teacher is pleased, O best of sages, we are truly blessed."
"But we all desire this boon granted by the Great Seer:
let not a sixth disciple of yours attain fame here; be gracious to us.
We are your four disciples, and the preceptor’s son is the fifth."
"May the Vedas be established here; this is the boon we desire.

Having heard these words of his disciples, the wise Vyāsa—the son of Parāśara, who knows the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas and contemplates the welfare of the world beyond—[acted accordingly].
The righteous-souled one spoke these words, consistent with dharma and leading to the highest good, to his disciples:
"The Veda should always be given to a Brāhmaṇa who is intent on hearing it,
by one who desires a permanent residence in the world of Brahmā."

"May you all be numerous; let this Veda be spread abroad. It must not be imparted to one who is not a disciple, nor to one who lacks vows, nor to one whose self is undisciplined. All these qualities of a disciple must be understood according to their true nature."
Knowledge should never, under any circumstances, be imparted to one whose character has not been examined.
Just as pure gold is tested by heating, cutting, and rubbing,
so too should students be scrutinized according to their lineage, virtues, and other such qualities.
"You must not direct your disciples toward what is improper or toward great danger;
knowledge will bear fruit according to their understanding and according to how they have recited it.
May everyone cross over all difficulties, and may everyone behold auspicious things."
One should cause the four castes to hear this, having placed a Brāhmaṇa at the forefront.
For this is indeed the study of the Veda, and that is remembered as a great task.
The Vedas were created here by the Self-born One for the purpose of praising the gods.
He who, out of delusion, should speak ill of a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas,
will undoubtedly suffer ruin through that malevolent thought toward the Brahmin.
This applies both to him who speaks unrighteously and to him who asks unrighteously.
One of those two either passes away or incurs enmity.
All this has been told to you regarding the rules for private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). You should act accordingly toward your disciples, and let this remain in your hearts.
12,315.001 Bhīṣma said: Having heard these words of their preceptor, the disciples of Vyāsa, possessed of great energy,
then embraced one another with joyful hearts.
"What has been spoken by the Blessed One is for our immediate and long-term welfare; it is firmly rooted in our minds, and we shall act accordingly.
Having thus honored one another with well-pleased hearts, they spoke once more.
Skilled in speech, they addressed their preceptor once more:
"O Great Sage, O Lord, it is our desire to go from this mountain to the earth,
provided that it pleases you to divide the Vedas into many parts."
Having heard the words of his disciples, the lordly son of Parāśara then replied with these beneficial words, consistent with dharma and worldly purpose:
"Whether you go to the earth or to the world of the gods, do as you please."
"And you must practice heedfulness, for the Veda is full of deceptions.
Then, having been thus permitted by their truthful teacher,
they all performed a circumambulation of Vyāsa and saluted him with their heads bowed.
Having descended to the earth, they then established the Cāturhotra sacrifice,
performing the *saṃyāja* rites for the Brahmins, the Kṣatriyas, and likewise the Vaiśyas;
being constantly honored by the twice-born, they rejoiced, devoted to their homes.
Devoted to officiating at sacrifices and teaching, they were illustrious and renowned throughout the world.
When his disciples had descended [to earth], the wise Vyāsa, accompanied by his son,
sat down in a secluded place, silent and absorbed in meditation.
Nārada, of great ascetic merit, saw him in the hermitage;
then, at the proper time, he addressed him with words of sweet syllables:
"O great ṛṣi, descendant of Vasiṣṭha, the sound of Vedic recitation does not proceed."
"12,315.012c Why do you sit alone, silent and intent on meditation, as if lost in thought?
12,315.013a Deprived of the sound of Vedic chanting, this mountain no longer shines;
it is like the moon eclipsed by dust and darkness."
It does not shine as it did before, like the dwelling of the Niṣādas;
though frequented by hosts of celestial sages, it is now deprived of the sound of the Vedas.
For the ṛṣis, the gods, and the Gandharvas of great power [no longer dwell there].
"Deprived of the sound of the Veda, they do not shine as they did before.
Having heard Nārada’s words, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana said:
"O great seer, O expert in the doctrines of the Vedas, that which has been spoken by you—"
"You ought to speak what is agreeable to my mind;
for you are all-knowing, all-seeing, and curious about everything. Whatever has occurred throughout the three worlds, all of it is established within your knowledge."
"O Brahmin-sage, give the command; tell me what I should do for you.
O Brahman-sage, declare that which must be performed by me. Separated from my disciples here, this mind of mine is not very joyful."
12,315.020 Nārada said:
"The lack of Vedic study is the impurity of the Vedas; the absence of vows is the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa.
The Vāhīkas are the impurity of the earth; curiosity is the impurity of women."
"May you study the Vedas together with your wise son,
dispelling the darkness caused by the fear of Rākṣasas with the sound of Vedic recitation.
Bhīṣma said:

Having heard the words of Nārada, Vyāsa, the knower of the supreme dharma and firm in his vows regarding the study of the Vedas, spoke joyfully, saying, "So be it. And he spoke once again to the highly wise Nārada.
"You have just now stated that the Bāhlikas are the stain of the earth.
Nārada said:
"O best of speakers, tell me, what are the Bāhlikas like?"
On this earth, there are four regions filled with sinful people:
the first is known as Yugandhara, and likewise Bhūtilaka;
the third is called Acyutacchala, the most wicked of all.
The fourth, however, is a great sinner known by the name Bāhlīka;
at Yugaṃdhara, people there drink the milk of deer, camels, and donkeys, and indeed,
the people in the land of Acyuta appear to be of a single uniform color.
Those wicked ones indeed discharge urine and excrement into the waters;
they constantly consume excessive amounts of food and drink that water while wearing sacred ash on their foreheads.
Furthermore, the Vāhīkas, who are excluded from the service of Hari, never remember Hari at any time.
"Those who increase their flesh and blood for the sake of worldly liberation—
those known as the Bāhlīkas— will be born in vain," so said the Piśāca, who is devoted to feeding on lotuses.
O great sage, listen to this concerning the formidable *muṣuṇṭhī* plant:
it is a Brahmin woman with many sons who has come to bathe at Puṣkara;
having drunk milk at Yugandhara, she is indeed accustomed to the sacred site of Acyuta.

"Having bathed at Bhūtilaka and indeed having beheld the Bāhlīkas, you have come here; why then, after bathing there, do you not go to heaven? Having said this, she smashed the Brahmin woman's vessel with a pestle.
The Piśācī Tīrthapālikā, her eyes copper-red with rage, said:
"This is how you behave during the day, but at night your conduct is quite different.
Go! Through your association with the Bāhlīkas, you have become impure; of this there is no doubt."
Those who hate the Great-Souled One and do not remember Janārdana—
there is no access for them to sacred pilgrimage sites, even for those merely associated with them.
A Brahmin woman, being afraid, set out together with her sons.

Remaining within her own body, she and her son, intent on meditation, thus chanted the pure twelve-syllabled name of the infinite Hari. When three years were completed, the Brāhmaṇī returned once more.
Accompanied by her son, the Piśācī spoke thus to the Tathāgata at Puṣkaradvāra:
"Salutations to you, O auspicious Brāhmaṇī! I have been purified by the sight of you.
Together with your son, perform the ritual ablution at the sacred ford (tīrtha), and be freed from evil."
"O virtuous woman, you ought to touch me with water while uttering the name of Hari.
Thus addressed, the brahmin lady of auspicious vows, together with her sons,
was delighted and sprinkled him with water accompanied by the twelve-syllable mantra.
At that very moment, the Piśācī became pure and possessed a divine form;
she indeed became a celestial Apsarā and went to the supreme heavenly world. And the Brāhmaṇī, devoted to Vāsudeva, [attained her goal] in due time.
Accompanied by her sons, she has gone to that supreme, auspicious abode of the Unfallen.
O wise sage, this has been told to you; the time has now arrived. O one of great wisdom, I shall depart, yet I will surely return again.
Having spoken thus, Nārada, the best among speakers, then departed.
But the blessed Dvaipāyana, having heard that from the best of sages,
then engaged in the study of the Vedas together with his son Śuka.
With a loud voice, like that of a student of phonetics (*śaikṣa*), as if filling the worlds with it,
while those two were thus practicing, proponents of various doctrines,
a wind blew with extreme force, driven by the gale from the ocean.
Then Vyāsa forbade his son, saying, "This is a time unfit for study. But Śuka, as soon as he was forbidden, being filled with curiosity,
asked his father, "O Brahmin, from where has this wind arisen?"
"You ought to relate to me the entire conduct of Vāyu.
Having heard these words of Śuka, Vyāsa was greatly amazed;
regarding this occasion of the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), he spoke these words.
Divine vision has arisen in you; your mind is healthy and stainless.
Abandoned by both darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas), you are established in goodness (sattva).
You behold the Self by means of the self, like one's own reflection in a mirror.
Having established [the Vedas] within yourself, reflect upon the Vedas with your own intellect.

O Viṣṇu, there are these two paths after death: the path of the gods (*devayāna*), which leads upward, and the path of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*), which is characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*) and leads downward. These two paths lead respectively to heaven and to the lower regions.

On the earth and in the intermediate space, wherever the winds blow— know these seven paths of the wind in their proper order. There, the hosts of gods known as the Sādhyas, possessed of great strength, came into being.
To them was born a son named Samāna, who was difficult to conquer.
Udāna was his son, and Vyāna was his son. After that, Apāna is to be known, and Prāṇa followed after him.
The invincible Prāṇa, the scorcher of enemies, became childless.
I shall now describe their individual functions exactly as they are:
the wind (Vāyu) sets in motion the various activities of living beings everywhere.
Because he causes all beings to breathe, he is called "Prāṇa. That wind which impels the masses of clouds— those born of smoke and those born of heat—
is the first wind on the first path, named Pravaha.
The second wind, named Āvaha, blows roaring in the sky with supreme splendor, drawing moisture from the clouds and lightning;
it is that which constantly causes the rising of the luminaries, beginning with the Moon.
Within the intermediate bodies, that which the great seers call *udāna* is the wind which sustains the water from the four oceans; having drawn up the waters,
the wind places them within the clouds in the sky.
He who, having joined the clouds with the waters, delivers them to Parjanya— he is named Udvaha,
the most excellent, the third wind, the ever-moving. By him the dark clouds are gathered together and then dispersed in many directions.
Those clouds, which bring about liberation for twelve thousand three hundred and fifteen years,
arise; by them, being compacted and pierced while roaring, they become rivers, and having come into existence for the sake of protection, they attain the state of clouds.
That wind which carries the celestial chariots of the gods through the sky,
the fourth wind named Saṃvaha, is the crusher of mountains; by that forceful, harsh, and crushing wind, the vital juices are shattered.

Driven by Vāyu, the clouds are dispersed and no longer exist as rain-bearing masses; this fifth wind, possessing great velocity and accompanied by thundering from the sky, is a movement of terrible portents, and it is named Vivaha.
In that revolving region, divine waters flow through the sky,
and the holy water of the celestial Gaṅgā remains supported there;
it is there that the sun, with its single ray, is struck back from afar.
The source of a thousand rays, by which the earth is illumined;
from whom the moon is nourished and who is the divine treasury of nectar— this wind, named Parivaha, is the foremost among the swift.
He who at the time of death casts out the vital breaths of all living beings— he whose path both Death and Vaivasvata follow—
[is seen] by those who examine correctly with an intellect that is peaceful and constantly fixed upon the inner self.
That which leads to immortality for those who delight in the practice of meditation;
having attained which with speed, the ten thousand sons of Dakṣa, the lord of progeny, reached the ends of the quarters.
"By whom [once] created, one who is overcome goes forth and never returns;
that supreme wind named Parāvaha is difficult to transcend. Thus are these sons of Aditi, the Mārutas, most wonderful."

12,315.053c Moving everywhere and supporting all things, they blow without resting. 12,315.054a But this is a great marvel, that this best of mountains has been suddenly shaken by that wind blowing forth.

"O dear one, when this wind that is Viṣṇu’s breath is suddenly stirred up by its own force, the world is then violently shaken. Therefore, those who know Brahman do not recite the Veda when the wind blows excessively."
"For it has been said that from wind comes the fear of wind; thus, that Brahman becomes afflicted.
Having spoken these words, the lordly son of Parāśara, after saying to his son, "Study [the Vedas]," then departed for the celestial Gaṅgā.
12,316.001 Bhīṣma said:
In that interval, while it was empty, Nārada approached Śuka,
who was intent on his private Vedic recitation and desired to explain the meanings of the Vedas.
Desiring to teach Śuka the various means to liberation that he had sought,
Śuka, upon seeing the celestial sage Nārada standing before him,
honored him according to the Vedic rite beginning with the offering of the *arghya*.
Then Nārada, being pleased, spoke joyfully: "O best among the knowers of Brahman, tell me, my son, with what supreme good shall I unite you?
Having heard Nārada's words, O Bhārata, Śuka replied:
"You ought to engage me in whatever may be for the benefit of this world.
Nārada said:
"Formerly, among the sages of purified souls who desired to know the truth..."
The blessed Sanatkumāra spoke these words:
"There is no eye equal to knowledge; there is no austerity equal to knowledge. There is no suffering equal to passion; there is no happiness equal to renunciation."
Abstaining from evil deeds, constant cultivation of virtuous character,
noble conduct, and proper behavior— this is the unsurpassed good.
Having attained this human state which is fraught with suffering, he who becomes attached to it is deluded.
That [attachment] is not sufficient for liberation from suffering; indeed, attachment is the very mark of suffering.
The intellect of one who is attached wavers, increasing the net of delusion. Enveloped by the net of delusion, one experiences suffering both in this world and in the next.

By every possible means, one who seeks the highest good must restrain both desire and anger, for these two are intent upon destroying that very good. One should always protect one's ascetic merit from anger and protect one's prosperity from envy.
One should protect one's learning from honor and dishonor, but protect oneself from negligence. Compassion is the supreme dharma, and forgiveness is the highest strength.
Self-knowledge is the supreme knowledge; there is nothing higher than truth.
The speaking of truth is excellent, yet that which is beneficial may even be superior to truth;
that which results in the ultimate welfare of living beings—this, in my view, is true. One who renounces the fruits of all undertakings, who is free from desire, and who possesses nothing.
He by whom everything has been renounced is wise and he is a scholar; here, with his senses under his own control, he moves among the objects of the senses,
unattached, tranquil in soul, changeless, and composed.
Whether together with those who have become his very self or even without them— those who are not that [self]—
he, being liberated, attains the supreme good before long.
He should always avoid seeing them, avoiding contact with them, and likewise avoiding conversation with them.
O Sage, he who dwells together with all beings attains the highest good.
One should not harm any living creatures; moved by a spirit of friendliness, one should conduct oneself accordingly. Having attained this human birth, one should not harbor enmity toward anyone.

12.316.019a Absence of possessiveness, perfect contentment, freedom from desire, and lack of restlessness— 12.316.019c these they call the supreme good for one who knows the self and has conquered his mind. 12.316.020a Having renounced all possessions, O dear one, become a master of your senses.
Abide in the state free from sorrow, which is fearless both here and in the hereafter.
Those who are free from worldly desire do not grieve; therefore, abandon worldly desire for yourself. By renouncing worldly desire, O gentle one, you shall be liberated from the torment of suffering.
By one who is constant in austerity, self-controlled, a sage with a restrained mind,
desiring to conquer the unconquered, one should remain unattached amidst attachments.
Unattached to the bonds of the *guṇas*, one should always delight in solitary wandering.

For a Brahmin, unsurpassed happiness comes very soon. Know that sage who delights alone among beings that find pleasure in pairs; he is satisfied by wisdom, and being satisfied by knowledge, he does not grieve.
Through auspicious deeds one attains divinity; through mixed deeds, human birth;
and through inauspicious deeds, one helplessly attains a lower birth.
Therein, one is constantly assailed by the sufferings of death and old age.
A living being is cooked in the cycle of existence; why do you not perceive this? You perceive what is harmful as beneficial, and what is unstable as stable;
you perceive what is worthless as valuable—why do you not perceive this?
Being enveloped by many threads of delusion born of yourself,
you do not perceive that you are wrapping yourself like a silkworm;
enough with this grasping, for grasping is fraught with fault.
For the silkworm is bound by its own cocoon; likewise,
living beings who are attached to their children, wives, and families perish,
like aged wild elephants sunk in the mud-flood of a lake.
Behold these beings, deeply afflicted, dragged by the net of affection as if fish were hauled onto dry land by a great net;
behold their family, sons, wives, bodies, and stores of wealth.
All that belongs to another is unstable; what is one's own? It is one's good and evil deeds.
Since you must inevitably depart, abandoning everything, why are you attached to what is worthless and do not attend to your own true welfare?
"How will you go alone along this path through the wilderness of darkness— unresting, without support, without provisions for the journey,
and without a guide? For when you have set out, no one at all will follow behind you."

"Both your good deeds and your evil deeds will follow you as you depart. Knowledge, action, valor, and extensive wisdom—all these are pursued for the sake of wealth; but one who has attained his goal is liberated."
This attachment to living in a village is a binding rope;
having severed it, those of good deeds depart, while those of evil deeds cannot sever it.
You see those of equal birth, age, and beauty who have been offered as victims to Death.
Indeed, there is no weariness in you, for your heart is made of iron. [It is] a river whose banks are forms, whose current is the mind, whose islands are tactile sensations, which carries flavors,
whose mud is fragrances, whose water is sounds, and which is difficult to traverse on the path to heaven.

One should cross the river by means of the boat of the intellect, which has patience for its oars, is made of truth, has the steadfastness of dharma for its keel, and moves swiftly with generosity as its wind.
Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
Abandon dharma through the absence of volition, and abandon adharma through non-violence.
Abandon both truth and falsehood through the intellect, and abandon the intellect through supreme certainty.
A body with bones for its pillars, bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, foul-smelling, and filled with urine and excrement;
it is possessed by old age and grief, a dwelling place of disease, and afflicted.
"Abandon this body, which is full of passion, impermanent, and the dwelling place of the elements—
this entire universe, both that which moves and that which is unmoving,
all of which consists of the great elements, whether it be vast or as small as an atom."
The great elements are space, wind, fire, water, and likewise earth;
consciousness is the sixth, which is called the self as the seventh;
the mind is to be known as the eighth, while intellect is recorded as the ninth.

The five sense organs, as well as darkness (*tamas*), goodness (*sattva*), and passion (*rajas*)— this group of seventeen is designated as the unmanifest (*avyakta*). Indeed, it is joined here with all the objects of the senses, both manifest and unmanifest.
This group of twenty-five consists of the manifest and the unmanifest qualities (guṇas).
When joined with all of these, one is designated as "Puruṣa" (the Spirit).
Herein lie the three aims of life, as well as pleasure, pain, birth, and death.
He who knows this in its true essence knows both the origin and the dissolution [of all things].
O son of Parāśara, whatever among the objects of knowledge is to be understood here—
whatever is perceived by the senses— that is the established nature of the manifest (vyakta).
That which is known as the unmanifest is to be understood as graspable through its marks and beyond the senses.
By means of his restrained senses, the embodied soul is satisfied as if by streams of water;
he beholds the Self spread out in the world and the world within the Self.
The power of one who perceives the higher and the lower does not see the limit of knowledge,
as he constantly beholds all beings in all their states. For one who has become Brahman, no contact with anything inauspicious occurs.
For one who has transcended the various afflictions born of delusion through knowledge,
the path of the world is not impaired by the light of wisdom in this world. [One perceives] the living being, which is without beginning or end, abiding within the self, and immutable.
The Blessed One, the knower of the sacred traditions, has declared that [the self] is both a non-doer and formless.
Yet, whatever living being is perpetually tormented by those various actions of its own making,
it kills other beings in many ways for the sake of warding off that suffering.
Then he undertakes yet another new and great amount of action;
he is tormented by that once more, like a sick man who has consumed unwholesome food. Thus, afflicted by delusion, he constantly perceives suffering as happiness.
Bound and churned by his own actions, he is constantly whirled about like a churning-stick. Then, having been released from that bondage through the ripening of his actions in this world,
he wanders through saṃsāra like a wheel, experiencing manifold suffering.
You, having ceased all bonds and having desisted from action,
become all-knowing, all-conquering, perfected, and free from worldly existence;
having halted new bondage through self-restraint by the power of austerity.
12,316.059c Many have attained perfection that is unimpeded and results in happiness.
12,317.001 Nārada said:
12,317.001a This scripture, which destroys sorrow, brings peace, and is auspicious, is called Aśoka.
Upon hearing this, one gains wisdom; having gained it, one prospers in happiness.
Thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for fear assail the fool day after day, but not the wise man.
Therefore, for the sake of destroying what is undesirable, learn from me this history;
if the intellect remains under control, one attains the destruction of grief arising from union with the unpleasant and separation from the beloved.

12,317.004c People of small intelligence are joined with mental sufferings. 12,317.005a One should not dwell upon those qualities belonging to things that have already passed away. 12,317.005c For one who disregards them, the bond of affection is released.
One should perceive the faults in that wherein passion arises; one should view what is beneficial as undesirable, and thus one quickly becomes dispassionate.
He who grieves over the past gains neither wealth, nor merit, nor fame.
Even if one were joined with non-existence, that [non-existence] does not cease for him.
Beings are joined with qualities and likewise separated from them;
this applies to all, for there is no ground for grief in this regard for anyone alone.

Whether it be dead or lost, he who grieves over what is past gains sorrow through sorrow and encounters two misfortunes. Those who, by means of their intelligence, perceive the continuity of existence in the worlds do not shed tears.
For one who perceives everything correctly, the activity of tears does not arise. When physical or mental suffering has arisen,
one should not dwell upon that which cannot be remedied by effort.
This is the medicine for suffering: that one should not dwell upon it. For when it is dwelt upon, it does not depart; rather, it increases all the more.
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom, and physical suffering with medicines.
This capacity of consciousness should not be equated with that of fools.
Youth, beauty, life, the accumulation of wealth, health, and dwelling with loved ones are all impermanent; a wise person should not be attached to them.
One person ought not to grieve alone for the suffering of the people;
rather, without grieving, one should take remedial action if one perceives a means to do so.
There is no doubt that in this life, suffering is far more abundant than happiness.
The unloveliness of death and the attachment to sense objects arise from delusion.
That man who abandons both suffering and pleasure attains the absolute Brahman; the wise do not grieve for him.

For wealth is indeed abandoned through suffering, and it brings no happiness in its maintenance; it is acquired with hardship, yet one should not worry about its loss. Indeed, men encounter various and distinct states of wealth.
The insatiable go to destruction; the wise attain contentment.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall. Unions end in separation; indeed, life ends in death.
There is no end to thirst; contentment, however, is the supreme happiness.
Therefore, the wise regard contentment alone as true wealth in this world.
For life, passing away even for the duration of a single blink of an eye, does not remain.
What could one constantly contemplate within these impermanent bodies?
Having reflected upon the non-existence of beings and having realized that which is beyond darkness,
those who have traversed the path do not grieve, beholding the supreme goal.
While he is still gathering [wealth], unsated in his desires, death seizes him and departs, just as a tiger seizes its prey. Yet,
one might also perceive a means for complete liberation from suffering.
Without grieving, one should indeed undertake [one's duties], remaining disciplined and free from vice.
In sound, touch, form, smells, and tastes,
there is nothing superior to their experience, whether for the wealthy or the poor.
Before the conjunction of the elements, there is no suffering, for it is free from affliction;
but because of separation from everything, one who remains established in their true nature should not grieve.
One should guard the genitals and the stomach with fortitude, and the hands and feet with the eyes.

Withdrawing his eye and ear through the mind, and his mind and speech through knowledge— having withdrawn his affection toward both those who praise him and others alike— he should wander without arrogance; he is happy and he is wise.
12,317.030a Seated, delighting in the inner self, indifferent and free from worldly desire,
12,317.030c he who should wander with only the self as his companion shall be happy.
12,318.001 Nārada said:

When the reversal of pleasure and pain occurs, neither wisdom, nor well-guided conduct, nor human effort can protect one from it. One should apply effort based on one's own inherent nature; the diligent person does not come to grief.
One should rescue one's dear self from old age, death,
and disease; for physical and mental illnesses afflict the body like sharp-pointed arrows discharged by firm archers.
For one who is diseased, trembling with the desire to know [the truth], longing for life,
and rendered helpless, the body is dragged toward destruction;
like the currents of rivers, they flow and do not turn back.
Taking away the life of mortals day after day and night after night,
this reversal between the bright and dark fortnights utterly consumes the mortal born; it does not pause for even a moment.
Wearing away the youth of all beings through their joys and sorrows, this undecaying sun indeed sets and rises again and again,
taking with him those unforeseen and unsuspected states of existence.

Nights pass away for men, taking with them both the desired and the undesired. Whatever desire a man might wish for, he would obtain each of those things if the fruit of human action were not dependent on another.
For men who are self-controlled, skillful, and wise are seen to be rendered fruitless and deprived of the results of their own actions;
while others, though foolish, devoid of merit, and the lowest of men, [attain success].
Even those devoid of blessings are seen to possess all their desires;
for there is another among living beings who is constantly intent on violence and the deception of the world, yet he grows old in very happiness.
Prosperity attends someone who remains inactive and sits still;
another, despite following his actions, does not attain what is to be gained. Tell me, is this the fault of man by his very nature?
The semen produced in one place goes again to another;
when it is joined with the womb, a fetus may or may not come to be.
For him whose cessation is perceived to be like the mango blossom, [there is no conception].
For some who desire sons and seek to continue their lineage, though they strive for success, no embryo is produced;
they tremble at the thought of conception as if before an enraged venomous serpent.
"How is it that a long-lived son is born, yet he is like a departed spirit even while still his father?
By worshipping the gods and performing austerities, those wretched men greedy for sons carry them in their wombs for ten months, only to give birth to the disgrace of their lineage."
Others, through those very auspicious rites, are born into great abundance of wealth, grain, and enjoyments accumulated by their ancestors,
having come together in sexual union with one another.
Like a calamity having entered, the embryo enters the womb; it is a living being within another body, devoid of skin,
its vital breaths obstructed, and its movements consisting only of flesh and phlegm.
The unstable foreign body, having been consumed by another foreign body,
perishes at the end of its destruction like one boat placed within another;
it was deposited as an insentient drop of semen into the womb through their union.
By what effort do you see the embryo living here? In that very same belly where food, drinks, and eaten edibles are digested,
why is the embryo not likewise digested like food?
The movement of the embryo, urine, and feces is determined by their own nature;
whether in their retention or their discharge, no power belongs to the agent.
For embryos flow out from the womb, and others are born in the same way.
Through sacred tradition, the destruction of others is brought about;
from this connection with the source of birth, he who is liberated while living obtains some offspring, yet again sinks into the pairs of opposites.

Of a hundred born together, they reach the seventh and tenth stages; beyond that, five do not survive to the age of a hundred. There is no doubt that for humans who do not exert themselves, there can be no spiritual attainments.

They are tormented by diseases like small deer by predatory beasts; though physicians strive with great effort, they cannot alleviate the agony of those being devoured by diseases while squandering vast wealth.
Even those skilled physicians, expert and well-provided with medicines,
are dragged down by diseases like deer tormented by hunters.
They drink decoctions and various kinds of clarified butters.
12,318.032c They are seen broken by old age, like elephants by superior elephants.
12,318.033a Who on earth treats those afflicted by disease—the beasts and birds?
12,318.033c Wild animals and the poor generally do not become afflicted.
"Even kings who are fierce, invincible, and of terrible splendor, Disease seizes by force, just as a butcher seizes his cattle.
Thus [he spoke] regarding the world, which is without refuge and overwhelmed by delusion and grief.
Like a stream suddenly cast by a powerful force and carried away by a stronger one,
innate dispositions— which are fixed within embodied beings— cannot be altered by wealth, nor by sovereignty, nor even by fierce asceticism.
They would not die, they would not age; all would have every desire fulfilled.
They would behold nothing unpleasant regarding the fruits of their exertion. Everyone desires to rise higher and higher above the world.
They strive according to their ability, yet it does not turn out as they intend. Intoxicated by the pride of sovereignty and the madness of liquor,
those who are vigilant, though deceitful and cruel, attend upon those who are powerful.
In some cases, afflictions cease without being examined;
in others, nothing at all is attained despite their respective efforts. Furthermore, a great disparity in results is observed within the junctions of karmic actions.
Some carry the palanquin while others go seated within it; among all those desiring prosperity, some have chariots preceding them,
as do men with hundreds of wives and widows by the hundreds.
Among beings who delight in pairs, men depart one by one.
Behold this other supreme truth; do not fall into delusion here. Abandon both dharma and adharma; abandon both truth and falsehood.
"Having abandoned both truth and falsehood, abandon that by which you abandon them.
This supreme secret has been told to you, O best of sages,
by which the gods, having relinquished the mortal world, went to heaven."
12,318.046 Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of Nārada, the highly intelligent Śuka, though steadfast, reflected in his mind but did not arrive at a certain conclusion.
"Great is the suffering caused by wife and children; great is the toil in the pursuit of sacred knowledge.
What, then, might be that eternal state which involves little suffering and yields great prosperity?
Having reflected for a moment, he determined his own course.
"O knower of the higher and the lower regarding the Dharma, [tell me] the supreme goal that leads to ultimate liberation.
How may I, remaining undefiled, attain the highest state,
so that I shall not return again to the ocean of the cycle of births?"
I truly long for that supreme state from which there is no returning again; having abandoned all attachments, I shall go to that certain destination of the mind where my self will attain peace.
"In that which is imperishable and immutable, where I shall abide eternally—
that supreme goal cannot be attained without yoga;
for the binding of one who is liberated by actions is no longer possible."
Therefore, having established myself in yoga and abandoned this body and home,
I shall become like the wind and enter the sun, that mass of splendor;
for it does not undergo decay, unlike the moon with its hosts of gods.
Trembling, he falls to the ground and ascends it once again;
for the moon is always waning and is filled once more.
Having understood this, I do not desire these repeated cycles of decline and increase.
The sun, with its fierce rays, scorches the worlds;
with its eternal, imperishable orb, it constantly draws up energy from all sides.
Therefore, it pleases me to go to the Sun of blazing splendor.
"O unassailable one, here I shall dwell with a detached inner self. While the sun scorches the world of moving and unmoving beings,
I shall cast this body into the abode of the sun."
Together with the sages, I shall go toward the solar radiance, which is exceedingly difficult to endure.
I take my leave of the trees, the serpents, the mountains, the earth, the quarters, and the sky;
and of the gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas.

"I shall enter all beings in the worlds, of this there is no doubt; let all the gods together with the seers behold my power of yoga. Then, having taken leave of that world-renowned seer Nārada, [he departed].
Having received permission from him, he went toward his father. Having saluted the high-souled seer, the sage Dvaipāyana, and having circumambulated him, Śuka, the silent sage, took leave of Kṛṣṇa.
Having heard those words of Śuka,
the high-souled seer was pleased and spoke to him again:
"O son, stay here for this day."
"I shall gratify your eyes for your sake.
Thus addressed by his father with a heart full of affection,
he did not entertain that desire, his inner self being free from attachment.
Becoming indifferent, free from affection, and released from all bonds,
that best of the twice-born fixed his mind on departing, contemplating only liberation; having completely abandoned his father, he went forth.
The vast plateau of Kailāsa, frequented by hosts of *siddhas*.
Bhīṣma said: O descendant of Bharata, having ascended the mountain plateau, the son of Vyāsa—

In a level, secluded place, free from all obstacles, he sat down; and the great sage, knowing the sequential application of yoga, held his self in accordance with the scriptures, proceeding in order through the limbs of the body beginning from the feet.
Then that wise man, facing the east not long after the sun had risen,
composed his hands and feet and sat down with humility.
There was no flock of birds there, nor any sound, nor even a sight [of anyone].
12,319.004c There, where the wise son of Vyāsa had begun to apply himself to yoga,
12,319.005a he then beheld his own self as completely released from all attachments. 12,319.005c Then Śuka, looking toward the sun, let out a great laugh.
Then, applying himself once more to yoga for the sake of attaining the path to liberation,
he became a great lord of yogins and ascended into the sky. Thereupon, he circumambulated the celestial sage Nārada.
Then he announced his own spiritual attainment to the supreme ṛṣi:
"The path has been seen; I have set out upon it. May it be well with you, O one whose wealth is asceticism!
Through your grace, O one of great luster, I shall go to my desired destination."
Permitted by Nārada, the son of Dvaipāyana then paid his respects and,
entering into yoga once more, ascended into the sky;
having leaped from the summit of Kailāsa, he then fell toward heaven.
Moving through the intermediate space, glorious, the son of Vyāsa was firm in his resolve.
All beings beheld that best of the twice-born as he rose up, possessing a splendor like that of Vainateya and a speed equal to thought or the wind.

Then, reflecting upon all three worlds with firm resolve, he set out upon the divine path, radiant as fire and the sun. As he traveled with one-pointed mind, undisturbed and free from fear, [the gods beheld him].

All beings, both mobile and immobile, beheld him; then, according to their power and in accordance with what was right, they paid him homage. And the denizens of heaven showered him with divine rains of flowers.
Seeing him, all the hosts of Gandharvas and Apsarases were struck with wonder,
and even the perfected sages were filled with supreme amazement:
"Who is this traveler of the air who has attained perfection through asceticism?"
With his lower body downward and his face turned upward, he was carried along by his eyes;
then, that supremely steadfast soul, renowned throughout the three worlds,
proceeded facing the east with speech restrained, gazing intently at the sun.
12,319.017 As if filling the entire sky in every direction with his sound,
12,319.018 O King, seeing him suddenly approaching, all the hosts of Apsarases were bewildered in mind and filled with supreme amazement.

12,319.018e Pañcacūḍā and the others, their eyes wide with wonder, [asked]: 12,319.019a "Which deity is this who has attained the supreme state? 12,319.019c Surely he comes here, liberated and free from desire."
Then he passed beyond the mountain named Malaya,
which Urvaśī and Pūrvacitti constantly frequent;
they both were filled with the greatest wonder at the sight of the son of a Brahmarṣi.
"Oh, what concentration of intellect this twice-born man possesses, devoted as he is to the study of the Vedas!
In a very short time, he moves through the sky like the moon;
through his service to his father, he has attained unsurpassed perfection."

Devoted to his father, firm in asceticism, and his father’s most beloved son—[all these] with palms joined in reverence and joyful minds offered praise. [They wondered: "How has he been abandoned by that father whose mind was focused on no other?"
Having heard the words of Urvaśī, Śuka, the knower of the highest dharma,
looked toward all the directions with his mind fixed on her speech.
He [beheld] the atmosphere and the earth itself, with its mountains, forests, and groves.
Then he beheld the lakes and likewise the rivers;
thereafter, all those deities, with palms joined in reverence, gazed upon the son of Dvaipāyana with great respect.
Then Śuka, the knower of the highest dharma, spoke these words to them:
"If my father should follow me, crying out 'Śuka!',
then an answer must be given by all of you with focused minds."
"You ought all to carry out these words of mine out of affection.
Having heard the words of Śuka, the quarters of the sky, along with the groves and forests,
the oceans, the rivers, and the mountains, replied to him from all sides.
"O Brahmin, as you command, so shall it be; 'Very well,' we shall respond when the Rishi has uttered his words. Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken these words, the Brahman-sage Śuka, of great ascetic merit, set forth toward perfection, abandoning the fourfold worlds;
for he cast off the eightfold darkness and relinquished the fivefold passion.
Then the wise one abandoned his being; it was like a marvel.
Thereupon, he became established in that eternal state—devoid of qualities, free from marks—in Brahman, blazing like a smokeless fire.
At that very moment, falling meteors, the burning of the quarters, and likewise earthquakes appeared; it was like a marvel. The trees shed their branches, and the mountains cast off their peaks.
With the sounds of thunderous crashes, Mount Himavat seemed to split asunder;
the thousand-rayed sun did not shine, nor did the fire blaze;
and the lakes, the rivers, and the oceans were all agitated.
Vāsava rained down water that was flavorful and fragrant,
and a pure wind blew, carrying divine scents.
He [stood] upon two incomparable, divine peaks born of the Himavat and Meru.

O Bhārata, he beheld two beautiful and auspicious mountains, one made of silver and the other of gold, joined together and colored white and yellow; they were a hundred yojanas in extent both horizontally and vertically,
situated in the northern direction.
With a mind free from hesitation, Śuka flew toward it in that very manner;
then, O great king, two mountain peaks were suddenly split in two, and it appeared as if a miracle had occurred.
Then, suddenly emerging from the two mountain peaks,
that best of mountains could not check his course;
thereupon, a great sound arose in the sky from all the inhabitants of heaven.
O Bhārata, when the Gandharvas, the Ṛṣis, and those who dwell upon the mountains saw Śuka pass through and the mountain split in two, a cry of "Excellent! Excellent! arose everywhere.
He was thus being honored by the gods, Gandharvas, and sages,
as well as by hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas and throngs of Vidyādharas;
the sky all around was strewn with celestial flowers.
O Great King, at that time, when Śuka was about to fly away, there were indeed 12,320.015c [leagues].
Then, traveling above the beautiful Mandākinī, the righteous-souled Śuka beheld the forest with its trees in full bloom. 12,320.016c–12,320.016c.
In that place, hosts of Apsarases, who were formless and naked, played with delight and bathed;
yet, seeing Śuka, they appeared empty and devoid of form. Perceiving that he was departing, his father, filled with affection, [approached].
Having attained the highest state, he followed behind him. But Śuka, having ascended from the wind to a path moving through the intermediate space,
displayed his own power and then became one with all beings.
Having risen with great ascetic fervor, Vyāsa, possessing the supreme state of great yoga,
traveled in the mere twinkling of an eye to where Śuka had gone. He saw that Śuka had reached his destination by splitting the mountain peak in two.

Then the sages recounted to him that various deed of his son. Thereupon, his father himself, with a loud voice, cried out "Śuka! in a long-drawn, phonetically precise accent, making the three worlds resound.
Having become all-pervading, the soul of all, and facing every direction,
the righteous-souled parrot replied, making the sound "Bhoḥ" resonate;
then, emitting that single-syllable sound "Bhoḥ" alone.

He caused the entire world, including all things mobile and immobile, to resound loudly. From that time until now, even today, whenever distinct sounds are uttered upon the ridges and in the caves of the mountains, they echo back toward Śuka.

Having displayed his power and then vanished, Śuka at that time abandoned the qualities such as sound and attained the supreme state. Having witnessed that greatness of his son of immeasurable splendor, [the father was filled with wonder].
12,320.027 He sat down on the mountain plateau, reflecting only upon his son.
12,320.028 Then, groups of Apsarases sporting on the banks of the Mandākinī,
upon encountering that seer, all became agitated and lost their composure.
Some hid themselves in the water, some took refuge in thickets,
and some gathered up their garments upon seeing that best of sages;
for the sage then recognized that his son had indeed attained liberation.
He was both pleased and ashamed at his own attachment.
Then the blessed Lord Śaṅkara, accompanied by gods and Gandharvas and honored by hosts of great seers, approached with the Pināka bow in hand.
Then Mahādeva spoke these words of consolation to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, who was then tormented by grief for his son:
"Of fire, earth, water, wind, and indeed of the intermediate space..."
"In the past, you chose from me a son equal to yourself in valor;
he has been born with such characteristics, nurtured by your ascetic power and my own majesty, pure and filled with the splendor of Brahman."

O brahmin-sage, he has attained the supreme state, so difficult to reach for those who have not conquered their senses, even by the gods; why, then, do you mourn for him? As long as the mountains shall endure, and as long as the oceans shall remain.

"O Great Sage, by my grace, your fame shall remain imperishable along with that of your son for as long as this world endures; and you shall always behold, throughout this entire world, a shadow resembling your own son that never departs from you."
O descendant of Bharata, having been thus entreated by the Blessed One himself as Rudra,
that sage turned back with supreme joy upon seeing his own shadow. Such,
O bull of the Bharatas, was the birth and the departure of Śuka.
"I have related to you in detail that which you asked of me;
O King, this was told to me long ago by the celestial sage Nārada and by the great yogi Vyāsa at every step in their discourses."
He who, devoted to tranquility, should retain this meritorious history, which is endowed with the meaning of the *mokṣadharma*, shall go to the supreme goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Whether he be a householder, a student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant,
whichever deity one who desires to attain perfection should worship—
from whom indeed does his certain heaven come, and from whom the supreme beatitude?
By what ritual should one offer oblations to the gods and likewise to the ancestors? Released [from the body], to what destination does one go, and what is the nature of liberation itself?
And having gone to heaven, what should one do so that one does not fall from the celestial realm?
"Who is the god of the gods, and likewise, who is the father of the ancestors? O Grandfather, tell me that which is even higher than him.
Bhīṣma said:
"O sinless one, you who are skilled in questioning ask me here a question that is profound. For this cannot be explained even in hundreds of years through mere reasoning,
O King, except by the grace of the gods or through the acquisition of transcendent knowledge."
"O slayer of enemies, this narrative is indeed profound; it must be explained to you.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Nārada and the seer Nārāyaṇa."

"Nārāyaṇa, the soul of the universe, eternal and possessing four forms, was born as the son of Dharma; thus did my father speak to me. O great king, this occurred long ago in the Kṛta Yuga, during the Svāyambhuva interval."
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa— among them,
the two imperishable ones, Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
having reached the hermitage of Badarī on a golden chariot, performed austerities.
That delightful vehicle was indeed eight-wheeled and drawn by living beings;
upon it sat those two original Lords of the World, emaciated and with veins clearly visible,
difficult even for the gods to behold because of their asceticism and splendor.
Only he whom those two gods grant their favor is worthy to behold them. Surely, impelled by the god of love within his heart and with their permission,
he has descended from the peak of Mount Mahāmeru to Gandhamādana.
Nārada, a being of great power, was wandering through all the worlds;
O King, he went swiftly to that region, the hermitage of Badarī.
At the time of their daily rites, curiosity arose within him.
This is that entire abode in which all the worlds are established—
along with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, together with the ṛṣis, kiṃnaras, and serpents.
This single form was born in the beginning, and subsequently became fourfold.
The great lineage of Dharma has been increased by these;
oh, how Dharma has been graced today here by these gods,
as well as by Nara and Nārāyaṇa and by Kṛṣṇa Hari.

There, Kṛṣṇa and Hari, for some particular reason, remained preeminent in righteousness and likewise established in asceticism. For these two are the supreme abode; what then could be their daily ritual?
"The illustrious parents of all beings are themselves deities;
which deity, then, do these two high-minded ones worship, or which ancestors?
Having thus reflected in his mind with devotion toward Nārāyaṇa, he [proceeded].
Then, suddenly, he appeared near the two gods;
and when the rites for the gods and the ancestors had been performed, he was beheld by them and honored according to the prescribed ritual as taught in the scriptures.
Having beheld that great wonder, an unprecedented and extensive ritual procedure,
the venerable seer Nārada sat down nearby,
well-pleased; gazing intently at Nārāyaṇa with a serene inner soul.
Having paid homage to Mahādeva, he spoke these words:
"In the Vedas, along with the Purāṇas and their limbs and sub-limbs,
you are celebrated as the unborn, eternal Creator, considered the supreme nectar."
12,321.024e This entire world, consisting of the past and the future, is established in you. 12,321.025a For all four stages of life, O Lord, have their root in the householder’s stage;
12,321.025c they worship you day after day, as you abide in various forms.
"You are the father and mother of the entire world, the eternal teacher. Which god do you worship today, and which father—whom we do not know?
O illustrious one, tell this to me who asks you."
The Blessed Lord said:
"O Brahmin, although this eternal secret of the Self is not to be spoken, I shall nevertheless tell it to you exactly as it is, for you are devoted to me."
That which is subtle, unknowable, unmanifest, immovable, and eternal;
which is devoid of the senses, the objects of the senses, and all elemental beings—
that indeed is called the inner self of all beings, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
This Puruṣa is conceived as being distinct from the three guṇas;

from him, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest (avyakta) consisting of the three guṇas was produced. That which exists as the state of the unmanifest yet remains manifest is the imperishable Prakṛti.
"Know that womb of ours to be that which consists of both being and non-being;
for it is he who is worshipped by us in the rites ordained for the gods and the ancestors.
Indeed, there is no other father, whether god or twice-born, higher than him."
"For that Self is to be known by us both; therefore, we shall worship it.
By that [Self], O Brahmin, this world-sustaining boundary was established:
'The rites for the gods and the ancestors must be performed'—such is its injunction."
Brahmā, Sthāṇu, Manu, Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, Dharma, Tapas, Dama, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
Vasiṣṭha, Parameṣṭhin, Vivasvat, and Soma.
Kardama, Krodha, and Vikrīta—
these twenty-one who have been mentioned are remembered as the Prajāpatis.
They honor the eternal ordinance of that god.
Having understood in truth his constant rites for the gods and the ancestors,
the best of the twice-born then recognize that all things are attained by the Self. Even those embodied beings who reside in heaven pay homage to him.

12,321.037c By his grace, they go to that destination which has been ordained as their fruit. 12,321.038a Those who are devoid of the seventeen qualities and indeed of [those] actions—having abandoned fifteen parts—they are liberated; this is the certainty.
O Brahmin, the destination of those who are liberated is designated as the *kṣetrajña* (the Knower of the Field).
For he is said to be all-pervading and devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). He is perceived through the yoga of knowledge, and it is from him that we two have issued forth.
Knowing that eternal Self to be thus, let us worship Him;
for the Vedas and the stages of life (āśramas), abiding in various forms,
worship that Primordial One with devotion, and He grants them their goal.
"But those in this world who are permeated by that [devotion] and have established themselves in single-mindedness— for them there is this further excellence, namely, that they enter into him.
Thus, O Nārada, has this summary of the secret doctrine been proclaimed to you.
"O brahmin-sage, through devotion, through love, and through our own devotion, this has been heard by you.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus addressed, that best of bipeds—"
Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Person,
spoke these words to Nārāyaṇa, the best among bipeds and the abode of the welfare of the world.
That purpose for which your birth occurred here by your own power— let that supreme goal, manifested in four ways in the house of Dharma,
be accomplished today for the sake of the welfare of the world.
"I go now to behold your primordial nature. O Lord of the World, the Vedas have been well-studied by me; austerity has been practiced, and never before have I spoken an untruth."
I constantly perform worship of my gurus; I have never previously disclosed the secrets of another. The four [secrets] are guarded by me according to the tradition.
I am always equal toward both enemy and friend; having constantly taken refuge in that primordial god, I choose him eternally with single-minded devotion.
"Purified by these special qualities,
why should I not behold the infinite Lord?
Having heard those words of Pārameṣṭhya," [he thought].
Nārāyaṇa, the protector of the Sātvata dharma—
O Lord, grant me your permission;
having seen him, I shall indeed have accomplished my purpose.
Having honored him with rites appropriate for his own station, he said to that Nārada, "Go";
then, having been dismissed, the son of Parameṣṭhin departed.
Having paid homage to that ancient seer,
he leapt into the sky with supreme speed and suddenly alighted upon Mount Meru.
There the sage remained for a moment; having reached a secluded spot on the mountain peak,
he gazed toward the north-west.
And he beheld a vast island, endowed with an exceedingly wonderful appearance, situated to the north of the Ocean of Milk,
renowned by the name Śveta.
Indeed, that [mountain] is described by the wise as being thirty-two thousand yojanas high above Meru; there,
beings are beyond the reach of the senses and free from hunger.
Free from movement, exquisitely fragrant,
white, and men who have departed from all evil,
they steal the sight of men who commit wicked deeds.
Their bodies consist of vajra-bones, equal in measure and proportion;
they possess divine lineage and forms, endowed with the essence of purity.
Their heads are shaped like parasols, and their voices resound like the roar of massed clouds.
Those who possess four excellent lotuses, a hundred lotuses on their feet,
sixty white teeth, and eight tusks; 12,322.011a.
With their tongues they lick from all sides his face,
which resembles the sun—
the God born of the universe— out of devotion.
Since all the worlds,
the Vedas, the dharmas, the peaceful sages,
and all the gods are born from him, they are his emanations.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How were those men born—beyond the senses, abstaining from food, motionless, and fragrant? What is their supreme destination?
"O best of the Bharatas, those men who become liberated here possess this very characteristic that belongs to the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa. Therefore,
sever my doubt, for my curiosity is great."
"For you are the garden of all stories, and we have indeed taken refuge in you.
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, this extensive narrative was heard by me in the presence of my father."

This very essence of stories is indeed what must be told to you; it is remembered as such. Nārada, the best of sages, recounted it to Śāntanu when he was questioned by the king in the past; I heard it there long ago.

There was a lord of the earth named Rājoparicara, famous as a friend of Ākhaṇḍala (Indra), who was devoted to Nārāyaṇa Hari. He was righteous, eternally devoted to his ancestors, and always unwearied in his service.
In former times, he attained universal sovereignty by virtue of a boon from Nārāyaṇa;
having adopted the Sātvata ritual that had previously issued from the mouth of the Sun,
he worshipped the Lord of Gods and, with the remnants of that offering, the Grandfathers.
Having distributed the remnants of his father's meal among the Brahmins and his dependents,
he ate only what remained; devoted to truth, he practiced non-violence toward all beings and worshipped Janārdana, the God of gods, with his whole being.
O crusher of enemies, to him who bore devotion toward Nārāyaṇa— the imperishable creator of the world, without beginning, middle,
or end— Śakra himself, the king of the gods, granted a single bed and seat.

"My self, my kingdom, my wealth, my wife, and my vehicles—all this belongs to the Blessed One"; thus he constantly regarded it. He performed the supreme sacrificial rites, both those performed for specific desires and occasional ones, as well as those done continuously.
Adopting the Sātvata ritual, he performed the rites with a concentrated mind.
In the home of that high-souled one, the foremost experts in the Pañcarātra ate the first portion of food,
which was declared by the Blessed One to be the proper way of taking their meal.
While that slayer of enemies was ruling the kingdom with righteousness,
no untruthful word ever arose from him, nor did his mind become corrupt;
nor did he commit even the slightest evil with his body.
For those renowned sages known as the Seven Citraśikhaṇḍins,
having attained a single-minded consensus, proclaimed that supreme scripture on the great mountain Meru, which was composed in accordance with the four Vedas.
From his seven mouths he uttered the unsurpassed law of the world:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, and the highly resplendent Vasiṣṭha— these are the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
These seven are indeed the primal natures, and Svāyambhuva is the eighth;
by these the world is sustained, and from them the scripture has issued forth.
[The sages] are single-minded, self-controlled, and devoted to restraint.

Knowing the past, the present, and the future, and devoted to the truth and the Dharma, they reflected in their minds upon the worlds and then composed this scripture, which is the highest good, the Brahman, and the unsurpassed benefit.
Therein, indeed, dharma, artha, and kāma were taught, followed by mokṣa;
as well as the various boundaries established for both heaven and earth.
Having propitiated the Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa through austerity, [he attained this].
For twelve thousand three hundred and twenty-two years and three days, they all remained together with the ṛṣis;
for then, at the command of Nārāyaṇa, the goddess Sarasvatī entered all those ṛṣis out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

Then, by the twice-born who were well-versed in austerity, this [Veda], born of the first creation, was properly set forth— concerning word, meaning, and cause. Indeed, from the very beginning, that scripture was adorned with the sound of the syllable *oṃ*.
In that place where the Compassionate One was indeed present, the sages meditated;
then the Blessed One, whose body remains unmanifest,
being invisible, spoke to all those sages, O Supreme Person.
This supreme work consists of exactly twelve thousand three hundred and twenty-two verses.
Since it is from this that the Dharma proceeds for the entire system of the world,
it shall serve as the source for both worldly engagement and renunciation.

12,322.037c It is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as by the Atharva-Āṅgirasa hymns. 12,322.038a Thus, O Brahmins, Brahmā was created by me from my grace, and Rudra was born from my wrath; you likewise are my primary manifestations.
The sun and the moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, and fire,
as well as all the hosts of constellations and whatever is designated as living beings— all these, O exponents of Brahman, perform their respective functions according to their own nature.
For just as all [other authorities] are authoritative, so too shall this supreme scripture be authoritative;
indeed, this teaching of mine shall be authoritative. From this, Svāyambhuva Manu himself will proclaim the laws of dharma.
When Uśanas and Bṛhaspati come into being,
they shall proclaim the scripture extracted from your own insights; for while the laws of Svāyambhuva endure, the scripture will have been composed by Uśanas.
And when this treatise composed by you has been promulgated among the worlds according to the doctrine of Bṛhaspati, O best of the twice-born, the protector of subjects, Vasu,
will then receive it from the presence of Bṛhaspati.
For that king shall be permeated by my being and shall be devoted to me;
by means of that scripture, he will perform all rites in the worlds.
Indeed, this is designated as the supreme scripture among all scriptures.
This is beneficial, righteous, and brings supreme fame;
by setting this in motion, you shall become possessed of offspring,
and that king, the great Vasu, shall be endowed with prosperity.
"When that king has passed away, this eternal scripture shall disappear; this is the truth I have told you. Having spoken these words, the Supreme Person vanished from sight.
Having dismissed all those sages, he departed for some unknown direction. Then those progenitors of the worlds, who contemplate the welfare of all the worlds,
set forth that eternal scripture, the source of dharma.
When the first age, the Kṛta Yuga, had begun, and Bṛhaspati had established the scripture along with its auxiliary branches and Upaniṣads within the lineage of Aṅgiras, those sages,
having resolved upon asceticism, departed for whatever regions they desired.
"By upholding [the teachings], they are the promulgators of all dharmas for all the worlds.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, after that great kalpa had passed, a son was born to Aṅgiras."
When the priest of the gods was born, the deities became filled with joy.
O King, the words *bṛhat*, *brahma*, and *mahat* are synonyms;
the learned Bṛhaspati was endowed with these qualities.
He had a preeminent disciple, King Vasu Uparicara,
who at that time had thoroughly mastered the scripture revealed by the Citraśikhaṇḍins.
That King Vasu had previously been purified by divine ordinance.
He protected the earth as Ākhaṇḍala protects heaven.
That high-souled king performed a great horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha),
for which Bṛhaspati served as the officiating priest and the Hotṛ.
And here, three sons of Prajāpati became the Sadasyas:
the great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita;
