as well as Dhanuṣākṣa, Raibhya, Arvāvasu, and Parāvasu.
The seer Medhātithi, the great seer Tāṇḍya,
the highly fortunate seer Śakti, as well as Vedaśiras,
and Kapila, the best of seers and grandfather of Śālihotra.
The first was Kaṭha, then Taittiri, the elder brother of Vaiśampāyana, Kaṇva, and Devahotra— these sixteen were proclaimed;
O King, all the necessary materials were gathered for that great sacrifice.

There was no slaughter of animals there; the king remained thus established. Non-violent, pure, noble, free from desire, and devoted to his duties, he prepared the portions of offerings prescribed in the *Āraṇyaka* texts.
Then the ancient Lord, the God of gods, being pleased with him,
revealed himself in person— though he is invisible to anyone else—
and having himself smelled the portion, he took the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
A portion was taken away by the invisible god Harimedhas.
Thereupon, Bṛhaspati, enraged and impetuous, raised his sacrificial ladle;
striking the sky with the blows of the ladle, he shed tears out of anger.
And he said to Uparicara: "This portion has been set aside by me;
it must indeed be accepted by the God himself in my presence, without a doubt.
For the sacrificial portions set aside here have been directly received by the gods."
"Why has that all-pervading Hari not come here to grant us his vision?
Then the great king Vasu,
along with all those members of the assembly, sought to appease that agitated sage.
Uparicara Vasu said:
"O Avadānin, there is no doubt that the entire portion of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) which was taken by the God of gods has been offered by you here before my very eyes."
Thus addressed by Vasu, the preceptor, filled with wrath, said:
"O sinless one, since I have been insulted by you here, I shall not perform the sacrifice;
furthermore, you have prevented the animal and substituted a beast made of flour."
Vasu said:
"O Lord, you behold the Divine eternally; how is it that I do not see Him?
Furthermore, the injury of animals has been forbidden by the mantras of the Yajurveda and other scriptures."
"I shall not prevent the violence; I shall see Hari alone.
Bhīṣma said:
"Therefore, you, my elder, must not feel anger toward me."
But Bṛhaspati, becoming enraged at Vasu as he spoke thus,
said to the officiating priests, "Why do you stop us from our ritual?
Then the great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita [intervened].
Undisturbed, they said to him: "You ought not to give way to anger.
Listen, my son, to these words spoken by us:
that you have given way to anger is not the dharma of the Kṛta Age."
For that god is free from anger, to whom this portion has been offered;
he cannot be seen by you or by us, O Bṛhaspati,
but only he upon whom he bestows his grace is worthy to behold him.
12,323.019 The Eka, Dvita, and Trita spoke; 12,323.019*0808_01 then the Citraśikhaṇḍins said:
"12,323.019a For we are indeed proclaimed to be the mind-born sons of Brahmā."
Indeed, for the sake of the highest good, they once went to the northern direction;
having performed supreme austerity for four thousand years,
standing perfectly on one foot, motionless as logs of wood, and deeply concentrated.
"On the northern side of Meru, along the shore of the Ocean of Milk,
is that region where we performed our most rigorous austerities.
How may we behold the Lord Nārāyaṇa there?"
To that most excellent one, the giver of boons, the eternal God of gods,
there then, at the concluding bath of his vow, an incorporeal voice spoke with a smooth and deep tone, O Lord, bringing great joy.
"O Brahmins, you have performed intense penance with a serene inner self. Being seekers and devotees, you wish to know how you shall behold that Lord.
To the north of the Ocean of Milk lies the Śvetadvīpa (White Island), which possesses great radiance."
There, the human beings devoted to Nārāyaṇa possess the luster of the moon; having attained a state of single-minded devotion, they are the devotees of Puruṣottama.
They enter the eternal God, who possesses a thousand rays.
"Beyond the senses, free from food, motionless, and fragrant—those men who dwell in Śvetadvīpa are devoted solely to the One. Go there, O sages; there my Self is revealed."

Then, having heard that incorporeal voice, we all proceeded toward that region by the path as described. Having reached the great White Island, our minds were fixed on it and we were eager to behold it.
Suddenly struck by his splendor, we were all rendered bewildered; consequently, our field of vision was then obstructed. With our sight stolen by that brilliance, we could not see the man.
Then there arose within us a superknowledge born of divine yoga.
Indeed, it cannot be perceived directly by one who has not performed intense austerity;
therefore, having again performed great penance for a hundred years appropriate to that time, [we beheld him].
At the conclusion of their vows, we beheld those most beautiful men— white as the moon, endowed with every auspicious mark,
standing with palms eternally joined in reverence, and chanting sacred mantras while facing the northeast.
That recitation which is performed by those great-souled ones is called *mānasa* (mental);
indeed, Hari becomes pleased by that one-pointedness of mind.
O tiger among sages, it is like the radiance of the sun at the end of a *yuga*.
The radiance of each individual among those men was indeed such that we considered that island to be an abode of splendor;
there was no one superior to another there, for they were all equal in brilliance.
Then, O Bṛhaspati, they suddenly beheld once more the radiance of a thousand suns risen all at once;
and those sons of Manu then ran together toward it with great speed.
With palms joined in reverence, joyful, and crying out "Homage!",
we then heard the great sound of those men as they addressed him:
"An offering is indeed being presented to that god by those men."
But we, our minds suddenly snatched away by his splendor,
could not see anything at all, for the power of our sight and our senses had been stolen. Yet, one sound was heard by us, uttered incessantly.

Filling all of space, endowed with every syllable of the sacred teachings—Victory is yours, O lotus-eyed one; homage to you, O creator of the universe! Homage be to you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.
"12,323.040c Thus was the sound heard by us, uttered with the phonemes of phonetics (śikṣākṣara).
12,323.041a In that interval, a pure wind, carrying all fragrances,
12,323.041c blew forth divine flowers as well as efficacious medicinal herbs."
Hari was worshipped by those men who knew the five times of the day, who were single-mindedly devoted,
and who were endowed with supreme devotion through their thoughts, words, and deeds; surely the Lord had arrived there, just as they had proclaimed in their speech.

"O best of the Aṅgirases, though we have returned the wind-god's strength and the sacrifice has been restored, we do not see him; we have been deluded by his power of illusion. With our minds agitated by anxiety, we have become distressed."
Among those thousands of men of pure birth,
no one honored us even with thought or glance;
yet those hosts of sages remained composed, devoted to a single-minded purpose.
Established in the state of Brahman, they did not direct their thoughts toward us. Then, to us who were utterly exhausted and emaciated by ascetic penance,
some bodiless being situated in the sky spoke there.
"O best of the twice-born, have you seen those white men who are devoid of all sense faculties? When they are seen, O supreme brahmins, the Lord of Gods has been seen.
All you sages, depart from here without delay, returning by the way you came."
That god cannot be seen by one who lacks devotion in any way whatsoever;
however, he may be seen by those who have attained single-minded devotion over a long period of time— that Blessed One, whose halo of radiance is difficult to behold.
"O best of the twice-born, a great task must be performed by you. When this Kṛta Yuga has passed and even when the reversal of time has occurred,
O Brahmins, then, upon the arrival of the Tretā Yuga in the Vaivasvata Manvantara."
"O Somapas, you shall indeed become our allies for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods.
Then, having heard those wonderful words, O Somapa,
through his grace we quickly reached the desired region.
"Even though we have performed such great austerities and likewise offered oblations to the gods and ancestors, that Lord has not been seen by us; how then do you deserve to see him?
Nārāyaṇa is the Great Being, the creator of the universe, the consumer of the oblations to the gods and ancestors."
12,323.053 *0814_01 Without beginning or end, unmanifest, worshipped by gods and dānavas.
12,323.054 Bhīṣma said:
12,323.054a Thus, according to the word of Ekata and the doctrine of Dvita and Trita...

Persuaded by the members of the assembly, the noble-minded Bṛhaspati then brought back the sacrifice and duly honored the deities. King Vasu, having completed the sacrifice, likewise protected his subjects.
Falling from heaven due to a Brahmin’s curse, he then entered the earth;
O tiger among kings, that monarch was devoted to truth and righteousness, and being ever fond of dharma, he remained within the depths of the ground.
Becoming devoted to Nārāyaṇa, he sang the name of Nārāyaṇa;
and by his very grace, he rose up once more from the surface of the earth and went to the station immediately following that of Brahmā.
"He has attained the supreme goal; he has reached the ultimate state directly. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When King Mahāvasu was a devotee of the Blessed One,"
12,324.001c For what reason did he, having fallen [from his state], enter a hole in the earth?
12,324.002 Bhīṣma said:
12,324.002a In this regard, they cite this ancient history (itihāsa).
O Bhārata, [this is] the dialogue between the ṛṣis and the gods:
"This earth is indeed the land of action; heaven is ordained for enjoyment.
Therefore, having reached the earth, Indra, consecrated and performing sacrifice,"
When the time for the *savanīya* animal sacrifice arrived, Bṛhaspati said,
"Let flour be brought here for the sake of the animal.
Hearing that, all the deities spoke thus to the best of the twice-born:
O subduer of enemies, those greedy for meat spoke separately to Bṛhaspati [regarding this matter]. The gods said to the best of the twice-born, "One should sacrifice with a goat (aja).
And that goat is to be known as a chāga; no other animal is intended—such is the established rule.
The sages said:
"It is indeed the Vedic revelation that one should sacrifice with seeds in the rites;
since goats are designated as 'seeds,' you ought not to kill them."
"O gods, this is not the dharma of the virtuous in which an animal is indeed slaughtered.
This is the most excellent Kṛta-yuga; how indeed could an animal be slaughtered? For your understanding is that of the Unborn (aja); therefore, the Unborn is called the seed."
12,324.006 Bhīṣma said:
While those sages were thus conversing with the gods,
Vasu, the best of kings, arrived at that place while traveling along the road.
12,324.006e The glorious one, moving through the atmosphere with his entire army and vehicles,
12,324.007a seeing him suddenly approaching as he traveled through the sky,
those twice-born ones said to the gods: "He will resolve our doubt."
"He is a performer of sacrifices, a preeminent lord of charity, and one who cherishes the welfare of all beings.
How could this great Vasu speak otherwise?
Having thus reached a consensus, the gods and the seers likewise [proceeded]."
Approaching suddenly, they questioned King Vasu from close by:
"O King, with what should one sacrifice—with a goat or rather with medicinal herbs? Cut through this doubt of ours; you are considered by us to be the authority."
12,324.011 With palms joined in reverence, Vasu questioned them: "Whose side is favored by each of you? Tell me the truth, for you have all assembled here.
12,324.012 The sages said:
"O lord of men, our position is that one should sacrifice with grains; however, O King, the position of the gods is considered to be that an animal is the offering. Tell us [which is right].
Bhīṣma said:
Having ascertained the opinion of the gods— that, due to Vasu’s taking of their side,
a goat should be sacrificed instead of a sheep— this was the speech uttered at that time.
Thereupon, all those sages, radiant as the sun, became enraged.
They spoke to Vasu, who was seated in his celestial chariot and speaking on behalf of the gods:
"Since you have taken the side of the gods, therefore fall from heaven! From this day forward, O King, your movement in the sky is obstructed."
"By the impact of our curse, O King, you shall pierce the earth and enter it,
if what has been spoken by us should be contrary to the Vedic sūtras; if we have uttered contradictory words therein, then let us fall [into hell]."
Then,
at that very moment, King Uparicara immediately descended and entered a cavity beneath the earth;
yet, by the command of Nārāyaṇa, his memory did not abandon him then.
Then all the gods together, with undistracted minds, reflected upon the liberation of Vasu from his curse, for that deed of the king was indeed well-performed;
"By this high-souled king, the curse has been incurred on our behalf."
"O dwellers of heaven, we must all together perform a service in return for this favor.
Having thus resolved with their intellects and quickly reached a decision, those lords,
with joyful hearts, then spoke to King Uparicara.
"You are devoted to Hari, the god who is the friend of Brahmins and the preceptor of both gods and demons;
surely he, with a pleased mind, will grant you release from the curse.
Yet, you must certainly show honor toward the high-souled twice-born."
"O best of kings, the fruit of their asceticism must inevitably come to fruition.
One who desires his own welfare must not speak what is contrary to the Vedic scriptures;
for this reason, you have suddenly fallen from the sky to the surface of the earth."

"O best of kings, such a calamity has befallen you on account of our side; however, O sinless one, we shall grant you this one favor for as long as you endure the duration of time due to the fault of the curse."
Having entered a cavity in the earth, you shall remain there for that same length of time; yet,
through our grace, you shall receive the stream of clarified butter (*vasordhārā*) well-offered in sacrifices by high-souled Brahmins,
and let no exhaustion touch you.
O Indra among kings, hunger and thirst shall not exist within the cavity of the earth,
because [the beings there] have drunk the stream of Vasu and are nourished by his splendor.
You are a devotee of that Great-Souled One, the eternal God of gods.
"12,324.025c Because of our boon, that god will indeed lead you to the world of Brahmā, being well-pleased.
12,324.026a Having thus granted the boon to the king, all those dwellers of heaven there, having completed the sacrifice with flour at the word of the sages, [departed]."

The gods and the sages rich in asceticism returned to their own abodes; having received their sacrificial fees, they all went back to their respective hermitages. And Śakra, after reflecting upon Vasu, entered Amarāvatī.

O Bhārata, Vasu, having become free from passion there as a result of his teacher’s instruction regarding falsehood, constantly performed worship to Viṣvaksena and continuously recited the mantra issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa.
Even there, O subduer of enemies, though dwelling within a hole in the earth, he worshipped Hari, the lord of the gods, with five sacrifices at the five appointed times.
Thereupon, the blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, was pleased with his devotion.
To Garuḍa,

who stood nearby with great speed, the blessed Lord Viṣṇu, the bestower of boons, spoke as if smiling to that best of the twice-born, who was single-mindedly devoted, intent on him, and self-controlled.
"O most excellent of the twice-born, O highly fortunate one, please go at my word. The righteous sovereign named Vasu, having taken refuge with me,
has entered beneath the surface of the earth due to the wrath of the brahmins."
"Those lords of brahmins have been honored by you; now go, O best of the twice-born!
By my command, O Garuḍa, bring that best of kings, who moves upon the earth, up here into the sky, hidden within a cavity of the ground; do not delay."
Then Garuḍa, possessing the speed of the wind,
spread his wings and entered a fissure in the earth where Vasu sat in silence;
then, having suddenly lifted him up, the son of Vinatā [departed].
Having suddenly seized that devoted Vasu from the surface of the earth,
he quickly flew up into the sky and released him there;
at that very moment, he was born again as King Uparicara.
O best of kings, that supreme ruler went to the world of Brahmā even with his physical body.
Thus, O son of Kuntī, by the command of the deity and due to a verbal transgression,
that high-souled one attained a destination unfit for a non-sacrificer because of the curse of a twice-born brahmin.
Because he had served Hari, the Supreme Lord, alone,
he quickly cast off that curse and attained the world of Brahmā. All this has been told to you, how human beings came into existence.
I shall tell you everything regarding how that sage Nārada went to Śvetadvīpa; listen with an attentive mind, O King.
Bhīṣma said:
Having reached the great white island, the venerable seer Nārada beheld those very same men— white, auspicious, and radiant as the moon;
they were without sense organs, without food, free from excretions, and fragrant.
With palms joined in reverence, joyful, and crying out "Victory to you!",
they were reciting the mantra of the Great Upaniṣad with its proper accents,
while those pure ones meditated in their minds upon the mantras of the five Upaniṣads.
To those who were chanting the supreme, eternal Brahman; who possessed the luster of the sun;
who were intent on worship and offered oblations; who were praising the Parameṣṭhin; whose minds were one-pointed; who were self-controlled; and who had taken refuge in single-minded devotion.

He honored him with his head and his mind, and being honored by them in turn, the brahmin, that great sage, stood with arms upraised, desiring to see [him], intent on recitation, and enduring all hardships, with a one-pointed mind.
He sang a hymn of praise to the All-pervading One, who is devoid of qualities and possesses a great self.
Nārada said:

"Salutations to you, O God of gods! You who are actionless, devoid of qualities, the witness of the world, the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the infinite, the primordial person (*puruṣa*), the Great Person (*mahāpuruṣa*), and the possessor of the three qualities (*triguṇa*)."
