[170-171]
12,326.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,326.001a Thus praised with secret and truthful names, the Blessed One,
assuming his universal form, revealed himself to that sage Nārada.
In some parts his self was as pure as the moon, and in others he surpassed the moon; in some parts the lord had the color of fire, and in others the form of a celestial mansion;
in some parts he had the color of a parrot’s wing, and in others the luster of crystal.
In some places it resembled a heap of blue collyrium, and in others it shone with the luster of gold;
in some places it had the color of coral sprouts, and in others it appeared white;
in some places it gleamed with the hue of refined gold, and in others it was like lapis lazuli.
Resembling blue lapis lazuli, in some places like sapphire;
shining with the color of a peacock's neck, and in some places like a string of pearls—
the Eternal One bears these many kinds of colors within his form.
The glorious one with a thousand eyes, a hundred heads, and a thousand feet; he who has a thousand bellies and a thousand arms, and who is sometimes called the Unmanifest;
emitting the syllable *Oṃ* from his mouth and the *Sāvitrī* mantra following it.
And from his remaining mouths,
O lord of the earth, he vomited forth the wealth arising from the four Vedas, uttering the four Vedas along with all their supplements.
The self-controlled Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa recited the Āraṇyaka;
he [carried] the sacrificial altar, the water-pot, the darbha grass, the stones in the form of jewels,
the deerskin, the wooden staff, and the blazing fire.
Then the Lord of Gods, the Master of Sacrifice, held [the weapon] with his hands. To him,
who was gracious, Nārada— the best of the twice-born, his own soul serene—
having become restrained in speech and purified, paid homage to the Supreme Lord.
To him who was bowing with his head, the immutable Origin of the gods said:
"The great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita have arrived at this place, longing for a vision of me."

Neither did they see me, nor shall anyone else see me, except for the most excellent of those who are single-mindedly devoted; and you, O twice-born one, are considered such a single-minded devotee. These excellent forms of mine were born in the house of Dharma.
"Always honor them and accomplish your purpose as you have come.
And choose a boon from me, O Brahmin, whatever you desire here;
for today I am pleased with you here, I who am the immutable form of the universe."
Nārada said:
"O Lord, today I have indeed obtained the immediate fruit of my austerity, self-restraint, and observance, since I have beheld your blessed self."
"This is the supreme boon for me, that you, the eternal one, the Blessed Lord, the all-seeing Lion, whose form is everything, the Great Master, have been beheld by me. Bhīṣma said:
Having thus instructed Nārada, the son of Parameṣṭhin, he spoke these words once more: "Go, Nārada, without delay!
For these devotees of mine, who possess the luster of the moon, are without sense organs and do not consume food."
"Let them contemplate me with one-pointed minds so that no obstacle may arise for them.
For these highly fortunate ones were formerly single-minded devotees;
freed from the qualities of darkness and passion, they will undoubtedly enter into me."
That which is not visible to the eye, nor touchable by the sense of touch,
nor to be smelled by scent, and devoid of taste; indeed,
the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* do not affect it.
And he who is the all-pervading witness, called the Self of the world,
does not perish when the bodies of the collection of beings perish;
he is unborn, eternal, perpetual, devoid of qualities, and likewise partless.
That which is known as the twenty-fifth principle, beyond the twice-twelve principles, is called the Puruṣa; it is indeed inactive and is said to be perceivable through knowledge.
O best of the twice-born, having entered into this, beings here indeed become liberated.
He is to be known as Vāsudeva, the eternal Supreme Self (paramātman). Behold, O Nārada, the majesty and the greatness of this God; even the sages do not know his true nature, O bull among sages.
He who is never stained by auspicious or inauspicious actions—
these they call the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*;
these abide and move within all bodies.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) enjoys these qualities, but he is not enjoyed by them. Behold the majesty of the living soul (jīva), who thus is the enjoyer of the qualities;
having moved slightly and lightly, the qualities do not become his enjoyers.

Abiding in all, going everywhere, the universe itself, the enjoyer of qualities though devoid of qualities; I am the food, I am the feeder, I am the eater, and I am the fire within the belly that digests;
I am this entire multitude of beings, with their diverse actions and diverse faces.
I abide in my primordial nature, yet I do not abide as one possessing form; having entered and presided over the body by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths,
O twice-born one, I alone am the cause of the closing and opening of the eyes of all living beings.
"But know me, O brahmin-sage, to be the all-pervading Lord, the Puruṣa—
devoid of qualities yet the enjoyer of qualities, the creator of qualities, and transcendent of qualities. O celestial sage, the earth, the foundation of the world, dissolves into water."
In the light, the waters dissolve; the light dissolves into the wind;
the wind goes to dissolution in space, and space likewise into the mind. For Time is the supreme element; it dissolves into the mind.
For the mind is the supreme element; it dissolves into the unmanifest (*avyakta*).
O Brahmin, the unmanifest dissolves into the inactive Puruṣa. There is indeed nothing higher than that eternal Puruṣa.
"Know me, O Brahman-sage, to be the all-pervading Lord, the Supreme Person.
For there is no being, whether stationary or moving, that exists eternally in this world,
except for that one eternal Person, Vāsudeva."
For Vāsudeva, the mighty one, has become the self of all beings.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth—
these great elements combined together are designated by the term "body."
O Brahmin, he who enters it is invisible and swift in his movement;
as soon as he is born, the Lord exists, setting the body in motion.
Nowhere does a body exist without a collection of constituent elements (dhātu).

O Brahmin, the elements do not move without the *jīva*, yet they remain eternally distinct from it; likewise, the *kṣetrajña* is eternally separate. Furthermore, the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are not its enjoyers.

These [five] are conceived within the five elements residing in the body; that is reckoned as the *jīva*, the remainder, the Lord Saṃkarṣaṇa. From him, one may obtain the state of Sanatkumāra through one's own karma.
And he in whom all beings go to dissolution at the time of destruction is taught as the mind (manas) of all beings, Pradyumna. From him is born the agent, who is both the effect and the cause.
From whom the entire world, both stationary and moving, originates—
he is Aniruddha, he is Īśāna, and he is the manifestation in all actions.
He who is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), whose nature is beyond the qualities (nirguṇa).
That very Lord is to be known as the individual soul (jīva), the powerful Saṃkarṣaṇa;
from Saṃkarṣaṇa comes Pradyumna, who is said to be the mind (manas);
and he who is Aniruddha from Pradyumna is the ego (ahaṃkāra), the Great Lord (maheśvara).
From me alone everything arises— the entire world, both stationary and moving,
O Nārada, as well as the imperishable and the perishable, and both the existent and the non-existent.
Those devotees of mine who enter into me become liberated here in this world.

For I am to be known as the Person, the twenty-fifth, devoid of action; I am without qualities, without parts, free from dualities, and without possessions. This should not be understood by you [merely] as "he who is seen possessing form."
"O Nārada, if I so desired, I—the Lord and Teacher of the universe—could vanish in a moment. This which you see me as, O Nārada, is indeed an illusion created by me;
you ought not to understand me as being thus endowed with the qualities of all beings."

12,326.043e I have thus correctly described to you my fourfold form. 12,326.044a For these highly fortunate men have become single-minded devotees; freed from darkness and passion, O sage, they shall enter into me.
"O Nārada, I am the agent, the action, and also the instrument;
for I indeed am known as the individual soul (jīva), and the life-force is established within me. Let not such a thought arise in you here, that 'the individual soul has been seen by me.'"

"O Brahmin, I am all-pervading, the inner self within the multitude of beings. When the bodies of the multitude of beings perish, I do not perish. I am Hiraṇyagarbha, the origin of the worlds, four-faced, and the knower of etymological definitions."
The eternal god Brahmā is my counselor for many matters;
and from my forehead, the god Rudra emerged out of my wrath. Behold my eleven Rudras stationed upon my right side.
Behold the twelve Ādityas stationed on my left side;
and see the eight Vasus, the best of gods, in front of me; and behold Nāsatya and Dasra, the two physicians, at my back.
Behold all the Prajāpatis; behold also the seven Ṛṣis.
Behold the Vedas and sacrifices by the hundreds, as well as immortality and medicinal herbs. Behold also the austerities, the observances, and the various kinds of restraints.
Behold the eightfold sovereignty gathered together in embodied form;
behold Śrī, Lakṣmī, Kīrti, and Pṛthivī, the mountain-like Earth;
and behold the goddess Sarasvatī, the mother of the Vedas, who abides within me.
"O Nārada, behold Dhruva, the best of luminaries, moving through the sky;
likewise, behold the clouds, the oceans, the lakes, and the rivers.
O best of beings, behold also the four classes of ancestors (pitṛgaṇas) in their embodied forms."
Behold these thirty qualities, free from form, residing within me.
O sage, even the rites for the gods are surpassed by the rites for the ancestors;
for I alone am the primordial father of both the gods and the ancestors.
Having assumed the form of Hayashiras in the northwestern ocean,
I drink the well-offered oblations to the gods and the ancestors accompanied by faith.
In ancient times, Brahmā was created by me, and he himself performed a sacrifice to me.
Then, being pleased, I granted him unsurpassed boons:
the status of being my son at the beginning of the kalpa, the office of the Overlord of the World,
and also a name consisting of ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*) that expresses various synonymous meanings.

No one whatsoever shall transgress the boundary established by you. And you, O Brahman, rich in asceticism, shall be the granter of boons to those who desire boons among the hosts of gods, asuras, and sages.
O highly fortunate one of constant and firm vows, you shall always be worthy of worship by the ancestors and by various classes of beings; and I, too,
shall always manifest myself for the sake of the gods' affairs.
"O Brahmin, you must instruct and direct him like a son. To Brahmā of immeasurable splendor,
and likewise to Rudra, Manu, and Indra of immeasurable splendor, he spoke these and other pleasing words.
12,326.062c Having granted the boons, I became joyful and intent upon cessation (nivṛtti).
12,326.063a Nirvāṇa is the cessation of all phenomena; cessation is remembered as the supreme state.
12,326.063c Therefore, having attained cessation, one should conduct oneself with complete tranquility in every limb.

The teachers, who have reached certain conclusions through the Sāṃkhya system, declare me to be Kapila— the eternal one, accompanied by knowledge, residing within the sun. This blessed Hiraṇyagarbha is well-praised in the Vedic hymns.
O Brahmin, I am that one whose course is Yoga, as proclaimed in the Yoga-shastras;
having manifested myself, I remain eternally in heaven. Then, at the end of a thousand yugas, I shall again withdraw the universe.
"O best of the twice-born, having established all beings— both stationary and moving— within myself, I shall dwell alone together with my knowledge; thereafter,
I shall once again create this entire world here by means of that knowledge."
That fourth form of mine which is *asman* (the stone) created the imperishable Śeṣa;
he is indeed called Saṃkarṣaṇa, and he in turn begot Pradyumna. From Pradyumna I was born as Aniruddha; such is my creation again and again.
From Aniruddha, likewise, Brahmā arises there, born from the primordial lotus;
from Brahmā come all beings, both moving and stationary. Know this to be the creation that occurs again and again at the beginnings of the kalpas.
Just as the rising and setting of the sun from the sky here have vanished, yet Time of immeasurable luster forcibly brings them back again,
so too shall I forcibly [recover] the earth for the welfare of all beings.
Bhīṣma said:
Then Nārada questioned the Blessed Janārdana. The Blessed One said:
"In what various forms, O Lord, are you to be seen by me?
"Listen, O Nārada, great sage, to the manifestations in their true essence:
the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf."
Rāma, Rāma, and Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Kalki—these are the ten [incarnations].
First, I shall become a fish and establish the subjects;
I shall uphold the worlds and the Vedas as they are sinking in the great ocean.
"O best of the twice-born, my second form is remembered as that of a tortoise, resembling Mount Hemakūṭa; for the sake of the nectar, I shall support Mandara,
which has again become submerged in the terrible great ocean and overwhelmed by its weight."
Assuming the form of a boar, I shall bring back to its own place this earth, girt by the oceans, whose every limb was overrun by beings and which had been lost;
and I shall slay Hiraṇyākṣa, the son of Diti, who is arrogant in his strength.
"Assuming the form of Narasiṃha once more, I shall slay Hiraṇyakaśipu, the son of Diti and destroyer of sacrifices, for the sake of the gods' mission. Furthermore,
Virocana’s son is the powerful and great Asura Bali."
He shall be invulnerable to all the worlds, including the gods, asuras, and rākṣasas;
he will even displace Śakra from his own sovereignty. When the three worlds have been seized by him and the Lord of Śacī has turned away in defeat, [this shall come to pass].
As the twelfth son born of Aditi from Kaśyapa, I shall come into being;
having gone to the sacrificial assembly with matted hair while being praised by the best of the twice-born,
I shall perform a hymn of praise for the sacrifice, and upon hearing it, Bali will be pleased.
"O boy, tell me what you desire," he was told; "I shall ask for a great boon.
"Let only three paces of land be given," I requested of the great Asura. "He would have granted it to me out of affection," but he was forbidden by his ministers.
"O Nārada, when water has come into my hands, encompassed by three strides, then I shall bestow the kingdom upon Śakra of immeasurable splendor and re-establish the gods in their own abodes."

I shall offer oblation even to that Dānava, the best among the strong, who dwells in the depths of Pātāla and is invincible by all the gods; and in the Tretā Yuga, I shall become Rāma, the upholder of the Bhṛgu lineage.
In the twenty-second cycle of the yuga,
I shall become a powerful seer there, Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, endowed with the strength of my arms.
I shall utterly destroy the Kṣatriya order, along with its abundant forces and vehicles.
When the transition between the Tretā and Dvāpara ages has arrived,
I shall become the Lord of the World by taking birth as Rāma, the son of Daśaratha.

"Due to the injury inflicted by Trita, the two sages, sons of Prajāpati, shall each incur deformity— first one, and then likewise the other— and they shall indeed attain the state of monkeys. Moreover, those who are born in their lineage shall become forest-dwellers."

"O twice-born one, those of great strength and great heroism, whose prowess is equal to that of Śakra, shall become my allies in the task of the gods. Then [I shall slay] the terrible lord of the Rākṣasas, the disgrace of Pulastya’s lineage."
I shall slay Rāvaṇa, that thorn of the worlds, along with his hosts in battle; I shall establish the stainless Vibhīṣaṇa in his kingdom,
and I shall lead all the inhabitants of Ayodhyā to the imperishable world.
I shall bestow the kingdom upon Vibhīṣaṇa in due order at the conclusion of the junction between the Dvāpara and Kali ages; then,
for the sake of Kaṃsa, my manifestation will take place in Mathurā.
In the twenty-eighth cycle of four ages, during the junction between the Kali and Dvāpara yugas, I,
the upholder of the Vṛṣṇi clan, shall again manifest myself in Mathurā under the name Vāsudeva for the sake of Kaṃsa.

The third Rāma, the powerful son of Vasudeva, will indeed be known by that name. Having slain there many Dānavas who are thorns to the gods, I shall establish my residence in the city of Dvārakā, the city of Kuśasthalī.
Dwelling there in that city, I shall indeed slay Naraka, the son of the Earth, who causes Aditi displeasure, as well as the Dānavas Mura and Pīṭha;
and [I shall take] the beautiful city of Prāgjyotiṣa, which is filled with various riches.

Having slain the foremost of the Dānavas, I shall lead [you] to Kuśasthalī; and I shall indeed liberate Nṛga, who has become a chameleon. Then, for the sake of my grandson, I shall go to the city of Śoṇita.
Having gone to the city of Bāṇa, I shall wage a great slaughter;
and I shall defeat Śaṅkara and Mahāsena, who desire the welfare and pleasure of Bāṇa, even though they are prepared for battle and honored by the world of the gods.
Then, having conquered Bāṇa, the thousand-armed son of Bali,
I shall destroy all the inhabitants of Saubha—
Kaṃsa, Keśin, as well as the cruel Ariṣṭa and the great asuras.
Having brought under his control the immensely powerful Cāṇūra, the exceedingly strong Muṣṭika,
as well as Pralamba, Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa in the form of a bull,
and Kālīya in the great lake of the Yamunā;
Thereafter, for the sake of the cattle in the cow-pens,
I shall sustain this great mountain for seven nights while Indra pours down rain; once the rain has ceased, I shall remain stationed upon the summit of the mountain.
"O twice-born one, when I enter into a conversation with Indra,
then that one known as Kālayavana, who is enveloped by the splendor of Garga,
shall meet his death at my hands alone, O best of the twice-born."
Having swiftly seized all the wealth from Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva,
the powerful Jarāsaṃdha, who opposes all kings,
will become a prosperous Asura and ruler of the earth in Girivraja.
"By the movement of my intellect, his death shall come;
indeed, I shall slay Śiśupāla at the sacrifice of the son of Dharma,
through the transgression of Duryodhana and by virtue of Yudhiṣṭhira."
When all the kings of the earth have assembled with their forces,
the son of Vāsava will indeed be my sole effective ally;
I shall then establish Yudhiṣṭhira in his own kingdom along with his brothers.
Thus the worlds will say: "The two sages Nara and Nārāyaṇa, the lords, being exerted for the sake of the world's purpose, are consuming the Kṣatriyas;
all the kings fallen by weapons shall indeed go to heaven."
Having relieved the burden of the earth as desired,
while Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, was once again ruling the kingdom,
O best of men, [he departed] from Dvārakā along with all the foremost of the Sātvatas.
"I shall bring about a terrible dissolution, destroying myself and my own kin. Bearing four forms, I possess immeasurable deeds;
having performed them, I shall go to my own worlds, honored by Brahmā."
Then, at the beginning of the Kali Yuga, having taken recourse to the royal tree,
he spoke in the Māgadha language within the palace of the King of Dharma—
clad in saffron robes, shaven-headed, and possessing white teeth.
The Buddha, son of Śuddhodana, will delude the young brahmins. When I have attained Buddhahood, Śūdras will be fed at the śrāddha rites.
All men will become shaven-headed and clothed in saffron robes.
There will be times unfit for study (*anadhyāya*), and Brahmins will be deprived of their sacred fires.
The *agnihotra* sacrifices will falter, and the honoring of teachers will perish.
Sons will not listen to their fathers, nor will daughters-in-law or mothers.

Neither friend nor wife shall remain, for indeed all will be turned upside down; thus the entire world in the Kali age will become devoid of the Śruti and Smṛti, naked, impure, and a mixture of castes.

From their presence shall arise men who hate the gods and Brahmins, ignorant of the Dharma, impure, and speakers of sophistry under the guise of logic; those who listen to the teachings of the naked ones are equal to those of evil resolve.
Therefore, those who seek their own welfare should neither converse with nor touch these [persons].
To purify oneself from contact with them, one should observe three days of fasting. Then, at the end of the Kali Yuga, there will be a Brāhmaṇa, tawny like Hari.

Kalki, the son of Viṣṇuyaśas, with Yājñavalkya as his domestic priest and all the Brāhmaṇas as his companions— accompanied by them, I shall once again utterly exterminate the Mlecchas and the heretics.
Having indeed slain the six heretics during that internal dissolution,
O best of the twice-born, I shall thereafter manifest as Haṃsa and Hayaśiras, ever devoted to sacrifices.
Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Vāmana, and Rāma;
Rāma the son of Daśaratha, Sātvata, and Kalki as well—
when the Vedic revelation was lost, it was then restored by me.
In the former Kṛta Yuga, twelve thousand three hundred and twenty-six ages, along with their respective Śrutīkas, were established;
these have passed away, as you have heard in the Purāṇas or perhaps elsewhere.
Moreover, many other supreme manifestations of mine have likewise passed away.
This entire world is indeed the Person (*puruṣa*), inexhaustible and immutable. Having performed the works of the worlds, they return again to their own primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
For such a vision as this was never attained even by Brahmā.

"O Brahmin, O best of beings, all this— both the past and the future, along with its secret mysteries— which you have attained here today with a mind focused in solitude, has been narrated by me to you because of your devotion."
Thus that Blessed Lord, the imperishable deity who assumes the universal form,
having spoken these words, vanished right there.
And Nārada, possessed of great splendor, having obtained the desired favor, [departed].

He rushed to the hermitage of Badarī to see Nara and Nārāyaṇa. This Great Upaniṣad, which is endowed with the four Vedas and composed through Sāṃkhya and Yoga, was proclaimed by him as the Pañcarātra.
Nārada recited once more, in the abode of Brahmā, O dear one, what had been sung from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, exactly as it was seen and heard;
having heard it from the mouth of Brahmā, Rudra recounted it again to the Goddess.
Thus has this been handed down in succession; this was heard by Śantanu.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Indeed, this greatness of that wise one is truly wonderful."
Does Brahmā not know [this], since he heard it from Nārada? For the Blessed Grandfather is next in rank to that god;
how could he not know the power of him who possesses immeasurable energy?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Indra among kings, thousands and hundreds of great kalpas, as well as creations and dissolutions, have passed away."
At the beginning of creation, the Lord Brahmā is remembered as the creator of progeny;
he knows the foremost of gods, and furthermore, O King,
he knows the Supreme Self, the Ruler, and likewise his own origin.
To those other hosts of perfected beings (siddhas) who had assembled in the abode of Brahmā,
he caused that Purāṇa, equal to the Vedas, to be heard. And Sūrya, having indeed heard it from them— those whose souls were purified— [proceeded].
O Bhārata, he caused the Brahman to be heard by those who followed him—
sixty-six thousand rishis of purified souls,
who had been created as precursors by the sun as it heats the worlds.
Sūrya spoke this to all of them, whose souls were purified:
"O dear one, by those high-souled ṛṣis who follow Sūrya,
the gods assembled on Mount Meru have been made to hear this supreme teaching."

O Indra among kings, having heard this from the presence of the gods, the twice-born Asita, that best of sages, caused it to be heard by the ancestors. And my father Śaṃtanu, O dear one, related it to me as well.
12,326.111c Having heard this from him, O Bhārata, I have now recounted it to you;
12,326.111d I obtained this ancient lore in the past from the celestial sage Nārada.
12,326.112a Whether by the gods or by the sages, those who have heard this ancient lore [shall attain their goal].
All of them worship the Supreme Self again and again. O King, this narrative concerning the seers, which has been handed down through tradition,
must never be given by you to one who is not a devotee of Vāsudeva.
O King, that devoted man who, having become pure and composed, always causes this supreme narrative to be heard,
shall before long attain the eternal world of Viṣṇu.
O King, from the hundreds of other righteous narratives that you have heard besides this one, this essence has been extracted,
just as the nectar was extracted by the gods and demons after churning the ocean.
Thus was this nectar of stories extracted here in the past by the brahmins.
That man who constantly recites this, or that man who hears it, having attained a state of single-minded devotion and being well-composed in solitude—

Having reached the great white island and become a man with the radiance of the moon, he shall enter the god of a thousand rays; of this there is no doubt. Likewise, one who is afflicted shall be freed from disease by hearing this narrative from the beginning.
One who desires knowledge attains his wishes, and the devotee goes to the destination of the devotees.
O King, you too must constantly worship Puruṣottama;
you should listen to the teachings concerning the high-souled Vāsudeva according to the prescribed rites.
For he is indeed the mother, the father, and the preceptor of the entire world;
may the eternal Lord, the divine protector of Brahman, be pleased with you,
O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, [and] Janārdana of the mighty arms.
He is always to be honored by sages who have mastered the Vedas, remaining ever undistracted.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this excellent narrative, O Janamejaya, the King of Dharma...
And all those brothers of his became devoted to Nārāyaṇa,
O Bhārata, thinking, "Victory has been won by that Blessed One, the Supreme Person. Constantly intent on recitation, they uttered the Sarasvatī mantra.
For our most excellent preceptor, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
having gone from the atmosphere to the Ocean of Milk, the eternal abode of nectar, recited this supreme mantra for silent recitation while invoking Nārāyaṇa.
Having worshipped the Lord of Gods, he returned once more to his own hermitage.
Bhīṣma said:
"I have thus related to you all this that was spoken by Nārada and recounted by me."
"For this has come down through tradition, as it was told to me by my father in the past.
Sūta said:
"All of this has been narrated to you, as proclaimed by Vaiśampāyana."
Having heard this, Janamejaya performed [the sacrifice] correctly according to the prescribed rules; for you all have performed austerities, have fulfilled your vows,
are preeminent knowers of the Vedas, and are residents of the Naimiṣa forest.
All the best of the twice-born arrived at the great sacrificial session of Śaunaka. "Worship the Supreme Lord, the Self, with well-offered sacrifices.
Janamejaya said:
How is it that the Blessed Lord, the God who is the foremost recipient in sacrifices and the Sovereign,
is the perpetual upholder of sacrifice, as well as the knower of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
how is it that he abides in the dharma of renunciation, is the source of security, and is dear to his devotees?
That very Lord, the Sovereign, ordained the dharmas of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*). How were the deities made entitled to shares within the dharmas of engagement?
And how were the dharmas of cessation (*nivṛtti*) established for those whose minds are turned away [from worldly life]?
"O Brahmin, sever this secret and eternal doubt of ours;
for you have indeed heard the discourse concerning Nārāyaṇa, which is consistent with Dharma.
Sūta said:
O best of the Śaunakas, I shall proclaim to you that ancient account which was related by the disciple of the wise Vyāsa when he was questioned by Janamejaya,
after hearing of the majesty of this Supreme Self within embodied beings.
The highly wise Janamejaya said to Vaiśampāyana:
"These worlds, including Brahmā, along with the gods, asuras, and humans,
are seen everywhere to be attached to ritual actions prescribed for worldly prosperity."
"O Brahmin, you have spoken of liberation (mokṣa), which is Nirvāṇa, the supreme bliss.
We have heard that those who become liberated here, freed from both merit and sin, enter the God of a thousand rays."

12,327.007a Alas! Truly, the eternal dharma of liberation is difficult to practice, 12,327.007c for having abandoned it, all the deities became consumers of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors.
12,327.008a How is it that Brahmā, Rudra, and Śakra, the lord who slays Bala, [have done so]?
The sun, the lord of the stars, Vāyu, Agni, and Varuṇa as well,
along with Ākāśa, the earth, and all the remaining inhabitants of heaven,
do not perceive their own dissolution brought about by final extinction (parinirmita).
Then they did not abide in that path which is certain, imperishable, and immutable;
for those who, having remembered the measurement of time, remained fixed in worldly activity,
there is this great fault regarding the measurement of time for those engaged in action.
"O Brahmin, this doubt of mine is fixed in my heart like a thorn.
Sever it by recounting an ancient history (itihāsa), for my curiosity is great. O twice-born one, how are the deities said to be the recipients of shares in the sacrifices?"
O Brahmin, for what purpose are the dwellers of the third heaven sacrificed to in the ritual? O best of the twice-born, as for those who receive their shares in the sacrifices—
when they themselves perform great sacrifices, to whom do they indeed give the shares?
12,327.014 Vaiśampāyana said:
12,327.014a "O lord of men, this question you have asked is most profound;
for it cannot be understood by one who has not practiced austerities, nor likewise by one who is ignorant of the Vedas."
This cannot be correctly expounded even by one who does not know the Purāṇas.
Come, I shall tell you that which my preceptor asked in the past—
the great seer Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa, the arranger of the Vedas.
Sumantu, Jaimini, and Paila of firm vows—
I am the fourth disciple, and Śuka is remembered as the fifth.
All these five disciples, endowed with self-restraint, were gathered together.

On Mount Meru, the most excellent and delightful mountain frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, he taught the Vedas— with the *Mahābhārata* as the fifth— to those endowed with purity and right conduct, who had conquered anger and mastered their senses.
As they were practicing the Vedas, a doubt once arose among them:
"Is it Brahmā, or Rudra, or perhaps the Ṛṣis who are the deities? For most are established on the path of worldly activity; by whose command [do we act]?"
Who indeed abide on the path of cessation? By whose teaching [do they do so]?
Who among them all perform sacrifices? And who is their supreme Lord?
This very person about whom you asked has been described to you by him.
12,327.019 Then, O Bhārata, that which was heard by me must also be told to you today:
12,327.020 Having heard the words of his disciples, the illustrious Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara and the dispeller of the darkness of all ignorance, spoke these words.

"O best of beings, I have indeed performed a most great and extremely severe austerity so that I might know the past, the present, and the future. For me, whose austerity has been practiced and whose senses are restrained— "
By the grace of Nārāyaṇa and through the favor of the Ocean of Milk,
this knowledge pertaining to the three periods of time has appeared according to my desire; listen to that, for I shall declare this supreme resolution according to my understanding.
12,327.023 Just as it actually occurred at the beginning of the kalpa, so was it seen by me with the eye of knowledge (jñānacakṣus).
12,327.024 Those people who know Sāṃkhya and Yoga call him the Supreme Self (paramātman);
he receives the designation "Great Person" (mahāpuruṣa) through his own action.
Therefore, the wise know that the unmanifest *pradhāna* was produced from Him;
from the unmanifest, the manifest arose through the Lord for the purpose of creating the worlds.
Indeed, Aniruddha is called the Great Self (*mahān ātmā*) within the worlds.
He who attained manifestation and created the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) is called Ahaṃkāra; for he consists of all splendor. Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth [are his manifestations].
O Bhārata, the great elements were produced from the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Having created the great elements, he then fashioned their qualities. Now hear of those eight embodied beings who were produced from the elements.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu,
the high-souled Vasiṣṭha, and likewise Manu Svāyambhuva—
these eight should be known as the primary natures (prakṛtis) upon which the worlds are established.

Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created these highly exalted sages— the grandfathers of the world— who were masters of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences and of the sacrifices along with their constituent parts, for the sake of the perfection of the worlds.
From these eight primal sources, this entire world was born. Rudra, whose nature is wrath, was born; he himself created ten others.
These eleven Rudras are known as the transformed manifestations of Puruṣa.
Those Rudras, as well as Prakṛti and all the divine seers (surarṣis),
having been born for the sake of the world’s success, approached Brahmā and said:
"O Blessed One, we have indeed been created by you, the All-Powerful."
"O Grandfather, by whom and in which office one must function— specifically,
that office for the consideration of affairs which has been designated by you—
how should that office be maintained by the official who holds it?"
"Bestow strength upon him who is the overseer of administrative affairs.
Thus addressed, Mahādeva spoke this to those gods:
"O gods, I have been well informed by you; may it be well with you."
This very same thought that you have conceived has arisen in me as well:
"How is the entire system of worldly governance to be maintained?
How can there be no loss of strength for you, nor for myself?"
"Let us all go from here for refuge to the Witness of the World, the Great Being, the Unmanifest; he will tell us what is for our welfare.
Then those sages and gods, together with Brahmā, [proceeded].
Desiring the welfare of the world, they went to the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk.
There they undertook a severe ascetic practice known as the Mahāniyama, which was ordained by Brahmā and fashioned according to the Vedas.
Their gaze was directed upward, their arms were raised, and their minds became one-pointed.
Standing perfectly on one foot, motionless as logs of wood, they remained in deep concentration. Having performed that supreme austerity for a thousand divine years, they [attained their goal].
They heard a sweet voice, adorned with the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas:
"O gods, including Brahmā, and you sages whose wealth is asceticism! Having honored you all with a welcome, I shall cause you to hear these most excellent words."

"O gods, I have understood your purpose, which is great and for the welfare of the world. You must perform that which is joined with active exertion and which strengthens your vital breaths. O gods, you have performed intense austerities out of a desire to propitiate me."
"O Great Beings, you shall enjoy the supreme fruit of this austerity. This is Brahmā, the teacher of the world and the grandfather of all worlds;
and you, O best of the gods, worship me with concentrated minds."
"O lords, all of you, constantly assign shares for me in the sacrifices;
I shall ordain your welfare according to your respective offices. Hearing these words of the God of gods, their hair stood on end with joy.

Then all those gods, Brahmā, and the great seers performed a sacrifice dedicated to Viṣṇu according to the rite prescribed in the Vedas. At that sacrificial session, Brahmā himself assigned his own portion.
12,327.049 All the gods and the celestial sages likewise assigned their respective portions. 12,327.050 Those portions, characterized by the dharma of the Kṛta age and most highly honored,
reached that Person, radiant as the sun, who is beyond darkness.
[To] the great, all-pervading god, the sovereign, the granter of boons, the Lord—
then, thereafter, the boon-granting god Maheśvara, remaining bodiless in the sky, spoke these words to all those immortals standing there.
"By whatever portion each of you was imagined, so has it come to pass. I am pleased; today I bestow upon you a fruit characterized by return. O gods, this is your mark, arising from my grace."
"Being worshipped with sacrifices accompanied by the completion of excellent sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*),
you shall, in age after age, become the enjoyers of the fruits of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*). And those gods who, throughout all the worlds, shall indeed worship with sacrifices— "

"12,327.054c They shall assign to you your portions, those men who have been ordained by the Vedas. 12,327.055a Whosoever has assigned my portion in this great sacrifice, he is thus entitled to a share of the sacrifice; he has been established by me in the Vedic sūtras."

"Supported by the fruits of the sacrificial portions, you shall sustain the worlds; you have been created according to your respective offices as the overseers of all matters in the world. Those rites which shall be performed, honored by the fruits of worldly activity,"
With your strength nourished by them, you shall indeed sustain the worlds;
for you shall be honored in the world by men in all sacrifices, and through that,
you shall honor me— this is my intention for you.
For this purpose the Vedas, along with the sacrifices and medicinal herbs, were created.
Indeed, when these are properly employed, the deities on earth are gratified. This creation of yours is fashioned according to the quality of worldly activity (*pravṛtti-guṇa*).
"O best of gods, this has been performed by me until the end of the kalpa. "O lords, consider the welfare of the world according to your respective jurisdictions.
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu—

Vasiṣṭha—these seven were indeed created from [Brahmā’s] mind. They are the foremost knowers of the Vedas and are ordained as teachers of the Vedas; they are established in the path of active worldly duty (pravṛttidharmin) and are fashioned according to the nature of Prajāpati.
This eternal path of those engaged in action has become manifest;
he is proclaimed as Aniruddha, the Lord who effects the creation of the worlds. [From him arise] Sana, Sanatsujāta, Sanaka, and Sanandana.
Sanatkumāra, Kapila, and Sanātana as the seventh—
these seven are declared to be the mind-born ṛṣis, the sons of Brahmā;
they have attained self-arisen knowledge and are established in the dharma of renunciation.

These are the foremost knowers of Yoga and likewise knowers of the Sāṃkhya doctrine; they are teachers in the science of liberation and promoters of the dharma of liberation. From me, who am unmanifest, the Great One (Mahat) consisting of the three qualities first emanated.
That which is conceived as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), who is beyond even that [the Unmanifest],
is I myself— the path for those engaged in action, from which return is difficult to attain. Whatever creature is fashioned in whatever manner, and for whatever specific task, [it is directed].
Whether in the state of active engagement or withdrawal, he inevitably experiences the fruit thereof.
He is the preceptor of the world, Brahmā, the Lord who is the primordial creator of the universe;
he is indeed your mother, your father, and your grandfather.
Instructed by me, he shall become the bestower of boons upon all beings. And his younger brother Rudra, who has arisen from my forehead,
instructed by Brahmā, shall likewise become the bestower of boons everywhere.
"Go, attend to your respective duties according to the prescribed rule. Let all activities proceed without delay in all the worlds,
and let the actions and the destinies of living beings be made manifest."
O best of gods, the lifespans of the beings created by transformation will be twelve thousand three hundred and twenty-seven years.
This period known as the Kṛta Yuga, the most excellent of times, now proceeds;
and in that age, Dharma will exist with three-quarters remaining.
"In this age, sacrificial animals are not to be harmed; this shall not be otherwise.
O gods, here indeed the entire four-footed Dharma will prevail.
Thereafter comes the age called Tretā, wherein the Trayī (the three Vedas) shall exist."
Where animals sprinkled for sacrifice shall indeed meet their slaughter in the ritual,
there the fourth quarter of Dharma will no longer exist;
thereafter, the mixed age known as Dvāpara shall come to pass.
In that age, Dharma will be deficient by two quarters;
there, animals will be slaughtered, bound to sacrificial posts. Then, when the Tiṣya age has arrived, the Yuga presided over by Kali.
"Wherever the Dharma shall remain standing on but a single foot, there [it will be].
To that teacher who spoke thus, the gods and the celestial sages said:
The gods said:
"When the Dharma stands on only one foot and is liable to go wherever it may, O Blessed One, how should we act? Tell us that.
The Blessed One said:
"You must dwell where teachers who are of virtuous conduct and endowed with tranquility are honored; where dharma does not decline;
and where the Vedas, sacrifices, austerity, truth, and self-restraint likewise prevail."
"Let the best of gods move about joined with the dharma of non-violence;
indeed, that region should be inhabited so that unrighteousness may not touch you with its foot.
Vyāsa said:
Having been thus instructed by the Blessed One, those gods along with the hosts of sages paid homage to the Blessed One and departed for their desired destinations.
When the inhabitants of the triple heaven had gone, Brahmā alone remained there.
Desiring to see the Blessed One abiding in the body of Aniruddha,
the Lord revealed himself to him, having assumed a great horse-head;
holding a water-pot and a rosary, he was reciting the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs.
Then, having beheld that god of immeasurable splendor with the horse's head,
the Lord Brahmā, the creator of the worlds, desiring the welfare of the worlds,
bowed his head in salutation to the granter of boons and stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
Then, having been embraced by the God, he was addressed with these words:
"Reflect upon all the courses of worldly affairs according to the prescribed rule;
you are the ordainer of all beings, the sovereign, and the teacher of the universe."
"Once the burden has been entrusted to you, I shall immediately attain composure.
And when your task for the gods becomes unbearable,
I shall manifest myself as the teacher of self-knowledge."
Having spoken thus, the Horse-headed One vanished on the spot;
instructed by him, Brahmā also went to his own world before long.
Such is this eternal and illustrious Padmanābha.

He was proclaimed as the foremost recipient of offerings in sacrifices and the eternal upholder of sacrifice; established in the dharma of cessation (nivṛtti), he attained the state of those whose nature is imperishable,
yet he ordained the dharmas of worldly activity (pravṛtti), creating the diversity of the world.
He is the beginning, the middle, and the end of all creatures;
he is the sustainer, that which is sustained, the agent, and the action. At the end of the age, having thoroughly withdrawn the worlds, he sleeps.
Awakened at the beginning of the age, he emitted the world;
he is the beginning and he is indeed the middle—the Buddha who creates the world.
Bow down to that god, who is beyond qualities yet whose self consists of the qualities.
To the unborn one of universal form, the abode of all the dwellers of heaven;
likewise to the lord of the great elements, the lord of the Rudras,
the lord of the Ādityas, and also the lord of the Vasus.
To the Lord of the Aśvins and likewise to the Lord of the Maruts; to the Sovereign of the Vedas and sacrifices, and also to the Lord of the Vedāṅgas;
to Hari, who dwells eternally in the ocean and has hair like muñja grass.
To the one who brings peace to all beings, who proclaims the dharma of liberation; to the lord of austerities and of splendors, and likewise of fame;
to the eternal lord of speech and also of the rivers.
To Kapardin, to Varāha, to the wise Ekaśṛṅga; to Vivasvat, to Aśvaśiras, who always assumes four forms;
to the secret one, visible through knowledge, the imperishable, and the perishable.
This god moves about, omnipresent and imperishable.
Thus was this seen by me in the past through the eye of knowledge;
and all of that has been told to you by me in truth, as I was questioned.
"O disciples, let my word be done: serve Hari, the Lord;
sing his praises with the words of the Vedas, and worship him according to the prescribed rites.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Thus addressed by that wise Vedavyāsa, we all became his disciples, as did his son Śuka, who was a knower of the supreme dharma; and he,
O lord of the people, was our preceptor along with us."
And with verses arising from the four Vedas, he praised him.
"All this that you asked me has been related to you;
thus, O King, did my preceptor Dvaipāyana relate it to me in the past."
The man who would constantly hear this, and who would recite it,
having paid homage to the Blessed One with a concentrated mind,
becomes free from disease, radiant, and endowed with strength and beauty.
The sick man is freed from disease, and the bound man is released from bondage. One who desires objects of desire shall obtain his desire, and he shall attain long life.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of all the Vedas, and a Kṣatriya shall be victorious.
A Vaiśya shall obtain abundant profit, and a Śūdra shall attain happiness.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a maiden obtains a desired husband. A woman who has conceived shall be delivered safely, and a pregnant woman shall give birth to a son.
A barren woman obtains offspring, enriched with sons and grandsons;
he who recites this on the road shall travel his journey in safety;
and whatever desire one may cherish, that one shall certainly attain.
Thus spoke the blessed Lord Vyāsa, the son of Parāśara, the master:
"This is the definitive word of the great seer,
the glorification of that high-souled, best of men."
"Having heard this account of the assembly of the seers and the celestial dwellers, the devoted obtain great happiness.
Janamejaya said:

Vyāsa, together with his disciples, praised this Madhusūdana with various names; O Blessed One, you ought to explain the etymology of these for me, who am eager to hear, as I listen to [the praise] of Hari, the Lord of the Lords of Creatures.
"Having heard this, may I become purified and stainless like the autumn moon.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O King, hear how the all-pervading Hari spoke to Phalguna."

With a serene mind, O King, Phalguna, the slayer of enemy heroes, questioned Keśava regarding the etymological derivation (*nirukta*) of the names of the Great-souled Keśava— names born of his qualities and actions— which had been proclaimed by those very names.
Arjuna said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, Creator of all beings, Imperishable One,
Abode of the worlds, Lord of the universe, Bestower of fearlessness upon the worlds!

O Lord Keśava, I desire to hear from you the etymological explanation of those names of yours which have been proclaimed by the great seers in the Vedas and Purāṇas, and those which are secret due to their ritual actions.
12,328.007c For no one else could have expounded the etymology of these names except for you, O Lord. 12,328.008 The Blessed Lord said:
12,328.008a In the Ṛgveda, in the Yajurveda, and likewise in the Atharva and Sāma Vedas...
O Arjuna, in the Purāṇas together with the Upaniṣads, as well as in Jyotiṣa,
in Sāṃkhya, in the Yoga-śāstra, and likewise in Āyurveda,
many of my names have been proclaimed by the great seers.
In that regard, there are certain names that are figurative and others born of action.
O sinless one, listen with a disciplined mind as I explain the etymologies of those names born of action;
for you, my dear, have been remembered of old as half of my own self.
Salutations to that most illustrious one, the supreme Self of all embodied beings,
to Nārāyaṇa, the universe itself, who is devoid of qualities yet whose nature consists of the qualities;
from whose grace Brahmā was born, and from whose wrath Rudra arose.
O best among those possessed of being, that which is the source of all things, both stationary and moving— that essence consisting of eighteen qualities—
is my supreme *prakṛti*, which sustains heaven and earth through yoga.
The eternal, true, and unconquerable [Prakṛti], known as the Self of the worlds,
from which all the transformations of creation and dissolution proceed;
from that [proceeds] the sacrifice, the sacrificer, and the ancient Virāṭ Puruṣa.

He who is called Aniruddha is the source and the dissolution of the worlds. When the end of Brahmā’s night had arrived, by the grace of that one of immeasurable splendor, a lotus appeared, O lotus-eyed one.
Therein Brahmā came into being, born from his very grace; likewise,
at the end of the day,
Rudra, the agent of destruction, was born from the forehead of that god when he was overcome with wrath.
These two, the best among the wise, are known to arise from grace and wrath;
following the paths ordained by Him, they are the agents of creation and destruction. They are merely the instrumental causes here, granting boons to all living beings.
Kapardin, Jaṭila, Muṇḍa, the one who dwells in the cremation ground; Rudra, the observer of fierce vows, the Yogi, the destroyer of Tripura;
the destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, and likewise the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes.
O son of Pāṇḍu, he who is the essence of Nārāyaṇa is to be known in age after age.
He who is Rudra, I am that; he who is I, Śiva, is the Supreme. As is Rudra, so am I; there is no difference between us two.
For when that Maheśvara, the god of gods, is worshipped,
O Pārtha, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is thereby worshipped.
For I am the Self of all the worlds, O son of Pāṇḍu.
Therefore, I shall first worship Rudra himself. For it is my firm conviction that if I do not worship the Lord Śiva, the giver of boons,
no one else would worship themselves.

12,328.022 "For the world follows whatever standard I have established. 12,328.023 Standards indeed are to be honored; therefore, I honor them. 12,328.023c He who knows that [standard] knows me; he who follows that [standard] follows me."
Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are indeed a single essence divided into two;
O son of Kuntī, he moves through the world, established in manifest form amidst all activities.
Indeed, no boon can be granted to me by anyone, O joy of the Pāṇḍavas.
Having thus reflected in my mind upon the ancient Lord of the Universe,
I worshipped the Self by means of the self for the sake of a son;
for Viṣṇu does not bow down to any other deity.
"Thinking 'He is indeed the Self,' I therefore worship Rudra;
yet Brahmā, the Rudras, Indra, the gods along with the sages,
all worship the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the foremost of the immortals."

O Bhārata, among all those who will be, those who exist, and those who have been, Viṣṇu is the foremost; he is to be served and worshipped eternally. Bow down to Viṣṇu, the giver of oblations, and likewise bow to him, the giver of refuge.

"O Kaunteya, bow down to the Giver of Boons; bow down to the consumer of the sacrificial offerings (havya) and the ancestral oblations (kavya). It has indeed been heard by you that my devotees are of four kinds. Among them, the single-minded ones are the best, for they have no other deity."
I alone am the refuge for those who perform actions free from desire;
as for the other three types of devotees, they are indeed considered to be seekers of fruits.
All of them are subject to falling away, but the one who has awakened possesses the highest state.

Brahmā, Śitikaṇṭha, and whatever other deities are remembered— those of preeminent awakening serve me alone, for they shall go to that which is supreme. This specific distinction regarding my devotee has been proclaimed to you, O Pārtha.
"O Kaunteya, you and I are known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
indeed, for the purpose of relieving the earth's burden, we have entered human bodies. O Bhārata, I know the yogas of the supreme self (adhyātma), who I am, and from whence I come."

The Dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*), as well as that which leads to worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), is known as the refuge for men; I alone am the eternal one. Water is called *nārāḥ*, for water is indeed the offspring of Nara.
That was my primordial course; therefore, I am indeed Nārāyaṇa.
Having become like the sun with its rays, I cover the entire universe. And because I am the abode of all beings, I am Vāsudeva.

O Bhārata, the movement of all beings and of all creatures is pervaded by me; O Pārtha, heaven and earth are encompassed by me, and my splendor is supreme. At the end, I am the presiding principle over all beings; desiring that [state], O Bhārata, I exist as such.
And because of my three strides, O Pārtha, I am designated as Viṣṇu. Indeed, people who desire to attain perfection through self-restraint long for me;
because I pervade heaven, earth, and the space between, I am Dāmodara.
Food is called *pṛśni*, as are the Vedas, the waters, and likewise nectar (*amṛta*). Since these have always been within my womb, I am therefore *Pṛśnigarbha*.
Thus did the seers address me when I was cast into the well by Trita.
"O Pṛśnigarbha, protect Trita!"— thus [he cried] when struck down by Eka and Dvita.
Thereupon, that first son of Brahmā, the excellent seer Trita,
indeed rose up from the well by means of the recitation of the *pṛśnigarbha* hymns.

The rays that shine forth from the sun as it heats the worlds, and likewise from fire and the moon— these are known as my hair. Because they are all-knowing, the best of the twice-born call me Keśava.
A fetus had been placed within his own wife by the high-souled Utathya;
and when Utathya had disappeared through divine power,
Bṛhaspati then found that wife of his, O Bhārata.
Then, O son of Kuntī, while that best of sages was thus engaged in sexual union, the embryo—endowed with the five elements—spoke:
"O giver of boons, I arrived first; you ought not to distress my mother."

12,328.046 Upon hearing this, Bṛhaspati became enraged and uttered a curse: 12,328.047 "Since I was prevented by you while engaged in sexual union, you shall therefore be born blind because of my curse; of this there is no doubt."
Due to the curse of that foremost of sages, he entered into long-lasting darkness;
for he was formerly known by the name of the sage Dīrghatamas.
Having acquired the four eternal Vedas along with their limbs (Aṅgas) and sub-limbs (Upāṅgas),...
Then he employed this secret name of mine according to the prescribed sequence, calling out "Keśava" again and again;
he regained his sight and Gautama was restored once more.
"O Arjuna, for this reason my name is Varada and Keśava. Furthermore,
Agni, joined with Soma, was made the single source and the mouth for all the gods and the high-souled ṛṣis."
Therefore, the entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of Agni and Soma.
For it is also stated in the Purāṇa:
"Agni and Soma have a single source."
"12,328.053C 'The gods have Agni as their mouth,' and 12,328.053D 'Because they share a single origin, they magnify one another and sustain the worlds.
Arjuna said:
"How were Agni and Soma formerly produced from a single source?
This doubt has arisen in me; resolve it, O Madhusūdana.
The Blessed Lord said:

"Behold, O son of Pāṇḍu, I shall relate to you this ancient account arising from my own splendor; listen to me with a one-pointed mind, O Pārtha. When the time for universal purification had passed, at the end of the fourth thousand yugas—"
When all beings, both stationary and moving, have dissolved into the unmanifest;
when the world has become a single ocean of water, devoid of light, earth, and wind, and is shrouded in blind darkness;
when everything is overcome by darkness alone—devoid of consciousness and established in non-duality.
12,329.003E Neither in night nor in day, neither in being nor in non-being, neither in the manifest nor in the unmanifest was he established.

12,329.003F In this state, from that which is the refuge of Nārāyaṇa’s qualities—imperishable, ageless, beyond the senses, ungraspable, unborn, true, non-violent, preeminent, and characterized by various specific manifestations;
12,329.003G from that which is imperishable, ageless, immortal, formless, all-pervading, the creator of all, and eternal—from that darkness, the Person appeared: Hari, the undecaying.
For there is also an illustration here:
"There was neither day nor night;
there was neither being nor non-being."
"Darkness alone existed in the beginning, multiform;
she is the mother of the universe"—thus is its meaning restated.
Now, upon the manifestation of that lotus-born Brahmā, who is the Puruṣa born from darkness, that Puruṣa, desiring to emit creatures, created Agni and Soma from his two eyes.
12,329.005B Then, when the creation of beings had commenced, the Brahman and the Kṣatra appeared according to the sequence of progeny.
12,329.005C That which is Soma is the Brahman; those who are the Brahman are the Brāhmaṇas.
12,329.005D That which is Agni is the Kṣatra; the Brahman is more powerful than the Kṣatra.
12,329.005E Why? Because this is a quality perceptible to the world, just as:
12,329.005F "No being superior to the Brahmins has ever been born," and "I say that one should offer oblations while the fire is blazing. 12,329.005G Thus I speak.
12,329.005H The creation of beings was performed by Brahmā, and having established the beings, the three worlds are sustained. 12,329.006A For there is also a Vedic mantra:
12,329.006B "O Agni, you are the invoker of all sacrifices."
"12,329.006C Among gods and among the human race...
12,329.006D And here there is an illustration:
12,329.006E "O Agni, the invoker of all sacrifices..."
12,329.006F "The person [is] with the gods and with humans in the world.
12,329.006G For Agni is the *hotṛ*, the performer of sacrifices.
12,329.006H And that Agni is Brahman.
12,329.007A For there is no offering without a mantra;
12,329.007B austerity does not arise without a person. 12,329.007C Through this, the worship of the mantras as the oblation exists for gods and humans; by this you are appointed as the *hotṛ*.
12,329.007D And those human offices pertaining to the *hotṛ* functions,
12,329.007E for it is ordained that officiating at sacrifices belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, not to the Kṣatriya or the Vaiśya, even though they are twice-born;
12,329.007F therefore, the Brāhmaṇas, having become the very fires, carry forth the sacrifices.
12,329.007 G. Sacrifices satisfy the gods; the gods nourish the earth.
12,329.008 A. For in the *Śatapatha* there is this Brāhmaṇa passage: 12,329.008 B. "When the fire is kindled, he who is wise offers the oblation of giving into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa."
12,329.008C Even so, the wise Brahmins who have become fire meditate upon fire.
12,329.008D Agni is Viṣṇu; having entered all beings, he sustains their vital breaths.
12,329.008E Moreover, there are verses sung by Sanatkumāra on this subject:
In the beginning, Brahmā, the source of all and free from blemish, created the universe.
The immortals, whose origin is Brahman, abide in heaven with the sounds of Vedic recitation.
The thought, speech, action, faith, and austerities of the Brāhmaṇas [are likewise rooted in that].
They sustain both the earth and the heavens through their coolness, like water that is as refreshing as nectar.
There is no dharma higher than truth; there is no teacher equal to a mother. For the welfare of beings both in this world and after death, there is nothing superior to the Brahmins.
Neither do their oxen grow, nor do their draft animals;
the *gargara* vessel is not stirred during the distribution.
They become outcastes, turned into *dasyus*.
In whose kingdom the Brahmins are deprived of their livelihood—
[for it is established] by the authority of the Vedas, Purāṇas, and Itihāsas that Brahmins are the very mouth of Nārāyaṇa, the self of all, the creator of all, and the source of all existence;
for at the very moment of the speech of that boon-granting God, the Brahmins first appeared, and from the Brahmins the remaining castes appeared.

12,329.013 C. And thus, when the Brahmins—distinguished even among gods and demons—were formerly created by me myself while I was in the state of Brahmā, the gods, demons, and great seers were established as specific classes of beings and restrained. 12,329.014 A. Indeed, on account of his assault upon Ahalyā, Indra acquired a tawny beard from Gautama; and on account of Kauśika, Indra underwent the loss of his testicles and attained the form of a ram’s scrotum.

12,329.014C The arm of Purandara, who was raising his thunderbolt to strike down the Aśvins’ sacrificial vessel, was paralyzed by Cyavana. 12,329.014D And by Dakṣa, who was filled with rage upon the slaughter of his sacrifice, another eye in the form of an organ was produced on Rudra’s forehead after he had further disciplined himself through asceticism. 12,329.015A When Rudra had entered into initiation for the sake of destroying Tripura, Uśanas cut off the matted locks from his head and hurled them [at him].
12,329.015B Then serpents appeared;
12,329.015C his throat, being pressed by those serpents, was brought to a state of blueness.
12,329.015D Or rather, in the previous Manvantara, that of Svāyambhuva, he attained the state of having a blue throat due to being seized by the hand of Nārāyaṇa.

12,329.016A While Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, was performing the preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*) for the production of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), the waters did not become clear as he touched them. 12,329.016B Thereupon, Bṛhaspati became enraged at the waters.

12,329.016C "Since the waters have become turbid and failed to become clear while I was touching them, therefore from this day forward they shall be filled with crocodiles, sea-monsters, fish, tortoises, and various creatures, and shall remain turbid."
From that time forward, the waters became infested with sea-monsters.
Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, was indeed the domestic priest of the gods and the sister’s son of the Asuras;
he gave the portion to the gods openly, but to the Asuras in secret.
12,329.018A Then, placing Hiraṇyakaśipu at their head, the Asuras requested a boon from their sister, the mother of Viśvarūpa:
12,329.018B "O sister, this son of yours, the three-headed Viśvarūpa, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, has been the domestic priest of the gods; he gave the sacrificial portion openly to the gods, but secretly to us.
12,329.018C Consequently, the gods are prospering while we are wasting away."
12,329.018 D "Therefore, you ought to restrain him so that he may turn toward us.
12,329.019 A Then, when Viśvarūpa had arrived at the Nandana grove, his mother said:
12,329.019 B "Son, why do you, while increasing the faction of the enemy, destroy your own maternal uncle's faction?"
"You ought not to act in this way.

Thinking that his mother's word was not to be transgressed, Viśvarūpa paid her honors and went to Hiraṇyakaśipu. And from Vasiṣṭha, the son of the Golden Womb (Hiraṇyagarbha), Hiraṇyakaśipu received a curse.
"12,329.020 Because you have chosen another as your *hotṛ*, therefore, with your sacrifice incomplete, you shall meet death from a previously unknown species of being.
12,329.020C Due to that pronouncement of a curse, Hiraṇyakaśipu met his death.
12,329.021A Viśvarūpa, who strengthened his mother’s side, became excessively devoted to ascetic penance (*tapas*).
12,329.021B To cause him to break his vow, Indra dispatched many beautiful apsarases.
12,329.021C Upon seeing them, his mind became agitated, and he was soon attached to those apsarases.
12,329.021D Perceiving that he was attached, the apsarases said, "We shall now depart as we came."
12,329.022A Tvaṣṭṛ’s son said to them:
"Where will you go? Stay with me for a while; it will be for your benefit. 12,329.022C They said to him:
"O celestial nymphs, we choose Indra, the granter of boons, the powerful lord of old," they said.
Then Viśvarūpa said to them, "This very day, the gods together with Indra shall cease to exist.
Thereupon, he muttered sacred mantras.
By means of those mantras, Triśiras grew in power.

With one mouth, he drank the Soma well-offered in sacrifices by the twice-born performers of rites throughout all the worlds; with another, he drank water; and with the third, he drank the gods together with Indra.
Then Indra, seeing him thus increasing and his entire body nourished by the drinking of Soma, fell into deep anxiety.
12,329.024A Those gods, together with Indra, approached Brahmā and said:
"12,329.024B Soma, well-offered at all sacrifices by Viśvarūpa, is being drunk;
12,329.024C we have become deprived of our shares."
"12,329.024 D The faction of the Asuras is increasing, while we are diminishing. 12,329.024 E Therefore, you ought to ordain for us that which is our immediate welfare.
12,329.025 A To them Brahmā said: "The seer Dadhīca, the descendant of Bhṛgu, is performing austerities."
"Let him be entreated for a boon so that he may cast off his body,
and let a thunderbolt be fashioned from his bones.
Then the gods went to the place where the venerable rishi Dadhīca was performing austerities.
The gods, together with Indra, approached him and said, "O Blessed One, is your asceticism proceeding well and without hindrance?
Dadhīca replied to them, "Welcome to you all; what may be done for you?
Whatever you shall say, that I will do."
12,329.026E They said to him, "The Blessed One ought to perform the renunciation of his body for the sake of the welfare of the world.
12,329.026F Then Dadhīca, being likewise undisturbed in mind, a great yogi equal in pleasure and pain, composed himself and performed the renunciation of his body.
12,329.026*0871_01 Having been addressed thus, Dadhīca spoke to them: 1/
"If I were to abandon [my life], the station of Indra would be attained by me after a thousand years," [he said].
Having said, "So be it," Indra [departed].
Having assigned him his own place, the ascetic became [established];
Indra became Dadhīca.
When that period was complete, the gods, including Indra, arrived, saying, "This is the time for the casting off of the body."
There is also a Vedic revelation on this point:
"Indra [acted] with the bones of Dadhyañc" (Ṛgveda 1.84.13a).
12,329.027A When he had been surrendered to the Supreme Self, the Creator gathered those bones and fashioned a thunderbolt.
12,329.027B With that thunderbolt—indestructible, invincible, produced from the bones of Brahmā, and entered by Viṣṇu—Indra struck Viśvarūpa and severed his heads.
12,329.027C And he performed the decapitation of him.
Immediately thereafter, Indra slew Vṛtra, the enemy produced by Tvaṣṭṛ from the churning of the body of Viśvarūpa.
Having said, "I give you the head of the sacrificial animal," to the axe,
when that Brahman-murder had been split in two, Indra, out of fear, abandoned his sovereignty over the gods and took refuge in a cool lotus plant growing in the waters of Lake Mānasa.
There, by virtue of his sovereign power, he became as minute as an atom and entered the knot of a lotus fiber.
Then, when the Lord of the Three Worlds, the husband of Śacī, had fled out of fear of the sin of killing a Brahmin, the world became leaderless;
darkness and passion (rajas) entered the gods.
The mantras of the great seers did not function;
Rākṣasas appeared;
and the Veda went into decline.
