by these words of truth, I accomplish all my purposes.
Formerly, this was related by Nārada to my preceptor while the sages,
the Pāṇḍavas, Kṛṣṇa, and Bhīṣma were listening;
it concerns how he reached the great White Island and beheld the imperishable Hari.
Having returned, O King, Nārada swiftly went to Mount Meru,
carrying in his heart the burden of what had been spoken by the Supreme Soul.
Afterwards, O King, a great trepidation arose within him.
Having traveled a long distance on the road and returned here safely,
he then departed from Mount Meru for Mount Gandhamādana;
and from the sky, he quickly descended toward the vast Badarī.
Then he beheld those two ancient gods, the best of sages, performing very great austerity, established in the self, and observing mighty vows;
they surpassed even the sun in brilliance, which illuminates all the worlds.
Adorned with the *śrīvatsa* mark, worthy of worship, and wearing circles of matted hair,
they had webbed feet and hands, and the marks of wheels upon their feet;
they were broad-chested, long-armed, and possessed four testicles.
They had sixty teeth and eight tusks, and their voices were like the roar of a mass of clouds;
they possessed beautiful faces and broad foreheads, with fine jaws, eyebrows, and noses; and the heads of those two gods resembled parasols.
Seeing those two endowed with such marks and designated as Great Beings (mahāpuruṣa),
Nārada was delighted and honored by them;
having addressed them with a welcome, he was then asked about his health.
Having gazed upon those two Supreme Persons, his mind became absorbed within them; for those who were present there in that assembly, honored by all beings,
were exactly like the two best of sages whom I had seen in Śvetadvīpa.
Having reflected thus in his mind and having performed a circumambulation,
he sat down there upon an auspicious seat made of *kuśa* grass. Then those two, who were the abodes of asceticism, fame, and splendor—
O King, having performed their morning rites and being endowed with self-restraint and tranquility, the two sages then honored Nārada with water for his feet and the respectful offering (*arghya*),
and sat down upon two seats after completing their hospitality and daily observances.

When they were seated there, that place shone brilliantly, like a sacrificial arena with fires whose great flames are fed by offerings of clarified butter. Then Nārāyaṇa spoke these words to Nārada there.

12,331.034c Once he was comfortably seated, rested, and established in happiness after having been offered hospitality, [Nārada asked: 12,331.035a "Has that Blessed One, the eternal Supreme Self, the supreme source of us both, been seen by you in Śvetadvīpa? 12,331.035c [Nārada replied: "He has been seen. 12,331.036a "And have you heard from him the supreme dharma, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.036c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.037a "And have you also seen that great-souled one who is the source of all beings, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.037c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.038a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.038c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.039a "And have you seen that ancient one, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.039c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.040a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.040c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.041a "And have you seen that ancient one, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.041c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.042a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.042c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.043a "And have you seen that ancient one, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.043c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.044a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.044c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.045a "And have you seen that ancient one, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.045c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.046a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.046c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.047a "And have you seen that ancient one, the one who is without beginning or end, the one whose form is the universe, and who is the creator of all worlds? 12,331.047c "I have seen him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.048a "And have you heard from him the dharma consisting of the knowledge of Brahman, which is the means for attaining liberation? 12,331.048c "Indeed, I have heard it from him, O best of the twice-born. 12,331.049
Nārada said:
"I have seen that glorious, imperishable Person who bears the universal form;
for all the worlds, as well as the gods together with the ṛṣis, abide within him."
Even now, while beholding you two who are eternal, I see him as well;
for you two, who bear manifest forms, are endowed with those very same characteristics that Hari, who assumes an unmanifest form, possesses.
"I saw you two there by the side of that god;
and today I have come here, having been dismissed by that Supreme Self.
For who indeed could equal him in splendor, fame, and glory?"
"O sons of Dharma, you two are peerless in the three worlds;
therefore, he previously told me my name known as Kṣetrajña,
and he also described how my future incarnations will occur."
There, those white men who are devoid of the five senses are all awakened and are devotees of Puruṣottama. They always worship the God, and He rejoices together with them.
For the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Self, who is dear to the twice-born, is indeed devoted to his devotees;
being worshipped, he who is fond of his devotees always rejoices. He is the consumer of the universe, the omnipresent God, our kinsman, and one who is affectionate toward his devotees.
He of exceeding power and splendor is the agent, the cause, and the effect;
he of great renown is the motive, the ordainer of knowledge, and the reality itself. Having disciplined himself through austerity, he is indeed that which is beyond Śvetadvīpa.
That which is renowned as *tejas* (splendor), illuminated by its own radiance,
is peace (*śānti*) throughout the three worlds for the perfected ones of purified soul. Through this auspicious understanding, he has established himself in the lifelong vow (*naiṣṭhika-vrata*).
There the sun does not shine, nor does the moon radiate;
the wind does not blow while the Lord of Gods performs his difficult penance.
Having established upon the earth an altar eight spans high, the Eater of All (Viśvabhuj) remains there.

Standing on one foot with arms raised and facing north, the god performed most difficult austerities while reciting the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches— those very same austerities that Brahmā, the sages, and Paśupati himself had performed.
And the remaining best of the wise— the Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas;
the Nāgas, Suparṇas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and those who are royal seers—
constantly offer oblations to the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rites.
All those actions performed with minds focused on the One alone approach the feet of that God; indeed,
the God himself receives them all with his own head.

There is no one else dearer to him than the awakened great-souled ones in the three worlds; therefore, I have attained absolute certainty. And so, having been sent by that Supreme Self, I have come here.
Exclusive devotion to no other deity, single-mindedness toward Hari; the state of being served by none other than Viṣṇu, and likewise the state of being worshipped by none other;
equality with Brahmā, Rudra, and the rest, and indeed the absence of [ordinary] intellect.
Not going to the abodes of other gods, not looking toward other devotees and so forth,
and likewise non-attachment to the fruits of action— this is considered one-pointedness (*ekāntitva*).
Thus the Blessed Lord Hari himself declared this to me.
"12,331.052c Having become intent upon that, I shall always dwell together with you both.
12,332.001 Nara and Nārāyaṇa said: 12,332.001a "You are blessed and you are favored, since the Lord himself has been seen by you."
For no one has ever seen him, not even the Lotus-born One himself;
the Blessed One, the Supreme Person, whose source is unmanifest, is difficult to behold.
O Nārada, these words spoken by me are indeed the truth.
There is no one in the world dearer to him than his devotees;
therefore, O best of the twice-born, he revealed his own self to you.
For that is the station of the Supreme Self for one who performs penance.
"O best of the twice-born, no one can attain that place except for the two of us;
for the splendor of that abode, shining by its own power, would be equal to the combined radiance of a thousand suns."
From that god, the lord of all beings, O Brahmin,

there arises *kṣamā* (patience/earth), O best of the patient, by which the earth is joined together. And from that god there also arises *rasa* (taste/flavor), which is beneficial to all living beings.
For by that [substance] the waters are joined and attain fluidity;
from that very same [substance] light is produced, whose nature consists of the quality of form (rūpa),
and by which the sun is joined and thereby illumines the worlds.
From that god, Puruṣottama, touch was produced; by which the wind is joined, and from that it blows through the worlds. And from that Lord, the Master of all the worlds, sound arises.
That by which space is joined remains unobstructed;
from that deity arises the mind present in all beings,
by which the moon is conjoined and maintains its quality of luminosity.

That place, known as Vedasaṃjñita, is called the producer of the six elements; there dwells the Blessed One, the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, accompanied by Knowledge. For those in this world who are stainless and free from both merit and sin [reside there].
O best of the twice-born, for those traveling along that secure path,
the Sun— the destroyer of darkness for all the worlds— is said to be the gateway;
he is garlanded with flames, possessed of great splendor, and by him this universe is sustained.
With all their limbs consumed by the sun, they become invisible anywhere to anyone;
having become like atoms, they enter into that god. Released even from that, they abide within the body of Aniruddha.
Then, O best of Brahmins, those who have become mind further enter into Pradyumna;
and having been released from Pradyumna, they likewise enter Saṃkarṣaṇa, the individual soul (jīva),
along with the followers of Sāṃkhya and the Bhāgavatas.
Then, O best of the twice-born, freed from the three qualities (guṇas), they directly enter the Supreme Self— the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) whose nature is beyond qualities,
Vāsudeva, the abode of all; know him as the Knower of the Field according to the truth.
With minds concentrated, disciplined, and with senses restrained,
those who have attained the state of single-minded devotion enter Vāsudeva.
And we two also, O best of the twice-born, were born in the house of Dharma.

Having resorted to that delightful and vast [hermitage], they established themselves in fierce asceticism. O twice-born one, may there be well-being for those manifestations of that very god, beloved by the gods, who will appear while residing within the three worlds.

O best of the twice-born, according to their own prescribed rules as before, those two undertook that supreme vow consisting of all the *kṛcchra* penances; being joined with the ritual for his own purpose, he remained steadfast in the *kṛcchra* vow involving all hardships.
"O ascetic, you were seen by us both in Śvetadvīpa when you had come together with the Blessed One and engaged in conversation;
for everything that occurs in the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, is known to us."
"Whatever is yet to be, has already occurred, or is currently happening— whether auspicious or inauspicious—
the God of gods has told you all of that, O great sage.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words of theirs, Nārada, devoted to Nārāyaṇa, turned toward fierce asceticism; with palms joined in reverence,
he chanted according to the rules many mantras dedicated to Nārāyaṇa.
For twelve thousand three hundred and thirty-two years and two and a half days, the illustrious and highly energetic seer Nārada dwelt in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
worshipping that very deity and those two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
12,333.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, after some time had passed, Nārada, the son of Parameṣṭhin,
having performed the rites for the gods according to the rule, thereafter performed the rites for the ancestors.
Then the lord, the eldest son of Dharma, spoke these words to him:
"O best of the twice-born, who is being worshipped by you in this rite ordained for the gods and the ancestors? O best among the wise, tell me that according to the sacred tradition."
"What is this action being performed, and what is its fruit desired?
Nārada said:
'This which you have previously stated—that destiny must be acted upon—'"

The deity and the supreme sacrifice is the eternal Supreme Self; therefore, being constantly absorbed in that state, I worship the imperishable Vaikuṇṭha. And from Him, in the beginning, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, was brought forth.

The Supreme Lord, being pleased, indeed begot my father; I am his son, born of his will, conceived at the very beginning of the kalpa. O virtuous one, I perform the sacrifice to the ancestors according to the rite of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus, that very Blessed One is the father, the mother, and the grandfather;
the Lord of the World is constantly worshipped by me in the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña). Furthermore, O God, another Vedic text states: "The ancestors indeed sacrificed to their sons."
The Vedic revelation had been lost and was taught once again by their sons;
therefore, those sons who imparted the mantras attained the status of fathers. Surely this was known to you both in the past, O you of purified souls.
12,333.009c Sons and fathers indeed honored one another.
12,333.010a "Having first laid down three *piṇḍas* upon the earth and having offered *kuśa* grass," 12,333.010c "How did those ancestors in ancient times receive the designation of *piṇḍa*?"
Nara and Nārāyaṇa said: "Indeed,
in former times,
Govinda, having assumed the form of a boar, swiftly lifted up this earth, which had been submerged and was girt by the oceans."
Having established the Earth in her own place, Puruṣottama—
his limbs smeared with water and mud— was intent on performing his worldly duties;
and when the time for his daily rites arrived, as the sun reached its meridian.
Having suddenly shaken off the lumps of clay clinging to his fangs, the Lord,
O Nārada, spread out *kuśa* grass upon the earth and established them there. Then,
with those [lumps] in view, he performed the ancestral rites (*pitrya*) for himself according to the prescribed rule.
Having formed three *piṇḍas* according to his own ritual procedure, the Lord,
facing eastward, himself performed the rite of final liberation (*apavarga*), sprinkling them with sesame seeds that were infused with oil and produced from the warmth of his own body.
And for the purpose of establishing the boundaries [of the worlds], he then spoke these words:
"I, the creator of the world, am myself intent upon creating the ancestors.
As I was immediately contemplating the supreme ritual procedure for the ancestors—"

"Shaken out by my two fangs, these balls of food have fallen to the earth toward the southern direction; therefore, they are indeed your ancestors. For those three who were previously formless have now assumed the form of these funeral cakes."
"May the eternal Pitṛs created by me exist in the world.
The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather—
I myself am to be known as residing here within these three *piṇḍas*."
"There is no one superior to me, nor is there anyone who should be worshipped by me myself. Who in this world is my father? I alone am the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
And even the father of the Grandfather—I alone am the cause here."
Having spoken these words, O Brahmin, Vṛṣākapi, the God of gods,
offered elaborate funeral cakes on Varāha Mountain,
and after honoring himself, vanished right there.
For this reason, O one of auspicious mind, the ancestors known as *piṇḍas* constantly receive worship, according to the word of Vṛṣākapi;
for those who sacrifice to the ancestors, the gods, their gurus, and likewise to guests.
The cows, the foremost of the twice-born, and likewise the Earth, their mother—
they worship Viṣṇu alone through action, mind, and speech;
for that Blessed Lord dwells within, residing in the bodies of all living beings.
"Equal toward all beings, the Lord over pleasure and pain,
the Great One, the Great-Souled One, the Soul of All— He is celebrated as Nārāyaṇa.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard these words spoken by Nara and Nārāyaṇa, Nārada,
possessing extreme devotion to the God, attained the state of single-minded dedication (ekāntitva).
After staying for a thousand years in the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, he departed.
Having heard the narrative of the Blessed One and having beheld the imperishable Hari,
he went quickly to the Himalayas where his own hermitage was located. Those two sages, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, renowned for their asceticism, [also departed].
In that very delightful hermitage, they performed supreme austerities.
You too, O one of immeasurable prowess, the upholder of the Pāṇḍava lineage,
have today become purified in soul by hearing this story from the beginning.
O best of kings, neither this world nor the next belongs to him who hates the imperishable Viṣṇu in deed, thought, or speech;
his ancestors sink into hell for eternal years.
"O best of the wise, how could anyone ever hate the god Nārāyaṇa, Hari? For how indeed could one's own self (ātman) be an object of hatred for anyone?
O tiger among men, it is an established truth that Viṣṇu is to be known as the Self."
"O dear one, this which is our guru, the ṛṣi who is the son of Gandhavatī—
he recounted this majesty of the Supreme Self;
from him I heard it, and I have now related it to you, O sinless one."
Know that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa is the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself;
for who else, O tiger among men, could be the author of the Mahābhārata? And who but that Lord could proclaim the various kinds of dharma?

"Let your great sacrifice proceed exactly as you have intended; for you have resolved upon the horse-sacrifice and you have heard the Dharma in its true essence. Having heard this great narrative, King Parīkṣit—
Then, for the sake of completing the sacrifice, he undertook all the necessary rites.
This narrative concerning Nārāyaṇa has been told by me to you,
O Śaunaka and others, dwellers of the Naimiṣa forest, as you requested.
"O King, this was formerly related by Nārada to my preceptor in the presence of the ṛṣis,
the Pāṇḍavas, and while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma were listening;
for he is the supreme preceptor and the lord of the worlds."
May Hari, the upholder of the earth, the treasure-house of tranquility and self-restraint, the repository of sacred learning and discipline, the supreme benefactor of the twice-born,
and the one who is free from death, be your refuge.
He is the treasury of great austerities, the vessel of immense glory, the destroyer of misfortune, the refuge for those who are single-mindedly devoted, and the giver of fearlessness.
May he, who bestows the [proper] destination upon you, who receives his portion of the sacrifice,
who transcends the three qualities (guṇas), who holds the four and five [Vedas],
and who takes the share of the fruit of meritorious works and sacrifices— may he protect you.
The eternal, unconquered, and exceedingly powerful one ordains for the sages who have performed good deeds a destination within his own self;
he is that unborn Person, the witness of the world.
O ascetics, with one mind, bow down many times to him who has the color of the sun and the gait of a lord;
even he who was born from the water bowed to that seer.
For he is the source of the world, the station of immortality—
subtle, ancient, immovable, and supreme;
it is upheld with noble resolve by those who practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
It is known constantly by those who have restrained their selves through their intellect.
Janamejaya said:
"I have heard, O Blessed One, of the majesty of that Supreme Self."
The birth in the abode of Dharma, consisting of Nara and Nārāyaṇa;
the ancient origin of the physical body created by Mahāvarāha;
and how each [being] is conceived according to the path of worldly engagement (*pravṛtti*) and the path of withdrawal (*nivṛtti*).
O sinless Brahmin, that which has been heard by us as you have narrated it,

and that great Horse-headed form (Hayaśiras) of Viṣṇu, the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, which was previously described by you as being in the north-eastern part of the great ocean— [all this we have heard].

And that was seen by the Blessed One, Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. What was that which had been produced previously by Hari, the sustainer of the world, that unprecedented form of those who possess great power and are the best among the wise?
"O Sage, having seen that foremost of the gods, unprecedented and of immeasurable splendor—
that holy Aśvaśiras— what did Brahmā do?
O Brahmin, resolve this doubt of ours, which has arisen from our knowledge of the Purāṇas."
"O you of supreme intelligence, tell us of that which was created by the Great Being.
O Brahmin, we have been purified by you as you recount this meritorious tale.
Vaiśampāyana said:
I shall relate to you in its entirety that ancient narrative equal to the Vedas,
which the blessed Vyāsa sang for the king, the son of Dharma;
I shall proclaim all of that to you, so listen, O Śaunaka.
Yudhiṣṭhira, the king of kings and son of Parīkṣit, questioned the seer Vyāsa Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana— the lord and treasury of the Vedas—
after he had heard of the form of the horse-headed god Harimedhas.
With doubt having arisen, the king questioned him further.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"That which Brahmā showed you—the deity bearing the horse-head—"
"For what purpose did that body fashioned by the gods come into being?
Vyāsa said:
"O lord of the people, whatever exists here in this world bound to a physical body..."
All [this] is pervaded by the five elements born from the intellect of the Lord.
For the Lord is the creator of the world, the sovereign Virāṭ Nārāyaṇa;
he is the inner self of all beings, the bestower of boons, both possessed of qualities and devoid of qualities.

12,335.011e Hear now, O best of kings, about the dissolution of the elements into the unmanifest (avyakta). 12,335.012a In ancient times, when the earth had dissolved into the waters and there was but a single ocean,
and when the water had become light and dissolved into light, and that light dissolved into wind;
When the wind has merged into space, and space follows the mind; when the manifest has merged into the mind, and the manifest has reached the state of the unmanifest;
when the unmanifest has gone into the Puruṣa, and the Puruṣa has entered the all-pervading—
All was indeed darkness; nothing at all could be discerned. From that darkness, Brahman was born—darkness-rooted and having truth as its essence.
That [Brahman], which culminates in the designation of universal existence, assumed a human form.
He is called Aniruddha; they declare him to be Pradhāna. O best of kings, that should be known as the Unmanifest (avyakta), consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa).
The Lord Hari, Viṣvaksena, is accompanied by Vidyā as his companion.
Hari, the immeasurable Lord and the primordial cause of all beings,
having entered into the yoga of sleep, made his bed upon the waters alone;
he lay there contemplating the manifold creation of the world, which arises from many qualities.
As he was contemplating creation, the Great Principle (Mahat) is said to have arisen from his own nature; from that, the ego-sense (Ahaṃkāra) was born as Brahmā, the auspicious four-faced one,
the Lord Hiraṇyagarbha, the grandfather of all the worlds.
Then, from Aniruddha, he who has eyes like lotuses was born within a thousand-petaled lotus; seated there,
the radiant and eternal Lord beheld the worlds consisting of water, appearing most wonderful.
Established in *sattva*, that Parameṣṭhin then created the hosts of beings.
Furthermore, previously upon a lotus petal as radiant as the rays of the sun,
there were two drops of water produced by Nārāyaṇa, preeminent in their qualities.
The Blessed One, who is without beginning or end and is infallible, beheld them;
there, a single drop appeared, honey-colored and of radiant luster.
By the command of Nārāyaṇa, that Madhu was then born from the quality of darkness (tamas).
But another drop was Kaṭhina; he was Kaiṭabha, characterized by the quality of passion (rajas).
Those two foremost ones, endowed with the qualities of darkness (tamas) and passion (rajas), powerful and mace in hand, pursued him along the stalk of the lotus.
They beheld Brahmā of immeasurable splendor seated upon a lotus,
creating first the four Vedas of beautiful form;
then those two foremost of Asuras saw the Vedas embodied.
While Brahmā looked on, they both suddenly seized the Vedas. Then those two foremost of Dānavas, having taken the eternal Vedas,
quickly entered the subterranean realm (Rasātala) in the great ocean to the northeast.
Then, when the Vedas had been stolen, Brahmā was overcome by dejection.
Deprived of the Vedas, he spoke these words to Īśāna:
"The Vedas are my supreme eye; the Vedas are my supreme strength."
"The Vedas are my supreme abode; the Vedas are my highest Brahman.
All my Vedas have been forcibly taken from here by the two Dānavas. Deprived of the Vedas, my worlds have indeed become shrouded in darkness."

"Without the Vedas, what indeed could I do, intent as I am on creating the worlds? Alas! What great sorrow has arisen for me from the destruction of the Vedas; it pierces my heart, rending it with intense grief."
"Who indeed shall now rescue me, submerged as I am in this ocean of grief?
Who shall bring back those lost Vedas, and to whom shall I become dear?"—
O best of kings, as Brahmā was speaking thus, [the Lord appeared].
O best among the wise, his intellect was awakened for the purpose of praising Hari; then the Lord, with palms joined in reverence, sang this supreme prayer:
"Salutations to you, O heart of Brahman; salutations to you, my elder brother."

O primordial of the worlds, best of beings, treasure-house of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, all-pervading Lord; O inconceivable one who manifests both the manifest and the unmanifest, you who abide on the path of security; O consumer of the universe, inner self of all beings, not born from a womb.
"I am born of your grace, O self-existent source of the worlds. My first birth from you was mental, honored by the twice-born;
my second ancient birth was indeed from your eye."
"O Great One, by your grace, this is my third birth, the great one born of speech;
O Lord, this is also my fourth birth, born from hearing you;
and my fifth birth is said to be that of the nose, also from you."

My fifth birth was also fashioned from you as one born from an egg; this is my sixth birth, O one of immeasurable splendor, and this seventh birth of mine is from a lotus. Indeed, in every creation, I am your son, though devoid of the three *guṇas*.
O lotus-eyed one, you are renowned as being fashioned from the primary qualities;
you are the Lord by nature, the self-existent Supreme Person.
Indeed, I have been created by you, possessing the eye of the Vedas and transcending old age.
"Those Vedas have been taken from me; my sight is gone and I am born blind. Be watchful!
Grant me back my two eyes; I am dear to you, and you are dear to me.
Thus was the Blessed One, the Puruṣa whose face is turned in every direction, praised.
Then, exerting himself for the sake of the work of knowledge, he abandoned sleep;
by means of his sovereign power, he assumed a second body. Having then become one with a beautiful nose, he possessed a radiance like that of the moon.
Having fashioned the auspicious Hayashiras, the abode of the Vedas, the Lord [created it];
heaven, together with its constellations and stars, became his head,
and his long hair was as radiant as the rays of the sun.
His two ears were the sky and the netherworld; his forehead was the earth-sustainer;
the holy Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, those great rivers, became his two eyebrows;
the moon and the sun were his two eyes; and the twilight was remembered as his nose.
The syllable *oṃ* was his refinement (*saṃskāra*), and lightning was fashioned as his tongue;
O King, the ancestors known as the Soma-drinkers were his teeth,
and Goloka and Brahmaloka were the two lips of that Great-souled One.
O King, his neck became the Night of Doom (Kālarātri), superior in its qualities.
Having assumed this horse-headed form, which was encompassed by various manifestations,
that Lord of the Universe, the Sovereign, vanished and entered the subterranean realm (rasā).
Having entered the earth once more and established himself in supreme yoga,
he adopted the voice of a learner and uttered the sound "Oṃ.
That sound was resonant, all-pervading, and indeed smooth.
12,335.051c He became internalized within the earth, yet he was exalted by the qualities of all beings.

12,335.052a Then, having bound those two Asuras with a covenant regarding the Vedas, and having cast them down into the netherworld (rasātala), they fled swiftly toward wherever the sound [of the Vedas] went.
In the meantime, O King, the Lord Hari, assuming the form of the horse-headed one,
retrieved all the Vedas that had gone to the netherworld; he then gave them back to Brahmā and returned to his own original nature.
Having established the Hayashiras [form] in the great ocean to the north-east,
the Ashvashiras then became the abode of the Vedas. Then,
the two Dānavas, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, could not see anything at all.
Then those two, moving with great speed, returned once more to that place while others looked on;
yet that spot where the Vedas had been deposited was entirely empty.
Thereupon, those two best among the powerful assumed the highest possible speed.
Then they both quickly rose again from that abode of the essences (rasas),
and they beheld that very same Lord, the primordial creator,
white and radiant as the pure moon, abiding within the body of Aniruddha.

Furthermore, Amitavikrānta had entered into a state of yogic sleep upon a bed fashioned to his own proportions, constructed above the waters, enriched by the coils of a serpent, and enveloped in garlands of flames.
Seeing him endowed with stainless goodness and radiant splendor,
those two lords of the Dānavas let out a great laugh;
possessed by passion and darkness, they both spoke.
12,335.060c This is that white man who lies there, having fallen into sleep.
12,335.061a Surely by him the Vedas have been brought up from the netherworld (rasātala).
12,335.061c Whose is he? Who indeed is this, and why does this enjoyer sleep?
Having uttered these words, the two of them awakened Hari.
Recognizing that they were seeking battle, the awakened Puruṣottama looked upon those two lords of the asuras and then set his mind on war.
Awakened, the one of great splendor fought both of them;
then a battle took place between them and Nārāyaṇa.
Both Madhu and Kaiṭabha had bodies permeated by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas).
While performing a service for Brahmā, Madhusūdana slew [the demons].
Then, by the swift slaying of those two and by the recovery of the stolen Vedas,
Puruṣottama brought about the removal of Brahmā’s grief.

Then Brahmā, his enemies destroyed and honored by the Vedas, surrounded [by them], created at that time all the worlds, both stationary and moving. Having bestowed upon the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) the supreme intelligence for the emanation of the worlds, he acted.
There, the Lord Hari vanished just as he had come;
having slain those two Dānavas, Hari assumed the form of Hayagrīva and,
for the sake of the religion of active worldly life (*pravṛtti-dharma*), resumed that very same body once again.
Vaiśampāyana said:
O lord of the people, thus did that blessed Vyāsa, my preceptor,
the knower of dharma and best of the twice-born, speak to Dharmarāja.
Thus did the illustrious Hari become Aśvaśiras;
this is declared to be the ancient form of the Lord that bestows boons.
For whatever brahmin should constantly hear or retain this [account], [he shall attain his desires].
His study shall never come to ruin;
for, having propitiated the horse-headed god with fierce asceticism,
Pāñcāla obtained the *krama* method on the path shown by Rāma.

O King, this ancient narrative of Hayashiras, equal to the Vedas, which you asked me about, has now been recounted to you. Whatever form the God may wish to assume in the performance of any particular task, [he can do so].
Transforming himself by his own power, he manifests each of those various forms.
He is the glorious treasury of the Vedas; he is indeed the treasury of asceticism. He is Yoga and Sāṃkhya, and he is the supreme Brahman—the all-pervading Hari.

The Vedas have Nārāyaṇa as their supreme goal; sacrifices have Nārāyaṇa as their essence. Austerity has Nārāyaṇa as its highest aim; the ultimate destination has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme object. Truth has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme goal; cosmic order (*ṛta*) has Nārāyaṇa as its very self.
Dharma centered on Nārāyaṇa makes a return to worldly existence difficult to attain;
indeed, even the dharma characterized by worldly activity has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
It is traditionally held that among the qualities of the earth, fragrance is the most excellent, and it has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
O King, the quality of water is taste, which has Nārāyaṇa as its essence; the quality of light is form, which is traditionally held to have Nārāyaṇa as its essence;
and touch, the quality of wind, is likewise traditionally held to have Nārāyaṇa as its essence.

Sound, which arises from space, is also of the nature of Nārāyaṇa; and from that, the mind was born, characterized by the qualities of the unmanifest. Time, as well as the course of the luminaries, has Nārāyaṇa as its supreme source.
Fame, Śrī, and Lakṣmī are deities devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
Sāṃkhya is centered on Nārāyaṇa, and Yoga has Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
For those for whom Puruṣa is the cause, Pradhāna is also the cause.
Intrinsic nature, actions, and destiny are the causes;
likewise, the locus, the agent, and the various instruments,
as well as diverse efforts— destiny is the fifth among these.
Enumerated through five causes, Hari is indeed the ultimate reality everywhere;
for those desiring to know the truth through all-encompassing reasons,
the truth is the one Great Yogi, Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa.
Keśava knows the intentions of the worlds including Brahmā, of the high-souled ṛṣis, and also of the Sāṃkhyas, the Yogins, and the ascetics who know the Self; but they do not know his.

"Whatever rites for the gods or ancestors are performed in all the worlds, whatever gifts are bestowed, and whatever great austerities are practiced— Viṣṇu, established in his sovereign ordinance, is the refuge of them all."
He is called Vāsudeva because he is the dwelling place created by all beings. For he is eternal, the supreme great seer,
possessed of great majesty, endowed with qualities, yet known as being beyond qualities.
He quickly attains union with the qualities,
just as time is joined with its respective seasons;
they do not perceive the course of this great-souled one.
And no one here perceives its departure;
the self-knowing great seers, possessed of self-restraint, constantly behold the Puruṣa who transcends the qualities (guṇas).
Janamejaya said:
"Aha! Indeed, the Blessed Lord Hari delights all those who are single-mindedly devoted;
the Blessed Lord himself accepts the worship performed according to the prescribed rules."
But those in this world whose fuel is consumed and who are freed from both merit and sin—
for them you have pointed out the destination attained through successive tradition;
they go to the Supreme Person by means of that very fourth destination.
But those persons who are single-mindedly devoted go to the supreme state.
Surely this dharma of exclusive devotion is the most excellent and dear to Nārāyaṇa, since,
without passing through the three other states of existence, they go to the imperishable Hari.

I know that the goal of men who are single-mindedly devoted is superior to that of those Brahmins who, properly established in their duty, recite the Vedas along with the Upanishads according to the prescribed rule, as well as those who follow the dharma of ascetics.
By whom was this dharma taught—by a god or by a seer?
And what is the practice for those who are single-mindedly devoted, and when was it first originated, O Lord?
Cut through this doubt of mine, for my curiosity is great indeed.
12,336.008 Vaiśampāyana said: When the armies of the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas were drawn up for battle and Arjuna was despondent, the Gītā was spoken by the Blessed One himself.
I have previously explained to you both the coming and the going;
for this dharma is indeed profound and difficult to understand by those who have not disciplined themselves. It was composed in accordance with the Sāmaveda and established in the primordial age.
"O King, this [universe] is indeed sustained by the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself.
O great king, having been questioned regarding this matter by Pārtha in the midst of the ṛṣis, the highly fortunate Nārada spoke while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma were listening."
O best of kings, this was also told to me by my preceptor;
hear it now exactly as it was told there by Nārada.
Regarding that which occurred at the time of his mental birth, emerging from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa:
O protector of the earth, at that time Nārāyaṇa himself, as Brahmā,
performed the rites for the gods and the ancestors according to that dharma, O Bhārata;
and the Phenapa sages likewise adopted that dharma.
The Vaikhānasas received this dharma from the Phenapas;
from the Vaikhānasas it went to Soma, who then disappeared once more.
O King, this occurred during the second birth of Brahmā, that of Cākṣuṣa.
Then, O King, from the Grandfather Soma, who had learned this dharma, he gave it to Rudra; and that [dharma], which has Nārāyaṇa as its essence, was bestowed upon Rudra.
Thereafter, O King, in the ancient Kṛta age, Rudra remained established in yoga.
He taught this dharma to all the Vālakhilya sages;
then, by the illusory power (*māyā*) of that god, he vanished once more. The high-souled Vālakhilyas then imparted it to Dharma.
O King, when the third great birth of Brahmā occurred from Speech, this Dharma arose there spontaneously from Nārāyaṇa himself. The sage named Suparṇa received it from that Supreme Person.
By means of well-performed austerity, self-restraint,
and religious observances, Suparṇa has circumambulated this supreme dharma three times; therefore, this vow is called *Trisauparṇa* here.
This vow, recited in the *Ṛgveda*, is indeed difficult to perform;
this eternal dharma was also obtained from Suparṇa,
O best of bipeds, and proclaimed by Vāyu, the life-breath of the world.
And from Vāyu, it was obtained by the ṛṣis who subsist on the remains of sacrificial offerings (vighasāśins). From them, the Great Ocean received this supreme dharma.
Thereafter, it vanished once more, absorbed into Nārāyaṇa.
O tiger among men, listen as I recount how, when there was once again a creation born of hearing from the high-souled Brahmā,
the divine Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa himself became intent on creating the world.

The Lord meditated upon the Supreme Person who brings about the creation of the world. Then, as he was thus meditating, a person emerged from his two ears; Brahmā, the creator of progeny, spoke to that Lord of the World.

"Create all beings, my son, from your mouth as well as from your feet. I shall provide for your welfare, O observer of noble vows, and bestow upon you strength and splendor. And receive from me the Dharma known by the name Sātvata."

"By that [measure], establish the entire Kṛta-yuga according to the prescribed rule. Then Brahmā paid homage to the god Harimedhas and received the supreme Dharma, together with its secret doctrines and its compendiums.

Having taught that Dharma—which emerged from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa together with the Āraṇyaka, consisting of 12,336 verses, pertaining to the duties of the Kṛta Age, and characterized by action
