12,336.029c
12,336.029e He went to the further shore of darkness, where the unmanifest (avyakta) is established.
12,336.030a Then, the boon-bestowing god, the Grandfather of the worlds of Brahmā,
12,336.030c created at that time all the worlds, both stationary and moving.
Then, at the beginning, the auspicious Kṛta Yuga commenced;
for it was then that the Sātvata dharma, having pervaded the worlds, remained established. By means of that very primordial dharma, Brahmā, the creator of the world, [proceeded].
He worshipped Hari Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of gods and the Sovereign; and then,
for the sake of establishing righteousness and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, he instructed Svārociṣa Manu.
Then, O King, in ancient times, the powerful Svārociṣa, the lord of all the worlds, himself calmly taught his son Śaṅkhapada. Then Śaṅkhapada, in turn, [taught] his own legitimate biological son.
"O Bhārata, he taught the *Diśāpāla-sudharma* to [the seers];
then, when the Tretā Yuga arrived once again, he vanished from sight.
O best of kings, this occurred long ago at the time of Brahmā’s birth from the nose."
Then, while Brahmā looked on, the lotus-eyed Lord Hari Nārāyaṇa himself vomited forth this Dharma;
O King, the blessed Sanatkumāra subsequently studied it from him.
And from Sanatkumāra, O tiger among the Kurus, the Prajāpati Vīraṇa indeed studied this dharma at the beginning of the Kṛta age; and Vīraṇa,
having studied it, gave it to Manu Raucya.
Raucya gave it to his son Śuddha, who was virtuous, well-disciplined, and highly intelligent;
he then bestowed it upon the righteous Kukṣi, the protector of the quarters.
Thereafter, that [mantra], having issued from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa, vanished once more.
O King, at the birth of the egg-born Brahmā from Hari as his source,
this Dharma emerged once more from the mouth of Nārāyaṇa;
it was received by Brahmā and applied according to the prescribed rule.
O King, the sages named Barhiṣads were taught [the Veda] by him;
from the Barhiṣads it passed to a twice-born man who had reached the end of the Sāmaveda, renowned by the name Jyeṣṭha and devoted to the Jyeṣṭhasāman vow. Hari [then received it].
O King, having passed from Jyeṣṭha to King Avikampana,
this Dharma of the Lord Hari then disappeared.
O King, this which is the seventh birth of Brahmā as the lotus-born is [the end of that lineage].
12,336.044c This very dharma was indeed proclaimed there by Nārāyaṇa himself,
12,336.045a to the pure Pitāmaha, the sustainer of the worlds, at the beginning of the Yuga;
12,336.045c and in ancient times, Pitāmaha bestowed this dharma upon Dakṣa.

Then, O best of kings, Dakṣa gave [the knowledge] to his eldest daughter’s son, Āditya, the eldest son of Savitṛ; Vivasvat then received it from him. And at the beginning of the Tretā Yuga, Vivasvat gave it again to Manu.
And Manu, for the sake of the welfare of the world, gave it to his son Ikṣvāku;
and having been recounted by Ikṣvāku, it remained pervading the worlds. And at the end of the dissolution, O King, it shall return once more to Nārāyaṇa.

O best of kings, that dharma which pertains even to those observing vows was previously told to you by Nārada in the *Harigītās*, arranged according to its concise rules; it was received by him along with its secret doctrines and its compendium.
"O King, this Dharma was received directly from Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of the World.
Thus, O King, this great, primordial, and eternal Dharma is difficult to understand and difficult to perform, yet it is always maintained by the Sātvatas."

By this well-applied action of dharma-knowledge, joined with the dharma of non-violence, Hari, the Lord, is pleased. Sometimes he has a single manifestation, or in some cases he is designated as having a twofold manifestation.
He is reckoned as having three manifestations (*trivyūha*), and he is also seen as having four manifestations (*caturvyūha*).
Indeed, Hari alone is the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), free from the sense of "mine," and likewise partless (*niṣkala*);
he is the individual soul (*jīva*) within all beings, transcending the qualities of the five elements.

And the mind, O King, is renowned as the impeller of the five senses; it is the wise treasury of the worlds and the creator of the world's emanation. It is both the non-doer and the doer, the effect and the cause itself.

O King, the imperishable Person sports in whatever way he desires. O best of men, I have proclaimed to you this dharma of exclusive devotion, which, by the grace of my teacher, is difficult for those of unrefined soul to understand.
"O King, men who are single-mindedly devoted are indeed rare in great numbers.
O joy of the Kurus, if this world were filled with those who are single-mindedly devoted—
non-violent, knowers of the Self, and intent on the welfare of all beings— "
12,336.058 "The attainment of the Kṛta Yuga occurs for those who are free from the performance of ritual prayers and works.
12,336.059 Thus, O lord of the people, that Blessed One Vyāsa, the best of the twice-born and knower of dharma, my own preceptor, spoke to Dharmarāja.
O King, in the presence of the ṛṣis, while Kṛṣṇa and Bhīṣma were listening,
Nārada, who possesses great ascetic merit, previously described to him that supreme deity,
the Brahman, white as the moon and imperishable.
12,336.061 Where those who are single-mindedly devoted and intent upon Nārāyaṇa go, that alone shall be the exclusive, supreme abode of the liberated. 12,336.062 Janamejaya said:
"12,336.062a Thus, why do other Brahmins, established in various vows, not practice this manifold dharma followed by the enlightened ones?
12,336.063 Vaiśampāyana said:"

"O King, descendant of Bharata, three natures are fashioned within the bonds of the body: the *sāttvika*, the *rājasa*, and the *tāmasa*. Among those bound in bodies, O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, the person of *sattva* is the best."

O tiger among men, one who is established in *sattva* is resolved upon the goal of liberation. In this state as well, he recognizes the Person who abides in Brahman; since liberation is centered on Nārāyaṇa, it is therefore remembered as being of the nature of *sattva*.
And by meditating upon the Supreme Person, one attains whatever is desired;
for those wise ones who are ascetics seeking liberation possess constant single-minded devotion and are entirely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
For those whose thirst has indeed been severed, Hari brings about security and well-being (yogakṣema).
For whatever person Madhusūdana beholds at the moment of birth,
he should be known as one characterized by *sattva*, and he will be certain of liberation.
For dharma practiced with single-minded devotion is indeed equal to Sāṃkhya and Yoga;
through that, they go to the supreme goal in liberation whose essence is Nārāyaṇa. And when a man is beheld by Nārāyaṇa, he becomes awakened.
Thus, O King, one who is awakened by his own will is not born again.
The *rājasa* and *tāmasa* natures are known to be mixed; for a person born with those as his essence, O Lord of the People, [is subject to rebirth].
Hari himself does not look upon that which is joined with the characteristics of worldly activity;
Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, beholds him as he is being born,
yet he sees the human being as overwhelmed by passion and darkness.
"O best of kings, although the gods and the ṛṣis abide in *sattva*, they are deficient in subtle *sattva*; therefore, they are known as *vaikārika* (transformative). Janamejaya said:
"How may a person subject to transformation go to the Supreme Person?
Tell me everything as it was seen, and the process of manifestation in its proper order.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Endowed with a most subtle essence and joined with the three syllables,
the inactive Puruṣa should go to the twenty-fifth Puruṣa.
Thus, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the Vedāraṇyaka are indeed one.
These constituent parts, numbering twelve thousand three hundred thirty-six and six-tenths, are declared to be the *Pañcarātra*.
This is the dharma of those who are single-mindedly devoted, having Nārāyaṇa as their supreme self.
It is like the floods of water that have issued forth from the ocean.
O King,
these great floods of the water of knowledge likewise enter back into that very same Nārāyaṇa.
"O kinsman of the Yadus, this Sātvata dharma has been recounted to you. O Bhārata, perform it according to the rule, if you are able.
For it was thus that the highly blessed Nārada spoke to my preceptor."

Vyāsa joyfully recounted this undecaying, solitary goal of white-clad ascetics to the wise son of Dharma; that very same teaching, having been transmitted from my teacher, has now been told by me to you.
"O best of kings, this dharma is indeed difficult to practice;
for while you follow it, others do not, being utterly deluded. For Kṛṣṇa alone is the creator of the worlds, as well as their deluder."
"O lord of the people, he is indeed the agent of dissolution and the cause.
Janamejaya said:
"Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, and likewise the Vedāraṇyaka—"
"O Brahmarṣi, these various forms of knowledge indeed circulate throughout the worlds. O Sage, are they all established in a single foundation, or do they have separate foundations?
Being asked by me, please explain their origin and their sequence."
12,337.003 Vaiśampāyana said:
He was born as a son in the midst of the island, one who was deeply learned, supremely noble, and self-possessed.
From Parāśara, Gandhavatī bore the great seer;
homage to him, the dispeller of the darkness of ignorance.
They declare him to be the sixth [Purāṇa], beginning with the Grandfather (Brahmā).
The great seer endowed with the power of the rishis,
the sole son born from a portion of Nārāyaṇa, Dvaipāyana, the great treasury of the Vedas; 12,337.004c.
In the primordial ages,
Nārāyaṇa, possessed of great majesty and sublime splendor, created Brahmā— the great repository of the Vedas— for the sake of obtaining a son.
The ancient, unborn, and great-souled Vyāsa [spoke].
Janamejaya said:
"O best of the twice-born, you yourself previously described his birth."
Śakti was the son of Vasiṣṭha, and Parāśara was the son of Śakti;
the heir of Parāśara was the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana,
whom you yourself further describe as the son of Nārāyaṇa.
"O one of supreme intelligence, tell me what was Vyāsa’s previous birth, born before this one of immeasurable splendor— his birth originating from Nārāyaṇa. Vaiśampāyana said:
While my preceptor— most righteous, a treasury of asceticism, devoted to knowledge, and desiring to know the meaning of the Vedas— was dwelling at the foot of the Himalayas,
that wise sage, having composed the narrative of the *Bhārata*, became weary from his austerities.
O King, we were then entirely devoted to serving him;
Sumantu, Jaimini, Paila of firm vows,
I as the fourth disciple, and likewise Śuka, the son of Vyāsa.
Surrounded by these five excellent disciples, Vyāsa shone at the foot of the Himalayas like the Lord of Beings (Śiva) amidst his attendants;
he was reciting the Vedas with their auxiliary branches and the entire meaning of the Mahābhārata.

12,337.013c We attend upon him, who is self-controlled and single-minded, with disciplined focus. 12,337.014a Then, on a certain occasion during our conversation, that best of the twice-born was questioned by us regarding the meaning of the Vedas, the meaning of the *Mahābhārata*, and likewise his birth from Nārāyaṇa.
Having first explained the meaning of the Vedas and the meaning of the Mahābhārata, he, the knower of reality,
began to relate this birth from Nārāyaṇa:
"Listen to this supreme and excellent narrative concerning the seers."
O Brahmins, this [knowledge], which arose at the beginning of time and was attained by me through austerity,
was revealed when the seventh creation of beings had arrived— that creation born from the lotus—
by Nārāyaṇa, the great yogi who is devoid of both good and evil.
From his navel, he brought forth as a son Brahmā, of immeasurable splendor.
Then he appeared, and [the Lord] spoke these words to him:
"Born from my navel, you are the lord who shall effect the creation of progeny."
"O Brahmā, create various offspring, both the ignorant and the wise.
Thus addressed, he turned away, his mind agitated by anxiety;
bowing down to the boon-granting god, the Lord Hari, he spoke.
"O Lord of Gods, what power do I have to create progeny? Salutations be unto you! O God, I am devoid of wisdom; ordain what must be done next.
Having been addressed in this way, the Blessed One then vanished from that place.

12,337.022c The Lord of Gods, the best among the wise, reflected upon his own intellect (buddhi). 12,337.023a Then Intellect, in her own embodied form, approached the Lord Hari; 12,337.023c and he, who is himself beyond yoga, then employed her through the power of yoga.
The imperishable Lord, the God, spoke these words to that intelligent and powerful *buddhi*, who was established in the application of sovereignty:
"Enter into Brahmā for the sake of accomplishing the creation of the worlds."
Then, commanded by the Lord, that Intelligence quickly entered him. Then Hari beheld him once more, endowed with intelligence, and spoke these words to him again: "Create these various creatures."
Saying "So be it," the righteous Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, accepted the command of Hari with his head and acted accordingly.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
In a mere moment, he reached his own abode known as Deva;
having returned to that very primordial state, he became one with it.
Then, indeed, another thought arose within him once again.
All these creatures were created by Brahmā Parameṣṭhin,
crowded with hosts of Daityas, Dānavas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas; indeed,
this poor Earth has been born overwhelmed by their burden.
"Many powerful Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas will arise on earth; endowed with ascetic power, they will obtain excellent boons. By virtue of those boons, they will all inevitably become arrogant."
The hosts of gods and the sages whose wealth is asceticism must be protected;
therefore, it is right for me to perform this removal of the earth’s burden. Then, [I shall act] through various manifestations upon the earth in due order.
By the suppression of the wicked and the support of the virtuous,
I shall uphold this earth, which is true and ascetic;
for she is indeed supported by me, who dwell in the netherworld as a serpent.
"Supported by me, she indeed sustains the entire world with its mobile and immobile beings;
therefore, having come into birth, I shall effect the protection of the earth.
Having reflected thus, the Blessed One Madhusūdana—
He created many forms for the sake of manifestation:
the boar, the man-lion, the dwarf, and likewise the human form.
By these, I must slay the ill-behaved enemies of the gods.
Then the Creator of the World, making the sound "Bhoḥ" resound, uttered Sarasvatī; there the son of Sarasvatī was born.
The son of the Lord, born from Speech, was named Apāntaratamas.
The Knower of the past, present, and future, the speaker of truth, firm in his vows—
the imperishable Source of the gods— spoke to him as he bowed his head:
"O best among the wise, you must apply yourself with focused hearing to the exposition of the Vedas."
"Therefore, O Sage, carry out these words as commanded by me.
By him, the Vedas were then divided during the interval of Svāyambhuva Manu. Thereupon, the Blessed Lord Hari was gratified by that deed of his.
Through well-performed austerity, self-restraint, and observance,
the Blessed Lord said:
"O son, in the various Manvantaras, you shall likewise be the promoter of the world."

"O Brahmin, you shall be immovable and forever invincible. Furthermore, when the Kali age (Tiṣya) arrives again, there will arise high-souled kings known as the Kurus, descendants of Bharata, renowned throughout the earth."

"O best of the twice-born, among those born from you, there will be a division of lineages for the sake of mutual destruction, with the exception of yourself. Even then, endowed with ascetic power, you shall divide the Vedas into many parts."
When the dark age (Kali-yuga) has arrived, you will become dark-complexioned;
you will be the performer of various duties and the source of knowledge,
yet though endowed with austerity, you shall not be liberated from passion.

"And your son shall be free from passion and shall become the Supreme Self (Paramātman) through the grace of Maheśvara; this word shall not be otherwise. He whom they indeed call the mind-born son (Mānasa-putra);"
Vasiṣṭha, the foremost treasury of ascetic power, who outshines even the sun, was endowed with the supreme intellect of his grandfather. 12,337.047c.
In his lineage,
there was then a great seer named Parāśara, of immense power; he was your father, the most excellent treasury of the Vedas.
You shall indeed be a great ascetic, an abode of penance;
born from the womb of a father’s maiden,
you will become the son of that sage.
Having severed all doubts regarding the meaning of the past, present, and future,
you— endowed with ascetic power— shall behold all those thousands of cycles of ages that have passed away in the past, as they are pointed out by me.
O Sage, after the passing of many thousands of yugas, you shall behold me again in this world— me, who am without beginning or end, bearing the discus in my hand;
for by virtue of your meditation upon me, O Sage, these words shall not be otherwise.
O Mahāsattva, you shall possess incomparable renown; you will become Śanaiścara, the son of the Sun, and a great Manu. And in that Manvantara, you shall be preceded by the host of the Seven Sages.
"O child, by my grace you yourself shall become [that], of this there is no doubt.
Whatever exists in the world, all that is fashioned by me; for while one person thinks of another, I ordain everything according to my own will."
Vyāsa said:
Having thus spoken these words to the sage Apāntaratamas, the son of Sarasvatī, the Lord then said, "Accomplish [this]."
By the grace of that god Harimedhas, I was then born by the command of Hari under the name Apāntaratamas;
and once again, I was born as the renowned joy of the family of Vasiṣṭha.
Thus have I related this former birth of mine,
born through the grace of Nārāyaṇa and as a portion of Nārāyaṇa himself;
for I indeed performed most great and extremely rigorous ascetic penance.
O best among the wise, through supreme concentration, I have previously related all this to you which you asked of me, my sons—
concerning past births and the future— out of affection for my devotees.
12,337.058 Vaiśampāyana said:
12,337.058a O King, this origin of our teacher Vyāsa, whose mind is untroubled, has been told to you as previously requested; listen again.

"O royal sage, know that Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata— these are indeed various systems of knowledge. Kapila is said to be the supreme seer who is the proponent of Sāṃkhya."
Hiraṇyagarbha, the ancient one, is the knower of yoga and none other;
he is also called Apāntaratamas, the teacher of the Vedas,
whom some here proclaim to be the sage Prācīnagarbha.
Umāpati, Bhūtapati, Śrīkaṇṭha, the son of Brahmā—
Śiva, being composed, has declared this Pāśupata knowledge. Furthermore,
the Blessed One himself is the knower of the entire Pañcarātra.
O best of kings, within all these branches of knowledge, it is seen—
according to tradition and according to wisdom— that the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate goal.
Yet, O lord of the people, those who are shrouded in darkness do not know him in this way.
The wise proclaim that very author of the scripture to be the sage Nārāyaṇa, the ultimate goal; they declare that there is no other,
for Hari dwells eternally within all things that are free from doubt.

Mādhava does not dwell upon those who possess doubt and rely on the power of logical arguments. But those who know the Pañcarātra, O King, who are devoted to the proper sequence and have attained single-minded devotion, indeed enter into Hari.
O King, both Sāṃkhya and Yoga are eternal,
as are all the Vedas in their entirety;
they have been expounded by all the ṛṣis together.
Nārāyaṇa is this ancient universe;
whatever auspicious or inauspicious action has been set in motion proceeds throughout all the worlds.
"Therefore, one should know that it comes from that seer,
whether in heaven, in the intermediate space, on earth, or even in the waters.
Janamejaya said:
"O Brahmin, are there many Puruṣas, or is there indeed only one? For which among these is the Puruṣa the most excellent, and what is said here to be the source?
Vaiśampāyana said:

"O scion of the Kuru lineage, many are the persons in this world who investigate Sāṃkhya and Yoga; they do not accept that there is but one Person (puruṣa). And as it is said that there is but a single source for the many persons,"
Thus I shall explain that universal Person, who is preeminent in qualities;
having paid homage to my guru Vyāsa, who possesses immeasurable splendor,
who is devoted to austerity, self-controlled, and worthy of worship, that supreme seer.
O King, this Puruṣasūkta is indeed renowned throughout all the Vedas as both *ṛta* and *satya*, having been contemplated by that lion among sages;
it has been established through general rules and exceptions by the sages beginning with Kapila.
O Bhārata, relying upon contemplation of the inner self, the scriptures have been spoken;
and that which Vyāsa has stated in brief regarding the oneness of the Puruṣa—
that I shall declare to you through the grace of him of immeasurable splendor.
In this regard, O lord of the people, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Tryambaka and Brahmā.
In the midst of the Ocean of Milk, there was [a mountain] with the luster of gold.
O King, there is a preeminent mountain known as Vaijayanta. There, the Lord, contemplating the state of the supreme self alone, constantly frequents Vaijayanta in the abode of Vairāja.
Then, while that wise four-faced one was seated there,
his son Śiva,
the three-eyed Lord and master of yoga, arrived by chance through the sky from of old.
Then he quickly descended from the sky onto the summit of the mountain and,
standing before him with joy, prostrated at his feet.
Seeing him fallen at his feet, [the Lord] took hold of him with his left hand.
Then the Lord, the sole Prajāpati, raised him up;
and the Blessed One spoke to his son, who had returned after a long time: "Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one! By good fortune have you come into my presence."
"Is all well with you, my son, regarding your constant study and asceticism? Since you are always one of fierce austerity, I ask you this again.
Rudra said:
"O Blessed One, by your grace, my own study and asceticism are well and undecaying, as is the welfare of the entire world. Indeed,
it has been a long time since I last beheld the Blessed One in the abode of Vairāja."
"Then I reached this mountain, which is frequented by your feet. For I have a great curiosity regarding your journey to this solitary place;
O Grandfather, this cause must surely not be a trivial one."
What indeed is that most excellent abode, free from hunger and thirst, inhabited by gods and asuras, and by sages of immeasurable splendor,
and constantly frequented by gandharvas and apsaras?
"Having abandoned this best of mountains, you have arrived here alone.
Brahmā said:
"The Vaijayanta, the best of mountains, is constantly frequented by me."
12,338.021c Here, with a one-pointed mind, the Puruṣa Virāj is meditated upon.
12,338.022 Rudra said:
12,338.022a "O Brahmā, many Puruṣas have been created by you yourself, O Self-born One."
"O Brahman, others are being created, yet he alone is the Virāj Puruṣa. O Brahman, who indeed is this Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) whom you meditate upon?
Explain this doubt of mine to me, for my curiosity is great."
Brahmā said:
"O son, as for the many Puruṣas that you have mentioned, this matter has already been transcended;
it should be viewed neither as 'thus' nor even as 'not thus'."
I shall now declare to you the substratum of that one Puruṣa,
how he is called the single source of many Puruṣas— such is that Puruṣa, the universal, the supreme, and the most great.
12,338.025e Having become devoid of qualities, they enter the eternal, which is itself devoid of qualities.
12,339.001 Brahmā said:
12,339.001a Listen, my son, to how this Puruṣa is indeed eternal and immutable.
He is described as imperishable, immeasurable, and all-pervading. O best of beings, he cannot be seen by you, nor by me, nor by others;
for he is remembered as being both with qualities and without qualities, universal, and visible only through knowledge.

12,339.003a This [Self], though bodiless, dwells within all bodies; 12,339.003c even while dwelling within bodies, it is not tainted by actions. 12,339.004a My inner self, yours, and those of others who are designated as "bodies" [are one].
He is the witness of all; he should not be apprehended by anyone anywhere.
With the universe as his head, the universe as his arms, and the universe as his feet, eyes, and nose, he moves alone through the fields, wandering at will according to his pleasure.
For the fields are the bodies, and the seeds are the auspicious and inauspicious [karmas];
he knows them through his yogic nature, and therefore he is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Neither his coming nor his going is to be perceived by any being whatsoever.

According to the method of Sāṃkhya and likewise through Yoga in their proper order, I contemplate his course; yet I do not know his supreme course. Nevertheless, I shall describe that eternal Puruṣa according to my knowledge.
His oneness and his greatness are such that he is remembered as the one Puruṣa; being alone and eternal, he bears the title of Mahāpuruṣa. He is the single fire that is kindled in many ways.
The sun is one, the source of all heat; there is but one wind that blows in many ways throughout the world;
and the great ocean is the single source of all waters.
And there is one Puruṣa, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa) and universal in form;
they enter that quality-less Puruṣa,
having abandoned everything composed of the qualities (guṇamaya) and having cast off both auspicious and inauspicious karma.
Having thus abandoned both truth and falsehood, one becomes free from qualities (nirguṇa). Having realized that inconceivable and subtle fourfold state of being,
the disciplined ascetic who wanders [thus] shall go to the Lord Puruṣa.
For in this way, some wise men desire the supreme self (paramātman),
while other contemplators of the inner self (adhyātmacintaka) likewise [desire] the single self (ekātman). Among these,
that which is indeed the supreme self is traditionally held to be eternally devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).
For he is to be known as Nārāyaṇa, the universal self, for he is indeed the Puruṣa;
he is not smeared by the fruits [of action], just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
But that other one, who is the *karmātmā* (the self of action), is joined with both liberation and bondage.
For he is indeed joined with even the group of seventeen;
thus has the Puruṣa been described to you in its many forms according to sequence—
that which is the entire abode of the cosmic order.
The object of knowledge is the supreme, that which is to be awakened, together with the awakener;
the thinker and the object of thought, the eater and the object to be eaten; the smeller and the object to be smelled, the toucher and the object to be touched.
The seer and the object to be seen, the hearer and that which is to be heard;
the knower and the object to be known, both with qualities and without qualities—
that which is indeed called Pradhāna, the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇasāmya).
This is eternal, constant, and imperishable— indeed,
that which is the primordial treasure produced by the Creator; that,
the wise proclaim to be Aniruddha.
Whatever Vedic rite in this world is performed well and is joined with a prayer for blessings, that indeed is to be enjoyed by him. All the gods and the sages are virtuous and self-controlled.
Therefore, they worship Him first with sacrifices as their share of the sacrifice.
I am the primordial Brahmā, the Lord of creatures; from Me you were born, and you have been produced by Me.
From me, O son, the world— both moving and stationary— and all the Vedas along with their secret doctrines (rahasya) have proceeded;
that Puruṣa, divided into four parts, sports according to his will.
Thus that very Blessed One was awakened by means of knowledge.
This has been told to you, my son, exactly as you asked;
it has been described precisely according to the Sāṃkhya knowledge and likewise according to Yoga.
Yudhiṣ�ṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you have spoken of the auspicious duties pertaining to the dharma of liberation;
it behoves your lordship to tell me the foremost dharma for those in the various stages of life."
Bhīṣma said:
Dharma, which leads to heaven and results in the fruit of truth, is ordained for all circumstances.
For dharma, which has many doors, there is no action here that is fruitless.
"O best of the Bharatas, whatever object a person reaches a firm conviction regarding, he recognizes only that and nothing else.
Moreover, O tiger among men, you ought to hear this story from me."
Long ago, this was told to Śakra by the celestial sage Nārada.
O King, the celestial sage Nārada is a perfected being honored throughout the three worlds;
he traverses the worlds in succession, unhindered like the wind.
Once, O great archer, he went to the abode of the king of the gods;
having been honored by Mahendra, he sat down in his presence. As he sat there at his leisure, the lord of Śacī questioned him.
"O Brahmarṣi, O sinless one, has anything wonderful been seen by you?
For even you, O brahmin-ṛṣi, wander through the three worlds with all that is mobile and immobile, always filled with curiosity like a witness who has attained perfection."
"O celestial sage, there is indeed nothing in the world unknown to you—whether heard, experienced, or seen; tell it to me. O King, to that lord of the gods, Nārada, the best among speakers, replied:
To him who was seated and had approached him, that best of the twice-born related a vast narrative; just as and in whatever manner he,
being questioned, told that story to him, so too do you listen to it from me.
Bhīṣma said:
O best of the Kurus, it is said that in the excellent city of Mahāpadma,
on the southern bank of the Gaṅgā, there lived a certain composed brahmin.

He was gentle, born in the lineage of Soma, one who had traversed the path of the Veda and severed all doubt; he was constant in dharma, having conquered anger, eternally contented, and mastered his senses.
He was ever devoted to non-violence, truthful, and esteemed by the virtuous.

Endowed with wealth acquired through righteous means and possessed of his own noble character, he maintained an eminent way of life within a great and renowned family, esteemed for its vast network of kinsmen, relatives, and friends.
Seeing that he had many sons established in extensive works,
O King, he remained devoted to the family traditions and became intent on the practice of dharma.
Thereupon, he [performed] the dharma declared in the Vedas and exactly as prescribed in the scriptures.
Reflecting in his mind upon the conduct of the virtuous and the threefold Dharma, he constantly worries:
"What would be auspicious for me to do? What is appropriate? What is my ultimate refuge?
Thus he remains perpetually distressed and reaches no certain conclusion.
While he was thus distressed, a highly composed brahmin guest arrived at one point; established in the supreme Dharma,
he performed hospitable rites for him with all due ritual propriety.
When he had rested and was seated, the Brahmin spoke these words to him: The Brahmin said:
"O sinless one, I have been won over by the sweetness of your speech; thus I have revealed my name to you."

"O best of Brahmins, having entered into friendship with you, I shall say something; listen to that. O foremost of the twice-born, what path would it be for me to perform the supreme duty by entrusting the duties of a householder to my son?"

I am the Self, established within the self; standing alone in the Self, I do not desire to act, being bound by common qualities (*guṇas*). As long as my youth has not yet passed away, it remains dependent upon the fruit of having sons.
"For so long I have desired to take provisions for the journey to the next world;
indeed, as I seek the further shore in this succession of worlds, this thought has arisen in me: 'Whence shall I obtain a boat made of Dharma?'"
Having heard of the virtuous deeds being gathered together in the world and those being bestowed,
and having seen the rows of banners and standards of righteousness;
My mind does not take pleasure in the time of enjoyment when it is showered upon living beings,
for I have seen ascetics seeking [liberation] in the world beyond.
"Therefore, O guest, by relying on the power of your intellect, do you direct me toward the true essence of dharma and artha.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard those words of the one who desired righteousness, that wise guest spoke these gentle words in a sweet voice:
"I too am bewildered in this matter; this is my own desire as well."
I do not reach a firm conclusion regarding this triple-heaven with its many doors;
some twice-born ones praise liberation, some the fruit of sacrifice,
while others have taken refuge in the forest-dwelling stage of life or the householder stage.
Some took recourse to the duties of kings, some to their own fruits [of action],
some to the service of their gurus, and some took recourse to that which is the Word; others, by serving their mother and father, have gone to heaven.
Some have gone to heaven through non-violence, and others likewise through truth; some, slain while facing the enemy in battle, have gone to heaven;
and some, perfected by the vow of gleaning, have taken their stand upon the path to heaven.
Some, auspicious and devoted to Vedic vows, were intent on study;
being wise, self-contented, and masters of their senses, they have gone to heaven. Others, endowed with uprightness, were slain by people devoid of uprightness.
"Those of pure soul, being upright, are indeed established upon the surface of the celestial vault.
Thus, because there are so many various doors to dharma in the world that are never closed,
my mind is agitated like a streak of cloud by the wind."
The guest said:
"O Brahmin, I shall give you instruction according to the sacred tradition, exactly as it was explained to me by my preceptor; hear that from me in its true meaning."
Thus, having understood the meaning exactly as it was explained by his preceptor, [he went] to that very place where,
in a former creation, the Wheel of Dharma was set in motion— at Naimiṣa, on the banks of the Gomatī, there is a city called after the Nāgas.
O bull among the twice-born, all the thirty gods performed a sacrifice there,
where Māndhātṛ, the best of kings and a righteous soul, surpassed even Indra;
there the great serpent Cakṣuḥśravas had made his dwelling.
The illustrious Padmanābha, renowned as Padma,
O bull among the twice-born, remains established in the threefold path and propitiates all beings through his speech, his actions, and his mind.
By means of conciliation, gifts, sowing dissension, and force— these four methods—
he protects his own people and those who are in distress with the vision of meditation.
You ought to approach him according to the prescribed rite and ask what you desire.
He will show you the supreme Dharma, for he is not one of false view; that Naga is a host to all, proficient in wisdom and the scriptures,
and endowed with all unsurpassed and desirable virtues.
By nature ever devoted to water and constantly engaged in study, he was endowed with austerity and self-restraint, as well as with conduct that was not inferior;
he was a performer of sacrifices, fond of giving, patient, and established in the highest conduct.

He was truthful in speech, free from malice, possessed of virtuous conduct, and relied upon by others; he ate only the remnants of food, was compliant in his words, and was distinguished by his benevolence, uprightness, and gratitude for what had been done for him.
Free from enmity, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
and born of a lineage as pure as the waters of a pool in the Ganges,
the Brahmin said: The Brahmin said:

To you who were striving under an excessive burden, these words of mine—which remove that great weight and provide supreme consolation—have been heard: "For one exhausted by the journey, there is rest; for one exhausted by standing, there is a seat."
It was like water for the thirsty, food for one afflicted by hunger,
like the attainment of desired food when a guest arrives at the proper time,
or like a son obtained at the right moment for an old man who has long been longing for one.
The sight of these words uttered by you gladdens me, like seeing one who is dear and affectionate, just as one might have imagined in the mind.
Like one who has been granted vision in the sky, I both behold and reflect upon them.
"Since this instruction has been given to me by you, who possess such wisdom,
I shall certainly do exactly as you tell me. O virtuous one, please dwell here with me for this night."
"At dawn, you shall depart, refreshed and having rested well;
for that blessed sun has its rays dimmed and is now turned downward.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O slayer of enemies, having been offered hospitality by him,
that guest indeed spent the night with that twice-born man. And as they were conversing at that time, their discourse was joined with righteousness.
That entire night passed happily, like a day,
for that best of Brahmins and for his guest as well, O Bhārata. Then, at the time of dawn, that guest was honored by him.
12,344.009c By a Brahmin who desires his own welfare, this should be done according to his ability.
12,344.010a Then that brahmin, having reached a firm resolve regarding dharma and being permitted by his kinsmen, being himself a knower of dharma—
12,344.010c As instructed, he who was single-mindedly resolved upon his meritorious deed went at the appointed time to the abode of the Lord of Serpents;
12,345.001 Bhīṣma said:
Passing through various forests, sacred fords, and lakes,
he approached a certain sage in due course. That brahmin [then] [inquired about] the elephant as it had been described by that brahmin.
Having heard it, he departed according to the proper custom; then,
that knower of purpose, having reached the abode of the Nāgas exactly as described,
spoke these words adorned with the honorific "bhoḥ," saying, "I am here."

Then, having heard his words, the serpent’s wife, who was devoted to dharma and possessed of beautiful form, revealed herself to that brahmin as a woman faithful to her husband. Devoted to righteousness, she performed worship for him according to the prescribed rites.
Having welcomed him with a "Welcome," she asked, "What shall I do for you?
The brahmin said:
"I have been rested and honored by you with your gentle words."
"O lady, I wish to see that supreme divine Naga;
for this is my highest purpose and this is the fruit I desire.
It is for this reason that I have today arrived at the abode of the serpents."
The Naga wife said:
"O noble Brahmin, he who travels for a month has gone to draw the chariot of the Sun;
in seven or eight days, he will undoubtedly show himself to you."
"O Noble One, you know this cause of my exile;
tell me, what else should be done for my husband? Speak to me.
The Brahmin said:
"O virtuous lady, it was by this resolve that I arrived here;
O Queen, awaiting his arrival, I shall dwell in this great forest. As soon as he has arrived, I must inform him of my presence here without any agitation."
"When you have come to meet me, you must speak these words to him:
'I too shall dwell here on the auspicious bank of the Gomatī,
subsisting on limited food and observing the prescribed rule.'"
12,345.013 Bhīṣma said: 12,345.013a Thereupon, that brahmin, the bull among brahmins, having repeatedly consoled the female serpent, returned once more to that very sandbank of the river.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O best of men, because that ascetic Brāhmaṇa lived there without food, those serpents became distressed."
All the kinsmen of that nāga, his brothers, sons, and wives, having gathered together in unison, went toward that brahmin. On a secluded sandbank, they beheld him indeed, firm in his vows.

To that twice-born man who was seated, fasting, and devoted to silent recitation, all those kinsmen of the host approached, honored the Brahmin repeatedly, and spoke these words without hesitation: 12,346.003c [They saw] the twice-born man seated, fasting, and devoted to silent recitation. 12,346.004a They all, having approached and repeatedly honored the Brahmin, 12,346.004c spoke these words without doubt, being the relatives of the host.
"O ascetic, today is indeed the sixth day since you arrived here;
yet, O lover of dharma, you do not desire any food. You have come to us, and we have presented ourselves before you."
"O best of the twice-born, hospitality must be performed by us, for we are all householders. O Brahmin, you ought to partake of roots, fruits, leaves, milk, or food for the sake of sustenance."
"By you, who have renounced food and dwell in the forest,
all these people— both young and old— are being afflicted by this crisis of righteousness. For the sake of showing us favor, you ought to take food."
"O Brahmin, if you do not eat, we shall go to hell;
for among us there is no one who has killed an embryo, nor anyone hostile to the king, nor even a liar, nor anyone who eats before the gods, guests, and kinsmen in this family."
The Brahmin said:
"By means of your instruction, this food has been chosen by me;
indeed, it is two nights short of ten days until the arrival of the Naga."
"If the serpent does not arrive when eight nights have passed, then I shall take my food; for his sake, this vow must be observed. You should feel no distress and may go back the way you came."
"Therefore, you ought not to break this vow of mine here.
Bhīṣma said:
"Having been thus permitted by that Brahmin, those serpents—"
12,346.013c They returned to their own abodes, O bull among men, their purpose unfulfilled.
12,347.001 Bhīṣma said:
12,347.001a Then, after a long period of time had passed, the serpent arrived.
Having completed his duties for the Sun and been granted leave, he returned to his own home. His virtuous wife approached him with services such as washing his feet;
and the serpent questioned that excellent woman who was thus attentive to him.
"O auspicious lady, are you indeed endowed with the same devotion toward the worship of deities and guests as was previously described by me? For surely,
one who has not fulfilled her purpose would not be softened by the common intellect of women."
"O fair-hipped one, through separation from me, you have been separated from the bridge of dharma.
The Naga's wife said:
"For disciples, service to the teacher; for Brahmins, the mastery of the Vedas."
Obedience to the master’s word for servants, the protection of the world by kings,
and the preservation of all beings— this is declared here as the duty of the Kṣatriya. For Vaiśyas, it consists of the performance of sacrifices accompanied by hospitality.
Service to the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas is the duty of a Śūdra.
O Lord of Nagas, the dharma of the householder consists in seeking the welfare of all beings,
constant moderation in diet, and the performance of vows in their proper sequence.
For dharma, through its connection with dharma, is the qualifier of the senses.
"To whom do I belong? From where have I come? Who am I?
And who might be mine?"—one who has entered the stage of life for liberation (mokṣāśramī) should always possess such a purposeful mind.
"Devotion to her husband is said to be the supreme duty of a wife.
O Lord of Nagas, through your instruction, I indeed understand that truth in its true essence. Thus, knowing my duty while you remain ever devoted to righteousness,"

12,347.011c Having abandoned the true path, how could I travel upon a treacherous road? 12,347.012a O illustrious one, my practice of dharma toward the deities does not decline; 12,347.012c And I am ever-diligent and unwearied in the hospitable reception of guests.

"Today is the seventh or eighth day since that brahmin arrived here; he has not disclosed his business to me and desires an audience with you. Eager for a sight of you, he is on the sandy bank of the Gomatī."

Seated, reciting the Veda, that Brahmin of firm vows was constantly devoted to austerity and meditation, true to his word, and a master of his senses. But I, O Lord of Nagas, was won over by him through conciliatory words.
"O best of serpents, he has arrived; he must be sent into my presence.
Having heard this, O highly wise one, you ought to go there. Or rather, O you who hear with your eyes, you ought to grant him an audience."
The Naga said:
"Then, O lady of pure smiles, whom do you perceive as that one in the form of a Brahmin— is he merely a human brahmin, or is he a god?"

"O illustrious lady, what mortal man, desiring to see me, would dare to speak such words with such audacity, especially when he has a longing for my sight? O beautiful woman, [this applies even] to the hosts of gods and asuras, and to the celestial rishis."
"Are not the Nāgas of great heroism, the sons of Surasā, full of speed?
Are we not worthy of homage, granter of boons, and followers even of men—especially as the masters of wealth? Such is the tradition."
The Naga wife said:
"O eater of air, through my straightforwardness I recognize that he is not a god; however, I know one thing of him: he is exceedingly wrathful yet possessed of great devotion."
He who is devoted here to the twice-born, who knows the proper time, and who is fierce in his wrath against the Kali age— he,
O wind-eater, having fulfilled the purpose ordained by his resolve,
attains the supreme world of those who seek refuge and enjoys foremost renown.
"O sinless one, O Lord of Nagas, let no one in your family be a destroyer of desired objects;
for even when possessing the power [to prevent it], he sinks into hell. He is like a *stokaka* bird longing for water while seeking some other task."
For twelve thousand three hundred and forty-eight years and six months, this bird, who loves the rainy season, has longed for a sight of you.
Indeed, no deity whatsoever would wait with such anxiety;
for among those born of equal lineage, no one remains in attendance upon another.

Abandoning that innate anger, you ought to look upon him; you should not burn yourself today by cutting off his hope. For those who have approached you with hope, you have failed to wipe away their tears.
Whether it be a king or a prince, he is joined with the very sin of killing an embryo. Through silence, one attains the fruit of knowledge; through giving, great fame;
and through truthful speech, eloquence, and one is glorified in the next world.
By the gift of land, one attains a destination equal to that of the hermitages;
by restoring lost property, one enjoys the fruit [of that merit]. Having performed a desired action that is free from affliction and devoid of selfish longing, one attains the same.
"Those who know the Dharma understand that no one goes to hell.
The Naga said:
"Indeed, through the fault of my birth, I possess great pride born of arrogance."
"O virtuous lady, that anger born of resolve has been consumed by you with the fire of your speech. O virtuous lady, I do not see any darkness greater than anger,
for it is because of it that serpents become especially subject to reproach."
For having fallen under the sway of passion, the powerful Ten-necked one,
who rivaled Śakra himself, was slain by Rāma in combat;
hearing that his calf had been carried away by Rāma from within the inner apartments, [he acted].

Agitated by rage due to the insult, the sons of Kārtavīrya were slain by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni. In that battle, the immensely powerful Kārtavīrya, who resembled the thousand-eyed Indra, was struck down out of wrath.
Likewise, Māndhātṛ, who rivaled Śakra himself, was brought under the sway of anger and slain in battle here by the Rākṣasa Lavaṇa. Therefore,
this [anger] is the enemy of austerities and the destroyer of prosperity.
"Upon hearing your words alone, my anger was restrained by me.
And I especially praise myself,
O constant one, since you, endowed with every virtue, are my wife, O large-eyed lady."
"I shall go right there where that twice-born man stays. Having spoken these words, he will by no means depart without having accomplished his purpose.
Bhīṣma said:

12,349.001a That lord of serpents proceeded there toward the brahmin, 12,349.001c meditating upon him alone in his mind and reflecting on the urgency of his purpose. 12,349.002a Approaching him, O lord of men, that wise king of snakes—
12,349.002c He, who by nature was fond of righteousness, spoke these sweet words: 12,349.003a "O sir, I address you with forgiveness; you ought not to be angry.
For what purpose have you arrived here, and what is your business?"
"O twice-born one, having approached you out of a desire for your welfare, I ask you out of affection:
why do you sit in worship upon this secluded bank of the Gomatī?
The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Know me to be Dharmāraṇya, who has come here to see the Naga;
O best of the twice-born, my business lies with Padmanābha there.
I have heard that he is absent, having departed."
I await that kinsman as a farmer awaits the rain-cloud. Free from affliction and composed in well-being, I practice ten thousand repetitions of the sacred *brahman*, absorbed in yoga.
The Naga said:
"O, you are of auspicious conduct; you are truly kind to the virtuous. O illustrious one, you are rich in learning and look upon others with supreme affection."
"I am that Naga, O brahmin-sage, whom you have now recognized. Command me as you wish; what dear service may I perform for you?
Having heard that you had arrived here from among your own kinsmen, I have come before you."
"Therefore, O twice-born one, I have come here myself to see you.
Having arrived today, you shall depart with your purpose fulfilled.
O best of the twice-born, you may confidently engage me in whatever matter you wish."
"For we have all been purchased by your virtues, especially since you,
disregarding your own welfare, attend to me alone here.
The Brahmin said:
"O illustrious one, I have come here, longing for a sight of you,
O serpent, desiring to ask about a certain matter of which I am ignorant. Abiding in the self, I seek that which is beneficial for my own soul."
O one of great wisdom, I indeed seek refuge in you, who are powerful and desirous of providing shelter.
You are illuminated by your own virtues, which are like the rays of the moon’s womb of glory— delightful to the heart and manifesting your very self through the touch of the moonbeams.
"O eater of air, please resolve this question that has arisen within me.
Afterwards, I shall state my business; you ought to listen to me.
The brahmin said:
In turn, he goes to the abode of Vivasvat;
may you, O Lord, draw that single-wheeled chariot,
should there be anything at all wondrous therein.
"You have seen it; you ought to describe it.
The Naga said:
"The Blessed Sun is the foundation of many wonders."
From whom all beings proceed, who are honored throughout the three worlds;
upon whose thousands of rays the perfected sages dwell together with the gods, like birds perched upon branches.
"O Brahmin, what could be more wonderful than this: that the great wind, having issued forth and taken refuge in the rays of the sun, expands within the sky?
O Brahmin-sage, let it be divided out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures."

That he creates water during the rainy season— what is more marvelous than this? That the Great-Souled One, stationed in the center of his orb, blazing with supreme radiance, beholds the worlds— what is more marvelous than this?
With jars marked by rainbows and possessing bellies like water-pots,
he whose foot named Śukra is dark and who is a cloud in the sky releases water during the rains— what could be more wonderful than this?

What could be more wonderful than this: that he, whose very self is eternally established in his extraordinary splendors, again takes up at the proper time the water that was abandoned by the pure-rayed sun during the eight months?
Since this earth, which supports all things moving and unmoving, is sustained by the seed [of the Lord],
and since within it dwells the mighty-armed, eternal, supreme, and imperishable God,
who is without beginning or end, O Brahmin— what could be more wonderful than this?
The god consists of mantra, is beginningless, the self of time, and a treasury of splendors;
he is the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) within that which comprises the universe—what could be more wondrous than that?
Yet, hear from me this one thing which is the wonder among wonders.
12,350.008c That which I saw in the stainless sky, due to its proximity to the sun—
12,350.009a formerly at the time of midday, while the sun was scorching the worlds—
12,350.009c appeared on all sides resembling a second sun.
Illuminating all the worlds with his splendor and his own radiance,
he approaches facing the sun, as if cleaving the sky; like an oblation offered into the fire, he pervades the heavens with rays of light.
With an indescribable form, like a second sun, he appeared. Upon his arrival, Vivasvat extended his hand;
and he, desiring to offer honor in return, extended his right hand.
Then, having pierced the sky, it entered the solar disc;
and that energy, becoming unified, attained the state of the sun in an instant.
At that meeting of their two splendors, a doubt arose within us.
"Of these two, which one standing on the chariot is the Sun who has arrived here?
Having conceived this doubt, we questioned the Sun:
'Who is this who, having ascended to heaven, has come like a second Sun?'"
Sūrya said:
"This is not a god, nor a friend of the wind (Vāyu), nor an asura, nor a serpent;
this is a sage who, perfected through the vow of the *uñcha* mode of life, has ascended to heaven."
This brahmin remained concentrated in meditation, subsisting on roots and fruits, then eating withered leaves, and later living on water and air alone.
Furthermore, this brahmin recited the *Ṛg-veda* hymns according to various *saṃhitās*.
O serpent, this brahmin— who made an effort toward the gate of heaven and thus went to the third realm—
was steady-minded, free from longing, and constantly subsisted on gleaned grains;
he was ever devoted to the welfare of all beings.
By his own power, he has attained this stainless state;
those like you long for such merit through his diligent effort.
Indeed, neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the asuras, nor the pannagas [are his equal].
"O twice-born one, such a wonder as this was seen by me there, concerning those beings who have attained the supreme goal.
The Naga said:
"O twice-born one, such a wonder as this was seen by me there."
"12,351.006c This perfected human body, which has attained the state of a Siddha,
12,351.006e revolves around the earth together with the sun, O Brahmin.
12,352.001 The Brāhmaṇa said:
"O serpent, there is no doubt that this is wonderful; I am well-pleased. By your words, which are consistent with their true meaning, the path has been shown to me.
May it be well with you; O virtuous one, best of serpents, I shall now depart."
"I am to be remembered by you through the sending of messages and commissions.
The Naga said:
"Without having stated the task concerning me, where have you now set out?"

"O twice-born one, let it be told what must be done and for what purpose you have come here. O bull among brahmins, whether the task has been stated or unstated, once it is completed, you shall take leave of me and then depart, O brahmin, with my full permission."
"O brahmin-sage, you ought not to depart from here after seeing me alone and casting aside your affection, as if you were merely sitting at the foot of a tree.
O best of the twice-born, I am yours and you are mine; of this there is no doubt."
"O sinless one, this entire world belongs to you; what anxiety do you have regarding me?
The Brahmin said:
"It is even so, O highly wise serpent, you who have understood the truth."
"The gods are not superior to you in any way whatsoever; this is exactly as it is.
O serpent, whoever I am, that very same person you are. Both I and you, as well as all beings, are always omnipresent."
"O Lord of Enjoyments, I had a doubt regarding the accumulation of merit.
Therefore, O virtuous one, I shall practice the vow of gleaning, perceiving it as the true goal. This is my firm resolve, O virtuous one, made for a most compelling reason."
"I bid you farewell; may it be well with you. I have accomplished my purpose, O serpent.
Bhīṣma said:
Having thus addressed the best of serpents, that Brahmin remained firm in his resolve.
O King, desiring initiation, he then took refuge with Cyavana Bhārgava. Having been consecrated by him, he devoted himself solely to dharma;
and in that same manner, O King, he then related this very story.
O king of kings, this meritorious story was also told by Bhārgava in the abode of Janaka to the high-souled Nārada;
and by Nārada, O king of kings, it was told in the abode of the lord of the gods.
O best of the Bharatas, this auspicious story was told in the past by the King of the Gods, whose deeds are untiring, when he was questioned;
it was related to all the most praiseworthy Vasus, O lord of the earth.
"And when my battle with Rāma was exceedingly fierce,
O King, this story was told to me by the Vasus.
It was related to you by me in its true essence, O Lord of the People, as you were questioning me."
O best among the upholders of dharma, this meritorious and righteous discourse has been told.
O Bhārata, that which you ask me is the supreme dharma:
[to be] one whose mind is not distracted and who does not crave [worldly gain], while performing the duties of dharma and artha, O King.
And that best of the twice-born, having made his resolve and having been instructed in his duty by the Lord of Serpents,
became absorbed in self-restraint and observances at the edge of the forest.
Having entered [the forest], he subsisted on a measured diet of gleaned grains.
